units.tr: To the most serene and most powerful prince and lord, Lord Maximilian, King of Bohemia and Hungary, Archduke of Austria, Burgundy and Silesia, etc., his most gracious lord: S. D.

units.la: ADmonet me, Serenissime Rex, hoc tempus, quo festum S. Michaelis celebratur, ut de conditione, custodia, atque defensione castorum angelorum, per quos Deus coetum suum ab omnibus calamitatibus in hac vita tueri vult, pauca quaedam dicere proposuerim. Quibus deinde addam, quo modo sanctos quoque ad nos possimus angelos allicere; ut fidelem nostri curam gerant, ab omnibusque periculis tueantur: denique, qua id ratione fiat, ut boni saepe custodis loco, malus homini adiungatur & attribuatur genius.
units.tr: Most serene King, this time, when the feast of St Michael is celebrated, urges me to set out a few points about the nature, custody and defence of the holy angels, through whom God wills to protect his congregation from all calamities in this life. To these I will then add how we may also attract the holy angels to ourselves, so that they take faithful care of us and shield us from all dangers; and finally, by what means it comes about that an evil spirit is often attached and assigned to a man in place of a good guardian.

units.la: Initio autem angelos esse, nemini pio sanaeque mentis dubium est. Id enim & sacra passim Scriptura nobis testa-tur: & etiam experientia, recte rem consideremus, verū esse demonstrat. Abrahamo namq; & Lotho legimus angelos ante Sodomæ & reliquarū circumiacentiū urbium euersionem apparuisse: ut est in Genesi cap 28 & 29. Et habemus inter cætera illustre sanè pulcherrimumq; huius rei testi-monium Exodi 4. ubi angelus Do-mini eo ipso tempore, quo populum Iudaicū hostiliter persequebatur Pha-rao, castra Israelitica conspectus est præire. Iosuæ consimili ratione, cum prelium contra hostes ingrederetur, angelus in albēti præcesit equo: qui pro populo Dei strenuè pugnare ui-sus est. Ita & in Nouo testamento le-gitur, Iosepho apparuisse in somnis angelum: qui monebat eum, ne Ma-riam grauidam Spiritus sancti virtu-te facta deserteret. Et cum Herodes, crudelis ille tyrannus, pueri I E S V uitæ insidiaretur: angeli solùm com-monefactione ab imminēte periculo Ioseph cū puero IESV ac matre est conseruatus. Præterea in Actis Apostolicis historia memorabilis est de S.Petro, qui præter omnium expectationē mirabiliter angelica cura è carcere eductus, Ecclesiæ fidelium restituitur. Plura similia passim exempla & Veteris & Noui testamenti historiæ suppeditant, quib. idem probari posset: sed hæc pauca, quæ adduximus, in præsentia sufficiant.
units.tr: At the outset, that there are angels is doubted by no one who is pious and sound in mind. Scripture bears witness to this everywhere, and experience too, if we consider the matter rightly, shows it to be true. For we read that angels appeared to Abraham and to Lot before the overthrow of Sodom and the neighbouring cities, as in Genesis chapters 18 and 19. Among other things we have a most clear and most beautiful testimony of this in Exodus 4, where the angel of the Lord was seen going before the camp of Israel at the very time when Pharaoh was hostilely pursuing the Jewish people. In a similar way, when Joshua entered battle against the enemy, an angel went before him on a white horse, and he seemed to fight valiantly for the people of God. So too in the New Testament we read that an angel appeared to Joseph in a dream, warning him not to abandon Mary, who was pregnant by the power of the Holy Spirit. And when Herod, that cruel tyrant, lay in wait for the life of the boy Jesus, Joseph was preserved with the boy Jesus and his mother from the imminent danger by an angel's warning alone. Moreover, in the Acts of the Apostles there is a memorable story about St Peter, who, beyond everyone's expectation, was wonderfully led out of prison by angelic care and restored to the faithful congregation. Histories of the Old and New Testaments supply many other similar examples everywhere, by which the same could be proved; but these few we have cited are enough for the present.

units.la: Iam dicendū est, quales nos oportet esse homines, si uelimus ut angelici chori in suam nos tutelam suscipiant, atqș etiā retineant. Ac tametsi illud satis pro dignitate nullo modo facere possumus: tamen quantum in nobis diuini spiritus fauore atqș gratia fieri potest, rem paucis adumbrare conabimur. Fiunt quidē boni angeli, nostri quasi familiares & ministri, ut loquitur epistola ad Hebreos: quando diligenter tractamus sacram scripturam, uerbumqș Dei studiose audimus & meditamur: uitamqș precipue & sacra passim Scriptura nobis testatur: & etiam experientia, recte rem consideremus, uerũ esse demonstrat. Abrahamo namq; & Lotho legimus angelos ante Sodomæ & reliquarũ circumiacentiũ urbium euersionem apparuisse: ut est in Genesi cap 28 & 29. Et habemus inter cætera illustre sanè pulcherrimumq; huius rei testimonium Exodi 4. ubi angelus Domini eo ipso tempore, quo populum Iudaicũ hostiliter persequebatur Pharao, castra Israelitica conspectus est præire. Iosuæ consimili ratione, cum prelium contra hostes ingrederetur, angelus in albeti præcessit equo: qui pro populo Dei strenuè pugnare uisus est. Ita & in Nouo testamento legitur, Iosepho apparuisse in somnis angelum: qui monebat eum, ne Mariam grauidam Spiritus sancti virtute facta deseret. Et cum Herodes, crudelis ille tyrannus, pueri IESV vitæ insidiaretur: angeli solùm commonefactione ab imminẽte periculo Ioseph cū puero IESV ac matre est conseruatus. Præterea in Actis Apostolicis historia memorabilis est de S.Petro, qui præter omnium expectationē mirabiliter angelica cura è carcere eductus, Ecclesiæ fidelium restituitur. Plura similia passim exempla & Veteris & Noui testamenti historiæ suppeditant, quib. idem probari posset: sed hæc pauca, quæ adduximus, in præsentia sufficiant.
units.tr: Now we must say what kind of people we ought to be, if we wish the angelic hosts to take us into their protection and also to keep us there. Although we can by no means do this as its dignity deserves, nevertheless we will try briefly to sketch the matter, as far as it can be done through the favour and grace of the divine Spirit within us. Good angels become, as the Epistle to the Hebrews puts it, our familiar friends and ministers, when we diligently handle Holy Scripture, zealously hear and meditate on the Word of God, and above all strive to lead our life, as long as we are in this world, honourably and according to the will of God. Scripture bears witness to this everywhere, and experience too, if we consider the matter rightly, shows it to be true. For we read that angels appeared to Abraham and to Lot before the overthrow of Sodom and the neighbouring cities, as in Genesis chapters 18 and 19. Among other things we have a most clear and most beautiful testimony of this in Exodus 4, where the angel of the Lord was seen going before the camp of Israel at the very time when Pharaoh was hostilely pursuing the Jewish people. In a similar way, when Joshua entered battle against the enemy, an angel went before him on a white horse, and he seemed to fight valiantly for the people of God. So too in the New Testament we read that an angel appeared to Joseph in a dream, warning him not to abandon Mary, who was pregnant by the power of the Holy Spirit. And when Herod, that cruel tyrant, lay in wait for the life of the boy Jesus, Joseph was preserved with the boy Jesus and his mother from the imminent danger by an angel's warning alone. Moreover, in the Acts of the Apostles there is a memorable story about St Peter, who, beyond everyone's expectation, was wonderfully led out of prison by angelic care and restored to the faithful congregation. Histories of the Old and New Testaments supply many other similar examples everywhere, by which the same could be proved; but these few we have cited are enough for the present.

units.la: Iam dicendū est, quales nos oporteat esse homines, si uelimus ut angelici chori in suam nos tutelam suscipiant, atqz etiā retineant. Ac tametsi illud satis pro dignitate nullo modo facere possumus: tamen quantum in nobis diuini spiritus fauore atqz gratia fieri potest, rem paucis adumbrare conabimur. Fiunt quidē boni angeli, nostri quasi familiares & ministri, ut loquitur epistola ad Hebræos: quando diligenter tractamus sacram scripturam, uerbumqz Dei studiose audimus & meditamur: uitamqz præcipue cipuè honestam iuxta Dei uoluntatem, quàm diu in hoc mundo sumus, degere conamur. Id si fecerimus, non tantum sancti angeli, uerum etiam tota Diuinitas in nobis habitare uult, & nostris corporib. tanquam hospitio quodã uti. iuxta illud Christi, Iohannis decimoquarto: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum seruabit, & pater meus diliget eum: & ad eum ueniemus, & mansionem apud eum faciemus. Seruare autem sermonem Dei est, fide & bona conscientia uerbo ipsius credere, quòd scilicet omnia peccata nobis remittantur propter Christum, quantumuis magna & grauia sint: ac rogare praeterea, ut Deus nos in illo pposito, modò nos uera poenitentia ducti ad Christum confugiamus, usq; ad beatę uitae terminum clementer cõseruare dignetur. At plura de hac re habet Paulus 1 Corinth. 3 & 6. Et praecipuè inuitat nos illo dicto Coloss. 3. Sermo Dei habitet in uobis opulenter. Hæc si faciemus, faciemus, contra conscientiam nihil quicquam agemus: omnino nobis persuadeamus, sanctos angelos in omnibus vitae nostrae actionibus praesto nobis futuros, omniaque pericula a nobis esse propulsuros.
units.tr: Now we must say what kind of people we ought to be, if we wish the angelic hosts to take us into their protection and also to keep us there. Although we can by no means do this as its dignity deserves, nevertheless we will try briefly to sketch the matter, as far as it can be done through the favour and grace of the divine Spirit within us. Good angels become, as the Epistle to the Hebrews puts it, our familiar friends and ministers, when we diligently handle Holy Scripture, zealously hear and meditate on the Word of God, and above all strive to lead our life, as long as we are in this world, honourably and according to the will of God. If we do this, not only the holy angels but the whole Godhead wills to dwell in us and to use our bodies as a kind of lodging, according to the saying of Christ in John 14: "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him." To keep God's word is to believe his word with faith and a good conscience, namely that all sins are forgiven us for Christ's sake, however great and grievous they are; and besides, to pray that God will graciously deign to preserve us in this state until the end of a blessed life, provided that, led by true repentance, we flee to Christ. Paul treats this matter more fully in 1 Corinthians 3 and 6, and above all he urges us with that saying of Colossians 3: "Let the word of God dwell richly in you." If we do this, we shall do nothing against conscience; let us be wholly persuaded that the holy angels will be at hand for us in all the actions of our life, and will drive off every danger from us.

units.la: Ex superioribus, quae diximus, iam facile aliquis colligere poterit, qui a spiritibus bonis regant̃. Restat nunc ut ostendamus, qui a malis agitentur geniis. In primis igitur omnes teneant hanc regulam, unde[?] qui a malo spiritu obsessi sunt, iudicari possunt.
units.tr: From what we have said above, anyone can now easily gather which people are ruled by good spirits. It remains for us to show which people are driven by evil spirits. First, then, let everyone hold this rule, by which those who are possessed by an evil spirit can be judged.

units.la: Omnis qui facit ac docet contraria verbo Dei, quod in Veteri & Novo testamēto nobis proponitur, id que pertinaciter defendit: is mali spiritus organum ac domicilium est.
units.tr: Whoever does and teaches things contrary to the Word of God, as it is set before us in the Old and New Testaments, and defends them obstinately, is an instrument and dwelling place of an evil spirit.

units.la: Haec tamen regula suas etiam admittit exceptiones. Aliud enim est, defendere contumaciter errorem contra verbum Dei: aliud vero, errare ex imbecillitate, aut ignorantia non affectata. Sic Iudas non ignarus, sed deliberato prius consilio, & diabolico surore incitatus, prodit innocentem Christum: sicut de eo Scriptura testatur, Sathanas intrauit in eum. Quamobrem statuamus, omnes eos mancipia & domicilia diabolica esse, qui in peccatis contra legem Dei & agnitam veritatem studiose perseuerarant. Præterea, si quis odiose loquatur de aliorum factis, aut aliter interpretetur quàm ab altero sunt suscepta, tantum ut ipse aliquid esse uidea tur, proximusque despiciatur: certò illum cōcludamus à dæmone agitari. Idem iudicium potest fieri de reliquis peccatis, quæ sunt contra singula Decalogi præcepta, quorū Paulus quædam in specie recenset Gal.5. 1 Cor.5.6. Ephef.4.
units.tr: Yet this rule also admits its exceptions. For it is one thing to stubbornly defend an error against the Word of God, and quite another to err through weakness or through unaffected ignorance. Thus Judas, not ignorant but acting on a deliberate plan and driven by diabolical frenzy, betrayed innocent Christ; as Scripture testifies of him, "Satan entered into him." Wherefore let us establish that all those are the bondslaves and dwelling places of the devil who have persisted in sins against the law of God and the truth they have acknowledged. Furthermore, if anyone speaks spitefully of the deeds of others, or interprets them otherwise than they were undertaken by the other, merely so that he himself may seem to be something and his neighbour be despised, let us certainly conclude that he is driven by a demon. The same judgment can be made concerning the remaining sins, which are against the individual precepts of the Decalogue, some of which Paul lists in particular in Galatians 5, 1 Corinthians 5 and 6, and Ephesians 4.

units.la: At hoc in loco quærere aliquis posset, quæ sit causa tanti odij, tantæq; inimicitiæ malorum spirituum contra Ecclesiam: & quare mali genis, non simili à Deo recipiantur modo, sicut homines? Ad hæc sic respōdetur: Summus ille princeps malorum lorum spirituum, cum uideret filium Dei coram coelesti patre suo adeò se humiliare: sese supra filium Dei extulit, ipsumq; contempsit. cuius rei causa de coelo deiectus, & omnibus donis, quib. cum Deus in creatione ornauerat, est priuatus. Ex eo tempore quasi naturali quodā odio ductus, cum suum virus in Deum effundere non posset, imbecillem ipsius naturam, hominem nimirum, ab amore & dilectione conditoris remouere, Deóque odiosam reddere totis uiribus conatur. Id quod clarè testatur historia lapsus primorum parentū, Genesis 3. Homo vero longè secus ac diabolus, nō temerè, sed instinctu ipsius lapsus, & à Deo auersus est. Quare etsi iustitia Dei illā regulam perpetuò aliàs seruet, ut in omnibus creaturis peccatum puniat: & magis mirum videatur, quòd Deus de sua lege dispensset, quàm quòd mundum condidit & conseruat: tamen sic dispensat de suo iure, ut filius suus unigenitus genitus fiat deprecator, & satisfaciat Patri pro peccatis generis humani, quòd diaboli fraudib.in æternæ abie ctionis miseriam præcipitatum erat. Hoc autem solatij hominibus est reli quum, quòd quicunque apprehen derit filium Dei fide, eiusq; beneficia sibi applicare potuerit, se nimirū sola ipsius obedientia seruari: ille certò sta tuat se hæredē esse uitæ æternæ: iux ta dictum Pauli ad Romanos 5: Iu stificati fide, pacem habemus apud Deum. & Rom.8: Hæredes Dei, co hæredes autem Christi. Quòd ue rò diabolus non recipiatur, causa est hæc: quòd ipse nō ex infirmitate, sed superbia ac fastu quodam, à Deo de sciuit: in quo furore & odio sic iam confirmatus est, ut nihil aliud in uo tis habeat, quàm ut omnia in odium & contumeliā nominis diuini faciat. quare quantum potest, nihil intenta tum relinquit, quo primùm ostendat suum iratum animū erga Deum: de inde, ut ipsum ad iram moueat, in eo quòd suam miseram creaturam ab eo seducit. His sceleribus maiorem ipse quoq; diuinam erga se poenam meretur & cumulat.
units.tr: At this point someone might ask: what is the cause of so great hatred and enmity of the evil spirits against the Church, and why are the evil spirits not received by God in the same way as men? To these questions the answer is as follows. That supreme prince of the evil spirits, when he saw the Son of God so humbling himself before his heavenly Father, exalted himself above the Son of God and despised him. For this cause he was cast down from heaven and deprived of all the gifts with which God had adorned him at creation. From that time, driven by a kind of natural hatred, since he could not pour out his poison against God, he tries with all his strength to turn the weak nature of man, namely the human being, away from love and affection for the Creator, and to make God hateful to him. This is clearly attested by the history of the fall of our first parents, Genesis 3. Man, however, was not, unlike the devil, turned away from God rashly, but by the instigation of that same fall. Wherefore, although the justice of God always keeps that rule in other cases, that sin be punished in all creatures, and it may seem more marvellous that God should dispense from his own law than that he created and preserves the world, yet he so dispenses with his right that his only-begotten Son becomes a suppliant, and makes satisfaction to the Father for the sins of the human race, which had been plunged by the devil's deceits into the misery of eternal rejection. This, moreover, is the remaining comfort for men: whoever has laid hold of the Son of God by faith and has been able to apply his benefits to himself, that is, to be saved by his obedience alone, let him confidently conclude that he is an heir of eternal life, according to Paul's saying in Romans 5: "Justified by faith, we have peace with God," and Romans 8: "heirs of God, and co-heirs of Christ." But that the devil is not received is for this reason: he fell from God not through weakness but through pride and a kind of arrogance, and in that fury and hatred he has been so confirmed that he has nothing else in his mind than to bring everything to the hatred and reproach of the divine name. Therefore, as far as he can, he leaves nothing untried by which he may first show his angry mind towards God, and then, in order to provoke God to anger, he seduces God's wretched creature away from him. By these crimes he himself also merits and heaps up a greater divine punishment upon himself.

units.la: Hæc sunt quę hic paucis de sanctis & malis angelis dicere uolui, si qui forte mecum ad recordationem diuinorum beneficiorum excitari per ea possent: quo sic instituamus omnis uitæ nostræ actiones, sicut Paulus iubet, pie, iustè, sobriè: ac preces nostras eò dirigamus, ut sancti angeli fiant custodes nostrorū corporum, et deductores animarum nostrarum: sicut de Lazaro in Luca diserte dicitur, quòd angeli ipsum in ęternam uitam deduxerint. Idq; ut nobis omnibus fiat, æternū patrem Domini nostri IESV Christi rogabimus: qui hæc ingentia beneficia quærentibus in filio, & per eum promisit.
units.tr: These are the things I wished to say briefly here about the holy and the evil angels, in case they might by any chance move others with me to remember the divine benefits. So may we order all the actions of our life as Paul bids, soberly, righteously and godly, and direct our prayers so that the holy angels become guardians of our bodies and escorts of our souls, as is said plainly of Lazarus in Luke, that the angels carried him into eternal life. May the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ grant this to all of us, he who has promised these great benefits, through the Son, to those who seek them.

units.la: Nunc uerò serenissime rex MAMILIANE, S. R. M. T. offero primitias huius mei laboris: quę ex prælectionibus Philippi Melanchthonis, thonis, aliísq; clarissimorũ uirorum relationibus, non sine studio atq; labore per multos annos collegi, ac in hunc ordinem digesi. Eum quidem non ingratũ futurum S. R. M. T. plane mihi persuadeo.
units.tr: Now, most serene King Maximilian, I offer Your Sacred Royal Majesty the first fruits of this my labour, which I have gathered over many years, not without zeal and toil, from the lectures of Philip Melanchthon and the accounts of very distinguished men, and have arranged in this order. I am quite persuaded that it will not be unwelcome to Your Royal Majesty.

units.la: Primùm enim audio, liberalia studia, eorum' que sectatores in tanto precio esse apud S. R. M. T. ut omnibus modis coseruare & promouere eos cupiat: & in primis eos coplecti atq; fouere, qui ad posteritatem propagare literas studeant. Quòd si tale quiddam (ut non diffido) in nostro hoc Opere inuenerít: id eo animo, quo ea offeruntur à me, ut accipiat, ac authoritate sua maleuolorum morsus à nobis repellat, etiam atq; etiam oro.
units.tr: For first, I hear that liberal studies and their devotees are held in such high esteem by Your Royal Majesty that you wish to preserve and promote them in every way, and above all to embrace and foster those who strive to hand letters down to posterity. If you find something of this kind in our present work (as I do not doubt), I earnestly beg you again and again to accept it in the spirit in which I offer it, and by your authority to repel the bites of ill-wishers from us.

units.la: Quòd uerò ausus fuerím S. R. M. T. hoc Opere adire, adhortati sunt me, & approbarũt institutum meum multa præclara Reipublicæ literariæ lumina, & ciues S. R. M. T. regnorũ, qui spem mihi faciebant nõ dubiam, fore ut hæc animi mei significatio sereno
units.tr: As for my having ventured to approach Your Royal Majesty with this work, I was encouraged, and my undertaking was approved, by many distinguished lights of the republic of letters and by citizens of Your Majesty's kingdoms, who gave me no doubtful hope that this declaration of my mind would meet with a serene

units.la: DEDICATORIA.
units.tr: DEDICATORY.

units.la: reno uultu à S.R.M.T. suscipéretur. Quod ut fiat, submísse oro. Denique me, & hunc meum laborē, quàm humilimè S.R.M.T. cōmendo. Omnipotēs Deus & pater Domini nostri IESV Christi, S.R.M.T. unà cum generosissima coniuge, illustrissimisq; liberis, longæuam incolumitatē, tranquillam gubernationem, omnisq; generis tam futurae q; huius uitæ bona cōcedat: ut uera fortitudine Samsonem, pietate Dauidem, sapientia Salomonem exprímat. Auertat etiam misericors Deus à S.R.M.T. totoq; eiusdem Imperio, per suos angelos, quicquid paci publicæ, ueraeq; pietati aduersatur: Amen. Datæ Basileæ, in festo Michaelis archangeli, anno reparatæ à Christo salutis M.D.LXII.
units.tr: with a serene countenance from Your Serene Royal Majesty. That this may come about, I pray with all humility. Finally, I commend myself and this my labour to Your Serene Royal Majesty as humbly as I can. May Almighty God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, grant to Your Serene Royal Majesty, together with your most noble consort and most illustrious children, long life and good health, a peaceful reign, and every kind of good thing, both of the life to come and of this present life; so that you may express in true fortitude a Samson, in piety a David, in wisdom a Solomon. May merciful God also turn away from Your Serene Royal Majesty and your whole Empire, through his angels, whatever is hostile to public peace and true piety: Amen. Given at Basel, on the feast of Michael the Archangel, in the year of salvation restored by Christ 1562.

units.tr: Johannes Manlius.

units.tr: Simon Sulzer to the kind reader, greetings.

units.la: VTarijs modis Deus æternus pater Domini nostri IESV Christi, suam in hoc mũdo ecclesiā omnib. retrò seculis collegit, collectam suauiter fouit atq; defendit: ita uel maximè his, in quæ incidimus, postremis temporibus, miráda dilectiõe & benignitate cœlestib. eandē thesauris perfundit, iuxta diuitias gratiæ suæ, de qua ubertim impartitur in omni sapientia & prudentia, & ut uerus oriens Sol ex alto lucis suæ radios emittit, quò dispulsa magis magisq; ignorantia & cæcitate, in qua mundus per principem tenebrarum detinetur, uerè contueri lætum Euangelij fulgorem, & frui die posit quem facit solíustitiæ CHRISTVS.
units.tr: In many ways, and above all in these last times, into which we have fallen, the eternal God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ has gathered his Church in the world from ages past. He has cherished and defended the Church he gathered, and with wonderful love and kindness he has showered it with heavenly treasures, according to the riches of his grace, from which he imparts abundantly in all wisdom and prudence. Like the true rising Sun, he sends out the rays of his light from on high, so that ignorance and blindness, in which the world is held by the prince of darkness, are increasingly dispelled, and we may truly behold the joyful brightness of the Gospel and enjoy the day which Christ, the Sun of righteousness, makes.

units.la: Quare par est, ut laudis sacrificium præstemus ei omnes pro beneficio tanto, quo sui in dilecto filio noticiam, quæ uera sapientia est, & radix immortalitatis, nobis misericorditer communicat.
units.tr: Therefore it is right that we all offer the sacrifice of praise to him for so great a benefit, by which he mercifully imparts to us the knowledge of himself in his beloved Son, which is true wisdom and the root of immortality.

units.la: Deinde uerò, ut sincero & ardenti pectore hæc ipsius dona amplectamur, augescentes incremento Dei proficia- mus constanter, ad perfectiora intenti: quandoquidem hic subsistere, deficere est. Postremò, quod pietatis est, & candoris, reuerenter de ijs etiam sentiamus & loquamur, quorum opera, uigilantia, fide, emolumenta tam salutaria Dominus confert. Inter cæteros autem diuinę lucis promos atq; ministros, nō postremum locum tenere cēsendus est uir doctissimus atq; sanctissimus, PHILIPPVS MELANCHTHON: cuius fama nominisq; celebritas ita doctis passim omnibus innotuit, ut operosa elogia haud quaquam requirat: neq; sit opus ceu è mortuis eū euocare ad cœtus hominū, cùm memoriam sui nunquam non refricet ipse lectoribus, illustribus utilibusq; monumentis. Prodit enim ipse, dum doctrina ipsius, Dei beneficio, in Scholis per fideles interpretes sonat: uel bonorum uirorum industria typis mandatur. nam cùm innumeras, easq; graues meditationes de uarijs doctrinæ Christianæ partibus, literis ipse mandarit: tum qua fuit ingenij felicitate, tota eius ὁμι-λία, qua nihil doctius ac piū magis, sem-per
units.tr: Then, indeed, that we may embrace these gifts of his with a sincere and burning heart, let us advance steadily, growing by the increase of God and aiming at what is more perfect, since to stand still here is to fall back. Finally, as is proper to piety and candour, let us think and speak with reverence of those also through whose labours, watchfulness and faith the Lord bestows such saving benefits. Among the other promoters and ministers of the divine light, the most learned and most holy man, PHILIPP MELANCHTHON, must be considered to hold no minor place. His fame and the celebrity of his name are so well known to all learned people everywhere that he needs no elaborate praise, nor is there any need to call him back from the dead to gatherings of men, since he himself never ceases to renew his memory for readers through his illustrious and useful monuments. For he still speaks, while his teaching, by God's blessing, resounds in the schools through faithful interpreters, or is committed to print through the diligence of good men. For although he himself committed to writing countless and weighty meditations on the various parts of Christian doctrine, yet by the felicity of his genius his whole homilia [ὁμιλία], than which nothing is more learned or more pious,

units.la: Note: the scan is cropped and the left-margin notes are illegible; not transcribed. per eos protulit fructus, qui hauriri ex ipso uel per occasione ad illustres sapientiae profectus possent, quos ipse siue in familiaribus colloquijs, siue in publicis praelectionibus ex diuitis pectoris penu depromsit, ut omnes & actiones, & sermones, bono publico aedificationique seruierint. Magnu est, una cum doctrinę ubertate & copia tantam esse sermonis moderationem, ut cum summa sapientia singularis suauitas perspicuitasq; coniuncta sit. Ac dici de hoc uiro potuit illud Horatij:
units.tr: ...has always brought forth such fruits, as could be drawn from him, even on occasion, for the attainment of distinguished wisdom. These he drew from the store of his rich heart, whether in familiar conversations or in public lectures, so that all his actions and words served the public good and edification. It is a great thing that, together with abundance and richness of doctrine, there should be such moderation of speech that singular sweetness and clarity are joined with the highest wisdom. And of this man one may rightly say that line of Horace:

units.la: Omne tulit punctum, qui miscuit utile dulci.
units.tr: He has won every vote who mixed the useful with the sweet.

units.la: Adeo ubiq; grauem comitatem, & comem grauitate, pietatemq; uel familiares eius sermones retulerunt. Accedebat huc artificiosa industria, ut quaecunque apud authores legisset, ad docendum & oblectandum felicissime accommodaret. Hac re effecit, ut reb. obscurissimis lucem & perspicuitatem afferret, cuius fuit studiosissimus: sicut omnis sophisticTes osor atq; insectator. Non aute uul garis est artificis, ex lectione uaria animaduertere spiritum & genium authorum, sapientiaeq; humanae: quod plurimi mi scripta doctorum tantum animi gratia percurrunt: interea non maiore inde fructu referentes, quàm solent aliquando trapezitæ, qui plurimam pecuniam tractantes, ipsi nihilo euadunt locupletiores: aut quàm solent ij qui terras peregrinas labore, impendio, & periculis nonnunquam lustrat: qui ut maximè situm regionum, ædificiorum magnificentiam, fontium amœnitatē, cursus fluminum, moles montium, gentium mores & uident & commemorant, at quomodo hæc referenda ad usum sint ignorát: nihilo magis uel ad sacrarum literarum professionem, uel ad publicam administrationem idonei, quàm ij qui nunquã pedes patria extulerunt: & sæpe cordatiores, prudentiaq; & dicendi facultate plenius instructi cernũtur, q apud suos solerter, cùm diligenti inspectione morum & exemplorum illustriū, documenta in omnes uitæ partes trahūt: tum observatione eorum, quæ serió, iocò, lepidè, grauiter, modestè, facetè, urbanè, salsè dicuntur, intelligēdi loquēdiq; facultatem sibi parant: idq; non ab ijs solùm qui sapientiæ nomine illustres habētur, sed etiam à rudioribus: quādo & olitor sæpè est opportuna locutus. Maximum quidē apud homines pondus ad persua dendū atq; cōmouēdos animos habēt, quæ ab excellentib. uiris prudenter & tempestiuè feruntur dicta. Salomon enim magnifieri testatur, si quid dicatur à potente: cum submisse sonet pauperis sermo. Cui astipulatur illud Hecubæ apud Euripidē: λόγος γὰρ ἐπ' ἀλοξύτων ἰὼν, καὶ τῶν ἀλοξύτων αὐτὸς, ἢ ταυτὸν ἀδυνέα [?]. Sed enim nec aliorū quoq; minus clarorū dicta & facta, in uita nobis occurrētia, negligenter & sine obseruatione erūt prætereunda. Neq; enim defecerūt adeò nostris temporib. ingenia: neq; euanuit ita spiritus operatio in senescētis hoc mūdi delirio, quin hodie audiātur apophthegmata, gnomæ, paroemiæ, quæ nec gravitate, nec acumine aut solertia priscis, quæ uetustatis nomine suspicimus, ullo modo cedunt. Quid, quod stultissimorum hominū inepti insulsiq; sermones, consilia, actus, utiliter cognoscuntur? ut ex oppositis tenebris, lucis veræ puritatisq; suavitas præstantiaq; plenius elucescat. Ad eum modum in hoc uitæ theatro uersatum PHILIPPVM, pientissimæ memoriæ uirum, apparet, ut oculis atqz auribus in omnia intétis, ex omnibus profectus occasionem hauserit, pectusqz repleuerit, ceu apis generosa sedulaqz, ex omnigenis floribus, pulcherrimarum rerum copia, uarietate & suauitate: quibus præleCtiones atqz scripta sua sic condire potuit, ut nemo non summa cum uoluptate attentioneqz docentem, aut etiam familiariter colloquentem audierit: & ceu Ognius Hercules, catena quadam minimè ingrata, ex remotissimis orbis Christiani plagis ad se pertraxerit discendi avidos, pertractosqz retinuerit citra fastidium: quòd non dubitarent fructum se relaturos, si limen optimi & doctissimi uiri tereret, ut Sapiens faciendum monet. & tantum abest ut familiaritate diminuta sit doctrina, & actus, quod plerisqz accidit: ut admiratio iudicij & uirtutum indies creuerit, apud omnes qui optimi clarissimiqz uiri consuetudine uterentur. Atque hæc cùm pridem solerter animadvertisset hic doctus & honestus uir M. IOANNES MANTIVS, in præceptore suo, seriò id peranNOS nos plurimos dedit operam, ut quæ ex ipso fidelissimus auscultator & observator audiret, sic exciperet, literisq; custodibus fidelissimis mandaret, ut & sibi &alijs olim usui esse possent: maximè cùm animadverteret, hæc lucubrationibus PHILIPPI non inseri, nec nisi à paucis fideliter teneri. Collegit ergo has veluti ex diuite mensa reliquias, ut quas non dubitaret & frugiferas, & gratas olim futuras esse, propter singulare gratiam, pondus, varietatem, & perspicuitatem: quæ ad ritè explicandam religio-nis & philosophię doctrinam, quantum valeant, norunt qui eas ritè in professo habent. Hinc ergo factum, ut operam e-ius studiumq; docti passim non solùm probarint: verum etiam, ut in publicum ederet, urgere, postulare, flagitare non desierint. Quorum piæ voluntati haud difficulter acquieuit, ut qui se suaq; stu-dia sanctificationi nominis Dei, juvandæq; quantum in ipso est Ecclesiæ, bonisq; studijs, pridem consecrasset. Cæterum quo maiore fructu, molestiaq; mi-nore, his frui studiosi possent, sylvam re-rum cōfusam, in Classes certas, & locos redegit: quò & explicationi Decalogi, alijsque capitibus doctrinæ Christianæ accommodari possent, & ad quamcunque rem inde sibi ornamenta non iniucunda petere. Commendanda ergo diligentia est, quæ documento studiosis discipulis omnibus esse debet, optimi uiri, in auscultando, excipiendoq;, tum in elaborando disponendoq; hoc Opere: quod nec sine sumptibus, neque ἰdιρῶτι mediocri, auxiliante Domino, tandem perfecit: ut si quibus parem occasionem facultatemq; Dominus concesserit, pari fide & sedulitate, publicis adesse cōmodis proponant. Deinde ut pientissimos doctissimi optimiqúe Manlij labores, quocunque possunt officio, fauore, gratiaq; & studio prosequantur & complectantur: Deumq; orent, ut Ecclesiam tot calamitatibus afflictam, benignè respiciat: & dispulsis externis internisq; tempestatibus, pacem in ea sanctam, ad gloriam nominis ipsius restituat. Bene uale: Basileæ, pridie Cal. Octobr.
units.tr: So widely have his familiar conversations also related his serious courtesy, his courtly gravity, and his piety. To this was added a skilful industry, by which whatever he had read in authors he applied most happily to teaching and delighting. By this he brought light and clarity to the most obscure matters, which he pursued most eagerly, being as much an enemy and pursuer of all sophistry as anyone. Yet it is not the mark of a common craftsman to perceive from varied reading the spirit and genius of authors and of human wisdom. Most people run through the writings of learned men merely for the sake of pleasure, and gain no greater profit from them than moneychangers, who handle a great deal of money yet are none the richer for it, or than those who sometimes traverse foreign lands at great labour, expense and danger. Such travellers see and report the sites of regions, the splendour of buildings, the pleasantness of springs, the courses of rivers, the mass of mountains, and the customs of peoples, but they do not know how these things are to be turned to use. They are no more fit for the profession of Holy Scripture or for public administration than those who never set foot outside their homeland. And they are often seen to be more discerning, and more fully equipped with prudence and skill in speaking, who at home, with diligent observation of the morals and examples of illustrious men, draw lessons for every part of life, and by observing what is said seriously, playfully, elegantly, gravely, modestly, wittily, courteously, or with salt, acquire for themselves the ability to understand and to speak. And this comes not only from those who are held famous for wisdom, but also from the less cultivated, since even a gardener has often spoken to the purpose. Indeed, sayings that are uttered prudently and at the right time by distinguished men carry the greatest weight among people for persuading and moving minds. For Solomon testifies that a word spoken by the powerful is held in high regard, whereas the speech of the poor sounds humble. To this agrees that line of Hecuba's in Euripides: λόγος γὰρ ἐπ' ἀλοξύτων ἰὼν, καὶ τῶν ἀλοξύτων αὐτὸς, ἢ ταυτὸν ἀδυνέα [λόγος γὰρ ἐπ' ἀλοξύτων ἰὼν, καὶ τῶν ἀλοξύτων αὐτὸς, ἢ ταυτὸν ἀδυνέα]. But neither should the words and deeds of other, no less famous men, which meet us in life, be passed over carelessly and without notice. For talents have not so failed in our times, nor has the working of the spirit so vanished in this world's senile folly, that there are no sayings, maxims and proverbs heard today which in gravity, sharpness or shrewdness yield in any way to those of antiquity that we admire for their age. And what of this: that the foolish, silly talk, counsels and deeds of the most foolish men are learned to good effect, so that from the contrasting darkness the sweetness and excellence of the true light and purity shine forth more fully? In this way it appears that Philipp, a man of most pious memory, moved about in this theatre of life, with eyes and ears attentive to everything, and drew an occasion for profit from everything, and filled his breast, like a noble and diligent bee, from flowers of every kind, with a store of most beautiful things, of great variety and sweetness. With these he was able to season his lectures and writings in such a way that no one heard him teaching or even conversing familiarly without the greatest pleasure and attention. And like the Ogmian Hercules, drawing men by a certain chain not unpleasant at all, he drew eager learners from the most remote regions of the Christian world to himself, and held them, once drawn, without weariness, since they did not doubt they would reap profit if they wore down the threshold of so good and so learned a man, as the Wise Man advises. And so far is doctrine from being diminished by familiarity, and his conduct, as happens with many, that among all who enjoyed the company of this best and most renowned man, admiration for his judgement and virtues grew daily. Since this learned and honourable man, Master John Mantius, had long ago carefully observed these things in his teacher, he took great pains in a serious matter, that he might receive in such a way what he heard from him as a most faithful listener and observer, and commit it to the most faithful guardian of letters, so that these might one day be of use both to himself and to others. He especially noticed that these things were not inserted in Philipp's lucubrations, and were kept faithfully by only a few. He therefore gathered these remnants, as it were, from a rich table, since he did not doubt they would one day be fruitful and welcome, on account of their singular grace, weight, variety and clarity. Those who have them in their proper use know how much they are worth for rightly explaining the doctrine of religion and philosophy. Hence it came about that learned men everywhere not only approved his labour and zeal, but also did not cease to urge, request and demand that he publish them. Mantius readily yielded to their pious wish, since he had long ago consecrated himself and his studies to the sanctification of God's name, to the helping of the Church as far as in him lay, and to good studies. But that studious readers might enjoy these things with greater profit and less trouble, he reduced the confused forest of material into fixed classes and headings, so that they might be adapted to the explanation of the Decalogue and to other heads of Christian doctrine, and so that from them one might seek pleasing ornaments for any subject whatever. The diligence of this excellent man, both in listening and receiving, and then in working out and arranging this work, is therefore to be commended, and it should be an example to all studious disciples. He completed it, not without great expense and no small labour, with the Lord's help. If the Lord grants similar opportunity and ability to others, let them likewise, with equal faith and diligence, set themselves to serve the public good. Furthermore, let all follow and embrace the most pious labours of the most learned and excellent Mantius with whatever duty, favour, goodwill and zeal they can, and let them pray to God that he will graciously look upon the Church, afflicted by so many calamities, and, having dispelled the external and internal storms, restore to it a holy peace, to the glory of his own name. Farewell. Basel, the day before the Kalends of October.

units.la: Anno Domini 1562.
units.tr: In the year of the Lord 1562.

units.la: PAVLI CHERLERI ELSTER-burgensis Elegia, in librum Ioannis Manlij, ad Lectorem.
units.tr: Elegy by Paul Cherler of Elsterberg, on John Manlius's book, to the Reader.

units.la: QVisquis amat varios rerum cognoscere casus,Quos hodie miri temporis ordo refert:Historiasq; graues, & multo sparsa leporeDognata, commixtis & pia dicta iocis:Hunc legat, emissum nuper sub luminis auras,Iudicio scriptas res moderante, librum.Plurima cognoscet, cognoscet plurima passim,Affectus animi quæ meditantis habent.Namq; ubi forte leget, miseris mortalibus anniSæpius ut mira conditione cadant:Hic velut ipse sibi mortem parit, alter ut illumTollit, & hunc rursum punit ut ipse Deus.Huic bonaceu blando multu fortuna iocatur,Dum facit ut cedant omine cuncta bono:Aspicit hinc alium duro velut invida multu,Dum facit ut cedant omine cuncta malo.Hæc ubi forte leget, vel dulcia gaudia carpet,Vel gemitus animo commiserante dabit.Interdum tacitè dicet: Proh Iuppiter alme,Quàm variis isto ludis in orbe modis.Sed neq; diversi solum sua pectora casus,Quos legimus miros sæpe fuisse, trahent.Doctrinis sed plena suis pulcherrima dicta,Omnibus in primis commoda mille ferent.Nam velut hortus alit varias amplissimus herbas,Vnde homini semper largior usus abit:Sic Liber hic etiam, tanquam pulcherrimus hortus,Herbarum & florum suggerit omne genus.Quo curis igitur gaudet sua corda levare,Vt mœstus veniat rebus amica quies:Hunc animo interdum vacuo spacietur in hortum,Et flores aliquos sedula carpat apis.
units.tr: Whoever loves to learn the varied fortunes of men, which the order of a wondrous age now brings forth, and serious histories sprinkled with much charm, and lessons mingled with pious jests, let him read this book, lately sent out into the light of day, its matter set down under the guidance of judgement. He will learn very many things, and above all the feelings of the mind that a meditating reader has. For when by chance he reads how wretched mortals often fall into strange conditions: here one, as if by his own hand, brings death upon himself; another is lifted up by God, and then again the same God punishes this one. For one man fortune plays with a kindly and generous charm, making all things turn out well for him; another she gazes on, as if jealous and harsh, making all things turn out badly. When he reads such things, he will either savour sweet joys or give way to groans as his mind feels pity. Sometimes he will say in silence: "O kindly Jupiter, how variously you play with us in this world!" Nor do the varied fortunes we read of, which have often been wondrous, alone move the heart. Yet this most beautiful book, full of its own teachings, will bring a thousand benefits above all else. For just as a generous garden nourishes many kinds of herbs, from which man always draws a richer use, so this book too, like a most beautiful garden, offers every kind of herb and flower. Therefore, whoever rejoices to lighten his heart of cares, so that quiet may come as a friend to the sorrowful, let him at times take a walk into this garden with an empty mind, and let the busy bee pluck some flowers.

units.la: Inde sibi poterit dulcissima fingere mella,Plurima quæ dubijs commoda rebus habent.
units.tr: Thence it can fashion for itself the sweetest honey, which holds much profit amid doubtful matters.

units.la: Vos autem fucos procul hinc procul esse iubemus:Nobis, non uobis, hortulus ille sacer.
units.tr: But you drones, we bid you keep far away from here: that sacred little garden is ours, not yours.

units.la: Vos bene degeneres depingit aranea, quondamPallade quæ talis facta iubente fuit.
units.tr: The spider depicts you as badly degenerate, you who once were made such by the command of Pallas.

units.la: Illa etenim ut fugit generoso è flore uenenum,Vnde premit dulcis munera mellis apis:
units.tr: For just as the bee flees the poison of a noble flower, from which it presses the gifts of sweet honey,

units.la: Sic uobis facile est huius de floribus horti,Pro dulci virus ducere melle nigrum.
units.tr: so for you it is easy, from the flowers of this garden, to draw black poison in place of sweet honey.

units.la: Tum uelut incautæ non parcit aranea muscæ,Cùm cadit in laxas præda petita plagas:
units.tr: Then, just as the spider spares no unwary fly, when the prey it has sought falls into its loose snares,

units.la: Sic ubi paulisper uobis data causa nocendi est,Omnia mordaci carpere dente iuuat.
units.tr: so when a chance to harm is given you for a little while, it delights you to tear everything with a biting tooth.

units.la: Qui sapit, & cuius mentem regit optima virtus,Ingenijs iudex æquior esse solet.
units.tr: He who is wise, and whose mind is ruled by the best virtue, is usually the fairer judge of talents.

units.la: Ille etiam, noster quem nunc tibi Manlius edit,Hunc animo librum candidiore leget:
units.tr: That reader of ours, whom Manlius now brings forth for you, will read this book with a more generous mind.

units.la: Et memor authori grates, laudemq; perennem,Præmia suscepto digna labore, feret.
units.tr: And mindful of the author, he will bear thanks and lasting praise, rewards worthy of the labour undertaken.

units.la: Basileæ, Anno Christi M. D. LXII. Mense Octobri.
units.tr: Basel, in the year of Christ 1562, in the month of October.

units.la: SAMVEL HOLZACHIVS Basiliensis, ad Lectorem.
units.tr: SAMUEL HOLZACH of Basel, to the Reader.

units.la: Integritate pia uir præstans, atq; laboriSocratico fausta sedulitate uacans,Hæc partim scripsit magno dictante PHILIPPO,Et partim ex alijs audijt ipse uiris:Nomine quos celebri sapientia rara beauit,Quod cernet tacitè crescere longa dies.Qui partim uiuunt, humanæ debita partimNaturæ fato persoluere suo.Principiò triados loquitur mysteria summæ,Te Genitor, Fili, Spiritus alme, colens:
units.tr: A man outstanding for pious integrity, devoted to Socratic labour and blessed with a happy diligence, partly wrote these things at the dictation of the great Philip and partly heard them himself from other men, whom rare wisdom has blessed with a celebrated name, a name which the long day, quietly growing, will see. Some of them still live; others have paid to fate the debt owed to human nature. First he speaks of the mysteries of the Triad of the highest, worshipping you, Father, Son and kindly Spirit:

units.la: Ex nihilo tua maiestas ut cuncta crearit,Queis mundi constat machina wasta, docet.
units.tr: How your majesty created all things out of nothing, of which the frame of the world is known to consist, he teaches.

units.la: Tempora continuo dicit labentia motu,Teq; uolans trini nuncia turba Dei.
units.tr: He tells of times slipping away in continual motion, and of you, the flying messenger of the threefold God.

units.la: Humanamq; dein tutantia ritè salutemAetherei regis facta stupenda refert.
units.tr: Then he relates the wondrous deeds of the heavenly King, which rightly protect human salvation.

units.la: Attingit Stygy regnum ferale tyranni,Nec de portentis, prodigysq; tacens.
units.tr: He touches on the deadly kingdom of the tyrant of Styx, and is not silent about portents and prodigies.

units.la: Res varie, quas producit natura, sequuntur:Est quæ mirandis ingeniosa modis.
units.tr: The various things which nature produces follow; there is one that is ingenious in wonderful ways.

units.la: Afferet obscuris hic codex lumina rebus,Haud unquam uulgo lumina visa prius.
units.tr: This book will bring light to obscure things, light never before seen by the common people.

units.la: In Testamentis oracula sacra duobusEdita, præcipuè respicit istud opus.
units.tr: It chiefly regards the sacred oracles published in the two Testaments.

units.la: Quæ digne satis hoc studium facundia laudet,Atq; ita, ne rebus verba minora sient?
units.tr: What eloquence could worthily praise this study enough, and so that the words are not less than the things?

units.la: Artes namq; aliæ peritureæ commoda vitæSpectant, vita quid hæc commoditatis habet?
units.tr: For other arts, doomed to perish, look to the conveniences of life; what convenience does this life have?

units.la: Vita brevis, duri plenissima vita laboris,Humana tolli qui nequit arte labor.
units.tr: Life is short and full of hard labour, a labour that human skill cannot remove.

units.la: Vani (divus ait Paulus) sapientia mundiOmnis ab æterno est infatuata Deo.
units.tr: Vain (says the divine Paul) is all the wisdom of the world, made foolish by the eternal God.

units.la: Discere mortales, quæ sit via certa salutis,E' sacris libris, haud aliunde, queunt.
units.tr: Mortals can learn what the sure way of salvation is only from the sacred books, not from anywhere else.

units.la: Felices animæ, quæ toto corde sequuntur,Quæ sacer ille Dei spiritus ipse docet:
units.tr: Happy are the souls who follow with their whole heart what that holy Spirit of God himself teaches.

units.la: Corpora cùm fuerint algenti clausa sepulchro,Gaudia vera illas, nec peritura manent.
units.tr: When their bodies have been shut up in the cold grave, those souls remain with true joys, which do not perish.

units.la: Quin & post cineres specie fulgente redibuntCorpora supremo clarificata die:
units.tr: Moreover, after the ashes, the bodies will return with a shining form, made bright on the last day.

units.la: Amplius ut non sint funestæ debita morti,Et cum mente pia cœlica templa petant.
units.tr: So that they are no longer subject to deadly death, and with pious mind they may seek the heavenly temples.

units.la: Observabis Lector, quoties literas hasce COLL. insertas videbis, ea quæ statim illis subiiciuntur, Collectoris, non D. PHILIPPI esse dicta. Quod vero ad consilium & laborem materiarum istarum pertinet, si quid ulterius scire cupies, Secundam horum Lotorū partem perlegas: ubi fusius pleraque declarabuntur.
units.tr: Reader, you will observe that whenever you see these letters COLL. inserted, what immediately follows them is said by the Collector, not by D. Philipp. As for the purpose and labour of these materials, if you wish to know more, read through the second part of these Loci, where most of it is explained at greater length.

units.la: DE DEO, TRINITATE, ET TRI-bus in Diuinitate per-sonis.
units.tr: DE DEO, TRINITATE, ET TRIBUS IN DIVINITATE PERSONIS.

units.la: Principium totius sacrae Scriptu-rae est: Ita omnino de Deo sentiendum, loquendum & cogitandum est, ut ipse se patefecit claro verbo, & minimè fallentibus testimonijs, ac editis miraculis Prophetarum Christi, & Apostolorum.
units.tr: The principle of all Holy Scripture is this: God must be felt, spoken of and thought of only as he has revealed himself, by his clear Word, by most trustworthy testimonies, and by the miracles performed by the prophets, Christ and the apostles.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Augustinus à quodam interrogatus, quid Deus ante mundi conditionem fecisset? Respondit: Parauit infernum de his interrogantibus. Doctor Pontanus eadem de re interrogatus, respondit: Sedit iuxta spinetum, & uirgas compegit talibus curiosis, de huiusmodi interrogantibus.
units.tr: When someone asked Augustine what God had been doing before the creation of the world, he replied: "He was preparing hell for those who ask such questions." Doctor Pontanus, asked the same thing, replied: "He sat beside a thicket and cut switches for curious people who ask such things."

units.la: Gratianus Imperator in epistola ad Ambro-sium inquit: Loquimur de Deo, non quantum debemus, sed quantum possumus. Sic quidam meos Locos uocat bona tenuia: sunt plus quàm tenuia, si modò sunt bona tenuia, tunc sum contentus, non irascor illi. plus enim quàm uerum dixit. Nemo sapientiam Dei immensam in omnem æternitatem exhauriet.
units.tr: The Emperor Gratian, in a letter to Ambrose, says: "We speak of God not as much as we ought, but as much as we can. Thus some call my Loci 'good thin things.' They are more than thin, if they are at least good and thin; then I am content and do not grow angry at him, for he has said more than true. No one will ever exhaust the immense wisdom of God through all eternity."

units.la: Doctor Io. Bugenhagius Pomeranus.
units.tr: Doctor Johannes Bugenhagius Pomeranus.

units.la: Quemadmodum si quis audiat noctu in templo pa-storem concionantem, scit eum adesse, sed non ip-sum intuetur: sic genus humanum Deum contem-plari non potest per densam caliginem, quae propter originis peccatum accessit.
units.tr: Just as, if someone at night hears a minister preaching in a church, he knows that he is present but does not see him, so the human race cannot contemplate God through the thick darkness that came in with the sin of origin.

units.la: Homerus uolens exprimere humanas cogita-tiones de Deo, fingit Thetidem quaerere Iouem in coelo, nec domi ipsum inuenire, ut qui esset ad-huc in conuiuio Aethiopum. Haec sunt humanae de Deo cogitationes. Lucianus ille ἀθεος fingit cancellos in coelo per quos Iupiter certo tempore homines respiciat, quo solummodo tempore petentes exaudiantur: qui autem alieno tempore inuo-cant, eorum precationem esse inane murmur.
units.tr: Homer, wishing to express human thoughts about God, pictures Thetis seeking Jove in heaven and not finding him at home, since he was still at the feast of the Ethiopians. These are human thoughts about God. That atheist Lucian imagines grates in heaven through which Jupiter looks down on men at set times, so that only those who pray at that time are heard; as for those who call on him at another time, their prayer is an empty murmur.

units.la: Simonides interrogatus quid esset Deus, petiuit sibi triduum ad cogitandum dari: triduo elapso, denuo sibi triduum concedi voluit. Denique cum diu secum ea de re deliberasset, & iterum interrogaretur, respondit: Quo diutius mecum cogito, eo minus inuenio. Sic humana ratio sine uerbo Dei nihil de Trinitate affirmare potest.
units.tr: When Simonides was asked what God was, he asked for three days to think it over. When three days had passed, he wanted another three days granted to him. At last, after he had deliberated on the matter for a long time and was asked again, he replied: the longer I think about it, the less I find. So human reason, without the Word of God, can affirm nothing about the Trinity.

units.la: Aesopus interrogatus, quid Deus in coelo ageret? Respondit: Ille frangit magnas ollas, & ex fustis alias novas componit. Significare voluit, quod Deus de sede potentes deponat, & humiles exaltet.
units.tr: When Aesop was asked what God was doing in heaven, he answered: He breaks great pots and makes new ones out of the broken pieces. He meant that God casts the mighty down from their seats and exalts the humble.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Non dubium est circulum esse imaginem Trinitatis. Ego sic accomodare, alius aliter: Centrum est Pater, circumferentia est Filius, area est Spiritus sanctus. Sicut centrum est principium circuli, sic Deus est princi-pium omnium rerum. Hæc ex lectione Euclidis sunt ex-cerpta.
units.tr: There is no doubt that the circle is an image of the Trinity. I adapt it in my own way, and others in theirs: the centre is the Father, the circumference is the Son, the area is the Holy Spirit. As the centre is the beginning of the circle, so God is the beginning of all things. These points are excerpted from the reading of Euclid.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Duæ similitudines à sole sumptæ, quibus ueteres utcunquæ Trinita-tem in Vnitate illustrauerūt.
units.tr: Two comparisons taken from the sun, by which the ancients in some measure illustrated the Trinity in the Unity.

units.la: Sol habet tres res in una substantia: primum est in eo circulus: postea est aureus fulgor; denique calor uiuificans res nascentes. Per circulū Patrem intelligebant: per fulgorem aureum, filium Dei, qui est fulgor æterni Patris, ut ipsum nominat Epi-stola ad Hebræos: per calorem uiuificantem, Spiri-tum sanctum, quo Pater Filium, & Filius Patrem complectitur, & postea Pater & Filius totam Ec-clesiam diligunt, & sibi eam adiungunt.
units.tr: The sun has three things in one substance: first, there is the circle in it; then there is the golden brightness; finally, there is the life-giving heat that quickens things that are born. By the circle they understood the Father; by the golden brightness, the Son of God, who is the brightness of the eternal Father, as the Epistle to the Hebrews names him; by the life-giving heat, the Holy Spirit, in whom the Father embraces the Son and the Son the Father, and afterwards the Father and the Son love the whole Church and join it to themselves.

units.la: Secunda parum dissimilis à priore.
units.tr: The second is only slightly different from the first.

units.la: Anima hominis est typus proximus Dei, sicut & sol. In sole sunt tres res considerandæ, radius ipse, lux & uirtus seu calor uiuificans: quæ res non realiter, sed tantum mutuum cogitatione discer-nantur. Radium Patrem esse asserunt: lucē Filiū, sicut ipsum symbolum nominat: Lumē de lumine, uel, ut au loānes, Lux illa uenit in mundū. Virtus altissimi. uocatur Spiritus sanctus in conceptione Christi ab angelo Gabriele.
units.tr: The soul of man is the nearest type of God, as the sun is too. In the sun three things are to be considered: the ray itself, the light, and the power or life-giving heat. These things are not distinguished in reality but only in thought, as it were by mutual reckoning. They say the ray is the Father, the light the Son, as the creed itself names him: "Light of light," or, as John says, "That light came into the world." "The power of the Highest" is what the angel Gabriel calls the Holy Spirit at the conception of Christ.

units.la: COLL. Similitudo sumpta ab homine, illustrans Trinitatem.
units.tr: COLL. A comparison taken from man, illustrating the Trinity.

units.la: Tria sunt præcipua in homine, mens, sermo seu cogitatio, & spiritus: νοῦς, λόγος καὶ πνεῦμα, quæ sunt pulcherrima imago Trinitatis. νοῦς enim seu mens gignit cogitationem aut sermonem, & habet se ut æternus Pater, qui sese cogitans & intuēs gignit Filium. λόγος habet se ut Filius, qui ostendit Patrem sicut cogitatio uel sermo mentem. πνεῦμα sicut Spiritus sanctus, qui commixtus nostris spiritibus excitat in nobis tales motus, qualis est ipse.
units.tr: There are three chief things in man: mind, speech or thought, and spirit [νοῦς, λόγος καὶ πνεῦμα], which are a most beautiful image of the Trinity. For the mind [νοῦς] or understanding begets thought or speech, and stands as the eternal Father does, who, thinking and contemplating himself, begets the Son. Speech [λόγος] stands as the Son does, who shows forth the Father as thought or speech shows forth the mind. Spirit [πνεῦμα] stands as the Holy Spirit does, who, mingled with our spirits, stirs up in us motions such as its own.

units.la: Trinitas secundum artes, descripta à Luthero.
units.tr: The Trinity according to the arts, described by Luther.

units.la: Deus Pater in diuinis est Grammatica: dat enim uoces, estq; fons ipse. Filius est Dialectica: dat dispositiones rerum, estq; uerbum λόγος, & dispounit omnia. Spiritus sanctus est Rhetorica: quia inspirat & mouet uiuificando.
units.tr: God the Father is in divine things like grammar: for he gives the words and is himself the source. The Son is like dialectic: he gives the arrangement of things, and he is the Word [λόγος], and he orders all things. The Holy Spirit is like rhetoric, because he inspires and moves by quickening.

units.la: Confabulatio inter Doctorem Martinum Lutherum & Philippum, quòd in creaturis reperiantur similitudines de Trinitate.
units.tr: A conversation between Doctor Martin Luther and Philip, that likenesses of the Trinity are found in creatures.

units.la: In fluminibus, substantia, fluxus & potentia: sic etiam in artibus. In Astronomia, motus, lumen & influentia. In Musica, re, mi, fa. In Geometria, tres dimensiones, linea, superficies, corpus. In Gra-matica, tres partes orationis. In Arithmetica, tres numeri. In Rhetorica, dispositio, elocutio et actio seu gestus. Inuentio nō est artis, sed naturæ. Sic quaelibet res habet pondus, numerum, & figuram.
units.tr: In rivers there is substance, flow and power; so also in the arts. In astronomy there are motion, light and influence. In music, re, mi, fa. In geometry, three dimensions: line, surface, body. In grammar, three parts of speech. In arithmetic, three numbers. In rhetoric, arrangement, delivery and action or gesture. Invention belongs not to art but to nature. So every thing has weight, number and shape.

units.la: ATTRIBVTA, & PROprietates Dei.
units.tr: The attributes and properties of God.

units.la: Plato: μόνῳ θεῷ γόρας ἐστὶν, εἶναι τελεάγωνον: Solius Dei honos seu decus est, inquit, esse perfectum. Videtis præstantes naturas subitò mutari. Igitur solius Dei decus est, quòd sit in eo perfectio uirtutis. Humana omnia sunt fragilia: sicut uidetis in Alexandro Magno, illam excellentē & præstantem naturam ita degenerasse à sese, & tam subitò sui factam esse dissimilem, ut mirum sit tantæ uirtutis, & tot honestarum actionum tam repentinā fieri posse mutationem.
units.tr: Plato: the prerogative of God alone is to be perfect [μόνῳ θεῷ γέρας ἐστὶν εἶναι τετράγωνον]. The honour or glory of God alone, he says, is to be perfect. You see how excellent natures are suddenly changed. Therefore it is the glory of God alone that perfection of virtue is in him. All human things are frail, as you see in Alexander the Great: that excellent and outstanding nature so degenerated from itself and became so suddenly unlike its former self that it is wonderful that such a great change of virtue and so many honourable deeds could come about so quickly.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: Collectanea

units.la: Mera est ignorantia Dei, nescire quòd Deus sit Deus uitæ & consolationis: id est, quòd Deus sit consolator afflictorum, lætitia & uita. Et econtrà verissima Dei cognitio est, scire quòd Deus non sit diabolus, sed simpliciter Deus. Est enim æquiuocum Deus, id quod euangelista Matthæus capite quarto indicat. Hic bene distingue diabolum, qui se Dominum omnium rerum uocat, ut à uero Deo discernatur, qui est huius uitæ sustentator.
units.tr: It is sheer ignorance of God not to know that God is the God of life and comfort: that is, that God is the comforter of the afflicted, the joy and the life. And conversely, the truest knowledge of God is to know that God is not the devil but simply God. For "God" is an equivocal term, as the evangelist Matthew indicates in chapter four. Here distinguish well the devil, who calls himself the Lord of all things, so that he may be told apart from the true God, who is the sustainer of this life.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: Collectanea

units.la: Cum Mileti inuentam auream mensam Apollo iussisset sapientissimo dari, ciuitas eam Thaleti dandam esse decreuit. Is magnitudinem huius laudis sibi non competere agnoscens, & libenter alteri uel impertiens uel cedens, misit Soloni. Solon ad eundem modum Bianti. Cum per omnes septem Græciæ sapientes uagata mensa ad Thaletem redijsseт, ait Thales: Nunc demum se oraculi sententiam intelligere, iussitq; mensam Apollini offerri, quòd Deus significasset hoc simuolucro, neminem mortalium, sed solum Deum sapientem esse.
units.tr: When the golden table that had been found at Miletus was ordered by Apollo to be given to the wisest man, the city decided it should be given to Thales. He, recognising that the greatness of this honour did not belong to him, and gladly either sharing it with another or yielding it, sent it to Solon. Solon sent it on in the same way to Bias. When the table, having wandered through all the seven wise men of Greece, had returned to Thales, he said that only now did he understand the sense of the oracle, and he ordered the table to be offered to Apollo, because God had signified by this symbol that no mortal, but God alone, is wise.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: Collectanea

units.la: Iupiter apud Homerum suspensus de catena dicitur. Expositum est ab Ethnicis, quòd Deus alligatus sit causis secundis. Imo credo potius uoluisse significare Homerum, illud numen æternum posse moderari causas secundas sua libertate.
units.tr: In Homer, Jupiter is said to be suspended from a chain. The heathen have explained this to mean that God is bound to secondary causes. Indeed, I believe rather that Homer meant to signify that this eternal power can govern secondary causes by its own freedom.

units.la: PROVIDENTIA ET contingentia.
units.tr: Providence and contingency.

units.la: Est apud Claudianum in bello Ruffini, ubi dicit se sæpè disputasse secum, an sit prouidentia: sed tamen se statuere, esse prouidentiā, postquā Ruffinus punitus sit. COLL.
units.tr: There is a passage in Claudian, in his poem on the war against Rufinus, where he says that he has often argued with himself whether there is providence; yet he has resolved that there is providence, now that Rufinus has been punished. COLL.

units.la: Diogenes dicebat de Harpago, qui rapuerat magnam pecuniam ex thesauro Alexandri, cuius fuerat thesaurarius: Harpagus locuples affert testimonium contra Deos, cum sit homo omnium pessimus.
units.tr: Diogenes said of Harpagus, who had stolen a great sum of money from the treasury of Alexander, whose treasurer he had been: "Harpagus, rich man, bears witness against the gods, though he is the worst of all men."

units.la: Erat Tubingæ optimus uir Franciscus Stadianus, mihi admodum familiaris, qui sæpius dicebat: Certissimè statuo, quòd sit prouidentia & contingentia: sed quomodo illa fiant plane ignoro.
units.tr: There was at Tübingen an excellent man, Franciscus Stadianus, very close to me, who often said: "I am most certain that there is both providence and contingency, but how these things come about I quite simply do not know."

units.la: Imago Dei in homine.
units.tr: The image of God in man.

units.la: Quare homo uocetur imago Dei? Respondeo: Quia est in eo quiddam iudicas, quod est mens et uoluntas, ac libertas aliqua electionis propter mentē.
units.tr: Why is man called the image of God? I answer: because in him there is something like a judge, namely mind and will, and some freedom of choice on account of the mind.

units.la: Ambrosius.
units.tr: Ambrose.

units.la: Non est imago Dei, in qua non habitat ipse Deus. Quod recte dicitur de renouata imagine.
units.tr: That is not the image of God in which God himself does not dwell. This is rightly said of the renewed image.

units.la: DE FILIO DEI. DE DVABVS NATVRIS in filio Dei.
units.tr: Concerning the Son of God. Concerning the two natures in the Son of God.

units.la: Viola habet pulcherrimā allegoriā ad designādū Christum. Purpureus color significat humanam naturam crucifixam: aureus significat diuinam in Christo. Item uiola significat concionatorem, seu pastorem Ecclesiæ. Purpureus color significat crucem: aureus uerbum Dei & fidem. Odor ille fragrātissimus significat illam fragrantiā uerbi Dei, id est Euangelij.
units.tr: The violet offers a very fine allegory for designating Christ. The purple colour signifies the crucified human nature; the golden colour signifies the divine nature in Christ. Likewise the violet signifies the preacher, or minister, of the Church. The purple colour signifies the cross; the golden, the Word of God and faith. That most fragrant odour signifies that fragrance of the Word of God, that is, of the Gospel.

units.la: Præcipuæ synodi: Antiochena refutauit Samosatenũ, qui affirmauit Christum tantum uulgarem hominem fuisse, & eum sicut alij homines, sapientia, gratia ac aliis donis profecisse. Nicæna condidit symbolum Nicænum, & illustrauit in primis articulum de duabus in Christo naturis. In Constantinopolitana quid actum sit, uide locum de Spiritu sancto. Ephesina damnauit Nestorium, qui extinxit hanc doctrinam: Non esse in Christo unitas duas naturas, sed λόγον adesse Christo, sicut amicus amico adest, aut sicut apud poetas Pallas adest Vlysi. Chalcedonensis damnauit Eutychen, qui confundebat naturas in Christo & fingebat humanam conuersam esse in diuinam, ut cum ex aqua & melle facta est mulsa.
units.tr: The principal synods: the Synod of Antioch refuted Samosatenus, who asserted that Christ was merely an ordinary man, and that he advanced, as other men do, in wisdom, grace and other gifts. The Synod of Nicaea framed the Nicene Creed and above all clarified the article concerning the two natures in Christ. For what was done at Constantinople, see the locus on the Holy Spirit. The Synod of Ephesus condemned Nestorius, who abolished this doctrine: that there is not a unity of two natures in Christ, but that the Word is present to Christ as a friend is present to a friend, or as Pallas is present to Ulysses among the poets. The Synod of Chalcedon condemned Eutyches, who confused the natures in Christ and imagined that the human nature had been changed into the divine, as when honey and water are made into mead.

units.la: In historia Samsonis est dictum: De forti exiuit dulcedo, id est: leo putrefactus gignit examen apum. leoni comparatur humana natura. Quo ænigmate etiam significatur, ex mortuo Christo prodire Ecclesiam & Euangelium.
units.tr: In the story of Samson there is the saying: "Out of the strong came forth sweetness," that is, the lion, when it had rotted, produced a swarm of bees. The human nature is compared to the lion. By this riddle is also signified that the Church and the Gospel come forth from the dead Christ.

units.la: Dionysius Areopagita uidens eclipsin solis in passione Christi contra naturæ ordinem existere, dixit: aut Deum naturæ pati, aut totam mundi machinam interituram esse. Unde satis clare liquet, in Christo uere Diuinam naturam fuisse.
units.tr: Dionysius the Areopagite, seeing that an eclipse of the sun occurred at the passion of Christ, contrary to the order of nature, said: either the God of nature is suffering, or the whole machinery of the world is about to perish. From this it is sufficiently clear that in Christ there truly was the divine nature.

units.la: DE OFFICIIS CHRISTI. COLL.
units.tr: ON THE OFFICES OF CHRIST. COLL.

units.la: Augustinus de imagine Christi pendentis in cru-ce inquit: Inspice uulnera pendentis Christi, sangui-nem morientis, precium redimentis, cicatrices re-surgentis. Caput habet inclinatum ad osculandum, cor apertum ad diligendum, manus extensas ad amplectendum, totum corpus expositum ad redi-mendum. Hæc quanta sint cogita, hæc in statero cordis tui perpende, ut totus figatur tibi in corde, qui totus pro te fixus fuit in crucem.
units.tr: Augustine, on the image of Christ hanging on the cross, says: Look at the wounds of the hanging Christ, the blood of the dying one, the price of the one who redeems, the scars of the one who rises. His head is bowed to kiss you, his heart is opened to love you, his hands are stretched out to embrace you, his whole body is exposed to redeem you. Consider how great these things are, weigh them on the balance of your heart, so that he who was wholly fixed to the cross for you may be wholly fixed in your heart.

units.la: Naturale odium est inter serpētem & pellica-num. Pellicanus cū auolat à suis pullis, quæsiturus eis cibum, interea irrepit in nidum ipsius serpens, & interficit pullos, super quibus mater reuertens, triduo lugere fertur. Deinde in pectore se uulne-rans, conspergit eos proprio suo sanguine, & sic à mortuis pullos resuscitat. Sanguine effuso, debili-tatur mater adeò, ut pulli cogantur exire & quæ-rere sibi uictum, quorum quidam naturali affectu matrem debilitatam pascunt. Quidam uerò degene-neres, matris nullam prorsus curam gerunt. Quòd mater animaduertens, receptis uiribus pullos se pa-scentes refouet: alios uerò ingratos à se reijcit, aut uiuere non permittit. Pulcherrima imago est, fi-lium Dei saluatorem nostrum representans. Dia-bolus naturali odio filium Dei, & eius pullos, id est, credentes, prosequitur, & eis uitam tandem crudeliter eripit: Christus uero, qui est uita & dator uitae, nostra calamitate motus uulnerat se in pectore, & uitam suam pro nobis æterno Patri offert, suoq; sanguine nos à serpentis ictibus in uitam æternam restituit. Sed quid fit? Quidam pulli illud beneficium amplectuntur, & sunt grati erga matrem Ecclesiam & Christum: quidam uero degeneres negligunt beneficia, & erga matrem Ecclesiam sunt ἀτεκνοι, quos tandem filius Dei ex Ecclesia exterminabit, & in extremo iudicio iudicabit.
units.tr: There is a natural hatred between the serpent and the pelican. When the pelican flies off from its young to seek food for them, a serpent meanwhile creeps into the nest and kills the chicks. The mother, returning, is said to mourn them for three days. Then she wounds herself in the breast and sprinkles the chicks with her own blood, and so raises them from the dead. With her blood poured out, the mother is so weakened that the chicks are forced to go out and seek their own food. Some of them, out of natural affection, feed their weakened mother. Others, degenerate, take no care of her at all. The mother, noticing this, when she has recovered her strength, cherishes the chicks that feed themselves, but casts off the ungrateful ones or does not allow them to live. It is a most beautiful image, representing the Son of God, our Saviour. The devil, out of natural hatred, pursues the Son of God and his chicks, that is, believers, and at last cruelly snatches their life away; but Christ, who is life and the giver of life, moved by our calamity, wounds himself in the breast, offers his life to the eternal Father for us, and by his blood restores us from the serpent's strikes to eternal life. But what happens? Some chicks embrace that benefit and are grateful to their mother the Church and to Christ; but others, degenerate, neglect the benefits and are childless [ἀτεκνοι] toward their mother the Church, whom the Son of God will at last banish from the Church and judge at the last judgment.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Cedrus est imago officiorum Christi. Quemadmodum enim cedrus apposita cadauera prohibet à putrefactione & arrosione uermium, nec uiuos patitur: sic Christus reddit mortuis uitam, uiuentibus adfert mortem.
units.tr: The cedar is an image of the offices of Christ. For just as cedar, when placed beside corpses, keeps them from putrefaction and from being gnawed by worms, yet does not let living things remain, so Christ restores life to the dead and brings death to the living.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Sicut adamas tanta duritie est, ut nulla ui possit frangi nisi adhibito sanguine hircino: ita diaboli potentia maior est, quàm ut possit ab ulla creatura debilitari: sed solo cruore filij Dei frangitur & debilitatur.
units.tr: Just as the adamant is of such hardness that it cannot be broken by any force unless goat's blood is applied, so the power of the devil is too great to be weakened by any creature; but it is broken and weakened by the blood of the Son of God alone.

units.la: POENA CONTEMPTVS officiorum filij Dei. COLL.
units.tr: PUNISHMENT FOR CONTEMPT OF THE OFFICES OF THE SON OF GOD. COLL.

units.la: Iulianus apostata cùm bello Parthico abesset, Liba-
units.tr: Julian the Apostate, while he was away on the Parthian war, Liba-

units.la: Libanius impius sophista Antiochiæ ludimagistrũ interrogat, Christianã irridendo religione: Nunc inquit, fabri filiũ quid putas facere? At ludimagister Spiritus sancti instinctu prædixit, quod paulo post accidit. Respondit enim: O sophista, creator omniũ rerũ, quẽ tu fabri filiũ appellas, loculũ Iuliano concinnat. Post paucos dies Iulianus telo (de quo incertus erat unde erat missum) traiectus interijt, ac loculo impositus Antiochiã est aduectus. Ita qui in cœlis est irridet eos, & vicissim subsannat hostes suos.
units.tr: Libanius, the impious sophist, asked a schoolmaster at Antioch, mocking the Christian religion: "Now, what do you think the son of the carpenter is doing?" But the schoolmaster, moved by the Holy Spirit, foretold what happened a little later. For he replied: "O sophist, the creator of all things, whom you call the son of a carpenter, is making a coffin for Julian." A few days later Julian was pierced by a weapon (of which it was uncertain where it had been sent from) and died; laid in a coffin, he was carried to Antioch. Thus he who is in heaven laughs at them, and in turn mocks his enemies.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Cũ ageretur in quodã celebri loco tragœdia de passione & morte Domini nostri Iesu Christi quidã agẽs personã pendentis in cruce Saluatoris nostri, acceptoin corde lethali uulnere, ab alio t e ẽte uesicã cruore impletã, et lateri ipsius alligatã, mortuus cõcidit: aliũ etiã, qui deflentis sub cruce personã repræsentabat, lapsu interemit, cuius mortẽ frater uindicãs in eo, qui ipsum in ligno pendentẽ sauciauit, capitali supplicio affectus est. Ita quatuor occubuerũt nõ sine suspicione, quòd homines in tã seriis reb. ludãt: præsertim cùm id fieri nõ possit sine offensione piorũ hominũ ac Deũ timentiũ. Est etiã pœna, qua Deus irã suã uult ostendere aduersus cõtemptores passionis Domini nostri IESV Christi, quam amplius repræsentari non uelit.
units.tr: When a tragedy about the passion and death of our Lord Jesus Christ was being performed in a certain famous place, one man, playing the part of our Saviour hanging on the cross, received a deadly wound in the heart from another actor, and, with a bladder filled with blood tied to his side, fell dead. Another, who was representing a person mourning beneath the cross, was killed by a fall; his brother, avenging his death, struck down the one who had wounded the man hanging on the wood, and was put to death by capital punishment. Thus four died, not without suspicion that men are playing with such serious matters, especially since this cannot happen without offence to pious men and those who fear God. There is also a punishment by which God wishes to show his anger against those who despise the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, which he does not wish to be represented any further.

units.la: DE SPIRITV SANCTO. COLL.
units.tr: CONCERNING THE HOLY SPIRIT. COLL.

units.la: INhistoria Ambrosij est, quòd quando enarra-uerit hæc uerba: Sicut ouis ducitur ad mactan-dum, tunc scriba eius uidit flammam ex ore ipsius erumpere, quæ uerè fuit Spiritus sanctus.
