De Elia idem scriptum est ab Epiphanio in uitis Patrum, quòd quando solitus est infantulus lambere papil-las matris, mater & alij uiderunt eum non trahere lac, sed flammam. Significatū est futurum eum plenum Spiritu sancto.
units.tr: In the history of Ambrose it is related that when he was expounding these words, "As a sheep is led to the slaughter," his scribe saw a flame break out of his mouth, which was truly the Holy Spirit. Of Elijah the same thing is written by Epiphanius in the Lives of the Fathers: when the little child was accustomed to suckle at his mother's breasts, the mother and others saw that he did not draw milk but a flame. It was signified that he would be full of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Quidam dicunt Spiritum sanctum dari non essentialiter, ignorantes quid dicant. Quando Spi-ritus sanctus mouet cor, mentem, & brachia Dauidis in prælio, ipse Spiritus sanctus fuit in eo substā-tialiter, id est: nō est eadē persona, sed est in eo tā-quam in domicilio, & tanquam in templo separa-biliter, ac tamē adest substātialiter, permiscetq; se ipsius spiritibus in cerebro & in corde, agitat, & eum mouet, quod est magnum Dei beneficium, quòd Diuinitas ita se nobis permiscet. Hoc quid sit, inde potest intelligi, quia in Scriptura sæpè dicitur: Misit spiritum Filij sui in corda uestra.
units.tr: Some say that the Holy Spirit is given not essentially, not knowing what they are saying. When the Holy Spirit moves the heart, the mind and the arms of David in battle, the Holy Spirit himself was in him substantially, that is, not as the same person, but he is in him as in a dwelling and as in a temple separable from him, and yet he is present substantially, mingles himself with the spirits in the brain and in the heart, stirs and moves him; and this is a great benefit of God, that the Godhead thus mingles itself with us. What this means can be understood from the fact that Scripture often says: "He sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts."

units.la: Constantinopolitana synodus defendit hunc articulum Spiritum sanctum esse personam procedentem à Patre & Filio.
units.tr: The Council of Constantinople defended this article, that the Holy Spirit is a person proceeding from the Father and the Son.

units.la: DE CREATIONE.
units.tr: ON CREATION.

units.la: DE MVNDO & TEMPORE.
units.tr: ON THE WORLD AND TIME.

units.la: Quidam scripsit mundum esse æternum, quia homines paulatim essent facti sapientiores: dicit etiam Homeri tempore non fuisse literas. Quanta stultitia est putare se sapientiorem esse quàm fuerunt illi præstantissimi uiri, Adam, Noha, Abraham & alij?
units.tr: Someone has written that the world is eternal, because people have gradually become wiser. He also says that in Homer's time there were no letters. How foolish it is to think that we are wiser than those most excellent men, Adam, Noah, Abraham and others?

units.la: De duratione Mundi, dictum prophetæ Eliæ, uel traditio domus Eliæ.
units.tr: On the duration of the world: a saying of the prophet Elijah, or a tradition of the house of Elijah.

units.la: Sex millia annorum mundus, & deinde confla-
units.tr: The world lasts six thousand years, and then the conflagration-

units.la: Duo millia inane. (gratio.
units.tr: Two thousand years void (of grace).

units.la: Duo millia lex Moysi.
units.tr: Two thousand years the law of Moses.

units.la: Duo millia dies Messiah.
units.tr: Two thousand years the days of the Messiah.

units.la: Et propter peccata nostra, quæ multa & magna sunt, deerunt anni ex his, qui deerunt.
units.tr: And because of our sins, which are many and great, some of the years will be lacking from those that remain.

units.la: Scriptum anno 1560. postquam natus est Christus ex uirgine: anno post creationem mundi 5522.
units.tr: Written in the year 1560 after Christ was born of the virgin, in the year 5522 after the creation of the world.

units.la: De duratione Mundi, dictum Irenæi martyris.
units.tr: On the duration of the world: a saying of the martyr Irenaeus.

units.la: Quot diebus factus est hic mundus, tot & millenis annis consummetur. est enim dies Domini, quasi mille anni. In sex autem diebus consummata sunt quæ facta sunt: igitur consummatio eorum septimus millesimus annus est.
units.tr: As many days as this world was made in, so many thousand years will it be brought to an end. For a day of the Lord is as a thousand years. Now in six days the things that were made were finished; therefore their completion is the seventh thousandth year.

units.la: Ego in antiquo codice scriptum legi: Im 1580 Ian. lar, geschicht nichts newes, so zergeth die welt gar. id est: anno 1680. si nihil noui accidat, totus mun-dus peribit. Habeo etiam aliam coniecturam. Nā tempus constitutæ politiæ Moysaicæ, id est, ab exi-tu ex Aegypto, usq; ad eiusdem politiæ destruction-nem, cum duratione mundi plane congruere existi-mo. Stetit uero politia Mosaica annos 1582 usque ad ultimam destructionem sub Tito. Igitur, mundi post destructionem illius politiæ ultra illos annos duraturum esse, haud puto.
units.tr: I have read in an old codex this writing: "In 1580, January: if nothing new happens, the whole world will go to ruin." I have another conjecture as well. For I think the period from the establishment of the Mosaic polity, that is, from the exodus from Egypt, down to the destruction of that same polity, agrees exactly with the duration of the world. Now the Mosaic polity stood for 1582 years, until its final destruction under Titus. Therefore I do not think the world will last beyond those years after the destruction of that polity.

units.la: De anno Clymacterico.
units.tr: On the climacteric year.

units.la: Clymactericus annus facit mutationes in statu & conditionibus hominum. Est autem septimus annus, qui semper multiplicatur ut: 14. 21. 28. 35. 42. 49. 56, &c. Ego egregios & præstantes uiros noui, qui 56 anno ex hac uita decesserunt. Iacobus Micyllus, bonus & præstans uir 56 anno morieba-tur: similiter Durerus excellens pictor 56 anno est mortuus, & alios multos possem nominare, tem-peranter etiam uiuentes, anno eodē mortuos. Estq; in primis annus Clymactericus, quando septena-rius cùm nonario multiplicatur, ut: annus 63 ualde multos tollit, qui est annus mortis Aristotelis, Vir-gilij & ducis Friderici Electoris Saxoniæ. Concur-runt in illo anno hi duo numeri septimus et nonus.
units.tr: The climacteric year brings changes in the state and conditions of men. It is the seventh year, which is always multiplied, as: 14, 21, 28, 35, 42, 49, 56, etc. I have known outstanding and excellent men who died in their 56th year. Jacob Micyllus, a good and excellent man, was dying in his 56th year; likewise Dürer, an excellent painter, died in his 56th year; and I could name many others, temperate men also, who died in the same year. But the chief climacteric year is when the septenary is multiplied by the nonary, as the 63rd year, which carries off very many. It was the year of the death of Aristotle, Virgil, and Duke Frederick, Elector of Saxony. In that year the two numbers, the seventh and the ninth, meet.

units.la: De anno Iubileo.
units.tr: On the year of Jubilee.

units.la: Leuitici uigesimo quinto capite, constituitur lex de anno Iubileo, ut facultates ad priores suos dominos redeat. Significauit uero ille annus Iubileus populo Israelitico uniuersale Euangelij praedicatione, & uera remissione omnium peccatorum, quae est Ecclesiae propria omnib. temporibus. Habuit etiam praeter hanc significationem alias multas utilitates politicas & singulares. Voluit Deus facultates in illo populo manere, & apud illas familias, quibus lege Moysi à Iosua antea erant traditae, sicut apud nos fit in feudis, quae vasalli non possunt, nec debent sine consensu domini feudi alienare. Haec ratio hanc ipsam ob causam adhuc seruatur, ut maneant facultates apud suas familias. Occurrit etiam Deus hac lege bis utrisq;, prodigis & auaris. Hi inhiat alienis facultatibus, & illas uarijs artib. ad se rapere conantur: illi uedut suas paternas facultates, & inanib. sumptib. consumut. Sed in magnis imperijs haec consuetudo seruari non potest, ut cu Romanum imperiu crescebat, multi habuerut praedia & facultates in Aphrica, Europa et Asia, quae ad pri-stinos dominos ppter multiplices possessores redire non potuerunt. Legim9 de Seneca, habuisse cu pulcherrima & fertilissima praedia in Aphrica, quae (ut de Aphricae fertilitate constat) singulis annis centuplu proferrent, ita ut unus modius centum daret.
units.tr: In Leviticus, chapter 25, a law is laid down concerning the year of Jubilee, that property should return to its former owners. That Jubilee year signified for the people of Israel the universal preaching of the Gospel and the true remission of all sins, which belongs to the Church at all times. Besides this signification it also had many other political and particular benefits. God willed that property remain among that people and with those families to which it had been earlier allotted by Joshua under the law of Moses, just as with us in fiefs, which a vassal cannot and ought not alienate without the consent of the lord of the fief. This same principle is still observed for this very reason, so that property remains with its families. God also addresses by this law both extremes, the spendthrift and the miser. The one covets others' property and tries to seize it by various arts; the other sells his paternal property and squanders it on empty expenses. But in great empires this custom cannot be kept. For when the Roman empire was growing, many had estates and property in Africa, Europe and Asia, which could not return to their original owners because of the many possessors. We read that Seneca had very beautiful and very fertile estates in Africa, which (as is well established about the fertility of Africa) yielded a hundredfold each year, so that one measure gave a hundred.

units.la: Sic ad imitationem huius legis Moysaicae [illegible, ~8 letters] [illegible, ~10 letters], Papa propter suu quaestm constituit an-num num Iubileum, quem nominat annum remissionis peccatorum, sumpta initiò occasione à relaxatione veterum Canonum poenitentialium, quibus ita uexabantur homines, ut prae earum duritie uix seruari posse uiderentur. Itaq; quo illos canones relaxaret, excogitauit idem illo anno singularem remissionem, ut quando quidam commiserat adulterium, septem annos ieiunare, & à coniugio abstinere oporteret: & similia multa monstra contra uerbū Diuinum finxit, quae adeò atrocia fuerunt, ut nihil mirum sit, si etiam bonorum hominum conscientias in desperationem & dubitationem uariam impulerint. Postea paulatim relaxarunt illos Canones poenitentiales, accepta pecunia ab hominibus, quam remissionem uocarunt indulgentias.
units.tr: [illegible, ~8 letters] [illegible, ~10 letters] Thus, in imitation of this law of Moses, the Pope, for the sake of his own profit, established a Jubilee year, which he called the year of the remission of sins. At first he took the occasion from the relaxation of the old penitential canons, by which men were so harassed that, because of their harshness, they seemed scarcely able to keep them. So in order to relax those canons, he devised in the same year a special remission, so that whoever had committed adultery had to fast for seven years and abstain from marriage; and he invented many similar monstrosities against the divine Word, which were so atrocious that it is no wonder they drove even the consciences of good men into despair and various doubts. Afterwards they gradually relaxed those penitential canons, for money received from men, and this remission they called indulgences.

units.la: Dicunt Bonifacium Octauum autorem huius anni Iubilei fuisse, quo homines Romae pecunia redimerent sua peccata, annunciata eis à Papa remissione peccatorum. Fertur saepe tanta hominum frequentia Romae fuisse, ut in illa hominum constipatione multi hac mutua collisione sint extincti.
units.tr: They say that Boniface VIII was the author of this Jubilee year, in which men at Rome would buy off their sins with money, once remission of sins had been proclaimed to them by the Pope. It is often reported that the crowd of people at Rome was so great that many were killed in that press of people by this mutual collision.

units.la: Illud pecuniae aucupiū ante nostra tempora adeò creuerat, ut Papa Cardinales in Germaniam uenditione harum indulgentiarum ad magnam summam pecuniae colligendam mitteret. eiusmodi annum Iubileum Papa 1550 anno iterum celebrauit Romae. Habet autem nomen à buccina seu tuba, qua ba, qua Iudæi in magnis solennitatibus & festis populum conuocabant, sicut nos campanis plebem ad conciones & alias res sacras peragendas, conuocare solemus.
units.tr: This business of catching money had grown so much before our time that the Pope sent cardinals into Germany to sell these indulgences and collect a large sum of money. In the year 1550 the Pope again celebrated such a Jubilee year at Rome. It takes its name from the trumpet or horn with which the Jews used to summon the people at great solemnities and feasts, just as we are accustomed to summon the common folk with bells to sermons and other sacred services.

units.la: D.Erasmus Roterodamus.
units.tr: Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam.

units.la: Ἐγὼ νέων βαλλὰ δὲ μέσων σύχαί τε γερόντων. Siquidem si quis à trigesimo usq; ad sexagesimum annum laboribus deditus atq; defatigatus fuerit, quietem meruisse uidetur, sicuti fuit ætas militaris Romæ, ubi militabant annis triginta: uidelicet à trigesimo usq; ad sexagesimum. Postea sexagenarij sunt idonei consilijs, secundũ ueterẽ uersum, ἰωπω γηράσκοντι τὰ μείονα νῦν' ἐπιβάλλε. id est: Senescenti equo da mitiora cicela, hoc est frenos. Aetas uero post septuagesimum annum iam est imbecillior.
units.tr: Neither for the young, nor for the middle-aged, nor for the old... Indeed, if a man has been given over to labour and worn out from thirty to sixty years of age, he seems to have earned rest, just as the military age at Rome was: men served there for thirty years, namely from thirty to sixty. Afterwards those of sixty are fit for counsel, according to the old verse: "To an aging horse give gentler bits, that is, reins." But after the seventieth year age is already weaker. [Ἐγὼ νέων βαλλὰ δὲ μέσων σύχαί τε γερόντων.]

units.la: Erasmus, cum ei semel scriberem, ut curaret, ut ipsius actus postremus esset congruens ipsius auctoritati: respondit mihi, ὅρᾳ γε νέων βελτίων δὲ μέσων σύχαί τε γερόντων.
units.tr: When I once wrote to Erasmus, asking him to take care that the last act of his life should accord with his authority, he replied to me: "Behold, it is better than the young, better than the middle-aged and the old." [ὅρᾳ γε νέων βελτίων δὲ μέσων σύχαί τε γερόντων.]

units.la: Aetates mundi conueniunt cum potentijs animæ. In prima ætate floruit ἡγεμονικόν: in secunda ætate regnauit θυμικόν, id est, militares homines, gigantes, ueluti Samson, Dauid & Achilles, qui fuerunt coætanei. In illa ætate Iulium Cæsarem facio ultimum. ἐπιθυμητικόν est tertia ætas, in qua nos indulgentes cibo & potui uiuimus. Nam nos non possumus ferre labores & molestias militares, quæ in secunda ætate existentes pertulerunt.
units.tr: The ages of the world correspond to the powers of the soul. In the first age the ruling part [ἡγεμονικόν] flourished; in the second age the spirited part [θυμικόν] reigned, that is, military men and giants, such as Samson, David and Achilles, who were contemporaries. To that age I assign Julius Caesar as the last. The third age is the appetitive part [ἐπιθυμητικόν], in which we live indulging in food and drink. For we cannot bear the labours and hardships of war, which those living in the second age endured.

units.la: Astrologi dicunt, hanc nostram ætatem esse lunarem, regnareq; trigonum lunarem, qui habet insignes mutationes. Lunaris trigonus est piscium, cancri & scorpij, mixtus ex Marte, Venere & Luna: uidemus enim uariam huius seculi mutationem.
units.tr: The astrologers say that our age is lunar, and that the lunar trigon rules, which has remarkable changes. The lunar trigon is that of Pisces, Cancer and Scorpio, mixed from Mars, Venus and the Moon; for we see the varied change of this age.

units.la: Ioannes Stigelius.
units.tr: John Stigel.

units.la: Natura hominis post lapsum est tanquam fractum horologium, in quo semper aliquid sarciendum est, neque unquam in hoc seculo perfectum fiet. Simile reperitur in horologio summi templi Basiliensis.
units.tr: Human nature after the Fall is like a broken clock, in which something always needs mending, and it will never be made perfect in this age. A similar thing is found in the clock of the great church at Basel.

units.la: Fert omnia tempus.
units.tr: Time brings all things.

units.la: Der Welt anfang mittel vnd endt/ Mût, zeit, stundt vnd tag verwendt.
units.tr: The world's beginning, middle and end; toil, time, hour and day are spent and consumed.

units.la: DE ANGELIS, LIBERATIONIBUS & defensionibus Dei miraculosis.
units.tr: On Angels, Deliverances and the Miraculous Defences of God.

units.la: ANgeli ideo creati sunt, ut defendant & tuentur nos homines, sunt enim λειτουργικὰ πνεύματα. Nisi enim adessent Angeli boni hominibus, una hora, imò momento, diabolus totum mundum inuerteret. Quia & diaboli & boni angeli prope homines sunt undicunq;, sed unus bonus angelus fortior est mille diabolis.
units.tr: Angels were created so that they might defend and guard us men, for they are "ministering spirits" [λειτουργικὰ πνεύματα]. Unless good angels were present with men, the devil would overturn the whole world in one hour, indeed in a moment. For both the devils and the good angels are near men wherever they are, but one good angel is stronger than a thousand devils.

units.la: Quidam pastor dixit: Est difficile de Angelis concioconcionari, quia nullus scit quis sit uir, & quæ sit fœmina, & wer ein Sie, oder ein Er ist.
units.tr: A certain minister said: "It is difficult to preach about angels, because no one knows who is a man and what is a woman, whether it is a She or a He."

units.la: Audiui à quodam graui uiro, & fide digno, se cõpertum habere, sibiq; de ueritate facti huius cõstare. In quodam pago uicino urbi Cygneæ, mulier quædam iußit filium suum adducere boues, in proximo syluæ aditu pascentes. & cùm puer aliquando diutius commoraretur, incidit magna nix, quæ totos illos montes obtegebat, noste ingruente, nec poterat puer ex illis montibus egredi. Parentes postridie solliciti non amplius de bobus, sed de filij uita, expectabant aduentum filij, nec poterant præ niuis altitudine egredi ex illis montibus quæsitum filium. Tertio die egredientes, quærunt puerum, tandemq; inueniunt ipsum in aprico syluæ loco, ubi nulla nix erat, sedentem, & parentibus aduenientibus arridentem. Interrogatus autem puer, quare non rediret domum? respondit, se expectare donec adueniret uesper, nesciens iam diem præteriisse, nec ullam niuis molestiam aut tempestatem passus. Et cùm amplius interrogaretur, an etiam aliquid comedisset? dixit, aduenisse quèdam uirum, qui porrexerit sibi panem cum caseo. Ita haud dubiè per Angelos seruatus est iste puer in media bruma: & sine dubio Angelus fuit ille uir, qui puero panem cum caseo porrexit.
units.tr: I heard from a certain grave and trustworthy man that he had found this out and that he was certain of the truth of the event. In a certain village near the town of Schweinfurt (Cygnea), a woman ordered her son to bring the oxen, which were grazing near the edge of a wood. When the boy stayed out rather long, a heavy snow fell, covering all those mountains, and night came on, and the boy could not come down from those mountains. The parents, anxious the next day not about the oxen but about the boy's life, waited for his return, and because of the depth of the snow they could not go up into those mountains to look for him. On the third day they set out and searched for the boy, and at last they found him sitting in a sunny spot of the wood, where there was no snow, smiling at his parents as they came up. When he was asked why he had not come home, he answered that he was waiting until evening came, not knowing that the day had already passed, and he had suffered no discomfort or storm from the snow. When he was asked further whether he had eaten anything, he said that a certain man had come and handed him bread with cheese. Thus without doubt this boy was preserved by angels in the midst of winter, and undoubtedly it was an angel who was that man who handed the boy bread with cheese.

units.la: Cũ essemus Spiræ in cõuentu, cõcionabatur Faber, & ber, & multa dicebat tetra de transubstantiatione, & adoratione panis consecrati. Quæ cum audiisset Grynæus, finito sermone, hominem accepit, dicitq; se quandoquidem audiuerat ipsius concionem, de sacramento cupere magnopere de eadem re priuatim cum ipso colloqui. Quod cum audiret Faber, humanissimis uerbis & uultu beneuolo respondebat, & ipsi optatissimum fore istum diem, quo cum Grynæo esset collocuturus, præsertim de re tali, iubebatq; ipsum postridie ad suas ædes redire. Grynæus nihil mali suspicans, discedit: rediens ad nos, dicit, se cras disputaturum esse cum Fabro. Sed ille interea temporis Grynæo insidias struit, accedit quendam illustrem uirum, ac totum ipsi negocium exponit: ac tandem obtinet ut hic illustris uir in uincula per Senatum, Grynæum coniici mandet. Cùm prandium uix inchoassemus, uenit uir quidam senex in nostrum diuersorium, ac me à prandio ad se ante fores euocat, interrogans de Grynæo, an intus esset? cui respondi, esse. subiecit ipse, imminere ei periculum, quod si uitare uellit, quàm primùm fugiat. Quæ cùm Grynæo nunciassem, suasi ei fugam: ille obtemperat. Surgimus à prandio ego, D. Crucigerus & ipse: nos procedebamus, ministri nostri sequebantur, in medio ibat Grynæus. Non transieramus quatuor aut quinque domos, statim in hospitio aderant lictores, quærentes. tes Grynæum: sed cùm non inuenissent eum in diuersorio, nihil ulterius fecerunt, uel iussi ut tantum ibi quærerent, uel personas nostras non agnoscentes, aut alioqui nihil crudele facere cupientes. Interrogaui multos, utrum hunc uirum nosset? uolens illi pro hoc beneficio gratias agere, sed nullus mihi indicare potuit, quis fuisset, neq; unquam amplius ipsum uidere potui. Hunc uirum omnino fuisse Angelum puto. Grynæus, cum deduxissemus ipsum usque ad Rhenum, conscendit nauim, & traiecit nobis expectantibus, ac postea nostrum aduentum Heydelbergæ expectauit.
units.tr: When we were at Speyer at the convention, Faber preached, and he said many foul things about transubstantiation and the adoration of the consecrated bread. When Grynaeus heard these things, after the sermon he approached the man and said that, since he had heard his sermon, he very much wished to speak privately with him about the sacrament. When Faber heard this, he replied in the most courteous words and with a kindly expression, and said that the day on which he would confer with Grynaeus, especially on such a matter, would be most welcome to him; and he bade him return to his house the next day. Grynaeus, suspecting no harm, left. Coming back to us, he said that he would debate with Faber the next day. But in the meantime Faber laid a trap for Grynaeus: he approached a certain distinguished man and explained the whole affair to him; and at last he obtained that this distinguished man should order, through the Senate, that Grynaeus be thrown into chains. When we had barely begun dinner, a certain old man came into our inn and called me from the meal to him at the door, asking about Grynaeus, whether he was inside. I answered that he was. The old man added that danger threatened him, and that if he wished to avoid it he should flee as soon as possible. When I had reported this to Grynaeus, I urged him to flee, and he complied. I rose from dinner, together with Master Crucigerus himself; we went forward, our servants followed, and Grynaeus walked in the middle. We had not passed four or five houses when at once the constables were present at the inn, asking for Grynaeus. But when they did not find him at the lodging, they did nothing further, either because they had been ordered to search only there, or because they did not recognize our persons, or because they were otherwise unwilling to do anything cruel. I asked many people whether they knew this man, wishing to thank him for this kindness, but no one could tell me who he was, and I could never see him again. I think that this man was certainly an angel. When we had escorted Grynaeus as far as the Rhine, he boarded a ship and crossed over while we waited, and afterwards he awaited our arrival at Heidelberg.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Magister Spangenbergius pastor Northusanus, conferens se cum filijs suis in balneum, ibi aliquot horas lauando consumpsit. Egresso è balneo cum filijs, statim hypocaustum corruit. Testatus est pater cœlestis, nos illi curæ esse, & uerè Angelos esse custodes nostrorum liberorum, parentum, cognatorum: & omnes nostras facultates per suos ministros tueri & protegere.
units.tr: Master Spangenberg, minister at Nordhausen, went with his sons to the bath, and spent several hours there washing. As he came out of the bath with his sons, immediately the hypocaust collapsed. The heavenly Father bore witness that we are his concern, and that the angels are truly the guardians of our children, parents and kinsfolk, and that through his ministers he defends and protects all our possessions.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: In Prussia accidit memorabile factum. Cum nasceretur quidam puer, statim accesit eum genius (uel quidquid illud tandem fuerit, id iudicandum aliis relinquo) qui ita curam infantis habuit, ut ipsi non fuerit opus alterius ullius ministri aut famulæ ministerio. Cum hic adolescceret, simili ratio-ne curam ipsius egit, ut cum ipso scholas uisitaret, ita tamen ut neq; ab ipso, neque ullo alio conspice-retur, exuit caligas adolescentis, ut famulus. Etsi quod imminere periculum adolescenti uideretur, uel strepitu claro prædixit: deinde facto adolescē-te Canonico, cum aliquando largius se ingurgi-tasset bibendo, exorto subito fragore, omnes sunt perterrefacti. Tunc ille adolescens, inquit: Nolite timere, mea res nunc agitur, altero die incidit in febrim, & totum triduum, donec abiret in suas ædes, eiulatus est auditus. Hic Canonicus Copernico Mathematico optime fuit notus.
units.tr: In Prussia a memorable event occurred. When a certain boy was born, a genius (or whatever it was, I leave it to others to judge) at once came to him, and it took such care of the infant that no other servant or maid was needed for his service. When this boy grew up, it looked after him in the same way, so that it visited the schools with him, yet in such a way that it was seen by neither him nor anyone else; it took off the young man's shoes like a servant. Also, if some danger seemed to threaten the young man, it warned him with a loud noise. Then, when the young man had become a canon, once when he had gorged himself rather freely on drink, a sudden crash arose, and everyone was terrified. Then that young man said: "Do not be afraid, my affair is now at stake." The next day he fell into a fever, and for three whole days, until he went home to his house, he was heard wailing. This canon was very well known to the mathematician Copernicus.

units.la: Heidelbergæ audiui à docto uiro, filio Doctoris Medicinæ, quòd is cùm esset puer exiuerit in hor-tum deambulatum cum fratre. Pueri ambo simul euntes, & tenentes se mutuis brachijs, insolentia quadam errauerunt in ponte, ut ambo de ponte in flumen delaberentur, qui tunc non erat munitus, sicut hic pons in Albi, quem iam lapideum eo in loco extruxerunt. Ego noui utrumq;, & iam sunt uiri, qui ad iustam ætatem peruenerunt. Ancilla uerò, quæ illos sequebatur, statim desilijt de ponte in flumen, & apprehendit utrosq;, & sic eos seruauit. Si fuisset imbecillis naturæ, disputasset secum: Tu peribis, non poteris euadere incolumis: sed illa eiuncitur naturali obligatione,
units.tr: At Heidelberg I heard from a learned man, the son of a doctor of medicine, that when he was a boy he had gone out into the garden to walk with his brother. The two boys, walking together and holding each other by the arm, carelessly stumbled on a bridge, so that both fell from the bridge into the river, which at that time was not railed, unlike this bridge on the Elbe which they have now built of stone at that spot. I know both of them, and they are now men who have reached a proper age. But the maidservant who was following them at once leapt from the bridge into the river, seized both of them, and so saved them. If she had been of a weak nature, she would have reasoned with herself: "You will perish, you will not be able to escape unharmed." But she was impelled by a natural obligation,

units.la: Noui uirum nobilem in oppido Franconiæ,no mine Creutzberg,qui adhuc uiuit,cuius filius de-cidit ex fenestra arcis in fossā aquea circa arcē. An cilla cucurrit ad famulū,qui erat in inferiore ædiū parte,& dicit puerū in aquas incidisse. Ibi accur-rit seruus magnitudine animi fretus, dimisit se in fossam,& liberauit puerū adhuc incolumē:etsi ali qua mora intercessisset,tamen diuino auxilio puer seruatus est.
units.tr: I knew a noble man in a town of Franconia, named Creutzberg, who is still alive, whose son fell from a window of the castle into a water-filled moat around the castle. A maidservant ran to a servant who was in the lower part of the building, and told him that the boy had fallen into the water. Thereupon the servant ran there, relying on greatness of spirit, let himself down into the moat, and freed the boy while he was still unharmed. Although some delay had intervened, nonetheless by divine help the boy was saved.

units.la: Imperator Carolus V. sæpè in magnis peri-culis quorū illud inter cætera non minimum fuit, cùm in expeditione Aphricana reliquas iuxta se naues mergi,sibiq; idē periculū instare uideret:ta-men diuinitus ex hoc,sicut ex plurimis alijs,serua-tus est:sicut dixit ad me Granuelus. O malum ho-spicium,ô malum hospicium mare.
units.tr: The Emperor Charles V was often in great dangers, of which this was not the least among the others: when, on the African expedition, he saw the ships beside him being sunk, and saw that the same peril threatened him, nevertheless he was preserved from this by God, as he was from very many other dangers; so Granvelle told me. "O bad inn, O bad inn, the sea!"

units.la: Pinxerunt quidam Imperatorem Carolum V. dormientē,& Christum abigentē illi muscas, qd̈ fecerūt in ignominiā Pauli papæ, cuiº silus [?] Cæsari struxerat insidias,quæ tñ diuinitus impediebātur.
units.tr: Certain men painted the Emperor Charles V sleeping, and Christ driving flies away from him; they did this in mockery of Pope Paul, whose plot had laid traps for Caesar, but these were impeded by God.

units.la: Est in historia Megalopolensiū principū, quo-modo aliquis ex ducib.in bello aduersus Turcas ca-ptus postea in Aegyptū ductus sit,ut ibi seruiret.E-lapso aliquo tēpore Liuoniēsis quidā magister tor-mētorū,factº est Soldanus Aegypti.Hic cùm nouis-set illū ducē,uocat eū ad se,dicēs:Vetº fuit inter nos amicicia, et ego tecū sub patre tuo militaui,à quo pluriplurima in me beneficia sunt collata, pro quibus meam erga te gratitudinem iterū declarabo. Memor igitur illius nostræ veteris amicitiæ, & beneficiorum tui patris mittam te in patriam. Dux aliquādiu Soldano acquiescere noluit, dicens se non ægrè ferre seruitutem, quam tamen, si ipse magis lenire uellet, sibi gratum fore: quod si faceret se non admodum cupere in patriam reuerti, quòd uerere tur nec suos ipsi fidem habituros esse, & arbitratu ros quòd esset impostor. Adhortanti Soldano, tandem acquiescit: is nauim ipsi prospicit, addito uiatico & mediocri comitatu. Ibi cum præternauigarent Macedoniam, rursus in mari à Piratis capitur, & in Aegyptum ad eundem Soldanum reducitur, cui dixit: Vides, Deum me redire in patriam non uelle, manebo potius hic. Sed Soldanus ducem denuò instructum uiatico, & maiore comitatu mittit in Cyprum, ubi inuenit (Dei prouidentia sic ordinante) suam coniugem, cum qua in patriā profectus est. Postea uerò per totam uitam ipse cū suis pro hac liberatione Deo gratias agere solitus est.
units.tr: In the history of the princes of Mecklenburg there is an account of how one of the dukes, captured in a war against the Turks, was afterwards led into Egypt to serve there. After some time a certain master of artillery from Livonia became Sultan of Egypt. When he had recognized that duke, he summoned him and said: "Once there was friendship between us, and I served under your father, from whom I received very many kindnesses; in return I will now again show my gratitude to you. Mindful therefore of that old friendship of ours and of the kindnesses of your father, I will send you back to your homeland." The duke for some time was unwilling to agree to the Sultan's wish, saying that he did not bear his servitude badly, but that if the Sultan wished to ease it for him he would be grateful; and that if he did so, he would not very much want to return to his homeland, because he feared that his own people would not believe him, and would think he was an impostor. At the Sultan's urging, he at last agreed. The Sultan provided him with a ship, with travelling money and a modest retinue. As they sailed past Macedonia, he was again captured at sea by pirates and led back to Egypt, to the same Sultan, to whom he said: "You see that God does not want me to return to my homeland; I will rather remain here." But the Sultan again equipped the duke with travelling money and a larger retinue, and sent him to Cyprus, where, by God's providence so ordering it, he found his wife, with whom he set out for his homeland. Afterwards, throughout his whole life, he and his people were accustomed to give thanks to God for this deliverance.

units.la: Ludouicus duodecimus Rex Galliæ, qui proximus fuit ante Franciscum, postquam diu exul apud Imperatorem Maximilianum fuisseт, uocatus est rursum ad regnum. Erat autem pulsus in exilium à Carolo Gibboso, & euaserat in habitu mulieris. Veniebat igitur ad imperatorem Maximilianum, apud quem uiuebat, donec iterum in regnum Galliæ reuocaretur. Ita diuinitus est custoditus, & in regnum suum restitutus.
units.tr: Louis XII, King of France, the immediate predecessor of Francis, was called back to the kingdom after a long exile with the Emperor Maximilian. He had been driven into exile by Charles the Hunchback, and he had escaped disguised as a woman. He therefore went to the Emperor Maximilian, with whom he lived until he was restored to the kingdom of France. Thus he was preserved by God's providence and restored to his realm.

units.la: Duces Saxoniæ, Fridericus Elector et Ioannes, fratres, aliquando in Albi Torga Vuitenbergam usque nauigauerunt: cumq; recenter solutæ glaciei magna moles innataret, ita nauim utrinq; quassauit, ut cum Vitebergæ in ripam uicinam essent egressi, carina nauis fissa, & asseres dissoluti diffluxerunt. Intuentur igitur spectaculum principes, stantes in ripa, cū magna administratione, cogitantes quāto in periculo fuerint: agnoscūt diuina ope nauim esse seruatam, donec ipsi egressi essent: denique post longum silentium, inquit Dux Fridericus ad fratrem: Fateamur nos esse seruatos diuinitus, & grati beneficium Dei celebremus, qui nos in hoc periculo & in aliis protexit. Quòd autem nobis egressis nauis dilacerata sit, profectò metuo post nos nostræ nauis, id est, domus Saxoniæ dilacerationem portendere.
units.tr: The dukes of Saxony, Frederick the Elector and John, brothers, once sailed on the Elbe from Torgau as far as Wittenberg. When a great mass of newly melted ice was floating on the river, it struck the boat so violently on both sides that, after the princes had landed on the nearby bank at Wittenberg, the keel of the boat split and the planks came apart and drifted away. The princes, standing on the bank, watched this sight with great anxiety, considering how great the danger had been. They acknowledged that the boat had been preserved by divine help until they themselves got off it. At last, after a long silence, Duke Frederick said to his brother: "Let us confess that we have been saved by God, and let us celebrate the benefit of God, who has protected us in this danger and in others. But as for the fact that the boat was torn to pieces after we had got out of it, I greatly fear that it foreshadows the dismemberment of our boat, that is, of the house of Saxony after us."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Historia memorabilis accidit Maximiliano optimo principi, filio Ferdinandi, regis Romani. Cùm enim absens Imperator Carolus V. in Germania res nondum pacatas componeret, accersitus est Maximilianus princeps ad gubernationem Hispaniæ, & uicinorum regnorum. Ibi dum uel animi causa, uel exercendi corporis gratia, uenationi ad Granatam uacaret, cumq; in ea uenatione cupi-ditate insequendi feram oblatam, longius à comita-tu suo discederet, à suis relictus diu in densissimis syluis uagatus est. accedente iam nocte, sollicitus (ut qui sibi à feris in illis locis immanissimis, & alijs no-ctis incommodis timeret) circumspectat, si quis sibi lo-cus daretur, quò se in tutū reciperet. Itaq; procul conspecta pastoris casula, citato equo ad eam per-uenit: rogatoq; pastore, ut sibi apud eum diuersa-ri ea nocte liceret. is omnia benignè pollicitus, de-scendere de equo iubet, & tugurium ingredi. E-rant porrò domi apud pastorem sex numero: utiq; praeter illum, filius circiter viginti annos natus, tum opilio robustus, & ad quoduis facimus aggre-diendum idoneus: praeterea uxor cum paruula fi-lia & nuru, quae paulo ante noua nupta in fami-liam rustici concesserat. Princeps ubi ad terram equo desiluisset, eumque tradidisset opilioni cu-randum, casam ingreditur: ac dum tenuis coenu-la sibi paratur, ad ignem assidet, nihil quic-quam suspicans mali. Interea quum ij, qui do-mi erant, Maximilianum minimè nossent: ne-que ipse, quis nam esset cuiquam aperuisset: illi tamen eum eleganter amictum, & praeclaris alijs ornamentis corporis & animi ornatum uiderent, ratique eum esse magnum omnino aliquem, atq; opu-lentum. tentum uirum,opimæ inhiantes prædæ, fœda te-terrimaq; de illo perdendo consilia ineunt. Itaq; cœnati,cubile (in perangusto cubiculo , quod quidem hostiolo uetustate putri,& cardinibus diluxatis,ac male cohærentibus ægrè claudebatur ) ei conster-nunt. Dumq; ea parantur, noua nupta filij , siue quòd huiusce consilij ab initio particeps fuisset.fa-ctiq; conscia, cuius postmodum eam pœnituis-set: siue (id quod credibilius est ) non adhibita consilijs, tantum ex nutibus,ipsorum & concur-sationibus rem persensisset : tandem uel atroci-tate rei commota , uel egregij principis sibi igno-ti uicem miserata , fidem ab eo stipulata, ne se proderet , illi perdita consilia detegit. licet facile potuisset , aperte fassus, quis nam esset, illud periculum declinare: maluit tamen uirtuti propriæ quàm fidei pastorum , & co-rum præsertim quos semel infidos atque im-pios expertus esset , sese committere. Itaque magno & erecto animo statuit , ut periculum potius, quàm eorum perfidiam subiret. Quamobrem in cubiculum sibi ad insidias parā-tum , ab hospite perductus , haud grauatim se re-cipit:ibi'que occlusoostio, eoq;, obiectu gravio-ris arcæ,bene oppilato: tum in manu sumpta bom-barda ad omnes casus subeundos , parata, cœpit intreintrepidus obseruare quò res caderet. Pastor cùm illum de uenatione ac uia fessum uidisset, ubi somno pressum dormire credidit, suspenso gradu ad ostium accedit: ac manu prætentat, nihil ratus, fore, ut id clausum interius offenderet. Quod ubi præter spem illi accidisset, petit à Maximiliano, ut sibi ostium aperiat: esse cur uelit nescio quid straguli ex arca promere. Is uerò cùm omnia persensisset, ut qui nihil dormiret: Apage te (inquit) cum tua ista importuna diligentia: ego iam in somno compositus, nihil est cur ostium recludam. Tum ille primùm indignari, clamare, quiritari, se perditum ac proditū prohiberi rebus suis: deinde ad arma currere, uim apertam parare: postremò palàm cædem quoq; minari, nisi domus sua tota sibi patêret, ac ille se sese ipsi protinus dederet. Et iam pastores coeperant hostium amoliri, alius autem per fenestram cubiculi eò tentare irrumpere: eoq; obnixius rem coeptam perficere conabantur, quod iam sua consilia detecta esse facilè intelligebant. At uerò Maximilianus quum rem in iniquissimo loco sitam uideret, fortiter pugnandum ratus, intentatum ad fores bombum displodit: quo glandis ictu ostium traiecit, pastorem prosternit, nec mora, dimota arca, patefactoq; hostio foras erumpit: pastoris filium obtruncat, opilionem ense stricto persequitur, inq; fugam uertit. Neque tamen protinus omni periculo delo defungitur.nam & uociferationibus uxoris, & tumultu insueto exciti, qui circum aderant alij pa-stores, raptis undiq; telis cõcurrunt: domum ipsam armati circumsistunt: iuuenem principem ad cædē & supplicia deposcunt. Ille autem dum primo illo insano rusticorum furore ( quo nihil iniquius est ) sibi caueret, nihil præterea territus, ubi iam illuce-scente aurora, magnam rusticorum turbam illo cõ-fluxisse uidet: audacter, quis nam ipsius esset, ape-rit: atq; intrepidus, autoritate illa, qua se digna e-rat, Hispaniarum sese præsidem ac moderatorem esse ostendit: extremum omnibus supplicium minat-tus, ni se omnes totis uiribus seruatum uellent. Si sibi parum fidei habendum putarent, à præsenti cæde abstinerent: sese cognitioni magistratus animaduersionió; reseruarent. quod si id facere negligerent, id non sibi solum fraudi, uerumetiam ipsis excidio atq; internecioni futurum. Illi, tametsi & heroica præstantissimi iuuenis principis indole & constanti oratione permoti, facilè crederent illum ipsum esse, quem præ se ferret, à cæde quidē abstinent: cæterùm ne ab ingenio suo rusticano discederent, eum comprehensum manibus uinciunt, itaq; colligatum atq; obstrictum summo mane ad uicini oppidi præfectum perducunt. Iam eodem peruenerant ex principis satellitibus, eum quæri-tantes: quem quum ita uinctum, atq; in dignisi-mis mis acceptum modis uiderent, parum abfuit, quin in turbam illam pastorum inconditam ac tumul-tuantem irruerent : sed ab ipso admoniti, ut à ui & armis temperarent, ægrè abstiterunt incœpto.
units.tr: A memorable event happened to Maximilian, an excellent prince, son of Ferdinand, King of the Romans. While the Emperor Charles V, who was absent, was still settling affairs in Germany that were not yet pacified, Prince Maximilian was summoned to govern Spain and the neighbouring kingdoms. While he was hunting near Granada, whether for relaxation or for exercise of the body, he was carried by eagerness to pursue a beast that had appeared, and went too far from his company. Abandoned by his men, he wandered for a long time in very dense woods. As night was already coming on, he, anxious (as one who feared wild beasts in those most savage places and other dangers of the night), looked about to see whether any place was available where he could withdraw to safety. So, having caught sight from afar of a shepherd's hut, he rode quickly to it. He asked the shepherd whether he might lodge there that night. The shepherd promised everything kindly, bade him dismount and enter the hovel. Moreover, there were six people in the shepherd's house: besides himself, a son about twenty years old, a sturdy herdsman fit for undertaking any deed; then the wife with a small daughter, and a daughter-in-law, who had recently married and come into the peasant's family. When the prince had got down from his horse and handed it to the herdsman to be cared for, he entered the cottage, and while a meagre supper was being prepared for him, he sat by the fire, suspecting no harm at all. Meanwhile, those who were in the house did not know Maximilian at all, nor had he himself told anyone who he was. Yet they saw him elegantly dressed and adorned with the distinguished ornaments of body and mind, and thinking that he was certainly someone great and wealthy, and longing for a rich prey, they formed wicked and most foul plans to destroy him. So, after supper, they made up a bed for him in a very narrow room, which was hardly closed by a little door rotten with age and with its hinges loosened and poorly fitting. While these things were being prepared, the son's new bride, either because she had been a party to this plot from the beginning and had become an accomplice, of which she later repented, or (what is more likely) not having been admitted to the plans but having perceived the matter from their nods and whisperings, at last, moved either by the atrocity of the deed or by pity for the unknown and excellent prince, extracted from him a pledge that he would not betray her, and revealed the wicked plans to him. Although he could easily have avoided that danger by openly declaring who he was, he preferred to trust his own courage rather than the good faith of the shepherds, especially of those whom he had found faithless and wicked once already. So with a great and resolute spirit he decided to face the danger rather than their treachery. Therefore, led into the room prepared for the ambush by his host, he withdrew without hesitation; there, with the door closed and well barricaded by a heavy chest placed against it, he took a gun in hand, ready for any outcome, and began to watch fearlessly how the matter would turn out. When the shepherd saw him tired from the hunt and the journey, he believed that he was lying asleep, and approached the door with cautious steps and felt it with his hand, thinking it would be no surprise to find it shut from inside. When this happened contrary to his hopes, he asked Maximilian to open the door for him, since he had some bedding to take out of the chest. But Maximilian, who had sensed everything and did not sleep at all, said: "Be off with your tiresome diligence! I am already settled in sleep, and there is no reason for me to open the door." Then the shepherd first began to be indignant, to shout and complain that he was being kept from his own goods, lost and betrayed; then he ran to arms and prepared open force; finally he openly threatened slaughter as well, unless his whole house was thrown open to him and the prince at once surrendered himself. And now the shepherds had begun to force the doors, while another tried to break in through the window of the room; they strained the harder to complete the undertaking because they readily understood that their plans were already discovered. But Maximilian, seeing that he was in a most unfavourable position, judged that he must fight bravely; he fired his gun at the door as it was being attacked, and the shot of the ball pierced the door, struck down the shepherd, and without delay, after moving the chest and opening the door, he burst out. He cut down the shepherd's son and pursued the herdsman with drawn sword, turning him to flight. Yet he was not at once freed from all danger; for the other shepherds who were nearby, roused by the screams of the wife and by the unaccustomed uproar, ran together from every side with seized weapons, surrounded the house itself armed, and demanded the young prince for slaughter and punishment. But he, while guarding himself against that first mad fury of the peasants (than which nothing is more unjust), and not otherwise frightened, when the dawn was already brightening and he saw a great crowd of peasants had gathered there, boldly declared who he was, and fearlessly, with that authority which was fitting for him, showed himself to be the governor and ruler of the Spains, threatening all with the extreme penalty unless they wished to be saved by all their strength. If they thought he was not to be trusted, they should refrain from the present slaughter and reserve him and themselves for the judgment of the magistrate and for punishment; but if they neglected to do so, this would bring ruin not only to him but also to themselves, and to their total destruction. They, although moved by the heroic character of the most excellent young prince and by his steady speech, and readily believing that he was the very man he claimed to be, did indeed refrain from slaughter; yet, not to depart from their rustic nature, they seized him with their hands, bound him, and at early morning led him, tied and bound, to the prefect of a neighbouring town. Men from the prince's attendants had already arrived there, seeking him; when they saw him so bound and treated with the most undeserved indignities, they came close to rushing upon that disorderly and uproarious crowd of shepherds, but, admonished by him to restrain themselves from violence and arms, they hardly held back from their undertaking.

units.la: Tum uerò horum aduentu re omni, ut erat, detecta, qui tanti sceleris fuerunt conscij, indignissimi facti poenas dederunt. Opilio ad extremum suppli-cium pertractus: scelerata domus tam impij faci-noris particeps flammis consumpta : noua nupta quæ indicium fecerat, multis & magnis muneri-bus affecta apud ipsum principem, suosq; in ma-gno precio est habita. Sic princeps ille iuuenis mi-rabili Dei bonitate in periculosissimo illo casu co-seruatus, & ex illo liberatus est. Caterum, ut æternus Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi hunc se-renissimum regem Bohemicum, & sapientissimum principem, unà cum S. S. R. M. coniuge omni-bus uirtutibus præstantissima, & liberis, de qui-bus magna spes est posteritati, à tragicis, & pe-riculosis casibus Reipublicæ orbis Christiani diu incolumem conseruet & tueatur, mecum omnes precari uelint.
units.tr: Then, indeed, upon their arrival, the whole matter was revealed as it was, and those who had been party to so great a crime paid the penalties of their most shameful deed. The herdsman was dragged to the extreme punishment; the wicked house, party to so impious a deed, was consumed by flames; the new bride who had given the information was honoured with many great gifts by the prince himself, and was held in high esteem by her own people. Thus that young prince, preserved in that most perilous accident by the wonderful goodness of God, was freed from it. Moreover, may all of you join me in praying that the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ may long keep safe and protect this most serene king of Bohemia, a most wise prince, together with his consort, Her Sacred Royal Majesty, most outstanding in every virtue, and their children, from whom great hope rests for posterity, from the tragic and perilous calamities of the commonwealth of the Christian world.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Cum in collectione horum locorum uersarer, cădidissime Lector, inueni hanc historiolam prae-dicta aliter ab alijs recenseri. Ego tamē usus cōsilio doctorū uirorū, nolui eius fructu lectore fraudare.
units.tr: As I was working on the collection of these passages, most candid reader, I found that this story has been related in a different way by others. Nevertheless, on the advice of learned men, I did not want to deprive the reader of its benefit.

units.la: Quãuis igitur eam diuersis circũstantijs ab alijs referri audiuissem, & meũ quoq; exẽplar iam conceptum nonnihil ab hoc uariaret, tamen cum inciderem in Ioan. Iustiniani Cretensis epistolas, ipse mihi autor dignißimus uidebatur, quem sequerer. Itaq; ad ipsius relationem & meum exemplar, immutandum atq; conformandum duxi.
units.tr: Although I had heard that others report it with different circumstances, and my own copy, already drafted, differed somewhat from theirs, nevertheless, when I came upon the letters of John Justinian of Crete, he seemed to me the most worthy authority to follow. So I decided to alter and conform my own copy to his account.

units.la: Mihi aliquãdo diuertendũ forte fuit in quodam oppido Papistico, ubi quoq; hospicio erat exceptus sacerdos qdã Papisticus, cũ certo numero satellitũ. Aderat aut una comes à Khonigstein, et alius quidã uir eruditus, qui à mea parte erat. Tũ inter cœnam dũ mihi unũ atq; alterũ uerbũ excidit ex Homeri Odißea, quã forte in manib. habebã. Ibi statim satellites cœperũt suspicari nos esse Lutheranos, & uitæ nostræ insidiabãtur: et nisi comes à Khonigstein mãdassset hospiti, ut nos occultaret in inferiore parte ædiũ, ꝑ puteũ ꝑ noctẽ, & summo mane nos dimitteret, certè actũ fuisset de nobis. Sic nusq; nõ odiũ ueteris serpẽtis aduersus Christianos, & ecõtrà Dei clementißima defensio erga suos apparet.
units.tr: It once happened that I had to lodge in a certain Papist town, where I was received as a guest by a Papist priest with a certain number of attendants. A companion from Königstein was with me, and another learned man who was on my side. Then, during supper, a word or two from Homer's Odyssey, which I happened to have in my hands, slipped out of me. At once the attendants began to suspect that we were Lutherans and plotted against our lives. Unless the companion from Königstein had ordered the host to hide us in the lower part of the building, by the well, through the night, and let us go early in the morning, it would certainly have been all over for us. So everywhere the hatred of the old serpent against Christians appears, and at the same time God's most merciful protection of his own.

units.la: Noui quendam pastorẽ in Thuringia non procul à Gotha, cuius mater matrona nobilis, uicina partui, cum in festo assumptionis Mariæ, quando dedicabantur herbæ, staret ad aram in templo, & iam essẽt afflata illarũ herbarũ graui odore, incidit in lipothymiã tãtã, ut in terrã cadẽs existimaretur esse esse mortua. Postquam res perfertur ad maritum, hominem nobilem, & ab ipso quaereretur, utrū uel let eam sic sepeliri, an uero ipsi catenas aureas et similia ornamenta demi? Respondit, se cā sic remissurā esse Deo, sicut euocasset illam ex hac uita, nec voluit illa ornamenta auferri. Ponitur in pheretrum, iacet sic in templo integro die. Noctu cum quidam homo sceleratus accederet ad pheretrum, spoliaturus eam, & corpus attrectaret, incœpit ipsa se movere: ille perterritus putat spectrum esse, & concitato cursu & clamore, fugit ex templo. Mulier autem paulatim sese colligens ex illo strepitu & clamore, uidet tandem quo in loco sit, incipit & ipsa uociferari: accurrunt uicini, & uident quid cū ipsa actum sit, deducuntq; eam rursum ad maritum in arcem, quae non procul a templo aberat, ibi cum ipsa incaluisset in uaporario, incipit parturire. Maritus statim uotū facit se dedicaturum esse Deo quicquid peperisset. Postquā igitur peperisset masculum, eundem, ubi paululum adoleuisset, monachum Franciscanum effecit: sed idem postea depositio errore & superstitione, factus est pastor in quodam loco Thuringiæ. Ita clementer illam honestam matronam Deus cum infante diutius in uiuis retinuit.
units.tr: I know of a certain minister in Thuringia, not far from Gotha, whose mother, a noblewoman near her time of childbirth, was standing at the altar in the church on the feast of the Assumption of Mary, when the herbs were blessed. She was already overcome by the heavy odour of those herbs and fell into such a faint that, collapsing to the ground, she was thought to be dead. When the matter was reported to her husband, a nobleman, he was asked whether he wished her buried just as she was, or whether the gold chains and similar ornaments should be taken off her. He replied that he would return her to God just as he had been called to call her out of this life, and he would not allow the ornaments to be removed. She was laid on a bier and lay in the church for a whole day. At night a wicked man came to the bier, intending to strip her, and laid hands on the body; then she began to move. He, terrified, thought it was a ghost, and fled from the church in a rush, shouting. The woman, however, gradually came to herself from the noise and the shouting, and at last saw where she was and began to cry out too. Neighbours ran up, saw what had happened to her, and led her back to her husband in the citadel, which was not far from the church. There, as she was warmed in the steam room, she went into labour. Her husband at once made a vow that he would dedicate to God whatever she bore. When she had given birth to a son, he made him a Franciscan monk once the boy had grown a little. Later, however, the same man, having laid aside error and superstition, became a minister in a place in Thuringia. Thus God mercifully preserved that honourable matron and her infant for a longer time in this life.

units.la: DE MALIS SPIRITIBVS seu diabolis, & ipsorum operibus.
units.tr: ON EVIL SPIRITS, OR DEVILS, AND THEIR WORKS.

units.la: VIdi Tubingæferè singulis noctibus aliquas flammas, quæ cum diu flagrarent, tandem in magnum & amplum fumum dissolutæ sunt, & ita evanerunt. Similiter cùm viuerem Heydelbergæ, apparuerunt spectra, quales sunt stellæ cadentes, quæ veniebât singulis noctibus. Dormiui semel ad fenestram in lecto eiusdem cubiculi, in quo dormiebat alius, qui sequente die missam primam essèt celebraturus, quò veniebat spectrum ad fenestram, & conclaue ingrediens, libros in eo repositos aperiebat, uoluebat et uertebat folia, & uno libro depositio semper sumebat alterum, donec oēs euolauisset. Deniq; accedebat ad parietē cū strepitu, ut ab omnib. nobis audiretur, tandēq; evanescebat: id fiebat singulis noctibus: nec uni soli, sed omnib. in illo cubiculo dormientibus apparuit. Sic non est cogitandum, spectra nihil esse: sunt diaboli (non est dubium (qui semper inter homines uagentur siue conspiciantur, siue non: non sunt animæ, aut aliæ res ex materia quadam conflatæ, sed prorsus diaboli.
units.tr: I saw at Tübingen almost every night some flames which, after burning for a long time, finally dissolved into a large, thick smoke and so vanished. Likewise, when I lived at Heidelberg, there appeared spectres like falling stars, which came every night. Once I was lying down by the window, in the bed of the same chamber where another man was sleeping, who was to celebrate the first Mass the next day. A spectre came to the window and, entering the room, opened the books stored there, turned over and leafed through the pages, and took up one book after another until it had flown through all of them. Finally it went up to the wall with a noise, so that all of us could hear it, and then it vanished. This happened every night, and it appeared not to one person only but to all who slept in that room. So we must not think that spectres are nothing. They are devils (there is no doubt about it), which always wander among men, whether they are seen or not. They are not souls, nor things made of some matter, but altogether devils.

units.la: Doctor Martinus Lutherus.
units.tr: Doctor Martin Luther.

units.la: Similis ratio est, cum Nixis in aquis habitantibus, & homines in aquas submergentibus, cum qui bus aliquæ uirgines familiaritatem habent. Non diabolos contemnamus.
units.tr: The case is similar with the Nixies, who live in the waters and drown men in them, as well as with those with whom some maidens have familiarity. We should not despise the devils.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: In Salinis Sueuicis quidam adolescens, filius honesti & docti uiri, ac de multorum studijs beneme-riti, suffocatus est in aquis, eo loco, ubi nocturnæ fac◦ces multis annis sunt conspectæ. Iudicant autem docti uiri, in illis profundis aquæ locis uersari malos spiritus, qui etiam bonis hominibus nocent. Iá sunt circiter 12 aut 14 anni quâdo illud factum est.
units.tr: In the Swabian salt-works a certain young man, the son of an honest and learned man who had deserved well of many by his studies, was drowned in the water at the place where nightly torches had been seen for many years. Learned men judge that evil spirits dwell in those deep places of the water and harm even good men. It is now about twelve or fourteen years since this happened.

units.la: Theodorus Gaza habuit prædium in Campania, quod pertinebat ad sacerdotium, quo donatus erat à Nicolao pontifice. In illo prædio cùm colonus effodisset urnam, in qua fuerunt ossa cadaueris (Fuit enim uetus consuetudo non tantum apud Gentes, sed etiam apud Iudæos, ut quilibet in suis prædijs sepelirentur. Inde conijci potest, illa ossa fuisse ex corpore coloni ante multos annos eo in loco habitantis, uel illud prædium possidentis) apparet illi spectrum, iubens eum rursus sepelire urnam, in qua erant ossa, additis his uerbis: nisi iterum ossa conderet, fore ut filius ipsius moreretur. Cum id colonus negligeret, eius filius paulo post noctu interficitur: sicut possibile est diabolo hominem, præsertim à Deo derelictum, interficere. Post aliquot dierum interuallum reuertitur spectrum, indicans colono, se etiam alterum terum filium interfecturum, nisi ossa reponat & honeste sepeliat. Colonus admonitus priore damno, uidens etiam alterum filium aegrotare, rem Theodoro refert. Gaza proficiscitur cum eo in praedium, & in eo loco ubi eruerat colonus urnam, ibi rursus facto sepulchro, urnam cum ossibus sepeliunt. Repositis ossibus in priorem locum, statim filius coloni convaluit. Hanc historiam Theodorus Gaza saepius multis suis amicis narravit, & addidit hunc versum: Sunt aliquid manes, lethum non omnia finit. Possem multa alia narrare, quae mihi & aliis multis acciderunt.
units.tr: Theodore Gaza had an estate in Campania, which belonged to a priesthood with which he had been endowed by Pope Nicholas. When a tenant on that estate dug up an urn containing human bones (for it was an old custom not only among the Gentiles but also among the Jews that each man should be buried on his own estates; so it may be conjectured that those bones came from the body of a tenant who had lived in that place many years before, or who had possessed that estate), a spectre appeared to him, ordering him to bury the urn with the bones again, and adding these words: unless he put the bones back, his son would die. When the tenant neglected this, his son was killed a little later at night, just as it is possible for the devil to kill a man, especially one forsaken by God. After an interval of some days the spectre returned, telling the tenant that it would also kill his other son unless he put back the bones and buried them honourably. The tenant, warned by the earlier loss and seeing his other son also sick, reported the matter to Theodore. Gaza went with him to the estate, and in the place where the tenant had dug up the urn, a grave was made again and the urn with the bones was buried. Once the bones were returned to their former place, the tenant's son immediately recovered. Theodore Gaza often related this story to many of his friends and added this line: "Ghosts do exist, and death does not end everything." I could tell many other stories that happened to me and to many others.

units.la: Non crederem esse Satyros, nisi experientia compertum esset. Quando Sylla redijt ex bello Mithridatico versus Romam propter Marium, qui optimates & praecipuos Romanos senatores interfecerat, ibi in itinere Satyrus utcunq; humana specie ad eum adducebatur, iussus est loqui, sed tantum edidit quoddam murmur stridens, quod non est ab ullo homine intellectum. Et credo illud spectrum fuisse diabolum: significauit enim quales cives Sylla Romae esset inuenturus.
units.tr: I would not believe there are Satyrs, were it not known from experience. When Sulla returned from the Mithridatic war towards Rome, on account of Marius, who had killed the optimates and the leading Roman senators, a Satyr, somewhat human in appearance, was brought to him on the road. He was ordered to speak, but he only gave out a certain shrill murmur, which no man understood. And I believe that spectre was a devil, for it signified what kind of citizens Sulla would find at Rome.

units.la: Ita ante paucos annos dicunt filium Imperatoris Caroli V. Philippum regem Hispaniarum circumduxisse secum duos Satyros, pilosos hominiculos, uel omnino similes hominibus, bestialem alioqui figuram, hominum uero speciem imitantes, solitos stridere obscurum quiddam, quod non intelligebatur. Isti haud dubiè aliquid portenderunt.
units.tr: So too, a few years ago, they say that Philip, king of Spain, son of the Emperor Charles V, took two Satyrs about with him, hairy little men, or altogether like men, otherwise of bestial form but imitating the human appearance, which were accustomed to utter some obscure sound that was not understood. Those creatures undoubtedly portended something.

units.la: In historia sancti Ambrosij est, apparuisse ei Satyros: existimo fuisse diabolos.
units.tr: In the history of Saint Ambrose it is told that Satyrs appeared to him. I think they were devils.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Ante paucos annos in Bohemia, cuidam dormienti spectrum apparet: Surge, inquit, & uade mecum. Ille confirmatus, respondit: Non ibo tecum. Secunda nocte redit, & sic quoque tertia, inquiens: Surge, abeamus. Respondit ille: Non abibo. Tunc spectrum inquit: Nisi surrexeris, male tecum agetur: ipse metuens sibi malum, surgit. Ductus est ab eo in apertum & planum campum, ubi cum esset, interrogat eum spectrum: Quid vides? Respondit: Video ab una parte ingentem exercitum, quasi Turcarum. Quid vides amplius? Ab altera parte exiguam quasi Christianorum turbam paratam ad prælium. Quid ulterius? Video victoriam penes Christianos esse. Tunc ait spectrum: Hæc breui sic euenient, ut uidisti, & statim euanuit.
units.tr: A few years ago in Bohemia, a spectre appeared to a man who was sleeping: "Get up," it said, "and come with me." He, having been strengthened, replied: "I will not go with you." On the second night it returned, and likewise on the third, saying: "Get up, let us be off." He answered: "I will not go." Then the spectre said: "Unless you get up, it will go badly for you." He, fearing harm to himself, got up. He was led by it onto an open and level plain, and when he was there, the spectre asked him: "What do you see?" He replied: "I see on one side a huge army, like that of the Turks." "What do you see further?" "On the other side a small crowd, as it were of Christians, ready for battle." "What next?" "I see that victory lies with the Christians." Then the spectre said: "These things will happen soon, just as you have seen," and at once it vanished.

units.la: Athenæus dicit fuisse in Aphrica tale animal, quod cum homines aspicerent, obstupescebant, & id multis militibus in exercitu Marij accidisse. Marius dolum sentiens, unicuilibet militi speculum curat, ibi animal ex suo contuitu interficitur. Existimo illud spectrum fuisse diabolum.
units.tr: Athenaeus says that in Africa there was a certain animal which made men who looked at it stupefied, and that this happened to many soldiers in the army of Marius. Marius, sensing the trick, had a mirror brought to each soldier, and by its reflection the animal was killed. I think that spectre was a devil.

units.la: Quidam docti iuri in concilio Basilien si, in quo doctißimi & excellentes uiri fere omnes eo tempore existentes congregati fuerunt, recreatio-nis causa extra urbem, ad quandam syluulam se contulerunt, ut amicè de controuersijs illius tempo-ris conferrent : inter eundum forte auiculam in modum lusciniæ dulcissimè canentem audiunt, ad-mirantur initiò dulcedinem uocis, & dubitant cu-ius auis sit cantus: cum non possint ipsum ab alia-rum auium cantu discernere. Ingredientes porrò syluulam, ueniunt ad arborem, in qua sedebat aui-cula. Deliberant communi consensu, ut eam adiu-rent. Tunc is qui cæteris cordatior uideri uolebat, alloquitur his uerbis auiculam : Ego adiuro te in nomine Iesu Christi, ut nobis indices, quis sis ? Re-spondit eis, se esse unam ex damnatis animabus, & destinatam esse ad eum locum usq; ad diem nouissi-mum, & tunc supplicium æternum subeundum es-se: neq; ullam sibi liberationem restare. His dictis auolauit ex arbore, clamitans : O ewig, ô ewig, swie ist das ein lange zeit, id est: ô quàm diuturna & immensa est æternitas. Iudico suisse diabolum in illo loco habitantem. Omnes uerò qui huic ad-iurationi intersuerunt, uehementer ægrotare incoe-perunt, & paulo post mortui sunt.
units.tr: Some learned men at the Council of Basel, at which almost all the most learned and excellent men of that time were gathered, went out of the city to a small wood for recreation, in order to discuss amicably the controversies of that time. On the way they happened to hear a little bird singing most sweetly, like a nightingale. At first they marvelled at the sweetness of its voice and wondered whose song it was, since they could not tell it apart from the songs of other birds. Entering the little wood, they came to the tree in which the little bird was sitting. By common consent they resolved to adjure it. Then he who wished to seem the most prudent of the others addressed the little bird in these words: "I adjure you in the name of Jesus Christ to tell us who you are." It answered them that it was one of the damned souls, destined to remain in that place until the last day, and that then it would have to undergo eternal punishment, and that no deliverance remained for it. Having said this, it flew off the tree, crying: "O ewig, ô ewig, swie ist das ein lange zeit" [O eternity, O eternity, how long a time that is!]. I judge it was a devil dwelling in that place. Yet all who took part in this adjuration began to fall gravely ill, and a little later they died.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam Monachus Erphordiæ in monasterio Sebaldi, homo doctus, & in lingua Græca exerci-tatus, tatus, qui cognito uerbo Dei, cùm papistas reliquisset, & puram iam Euangelij doctrinam amplecteretur, uocatus est à Vinarien-sibus senatoribus Vinariam, ut ibi Euangelium concionare-tur. Cum igitur suggestum ascendisset, & locum quendam tractandum et interpretandum sumpsis-set, uisa est auis in eius capite per totam concio-nem ipso nesciente sedere. Quanquam multi homines uidebant, tamen ne forte tumultus excita-retur inter concionandum, nullum uerbum de hac re dicere uoluerunt. Finita uero concione, cùm ex suggesto abiret, auis etiam euanuit. Ibi varij sermones sparsi sunt: quidam mortem concionatoris significari dixerunt, quod & factum est. nam post triduum optimus uir moriebatur.
units.tr: A certain monk at Erfurt, in the monastery of St Sebald, a learned man practised in Greek, had come to know the Word of God, left the Papists, and was now embracing the pure doctrine of the Gospel. The senators of Weimar summoned him there to preach the Gospel. When he had climbed into the pulpit and taken up a passage to treat and expound, a bird was seen sitting on his head throughout the whole sermon, though he himself did not know it. Many people saw it, but lest a tumult be stirred up during the sermon, they chose not to say anything about it. When the sermon was over and he was leaving the pulpit, the bird also vanished. Various talk spread: some said that the death of the preacher was signified, and this came to pass, for after three days that excellent man died.

units.la: In quodam loco fuit quidam Doctor medicinæ, magna cum felicitate morbos curans, cum aliqua ignorare pudebat. Confugit igitur ad diabolum, quem in uitrum inclusum de rebus dubijs consule-bat, qua impietate sua, magnas filijs suis facultates reliquit, ita ut supra 26000 florenos patre mortuo ex hæreditate consequerentur. Voluit ante agonem pœnitentiam agere, at instar Aiacis furere cœpit, & semper istum suum consiliarium uocauit, horribilesq; blasphemias contra Spiritum sanctum protulit, in quo furore denique ex hac uita discessit.
units.tr: In a certain place there was a doctor of medicine who cured diseases with great success, but he was ashamed to be ignorant of anything. So he took refuge with the devil, whom he consulted about doubtful matters, shut up in a glass. By this impiety he left great wealth to his sons, so that after their father's death they obtained more than 26,000 florins from the inheritance. Before his death he wanted to repent, but he began to rage like Ajax, always calling that devil his counsellor, and he uttered horrible blasphemies against the Holy Spirit. In this frenzy he finally departed this life.

units.la: Fuit alius quidam multas à diabolo tentationes patiens, qui dixit, diabolum in forma muscæ aut crabronis suis genis et oculis cum magna gravitate imhærere, ut vix gestari posset.
units.tr: Another man, who suffered many temptations from the devil, said that the devil, in the form of a fly or a hornet, clung to his cheeks and eyes with such heaviness that he could scarcely be carried about.

units.la: Erphordiæ quidam miser homo cum esset in magna inopia, sollicitus fuit de victu & de vitæ instituendæ ratione, in tali dolore animi inui-tauit ad se diabolum, qui statim aduenit, dicens: Si vis te mihi addicere, docebo te artem ex qua significabitur, quo res furto, vel alijs modis ablatæ peruenerint. Miser conditiones accepit: diabolus etiã se monstratorem rerum ablatarũ fore pollice-tur. Cum ergo hãc artem diu professus esset, factus est ad eũ magnus hominũ concursus, ita ut multi eũ consulerent: sed tandem diabolus destituit eum, & cum multos honestos & innocentes homines falsò furti arguéret, à senatu captus, ibi statim confessus est, se cum diabolo pactũ habuisse. Multum negocij fecit pastoribus eum consolantibus, quia contende-bat se non posse conuerti: sed tamen conuersus est, & accepit consolationem, cùm concionatores dicerent, eum quidem impiè fecisse, sed esse man-datum Dei, ut omnes peccatores ad filium Dei generis humani saluatorem confugerent, & om-nes ad ipsum conuersos, & ipsius auxilium im-plorantes contra Sathanam, fuisse exauditos: & quamuis se illi addixisset, tamen tale pactum fore irritum, quia nemo posset alteri polliceri aliquid, quod non sit in sua potestate.
units.tr: At Erfurt a wretched man, who was in great want and anxious about food and about how to order his life, in such grief of mind invited the devil to himself. The devil came at once, saying: "If you want to devote yourself to me, I will teach you an art by which it will be shown by what means goods taken by theft or other means have come to be found." The wretch accepted the conditions, and the devil promised to be the revealer of stolen goods. So when he had long professed this art, a great crowd of people came to him and many consulted him. But at last the devil abandoned him, and when he falsely accused many honest and innocent men of theft, he was seized by the senate, and there at once confessed that he had made a pact with the devil. The ministers took much trouble to console him, because he insisted that he could not be converted. Yet he was converted and received consolation, when the preachers said that he had indeed acted impiously, but that it is God's command that all sinners should flee to the Son of God, the Saviour of mankind, and that all who turned to him and implored his help against Satan had been heard. And although he had given himself over to the devil, nevertheless such a pact would be void, because no one can promise another anything that is not in his own power.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Similis historia accidit anno 1558. in pago, vix dimidiû miliare ab oppido Ihena distante. Quidam magus variis indicatis à diabolo, herbis, ægrotos non paucos sanitati restituit: tandem inter ipsum & eius vicinum fabrum lignarium rixæ sunt ortæ, sic ut faber scommatibus aliquibus acerbioribus in ipsum inueheret, unde magi animum sauciauit. Elapsis iam aliquot mensibus, faber in morbum periculosum incidit. Mittit igitur ad magum, ut ipsi iniuriam aliquando in ipsum illatam condonet, & sibi in hoc periculoso morbo subueniat & opituletur. Magus uerò, sicut callidus & uersutus, etsi fabro illius delicti remissionem promittat: tamen iniurias ipsi illatas ulciscitur, hoc modo: Iubet fabrum uti radice in potione, cui à uerre nomen est inditum, cum alijs uenenatis herbis, qua potione ad sed sumpta, ingentes corporis cruciatus sensit, quibus indies magis magisq; crescentibus, denique in eis moritur. Mulier uerò fabri cum eius agnatis, accusant magum homicidij. Delata itaq; causa ad senatum Ihenensem, qui, sicut honestos uiros decet, magum in uincula conijci curant. Cùm uerò magus in tortura de suis sceleribus peractis examinaretur, retur, totum negocium confessus est, in primis quòd interfecisset illum fabrum, qui semel ipsum læserat, & quòd magiam suam à quadam uetula in uicinia Harciniæ syluæ habitante didicerat. Itē semper ipsi affuisse diabolum, de hominibus ad ipsum aduenientibus commonefacientem, & inspi-rantem ei, quid præsentibus & absentibus, ipsumq; consulentibus largiri deberet. His itaq; compertis palo infixus, & combustus est.
units.tr: A similar story happened in the year 1558 in a village scarcely half a mile from the town of Jena. A certain magician, using various herbs revealed to him by the devil, restored not a few sick people to health. At length a quarrel arose between him and his neighbour, a carpenter, and the carpenter attacked him with some rather bitter taunts, which wounded the magician's spirit. After some months had passed, the carpenter fell into a dangerous illness. He therefore sent to the magician, asking him to forgive the wrong once done to him and to help and relieve him in this dangerous illness. But the magician, being crafty and cunning, although he promised the carpenter forgiveness, nevertheless avenged the injury in this way: he ordered the carpenter to drink a root called "verre", mixed with other poisonous herbs. After drinking it he felt huge bodily torments, which grew daily until at last he died of them. The carpenter's wife and kinsmen accused the magician of homicide. The case was referred to the senate of Jena, which, as honourable men should, had the magician thrown into chains. When he was examined under torture about the crimes he had committed, he confessed the whole affair: first, that he had killed that carpenter who had once injured him; and that he had learned his magic from an old woman living in the neighbourhood of the Harz forest. He also confessed that the devil had always been present with him, reminding him of the people who came to him and inspiring him what he should bestow on those who consulted him, whether present or absent. These things having been established, he was impaled and burned.

units.la: Anno 53 captæ sunt Berlinæ duæ incantatrices mulieres, quæ glaciem ad perdendas fruges per-ficere conatæ sunt. Eaeq; mulieres rapuerunt furto alterius uicinæ mulieris infantulum, & ipso diffe-cto coxerunt. Factum est diuinitùs, ut mater quæ-rens infantē interueniret, ibiq; in ollam impositā amissi infantis membra uideret. Captis itaq; mulie-ribus, & in tortura examinatis, dixerunt, si proce-sisset coctio, tunc futura fuisset ingens glacies, ita ut omnes fruges perderentur.
units.tr: In the year 1553 two sorceresses were seized at Berlin, who tried to bring about an ice to destroy the crops. These women had stolen the little child of another woman, a neighbour, and when it was dead they boiled it. By divine providence it came about that the mother, seeking her infant, came upon them, and there saw the limbs of her lost child in a pot. The women were seized and examined under torture, and they said that if the boiling had gone on, there would have been a huge ice, so that all the crops would have been destroyed.

units.la: Cardinalis quidā hospitibus inuitatis spectacu-lum exhibuit, in quod produxit mulieres magicas, quæ fecerunt tempestatem: repressa autem tempe-state, euanuerunt.
units.tr: A certain cardinal, having invited guests, put on a spectacle in which he produced magic women who made a storm; but when the summer weather was restored, they vanished.
