units.la: Heydelbergæ minister Doctoris Theologiæ, bo-nus homo, & non alienus à nostra doctrina, aliquā do profectus in patriam, cùm rediret, & non pro-cul abesset Heydelberga, ibi eques quidam arduo equo uectus se demittit, & ipsum nihil tale uolen‑tem equo imponit: ille uero cum uellet apprehen‑dere sessorem in equo, ut se teneret, sensit eum euanuisse. ipse solo equo in altum tanta celeritate uectus est, ut pene sit extinctus. Cum igitur uenit propè urbem Heydelbergam, abijcitur iuxta pon‑tem, ubi iacet per aliquot horas attonitus, quasi mortuus: reuersus ad se ac circumspiciens, uidit se esse Heydelbergæ, ingressusq; domũ ægrotat per dimidium annum. Hæc ipse nobis narrauit.
units.tr: At Heidelberg there was a minister, a Doctor of Theology, a good man and not unfriendly to our doctrine. Having gone some time ago to his homeland, he was returning, and was not far from Heidelberg, when a certain horseman, riding a tall horse, came down and set him, who wanted nothing of the sort, up on the horse. But when he tried to grasp the rider so as to hold himself on, he felt that the man had vanished. He himself, alone on the horse, was carried aloft with such speed that he was nearly killed. When he came near the city of Heidelberg, he was cast down beside the bridge, where he lay for some hours, stunned and as if dead. Coming back to himself and looking around, he saw that he was at Heidelberg; he went into his house and was ill for half a year. He himself told us these things.

units.la: In Italia leuiter curat doctrinã Astronomicã, sed excellétes sunt in arte magica. Papa Paulus erudi‑tissimus in omnib. doctrinis, erat etiam studiosus ar‑tis magicæ. huius igitur artis prouidentia ductus, quondam Aloisio filio suo suo scripsit, ut illũ diem caueret, quo illum interficiendum præuiderat. Hic autem cauit quidem, nec tota die uoluit egredi ex sua arce seu palatio. Sed cum iam accessisset uespe‑ra, & sperasset iam se perfunctum periculo, iussit se gestari in aggerem ad inspiciendas ædificatio‑nes: egrediuntur cum eo coniurati, & regrediun‑tur. Cũ igitur ille collocaretur in suo cubiculo, isti ingrediuntur, interficiunt eũ, suspendunt̄q; ipsum pudendis e fenestra: fuerat enim homo libidinosus. Hoc non potest dici Astronomia.
units.tr: In Italy astronomical learning is lightly cultivated, but they excel in the magic art. Pope Paul, most learned in all disciplines, was also devoted to the magic art. Led therefore by the foresight of this art, he once wrote to his son Aloysius, warning him to beware the day on which he had foreseen that he would be killed. Aloysius did take care, and did not want to leave his citadel or palace the whole day. But when evening came and he hoped he had got through the danger, he ordered himself to be carried to the embankment to inspect the buildings. Conspirators went out with him and came back with him. When he was placed in his bedchamber, they came in, killed him, and hanged him from the window by his genitals, for he had been a lustful man. This cannot be called astronomy.

units.la: Abbas Trittenhemius seu Spaheimensis fuit magnus magus, in quodam forte itinere ( sicut mihi Pirchaimerus narrauit) cum uenissët in diuersoriū non bene instructum, quidam per iocum dixerūt: Domine Abbas, cura nobis bonum ferculum piscium. ille tantum pulsauit fenestram, ac statim uenit quidam portans lancem instructam lucijs coctis.
units.tr: Abbot Trithemius, or of Spanheim, was a great magician. On a certain journey (as Pirckheimer told me), when he had come to an inn that was not well supplied, some people said in jest: "Lord Abbot, get us a good dish of fish." He merely tapped on the window, and at once a man came in carrying a platter loaded with cooked pike.

units.la: Noui quendam nomine Faustum de Kundling, quod est paruum oppidum, patriæ meæ uicinum. Hic cum esset scholasticus Cracouiensis, ibi magiam didicerat, sicut ibi olim fuit eius magnus usus, & ibidem fuerunt publicæ eiusdem artis professiones. Vagabatur passim, dicebat arcana multa. Ille Venetijs cùm uellet ostendere spectaculum, dixit se uolaturum in cœlum. Diabolus igitur subuexit eum, & afflixit adeo, ut allisus humi pene exanimatus esset: sed tamen non est mortuus.
units.tr: I knew a man named Faustus of Kundling, a small town near my homeland. When he was a scholar at Kraków he had learned magic there, since the art was once much practised there and there were public professions of it. He wandered about everywhere and claimed to know many secrets. When at Venice he wished to show a spectacle, he said he would fly up into heaven. The devil therefore carried him aloft and dashed him down so violently that, struck against the ground, he was nearly dead, yet he did not die.

units.la: Ante paucos annos idem Ioannes Faustus, postremò die sedit admodum mæstus in quodam pago ducatus Vuirtenbergensis. Hospes ipsum alloquitur, cur mœstus esset præter morem et consuetudinem (erat alioqui turpissimus nebulo, inquinatissimæ uitæ, ita ut semel atq; iterum pene interfectus sit propter libidines) ibi dixit hospiti in illo pago: Ne perterrefias hac nocte. Media nocte domus quassata est. Mane cum Faustus non surgeret, & iam esset fere meridies, hospes adhibitis aliis, ingressus est in eius cœlaue, inuenitq; eum iacentem prope lectum inuersa facie, sic à diabolo interfectus. Viues, adhuc habebat secum canem, qui erat diabolus, sicut iste nebulo qui scripsit De uanitate artium etiam habebat canem, secum currentem, qui erat diabolus. Hic Faustus in hoc oppido Vuittenberga euasit, cum optimus princeps dux Ioannes dedisset mandata de illo capiendo. Sic Norimbergae etiam euasit, cum iam incipceret prandere, æstuauit, surgitq; statim, soluens quod hospiti debebat. uix autem uenerat ante portam, ibi ueniunt lictores, & de eo inquirunt.
units.tr: A few years ago this same John Faustus sat, on his last day, very sad in a certain village of the Duchy of Württemberg. His host addressed him and asked why he was sadder than usual. (He was otherwise a most disgraceful scoundrel, of a most polluted life, so that more than once he was nearly killed on account of his lusts.) There he said to the host in that village: "Do not be frightened tonight." At midnight the house was shaken. In the morning, when Faustus still did not get up, and it was already nearly noon, the host called in others and entered his chamber. He found him lying near the bed, face down, thus killed by the devil. While alive, he still had with him a dog, which was the devil, just as that scoundrel who wrote On the Vanity of the Arts also had a dog running with him, which was the devil. Faustus escaped at Wittenberg in this town, although the most excellent prince, Duke John, had issued orders for his capture. So too he escaped at Nuremberg. He was just beginning to dine when he grew agitated, got up at once, and paid what he owed the host. Scarcely had he come before the gate when the officers arrived there and inquired about him.

units.la: Idem Faustus magus, turpissima bestia, & cloaca multorum diabolorum, uane gloriabatur de se omnes uictorias, quas habuerunt Caesariani exercitus in Italia, esse partas per ipsum sua magia. idq; fuit mendacium uanissimum. Id enim dico propter iuuentutem, ne statim talibus uanis hominibus assentiantur.
units.tr: This same Faustus, the magician, a most vile beast and sewer of many devils, boasted vainly that all the victories which the imperial army won in Italy had been achieved through his magic. This was a most empty lie. I say this on account of the young, lest they at once assent to such empty men.

units.la: In Liuonia Moscouitae exercent horribilem crudelitatem, suspendunt paruos pueros, & dissecant mulieres grauidas, ac ex pueris eximunt corda ad incantationes: ducunt secum milites multa millia mulierum, quarum plurimae sunt uenefica: harum consilijs pugnant: castra metantur, quae ad suas incantationes utuntur corculis puerorum. Cum magia etiam semper fuerunt coniuncta infanticidia.
units.tr: In Livonia the Muscovites practise horrible cruelty. They hang small boys, cut open pregnant women, and take hearts from the boys for incantations. They lead with them, as soldiers, many thousands of women, most of whom are witches. They fight by their counsels and pitch camps, and they use the little hearts of boys for their incantations. Infanticide has always been joined with magic.

units.la: Marius quando duxit exercitum contra Cimbros, habuit secum Iudaicam mulierem in castris uatiuatidicam, ex cuius prædictionibus multa constitu-it. Nominata est Martha: de qua plura in Plu-tarcho.
units.tr: When Marius led his army against the Cimbri, he had with him in camp a Jewish woman, a prophetess, from whose predictions he decided many things. Her name was Martha. More about her is found in Plutarch.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Reperiuntur quidam præstigatores in Asia, cir-cumeuntes per totas insulas, & gerentes serpen-tes, quibus saltantibus existimatur purgari domus, quòd nihil possit nocere illi domui uel familiæ, in qua suam artem exercuerint. Gestant in uase cu-preo unum atq; alterum serpentem: uenientes ue-rò in domum aliquam, incipiunt ludere tympa-nis: ad quem strepitum paulatim assurgit serpens, & aperit rictum, ac caput promit. Illo ludente saltat, tandem decidit serpens, quasi exanimis: quia diabolus cruciat eum.
units.tr: There are certain charlatans in Asia who travel through all the islands carrying snakes. When they dance with them, it is thought that the house is cleansed, because the snakes can do no harm to that house or family in which they have practised their art. They carry one or two snakes in a copper vessel. When they come into some house, they begin to play on drums. At this noise the snake gradually rises, opens its jaws, and thrusts out its head. While the charmer plays, it dances; at last the snake falls down as if lifeless, because the devil torments it.

units.la: Nos meminimus Francosordiæ ad Oderam puel-lam fuisse, quæ quicquid manibus arriperet uerte-bat in argentum, quod comedebat. Aliquando abreptum est ex eius manibus, & missum ad prin-cipem, & ad nos etiam.
units.tr: We remember that at Frankfurt on the Oder there was a girl who turned into silver whatever she seized with her hands, and then ate it. Sometimes it was snatched from her hands and sent to the prince, and to us as well.

units.la: Viennæ fuerunt duo magi, quorum alter deuo-rauit alterum, id est: diabolus abduxit alterum in specum, in quo tridno latuit, deinde reuersus est.
units.tr: At Vienna there were two magicians, one of whom devoured the other; that is, the devil carried one off into a cave, where he lay hidden for three days, and then he returned.

units.la: In Italia fuit quædam virgo à diabolo obsessa, etsi ea ignorabat Latinè loqui, tamen interrogata à Lazaro Bonamico, professore Bononiæ, quis es-set optimus uersus in Vergilio? Respondit diabo-lus lus per eam: Discite iusticiam moniti, & non tenere diuos, hoc sciuit diabolus.
units.tr: In Italy there was a certain virgin possessed by the devil, although she did not know how to speak Latin. Yet when she was asked by Lazarus Bonamicus, professor at Bologna, which was the best verse in Virgil, the devil answered through her: "Learn justice, be warned, and do not scorn the gods." The devil knew this.

units.la: Ante paucos annos fuit similis mulier in ducatu Luneburgensi, ignara aliàs latinæ & græcæ linguæ: tamen obsessa à diabolo, perfectè Latinè & Græcè loquebatur.
units.tr: A few years ago there was a similar woman in the Duchy of Lüneburg, otherwise ignorant of Latin and Greek. Yet, possessed by the devil, she spoke perfect Latin and Greek.

units.la: Dixit reuerendus, piæ memoriæ, Philippus, se audiuisse ex fide dignis uiris Christophoro Groß et Sigismundo Gelenio, de quadam uirgine Bononica, quæ biennium post mortem inter homines est uersata: inuitata uero ad conuiuia, parum cibi degustare uisa est. Cùm autem aliquando inter alias uirgines in choreis incederet, forte adest alius magus, ad astantes inquiēs: Hæc uirgo pallida, est mortua. Quo modo, respondent ei, est mortua, cùm eam incedere uideas? Videte, inquit, monstrabo uobis: accedens ad eam, submouet sub dextro humero fascinum, quo sublato concidit, & ut cadauer mansit. Illud fascinum ab alio mago erat impositum. ita diabolus hoc corpus toto tempore circumgestauit.
units.tr: The reverend Philip, of pious memory, said that he had heard from trustworthy men, Christoph Groß and Sigismund Gelenius, about a certain virgin of Bologna, who for two years after her death moved among men. When invited to banquets, she seemed to taste little food. Once, however, as she walked among other virgins in the dances, another magician happened to be present, and said to the bystanders: "This pale virgin is dead." "How so?" they replied. "She is dead, when you see her walking?" "Look," he said, "I will show you." Going up to her, he removed a charm from under her right shoulder, and when it was lifted she fell and remained like a corpse. That charm had been placed there by another magician. So the devil carried this body about the whole time.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Qui dã habitu & uestitu precioso indutus, cũ tibicine et fidicine prope Rotẽburgã ad Thubarã boni uiri ædes sæpius accesṡit, ac in eis cõuiuia & choreas instituit, prætextu ducẽdi illius patrisfamiliâs honestã filiã: affirmauit etiã se esse natũ ex nobili stirpe, atq; in longinquis terris plurimas arces, præsidia, oppidula, aliaq; eiusmodi habere, sibiq; deesse nihil q; in hoc mundo ab ullo homine desiderari possit, nisi uxor excellētib. morib. prædita. Displicuit patrifamiliâs hospitis cū suis socijs importuni tas, et ipsi suā filiā, quæ esset ignobilis, recusauit, ac redire prohibuit. At hospes cū suis duob. socijs adeò fuit impudēs, ut circa uesperā ornatus suis ornamētis aliquoties rediret, suūq; negociū institutū pficere conaretur. Postremò uero ex multis cōiectu ris dolū ac fraudē patersamiliâs olfaciēs, inuitauit ad se illius loci uerbi Diuini ministrū, cū quo præ- sente illo peregrino hospite de uarijs sacræ Scriptu ræ locis cōfert, quæ colloqua hospes & duo eius socij ægre ferētes, dixerūt, esse multas alias facetias & sales qb. cōuiuæ potius quàm sacræ Scripturæ in- terpretatiōe exhilarari posset, rogareq; ne esset eis ulterius molesti sacra Scriptura. Ad quæ patersami liâs iā satis cōfirmatus cōtra sathanæ insidias respō dit, & his uerbis eos interpellat: Abite uos nebulo- nes, insidiatores nostræ uitæ, nec quicquam negocij mecū, neq; cū meis mihi à Deo cōcessis habete: nos enim baptisati & redēpti sumus preciofo sangui- ne Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui nos cōtra insidias & astutias uestras diabolicas desēdere et tueri uult. Postquā hæc dixisset, nequā ille cū suis socijs ma- gno strepitu, relinquēs post se intolerabilē fœtorē & trium hominum suspensorū cadauericb in hi- pocausto, euanuit. Sic ille bonus paterfamiliâs cum suis liberatus & defensus est.
units.tr: A certain man, dressed in splendid clothes, came several times with a flautist and a lute-player to the house of a good man near Rothenburg on the Tauber. There he held banquets and dances, under the pretext of leading away the householder's honest daughter. He also affirmed that he was born of noble stock, that in distant lands he had very many citadels, garrisons, little towns and the like, and that he lacked nothing in this world that any man could desire, except a wife endowed with excellent morals. The householder was displeased by the importunity of the guest and his companions, and he refused to give them his daughter, who was of low birth, and forbade them to come back. But the guest, with his two companions, was so shameless that near evening, decked out in his finery, he returned several times and tried to bring his undertaking to completion. At last, however, the householder, smelling a trick and fraud from many signs, invited to his house the minister of the Divine Word of that place. In the presence of that strange guest, he conferred with him on various passages of Holy Scripture. The guest and his two companions, taking it badly, said that there were many other witticisms and jokes by which a company could be cheered at a banquet rather than by the interpretation of Holy Scripture, and they asked that Scripture not trouble them any further. To this the householder, now sufficiently strengthened against the snares of Satan, answered and addressed them with these words: "Go away, you scoundrels, plotters against our life. You have nothing to do with me or with what has been granted to me by God. For we are baptized and redeemed by the precious blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, who wishes to defend and protect us against your diabolical snares and cunning." When he had said this, that wicked one, with his companions, departed with a great noise, leaving behind an intolerable stench and the bodies of three hanged men in the hypocaust, and vanished. Thus that good householder, with his household, was freed and defended.

units.la: Amen. Ihenæ uenicbat ad me homo, qui querebatur, quòd spectrum quoddam se à genis suis suspenderet, & esset ei molestissimum, iubens ut se interficeret. Petebat à me consilium, quid sibi faciendum esset. Respondi: Hoc genus dæmoniorum, non expellitur, nisi precationibus & ieiunijs. Dixit mihi etiam, qua occasione primùm ipsi hoc acciderit.
units.tr: Amen. A man came to me at Jena who complained that a certain spectre hung from his cheeks, was very troublesome to him, and urged him to kill himself. He asked my advice on what he should do. I replied: this kind of demon is not expelled except by prayers and fasting. He also told me on what occasion this had first happened to him.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Cum Coburgi subsisteremus in eremo, quater accidit, ut semper post apparitiones nocturnarum facium Doctor Lutherus graui capitis morbo agitaretur. Accidit autem, ut cum præcedente nocte tres ciusmodi uolantes faces uidisset, ferè incidisset in syncopen Doctor Martinus. Præsentiens autem morbum, ministrum suum uocabat, is amygdalinum oleum instillabat in aurem, item oleum nucis muscatæ, & subinde pedes fricabat calefactis linteis. Tandem iussus minister legere epistolam Pauli ad Galatas, sic ei somnus conciliabatur. Cum iam euasisset periculum, dicebat Doctor: Venite in contemptum diaboli, Psalmum De profundis quatuor uocibus cantemus.
units.tr: While we were staying at Coburg in the hermitage, it happened four times that Doctor Luther was always troubled by a severe headache after the appearances of nocturnal lights. It once happened that, on the night before, he had seen three such flying torches, and Doctor Martin nearly fell into a swoon. Sensing the illness coming on, he called his attendant, who dripped almond oil into his ear, and also oil of nutmeg, and from time to time rubbed his feet with cloths warmed by the fire. At last, when the attendant was ordered to read Paul's Epistle to the Galatians, sleep came to him. When he had got past the danger, the Doctor said: "Come, let us sing the Psalm De profundis in four voices, in contempt of the devil."

units.la: DE SIGNIS PORTENTIS ac prodigijs.
units.tr: ON SIGNS, PORTENTS AND PRODIGIES

units.la: Est mirabilis & pulcherrima dispositio ortus & occasus stellarum, quæ adferunt rebus nascentibus conuenientes serenitates & pluuias, præpræsertim quando anni sunt regulares. Sed turbantur sæpè tempestates anni uel propter hominum peccata, uel positum stellarum, ut hoc tempore (erat enim in principio noui anni) uidetis, quantum sit pluuiarum, quia Saturnus est in tauro, accedens iam ad hyades, quæ natura sunt humidæ, & humiditates adferunt, & Iupiter in piscibus: illæ stellæ augent humidas tempestates. Verùm dicamus de an-nis regularibus. In uere seu Aprili sol accedit ad pleiades, ibi res nascentes indigent humiditate. Po-stea ad geminos, ibi aura uel aer est temperatior. Item quando sol uenit ad cancrum, & ad præsepe, iterum opus est pluuijs. Postea opus est æstu & siccitate, ut fruges possint maturescere. Vbi accedit ad leonem & syrium, tunc fiunt æstus, & est tem-pus siccum propter frugum maturationem. Dein-de rursus est opus humiditate in satione, uidelicet quando sol uenit ad scorpium. Deniq; sequuntur frigora, quando uenit Orion oppositus soli, tunc rursum multum tempestatum humidarum habetis.
units.tr: The arrangement of the rising and setting of the stars is wonderful and beautiful; they bring to growing things fitting fair weather and rains, especially when the years are regular. But the seasons of the year are often disturbed, either by the sins of men or by the position of the stars, as at this time (for it was at the beginning of the new year) you can see how much rain there is, because Saturn is in Taurus, now approaching the Hyades, which are by nature moist and bring moisture, and Jupiter is in Pisces; those stars increase wet weather. But let us speak of regular years. In spring, or April, the sun approaches the Pleiades; there growing things need moisture. Afterwards it comes to Gemini, where the air is milder. Likewise when the sun comes to Cancer and the Manger, again rains are needed. Afterwards there must be heat and dryness, so that the crops may ripen. When it approaches Leo and Sirius, then the heats come, and it is a dry time for the ripening of the crops. Then again moisture is needed for sowing, namely when the sun comes to Scorpio. Finally the cold follows, when Orion rises opposite the sun; then again you have much wet weather.

units.la: Fuit quidam Doctor, qui contra rerum natura-lium inquisitionem & astronomiam sic garriebat: Ho, mei rustici non indigent Calendario, quia bene norunt, quando sit hyems aut æstas: similiter quan-do meridies aut uespera. Doctor Martinus me in-tuebatur, metuens ne quid ei durius responderem. Nihil ei aliud respondebam, quàm: Hæc oratio non Doctori conuenit, Es ist ein vndoctorliche rede. Veniebant quidem mihi duriora in mentem, sed me represi. Hæc responsio Doctori Ionæ & Doctori Martino, & multis alijs doctis uiris per totā cœnam iocus fuit.
units.tr: There was a certain teacher who, speaking against the study of natural things and astronomy, prattled thus: "Oh, my country folk have no need of a calendar, since they know well when it is winter or summer, and likewise when it is noon or evening." Doctor Martin looked at me, fearing I might answer him too harshly. I answered him nothing other than: "This speech is not fitting for a doctor; Es ist ein vndoctorliche rede" (that is, an unlearned way of talking). Harsher things indeed came into my mind, but I restrained myself. This answer became a joke for Doctor Jonas, Doctor Martin and many other learned men throughout the whole dinner.

units.la: Ante expeditionem nostri Imperatoris Caroli V. in Galliam Narbonensem, in solitis motibus Alpes tremuerunt, & ex altissimis montibus & pluribus locis erupit aqua, ita ut esset admirationi multis hominibus. Sed habet physicas causas. Nam ubicunque in cauernis terræ sunt halitus, ibi sunt etiam aquæ, quæ apertis cauernis erumpūt & collapsis cauernius mutantur cursus flumi-num. Ita etiam erumpunt salinæ, quando terra ter-ræmotu concutitur, quia in eo loco sunt salinæ: in quo per longū tractū sunt cauernæ sicut cellæ-quando uerò decidunt illi specus tunc necesse est aquam alibi erumpere. Sunt magnum beneficium Dei salinæ, neq; sunt durabiles.
units.tr: Before the expedition of our Emperor Charles V into Narbonese Gaul, the Alps trembled in their usual movements, and water burst forth from the highest mountains and in many places, so that it was a wonder to many people. But it has natural causes. For wherever there are vapours in the caverns of the earth, there are also waters, which burst out when the caverns open, and when the caverns collapse the courses of rivers are changed. Salt springs also burst forth in the same way when the earth is shaken by an earthquake, because in that place there are salt deposits; where, over a long stretch, there are caverns like cells, when those hollows fall in, the water must break out elsewhere. Salt springs are a great benefit from God, and they do not last.

units.la: Anno 54, à Mansfeld usq; Misniam fuerunt tanti terræmotus, ut tota Misniafere sit quassata, sed nos nihil in hac ripa Albis animaduertimus.
units.tr: In the year 1554, from Mansfeld as far as Meissen, there were such great earthquakes that almost all of Meissen was shaken, but we noticed nothing on this bank of the Elbe.

units.la: Quando nostèr Imperator Carolus V. anno 32. ascendit ad conuentum Rabisbonensem, fuit hospes principis Palatini prope Heydelbergam. Ibi cum in uenatione instituta uideret ceruū, eum que insequeretur, occurrit ei lupus: ille relicto ceruo adoadoritur lupū. Intereaq; ex equi lapsu fregit crus, quod non posse uidebatur sanari, nisi pes abscinderetur. Cùm itaq; iam Chirurgi adferrent instrumenta, et se appararent ad abscindendum pedem, interuenit rex Ferdinandus, seuerissimè prohibens minitans que se uelle omnes suspendere, qui sectioni interessent, eam'que adiuuarent. Quibus perterriti Chirurgi abstinuerunt. Deinde consuluit Rex Ferdinandus, ut imperater Carolus V. proficisceretur ad uicinas thermas, quibus sanatum est crus. Hoc casu fortasse postrema ipsius ætas significata est.
units.tr: When our Emperor Charles V came to the Diet of Regensburg in the year 1532, he was the guest of the Count Palatine near Heidelberg. There, while a hunt was under way and he saw a stag and was pursuing it, a wolf met him; leaving the stag, he attacked the wolf. Meanwhile, by a fall from his horse, he broke his leg, which seemed unable to be healed unless the foot were cut off. When the surgeons were already bringing their instruments and preparing to amputate the foot, King Ferdinand intervened, most sternly forbidding them and threatening to hang all who should take part in the operation or assist in it. Terrified by this, the surgeons held back. Then King Ferdinand advised that Emperor Charles V should go to the nearby hot springs, by which the leg was healed. Perhaps by this accident his final age was signified.

units.la: Cercopithecus me aliquando ferè interfecissēt, nisi comes, ad cuius mensam asidebam, auulsisset. Quòd fuit signum multorum meorum præsentiū & futurorum cercopithecorum morsuum.
units.tr: A long-tailed monkey once nearly killed me, had not a companion, at whose table I was sitting, pulled it off. This was a sign of many bites from monkeys, both present and future, that I have had.

units.la: Conspectus est in aere ante quendam conuentum Schmalcaldensem in Thuringia exercitus equi tum: deinde numerus quidam rusticorū: tertiò draco magnus. Et puto significari per exercitum primū bellum principum: per rusticos, motum rusticanum: per draconem, hoc præsens bellum intricatum, & alia bella secutura.
units.tr: Over a certain assembly at Schmalkalden in Thuringia there appeared in the air the image of an army of horsemen; then a number of peasants; thirdly a great dragon. I think that the army signifies the first war of the princes, the peasants the peasants' uprising, and the dragon this present tangled war, and other wars that will follow.

units.la: Bambergæ est sepulchrum Heinrici Imperatoris, in quod est incisa iusticia, tenēs libra in manu. Iam libra ita est facta, ut lingula bilancis non sit in trutina, sed declinet paululum ad alteram partem. De hoc uetus apud ipsos sermo spargitur: quando lingula in trutinam redierit, tunc adfutu rum esse exitium urbis.
units.tr: At Bamberg there is the tomb of Emperor Henry, on which is carved Justice holding a balance in her hand. Now the balance is so made that the tongue of the scales is not in the middle but leans a little toward one side. An old saying about this is spread among them: when the tongue returns to the middle, then the destruction of the city will come.

units.la: Hic annus 56 tristissimus erit, quod significant multa horribilia signa. Recens fuit terræmotus Egræ, alio loco pluit sanguinem, cometa flagrat, erit etiam deterrima coniunctio Saturni & Martis, quæ magnas siccitates significat, fortassis etiam sterilitates. Hæc non tantum in hoc anno, sed etiam in sequentibus suas efficacias ostendent. Oremus ut Deus leniat imminentia pericula. Nunc simul congregati sunt legati Turcici, Papæ, Regis Galliæ, &c. Qui certè aliquid noui concludent, nisi Deus prohibeat, ita ut metuenda sint tristissima pericula Germaniæ: sicut uenient maximi tumultus paulo ante diem extremi iudicij.
units.tr: This year, 1556, will be very sad, as many dreadful signs indicate. Lately there was an earthquake at Eger, in another place it rained blood, a comet is blazing, and there will also be a most evil conjunction of Saturn and Mars, which signifies great droughts and perhaps even barrenness. These things will show their effects not only in this year but also in the following ones. Let us pray that God may soften the impending dangers. Now the envoys of the Turk, of the Pope, of the King of France, and others have assembled together. They will certainly conclude something new, unless God forbid it, so that the most dreadful dangers for Germany are to be feared, just as the greatest tumults will come shortly before the day of the last judgement.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: In mundo sunt duo lumina, Oeconomia & politia. In cœlo quoq; duo, Sol & Luna. Sol politiam designat ac magistratus. Luna Oeconomiam seu uulgus. Si Sol eclipsin patitur, minatur imperantibus. Si Luna, uulgo & subditis. Sic anno 25 seditionem rusticanam præcessit eclipsis Lunæ. Christianis illa signa nihil minantur. Sunt enim supra Solem & Lunam, & mortui ubi resurrexerint, clarius lucebunt quàm Sol & Luna.
units.tr: There are two lights in the world, the household (oeconomia) and the state (politia). There are also two in the heavens, the Sun and the Moon. The Sun signifies the state and the magistrates; the Moon signifies the household, or the common people. If the Sun suffers an eclipse, it threatens rulers; if the Moon, it threatens the common people and subjects. So in the year 1525 an eclipse of the Moon preceded the Peasants' War. Such signs threaten nothing to Christians, for they are above the Sun and Moon, and the dead, when they have risen, will shine more brightly than the Sun and Moon.

units.la: Audiui ex uentis facilimè posse de euentu prælij iujudicari . Quando ante annos quinquaginta aut circiter rex Scoticus est captus, illo tempore quidam in Anglia captiuus tenebatur, cui cum custos carceris commissum esse praelium significaret: Si (inquit captiuus) eo die pugnarint, tunc jam scio quis uicerit, noster Rex uicit Scoticum. Interro-gatus, unde cognouisset? Respondit, ex uentis se coniecisse: nam uentos fuisse Scotis eo die ualde contrarios.
units.tr: I have heard that the outcome of a battle can very easily be judged from the winds. About fifty years ago or so, when the Scottish king was captured, a certain man was held prisoner in England. When the jailer told him that a battle had been fought, the captive said: "If they fought on that day, then I already know who won: our king has defeated the Scot." Asked how he had known, he replied that he had guessed from the winds, for the winds on that day had been very much against the Scots.

units.la: Quando habetis flatus in peregrinatione aduersos, tunc uestra negocia difficulter perficietis. Quia boni angeli & diaboli inter se dimicant: quod existimo uniuersaliter uerum esse.
units.tr: When you have adverse winds on a journey, you will find your business difficult to carry through, because good angels and devils contend with one another; I think this is universally true.

units.la: In propinquo oppido Locha erat ceruus, qui singulis annis in mense Septembri die Egidij muros transiliebat, & in syluam ad ἐποχλὴν[?], id est, ad admissionem currebat, & in mense Octobri reuertebatur, idq; per multos annos faciebat. Sed ultimo anno, quo Dux Fridericus mortuus est, non est reuersus, quia ad nouum dominum redire noluit.
units.tr: In the nearby town of Locha there was a stag which every year, on the feast of St Giles in September, leapt over the walls and ran into the forest for [ἐποχλὴν], that is, for admission, and returned in October; and it did this for many years. But in the last year, when Duke Frederick died, it did not return, because it was unwilling to go back to a new lord.

units.la: Duo principes in conuentu Francofordiensi ante uiginti annos aut circiter habito, deambulatum extra portam urbis iuerunt, ibi falconibus uolantibus forte immiscet se pica, super quo falcones ita se collidunt, ut decidant, & ambo moriantur, pica manente incolumi: quae tamen attonita decidens, antequam auolare posset, à cane devoratur. Sic arbitror. bitror idem nobiscum fore: illi duo perierunt, nos per Turcam, aut alio modo peribimus.
units.tr: About twenty years ago, when a diet was held at Frankfurt, two princes went for a walk outside the city gate. There, while falcons were flying, a magpie happened to get among them, and the falcons collided with each other so that they fell, and both died, while the magpie remained unharmed. Yet the magpie, stunned, fell before it could fly away and was devoured by a dog. I think it will be the same with us: those two perished, and we shall perish through the Turk or in some other way.

units.la: Cùm dux Fridericus cum episcopo Moguntinē si eodem tempore quo mortuus est imperator Maximilianus, in arce Locha recreationis causa extra fenestrā prospiceret de suis negocijs & Republica colloquentes, tunc subitò regulus imuolauit fenestram, ubi semel atq; iterū circumuolitans decidit mortuus. Quò proculdubio significata est Cæsaris Maximiliani mors.
units.tr: When Duke Frederick, together with the Archbishop of Mainz, was in the castle of Locha for recreation, at the very time when Emperor Maximilian died, looking out of a window and conversing about their affairs and the commonwealth, a little bird (a wren) suddenly flew in through the window; flying round once and again, it fell dead. Without doubt this signified the death of Emperor Maximilian.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Memini in quodam monasterio ante mutationem, quæ secuta est, ursum, qui ibi alebatur erupit se ex sua cauerna, & uenisse in medium chorum stantibus & canentibus monachis. Aliqui fugiebant, pauci stabant corripientes cuspides quibus occurrerent urso, eūq; repellerent: inter quos nouus quendam cuius tanta fortitudo erat, ut in primis correpto cuspide repulerit ursum. Hoc fuit signum mutationis paulo post secutæ.
units.tr: I remember that in a certain monastery, before the change that followed, a bear which was kept there broke out of its den and came into the middle of the choir while the monks stood and sang. Some fled; a few stood gripping spears with which to meet the bear and drive it back. Among them was a novice of such great strength that he was the first to seize a spear and drive the bear back. This was a sign of the change that followed shortly afterwards.

units.la: Absque dubio magni uiri certis ac proprijs signis de rerum mutatione admoneri solent. Videte quale signum habuerit Hannibal? Ille uidit in somno ingentem draconem uagari per Italiam, & facere uastationem totius Italiæ. ille ipse fuit. Item quando Iulius Cæsar ante pugnam Pharsalicam uesperi circumiuit in castris, inspecturus excubias, ibi ardere uisa est galea, quæ flamma ardens aliquandiu supra galeam est conspecta: fuit singulare signum.
units.tr: Undoubtedly great men are usually warned of changes in affairs by certain and particular signs. See what sign Hannibal had: he saw in a dream a huge dragon wandering through Italy and laying waste the whole of Italy; he himself was that. Likewise, when Julius Caesar, before the battle of Pharsalus, went round the camp in the evening to inspect the watches, a helmet was seen to blaze there, and a flame was seen burning for some time above the helmet. It was an extraordinary sign.

units.la: In Franconia, ante bellum ad Ingolstadium, nascebatur puer, cui ex uentre erupit culter. Significauit autem diabolus in Germania fore bellum ciuile. Non enim culter in uentre creuit aut ortus est, sed diaboli præstigijs effectum est, ut ex eo prodire uisus sit.
units.tr: In Franconia, before the battle at Ingolstadt, a boy was born from whose belly a knife burst forth. The devil signified that there would be civil war in Germany. For the knife did not grow or arise in the belly; rather, by the devil's trickery it was brought about that it seemed to come out of it.

units.la: Cum aliqua mulier in oppido Newmarck infantem lauans audiret alterum cultro se læsisse, & tanquam moribundum uocare matrem, ipsaq; ad puerū intrepidè accurreret, non habita ratione infantes, qui in labro abeunte ipsa suffocaretur: tum huic spectaculo maritus interueniens (arbitratus est matris socordia periisse infantem) statim coniugem conspectam pugione confodit. Audiens postea causam coniugis abitus, seipsum strangulauit. Illud factū portendit alias calamitates Germaniæ, quarū aliquas uidimus, & reliquas ulterius uidebimus.
units.tr: When a certain woman in the town of Neumarkt was bathing an infant, she heard the other child say that it had been wounded by a knife, and it called to its mother as if dying. She ran fearlessly to the boy, not heeding the infant, which was suffocated in the tub while she was away. Then her husband came upon this sight and, thinking the infant had perished through his wife's carelessness, at once stabbed the woman he saw with a dagger. Hearing afterwards the cause of his wife's absence, he strangled himself. That deed portended other calamities for Germany, some of which we have seen, and the rest we shall see further on.

units.la: In Marchia nequa quida interfecit mulierē grauidā, cui execuit infantē, ac præcidens ei manū, quā voluit afferre latronibus ad incantationes magicas. Credo non esse tam crimen quàm portentum Xanthi pepēdit mulier habens suspēsum filiū de collo suo, et facē in manu, qua incēderet domū. Illud portentū obsidente Bruto philosopho accidit.
units.tr: In the March, a certain wretch killed a pregnant woman, cut the infant from her womb, and cut off her hand, which he wanted to bring to robbers for magic incantations. I think this is not so much a crime as a portent. At Xanthus a woman hanged her son from her neck, with a torch in her hand with which she would set fire to the house. That portent occurred while the philosopher Brutus was besieging the city.

units.la: Ante aliquot annos magnis agminibus in Germania cicadæ uolarunt. erat talis figura corporis, quæ imitabatur Turcicū pileum, & Turcicam uestem. Significauit aduentum Turcarum, uel peregrinarum nationum.
units.tr: Some years ago, great swarms of cicadas flew about in Germany. They had a body-shape which imitated the Turkish cap and Turkish dress. It signified the coming of the Turks, or of foreign nations.

units.la: Magdeburgi ante bellum Smalcaldicum in templo audiebantur sonitus, tanquam collisorum aßerum fragor: ego ipse audiui. nam illo tempore non procul habitabā à tēplo. Porro Doctor Huldrichus Sizinger similiter accedens propius ad templum, audiuit. Item ante obsidionem oppidi Vuittenbergensis in templo arcis, similes tumultus audi-ti sunt, quos audiuit pius senex Doctor Melchior Fendius. Item ante seditionem rusticanam in templo Bambergensi multi magni sonitus auditi sunt.
units.tr: At Magdeburg, before the Smalcaldic War, sounds were heard in the church like the crash of planks colliding; I myself heard them, for at that time I did not live far from the church. Likewise Doctor Huldrich Sizinger, approaching the church more closely, heard them. Again, before the siege of the town of Wittenberg, similar tumults were heard in the church of the castle, and the pious old man Doctor Melchior Fendius heard them. Likewise, before the Peasants' War, many loud noises were heard in the church at Bamberg.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Octo uel decem menses ferè ante obsidionem oppidi, Vuitenbergæ conspecti sunt in loco uicino cœmiterij crebri ignes multis noctibus: alij manebant in uno loco, alij uerò discurrebant. Hinc Iohannes Vuick ciuis huius oppidi, peritus rei militaris, colligebat, fore ut oppidum cingeretur, sednon caperetur. Illud poterat iudicare ex ignibus durantibus, & non citò pereuntibus, quod etiam factum est.
units.tr: Eight or ten months before the siege of the town of Wittenberg, many fires were seen for several nights in a place near the cemetery. Some remained in one spot, while others ran about. From this, John Vuick, a citizen of this town and skilled in military affairs, concluded that the town would be surrounded but not taken. He could judge this from the fires lasting and not quickly dying out, which in fact happened.

units.la: In proxima oppugnatione Rhodi, mulier stetit cum duobus filijs in muro, defenditq; illam mœnio-rum rum partem, quam diu potuit: & cum non posset sese diutius defendere, interfecit filios spectantibus Turcis, deinde sibi ipsi conscinuit mortem. Est res valde horrenda & terribilis, quæ significauit Turcos urbe Rhodiana esse potituros.
units.tr: In the recent siege of Rhodes, a woman stood with her two sons on the wall and defended that part of the fortifications for as long as she could. When she could no longer defend herself, she killed her sons while the Turks looked on, and then took her own life. It is a very dreadful and terrifying thing, and it signified that the Turks would gain possession of the city of Rhodes.

units.la: Albis est inuidum & insidiosum flumen: in quo cum aliqui perituri fuerint, plerunq; ignes seu faculæ super aquas saltantes conspiciuntur. Quotiescunq; autem huiusmodi signa conspecta fuerunt, uniuersali experientia compertum est, omnino aliquos perire.
units.tr: The Elbe is a treacherous and deceitful river. When some people are about to perish in it, fires or torches are often seen leaping over the water. Whenever such signs have been seen, it has been established by universal experience that some people certainly perish.

units.la: Ante pugnam Electoris Ioannis Friderici ducis Saxoniæ, solis ferruginem uidimus. Item ante pugnam proximam Saxonicam pridie eius diei, quo pugna commissa est, etiam solis ferrugo conspiciebatur.
units.tr: Before the battle of Elector John Frederick, Duke of Saxony, we saw an eclipse of the sun with a rust-coloured hue. Likewise, before the next battle in Saxony, on the day before the battle was joined, a rust-coloured sun was also seen.

units.la: Initio belli Peloponnesiaci tanta eclipsis solis conspecta est, ut in die perinde ac in nocte stellæ lucerent. Item auiculæ consternatæ inusitata caligine in terram prolapsæ sunt. Sic etiam in synodo Constantiensi similis eclipsis conspecta est. Constat magnas mutationes accidisse in Græcia tempore belli Peloponnensiaci. Post tempora item Ioannis Huß, Constantiæ propter doctrinæ Christianæ ueritatem combusti, quàtæ mutationes sint secutæ, nemo ignorat.
units.tr: At the beginning of the Peloponnesian War, such a great eclipse of the sun was seen that the stars shone in the day just as at night. Likewise, small birds, dismayed by the unusual darkness, fell to the ground. So too at the Council of Constance a similar eclipse was seen. It is established that great changes took place in Greece during the Peloponnesian War. Likewise, after the time of John Hus, who was burned at Constance on account of his defence of the truth of Christian doctrine, no one is ignorant of what great changes followed.

units.la: Ante obsidionem oppidi Curiensis, & arcis Blas Blaßenburgensis, anno 1552. fuit magnus terræ-motus in ditione Marchionis Alberti circa urbem Curiensem, ut quidam homines mundi interitum expectarent. Iudicatur iam ex euentu illum ter-ræmotum fuisse signum sequentis belli. Alia quo-que plurima exempla, quæ nostro tempore facta sunt, scimus.
units.tr: Before the siege of the town of Kur and of the fortress of Blaßenburg, in the year 1552, there was a great earthquake in the territory of Margrave Albert around the city of Kur, so that some people expected the end of the world. It is now judged from the outcome that this earthquake was a sign of the war that followed. We also know of very many other examples that have occurred in our own time.

units.la: HISTORIA DE CLADE accepta in Pannonia ad Mogaciũ, & Ludouici regis interitu, lucu-lenter à Ioachimo Came-rario descripta.
units.tr: An Account of the Defeat Suffered at Mohács in Pannonia and the Death of King Louis, Vividly Described by Joachim Camerarius

units.la: MVltis magnisq; rebus gestis, & elatus fuc-cessibus Turcarum rex Solymanus, bellũ intulit Pannoniæ, potiente regno illo Ludouico fi-lio Ladislai, cũ quo nupta fuit Maria Imperatoris Maximiliani neptis. Huic puero cõciliante matri-monium Maximiliano desponsata illa, adhuc & ipsa parua uirguncula fuerat, cum Viennæ ad Da-nubium Imperator & Pannoniæ ac Sarmatiæ re-ges congressi fuissent. Sed Ludouicum editum in lucem accepimus, nullam partem corporis cute integente, quæ tamen inunctionibus medicis po-stea producta fuit. Voluerat Ladislaus pater no-men filio indere Iulij: sed mater obtinuit, ut suæ gentis (erat enim Gallica) nomine potius appella-retur. Hæc animaduertentibus quibusdã ominosa statim uisa. Nam & nudum pelle corpus, nudationem: & omissum nomen fundatoris maximi imperij, deminutionem regni portendere credidere. Agebatur iam annus post salutiferum Christi partum M. D. XXVI. & conuentum procerum Germaniae Spirae habebat fratris Caroli Imperatoris loco Dux Ferdin. At infelix Pannoniae rex, implorare auxilium atque opem Christianitatis, crebrosque Spiram legatos mittere, qui & expeditionem Turcarum metuendam ac terribilem, & quam ipse ab omnibus rebus ad bellum cum parandum tum gerendum necessarijs esset imparatus, conuentui demonstrarent, & ab illis peterent, ut sibi subuenire, & regnum suum Christiano nomini conseruare uellent: neu committerent, ut per suam oppressionem aditus ad ipsos Tyranno crudelissimo & infestissimo hosti aperiretur. Satis iam illum, ac nimis longe, cum miseranda pernicie & ingenti calamitate populi Christiani progressum. Nec se tantum petere, sed quaerere uiam per regnum suum, qua libere inuehi in Christianitatem, & pro arbitrio grassari possit. Ferdinandi autem misericordiam & fidem, ut decuit, in primis implorare, cuius secum soror nupta esset: obsecrare, illam ut tueri, si negligendus ipse uideretur, non omitteret. His & similibus ad conuentum allatis credere quidam, & terreri animis, & censere quampri-mum mum copias comparandas, quæ in Pannoniam mit terentur. Quidam negocium esse magnum dicere, & deliberandum diutius. Non etiam nulli totam rem eludere, & uanum metum affirmare fingi à Pannonibus, qui cum scirent neminem facile è Germania ad sese usque perductum iri, pecunias auferri posse cõsiderēt. Erant etiam plerorumque inter se dubij animi & incerti, neq; quisquam sefrè alteri admodum sidebat. Itaq; hoc modo actum est, ut legatio decerneretur ad inspiciendum res Pannonicas. Sed Turca interea omnibus uiribus instare bello, & urgere expeditionem, accersereq; cum Epiroticas & Græcas, tum Asiaticas copias, quarum illis Abraimum, his Becranum ducem præfecit. Cumq; Taururum, Albam Græcam nunc uocant, uenisset, præmisit Balibeio duce equites. qui quàm longè lateq; possent, excurrendo hostium agros popularentur. Rex tum Budæ erat, & uel deserendum regnum, uel asserendum manu uidebat. Itaque quas potuit copias coegit: sed & Boemi & Germani aliquot, pontificis Romani (ut ferebatur) pecunia conducti aduenere. Verùm omnium numerus XXIIII millia excessisse negatur. Duces fortesq; uiri in illis fuere plurimi, ut hæc clades multo maior quàm in speciem appareat, acceptam esse, qui considerare uolet, facile sit intellectu rus. Erant ex Pannonicis cum rege inter alios duces, ces,& Gregorius Zepusius, frater Ioannis praesi-dis eius regionis, quam olim Iazigas incoluisse perhibent, nunc Septemcastrensis nominatur: qui ipse cum magna & ualida manu indies expectabatur. Et praesides multi, interq; illos unus praecipua audacia P. Tomoreus Colocensis familiae Franciscanae, homo imperitus & temerarius, sed & manu promptus, & animo imperterrito. Is, quia semel atq; iterum inconsultè euagatas turmas pauculas praedonũ uicinorum retuderat, & quia strenuũ olim egerat militem, ducis etiam opinionem conceperat. Cui laudi inhians, regè impellere, atq; penè cogere, ut hosti obuiam iret. Ergo infelix rex ætate penè adhuc puer, destitutus & prudentum uirorũ consilijs, & fortium atq; bellatorum copijs, etiam ut aliqui tradidere, & multa suspicari permittunt, circundatus fraude & insidijs suorum, Buda egreditur ut hosti occurrat, alacris & exultabundus, neq; formidinis aut timiditatis ullam significationem praebens, relicta Maria uxore ad Bresspurgum. Et ad Mogacium, quod intra Budam & Taurum situm est, castrapofuit. Balibeius, quem cum equitibus ad uastandam Pannoniam praemissum supra diximus, omissis agris, exercitum Regiũ observare & carpere, & à pabulatione atq; aquatione prohibere, diuisisq; suis equitibus quos habebat secum ad M. XX. in partes quatuor, ita infestis excurexcursionibus premebat regios, ut cũ una pars de diei quadrante fessa reciperet se, altera mox succederet, atq; huic deinde tertia, & isti postremò quarta, totus dies perpetua infestatione & uexatione hostiũ cõsumeretur. Exercitus Regius sese intra castra obiectis carris atq; plaustris cõtinere primùm: deinde cum usq; adeò in angustum redigeretur, ut iam ad fluuium nemo auderet accedere, cogerenturq; intra castra puteis effosiis aquam quærere, placuit Pannonibus, autore Tomoreo & Gregorio Zepusio, fortunam prælij experiri, minimè probantibus ac potius uehementissimè dissuadentibus Germanis & Boemis ducibus. qui censerent Ioannem Zepusium saltem operiendum, is enim aduenture iam nunciabatur. Conuenerant autem uniuersæ Turcicæ copiæ, ipseq; Solymanus aderat, neque pauciores habuit, ut certò cognitum est, ducentis millibus bellatorum. Sed urgentibus suis, Rex hoc modo dixisse fertur, se non esse timidum, neq; ignauissimum futurum, cupere ut quisq; uir fortis esse uelit, se suæ uitæ ac sanguini non decreuisse parcere. Ita productus exercitus regius, & instructa acies fuit à Tomoreo, permistis inter se equitib. ac peditibus, quo ordines dilatarentur: id quod ad ingentē hostiū multitudinē, ne includi sui atq; cingi possent, excogitauerat. Regem ego accepi in prima acie ita fuisse collocatum, ut ante eum non esset duoduobus illa densior, & ipse cū tertijs inuheretur, inq; cōflictu & impetu pugnæ ad primos protru-sum. Alij tradidere, seseparatim cum mille equitibus post aciē constitisse, qd exitus rei uidetur refellere. Bellicis machinis abundabant, ut solent, Turcæ: il-lisq; globis contra Regium exercitū directè im-missi, sed sine detrimento : sublimius enim lati illi, hastas modò quorundā perculere. Regiæ machinæ & paucæ & futiles non multum hostibus nocere potuerūt. Sed Turcæ tanto maiore numerosiorcq; multitudine undiq; exercitū regium non solùm se psere, sed etiā implicuerūt : neq; solū repugnantes profligare, sed etiam castra iam oppugnare ad quæ ipsa quoq; cum Regij duces respicerent, & defen-dere cuperent, diminuti pugnatores, & ordines distracti fuere. Itaq; celeriter fuga orta, ducibus plerisq; uiris strenuis, & qui suorum cladi super-esse nollent, interfectis. Præsules multi cæsi: interq; illos Tomoreus, magis intrepidus miles, quàm consultus dux, fortissimè dimicans cecidit. Capti pauci. Zepusius, dum in nauem cū citato equo in-silire nititur, neq; illā potest attingere, Danubij a-quis, delapsus in fluuium, obruitur. Rex fuga cum in equo uasto, ipseq; grauibus armis onustus, ad nō magnum amnem uenissēt, uno modò comitatus, qui ante eum, ut postea narrasse fertur, in ulterio-rem ripam euaserat, transiturus & ipse præcipi-tato tato equo, in aqua & limo suffocatur. Putabatur, amnis uadum à fugientibus quasi cauato alueo corruptum fuisse, ut minus iam peruium esset. Sunt qui tradiderint, appetentem equum ripam, retro actum super regem incidisse, itaq; illum oppressum. In illo non magno quidem neque celebri amne perijsse nobilissimum regem, & eximium a dolescentem, illius uerbis, qui unus comitatus eum esset, creditum: & corpus exanimum non procul ab indicato ab eodem loco paulo inferius postea repertum, sepulturæ mandatum est. Hoc prælium, quo anno diximus. IIII. Calend. Septemb. commissum. Solymanus autem uictoria metuendus & ferox, derisa hostium temeritate & imprudentia, ususq; fortunæ prosperitate, Budam statim occupat, arcemq; in deditionem præsidio accepto spoliat, atq; diripit. Fuerat ante illa studio quodam singulari regis Mathiæ, & operibus & instructione admirabili exculta, signisq; ac tabulis exornata: imprimis autem omni genere librorum dives. Nam Mathias, ut ueræ uirtutis amator, doctrinam & artes sapientiæ incredibili fauore atq; studio prosecutus fuit. Hac igitur, ut dixi, direpta ac spoliata, quia iam hyems prope erat, re melius quàm sperare auderet gesta, in Thraciam reduxit copias Turca, & uictoriam maxima festinitate celebrauit. At Maria regina tandem post longam dissimulatiolationem nunciorum, casu mariti, quem unicè dilexerat, & à quo maximo fuerat amore comprehensa, cognito, lamentis & uociferatione omnia loco complere, neque de se aut regno solicitari, sed solius mariti interitum ante oculos habere, illum deplorare, illum requirere, sine illo recusare uiuere, &c.
units.tr: After many great achievements and elated by his successes, the Turkish king Suleiman made war on Pannonia, whose kingdom was then held by Louis, son of Ladislaus, to whom Mary, granddaughter of the Emperor Maximilian, had been married. Maximilian had arranged this match for the boy, and she was still a little girl herself when the Emperor and the kings of Pannonia and Sarmatia met at Vienna on the Danube. We are told that Louis was born with no skin covering any part of his body, though this was later drawn out by medical ointments. His father Ladislaus wanted to name the boy Julius, but the mother prevailed, so that he was called by a name from her own people, who were French. Some saw these things as ominous at once: the bare body seemed to foretell nakedness, and the dropped name of the great founder of the empire seemed to foretell a diminishing of the kingdom. It was now the year 1526 after the saving birth of Christ, and Duke Ferdinand was presiding at the assembly of the princes of Germany at Speyer in place of his brother, the Emperor Charles. The unfortunate king of Pannonia implored the help and aid of Christendom and sent envoys again and again to Speyer. They were to explain to the assembly both the dreaded and terrible expedition of the Turks, and how unprepared he himself was, in every respect needed both to prepare and to wage war, and they were to ask the princes to come to his aid and wish to preserve his kingdom for the Christian name, and not allow his overthrow to open the way for the most cruel and hostile tyrant to the Christians themselves. The Turk had already advanced far enough and too far, with pitiable destruction and great calamity to the Christian people. He was not only asking for help but seeking a route through his kingdom by which the Turk could freely invade Christendom and rage at will. He begged, as was fitting, first of all for the mercy and good faith of Ferdinand, whose sister was his wife, and entreated him not to abandon her protection if he himself seemed to be neglected. When these and similar appeals were brought before the assembly, some believed them and were alarmed, and thought that troops should be assembled as soon as possible to be sent into Pannonia. Others said the matter was great and needed longer deliberation. Some even made light of the whole business and declared that the Pannonians had invented an empty fear, since they knew that no one could easily be brought from Germany all the way to them, and they were considering how to get money out of it. Moreover, the minds of most were doubtful and uncertain, and no one trusted another very much. And so it was resolved that a delegation should be appointed to examine the affairs of Pannonia. Meanwhile the Turk pressed the war with all his strength and hurried the expedition, summoning forces both from Epirus and Greece and from Asia; he set Abraimus over the one and Becranus over the others as leaders. When he came to Taurum, which they now call Alba Graeca, he sent ahead Balibeius with cavalry, to ravage the enemy's fields by raiding as far and wide as they could. The king was then at Buda and saw that he must either abandon the kingdom or defend it by force. So he gathered what troops he could, and some Bohemians and Germans arrived too, hired with the money of the Roman pontiff, as was reported. Yet it is said that the total number did not exceed 24,000. There were very many leaders and brave men among them, so that anyone who wishes to consider it can easily understand that this defeat was much greater than it appears at first sight. Among the other commanders with the king were the Pannonian lords, and Gregory Zepusius, brother of John Zepusius, governor of that region which they say was once inhabited by the Iazyges and is now called Siebenbürgen. John himself was daily expected with a large and strong force. There were also many governors, and among them one of remarkable boldness, P. Tomoreus of Kalocsa, of the Franciscan family, an inexperienced and rash man, but ready with his hand and fearless in spirit. Because he had once and again driven back small bands of raiders who had wandered out recklessly from neighbouring territories, and because he had formerly served as a vigorous soldier, he had also gained a reputation as a commander. Eager for this glory, he urged the king, and almost forced him, to go out and meet the enemy. So the unfortunate king, still almost a boy in years, deprived of the counsel of wise men and of the troops of brave soldiers, and, as some have reported and as many things allow us to suspect, surrounded by the treachery and snares of his own people, left Buda to meet the enemy, eager and exultant, showing no sign of fear or timidity, leaving his wife Mary behind. He pitched camp at Mohács, which lies between Buda and Taurum, and at Pressburg. Balibeius, whom we have said was sent ahead with cavalry to lay waste Pannonia, abandoned the fields and set about watching and harassing the royal army, keeping it from foraging and watering. Dividing the cavalry he had with him, about 20,000, into four parts, he pressed the royal forces with such hostile sallies that while one part, tired after a quarter of the day, withdrew, another at once took its place, then a third after it, and finally a fourth, so that the whole day was spent in constant harassment and vexation by the enemy. At first the royal army kept itself within its camp, with wagons and carts set up as a barrier. Then, when it was reduced to such straits that no one dared approach the river any more, and they were forced to seek water within the camp by digging wells, the Pannonians, on the advice of Tomoreus and Gregory Zepusius, decided to try their luck in battle. The German and Bohemian commanders strongly disagreed and urged them, rather, to wait at least for John Zepusius, who was reported to be coming. All the Turkish forces had gathered, and Suleiman himself was present, with no fewer than 200,000 fighting men, as was clearly established. But under pressure from his men the king is reported to have said that he was not a coward and would not be the most spineless of men; he wished that every man who wanted to be brave should be so, and he had resolved not to spare his own life or blood. So the royal army was led out, and the battle line was drawn up by Tomoreus, with cavalry and infantry mixed together so that the ranks would be extended. He had devised this so that they would not be surrounded and encircled by the enormous multitude of the enemy. I have been told that the king was placed in the front line in such a way that there were not more than two men deep in front of him, and that he himself rode in with the third rank and was thrust forward among the first in the shock and rush of the fight. Others have reported that he stood apart behind the line with a thousand cavalry; but the outcome of the affair seems to refute this. The Turks, as is their custom, had plenty of siege engines, and they hurled their missiles directly against the royal army, but without harm, for they flew too high and only struck the spears of some. The royal guns were few and feeble and could do little damage to the enemy. But the Turks, with a far greater and more numerous multitude, not only surrounded the royal army on every side but also enveloped it. They not only routed the men who resisted but began to attack the camp itself, which the royal commanders also looked back at and wished to defend; their fighters were reduced and their ranks were broken apart. So a rout quickly began, most of the brave leaders having been killed, for they did not wish to survive the ruin of their men. Many governors were slain, among them Tomoreus, a soldier more fearless than a skilled commander, who fell after fighting with great courage. Few were taken prisoner. Zepusius, while trying to leap onto a boat with his swift horse, could not reach it, slipped into the waters of the Danube and was drowned. The king fled on a large horse, himself weighed down with heavy armour. When he came to a river not very large, accompanied by only one man, who, as he later was reported to have said, had gone ahead of him to the farther bank, the king himself also tried to cross, but his horse plunged and he was suffocated in the water and mud. It was thought that the ford of the river had been spoiled by the fleeing men, as if the bed had been hollowed out, so that it was no longer passable. Some have reported that the horse, trying to reach the bank, was driven back and fell upon the king, so that he was crushed. The most noble king and the outstanding young man perished in that river, neither large nor famous, as was believed on the word of the one companion who had been with him. His lifeless body was found not far from that place, a little further downstream, some time later, and was given burial. This battle, as we have said, was fought on the fourth day before the Calends of September in the year mentioned. Suleiman, feared for his victory and fierce, scorned the rashness and imprudence of the enemy and, making use of the prosperity of fortune, at once seized Buda, took the citadel on the surrender of its garrison, and plundered it. Before that, Buda had been adorned, through the particular zeal of King Matthias, with buildings and admirable workmanship, decorated with statues and paintings, and above all rich in books of every kind. For Matthias, as a lover of true virtue, had cherished learning and the arts of wisdom with incredible favour and zeal. So, after this city had been plundered and despoiled as I have said, and since winter was nearly upon them, and because he had achieved more than he dared hope, the Turk led his troops back into Thrace and celebrated his victory with the greatest haste. But Queen Mary, when at last, after a long delay of messengers, she learned of the death of her husband, whom she had loved above all and by whom she had been held in the greatest affection, filled everything with laments and cries. She did not care for herself or for the kingdom, but kept before her eyes the death of her husband alone; she mourned him, she sought him, she refused to live without him, and so on.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Ante seditionē rusticanam Fridericus Marchio Brandenburgensis, & præpositus Herbipolensis, cum quodam suo fratre in ludo equestri congressus est, ubi thorax in illo uehementissimo concursu fuit apertus, ita ut pectus ipsi nudaretur. Id quidam docti interpretantur significasse tragicam calamitatem, in quam postea in obsidione arcis Herbipolensis incidit: nam erat in eadem à rusticis obsidione cinctus.
units.tr: Before the peasants' revolt, Margrave Frederick of Brandenburg, who was also provost of Würzburg, fought a tilting bout with a certain brother of his. In that very violent collision his breastplate was torn open, so that his chest was bared. Some learned men interpret this as signifying the tragic disaster into which he later fell, during the siege of the Würzburg citadel, when he was surrounded by the peasants in that same siege.

units.la: In Vngaria antequam interficeretur rex Ludo vicus, tam magni terræmotus fuerunt, ut inde domus corruerent. Non multò ante fuerunt apud Belgas & in Italia plurimi terræmotus. Qui tumultus illos secuti sint, audiuistis.
units.tr: In Hungary, before King Louis was killed, there were such great earthquakes that houses collapsed. Not long before, there had been many earthquakes among the Belgians and in Italy. You have heard what uprisings followed these.

units.la: Habui caniculam, quæ edidit fœtus in ipsa eclipsi, qui oēs mala morte perierunt. Doctor Milichius habebat unum, qui ab aliis canibus laceratus est, alter perijt incendio.
units.tr: I had a little bitch which gave birth to puppies during the eclipse itself, and all of them died a bad death. Doctor Milichius had one which was torn apart by other dogs, and another perished in a fire.

units.la: Minantur nobis eclipses, prodigia & positus stelstellarum his annis elapsis, ostensa, uarios bellorum apparatus, & mirabilia cosilia contra pios instrui, & fuisse instructa: contra quae omnia tamen Deus suam Ecclesiam, donec ipsi placuerit, seruabit, sicut mater in Nebra, Franconiae oppido, est seruata, etiamsi ambusta, & infantulus necatus est. Sic etsi quidam ex membris Ecclesiae pereant, corpus tamen Ecclesiae saluum manebit. Die 26 Iunij, anno 1555, in oppido Nebra, mulier honesta magna difficultate peperit filiam, quae edita, mox flamma ex matris aluo erupit cum sonitu, qualis fit emisso globo ex bombarda. Flamma uero etsi matrem aliquantulum combusserit ac laeserit, tamen non est extincta, sed recenter natam filiam circumdedit & necauit.
units.tr: Eclipses, portents and the positions of the stars displayed in the years just past threaten us. They show various preparations for war and wonderful plots being devised against the godly, and some already set in motion. Yet against all these things God will keep his Church for as long as it pleases him, just as the mother in Nebra, a town in Franconia, was preserved, though burned, while her little infant was killed. So even if some members of the Church perish, the body of the Church will remain safe. On 26 June 1555, in the town of Nebra, an honest woman with great difficulty gave birth to a daughter. As soon as she was born, a flame burst out of the mother's womb with a sound like a ball fired from a cannon. The flame scorched and injured the mother somewhat, but it was not extinguished; it encircled the newly born daughter and killed her.

units.la: Statua Iulij Caesaris in insula Tyberina posita, miro prodigio est conuersa. Nam latus quod erat uersus occidentem conuertit se uersus orientem. Eo prodigio significata est Caesaris aduersus Pompeium uictoria.
units.tr: A statue of Julius Caesar placed on the Tiber island was miraculously turned: the side that had faced west turned to face east. By this portent Caesar's victory over Pompey was signified.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Est pagus no procul a Gorlitz situs nomine Hirsdorf, ibi rusticus quidam uir fide dignus, cum in agrum suum ixisset ad colligendas segetes, quas paulo ante demessuerat, uidet ex stipulis copiosum sanguinem manantem, ita ut ducenti fere manipuli sanguine cotaminarentur. Rusticus uero hoc prodigio digio perterritus, statim alijs indicat: fit multorum hominũ concursus, qui admirati sunt hac prodigio sam rem.
units.tr: There is a village not far from Görlitz called Hirsdorf. There a certain countryman, a trustworthy man, went out into his field to gather the sheaves he had cut a little before, and saw copious blood flowing from the stubble, so that nearly two hundred bundles were stained with blood. The countryman, terrified by this portent, immediately told others, and a great crowd of people gathered, who marvelled at this strange thing.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Scripsit etiam huc doctor Medlerus in ducatu Brunsuicensi, è terra erupisse sanguinē, ceu fontis scaturiginē, ulnæ altitudine, & diu fluxisse. Nec uerò dubiū est hæc signa nobis minari bella, quia multi cuētus testātur talia prodigia nō esse inania. Nos uerò orabimus Deũ, què scimus misericordē esse, et precibus piorum moueri, ut pœnas leniat, & ut diuinæ suæ misericordiæ meminisse uelit.
units.tr: Doctor Medler has also written from the duchy of Brunswick that blood burst out of the earth like the gushing of a spring, a cubit high, and flowed for a long time. There is no doubt that these signs threaten us with wars, since many reliable witnesses testify that such portents are not empty. But we will pray to God, whom we know to be merciful and moved by the prayers of the godly, that he may ease the punishments and be willing to remember his divine mercy.

units.la: DE VARIIS ET MIRANDIS naturæ operibus.
units.tr: Of the various and wonderful works of nature.

units.la: In canibus exiguam quandam humani intellectus imaginem inesse, exemplis constare potest. In mea patria erat canis iuxta aliquod sacellū, qui omnes peregrinos illū locū prætereuntes cū rabie quadā allatrabat, nec ullum oppidanum: sed ab illis se attingi & contrectari patiebatur.
units.tr: That dogs have a small image of the human intellect inside them can be shown by examples. In my homeland there was a dog near some shrine which barked at every stranger passing that place with a certain fury, but never at any townsman; it allowed itself to be touched and handled by them.

units.la: Dicunt in insula Rhodo fuisse canes, qui uidentes urbem Rhodianam à Turcis esse occupatā, continuò in illos irruerūt, & quorumcunq; eis copia dabatur, ipsos dilaniauerunt: Christianis occurrentibus etiam ignotis blanditi sunt.
units.tr: They say that on the island of Rhodes there were dogs which, seeing that the city of Rhodes had been occupied by the Turks, immediately attacked them and tore apart whatever Turks were available to them; but they fawned on Christians who met them, even strangers.

units.la: Faciens aliquando iter, de uia dubitabam: cumque scirem equum eandem uiam sepenumero perambulasse, reliqui ei frenum & recte me uexit. Equus habet quandam memoriam: uerùm illa sunt umbræ, & simulachra habituum.
units.tr: Once when I was making a journey and was unsure of the road, I knew that the horse had often traversed that same way, so I let it have the reins, and it carried me correctly. A horse has a certain memory, but these are shadows and likenesses of habits.

units.la: Equus Alexandri Magni Bucephalus, neminem est passus passus assessorem, nisi ipsum Alexandrum, & quidem cataphractum. Idem dicunt de equo Iulij Cæsaris. Et Plinius narrat exemplum cuiusdam Germanici Principis, habentis egregium equum. Principe autem in prælio occiso victor uolens equum conscendere, ibi ab equo correptus, & dilaceratus est.
units.tr: Alexander the Great's horse, Bucephalus, allowed no one to be its rider except Alexander himself, and that only when he was in full armour. They say the same of Julius Caesar's horse. Pliny also tells the story of a certain German prince who had an outstanding horse. When the prince was killed in battle, the victor, wishing to mount the horse, was seized by it and torn apart.

units.la: Basilius diligentissimè descripsit multa animantia. Basilium deinde secutus Ambrosius, earundem animantium historiam in ennarratione operum sex dierum pene ad uerbum recenset: docetq; in illis proposita nobis esse à Deo tanquam picta plurimarum uirtutum simulachra, quæ nos officij nostri admoneant.
units.tr: Basil described many living creatures with great diligence. Following Basil, Ambrose in his exposition of the works of the six days recounts the history of those same creatures almost word for word, and teaches that in them God has set before us, as painted images, many virtues which remind us of our duty.

units.la: Pultarchus ait, extauris putrefactis nasci apes, ut & Vergilius in Georgicis scripsit, ex equis, crabrones, ex asinis, scarabeos, ex hominibus, serpentes. Typus uerò harum rerum hic est. Tauri erat victimæ. Sic igitur ex Christo victima, mel et apes, id est, Euangelium & Ecclesia oriuntur. Equi, id est equites degenerantes gignunt crabrones. Asini procreant plebeios homines, qui sunt scarabei, id est quatenus non regantur à magistratu, fiunt seditiosi, & inimici gubernatoribus ac legitimis imperijs. perijs. Ex homine uerò hanc ob causam nascuntur serpentes, quia serpens, id est diabolus, initiò uirus suum in hominem infudit. Quo admonemur, homine post lapsum in morte & contagione peccati manentem, sua natura serpenti diabolo non esse dissimilem.
units.tr: Plutarch says that bees are born from putrefied oxen, as Virgil also wrote in the Georgics; hornets from horses, scarabs from asses, and serpents from men. But the type of these things is this. The ox was a sacrificial victim. Thus from Christ the victim, honey and bees, that is, the Gospel and the Church, arise. Horses, that is, degenerate knights, produce hornets. Asses produce common people, who are the scarabs, that is, when they are not governed by the magistrate they become seditious and enemies of the governors and of lawful rule. Serpents are born from man for this reason: the serpent, that is, the devil, at the beginning poured his poison into man. We are reminded by this that man, remaining after the fall in death and the contagion of sin, is by his nature not unlike the serpent, the devil.

units.la: Hippocrates dissimilitudinem non solum regionum, sed etiam ingeniorum ac morum in diuersis regionibus docet oriri à cœlestibus causis.
units.tr: Hippocrates teaches that differences not only of regions but also of talents and morals in different regions arise from heavenly causes.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Ptolomeus ait: Sapiens anima adiuuat cœlestem operationem, quemadmodum optimus agricola arando expurgandoq; adiuuat naturam.
units.tr: Ptolemy says: A wise soul assists the heavenly operation, just as the best farmer assists nature by ploughing and clearing.

units.la: Ouidius: Est Deus in nobis agitante calescimus illo. Vult significare Poeta, quòd habitus fiant excellentiores quando adiuuantur diuinitùs. Quemadmodum noster Imperator Carolus V. diuina providentia factus est excellens Imperator.
units.tr: Ovid: "There is a God within us; by his stirring we grow warm." The poet means that dispositions become more excellent when they are aided by God. Just as our Emperor Charles V was made an excellent emperor by divine providence.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: De Alexandro dicitur, quòd habuerit apud se comicum Poetam, comœdias bellas facientem, de animalium inter se concertationibus & pugnis propter amores ac libidines. Quæ tamen comœdiæ Alexandro non placuerunt. Poeta ægrè ferens inquit: Rex, tu tragica facis, non comica, ideo ista tibi non placent.
units.tr: It is said of Alexander that he kept at his court a comic poet who wrote fine comedies about the contests and fights of animals among themselves over loves and lusts. Yet these comedies did not please Alexander. The poet, taking it badly, said: "King, you make tragedies, not comedies; that is why these things do not please you."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Fabula est apud Lucianum de quodam volenti regi Ptolemæo exhibere mirabile spectaculum. Docuerat simias repræsentare comœdias, quas introduxit, & regi comœdias agentes exhibuit. Alius volens illum eludere, eiusdem que ineptias reprehendere, obiecit simijs nuces. Ibi simiæ relicta omni actione colligerunt nuces. Inde dicitur in vulgari proverbio: Simia manet simia, etiamsi sit purpura in duta.
units.tr: In Lucian there is a story about a man who wanted to give King Ptolemy a wonderful spectacle. He had trained monkeys to act out comedies, which he staged, and he showed them performing comedies before the king. Another man, wishing to mock him and expose his foolishness, threw nuts to the monkeys. The monkeys dropped all their acting and gathered up the nuts. Hence the common proverb: A monkey remains a monkey, even when dressed in purple.

units.la: Artaxerxes Longimanus sic dictus, quia dextera longior fuit sinistra. Noster Imperator Carolus V. habebat pulcherrimos digitos. Recti digiti mediocri longitudine, significat magnitudinem animi, & beneficientiā: curti vero significant astutam naturam. Pulcherrimos etiam digitos habebat Henricus dux Saxoniæ & Misniæ, pater nostri Electoris Augusti.
units.tr: Artaxerxes was called Longimanus because his right hand was longer than his left. Our Emperor Charles V had very beautiful fingers. Straight fingers of medium length signify greatness of spirit and generosity; short ones signify a crafty nature. Henry, duke of Saxony and Meissen, father of our Elector Augustus, also had beautiful fingers.

units.la: Indicæ conchæ sunt omnium generosissimæ, sicut ibi plurimū generosissimarū rerū nascitur. Fit metio in Biblijs auri Ophir. Inde est aurū Obryzū, quod est præstantissimū. Crescunt deinde in India generosa aromata. Disputaui aliquādo in cōuentu Vuormatiensi cū Pistorio sene, præstātissimo medico ducis Friderici & Caroli V. Imperatoris, qui tunc laborabat. Ibi eidem Pistorio propter suum consilium, quod sequebantur cæteri medici donauit Imp[?] uit Imperator 1000 coronatos. Interrogabã eũ, quibus rebus peregrinis non possimus carere, cùm & nos habeamus pulcherrimas & generosissimas plantas? Diccbat multis audientibus: Sacchar̃o non possumus omnino carere.
units.tr: Indian pearls are the most noble of all, just as very many noble things are born there. Mention is made in the Bible of the gold of Ophir, and from this comes Obryzum gold, which is the most excellent. Noble spices also grow in India. I once disputed at the Worms assembly with old Pistorius, the most excellent physician of Duke Frederick and Emperor Charles V, who was then ill. There the Emperor gave the same Pistorius 1000 crowns for his advice, which the other physicians followed. I asked him which foreign things we could not do without, since we too have very beautiful and noble plants. In the hearing of many he said: We cannot by any means do without sugar.

units.la: Turca habet iam optimũ aurũ. Nam Aegyptiæ præfectus Bascha, quãdo mittit munera Turcico Imperatori, tunc mittit ipsi aliquas massas Arabici auri, qd̃ est ualde generosum, ut est aurũ Turcicũ.
units.tr: The Turk now has excellent gold. For when the Pasha, the governor of Egypt, sends gifts to the Turkish Emperor, he sends him some lumps of Arabian gold, which is very fine, just as Turkish gold is.

units.la: Vuitebergense solum est arenosum cum terreo mixtũ. Quando multũ terræ est admixtũ pauxillo arenæ, facilè quidem colitur, sed non est fœcunda. Circa Bambergã et Heydelbergã etiã est arenosum solum, sed ibi est felicior cultura quàm hîc Vuitenbergæ. Illa terra est optima, quæ est pinguis, halituosa, & dulcis. Nullum est dubium, quin corpora cum naturis terrarũ conueniant, sicut corpora in Thuringia sunt grandiora quàm hîc. Quia hîc sunt tenues, salsi & amari halitus, sicut etiam terra est: ideoq; corpora sunt rarefacta, marcida & tenuia. Quando scrobem in solo Lipsico aut Vuitenbergergensi effoditis, tunc non potestis rursus implere soueam terra effossa, quod est signũ raræ terræ. In Thuringia autem impleta fôssa, terra etiam est reliqua, quod significat terram densiorem & pleniorem.
