Item frumenta & uina degenerant, in aliam speciem propter terræ diuersitatem, ut quando feritis hic in arena triticum, tunc tertio anno fit robus. Quando feritis in Thuringia robum, tunc tertio anno fit triticum. Ita uina in alio solo degenerant. Credo etiam ingenia & corpora hominum in alijs locis degenerare: sicut illa pars Italiæ quæ dicitur Longobardia, habet robusta & procera corpora: quia Longobardi hauddubie sunt Saxones.
units.tr: The soil at Wittenberg is sandy, mixed with clay. When much earth is mixed with a little sand, it is indeed easily tilled, but it is not fruitful. Around Bamberg and Heidelberg the soil is also sandy, but cultivation there is more productive than here at Wittenberg. The best soil is that which is rich, vaporous and sweet. There is no doubt that bodies agree with the natures of lands, just as bodies in Thuringia are larger than here. Here the vapours are thin, salty and bitter, as the earth itself is, and so bodies are rarefied, wasted and slight. When you dig a pit in the soil of Leipzig or Wittenberg, you cannot refill the hole with the earth you dug out, which is a sign of thin soil. In Thuringia, however, when the ditch is filled, earth is left over, which signifies denser and fuller soil. Likewise grain and wine degenerate into another kind because of the difference of soil: when you sow wheat here in sand, in the third year it becomes rye; when you sow rye in Thuringia, in the third year it becomes wheat. So wines too degenerate in other soil. I believe that the talents and bodies of men also degenerate in other places. Thus that part of Italy called Lombardy has robust and tall bodies, because the Lombards are undoubtedly Saxons.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Alphonsus rex Neapolitanus indigens pecunia, quia susceperat bellum. Id consilij, aliquorum hominum sapientum persuasu, capiebat, ut sumeret plumbeum tectum, & illud plumbum coqueret, unde ingentem maßam auri inuenit.
units.tr: King Alfonso of Naples, lacking money because he had undertaken a war, took the following course on the persuasion of certain wise men: he took the lead off a roof and smelted it, and so found a huge mass of gold.

units.la: Dicunt hunc Turcicum Imperatorem nulla alia re magis delectari, quàm gemmis: ideo q; misisse Venetias optimas & pulcherrimas gemmas, ex quibus curauerit sibi fieri coronam, cùm ibi sint præstantißimi artifices. Sed Venetos postea addidisse unam gemmam, quæ pulchritudine & magnitudine superauerit reliquas omnes. Quo sanè munere nihil gratius Turcico Imperatori fuit.
units.tr: They say this Turkish Emperor delights in nothing more than gems. Therefore he sent to Venice the finest and most beautiful gems, so that a crown might be made for him from them, since the most excellent craftsmen are there. But afterwards the Venetians added one gem which surpassed all the rest in beauty and size. Indeed nothing was more welcome to the Turkish Emperor than that gift.

units.la: DE EVANGELIO.
units.tr: ON THE GOSPEL.

units.la: Nihil habetur de sancto Bartholomeo, nisi unicum dictum, quod in Dionysio reperitur: tur: Euangelium est longum & breue. Est breue scilicet, quod ad summas Dialecticas attinet: & lo-gum, quando explicantur illæ summæ, traduntur definitiones & diuisiones.
units.tr: Nothing is known of St Bartholomew except a single saying, which is found in Dionysius: The Gospel is both long and short. It is short as far as the highest principles of dialectic go; it is long when those principles are explained and definitions and divisions are set out.

units.la: Quidam medicus, uir doctus, dicebat nobis, se ualde fuisse familiarem alteri cuidã medico Italo, benefico uiro (sicut sunt Itali qui sunt eruditi) qui receperat ipsum ad se propter Græcam linguam. Volebat enim discere græcè, ut melius intelligeret Galenum. Cum apud eum biennium fuisset & ipsi ualde familiaris esset, cœpit ei concionari de doctri-na Ecclesiæ. Ibi dicebat, audiuit me satis humani-ter, cum autem multa dixissem de Euangelio & a-lijs articulis Christianæ doctrinæ, tandem gemens, inquit: Ah quàm pœnitet me mei de te iudicij? Pu-taui te eruditum uirum esse: nunc audio te adhuc delectari istis fabulis. Sic est humana ratio depra-uata iuxta Psalmi dictum: Dixit insipiens in corde suo, non est Deus.
units.tr: A certain learned physician told us that he had been very intimate with another Italian physician, a kindly man (as learned Italians often are), who had taken him into his house for the sake of Greek. For he wanted to learn Greek so as to understand Galen better. After he had been with him for two years and had become very close to him, he began to preach to him about the doctrine of the Church. He said: He listened to me quite courteously, but when I had said much about the Gospel and the other articles of Christian doctrine, at last he sighed and said: Ah, how I regret my judgement of you! I thought you a learned man; now I hear you still delight in these fables. So corrupt is human reason, according to the saying of the Psalm: The fool has said in his heart, There is no God.

units.la: Nazianzenus, contra hæreticos uolentes pro-bare Euangeliumt urbare politias, imò inquit: E-uangelium ita munit & ornat magistratum, ut nul-la uox unquam magis ornauerit in cœlo aut in terra.
units.tr: Nazianzen, against heretics who wanted to prove that the Gospel overturns states, says rather: the Gospel so strengthens and adorns the magistracy that no voice has ever adorned it more, in heaven or on earth.

units.la: Christus confert Euangelium margaritæ, quia Euangelium in corde accipitur tanquam ros cœle-stis, id est nouitas accipitur in corde à rore cœlesti, & fit generosissima gemma, quando tempestatibus turbatur quàm plurimis, id est, quando Ecclesia est subiecta cruci, aut quãdo Christus pendet in cruce, illa etiam gemma liquescit in aceto, quòd fit cùm Euangelium corrumpatur doctrina legis, & sapientia humana. Christus ipse pro sua persona est purissima gemma, id est, sine peccato, et tota massa generis humani plena est roris cœlestis, sic ut λόγος luceat in tota massa generis humani: et est amarissima gemma, id est: nemo sustinet tantos dolores, quantos ipse sustinuit. Sic Euangelium est purissima gemma, quæ viuificat & lætificat. Sed & amara est, id est, crux comitatur doctrinam.
units.tr: Christ compares the Gospel to a pearl, because the Gospel is received in the heart like heavenly dew; that is, the new life is received in the heart from the heavenly dew, and it becomes the most noble gem when it is most troubled by many storms, that is, when the Church is subject to the cross, or when Christ hangs on the cross. That gem also dissolves in vinegar, which happens when the Gospel is corrupted by the doctrine of the law and by human wisdom. Christ himself, in his own person, is the purest gem, that is, without sin; and the whole mass of mankind is full of heavenly dew, so that the Word [λόγος] shines through the whole mass of mankind. He is also the most bitter gem, that is, no one endures such great pains as he endured. So the Gospel is the purest gem, which gives life and gladdens; but it is also bitter, that is, the cross accompanies the teaching.

units.la: Audiui sæpè ex uiro præstante D. Hieronymo Schurpfio, se existimare primâ pernicie Euãgelij et originê corruptelarũ fuisse puræ doctrinæ, quòd doctores Ecclesiæ fastidiuisset usitatas Ecclesiæ formulas loquēdi, sæpius repetere, & populo eadẽ dicta inculcare: ideoq; quæsitas esse nouas & inusitatas formas loquēdi: quia homines sunt ἀξύνετοι καὶ φιλόναυοι.
units.tr: I have often heard from the excellent man Dr Hieronymus Schurpf that he judged the first ruin of the Gospel, and the origin of the corruptions of pure doctrine, to be this: the teachers of the Church came to dislike the customary formulas of the Church, which they repeated often and drummed into the people, so they sought new and unusual forms of speech. For men are unintelligent [ἀξύνετοι] and lovers of novelty [φιλόνεοι].

units.la: Prætor cuiusdã celebris urbis honestiss. uir non iniquus doctrinæ nostræ, cũ peteret Theologi illius loci institui inquisitionē (cui multi boni uiri sunt aduersati) interrogauit Theologũ quendã: Num sitis sanguinē aut pecuniam? At superior dominus eiusdem loci cùm resciscesceret, prohibuit fieri inquisitionem.
units.tr: The magistrate of a certain famous city, a most honourable man not unfriendly to our teaching, when a theologian of that place sought an inquiry to be instituted (to which many good men were opposed), asked one theologian: Are you thirsting for blood or money? But the superior lord of the same place, when he learned of it, forbade the inquiry to be made.

units.la: Quando Lipsiæ reformatio facta est Franciscanorum ante annos nõ multos, ibi fuit quidã Franciscanus inimicus superstitionibus: cum abijssent illinc reformatores, ipse cũ esset concionator, dixit: Boni auditores, uos miramini quid agãt nostri, fratres: si quidẽ cupitis scire, qualis sit nostra reformatio, dicam uobis. Prius in monasterio nostro comedebamus assata intus & foris: benè sapiebat. Nunc est mandatum, ut fruamur assatis foris: etiam bene sapit. Prius bibebamus uinum ex cantharis, nunc est mandatum' ut ex urceis bibamus, etiam benè sapit. Prius fuit mandatum ut incumberemus literis, & disceremus: nunc est mandatum, ut non discamus, quod non est bonum. Et ita conclusit. Fuit nominatus Fleck Voitlandus, mortuus est non procul à Bitterfeld, cum captiuus teneretur in monasterio. Cùm enim essent editæ propositiones Lutheri de indulgentijs, & ipse legisset, dixit: Iam aduenit monachus ille, qui uestros errores patefaciet. Vaticinatus est de mutatione illarum hypocrisium.
units.tr: When the reformation was carried out among the Franciscans at Leipzig not many years ago, there was a certain Franciscan, an enemy of superstitions. When the reformers had left, he, being a preacher, said: Good listeners, you wonder what our brothers are doing. If you want to know what our reformation is like, I will tell you. Formerly in our monastery we ate roast meat both inside and out, and it tasted good. Now it is commanded that we enjoy roast meat outside only, and that too tastes good. Formerly we drank wine from tankards; now it is commanded that we drink from pitchers, and that too tastes good. Formerly it was commanded that we apply ourselves to letters and learn; now it is commanded that we do not learn, which is not good. And with that he concluded. He was named Fleck of Vogtland; he died not far from Bitterfeld while held captive in a monastery. When Luther's propositions on indulgences had been published, and he had read them, he said: Now that monk has come who will expose your errors. He prophesied the overthrow of those hypocrisies.

units.la: Doctor quidam cum moriturus esset, & uenisset ad eum concionator Lipsicus nomine Morus, qui stans ad lectum hortabatur eum, ut se commendaret filio Dei ille sustulit oculos, & dixit: Creditis uos ist ? Quasi diceret, Quid mihi molesti estis istis fabellis?
units.tr: A certain doctor, when he was about to die, had the Leipzig preacher Morus come to him. Morus stood by the bed and urged him to commend himself to the Son of God. The doctor lifted his eyes and said, "Do you believe that?", as if to say, "Why do you bother me with these fables?"

units.la: Bernhardº: Homo semper proficit aut deficit, ue-rum rum est, natura nūquam manet in eodem statu, aut aut enim deficimus in cognitione uerbi diuini, aut proficimus.
units.tr: Bernard: "A man always either advances or falls back. This is true, for nature never remains in the same state. Either we fall away in the knowledge of the divine word, or we advance."

units.la: Quidam Monachus Franciscanus in urbe Isen naca (quæ sita est in Thuringia) nomine Iohannes Hilden, bonus et doctus uir (qui obijt ibidem in carcere) scripsit multos bonos libros, inter quos etiam commentaria in Danielem: & prædixit multa quæ sua manu scripta extant quæ euenerunt. In urbe Gotha scripsit propria manu, anno 1516 futuram esse mutationem doctrinæ religionis, & doctrinam Papisticam abrogatum iri.
units.tr: A Franciscan monk named John Hilden, a good and learned man who died in prison there, lived in the city of Eisenach in Thuringia. He wrote many good books, including commentaries on Daniel, and foretold many things that came to pass, as his handwritten works still extant show. In the city of Gotha, in 1516, he wrote in his own hand that there would be a change in religious doctrine and that the Papist doctrine would be abolished.

units.la: Quidam Monachus Spiræ toto tempore conuentus ita procedebat in suis concionibus, ut non attingeret religionis controuersias, cum tamen haberet auditorium frequens, quia mediocriter concionabatur. Tandem uero dixit: Ego scio uos desiderare, ut uobis indicem huius temporis controuersias, at certò consilio hactenus distuli. Attamen, ut satisfaciam uestræ expectationi, promitto me proxima Dominica de illis aliquid dicturum. Conuenit igitur tunc ingens multitudo. Ille uero perte-xit suam concionem usitato more ut antea, & ni-hil meminit in concione controuersiarum, tandem ferè in fine concionis dixit: Penè eram oblitus pro-ximæ meæ promissionis, reprehendo in hac re meâ negligentiam: tamen aliquid dicâ: Videtis esse ma-gnam gnam controuersiam. Vocantur in odium status Ecclesiastici, & status Laicorum: & sic dixit quædam generalia. Vos Laici accusatis clericos, & nos clerici uos accusamus. Postea in fine subiecit: Kher ein ieglicher sür seiner thür, so &wirdt es uberal rein, id est: multi reformant alios, se ipsos uerò negligunt, interimq; stabiliunt tetros errores. Simile noster Imperator Carolus V. in comitijs Ratisbo-nensib. dixit nos: Omnes indigemus reformatione.
units.tr: A certain monk at Speyer, throughout the whole time of the assembly, preached in such a way that he did not touch on the controversies of religion. Yet he had a crowded audience, because he preached moderately well. At last, however, he said: "I know you want me to point out to you the controversies of this time, but I have deliberately put it off until now. Nevertheless, to satisfy your expectation, I promise that I will say something about them next Sunday." A huge crowd therefore gathered then. He, however, went through his sermon in the usual way, as before, and made no mention of the controversies in it. Finally, almost at the end of the sermon, he said: "I had nearly forgotten my promise for next time. I blame my negligence in this matter. Yet I will say something: you see there is a great controversy. The ecclesiastical estate and the lay estate are being brought into hatred." And so he said some general things: "You laity accuse the clergy, and we clergy accuse you." Afterwards, at the end, he added: "Kher ein ieglicher sür seiner thür, so wirdt es uberal rein" (each should sweep in front of his own door, and then it will be clean everywhere). That is: many reform others but neglect themselves, and meanwhile they uphold foul errors. Similarly, our Emperor Charles V said at the Diet of Regensburg: "We all need reformation."

units.la: Capita Christianæ doctrinæ sine singulari in-uocatione & meditatione intelligi non possunt. Sicut dixit ad me Aegidius concionator in cōuentu Augustano: Vos habetis ualde difficile Theologiā, oportet aliquem multum orare, antequā eam in-telligat. Verè dixit.
units.tr: The chief points of Christian doctrine cannot be understood without special invocation and meditation. As Aegidius, the preacher in the congregation at Augsburg, said to me: "You have a very difficult theology; one must pray much before one understands it." He spoke truly.

units.la: Religiones sunt corruptæ iuxta diuersas natu-ras gentium. Aegyptiaca & Syriaca natio fuit su-perstitiosa. Græca fuit acuta & ingeniosa, quæ ge-nuit multas subtiles hæreses & allegorias. Italica uerò non genuit tales disputationes, sed mutauit religiones in regnum politicum: quia gens Italica est cupida dominationis. Germani sunt amantes libertatis, igitur iam uertunt religionem in liber-tatem, & securitatem carnalem.
units.tr: Religions are corrupted according to the different natures of peoples. The Egyptian and Syrian nations were superstitious. The Greek was sharp and clever, and it produced many subtle heresies and allegories. The Italian, however, did not produce such disputations but turned religion into a political kingdom, because the Italian people is greedy for domination. The Germans are lovers of liberty, so now they turn religion into liberty and carnal security.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Alexatus dixit ad Claudium Beuthler: Vos Ger-mani non retinebitis Euangelij doctrinam. Galli enim non possunt recipere, quia sunt oppressi seruitute. Itali nostri sunt impij & nimis obstinati. Sic dedit testimonium veritati, quia sic fit in mundos. Sapientes persequuntur veritatem, & ideo data est nobis barbaris.
units.tr: Alexatus said to Claudius Beuthler: "You Germans will not keep the doctrine of the Gospel. The French cannot receive it, because they are oppressed by servitude. Our Italians are impious and far too obstinate." Thus he bore witness to the truth, since it goes this way in the world: "The wise persecute the truth, and therefore it has been given to us barbarians."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Fuit hic doctor Iuris, optimus vir, qui volebat Euangelij doctrinam & Legum conciliare. Cum vero iam aliquot menses in ea re frustra consumpsisset, & res non succederet, atque ob id valde animo angeretur, sederetque aliquando valde solicitus, edens mirabiles gestus, puer paruulus, qui post fornacem dormiebat, expergefactus, videns hoc, dixit: Qualis senex fatuus? Ibi respondit doctor ille: Rectè dicis, & abiecto libro, monit ab illo puero, propositum suum mutauit.
units.tr: There was here a doctor of law, an excellent man, who wanted to reconcile the doctrine of the Gospel with the laws. But when he had spent some months on this in vain, and things did not go well, he was greatly troubled in mind and sometimes sat very anxious, making strange gestures. A small boy who was sleeping behind the stove woke up, saw this, and said, "What a foolish old man!" The doctor replied, "You are right." Throwing down his book, he changed his plan at the boy's prompting.

units.la: In Belgico quidam monachus dixit populo, se insequenti concione de veritate utriusque doctrinæ, Euangelicæ & Papisticæ, dicturum esse. Cum ergo finissset concionem, ita dixit: Ecce pene oblitus eram me promisisse de veritate verę religionis iudicium. Quare id iam paucis exponam: Veritas similis est aquæ lustrali, cui cum pistillum intingimus, quo homines conspergamus, unusquisque ab ea refugit. Eodem modo veritas, ita se habet, ut omnes eam fugiant.
units.tr: In the Low Countries a certain monk told the people that in the following sermon he would speak about the truth of both doctrines, the Evangelical and the Papist. When he had finished the sermon, he said: "Behold, I had nearly forgotten that I had promised a judgment on the truth of the true religion. So I will set it out briefly. Truth is like holy water, into which we dip the aspergillum with which we sprinkle people; each one shrinks back from it. In the same way, truth is such that everyone flees from it."

units.la: Dux Fridericus elector, Coloniæ ad se accersiuit Erasmum Roterodamum, in eo conuentu, quem habuit Carolus V. Imperator post coronationem, & eum amanter orauit, ut libere diceret, num erraret Lutherus in ijs cotrouersijs, de quib. praecipuè disseruisset. Ibi Erasmus plane dixit, rectè sentire Lutherum. Interrogauit etiam princeps eum inter caetera, dicēs: Domine Erasme, quid tādē peccauit ille miser meus monachus, quòd ipsi tam infesti sint omnes, & sic eum persequantur? Respondet Erasmus: O clementissime princeps, duo maxima peccata commisit, abstulit coronā Papæ, & episcopis, ac uentrem monachis.
units.tr: Duke Frederick the Elector summoned Erasmus of Rotterdam to Cologne, to the assembly that Emperor Charles V held after his coronation. He earnestly asked him to say freely whether Luther was wrong in those controversies which he had chiefly discussed. Erasmus plainly said that Luther thought rightly. Among other things, the prince asked him, "Master Erasmus, what on earth has my poor monk done wrong, that everyone is so hostile to him and persecutes him so?" Erasmus replied: "O most clement prince, he has committed two very great sins: he has taken away the crown of the Pope and the bishops, and the belly of the monks."

units.la: Ante annos 500 multi homines fuerūt in his terris Saxonicis, nondū cōuersi ad agnitionē nominis Christi, uel qualemcunque doctrinam de Christo. Inter illos fuit etiam quædam nobilis domina nupta principi uiro ethnico, quæ obsequijs suis conuertit eum ad ueram religionem. Historiographus uerò nomine Theodoricus, episcopus Merseburgensis, consiliarius Heinrici Bambergensis imperatoris, fundator episcopatus Libusiensis prope Francfordiam: O inquit, illa neglexit sua ieiunia, nec seruauit illa discrimina ciborum: instituens longā disputationem, num rectè fecerit quòd nō seruauerit illas traditiones: & post longam disputationē ita cōcludit. Sed ex illo facto multū boni secutū est, conconuersio uidelicet uiri.Et ita excusat illam, quod uiolauerit istas traditiones. Credo uero illam mulierem maiorem habuisse cognitionem doctrinae Christianae, quàm ipsum Episcopum.
units.tr: Five hundred years ago many people in these Saxon lands had not yet been converted to the knowledge of the name of Christ, or to any doctrine about Christ at all. Among them there was also a certain noble lady, married to a heathen prince, who by her good services converted him to the true religion. But the historian Theodoric, bishop of Merseburg, counsellor of Emperor Henry of Bamberg, and founder of the bishopric of Lebus near Frankfurt, says: "Oh, she neglected her fasts and did not keep those distinctions of foods." He then conducts a long discussion as to whether she did right in not observing those traditions. After the long discussion he concludes: "But from that deed much good followed, namely the conversion of her husband." And so he excuses her for having violated those traditions. But I believe that woman had a greater knowledge of Christian doctrine than the bishop himself.

units.la: Polyphemus Erasmi minister (sic enim nominatur) solebat acriter cum alijs disputare de controversijs Euangelij, & defendere veram doctrinam. Tandem cùm contenderet cum eo quidam tum multuosior, quem non poterat refutare argumentis, percutit eum libro noui Testamenti, què tenebat in manibus. Erasmus aspiciens, iocosè dicit: Hoc mihi mirum uidetur, Euangelium sic Euangelio defendi.
units.tr: Polyphemus, Erasmus's minister (for so he was called), used to argue vigorously with others about the controversies of the Gospel and to defend the true doctrine. At last, when a certain rather noisy man, whom he could not refute by arguments, contended with him, he struck him with the book of the New Testament that he was holding in his hands. Erasmus, looking on, said jokingly: "This seems strange to me, that the Gospel should be defended in this way, with the Gospel."

units.la: Doctor Aurbachius optimus uir, dicebat, instauratione m Euangelij fuisse detrimentosam omnibus artificibus, exceptis medicis. Omnes enim pictores, statuarij, aurifices conqueruntur se ualde esurire. Medicis uero prodest, quia post quam sancti desierunt curare morbos, iterum ad medicos homines confugiunt.
units.tr: Doctor Aurbach, an excellent man, used to say that the restoration of the Gospel was harmful to all craftsmen except physicians. For all painters, sculptors and goldsmiths complain that they are very hungry. But it benefits physicians, because after the saints ceased to heal diseases, men again flee to the doctors.

units.la: D. Martinus Lutherus.
units.tr: D. Martinus Luther.

units.la: Hæc tria deuastabunt religionem Christianam: Primùm, obliuio beneficiorum, quæ accepimus ab Euangelio. Secundò, securitas, quæ iam ubiq; regnat. Postremò, sapientia mundi, quæ omnia certo ordine uult comprehendere, & pacem communem cõsilijs impijs iuuare. Igitur sedulò orem°, ut Deus nos & posteros nostros in agnitione Euangelij sui retineat, ut id semper in Ecclesijs nostris cum fructu doceatur.
units.tr: Three things will lay waste the Christian religion: first, forgetfulness of the benefits we have received from the Gospel; second, the security that already reigns everywhere; and last, the wisdom of the world, which wishes to grasp all things in a fixed order and, by impious counsels, to serve the common peace. Therefore I earnestly pray that God may keep us and our posterity in the knowledge of his Gospel, so that it may always be taught in our churches with profit.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: In Ecclesijs benedicite Deo, Domino de fontibus Israel. Psal. 68.
units.tr: "In the congregations bless God, the Lord, from the fountains of Israel." Ps. 68.

units.la: Fontes Israel significant doctrinam cælestem, patefactam diuinitus, & traditam per Patres, Prophetas, Apostolos, & ipsum filium Dei in populo Israel. Ad hos fontes constitutæ & collectæ sunt Ecclesiæ inde usque ab initio mundi: ex his fontibus doctrinæ in populo Israel propagatæ sunt etiam Ecclesiæ in gentes, quæ ab Apostolis & Prophetis accipiunt doctrinam, & ab his testibus institutæ confirmantur, et etiam sciunt se veros cultus Deo præstare, fide, invocatione, & reliqua obedientia, iuxta doctrinam Euangelij.
units.tr: The fountains of Israel signify the heavenly doctrine, revealed by God and handed down through the Fathers, the Prophets, the Apostles, and the Son of God himself among the people of Israel. The Churches have been established and gathered at these fountains from the beginning of the world. From these fountains the doctrine spread among the people of Israel, and so the Churches among the nations also were founded. They receive their teaching from the Apostles and Prophets, are confirmed by these witnesses, and also know that they render true worship to God, by faith, by invocation, and by the rest of obedience, according to the doctrine of the Gospel.

units.la: DE IVSTIFI-catione.
units.tr: On Justification.

units.la: Cum essemus Augustæ, ubi & multa exempla confessionum à pluribus exhiberentur, ibi inter cæteros aliquis bonus sodalis offerebat etiam suam sententiam, quòd essemus iusti fide: dicebatq; hanc propositionem probari posse ex Platone, & Catone. Allegabat autem ex Catone dictum:
units.tr: When we were at Augsburg, where many examples of confessions were also being presented by several people, a certain good companion among the others offered his own opinion, that we are justified by faith. He said this proposition could be proved from Plato and Cato. He quoted this saying from Cato:

units.la: Si Deus est animus, nobis ut carmina dicunt, Hic tibi praecipuè sit pura mente colendus.
units.tr: "If God is a mind, as the poets say, he is to be worshipped by you above all with a pure mind."

units.la: Sed nihil ad propositum est. Docet enim tantum particulam legis Cato, & nihil scit de iustitia Evangelij, quae in Christo nobis ostenditur. Congruit cū Iuliano dicente, Phocylidem opponendum esse Salomoni, quia in Phocylide eadem praecepta contineri, quae in Salomone affirmat.
units.tr: But it has nothing to do with the matter. Cato teaches only a small part of the law and knows nothing of the justice of the Gospel, which is shown to us in Christ. It agrees with Julian, who said that Phocylides should be set against Solomon, because Phocylides contains the same precepts that Solomon affirms.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Audiui potentem uirum dicentem: Necesse est ociosos esse homines, qui ista negocia religionis curant. Alius quidam interrogatus de quadam sententia sacrae Scripturae, dicebat ad ducem Iohannem Fridericum: Illustrissime D. Princeps, quid interrogas me de quinque libris Moysi? quin potius interroga me de quinque pagis curandis, ibi respondebo melius.
units.tr: I heard a powerful man say: "It is necessary for those who take care of these matters of religion to be idle men." Another man, when questioned about a certain passage of Holy Scripture, said to Duke John Frederick: "Most illustrious Prince, why do you ask me about the five books of Moses? Rather, ask me about the care of five villages; there I will answer better."

units.la: Interfui semel in luctu grauissimo D. Martini Lutheri, aderant etiam Spalatinus & D. Hieronymus Schurpfius, qui eiusdem rei testes mecum esse possunt. Ibi nulla alia consolatione Doctor Martinus sustentabat se in grauissima tentatione, nisi crebberrima repetitione dicti Paulini: Conclusit Deus omnes sub peccato, ut omnium misereatur.
units.tr: I once took part in a very grievous mourning for Dr. Martin Luther. Spalatin and Dr. Hieronymus Schurpf were also present, and they can be witnesses of the same thing with me. There Doctor Martin sustained himself in his most grievous temptation with no other consolation than the very frequent repetition of the saying of Paul: "God has shut up all under sin, that he may have mercy on all."

units.la: Noui quendam Iudaeum Francofordiensem ante multos annos, admodum senem & uirum sapientem, cùm aliquando conueniremus, loquebamur de narijs uarijs rebus, & dicebam ad illũ, quòd uoluisset nos ante multos annos damnare. ille respõdit: Nos non damnamus uos, sed concedimus quicquid credatis, quòd, sicut Paulus inquit, iustus sua fide uicturus sit. At, dicebã: Hæc non seriò dicis, scio. Tandẽ ille fatebatur, & dicebat, oportere ipsos sic loqui, ne à nobis occiderentur. Ita uidetis, quomodo laceretur Scriptura, & quomodo uocabula gratia, fides, iustificatio, &c. uarijs sophismatibus corrumpantur.
units.tr: Some years ago I knew a Jew of Frankfurt, a very old man and a wise one. When we once met and were talking about various matters, I said to him that many years ago they had wanted to condemn us. He replied: "We do not condemn you; we grant whatever you believe, because, as Paul says, the just shall live by his faith." But I said: "You are not speaking seriously here, I know." At last he confessed, and said that they had to speak in this way, so that they would not be killed by us. So you see how Scripture is torn apart, and how the words grace, faith, justification, and so on are corrupted by various sophisms.

units.la: Doctoris Pomerani similitudo.
units.tr: A comparison of the Pomeranian doctor.

units.la: Annulum amamus propter gemmam, & magni facimus. Sic fide iustificamur, non propter ipsum annulum, id est, qualitatem, sed quòd fide accipiamus hanc gemmam, id est, filium Dei mediatorem.
units.tr: We love a ring because of its gem, and we value it greatly. So we are justified by faith, not because of the ring itself, that is, the quality, but because by faith we receive this gem, that is, the Son of God as Mediator.

units.la: Item simile argumentum: Sponsus accipit annulum à sponsa, non quòd amet annulum, sed quia est pignus & arrabo copulationis.
units.tr: Likewise a similar argument: The bridegroom receives a ring from the bride, not because he loves the ring, but because it is a pledge and earnest of the union.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Solus Psalmus 51 Miserere mei, &c. multis moriturus aperuit coelum. Scio, multos eundem Psalmũ præsenti mortis periculo orasse, quibus etiã in ipso papatu, regnũ Dei aperuerit: præcipuè cum hunc uersum meditarentur: Cor contritum & humiliatũ Deus non despicies. Sancti Bernhardi ultima uox in agone mortis hæc fuit: Sacrificium Deo spiritus contribulatus. Cor contritum & humiliatum non despicies. Non dixit sua me rita & monachatum, Deo esse sacrificium.
units.tr: Psalm 51, "Have mercy upon me," etc., alone opened heaven to many who were about to die. I know that many prayed this same psalm in the peril of imminent death, and that even in the papacy it opened the kingdom of God to them, especially when they meditated on this verse: "A broken and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise." The last words of St. Bernard in the agony of death were these: "A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit. A broken and humbled heart you will not despise." He did not say that my merits and my monastic life are a sacrifice to God.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Imperator Fridericus secundus fecit monetam coreaceam: ille coreaceus nummus ualet imputatione, aureus uerò nummus ualet per se recipsa. Sic nos non habemus aureum nummum, id est, perfectam qualitatem, sed coreaceum nummum, id est, imputatiuam & inchoatiuam iusticiam.
units.tr: Emperor Frederick II made a leather coin. That leather coin is worth by imputation, but a gold coin is worth in itself, by its own nature. So we do not have the gold coin, that is, perfect quality, but the leather coin, that is, imputed and inchoate righteousness.

units.la: Doctor Hieronymus Schurpfius dixit ad principes, cùm ipsi apologiam offerret: Iustificamur nō propter nostrum credere, sed propter filium Dei, & in quem credimus. Ita ille loquebatur.
units.tr: Doctor Hieronymus Schurpf said to the princes, when he offered them the Apology: "We are justified not because of our believing, but because of the Son of God, and in whom we believe." So he spoke.

units.la: Legatus quidam Parisiensis à Rege huc missus, cùm eadem de re inter nos sermo esset, loquens de dicto Pauli, inquit: Credidit Abraham Deo, & imputatum est ei ad iusticiam: Nō inquit, propter qualitatem, sed propter obiectum.
units.tr: A certain Parisian envoy, sent here by the King, when the same matter was under discussion among us, speaking about the saying of Paul, "Abraham believed God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness," said: "Not because of the quality, he says, but because of the object."

units.la: D. Martinus Lutherus.
units.tr: Dr. Martin Luther.

units.la: Audiui D. Lutherum inter concionandum sic templum Hierosolymitanum depingere: Primùm occurrebat atrium, ubi mactabantur pecora: deinde altare, ubi sacerdotes sacrificabant. Cæterùm in intimo aditu situm erat Sanctum sanctorum, cuius effigiem quandam refert quòd nos chorum appellamus, in quod introibat summus sacerdos semel in anno. Sic dicebat triplicem esse iusticiam. Atrium significat ceremonialem iusticiam: Altare, iusticiam moralem: Sanctum sanctorum, iusticiam fidei. Imago est bona.
units.tr: I heard Dr. Luther, while preaching, describe the Temple at Jerusalem in this way. First there was the court, where the cattle were slaughtered; then the altar, where the priests offered sacrifices. But in the innermost entrance lay the Holy of Holies, of which a kind of image is what we call the choir, into which the high priest entered once a year. So he said there is a threefold righteousness. The court signifies ceremonial righteousness; the altar, moral righteousness; the Holy of Holies, the righteousness of faith. It is a good image.

units.la: Disputaui semel cum quodam Iudæo ex capite 53 Esaiæ, qui voluit defendere illa dicta esse scripta de Ezechia: cum vero vinceretur, clausit librum, & aufugit.
units.tr: I once disputed with a certain Jew on the basis of chapter 53 of Isaiah. He wanted to maintain that those words were written about Hezekiah. But when he was being defeated, he shut the book and ran away.

units.la: Audiui admodum adhuc puer patrem meum (quia amisi cum adhuc puer: sed memini adhuc multos eius sermones. Erat enim illi consuetudo cum doctis viris, & exercitatis in doctrina conferre) cum colloqueretur cum doctis de remissione peccatorum & pœnitentia, dicere sæpe ad eos: Quare vos docetis me, quod debeam dubitare de remissione peccatorum & iustificatione, cum me symbolum Apostolorum iubeat dicere: Credo remissionem peccatorum. Ad quæ illi non potuerunt respondere. Mortuus est autem ante annos quinquaginta. Hæc autem anno 47. dixit.
units.tr: When I was still a very young boy I heard my father (I lost him while I was still a child, but I still remember many of his sayings; for he had the habit of conferring with learned men and those trained in doctrine) speaking with learned men about the forgiveness of sins and repentance. He often said to them: "Why do you teach me that I should doubt the forgiveness of sins and justification, when the Apostles' Creed bids me say: I believe in the forgiveness of sins?" They could not answer this. He died fifty years ago. He said this in the year 47.

units.la: Audiui adolescens Stœslerum & Capnionem de doctrina nostra disputantes, & dixerunt ad quendam Scotisticum doctorem: Cum nos legimus in nostris Bibliis, invenimus longe aliam Theologiam ac sententiam de iustificatione, quàm vos in vestris Glossis.
units.tr: As a young man I heard Stoessel and Capnio disputing about our doctrine, and they said to a certain Scotist doctor: "When we read in our Bibles, we find a theology and an account of justification quite different from what you find in your glosses."

units.la: Cardinalis Anglicus Eboracensis legens nostram apologiam confessionis Augustanæ tunc recens editam, dixit, nostram causam de iusticia fidei esse firmiorem in confirmatione, quàm in cõsutatione, qd'uerũ est: quia facilï est cõstruere in sophisticis, quàm destruere. Facilius uerò est destruere, quàm construere, in Physicis. Sic sapienter & uerissimè iudicabat. Multa illustria testimonia sacræ Scripturæ habemus ad cõfirmandã ueritatem. At quædam speciosa argumenta ab aduersarijs nostris nobis opponuntur, quæ diluere difficile est. Verùm præstat nos melius munitos esse ad retinendam ueræ doctrinæ sententiam, quàm sic munitos esse, ut omnibus cauillationibus satisfacere possimus. Sicut olim maiori ignominia notabatur, qui scutum amiserat, quàm qui gladium: quorum huius ad infligenda uulnera, illius ad defendenda corpora usus erat.
units.tr: The English Cardinal of York, reading our Apology of the Augsburg Confession, which had then just been published, said that our case concerning the righteousness of faith is firmer in its confirmation than in its refutation, which is true, because it is easy to construct in sophistical matters, but it is easier to destroy than to construct in natural philosophy. So he judged wisely and most truly. We have many illustrious testimonies of Holy Scripture for confirming the truth. But some specious arguments are set against us by our opponents, which are hard to dissolve. Yet it is better for us to be so well armed for keeping the teaching of the true doctrine, than to be armed in such a way that we can meet every quibble. Long ago, the man who had lost his shield was judged more disgraced than the man who had lost his sword; the one was used for inflicting wounds, the other for defending the body.

units.la: Fuit mihi aliquando disputatio cũ Vito Amerbachio collega nostro de illa sententia Paulina: Credidit Abraham Deo, & imputatũ est ei ad iusticiam. Hanc sententiã dicebat nõ esse rectè accomodatam à Paulo, & sic in ferebat: Moyses loquitur de fide Abrahæ expectante magnã posteritatẽ, & non de fide expectante remissionẽ peccatorũ: ita ab exemplo uolebat argumentari: Sicut Abrahã credidit in suo promisso negocio, ita unumquemquam oportet credere in suo promisso negocio. Nõ intellexit quid diceret, hæc erat ipsius cõcio uel potius delirium. rium, qua Moysen & Paulum conciliare uolebat.
units.tr: Once I had a disagreement with my colleague Vitus Amerbach about that Pauline saying: "Abraham believed God, and it was imputed to him for righteousness." He said this saying was not rightly applied by Paul, and argued thus: "Moses speaks of the faith of Abraham looking forward to a great posterity, and not of faith looking forward to the forgiveness of sins." He wanted to argue from the example in this way: "Just as Abraham believed in his own promised matter, so each one ought to believe in his own promised matter." He did not understand what he was saying; this was his own opinion, or rather delirium, by which he wanted to reconcile Moses and Paul.

units.la: Quidam Medicus intra cætera capita, de quibus rixabatur, cum doctore Fuchsio etiam hanc disputatione immiscebat, uolēs esse arbiter et cōciliator doctrinæ de fide & iustificatione coram Deo, & ita scribebat non esse realem controuersiam, Lutherū enim loqui de habitu, alios de actionibus, id est, operibus: ita congruere omnium sententias. Quia quod tribuitur habitibus, id etiam tribuitur efficaciæ uel actionibus, & ita non esse controuersiam. Sic suis concordantiis uolebat quemlibet in sua fide saluari, si seruaret legem naturæ.
units.tr: A certain physician, among the other points about which he was quarrelling, also mixed into this disputation with Doctor Fuchs, wishing to be the arbiter and reconciler of the doctrine of faith and justification before God. He wrote that there was no real controversy: Luther speaks of a habit, others of actions, that is, works; thus the opinions of all agree. For what is attributed to habits is also attributed to their efficacy or actions, and so there is no controversy. By his concordances he wanted anyone to be saved in his own faith, if he kept the law of nature.

units.la: Alius quidam homo facetus in conuiuio dixit, inanes esse disputationes de iustificatione, quia neminem esse iustum testimonio Psalmi: Non uidi iustum in terra. Ibi alter assidens increpat eum, inquiens: Tu asine, non legisti Psalmum? Sic enim habet textus: Non uidi iustum in terra derelictum, quod uocabulum tu omittis. Fuit calumnia, quia citauit textum mutilatum.
units.tr: Another witty fellow at a dinner said that disputations about justification are empty, since by the testimony of the Psalm no one is righteous: "I have not seen a righteous man on earth." Another man sitting there rebuked him: "You donkey, have you not read the Psalm? For the text says, 'I have not seen a righteous man forsaken on earth,' and you leave out the word 'forsaken.'" It was a slander, because he quoted the text in a mutilated form. ## The saying of the Pomeranian doctor.

units.la: Sententia Doctoris Pomerani.
Quando tu disputas de nostrorum meritorum dignitate, tunc dic: Etiamsi non sum dignus, nihilominus tamen sum indigens.
units.tr: When you dispute about the worth of our merits, then say: Even if I am not worthy, I am nevertheless in need.

units.la: Cochleus scribebat contra Doctorem Martinū Lutherū, dicēs: Quid dicis, Fide tātū iustificamur? ta mẽ etiam Deus iustificat, Spiritus sanctus iustificat, & multa similia ita coacervabat, non intelligens quid diceret. Deus est causa efficiens iustificationis: meritum filij Dei, est causa impulsiva. illa causa apprehenditur aliquo instrumento, quod est fides.
units.tr: Cochlaeus wrote against Doctor Martin Luther, saying: "What do you mean, we are justified by faith alone? Yet God also justifies, and the Holy Spirit justifies," and he heaped up many similar objections, not understanding what he was saying. God is the efficient cause of justification; the merit of the Son of God is the impulsive cause; that cause is apprehended through an instrument, which is faith. ## S. Bernard.

units.la: S. Bernhardus.
Quisquis pro peccatis compunctus esurit & sitit iusticiam, credit in te, qui iustificas impium, is per solam fidem iustificatus, pacem habebit apud Deum.
units.tr: Whoever, pricked by his sins, hungers and thirsts for righteousness and believes in you, who justify the ungodly, is justified through faith alone and will have peace with God.

units.la: Basilius quomodo particula Sola fide usus sit in concione de humilitate.
units.tr: How Basil used the particle "Sola fide" in his sermon on humility.

units.la: Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur, quòd Christus nobis factus sit sapientia à Deo, iusticia, sanctificatio, & redemptio, sicut scriptum est: Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur. Hæc enim perfecta & integra gloriatio à Deo, quando neq; propter iusticiam suam quisquis effertur, sed agnoscit se indigere vera iustitia, fide autem sola in Christum iustificari. Horum dictorum meminerimus propter aduersarios, quia obijciunt nobis, quòd nusquam veteres scriptores usi sint particula illa Sola.
units.tr: "Let him who glories glory in the Lord," because Christ has been made to us wisdom from God, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption, as it is written: "Let him who glories glory in the Lord." For this is a perfect and complete glorying before God, when no one is puffed up on account of his own righteousness, but acknowledges that he lacks true righteousness and is justified by faith alone in Christ. Let us remember these words on account of our opponents, who object to us that the ancient writers never used that particle "Sola."

units.la: DE VETERI ET nouo Testamento.
units.tr: On the Old and New Testament.

units.la: Avdiui Anabaptistā, qui postea cū alijs est decollatus, cū quo necesse erat disputare, dicentem: Si omnia Biblia in toto mundo hic essent posita, non emerem uno nummo. Scimus esse figuras literarum: sed tamen Deus per uerbum externum est efficax.
units.tr: I heard an Anabaptist, who was afterwards beheaded along with others, and with whom I had to dispute. He said: "If all the Bibles in the whole world were placed here, I would not buy them for a single penny. We know that the letters are mere figures, but God is nevertheless effective through the outward word."

units.la: Lectio noui & ueteris Testamenti quotidiana, omnibus hominibus necessaria.
units.tr: Daily reading of the Old and New Testament, necessary for all people.

units.la: Sæpe uos hortamur & obtestamur, ut propter uestram salutem faciatis uobis textus Bibliorum familiares. Quando mane surgitis, recitatis precibus uestris, legite unum caput in ueteri Testamēto cum aliquo psalmo, uesperi unum ex nouo, siue intelligatis siue non: tamen aliquid inde discetis, & proderit uobis illa lectio. Accenditur hac lectione inuocatio. est ualde magna bestialis uita & barbaries, surgere & ire cubitum sine cogitatione rerum diuinarum. Videtis puniri mundū propter carnalem securitatem, & uerbi Dei contemptum, & nos omnes sentire pœnas, quas ut leniat filius Dei toto pectore oremus.
units.tr: Often we urge and beseech you, for the sake of your own salvation, to make the texts of the Bible familiar to you. When you rise in the morning, after your prayers, read one chapter of the Old Testament with some psalm, and in the evening one from the New, whether you understand it or not. You will still learn something from it, and that reading will profit you. Invocation is kindled by this reading. To rise and go to bed without any thought of divine things is a very great bestial life and barbarism. You see the world punished for its carnal complacency and its contempt of the Word of God, and we all feel the penalties. Let us pray with all our heart that the Son of God would alleviate them.

units.la: Breuis ueteris & noui Testamenti summa.
units.tr: A brief summary of the Old and New Testament.

units.la: Moyses initiò loquitur de essentia Dei, secundò dò de creatiõe, tertiò de hominis formatiõe, quartò de peccato & lapsu hominis, & de edita promissio ne, per quã homo destitutus est, & coepit rursus Ec clesiã cõdere. Postea sequūtur illustriores promis-siones. Deinde in Exodo promulgatur lex, quæ est perpetua uox Dei, postulãs obedientiã, & inobedientes dãnans. In libris Regũ proponũtur exem pla obedietiæ & inobedietiæ: Dauid recipitur, po stea renouatur promissio : deniq; magis magisq; Prophetæ eadẽ illustrãt. In nouo Testamēto expres sè illustrãtur singuli articuli Christianæ doctrinæ.
units.tr: Moses speaks first of the essence of God, second of creation, third of the formation of man, and fourth of the sin and fall of man, and of the promise given, by which man was restored and began again to build the Church. Afterwards more illustrious promises follow. Then in Exodus the law is promulgated, which is the perpetual voice of God, demanding obedience and condemning the disobedient. In the books of Kings examples of obedience and disobedience are set forth. David is received, and afterwards the promise is renewed. Finally the Prophets illustrate the same things more and more. In the New Testament the individual articles of Christian doctrine are expressly set forth.

units.la: Fructus lectionis crebræ Psalmorum.
units.tr: The fruit of frequent reading of the Psalms.

units.la: Vtilitates lectionum Psalmorum multiplices sa-ne sunt: primò enim diligēs eorũ lectio formatiudi cium: deinde accenditur per eā pietas: tertiò Gram matica exercetur in huiusmodi exercitijs.
units.tr: The uses of reading the Psalms are indeed manifold. First, their diligent reading forms the judgment. Second, piety is kindled through it. Third, grammar is exercised in such exercises.

units.la: Prophetæ Danielis summa.
units.tr: Summary of the Prophet Daniel.

units.la: Daniel debet nobis esse notus propter multi-plicem doctrinam: multa enim præclara in eo con-tinentur uerò præcipuæ & ualde insignes ma-teriæ in Daniele sunt : Prima, historia est de con-uersione Nabuchodonosor. quàm gratũ exemplũ est, quòd Nabuchodonosor tantus tyrannus et ido-lolatra recipiatur & cõuertatur. Ibi debetis in me-moriam reuocare seriem totius historiæ, & concio-nes nes singulas Danielis, ut: Redime peccata tua eleemosinis. Adhibete etiam curam, ut recte intelligatis illas sententias. Item postea sunt duæ prædictiones: una de quatuor monarchijs, de statua Nabuchodonosor: altera vero visio de illis horribilibus bestijs, & de hominis figura, postea de leonis figura, item pardi figura, etiam de Romana lupa, quomodo sit pingenda, quam ipse præ admiratione non satis ex sententia depingere potest. Item prædicit mortem Christi, & tempus eius adventus: etiam excidium seu euersionem totius politiæ, quòd illa politia sit desitura. Item prædicit postremi mundi calamitates.
units.tr: Daniel ought to be known to us on account of his manifold teaching, for many excellent things are contained in him. The chief and most notable subjects in Daniel are these. The first is the history of the conversion of Nebuchadnezzar. What a welcome example it is that Nebuchadnezzar, so great a tyrant and idolater, is received and converted! There you ought to recall to memory the sequence of the whole history and each of Daniel's addresses, such as "Redeem your sins by alms." Take care also to understand those sentences rightly. Likewise there are afterwards two predictions: one about the four monarchies, concerning the statue of Nebuchadnezzar; the other a vision of those horrible beasts, of the figure of a man, then of the figure of a lion, likewise of a leopard, and also of the Roman she-wolf, and how it is to be painted, which he himself, from amazement, cannot paint sufficiently in accordance with the meaning. Likewise he foretells the death of Christ and the time of his coming, and also the destruction or overthrow of the whole polity, because that polity is to cease. Likewise he foretells the calamities of the last world.

units.la: Lazarus Bonamicus vir doctus, cum esset interrogatus, quomodo ei placeret Psalterium, respondit, placere sibi: recitari enim ibi egregias sententias de prouidētia: sed tamē nihilo melius esse, quàm Pindari poema. quod falsum est. Nam Pindarus etsi habet egregias sententias de prouidentia (nam totus fere Pindarus consumitur in testimonijs de prouidentia) tamen Pindarica sunt idolatrici. Deinde sunt tantum legalia in Pindaro. Dauid vero in Psalterio habet promissionem gratiæ.
units.tr: Lazarus Bonamicus, a learned man, when asked how he liked the Psalter, replied that he liked it, for excellent sentences about providence are recited there; but nevertheless it is no better than a poem of Pindar. That is false. For although Pindar has excellent sentences about providence (for almost the whole of Pindar is taken up with testimonies about providence), nevertheless the things in Pindar are idolatrous. Moreover, there is only legal matter in Pindar. But David in the Psalter has the promise of grace.

units.la: DE SACRAMENTIS.
units.tr: ON THE SACRAMENTS.

units.la: Maximilianus Imperator, quando oppugnaturus erat postridie ciuitatem in Belgico, inuitauit pridie capitaneos suos ad cœnā, inter quos erat comes quidam, qui cùm reliqui co-uiuæ se hilares præberent, ipse solus tristis in men-sa sedit. Interrogatus ergo à Maximiliano: Domine comes, quare tu tristaris, cùm cras tibi pugnandū sit? Respondit, se, si uerum fateatur, tristem esse. Maximilianus dicit ei: Indica mihi causam tuæ tri-stitiæ, si mea maiestas poterit tibi opitulari, faciet. Potest, inquit, comes. Tandem Imperator ab co re-quirit, quid nam sit, quòd tristis sit comes, respon-dit: Quoniam mihi cras præliandum est, et euentus belli sunt incerti, cogito etiam de animæ meæ salu-te. Præcipuè autem doleo, inquit, quòd debeam tria millia aureorum, quos exposui in multiplices usus rei militaris, de quib. non queo maiestati tuæ rationem reddere, &, ut maiestas tua hanc ingen-tem pecuniæ summam clementer remittere uelit, oro. Imperator primùm admiratus illam ma-gnam pecuniæ summam, tandem dixit, se libenter ei remittere debitum, modò crastino die se fortem & strenū uirū in prælio præberet. Comes, ut esset certus de remisso debito, dixit. Domine Imperator Maiestas tua mihi præbibat, ut sim certior de cle-menti illa remissione huius debiti. At Imperator: Age, ne de mea erga te beneuolentia dubites, & me ex animo tibi remittere scias, præbibo tibi bo-num haustum: & sic eum absoluit. Quod sacra-menti menti signũ non fuit obscurum. Deinde fuit hilaris, & fortiter se postero die gessit.
units.tr: When the Emperor Maximilian was about to attack a city in Flanders the next day, he invited his captains to supper the evening before. Among them was a certain count who, while the others were cheerful at table, sat alone and gloomy. Maximilian asked him: "Lord Count, why are you sad, when you have to fight tomorrow?" He replied that, if he was to tell the truth, he was sad. Maximilian said to him: "Tell me the cause of your sadness. If my majesty can help you, it will do so." "It can, my lord," said the count. At last the Emperor asked him what the reason was that the count was sad. He answered: "Because I have to fight tomorrow, and the outcome of battle is uncertain, I am also thinking about the salvation of my soul. But especially I grieve, he said, that I owe three thousand gold coins, which I spent on the many needs of war, and of which I cannot give your majesty an account. I beg that your majesty will graciously be willing to remit this great sum of money." The Emperor, at first astonished at so large a sum, finally said that he would gladly forgive him the debt, provided that the next day he showed himself a brave and vigorous man in battle. So that he might be certain of the remitted debt, the count said: "Lord Emperor, let your majesty give me assurance, so that I may be more certain of that gracious remission of this debt." But the Emperor said: "Come, do not doubt my goodwill towards you, and know that I forgive you from my heart. I will drink a good health to you," and so he dismissed him. This sign of the sacrament was not unclear. Afterwards the count was cheerful and acquitted himself bravely the next day.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Memini Maximilianum Imperatorem,& regem Galliæ,cùm mutuum inter se fœdus ferirent, ambos simul accefisse ad cœnæ Dominicæ communionem,unamq; hostiam in signum firmissimæ beneuolentiæ diuisam & distributam esse inter cos. Illud fuit signum mutui sæderis,& mutuæ amiciciæ inter Maximilianum, & Regem Galliæ.
units.tr: I remember that the Emperor Maximilian and the King of France, when they were making a mutual covenant, both came together to receive the Communion of the Lord's Supper, and that one host was divided and distributed between them as a sign of the most firm goodwill. That was the sign of the mutual covenant and mutual friendship between Maximilian and the King of France.

units.la: DE BAPTISMO.
units.tr: ON BAPTISM.

units.la: Scribũt in India adhuc retineri Circũcisionẽ, Baptismum,Sabbatum,& diem Dominicũ:et dicunt, quòd etiam ibi fœmellæ circumcidantur.
units.tr: They write that circumcision, baptism, the Sabbath and the Lord's day are still retained in India, and they say that even there girls are circumcised.

units.la: Herodotus scribit, se in tribus locis inuenisse Circumcisionē in Aegypto, quia multi ibi exulabant ex posteris Iacob, & filij Esau retinebant Circumcisionem in Arabia.nam Turci adhuc hodie eam quoq; retinent ab ijsdem populis acceptā. Deinde in Syria: postea in Colchica propter exulantes decem tribus, quæ inde uenerunt in Europam,& multi Iudæi fuerunt in Germania, & uicinis locis ante natum Christum.
units.tr: Herodotus writes that he found circumcision in three places: in Egypt, where many descendants of Jacob had gone into exile, and in Arabia, where the sons of Esau retained circumcision; for the Turks still retain it today, received from those same peoples. Then in Syria; and afterwards in Colchis, on account of the ten tribes that went into exile and from there came into Europe; and many Jews were in Germany and in neighbouring places before the birth of Christ.

units.la: Papistæ mouerunt hanc quæstionem:an asinus bibens ex baptismo bibat aquā baptismi,& sic asinus dicendus sit baptizatus? Est quæstio digna asinis. sinis. Non intelligunt asini isti, quid sit baptismus, quod inde ipsis accidit, quia ordinem prædicamentorum non didicerunt, nec animaduertunt.
units.tr: The Papists raised this question: whether an ass, drinking from a baptismal font, drinks the water of baptism, and so whether the ass is to be called baptized? It is a question worthy of asses. Those asses do not understand what baptism is, and this is what happens to them, because they have not learned, nor do they notice, the order of the predicaments.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: In Borussia sacerdos parum doctus cum aliquando delatus esset apud episcopum, quòd non iuxta ritum Ecclesiæ baptizaret infantes: Episcopus uolens experiri hanc rem, accusat sacerdotem de hoc negocio. Sacerdos negabat, dicens, se retinere communem morem baptizandi infantes. Vt autem certus de hac re esset episcopus, sic explorauit: Cum nullus infans baptizandus esset, subornat quosdam coponentes νῶφορ πρόσωπον (ut dicunt) ex stramine, quem fascijs inuolui iussit, & sic inscio sacerdote ad baptizandum adferri. Cumq; iam ad baptismum astaret episcopus & alij, sacerdos fraudè subolens, dixit: Baptizo te in nomine episcopi, in nomine meo, & in nomine compatrum. Episcopus statim erupit in hæc uerba: Domine, an hæc est forma baptizandi in Ecclesia? Respondit sacerdos. Qualis est puer, talis etiam est baptismus.
units.tr: In Prussia a poorly educated priest was once reported to the bishop for not baptizing infants according to the rite of the Church. The bishop, wishing to test the matter, charged the priest with this offence. The priest denied it, saying that he kept the common custom of baptizing infants. To make sure of the facts, the bishop devised the following test. When no infant was due for baptism, he got some men to make up a dummy child of straw (as they say), which he ordered to be wrapped in swaddling bands and brought to the font for baptism without the priest's knowledge. When the bishop and the others were already standing at the font, the priest, suspecting a trick, said: "I baptize you in the name of the bishop, in my name, and in the name of the godparents." The bishop at once burst out: "Sir, is this the form of baptism in the Church?" The priest replied: "Such as the child is, such is the baptism." [νήπιον πρόσωπον]

units.la: Torgæ erat aurifaber anabaptista, qui hanc habebat opinionem, quòd infantes nascerentur sine peccato originali. Ratio erat hæc: quia parentes eorum essent baptizati. Igitur in illis non esse amplius peccatum originale, qui ex parentibus sanctis nascerentur. Ibi Doctor Martinus respondit ei hac similitudine : Nescis ex quo culmen & frumentum in agro nascatur? Proijcitur seu semina tur granū, quod iam nō habet calamum, sed antea quidem habuit, cùm adhuc staret in agro. Attamen ex hoc nudo grano postea nascitur seges, quæ & granum & culmum habeat.
units.tr: At Torgau there was a goldsmith who was an Anabaptist and held the opinion that infants were born without original sin, because their parents had been baptized; so, he reasoned, original sin no longer remained in those born of holy parents. Doctor Martin answered him with this comparison: "Do you not know from what the stalk and the grain grow in the field? The seed is cast or sown, a grain which no longer has its stalk, though it did have one before, while it still stood in the field. Yet from this bare grain a crop afterwards grows which has both grain and stalk."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Consilium de baptizanda Iudæa.
units.tr: Counsel concerning the baptism of a Jewess.

units.la: Primò, nomen ipsi imponendum est, quod tamen ipsa elegerit.
units.tr: First, a name is to be given to her, which she herself may choose.

units.la: Secūdò, interroganda est, an teneat Decalogū, eumq; recitet.
units.tr: Second, she is to be asked whether she holds the Decalogue and can recite it.

units.la: Deinde quærendum: Credis ne te etiam esse peccatricem, in peccatis natā, egētemq; filio Dei Messia saluante à peccatis, à morte & potestate diaboli redimente nos.
units.tr: Then the question is to be put: do you believe that you too are a sinner, born in sins and in need of the Son of God, the Messiah, who saves from sins and redeems us from death and from the power of the devil?

units.la: Quartò: Credis ne etiam quòd Dominus noster Iesus Christus sit ille ipse Messias, per Prophetas passim promissus ex semine Abrahæ, et ex Dauidis progenie, natus ex pudica virgine Mariæ, et verus Deus & homo nobis in hoc à Deo patre datus, ut pro nostris peccatis pateretur, crucifigeretur, ac mortem tandem obiret, rursusq; ex morte resurgeret, ut nos à peccatis redemptos in æternum iustos ac vivos redderet per Spiritum sanctum, quem nobis absq; omni merito & dignitate nostra à Patre impetrauit atq; donauit? Hicq; iubeatur symbolum Apostolicum recitare.
units.tr: Fourth: do you also believe that our Lord Jesus Christ is that very Messiah, promised everywhere through the prophets, sprung from the seed of Abraham and from the family of David, born of the chaste virgin Mary, and the true God and man, given to us by God the Father in this way, that he should suffer for our sins, be crucified, and at last undergo death, and rise again from death, so that he might make us, redeemed from sins, righteous and alive for eternity through the Holy Spirit, whom he obtained and bestowed on us from the Father without any merit or worthiness of ours? Here she is to be told to recite the Apostles' Creed.

units.la: Quintò. Quandoquidem hæc fides, & talis spiritus, unum Deum sicut liberi parentem inuocant, iuxta dictum Ioelis: Omnis quicunq; inuocauerit nomen Domini saluus erit: itaque recita orationem Dominicam.
units.tr: Fifth: since this faith and this disposition call upon one God as free children call upon a parent, according to the saying of Joel, "Whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved," therefore recite the Lord's Prayer.

units.la: Conclusio fiat cum adhortatione, in hunc modum: Iam in posterum certa sis, nec ulla dubitatio oriatur, quin peccata tua tibi sint remissa, & vocaberis ac eris filia Dei per Iesum Christum unigenitum eius filium, in quem uerè credis. Gratia & pax Dei sit tecum. Et dicat baptizatus homo: Amen.
units.tr: The conclusion is to be made with an exhortation, in this manner: From now on be certain, and let no doubt arise, that your sins have been forgiven you, and you shall be called and shall be a daughter of God through Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, in whom you truly believe. The grace and peace of God be with you. And let the baptized person say: Amen.

units.la: DE COENA DOMINI. Ad quæstionem Vigelij, Doctoris Theologiæ.
units.tr: ON THE LORD'S SUPPER. In reply to the question of Vigelius, Doctor of Theology.

units.la: Certum est Deum non esse alligandum ad ullam rem, ad quam se ipse non alligat suo uerbo. Sicut peccant omnes, qui Deum magis ad hanc statuam, quam ad aliam exaudire imaginantur: & ex tali imaginatione omnes idolomaniæ ortæ sunt.
units.tr: It is certain that God is not to be bound to any thing to which he does not bind himself by his Word. Just as all those sin who imagine that God hears them more readily at this statue than at that one; and from such an imagination all the idolatries have arisen.

units.la: Non est igitur Deus ad panem & uinum extra usum institutum alligandus. Et merus furor est, fingere quòd dictis verbis à consecrante sic immigret corpus Christi in pane, ut ibi semper manere cogatur, sicut infusum vinum in cantharum manet, etsi rursus effundatur. Sed sacramenta sunt pacta & exhibitiones, & cùm sumuntur illæ res, simul adest Christus & est efficax. Hæc sacramentalis præsentia est voluntaria, non est inclusio Geometrica vel magica, quòd Christus cogatur manere in pane.
units.tr: God is therefore not to be bound to bread and wine outside the use he instituted. And it is sheer madness to imagine that, once the words have been spoken by the one consecrating, the body of Christ migrates into the bread in such a way that it is compelled to remain there always, just as wine poured into a cup remains there even if it is afterwards poured out. But sacraments are covenants and exhibitions, and when those things are received, Christ is present at the same time and is effective. This sacramental presence is voluntary; it is not a geometrical or magical enclosure, such that Christ is forced to remain in the bread.

units.la: Cùm baptizatur homo, in ipsa actione vere adest Spiritus sanctus, non manet in aqua extra actionem. Sunt igitur abominandæ illæ quæstiones, an mus, rodens panem consecratum, comedat corpus Christi? Et abominandus est mos circumferendi panem in spectaculis. Quare eæ, quæ post communionem reliquiæ sunt de pane & vino, quæ non manducantur ab ijs quorum sit intentio uti cœna Domini, non sunt sacramenta: quia actio tota est sacramentum. Sed propter imperitos reverentiam consulo, ut reliquum in poculo ebibat ultimus communicans, vel unus, vel plures.
units.tr: When a person is baptized, the Holy Spirit is truly present in the very action; he does not remain in the water apart from the action. Therefore those questions are detestable: whether a mouse gnawing the consecrated bread eats the body of Christ? And the custom of carrying the bread about in public shows is detestable. Hence those remnants of bread and wine which are left over after communion, and which are not eaten by those whose intention is to use the Lord's Supper, are not sacraments, because the whole action is the sacrament. But out of reverence for the unlearned, I advise that the last communicant, whether one or several, drink up what remains in the cup.

units.la: Philippus Melanchthon.
units.tr: Philip Melanchthon.

units.la: Venerabili viro, egregia virtute & sana doctrina prædito, D. IOHANNI TVRBIDINI, pastori ecclesiæ Gottensis, amico suo.
units.tr: To the venerable man, endowed with outstanding virtue and sound learning, Master John Turbidinus, minister of the church at Gotha, his friend.

units.la: Etsi multa sint disputata à multis de elevatione Sacramenti, tamen in Ecclesijs nostris placuit eum mo-
units.tr: Although many have disputed much about the elevation of the sacrament, nevertheless in our churches it has been decided to imitate the custom, because some who defended that elevation also upheld the custom of carrying the bread about and adoring it.

units.la: more imitari, quòd allegata hac elevatione, aliqui confirmabant more circūferendi & adorandi panem. Hac aūt circūgestationem cōstat extra rationē sacramēti esse, ut si aqua gestetur sumpta excere monijs Baptismi. Sunt enim Sacramenta actiones à Deo institutæ. Aqua nō est sacramentū, sed ipsa baptisatio, sonāte simul uerbo Dei. Sic de cœna Domini sentiatur. Panis & uinum ordinata sunt ad sumptionem, sed si circūferantur, tanquam spectaculū, in circumgestatione nequaquam est sacramentum. Non enim alligatus est Deus ad aliquam creaturā sine suo expresso uerbo. Post hæc horribilis error est, quòd sacrificulus offerat in hoc ministerio Filiū Dei pro uiuis & mortuis, & quidē quòd addūt id opus ualere ex opere operato, id est, (ut ipsi loquuntur) sine bono motu utentis: ad hāc persuasiōnē oblationē retinēt. Cū error iste dānabilis sit, aboleri uinculū erroris utile est, & prorsus homines de uero usu sacramēti, de cōfirmatione fidei, et gratiarū actione, docendi sunt. 18 Ianuarij, Anno 44.
units.tr: It is clear, however, that this carrying about lies outside the purpose of the sacrament. It would be like carrying water taken from the rite of baptism. Sacraments are actions instituted by God. The water is not the sacrament; the baptism itself is, when the Word of God is spoken along with it. The same should be thought of the Lord's Supper. Bread and wine are ordained for eating, but if they are carried about as a spectacle, there is by no means a sacrament in the carrying about. God is not bound to any creature without his express word. Next comes a horrible error: the little priest offers the Son of God in this ministry for the living and the dead, and they add that this work avails by the work done, that is (as they themselves put it) without any good disposition in the one who uses it. By this persuasion they retain the oblation. Since this error is damnable, it is useful to dissolve the bond of error, and people must be taught thoroughly about the true use of the sacrament, about the confirmation of faith, and about thanksgiving. 18 January, Anno 44.

units.la: In quodā regno aliquis phātasticus homo est, qui non uult celebrari cœnā Domini nisi uesperi. quāquā non refert, siue manè, siue uesperi sumatur: tamen turbat Ecclesias. Potestas seu magistratus debebat huiusmodi stultū carceribus coercere, donec animum mutaret. Vesperi ideo Christus dedit cœnā, quia illæ gētes tātūm cœnabāt, et nō prandebāt.
units.tr: In a certain kingdom there is a fanatical fellow who does not want the Lord's Supper celebrated except in the evening. Yet it makes no difference whether it is taken in the morning or in the evening; still, he disturbs the churches. The power or the magistrate ought to restrain such a fool in prison until he changes his mind. Christ gave the supper in the evening only because those peoples dined in the evening and did not take lunch.

units.la: Anno post natū Christiū 1510, die 19 Iulij, cōbusti sunt in Marchia Brandeburgēsi 38 Iudæi, qui sacramentalē hostiam à sacrilego quodam, emptam pugionibus & cultellis in ipsius Christi & Ecclesiæ Christianæ, ignominiam impiè cōsoderant, adiectis blasphemijs, quòd Christianorum Deus nullum haberet sanguinem, qui tamen miraculosè promanauit, adeò ut celari nullo modo potuerit. Quare comprehensi scelerati, omnes uiui sunt exusti, exceptis paucis, qui sacro baptismate conspersi, postridie capitis supplicio sunt affecti. Sacrilegus uerò ıste, qui uendiderat candentibus primùm forcipibus dilaceratus: uiuus etiam deinde combustus est.
units.tr: In the year after the birth of Christ 1510, on 19 July, thirty-eight Jews were burned in the Margraviate of Brandenburg. They had bought a consecrated host from a certain sacrilegious man and impiously stabbed it with daggers and knives, in insult to Christ himself and the Christian Church, adding blasphemies that the God of the Christians had no blood. Yet blood flowed out miraculously, so that it could in no way be hidden. For this reason the wicked men were seized, and all of them were burned alive, except for a few who, having been sprinkled with holy baptism, were put to death by beheading the next day. But that sacrilegious seller was first torn with red-hot pincers and then burned alive.

units.la: Iohānes Friderico, dux Saxoniæ, senior et Elector, in quodā cōuentu secū habebat filiū Iohannē Fridericū (cū quo fuit captus à Carolo V. Imperatore) adolescentulū adhuc. Cùm is audiret papistā cōcionante de dicto Bibite ex hoc oēs, et monachos disputaret particulā Omnes, restringendā esse ad solos sacerdotes, dixit dux Iohannes Fridericus iunior: Si hæc uera sunt, tunc in hac sententia Beati omnes, qui confidunt in eo, uocabulum Omnes, etiam de solis sacerdotibus intelligendum esset. Ita ille eruditus dux adolescens consuluit papistam.
units.tr: John Frederick, the senior duke of Saxony and Elector, was at a certain assembly with his son John Frederick, still a young man, who was captured with him by the Emperor Charles V. When the boy heard a Papist preaching about the words "Drink ye all of this," and the monks arguing that the word "all" must be restricted to priests alone, Duke John Frederick the younger said: "If these things are true, then in that saying 'Blessed are all who trust in him,' the word 'all' would also have to be understood as referring only to priests." Thus that learned young duke confuted the Papist.

units.la: Stuggardiæ fuit cōsuetudo, ut pastor Ecclesiæ quotannis à capitulo Constantiensi peteret potestatem sacramenta administrandi, sed quia magni sunt reditus
units.tr: At Stuttgart it was the custom that the minister of the church asked the chapter of Constance each year for the power to administer the sacraments. But because the income is large

units.la: {g} {z} marks in the margin of the text, not legible in detail. reditus (habet enim pastor quotānis circiter 800 florenos) princeps parochiam adolescenti cuidam nobili commendauit. (Antea autem docti uiri, ut Nauclerus, & alij, habuerunt illos reditus, & Brentius habet nunc eosdem.) Sed nobilis ille uenabatur, nec Ecclesiam curabat, atq; ita neglexit morem petendi administrationem Sacramentorum. Orta est igitur quaestio inter Theologos, an illi, qui interea temporis, dum fuit mos neglectus, usi fuerant sacramento, recte cœnam Domini sumpsissent? Ibi aliqui indocti disputauerunt, quòd non uero sacramento usi fuissent, sed doctiores, ut Capnio & alij quidam, dixerunt: Quamuis consuetudo petendi, ac ius porrigēdi sacramenta neglecta fuisset, nihilominus ueram administrationem facta fuisse. Nam ea, quae sunt iuris diuini, non mutantur, etiāsi aliqua traditio humana negligatur, praesertim quae non facta est ex contemptu. Hæc acciderunt, cùm D. Philippus ibi uiuerēt.
units.tr: {g} {z} marks in the margin of the text, not legible in detail. the income (for the minister receives about 800 florins each year), the prince committed the parish to a certain young nobleman. Earlier, learned men such as Nauclerus and others held that income, and Brentius holds the same income now. But that nobleman was given to hunting and did not care for the church, and so he neglected the custom of asking for the administration of the sacraments. A question therefore arose among the theologians: had those who, in the meantime, while the custom was neglected, received the sacrament, rightly taken the Lord's Supper? Some unlearned men argued that they had not in fact received a true sacrament. But the more learned, such as Capnio and certain others, said: "Although the custom of asking and the right of offering the sacraments had been neglected, nevertheless a true administration had taken place. For those things which are of divine right do not change, even if some human tradition is neglected, especially when it was not neglected out of contempt." These things happened while Master Philip was living there.

units.la: Quidam insignis monarcha comiti Vuilhelmo de Nassau, disputanti cum eo de multis Papisticæ doctrinæ erroribus, qui irrepserunt in Ecclesiam, cùm diu de multis tacuisset, & familiariter Comitem loquentem audiuisset, & tandem uentum esset ad reprehensionem Missæ, dixit: Vuilhelme, Missā mihi relinquas oportet: ea enim mihi, perinde atq; tor meum, chara est.
units.tr: A certain distinguished monarch, when Count William of Nassau was disputing with him about the many errors of Papist doctrine which had crept into the Church, had kept silent for a long time about many matters and had listened to the count speaking in a familiar way. At last they came to the criticism of the Mass, and he said: "William, you must leave me the Mass, for it is as dear to me as my necklace."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: De coena Domini.
units.tr: On the Lord's Supper.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Episcopus quidam Moguntinus ceperat quos- dam, qui sub utraq; specie usi erant Eucharistia, eosq; iussit conijci in carcerem,uolens ipsos fame necare. Quare mandauit procul illis ostendi panē & uinum,additis his uerbis:Accipite,comedite:ac cipite,bibite.
units.tr: A certain bishop of Mainz had seized some people who received the Eucharist in both kinds and ordered them thrown into prison, intending to starve them to death. He then had bread and wine shown to them from a distance, with these words added: "Take, eat; take, drink."

units.la: Habebamus Tubingæ Doctorem Theologiæ, uirum senem,qui pingebat nobis transsubstantia- tionem. Si tantùm adpinxisset aures asininas, re- ctè fecisset.
units.tr: We had at Tübingen a doctor of theology, an old man, who painted transubstantiation for us. If he had only painted asses' ears on it, he would have done right.

units.la: Quando Papa est in magna pompa, præcedit ipsum equus gestans panem consecratum in arcu- la,ϲὺν πυξωτίῳ, in der monstrantzen, ut ipse adore tur cum illo pane. Pompa illa à Persis sumpta est.
units.tr: When the Pope goes in great pomp, a horse carries the consecrated bread in a little case, in the monstrance (in der monstrantzen), so that he may be adored along with that bread. That pageant was taken over from the Persians.

units.la: Cùm essemus in conuentu Ratisbonensi,et hanc assereremus propositionē:Nihil habere rationē sa cramēti extra usum à Deo institutū. Ibi ipse ualde acerbè et acriter cōtra me disputabat. Postea cū fir missimis argūmētis esset cōuictus veritate,nec pos set amplius aliquid cōtradicere, ad tantā iram est adductus, ut supplosione pedum, & concussione manuum uideretur rem defensurus esse: & tandē uerò astantibus Granuelo & Electore Friderico ad Rhenum,alijsq; non infimæ authoriꝛtatis uiris dixit: Ego tamen tecum disputabo usq; ad ignem. Ita ira incensus,accessit ad Mundinensem ,qui nūc est Cardinalis, tunc erat episcopus Mundinæ, qui habebat optima uina Italica, apud quē largissimè bibit. Altero die dicebatur esse mortuus, cùm tantū decubuisset in acerrimo paroxismo, ita ut postea non potuerit recuperare ualetudinem, donec paulo post moreretur.
units.tr: When we were at the Regensburg assembly and I maintained this proposition, that nothing has the nature of a sacrament apart from the use instituted by God, he himself disputed against me very bitterly and fiercely. Afterwards, when he had been convicted by the truth of the most solid arguments and could contradict nothing further, he was driven to such anger that he seemed about to defend his case by stamping his feet and clapping his hands. Finally, with Granvelle and Elector Frederick on the Rhine standing by, and other men of no small authority present, he said: "Yet I will dispute with you even to the fire." Inflamed with anger in this way, he went to the Mundinensis, who is now a cardinal but was then bishop of Munda, and who had excellent Italian wines, and he drank very freely with him. The next day he was said to be dead, for he had collapsed in a most severe paroxysm, so that afterwards he could not recover his health, and shortly after he died.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Anno 1553 fuit minister cuiusdam sartoris Lipsiæ, qui cùm antea coena Domini usus esset utraque specie, postea persuasus sub Papatu una specie sumpserat.
