Deinceps uerò Lipsiæ rursus admonitus à suo sartore, ut ad sacra σωάξιν accederet, diu nihil respondit: tandem uerò cum ingenti & horribili boatu exclamat: O', ô, ego sum perpetuū diaboli mancipium, & cum impetu se per fenestrā præcipitauit, ita ut omnia sua uiscera interiora effunderet. Sic horribili morte est extinctus.
units.tr: In 1553 there was a journeyman of a certain tailor at Leipzig who, having previously received the Lord's Supper in both kinds, was later persuaded under the Papacy to take it in one kind only. Afterwards at Leipzig, admonished again by his master the tailor to approach the holy communion [σύναξις], he answered nothing for a long time. At last, with a huge and horrible roar, he cried out: "O, o, I am the devil's slave forever!" and threw himself headlong through the window, so that all his inner organs spilled out. He died a horrible death.

units.la: Quidā in Italia ut gratificaretur episcopo, sumpsit unicā speciē coena Domini (& usus est manca & mutila coena, qualē aduersarij nostri solēt populo distribuere) qui aliàs de reliqua doctrina Christiana nō male sentiebat. Mox ubi redijt domū, incidit in grauissimū morbū, & cùm decumberet in lecto, repetiuit sæpè hanc uocem: Ah, inquit, fieri non potest, ut remissionem peccatorum consequar: quia filius Dei factus est mihi aduersarius, & aduersa fronte mihi repugnat, accusans me coram æterno patre periurij & defectionis, quoniam ipsum negaui. Et cùm ipse mihi hostili animo repugnet, quæ potest esse spes reconciliationis? Si Christus pro me intercederet apud Deum, sicut pro aliis peccatoribus intercedit, & fungeretur officio Mediatoris & deprecatoris, bonam spem conciperem, fore, ut Deus mihi reconciliaretur, placatus precibus Filij. Sed cùm hic hostilem impressionem in me facit, cogor omnem spem salutis abijcere. Hac uoce subinde repetita, tandem miserabiliter extinctus est.
units.tr: In Italy someone, to please a bishop, took the Lord's Supper in one kind only (and it was a maimed and mutilated supper, of the sort our opponents usually distribute to the people). In other respects he did not think badly of the rest of Christian doctrine. As soon as he returned home he fell into a very grave illness, and while lying in bed he repeatedly cried out: "Ah, it cannot be that I obtain forgiveness of sins, for the Son of God has become my adversary and opposes me with a hostile face, accusing me before the eternal Father of perjury and apostasy, since I denied him. And since he resists me with a hostile mind, what hope of reconciliation can there be? If Christ were interceding for me with God, as he intercedes for other sinners, and performing the office of Mediator and advocate, I would conceive good hope that God would be reconciled to me, appeased by the prayers of the Son. But since he makes a hostile attack on me, I am forced to abandon every hope of salvation." Repeating this cry from time to time, he at last died wretchedly.

units.la: In bello Neapolitano, quod fuit ante quadraginta annos (in quo fuit ille senex, honestus ciuis, Roslerus) in castris magna fuit penuria aquæ. Milites dederunt panem consecratum asino, præcipitauerunt ipsum in mare, ut cieret aquas. Is in mare delapsus ciuit tantas tempestates, ut omnes perituros esse cogitauerint. Postea semper superfluam aquam habuerunt. Ita uidetis quid superstitio hominum efficiat.
units.tr: In the Neapolitan war, forty years ago (in which that old man, an honest citizen, Rosler, took part), there was great shortage of water in the camp. The soldiers gave consecrated bread to an ass and threw it into the sea, to stir up the waters. The ass, once fallen into the sea, stirred up such storms that everyone thought they would perish. Afterwards they always had more water than they needed. So you see what superstition of men can bring about.

units.la: DE SACRIFI-cijs.
units.tr: CONCERNING SACRIFICES.

units.la: Omnes gentes mactauerunt humanas hostias. Huiusmodi horrenda commiserunt per καταλλαγὴν, ubi homines sine mandato & absque ratione imitati sunt Patrum exempla: sicus sicut iam multi imitantur exemplum Lutheri. Quidam putant se similes esse Prophetis, quando omnibus maledicunt, ignorantes interim quid dicant.
units.tr: All nations have slaughtered human victims. They committed these horrors by way of reconciliation [καταλλαγή], when men, without command and without reason, imitated the examples of the Fathers, just as many now imitate the example of Luther. Some think they are like the Prophets when they curse everyone, while not knowing what they are saying.

units.la: Audiui Albertum Durerum narrantem, Hieronymum Hirs fuisse in insula quadam, ubi quotannis solebat fieri humanae hostiae, & diabolus clara uoce unum deposcebat.
units.tr: I heard Albrecht Dürer relate that Hieronymus Hirs was on a certain island where human victims used to be offered every year, and the devil demanded one with a loud voice.

units.la: Sextus Pompeius, cum hostem quendam suum in littore nauali uicisset, mersit in mari quinquaginta candidos equos, quos ita Neptuno sacrificare uoluit.
units.tr: Sextus Pompeius, having defeated an enemy of his on the shore of a naval station, sank fifty white horses in the sea, wishing to sacrifice them thus to Neptune.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: In Hungaria magnum habebant quaestum ex sacris funebribus. Interdum Parochi uno anno centum tauros accipiebant, & singulos quatuor aut quinque aureis uendebant. Apud nos etiam cum celebrarent ἀνυστάσια, homines multum panis, uini, & carnis offerebant. In summa, illa iusta & sacra fuerunt quaestuosa sacrificulis.
units.tr: In Hungary the priests made a great profit from funeral rites. Sometimes parish priests received a hundred oxen in one year and sold each one for four or five gold coins. Among us too, when they celebrated memorial feasts [ἀνυστάσια], people offered much bread, wine and meat. In short, those funeral rites, however right and sacred they were called, were profitable to the little sacrificers.

units.la: Cordatus, cum dicerem in lectione de ἐπιεικείᾳ, ubi Paulus dicit de sacrificijs familiarum, quae est satis larga, quam nunc nemo concederet, etiam quantumuis diues & indulgens, finita lectione pransus est mecum: & interrogaui eum, an ipse quoq; talia concederet? Ille respondit: Non certè facerem.
units.tr: When I was lecturing on forbearance [ἐπιείκεια] and said that Paul, in the passage where he speaks of the sacrifices of households, grants a fairly wide licence, one that no one would now concede, however wealthy and indulgent, Cordatus dined with me after the lecture. I asked him whether he too would grant such things. He replied: "Certainly I would not."

units.la: Eccius in conuentu Augustano, in consessu principum cipum, obiecit mihi argumentum tale ex Iesu Sy-rach, capite quinto: Non sis securus de propiciato peccato. Ergo semper de gratia dubitandum est. Respondi illi: Securitas opponitur duobus: scilicet doloris & dubitationi. Hic opponitur doloris. Non sis securus de propiciato peccato id est, semper maneat in te dolor admissi peccati. Hanc solutionem dedi in consessu principum, cui ipse acquieuit. Sed est responsio ad hominem, nō est realis. Vera solutio est, quòd textus loquitur de sacrificijs, id est, non consequeris externis sacrificijs, aut operibus sine fiducia mediatoris remissionem peccatorum, iusticiam & uitam aeternam. Et saepe sic necesse est dare solutiones ad homines, ubi non occurrunt reales, ut litigiosis & loquacibus imponatur silentium.
units.tr: At the Diet of Augsburg, in the assembly of princes, Eck objected to me an argument from Jesus Sirach, chapter five: "Do not be secure about a sin already forgiven." Therefore, he said, one must always doubt about grace. I answered him: security is opposed to two things, namely grief and doubt. Here it is opposed to grief. "Do not be secure about a sin forgiven" means that the grief over the sin committed must always remain in you. I gave this solution in the assembly of princes, and he himself assented to it. But it is an answer to the man, not a real one. The true solution is that the text speaks of sacrifices, that is, that you will not obtain forgiveness of sins, righteousness and eternal life by external sacrifices or by works without trust in the Mediator. And it is often necessary to give such solutions to men, where real ones do not occur to us, so that silence may be imposed on the quarrelsome and the talkative.

units.la: Magnates huius mundi plerunque sacrificia in pompam quandam & ostentationem conuertunt. Romanus quidam Imperator olim simul eodem tempore obtulit & mactauit mille tauros, mille leones, & mille aquilas. Hoc putarunt esse acceptissimum Deo sacrificium, & conuenientem & laudabilem tali imperio pompam & magnificentiam: cum interim ipsi astarent cum suis amasijs, nihil minus quàm diuinam gloriam quaerentes. Ita passim apud plerosque ceremoniae uertuntur in pompam.
units.tr: The great men of this world often turn sacrifices into a kind of pageant and display. A certain Roman emperor once offered and slaughtered at the same time a thousand bulls, a thousand lions and a thousand eagles. They thought this a sacrifice most acceptable to God, and a pomp and magnificence fitting and praiseworthy for such an empire, while meanwhile they themselves stood about with their mistresses, seeking anything rather than the glory of God. So in many places ceremonies are everywhere turned into pageantry.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam Rex, possecturus ad bellum Anglicum, & moturus castra, in principio itineris cremauit hominem propter religionem & confessionem uerae doctrinae, tanquam uictimam, ut felicius iter succederet.
units.tr: A certain king, about to make war on England and about to move his camp, at the start of the journey burned a man as a victim, because of his religion and his confession of the true doctrine, so that the journey might turn out more fortunately.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quaedam gentes in quodam loco Germaniae suos parentes senes ante 300 annos, tanquam inutilia terrae pondera iudicantes, sacrificarunt. Fertur enim, de quadam comitissa ibidem in quadam sylua iter faciente, talem parricidam deprehendisse, & parentem ab eo liberasse.
units.tr: Certain peoples in a certain place in Germany, judging their aged parents to be useless burdens on the earth, sacrificed them some three hundred years ago. For it is reported that a countess, travelling through a certain forest there, caught such a parricide and freed the parent from him.

units.la: DE CONFESSIONE & Absolutione.
units.tr: On Confession and Absolution.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Domino Doctore Luthero Erphordiae confessore existente, quaedam puella ex honesta familia & pudica, seruiuit cuidam mulieri diuiti uiduae, cuius filius adolescens, captus forma & amore puellae, sollicitauit eam ad concubitum. Indignum facinus auersans puella (sicut bonestam[?] decet) aliquoties à se repulit furiosum. viosum adolescentem: Denique cum quotidie magis magisque instaret, & in illicito proposito perseveraret, puella rei indignitate impulsa, ut famæ consuleret, & suam pudicitiam à summa infamia vindicaret, matri adolescentis rem ordine narrat, monet que ut filio insidias struenti frenum injiciat. Mater, re deliberata, iniuit rationem cum puella, & iubet eam in filij amorem consentire, ac certam horam noctis præscribere, ut hac occasione filium tam indigna conantem reprimeret. Consilio probat puella, inijtq; pactum simulatum cum filio. Filius, hora noctis constituta, se contulit ad locum propositum. Mater, quæ antea filij furores hac arte cohibere ac frenari secum constituerat, victa libidine & instinctu diaboli, filio corpus prostituit. Nascitur ex indigno incestu femella, quam expositam, & alio in loco clam educatam mater tandem ad se recipit. Idem filius omnium harum rerum ignarus, & hanc amare incipit, ducens eā in uxorem. Mater dubia & desperabunda in agone mortis, sentiens etiam conscientiæ morsum, peccata confitetur. Res igitur ad collegium Theologorum defertur. Cūq; diu de matre ambigeretur, ut in casu nō usitato, tandē lata est sententia ut afflictæ cōscientiæ matris cōsuleretur, cōmuni cōsensu totius collegij Theologici Erphordiensis. Mater itaq; cum adhortatione ad pœnitentiam & fidem absoluta est. Deinde statutum est, ut filio etiam matrimonium, iamdiu sponsalium solennitatibus, copulaq; carnali confirmatum, concederetur. Probauerunt docti uiri sententiā & decisionem Theologorum. Portam enim gratiæ seu absolutionis, ut nunc uocant, nunquam clausam debere esse peccatoribus, quibuscunq; peccatis sint contaminati, aut qualiacunq; peccata unquā perpetrauerint. Lauda uerunt etiā, rē occultè inter Theologos transactā.
units.tr: When Dr Luther was confessor at Erfurt, a girl from a respectable and chaste family was in service with a wealthy widow. The widow's young son, captivated by the girl's beauty and in love with her, pressed her to sleep with him. The girl, abhorring the shameful deed, repulsed the frenzied youth several times, as an honest woman should. At last, since he pressed harder every day and persisted in his unlawful purpose, the girl, moved by the outrageousness of the thing, and wishing to protect her reputation and save her chastity from utter disgrace, told the young man's mother the whole matter in order and urged her to curb her son as he plotted this. The mother, having considered the matter, came to an arrangement with the girl. She bade her feign consent to the son's love and fix a certain hour of the night, so that by this opportunity she might restrain her son from attempting such unworthy things. The girl approved the plan, and she made a pretended agreement with the son. When the appointed hour of night came, the son went to the place agreed. The mother, who had earlier resolved to check and restrain her son's frenzy by this stratagem, was overcome by lust and the prompting of the devil, and prostituted her body to her son. From this unworthy incest a daughter was born, whom the mother exposed, then had secretly raised in another place, and at last took back to her own home. The son, ignorant of all these things, began to love this girl and took her as his wife. The mother, doubtful and in despair in the agony of death, and also feeling the gnawing of conscience, confessed her sins. The matter was therefore referred to the college of theologians. Since the question about the mother was long debated, as being an unusual case, at last a judgment was given, by the common consent of the whole Erfurt theological college, that provision should be made for the troubled conscience of the mother. The mother was therefore absolved, with an exhortation to repentance and faith. Then it was decided that the son should also be granted marriage, which had long since been confirmed by the solemnities of betrothal and carnal union. The learned men approved the opinion and decision of the theologians. For the door of grace or absolution, as they now call it, ought never to be closed to sinners, however defiled they may be by their sins, or whatever sins they may ever have committed. They also praised the fact that the matter was settled secretly among the theologians.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Age tantum humanissime uir & candidissime amice, habes quod pollicitus sum, de Theologorum cautelis, sed propter temporis penuriam ad pauca redigo, & primùm historiam recito. ( hîc superior historia annexa erat) His postea adiecit Lutherus adhortationem, admonuitq; Theologos iuniores, qui fungerentur, uel aliquando functuri essent ministerio uerbi, ut cautè agerent cum pertur batis conscientijs, ne confitentibus peccata laqueum inijcerent, neq; afflictionem afflictis adderent. Visus est autem Lutherus hac ipsa historia reprehendere cuiusdam Theologi iniquam petulantiam in diuerso casu, quem etiam breuibus recito. Pastor quendam adulterum ad magistratum detulit. Senatus illius loci, non habita ratione ulla circumstantiarum, apud iudices Lipsenses quærit de iure. Lipsenses, casu nudè intellecto, ferùt sententiam iudicij capitalis. Eam exequitur ille senatus, decollans miserum. Breui, ubi patefactum est, hunc proditum à pastore, iudices Lipsenses palmo diam cecinerunt, & decollato factam iniuriam affirmant. Non enim iudicium criminis reum agere aliquem posse, qui à sacerdote apud magistratum sit delatus ex confessione, ubi sola remissio peccatorum impertitur: non igitur ministerium esse gladij. Vide de eo in Decretatilibus c. Si sacerd. extra. de officio iudicis ordinarij. uerba eius capitis haec sunt: Si sacerdos sciat pro certo, aliquem esse reum alicuius criminis, uel si confessus fuerit, & emendare noluerit (nisi iudiciario ordine quis probare possit) non debet eum arguere nominatim, sed indeterminatè: sicut Christus inquit: Unus uestrum me proditurus est. Sed si ille cui damnum illatum est petiuerit iusticiam, poteris excommunicare authorem damni, licet etiam ei confessus sit: sed non nominatim potest eum remouere à communione, licet sciat eum esse reum: quia non ut iudex scit, sed ut Deus: uerùm debet eū admonere, ne se ingerat. quia nec Christus Iudam à communione remouit. Haec tibi simpliciter narranda magis, quàm declaranda existimaui. Quàm autem fuerit necessaria admonitio, ex rei magnitudine intelligi potest.
units.tr: Come now, most courteous sir and dearest friend, you have what I promised concerning the theologians' cautions. But because of shortness of time I reduce it to a few points, and first I recite the story. (Here the preceding story was attached.) Afterwards Luther added an exhortation to it, and admonished the younger theologians who were serving, or would one day serve, in the ministry of the Word, that they should act cautiously with troubled consciences, not to lay a snare for those confessing their sins, nor add affliction to the afflicted. Luther seemed, moreover, in this very story to rebuke the unjust rashness of a certain theologian in a different case, which I also recite briefly. A minister denounced a certain adulterer to the magistrate. The council of that place, without taking any account of the circumstances, sought the law from the judges of Leipzig. The Leipzig judges, having understood the bare fact, pronounced a sentence of capital judgment. That council carried it out, beheading the wretched man. Shortly afterwards, when it became known that this man had been betrayed by the minister, the Leipzig judges publicly sang their triumph and declared that a wrong had been done by the beheading. For a person who has been reported to the magistrate by a priest on the basis of confession, where only the remission of sins is bestowed, cannot be brought to trial for a crime; therefore the office does not belong to the sword. See about this in the Decretals, chapter "Si sacerdos", extra, "de officio iudicis ordinarii". The words of that chapter are these: If a priest knows for certain that someone is guilty of some crime, or if he has been confessed to and is unwilling to amend (unless someone can prove it by judicial order), he ought not to accuse him by name, but indefinitely, as Christ said: One of you is going to betray me. But if the person to whom the harm was done seeks justice, you may excommunicate the author of the damage, even though he has confessed to you; but you cannot remove him from communion by name, although you know him to be guilty, because you know it not as judge but as God; yet you ought to admonish him not to thrust himself forward, because Christ did not remove Judas from communion either. I thought these things were to be told to you plainly rather than explained. How necessary the admonition was may be understood from the greatness of the matter.

units.la: Quare eam tibi cogitandam relinquo. Vale feliciter; citer. Vuitebergæ pridie idus Martij, anno 1544.
units.tr: Therefore I leave it to you to consider. Farewell, and fare well. At Wittenberg, the day before the Ides of March, in the year 1544.

units.la: Quidā nos erant calumniati apud Marchionē Iohannem, bonū & ingeniosum principem, quòd doceremus reos manifestorū scelerū non esse absoluendos, antequā redijssent in gratiam cum suo pa-store, & dixerant hoc esse papisticum. Quod cùm ipse princeps mihi narraret, dicebā : Illustrissime princeps, qui perseuerant in sceleribus contra cō-scientiā, donec non abijciunt propositum peccādi, non possunt absolui. Vt cùm aliquis offendit alium, & indicit ei bellum non necessarium, & hostiliter ipsum persequitur, donec retinet illud propositum, non est absoluendus. Ita docemus, & rectè. Ibi prin-ceps respondit: Iam satis intelligo, hæc non iniquè aut falsè doceri.
units.tr: Some men had slandered us before Margrave John, a good and clever prince, on the ground that we taught that those guilty of manifest crimes should not be absolved until they had been reconciled with their minister; and they had said this was Papistical. When the prince himself told me this, I said: Most illustrious prince, those who persist in crimes against conscience, so long as they do not cast off the purpose of sinning, cannot be absolved. Suppose someone offends another and declares an unnecessary war on him and pursues him with hostility; so long as he keeps that purpose, he is not to be absolved. This is how we teach, and rightly. The prince replied: Now I understand well enough that these things are not taught unjustly or falsely.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Tecelius monachus, qui huc attulit indulgentias à Papa, ualde multa impudenter dixit, et non procul hinc rursus pulchrè à quodam est illusus, qui interrogauit ipsum, num haberet potestatē absoluendi à futuris delictis? & promisit ei decem thaleros. Ille respondit, esse rem ualde difficilem: sed tamen sibi datam esse plenam potestatem à Pontifice, nec posse hanc absolutionem tam parua pecunia emi. Quare ita acta res est, ut numeratis ui-ginti aut triginta thaleris, ille per literas absol-ueretur à peccato comittendo. Postea idem e-ques ques monacho in itinere struxit insidias, & omnè pecuniam, quam collegerat ex oppido, eripuit. Tecelius redijt in oppidum ad Magistratū, & accusauit prædonem: qui proferens has literas, excusauit factū, quòd sibi ab ipso hoc factū esset concessum. Hoc modo ille euasit, & alter commonefactus est ut ageret prudentius.
units.tr: Tetzel, the monk who brought the indulgences from the Pope here, said many things very shamelessly. Not far from here, someone else cleverly made a fool of him. This man asked him whether he had the power to absolve from future sins, and promised him ten thalers. Tetzel replied that it was a very difficult matter, but that the Pope had given him full power, and that such an absolution could not be bought for so small a sum. So the matter was settled: once twenty or thirty thalers had been counted out, the man would be absolved by letter from a sin he was yet to commit. Afterwards the same knight laid an ambush for the monk on his journey and snatched all the money he had collected in the town. Tetzel returned to the town and complained to the magistrate about the robber. The knight produced these letters and excused the deed, saying that it had been granted to him by Tetzel himself. In this way he escaped, and the monk was warned to act more prudently.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Origenes cum forte in Ecclesia lectionem inchoaturus esset, sedit diu gemens & lachrymans, ac tandem exclamat: Peccatori autem dixit Deus, quare enarras iusticias meas? Hanc uocem sæpe repetens, questus est, se multa inconsideratè disputasse: ac ueniam erratorum non solùm à Deo, sed etiam ab Ecclesia petiuit, quæ assidens seni, lachrymis declarabat, se luctu ipsius misericordia affici. Non enim alius dolor, in bona mente acrior existere potest, quàm quæ oritur ex conscientia contemptæ cœlestis doctrinæ.
units.tr: When Origen was about to begin a reading in the Church, he sat for a long time groaning and weeping, and at last cried out: "But to the sinner God said, Why do you recount my righteousnesses?" Repeating this saying often, he lamented that he had disputed many things inconsiderately. He sought forgiveness for his errors not only from God but also from the Church, which, sitting beside the old man, showed by its tears that it was moved with pity at his grief. For no other sorrow in a good mind can be keener than that which arises from the conscience of having despised heavenly doctrine.

units.la: DE SATISFACTIONE.
units.tr: ON SATISFACTION.

units.la: Fuit Canonicus, qui locauit multum pecuniæ duobus scholasticis, ut pro eo recitarent horas Canonicas tempore morbi, quo morbo moriebatur. Heydelbergæ Doctor Theologiæ recitabat quotidie horas canonicas, sæpe incumbens in aliam cogitationem, sicut erat occupatus negocijs publicis, cùm interrogaretur ubi esset ? interdum animaduertebat, interdum non.
units.tr: There was a canon who paid two scholars a good sum to recite the canonical hours on his behalf during the illness of which he died. At Heidelberg a Doctor of Theology recited the canonical hours every day, often drifting off into other thoughts, since he was busy with public affairs. When asked where he had got to, sometimes he noticed and sometimes he did not.

units.la: Politianus canonicus Florentinus interrogatus, an legisset horas canonicas? dixit: Semel perlegi istū librum, & nunquam peius collocaui tempus.
units.tr: Politianus, a canon of Florence, was asked whether he had read the canonical hours. He replied: "I read that book through once, and I never spent time worse."

units.la: Habui amitam honestam matronam Heydelbergæ, quæ narrabat nobis, se post mortem mariti grauidam sedisse ad focum solam, ubi cùm sederet mœsta, descendit per gradus longus & procerus monachus Franciscanus, unaq; cum eo maritus, qui simul conuenerunt ad focum. Maritus uxorem salutauit, iussitq; monachum ingredi in hypocaustum, se enim habere multa colloquenda cum coniuge. Ingresso monacho, coepit loqui de restitutione alicuius debiti, & alijs rebus. Cùm diu protraxisset sermonem, iussit uxorem sibi porrigere manum. Illa metuens noluit primò porrigere, sed tandem persuasa, porrigit ei manum, quam ille apprehensam ita combusit, ut ipsa fieret sicut carbo: & sic discessit ab ipsa. Hæc ipsa nobis sæpe narrauit. Ego & multi alij, adhuc uiuentes in patria mea, uidimus manum sic adustam.
units.tr: At Heidelberg I had an honest matron as my aunt, who told us that after her husband's death, while she was pregnant, she was sitting alone by the hearth. As she sat there sad, a tall, lanky Franciscan monk came down the stairs, and with him her husband, and the two of them came together to the hearth. The husband greeted his wife and told the monk to go into the heated room, since he had much to discuss with his wife. When the monk had gone in, he began to talk about the repayment of a certain debt and other matters. After he had drawn out the conversation for a long time, he ordered the woman to hold out her hand to him. Fearful, she at first refused, but at last, persuaded, she gave him her hand. He seized it and burned it so that it became like charcoal, and then he left her. She often told us this herself. I and many others, who are still living in my homeland, saw the hand so scorched.

units.la: Habui olim præceptorem quendam, bonum & doctum uirum, multis notum, qui fuit concionator in Pfortzeim, et mortuus est nō ante multos annos.
units.tr: I once had a certain teacher, a good and learned man known to many, who was a preacher at Pforzheim and died not many years ago.

units.la: Hic narrauit mihi, ad se (cùm habuisset suam primam missam) dormientem solùm in cubiculo, uenisse aliquoties spectrum, uoluisse passim in libris chartas, sæpe etiā attraxisse lectum, adeoq; ipsum uexasse, ut non amplius solus dormire ausus fuerit, sed orauerit alium ex uicinis, ut apud se dormiret. Sequenti nocte iterum uenit illud spectrum ante lectum, & satis diu uexauit ambos. Et quia uerò paulo ante mortuus erat, quidam ex suis cognatis concepit opinionem, oportere pro ipso missam celebrari. Habita pro eo missa, spectrū ipsum dereliquit, & non amplius est reuersus. Sunt diaboli tentationes & illusiones, quibus superstitiones & idolomaniam apud homines stabiliat.
units.tr: He told me that when he had said his first Mass, and was sleeping alone in his room, a spectre came several times. It tossed papers about among the books, often even dragged the bed, and harassed him so badly that he no longer dared to sleep alone, but asked someone from the neighbourhood to sleep in his room. The next night the spectre came again before the bed and tormented both of them for quite a while. Because he had died shortly before, one of his relatives formed the opinion that a Mass ought to be celebrated for him. After a Mass was said for him, the spectre left him and never returned. These are the temptations and illusions of the devil, by which he establishes superstitions and idolatry among men.

units.la: Veteres distribuerunt horas canonicas in Psalmum, Beati immaculati. Fuit bonum institutum. Spiræ in conuentu habebamus hospitium apud sacrificulum, qui norat meos parentes & maiores. Quia mane surgebam meo more, ille etiam surgebat ad recitationem horarum Canonicarum. Assidebam illi male crucianti suum Psalterium, tandemq; dicebam: Domine Petre (sic erat ei nomen) tu habes tres passiones: primò crucias Deum: secundò Dauidem: tertiò teipsum. Scio, inquit, ista, non itaq; debes mihi exprobrare: sed oportet me illas preces legere. Dicebam ipsi: Tu es iam senex, non deberes mane surgere, sed prolixè dormire. Quia matumatutinus somnus valde prodest, præsertim senibus. Postea quando surrexeris, repete orationem Dominicam, Symbolũ: & lege unum caput in Bi-blijs, vel psalmum Miserere, seu De profundis. Et dum ego hic adsum, prælegam tibi epistolam Pauli ad Timotheum. Ipse obtemperauit mihi ac dormi-bat diutius. Cùm surrexisseт, finitis precibus, exponebam ei discrimen Machometicæ doctrinæ & Christianæ. Cùm ita docerem illum, pene ut pue-rum: Ah bone Deus, inquit, nunquam credidissem tam bona fuisse in Paulo, quæ plane non intellexi: acquiescam igitur tibi. Sic mihi postea obtemperauit.
units.tr: The ancients divided the canonical hours among the psalm "Blessed are the undefiled." That was a good arrangement. At Speyer, during the diet, we had lodgings with a priest who knew my parents and ancestors. Since I got up early, as is my custom, he too got up to recite the canonical hours. I sat beside him as he struggled badly with his Psalter, and at last I said: "Lord Peter (that was his name), you have three sufferings: first you torment God, second David, and third yourself." "I know that," he said, "so you ought not to reproach me; but I must read those prayers." I said to him: "You are now an old man. You should not get up in the morning but sleep in late, for morning sleep is very beneficial, especially for the elderly. Afterwards, when you have got up, repeat the Lord's Prayer and the Creed, and read a chapter of the Bible, or the psalm Miserere or De profundis. While I am here, I will read you Paul's letter to Timothy." He obeyed me and slept longer. When he got up, and had finished his prayers, I explained to him the difference between Mohammedan and Christian doctrine. As I was teaching him this, almost as if he were a boy, he said: "Ah, good God! I would never have believed there were such good things in Paul, which I plainly did not understand. I will therefore submit to you." And afterwards he did obey me.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Non ante multos, annos quidam mortuus est Brandenburgi, qui post mortem venit semel in fo-ro ad suam coniugem, & iussit pro se canere mis-sas. Illa inquit: Vade, tu non es meus uir, sed es dia-bolus. Quo audito, ille ita evanuit. Est uera historia.
units.tr: Not many years ago a certain man died at Brandenburg. After his death he came once to his wife in the marketplace and ordered her to have Masses sung for him. She said: "Go away, you are not my husband but a devil." On hearing this he vanished. It is a true story.

units.la: Doctor Martinus Lutherus in principio suarum disputationum (cùm esset oneratus multi-plicibus lectionibus, responsionibus & prædicationibus, & non posset recitare quotidie suas horas Canonicas) die Sabbathi quando erat ei ocium à lectionibus, septies adhuc recitabat horas istas Canonicas. Surgebat enim mane hora secun-da, & ut poterat celeriter pronunciabat, continuabat nuabat[?] recitatione usque ad horam quartam vespertinam. Nos mirabamur laborem, quem nullus nostrum potuisset perferre. Ambidorfius ad eum dicebat: Quid est, D. Doctor, quòd ita istas horas recitas? Quia si peccasti omissione, iam non potest corrigi peccatum per recitationem: rectè argumentabatur. Et dixi ipse ad eum, me quidem non irasci labori, sed pertinaciae, quòd immoreretur stulto isti labori. Tunc respondit iocans: Profectò pulchrè me laudas, cùm tribuis mihi pertinaciam. Sic tamen admonitus, destitit tandem à tam inutili labore, cum aliis necessariis negocijs occuparetur.
units.tr: Doctor Martin Luther, at the start of his disputations, when he was burdened with many lectures, replies and sermons, and could not recite his canonical hours every day, still recited those canonical hours seven times on Saturdays, when he had leisure from lectures. He rose early, at the second hour, and recited them as quickly as he could, continuing the recitation until the fourth hour in the evening. We marvelled at the labour, which none of us could have endured. Amsdorf (Ambidorfius) said to him: "What is it, Doctor, that you recite the hours in this way? For if you have sinned by omission, the sin cannot be corrected by reciting them now." He reasoned correctly. And I said to him that I was not angry at the labour, but at the obstinacy with which he kept at that foolish toil. Then he replied in jest: "Indeed you praise me finely, when you ascribe obstinacy to me." Yet, so admonished, he at last gave up such a useless labour, as he was occupied with other necessary business.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: Collation (COLL.)

units.la: Sacrificulus quidam, cùm in lecto iaceret potus, coepit recitare horas suas, ut vocant, Canonicas, & interim uomens, uentris crepitum edidit. Ibi diabolus arridens dixit: Qualis est oratio, tale etiam est thus.
units.tr: A certain priest, lying drunk in bed, began to recite his hours, as they call them, the Canonical hours; and meanwhile, vomiting, he let out a fart. Then the devil, grinning, said: "Such as the prayer is, such also is the incense."

units.la: Mihi fuit acerrima contentio cum quodam Gardiano, qui dixit, sacerdotem debere tot horas Canonicas legere, quot haberet sacerdotia. Imò ne ipse quidem Canon illud praecipit.
units.tr: I once had a very sharp dispute with a certain warden, who said that a priest ought to read as many Canonical hours as he held benefices. Nay, the Canon itself does not even command that.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: Collation (COLL.)

units.la: Quidam Sacrificulus in monasterio, cum legen-dae essent horae Canonicae, nihil aliud egit, quàm ut recitaret Alphabetum. Interrogatus, cur non horas Canonicas recitaret? Respondit: Non intelligo eas. Quid ergo faciam? Ego, inquit, semper mane recito Alphabetum, & dico: O Domine Deus, accipe tibi has literas, & fac tibi ex his horas Canonicas.
units.tr: A certain priest in a monastery, when the Canonical hours were to be read, did nothing but recite the alphabet. Asked why he did not recite the Canonical hours, he answered: "I do not understand them. What then should I do? I," he said, "always recite the alphabet in the morning and say: 'O Lord God, take these letters to yourself and make the Canonical hours out of them for yourself.'"

units.la: Quidam strenuus Papistarum defensor, solet cucullam circumgestare in diebus Quadragesimæ. Non secus factum videtur, ac si quis lupo cucullā indueret. Hac enim ratione pro suis peccatis uult satisfacere.
units.tr: A certain zealous defender of the Papists is in the habit of wearing a cowl about during Lent. It seems no different than if someone were to put a cowl on a wolf, for by this method he wishes to make satisfaction for his sins.

units.la: Audiui adolescens hominis satis ingeniosi concionem. Is cùm deberet concionari de indulgentijs, & declamaret quid essent indulgentiæ, dicebat: Sicut in scholis sunt anteprædicamenta, ita in Ecclesia sunt antesacramenta, ut illæ preces ante Baptismū: uera autē sacramenta ut ipse baptismus. Sed satisfactio est postsacramētum, & huius postsacramenti postsacramentum est indulgentia.
units.tr: I once heard a sermon from a young man of quite considerable talent. When he was to preach about indulgences, and was explaining what indulgences were, he said: "As in the schools there are pre-predicaments, so in the Church there are pre-sacraments, like those prayers before baptism; the true sacraments are like baptism itself. But satisfaction is a post-sacrament, and of this post-sacrament the post-sacrament is indulgence."

units.la: Est enim indulgentia relaxatio ueterum canonum pœnitentialium. Vt si cui pœnitentiæ nomine iniunctum esset, ut sex hebdomadas ieiunaret: id episcopus relaxabat accepta pecunia. Hæ sunt indulgentiæ et remissiones canonum pœnitentialiū: & uocabantur satisfactiones: quæ paulatim in Ecclesia ita creuerunt, & sine modo cumularentur.
units.tr: For an indulgence is the relaxing of the ancient penitential canons. So if someone had been enjoined, by way of penance, to fast for six weeks, the bishop would relax this for money received. These are the indulgences and remissions of the penitential canons, and they were called satisfactions; these gradually grew in the Church in this way, and were piled up without limit.

units.la: Eccius concionatus est Lipsiæ de indulgentijs, dixit: Non sunt magnificiendæ, & tamen non sunt contemnendæ. Ista fuit summa suæ conclusionis.
units.tr: Eck preached at Leipzig about indulgences, and said: "They are not to be magnified, and yet they are not to be despised." That was the sum of his conclusion.

units.la: Princeps quidam adulter, pro satisfactione suorum delictorũ die Parasceues, quo passionis Christi memoria solet celebrari, bibebat cereuisiam absynthiacam. Ita illo cruciatu uolebat sua peccata abluere, etiamsi aliàs sibi nimium indulgeret.
units.tr: A certain adulterous prince, in satisfaction for his offences, on Good Friday, the day on which the memory of Christ's passion is usually celebrated, drank wormwood beer. He wished by that torment to wash away his sins, even though otherwise he indulged himself too much.

units.la: Alloquebar fortè monialem: Cur, inquiens, recitatis preces, & cantilenas canitis non intellectas? Respondit illa: Ey, Deus noster bene intelligit. Sic uolebat fantasias ex satisfactione pro peccatis ortas eludere.
units.tr: I happened to speak with a nun: "Why," I said, "do you recite prayers and sing songs you do not understand?" She answered: "Ah, our God understands them well." In this way she wished to ward off the scruples arising from satisfaction for sins.

units.la: Domina Margaretha Imperatoris amita, ante annos uiginti in conuentu Augustano ordinauit, ut per totum annum corpus conseruaretur (sicut illi habent unguenta & aromata, quæ prohibent putrefactionem) & in monasterium monialium gestaretur in templum, & ad singulas horas Canonicas proponeretur ei cibus & potus, ut infimis monialibus. Habebat enim hanc imaginationem, quòd obseruatione talium rituum satisfactura esset pro suis peccatis, & etiam melius habitura in altera uita. Quod decretum Imperator rescisccns, statim aboleuit, & eam sepeliri curauit.
units.tr: Lady Margaret, aunt of the Emperor, twenty years ago at the Diet of Augsburg ordered that her body be preserved for the whole year (as they treat bodies with unguents and spices that prevent putrefaction), and that it be carried into the church of a convent of nuns, and at each of the Canonical hours food and drink be set before her, just as for the lowest of the nuns. For she held this notion, that by observing such rites she would make satisfaction for her sins, and would also fare better in the other life. When the Emperor learned of this decree, he immediately abolished it and saw to it that she was buried.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: Collation (COLL.)

units.la: Hodie est consuetudo sacerdotum Turcicorum, ut se uulnerent et lacerent. Qua satisfactione existimant stimant se præstare Deo cultum ex opere operato.
units.tr: Today it is the custom of Turkish priests to wound and lacerate themselves. By this satisfaction they think they render to God a worship ex opere operato.

units.la: DE PRAEDESTINATIONE
units.tr: DE PRAEDESTINATIONE

units.la: Sunt pauci anni, quando Dominus pastor & ego habebamus literas à quodam, qui quere-batur se toties relabi in idem uitium adulterij, ut inciperet desperare de electione Dei, cum quo no-bis multum erat negocij. Scribebamus esse iudi-candum ex uerbo Dei. Deum uero omnes agen-tes pœnitentiam, credentes & confugientes ad filium Dei, et promissiones diuinas uniuersales fi-de apprehendentes, recipere. Respondebat: Hæc es-set res mirabilis, quod Deus non haberet potestatem recipiendi & condemnandi quemcumq; uelit. Ve-rum Deus non est mendax, neq; tyrannus. Nos de-bemus de Deo sentire sicut se patefecit in uerbo suo. In huiusmodi tentationibus pulchrè etiam consulit Basilius in concione de filio prodigo: Tantum ue-lis, & Deus tibi præoccurret.
units.tr: A few years ago, when the Lord minister and I were at home, we received a letter from a man who complained that he kept relapsing into the same sin of adultery, so that he was beginning to despair of God's election. This case gave us a good deal of trouble. We wrote back that the matter must be judged by the Word of God, and that God receives all who repent, who believe and take refuge in the Son of God, and who lay hold of the universal divine promises by faith. He replied that it would be a strange thing if God had no power to receive and condemn whomever he wishes. But God is neither a liar nor a tyrant. We must think of God as he has revealed himself in his Word. In temptations of this kind Basil also gives excellent counsel in his sermon on the prodigal son: "Only will it, and God will run to meet you."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Prædestinatio est secreta sententia, qua Deus eligit aliquos ad uitam æternam.
units.tr: Predestination is the secret decree by which God chooses some to eternal life.

units.la: Causa efficiens, est æterna Dei uoluntas, ordinàs Christum, ut sit uictima pro saluandis, & propter Christum eligens aliquos gratuita misericordia.
units.tr: The efficient cause is the eternal will of God, which ordained Christ to be the victim for those who are to be saved, and which elects some, on account of Christ, by free mercy.

units.la: Materia circa quam, sunt angeli & homines electi. Non est autem electio universalis, iuxta illud: Multi sunt vocati, pauci vero electi.
units.tr: The matter concerning which predestination is exercised is the elect angels and men. Election, however, is not universal, according to the words: "Many are called, but few are chosen."

units.la: Causa vero discriminis cur aliqui eligantur, aliqui vero improbentur, non est ex voluntate Dei prorsus, quia promissio est universalis quod ad voluntatem Dei attinet. Deus vult omnes homines salvos fieri: sed aliquo modo (loquor de nostro iudicio ex verbo) causa discriminis et reprobationis, in nobis hominibus est, cum repugnamus verbo Dei. Electionis causa est, cum non repugnamus verbo, sed assentimur & promissionem fide accipimus. Ita necesse est scire, quod promissio sit universalis: hoc nisi retineatur, non potest effici fides: quia hanc oportet effici per verbum.
units.tr: As for the cause of the difference, why some are chosen and others rejected, it does not lie entirely in the will of God, since the promise is universal as far as God's will is concerned. God wills that all men be saved. But in a certain way (I speak according to our judgement from the Word) the cause of the difference and of reprobation lies in us men, when we resist the Word of God. The cause of election lies in us when we do not resist the Word but assent to it and receive the promise by faith. Thus it is necessary to know that the promise is universal; unless this is maintained, faith cannot be produced, since faith must be produced through the Word.

units.la: Formalis, est cogitatio in Deo seu Dei propositum.
units.tr: The formal cause is the thought in God, or God's purpose.

units.la: Finalis est salvatio, & sicut is finis est praedestinationis, ita idem finis est vocationis, & iustificationis. Nemo salvatur, nisi prius vocatus & praedestinatus.
units.tr: The final cause is salvation. Just as salvation is the end of predestination, so it is also the end of calling and justification. No one is saved unless he has first been called and predestined.

units.la: Effectus, est vocatio per verbum, iustificatio, donatio Spiritus sancti, renovatio & glorificatio.
units.tr: The effects are calling through the Word, justification, the gift of the Holy Spirit, renewal and glorification.

units.la: D. Martinus Lutherus.
units.tr: Doctor Martin Luther.

units.la: Non sis sollicitus de Dei praedestinatione, neque curiosè in hoc Dei sacrarium erumpas. Non enim poteris pro hebetudine oculorum tuorum tam alta mysteria tuo ingenio penetrare: sed audi Christum, in quo pater secretam suæ praedestinationis sententiam aperuit, in quo reuelatum [illegible, ~3 letters] diu
units.tr: Do not be anxious about God's predestination, and do not pry curiously into this sanctuary of God. For with your dull eyes you will not be able to penetrate such deep mysteries with your intellect. Instead, hear Christ, in whom the Father has opened the secret decree of his predestination, which had long lain hidden. Christ is to be heard.

units.la: b 4 diu Christus audiendus. diu latuerat. Nam per Christum certi facti sumus, omnem credentem à Patre esse prædestinatum. Quē enim prædestinauit, eū & uocauit per Euan-gelium, ut credat, & per fidem iustificetur. Pro-inde noli curare, an sis prædestinatus: cura po-tius ut credas in Christum, & per eum iustificeris, & hinc certus eris, te per Deum esse electum & prædestinatum. Pater non iudicat quenquam in-quit Christus apud Ioānē. Proinde, cùm animi an-guntur, et turbantur cura prædestinationis, ex hoc loco conscientiæ suæ pacem & solatium petant. Nam uerum est, Deum aliquos ex hominibus aliàs reiectis ad uitam æternam elegisse & destinasse antequam iacerentur fundamenta mundi: sed quia Deus in abscondito habitat, & iudicia eius occulta sunt, nec licet nobis tantam profunditatem assequi, itaque ad Christum est discedendum, cui Pater omne iudicium dedit, & in quo nobis reue-lauit occultam prædestinationis suæ sententiam.
units.tr: For through Christ we are made certain that every believer has been predestined by the Father. For whom he has predestined, them he also calls through the Gospel, that they may believe and be justified through faith. Therefore do not worry whether you are predestined; rather take care to believe in Christ and to be justified through him, and from this you will be certain that you are elect and predestined by God. "The Father judges no one," Christ says in John. Therefore, when souls are troubled and disturbed by the care of predestination, let them seek peace and comfort for their conscience from this passage. For it is true that God has chosen and destined some men, passed over others, to eternal life before the foundations of the world were laid; but because God dwells in secret and his judgements are hidden, and we cannot attain to such depth, we must withdraw to Christ, to whom the Father has given all judgement, and in whom he has revealed to us the hidden decree of his predestination.

units.la: Iam si te in Christo per fidem inueneris, in Christo electus es: sed si persequeris uerbum, & Christum contemnas aut ignores, scias te reiectum esse. Nã qualem te in Christo inueneris, talis es in Deo: quia Pater omne iudicium dedit Filio. Hoc est au-tem iudicium in Christo reuelatum, credentes sal-uari, incredulos autem condemnari. Nam uide quid illud sit, quod in Psalmo canitur: Cùm peruerso peruersus eris, et cū electo electus eris. Cæterum si diuino captu, quantum ad Dei immutabilitatem attinet, loquendum erit, firma sit sententia, quem Deus ante conditum mundum elegerit, eum non posse perire: (nemo eum rapiet de manu huius pa storis) quem uero reiecerit, eum non posse saluari, etiamsi omnia opera sanctorum fecerit: usq; adeo intractabilis est sententia Dei. Tu igitur in solam Domini eligentis misericordiam respice, ut salute per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum consequa ris. Augustinus: Prædestinatio Dei etsi apud nos, qui in præsentis uitæ periculis uersamur, incerta est, apud illum tamen qui fecit futura, incom-mutabilis permanet. Nec qui illuminauit, obcæcat: nec qui ædificauit, dissoluit: nec q plātauit, euellit. Ἀμεταμέλητα enim sunt dona & uocatio Dei, & firmum fundamentum Domini stat, habens signaculum hoc: Cognouit Dominus, qui sunt eius. Nullo ergo modo prædestinatio Dei facit, ut aliqui ex filijs Dei sint filij diaboli, aut ex templo Spiritus sancti templa facit dæmonum, aut ex membris Christi membra meretricum. Sed potius prædestinatio facit, ut ex filijs diaboli fiant filij Dei, & ex templo dæmonum templum Spiritus sancti, & ex membris meretricis fiant menbra Christi, quia ipse alligat fortem, & uasa eius rapit, eruens ea de potestate tenebrarum, & transferens ipsum de contu-melia tumelia in gloriam. Hic autem, de quibus dicitur, ex nobis exierunt, sed non erant ex nobis. Si enim fuissent ex nobis, mansissent utiq; nobiscum: uoluntate exierunt, uoluntate reciderunt: & quia profecti sunt, non sunt prædestinati. Essent aut prædestinati, si essent reuersuri, & in sanctitate & veritate permansuri. At prædestinatio multis causa est standi, nemini causa labendi.
units.tr: Now if you find yourself in Christ through faith, you are elect in Christ. But if you persist in despising the Word and despise or ignore Christ, know that you are rejected. For what you find yourself to be in Christ, such you are in God, since the Father has given all judgement to the Son. This judgement is revealed in Christ: those who believe are saved, and the unbelieving are condemned. See what that means in the Psalm which is sung: "With the froward you will show yourself froward, and with the elect you will be elect." Otherwise, if we must speak in terms of the divine comprehension, as far as God's immutability is concerned, the decision is firm: whom God has elected before the world was made cannot perish (no one will snatch him out of the hand of this shepherd); but whom he has rejected cannot be saved, even if he does all the works of the saints. So intractable is the decree of God. Therefore look only to the mercy of the Lord who elects, so that you may obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ. Augustine: "The predestination of God, although it is uncertain to us who live amid the dangers of the present life, nevertheless remains unchangeable before him who made the future. Neither does he who has enlightened blind anyone, nor does he who has built tear down, nor does he who has planted uproot. For the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable [ἀμεταμέλητα], and the firm foundation of the Lord stands, bearing this seal: The Lord knows those who are his. Therefore by no means does the predestination of God make some of the sons of God sons of the devil, or make temples of demons out of the temple of the Holy Spirit, or make members of harlots out of the members of Christ. Rather, predestination makes sons of the devil become sons of God, and temples of demons become temples of the Holy Spirit, and members of the harlot become members of Christ, because he binds the strong man and plunders his vessels, rescuing them from the power of darkness and transferring them from dishonour into glory. But those of whom it is said, 'They went out from us, but they were not of us,' for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us; they departed by their own will, they fell away by their own will, and because they went out, they were not predestined. They would have been predestined if they were going to return and remain in holiness and truth. But predestination is a cause of standing for many, and a cause of falling for no one.

units.la: DE RESVRRECTIONE mortuorum.
units.tr: On the Resurrection of the dead.

units.la: Certissimum argumentum, & ferè indissolubile, quòd anima sit immortalis.
units.tr: A most certain argument, and almost indissoluble, that the soul is immortal.

units.la: Homo debebat seipsum nosse, & omnes partes animæ ipsius habere perspectas: At hoc in hac uita non fit: Necesse est igitur restare aliam uitam ubi fiet.
units.tr: Man ought to know himself and to have all the parts of his soul thoroughly examined. But this does not happen in this life. It is necessary, therefore, that another life remain in which it will happen.

units.la: Aliud, idem probans.
units.tr: Another argument proving the same.

units.la: Oportet legem impleri: nisi enim hoc aliquando fiat, frustra lata est lex: At in hac uita non impletur: Ergo restat alia uita in qua implebitur.
units.tr: The law must be fulfilled. For unless this happens at some time, the law was given in vain. But in this life it is not fulfilled. Therefore another life remains in which it will be fulfilled.

units.la: Hoc argumentum pene est demonstratio, pulchrius etiam atq; firmius illo Platonico, quo ab illo affirmatur immortalitas animæ. Inquit enim Plato: Impossibile est mentem factam esse ex elementari tari materia, cùm habeat insitas et innatas noticias quibus homo differt à brutis, &c.
units.tr: This argument is almost a demonstration, and more beautiful and firmer than that Platonic argument by which Plato affirms the immortality of the soul. For Plato says: It is impossible that the mind was made from elementary matter, since it has implanted and innate notions by which man differs from the brutes, etc.

units.la: Papa Leo, bonus Epicureus, cùm audiuisset in disputatione de resurrectione mortuorũ pro & contrà disputari in mensa, respondit: Bene disputastis, sed ego faciam mihi bonũ uultũ ( sic enim in aliis negocijs loqui solent Itali) et adiecit uersiculũ Cornelij Galli de homine morituro: Et redit in nihilũ, q; fuit ante nihil. Versus est bonus, sed sententia est mala. Nõ decebat serijs reb. ipsisq; fidei articulis huiusmodi nugas & phātasias immiscere, quemadmo dũ quidã nugati sunt, dicētes, quòd pecora sint resurrectura in extremo iudicio. Sic quidã in aula Pomeranica, cùm hæc ibi narrarentur, alteri nobili ioco illusit, dicēs. O quàm malè tecũ agetur in extremo iudicio, cũ resurrecturi sunt lepores, quorũ tu multos interfecisti. Tales postea ludi ex talibus disputationibus oriuntur.
units.tr: When Pope Leo, a good Epicurean, heard a disputation at table about the resurrection of the dead, argued for and against, he replied: "You have argued well, but I will put on a good face (for so the Italians are accustomed to speak in other matters)," and he added a little verse of Cornelius Gallus about a man who must die: "And he returns to nothing, which was before nothing." The verse is good, but the sentiment is bad. It was not fitting to mix such trifles and fancies into serious matters and into the articles of faith itself, as some have trifled by saying that cattle will rise again at the last judgment. So too, in the court of Pomerania, when these things were being discussed there, a certain nobleman mocked another with a joke: "O how badly you will be treated at the last judgment, when the hares will rise again, many of which you have killed!" Such games arise afterwards from such disputations.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Iulius papa alebat duos in aula mēte captos, qui aliquādo cōtendebant de resurrectione mortuorũ. Cùm alter negabat esse resurrectionē mortuorũ, alter affirmabat. Tandē ambo prouocauerūt ad Papā, qui litē dirimeret. Papa uerò sic sententiā pronũciauit, rectè illũ dicere qui resurrectionē affirmaret, sed id afferre mentes tristes: alterum autem læta dicere, unde eo fieri mentes lætiores.
units.tr: Pope Julius maintained in his court two men who were out of their minds, and who sometimes quarrelled about the resurrection of the dead. When one denied that there is a resurrection of the dead, the other affirmed it. At last both appealed to the Pope, to settle the dispute. The Pope pronounced this judgment: the one who affirmed the resurrection spoke rightly, but that doctrine brings sad minds; the other, however, spoke of joyful things, whence his mind becomes happier.

units.la: DE CALAMITATIBVS & Afflictionibus.
units.tr: On Calamities and Afflictions.

units.la: INtueamur nostru Imperatore potentissimum et fortunatissimu Carolu V.nemo est,qui optaret accipere eius regna simul cu eius morbis. Ego quide laboro: sed nullo modo tam grauiter.Ipse dixit,mirari se quomodo uiuat. Miru est,homine ta fragilem tam multas miserias & morbos sustinere. Cogitate solam historiam de naufragio : quantam calamitatem sustinuit? Vidit nauem interire in suo conspectu,post triduum ipsius nauis cum alijs appellitur ad insulam, in qua est cõmoratus donec oblata maris tranquillitate nauigaret in Italiam.
units.tr: Let us look at our most powerful and most fortunate emperor, Charles V. No one would want to receive his kingdoms together with his diseases. I myself suffer, but not nearly so gravely. He himself said he wondered how he was still alive. It is remarkable that a man so frail endures so many miseries and diseases. Consider only the story of his shipwreck: what a calamity he endured! He saw the ship sink before his eyes. After three days he and the others were carried to an island, where he stayed until the sea grew calm and he could sail to Italy.

units.la: Noui bonum principem, qui ante paucos annos post acceptam cladem dicebat: Video me iam despectiorem esse quàm antea. Verum est,quando homines in calamitatibus uersantur, tunc uaria iudicia de eis feruntur.
units.tr: I knew a good prince who, a few years ago, after suffering a defeat, said: "I see that I am now held in lower esteem than before." It is true that when men are caught up in calamities, various judgements are passed on them.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Extat Publij Mimi de fragilitate humarum uirium pulcherrimum dictum:Cuiuis potest contingere,quod cuiquam contigit.
units.tr: There is a most beautiful saying of Publius Mimus on the frailty of human strength: "What has happened to anyone can happen to anyone."

units.la: Versantes in calamitatibus ab omnibus conculcantur,iuxta illud:Δρυὸς πεσόντος πᾶς ἀνὴρ ξυλέ-νεσθαι, id est, quercu lapsa , quiuis lignum aufert. Cùm Achilles interfecisset Hectore, oës etiã ignauissimi missimi coniecerunt stercus in cadauer Hectoris.
units.tr: Those who are caught in calamities are trampled by everyone, according to the saying: "When the oak falls, every man goes to chop wood" [Δρυὸς πεσόντος πᾶς ἀνὴρ ξυλένεσθαι], that is, when the oak has fallen, anyone can carry off a piece of wood. When Achilles had killed Hector, even the most cowardly and worthless men threw dung on Hector's corpse.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Nunquam periculum sine periculo uitatur: ut est antiquum dictum. Sic nos quando nitimur mederi malis, tunc incidimus in alia, iuxta dictum: Incidit in Scyllam cupiens uitare Charydim.
units.tr: A danger is never avoided without danger, as the old saying goes. So when we strive to remedy evils, we fall into others, according to the saying: "He fell into Scylla while trying to avoid Charybdis."

units.la: Apud Euripidem in Phœnissis cum mater interrogaret Polynicem, an magnum malum esset exilium? Respondit Polynices: Imò maius est, quàm uerbis dici possit.
units.tr: In Euripides' Phoenissae, when his mother asked Polynices whether exile was a great evil, Polynices replied: "Indeed it is greater than can be told in words."

units.la: COLL. Nullus hominum sine calamitate.
units.tr: COLL. No one among men is without calamity.

units.la: Rex Artaxerxes, mortua concubina sua unicè à se dilecta, cum audiuisset in Ionia Democritum doctum hominem esse, misit ad cum legatos petitū, ut resuscitaret mortuam. Respondit Democritus: Rem est magna & difficilis, sed huic posset mederi, si rex pararet remedia, quibus opus esset.
units.tr: King Artaxerxes, after his concubine, whom he loved alone, had died, heard that Democritus, a learned man, was in Ionia. He sent envoys to ask him to restore the dead woman to life. Democritus replied: "The thing is great and difficult, but it could be remedied if the king provided the remedies that would be needed."

units.la: Cùm hoc responsum esset ad regem illatum, dixit rex se curaturū ut haberet remedia, si indicaret, quæ ad hæc necessaria essent. Democritus respondit: Triginta nomina hominum inscribēda esse sepulchro talium, qui singsuli prouenissent ad annū uigesimum & nihil dolorum experti fuissent: tum uerò concubinam suam reuicturam. Sed rex hæc nomina inuenire non potuit. Significatum est hac narnarratione, nullum hominem uicturum esse, qui nō aliquas huius uitæ ærumnas senserit.
units.tr: When this reply had been brought to the king, the king said he would see to it that he had the remedies, if Democritus would say what things were needed for them. Democritus replied that the names of thirty men must be inscribed on the tomb, of such men as had each lived to the twentieth year and had experienced no sorrows; then indeed his concubine would come back to life. But the king could not find these names. By this story it is signified that no man will live who has not felt some hardships of this life.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Boetius lib. 2.
units.tr: Boethius, book 2.

units.la: Constat æterna positum ǫ; lege est, Vt constet genitum nihil.
units.tr: It is fixed by eternal law that nothing begotten should endure.

units.la: Id est: hoc unū constat, & ratum ac firmum est lege æterna, ut nihil genitum constet, idest, firmum sit & æternum.
units.tr: That is: this one thing is established and certain by eternal law, that nothing begotten is constant, that is, that it is firm and eternal.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Plura sunt αὐθαίρετα, quàm αὐτόματα mala, ut cū Constantinus summus ille princeps, quo nescio an maior fuerit quis in terra, interfecit suũ filium principem, appetētem regnū ante tēpus. Illa mala sunt αὐθαίρετα quæ sibijpsi filius accersiuit.
units.tr: There are more self-inflicted [αὐθαίρετα] evils than chance [αὐτόματα] ones, as when Constantine, that great prince, than whom I do not know whether there was a greater on earth, killed his own son, a prince who was seeking the kingdom before his time. Those are self-inflicted evils which the son brought upon himself.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Ludouicus Pius filium suum præfecerat Mediolano, cuius magna industria fuit, ita ut peruenisset ad Imperium, si fortunam suā expectare potuisset: quia tenuit iam aliquam imperij partem mandato patris. Sed quia molitus est defectionem contra patrem, pater decollauit eum & quidem ille pater, qui re ipsa nominatus est Ludouicus Pius, cum aliàs fuerit placidus & tranquillus. Ita filius illa αὐτόματα mala accersiuit.
units.tr: Louis the Pious had placed his son over Milan. He was of great industry, so that he would have come to the empire if he had been able to await his fortune, since he already held some part of the empire by his father's command. But because he plotted rebellion against his father, the father had him beheaded. And indeed that father, who in fact was named Louis the Pious, though otherwise he was gentle and calm, did this. Thus the son brought upon himself those self-inflicted evils [αὐτόματα].

units.la: Xenophon.
units.tr: Xenophon.

units.la: Γαῦ προσδοκᾶν δεῖ, ἀνθρώπου ὄντα: id est omnia nia oportet expectare eum, qui est homo. Nota autem mala sunt optima: quia iacula praevisa minus laedunt.
units.tr: One must expect [Γαῦ προσδοκᾶν δεῖ, ἀνθρώπου ὄντα], being a human: that is, one must expect everything, since one is a man. It is worth noting too that foreseen evils are the best, since missiles seen coming do less harm.

units.la: Idem.
units.tr: The same.

units.la: Omnibus bonis dij duo mala adiunxerunt: praestissimi sua mala æquo animo ferre sciunt.
units.tr: The gods have attached two evils to every good man: the most excellent know how to bear their evils with an even mind.

units.la: COLL. Poena contra insolentiam, tempore calamitatum publicarum.
units.tr: COLL. Punishment against insolence in a time of public calamity.

units.la: Romani tempore belli Punici ciuem prospicientem de fenestra coronatum, iusserunt in carcerem duci, tali tempore delitijs indulgentem.
units.tr: In the time of the Punic war the Romans ordered a citizen, who was looking out of a window wearing a garland, to be led off to prison, since in such a time he was indulging in pleasures.

units.la: Terra plena petulantibus hominib.
units.tr: The land full of wanton men.

units.la: Nuper dixit ad me quidam bonus & sanctus uir: Heu quanta est petulantia hominum, ut terra eam non amplius possit sustinere. Sic ante bellum Troianum dicunt terram petiisse à Ioue, ut se ab onerib. imuti libus leuaret, quia nimium premeretur iniustitia: ita Iouem praebuisse huius belli causam.
units.tr: Recently a certain good and holy man said to me: "Alas, how great is the wantonness of men, so that the earth can no longer bear it." So, before the Trojan war, they say the earth asked Jove to relieve it of its useless burdens, since it was too heavily pressed by injustice; thus Jove provided the cause of that war.

units.la: DE FAME.
units.tr: On Famine.

units.la: Tempore Ottonis Imperatoris tanta fuit sterilitas passim in Germania per triennium, ut multa millia interierint fame. Unde etiam nunc Erphordiae quotannis pinsitur panis paruulus, in memoriam eius perniciae. Nihilominus nos manemus usque; a deo intemperantes, feri ac ingrati, ut quasi putemus nihil nobis opus esse diuino auxilio, ut nihil aliud dicam.
units.tr: In the time of the Emperor Otto there was such barrenness throughout Germany for three years that many thousands perished of hunger. Hence even now at Erfurt a small loaf is baked every year in memory of that destruction. Nevertheless we still remain intemperate, savage and ungrateful towards God, so that we seem to think we have no need of divine help, not to mention anything else.

units.la: Famis ingentis exemplum.
units.tr: Example of a great famine.

units.la: Vidi aliquando totum Senatum & omnes sacertes Tubingenses nudis pedibus incedere tempore famis.
units.tr: I once saw the whole Senate and all the beadles of Tübingen walking barefoot in a time of famine.

units.la: Conseruationis diuinæ, famis tempore exemplum.
units.tr: Example of divine preservation in a time of famine.

units.la: Cùm essem Tubingæ, fuit magna caritas an-nonæ. Veni eodem tempore ego & alij mei condi-scipuli in domum cuiusdam rustici, ubi uidebamus eos comedere rapas coctas cũ crudis. Quæsiuimus utrum haberet panem? Respondit se neque pecu-niam, neq; panem habere. Ibi intelleximus Deum tam mirabiliter rusticum & eius familiam seruare & nutrire. Nā omnes in ipsius familia erant satis robusti, etsi ipse fuerit aliquantulum macilentus. Cum postea adferret nobis ligna Tubingam, dedimus ei plus pecuniæ, quàm ipsi debebamus, ad suæ familia sustentationem.
units.tr: When I was at Tübingen there was a great dearth of grain. At the same time I and other fellow students came into the house of a certain countryman, where we saw them eating boiled turnips with raw ones. We asked whether he had any bread. He replied that he had neither money nor bread. There we understood that God preserves and nourishes this countryman and his family in a marvellous way. For all in his household were quite robust, although he himself was somewhat thin. Afterwards, when he brought firewood to us in Tübingen, we gave him more money than we owed him, for the support of his family.

units.la: Frumenta & non gramina nutri-re, exemplum illustre.
units.tr: Grain, not grass, nourishes: a notable example.

units.la: Ante annos 30 magna fames grassabatur Venetijs ac in tota Italia: nam annis tribus continua famis fuit. Finito autem bello Veneto ante coronationem Imperatoris Caroli V. tunc multi homines reperti sunt in uijs iacentes, & tenentes gramina in ore. Sic habetis perspicuum exemplū quòd frumenta & non gramina nutriant.
units.tr: Thirty years ago a great famine raged in Venice and throughout Italy, for there was continuous famine for three years. Then, when the Venetian war had ended, before the coronation of the Emperor Charles V, many people were found lying in the streets and holding grass in their mouths. So you have a clear example that grain, and not grass, nourishes.

units.la: Beneficentia senatus Argentinen- sis tempore famis.
units.tr: The generosity of the Strasbourg senate in a time of famine.

units.la: Anno 1517. magna fames fuit: eo tempore urbs Argentinensis fuit benefica, distribuens uenale frumentum ciuibus & uicinis pro mediocri precio, ut consuleretur saluti ac uitæ subditorum.
units.tr: In the year 1517 there was a great famine. At that time the city of Strasbourg was generous, distributing grain for sale to its citizens and neighbours at a moderate price, so that the health and lives of its subjects were looked after.

units.la: MORS PIORVM, EORVMque qui propter Christi doctrinam interficiuntur.
units.tr: The death of the godly, and of those who are killed for the teaching of Christ.

units.la: Pij principis ex hac uita decessus.
units.tr: The death of a pious prince.

units.la: Theodosius moriturus dixit, se quidem libenter discedere ex hac uita, defessum & defatigatum mole imperij, sed magis se iam sollicitum esse de Ecclesiæ statu post ipsum, quàm de sua uita: scire se, Ecclesiam habituram nouos prædones, sicut factum est. Valês enim expulit ex Ecclesia recte docentes. Valentinianus quidem defendit: sed tamen magna Imperij quassatio est facta.
units.tr: When Theodosius was about to die, he said that he was indeed glad to leave this life, weary and worn out by the burden of empire, but that he was now more anxious about the state of the Church after his death than about his own life. He knew that the Church would have new plunderers, as has happened: for Valens drove the sound teachers out of the Church. Valentinian indeed defended it, but still a great shaking of the empire followed.

units.la: Exemplum omnibus pijs in agone mortis proponendum.
units.tr: An example to be set before all the godly in the agony of death.

units.la: Quando dux Fridericus erat in agone mortis, iussit sibi grandioribus literis multas sententias consolationum in tabulam scribere: quas sæpè legit, ijsque se confirmauit. Si quis addidisset picturam triumphi umphi Christi, benefecisset, & credo quòd fuisset ei uoluptati. Sic piè & sanctè mortuus est, sentiens ingentes cruciatus calculi. Interrogatus, an alios dolores haberet? respondit. Habeo cor tranquillū: uerùm in carne habeo dolores maximos, quos fero propter Christum.
units.tr: When Duke Frederick was in the agony of death, he ordered many sentences of comfort to be written in large letters on a tablet. He often read them and strengthened himself by them. If someone had added a picture of Christ's triumph, he would have done well, and I believe it would have given him pleasure. So he died piously and holily, feeling the intense torments of the stone. When asked whether he had other pains, he replied: "I have a quiet heart, but in the flesh I have very great pains, which I bear for Christ's sake."

units.la: Versus Bembi consolationis plenus.
units.tr: Bembo's verses, full of consolation.

units.la: Bembus Venetus nobilissimo genere natus, scripsis carmen pulchrum de S. Stephano, in quo posuit hunc uersiculum de eo:
units.tr: Bembo the Venetian, born of a most noble family, wrote a fine poem about St Stephen, in which he placed this little verse about him:

units.la: Ibat ouans animis, & spe sua damna leuabat.
units.tr: He went forth rejoicing in spirit, and by his hope he lightened his losses.

units.la: Innocentis necis & patientiae exemplum.
units.tr: An example of innocent death and patience.

units.la: Fui in aliquo loco, ubi sumebatur supplicium de aliquot praestatissimis uiris: inter quos senior quondam uir cum flecteret genua (quanquam non posset per seipsum procumbere, sed utcunq; sustentabat eum lictor) praebens ceruicem iam lictori, postremò dicebat: O Domine Deus, ego multis meis magnis peccatis merui mortem & supplicia: sed tamen tu scis quòd in ista causa sim innocens. Dixit se habere conscientiam bonā, in illa causa propter quam occideretur.
units.tr: I was once in a place where punishment was being inflicted on several most distinguished men. Among them was an old man who, when he knelt down (although he could not lie down by himself, and the executioner's assistant held him up as well as he could), offered his neck to the executioner. At last he said: "O Lord God, by my many great sins I have deserved death and punishment, but still you know that in this cause I am innocent." He said that he had a good conscience in the cause for which he was to be put to death.

units.la: Sancti Iacobi mors, ex insidijs interfecti.
units.tr: The death of St James, killed by treachery.

units.la: Iudæi interfecerunt Iacobum Alpheum, in illo interinteru illo quando abfuit Romanus magistratus, & expectabatur aduentus noui præsidis ex urbe Roma. Ibi iste Iacobus est necatus à suo pontifice, qui non habebat ius gladij. Sed tempora aliàs tunc erant plena seditionum. Quia quando instat finis alicuius regni, præcedunt multæ seditiones. Sicut iam paulatim sacra ædificia per partes ruunt: sic sensim ruunt etiam imperia. Quantus tumultus est iam in Germania? Sine ulla dubitatione instat mutatio aliqua.
units.tr: The Jews killed James the son of Alphaeus in the interval when the Roman magistrate was absent and the arrival of a new governor from the city of Rome was awaited. There this James was put to death by his high priest, who had no right of the sword. But the times were then full of uprisings, for when the end of a kingdom is at hand, many seditions go before it. Just as sacred buildings now gradually fall apart piece by piece, so empires too slowly collapse. How great is the tumult already in Germany? Without any doubt some change is at hand.

units.la: Mors triste spectaculum.
units.tr: A sorrowful spectacle: death.

units.la: Ante annos 36. aut circiter, bona & honesta matrona moriebatur: ad quam accedebat concionator iuuenis, de clamitans multa de mortis dulcedine. Ipsa uero pertæsa illius stultæ orationis, inquit: Ah tu nondum expertus es mortis cruciatus: ego confido in Deum, qui me iam ex omnibus illis calamitatibus & ærumnis eripiet.
units.tr: About thirty-six years ago, a good and respectable matron was dying. A young preacher came to her, and he kept loudly declaring much about the sweetness of death. But she, weary of his foolish speech, said: "Ah, you have not yet experienced the agonies of death. I trust in God, who will rescue me from all those calamities and troubles."

units.la: Insignis pij militis ex hac vita decessus.
units.tr: The notable departure from this life of a godly soldier.

units.la: Ioannes Huniades, pater Mathiæ, fuit magnanimus & felix bellator, qui unus reuera aliquid præclari contra Turcas gessit. In postrema autem pugna, qua fuit victor, magna cum gloria ex hac uita discessit. Sicut enim Epaminondas iam moribundus interrogauit gauit an saluᵒ esset clypeus? dixerūt esse saluū. Deinde: quæsiuit à qua parte staret victoria? Dixerūt victores esse suos ciues, quo audito, fortiter, ac læto animo mortuus est. Sic Iohannes Huniades cùm audisset profligatos esse suos hostes, agit Deo gratias, cui suam animam & corpus commenda-uit, & ita lætus est mortuus.
units.tr: John Hunyadi, father of Matthias, was a great-hearted and fortunate warrior, who alone truly achieved something glorious against the Turks. In his last battle, in which he was victorious, he departed this life with great glory. For just as Epaminondas, already dying, asked whether his shield was safe, and they said it was safe, and then asked on which side victory stood, and they said that his fellow citizens were the victors, and on hearing this he died bravely and with a glad mind; so John Hunyadi, when he had heard that his enemies were routed, gave thanks to God, to whom he commended his soul and body, and so he died joyful.

units.la: Papæ tyrannis & organorum eius sæuitia in pios
units.tr: The tyranny of the Pope and the savagery of his instruments against the godly.

units.la: Duo boni uiri in Elwagen, pastor & eius concionator supplicio afficti sunt, qui nihil aliud fecerāt, nisi quòd mollissimè taxaucrant crassissimos abusus papisticos. Concionatoris nomen erat Cræsus, qui fuit meus præceptor. Illi duo duxerunt uxores. Concionator erat perclarè doctus. Pastor uerò minus. Cùm essent in carcere, ille non fuit fortis, adeò ut pastor licet indoctior, confirmauerit illum. Postea ambo in bona confessione sunt decollati.
units.tr: Two good men at Ellwangen, a minister and his preacher, were put to death, although they had done nothing except gently rebuke the very gross Papist abuses. The preacher's name was Crasus, who was my teacher. Both of them had taken wives. The preacher was exceedingly learned, but the minister less so. When they were in prison, the preacher was not brave, so much so that the minister, though less learned, strengthened him. Afterwards both were beheaded after a good confession.

units.la: Aliud.
units.tr: Another example.

units.la: Papa iam in Italia comburit quicquid potest requiri librorū, non tantū Theologicorum sed etiā Philosophicorum. In primis autem omnes Erasmi Libros curat inquiri. Flaminium illum bonum uirum effodit mortuum & cōbusit cadauer, qui Psalmos reddidit uersibus: uult aboleri omnia scripta pta præter libros unius Thomæ Aquinatis omniū insulsissimi scriptorum.
units.tr: The Pope in Italy now burns whatever books of any kind can be found, not only theological but also philosophical. Above all he takes care that all the books of Erasmus are searched out. He dug up and burned the corpse of that good man Flaminio, who rendered the Psalms into verse. He wants all writings to be abolished except the books of Thomas Aquinas alone, the most insipid of all writers.

units.la: Alia in antiqua Ecclesia tyrannis.
units.tr: Another tyranny in the ancient Church.

units.la: In Ægypto fuit episcopus Cheræmon, uir admodum senex, expulsus ex urbe sua cum magna multitudine piorum hominum, antecessit agmen senex cum coniuge sna. Cùm autem interea missi essent equites, qui eos conculcarent & extinguerent, cumq; pius ille senex non posset perinde atq; alij iuniores festinando effugere, ibi ille cùm sua coniuge in cœlum subduci à reliquo agmine conspectus est. Euidens est exemplum præsentiæ Dei in Ecclesia, iuxta dictum Psalmistæ: Prope est Dominus omnibus, qui tribulato sunt corde.
units.tr: In Egypt there was a bishop, Cheremon, a very old man, who was driven out of his city together with a great crowd of godly people. The old man went ahead of the column with his wife. Meanwhile horsemen were sent to trample and destroy them, and since that godly old man could not escape by hastening as the younger ones did, he was seen by the rest of the column being taken up into heaven with his wife.
