It is a striking example of God's presence in the Church, according to the saying of the Psalmist: "The Lord is near to all who are of a broken heart."

units.la: Aliud.
units.tr: Another.

units.la: Cardinalis quidam in Anglia, interfecit optimos uiros Latomerum integerrimum octogenarium senem. Cum esset Paduæ scholasticus uadit ad auditorium, ubi monachus enarrauit epistolam Pauli ad Romanos, secum ferens meum commentarium, quasi improbans huius nugas. Sed iam scripsit pro Pontifice.
units.tr: A certain cardinal in England put to death excellent men, including Latomerus, a most upright old man of eighty. When he was a student at Padua, he went to the lecture hall where a monk was expounding Paul's Epistle to the Romans, carrying with him my commentary, as though he disapproved of its trifles. But now he has written for the Pope.

units.la: Veteris Ecclesiæ in pios tyrannis.
units.tr: The ancient Church and tyrants against the pious.

units.la: Magna lucta fidei est in Babyla Episcopo Antiocheno laudabili illo sene. Cùm ducebatur ad supplicium plicium senex cum duobus filijs tempore Decij, da-stitit ibi quoq; mater: & cum filij primo interfice-rentur, uicit illum dolorem fides in patre et matre. Postea pater est interfectus in confessione bona: mater uero non occidebatur.
units.tr: There is a great struggle of faith in the case of Babylas, the bishop of Antioch, that praiseworthy old man. When the old man was led to execution with his two sons in the time of Decius, the mother was also present there. When the sons were first put to death, faith overcame grief in both the father and the mother. Afterwards the father was killed, in good confession, but the mother was not put to death.

units.la: Velcurionis pius ex hac vi-ta discessus.
units.tr: The pious departure from this life of Velcurio.

units.la: Magister Velcurio cum aegrotaret, adeo ut et-iam morbo illo moreretur, cumq; caeteri magistri & doctores, accedentes ipsum, consolarentur, subi-to prorupit in haec uerba: Pater est amator, filius redemptor, spiritus sanctus consolator: quomodo itaq; tristicia affici posem?
units.tr: When Master Velcurio was sick, so sick that he was dying of that illness, the other masters and teachers came to him to console him, and he suddenly burst out with these words: "The Father is love, the Son is redeemer, the Holy Spirit is comforter; how then can I be affected by sadness?"

units.la: Mortem piorum & sanctorum homi-num sequi calami-tates.
units.tr: The death of pious and holy men is followed by calamities.

units.la: Sic Stillico mortuo, Ambrosio dixit: secu-turas esse magnas mutationes, & ita accidit. Nam mortuo Ambrosio, inuaserunt peregrinae gen-tes Italiam, & horribiliter eam vastauerunt. Mor-tuo Augustino, Vandali traiecerunt in Africam, & statim secuta est haeresis Arriana. Videte quid ac-cidit post mortem Doctoris Martini Lutheri.
units.tr: Thus, when Stilicho was dead, Ambrose said that great changes would follow, and so it came about. For after Ambrose died, foreign peoples invaded Italy and laid it waste in dreadful fashion. After Augustine died, the Vandals crossed into Africa, and immediately Arian heresy followed. See what happened after the death of Doctor Martin Luther.

units.la: Deus mitiget calamitates, & pro sua immensa misericordia nos tueatur.
units.tr: May God lessen these calamities and, in his immense mercy, protect us.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Exemplum insignis patientiæ in Mauricio.
units.tr: An example of remarkable patience in Maurice.

units.la: Mauricius Imperator bella gesit cum quodam rege Barbaro, à quo prælio superatus est: & maxima eius exercitus pars fugata, captiq; sunt plures duobus millibus militū. Barbarus obtulit Mauricio singulos redimendos uno numo. Hic propter nimiā auariciā noluit: Barbarus secundò obtulit, & hic secundò recusauit. Quare Barbarus motus iracundia uniuersam multitudinē captiuorū trucidauit. Tandem post exiguum temporis spaciū, uidit Mauricius in somnis imaginem Saluatoris nostri, in sublimi cruce pendentem, & iuxta eum stantem multitudinem trucidatorum, ipsum accusantium. Visum est igitur Mauricio se à Christo uocari. Accedit igitur ad Christum, sic interrogantem eum: Maurici, utrum uis luere pœnam pro captiuis his interfectis in hac uita, an in altera? Ille supplex procumbit, rogans ut sibi parceret in altera uita, ac in hac potiùs sumeret pœnas. Tũc Christus: Ergo si uis in altera uita nõ puniri, in hac uita lues tuorũ peccatorum pœnas: ideoq; tradã te in potestatẽ Phocæ, ut interficiat te cũ tota familia. Mane experge-factus Mauricius, ac nimium illo somno perterritus, ad se uocat Philippum, quem antea suspectum habuerat, dixitq; ad eum: Philippe, sæpe hubui te suspectū, quòd affectares meum regnū: iam uerò te omni suspitione libero. Hac nocte mihi reuelatum est, in somno, me interficiendum esse à Phoca. Quærit igitur qualis esset? Ibi Philippus inquit: Nihil est quod uerearis à Phoca: est enim homo timidus. Ibi statim Mauricius subiecit: Omnis timidus est homicida & crudelis. Paucos post dies annunciatum est Imperatori, Phocam cum exercitu uenire ad interficiendum ipsum. Imperator fugit ad amicum nescio quò: sed retractus est ex fuga, & prius in conspectu eius trucidati sunt filij. Postea cum infans quæreretur, dixit Mauricius, cum esse apud nutricem. Missum est ad illam ut auferretur infans. Nutrix misericordia mota erga Imperatoris filium, ipsum abdit in loco quodā secreto, & suum pro eo adfert. Pater agnouit suū non esse, nec uoluit alium infantem pro suo interfici. Dixit igitur ad Phocā: Iste nō est meus, parcas alieno innocenti sanguini, & iubeas adferri meū. Coacta est igitur nutrix adducere Imperatoris infantē, qui adductus, patre etiam intuente, est trāsfossus. Deniq; cùm & coniugem adductam ante oculos suos uideret interfici, exclamabat Mauricius: Iustus et Domine, & rectum iudicium tuum. Tandem & ipse Mauricius decollatus est, repetito iterum hoc uersiculo Psalmi: Iustus es Domine, & rectum iudiciū tuū. Cogitate quanta hæcfuerit rit poenitentia & obedientia in calamitatibus, atq; adeò ipsa morte. Nullus ei dolor tantus fuit, quem non fide mediatorem apprehendente uicerit.
units.tr: The Emperor Maurice waged war against a certain barbarian king, by whom he was defeated in battle. Most of his army was put to flight, and more than two thousand of his soldiers were taken captive. The barbarian offered to ransom them individually for one coin each. Maurice, out of excessive avarice, refused. The barbarian offered a second time, and he refused again. Therefore the barbarian, moved to anger, slaughtered the whole multitude of captives. Then, after a short space of time, Maurice saw in a dream the image of our Saviour hanging on a high cross, and beside him a multitude of the slaughtered, accusing him. It seemed to Maurice that he was being summoned by Christ. He therefore came to Christ, who asked him: "Maurice, do you wish to pay the penalty for these captives slain, in this life or in the next?" He fell down in supplication, asking that he be spared in the next life and that the punishment be taken in this life instead. Then Christ said: "So if you do not wish to be punished in the next life, you will pay the penalties for your sins in this life. Therefore I will hand you over into the power of Phocas, so that he may kill you with your whole family." Maurice woke early and, terrified by that dream, summoned Philip, whom he had earlier suspected, and said to him: "Philip, I have often suspected you of aiming at my kingdom; now, however, I free you from all suspicion. This night it was revealed to me in a dream that I am to be killed by Phocas." He then asked what sort of man Phocas was. Philip replied: "There is nothing you need fear from Phocas, for he is a timid man." Maurice immediately added: "Every timid man is a murderer and cruel." A few days later the emperor was told that Phocas was coming with an army to kill him. The emperor fled to a friend, I know not where, but he was dragged from his flight, and his sons were slaughtered before his eyes. Afterwards, when the infant was sought, Maurice said that he was with his nurse. A man was sent to her to take the infant away. The nurse, moved with pity for the emperor's son, hid him in a secret place and brought her own child in his place. The father recognised that it was not his own, and would not have another innocent infant killed in place of his. He therefore said to Phocas: "This one is not mine. Spare innocent blood that is not yours, and order mine to be brought." So the nurse was compelled to bring the emperor's infant, who, brought forward while his father looked on, was pierced through. Finally, when he saw his wife also brought before his eyes and slain, Maurice cried out: "You are just, O Lord, and right is your judgment." At last Maurice himself was beheaded, repeating once more this verse of the Psalm: "You are just, O Lord, and right is your judgment." Consider how great his repentance and obedience were in calamities, and even in death itself. No pain was so great that he did not overcome it by laying hold of the Mediator by faith.

units.la: Ante paucos annos quidam est decollatus, qui ante supplicium dicebat, se nolle suam uitam redimere uno numo: quia iam uicerat mortem uiuifi-catus per filium Dei: accensa in eo lætitia Spiritus sancti, qui est spiritus gratiæ & precum. Habuit enim illum non ex factis, sed sola fide, apprehen-dente misericordiam in filio Dei ostensam, qua su-perauerat suam mortem.
units.tr: A few years ago a certain man was beheaded who, before his execution, said that he was unwilling to redeem his life for one coin, because he had already conquered death, having been made alive through the Son of God. The joy of the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of grace and of prayers, was kindled in him. For he had this not from works but from faith alone, laying hold of the mercy shown in the Son of God, by which he had overcome his death.

units.la: Mors S. Mariæ matris Salua-toris nostri.
units.tr: The death of St Mary, mother of our Saviour.

units.la: Epiphanius putat Mariam coronatam marty-rio, & allegat hoc dictum Simeonis: Tuam ipsius animam pertransibit gladius. Sed tamen affirmat non constare, quo genere mortis sit extincta, aut ubi sit corpus eius in terra sepultum. Mortua au-tem est anno ætatis suæ quinquagesimonono, ut scribit Nicephorus, totidem videlicet annos nata ante mortem, quot Maximilianus. Credo, quòd co-ceperit anno vigesimo: alij volunt anno decimo-quinto ætatis suæ. Vixit autem post ascensionem filij quinq; aut sex annos, et fuit rectrix istius coetus.
units.tr: Epiphanius thinks Mary was crowned with martyrdom, and he cites the saying of Simeon: "A sword will pierce your own soul." Yet he affirms that it is not certain by what kind of death she died, or where her body lies buried in the earth. She died in the fifty-ninth year of her age, as Nicephorus writes, having been as many years old at her death as Maximilian. I believe she conceived in her twentieth year; others hold it was in her fifteenth year of age. She lived after the ascension of her Son five or six years, and was the leader of that assembly.

units.la: Pij principis morientis uotum.
units.tr: The vow of a pious prince on his deathbed.

units.la: Dux Saxoniæ Iohannes, iustus, sapiens, & mo-deratideratissimus princeps, ante obitum subinde haec uerba repetiuisse dicitur, se paterno animo semper erga suos fuisse subditos, sé que optare ut ad posteritatem etiã patria tranquilla sit, & paternis imperijs regatur.
units.tr: Duke John of Saxony, a just, wise and most moderate prince, is said to have repeatedly spoken these words before his death: that he had always been towards his subjects with a fatherly spirit, and that he wished the country to remain peaceful also for posterity, and to be ruled by paternal government.

units.la: Papæ & suorum contra pios tyrannis.
units.tr: Tyranny of the Pope and his followers against the pious.

units.la: Lugduni ante paucos annos, tres honesti uiri propter confessionem Euangelij sunt interfecti.
units.tr: A few years ago at Lyon three honest men were put to death for their confession of the Gospel.

units.la: Simile.
units.tr: A similar case.

units.la: In Anglia nunc filia regis est decollata, & caput eius abiectum in gremium principis cognati astantis, qui postea etiam est accusatus.
units.tr: In England recently the king's daughter was beheaded, and her head was thrown into the lap of a kinsman of the prince who was standing by, and who was afterwards also accused.

units.la: Simile.
units.tr: Simile.

units.la: Cùm in Belgico quidam Lutheranus duceretur ad supplicium, dixit: Ego oro uos propter Deum, ut tantum dicatis mihi, quid fecerim? Ibi responsum est, quòd propterea duceretur ad supplicium, quia Germanica Biblia excudisset. Ibi ille: Ago Deo gratias, quòd nullũ aliud crimẽ mihi obijcere positis, & lætus sum, quòd hanc rem ad Dei tribunal adferre possum.
units.tr: When a certain Lutheran was being led to execution in the Low Countries, he said: "I beg you, for God's sake, just tell me what I have done." He was told that he was being led to execution because he had printed the German Bible. Then he said: "I thank God that you have no other charge to bring against me, and I am glad that I can bring this matter before God's judgment seat."

units.la: Simile.
units.tr: Simile.

units.la: Episcopus quidam solebat dicere: Ego non soleo diu disputare cum Lutheranis, sed statim iubeo eos demergi in Rhenum. Postea ille ipse episcopus horribiliter est mortuus.
units.tr: A certain bishop used to say: "I am not in the habit of debating long with Lutherans; I at once order them to be drowned in the Rhine." Afterwards that same bishop died a horrible death.

units.la: Sequentes tres historiae sunt scriptae ad Lutherum Anno 1543. Prima.
units.tr: The following three histories were written to Luther in the year 1543. The first.

units.la: Quidam ciues in Austria profecti sunt ad vicinum oppidum, quod duobus milliaribus distat abeis, & ibi sumpserunt sacramentum sub utraq; specie. Papistici sacerdotes illius loci, postquam compererunt, iusserunt eos in vincula conijci: sed qui praefuerunt, id facere recusarunt.
units.tr: Some citizens in Austria went to a neighbouring town, two miles away from them, and there they received the sacrament in both kinds. When the Papist priests of that place found out, they ordered them to be thrown into chains; but the magistrates refused to do so.

units.la: Secunda.
units.tr: The second.

units.la: Ad eundem modum in regali Alba, quam Stul-weissenburg uocant, Euangelium docetur pure, & administrantur sacramenta iuxta Christi institutionem. Iusserunt autem Papistae cum doctorem Ecclesiae, tum ciues sacramentis usos, conijci in carcerem. Sed praeses oppidi rescripsit, se Deo potius obtemperare, quam hominibus: in caeteris omnib. facturum officium.
units.tr: In the same way, in the royal town of Alba, which they call Stuhlweissenburg, the Gospel is taught purely and the sacraments are administered according to Christ's institution. But the Papists ordered both the teacher of the Church and the citizens who had used the sacraments to be thrown into prison. But the governor of the town wrote back that he must obey God rather than men; in all other matters he would do his duty.

units.la: Tertia.
units.tr: The third.

units.la: In die Paschae, ex oppido Metensi ad vicinum monasterium, quod est comitis Vulhelmi a Fürstenberg, iuerunt ciues circiter ducenti cum uxoribus, ut ibi integro sacramento uterentur. Id cum Scapaniae gubernator resciuisset, cum aliquot equitibus impetum in monasterium fecit, & matronas in conspectu maritorum nudatas uestibus uio'auit. Quid a Turcis posset committi magis indignum?
units.tr: On Easter day, about two hundred citizens with their wives went from the town of Metz to a neighbouring monastery, which belongs to Count Wolfgang of Fürstenberg, in order to receive the sacrament whole. When the governor of Scapaniae learned of this, he attacked the monastery with some horsemen and, in the sight of their husbands, stripped the matrons naked and violated them. What could be done more shamefully even by the Turks?

units.la: COLL. Simile.
units.tr: COLL. Simile.

units.la: Romæ duo Augustani in cellis inuenti sunt præcisis capitibus, & linguis exectis. Tanta fuit crudelitas. Reprehenderant autem hi luxū Cardinaliū.
units.tr: At Rome two men from Augsburg were found in their cells, with their heads cut off and their tongues torn out. Such was the cruelty. They had, however, been rebuking the luxury of the cardinals.

units.la: Tyrannis Papæ, & suorum, contra Iohannem Hus & Hieronymum Pragensem
units.tr: The tyranny of the Pope and his followers against John Hus and Jerome of Prague

units.la: Cogitate, qualis fuerit dolor illorum duorum virorum, Iohannis Hus, & Hieronymi Pragensis in concilio Constantiensi. Ibi aduersatus est eis totus mundus. Gerson etiam fuit unus ex condemnatoribus, qui eo tempore fuit eruditus & magnus vir: & tamen fuit ex illorum numero, qui se sanguine innocentum & iustorum hominum polluerunt. Dicitur surrexisse ex Concilio Casparus Schlick, à quo est illa familia in valle Ioachimica, cum videret inclinationem fieri ad eorum condemnationem, nolens esse suffragator & approbator supplicij.
units.tr: Consider what the grief of those two men was, John Hus and Jerome of Prague, at the Council of Constance. The whole world was against them. Gerson too was one of their condemners; he was at that time a learned and great man, and yet he was among those who polluted themselves with the blood of innocent and righteous men. It is said that Caspar Schlick, from whom that family in the Joachimsthal valley descends, withdrew from the Council when he saw a move being made towards their condemnation, unwilling to be a voter for and approver of the execution.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Palatinus Ludouicus ille bonus: senex & pius princeps, ante paucos annos Idibus Martij mortuus est: cum quo etiam mortua & extincta pax Germaniæ. Hic paulo ante mortem uocauit ad se plurimos concionatores, cum quibus collocutus fuit de causis & controuersijs religionis, dixitque, illos sibi præ cæteris esse gratissimos hospites. Adfuit autem ei in agone mortis pastor Heydelbergensis, qui adhuc viuit. Mortuus est postea ille princeps in pia confessione doctrinæ Christianæ.
units.tr: The Palatine Louis, that good man, an old and pious prince, died a few years ago on the Ides of March; with him the peace of Germany also died and was extinguished. Shortly before his death he summoned to himself very many preachers, with whom he conferred about the causes and controversies of religion, and said that they were his most welcome guests above all others. The minister of Heidelberg, who is still alive, was present with him in his death struggle. That prince afterwards died in a pious confession of Christian doctrine.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Dicitur de Petro Apostolo, quòd fuerit vestitus pallio (quia tunica fuit interior vestis, & superinduerit pallium) habens in manu sudarium, quo solitus est uti propter assiduas lachrymas. Interrogatus verò, quare ita lachrymaretur? Respondit, se flere desiderio Domini. Sed credo eum flevisse propter calamitates generis humani potissimum, quibus genus humanum propter peccatum obnoxium est.
units.tr: It is said of the Apostle Peter that he was clothed in a cloak (since the tunic was the inner garment, and he had put the cloak over it), holding in his hand a handkerchief, which he was accustomed to use because of his constant tears. When he was asked why he wept so, he replied that he wept from longing for the Lord. But I believe he wept chiefly over the calamities of the human race, to which the human race is subject because of sin.

units.la: Tyrannis Saltzburgensis contra pios.
units.tr: The tyranny of the Archbishop of Salzburg against the godly.

units.la: Audiui de episcopo Saltzburgensi, quòd decem homines propter religionem coniecerit in carcerem, & cos ita fame necauerit, ut se mutuò devorarent. Quis unquam hoc audiuit in Phalaridis historia?
units.tr: I have heard of the bishop of Salzburg that he cast ten men into prison because of their religion, and so starved them that they devoured one another. Who has ever heard of such a thing even in the history of Phalaris?

units.la: Tragica mors patris & filij simul combusti.
units.tr: The tragic death of a father and son burnt together.

units.la: Ante paucos annos cùm quidam alligatus esset palo in Anglia, ut propter cõfessionem doctrinæ combureretur, ibi filius astans spectator suppliciij pacij paterni transfilijt in rogum ad patrem, & carnisex utrumq; com usit.
units.tr: A few years ago, when a certain man was tied to a stake in England so that he might be burnt for confessing the doctrine, his son, standing by as a spectator of his father's punishment, leapt into the fire to his father, and the flames consumed both of them.

units.la: Breuis de morte & confessione Iohannis Huss narratio.
units.tr: A brief narrative of the death and confession of John Hus.

units.la: Iohannes Huss Bohemus in Concilio Constantiensi publicè pronunciatus est hæreticus, & singulari ritu spoliatus iure sacerdotali, per episcopos damnatus ad supplicium ignis, & traditus seculari potestati. Cùm educitur ad locum supplicij, gestat in capite mitram episcopali similem, in qua depicti erant duo dæmones, cum inscriptione: Hæresiarcha. Subinde inter eundum has voces ingeminauit: Iesu Christe fili Dei uiui, qui passus es pro nobis, miserere mei. Tandem impositus rogo, eandem precationem aliquoties alta uoce repetens, fortiter supplicium pertulit. Hæc anno 45. recitauit.
units.tr: John Hus of Bohemia was publicly pronounced a heretic at the Council of Constance, and, stripped of his priestly rights in a singular ceremony, was condemned by the bishops to death by fire and handed over to the secular power. When he was led out to the place of execution, he wore on his head a mitre like a bishop's, on which were painted two demons, with the inscription: "Heresiarch." Meanwhile, as he went, he kept repeating these words: "Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who suffered for us, have mercy on me." At last, when he was placed on the pyre, repeating the same prayer several times in a loud voice, he bore the punishment bravely. He recounted these things in the year 1545.

units.la: Eberhardi ducis Vuirtenbergensis, decedentis ex hac uita, pia confessio & consolatio.
units.tr: The pious confession and consolation of Eberhard, duke of Württemberg, as he departed this life.

units.la: Eberhardi ducis Vuirtenbergensis pij & præstantis principis confessio: qui cum iacuisset totum triduum, & iam morituro præberetur corpus Domini, erigens se quasi conualuisset, dixit: Ago tibi æterne Deus pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi gratias ingentes, quòd ostendisti consolationem conscientiæ scientiæ meæ, per filium tuum, & reuocasti me ad pœnitentiam. Tandem cœpit hæc sequentia intenta uoce proferre: Deus, inquit, sicut omnes sumus imbecilles, & polluti horribilibus peccatis, si meũ regimen unquam fuit graue & molestum alicui ex meis subditis, aut alijs hominibus, punias me & sumas supplicium in hac uita de meo corpore, & postea animæ parcas.
units.tr: The confession of Eberhard, duke of Württemberg, a pious and outstanding prince. When he had lain for three whole days, and the body of the Lord was being offered to him as he was about to die, he raised himself up as if he had recovered and said: "I give you immense thanks, eternal God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, that through your Son you have shown consolation to my conscience, and have called me back to repentance." Then he began to say the following in a loud voice: "God, since we are all feeble and defiled by dreadful sins, if my government was ever heavy and burdensome to any of my subjects or other people, punish me, and exact the penalty in this life from my body, and afterwards spare my soul."

units.la: Pij principis confessio omnibus in agone mortis necessaria.
units.tr: The confession of a pious prince, necessary for everyone in the agony of death.

units.la: Cùm optimus & pius princeps dux Franciscus Luneburgensis multos cruciatus in crure sentiret, paulo ante mortem dixit: Isti cruciatus mei, multo minores sunt, quàm peccata mea merētur. Omnipotens Deus, ueni tandem, & miserere mei, propter filiũ tuum unigenitũ: & non abijce me, propter eundem filium tuum, ab æterna tua consuetudine. Hora illa extremi agonis adueniente, tum demum experientia discimus, quid antè in doctrina Euangelica profecerimus.
units.tr: When the most excellent and pious prince, Duke Francis of Lüneburg, felt many torments in his leg shortly before his death, he said: "These torments of mine are far less than my sins deserve. Almighty God, come at last and have mercy on me, for the sake of your only-begotten Son; and do not cast me off, for the same Son's sake, from your eternal fellowship." When that hour of final agony arrives, then at last we learn by experience how much we have progressed in the teaching of the Gospel beforehand.

units.la: Erasmi confessio ante mortem.
units.tr: The confession of Erasmus before death.

units.la: Erasmus Roterodamus moriturus, sæpe ingeminauit hanc uocem: Domine fac finem, fac finẽ, sed quid uoluerit, dicere non possum.
units.tr: Erasmus of Rotterdam, about to die, often repeated this cry: "Lord, make an end, make an end," but what he meant I cannot say.

units.la: Miserabilis mors piorum doctorũ.
units.tr: The wretched death of pious teachers.

units.la: Fuerũt tres uiri in Anglia, (ubi plurimi propter confessionẽ doctrinæ supplicio afficiũtur) q; hoc anno 56 miserrimè interfecti sunt, quorum non habuit ista natio similes, Latomerus senex octogenarius, Hugo episcopus Londinensis, & cardinalis Cantuariensis, docti & pij homines, cum alijs quàm plurimis. Hæc 19. Iunij narrauit.
units.tr: There were three men in England (where very many are put to death for the confession of doctrine) who were most miserably killed in this year 1556, and whom that nation has never had equals: Latomerus, an old man of eighty, Hugh, bishop of London, and the cardinal of Canterbury, learned and pious men, together with very many others. He related this on 19 June.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Insigne confessionis exemplum.
units.tr: A notable example of confession.

units.la: Ludi magister quidam in Anglia sub rege quodam scripserat ad quendam sacrificulum literas, & illu de crassioribus erroribus Papistarum admonuerat. Alter literas regi offert. Rex iubet ludimagistrum in carcerem conijci. Tandem uerò sententia ferebatur ut ille cõbureretur. Ibi amicus quidam ei uespe ri assatura attulit, quam cùm attingeret, & feruore motus digitos retraheret, risit: Ecce, inquit, ego nõ possum ferre hunc dolorem, quid fiet, cùm cras ipse assabor? Adductum itaq; in iudicium rex ipse alloquitur eũ, dicens: Si ipsi donaturũ esse uitam, si illam doctrinam quam in suis literis esset confessus, abnegaret. At ille: O serenissime rex, post Deum nihil magis quàm tuam serenitatem ueneror: sed à Deo & eius doctrina deficere non possum. Maluit hic pro veritate Euangelij subire supplicium, quàm adulatione uitam conseruare. Sic constantissimo animo, & confessione pia est mortuus.
units.tr: A schoolmaster in England, under a certain king, had written a letter to a certain priest and had warned him about the gross errors of the Papists. The other man presented the letter to the king. The king ordered the schoolmaster thrown into prison. Finally sentence was passed that he should be burned. That evening a friend brought him roast meat, and when he touched it and drew back his fingers from the heat, he laughed. "Look," he said, "I cannot bear this pain. What will happen when I myself am roasted tomorrow?" Then the king himself had him brought before the court and addressed him, saying that he would grant him his life if he would renounce the doctrine he had confessed in his letter. But he replied: "O most serene king, after God I revere nothing more than your serenity, but I cannot fall away from God and his doctrine." He chose to undergo punishment for the truth of the gospel rather than preserve his life by flattery. So he died with a most steadfast mind and a pious confession.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Cùm ægrotaret D. Munsterus, & ad eum accederent quidam ex eius amicis, uisuri quomodo ualeret, & misericordia afficerentur ob cruciatus quos ex ulceribus sui corporis sentiret: O, inquit, charissimi amici, & fratres dilecti in Christo, hæ sunt gemmæ & preciosa ornamenta Dei (ostendes eis simul ulcera) quibus Deus suos amicos ornat, ut eos ad se attrahat: quæ ornamenta preciosiora carissimus, quàm omne aurū aut opes huius mundi. Ita paulo post piè & tranquillè in Domino obdormiuit.
units.tr: When Dr. Münster was ill, some of his friends came to him to see how he was doing, and they were moved with pity at the torments he suffered from the sores on his body. "O, most beloved friends," he said, "and brothers dear in Christ, these are the jewels and precious ornaments of God" (and he showed them the sores at the same time) "with which God adorns his friends so as to draw them to himself. These ornaments are more precious, dearest friends, than all the gold or wealth of this world." Soon after, he fell asleep in the Lord, piously and peacefully.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Relata est à fideli Ecclesiæ Basiliensis doctore hæc historia, atq; erudite ad consolationes Euangelij applicata. Anno Domini 1525, id est biennium ante pugnam Ticinensem, Heluetij cū aliis Gallicis copijs obsiderunt urbem Beyrott: in qua quidã duces suaserunt, ut Heluetijs muros & aggerem transcendere permitteretur, quo plures eorum in oppugnatione ex illa securitate interficerentur. nam oppidani milites tam multas commoditates habebant, ut uix possibile uideretur Heluetios contra eos posse consistere. Ibi comes de Salma in hæc uerba prorupit, eaq; dissuadens dixit: Minimè cõsulo. Mihi enim, ut ueteri militi, satis cognita est illius gentis fortitudo & animositas pugnandi. nam
units.tr: This story was related by a faithful teacher of the Church of Basel and was aptly applied to the consolations of the gospel. In the year of the Lord 1525, that is two years before the battle of Pavia, the Swiss, together with other French troops, besieged the city of Beyrott. In it certain commanders advised that the Swiss be allowed to climb over the walls and the rampart, so that more of them might be killed in the assault, since the townsmen's soldiers had so many advantages that it seemed barely possible for the Swiss to hold their ground against them. Here the Count of Salm burst out and, dissuading them, said: "I do not advise it. For I, as an old soldier, know well enough the courage and fighting spirit of that people.

units.la: si concedamus ipsis de nostris commoditatibus spa-cium unius pedis, timendum nobis esset, ne magnā in nostros milites stragem faciant, & victores eua-dant. Quemadmodum ille bonus & prudens dux, nihil concedere in illa oppugnatione de suo iure voluit: ita & nos in spiritualibus & saevis tenta-tionibus diaboli nihil de nostro iure, id est haeredi-tate vitae aeternae, iustitia & remissione peccatorum, diabolo remittere debemus: considerantes, ipsum nequaquam esse segnem militem. siquidem Petrus eum describit rugientem leonem, quaerentem quem devoret. Praeterea neque ille dux iussit milites osci-tari, sed quibuscunque modis hostibus nocere man-dauit. Hic quoque ipsi obtemperarunt, ac egregie contra fortem hanc gentem se defenderunt, ac depule-runt ipsam ab hac oppugnatione, propter loci in-commoditatem: sic nos quoque non simus ignavi con-tra incursiones nostri hostis diaboli, variis modis insidias nobis struentis: & sequamur consilium cha-rissimi nostri ducis Salvatoris Domini Iesu Chri-sti, qui sub persona Apostolorum nos etiam admo-net de insidijs nostri hostis, cum inquit: Diabolus expetiit, ut vos cribaret. Apostoli enim hic to-tius Ecclesiae personam representant. Induamus ar-ma, simul etiam clypeum in manum sumamus, quem Paulus verbum Dei vocat. Quare si hostis nostrarum animarum iam tristem & perturbatam nostram consci-entiam
units.tr: If we were to yield to them a single foot of our position, we would have to fear that they would inflict great slaughter on our soldiers and come off as victors. Just as that good and prudent commander would concede nothing of his right in that siege, so too in spiritual and fierce temptations of the devil we must give up nothing of our right, that is, our inheritance of eternal life, righteousness and forgiveness of sins. We must consider that he is by no means a lazy soldier, since Peter describes him as a roaring lion seeking whom he may devour. Moreover, that commander did not order his men to lie idle, but commanded them to harm the enemy by whatever means they could. Here too they obeyed, defended themselves splendidly against this brave people, and drove them away from the siege because of the unfavourable nature of the place. So let us too not be slack against the assaults of our enemy the devil, who lays snares for us in various ways. Let us follow the counsel of our dearest leader, the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, who, in the person of the Apostles, also warns us about the snares of our enemy, when he says: Satan has desired to sift you. For the Apostles here represent the person of the whole Church. Let us put on armour, and at the same time take up the shield in our hand, which Paul calls the word of God. Therefore, if the enemy of our souls now tries to assail our sad and troubled conscience with his tricks,

units.la: Non sunt hae verbalia lineas integras, sed reliquae sunt in margine paginae. entiam suis dolis oppugnare conetur, faciamus id quòd fortes milites decet. ac si nobis consolationem quam ex baptismo habemus, ex conscientiis excutere uelit, ita ut nullam planè ex eo sentiamus consolationem: sumamus aliud, & sic consequenter, do nec nos planè relinquere cogatur. Quod tandem si fiat, ut si, Deo uolente, ex hac uita discessuri simus uictores, noster dux, Dominus noster Iesus Christus, nos æterno patri sistet, ac ut strenuos milites ipsi commendabit: ubi denique nostrarum in hac uita assiduarum oppugnationum & uictoriæ premium, uidelicet summa et æterna bona accipiemus. Idq; ut fiat quàm citissimè, omnes strenui milites Christiani assiduis gemitibus Deum æternum patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, unà cum Filio & Spiritu suo sancto precentur.
units.tr: These are not complete lines of text; the rest of them are in the margin of the page. conscience with his tricks, let us do what brave soldiers ought to do. If he wishes to shake from our consciences the consolation we have from baptism, so that we feel no consolation from it at all, let us take up another, and so on, until he is forced to leave us altogether. And if this happens, then, God willing, when we are about to depart from this life as victors, our leader, our Lord Jesus Christ, will present us to the eternal Father and will commend us to him as valiant soldiers. There at last we shall receive the reward of our constant struggles and victory in this life, namely the highest and eternal goods. And so that this may happen as quickly as possible, let all valiant Christian soldiers pray with constant sighs to the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, together with his Son and his Holy Spirit.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam pius & honestus ciuis Basiliensis, decedens ex hac uita, & iacens iam in agone mortis, interrogatus à fideli, eodemq; Euangelij concionatore, quò iam uellet proficisci? sustulit oculos in cœlum, & digito idem monstrauit. nam non amplius, propter mortis uicinitatem, loqui poterat. Paulo uerò post, tranquillo animo moriebatur. Sic sanctus hic uir monstrauit digito & oculis nobis illum locum, ad quem nos omniomnibus nostræ uocationis laboribus respicere debemus.
units.tr: A certain pious and honourable citizen of Basel, departing this life and already lying in the agony of death, was asked by a faithful preacher of the Gospel, who was also present, where he now wished to go. He lifted his eyes to heaven and pointed with his finger to the same place, for because of the nearness of death he could no longer speak. A little later he died with a tranquil mind. So this holy man, by pointing his finger and raising his eyes, showed us that place to which we ought to look in all the labours of our calling.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Fuit ante annos 300 Lantgrauius quidam Ifenaci in Thuringia, nomine Fridericus, uir summa authoritate præditus, qui magna bella summa cum uirtute gessit, & habuit multas uictorias. Vnde tanto hostibus suis terrori fuit, ut D. Martinus de eo dixerit, cùm calcaria sua in Thuringia indueret, auditum esse sonitum in Franconia. Huic seni Lãtgrauio exhibita est Comædia de decem uirginibus Matthæi 25. Cùm autem intellexisset ea similitudine taxari hominum mortuorum inuocationem, & doceri, quòd nihil consequi possemus meritis sanctorum, sed sola fiducia in Christum nos fieri hæredes uitæ æternæ, & esse propter obedientiam filij Dei acceptos: ita consternatus est, ut in morbum inciderit: quo cùm biennium conflictatus esset, interijt.
units.tr: About three hundred years ago there was a certain Landgrave at Eisenach in Thuringia, named Frederick, a man of great authority, who waged great wars with great courage and won many victories. He was so much of a terror to his enemies that Dr Martin said of him that when he put on his spurs in Thuringia, the sound was heard in Franconia. This old Landgrave was shown a comedy of the ten virgins from Matthew 25. When he understood that this parable condemned the invocation of dead men, and taught that we obtain nothing by the merits of the saints, but that by faith alone in Christ we are made heirs of eternal life and are accepted for the obedience of the Son of God, he was so dismayed that he fell into a sickness, and after struggling with it for two years, he died.

units.la: Causæ cur pij interficiantur: & mors Polycarpi, eiusq; in suppli-cio precatio.
units.tr: Chief causes why the godly are put to death; and the death of Polycarp, with his prayer under torture.

units.la: Duæ sunt causæ præcipuæ, quare pij doctores à tyrannis interficiantur. Prima est, quia Deus vult conspici testimonia de veritate doctrinæ in Ecclesia, quòd ipsi non quæstus aut utilitatis cau​sa hanc doctrinam Euangelij amplexi sint, sed stentur illi sancti uiri hanc doctrinam diuinitus esse traditam, cum eam omnibus bonis corporalibus anteferant. Altera causa est, quia uult illos summos uiros testes esse de extremo iudicio & immortalitate, quod restet aliud iudicium, in quo pij doctores fruentur æterna consuetudine Dei: & eregione tyranni & persecutores uerbi diuini habituros esse æternos cruciatus. Sic Polycarpus discipulus Iohannis, cum iam ageret fere nonagesimum annum, imponitur rogo ardenti, ut corpus ipsius igne torreatur, & longiore cruciatu consumatur. Hic, dum stat inter flammas, incipit his uerbis precationem suam clara uoce recitare: Deus pater dilecti filij tui Iesu Christi, per quem agnitionē tui accepimus, conditor uniuersæ naturæ, te inuoco, te confiteor uerum esse Deum, te glorifico per Pontificem dilectum filium tuum, cum Spiritu sancto, suscipe me, & fac me socium resurrectionis sanctorum tuorum. Hæc dum sic clara uoce clamitat, flamma se expandit, & cedit corpori: stat senex integer & alacris, non sentiens flammam (ut olim in Chaldæa seu Babylonica fornace seruati sunt tres uiri ab incendio, inter quos conspectus est candida luce quartus, angelus Michael, similis filio Dei) & celebrat hunc Deum patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Visis illis inusitatis rebus, sta-pant magistratus & carnifices stupefacti, cum uiderent derent senem illæsum uiuere. Tandem iubet tyran‐nus gladio senem illum transfodi, adiuncta hac uo‐ce: Minus hæc sæua fuerunt: permisit Deus seue‐rius extingui.
units.tr: There are two main reasons why godly teachers are killed by tyrants. The first is that God wills there to be visible testimonies in the Church to the truth of the doctrine, namely that they did not embrace this doctrine of the Gospel for gain or profit, but that those holy men stand firm in holding that this doctrine was handed down from God, since they value it above all bodily goods. The other reason is that He wills those outstanding men to be witnesses of the last judgment and of immortality, that there is another judgment remaining, in which godly teachers will enjoy the eternal fellowship of God, and, on the other side, tyrants and persecutors of the divine Word will have eternal torments. So Polycarp, a disciple of John, when he was already nearly ninety years old, was placed on a blazing pyre so that his body might be roasted by the fire and consumed with a longer torment. Standing amid the flames, he began to recite his prayer aloud in these words: "God the Father of your beloved Son Jesus Christ, through whom we have received the knowledge of you, Creator of all nature, I call upon you, I confess you to be the true God, I glorify you through the High Priest, your beloved Son, together with the Holy Spirit. Receive me, and make me a partner in the resurrection of your saints." While he cried out these words in a loud voice, the flame spread out and yielded to his body. The old man stood unhurt and cheerful, not feeling the fire (just as of old in Chaldea, in the Babylonian furnace, three men were kept safe from the burning, and among them a fourth figure was seen in bright light, the angel Michael, like the Son of God), and he praised this God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. At these unusual sights the magistrates and executioners were struck dumb with amazement, seeing the old man living on unharmed. At last the tyrant ordered that the old man be pierced through with a sword, adding these words: "These flames were not cruel enough; God allowed him to be put out more harshly."

units.la: Matronæ pie morientis exemplū.
units.tr: Example of a godly matron dying.

units.la: Moriebatur honestissima quædā matrona Ihe‐næ, quæ cùm honestissimè uixisset, & multum ha‐buisset calamitatis in uita (habuit enim maritū mo‐rosum & belluonem, à quo multa perpessa erat) tandē Deus misertus illius, sustulit eam ex hac ui‐ta. Hæc per triduum iacuit in agone, & tandem ad pastorem D. Antonium Musam dixit: O Do‐mine Antoni, ego ago gratias Deo, ostendenti mi‐hi mea peccata, et rursus me cōsolanti per uerbum suū, in quo mihi proponitur remissio omniū meo‐rū peccatorū. Iam enim intelligo hæc uerba, Re‐mittuntur tibi peccata tua. et ita post triduū in ma‐gna læticia et fiducia Saluatoris nostri mortua est.
units.tr: A very honourable matron of Jena was dying. Though she had lived most honourably and had suffered much hardship in life (for she had a surly, brutish husband, by whom she had endured much), God at last took pity on her and took her out of this life. She lay in agony for three days, and at last she said to the minister, Dr Antonius Musa: "O Lord Antonius, I give thanks to God, who showed me my sins and again comforted me through His Word, in which the forgiveness of all my sins is set before me. For now I understand these words: 'Your sins are forgiven you.'" And so, after three days, she died in great joy and in trust in our Saviour.

units.la: S. matronæ in confessione mo‐rientis pictura.
units.tr: Picture of a matron dying in confession.

units.la: Habetis pulchram historiā de muliere Romana Sabina, quæ grauida in carcere fuit cōi ecta pro‐pter confessionē. Cùm aūt tēpus partus immineret, & ingentes sustineret cruciatus propter partū, ibi astitit custos carceris, et dixit: Quare iam adeò gra‐uiter sers dolorē partus? quid fiet cras aut post bi‐duū, cùm non paries, sed ipsam mortem aggredie‐ris. ris? Iam, inquit illa, patior ut mulier, mersa in hos dolores propter mea peccata, ut dicitur in Genesi: In dolore paries filios: Cras aut post biduū non ego patiar, sed in me Christus.
units.tr: You have a fine story about a Roman Sabine woman, who, pregnant, was thrown into prison on account of her confession. When the time of her delivery drew near and she was suffering great pains in labour, the jailer stood by her and said: "Why do you already bear the pain of labour so heavily? What will you do tomorrow or the day after, when you are not giving birth but facing death itself?" "Now," she replied, "I suffer as a woman, plunged into these pains because of my sins, as it is said in Genesis: 'In pain you shall bring forth children.' Tomorrow or the day after, it will not be I who suffers, but Christ in me."

units.la: Dionysij Areopagitæ mors.
units.tr: Dionysius the Areopagite's death.

units.la: Dionysius Areopagita conuersus à Paulo Lutetiì docuit, & ibi supplicio affectus est. Primùm est obiectus bestijs: cùm bestiæ ipsi pepercissent, detruncatus est capite. Ibi trucus, caput præcisum apprehendit, & ad sepulchrū portauit. Hæc Suidas.
units.tr: Dionysius the Areopagite, converted by Paul, taught at Paris, and there he was put to death. First he was thrown to the beasts; when the beasts spared him, he was beheaded. Then the executioner picked up the severed head and carried it to a tomb. So Suidas.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Scriptū est ad doctum uirū, cuiusdam uiri uxorem Cygneæ aliquot horas in lipothymia iacuisse, ita ut oēs eam mortuā existimarent. Cùm itaq; maritus abijsset, & curaret ipsi sepulchrū, interea tempóris mulier rursus cōualescit, & uiro redeunti obuiā uenit. cui mox maritus dicit: Curauerā tibi iam habitaculū. At mulier: Ego interea temporis fui in cœlo, & uidi beatos angelos & homines celebrantes Deum, uidiq; illum & illam (homines quosdā nominans, qui paulo antè mortui erāt) uidissem libenter Deū, sed eum uidere non poteram.
units.tr: It is written of a learned man that the wife of a certain man at Cygnea lay for several hours in a faint, so that everyone thought her dead. When her husband had gone away and was arranging her tomb, the woman meanwhile revived and came to meet him as he returned. Her husband at once said to her, "I have already arranged a dwelling for you." But the woman said, "In the meantime I was in heaven, and I saw the blessed angels and men praising God. I saw him and her (naming some people who had died shortly before). I would gladly have seen God, but I could not see him."

units.la: Scriptum est Vuitenbergā de duce Vngarico à Turcis capto, cum ipsi uitæ incolumitas non alia cōditione permitteretur, quàm si deficeret à cōfessione Christiana, cōstantiß. denegauit, et fide cōstanti doctrinā nostrā cōfessᵒ est: & doctrinā pariter Machometicam meticam refutauit. Postea coram Turcico Bascha est dissectus. Habetis simile exemplum in libro Ma-chabæorum, ubi mater uidit necem filiorum. Magnum robur est in matre, uidere illa, & confirmare filios in agone.
units.tr: It is written from Wittenberg that a Hungarian duke was captured by the Turks. His life would be spared only on the condition that he renounce the Christian confession. He steadfastly refused, and with a constant faith he confessed our doctrine, and at the same time he refuted the Muhammadan doctrine. Afterwards he was cut to pieces in the presence of the Turkish pasha. You have a similar example in the book of the Maccabees, where a mother watched her sons being put to death. Great is the strength a mother has when she sees this and encourages her sons in their agony.

units.la: Consolatio pro morituris & afflictis, 1556. ad Baronem de Vngnad.
units.tr: A consolation for the dying and the afflicted, 1556, addressed to Baron Ungnad of Hungary.

units.la: Quæ debeant esse in Christiano moriente, & in omnibus afflictionibus. Quando tibi moriendum est (Deus autem per suam gratiam det tibi longam uitam, & post eam deniq; felicem in fide discessum) hæc omnia tibi debent esse cogitata (quia singuli homines debemus esse parati ad mortem) In primis cogitabis filium Dei esse datorem iustitiæ, & uitæ æternæ, quam nos fide accipiamus, iuxta hoc dictum: Iustificati fide pacem habemus. Item: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut unigenitum filium suum daret, ut omnis qui credit in ipsum, nō pereat, sed habeat uitam æternam. Debes igitur primùm petere à Deo propter filium remissionem peccatorum, & reconciliationem: & consolari teipsum firmissimè, quòd illa acceperis & habeas certò propter filium, gratis, & per eum.
units.tr: What a Christian who is dying, and anyone in any affliction, ought to have in mind. When you must die (may God grant you a long life through his grace, and at last a happy departure in faith), all these things ought to be in your thoughts, because each of us ought to be ready for death. First, you will consider that the Son of God is the giver of righteousness and of eternal life, which we receive by faith, according to the saying: "Justified by faith, we have peace" (Rom. 5). Likewise: "God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life" (John 3). You ought therefore first to ask God, for the sake of the Son, for the forgiveness of sins and reconciliation, and to comfort yourself most firmly that you have received these things, and have them with certainty, for the Son's sake, freely and through him.

units.la: Piæ matronæ confesio ante mortem.
units.tr: The confession of a pious matron before death.

units.la: Lipsiæ honesta matrona, cum ei iam mors appropropinquaret, dicebat: Ego meos liberos nondum educatos Deo iam cõmendaui, qui meorũ orphanorũ curã habebit. Ego uerò iam nihil oro aut peto, nisi ut Deus hanc suam consolationem, quam per suum uerbum in corde meo incendit, ad extremum uitæ meæ halitum in me conseruet. Sic tranquillo animo ex hac uita decessit.
units.tr: At Leipzig an honourable matron, when death was already drawing near, said: "I have already commended my children, who are not yet brought up, to God, who will take care of my orphans. As for me, I now ask and seek nothing except that God would keep in me, to the last breath of my life, this consolation which he has kindled in my heart through his Word." So she departed from this life with a calm mind.

units.la: EXITVS IMPIORVM Ethnicorum ex hac uita, eorundemque qui iniustè apud Ethnicos sunt oppressi.
units.tr: EXITS OF THE WICKED: of the Gentiles from this life, and of those who were unjustly oppressed among the Gentiles.

units.la: COLL. Tristis ex hac uita discessus.
units.tr: A sad departure from this life.

units.la: Agrippina mater Neronis, cum percussores ad eam misi essent, & multis uulneribus eam sauciassent, clamauit: Fodias uentrem, qui gestauit illud monstrum, & perniciem generis humani. & ita cum gemitu est extincta.
units.tr: When Agrippina, the mother of Nero, sent assassins to her and they had wounded her with many blows, she cried out: "Strike the belly that bore that monster and the ruin of the human race." And so she was put to death, with groaning.

units.la: COLL. Palamedes iniustè oppressus.
units.tr: Palamedes unjustly overthrown.

units.la: Palamedes unus ex principibus Græcis, ad Troiam profectis, familiaris Achilli, ipsiusq; grammateus, magno usui Reipublicæ non solùm in eo bello, uerùmetiam in pace fuit. Fertur aliquot literas apud Græcos primò repperisse: adeoq; vir prudens & sapiens fuisse, ut multa perniciosè ab Agamem-none tentata, ipsius consilio & autoritate impedi-ta fuerint. Ob quam eius uirtutem inuidia moti A-gamenon & Vlysses, in ipsius necem cõspirant. Falso igitur proditionis ipsum accusari procurant. De qua, ut conuinceretur, Vlysses prius clàm the-saurum in eius tentorio defodi curauit, fictasq; li-teras tanquam ab hostibus missas, ad ipsum Pala-medem cum mentione eius thesauri & proditio-nis, sparsit. Quibus literis repertis, & in iudicium productis, simulq; thesauro effosso, falsò proditio-nis damnatur. Huius historia refertur inter exem-pla per inuidiam oppressorum.
units.tr: Palamedes, one of the leading Greeks who set out for Troy, was a close friend of Achilles and his secretary, and he was of great service to the commonwealth not only in that war but also in peace. He is said to have been the first to devise several letters among the Greeks. He was so wise and prudent a man that many schemes that Agamemnon attempted in a harmful way were blocked by his counsel and authority. Moved by envy of his virtue, Agamemnon and Ulysses conspired for his death. They therefore arranged for him to be accused falsely of treason. To convict him, Ulysses first had a treasure secretly buried in his tent, and then scattered forged letters, as if sent by the enemy, addressed to Palamedes himself, mentioning that treasure and the treason. When these letters were found and brought before the court, and the treasure was dug up at the same time, he was condemned for a treason he had not committed. His story is related among the examples of men oppressed through envy.

units.la: COLL L.
units.tr: COLL L.

units.la: Socratis mors.
units.tr: The death of Socrates.

units.la: Sic & Socrates per inuidiam maleuolorum in-iustè est oppressus. Socrate autem interfecto Athenis, recitata est tragœdia ab Aristophane de Palamede, qui interfectus est à Græcis ad Troiam. In hac hi-uersus habentur: Εὐξαίνετε ἐὐξαίνετε ἀρίσγον τῶν ἐλλιίων, Τλὶν ἀνδλίαν μυδλνὰ βλάψαντα,
units.tr: So too Socrates was unjustly oppressed through the envy of evil men. After Socrates had been put to death at Athens, Aristophanes' tragedy about Palamedes, who was killed by the Greeks at Troy, was performed. In it there are these lines: "Card him, card him, the best of the Greeks, the man who has done countless harm to men" [Ἐξαίνετε, ἐξαίνετε ἄριστον τῶν Ἑλλήνων, πρὶν ἄνδρα μυρία βλάψαντα].

units.la: Hos uersus cùm recitari audirent, ita commoti sunt ciues, ut statim authores interfecti Socratis ap-prehenderent. Sic hisce nostris temporibus multi sancti & pij homines passim interficiuntur. Sicut ab initio mundi Abel propheta: ita postea Chri-stus stus ipse, Apostoli, & infiniti alij, qui ipsius vestigia sequuntur.
units.tr: When the citizens heard these lines recited, they were so moved that at once they seized the authors of Socrates' death. So in our own times many holy and pious men are killed everywhere, just as from the beginning of the world Abel the prophet was killed, and afterwards Christ himself, the apostles, and countless others who follow in their footsteps.

units.la: Catonis mors.
units.tr: The death of Cato.

units.la: Marcus Cato, priusquam sibi mortem consciscere, aliquoties legit librum Platonis de immortalitate animæ, ut acerbissimo dolori, quem ex Pompeij casu cæperat, remedium adhiberet: nec tamen potuit in eius scripti sententia acquiescere, sed doloris magnitudine fractus, librum abiecit, & ferro sibi mortem conscivit. Inde verissimum est, quòd est apud Platonem: Consolationes philosophicas esse λόγως καὶ φυναρίας, id est meras nugas.
units.tr: Marcus Cato, before he took his own life, read several times Plato's book on the immortality of the soul, in order to apply a remedy to the most bitter grief he had conceived from the fall of Pompey. Yet he could not find rest in the argument of that writing; broken by the greatness of his sorrow, he threw the book aside and took his own life with a sword. Hence what Plato says is most true: that philosophical consolations are "words and trifles" [λόγως καὶ φυναρίας], that is, mere nonsense.

units.la: COLL. Tragicæ mortis exemplum.
units.tr: COLL. An example of a tragic death.

units.la: Nullus est tam ferreus, qui sine consternatione animi legat fratrum Thebanorum certamē, & matris Locastæ exitum: quæ direptura prælium inter fratres, cùm tardius venisset, ex alterius filij vulnere ensem extrahit: & hoc ense, qui filij cruore manabat, miserrima mater se transfigit, posteáq; se mediam inter filios abijcit, spargens brachia, quasi in utriusq; complexu moritura.
units.tr: No one is so hard-hearted that he can read without dismay of the fight of the Theban brothers and the end of their mother Jocasta. She, having come too late to part her sons who were fighting, took a sword from the wound of one son, and with this sword, dripping with her son's blood, the most wretched mother stabbed herself. Then she threw herself down between her sons, spreading her arms, as if about to die in the embrace of both.

units.la: Aliud simile.
units.tr: Another similar case.

units.la: Cornelius Gallus, Augusti miles & familiaris, tantæ fuit apud eum authoritatis & fidei, ut commendaret ipsi Aegyptum, ubi maximus metus erat: & tamen postea in eius odium incurrit, propter suspicionem affectati regni. Quamobrem tantum animi dolorem concepit, ut sibi ipsi mortem conscIuerit. Fuit bonus miles atq; poeta, & amicus quondam Virgilij, cuius etiam meminit in decima Aegloga, hoc uersu: Galle quid insanis? Hic cū in summis doloribus uersaretur, composuit eruditissimam querelam de miserijs humanis, in quo scripto reperitur:
units.tr: Cornelius Gallus, a soldier and friend of Augustus, enjoyed such authority and trust with him that Augustus entrusted Egypt to him, where the greatest fear lay. Yet afterwards he fell into Augustus' hatred, on suspicion of aiming at kingship. Because of this he conceived such bitter grief that he took his own life. He was a good soldier and a poet, and a former friend of Virgil, whom he also mentions in the tenth Eclogue with the line: "Gallus, why are you mad?" While he was in the depths of his grief, he composed a most learned lament on human miseries, in which this is found:

units.la: Et redit in nihilum, quod fuit ante nihil.
units.tr: And it returns to nothing, which was nothing before.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Cornelij Agrippæ mors.
units.tr: The death of Cornelius Agrippa.

units.la: Cornelius Agrippa agens agonem mortis, uocauit ad se canem, qui cum ipso circumiuit, eumq; his uerbis alloquitur: Abi à me perdita bestia, quæ me perdidisti. Sic statim canis ab eo discedens, se in aquam præcipitauit.
units.tr: Cornelius Agrippa, struggling in the agony of death, called to himself a dog, which went around with him, and addressed it with these words: "Away from me, you lost beast, who have lost me!" At once the dog, leaving him, threw itself into the water.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Epigramma de quodam doloris extincto.
units.tr: An epigram on a certain man who died of grief.

units.la: Græci habent Epigramma de quodam, quem ita excruciauit forma illa sophisticorum argumentorum, ut mortuus sit præ dolore: Ξεῖνε λόγων ψευδομένος με ἀπόλεσε φίλων. id est: Hospes perdidit me illa forma argumenti, quæ est malorum sermonum. Hoc Epigramma recitat Athenæus: & nominat eum, de quo scriptum est, Phileten.
units.tr: The Greeks have an epigram about a man whom that form of sophistical argument tormented so much that he died of grief: "Stranger, the false words of friends have destroyed me" [Ξεῖνε, λόγων ψευδομένος με ἀπόλεσε φίλων]. That is: the stranger destroyed me, that form of argument which belongs to evil speeches. Athenaeus quotes this epigram, and names the man it is about as Phileta.

units.la: COLL. Alius eodem modo mortuus.
units.tr: COLL. Another who died in the same way.

units.la: In academia Friburgensi, quidam antagonista Eccij, cùm Eccius acerrimè disputaret contra ideas, id est uniuersalia Scoti, alter Scotista uoluit defendere suam sectam: sed cùm uideret se conuici, conscìuit sibi mortem præ dolore, eo quòd superabatur. Illi etiam potuit subscribi superius Epigramma. Sic ualde multos perdidit Sophistica.
units.tr: At the University of Freiburg, a certain opponent of Eck, when Eck was disputing hotly against the ideas, that is the universals of Scotus, wished to defend his sect as a Scotist. But when he saw that he was being refuted, he took his own life out of grief, because he was being overcome. The epigram cited above could also be applied to him. In this way sophistry has destroyed very many.

units.la: COLL. Homeri mors.
units.tr: COLL. The death of Homer.

units.la: Homerus iam senex mortuus esse dicitur, eo quòd non potuerit soluere Aenigma de pediculis. sed existimo esse, fabulam à quodam Homeri osore esse excogitatam.
units.tr: Homer is said to have died when already an old man, because he could not solve the riddle about the lice. But I think this fable was invented by someone who hated Homer.

units.la: COLL. Aristotelis mors.
units.tr: COLL. The death of Aristotle.

units.la: Aristoteles dicitur demersisse se in Euripum, eo quòd causam eius inuestigare non posset: atq; ita extinctus esse. Sed non credo esse uerum. Nazianzenus quidem narrat, sed non est in ueteribus. Forsitan aliqui qui malè senserunt de Aristotele, sparserunt istam fabellam, quòd Aristoteles stans in littore, & cogitans de causa Euripi, cùm eam cogitando assequi non posset, abiecerit se in mare, dicens: Quia Aristoteles non capit, Euripus capiat Aristotelem.
units.tr: Aristotle is said to have plunged himself into the Euripus because he could not discover the cause of its currents, and so to have died. But I do not believe it is true. Gregory of Nazianzus does relate it, but it is not found in the ancient writers. Perhaps some who thought ill of Aristotle spread this little tale: that Aristotle, standing on the shore and thinking about the cause of the Euripus, since he could not grasp it by thinking, threw himself into the sea, saying: "Since Aristotle cannot grasp the Euripus, let the Euripus grasp Aristotle."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Fabula est de Aristeo, quòd fuerit etiam inter Gigantes. sed dij pepercerunt ipsi propter pietatem, quia nō consensit in bellum contra deos. Opinor fabulā esse natam ex imitatione historiæ de diluuio, ubi solus Noe seruatur, reliqui moriūtur.
units.tr: There is a fable about Aristaeus, that he was also among the Giants. But the gods spared him because of his piety, since he did not consent to the war against the gods. I suppose the fable arose from an imitation of the story of the Flood, where only Noah is preserved and the rest die.

units.la: Pompeij mors.
units.tr: The death of Pompey.

units.la: Iulius Cæsar aspexit caput Pompeij lachrimās, & sepeliri curauit. Fuit aūt Pompeius interfectus anno ætatis suæ 59. qui fuit unus ex præcipuis uiris, qui inter Ethnicos uixerunt eo tempore. Cicero ad Cornelium scribens, pulchrè eius laudes amplificat: sed accidit ei id quod uulgo dicitur, ᴈwer einem vom galgen hilfft, der hilfft im selbst dran.
units.tr: Julius Caesar looked upon the head of Pompey with tears and had it buried. Pompey was killed in the fifty-ninth year of his age. He was one of the leading men who lived among the heathen at that time. Cicero, writing to Cornelius, magnificently extols his praises, but it befell him what is commonly said: he who helps someone down from the gallows helps himself up to it.

units.la: Est igitur mors Pompeij testimonium de instabilitate fortunæ, & quòd magni uiri accersant suis erratis magnas miserias: ut Osias rex Israel suo errato sibi & suis ingentes calamitates accersiuit. Cæsaris Iulij mors est testimonium, quòd fortuna tantum sit instabilis.
units.tr: The death of Pompey is therefore a testimony to the instability of fortune, and that great men by their errors bring great miseries upon themselves, just as Azariah, king of Israel, by his error brought great calamities upon himself and his people. The death of Julius Caesar is a testimony that fortune is only unstable.

units.la: DE CONSOLATIONIBUS.
units.tr: ON CONSOLATIONS.

units.la: De bona conscientia, Dicta.
units.tr: On a Good Conscience: Sayings.

units.la: Est aliquid magnis crimē abesse malis: Ouid. Pindarus: Bona conscientia dulcis auctrix senectæ. Hanc sententiam ego olim scripsi ad doctorem ctorem Lamingium. Rescripsit mihi, se ualde ea sententia delectatum fuisse, eamq; multum solatij sibi attulisse, quia antea non audiuerat. Et uerum est sane, homines ualde erigi ac lætari, arrepto aliquo dulcissimo dicto. Salomon scripsit integrum librum talium Sententiarum.
units.tr: It is something to be free of great crimes, as Ovid says. Pindar: "A good conscience is a sweet bringer of old age." I once wrote this saying to Doctor Lamingius. He wrote back that he had been greatly delighted by it, that it had brought him much comfort, because he had never heard it before. And it is indeed true that people are greatly lifted up and cheered when they seize on some very sweet saying. Solomon wrote a whole book of such sayings.

units.la: Philosophicæ consolationis finis.
units.tr: The Goal of Philosophical Consolation.

units.la: Finis consolationis aut doctrinæ humanæ non est consolatio, sed ut habet ille uersus Vergilij, Vitaq; cum gemitu fugit indignata sub umbra.
units.tr: The aim of human consolation or teaching is not consolation itself but, as that line of Vergil has it, "and life flees with a groan under an indignant shade."

units.la: Euangelicæ consolationis finis.
units.tr: The Goal of Evangelical Consolation.

units.la: Finis consolationis in Ecclesia, est uita æterna, iuxta symbolum: Credo uitam æternam. Item: Hæc est uita æterna, ut cognoscant te solum Deum, & Christum esse Iesum. Item, Si quis diligit me, & sermonem meum seruauerit, pater meus diliget eum, & ueniemus ad eum, & mansionem apud eum faciemus.
units.tr: The aim of consolation in the Church is eternal life, according to the creed: "I believe in life everlasting." Likewise: "This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent" (John 17:3). Likewise: "If anyone loves me and keeps my word, my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him" (John 14:23).

units.la: Dixit ad me illustrissimus princeps Lantgrauius Dresdæ, anno 1556, mense Iunio, sibi impossibile fuisse sustinere tanta pericula, nisi habuisset consolationem ex uerbo diuino in suo corde. Die enim & nocte circumsteterunt eum aliquot cohortes militum, quibus custodia mandata fuit.
units.tr: The most illustrious Prince, the Landgrave, told me at Dresden in June 1556 that it would have been impossible for him to endure such dangers had he not had consolation from the divine word in his heart. For several companies of soldiers, to whom his guard had been entrusted, surrounded him day and night.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Gerson: Multo plures sunt gratiæ priuatiuæ, q; posipositiuæ.id est,illa beneficia, quòd Deus custodit nos,ne incidamus in mala (quæ ipse nominat priuatiua)plura sunt,quàm beneficia positiua:id est, res exhibitæ, uel dona quæ possidemus, ut quòd Deus uocauit te ad hoc uel illud munus.
units.tr: Gerson: The privative graces are far more numerous than the positive ones. That is, those benefits by which God keeps us from falling into evils (which he calls privative) outnumber the positive benefits, that is, the things bestowed or the gifts we possess, such as that God has called you to this or that office.

units.la: Liberatio & auxilium Dei contra causas secundas, & mirabile Dei auxilium in summis ærumnis.
units.tr: God's Deliverance and Help against Secondary Causes, and God's Wonderful Help in the Greatest Distress.

units.la: Christianus rex Danicus, bonus & pius princeps, ægrotauit aliquàdo, ut plane de eius uita oës medici desperarent, & iuberent eum se præparare ad mortem, nullam dicentes esse reliquam spem suæ uitæ. Rex illis agit gratias, quòd omnia quæ fieri potuerint, diligenter ad sanitatem constituendam curauerint. se quoque curasse in suo testamento, ut honestè pro labore ipsorum acciperent præmia. Cõpositis itaq; omnibus ad mortem paratis, rex tertio die post conualuit. Hæc & similia exempla sunt obseruanda. Admouet autem nos hæc historia, de mirabili liberatione Dei ex calamitatib. etiam in summis periculis, ne spem auxilij diuini & inuocationem in talibus periculis amittamus.
units.tr: The Christian King of Denmark, a good and pious prince, once fell so ill that all his physicians utterly despaired of his life and told him to prepare himself for death, saying that no hope of his life remained. The king thanked them, because they had carefully done everything that could be done to restore his health. He also made provision in his will that they should receive honourable rewards for their labour. Then, with everything arranged and ready for death, the king recovered on the third day. Such examples and similar ones are to be noted. This story reminds us of God's wonderful deliverance from calamities, even in the greatest perils, so that we do not lose hope of divine help or cease to call upon God in such dangers.

units.la: Consolationes Papisticæ homines in dubitationibus relinquunt.
units.tr: Papist Consolations Leave People in Doubt.

units.la: Heydelbergæ cum puer quãdam moreretur (ubi & ego interfui) quidam doctor Theologiæ cum monacho, morienti puero semper præcinebat cã- tilenam: Maria mater gratiæ, nos in hora mortis suscipe. Talis solet esse consolatio Papistica apud morientes.
units.tr: At Heidelberg, when a boy was dying (and I was present there too), a certain doctor of theology together with a monk kept singing to the dying boy the ditty: "Mary, mother of grace, receive us in the hour of death." Such is the Papist consolation usually offered to the dying.

units.la: Consolatio pro pijs, in calamitatibus uersantibus.
units.tr: Consolation for the Godly Who Are Caught in Calamities.

units.la: In silentio & spe erit fortitudo uestra: id est, nõ fremite aduersus Deũ, non fugite Deũ si differtur auxilium (hæc crebra admonitio fuit D. Philippi) Ista dicta & similia intelliguntur ab ijs, quorum ætas aliquantulum maturuit, ut illa possint perpendere. Iuuenes uero id non intelligunt.
units.tr: "In quietness and in trust shall be your strength" (Isa. 30:15): that is, do not rage against God, and do not flee from God if help is delayed. This was a frequent admonition of Dr Philip. These sayings and others like them are understood by those whose age has ripened somewhat, so that they can weigh them; young people, however, do not understand them.

units.la: Consolatio pro sontibus, & à magistratu interficiendis.
units.tr: Consolation for the Guilty Who Are to Be Executed by the Magistrate.

units.la: Quomodo, si quis ad supplicium capitale producatur, est consolandus?
units.tr: How is a man to be consoled if he is led out to capital punishment?

units.la: Audiat initio uerbum Euangelij de redemptione per Christum, illudq; fide suscipiat, credens se habere remissionem peccatorũ et vitam æternam propter Filium Dei. Sic quoq; secum reputet, Deũ huiusmodi cruces & laqueos aliaq; pœnarũ genera ordinasse, ad ostendendam suã iusticiam, ut qui malefi-cia nolit esse impunita. Quare non cogitet se ea passione aut opere ullam mereri remissionẽ peccatorũ: sed potius tale opus esse, quo Deus vult obedientiã erga se experiri ac declarare: sicut obedien-tiam tiam uoluit ostendere in castitate Ioseph. Sciat uero ac certò statuat peccata sua sibi esse remissa gratuitò, propter Christū, qui pro ijs satisfecit. Hac enim ratione cor seu cõscientia uerū solatiū percipit per Spiritū sanctū, qui operatur uerbo uocali, & sacramentis. Adhæc agnoscat se patientem esse decere, propter Deum, qui sic iusticiam suam ostendit, dum delicta omnēq; iniusticiā, aut immediatè per se, aut mediatè per Magistratum punit. Ita cõfirmatio fidei fit per uerbum & sacramenta, & cum uerbo spiritus sanctus datur, & est efficax.
units.tr: First let him hear the word of the Gospel about redemption through Christ, and let him receive it by faith, believing that he has the forgiveness of sins and eternal life for the sake of the Son of God. Let him also reflect in this way: God has ordained crosses and nooses and other kinds of punishment of this sort to show his justice, since he does not wish wrongdoing to go unpunished. Therefore let him not think that by this suffering or deed he merits any forgiveness of sins; rather, this is a work by which God wills to test and display obedience toward himself, just as he wished to show obedience in the chastity of Joseph. Let him know, and firmly determine, that his sins have been forgiven him freely, for the sake of Christ, who made satisfaction for them. For in this way the heart or conscience receives true comfort through the Holy Spirit, who works through the spoken word and the sacraments. Furthermore, let him acknowledge that it is fitting for him to be patient, for God's sake, who thus shows his justice, since he punishes sins and all injustice, either directly by himself or indirectly through the magistrate. Thus the confirmation of faith comes through the word and the sacraments, and with the word the Holy Spirit is given and is effective.

units.la: Præcipua consolatio, qua se Adam & Eua sustentauerit.
units.tr: The Chief Consolation by Which Adam and Eve Sustained Themselves.

units.la: Facilè quiuis perpendere potest, quanto mœrore Adã atq; Eua affecti fuerint, cũ unus filiorũ alterũ trucidasset. Memini honestā matronā in tanto luctu & mœrore uersatā esse, ut nullā consolatione nisi illud Adæ et Euæ exemplū seu triste spectaculū admitteret. Breui enim tempore amiserat maritum & filiũ. Maritus deciderat de curru, & fractis costis uitam miserabiliter finiuit. Filius uero, paulo ante in aquis suffocatus, extinctus erat.
units.tr: Anyone can easily grasp how great the grief of Adam and Eve must have been when one of their sons slew the other. I remember a certain honourable matron who, while caught in such great sorrow and mourning, would admit no consolation except the example of Adam and Eve, or rather their sad spectacle. For in a short time she had lost her husband and her son. Her husband had fallen from a cart and, with his ribs broken, miserably ended his life; her son, a little before, had been drowned in the waters and was dead.

units.la: Calamitates docent homines, ex uerbo diuino consolationes haurire.
units.tr: Calamities teach people to draw consolations from the divine Word.

units.la: Memini uidu ã Doctoris Martini Lutheri, honestam matronā, ferè tempore belli in exilio nostro, cum legeret Psalmos, dicere: Iam primùm in his nostris
units.tr: I remember seeing an honest matron of Doctor Martin Luther's household, at about the time of the war while we were in exile, reading the Psalms and saying: "Only now, in these our calamities, do I understand many Psalms which I did not understand before, since I was not living in such distress. So from them I receive more consolation and instruction than I ever felt apart from such calamities."

units.la: Adam & Eua exm conso. latiuncs stris calamitatibus intelligo multos Psalmos, quos antea non intellexi, non uersans in illis ærumnis. Vnde plus consolationis & doctrinæ percipio, quàm aliàs extra illas calamitates sensi.
units.tr: Now, in our calamities, I understand many Psalms which I did not understand before, not having experienced such troubles. Hence I receive more consolation and teaching from them than I ever felt at other times outside such calamities.

units.la: COLL. Consolatio pro destitutis auxilio diuino.
units.tr: COLL. Consolation for those deprived of divine help.

units.la: Fuit ante aliquot annos Madeburgensis episcopus, Ioannes à Beichlingen. Is cùm à collegio ad episcopatū esset pertractus, forte accidit, ut quidā dux ob simultatem aliquam bellum ei inferre pararet. Episcopus tanquā altum somnum dormiens, nihil contra talem uim parabat: sed curabat Ecclesiam suā, in qua frequenter uitia corrigere lectione & oratione diligenti conabatur, perinde ac si nullus esset belli metus. Cū autem idem dux speculatores mitteret in aulam Episcopi: illiq; easdem res, quas uiderant, retulissent: statim ab optimo Principe intermissa est expeditio, & dimissi sunt milites. Ita enim respondit, Se longè inferiorē esse, quàm ut cum ea pugnaret, qui socium haberet pugnæ Deū. Ideo nō fallit consolatio, & spes in diuinū auxiliū.
units.tr: Some years ago there was a bishop of Magdeburg, Johann von Beichlingen. When he had been elected bishop by the cathedral chapter, it happened that a certain duke, out of some quarrel, prepared to make war on him. The bishop, as if sleeping a deep sleep, made no preparation against such force, but went on caring for his Church, in which he diligently tried to correct faults by reading and prayer, just as if there were no fear of war at all. When the same duke sent scouts to the bishop's court and they reported what they had seen, the expedition was at once called off by that excellent prince, and the soldiers were dismissed. For he replied that he was far too weak to fight against one who had God as his companion in the fight. Therefore consolation and hope in divine help do not deceive.

units.la: Dictū, quod cùm ad Philosophicas, tū ad Euangelicas referri potest.
units.tr: This is a saying which can be referred both to the philosophers and to the Gospel.

units.la: In consolationib. plerunq; traditur hæc sentētia, τέον καὶ ἐλπιστέον: id est, ferendū & sperandū, id à magnis uiris esse scriptum in parietibus,
units.tr: In consolations this maxim is commonly handed down: must be endured and must be hoped for [τλητέον καὶ ἐλπιστέον]; that is, one must bear and one must hope. I remember that this was written by great men on walls, as a motto.

units.la: pro symbolo. Ac memini à quodã doctore, erudito ac ualdè præstanti uiro, qui erat magnorũ principũ consiliarius, esse scriptum ante annos 8 o.
units.tr: I also remember that it was written, some eight years ago, by a certain teacher, a learned and very distinguished man who was counsellor to great princes.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Consolatio contra diabolicas tentationes.
units.tr: A consolation against diabolical temptations.

units.la: Cùm Friburgi in Misnia quidam ualdè pius & uenerandus senex graui morbo decũberet, & iam ultimum diem obiturus eßet, aliquãdo ipso relicto solo, uenit diabolus amictus Pontificali ueste, & mi serum senem iam in ipso mortis agone ualdè exagitauit, uolens eum ui cogere, ut ipsi singula delicta, quæ in tota sua uita comisisset, enarraret. Volebat enim ipse, habens chartam & atramentũ, omnia signare. Verùm cùm pius senex diu uehemêter per sacras literas obstreperet, nec persuaderetur, & tamẽ diabolus uehemêter illã narratione urgeret, tandẽ bonus senex dixit: Quandoquidẽ igitur omnino hoc uis, ut tibi singillatim delicta mea enarrem: scribe itaq; huiusmodi primùm facto exordio, Semen mulieris conteret caput serpentis, &c.
units.tr: When a certain very pious and venerable old man lay sick with a grave illness at Freiberg in Meissen, and was now about to die, the devil one day, with the old man left alone, came in the guise of a pontifical vestment and violently harassed the wretched old man, who was already in his death agony, trying to force him to recount each of the sins he had committed in his whole life. For the devil himself, holding paper and ink, wanted to write them all down. But when the pious old man had for a long time vigorously resisted with the words of Holy Scripture and would not be persuaded, and the devil still pressed hard for this confession, at last the good old man said: "Since you so insist on it, that I should recount my sins to you one by one, then write this down first, as the beginning: 'The seed of the woman shall bruise the head of the serpent,' etc."

units.la: Diabolus hoc audiens, proiecit chartã unà cũ atramento in terram, & relicto post se ingenti fœtore aufugit. Senex uerò ille pius paulo pòst placida morte in bona confessione mortuus est.
