units.tr: When the devil heard this, he threw the paper, together with the ink, onto the ground, and fled, leaving a great stench behind him. But that pious old man, a little later, died a peaceful death in a good confession.

units.la: Consolatio ex dicto Pauli ad Romanos octauo capite: Quis nos separabit à dilectione Dei?
units.tr: A consolation from the saying of Paul in Romans, chapter eight: "Who shall separate us from the love of God?"

units.la: Vxor Camerarij aliquando audiuerat Sarceriũ explicantem dictum Pauli, Quis nos à dilectione Dei separabit, reuersa domũ: Ah, inquit, ego iam audiui aliquid in concione, quod nunquam obliui scar. Interrogo quid sit? Respondit illa: Sæpe cogitaui, quando hoc dictum audiui legi, Quis separabit nos à dilectione Dei: O bone Deus, quid de te fiet? tu non amas Deum, ergo es à Deo tibi irascen te derelicta. Sed iam ex hac concione didici, quòd dictum non sit intelligendũ de nostra dilectione, qua nos Deum diligimus: sed de dilectione, qua Deus nos diligit, à qua nemo poterit nos separare.
units.tr: Once the wife of Camerarius had heard Sarcerius expounding Paul's saying, "Who shall separate us from the love of God," and on returning home she said: "Ah, I have now heard something in the sermon that I shall never forget. I ask what it is? She replied: I have often thought, whenever I heard or read this saying, 'Who shall separate us from the love of God?', O good God, what will become of us? You do not love God, so you have been forsaken by God, who is angry with you. But now from this sermon I have learned that the saying is not to be understood of our love, by which we love God, but of the love by which God loves us, from which no one can separate us."

units.la: Hoc ideo recito, ut firmius & melius retineatis, dictum hoc esse intelligendum passiuè, non actiuè.
units.tr: I recite this so that you may hold it more firmly and more clearly: this saying is to be understood passively, not actively.

units.la: Ducis Luneburgēsis decedentis ex hac miseriarum ualle, Christiana confessio & consolatio.
units.tr: The Christian confession and consolation of the Duke of Lüneburg, departing from this vale of miseries.

units.la: Dux Luneburgensis, bonus & pius princeps, qui præcisus est pes ante paucos annos, moriebatur iuuenis, & in magno dolore: tamen edebat confessionem insignem, dicens: Ego certò scio, quòd mea peccata mihi remißa sunt propter filiũ Dei: & illi dolores tantum sunt commonefactiones pœnitentiæ.
units.tr: The Duke of Lüneburg, a good and pious prince, whose foot was cut off a few years ago, was dying young and in great pain. Yet he made a remarkable confession, saying: "I know for certain that my sins have been forgiven me for the sake of the Son of God, and these pains are only reminders of repentance."

units.la: Consolatio Doctoris Martini Lutheri, contra spirituales tentationes.
units.tr: The consolation of Doctor Martin Luther against spiritual temptations.

units.la: Ipse uideriť ubi anima mea mansura sit, qui pro ea sic solicitus fuit, ut uitā seu animā propriam pro ea posuerit, ut meam redimeret. Ille est optimus pastor, & benedictus episcopus animarum in se credentium. Neq; enim in me primùm docet animas sibi credentes curare, neq; eam ipsam uolo in mea manu aut cura positam esse, alioqui in momento à diabolo devoraretur: sed ipse in manu habeat, cui nemo rapere potest. Nunc sufficit nosse, in domo patris mei esse multas habitationes.
units.tr: He himself will see where my soul is to remain, he who was so anxious for it that he laid down his life and soul for it, to redeem mine. He is the best minister and the blessed bishop of the souls that believe in him. For he does not teach me that I am to take care of the souls entrusted to him, nor do I want that soul itself to be placed in my hand or care, otherwise it would at once be devoured by the devil; rather let him keep it in his hand, from which no one can snatch it. For now it is enough to know that in my Father's house there are many dwelling places.

units.la: DE INVOCATIONE.
units.tr: DE INVOCATIONE.

units.la: Ore & expressis uerbis precationes fiant.
units.tr: Prayers should be made aloud and in express words.

units.la: CVm Cyclopicus homo irrideret quendam precantem, & uerba suæ precationis expressa uoce dicentem, cui assidebat Doctor Hieronymus Schurpf: hic ægrè ferens istius ineptias, inquit: Scriptum est de precatione, Precantes dicite: ac aliquoties uocabulum, Dicite, urgebat.
units.tr: When a Cyclops-like boor was mocking a man who was praying and speaking the words of his prayer aloud, Doctor Hieronymus Schurpf, who was sitting beside him, was annoyed at the fellow's silliness. He said: "Scripture says about prayer, 'When you pray, say,'" and he kept pressing the word "say" several times.

units.la: Ignauiæ in recitatione precum taxatio.
units.tr: The censure of laziness in reciting prayers.

units.la: D. Philippus taxans negligentiam in recitatione precum, sæpe dicere solebat: Turpe ac detestandum est, uos mane surgentes non dicere orationem Dominicam, cum recitatione alicuius psalmi & symboli Apostolici, aut cū gratiarūactione pro beneficijs acceptis. Multi dicūt, Cor loquitur cū Deo. Verum est, recitationem uerborum ore, sine corde, esse hypocrisin: sed tamen etiā palàm nostrā fidem confiteri oportet: & qui dicunt, cor orat, illi tantū prætendunt excusationē negligentiæ & pigritiæ suæ in omittenda plane omni precatione. Itaq; German manicum prouerbiū uerè idem exprimit: <bl>Swes das herȝ vol ist, des ghet der mundt über.</bl> Quod sic exprimit Salomō: Ex abūdatia cordis os loquitur. Ergo dū nihil egreditur, nihil inest pectori. Quare nō tātū murmurate, aut apud uos ofcitātes precatione cogitate, sed etiā expressa uoce attentione excitate.
units.tr: Doctor Philip, censuring carelessness in the recitation of prayers, used often to say: "It is shameful and detestable that you, rising in the morning, do not recite the Lord's Prayer, together with some psalm and the Apostles' Creed, or a thanksgiving for benefits received. Many say, 'The heart speaks with God.' It is true that reciting words with the mouth without the heart is hypocrisy, but still we ought to confess our faith openly. Those who say 'the heart prays' only put forward an excuse for their carelessness and laziness in omitting prayer altogether. So the German proverb expresses the truth: <bl>Where the heart is full, the mouth overflows.</bl> Solomon expresses the same thing: 'Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.' Therefore, when nothing comes out, nothing is within the breast. So do not merely mutter, or yawn among yourselves while thinking about prayer, but rouse your attention with an audible voice."

units.la: De sanctorum inuocatione, Doctoris Martini Lutheri iudicium.
units.tr: On the invocation of the saints: the judgment of Doctor Martin Luther.

units.la: Doctor Martinus sæpe dicebat, quod est dignū memoria: Etiamsi inuocatio hominū mortuorum non propter multas alias causas esset detestanda, tamen propter hoc esset detestāda, quòd obscurat meritū et obedientiā filij Dei, qui pro peccatis generis humani satisfecit.
units.tr: Doctor Martin often said, and it is worth remembering: "Even if the invocation of dead men were not to be condemned for many other reasons, it would still be condemned for this: that it obscures the merit and obedience of the Son of God, who made satisfaction for the sins of the human race."

units.la: Simile.
units.tr: A comparison.

units.la: Viennæ ante paucos annos cōcionator Regius, differēs de inuocatione sanctorū dixit: Nos nō debere inuocare sanctos, sed cū eis. Dictū est ingenio si hominis, sed quomodo idē declarauerit, non scio.
units.tr: A few years ago at Vienna a royal preacher, speaking about the invocation of the saints, said: "We ought not to invoke the saints, but to invoke with them." It was a witty saying of the man, but I do not know how he explained it.

units.la: Δεῖ cὺ σὺφμίᾳ ἀποθανεῖν. Oportet mori in precatione. Ita uidetis Christum cruce pendentem in precatione mori, ac dicere: Pater ignosce illis, quia nesciunt quid faciunt. Et notum est dictũ:Beati mortui, qui in Domino moriũtur:id est,in agnitione,inuocatione,uera fide et fiducia mediatoris. Item: Si quis perseuerauit usque ad finem, saluus erit.
units.tr: One must die in prayer [Δεῖ συνευφημίᾳ ἀποθανεῖν]. Thus you see Christ dying on the cross in prayer, saying: "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do." And it is a well-known saying: "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord," that is, in knowledge, invocation, true faith and trust in the Mediator. Likewise: "He who has persevered to the end will be saved."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam eremita orauit Deũ sibi ostendi,qualem cultum peteret.Respondit ei oraculum: Da mediam lunam,solem,simul & canis iram. Ille bonus pater ualdè anxius mirabatur,quomodo uellet cœlo lunam detrahere, & multo magis solem?cum hoc uelit, Da { Mediam lunam } Id est { C O R } Solem. Canis iram
units.tr: A certain hermit prayed that God would show him what kind of worship he should seek. An oracle answered him: "Give the half-moon, the sun, and the dog's wrath." That good father, very anxious, wondered how he was to take the moon from the sky, and much more the sun, since it wills this: Give { the half-moon } That is { the HEART } the sun. The dog's wrath.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Bernhardus:Semper precatio,aut hoc quod petit impetrat,aut aliquid melius.
units.tr: Bernard: Prayer always either obtains what it asks, or something better.

units.la: Mos supplicum pulchrè accômodatus ad inuocationem.
units.tr: A suppliant's custom aptly applied to invocation.

units.la: Fuit uetus mos fieri supplicè,ita ut manu supplex teneret filium illius cui supplex fiebat. Themistocles mistocles uenit ad regem Molossorum, petiturus hospitium, ne interficeretur: stetitq; supplex ad aram, cum ueniret rex, filium paruulum tenens in manibus: et ostenso filio, petiuit sibi parci. Talis fuit ritus supplicum, hauddubie à primis patribus, Adam, Seth, Sem & Abraham usurpatus. Nos simili modo accedentes ad Deum, stamus coram eo supplices, tenentes filiū suum unigenitum fide in corde nostro: & obtestamur æternum patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, ut nostras preces propter filij sui pro nobis crucifixi & resuscitati obedientiam exaudiat.
units.tr: There was an ancient custom of making supplication, so that the suppliant held in his hand the child of the one to whom he made supplication. Themistocles came to the king of the Molossians, seeking hospitality, so that he might not be killed. He stood as a suppliant at the altar when the king came, holding a small child in his arms; and, showing the child, he asked that he be spared. Such was the rite of suppliants, doubtless used from the first fathers, Adam, Seth, Shem and Abraham. Coming to God in a similar way, we stand before him as suppliants, holding his only-begotten Son in our hearts by faith, and we beseech the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ to hear our prayers for the sake of the obedience of his Son, who was crucified and raised again for us.

units.la: Tres causæ, quare propagatio longioris uitæ sit petenda.
units.tr: Three reasons why a longer life should be asked for.

units.la: Prima, ut ipsi doctrinam de Deo discamus.
units.tr: First, that we may learn the doctrine of God ourselves.

units.la: Secūda, ut eam in uitæ periculis, pœnitentia, & quotidiana inuocatione exerceamus, & in nobis ueram fidei sententiam confirmemus.
units.tr: Second, that we may exercise it in the dangers of life, in repentance and in daily invocation, and confirm in ourselves the true judgment of faith.

units.la: Tertia, ut alios erudiamus, cōfirmemus, & uerā Dei agnitionem ad posteros propagemus.
units.tr: Third, that we may teach and strengthen others, and spread the true knowledge of God to posterity.

units.la: Cassita admonitrix sedulæ inuocationis.
units.tr: The lark as a reminder of diligent invocation.

units.la: Cassita est monitrix duarū rerū. Initiò est laudatrix Dei: quia quotidie canit ter mane, paulo ante solis ortum, meridie & vesperi. Docet nos illa tempora distribuere precationi, & gratiarum actioni. Deinde est monitrix operum agricolarū. opera enim rustica inchoantur, quādo primùm ue-nit casita in vere.
units.tr: The lark is a reminder of two things. First, it is a praiser of God, since it sings every day three times: early in the morning, a little before sunrise, at midday, and in the evening. It teaches us to distribute those times to prayer and to thanksgiving. Second, it is a reminder of the work of farmers, for rustic labours begin as soon as the lark comes in spring.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Salsum dictum, quo diabolus ab inuocante est depulsus.
units.tr: A witty saying by which the devil was driven off by one who prayed.

units.la: Mementote historiā, uel potius fabellā de Sancto Bernhardo. est enim erudita fabella, cuiuscunq; sit. Bernhardus sedens in latrina, recitans preces, cum ueniret ad eum diabolus, quærens quare tam sancta eo in loco recitaret. Respondit: Quæ sancta uerba ex ore profero, ad Deum perfero: quæ per inferiora decidunt, hæc tu excipe.
units.tr: Remember the story, or rather the little tale, about Saint Bernard. It is a learned little tale, whoever its author. Bernard was sitting in the privy, reciting his prayers, when the devil came to him and asked why he recited such holy words in such a place. He replied: "The holy words that come from my mouth I carry up to God; whatever falls downward, you may take for yourself."

units.la: Regula precantibus perpendenda.
units.tr: A rule to be weighed by those who pray.

units.la: Promissiones diuinæ sunt ratæ & firmæ, scilicet cum exceptione castigationis & crucis. & hic retinetè practicatur tertia petitio orationis Dominicæ, quæ sic sonat: Fiat voluntas tua, sicut in cœlo, sic etiam in terra.
units.tr: The promises of God are sure and firm, namely with the exception of chastisement and the cross. And here the third petition of the Lord's Prayer, which runs thus, is rightly applied: "Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth."

units.la: Nobilis quidā, qui in maximas tentationes, & penè in desperationem inciderat, is mihi & Doctori Martino Luthero hoc argumentum proponebat, & magnis vociferationibus dicebat:
units.tr: A certain nobleman, who had fallen into very great temptations and nearly into despair, put this argument to me and to Doctor Martin Luther, and said with loud outcries:

units.la: Deus promisit se exauditurum nos, ipsum invocantes.
units.tr: God has promised that he will hear us when we call upon him.

units.la: Ego istam calamitatem sæpe deprecatus sum, et adhuc quotidie deprecor: sed tamen non liberor, et relinquor in ista calamitate.
units.tr: I have often prayed, and still pray every day, to be freed from this calamity; yet I am not freed, and I am left in this calamity.

units.la: Ergo, Deus non est uerax in suis promissionib. Respondeo ad maiorem : Deus promisit se nos exauditurũ esse in calamitatib. Promissio uerò illa intelligenda est cum exceptione castigationis, & crucis: plerũq; uerò calamitates sunt castigationes.
units.tr: Therefore God is not truthful in his promises. I answer the major premise: God has promised that he will hear us in calamities; but that promise must be understood with the exception of chastisement and the cross, and for the most part calamities are chastisements.

units.la: Sanctorum pro Ecclesia perpetuæ preces.
units.tr: The perpetual prayers of the saints for the Church.

units.la: In cõuentu Ratisbonensi, cùm quidã ex collocutoribus multos locos ex Augustino & alijs ueteris Ecclesiæ scriptoribus citaret, quod sancti scirent aliquid de uiuentibus, quibus sanctorũ inuocationem uolebat probare: ego deniq; respondi : Quid tã multa dicta ex Augustino et alijs ueteris Ecclesiæ scriptorib. citas, quasi Augustino & alijs Ecclesiæ scriptorib. sit tantũ habenda fides, & ex illis scriptis solummodo aliquid iudicandũ, & nullũ in sacris literis haberemus. Imò dicã tibi manifestũ testimoniũ ex nouo Testamento, probans quòd mortui sint soliciti de ecclesia et de nobis. Ita enim ait Matthæus: Elias & Moyses loquebantur cum Christo de rebus futuris. Ibi dixit Granuelus: Est bonum testimoniũ. & approbauit illud. Nõ dubium est, quin sancti ipsi qui sunt in cœlo, nostri cura erga Ecclesiã in terra uiuentem afficiantur, sicut illi ibi disputabant cum Christo de ipsius passione & collectione Ecclesiæ per totum terrarum orbem. Non tamẽ propterea sequitur, sanctos esse inuocandos.
units.tr: At the Regensburg conference, when one of the interlocutors cited many passages from Augustine and other writers of the ancient Church, to prove that the saints know something of the living, and so to prove the invocation of saints, I finally replied: "Why do you cite so many sayings from Augustine and other writers of the ancient Church, as if faith were to be placed in Augustine and the other writers of the Church alone, and we were to judge only from their writings and had no testimony in the sacred letters? Rather, I will give you a plain testimony from the New Testament, proving that the dead are concerned for the Church and for us. For so Matthew says: Elias and Moses talked with Christ about future things." Granuelus said: "It is a good testimony," and he approved it. There is no doubt that the saints who are in heaven are affected with care for the Church living on earth, just as those men were there disputing with Christ about his passion and the gathering of the Church through the whole world. Yet it does not follow from this that the saints are to be invoked.

units.la: Elusio invocationis sanctorum:
units.tr: Evasion of the invocation of saints.

units.la: Præfecto cuidam in mea patria, alius quispiam aulicus volebat persuadere opinionem de invocatione sanctorum, sic inquiens: Non ne vides, in aulis oportere aliquē, volentem sua negocia promover, habere intercessorem et deprecatorem pro se apud reges & alios potentes dominos? respondit Præfectus: ô Domine, si in cœlo talis vitæ status futurus est, qualis in hac vita status aulicus, ego ne quidem optarem venire in cœlum. In aulis enim est προσωπολη̃psia: in regno vero cœlesti non erit acceptio personarum.
units.tr: To a certain prefect in my homeland, another courtier was trying to persuade him of the opinion about invoking the saints, saying: "Do you not see that in courts someone who wishes to promote his affairs must have an intercessor and advocate on his behalf with kings and other powerful lords?" The prefect replied: "Sir, if the condition of life in heaven is to be like the condition of a courtier's life in this world, I would not even wish to come to heaven. For in courts there is respect of persons; but in the heavenly kingdom there will be no acceptance of persons."

units.la: Ante aliquot annos quispiam in quodam loco concionabatur, quòd sancti non essent invocandi, orta sic concione: Nulli sancti sunt in cœlo, & omnes sancti dormiunt. Coepit materiam alienissimam, nunquam ab hominibus illius loci auditam, qua voluit evertere cultum sanctorum. Quare statim explosus & eiectus est. Sic recte ipsi accidit. Nam sancti sunt in cœlo, ut apparet ex apparitione Eliæ & Moysi in monte Thabor.
units.tr: Some years ago someone was preaching in a certain place that the saints were not to be invoked, and his sermon began thus: "There are no saints in heaven, and all the saints are asleep." He began a subject quite alien, never heard before by the people of that place, by which he wished to overturn the cult of the saints. For this reason he was at once hissed down and driven out. So it fittingly happened to him; for the saints are in heaven, as appears from the appearance of Elias and Moses on Mount Tabor.

units.la: DE TRADITIONIBVS humanis.
units.tr: On human traditions.

units.la: IN Hassia bonus vir concionator, in mutatione illorum ritu̇um, cùm hortaretur populū de abolendo discrimine ciborum, dixit: Vtitur utiq; hac liberlibertate ipse Princeps noster. Significans, Latgra- uium ipsum uesci carnibus. & obtinuit. Postea in- cidit in morbū in Quadragesima. Ibi petiit rur- sus à populo, ut abstinerent à carnibus, saltem in hac Quadragesima : ne uideretur à se ortum esse initium mutationis illorum rituum in Ecclesia.
units.tr: In Hesse a good preacher, while urging the people to give up the distinction between foods during the change of their ceremonies, said: "Our own Prince makes use of this liberty." He meant that the Landgrave himself eats meat, and he won his point. Afterwards he fell ill during Lent. There he asked the people again to abstain from meat, at least during this Lent, so that it would not appear that he had started the change of those ceremonies in the Church.

units.la: Recitatur historia de Spiridone Cyprio episcopo, digna memoratu. Cùm ad eum uenisset hospes die ieiunij, nec subitò promi aut parari cibi usitati illo die possent, iubet carnes, quas reconditas habebat, apponi: Non uescor his, inquit hospes, hodie. sum enim Christianus. Tum Spiridon: Et hanc ipsam ob causam te uesci decet, quia es Christianus. Nam om nis creatura Dei bona est, & nihil reijciendum quod cū gratiarū actione sumitur. Obtēperat hos- pes monitus hoc exemplo, et discit longè alios maiores cultu Deo præstādos esse, q; hæc ciborū discrimina.
units.tr: There is a story worth recalling about Spyridon, bishop of Cyprus. When a guest came to him on a fast day, and no ordinary food for that day could be quickly produced or prepared, he ordered the meat he had stored away to be set before him. "I do not eat these things today," said the guest, "for I am a Christian." Then Spyridon said: "For that very reason you ought to eat them, because you are a Christian. For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving." The guest, warned by this example, complied, and learned that far greater things than these distinctions of food are to be performed in the worship of God.

units.la: Papa Hadrianus, qui fuit præceptor Caroli V. Imperatoris, scripsit longum librū de traditionib. humanis, in hanc sententiā, quòd episcoporū tra- ditiones obligent homines: id est, quòd sit peccatum mortale, uiolare traditiones Pontificum, sicut ille nominat. Sic uerò argumentatur:
units.tr: Pope Hadrian, who was the tutor of the Emperor Charles V, wrote a long book on human traditions to this effect: that the traditions of bishops bind men, that is, that it is a mortal sin to violate the traditions of the popes, as he calls them. He argues as follows:

units.la: Nō obedire parentibus, est peccatū mortale.
units.tr: Not to obey parents is a mortal sin.

units.la: Pontifex autem & episcopi, sunt loco parentum in ecclesia.
units.tr: But the pope and the bishops stand in the place of parents in the Church.

units.la: Ergo nō obedire Pontifici & episcopis, est peccatum mortale.
units.tr: Therefore not to obey the pope and the bishops is a mortal sin.

units.la: Respondeo: Maior est uera: Qui maledixerit patri suo, morte moriatur. Minorē concedo, in his quae sunt ministerij: non in illis quae sunt extra ministerium. Deus ipse prohibet pastoribus, condere leges de discrimine ciborum. Ita ille errat in hypothesi falsa.
units.tr: I reply: the major premise is true: "Whoever curses his father or mother shall surely be put to death." I grant the minor premise, in matters that belong to the ministry, but not in those that lie outside the ministry. God himself forbids ministers to make laws concerning the distinction of foods. Thus he errs with a false hypothesis.

units.la: Quidā ante annos 12, cuiusdā sui uicini einovo-μάχς, eijcientis statuas ex templo, easq; cōburentis fidem sic explorauit. Cuidam statuae impositū puluerem tormentariū, ignorante suo uicino, qui pro more statuas imponebat in fornacem. post paruum interuallum, puluere incenso, excussit fornacem, et omnes fenestras. Ibi consternatus einovομάχος, currit ad uicinum, conquerens ipsi de illo casu. Existimabat enim, illam poenam diuinitus inflictam esse, propterea quòd statuas, nulla habita ratione, multis cōtumelijs afficeret. Tum uicinus inquit: Tu puniris hanc ipsam ob causam. Elapso uero triduo, einovομάχος rursus conuenit uicinum. Ibi uicinus auditis iterum ipsius querelis, tandem inquit: Qualis est tua fides & constantia in doctrina Euangelij? tu fatue, ego impositi puluerem in statuam, ut examinarem te in doctrina Christiana, & qualis esset tua constantia in hac statua experirer. Quid enim facturus esses, si tibi dicenda esset confessio coram toto mundo propter Euangelium, cùm in hac tam leui re sis tam perterritus?
units.tr: Some twelve years ago, a neighbour of mine, an image-breaker [εἰκονομάχος], who was throwing statues out of a church and burning them, tested the faith of a certain neighbour in this way. Gunpowder was placed in one of the statues, without the knowledge of his neighbour, who, as was his custom, was putting the statues into the furnace. After a short interval, the powder was ignited, and it blew out the furnace and all the windows. The image-breaker was dismayed, and ran to his neighbour, complaining to him about the accident. For he thought that this punishment had been inflicted by God, because he had treated the statues with insults without any restraint. Then the neighbour said: "You are being punished for this very reason." But after three days had passed, the image-breaker met his neighbour again. There the neighbour, having heard his complaints once more, finally said: "What sort of faith and constancy do you have in the teaching of the Gospel, you fool? I put the powder in the statue so that I might test you in Christian doctrine, and find out how steadfast you were in regard to this statue. For what would you do if you had to make confession before the whole world for the sake of the Gospel, when you are so terrified in this trivial matter?"

units.la: Doctus & ingeniosus uir, huius oppidi Vuittebergensis pastor, frater Doctoris Pontani, cum esset ualetudinarius, propter crebra bonorū amicorum colloquia adebat cōmensales. Accidit uerò, ut cum eius conuictores luderent in illis diebus hilariū seu bacchanalijs, ipse disputaret cū Hieronymo Baumgartnero, et alijs, proponēs hanc quæstionē: Quare uultis seruare illos ludos hilariū, & nō seruare iciuniū, uel quadragesimā? Postulabat primò rationē. deinde duriter eos obiurgabat, quòd nullam scirent adducere. Ita quidam uenit in illis ludis hilarium, Quid, inquiens, an ego existimem hic esse Christianos, cùm uideā tales choreas? pridie enim auditores Iurisconsultorū instruxerāt cœnā, ad quam uocauerāt omnes Doctores cū eorum coniugibus & filiab. ac deinde choreas instituerāt. quem ego obiurgabam dicens: Quare sumis tibi iudicium de Ecclesia? Postea cum esset refutatus, modestius est locutus. Fecit sicut quidam pastor in loco vicino, qui inceptè concionabatur contra suos dominos, descendentes in illis diebus hilarijs personas ad quorundam ciuium familias. Imò hæc fuit magna benevolentia, & familiaritas superiorum ad inferiores.
units.tr: A learned and clever man, pastor of this town of Wittenberg and brother of Doctor Pontanus, was in poor health, and because of frequent conversations with good friends he used to visit his dinner companions. It happened that, while his fellow guests were making merry in those days of festivity or bacchanalia, he disputed with Hieronymus Baumgartner and others, putting this question: "Why do you wish to keep those festive games, and not keep the fast or Lent?" At first he demanded a reason, and then he rebuked them harshly because they could bring none. So one of them, who had come to those festive games, said: "What, do you think there are Christians here, when you see such dances? For the day before, the students of the lawyers had prepared a dinner, to which they had invited all the teachers with their wives and daughters, and afterwards they had arranged dances." I rebuked him, saying: "Why do you take upon yourself the judgement of the Church?" Afterwards, when he had been refuted, he spoke more modestly. He did as a certain pastor in a nearby place did, who, in a rash sermon, attacked his masters for going about in those festive days to the households of certain citizens. Indeed, this was great kindness and familiarity of superiors towards their inferiors.

units.la: Nūc uenio ad quæstionē: Est'ne licitū Christianis seruare bacchanalia(ut uocant)nec ne? Respōdeo: Ieiunium est superstitio, si fiat cum obseruatione opinionis cultus & necessitatis.
units.tr: Now I come to the question: is it lawful for Christians to keep the bacchanalia (as they call them), or not? I reply: fasting is superstition, if it is done with the observance of an opinion of worship and of necessity.

units.la: Superstitiões et impios cultus necesse est aboleri.
units.tr: Superstitions and impious forms of worship must necessarily be abolished.

units.la: Ieiunium, quod fit cum obseruatione opinionis cultus aut necessitatis; est impius cultus.
units.tr: Fasting that is done with the observance of an opinion of worship or of necessity is an impious form of worship.

units.la: Ergo tale ieiunium est abolendum. Illa uerò relaxatio animorum, est consuetudo politica. Cõsuetudines aūt politicæ honestæ possūt retineri. Ergo et illa honesta politica cõsuetudo retineri debebat.
units.tr: Therefore such fasting is to be abolished. But that relaxation of spirits is a political custom. Honourable political customs may be retained. Therefore that honourable political custom ought also to have been retained.

units.la: Explicatio dicti: Omnis creatura sanctificatur per precationem.
units.tr: Explanation of the saying: Every creature is sanctified by prayer.

units.la: Omnis creatura sanctificatur per precationē: id est, placet Deo, est concessa, eius usus fit sanctus. Fuit hic longa disputatio, an liceret Iurisconsulto dicere causam. Doctor Hieronymus acerrimè disputabat. Doctor Pontanus, bonus et honestus uir, uolebat professionem suam abijcere. Sed illa res est diligenter, Dei beneficio, explicata. Omnis creatura sanctificatur: id est, usus eius fit concessus & sanctus.
units.tr: Every creature is sanctified by prayer: that is, it pleases God, it is permitted, and its use becomes holy. There was a long dispute here over whether it was lawful for a jurist to plead a case. Doctor Hieronymus argued most sharply against it. Doctor Pontanus, a good and honest man, wanted to give up his profession. But the matter was carefully settled, by God's blessing. Every creature is sanctified: that is, its use is made permitted and holy.

units.la: τέλος σὺν θεῷ.
units.tr: The end, with God [τέλος σὺν θεῷ].

units.la: LOCORVM COMMVNIVM A' IOANNE
units.tr: THE COMMON PLACES, VOLUME 1, BY JOHN

units.la: Manlio collectorum,
units.tr: of Manlius's collections,

units.la: TOMVS II.
units.tr: VOLUME II.

units.la: In quo, præter aliaʒuariæ[?] quoque
units.tr: In which, besides various other matters, there are also treated

units.la: materiæ ad seriem Decalogi accommodatæ tractan-
units.tr: matters suited to the order of the Decalogue,

units.la: tur.
units.tr: are treated.

units.la: IOANNIS MANLII IN SECUNDAM huius Operis partem PRAEFATIO.
units.tr: JOHN MANLIUS'S PREFACE TO THE SECOND PART OF THIS WORK.

units.la: In qua ea exponuntur, de quibus præcipuè Lector admonendus fuit.
units.tr: In which are set out the matters about which the reader in particular ought to be warned.

units.la: NON temerè aut inconsideratè labor hic noster, amice Lector, collectus ex ore D. PHILIPPI Melanchthonis, aliisq; clarissimis uiris (qui nunquam cogitarunt fore ut ipsorum dicta typis commendarentur) in lucem prodit: sed multi uiri doctrina & pietate excellentes, occasionem mihi dederunt, primùm ut eum susciperem, deinde quoq; typis uulgari paterer. Hi enim cùm uiderent, me plurima exempla partim ex lectionibus PHILIPPI Melanchthonis, partim etiam ex aliorum doctissimorum quorundam relationibus collegisse: seduli adhortatores fuerunt, ne solus illis ipse fruerer, sed aliis quoq; communicarem. Id quòd ea fieri ratione uel optimè posse, si in publicum ea, ad studiosorum utilitatem, emitterem.
units.tr: This labour of mine, kind reader, gathered from the mouth of Dr Philip Melanchthon and other most distinguished men (who never imagined their sayings would be commended to print), does not come forth to the light rashly or thoughtlessly. Rather, many men excellent in learning and piety gave me the occasion, first to undertake it and then to allow it to be made public in print. For when they saw that I had collected very many examples, partly from the lectures of Philip Melanchthon and partly also from the accounts of certain other most learned men, they were diligent in urging me not to enjoy them alone but to share them with others. This could be done best of all, they said, if I put them out to the public for the benefit of students.

units.la: Horum uerò petitioni tametsi primùm propter multas & graues causas ualde reluctatus fuerim: tamen uictus tandem, & persuasus, ne prorsus ex omnium manibus, & praesertim meo usu exciderent (quod propemodum aliquando accidisset) cum mihi obijceretur illud aliquoties uitium, me inuidere ipsis, ipsorumq; posteris materias illas, eorum tandem uoluntati acquieui. In disponendis autem his Exemplis, ordo in hoc nostro labore non parum negocij mihi facessebat: uerùm postea serió rem & exactè perpendéti, succurrebat uulgaris admonitio illa:
units.tr: Although at first I struggled hard against their request, for many weighty reasons, yet at last I was overcome and persuaded, lest these materials should altogether slip from the hands of everyone, and especially from my own use (which had nearly happened at one point). Since I was often reproached with the fault of begrudging them to others and to their descendants, I finally yielded to their wishes. In arranging these examples, the order in this work of ours caused me no small trouble; but afterwards, when I weighed the matter seriously and carefully, that common warning came to mind:

units.la: Crede mihi, sapere non nimium sapere est.
units.tr: Believe me, not to be too wise is to be wise.

units.la: Obseruauimus autem ordinem seu methodum locorum communium, quę in locis extra Decalogum, atq; in Decalogo obseruata est. Interdum bis terue diuersis locis unum exemplum inserui-mus: id quod non inconueniens visum fuit, ob varias unius materiae applica-tiones ad diuersa argumenta. Quod attinet ad signum C O L L. sciendum est, non esse ea Philippi, quae post hoc signum inueniuntur: quamuis forte semel atq; iterum illud non obseruatum est. Preterea rea quaedam nomina in quibusdam nar-rationibus sunt suppressa: quod fecimus non sine consilio quorundam doctorū & bonorum uirorū. Huc accedit, quòd aliquas res passim è Germanico in Latī-nam linguam uertimus, ea quidem proprietate, qua unquam fieri potuit, ut sen-tentia authorum retineretur. Idq; factū est hanc ipsam ob causam, ut peregrinis nationibus hoc nostro quoq; labore in-seruiremus: quaedam Germanicè relicta sunt & id propter gratiam & emphasin, quę fuit in proprietate linguę Germani-cæ. Iam uerò praeuideo, quosdā nō di-co famelicos, sed auaros typographos, cum meo incōmodo, in hunc meum la-borem (sicut corui solent) inuolaturos esse: quos tamen suis pennis amici mei suo tempore satis delineabunt: neq; mi-hi etiam desunt rationes, quibus de sua praeda frustrabuntur. Deniq; non igno-ro, ut in omnibus honestis coeptis fieri solet, sic etiam has meas lucubrationes, sciolos & calumniatores sinistrè inter-pretaturos esse: mihi tamen interea suffi-cit, eas à multis doctis & pijs uiris ap-probari. Haec tibi necessariò, Lector, de meis
units.tr: I have observed the order and method of the commonplaces which was followed in the places outside the Decalogue, and in the Decalogue. Sometimes I have inserted one example in two or three different places; this seemed not out of place, on account of the various applications of a single subject to different topics. As for the sign C O L L., it should be known that the items which follow this sign are not Philip's, although perhaps once or twice this has not been observed. Moreover, certain names have been suppressed in some narratives; we did this not without the counsel of certain learned and good men. In addition, we have translated some things here and there from German into Latin, with as much fidelity to idiom as could ever be managed, so that the sense of the authors might be kept. This was done for this very reason, that we might serve foreign nations with this labour of ours too; some things have been left in German, on account of the force and emphasis which lies in the idiom of the German language. Now indeed I foresee that certain men, I do not say starving but greedy printers, will swoop down upon my labour, to my inconvenience, as crows usually do; yet my friends will in due time sufficiently pluck them of their feathers, and I do not lack reasons by which they will be cheated of their prey. Finally, I am not unaware that, as usually happens with all honest undertakings, smatterers and slanderers will interpret these my labours unfavourably; nevertheless it is enough for me meanwhile that they are approved by many learned and pious men. These things, reader, I have necessarily set before you concerning my own

units.la: PRAEFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: meis uigilijs significanda esse duxi: quae quanti mihi constiterint, plurimi optimi & doctissimi uiri norunt. Tu uero, eo animo, quo tibi trado, suscipe: ac Vale.
units.tr: I thought these matters had to be made known to you, Reader, through my own labours; how much they have cost me, very many excellent and learned men know. But you, receive them in the spirit in which I hand them over to you. Farewell.

units.la: AD STVDIOSVM LEctorem Carmen.
units.tr: To the Studious Reader, a Poem.

units.la: SI tibi sint curæ cœlestia scripta Philippi,Cui docti acceptum, quod didicêre, ferunt:Nam tulit è tenebris ad splendida tempora PhœbiDoctrinæ solida cum pietate decus:Hinc est lingua triplex, rerumq; peritior usus,Hinc est saluifico turba dicata duci:Hinc cum Cecropio Germani uerba Pericle,Hinc bene creduntur cum Cicerone loqui:Hinc tot Apollinea iuuenes nascuntur ab arte,Proditor haud Troiæ quot numeraret equus.Nunc etiam placeant deducta Melanchthonis ore,Manlius in seros quæ cupit ire dies.Bis seni tacitis abierunt mensibus anni,Dum fœcunda tenax miles ad ora stupet.Est operosa quidem res audiisse Philippum,Et præclara sua scripta notasse manu:Quæ fingunt animos studijs, & pectora mulcent,Quæ fugienda uetant, quæq; sequenda docent.Non rudis ingenio, non experientia rerumNobile præcipui nomen honoris habent:Pendet ab arte uagæ sortis sapientia uictrix:Is non, Pieria qui caret arte, sapit.Si tibi uis igitur sapientis quærere famam,Tristibus hic curis dulce leuamen habe.
units.tr: If the heavenly writings of Philip are of concern to you, to which learned men say they owe whatever they have learned, then, since he brought the glory of solid learning together with piety out of darkness into the bright times of Phoebus, here you have a threefold tongue and a more experienced practice in affairs. Here is a crowd dedicated to the saving leader. Here the Germans are believed to speak words as Pericles of Athens did, and to speak well as Cicero did. Here so many young men are born by Apollo's art that the horse of Troy could not count as many betrayers. Now too, let the things drawn from the mouth of Melanchthon please you, things that Manlius wishes to last into late days. Twelve years have passed in silent months while the tenacious soldier stands amazed at his fruitful words. It is indeed a laborious thing to have heard Philip and to have noted his famous writings with one's own hand. These things shape minds for study and soothe hearts, they forbid what must be shunned and teach what must be followed. Wisdom that conquers does not depend on a rude mind or on lack of experience of affairs; a noble name of distinguished honour is held by those who are practised in these arts. Wisdom that conquers depends on the art of a wandering lot. He who lacks the Pierian art is not wise. So if you seek the fame of a wise man, here you may have a sweet relief from sad cares.

units.la: Multum hic inuenies, quorum meminisse iuuabit.Perlege: sic lecto codice doctus eris.
units.tr: You will find much here whose remembrance will be a pleasure. Read it through: once you have read this book, you will be learned.

units.la: M. Iustus VirfusiusBlackenburgensis.
units.tr: M. Iustus Virfusius of Blankenburg.

units.la: SAMVELIS HOLZACHII IN primum, secundum, tertium, quartum, & quintum præceptum Decalogi, Carmen.
units.tr: Samuel Holzach's Carmen on the First, Second, Third, Fourth and Fifth Commandments of the Decalogue.

units.la: Diuina de lege sonat uox, deq; sacrorumRitibus omnigenis, officioq; fori.
units.tr: The voice of divine law resounds, and of all kinds of sacred rites, and of the duties of civil life.

units.la: Hinc quos impietas, & uana superbia ducit,Culpans, fert laudem turba modesta tibi.
units.tr: Hence the modest crowd praises you, condemning those whom impiety and vain pride lead astray.

units.la: Comminuit statuas, stultissima pectora ducensIllas pro uero quæ coluere Deo.
units.tr: He smashes the statues, showing that the most foolish hearts worship as the true God those things which are not God.

units.la: Contemptumq; Dei simul ac periuria pœnisAfficit hinc, sequitur præstita deinde fides.
units.tr: He punishes contempt of God and perjury alike with penalties; hence follows the faith once pledged.

units.la: Proditur in cognoscendis incuria festis,Nobile Iudaicæ pingitur ædis opus.
units.tr: Neglect in keeping the festivals is exposed, and the noble work of the Jewish temple is portrayed.

units.la: Hinc explere iubet, cura non deside, munus,Ad quod te cernis cunq; uocare Deum.
units.tr: Hence he bids you perform your duty with unwearied care, wherever you see God calling you.

units.la: Hinc scribit qua chara domus sit lege regenda,Deq; animi motu se uariante docet.
units.tr: Hence he writes how the dear household is to be governed by law, and teaches of the changing motions of the mind.

units.la: In natos celebrat pietatem deinde parentum,Natorum hinc, fratrum deinde relatus amor.
units.tr: Then he celebrates the piety of parents towards children; hence the love of children, and then of brothers, is related.

units.la: Estq; magistratus tenuem narrata potentisIn plebem, sed nec plebis omissa fides.
units.tr: He narrates the power of the magistrate over the common people, but the faith of the common people is not left out either.

units.la: Qua ratione, docet, siet instituenda iuuentus, Afferat ut patribus gaudia læta suis. Gratos ingratosq; parentibus atq; magistris, Et bene promeritis, ordine deinde refert. Ergo & amicitiæ positum uenerabile nomen, Estq; fides titulo falsa notata suo. Firmantem tractat mox publica commoda pacem: Ira debinc, iræ tum moderamen adest. Dicit quos poscant Mauortia bella paratus, Nec de lugubri deditione tacet. Consilijsq; ducum uersutis addita charta, Cædibus ac tragicis casibus inde locus.
units.tr: He teaches in what way youth is to be instructed, so that it may bring joyful delights to its fathers. He sets out in order those who are grateful and ungrateful to parents and teachers, and to those who have deserved well. Then the venerable name of friendship is set forth, and faithfulness, falsely marked with its title. Next he treats of public advantages and a firm peace; then comes anger, and then the restraint of anger. He says whom Mars's wars demand, and he is ready; nor is he silent about the lamentable surrender. A page is added on the crafty counsels of generals, and then slaughter and tragic chances take their place.

units.la: Eiusdem in sextum, septimum, & octauum præceptum, Carmen.
units.tr: Another Carmen by the same author, on the Sixth, Seventh and Eighth Commandments.

units.la: Hoc quoq; materia scriptum non simplice constat: Hinc uitiosus amor, connubijq; fides. Hic & auaricia est, & opum laudabilis usus, Nudaq; simplicitas, fraudsq;, leuesq; ioci. Cuncta quid ulterius recitemus nomina rerum, Quod tamen in geminis fecimus ante locis? Ordine legisti iam præcedentia scripta, Vt tibi materies nota sit, atq; stylus. Copia par hic est, exempla disce priorum, Quam sit materiæ diuitis istud opus. Est hæc cum suaui dulcedine copia iuncta, Nullibi non doctis nota futura uiris.
units.tr: This also, written on a subject that is not simple, consists of: hence vicious love and the faith of marriage. Here too are avarice and the laudable use of wealth, naked simplicity, fraud and light jests. Why should we recite further all the names of things, which we did nonetheless set down in the two earlier places? You have already read the preceding writings in order, so that the subject and style are known to you. The abundance here is equal; learn the examples of earlier times, and how rich this work is in material. This abundance is joined with a sweet pleasantness, and will be known nowhere that is not known to learned men.

units.la: Accipe & hoc ergo Lector studiose uolumen,Scriptoriq; pijs fausta precare sonis.Ingenium natura dedit, labor improbus artem,Doctorumq; fides, Manle diserte, tibi.Fata uiros audire tibi tribuere benigna,Queis maius norunt secula nostra nihil.Doctrinis in te pietas sanctissima certat,O' uir doctrinas nate iuuare bonas.
units.tr: Take this volume too, studious reader, and wish good fortune to the writer with pious sounds. Nature gave the talent, unremitting labour the skill, and the trust of learned men is given to you, eloquent Manlius. Kindly fates have granted you to hear men than whom our age knows nothing greater. In your teachings the most holy piety strives, O man born to help good teachings.

units.la: Aliud carmen boni cuiusdam uiri, in laborem Ioannis Manlij.
units.tr: Another poem by a certain good man, on the labour of Johann Manlius.

units.la: Præmia uirtutis, scelerum & tormenta, uenustisHistoriæ præbent conspicienda typis.Corripiunt pœnis reprobos, summumq; timereErudiunt uera cum pietate Deum.Mercedem sperare pios, & conscia rectiCorda iubent, aura nec trepidare leui.Quod fuerat uitijs durum, fit mobile pectus:Conuersumq; cupit iam meliora sequi.Quandoquidem superos metuit, tædetq; pigetq;Iam scelerum, cœli iam meditatur iter.Exemplis igitur quisquis non flectitur istis,Durius Hyrcana tigride pectus habet.Post sapiet serus, uerùm spe elusus inani:Et cùm nil metuet, pœna sequetur atrox.Vtere mortalis uitæ pictoribus istis,Qui uelut in speculo pulchra sequenda monet.
units.tr: The rewards of virtue and the torments of crimes, the history sets before us in charming pictures to be looked at. They seize the reprobate with punishments, and teach them to fear God truly with piety. They bid the pious hope for reward, and hearts conscious of uprightness not to tremble at every light breeze. What was hard for vices becomes a pliant breast, and, converted, it now desires to follow better things. Since it fears the heavens, and is weary and sorry for its crimes, it now contemplates the way to heaven. Therefore whoever is not moved by these examples has a breast harder than a Hyrcanian tigress. He will grow wise too late, deceived by vain hope; and when he fears nothing, savage punishment will follow. Use these pictures of mortal life, which, like a mirror, show what is to be followed.

units.la: Hoc filo ductus, culpæ vestigia linque,Atqʒ; piè soli viuere disce Deo.
units.tr: Led by this thread, leave the traces of guilt, and learn to live piously to God alone.

units.la: Hunc etiam legito: nec te labor iste molestet,Fert secum breuis hic commoda multa Liber:
units.tr: Read this one too; may its labour not trouble you. This little book brings with it many advantages.

units.la: DE LEGE▸ Præcipuæ Decalogi uirtutes, obiter in quadam lectione à Domino Philippo recitatæ.
units.tr: On the Law: the chief virtues of the Decalogue, mentioned in passing in a lecture by Master Philip.

units.la: [P]Rimæ tabulæ uirtutes sunt, agnitio ueri Dei, fides, timor, dilectio: item aliæ uirtutes ibi comprehensæ, ut: celebratio, inuocatio ueri Dei, propagatio doctrinæ, conseruatio ministerij. In secunda tabula, pietas erga parentes, obedientia erga magistratus & gratitudo. In quinto & sexto, iustitia particularis. In septimo, iustitia commutatiua & distributiua. In octauo, ueritas, candor, constantia: & in nono & decimo, originalis iustitia.
units.tr: The virtues of the first table are the knowledge of the true God, faith, fear, and love. There are also other virtues contained there, such as the celebration and invocation of the true God, the propagation of doctrine, and the preservation of the ministry. In the second table are piety towards parents, obedience towards the magistrates, and gratitude. In the fifth and sixth commandments is particular justice. In the seventh is commutative and distributive justice. In the eighth are truthfulness, candour, and constancy. In the ninth and tenth is original justice.

units.la: Decalogus debet esse norma uitæ, iuxta dictum: Lucerna pedibus meis, uerbum tuum.
units.tr: The Decalogue ought to be the rule of life, according to the saying: "Your word is a lamp to my feet."

units.la: Doctor Martinus Lutherus.
units.tr: Doctor Martin Luther.

units.la: Peccata primæ tabulæ afferūt simpliciter desperationem. Reliqua peccata secundæ tabulæ afferūt secum contritionem, & spem pœnitentiæ. Illa peccata adhuc circa misericordiæ obiectū uersantur.
units.tr: The sins of the first table bring simply despair. The remaining sins of the second table bring with them contrition and the hope of repentance. Those sins still concern the object of mercy.

units.la: Idem.
units.tr: The same.

units.la: Decalogus est semper prædicandus: quia enim caro nostra infirma est, ideò sub carcere legis tenenda est, donec ad agnitionē sui in Christo per ueniat. Quanquam sathan non cessat suos uexare, ut indies contra Decalogum uiuant, & præcipuè contra primam tabulam, ubi diaboli sæuissimi contra nos ductores exercitus sunt. In secunda, nō senioribus & magistratui obedire, irasci, occidere, scortari, idem diaboli efficiunt. Decalogus est eruditio eruditionum. Fides est uirtus uirtutum. Oratio Dominica est letania letaniarum. Nā sicut Decalogus omnia pulcherrimè & copiosissimè docet & exhortatur: ita fides quàm proprissimè facit, ut oratio Dominica quàm pijssimè roget & impetret. Ideo hæc trinitas perficit & absolutum reddit hominem in cogitando, dicendo, & agendo, id est, linguam, mentem, caput excolit ad summam perfectionem: quid uis amplius?
units.tr: The Decalogue must always be preached. For since our flesh is weak, it must be kept under the prison of the law until it comes through to the knowledge of itself in Christ. Yet Satan does not cease to harass his own, so that they live daily against the Decalogue, and especially against the first table, where the most savage devils are the leaders of the armies against us. In the second table, to disobey elders and magistrates, to be angry, to kill, to commit fornication: these too are the work of devils. The Decalogue is the teaching of teachings. Faith is the virtue of virtues. The Lord's Prayer is the litany of litanies. For just as the Decalogue teaches and exhorts all things most beautifully and most fully, so faith effects them most aptly, and as the Lord's Prayer asks and obtains most piously. Therefore this trinity completes and makes the man whole in thinking, speaking, and acting; that is, it cultivates the tongue, the mind, and the head to the highest perfection. What more do you want?

units.la: Clementis dictum: Δικαιοσύνη ἐστὶ κοινωνία θεῖ μετὰ ἰσότητος. Iusticia est cōmunicatio, qua Deus se nobis communicat, cum æqualitate.
units.tr: A saying of Clement: Justice is the fellowship of God with equality [Δικαιοσύνη ἐστὶ κοινωνία θεοῦ μετὰ ἰσότητος]. Justice is a communion by which God communicates himself to us, with equality.

units.la: In hoc dicto est declaratio primæ tabulæ & secundæ. Quando dicit cum æqualitate, secundam tabulam complectitur. Iurisconsulti nihil aliud agunt in illis magnis uoluminibus, nisi ut quærant æqualitatem. Doctrina Iurisconsultorum, est doctrina recitans leges naturales, & alias leges necessarias, uel probabili consequentia inde extructas, sancitas ordinaria authoritate & interpretationes[?]. tione rectorum doctorum Bartoli, Baldi, &c.
units.tr: In this saying there is a statement of the first table and of the second. When he says "with equality," he embraces the second table. The jurists do nothing else in those great volumes than seek equality. The doctrine of the jurists is a doctrine reciting the natural laws, and other necessary laws, or laws built from them by probable consequence, sanctioned by ordinary authority and by the interpretation of learned doctors such as Bartolus, Baldus, and others.

units.la: Ante 50 annos sunt editi libelli, in quibus triū legum fit mentio. Primam legem uocarunt legem naturæ, qua homines ante Moysem sunt saluati. Secunda Moysi dicitur, & illam tantum de externorum membrorum gubernatione, seu externa disciplina sunt interpretati. Tertiam legem uocarunt Euangelicam, quam quidam homo exposuit esse omnium perfectissimam: & quemadmodum homines uiuentes sub politia Moysaica, sua lege saluati sunt, ita nos in regno Christi nunc uersantes iusticiam, reconciliationem coram Deo, remissionem peccatorum, & uitam æternam illa Euangelij perfectione consequi. At unica est æterna immota lex, & omnibus temporibus omnes homines obligans, & hæc uocabulo satis tenui lex moralis nominatur.
units.tr: About fifty years ago there were published little books which mention three laws. They called the first the law of nature, by which men were saved before Moses. The second is said to be Moses', and they explained it only as the governance of the outward members, or outward discipline. They called the third the Evangelical law, which a certain man declared to be the most perfect of all; and just as men living under the Mosaic polity were saved by their law, so we, now living in the kingdom of Christ, obtain justice, reconciliation before God, forgiveness of sins, and eternal life by that perfection of the Gospel. But there is one eternal and unchanging law, binding all men at all times, and this is called the moral law by a rather thin word.

units.la: Ioannes Syluius Egeranus cōcionator Cygneæ, & in ualle Ioachimica, erat homo doctus, sed profanus: scribebat contra nostras ecclesias, edebatq; libros plane tetros, nominabat Sophisma, quòd di ceremus, homines non posse implere legem. Et gratiā gratuitā & reconciliationē coram Deo, quam sola fide propter mediatorem apprehendimus, intelligebat promulgationem doctrinæ legis.
units.tr: John Sylvius Egranus, preacher at Cygnea and in the valley of Joachimsthal, was a learned man, but profane. He wrote against our churches and published thoroughly foul books. He named it a "sophism" when we say that men cannot fulfil the law. And he understood the free grace and reconciliation before God, which we apprehend by faith alone on account of the mediator, to be the mere promulgation of the doctrine of the law.

units.la: Quidam uociferatur, summam artem Christianorum esse nescire legem. Quanta insulsitas est, ac si sic diceret: Summa ars Christianorum est, esse asinum, & nihil studere: summum decus est, manere asinum. Omnes in suis uocationibus negligentes, discunt illius asiini artem.
units.tr: Someone cries out that the highest art of Christians is not to know the law. How foolish this is, as if he said: "The highest art of Christians is to be an ass and to study nothing; the highest honour is to remain an ass." All who neglect their callings learn the art of that ass.

units.la: Nos in prima inspectione Ecclesiarum uenimus ad quendam pastorem, quem interrogauimus, an etiam doceret Decalogum. Respondit nobis, se non habere illum librum. Nesciuit quid esset Decalogus. Bone Deus quàm uehementer commouebatur Doctor Hieronymus Schürpf, & alij uisitatores qui aderant, ac illam insciitiam deplorabant, sicut erat deploranda: & non modo deploranda, sed potius uinculis seu carceribus puniëda. Vixerat ille antè in uita monastica, & tamen adeò fuit rudis, uerè non habuit illum librum: sed habuit artem illius asini, qui dixit: Summa ars est Christianorum, nescire legem.
units.tr: On our first visitation of the churches we came to a certain minister, whom we asked whether he also taught the Decalogue. He answered us that he did not have that book. He did not know what the Decalogue was. Good God, how greatly Doctor Hieronymus Schürpf and the other visitors who were present were moved, and they lamented that ignorance as it deserved to be lamented; and it should be punished not only with lamentation but rather with chains or prison. That man had lived earlier in the monastic life, and yet he was so untaught that he truly did not have that book; but he did have the art of that ass, who said: "The highest art of Christians is not to know the law."

units.la: Monachi finxerunt uaria deliramenta de statu perfectionis. Vocarūt uerò in statu perfectionis uiuere, exercere se iuxta aliqua electa opera, nōminatim in Decalogo expressis uerbis praescripta: sicut dicitur de quodā iuuene monacho, ante professionē recepto in quoddā monasterium, cùi dabantur in prādio & cœna duo cāthari, unus uino, alter ceruisia, completi. Iuuenis uerò monachus duos mēses cum illis agēs, uidit reliquos omnes suos cātharos ebibere, & suā naturam tantū potus, quanquātum reliquorū non ferre : accedit Abbatē, ac se rursus ex coenobio dimitti petit. Interrogatus ue rō ab Abbate, quæ res ipsum moueret ex tā opimo stabulo discedere? O' inquit, Domine pater, ordo est nimis difficilis, ordo est nimis intolerabilis: nam ego non possum exhaurire meos cantharos, sicut ab alijs fieri uideo. Hæc est ipsorum uitæ per- sectio, cui hodie adhuc sunt addicti.
units.tr: The monks have invented various follies about the state of perfection. They called it living in the state of perfection to exercise oneself in certain chosen works, prescribed by name in the Decalogue in express words. So it is told of a certain young monk who, before his profession, was received into a monastery, where two tankards were given him at dinner and supper, one full of wine and the other of beer. The young monk, spending two months with them, saw all the others drain their tankards, and found that his nature could not bear as much drink as the rest. He approached the Abbot and asked again to be dismissed from the cloister. When the Abbot asked what moved him to leave so rich a stable, he said: "O Lord Father, the order is too difficult, the order is too intolerable; for I cannot empty my tankards as I see others do." This is the perfection of their life, to which they are still devoted today.

units.la: DE LEGIBVS FORENSIBVS & ceremonialibus Moysi.
units.tr: On the Forensic and Ceremonial Laws of Moses.

units.la: Struthius tempore seditionis rusticorū scri- bebat agros liberandos esse annuis pensionibus, cum lex Moysi præcipiat, quinquagesimo anno re dire fundos ad hæredes priores.
units.tr: Struthius, at the time of the peasants' rebellion, wrote that the fields should be freed from annual payments, since the law of Moses commands that estates return to their original heirs in the fiftieth year.

units.la: Ego hic sedes in nouo Collegio, disputaui con- traaliquē uolentē omnes forenses controuersias ex legibus Moysaicis iudicari, & sic arguebat.
units.tr: I, sitting here in the new college, disputed with someone who wanted all forensic controversies to be judged by the Mosaic laws, and he argued thus.

units.la: Vbicūq; sunt scripta Prophetica, ibi est Ecclesia. Iudæi retinent scripta Prophetica, uel apud Iu- deos sunt scripta Prophetarum.
units.tr: Wherever the prophetic writings are, there is the Church. The Jews retain the prophetic writings, or among the Jews are the writings of the prophets.

units.la: Ergo Iudæi sunt Ecclesia.
units.tr: Therefore the Jews are the Church.

units.la: Respondeo per distinctionem ad minorem: Iu- dæi retinent quidem scripta Prophetica iuxta li- teram: alioqui re uera nego minorem. Non enim uerè retinēt, sed corrumpunt, & alias peregrinas sententias affingunt. Libros quidem retinent, at nouas & inusitatas sententias addunt.
units.tr: I reply by distinguishing the minor premise: the Jews indeed retain the prophetic writings according to the letter; otherwise I deny the minor premise in its true sense. For they do not truly retain them but corrupt them, and attach to them alien opinions of their own. They keep the books, indeed, but add new and unusual interpretations.

units.la: De Lege.
units.tr: On the Law.

units.la: Idem aliquando in templo arcis habuit longâ concionem, & contentiosè dixit, controuersias forenses, & negotia forensia ex lege Moysi iudicanda esse. In alia uerò concione habuit contrariam orationem, quæ grata fuit multis, ita ut ipsi describerent.
units.tr: On one occasion he gave a long sermon in the temple of the citadel, and argued vehemently that legal disputes and forensic business are to be decided by the law of Moses. In another sermon, however, he delivered the opposite teaching, which pleased many so much that they wrote it down.

units.la: Doctor Martinus Lutherus habuit bonam imaginationem de duabus tabulis Moysi: dixit, duas tabulas esse perfossas per singulas literas, ita ut ab utraq; parte legi possent. Illud quidam sic intellexerunt: alius est literalis intellectus legis, alius est spiritualis. Alij fecerunt duos cultus, alium externum alium internum.
units.tr: Doctor Martin Luther had a fine image of the two tablets of Moses. He said that the two tablets were pierced through by each letter, so that they could be read from either side. Some understood this to mean that the law has one literal sense and another spiritual sense. Others made two kinds of worship, one external and one internal.

units.la: Causæ constitutæ politiæ Moysaicæ.
units.tr: The causes for establishing the Mosaic polity.

units.la: 1 Vt esset aliqua certa sedes, in qua se Deus patefaceret.
units.tr: (1) That there might be a certain fixed seat in which God would reveal himself.

units.la: 2 Vt esset publicus aliquis coetus, qui rectè invocaret Deum, & esset custos fidelis doctrinæ à Deo patefactæ.
units.tr: (2) That there might be a public assembly which would rightly call upon God and be a faithful guardian of the doctrine revealed by God.

units.la: 3 Præcipua est, ut esset certa familia nota, in qua nasceretur Christus, moraretur, & ostenderet se generi humano.
units.tr: (3) The chief cause: that there might be a certain known family in which Christ would be born, dwell, and show himself to the human race.

units.la: 4 Vt essent certi & fide digni testes in hac politia suarum promissionum, & suorum miraculorum.
units.tr: (4) That there might be sure and trustworthy witnesses in this polity to his promises and his miracles.

units.la: Causæ deletæ illius politiæ, & ceremoniarum Moysi.
units.tr: The causes for abolishing that polity and the ceremonies of Moses.

units.la: Prima iustitia Dei est, quæ est immutabilis, qua Deus punit atrocia delicta atrocibus pœnis: ut Herodotus ait. Horribilibus idolatriis, & libidinibus hic populus contaminatus erat. Deus igitur eum propter hæc & similia peccata puniuit: ut ex historijs patet.
units.tr: The first is the immutable justice of God, by which God punishes atrocious crimes with atrocious penalties, as Herodotus says. This people had been defiled by horrible idolatries and lusts. God therefore punished them for these and similar sins, as is clear from the histories.

units.la: Secunda est, Vt extaret illustre testimoniū iræ Dei aduersus persequentes filium, quem unicè pater diligit, ut testatur inquiens: Hic est filius meus dilectus, &c.
units.tr: The second: that there might stand a notable testimony to the wrath of God against those who persecuted the Son, whom the Father alone loves, as he testifies, saying: "This is my beloved Son," etc.

units.la: Tertia, Est illustre testimoniū, quòd homines nõ iustificëtur ex operibus legis, & obseruatione cultu̇ã: quia etiam gentes admittebantur ad Ecclesiā.
units.tr: The third: it is a notable testimony that men are not justified by the works of the law and the observance of worship, since even the Gentiles were admitted to the Church.

units.la: Quarta, Voluit Deus esse illustre testimonium exhibiti Messiæ, quia Micheas inquit: Secundum templū illustrius est illo, quod Salomõ ædificauit.
units.tr: The fourth: God willed it to be a notable testimony to the manifestation of the Messiah, since Micah says: "The latter temple will be more glorious than that which Solomon built."

units.la: Quinta, Voluit Iudæis præripere prærogatiuam, & æquare gentes Iudæis.
units.tr: The fifth: he wished to snatch away the prerogative from the Jews and to make the Gentiles equal to the Jews.

units.la: Sexta, Abrogatio politiæ istius ostendit, Christi regnum non esse de hoc mundo, sed spirituale.
units.tr: The sixth: the abolition of that polity shows that the kingdom of Christ is not of this world, but spiritual.

units.la: Iudæus quondam mecum disputabat, dicens: Vos non estis populus Dei. Quare? inquam: Quia non seruatis legem. Respondebam ei: Imo tu non seruas. Deinde, inquit: Vos docetis contra legē. Quomodo? Quia, inquit, nõ seruatis sabbathum. Putabat legem seruari, quando externis gestibus & laboribus manus abstineret.
units.tr: A Jew once debated with me, saying: "You are not the people of God." Why? I asked. "Because you do not keep the law." I answered him: "On the contrary, you do not keep it." Then, he said: "You teach against the law." How so? "Because," he said, "you do not keep the sabbath." He thought the law was kept when a man abstained from work and held his hands from labour by outward gestures.

units.la: Duę insignes causæ, cur Deus Iudæis carnem suillam prohibuerit.
units.tr: Two notable reasons why God forbade the Jews to eat pork.

units.la: D. Philipus piæ memoriæ dicebat: deum uoluisse cauere, ne à porcis horti & agri, qui erant in illis locis amœnissimi, & multis terræ fructibus oleis & aromatibus ornati, ut balsamo &c. uastarentur: sunt enim porci genus animalis uastans & perdens res etiā preciosissimas, & radices è terra eruens: alioqui, quod ad usum attineret, se nullam aliam causam scire, cum apud omnes medicos caro illa saluberrima habeatur.
units.tr: Master Philip, of blessed memory, used to say that God wished to guard against the swine ravaging the gardens and fields, which were most pleasant in those regions and adorned with many fruits of the earth, olives and spices, such as balsam, etc. For swine are an animal that lays waste and destroys even the most precious things, rooting up plants from the earth. Otherwise, as far as its use is concerned, he said he knew no other reason, since that flesh is held by all physicians to be most wholesome.

units.la: Alius quidam doctissimus uir aliquando dixit, se sæpius cogitasse ea de re, & se hanc etiam causam esse existimare, quòd caro suilla facilè in male affectis corporibus putrescat. Alioquin etiam sanis corporibus conueniens & salubris est. Cùm igitur Iudæi pluribus morbis obnoxij fuerint, ut lepræ, paralysi, uoluisse Deum cauere usum taliũ carnium, ne augerent morbos. Et hanc etiam iudicat causam esse, cur Iudæis Deus leporina carne uesci prohibuerit.
units.tr: Another very learned man once said that he had often thought about this matter and judged that this was also the reason: pork easily putrefies in ill-conditioned bodies, though otherwise it is suitable and wholesome even for healthy bodies. Since the Jews were liable to many diseases, such as leprosy and paralysis, God therefore wished to guard against the use of such meats, lest they increase the diseases. He also judges this to be the reason why God forbade the Jews to eat hare flesh.

units.la: DECALOGVS.
units.tr: DECALOGUE.

units.la: Primum præceptum. IMPIVS CVLTVS seu IMPIETAS.
units.tr: The First Commandment. IMPIOUS WORSHIP, or IMPIETY.

units.la: Quando Demetrius se in numerum deorum referri uolebat, ibi multi non assentiebantur, & illam iniustam petitionem ægre ferebat. Tunc quidam ex adulatoribus dixit: Videte ne dum cœlum defenditis, terram amittatis. Illa nō solùm est uox aulica, sed est cōmunis phantasia omniū hominū.
units.tr: When Demetrius wanted to be counted among the gods, many did not agree and bore that unjust request with difficulty. Then a certain flatterer said: "Take care that while you defend the heavens you do not lose the earth." That is not only a courtly saying but the common fancy of all men.

units.la: Caligula suam statuam in templū Capitolinum Romæ collocari curauit, ut à latere quodam Iouis Capitolino adstaret, cui aliqua in aurem susurraret, ac sacerdotes ei sacrificarent. Talis fuit insania illius seculi.
units.tr: Caligula had his statue set up in the Capitoline temple at Rome, so that it stood beside Jupiter of the Capitol, and whispered something into his ear, while priests offered sacrifice to him. Such was the madness of that age.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Romanum præsidium in Aegypto interfectum est, eo quòd unus ex militibus Romanis interfecisset Felem deum Aegyptium: unde ciuitas tota mouit seditionem aduersus præsidiarios, & septem millia hominum (ut dicit Diodorus Siculus) fudit. Id tempore Tyberij accidit.
units.tr: A Roman garrison in Egypt was killed because one of the Roman soldiers had killed Felis, the Egyptian god. Thereupon the whole city rose in revolt against the garrison soldiers, and (as Diodorus Siculus reports) destroyed seven thousand men. This happened in the time of Tiberius.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quando Romæ templum Iouis ictum fuit fulmine, & statuæ Iouis in illo templo est decussum brachium, significauit Deus se uelle destruere impium illum cultum.
units.tr: When the temple of Jupiter at Rome was struck by lightning, and the arm of the statue of Jupiter in that temple was broken off, God signified that he wished to destroy that impious worship.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Cum Alexander Seuerus Imperator paulò post esset periturus, hac etiam occasione est mota noua persecutio aduersus Christianos, qui sunt expulsi urbe: postea est restitutus ille cultus. Cum sacrificarent carent in eodem loco, rursus est fulmine ictum idem templum, sacerdotesq; fulmine cõflagrarūt: & persecutio facta est multo grauior, donec cõsul unà cũ coniuge & liberis factus esset Christianus.
units.tr: When the emperor Alexander Severus was about to die shortly afterwards, a new persecution was stirred up against the Christians on this occasion, and they were driven out of the city. Afterwards that worship was restored. When they were again offering sacrifice in the same place, the same temple was struck by lightning again, and the priests were burned up by the fire. The persecution became much more severe, until the consul, together with his wife and children, became a Christian.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Obseruate fabellam non illepidam ex Ecclesiastica historia. Persicus quidam sacrificulus gloriabatur suum deum, cuius ipse esset minister, esse uerum deum, quippe qui omnium aliarum gentium deos superaret, imò & consumeret. Fuerunt enim talium idolorum imagines aureæ, argenteæ, æneæ, ferreæ, & ligneæ, aut cuiuscunque materiæ: quæ si non consumitur, tamen mutat artificialem formam Ignis deus Persicus. Hic tandem peruenit in Aegyptum, & cum incidisset in Canopi sacerdotem eadem disputatione, ibi sacerdos vicissim deum Canopum extollit, illum præferens numini Persico & Chaldaico: unde magno certamînis præmio, ingens pecunia victori est proposita.
units.tr: Notice a not unpleasant little tale from ecclesiastical history. A certain Persian priest boasted that his god, whose minister he was, was the true God, since he surpassed the gods of all other nations and even consumed them. For there were images of such idols made of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, or any other material; and if fire did not consume them, it at least altered their artificial form. This Persian god (Fire) at last came to Egypt, and when the Persian met a priest of Canopus in the same dispute, the Egyptian priest in turn exalted the god Canopus, preferring him to the divinity of the Persians and Chaldeans. Thereupon a great sum of money was offered as the prize of the contest to the winner.

units.la: Persicus sacrificulus suum deum Ignem adfert. Interim Canopi minister, hydriam pluribus foraminibus perfluentē (quales sunt in istis regionib. ustatæ, & frequentes ad decolandū aquam) adornat, & cera obstructis foraminib. omnib. implet aqua. Tempore constituto Persicus sacerdos cum suo numine Igne aduenit: vicissim suum Canopum Ae-gyptius gyptius sacrificulus etiam adducit, quem ille igni supponit, certa spe ductus fore, ut tandem quæcunque esset statuæ materia dissolueretur, aut frangeretur calore ignis. Sed cum testa hydriæ calcfieri cœpit, tunc simul incipit liquescere cera, & aqua effluens ex foraminibus hydriæ ignem extinxit. Sic euasit Aegyptius victor, ostendens suum numen esse potentissimum, ut quod deum Persicum, qui summus aliorum deorum esset habitus, superasset. Est lepida fabella, quæ si nihil aliud docet: tamen ostendit vanitatem talium religionum. Prætule-[?]unt Persæ Ignem regibus in publicis pōpis, ut historiæ etiam ostendunt. Narratur in historia de rebus gestis Alexandri, quòd hic Ignis argenteis altaribus toto agmini Darij euntis ad pugnā Alexandri prælatus sit, comitantibus 365 iuuenibus sacerdotibus, & carmen canentibus ad numerum dierum circuitus anni.
units.tr: The Persian priest brought his god Fire. Meanwhile the minister of Canopus prepared a water jar pierced with many holes (such as are used in those regions for cooling water), and stopped all the holes with wax and filled it with water. At the appointed time the Persian priest came with his god Fire. In turn the Egyptian priest brought his Canopus, which the other placed over the fire, led by the confident hope that the statue, whatever its material, would at last dissolve or be broken by the heat of the fire. But when the clay of the jar began to grow hot, the wax began to melt at the same time, and the water flowing out through the holes of the jar put out the fire. So the Egyptian came off the victor, showing that his divinity was most powerful, since it had overcome the Persian god, who was thought to be the highest of the gods. It is a charming tale, and even if it teaches nothing else, it shows the vanity of such religions. The Persians placed Fire ahead of kings in public processions, as histories also show. It is related in the history of the deeds of Alexander that this fire was carried on silver altars before the whole army of Darius as it marched to battle against Alexander, with 365 young priests accompanying it and singing a song for the number of days in the year's circuit.

units.la: HVMILITAS & MODESTIA.
units.tr: HUMILITY AND MODESTY.

units.la: Pindarus ait, quòd, qui vclit ultra columnas Herculis, sit fatuus, id est: præcipit, ut simus modesti ac humiles.
units.tr: Pindar says that whoever sails beyond the pillars of Hercules is foolish; that is, he urges us to be modest and humble.

units.la: Agathocles in Sicilia, bellicosus uir, instructusque pecunia ad militandum, peruenit ad regnum: sed miserabilibus cruciatibus est mortuus. voluit hic habere famam modestiæ, quia eius pater fuit figulus. habebat pocula ex uasis testaceis, quæ erant facta ex terra Samiæ. Hinc hi uersus sunt: Fama est fictilibus cœnasse Agatoclea regem, Atq; abacum Samio sæpe onerasse luto. Quæsitus causam, respondit: Rex ego qui sum, Sicaniæ figulo sum genitore satus. Fortunam reuereter habe, quicunq; repente Diues ab exili progrediere loco.
units.tr: Agathocles in Sicily, a warlike man, provided with money for waging war, came to the kingdom, but died in wretched torments. He wished to have a reputation for modesty, because his father had been a potter. He had drinking cups made of earthenware, which were fashioned from the clay of Samos. Hence these verses: "It is said that King Agathocles dined from earthen vessels, and often loaded his sideboard with Samian clay. When he was asked the reason, he answered: 'I am king, though born of a Sicanian potter as my father. Respect fortune, you who suddenly rise from a humble place to wealth.'"

units.la: Non habetis post Christum pulchrius humilitatis & modestiæ in toto mundo exemplum, quàm Ionathæ filij Saulis, qui sumit coronam, quasi de suo capite, & Dauidi imponit.
units.tr: Since Christ, you do not have in the whole world a more beautiful example of humility and modesty than that of Jonathan, son of Saul, who takes the crown, as though from his own head, and places it on David.

units.la: Noster Imperator Carolus V. cum cepisset regem Galliæ, annunciata ei uictoria ab eis, qui à partibus Gallorum fuerant, ut gratularentur ipsi de uictoria: dicitur ex arce, in qua fuerat, secessisse solus in monasterium quoddam, donec illi abiret. Prohibuit etiam ne quis ad ipsum admitteretur, inquiës: Non decere instituì triumphũ, capto rege, præsertim cùm ipse nihil mali fecerit: memorem enim se esse dicebat humanæ fortunæ, quòd ipse quoq; in manus hostium uenire posset.
units.tr: Our emperor Charles V, when he had taken the king of France, and when news of the victory was brought to him by those who had been on the side of the French, so that they might congratulate him on the victory, is said to have withdrawn alone from the citadel where he was to a certain monastery, until they had gone away. He also forbade anyone to be admitted to him, saying that it was not fitting to institute a triumph when a king had been taken, especially since the king had done no wrong; for he said he was mindful of human fortune, since he himself too could fall into the hands of enemies.

units.la: Modestia Atheniensium & ducis Vuirtenbergensis.
units.tr: The modesty of the Athenians and of the duke of Württemberg.

units.la: Athenienses cum Arcadibus contendunt, postulantq; se collocari ante ipsos in pugna ad plateas: Tandem Athenienses dicebant, se permittere hanc rem ducibus, ubicunq; collocarentur futuros esse fortes uiros, & sic nihil disputant amplius de loco. Semel in conuentu Schmacaldensi oriebatur contentio de loco, dicebat dux Vuirtenbergensis, ducis pater: Collocetis me post fornacem, nō uro, modò efficiamus ea, propter quæ conueni-mus. Ita uerissimum est illud Senecæ: Nihil magnū quod non est placidum.
units.tr: The Athenians contended with the Arcadians, who demanded to be placed before them in the battle at the plateae. In the end the Athenians said they would leave the matter to the commanders, since wherever they were placed they would be brave men, and so they disputed no more about the place. Once at the assembly at Schmalkalden a dispute arose about place. The duke of Württemberg, the father of the duke, said: "Put me behind the stove. I will not burn, provided we accomplish what we have met for." So true is that saying of Seneca: "Nothing is great that is not calm."

units.la: Imperator Carolus V. cum ipsi indicaretur du-cē de Alba periculosè decumbere, ita ut uideretur imminere mors, inquit: An nunc primùm didi-cit se esse mortalem, ego quotidie in meo corpore experior: & Deus mihi morbos multos commo-nefactores addidit, qui me de fragilitate humana-rum uirium admonent.
