units.tr: When the Emperor Charles V was told that the Duke of Alba was seriously ill, so that death seemed near, he said: "Is he only now learning that he is mortal? I experience it every day in my own body, and God has added many reminders of illness to me, who warn me of the frailty of human strength."

units.la: Dicunt de eodem, quòd statim à prima adole-centia, compertus sit natura innimicus esse glo-riosis & infolētioribus. Solitus enim astare spectā-tęq; cursu certantes: ibi si quem forte gloriosio-rem & magis superbum uideret, occultè ei pedem opposuit, ut cadens non uinceret.
units.tr: Of the same duke they say that from his earliest youth he was known to be by nature an enemy of the boastful and the more insolent. He used to stand by and watch those racing, and if he saw someone who seemed more boastful and proud, he secretly put a foot in his way, so that the man, falling, would not win.

units.la: Idem Imperator noster Carolus V. & frater ipsius Rex Ferdinandus, ibāt in nuptijs Ducis Ba-uariæ Ratisbonæ in templū: & cum uentū esset ad templum, neuter ipsorum uoluit procedere. Rex Ferdinandus nunciauit fratri, ut præcederet, quia esset Imperator: at Imperator renunciauit, esse ho-nestum, ut pater sponsæ præcederet, & conuenire illud ipsi in hoc loco, ut in nuptijs filiæ suæ. Adhæc respondit Ferdinandus, Imperatorē esse & patrem & Imperatorē. Ita Imperator coactus est præcedere. In choro deinde, ut uocāt, iterū se honorificè & officiosissimè salutarunt, certaueruntq; uter præcederet. Tandem Imperator præcessit. Hæc humilitas suit officiosa, & in loco.
units.tr: The same Emperor Charles V and his brother King Ferdinand were going into the church at the wedding of the Duke of Bavaria at Regensburg. When they came to the church, neither wanted to go in first. King Ferdinand told his brother to go ahead, since he was the emperor. But the emperor replied that it was proper for the father of the bride to go first, and that this place fitted him, as it would at his own daughter's wedding. To this Ferdinand answered that the emperor was both father and emperor. So the emperor was compelled to go first. Then in the choir, as they call it, they again greeted each other with honour and great courtesy, and contended over which of them would go first. At last the emperor went first. This humility was courteous and fitting to the place.

units.la: Recitaui uobis sæpius historiam Alphonsi sapientissimi regis, qui paulo ante nostrā ætatem discipulus Pontani fuit. Fridericus Imperator fuit apud eum Neapoli, & cùm obiurgaretur Alphonsus à suis consiliarijs, quòd Fridericum sibi præferret, obiurgauit illos assentatores, inquiens, se scire gradus Regum, illum esse Imperatorem, & Imperatori esse tribuendum suum honorem in orbe Christiano, quamuis aliorum esset maior potētia. Multa sunt in ipsius historia memorabilia, & habuit uariabilem fortunam. Dedit etiam se uoluptatibus, quamobrem castigatus & è regno eiectus: postea tamen reductus est. Deus ita restituit eum, sicut Dauidem.
units.tr: I have often recounted to you the story of Alphonso, the most wise king, who was a pupil of Pontanus shortly before our own time. The Emperor Frederick was with him at Naples, and when Alphonso was rebuked by his counsellors for placing Frederick above himself, he rebuked those flatterers, saying that he knew the ranks of kings: that the other was emperor, and that the emperor's honour was to be rendered to him throughout the Christian world, although others had greater power. Many memorable things are recorded in his history, and he had a changeable fortune. He also gave himself to pleasures, for which he was chastised and driven from his kingdom; afterwards, however, he was restored. God restored him just as he restored David.

units.la: Vera gloria propter Deum est appetenda, illa non est superbia sed humilitas: ut cum aliquis me baccalaureum Kembergensem appellat, aut locatum Vuitebergensem, ut quidā faciunt, ille reipsa nihil me lædit. Vtinam essem bonus Baccalaureus.
units.tr: True glory is to be sought for God's sake, and that is not pride but humility. So when someone calls me "Baccalaureus of Kemberg," or "placed at Wittenberg," as some do, that in reality does me no harm. Would that I were a good bachelor!

units.la: Antuerpienses dono dederunt aulæum Imperatori
units.tr: The Antwerpers gave the Emperor Charles V a tapestry as a gift,

units.la: atori Carolo V. in quo pulcherrimè picta erat victoria belli cum rege Galliæ gesti, eiq; addita e- ant nomina regis Galliæ, & aliorū principū, qui prælio fuerant. Imperator autem recipere noluit, ne uideretur lætari aliorum calamitate & mise- ris. Admoniti igitur, qui obtulerunt, sustulerunt nomina & tunc accepit, placuitq; ipsi mirificè. Sic placet magnis uiris inuoluere historias fabulis: quia nolunt res suas clarè narrari coram populo: ideoq; fingunt cantilenas, qualis est illa: Der schef vr von der Newenstadt.
units.tr: in which the victory of the war waged against the king of France was beautifully painted. The names of the king of France and of the other princes who had fought in the battle had been added to it. The emperor, however, did not wish to receive it, lest he seem to rejoice in the misfortunes and miseries of others. So those who had offered it, being admonished, removed the names, and then he accepted it and was wonderfully pleased. So great men like to wrap their histories in fables, because they do not want their deeds told openly before the people; therefore they make up songs, such as that: "Der schef vr von der Newenstadt."

units.la: Cum Cyrus & Cyaxares essent in ijsdem castris, iuit Cyrus in tentorium Cyaxaris, uiditq; eum la- crimantem, miratur quid causæ esset. At ille: Non uoleam? Ego sum Rex, & uideo præcipuos exerci- tus duces apud tuum tentorium uersari, te colere & ne regem negligi. Cyrus inquit, se libenter depositu- rum imperium, & statim capitaneis mandat, ut e- at ad Dominum, ipsi adsint, eumq; sequantur.
units.tr: When Cyrus and Cyaxares were in the same camp, Cyrus went into the tent of Cyaxares and saw him weeping, and he wondered what the cause was. But Cyaxares said: "Should I not weep? I am the king, and I see the chief commanders of the army gathering at your tent, paying you court, while the king is neglected." Cyrus replied that he would gladly lay down his power, and at once ordered his captains to go to the lord, to be present with him and to follow him.

units.la: Cum Rex Galliæ Franciscus captiuus ab Caro- lo V. Imperatore teneretur, & in pariete scriptum uideret Symbolum Imperatoris, PLVS VLTRA, scripsit, hodie mihi, cras tibi. Quod cum Impera- tor uidisset, subscripsit, Fateor me esse hominem.
units.tr: When King Francis of France was held captive by the Emperor Charles V, and saw the emperor's motto, PLVS VLTRA ("further beyond"), written on a wall, he wrote beneath it: "Today to me, tomorrow to you." When the emperor saw this, he signed beneath it: "I confess that I am a man."

units.la: SVPERBIA & INSOLENTIA.
units.tr: PRIDE AND ARROGANCE.

units.la: Demosthenes Aeschini exprobranti ipsi fortu- nam, respondit: Nemo hominum scit an ad uesperam sit habiturus eandem fortunam.
units.tr: When Aeschines reproached Demosthenes for his fortune, Demosthenes replied: "No one knows whether he will have the same fortune by evening."

units.la: Perseus introspiciens in Gorgonem uertitur in saxum, id est: post res secundas homines fiunt superbi. Illa considerarunt homines sapientes, exemplorum assiduitate commonefacti.
units.tr: Perseus, looking into the Gorgon, is turned into stone; that is, after prosperous circumstances men become proud. Wise men considered these things, reminded by the constant repetition of examples.

units.la: Timotheum Atheniensem, & Platonis socium pinxerunt Athenienses dormientem, & Fortunā (quia fuit ualde fortunatus) circa eum stantem & implentem rete. Postea uero uenit semel in concionem & dixit: Hoc ego feci & non Fortuna. Illis dictis, dixerunt cum semper fuisse infortunatum.
units.tr: The Athenians painted Timotheus of Athens, a companion of Plato, asleep, with Fortune (because he was very fortunate) standing beside him and filling his net. Later, however, he came once into an assembly and said: "I did this, and not Fortune." After he had said these words, they said that he had always been unfortunate.

units.la: Heroici uiri sæpe incidunt in tales furores, in quales Rex Babyloniæ Nabuchodonosor, quia sunt insolentes. Hercules ita insaniuit, ut interficeret coniugē & filios. Insaniuit etiā Pompeius quādo intrauit in templū, deinde mouit bellum ciuile.
units.tr: Heroic men often fall into such frenzies as Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, because they are insolent. Hercules went mad so that he killed his wife and sons. Pompey too went mad when he entered the temple, and then waged civil war.

units.la: Erat apud me simplex homo, cui dabam literas ad locum ubi habiturus erat conditionem: monebam eum multa de quibusdam rebus, de quibus erat monendus. Respondit: Non necesse est me multa monere, scio uti foro. Ita multum est in nobis fiduciæ & inanis ostentationis, cum simus fatui, & parū sciamus, cùm in Ecclesiasticis tum in politicis controuersijs.
units.tr: I had a simple man with me, to whom I gave letters for the place where he was about to take up a position. I advised him on many matters on which he needed advice. He replied: "There is no need for you to advise me on much; I know how to manage the forum." So there is much confidence and empty display in us, when we are fools and know little, both in ecclesiastical and in political controversies.

units.la: Milo Crotoniata fuit tantæ fortitudinis uir, ut arbores dilaceraret: tandem hæsit ipse in trunco & à lupo laceratus est. Ita homines, quibus rebus confidunt, ijs maximè euertuntur.
units.tr: Milo of Croton was a man of such strength that he tore trees apart. At last he got his own hand stuck in a trunk, and was torn to pieces by a wolf. So men are most overthrown by the very things in which they trust.

units.la: Perseus habuit clypeum uel gorgonē, quo uertit alios in saxa: & prohibitum est ci, ne aspiceret suum clypeum, id est, non admiraretur suam potentiam & uires.
units.tr: Perseus had a shield, or the Gorgon's head, by which he turned others into stone, and he was forbidden to look at his own shield; that is, he was not to admire his own power and strength.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Rex Aegyptius circumnauigauit totam terram inhabitabilem, sicut fuit olim studium regum inquirere fines terrae, discere doctrinā cosmographiae. Ille Rex uenit in insulam Thulam, & cùm nihil restaret amplius, fecit finem peregrinationum, editq; insulae nomen Thulae. Postea rediēs in Aegyptum interrogauit oraculū: Num esset aliquis maior ipso. Oraculum reprehendit eum, quòd se extolleret, & magnificaret supra quàm hominem conueniret, ac respondit: πρῶτα θεὸς μὲν ἔπειτα λόγος καὶ πνεῦμα σὺν αὐτοῖς.
units.tr: The Egyptian king travelled around the whole uninhabitable earth, as kings once made it their business to explore the ends of the earth and to learn the science of cosmography. This king came to the island of Thule, and when nothing further remained, he brought his travels to an end and named the island Thule. Afterwards, returning to Egypt, he asked the oracle whether anyone was greater than himself. The oracle rebuked him for exalting himself and magnifying himself beyond what befits a man, and answered: "First God, then Word and Spirit with them" [πρῶτα θεὸς μὲν ἔπειτα λόγος καὶ πνεῦμα σὺν αὐτοῖς].

units.la: Hoc dictum in historia regis Thulae in Suida reperitur. Puto esse uersum ex Sibyllinis, tres personas Diuinitatis comprehendentem. Vlterius est oraculum locutum: Tu miser homo egredere è tendo, & malè peribis. Occisus est igitur statim à suis egrediens. Sic dedit poenas superbiae.
units.tr: This saying is found in Suidas, in the story of the king of Thule. I think it is a verse from the Sibylline books, which embraces the three persons of the Godhead. The oracle then spoke further: "You wretched man, go out of your tent, and you will perish miserably." So he went out, and was at once killed by his own people. Thus he paid the penalty for his pride.

units.la: Aliud insolentię, & modestiae exemplum.
units.tr: Another example of arrogance and of modesty.

units.la: De quodam rege dicitur quòd aliquando iurauerit, se futurum Carolum de Austria (sic enim nominanominabat Imperatorem nostrum) & cò reda-cturum, ut iterum fieret comes de Habspurg. Im-perator nihil iussit ei respondere, nisi ut cogitaret se iam esse senẽ regem, & debere cogitare de com-muni orbis terrarum cõcordia. Est hoc modestissi-mum responsum.
units.tr: It is said of a certain king that once he swore that he would make Charles of Austria (for so he named our Emperor) and bring it about that he again became count of Habsburg. The Emperor ordered that he be given no answer except that he should consider that he was now an old king, and should think about the common concord of the world. This is a most modest reply.

units.la: Quando Hadrianus, qui fuit præceptor Ca-roli V. factus est Papa, ibi celebrata res est Lo-uanij in magna pompa, quòd iste magister Loua-niensis factus esset Papa. suspensa sunt aulea, in quorum uno fuit hoc: Traiectum plantauit, Lo-uanium rigauit: Cæsar incrementum dedit. Nihil cogitarunt nisi de rebus secundis uel humanis. Quare non ineptè aliquis facetus ascripsit: Hic Deus nihil fecit. Sæpe ita cogitant homines, obli-uiscuntur Dei, & fiunt insolentes, quando acci-piunt talia beneficia.
units.tr: When Hadrian, who had been the tutor of Charles V, was made Pope, there was a celebration at Louvain with great pomp, because this master of Louvain had become Pope. Hangings were displayed, on one of which was this: "He planted Utrecht, he watered Louvain; Caesar gave the increase." They thought of nothing but worldly and human good fortune. Not without wit, someone wrote beneath it: "Here God did nothing." Men often think in this way; they forget God and become arrogant when they receive such benefits.

units.la: Omnibus hominibus contëptus dolorẽ adfert, nec ulla est tanta humilitas quæ non ægre ferat se contemni: sicut dicitur de quodam uidente quen-dam suorum subditorum stare in tecto facientem opera, qui voluit experiri suam artẽ iaculãdi, col-lidit, ut miser de tecto labaretur. Ille uerò uicissim miserabiliter mortuus est.
units.tr: Contempt brings pain to all men, and there is no humility so great that it does not bear with difficulty being despised. It is told of a certain man who, seeing one of his subjects standing on a roof doing some work, wished to test his skill at throwing, struck him so that the unhappy man fell from the roof. But he in turn died miserably.

units.la: Paufanias adolescens, eques & dux Spartanus (qui fuit summus in illa pugna, qua Lacedæmo-nes uicerunt ad plateas decem millia, plurimos strucidarunt) rucidarunt) sedet in conuiuio, in quo unà aderat Simonides, qui existimabatur tunc temporis sapiens esse, sicut & magnus uir fuit. Ille itaq; forte Pausanias, ut derideret Simonidem, dixit ad eum: Simonides, dic aliquid sapienter. Hic nihil aliud respondit, nisi, ὦ Παυσανία, μέμνησω ἀνθρωπόν σε εἶναι. O Pausania, memineris te hominem esse. Ille ipse Pausanias paulò post captus, in carcere necatus est, & mater sua primum lapidem ad ostium carceris admouit, ut filius inclusus ibi fame necaretur. Sic suæ insolentiæ pœnas dedit.
units.tr: Pausanias, a young nobleman and Spartan commander (who was supreme in that battle in which the Lacedaemonians defeated the Persians at Plataea and slew very many, ten thousand), sat at a banquet, at which Simonides was also present, who was then thought to be wise, as he was also a great man. So Pausanias, wishing to mock Simonides, said to him: "Simonides, say something wise." He replied only: "O Pausanias, remember that you are a man" [ὦ Παυσανία, μέμνησο ἀνθρωπον σε εἶναι]. Pausanias himself, shortly afterwards captured, was starved to death in prison, and his mother placed the first stone at the prison door so that her son, shut in there, would die of hunger. Thus he paid the penalty for his arrogance.

units.la: Erat monachus Tubingæ, cui cum diceret Ecclesius: Superbus es monachus. Respondit monachus, mi Domine Doctor: Si multum humilitatis habeas, quæso mihi quoq; drachmam uendas. Notauit rursus Eccij superbiam, qui erat naturâ superbissimus.
units.tr: There was a monk at Tübingen, to whom Eck said: "You are a proud monk." The monk replied: "My lord Doctor, if you have so much humility, I beg you, sell me a drachma's worth of it too." He again remarked on Eck's pride, for Eck was by nature most proud.

units.la: Dicitur de rege quodam tempore Othonis primi ipsum indixisse his uerbis Imperatori bellum: sementurum in Germaniâ, & allaturum plures gallinas, quàm ipse in Germania haberet stramineos pileos. Otho Imperator derisit illam stultam insolentiam: significans non decere insolentiam in sermone, iubens omnes milites suos stramineos pileos gerre. Ita ex illa insolentia rex est captus.
units.tr: It is said that a certain king, in the time of the first Otto, declared war on the Emperor in these words: that he would sow in Germany and bring more hens than he had straw hats in Germany. Emperor Otto mocked that foolish arrogance, showing that arrogance in speech is unbecoming, and ordering all his soldiers to wear straw hats. So the king was captured because of that arrogance.

units.la: Quidam dixit se habere cor Imperatoris Caroli V. quæ est uox arrogans, minimè conueniens iuueni. Pater ipsius vir prudens & consiliarius, nequaquam tam superbum dictum proferre ausus fuisset.
units.tr: Someone said that he had the heart of the Emperor Charles V, which is an arrogant saying, very unsuitable for a young man. His father, a prudent man and counsellor, would by no means have dared to utter so proud a statement.

units.la: Quidem monachus in quodam monasterio, magnam sanctitatem præ se ferens, semper incedens obliquo capite terram spectans, quem propter vitæ innocentiam & probitatem reliqui fratres in Abbatem elegerunt. Factus vero Abbas, cito cum fortuna mores mutauit, & ut antea fuerat simplicissimus, ita postea factus est nequissimus. Quod cum alij mirati fuissent, tandem interrogauerunt, cur antea probitatem & simplicitatem simulasset, terramq; semper spectasset. Respondit ille: Quærebam claues monasterij, quibus inuentis, id est, delato mihi hoc honore, iam rectus incedo, & clauibus pro libitu utor.
units.tr: A certain monk in a monastery, who showed great holiness, always walked with his head bowed, looking at the ground, and the other brothers, on account of his innocent and upright life, chose him as abbot. But once made abbot, he quickly changed his manners with his fortune, and as he had been most simple before, so afterwards he became most wicked. When others marvelled at this, they finally asked why he had earlier feigned uprightness and simplicity and had always looked at the ground. He replied: "I was looking for the keys of the monastery; once I had found them, that is, once this office was conferred on me, I now walk upright and use the keys as I please."

units.la: Non debetis esse tam superbi & insolentes, ut illi hypocritæ, qui iactitant se omnia scire & volunt esse omniscij. ualde parum sciunt, & nihil sciunt sicut dixit quidam impudens Theologus: indignum esse, si Theologus interrogaret alios, & non esse Theologum, qui alios interrogaret quædam de doctrina. Talis est hypocrisis in multis, ut nihil aliud dicam, tument persuasione excellentis sapientiæ & doctrinæ: putant se esse sapientes, cum stulti sint, & non intelligant quid dicant.
units.tr: You must not be so proud and arrogant as those hypocrites who boast that they know everything and want to be thought all-knowing. They know very little, and nothing at all, just as a certain shameless theologian said: that it would be unworthy for a theologian to ask others, and that he would not be a theologian who asked others about points of doctrine. Such is the hypocrisy of many, that, to say nothing else, they swell with the conviction of their excellent wisdom and learning; they think they are wise when they are foolish, and do not understand what they are saying.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Noui rusticum quendam, qui cùm amplissimas opes ex fodinis nancisceretur, ita se extulit, ut cũ potentissimis ciuibus, splendore, uestibus, ciborum lauticia certaret. Hoc cùm uideret Georgius dux Saxoniæ, suauiter eum deridebat, dicens: Ecce ille rusticus certè, si posset, deos superaret. Tales sunt homines plebei, qui bonis à Deo datis insolenter utuntur, iuxta illud: Asperius nihil est misero, cum surgit in altum.
units.tr: I knew a certain peasant who, having acquired very great wealth from the mines, so exalted himself that he vied with the most powerful citizens in splendour, clothing and lavish feasting. When Duke George of Saxony saw this, he mocked him pleasantly, saying: "Look, that peasant would surely overcome the gods, if he could." Such are the common people who use the goods given them by God insolently, according to the saying: "Nothing is harsher to the wretch than when he rises high."

units.la: Vulgari fertur prouerbio: Duo montes non facile iunguntur, quo significatur, superbos non facilè inter se conuenire.
units.tr: There is a common proverb: "Two mountains do not easily join together," meaning that proud men do not easily agree with one another.

units.la: Pompeius Magnus olim ingressus est in Sanctũ Sanctorum, id est: in chorum & secretum locum templi, in quo erat arca fœderis collocata, & sedes Dei. Ex illa insolentia statim secuta est mutatio suæ fortunæ, & paulo post in conspectu templi est interfectus.
units.tr: Pompey the Great once entered the Holy of Holies, that is, the inner and secret place of the temple in which the ark of the covenant and the throne of God were placed. Immediately after that act of insolence came a change of his fortune, and shortly afterwards he was slain in full view of the temple.

units.la: Cùm aliquando Episcopus quidam, iam recens electus, gereret se paulo insolentius & crudelius cum comitibus uicinis confisus potentia Cæsaris, doloensq; nostram doctrinam delere funditus, dixit ad eum Dominus à Stein: Domine princeps uideris multis sapientibus uiris longè insolentior, produxitq; multa exempla similia Italica, ex quibus intelligeret multas mutationes in Italia secutas esse. Respondit princeps: Vtendum est tempore. Ad hæc Dominus à Stein: Domine episcope, tu es princeps, ego uerò nequaquam: scio itaq; tibi deberi reuerētiam. Præterea tu etiam es Doctor, & ego nō: sed anteeo te ætate, & uidi multa talia exempla. Dedicatio est iam in superiori pago, sed quando erit in inferiore, certè male nobiscum agetur.
units.tr: Once a certain bishop, newly elected, was behaving somewhat too insolently and cruelly towards his neighbouring nobles, trusting in the power of the Emperor and resolving to destroy our doctrine root and branch. Lord von Stein said to him: "Your Highness seems far more arrogant than many wise men." He brought forward many similar examples from Italy, from which the bishop might understand that many upheavals had followed in Italy. The prince replied: "One must use the time." To this Lord von Stein said: "Lord Bishop, you are a prince, but I am not at all; I therefore know that reverence is owed to you. Moreover, you are also a Doctor and I am not; but I am older than you, and I have seen many such examples. The dedication is already in the upper village, but when it comes to the lower one, things will certainly go badly for us."

units.la: Rana prope bouem, miratur bouis magnitudinem, ita ut crepat. Est imago omnium superborum & non habentium facultates. Augustus est bos coram Antonio, & Antonius rana coram Augusto, donec crepat.
units.tr: A frog near an ox marvels at the size of the ox, so that it bursts. It is an image of all the proud who have no means. Augustus is the ox in the presence of Antony, and Antony is the frog in the presence of Augustus, until he bursts.

units.la: Prædicator Argentinensis Keisersberger voluit taxare superbiam alicuius uetulæ, quæ nuper nupserat uiro, dixit in concione: Colores sunt pulchri, sed non recte distributi. Nam oculi sunt rubri, qui color debebat esse in labijs, & dentes oculorum nigritudinem habent, cum debebant esse albi. Sed maxillæ sunt pallidæ, & alia similia recitabat: nam alias erat eloquens.
units.tr: The preacher of Strasbourg, Keisersberger, wanted to rebuke the pride of a certain old woman who had recently married a man. He said in a sermon: "The colours are beautiful, but not rightly distributed. For the eyes are red, which colour ought to be on the lips, and the teeth have the blackness of the eyes, when they ought to be white. But the cheeks are pale," and he recited other similar things, for in other respects she was eloquent.

units.la: Omnes fatui sunt superbi, & econtrà omnes superbi fatui: & siquidem tibi bene cum ipsis conuenire uelis, tantummodo cures, ut laudes eos. Quo magis est aliquis excellens, eo magis miratur artem, ac magis se subijcit. Audiui à Durero, qui dicebat se mirabiliter delectari pictu-ris suis ris suis recens factis: postea cum ex interuallo temporis easdem aspiceret, earum ipsum ualde pudere.
units.tr: All fools are proud, and conversely all the proud are fools. And if you wish to get on well with them, you need only take care to praise them. The more excellent someone is, the more he admires his art, and the more he submits himself. I heard from Dürer, who said that he took wonderful delight in his pictures when they were freshly made; later, when he looked at the same ones after an interval of time, he was greatly ashamed of them.

units.la: Memini, cùm quidam moueretur æmulatione contra Lutherum,eum hæc uerba dixisse: Ego nō minus honorari ac uenerari cupio, quàm ipse. Deus autem Luthero eum honorē addidit. Ille ue-rò sua uocatione contētus esse debuisset. Non om-nium eadem aut par uocatio esse potest. Est exem-plum æmulationis, inuidentiæ & superbiæ.
units.tr: I remember that when a certain man was stirred by rivalry against Luther, he said these words: "I desire to be honoured and revered no less than he is. God, however, has added that honour to Luther. But he ought to have been content with his calling. No one's calling can be the same or equal to another's." This is an example of rivalry, envy and pride.

units.la: Erasmus si quando homines superbos & arrogā-tes notare & deridere uellet, scripsit eis, Absolutæ eruditionis & pietatis uiris, &c. Sic scripsit Theo-logis Parisiensibus. Significat autem absolutæ e-ruditionis & pietatis, alienos ab omni eruditione & pietate.
units.tr: When Erasmus wished at any time to mark and deride proud and arrogant men, he wrote to them: "To men of absolute learning and piety," and so on. He wrote thus to the Parisian theologians. But "of absolute learning and piety" means men estranged from all learning and piety.

units.la: Dux Luneburgensis auus horum ducum nunc iuuentium, ingeniosissimus & felicissimus fuit in componendis cantilenis. Fertur hoc eius esse: Der guckguck hat sich zu todt gefallen uon einer hochē weiden: wer will uns diese sommer zeit die lange weil uertreiben. Accidit aliquid aduersi alteri principi, qui multa aliis minatus erat: at impeditus perficere non poterat.
units.tr: The Duke of Lüneburg, grandfather of these dukes who are now young, was a most gifted and most fortunate composer of songs. This is said to be his: The cuckoo has fallen to death from a high willow: who will now drive away the long tedium of this summer time for us? Something adverse happened to another prince, who had threatened many others, but being hindered he could not carry it out.

units.la: Dicunt nullam aliam fuisse causam, quare Soli-manus Turcicus Imperator interfecit Imbre Vua-scha, nisi quod Imbre Vuascha(si quādo Imperator exiret in arcem uel alió) semper splēdidiori habitu indutus fuerit, quàm Solimānus, ita ut praecipui capitanei Turcici sint secuti Imbre Vuascha. Imperatoris comitatus, respectu Imbre Vuascha, fuit tanquam solitudo. Ista res offendit Imperatorem, ideo eum interfecit.
units.tr: They say there was no other cause why Suleiman the Turkish Emperor killed Imbre Vuascha, except that Imbre Vuascha, whenever the Emperor went out to the citadel or elsewhere, was always dressed in a more splendid garb than Suleiman, so that the chief Turkish captains followed Imbre Vuascha. The Emperor's retinue, in comparison with Imbre Vuascha, seemed like a mere solitude. This matter offended the Emperor, and therefore he killed him.

units.la: Episcopus Mersburgensis creuit Moguntiæ cōcionibus, quibus inflexit se ad hominum sensus. quædam dixit accersita ex harum Ecclesiarum doctrina. factus uero Episcopus Augustæ, postridie equitabat in equo, cui os fiscella campistratum erat. illud uidens D. Antonius Fuggerus inquit: Iste Episcopus non amplius mihi placet. Vidit enim eum statim factum esse insolentiorem.
units.tr: The Bishop of Merseburg grew in Mainz through sermons, by which he bent men's minds to himself; he said certain things drawn from the teaching of these Churches. But when he became bishop at Augsburg, the next day he rode on a horse whose muzzle had a basket-like covering spread over it. Seeing this, Lord Anton Fugger said: "That bishop no longer pleases me." For he saw that he had at once become more insolent.

units.la: Quando pauper aliquis aut mendicus superbire nititur, tum locum habet illud Germanicum prouerbium: An arme hoffart wischt der teufel den ars. Nostris tamen temporibus inuenias sæpe egenos & quasi mendicos insolentiores & magis iactabundos, quàm quosdam diuitijs & opibus potentes ac excellentes.
units.tr: When some poor man or beggar strives to be proud, then the German proverb applies: "The devil wipes his backside with poor pride." Yet in our times you will often find the needy and almost beggarly more insolent and more boastful than certain men who are powerful and eminent in riches and wealth.

units.la: SECVNDVM PRAEceptum.
units.tr: SECVNDVM PRAEceptum.

units.la: IDOLOLATRIA.
units.tr: IDOLOLATRIA.

units.la: Imperator quidam postquam induisset induisium S.Georgij, quod est Bamberge (fortasse fuit alicuius equitis senio confecti) procedens inter ictus bombardarum, habebat hanc persuasionem, se non posse feriri globo.
units.tr: A certain emperor, after he had put on the St George's surcoat that is kept at Bamberg (perhaps it had belonged to some old knight), went out amid the blasts of the cannon and was persuaded that he could not be struck by a cannonball.

units.la: Quaedam mulier interrogata Coloniae à suo filio, cur adoraret imagines trium magorum, qui non possent exaudire eam, (sicut omnes statuae sunt tantum opera ab hominibus sculpta uel fabricata) inquit: Non ego ipsos alloquor, sed tantum recito ibi orationem Dominicā. Pater noster qui es in coelis &c. Sic illā impietatē hoc praetextu tegebat. qualis furor est illa adoratio statuarum.
units.tr: A certain woman at Cologne was asked by her son why she worshipped the images of the three Magi, which could not hear her (since all statues are merely works sculpted or fashioned by men). She replied: "I do not address them myself, but I only recite there the Lord's Prayer: Our Father, who art in heaven, etc." Thus she covered that impiety with this pretext. What madness is that worship of statues!

units.la: Contentiones de statuis uocarūt εἰνοvομαχίαν, sicut notum est etiam nunc uehementes de ijs esse contentiones. Iam quidem de ijs subtiliter disputare nolo, sed tamen manifestum est, statuas & imagines maximam praebuisse occasionem multiplici idolatriae. Quare satius fuisset nullas unquā fuisse statuas. Sic Granuelus, nō de hac re sed de inuocatione Sanctorū, multis nobis audiētib. dixit: Quāquam non possum hoc asseuerare, quòd non liceat dicere, ora pro me sancte Petre: tamen tantum est abusuū in omni inuocatione Sanctorum, ut uelim prorsus nullam esse. Illa uerba dixit Grāuelus in colloquio Ratisbonæ, cùm de ea re disputaremus.
units.tr: Disputes over statues the Greeks called "image-battles" [εἰκονομαχία], just as even now the disputes about them are known to be fierce. I do not wish to dispute about them in detail, but it is nonetheless plain that statues and images have given the greatest occasion for manifold idolatry. Therefore it would have been better if there had never been any statues at all. So Granvelle, speaking not on this matter but on the invocation of the saints, said in the hearing of many of us: "Although I cannot affirm that it is not lawful to say, 'Pray for me, holy Peter,' yet there is so much abuse in every invocation of the saints that I would wish there were none at all." Granvelle spoke those words at the colloquy of Regensburg, when we were disputing on that matter.

units.la: Bonum est nos talia dicta sapientum uirorum sci re, qui quamuis non fuerint nec voluerint esse in nostro coetu: tamen improbauerunt hos maximos abusus. Idem quoq; mihi licet dicere de statuis.
units.tr: It is good for us to know such sayings of wise men, who, although they were not and did not wish to be in our assembly, nevertheless disapproved of these great abuses. I may say the same thing myself about statues.

units.la: Erat puella quædam apud Rhenum, quæ certis horarum periodis iacebat, quasi esset exanimis multis horis, interdū uiginti quatuor, interdū triginta sex. Postea cùm ad se redijsset, multa narrabat de inferis, & dicebat se fuisse in purgatorio: & quas animas ibi uidisset, narrabat. Ita crescebat lucrum sacrificulis.
units.tr: There was a certain girl by the Rhine who, at fixed intervals of hours, lay as though lifeless for many hours, sometimes twenty-four, sometimes thirty-six. Afterwards, when she came to herself, she would tell much about the lower world, and said she had been in purgatory; and she would relate what souls she had seen there. Thus the profit of the little priests grew.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Nouimus homines cucurrisse ad Grimmenthal, qui amētes fuerunt, & iacuerunt ante ciuitatem per aliquot horas, postea redierunt ad se. Hæc dixerunt esse miracula sanctæ Mariæ.
units.tr: We know of people who ran to Grimmenthal, who were out of their minds, and lay before the town for some hours, and afterwards came to themselves again. They said these were miracles of the holy Mary.

units.la: Scio aliū locum in Germania, quē honoris causa nō nomino, ut parcā illis hominibus, in quo mulieres steriles cogebantur certo tēpore nudē circumire altare, & gestare agniculum. Interea stabant monachi illi nebulones in suis cancellis, & mulieres nudas spectabant.
units.tr: I know of another place in Germany, which I do not name out of respect, so as to spare those people, where barren women were compelled at a set time to go naked around the altar and carry a little lamb. Meanwhile those wicked monks stood in their enclosures and looked at the naked women.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam cum audiuisset cantilenam: Ein feste burck ist unser Gott, dixit: Ich will helffen die burck zerschiessen, oder ich will nit leben. Post triduum est mortuus sine cōfessione, ac sine agnitione filij Dei.
units.tr: Someone, when he had heard the song "A mighty fortress is our God," said: "I will help shoot the fortress to pieces, or I will not live." After three days he died without confession and without acknowledging the Son of God.

units.la: Tubingæ quedā uetula mihi optime nota, suspēdit donū ad quandam arā sanctæ Mariæ, dicēs, se adiutam se adiutam esse à Maria in quodam negocio etiam malo, mihi non ignoto. Ibi pastor statim ascēdit in suggestum, & in concione egit gratias Deo, quòd tam propitia esset beata Maria huic oppido, & iußit eam magis colere, & plura dona adferre. Ita diabolus hac occasione idololatriam stabiliuit.
units.tr: At Tübingen a certain old woman, very well known to me, hung a gift at a certain altar of the holy Mary, saying that she had been helped by Mary in a certain matter, even an evil one, which is not unknown to me. Thereupon the minister at once climbed into the pulpit and in his sermon gave thanks to God that the blessed Mary was so favourable to this town, and he ordered that she be honoured more and that more gifts be brought. Thus the devil, on this occasion, established idolatry.

units.la: Ego & Doctor Martinus Lutherus, & alij quidam uidimus αὐτόμα in urbe Ifenach artificiosè à Papistis factū, ad suos quæstus retinendū. Erat aūt statua Mariæ tenētis puerū Iesum, & ita facta, ut si retro iaceret, monachus posset eam regere, ut aut Maria aut puer caput ad accedentē aduertens a-spiceret, si quis pecuniā largiretur: aut retrorsum caput auerteret, si nullum donum afferret.
units.tr: I, and Doctor Martin Luther, and certain others saw at the city of Eisenach an automaton artfully made by the Papists to keep up their profits. It was a statue of Mary holding the boy Jesus, and it was so made that, if it lay on its back, a monk could guide it so that either Mary or the boy would turn the head toward the approaching person and look at him, if someone gave money; or would turn the head backwards if he brought no gift.

units.la: In quodam Papistico loco, ante annos aliquot aliqui boni homines abstulerunt statuā Mariæ ex uico quodā, ad quam cōcurrebatur, & fiebāt adorationes. Dominus illius loci postridie iußit fieri inquisitionem seuerissimā, ut perpetratores huius facinoris inquirerentur, curauitq; in eum locū argenteā statuā reponi, cùm antiqua nō posset inuenīri. Fecit perinde sicut Caligula qui uoluit collocari suam statuā in templum Hierosolymitanum.
units.tr: In a certain Papist place, some years ago, some good men carried off a statue of Mary from a village to which people were flocking and where adorations were being made. The lord of that place the next day ordered a most severe inquiry to be made, so that the perpetrators of this crime might be sought out, and he took care that a silver statue be placed in that spot, since the old one could not be found. He did just as Caligula did, who wished his own statue to be placed in the temple at Jerusalem.

units.la: Quidam impostor indulgentiarius uendebat indulgentias, & ubiq; circumferebat. Hic aliquādo ascensø suggesto in cōcione dixit: Quicūq; meßs indulgētias osculabitur non morietur hoc anno peste, eritq; liber ac tutus à pestis contagio. Dux Vuirtenbergensis Eberhardus iußit eum ad se accersi, cumq; venißet, dixit: Quare hoc in concione dicis? Respondit: Verũ est domine, sed ipsi osculantur tantum uitrum, non indulgentias. Abi, inquit, Dux, cum tua sophistica excusatione. Credo si non statim discessississet, tunc ipsum suspendi mandasset, & iuste fecississet.
units.tr: A certain impostor, a seller of indulgences, was selling indulgences and carrying them about everywhere. Once, having mounted the pulpit in his sermon, he said: "Whoever kisses my indulgences will not die this year of plague, and will be free and safe from contagion of the plague." Duke Eberhard of Württemberg ordered him to be summoned to him, and when he came, said: "Why do you say this in the sermon?" He answered: "It is true, my lord, but they kiss only the glass, not the indulgences." "Begone," said the Duke, "with your sophistical excuse. I think, if he had not at once departed, he would have ordered him hanged then and there, and would have acted justly."

units.la: Dicitur de legatis Turcicis uenientibus Cracouiam, cū honoris gratia adhiberētur ad pompam die Palmarum, & uiderent sacerdotes flexis genibus procidere ante asinum, qui circumducebatur, eleuatis brachijs in publico eos exclamasse: O quanta impietas & dedecus est, adorare asinum creaturā? Es steht dennoch nit woll, multos asinos adorare unum.
units.tr: It is said that Turkish envoys coming to Kraków, when they were brought, out of courtesy, to the procession on Palm Sunday, and saw the priests falling on their knees before the donkey which was led about, raised their arms and cried out in public: "O what impiety and disgrace it is to adore a donkey, a creature! Yet it is not good that many adore one donkey."

units.la: Consuetudo fuit olim, ut homines ad statuam sancti Viti currerent, ibiq; totum diem saltarent usq; ad animæ deliquium: ita ut eos linteis stragulis inde asportare necesse fuerit, tandem prostrati liberabantur.
units.tr: It was once the custom for people to run to the statue of St Vitus, and there to dance the whole day until they swooned; so that it was necessary to carry them away on coverlets, and at last they were freed when they lay prostrate.

units.la: In Lotharingia ad S. Athanasium à malis spiritibus, obsessi adserebantur, ubi ita liberabantur, ut integrum annum à morbis liberi essent.
units.tr: At Saint Athanasius in Lorraine, people were said to be possessed by evil spirits, and were freed there in such a way that they were free from diseases for a whole year.

units.la: Ad sanctam Mariam Ratisbonensem homines ultra uiginti milliaria, nec bibentes nec comedentes currebāt, quò cùm uenissent, iacebāt prostrati quatuor horas, posteaq; liberabantur.
units.tr: To the holy Mary of Regensburg people ran from more than twenty miles away, neither drinking nor eating; when they had come there, they lay prostrate for four hours, and afterwards were freed.

units.la: Vuitebergæ ante hæc tempora mõstratum est memorale S. Frãcisci. Augustæ etiam homines coierunt Symphorianum contra crubonem, alludẽ es ad uulgatum nomen semper. Est enim ibidem ara cum statua eiusdem in templo S. Vlrici, quæ est uere idolum alicuius magnatis, eoq; multorum magnatũ donaria sunt allata. Ad hoc idolum confugiebant laborãtes morbo Gallico, ut ab illo liberentur. Sed post comitia Augustana istam remo┬ruerunt statuam. Colere Annam locupletatricem, nihil aliud est, quàm colere Iunonem.
units.tr: At Wittenberg, before these times, the memorial of St Francis was displayed. At Augsburg too people gathered at Symphorian against the swelling, playing on the commonly used name "semper." For there is in that same place an altar with a statue of him in the church of St Ulrich, which is truly the idol of some great man, and therefore gifts of many great men were brought to it. To this idol those suffering from the French disease fled, that they might be freed from it. But after the Diet of Augsburg they removed that statue. To worship Anne the enricher is nothing other than to worship Juno.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Fuit Vuitebergæ, paulo ante restaurationem huius doctrinæ sanioris, sacrificulus ualde robustus & crassus, ac bonus potator, iste quotannis solebat Dominica misericordiæ Domini, & in die omnium sanctorum ostendere reliquias sanctorũ, ad quam ostensionem confluebant multa millia hominum ex finitimis undiq; locis, etiam ultra viginti aut tringinta milliaria distantibus. Habebat autem sacrificulus magnum catalogum, ex quo ordine legebat reliquias hominum mortuorum in illo libro inscriptas, easq; simul etiam ostendebat. Nos autem qui eramus in aula principis, ea etiam sorte uidebamus. Itaq; cum sacrificulus iste mane facturus erat ordinem reliquiarum, scriptum in isto libro, & uesperi bene potus esset: facetus qui‐dã homo Musicus in aula, pingebat inter illos arti‐culos issdẽ literis, quib. reliqui erat pictì, talia uer‐ba: Ein mercklicher partikel uon Sancti Francisci bruch. Sacrificulus ignarus harum rerũ, mane mo‐re solito ex libro declamat ordine singulas parti‐culas reliquiarũ, & cum uenisset ad uerba nõ pri‐us lecta aut considerata, alta uoce clamabat: Ein mercklicher partikel uon Sant Francisci bruch. Ibi inter dicẽdum admonitus de uocabulo Bruch, statim addit correctionẽ: Ey nein,nein, uon Sanct Francisci buch solt ich sagen.
units.tr: Shortly before the restoration of this sounder doctrine, there was a priest at Wittenberg, a very sturdy and stout man and a good drinker. Every year on the Sunday of the Lord's mercy and on All Saints' Day he used to display the relics of the saints, and many thousands of people flocked to this display from the neighbouring regions on every side, some even from twenty or thirty miles away. The priest had a large catalogue, from which he read in order the relics of dead men written in that book, and he showed them at the same time. We who were at the prince's court also watched this. Now when this priest was to go through the list of relics written in the book the next morning, one witty man among the court musicians, in the evening, wrote among those entries, in the same lettering as the rest, these words: "Ein mercklicher partikel uon Sancti Francisci bruch" [A notable particle of St Francis's hernia]. The priest, unaware of these things, next morning, as usual, read the particles of relics from the book one by one in order. When he came to these words, which he had not read or looked at beforehand, he cried out in a loud voice: "Ein mercklicher partikel uon Sant Francisci bruch." Then, reminded by the word "Bruch" in the middle of his reading, he at once added a correction: "Ey nein, nein, uon Sanct Francisci buch solt ich sagen" [Oh no, no, I should have said "of St Francis's book"]. ## CONTEMPTORS, BLASPHEMERS AND CURSERS: THEIR PUNISHMENTS

units.la: CONTEMPTORVM, BLASPHE‐morum,& execrantium pœnæ.
units.tr: CONTEMPTORVM, BLASPHEMORUM, & EXECRANTIUM POENAE.

units.la: Hoffman iturus ad conuentum Ratisbonensem, non procul ab Vlma,est mortuus in horribilibus mugitibus.
units.tr: Hoffman, setting out for the Diet of Regensburg, not far from Ulm, died amid dreadful bellowing.

units.la: Heliodorus subita consternatione oppressus est, cùm templum in urbe Hierosolyma spoliatu‐us esset.
units.tr: Heliodorus was overwhelmed by a sudden terror when he was plundering the temple in Jerusalem.

units.la: Latomus theologus Louaniensis moriturus mugijt sicut bos, & uociferatus est de suo dolore & peccato, quòd fuisset persecutus homines san‐ctos,& adiuuisset consilia necis cõtra conscientiã.
units.tr: Latomus, the theologian of Louvain, bellowed like an ox as he was dying, and cried out about his pain and his sin, that he had persecuted holy men and aided plots to murder against his conscience.

units.la: Dominicaster monachus monastenij in ipsa cō‐cione percutiebatur fulmine, cùm clamaret cõtra Euangelicam doctrinam:& ita est mortuus.
units.tr: Dominicaster, a monk of the monastery, was struck by lightning in the very middle of his sermon, while he was shouting against the evangelical doctrine, and so he died.

units.la: Ante paucos annos adolescētes duo inter se cer- tauerunt, uter posset dicere atrocissimas execrationes : alter cœpit omnino furere in ipso certamine: ita Deus punit blasphemos.
units.tr: A few years ago two young men quarrelled with each other as to which of them could utter the most atrocious curses. One of them began to rage completely in the very contest. Thus God punishes blasphemers.

units.la: Basileæ est editus liber de sceleribus Georgij Dauidis, qui fuit incola Hollandiæ, & multis finitimis regionibus notus. Ille impostor collegit ingentem pecuniam istis imposturis simulatione pietatis, ita ut aliquot millia aureorum collegerit, multos homines mirabiliter decepit suis fallacijs: postea factus est ciuis Basiliensis, emit arcem & egregia prædia. Mortuus quidem est sine supplicio: postea uero re comperta, effossus & combustus est. Quanta scelera docuerit & fouerit, inuenietis in scripto ab academia Basiliensi edito, quod ueram vitæ ac dogmatum huius Dauidis narrationem continet. Fuit mirabilis impostor: excitauit manas turbas in Holandia & uicinijs, deterioresq; blasphemias, quàm sunt Anabaptistarum. Scripta ipsius vere antinomiæ sunt, quando uocant se spirituales, tum affirmat se habere libertatem iuxta quamcunq; quouis etiam loco receptam doctrinam aut politiam uiuendi, omniaq; externa, siue in religione, siue in politijs ipsis libera & adiaphora habentur, modo istius Tertij Dauidis Georgij spiritum habeant.
units.tr: At Basel there was published a book on the crimes of David George, who lived in Holland and was known in many neighbouring regions. This impostor gathered a huge sum of money by these deceits, under a pretence of piety, so that he collected several thousand gold coins, and by his trickery he wonderfully deceived many people. Afterwards he became a citizen of Basel, bought a castle and excellent estates. He indeed died without punishment, but later, when the facts were discovered, he was dug up and burned. You will find how many crimes he taught and fostered in the writing published by the academy of Basel, which contains a true account of the life and doctrines of this David. He was a remarkable impostor. He stirred up great disturbances in Holland and the neighbouring regions, and blasphemies worse than those of the Anabaptists. His writings are truly antinomian: they call themselves "spiritual," and they affirm that they have freedom to live according to any doctrine or polity whatever, received anywhere, and that all external things, whether in religion or in civil affairs, are free and indifferent, provided they have the spirit of this third David George.

units.la: Ante paucos annos frater Tameri suspēdit se, eo quòd cùm antea docuisset purè Euangelium de Christo, postea per fratrem esset abductus à uera sententia: sicq; pœnas dedit.
units.tr: A few years ago a brother of Tamer hanged himself, because, having once taught the Gospel of Christ purely, he was afterwards drawn away from the true opinion by a brother, and so he paid the penalty.

units.la: Fuit eques in urbe Eslingen die sanctæ Cathá-rinæ, quo ibi frequens est mercatus. Hic postquam multum pecuniæ lusu perdiderat, uolens abire, ius-so ministro adducere equos, usus est horrendis & abominandis execrationibus. Seruus dixit: Quare uis iam abire sub noctem: uiæ sunt difficiles, inci-demus fortasis in aquas (sicut ibi uiæ sunt malæ) expectemus crastinum diem. Ille pergit furere in illis execrationibus: seruus obtemperat: egredi-untur, fuerunt eorum tres. Nam præter equitem nobili aderat alius quidam adolescens, ex quo hanc narrationem audiui, postquam iam adole-uerat: erat honestus uir, dicebatq; se fuisse tunc istius ministrum. His ita non longe progressis, oc-currunt equites plurimi magno cum sonitu com-plectentes in medio ipsum nobilem, & utrinq; collidentes, ita ut decideret de equo, quasi exani-matus. Sed tantum fuit roboris in illo adolescente, qui habebat bonam adhuc consoientiam, ut pene-traret illum equitatum & dominum duceret. Sed uiarum errore (cùm tamen non sit facilis erra-tio, sicut ipse dicebat) uagantibus & impeditis, tota illa nocte auditus est molestus ille equitum strepitus in altero latere: ad aliud uerò latus, ubi erat adolescens, equitatus non peruenit, eò quòd ipsi non possent diaboli nocere. Deinde deducūt dominum circa auroram ad monasterium Behen-hausen. Ibi decubuit ille triduo, & postea moritur. Talis est exitus taliū horribilium execrationum.
units.tr: There was a nobleman in the city of Esslingen on St Catherine's day, when the market there is busy. After he had lost a great deal of money at gambling, he wished to leave, and, ordering a servant to bring the horses, he used horrible and abominable curses. The servant said: "Why do you want to leave now, toward night? The roads are difficult; we may perhaps fall into the waters (the roads there are bad). Let us wait for tomorrow." He went on raging in those curses, and the servant obeyed. They set out, three of them; for besides the nobleman there was another young man, from whom I heard this account after he had grown up. He was an honest man, and he said that he had then been the nobleman's servant. Having not gone far, they met many horsemen with a great noise, who surrounded the nobleman in the middle and jostled him on both sides, so that he fell from his horse as if lifeless. But there was so much strength in that young man, who still had a good conscience, that he broke through that troop of horsemen and led his master out. But while they wandered, hindered by a mistake on the road (though the road is not easy to go astray on, as he himself said), that troublesome noise of horsemen was heard all night on the other side; but on the other side, where the young man was, the horsemen did not come, because they could not harm him. Then, about dawn, they brought their master to the monastery at Behenhausen. There he lay sick for three days and afterwards died. Such was the end of such dreadful curses.

units.la: Accidit in loco quodā uicino, ubi iuuenes quidam exhibuerunt ludos circa dies Bacchanaliorū: postea uerò sunt conuiciati inuicem, & certauerunt, quis posset dicere atrocissimas execrationes . Primus factus est mutus, secundus furiosus: & quid de cæteris fit, ignoro. Nondum enim recte factum inquisiui. Memini Tubingæ puero exectam linguam esse, quod nouas horrendas execrationes usurpauerit.
units.tr: It happened in a certain neighbouring place, where some young men put on games around the days of the Bacchanalia, that afterwards they abused one another and quarrelled over who could utter the most atrocious curses. The first became dumb, the second mad; and what became of the rest I do not know, for I have not yet carefully inquired. I remember that at Tübingen, when I was a boy, a tongue was cut out because its owner had come up with new and dreadful curses.

units.la: Retulit mihi bonus amicus, propositam esse in Silesia cantilenam, continentem blasphemiam contra ministerium, in cuius principio inter cætera iactatur, concionatores Euangelicos dicere, quòd Deus ipsorum potestati sit alligatus, & cogatur facere, quodcunq; ipsi uelint. Tales plures execrandæ et detestandæ uoces in illa cantilena recitātur. Illa peccata Deum irritabunt, ut sint uenturæ pœnæ Turcicæ. Potestas etiā debebat seuerißimè tales blasphemantes punire, & tollere.
units.tr: A good friend told me that a song had been published in Silesia containing blasphemy against the ministry. At its beginning, among other things, it boasts that evangelical preachers say that God is bound to their power and is compelled to do whatever they wish. Many such detestable and execrable utterances are recited in that song. Such sins will provoke God, so that the Turkish punishments will come. The civil authority ought also to punish such blasphemers most severely and remove them.

units.la: Anno 1551 in ferijs Pentecostes in Marchia, ex pago quodam diabolus uisibili specie mulierem proferētem diras execrationes, in aerem subduxit,
units.tr: In the year 1551, during the Pentecost holidays, in the March, a devil in visible form carried off into the air a woman who was uttering dreadful curses from a certain village,

units.la: multis spectantibus, eamq; postea præcipitauit in vicinam uliginem. Factus est concursus hominum volentium videre quò abduceretur. Cùm verò ad eum locum venirent, ubi mulier iaceret, invenerunt eam obtorto collo iacentem, ac mortuam.
units.tr: in the sight of many, and afterwards hurled her down into a neighbouring swamp. A crowd of people gathered, wanting to see where she had been taken. When they came to the place where the woman lay, they found her lying dead, with her neck twisted.

units.la: Ante aliquot annos in Thuringia, diabolus etiam propter blasphemiam abducere volebat adolescentem multum luctantē & repugnantem, qui tamen est seruatus: & egit statim pœnitentiam. Profecto species hæ diaboli non sunt inanæ terriculamentum, sed verè horrenda exempla. Observate diligenter historias tales, ut sitis modestiores & diligentiores in uitandis execrationibus, & blasphemijs nominis diuini, simulq; cogitetis de dicto Ioannis: Filius Dei apparuit ut destruat opera diaboli. Deus nobis adsit & nos doceat. Hoc tempus in quo nunc uiuimus est periculosum, non tantum propter inclinationem stellarum infelicē, sed etiam propter diaboli insidias, qui acerrimè iam ex omnibus partibus oppugnat Ecclesiam.
units.tr: Some years ago in Thuringia, a devil also, on account of blasphemy, wanted to carry off a young man who struggled and resisted greatly, but he was saved, and he at once repented. Indeed these appearances of the devil are not empty scarecrows but truly dreadful examples. Observe such stories carefully, so that you may be more restrained and diligent in avoiding curses and blasphemies against the divine name, and at the same time think of the saying of John: "The Son of God appeared that he might destroy the works of the devil." May God be with us and teach us. This time in which we now live is dangerous, not only because of the unlucky conjunction of the stars, but also because of the snares of the devil, who now attacks the Church most fiercely from every side.

units.la: DE PERIVRIIS.
units.tr: ON PERJURIES.

units.la: Cum quidam Cygneæ peierassēt propter quasdam fodinas in oppido Schneberg, dicūt curiæ testitudinem egisse rimas, quæ etiam nūc apparēat, & deinceps nihil metalli in fodinis repertum esse: ac adhuc audio inutiles sumptus in illis fodinis extruendis collocari.
units.tr: When some men of Zwickau had sworn falsely about certain mines in the town of Schneeberg, they say that the tortoise of the court made cracks, which can still be seen even now, and that afterwards no metal was found in the mines; and I hear that to this day useless expenses are still being laid out on building those mines.

units.la: Secundum praeceptum.
units.tr: The second precept.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Nobilis quidam hostis imperij, siue Sueuici fœderis, captus erat à Palatino, à quo, ut ueniam ad sua negocia discedendi impetraret, iureiurando promisit se rediturum ad certum tempus in aulam Heidelbergensem. Postquam res uerò ita esset constituta, ut parceretur eius vitæ, Palatinus ipsi discessum permisit, hac conditione, ut iuramentum præstaret, quòd certo tempore rediret, ac se iudicio sisteret. Ille uerò, neglecto iuramento, non redijt: unde paulò post à Iudæo hospite suo, non procul à ualle Ioachimica proditus, ac bombarda ictus est. Talis fuit exitus illius periurij.
units.tr: A certain noble, an enemy of the empire or of the Swabian league, was captured by the Palatine. In order to obtain leave to go and attend to his affairs, he swore an oath that he would return to the court at Heidelberg at a set time. When the matter had been arranged so that his life was spared, the Palatine let him leave on this condition: that he swear to return at a certain time and submit himself to judgment. He, however, neglected the oath and did not return. Shortly afterwards he was betrayed by his Jewish host, not far from the valley of Joachimsthal, and struck by a cannon-shot. Such was the end of his perjury.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Anno 1528 quidam gregarius miles in Marchia, forte in oppido quodam aduersa ualetudine retentus est. Ibi cum decumberet, tradidit saccum refertum magna pecunia hospiti custodiendum. Post aliquot dies cum conualesceret reposcit saccum. Mulier hospitis auara, egrè tantam predam amittens, deliberat cum uiro, utrum pecuniā redderet an non? Iniuerunt consilium, ut mulier neget depositum. Quare cum miles suum repeteret, illa confidenter negat se quicquam accepisse, ac simulat se mirari impudentiam militis, audentis aliquid postulare, cum nihil asseruandum dederit, & inuehitur in militem conuitijs rabiosissimè. Miles indignidignitate rei uictus obijcit uicissim mulieri perfi-diam. Quare maritus tanquam defensurus coniu-gem,extrudit militem domo.Is autem foris irrita-tus scelere hospitis,stringit gladium,tanquam im-petum facturus in hospitem,& fregit ianuam. Ho-spes implorat fidem ciuium, & queritur suas aedes oppugnari. Accurrunt lictores, & militem,quòd uim publicam fecisset, abducunt in carcerem. Post aliquot dies Senatus oppidi alio mitti narratione facti, & sententiam rescribi petit. Constabat,æ-des publicè oppugnatas esse: quare fertur senten-tia,ut miles ultimo supplicio afficiatur . Cumq; iam instaret dies iudicij , uenit diabclus in carcerem ad captiuum , indicans ei, quam sententiam Iudi-ces laturi sint, & pollicetur se hoc periculo eum liberaturum esse,hac conditione,ut se diabolo de-dat. Miles constanter respondit,se potius moritu-rum esse,quamuis sit innocens . Cum uero diabo-lus uerbis multis exaggerasset periculu,nec tamen inflexisset militis animum:tandem pollicetur libe-rationem sine ulla conditione:Et cum veneris, in-quit, in iudicium , dic te imperitum esse foren-sium negociorum,& patrono indigere:ibi astabo caeruleo pileo tectus,& ornato pennis:pete igitur ut me iubeant causam dicere . Miles qui hoc sine impietate facturus uidebatur , ait se hoc consilio usurum esse. Postridie in iudicium ducitur , adest etiam Orator tectus cæruleo pileo : ibi cùm actor peteret militè propter uim publicam capitali supplicio affici, miles respondit: se imperitum forensium negociorum, petere ut liceat isti suo aduocato pro se dicere: concedunt Iudices. Ibi diabolus de iure erudite disputat, non esse capitali supplicio afficiendum eum, à quò non sit ortum rixæ & tumultus initium: ait ab hospite militem ui extrusum, & spoliatum esse. Iubet quæri saccum, & locum monstrat. Ibi cum hospes uehementer negaret, addens etiā diras imprecationes, ut ipsum abreptum diabolus perderet, si fecisset. Hanc imprecationem cum inuocatione diaboli cùm aliquoties repetiuisset, ibi Causidicus omissa iam disputatione adoritur hospitem, & comprehēsum per fenestras & medium forum omnibus perhorrescen tibus cum fragore abducit: nec postea unquam corpus hospitis inuentum est. Hoc exemplo punivit Deus hospitis perfidiam.
units.tr: In 1528 a common soldier in the Mark was detained by illness in a certain town. While he lay sick there, he handed a sack full of a great sum of money to his host for safekeeping. Some days later, when he was recovering, he asked for the sack back. The host's wife, greedy and very reluctant to lose so great a prize, discussed with her husband whether they should return the money or not. They resolved that the wife should deny the deposit. So when the soldier demanded his property, she confidently denied that she had received anything, pretended to marvel at the soldier's impudence in demanding something when he had given nothing to keep, and launched into the most furious abuse of him. The soldier, overcome by the injustice of it, in turn charged the woman with treachery. Then the husband, as if to defend his wife, thrust the soldier out of the house. Outside, the soldier, enraged by the host's crime, drew his sword as though about to attack the host, and broke down the door. The host called on the citizens for help and complained that his house was being assaulted. The bailiffs ran up and led the soldier off to prison, because he had committed a breach of the public peace. After some days the town council asked for the account of the deed to be sent to another place, and for the sentence to be written back. It was established that the house had been attacked in public, so sentence was passed that the soldier should be put to death. When the day of the trial was already at hand, the devil came into the prison to the captive, told him what sentence the judges were about to pronounce, and promised that he would free him from this danger on condition that he surrender himself to the devil. The soldier firmly replied that he would rather die, though innocent. When the devil had magnified the danger with many words and yet had not bent the soldier's mind, he at last promised liberation without any condition. "And when you come into court," he said, "say that you are unskilled in legal business and need an advocate. I will stand beside you, covered with a blue cap and adorned with feathers, so ask that they allow me to plead the case." The soldier, who seemed willing to do this without impiety, said that he would use this plan. The next day he was led into court; the advocate also came, covered with the blue cap. There the plaintiff demanded that the soldier be put to death with capital punishment for breach of the public peace. The soldier replied that he was unskilled in legal business and asked that his advocate be allowed to speak on his behalf. The judges agreed. Then the devil argued learnedly on the law that he should not be put to capital punishment, since the quarrel and the disturbance had not begun with him; he said the soldier had been forced out of the house by the host and robbed. He ordered that the sack be sought and showed the place. When the host vehemently denied it, adding even dreadful curses that the devil should destroy him, if he had done it, the devil repeated this curse several times, invoking himself. Then the advocate, abandoning the argument, attacked the host, seized him, and carried him off with a crash through the windows and across the middle of the marketplace, while everyone looked on in horror. Nor was the host's body ever found afterwards. By this example God punished the host's treachery.

units.la: Iuramentum seruantis exemplum.
units.tr: An example of keeping an oath.

units.la: Quidam nobilis indicens bellum Georgio Duci Saxoniæ, cepit forte D. Fachium, ipsumq; diu captiuum detinuit, nec prius dimisit, quàm promitteret se soluturum tria millia aureorum. hic ita redijt domum, hac promissione cum iuramento facta. Cùm igitur liberatus esset, ibat ad iudicium cium publicum, (zum Hoffgeriht.) & ueniens ad aulam Ducis Georgij, petebat æquitatem consi-derari, & sui infortunij rationem haberi, quādo-quidem in publico negocio esset captus. Dux Ge-orgius respondit, se non uelle eius nomine obulū soluere, nec uelle confirmare latrocinia, sicut erat seuerus, ille tamen voluit seruare fidem promis-sam in iuramento: tandem Moguntinus qui iam mortuus est, dedit illi mille aureos, & Dominus item de Schonberg dedit illi alteros mille aureos, & ipse de sua atq; amicorum contributione etiam mille collegit. Ita tradidit ei qui ipsum captiū te-nuerat, tria millia aureorum, & seruauit iuramen-tum, quod promiserat. Viuit iam, & bene cum ipso agitur.
units.tr: A certain nobleman, declaring war on Duke George of Saxony, happened to capture Sir Fach, and held him captive for a long time, and did not release him until he promised to pay three thousand gold coins. He went home with this promise made under oath. When he had been freed, he went to the public court (zum Hoffgeriht) and, arriving at the court of Duke George, asked that fairness be considered and his misfortune be taken into account, since he had been captured in a public cause. Duke George replied that he did not wish to pay a ransom on his behalf, nor to confirm robbery; he was stern, yet he wished to keep the promise he had made under oath. At last the Elector of Mainz, who has since died, gave him a thousand gold coins, and the lord of Schönberg likewise gave him another thousand, and he himself collected a further thousand from his own and his friends' contributions. So he handed over to the man who had held him captive three thousand gold coins, and kept the oath he had sworn. He is still alive, and things go well for him.

units.la: TERTIVM PRAECEP-tum.
units.tr: The Third Commandment.

units.la: DE NEGLIGENTIA IN CO-gnitione festorum, aliaq; eiusmo-di ad hoc praeceptum per-tinentia.
units.tr: On negligence in knowing the feasts, and other matters pertaining to this commandment.

units.la: Reuerendus D. Philippus aliquando quendam interrogauit, quale esset festum? respondit, festum trium regum, cū esset festum purificationis Mariæ.
units.tr: The Reverend Dr. Philip once asked a certain man what feast it was. He answered: the feast of the three kings, when it was the feast of the purification of Mary.

units.la: Fuit Athenis pessimus homo Cynesias, qui ut derideret religionem, egit contraria festa populo: quando illi læta celebrabant, tunc ipse celebrabat funebria. Tales omni tepore reperiuntur.
units.tr: There lived at Athens a most wicked man, Cynesias, who, in order to mock religion, held festivals contrary to those of the people: when they celebrated joyful days, he then celebrated funerals. Such people are found in every age.

units.la: Venerunt ad Alphonsum, regem Hispaniæ, qui patrum nostrorum memoria uixit, indie Natalis Christi quidam eius capitanei, dicentes, facilè & opportunè posse opprimi hostes. Ibi respondisse eū ferunt: Pluris facio istum diem, quam ullam victo riam, tamen postea feliciter uicit.
units.tr: Some men of Alphonsus, king of Spain, who lived within our fathers' memory, came to him on Christmas Day, saying that the enemies could easily and opportunely be crushed. He is reported to have answered: I value this day more than any victory; yet afterwards he conquered happily.

units.la: Noui ciuitatem, in qua concionatores die Natali singuli finita concione redierunt ad suas ta bernas, & fecerunt usitata sua opera, sicut alio die professo. Quia superstitionem esse, discernere dies, affirmabant. Est hyperbole.
units.tr: I know of a city in which the preachers, on Christmas Day, after the sermon ended, each returned to his shop and did his usual work, as on any other day. They affirmed that it was superstition to distinguish days. This is hyperbole.

units.la: Vidi Iudæum fœneratorem, qui solebat Typo graphis quibusdam pecuniam credere, propter u suram. Hunc si quando impressores accedebant die sabbathi, ipsi quidem religio erat numerare eis pecuniam, sed dabat tantum illis clauē ad men sam, iubebatq; numerare quātum uellent: ipse in terea astans aspiciebat, ne fraudem aut dolum co mitterent. Idq; hanc ob causam fecit, ne uiolaret præceptum tertium, cum tamen ipse aspiciendo quoq; numeraret, deinde etiā ne manibus cōmitte ret peccatum, quibus pecuniā ad usuras dedisset.
units.tr: I saw a Jewish moneylender who used to lend money on usury to certain printers. If the printers came to him on a Sabbath, it was a scruple for him to count out the money to them himself; instead he gave them only the key to the table and bade them count out as much as they wished, while he stood by and watched, lest they commit fraud or deceit. He did this for this reason: so that he would not violate the third commandment; yet while watching he counted the money too; and further, so that he would not commit a sin with the hands with which he had lent the money at usury.

units.la: Memini phantasticum hominem prædicantem die Natiuitatis historiam passionis Christi, & ecōtrà tempore Passionis, Natiuitatem: ut tantum non effet papista. Tales inepti & importuni homines, omnibus temporibus multi reperiuntur. Non dubium est, quin angeli in cœlo feruant illa festa, Deoq; agunt gratias in excelsis pro istis immensis beneficijs, commonefacti de tempore. Si quis uero non aliter tempus accedendi templum atq; balneandi obseruare uellet, qualis esset confusio? quanquam illud opus sua natura non esset peccatum: tamen propter illa inordinatione magistratus est, huiusmodi non impunita relinquere.
units.tr: I remember a fanatical man who, preaching on the day of the Nativity, related the history of Christ's passion, and conversely at the time of the Passion, the Nativity; so that he was hardly not a Papist. Such foolish and troublesome people are found in every age. There is no doubt that the angels in heaven keep those feasts and give thanks to God on high for these immense benefits, being reminded of the time. But if someone wished to observe no other time for going to church and for bathing, what confusion would there be? Although that act in its own nature would not be a sin, nevertheless, because of such disorder, it is the duty of the magistrate not to leave such things unpunished.

units.la: Accidit Magdeburgi, ut die sabbathi Iudæus in cloaca incideret, ibi Iudæi tati faciebant suu sabbathum, ut ipsum eo die extrahere nollent. Re delata ad episcopum Magdeburgensem Ernestum, inquit: Cum Iudæi tanti faciant suum sabbathum, ut hominem ex cloaca extrahere nolint, ergo etiam nostrum sabbathum tanti faciamus, ac prohibuit ne die Dominico Iudæus extraheretur. ita oportuit illum Iudæum biduum manere in cloaca. Tertio tandem die extractus est.
units.tr: It happened at Magdeburg that on a Sabbath a Jew fell into a sewer, and the Jews made so much of their Sabbath that they were unwilling to pull him out on that day. The matter was reported to Ernest, bishop of Magdeburg, who said: Since the Jews make so much of their Sabbath that they will not draw a man out of a sewer, therefore let us also make so much of our Sabbath; and he forbade that the Jew be drawn out on the Lord's Day. So that Jew had to remain in the sewer for two days. On the third day at last he was drawn out.

units.la: Vidi aliquado, quod Iudæi in sabbatho conducerent quendam Christianum, qui calefaceret, coqueret, & mucos candelarum decerperet.
units.tr: I once saw Jews on the Sabbath hire a certain Christian to light the fire, cook, and snuff out the candle wicks.

units.la: Templi Hierosolymitani structura. COLL.
units.tr: The structure of the Temple at Jerusalem. COLL.

units.la: Templum Hierosolymitanum oblongum fuit, ante quod foris in atrio extructum erat altare holoholocausti, in quo boues aliáq; animalia oblata in sacrificijs cremebantur. In ipso enim templo hæc comburere periculosum propter ignem & fumum fuisset. Sic quoq; lauacra, in quibus cùm animalia mactata, tum etiam ipsi sacerdotes lauarentur, foris collocata fuerunt. Postea in ipso templi corpore, situm fuit altare thymiamatis, in quo fumigationes fiebant, quemadmodum etiam nunc apud Papistas similes fere fumigationes in usu sunt. Ad alterum uerò latus altaris thymiamatis stetit candelabrum, cum alioqui templum obscurum esset. Populus uerò nõ intrauit templũ, sed foris extra templum stetit, & solus sacerdos templum ingressus est. Deinde ulterius in templo fuit Sanctum Sanctorum, eodem fere modo sicut adhuc chorus est distinctus à reliquo templi spacio, seu corpore, in antiquis templis (non loquor de barbarie harum gentium) quod generaliter aditum appellare possumus, seu locum secretiorem: unde populus arcebatur, nec quisquam eo ingredi audebat, nec alius sacerdos, nisi summus semel in anno. Eo in loco collocata erat arca fœderis, sub eam positum fuit operculum, quod nominarunt Propiciatorium, sub quo duo Cherubin fuerunt.
units.tr: The Temple at Jerusalem was oblong. Before it, outside in the court, stood the altar of holocaust, on which the oxen and other animals offered in sacrifices were burnt. For to burn these within the temple itself would have been dangerous because of the fire and smoke. Likewise the washing places, in which the animals were slaughtered and the priests themselves washed, were placed outside. Afterwards, in the body of the temple itself, the altar of incense was situated, on which the fumigations were made, just as even now among the Papists similar fumigations are in use. On the other side of the altar of incense stood the candelabrum, since otherwise the temple would be dark. The people, however, did not enter the temple but stood outside it, and only the priest entered the temple. Further inside the temple was the Holy of Holies, in almost the same way as the choir is still set apart from the rest of the temple space or body in ancient churches (I am not speaking of the barbarism of these peoples), which we may generally call the entrance, or the more secret place: from it the people were kept away, nor did anyone dare to enter it, nor any other priest, except the high priest once a year. In that place the ark of the covenant was set, and over it was placed a lid, which they called the Propitiatory, under which there were two cherubim.

units.la: QVAR-
units.tr: QVAR-

units.la: QVARTVM PRAECEPTUM.
units.tr: THE FOURTH PRECEPT.

units.la: DE VOCATIONE, SEDVLITATE ac diligentia in ea.
units.tr: ON VOCATION, DILIGENCE, AND CARE IN ONE'S CALLING.

units.la: Contrariæ orationes Virtutis & Voluptatis, ad Herculem deliberantem utram uitæ uiam ingrediatur, Voluptatis ne an Virtutis, ex Prodici libro transcriptæ.
units.tr: The contrary speeches of Virtue and Pleasure to Hercules, as he deliberates which way of life to enter, that of Pleasure or that of Virtue, transcribed from the book of Prodicus.

units.la: Cum Hercules ex pueritia egressus, iamq; prope pubertatem esset, qua ætate sua compotes facti adolescentes significant, utram uiam uirtutis an ignauiæ ingredi uelint, exijt in solum locū, seditq; tacitus deliberans, utram uiam iniret. Hic apparuerunt ei duæ mulierculæ, maiores humana specie, quarū altera uultu modesto, & liberali erat, nullo peregrino cultu aut fuco ornata, sed genuina bonitas formæ apparebat: in corpore mundicies, in oculis pudor, in incessu modestia: uestem præterea candidam gerens. Altera erat habitior & fucata. Nam & rubor & candor maior erat natiuo, & incedebat supina, oculos latè pandens, ueste induta, quæ formam maximè commēdabat, contemplans interim se, & circumspectans, an alij se uiderent, nonnunquam etiam umbram suam respiciens. Postquam autem propius uentum est, illa prior modestè pergebat. Hæc autem ut anteuerteret accurrit ad Herculem, ac inquit: Video te ôHercules,deliberare utram uiâ ad uitam ingre- diaris:quòd si me tibi adiunxeris, ducâ te iucũdissi- ma & facilima uia. Nulla res iucunda est,qua nõ potieris, & molestiâ nullâ perpetieris. neq; enim aut bella aut alia negocia curabis: sed hoc unũ co- gitabis ac quæres, ubi aut cibũ aut potũ suauiorẽ, aut quod delectet oculos, aut unde olfaciendo,aut tangendo aliquam uoluptatem percipias, aut ubi timorib.perfruaris,aut quomodo mollissimè cubes aut quomodo hæc omnia sine aliquo labore conse- quaris. Et si quis inciderit metus egestatis, nõ est quod timeas me tibi aliquid laboris impositurum esse.Efficiam enim, ut fruaris his quæ alieno labo- re parta sunt in promptu: nec ulla re abstinebis, unde modo speres te aliquam uoluptatem posse lucrifacere. Ego enim meis sodalibus potestatem facio ex omnibus rebus uoluptatem decerpere.
units.tr: When Hercules had left boyhood and was nearly at puberty, the age at which young men show whether they are masters of themselves, and whether they wish to enter the way of virtue or of idleness, he went out into a lonely place and sat there in silence, pondering which road to take. Then two women appeared to him, taller than human stature. One had a modest and noble countenance and was adorned with no foreign finery or paint; her natural goodness of form was visible: cleanliness in her body, modesty in her eyes, restraint in her bearing, and she wore a white garment. The other was more showy and painted. Her blush and whiteness were greater than nature gave, she walked with an upright carriage, her eyes wide open, and she wore clothing that set off her figure most. Meanwhile she kept looking at herself and glancing round to see whether others were watching her, and now and then she even looked back at her own shadow. When they came nearer, the first went on with modest steps. The second, to get ahead, ran up to Hercules and said: "I see you, Hercules, deliberating which road in life to take. If you join yourself to me, I will lead you by the most pleasant and easiest way. There is no delight you will not enjoy, and you will suffer no discomfort. You will not concern yourself with wars or other business; you will think and seek only this: where you may find food or drink more delicious, what will delight your eyes, where you may perceive some pleasure by smell or touch, where you may enjoy the company of lovers, how you may lie most softly, and how you may obtain all these things without any labour. And if any fear of want arises, you need not worry that I will impose any toil on you. For I will make sure you enjoy, ready to hand, what others have won by their labour; nor will you hold back from anything from which you hope to gain some pleasure. For I give my companions the power to pluck pleasure from every thing."
