units.la: Hæc Hercules audiens,inquit:Mulier,quod est tibi nomen?Tum illa:Mei sodales uocant me Felici- tatem,qui me aspernantur, uocant me Ignauiam.
units.tr: When Hercules heard this, he said: "Woman, what is your name?" She replied: "My companions call me Happiness; those who despise me call me Idleness."

units.la: Interea accesit & altera mulier, dixitq; : Venio & ego ad te, adolescens. Noui autem & genero- sos parentes tuos, & indolem educationemq; tuã. Hæc mihi spem faciũt fore,ut si me secutus fueris, magnas & honestas res geras, & me multo apud homines clariorem efficias, nec te longa prefatione, quæ ad voluptatem fingi solet, morabor, sed simpliciter id quòd res est, vereq; narrabo, quod dij constituerunt. Nulla verò bona sine labore curaq; mortalibus dij dedcrunt: sed siue deos tibi uis esse propicios, placandi sunt, siue ab alijs diligi uis, beneficijs adiungendi sunt, siue honore affici à ciuibus cupis, bene mereri te de patria oportet, siue uis in admiratione esse apud omnes Græcos, benefactis id consequi oportet: siue uis, ut terra tibi pariat fruges, colenda est: siue ex pecudibus ditescere uis, pascēdæ sunt: siue bello opes tuas augere uoles, ut socios in libertatem asseras, & inimicos in seruitutem redigas. bellicæ artes discēdæ sunt ab illis, qui eas nouerunt, & exercendæ, vt quomodo eis utendum sit scias. Si robur corporis uis confirmare, consuefaciendum est, ut rationi obediat, & exercendum magno labore, ac sudore.
units.tr: Meanwhile the other woman also approached and said: "I too come to you, young man. I know your noble parents and your upbringing, and these give me hope that, if you follow me, you will achieve great and honourable things and make yourself far more famous among men. I will not delay you with a long preamble of the kind that is usually devised to lure men to pleasure, but will speak simply and truthfully, as things really are. For the gods have given mortals no good thing without labour and care. If you want the gods to be favourable to you, they must be propitiated; if you wish to be loved by others, you must win them by kindnesses; if you desire to be honoured by your fellow citizens, you must deserve well of your country; if you want to be admired by all the Greeks, you must achieve it by noble deeds; if you want the earth to bear fruit for you, it must be cultivated; if you wish to grow rich from livestock, they must be pastured; if you want to increase your wealth by war, so as to bring allies into freedom and reduce enemies to slavery, the arts of war must be learned from those who know them and practised, so that you know how to use them. If you want to strengthen the strength of your body, it must be trained to obey reason and exercised with great labour and sweat."

units.la: Quod cùm dixisset Virtus interpellat eam Ignauia, inquiens: Vides, Hercules, quàm asperā & longam uiam ad felicitatem hæc mulier ostendat, ad quam ego tibi compendiarum & planam uiam monstraui. Tum Virtus: O` misera, dic, nunquid habeas boni, & nunquid suaue unquam cognoueris, quæ nullum laborem uis illorum consequendorum causa suscipere? Et ne quidem expectes
units.tr: When she had said this, Idleness interrupted her, saying: "You see, Hercules, how harsh and long a road to happiness this woman points out, whereas I have shown you a short and smooth road to it." Then Virtue said: "O wretched one, tell me, do you have any good thing, or have you ever known anything sweet, you who are unwilling to undertake any labour in order to obtain such things? You do not even wait for the natural desire for pleasant things,

units.la: Tes naturale desiderium suavium rerum, sed an-equam natura expetat eas, imples atq; obruis te-dis, priusquam esuris: bibis antequam sitis: con-vimenta varia ad irritandum famem excogitas: ina praeciosa, ut inuites sitim coparas. Et ut sua-iter dormias, non modo mollia strata, sed etiam ectos facis. Somnium enim accersis, non ut per la-boris interualla quiescas, sed inopia negocij: sine udore ac legum metu, amori, operam das: nocte buteris, & optimam diei partem somno perdis. t cum deam te esse glorieris, ex deorum nume-o eiecta es. Asspernantur te & honesti homines, eq; unquam suauissimum carmen tuas laudes ce-brans audiuisti: & pulcherrimum spectaculum unquam uidisti. Nullum enim unquam recte fa-ctum tuum spectasti. Quis tibi improba credet? uis egenti dabit aliquid? quis sanae mentis in tuo choro esse uelit? Vbi iuuenes imbecilli corpore unt, senes fatui, qui cum adolescentiam in otio perdiderint, senectutem miseram & calamito-am agunt, tunc & pudet ante actae vitae, & piget rimum quaerere necessaria aetati subsidia: suauia adolescentia ante tempus praecerpserunt, labo-rem & aerumnas in aetatem eam distulerunt. Ego vero apud deos uersor, & apud honestos homi-es: nullum honestum facinus neq; dij, neq; ho-ines sine me faciunt, Ideoq; me & dij & homi-nes nes honore afficiunt. Grata sum opitulatrix artifi-ficum, fida custos familiæ dominorum, benevola adiutrix seruorum, iucunda comes laborum, in pa-ce firma periculorum, in bello auxiliatrix, optima amiciciæ socia: & mei amici suaues uoluptates si-ne fastidio percipiunt ex cibo & potu. Expectant enim illorum naturale desiderium, somnus etiam sua-uior eis est, quàm ociosis, quæ etiam si opus est si-ne molestia abrumpũt, ne propter hunc necessa-ria intermittat. Iuuenes senum laudibus gaudent: & senes delectantur iuuenum honoribus, & incre-dibili uoluptate rerũ à se gestarum meminerunt, & sine difficultate præsentes labores conficiunt. Per me dijs clari, amicis chari ac patriæ. Et cum ex hac uita discedendum est, non obscuri aut igno-ti iacent, sed laudes eorũ perpetuo à posteris præ-dicantur. Hæc tibi, ô fili bonorum parentum Her-cules, contingent, & ueram felicitatem stabilemq; ita consequeris, si laborem non defugias.
units.tr: but before nature craves them, you fill and overwhelm yourself with feasts; you eat before you are hungry and drink before you are thirsty; you devise varied dishes to provoke appetite, and you procure costly wines to invite thirst. And so that you may sleep soundly, you make not only soft coverings but even couches. For you summon sleep not so that you may rest in the intervals of toil, but out of lack of business; without sweat or fear of the laws you give yourself to love; you stay awake at night and waste the best part of the day in sleep. And though you boast of being a goddess, you have been cast out of the company of the gods. Honest men shun you. Have you ever heard a sweet song celebrating your praises, or ever seen a fine spectacle? For you have never looked upon any good deed of yours. Who will trust a wicked woman like you? Who will give anything to a needy one? Who of sound mind would wish to be in your company? Young men, weak in body, and foolish old men, who have squandered their youth in idleness, lead wretched and miserable old age; then they are ashamed of their past life, and it grieves them to seek late the supports their age requires. They have plucked the sweets of youth before their time, and have put off labour and hardship to that age. But I dwell with the gods and among honest men: no honourable deed is done, by gods or men, without me. Therefore both gods and men honour me. I am a welcome helper of craftsmen, a faithful guardian of masters' households, a kindly assistant of servants, a pleasant companion in toils, steadfast in dangers, a help in war, the best partner in friendship. My friends enjoy sweet pleasures without disgust, from food and drink; for they wait for their natural desire, and sleep is sweeter to them than to the idle, and they cut it short without distress, if need be, so that it does not hinder necessary tasks. Young men rejoice in the praise of their elders, and old men take delight in the honours of the young, and they recall with incredible pleasure the deeds they have done, and they finish present labours without difficulty. Through me they are famous among the gods, dear to their friends and to their country. And when they must depart from this life, they do not lie obscure or unknown, but their praises are proclaimed by posterity forever. These things, O Hercules, son of good parents, will be yours, and so you will attain true and lasting happiness, if you do not shrink from labour."

units.la: Cum Alexander uulnus in prælio accepisset, cla-mauit miles Beotius: Agentẽ fortiter oportet ali-quid pati: τὸν ἀρῶντα ἀεινὰ καὶ παθεῖν δεῖ. Est dictũ Pindari cum Alexander iussisset inquiri, quis esset: significatum est esse quendã Thebanum: cuius fortitudine motus, deinceps poenitentia ductus est, quòd antea tantã urbẽ Thebanam deleuisset, benefecitq; singulis Thebanis, qui ad eum uenirẽt. Illiũ tutem militè ad se adduci iußit, ac honorifico mu-nere ornauit, ita singulis, & quidè sedulis in sua uocatione multa ferenda & patienda sunt.
units.tr: When Alexander had received a wound in battle, a Boeotian soldier cried out: "The one who ploughs must always also suffer [τὸν ἀρῶντα ἀεινὰ καὶ παθεῖν δεῖ]." It is a saying of Pindar. When Alexander ordered an inquiry into who the man was, it was reported that he was a certain Theban, whose courage moved Alexander; afterwards, led by regret that he had earlier destroyed the great city of Thebes, he did a kindness to every Theban who came to him. He ordered this soldier brought to him and honoured him with a gift of distinction. So too each person, and especially the diligent, must bear and endure many things in their own calling.

units.la: Durerus, cùm Maximilianus Imperator carbo-e imaginem aliquà deliniasset, quam ab ipso pin-gi uolebat, & carbo aliquoties fractus esset, eandē postea expeditius pinxit. Ibi Maximilianus quæsi-it à Durero, quomodo fieret, ut ipsius carbo non frangeretur. Subridès Durerus respondit: Clemē-ssime Cæsar, nollem equidē Cæsareā tuam maie-statē tam artificiosè pingere posse atq; ego: quasi diceret: in hac re ego me exercui, & hæc est mea vocatio: tua maiestas habet graviora negocia, & aliam uocationem, iuxta illud commune proue-rbium: Aliud est sceptrum, aliud plectrum.
units.tr: When Dürer had sketched some image in charcoal, which the Emperor Maximilian wished to have painted by him, and the charcoal had broken several times, he afterwards painted it more readily. Then Maximilian asked Dürer how it came about that his charcoal did not break. Smiling, Dürer replied: "Most gracious Caesar, I would not wish to be able to paint your Caesarean majesty as skilfully as I can." He meant: in this matter I have trained myself, and this is my calling; your majesty has weightier business and another calling, according to the common proverb: "The sceptre is one thing, the plectrum another."

units.la: Princeps Moscouiæ in acie alium principem hostium hostem cepit, eumq; interfecit, & ex interempti cranio curauit sibi poculum fieri, cum hac scriptione, in contumeliā interfecti: Quia alie-na appetiuisti, propria amisisti.
units.tr: The prince of Muscovy, in battle, captured another prince who was his enemy, killed him, and had a drinking cup made from the dead man's skull, with this inscription added in mockery of the slain man: "Because you coveted what belonged to others, you lost what was your own."

units.la: Aristoteles dicit: Beatā fore uitam hominum, artifices iudicarent de artibus. Fuit excellens pi-ctor Romæ, tempore Traiani. Hadrianus autem polypragmō erat. Cùm ergo Imperator proponeret formā ædificij, Hadrianus eā quoq; pinxit suo iudicio. Pictor uerò dixit ad eū: Vade & pinge tu cucurbitas, quo respōso irritatus Hadrianus, post-quam quam peruenit ad imperiū, interfecit hunc pictorem. Cucurbitas enim quiuis pingere potest, quia inæqualiter crescunt: & eò facilius, quòd habeãt magnum aliquem uentrem, cui petiolum aliquem facilè ineruditi etiam artis pictoriæ adiungere possunt.
units.tr: Aristotle says that human life would be happy if craftsmen were the judges of their crafts. There was an excellent painter at Rome in the time of Trajan. Hadrian, however, was a busybody. When the Emperor once set out the plan of a building, Hadrian, on his own judgement, painted it too. The painter then said to him: "Go and paint the gourds yourself." Hadrian was angered by this answer, and once he had come to the throne he had this painter put to death. Anyone can paint gourds, since they grow unevenly, and it is all the easier because they have a large belly to which even the unlearned in the art of painting can easily attach a little stalk.

units.la: Propria curanda in uocatione.
units.tr: Each man should attend to his own calling.

units.la: De Seuero Imperatore dicitur, quòd curarit res ipsas agendas, ea uerò quæ de ipso dicebantur à uulgo contempserit. Idem dicitur de Fabio: Non ponebat enim rumores ante salutem.
units.tr: It is said of the Emperor Severus that he took care to carry out affairs himself, but he despised what the common people said about him. The same is said of Fabius: "For he did not set rumours above safety."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Non improbanda Italorum consuetudo est, qui se dedant uni tantum rei, idq; ita, ut prorsus cæte-ra negocia & studia negligant. Germanorum nō est ista consuetudo, ut in uno excellant, & cætera negligant. In Italia habent peculiares sartores caligarum, & peculiares sartores thoracum & aliarum vestium.
units.tr: The custom of the Italians is not to be disapproved, for they devote themselves to one thing only, and so completely neglect all their other business and studies. The Germans do not have this custom, of excelling in one thing and neglecting the rest. In Italy they have special tailors for hose, and special tailors for breastplates and other garments.

units.la: ἱππεὺς ἱππέυειν ἱσέσαι, ἀοτπλόσ τε ικὰι ἄδλειν
units.tr: A horseman knows how to ride a horse, and a sailor how to sail. [ἱππεὺς ἱππέυειν ἱσέσαι, ἀοτπλόσ τε ικὰι ἄδλειν]

units.la: Aristophanes de Cleone dixit, ipsum alterum pedem habere in curia, & alterum in castris, id est, uoluisse omnia regere, quæ non essent sui officij. Sententia est bona: significans debere esse magnitudinem animorum coniunctam cum moderatione, ita ut non temerè pugnemus.
units.tr: Aristophanes said of Cleon that he had one foot in the senate house and the other in the camp, that is, that he wanted to control everything, including what was not his office. The saying is a good one, signifying that greatness of spirit ought to be joined with moderation, so that we do not fight rashly.

units.la: Leontinus episcopus, Constātino Imperatori, Volenti multa de religione disputare, dicebat Imperator πρὸς ἕτερα ταχθεὶς, ἕτερα πράττεις: ad alia ordinatus, alia facis.
units.tr: The bishop of Leontini, speaking to the Emperor Constantine, who wanted to dispute at length about religion, said: "You were appointed to other things, and you do other things." [πρὸς ἕτερα ταχθεὶς, ἕτερα πράττεις] That is: "Ordained for other things, you do other things."

units.la: Spartam nactus es, hanc orna.
units.tr: You have obtained Sparta; adorn it.

units.la: Hoc est symbolum Ducis Iuliacensis. Sparta autem fuit præcipua urbs in Laconia, iam uocata Lymachus, id est solutio exercituum: Græcia enim iam nota est in seruitute. Hîc prouerbialiter ponitur, pro eo quod est, habes honestum locum, bonam functionem, illam orines, non curiose quæras aliena, non ingeras te alienis negocijs aut functionibus. In Epistolis Ciceronis ad Atticum, bis ponitur hoc prouerbium, de uitanda curiositate in aliorum studijs aut negocijs.
units.tr: This is the motto of the Duke of Jülich. Sparta was the chief city of Laconia, and it was once called Lymachus, that is, the dissolution of armies; for Greece was already known to be in servitude. Here it is used proverbially to mean: you have an honourable place and a good office; be content with it, do not eagerly seek what belongs to others, and do not thrust yourself into other men's business or duties. In Cicero's Letters to Atticus this proverb occurs twice, concerning the avoiding of officiousness in the affairs or business of others.

units.la: Quæ præcipua sit causa successuum in uocationibus, earumq; laboribus.
units.tr: What is the principal cause of success in callings, and of their labours.

units.la: Ouidius de felici labore Poetarum (quod idem omnium labore intelligi potest) inquit: Est Deus in nobis agitante calescimus illo.
units.tr: Ovid, speaking of the happy labour of poets (which may be understood as the labour of all), says: "There is a God within us; when he stirs, we grow warm."

units.la: Vult hic Ouidius significare, quod tum demum habitus sint excellentes, quando adiuuantur diuitus. Noster Imperator Carolus V. est excellens bellator, eò quod concilia & conatus eius diuina prouidentia gubernantur.
units.tr: Ovid here means that men become excellent only when they are helped by God. Our Emperor Charles V is an excellent warrior, because his counsels and endeavours are governed by divine providence.

units.la: Quartum præceptum.
units.tr: The Fourth Precept.

units.la: Negocia in uocatione urgenda.
units.tr: Business must be pursued in one's calling.

units.la: Noster Imperator Carolus V. habebat diu hãc consuetudinem, ut urgeret negocia, & habebat librum in quo solebat notare: Hoc negocium eo tempore, uel die est urgendum, & perficiendum: sed cum senuisset, interdum negocia alijs curanda reliquit.
units.tr: Our Emperor Charles V had for a long time this habit of pressing on with his business, and he kept a book in which he used to note: "This business must be pursued and completed at this time or on this day." But when he grew old, he sometimes left business to be taken care of by others.

units.la: Seneca:
units.tr: Seneca:

units.la: Difficile est unum hominem agere, id est, non extra metas uocationis euagari. Stultus qui parata relinquens, quærit non parata.
units.tr: It is hard for one man to do many things, that is, not to wander beyond the bounds of his calling. Foolish is he who, leaving aside what is ready to hand, seeks what is not ready.

units.la: In quadam arce Gallica inuenitur uetus aulæum, in quo depicta sedet mulier nens, cui adiunctus est hic uersus: Nenti fila Deus & mentem iungit Olympo.
units.tr: In a certain French citadel there is found an old tapestry, on which a woman is depicted spinning, and to which this verse is attached: "God joins the threads to the spinner, and the mind to Olympus."

units.la: Hoc aulæum Rex Franciscus sæpe aspexisse dicitur, ac disputasse de ea sententia. Miratus est merito sententiam, ut sapiens & unus ex præstantibus regibus, quales olim magnifici reges fuerunt, sapientia & magnitudine animi excellentes. Est autem sensus carminis. Nenti filia Deus iungit, id est: Deus iuuat laborem uocationis, ipsumq; suo auxilio regit, & mentem iungit Olympo, id est: Deus addit præliatori animum, & gladium eius in acie gubernat. Et sic inter nendum cogitat de Deo, simulq; idem miles inter præliandum eiusdem auxilium imuocat.
units.tr: King Francis is said often to have looked at this tapestry and to have debated the saying. He rightly admired the sentiment as the work of a wise man, and of one of those outstanding kings, such as the magnificent kings of old were, excellent in wisdom and greatness of spirit. The sense of the verse is this: "God joins the threads" to the spinner, that is, God helps the labour of one's calling and himself guides it with his aid; "and joins the mind to Olympus," that is, God adds courage to the warrior and steers his sword in battle. And so, while spinning, the woman thinks of God, and at the same time the soldier, while fighting, calls upon the same help.

units.la: Seneca
units.tr: Seneca

units.la: Quartum praeceptum. Seneca.
units.tr: Fourth precept. Seneca.

units.la: Magna pars uitæ hunanæ elabitur nihil agëdo: maior pars male agendo: maxima aliud agendo, quod est, non necessaria agendo.
units.tr: A great part of human life slips away in doing nothing, a greater part in doing evil, and the greatest part in doing something else, that is, in doing things that are not necessary.

units.la: Pictor quidam uenit ad Apellem, monstrans ei tabulam quandam, & excusans se, quòd non arte pinxisset. Ibi Apelles, inquit: Non est opus isto præ-conio, nam & ego idipsum optimè uideo. Repre-hendit in eo laboris negligentiam & ignauiam.
units.tr: A certain painter came to Apelles, showing him a panel and apologising that he had not painted it skilfully. Apelles said: "There is no need for that announcement, for I see that very thing well enough myself." He rebukes in him negligence and idleness in his work.

units.la: Columella in præceptis quæ patrifamiliâs præ-scribit, scriptum reliquit: Nihil agendo homines male agere discunt.
units.tr: Columella, in the precepts he lays down for the head of a household, left this written: "By doing nothing, men learn to do badly."

units.la: Erat hic in uicino quodâ oppido Diaconus, qui vocabatur à ciuibus Pricensibus ad conditionem pastoris. Hic cùm doctor Martinus eum alloque-retur, an uellet hanc conditionē suscipere, respon-dit aliquoties: Quicquid Deus uult, quicquid De-us uult: cui Dominus Philippus dicebat: Ey opor-tet etiam accedere tuam uoluntatem. Cui tandem uocationi obtemperauit.
units.tr: There was a deacon in a nearby town, who was called by the citizens of Prizen to the office of minister. When Doctor Martin asked him whether he would accept this office, he answered again and again: "Whatever God wills, whatever God wills." Lord Philip said to him: "Your own will must also yield." At last he obeyed this call.

units.la: Siculus quidam in conuentu Ratisbonensi faci-ebat ex cartha cantharum, & alia similia, quibus multos spectatores alliciebat, propterea duceba-tur in cuiusdam aulam. Sic quidam, qui assueuerat iacere grana per foramen acus, cùm esset dedu-ctus ad Alexandrum, ut eius fantasias aspiceret, ui-sis illis, Alexander iußit ei dari modium grano-rum. rum, ut haberet quod deijceret.
units.tr: A certain Sicilian at the Regensburg assembly made cups and other similar things out of paper, and by this he drew many spectators, so he was taken into the hall of a certain nobleman. Likewise, a man who was accustomed to pass grains of corn through the eye of a needle was brought before Alexander to show his tricks. After Alexander had watched them, he ordered that a bushel of grain be given to him, so that he would have something to throw through the needle's eye.

units.la: Camelus appetens cornua, amisit etiam aures.
units.tr: The camel that craved horns lost even its ears.

units.la: Est pulcher apologus, si quis accommodet ad vocationis exempla: alius appetens alienum principatum, amisit suum. Cera uolebat imitari lateres, & iniecit se in ignem, uoluit durari, sed igne consumitur: sic quando is uult esse aulicus, qui non est idoneus, tunc coijcit se in ignem & cosumitur. Plerumq; conijcimus nos in ingētia negocia, quib. nō sumus pares, cuius contrariū docet hic uersiculus:
units.tr: This is a fine fable, if one applies it to examples of vocation: another man, coveting a principate that was not his, lost his own. Wax wanted to imitate bricks and threw itself into the fire; it wished to harden, but the fire consumes it. So when someone wants to be a courtier though he is not suited to it, he throws himself into the fire and is consumed. Very often we throw ourselves into huge undertakings for which we are not equal, whereas the opposite is taught by this little verse:

units.la: Quod sis, esse uelis, nihilq; malis.
units.tr: Be what you are, wish to be that, and prefer nothing else.

units.la: Fingunt apud inferos Sisyphum immane saxū in aduersum montem uoluere, quod iterum è summo iam uertice rursus labitur, & plane raptim petit æquora campi. Significari scribunt isto commento, irrito labore multos mortales confici.
units.tr: They fable that in the underworld Sisyphus rolls a huge stone up a hill, which again slides down from the summit and rushes headlong to the level plain. They write that by this fiction is signified that many mortals are worn out by fruitless labour.

units.la: Quidam pictor picturus uenationem cuidam Domino, cum pinxisset magnas arbores, lepores autem & canes ita, ut uix discerni possent, displicuit pictura domino dicenti, se non posse dignoscere lepores à canibus. ibi pictor accepto carbone inscripsit canibus Hund, & leporibus hasz:ita curiosus fuit circa parerga, neglectis ergis.
units.tr: A painter, about to paint a hunt for a certain lord, painted large trees, but the hares and dogs so that they could scarcely be told apart. The lord was displeased with the picture, saying he could not distinguish hares from dogs. Then the painter took a piece of charcoal and wrote "Hund" on the dogs and "Hasz" on the hares. So curious was he about the accessories, while neglecting the main things.

units.la: Pindarus laudat Hieronem Siculum, principem suæ ætatis, propter quatuor uirtutes, quarum una est, quòd præsentia sapienter faciat, & non corrumpatur spe aut metu.
units.tr: Pindar praises Hiero of Sicily, the foremost prince of his age, for four virtues, one of which is that he acts wisely in the present and is not corrupted by hope or fear.

units.la: Noster Lucas senior fuit septuagenarius, is ut bonus & honestus vir, fuit sedulus in sua vocatione, & pinxit totos dies quando fuit domi: surgebat ante familiam, pingebat etiam vesperi ad lychnum. Illa diligentia vocationis fuit ipsi summæ suauitatis. Putas'ne Stigelio esse molestum, facere uersus? Mihi & tibi est magna molestia: ipsi est tā naturale, quàm aui uolare in aere, sicut dicitur: Marti arma non sunt oneri.
units.tr: Our Lucas the Elder was a septuagenarian. As a good and honest man he was diligent in his calling, and he painted all day whenever he was at home. He rose before the household and painted even in the evening by lamplight. That diligence in his vocation was to him the greatest pleasure. Do you think it is a burden to Stigelius to write verses? For me and for you it is a great labour, but for him it is as natural as for a bird to fly in the air, as the saying goes: "Arms are no burden to Mars." ## COLL.

units.la: COLL.

Cùm ad Philippum regem Macedonicum missi essent legati Attici, & ipse Philippus tunc quidem dormiret: Parmenio ante ianuam cubiculi stans, iussit eos paululum expectare. Ipsi superbi egreferebant illam moram, ibi Parmenio dixit ad eos: Sinite illum paulisper dormire, nam tunc cum eos dormiretis (scilicet in Republica) ipse uigilauit. Erat acutum responsum, monēs oportere esse intentos in occasionem eos, qui uolūt aliquid in sua uocatione feliciter perficere.
units.tr: When Athenian envoys were sent to Philip, king of Macedon, Philip himself was then asleep. Parmenio, standing before the bedchamber door, told them to wait a little. Proud, they resented the delay. Then Parmenio said to them: "Let him sleep a little, for while you were sleeping (namely in the commonwealth) he was awake." It was a sharp reply, warning that those who want to carry something through successfully in their calling must be alert to the opportunity.

units.la: OECONOMIAE GVBERNATIO.
units.tr: THE GOVERNMENT OF THE HOUSEHOLD.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Audiui ex mea matre, agriculturam distribuen-dam esse in tres tertias, seu in tres partes: unam partem absumere ipsam agriculturam, alteram partem esse collocandam in sustentandam familiā. Reliquam uerò dari Magistratibus, & si quid reliquum fuerit reponendum.
units.tr: I have heard from my mother that farm income should be divided into three thirds, or three parts: one part to be spent on the farm itself, a second part to be set aside for supporting the household, and the remainder to be given to the magistrates, with whatever is left over to be put by.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Ferunt de coniuge Imperatoris Ferdinandi, quod illa ægerrimè tulerit, quando uideret filijs apponi lauticias ciborum, ita ut semper dixerit: Non educate ipsos ad apparatum splendidum, date illis cibos plebeios, quibus uti assuescant: ut si hodie uel cras fortuna mutaretur, ferre inopiam possent.
units.tr: They tell of the wife of the Emperor Ferdinand that she took it very badly when she saw lavish dishes set before her sons. She always said: "Do not bring them up to a splendid display. Give them plain food, so that they grow accustomed to it, and if fortune should change today or tomorrow, they will be able to bear poverty."

units.la: εἷς ἐστὶ δῆλος οἰκίας ὁ Δεσπότης, id est:
units.tr: That is, the master of the household is one [εἷς ἐστὶ δῆλος οἰκίας ὁ Δεσπότης], that is:

units.la: In quaq; seruus unus est herus domo.
units.tr: In every household, one servant is the master.

units.la: Ille uersus Doctori Martino adeò placuit, ut his sequentibus rythmis eum transtulerit: Es ist gewiß ein frommer mann, Der sich umb sein weib nimmet ann. Es ist gewiß ein frommes weib, Two sie bei einem manne bleibt. Ein eheman soll geduldig sein, Sein weib nit halten als ein schwein. Ein hauffraw soll uernunfftig sein, Des mannes weise lernen sein. Da wurdt Gott geben gnad dazu, Das inen die ehe gar sanffte thu. Vnd wirdt dem teuffel weren woll, Das er sein list nit enden soll. Der mann muß selber sein der knecht,
units.tr: That verse pleased Doctor Martin so much that he rendered it in the following rhymes: It is surely a pious man who takes his wife under his care. It is surely a pious wife who stays with one husband. A married man should be patient and not treat his wife like a pig. A housewife should be sensible and learn her husband's ways. Then God will grant grace for this, so that marriage goes very gently. And the devil will be well defended against, so that he shall not finish his tricks. The man must himself be the servant,

units.la: Quartum præceptum.
units.tr: Fourth commandment.

units.la: Vuill erß im hause finden recht.Die fraw muß selber sein die magd,Vuill sie im hauße schaffen rath.Gsinde nimmermehr bedenckt,Was schadt und nutz im hauße brengt.Es ist inen nit gelegen dran,Weil sie es nit fur eigen han.
units.tr: If you want to find justice in the house, the wife must herself be the maid, if she wants to manage the household well. Servants never consider what brings harm or profit to the house. It is no concern of theirs, since they do not hold it as their own.

units.la: Alij rythmi D.Philippi.
units.tr: Other rhymes of Dr Philip.

units.la: Almusen geben armet nicht,Kirchen gehen seumet nicht,Vnrecht gut faselt nicht,Gottes wort treuget nicht.
units.tr: Giving alms does not make a man poor; going to church does not make him lazy; ill-gotten goods do not last; the word of God does not deceive.

units.la: Alij eiusdem.
units.tr: Others of the same.

units.la: Vuer da mehr wil uerzeren,Dann sein pflug kan erehren:Der muß zu lezt uerderben,Oder uileicht am galgen sterben.
units.tr: Whoever wants to spend more than his plough can earn will in the end come to ruin, or perhaps die on the gallows.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Interrogatus Libycus, qua re optimè stercora-retur ager, respõdit: Stercore, quod cadit de calceis Domini, iuxta illud: Oculus Domini saginat equū.
units.tr: When the Libyan was asked by what means a field might be best manured, he answered: with the dung that falls from the Lord's shoes, according to the saying: "The eye of the Lord fattens the horse."

units.la: Non emas, quod opus, sed quod necessarium est.
units.tr: Do not buy what is pleasing but what is necessary.

units.la: Item: Oportet patre familiâs esse uendacem, non emacem. Hæc & similia pertinent ad prudentiam oeconomicam.
units.tr: Likewise: a householder ought to be a seller, not a buyer. These and similar sayings belong to economic prudence.

units.la: Doctor Martinus Lutherus solebat dicere: Minus nocet ignauus fur, quàm segnis minister.
units.tr: Doctor Martin Luther used to say: a lazy thief does less harm than a slack minister.

units.la: dd
units.tr: dd

units.la: Est pulchrum & argutum dictum.
units.tr: It is a fine and witty saying.

units.la: Columella.
units.tr: Columella.

units.la: Bona nomina oportet sæpe interpellari, ne fiant incerta, id est: fideles debitores etiam sæpius admonendi, ne obliuiscantur debiti.
units.tr: Good debtors must often be pressed, lest their debts become uncertain; that is, faithful debtors must be reminded even more often, lest they forget what they owe.

units.la: De optimo thesauro patrisfamiliâs.
units.tr: On the best treasure of the head of a household.

units.la: Cum Eberhardus Dux Vuirtembergensis esset Florentiæ, hospes suus præstantissimus uir, monstrauit ipsi sua armamenta, argentea & aurea uasa. Tertio idem hospes die dixit ad illustrissimum Ducem: Monstrabo tibi adhuc pulcherrimum & præstantissimum thesaurum, duxitq; eum in conclaue, ubi stabant ordine liberi cum præceptore Politiano, & ab altera parte coniunx cum filiabus. Sapientissimus Dux cum magna admiratione, huius sui hospitis familiā intuetur: Quid, inquit, pulchrius esse potest hoc ordine?
units.tr: When Duke Eberhard of Württemberg was at Florence, his most excellent host showed him his armoury, his silver and gold vessels. On the third day the same host said to the most illustrious Duke: "I will now show you a most beautiful and excellent treasure." He led him into a room where the children stood in order with their tutor Politian, and on the other side the wife with the daughters. The wisest Duke gazed with great admiration at his host's family and said: "What can be more beautiful than this order?"

units.la: Iurisconsultorum dictū: Naturale est, ut quod multis committitur, negligenter fiat.
units.tr: A saying of the jurists: it is natural that what is committed to many is done carelessly.

units.la: Xenophon dicit de Cyro, quòd mandaturus aliquid, nunquam dicere solitus sit: Hoc aliquis faciat, sed addidit nominatim: Hoc tu facias.
units.tr: Xenophon says of Cyrus that when he was about to order something, he was accustomed never to say, "Let someone do this," but named the person: "You do this."

units.la: Aristoteles dicit, duplicem esse mercaturam οικονομικὴν καὶ καπηλευτικὴν. οικονομικὴ honesta censetur, estq; quando quis ea uendit, quæ sibi domi suæ, uel natura, uel industria prouenerunt, & ad ȳ ad suæ familiæ sustentationem supersunt. Hu-smodi quiuis paterfamiliâs honestè uendit, etiâsi el nobilis sit. ναυτυλεντινὴ est res paruas emere, ꝑ postea alijs uendere, ut faciunt propolæ, item προξενητὰ seu parariû agere. Hoc sanè genus mercaturæ, uirũ nobilẽ aut honestũ minimè decet.
units.tr: Aristotle says there are two kinds of trade, the economic [οικονομικὴ] and the retail [καπηλευτικὴ]. The economic is considered honourable, and it is when someone sells what has grown on his own land, by nature or by his own labour, and what is left over to support his family. Such a head of household sells honourably, even if he is noble. The retail trade [καπηλευτική] is buying small goods in order to sell them on to others, as shopkeepers do, and likewise acting as a go-between [προξενητική] or agent. This kind of trade is certainly not at all fitting for a noble or honourable man.

units.la: AFFECTVS.
units.tr: AFFECTS.

units.la: Disputabat quidam ante aliquot annos Lipsiæ, non esse Christianum irasci: sed uanum est discere, affectus non esse in homine. Nam de Christo ipso dicitur in Luca, quod circumspexerit iratus: ira est affectus, conditus à Deo in natura. Quòd enim inordinatè irascamur, id fit uitio corruptæ natu-ræ, sicut inordinatè amamus, Deus ipse, Chri-stus & angeli eius irascuntur diabolis, & organis eius blasphemantibus.
units.tr: Some years ago a certain man argued at Leipzig that it is not Christian to be angry. But it is vain to teach that the affections are not in man. For it is said of Christ himself in Luke that he looked around in anger. Anger is an affection, implanted by God in nature. For when we are angry inordinately, this happens through the vice of corrupted nature, just as we love inordinately. God himself, Christ and his angels are angry with the devils and with those who blaspheme with his organs.

units.la: Timantes pictor pinxit maclationem Iphige-niæ, & quia non potuit pingere uultum patris mæstum, pinxit illum tectum. Quia dolores & af-sectus animi non possunt satis exprimi.
units.tr: Timanthes the painter painted the sacrifice of Iphigenia, and because he could not paint the sorrowful face of the father, he painted him covered. Because the pains and affections of the mind cannot be sufficiently expressed.

units.la: Quare sint conditæ προγὰι in na-tura hominum.
units.tr: Why the first movements [προπάθειαι] were implanted in the nature of human beings.

units.la: Vt sint initia uirtutum. Vt sint testimonia de amore Dei, erga genus hu-manum. In diabolis non sunt προργὰι, quia sunt ni-chis rabiosi.
units.tr: So that they may be the beginnings of virtues. So that they may be testimonies of God's love toward the human race. In devils there are no first movements, because they are nothing but raging.

units.la: Quare habent uaccę sua uberá in ima parte uentris?
units.tr: Why do cows have their udders in the lowest part of the belly?

units.la: Propter coctionem.
units.tr: On account of digestion.

units.la: Vbi habet mater sua ubera?
units.tr: Where does the mother have her breasts?

units.la: In pectore: quia non tantum alit, sed debet docere & trāsmittere cor, id est, σοργὴν in sobolem. Bruta sui mutuo obliuiscuntur: quòd homines non decet facere: quamuis etiam de equis dicatur, in ijs esse σοργὴν, quod est credibile, & exempla commemorantur.
units.tr: In the breast, because it not only nourishes but ought also to teach and to transmit the heart, that is, affection [στοργή] toward the offspring. Beasts forget one another mutually, which human beings ought not to do; although it is also said of horses that there is affection [στοργή] in them, which is credible, and examples are recorded.

units.la: ΣΤΟΡΓΑΙ PARENTVM ERGA sobolem, & econtrà liberorum erga parentes
units.tr: Parental affection [στοργαί] toward offspring, and children's affection toward parents

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Apud Euripidem Andromache offert se ad necem ut parcatur filio: quo exemplo Poeta pulchrè illum naturalem matris affectum erga filium depingit. Simile est in historia Salomonis.
units.tr: In Euripides, Andromache offers herself for slaughter so that her son may be spared. In this example the poet portrays well a mother's natural affection for her son. There is a similar case in the story of Solomon.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Cum Agesilaum regem Spartanorū, domi suæ cum liberis paruis in baculo equitantem deprehendisset, quidam ex ducibus casu interueniens, atq; admirans regem, & quidem talem, quo illa ætate nullus uir præstantior in tota Græcia esse iudicabatur, hoc modo cum pueris colludere: petit Agesilaus ueniam ab isto, siquidem hic ludus uideretur alienus à regia grauitate. Deinde addit, se nō tantū oneris ipsi imponere, ut perpetuò hãc rem taceat, sed rogat, ut tantisper sileat, donec ipse liberos haberet: significans eum, qui liberos, non haberet, non intelligere, quid habeāt hi lusus, non modo voluptatis, sed etiam utilitatis. Quamuis enim per se ridiculæ res sunt: tamen ad disciplinam & mores formandos pertinent. Et prudens pater intelligit, magnam esse uim assuefactionis in tenera ætate, etiam in his leuissimis exercitijs.
units.tr: When King Agesilaus of the Spartans was found at home playing on a stick-horse with his small children, one of his commanders happened by, was astonished that the king, who was judged the most outstanding man in all Greece at that time, should play like this with children, and asked his pardon, since this game seemed unworthy of royal dignity. Agesilaus then replied that he would not only impose a burden on him by asking him to keep this matter silent forever, but asked him to be silent for a while, until he himself had children. He meant that a man without children does not understand what these games are good for, not only for pleasure but also for usefulness. For though in themselves such things are ridiculous, they nevertheless contribute to training and forming character. A wise father understands that habit has great power in tender years, even in these very trivial exercises.

units.la: Amor descendit: Vnde amatores in ipsorũ rythmis flammas descendentes pingunt. eodem etiā modo summi reges & principes in tapetis flammas descendētes habēt, precipuè in stragulis equorũ. Significāt his flammis descēdentibus, quòd diligant subditos, et quòd uelint benefici esse erga subditos, ipsosq; fouere, & cōtra iniurias notorias defendere.
units.tr: Love descends. Hence lovers paint flames descending in their verses. In the same way the greatest kings and princes have flames descending on their tapestries, especially on the horse-cloths. By these descending flames they signify that they love their subjects, that they wish to be generous towards them, to cherish them, and to defend them against open wrongs.

units.la: Cum Archidamus esset reuersus in patriam, parta uictoria & superato hoste prodierunt illi obuiam ciues ac amici: ibi scribit Xenophon, quòd pater conspecto filio lachrymauerit. Quemadmodum & Fridericus Imperator, cùm filius Maximilianus Imperator crearetur, stetit senex ille & cœpit lachrymare. Quanquam & hic noster Imperator Carolus, cum traderet filio Philippo coram statibus Burgundicis & alijs regionibus, summam illarum gubernationem lachrymauerit, inquiens: Non miremini, illa sunt senectæ, senectæ, senes facilè lachrymantur, ut est in uersu Homeri: ἀριϛλάκηςυες ἀνδρες, id est: boni uiri facilè lachrimantur. Vidi doctorem Martinum Lutherum in aliena causa effusissimè lachrymantem, cum esset in suis calamitatibus animosissimus. Domi cum uideret filiam morientem, effundebat profusissimas lachrymas. Cum autem prodiret in funus suæ filiæ, ibi in publico repressit se, ita, ut ne quidē guttula lachrymarum in ipso conspiceretur.
units.tr: When Archidamus had returned to his homeland, victory won and the enemy overcome, his citizens and friends came out to meet him. There Xenophon writes that the father, on catching sight of his son, wept. Likewise the Emperor Frederick, when his son Maximilian was being crowned emperor, stood there as an old man and began to weep. Our own Emperor Charles also, when he handed over to his son Philip, before the estates of Burgundy and the other regions, the supreme government of those lands, wept, saying: "Do not be surprised; these are the tears of old age, old men weep easily, as in the verse of Homer: [ἀριστολάκηες ἄνδρες], that is, good men weep easily. I have seen Dr. Martin Luther weeping most profusely over another's cause, though he was most spirited in his own calamities. At home, when he saw his daughter dying, he shed the most abundant tears. But when he went out to his daughter's funeral, there in public he restrained himself so that not even a drop of tears could be seen on him.

units.la: Apud Philosophos est quæstio, an pater magis diligat filium quàm filiam: Respondetur quòd magis diligat filiam, quia antefert hoc, quod est imbecillius. Asina salit per ignem, ut opituletur pullo. Estualde mirabile in draconibus, & euidens simulachrum talium adfectuum, quod est apud Platonem. Draco incidit in uiatorem, quem adducit secum ad specum, ubi erant dracunculi sui, quo cùm uentum esset, intelligit uiator eos eximendos esse ex illo specu, & exemit. ibi circuit eum draco, tanquam gratulabundus, illumq; dimittit incolumem.
units.tr: Among the philosophers there is the question whether a father loves his son more than his daughter. The answer is that he loves the daughter more, because he prefers what is weaker. A she-ass leaps through fire to help her foal. There is something truly wonderful about dragons, and a clear image of such affections, which is found in Plato. A dragon fell upon a traveller, whom it led with it to its cave, where its little dragons were. When they had arrived there, the traveller understood that he had to rescue them from that cave, and he did so. Then the dragon circled around him, as if rejoicing, and let him go unharmed.

units.la: Epaminondas interrogatus, quid ei in tota uita iucundissimum accidisset: Respondit, inde se maximam uoluptatem cepisse, quòd uiuis parentibus liberasset seruitute patriam, uictis ingenti præmio Lacedæmonijs, & quòd parentes suos adhuc uiuos haberet suorum honorum spectatores.
units.tr: Epaminondas, when asked what had given him the greatest joy in his whole life, answered that he had felt the greatest pleasure in this: that, while his parents were still alive, he had freed his country from slavery, after the Lacedaemonians had been defeated, and that his parents were still alive to witness his honours.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Iohannes Murmellius, cum in enarratione Virgilij, incidisset in uersiculum: Omnis in Ascanio chari stat cura parentis. O dicebat ad suos discipulos, hunc uersiculum nemo uestrum intelliget, priusquam ille liberos habuerit.
units.tr: John Murmellius, when in his lecture on Virgil he came upon the little verse, "Omnis in Ascanio chari stat cura parentis," said to his pupils: "None of you will understand this verse before he has children."

units.la: Clemens citat contra phanaticos homines, qui uolebant constituere in Ecclesia ἀπράθεια, quod Petrus dixerit se dolere cum uideret coniugem duci ad supplicium, & affatus sit eam clara uoce, ut esset memor Domini. Ipse est Romæ interfectus à Nerone, teste Aegesippo, cui credo, quia scriptum eius uetus est.
units.tr: Clement cites against fanatical people, who wanted to establish apatheia [ἀπάθεια] in the Church, that Peter said he grieved when he saw his wife led to execution, and addressed her in a loud voice, so that she would remember the Lord. Peter himself was put to death at Rome by Nero, according to the testimony of Hegesippus, whom I believe, because his writing is ancient.

units.la: D. Martinus Lutherus.
units.tr: Dr. Martin Luther.

units.la: Iuniores infantes recens nati plus diliguntur & plus afficiunt parentes, quia illi liberi plus indigent affectuũ, ut diligenter custodiantur: cæteri uero paulo magis adulti, & iam fari ualentes non tantum curæ requirunt. Ideo amor parentum, semper & simpliciter magis descendit ad nouiter natos.
units.tr: Younger infants, newly born, are loved more and move their parents more, because those children need more affection so that they may be carefully looked after; but the others, somewhat older and already able to speak, do not require so much care. So parental love always and simply descends more towards those newly born.

units.la: Carens γόργη illa naturali.
units.tr: Lacking that natural affection [στοργή].

units.la: Monetarius autor seditionis in Thuringia, cum natus esset ei filius, sedens inter pocula, dixit ad nuncios, gratulantes ipsi de nato infante: Videte amici ego planè affectibus careo, & à consideratione creaturarum abreptus sum: uerùm à stultitia & fatuorum affectibus non erat abreptus.
units.tr: A minter, the instigator of the sedition in Thuringia, when a son had been born to him, sitting among his cups, said to the messengers who congratulated him on the newborn infant: "Look, friends, I am plainly without affections, and I have been carried away from the contemplation of creatures; but I was not carried away by foolishness and the affections of fools."

units.la: ΣΤΟΡΓΑΙ FRATRVM.
units.tr: Brotherly affection [στοργαί]

units.la: Vidi optime consentientes fratres laudatissimos principes Palatinos, erat lætissimi & hilares, quàdo conueniebāt. Eratq; inter eos magna στοργή. Episcopus Ratisbonensis erat festiuus sæpe exhilarabat fratrem, sumebat personam aurigæ Norimbergæ, uendebatq; cocta ova uilissimo precio mulieribus, & multa in culinam fratris, qui tunc temporis erat Norimbergæ, perueniebāt. Frater conquerebatur de fraude & dolo uenditoris ouorū. Indicata causa, hoc lepōre, eo tempore fratrem eiusq; hospites exhilarabat.
units.tr: I have seen the most praiseworthy Palatine princes, brothers, agreeing very well. They were very joyful and cheerful whenever they met, and there was great affection [στοργή] between them. The Bishop of Regensburg was jovial and often cheered his brother. He would take on the role of a Nuremberg coachman and sell cooked eggs to women at a very low price, and many of them found their way into the kitchen of his brother, who was then in Nuremberg. The brother complained of the fraud and trickery of the egg-seller. When the matter was revealed, this joke cheered his brother and his guests at that time.

units.la: Xerxes & frater, cùm certarēt nō de tribus capellis, ut dicitur: sed de illo pulcherrimo regno Persarū, quo postea nullum fuit pulchrius, ibi de tanto regno ita certarūt, ut interea nulla iracundiæ, aut odij labes esset in animo, sed potius maioribus inter se officijs certarent. De ipsa autem controuersia patrem iudicem constituerunt.
units.tr: Xerxes and his brother quarrelled, not over three goats, as the saying goes, but over that most beautiful kingdom of the Persians, than which none was more beautiful afterwards. They contended over so great a kingdom in such a way that meanwhile no stain of anger or hatred entered their minds; rather, they vied with each other in greater acts of kindness. They appointed their father as judge of the dispute itself.

units.la: Inter Fridericum & Vuilhelmū duces Saxoniæ fratres, gestū est bellum ad triennium fere, ibi cum Vuilhelmus ad Lipsiā oppugnādā proficisceretur cum exercitu, eodē se Fridericus ad defendendā urbem cōtulit. Consiliarij utriusq; pacem suaserunt, ita ut dissensio inter fratres componeretur. idq; iudicarunt non commodius fieri posse, quàm si principes ipsi inter se colloquerentur. Fide data & accepta, convenerunt principes soli in quodam tumulo prope Lipsiam, & aliquandiu clausis galeis colloquuti sunt. Tandem apertis galeis, & abiectis chirotecis ferreis sese mutuò complexi sunt: ibi clamor & exultatio utrinq;, facta est, & accesserunt quidam è præcipuis consiliarijs, qui cum intelligerent pacem ab ipsis principibus inter se factam, de modis & rationibus pacis consultauerūt. Ibi Fridericus, qui æquior erat, & pater patriæ, ac bonus princeps, respondit, ut ea in aliud tempus differrentur, citans uersum Psalmi 127. Non confundetur, cum loquetur inimicis suis in porta: iubens ut conuenirent in monasterio Portensi apud Naumburgum, ibi postea deliberationes de rationibus pacis habitæ & descriptæ sunt. Hanc historiam mementote, cum aliquando iuxta illum locum iter feceretis.
units.tr: Between Frederick and William, the dukes of Saxony and brothers, a war was waged for nearly three years. When William set out with an army to besiege Leipzig, Frederick hastened to the city to defend it. The counsellors of both urged peace, so that the dispute between the brothers might be settled. They judged that this could be done no more conveniently than if the princes themselves talked together. With faith given and received, the princes met alone on a certain hill near Leipzig and talked for some time with their helmets closed. At last, with their helmets opened and their iron gauntlets cast aside, they embraced each other. There was shouting and rejoicing on both sides. Some of the chief counsellors came up, and when they understood that peace had been made between the princes themselves, they consulted about the terms and manner of the peace. Then Frederick, who was the fairer of the two, a father of his country and a good prince, replied that these matters should be deferred to another time, citing the verse of Psalm 127: "They shall not be put to shame when they speak with their enemies in the gate." He ordered them to meet in the monastery of Pforta near Naumburg, and there the deliberations on the terms of peace were afterwards held and recorded. Remember this story when you travel past that place some day.

units.la: Inter Duces Bauariæ Vuilhelmum & fratrem eius, post mortem patris orta est dissensio de diuisione ditionis, quam detulerunt ad Maximilianum Imperatorem. Ipsi inter se interim mutuis officijs beneuolentiam conseruarunt: & alter alteri se libenter cessurum ex ditione pollicebatur. Nam testamento paterno prohibebatur, ne adiret hereditatem tatem iunior: sed tantum ille honos & titulus co-mitis exhiberetur, quem illi authores testamenti paterni eripere quoq; volebant: sed Imperator a-boleuit illud testamentum, tanquam iniustum, & decernit, ut juniori titulus Ducis non eriperetur. Servivit autem ille deinde fratri seniori in quadā præfectura tanquam minister, & non tanquam æ-qualis, ac quidem diligentius seruiuit, quàm ullus ex equitibus aut ministris: nec aliter appellauit il-lam partem ditionis à fratre sibi traditam quàm suam præfecturam, & non suum dominium. Tanta beneuolentia fuit inter illos duos fratres, ut etiam in certamine illo coram Imperatore mutuis beneuolentiæ & amicitiæ officijs certarent.
units.tr: After the death of their father, a dispute arose between the dukes of Bavaria, William and his brother, over the division of the territory, and they brought it before the Emperor Maximilian. Meanwhile they kept up goodwill between themselves by mutual services, and each readily promised to yield his share of the territory to the other. For by their father's will the younger was forbidden to enter the inheritance, but was to be given only the honour and title of count, which the authors of the father's will also wanted to take from him. The Emperor, however, annulled that will as unjust and decreed that the younger should not be deprived of the title of duke. He afterwards served his elder brother in a certain office as a minister, not as an equal, and indeed he served more diligently than any of the knights or servants. Nor did he call that part of the territory handed over to him by his brother anything but his own administration, not his own dominion. So great was the goodwill between those two brothers that even in that contest before the Emperor they vied with each other in offices of mutual goodwill and friendship.

units.la: Principes ab Anhaldt fuerunt viri proceri ac robusti, pulchris corporibus præditi. Horum unus Rodolphus, qui fuit capitaneus in bello Veneto. In prima adolescentia, diu Moguntiæ operam li-teris dans, vixit non secus atq; aliquis ex equestri ordine, nec unquam ultra eum statum sese extulit. Postea verò secutus bellum Venetum, primùm cæ-pit militare, & per labores militares clarus factus est. Ibi primùm significatum est Imperatori Maxi-miliano, quis esset, ac postea ob virtutes singulares per totam vitam Imperatori charus fuit. Hi præ-stantissimi principes eo tēpore existētes, simul a-micè vixerunt, tanquā in una familia, sine discor-dia,ac dia, ac in illa sua qualicunq; mediocritate uictus se se mutuo uarijs officiorum generibus oblectarunt.
units.tr: The princes of Anhalt were tall and sturdy men, endowed with handsome bodies. One of them, Rudolf, was captain in the Venetian war. In early youth, while studying for a long time at Mainz, he lived no differently from any man of the knightly order, and never raised himself beyond that station. Afterwards, following the Venetian war, he first began to serve as a soldier and became famous for his military labours. There it was first made known to the Emperor Maximilian who he was, and afterwards, on account of his singular virtues, he was dear to the Emperor throughout his life. These most excellent princes, living at that time, lived together as friends, as in one family, without discord, and in their modest condition, whatever it was, they delighted one another with various kinds of services.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: Comparisons

units.la: Comites etiam de Mansfeld olim non dissimili ratione mutuis inter se beneuolentiæ & fraternitatis officijs certauerunt: sic ut nulla odia aut simultates multis annis inter eos extiterint. Quare non immerito uirtutes hæ, aliæq; ipsorum clementia & paterna uoluntas erga suos subditos, datis occasionibus, ab omnibus cebrantur.
units.tr: The counts of Mansfeld also, in former times and by a not dissimilar method, vied with each other in offices of mutual goodwill and brotherly kindness, so that for many years no hatreds or quarrels arose among them. Therefore these virtues, together with their clemency and fatherly care for their subjects, are rightly celebrated by everyone whenever the occasion arises.

units.la: ΣΤΟΡΓΑΙ SVPERIORVM erga scribditos, & econtrà.
units.tr: ΣΤΟΡΓΑΙ SVPERIORVM erga scribditos, & econtrà.

units.la: Heydelberæ principi Palatino Friderico quidam rusticus dono dedit calathum, plenum pyris optimis, simulq; petijt aliquid ignoro quid. Princeps beneuolus pyra statim accipiens, mandat id, quod rusticus ab ipso petiuerat, perfici. Hoc beneficio impetrato, rusticus agit gratias principi quàm plurimas, & à principe tam beneuolo discedit.
units.tr: At Heidelberg a certain countryman gave the Palatine prince Frederick a basket full of the best pears, and at the same time asked for something (I do not know what). The kindly prince at once accepted the pears and ordered that what the countryman had asked of him be carried out. Having obtained this favour, the countryman thanked the prince as warmly as he could and departed from so kind a prince.

units.la: Portauit puer ad aulam Palatini principis electos canes, quos mittebat principi noster hospes. Et mea quoq; mater misit Friderico Palatino poma nostratia: ille statim remisit poma, alia quæ ex Belgico attulerant. Hæc sunt significationes humanitatis & beneuolentiæ non exiguæ.
units.tr: A boy brought to the court of the Palatine prince some choice dogs which our host was sending to the prince. My own mother also sent Frederick the Palatine some of our local apples; he at once sent back the apples and others which they had brought from the Low Countries. These are no small signs of courtesy and kindness.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Cum dux Saxoniæ Fridericus esset mortuus, ad primum rumorem conuenerunt huc rustici, & circa molam in uia prosternebat se, subinde iterantes hanc uocem, Ah amisimus patrem nostrum.
units.tr: When Duke Frederick of Saxony had died, at the first report the country folk gathered here, and lay prostrate on the road near the mill, repeating again and again this cry: "Ah, we have lost our father."

units.la: DE INSTITVTIONE liberorum.
units.tr: DE INSTITVTIONE liberorum.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Maior est habenda ratio rectæ institutionis liberorum, quàm ullarum diuitiarum. Qui uero secus faciunt, persimiles mihi uidentur ijs qui calceos curant, pedes ipsos negligunt, cùm eis tuendis calcei sunt inuenti. Sapienter igitur Crates ille antiquus, consc̈ensa urbis altissima parte, exclamandū censuit: Quò quò ferimini ciues? itáne conuenit in opibus parandis maximè occupari? in ijs uero quorum causa quæruntur, nihil laborare, ac minimè esse sollicitos? Credite mihi, non potest melior hæreditas liberis à parentibus relinqui, quàm si bene educati, & ad uirtutem rectè ab ineunte ætate sint instituti: hoc eis perpetuum manet patrimonium, neq; à fortunæ procellis labefactari potest.
units.tr: A right upbringing of children is to be held of greater account than any riches. Those who act otherwise seem to me very like those who take care of shoes and neglect the feet themselves, when shoes were invented for the sake of protecting the feet. Wisely, therefore, that old Crates, climbing to the highest part of the city, thought he should cry out: "Where, where are you rushing to, citizens? Is it fitting to be so busy in acquiring wealth, and yet to take no pains and be in no way anxious about those for whose sake it is sought? Believe me, no better inheritance can be left to children by their parents than if they are well brought up and rightly trained to virtue from an early age. This is a lasting patrimony for them, and it cannot be shaken by the storms of fortune."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Vt neq; equus indomitus, quamuis natura bonus ad eas utilitates, quæ ab eo desiderantur, idoneus est: ita nec ab homine indocto, quantumuis ingeniosus sit, uirtutis fructum possis elicere. Simile mile dixit Durerus: Homo indoctus, est quasi impolitum speculum.
units.tr: Just as a horse that has not been broken, though naturally good and fit for the uses that are required of it, is of no service, so too you cannot draw the fruit of virtue from a man who is untaught, however gifted he may be. Durer said something similar: "An untaught man is like an unpolished mirror."

units.la: GRATITVDO.
units.tr: GRATITUDE.

units.la: Χαρίτων δέ τε θυμὸς ἄχαρις. Mens est optima in beneficijs.
units.tr: Χαρίτων δέ τε θυμὸς ἄχαρις. A mind is best shown in benefits. [Χαρίτων δέ τε θυμὸς ἄχαρις: "but the spirit of the graces is ungracious"].

units.la: Fridericus Imperator miserat ad filium Maximilianum initio noui anni legatos, per quos ipse precatus erat felix & faustũ auspiciũ noui anni: simulq; misit pulchra poma in argentea lance, inspersis uiginti uel triginta nouis aureis. Filius Imperatoris Maximilianus modestè respondens legatis, summa cum reuerentia donum illud accepit, gratias agens domino Patri, & uicissim felicem ac faustum cursum anni ipsi optans. Deinde diligenter ministris ac sodalibus suis mandauit, dicens: Non attingatis uos mihi hæc poma, quia mea sunt, & mihi uolo reseruari: sed aureos proiecit inter socios. Postea cùm legati redijssent domum, interrogati à patre Imperatore, quomodo sese gesssisset filius (quia voluit filij ingenium conspicere) responderunt, ipsum poma seruasse, & dixisse: Hoc meum est munus, sed pecuniâ proiecit se inter sodales, ut ipsi partirētur. Tũc Imperator dixit: Præuideo filium meum dissipatorem diuitiarum futurum. Et uerè Maximilianus ita liberalis & gratus erga benemeritos fuit postea in tota uita.
units.tr: The Emperor Frederick had sent envoys to his son Maximilian at the beginning of the new year; through them he himself wished him a happy and fortunate beginning of the new year, and at the same time he sent fine apples on a silver dish, with twenty or thirty new gold coins scattered among them. The son, the Emperor's Maximilian, replied modestly to the envoys, received the gift with the greatest respect, thanked his lord father, and in turn wished him a happy and prosperous course of the year. Then he carefully ordered his attendants and companions, saying: "Do not touch these apples, for they are mine, and I wish to keep them for myself"; but he threw the gold coins among his companions. Afterwards, when the envoys had returned home and were asked by his father the Emperor how his son had behaved (for he wished to observe the son's disposition), they replied that he had kept the apples and said: "This gift is mine, but he threw the money among his companions so that they might share it." Then the Emperor said: "I foresee that my son will be a squanderer of wealth." And indeed Maximilian was afterwards so generous and grateful towards those who had deserved well of him all his life.

units.la: οἱ ἀγαθοὶ αὐτὶ μικρῶν οἰδλασιν χάριν.
units.tr: οἱ ἀγαθοὶ αὐτὶ μικρῶν οἰδλασιν χάριν. [The good feel gratitude even for small things.]

units.la: Boni pro paruis etiam sunt grati. Iulius dederat agros suis militibus. Venit qui dam accusans militem, quòd teneret agrum, qui non debuisset uenire in distributionem. Iulius actori respondit: Veram habes causam: militi uerò: Tu cede ei. Miles ait: Meministi Imperator in pugna quadã te excedere ex pugna, & residere sub arbore? Inquit Cæsar: Memini. Meministi'ne militem tibi adferre aquam in galea? Memini. Túne es ille? Ego sum, in quit. Imo nõ es: quia ille erat integer, saluis oculis. Rectè, inquit: in prælio alterum oculum amisi. Ibi Iulius mox numerauit colono precium pro prædio quanti erat, ut illud miles retineret.
units.tr: Good men are grateful even for small things. Julius had given fields to his soldiers. A man came accusing a soldier, because he held a field which ought not to have come into the distribution. Julius answered the accuser: "You have a true case." To the soldier he said: "You, yield it to him." The soldier said: "Do you remember, Emperor, that in a certain battle you withdrew from the fight and sat down under a tree?" Caesar said: "I remember." "Do you remember that a soldier brought you water in his helmet?" "I remember." "Are you that man?" "I am," he said. "No, you are not, for he was whole, with both eyes saved." "Rightly," he said; "in the battle I lost one eye." Then Julius at once counted out to the farmer the price the farm was worth, so that the soldier might keep it.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Plauti dulcissimum & grauissimum dictum: Hoc demum graue & gratum est, bonis quod bene fit Graue, id est: grauiter, sapienter collocatum, respicit dantis personam: gratum accipientis. Existimo Plautum ad uocabulum Grecum σεμνὸν respicere: nam σεμνότης grauitas, uirtus est.
units.tr: Plautus' sweetest and most weighty saying: "This at last is heavy and welcome, that good things are done for good men." "Heavy," that is, weightily and wisely bestowed, refers to the person of the giver; "welcome" to the recipient. I think Plautus alludes to the Greek word σεμνόν, for σεμνότης is gravity, which is a virtue.

units.la: Gratitudo erga parentes.
units.tr: Gratitude towards parents.

units.la: Cum Noribergæ bonus quidam senex, obiurgaret ancillam, illa dixit: Tu nescis, quid dicis, tu es delirus senex, filius astans tacet. Pater discedente ancilla filium alloquitur, inquiens: Tu audiuisti hoc conuicium tuæ ancillæ, & tacuisti. Nam ego uixi in tali flore ætatis, in quo tu nunc es. Cogita etiam te senem fore, & eadem tibi accidere posse, quæ mihi iam accidunt. Ibi filius statim ancillam domo exire iußit.
units.tr: At Nuremberg a certain good old man was rebuking a maidservant, and she said: "You do not know what you are saying; you are a doting old man." The son, standing by, kept silent. When the maidservant had left, the father addressed his son, saying: "You heard this insult to your servant and said nothing. For I too lived in such a flower of age as you are in now. Consider also that you will become old, and the same things may happen to you that now happen to me." Thereupon the son at once ordered the maidservant out of the house.

units.la: Gratitudo erga præceptores.
units.tr: Gratitude towards teachers.

units.la: Fridericus à Dőn uir nobilis & eloquens, rogatus à quibusdam, ut pro ipsis causam diceret, promisit se facturum: postea cum uentum esset ad iudicium, & ipse uideret in altera parte esse præpositum templi Arcis Vuitebergensis, qui erat doctor Iuris, & cancellarius ducum Saxoniæ, petiuit differri cognitionem istius controuersiæ, dicēs, se nolle agere causam contra illum suum præceptorem, & quicquid ipse in dicendo posset, illud ipsum ab hoc uiro habere.
units.tr: Frederick von Dön, a noble and eloquent man, was asked by some people to plead their case for them, and promised he would do so. Afterwards, when the matter came to court and he saw that on the other side was the provost of the Castle Church of Wittenberg, who was a doctor of law and chancellor of the dukes of Saxony, he asked that the hearing of that dispute be deferred, saying that he was unwilling to argue a case against his own teacher, and that whatever ability he had in speaking he had from this man.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Inter antiquas leges præcipitur ἐάν τις μὴ τρέφει γονεῖς, ἄτιμος ἔσω. Hanc iustissimam legē, quanati obligantur parentibus, filia Cimonis nouo & inaudito exemplo præstitit. Nam cùm ad captiuum patrem lachrymis emollito custode, intromissa esset, parentem suum senio & mœrore ac inedia intolerabili exhaustum, excrtis mamillis iam uelut ultimæ senectutis infantem lactauit, nouoq; modo γοργὸν καὶ ἀντιπελάργησιν expressit, dum debita parenti ἀντιτρεφωτροφίαν compensauit. Aiunt olim tantam fuisse uim huius picturæ, ut ubiubicunq; in theatris effet exposita, statim & men tes & oculi spectatorum admiratione incredibili stupescerent. Huc congruit & descriptio Cico-niarum, quæ ab Aristophane non insuauiter recitatur. Vtinam nos singuli hoc insigne exemplum imitaremur, & simili pietate erga sanctissimam nostram parentem Ecclesiam, nunc mœstã & humanis præsidijs orbatam, affecti essemus, & no-stra gratitudine omnibus officijs ostenderemus.
units.tr: Among the ancient laws it is prescribed: "If anyone does not support his parents, let him be without honour." The daughter of Cimon showed a new and unheard-of example of this most just law, to which children are bound toward parents. For when, with the guard softened by tears, she was admitted to her captive father, who was worn out by old age, grief and intolerable hunger, she bared her breasts and nursed him, as if he were an infant in his last old age; and in a new way she portrayed the "gorgon" and the stork's requital, while she repaid the nourishment owed to a parent. They say this picture once had such power that wherever it was displayed in the theatres, the minds and eyes of the spectators were struck with incredible admiration. The description of the storks, which Aristophanes recites not unpleasantly, agrees with this too. Would that each of us imitated this distinguished example, and were moved by similar piety towards our most holy mother the Church, now sorrowful and bereft of human protection, and showed our gratitude by all services.

units.la: INGRATITVDO ERGA parentes, cognatos & præceptores.
units.tr: Ingratitude towards parents, relatives and teachers.

units.la: Mahometus, qui cepit Constantinopolim interfecit duos fratres paruulos, & alterum paruulum in sinu matris.
units.tr: Mahomet, who took Constantinople, killed two small brothers, and another small child in its mother's bosom.

units.la: Selinus pater huius Solimanni, interfecit & patrem fugientem, & fratrem, & in eo ipso loco ubi pater est interfectus, iuxta Baiarum ulcere sæuissimo diuinitùs inflicto mortuus est. Locus ostenditur in Macedoniam iter facientibus per Hungariam.
units.tr: Selim, father of this Suleiman, killed his fleeing father and brother, and in the very place where his father was killed he died, struck by God with a most savage ulcer near Baiae. The place is shown to those travelling through Hungary into Macedonia.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Aristoteles in nono libro de Anima scribit, cuculum propter impietatem, quam in ipso insignem esse compertum est, non facere proprium nidum, nec suos pullos excludere, sed deponere ouâ oua in alieno nido, ac plerumq; in currucæ. Hæc cum reperit oua cuculi inter sua, simul etiam his incubat: deinde pullis exclusis, quia cucu-lus magnitudine & uiribus superat reliquos, quic quid sedula mater cibi affert suppositicius iste præripit: ita fit, ut cæteri pulli fame morian-tur. Putant etiam matrem eo maiore cura hunc fouere, quia magis hunc miratur & amat, pro-pter corporis magnitudinem. Interdum ipse cu-culus factus robustior cæteros pullos devorat: interdum senior cuculus exorbet oua currucæ, adeo multiplex est in hoc genere crudelitas. Po-stremo ubi adoleuit sceleratus & impius cuculus, addit nefariam, & plus quàm tragicam catastro-phen.Nam currucâ,qua incubante natus & à qua magna assiduitate nutritus est, crudeliter lacera-tam devorat. Hanc pro maternis beneficijs, & pro nutricatione vicem iste ἀχάρις rependit, qui dignus, ut perpetua scabie notatus sit, & quem oderunt ac fugiunt reliquæ aues ceu dirum portentum. Ita enim natura fertur illum damnasse im-pietatis, ut uerè erret, sicut pollutum animal sine ni-do, & sine ulla societate, sicut apud Homerum de pœ-na impiorum dicitur, ἀνάστιος καὶ ἀφεγγὴς ωρ: solus enim sine societate sui generis, aut aliarum auium uagatur. Imago proposita est in tetra uolucri, ut uideamus turpissimæ beluæ similitudinem habere ingratos sicut in aliis foedis animalibus aliorum ui ciorum similitudo proposita est: ut cognita turpi-tudine bestiæ, homines magis abhorrent à similibus vitijs: ut in lupo inest rapacitas & crudelitas: in polipo tanta libido, ut extinguatur in cõcubitu. Sed longum est exempla persequi. Cuculus etiam affectat musicam laudem dulcißimæ canentis luscinïæ, eò aduolat, & excitatus cantu illius, cum ea certare studet. Hinc intelligi potest, in quo genere hominum ingrati significentur, nempe inter eos qui obstrepunt melioribus in dicenda sententia, in studijs, in rebus Ecclesiasticis, & alijs quæ uitæ conducunt. Sic Homero obtrectabat Zoilus ceu luscinïæ cuculus: Ciceroni Clodius, & alij multi. Habuerunt & suos cuculos omnes docti & heroici quolibet tempore: Scipioni obtrectabat Carbo, Alcibiadi Hyperbolus. Habet & nostrum seculum perplurimos cuculos, qui matri, id est: Ecclesiæ, & alijs de se bene merentibus, quales gratias reddant, uidemus.
units.tr: Aristotle, in the ninth book of On the Soul, writes that the cuckoo, because of the impiety that is known to be outstanding in it, does not build its own nest or hatch its own young, but lays its eggs in another's nest, and most often in a warbler's. When the warbler finds the cuckoo's eggs among her own, she sits on them as well. Then, once the young have hatched, the cuckoo, because it surpasses the others in size and strength, snatches away whatever food the diligent mother brings, so that the other chicks die of hunger. They think too that the mother cherishes this one with greater care, because she admires and loves it more for its bodily size. Sometimes the cuckoo, grown stronger, devours the other chicks; sometimes, when it is older, it sucks out the warbler's eggs. So manifold is cruelty in this kind. Finally, when the wicked and impious cuckoo has grown up, it adds an unholy and more than tragic catastrophe. For it devours the warbler, under whose brooding it was born and by whose constant care it was nourished, tearing her cruelly to pieces. In return for maternal kindness and nurture, this ungrateful creature repays her, and it deserves to be marked with perpetual mange; the other birds hate and shun it as a dire portent. Nature is said to have condemned it for its impiety, so that it truly wanders like a polluted animal, without a nest and without any fellowship, as Homer says of the punishment of the impious: ἀνάστιος καὶ ἀφεγγὴς [anastios kai aphengēs], hearthless and without light. For it wanders alone, without fellowship either of its own kind or of other birds. The image is set before us in a foul bird, so that we may see that the ungrateful have the likeness of a most shameful beast, just as in other foul animals the likeness of other vices is set forth, so that, having recognised the baseness of the beast, people may shrink more from similar vices. Thus the wolf has rapacity and cruelty; the polyp has such lust that it is extinguished in intercourse. But it would be long to pursue examples. The cuckoo also aspires to the musical praise of the sweetest-singing nightingale; it flies thither and, roused by her song, strives to vie with her. From this it can be understood which kind of men are signified as ungrateful: namely, those who clamour against their betters in speaking their opinion, in studies, in ecclesiastical affairs, and in other matters that serve life. So Zoilus railed at Homer like a cuckoo against the nightingale; Clodius railed at Cicero, and many others. All learned and heroic men at every time have had their cuckoos: Carbo railed at Scipio, Hyperbolus at Alcibiades. Our own age too has very many cuckoos, and we see what thanks they render to their mother, that is the Church, and to others who have deserved well of them.

units.la: Alia allegoria parum dissimilis à priore.
units.tr: Another allegory hardly different from the previous one.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Cuculus ebibit currucæ oua, & sua in locum ipsius reponit: postea exclusi non possunt foveri, quare semper sunt leprosi. Tandem uorat matrem & non potest ferre luscinïa. Papa est cuculus, iste uorat Ecclesiæ oua sua, & caeat Cardinales: uult postea quoq; deuorare matrem ipsam Ecclesiam, in qua natus est, & educatus: nec potest ferre piorum hominum cantilenam.
units.tr: The cuckoo sucks out the warbler's eggs and puts its own in their place; afterwards the hatched young cannot be fostered, so they are always sickly. At last it devours the mother, and the nightingale cannot bear it. The Pope is the cuckoo: he devours the eggs of the Church and creates Cardinals. Afterwards he also wants to devour the mother herself, the Church in which he was born and reared, and he cannot bear the singing of pious men.

units.la: In epistola Diogenis scriptum extat: Non debemus gratiā parentibus, quia voluptatis suæ causa educant sobolem. Est planè diabolica oratio. Voluptas non est causa finalis in parentibus educandi sobolem. Causa impulsiva est, potius mandatum Dei, ut educent sobolem. Hæc fuit vanitas Græciæ, sic ludere, ut nunc est illorum tribunorum qui inaudita, & insulsa excogitant.
units.tr: In a letter of Diogenes it is written: "We ought not to owe gratitude to parents, because they rear offspring for the sake of their own pleasure." This is plainly a diabolical saying. Pleasure is not the final cause of parents rearing offspring; the impelling cause is rather God's command that they should rear offspring. This was the vanity of Greece, to trifle in this way, as is now the case with those tribunes who devise unheard-of and silly things.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Accidit ut homo quidam dives haberet patrem pauperem, & valde quoq; senem, sic ut sibi labore suo victum non amplius comparare posset. Quia igitur nolebat, ut mendicaret, cum illi hoc ignominiosum fuisset, cogebatur illum alere. Sed cum non libenter faceret, die quodam accidit, ut cum filius prandens, haberet in mensa lautum quoddam ferculum, & videret patrem suum iam senio confectum venientem ad prandium, iuberet illud seponi, donec rursus abijsset. Cùm autem pater more solito, postquam pransus erat, rursus abiret, iussit filius depromi ferculum, quod absconditum erat. Ibi servus renunciauit patinam plenam esse serpentū. Quod cum ille procurrens videre vellet, ecce ibi statim ingens serpens in os ipsius illapsus est, suum os ori ipsius adiungens, ita ut semper, quando ipse comederet, cogeretur quoq; cibare serpentem, quem ille ita secum circumgestauit quoad uixit.
units.tr: It happened that a certain rich man had a poor father, who was also very old, so that he could no longer procure his own food by his labour. Because the son did not want him to beg, which would have been disgraceful to him, he was compelled to feed him. But since he did this unwillingly, it happened one day that, while the son was dining, a choice dish lay on the table, and seeing his father, now worn out with age, coming to dinner, he ordered it to be set aside until the old man had gone away again. When the father, as usual, had dined and went away again, the son ordered the dish, which had been hidden, to be brought out. There the servant reported that the dish was full of serpents. As the son ran forward wanting to see this, behold, at once a huge serpent slid into his mouth, joining its mouth to his, so that whenever he himself ate, he was forced to feed the serpent too; this he carried about with him thus for as long as he lived.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Audiui ab alio uiro honesto & docto simi-lem historiam, ubi etiam pauper quidam senex accessit filium suum, qui factus erat opulentus, pe-tens θρεπτήρια, id est, præmia & officia educatio-nis. Filius uerò probri loco sibi à multis obijci posse iudicans, quòd haberet patrem pauperem ac e-genum, palàm negauit se non esse illius senis pau-peris filiū, ac iussit ut statim ex ædib. suis discede-ret.
