Pater lacrymans abijt: ipso abeunte, filius sta-tim furere incipit, & in isto furore etiā moritur. Sic Deus pœnam ingratitudinis erga parentes in isto ostendere uoluit.
units.tr: I have heard from another honest and learned man a similar story, in which a poor old man also came to his son, who had become wealthy, asking for the threptéria [θρεπτήρια], that is, the rewards and duties owed for his upbringing. The son, however, judging that he would be taunted by many people for having a poor and needy father, openly denied that he was the son of that poor old man and ordered him to leave his house at once. The father went away in tears. As he left, the son immediately began to rage, and in that madness he also died. In this way God wished to show the punishment of ingratitude towards parents.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Narrant fuisse quendam, qui suum patrem ma-le cæsum capillis ad limen domus usq; protraxe-rat. Deinde cum & ipse senesceret, multò dete-rius à filio tractatum fuisse, & extra limen domus protractum in luto prouolutum esse, donec & ip-se pater clamaret: Parce fili, ego meum parentem tantū ad limen domus protraxi. Sic Deus plerun-que eodem genere, in quo quis peccat, punit.
units.tr: They tell of a certain man who had beaten his father badly and dragged him by the hair to the threshold of the house. Later, when he himself grew old, he was treated much worse by his own son: he was dragged outside the threshold of the house and rolled in the mud, until at last the father himself cried out: "Spare me, son! I only dragged my own father to the threshold of the house." In this way God often punishes by the same kind of sin in which a man has sinned.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Recitatur similis fere historia, quod quidam parentem iam senio confectum in carcerem incluserit, & miserit illi per filium uilem pannum ad tunicam. Filius diuinitus fortasse lacerat pannum. Quo uiso, dixit pater: Quid agis peruersissime? Ibi filium respondisse dicunt: Hac parte panni mihi reseruabo, donec & tu senueris, tunc similiter te tractabo. Audito hoc, pater iussit senem parentem reduci, & honorifice eum ad extremum halitum tractauit.
units.tr: A story almost like this is told: a man had shut his father, already worn out with age, in prison, and sent him a worthless rag for a tunic through his son. The son, perhaps divinely prompted, tore the rag. When the father saw this, he said: "What are you doing, most perverse fellow?" They say the son replied: "I will keep this part of the rag for you, until you too grow old; then I will treat you in the same way." When the father heard this, he ordered the old man, his own father, to be brought back, and he treated him with honour until his last breath.

units.la: Fuit hic rex Mauritaniæ in obsidione Vuitebergensi apud Imperatorem Carolum, quem filius non solum excæcauerat, uerumetiam regno expulerat. Illud non solum ingratitudinis, sed etiam tyrannicæ barbariei exemplum est.
units.tr: There was once a king of Mauritania at the siege of Wittenberg with the Emperor Charles, whom his son not only had blinded but had also driven from his kingdom. This is an example not only of ingratitude but also of tyrannical barbarity.

units.la: Erat Francofordiæ ad Mœnum bombardarius, qui cùm mitteret puluerem in bombardam adhuc calidam, ex puluere incenso illius est solo, ita ut moreretur. Omnes dicebant eum fuisse bonum artificem, & ingeniosum: sed illud accidisse ei, quia in iuuentute male tractauerat matrem.
units.tr: There was a gunner at Frankfurt on the Main who, while he was putting powder into a cannon that was still hot, was killed when the powder caught fire, so that he died. Everyone said that he had been a skilled and clever craftsman, but that this had happened to him because in his youth he had treated his mother badly.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Vidimus hic quandam matrem ducentem secum miserrimam puellam, quæ obsessa fuit à diabolo. Hoc mater confessa est filiæ accidisse ex imprecatione sua. Cùm enim dixisset ad illam: Inuolet in te diabolus, statim eadem hora actam esse in furore, Hæc publicè comperta sunt, cùm hic puella & mater examinarentur: unde & postea factæ sunt publicæ præcationes pro puella. Porrò cùm piæ memoriæ Doctor Martinus Lutherus dixisset ad diabolum, citans dictum ex Epistola Iacobi: Increpet te Deus: respondit murmure quodam diabolus per labia puellæ: Increpet, increpet: ut satis appareret uerè puellam obsideri à diabolo.
units.tr: Here we saw a mother bringing with her a most wretched girl who had been possessed by the devil. The mother confessed that this had happened to her daughter through her own curse. For when she had said to the girl, "May the devil fly into you!", at that very hour the girl was seized by a fit of frenzy. These things were publicly established when the girl and her mother were examined here; and afterwards public prayers were offered for the girl. Moreover, when the late Doctor Martin Luther, of pious memory, said to the devil, quoting the saying from the Epistle of James, "The Lord rebuke you", the devil answered with a certain murmur through the girl's lips: "Rebuke, rebuke!" so that it was quite clear that the girl was truly possessed by the devil.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: In oppido Freiberg in Misnia, accidit ante paucos annos, ut quidam iracundus & ad malè imprecandū pronus senex filio quoddā negociū citò expedire mādaret: quod parētis mandatū filius parui faciens, in loco quodam, ac si illud non audiuisset, aliquandiu commoratur: qua ex re pater, aliàs satis morosus, mirum in modum furore accenditur, ac filio, ne unquam uiuus ex eodem loco discedat, horribiliter imprecatur. Facta ea imprecatione, filius continuò ibidem stare incipit, nec potuit ulla ratione uel medio uiuus inde auelli.
units.tr: A few years ago, in the town of Freiberg in Meissen, it happened that an irascible old man, prone to cursing, ordered his son to carry out a certain task quickly. The son, caring nothing for his father's command, lingered for a while in a certain place, as if he had not heard it. Because of this, the father, otherwise rather peevish, was wonderfully inflamed with rage and cursed his son dreadfully, that he should never leave that place alive. Once this curse was uttered, the son immediately began to stand there, and by no means or remedy could he be pulled away from it alive.

units.la: Nocturno tempore coacti sunt ei parētes pulpitū apponere, cui aliquantulum dormiturus sese inclinaret. Conspiciuntur autem hodie adhuc manifestà in pauimento, ubi totum illud triennium constiterat, pedum uestigia. Tandem elapso triennij spacio, pœna piorum precibus, quæ quotidie pro eo fiebant, ita mitigata est, ut in uicino loco integrum iam quadriennium sedere potuerit. Sedet autem macilento admodum uultu, parum comedit, pauca etiam interdum loquitur. Interrogatus uero à quibusdam hominibus honestis, quomodo res sese cum ipso haberet, nihil propemodum aliud respondit, quàm diuinitus quidem se castigari, & in manu Dei situm esse, quid tandem de eo fiat: non tamen de æterna salute per solum Christum nobis acquisita se quicquam desperare. Postea uero elapsis illis septem annis, mortuus est in agnitione & fiducia mediatoris Domini nostri Iesu Christi, anno 1552 die undecimo Septembris.
units.tr: At night his parents were compelled to put a footstool there, on which he might rest and sleep a little while leaning forward. Even today the footprints can be seen in the floor where he had stood for those three years. At last, when three years had passed, his punishment was softened by the prayers of the pious, which were offered for him every day, so that in a nearby place he was able to sit for a whole four years. He sits with a very wasted face, eats little, and sometimes speaks only a few words. When some respectable men asked him how things stood with him, he answered almost nothing else than that he was indeed being chastised by God and that he was in God's hand, to be done with as God would finally decide; yet he did not despair at all of his eternal salvation, which has been won for us by Christ alone. Afterwards, when those seven years had passed, he died, in the knowledge and trust of our Mediator, the Lord Jesus Christ, on 11 September 1552.

units.la: Linus praeceptor Herculis est ab Hercule, illi sacapiti eius tabula, interfectus. Tale praemium plurimi pro beneficijs acceptis reddunt.
units.tr: Linus, the teacher of Hercules, was killed by Hercules, who struck his sacred head with a tablet. Many men repay benefits received in just such a reward.

units.la: Alexander quanquam non laesit suum praeceptorem Aristotelem, sicut Hercules Linun: tamen ab ipso fuit, alieniore animo, & Callisthene Aristotelis ex sorore nepotem miserabiliter cruciauit.
units.tr: Alexander, although he did not harm his teacher Aristotle as Hercules harmed Linus, nevertheless treated him with a more estranged spirit, and he cruelly tortured Callisthenes, the nephew of Aristotle through his sister.

units.la: Plutarchus recitat dictum cuiusdam Philosophi, dicentis, se dextra tradere doctrinam, sed multos sinistra accipere.
units.tr: Plutarch relates a saying of a certain philosopher, who said that he handed over his teaching with his right hand, but that many received it with their left.

units.la: Ioannes Damascenus, qui uixit tempore Theodosij, uel Valentiniani Imperatoris, habuit apud se discipulum Persicum, quem diligenter erudiebat. Ille discipulus aliquando nactus scribendi occasionem sionem, scripsit epistolam nomine Ioannis Damascenī præceptoris sui & illius manum imitatus est. Erat autem argumentum epistolæ: Ego Ioannes Damascenus significo regi Persico, ut si uelit, veniat, iam posse cum capere Imperatorem Valentinianum, propter illas & alias occasiones. Hanc deinde epistolam sparsit in aula regis Persici, quæ cum offerretur regi Persico, misit eam mox Imperatori Valentiniano. Imperator uero ad se uocans Damascenum, monstrauit illi literas, & interrogauit, quare hæc scripsisset? Ille diligenter inspiciens literas, dixit: Domine Imperator, ego agnosco meam manum, eamq; non possum negare, sed sanctè iuro, me nihil unquam tale cogitasse, minus uero scripsisse. Imperator dixit, non potes negare, est enim manus tua. Ita ille uictus, dextra manu mutilatus est. Talem gratiam & mercedem ille ingratus discipulus suo præceptori reddidit.
units.tr: John of Damascus, who lived in the time of the Emperor Theodosius or Valentinian, had with him a Persian disciple whom he instructed diligently. That disciple, once having the opportunity to write, wrote a letter in the name of his teacher John of Damascus, imitating his hand. The content of the letter was this: "I, John of Damascus, inform the king of Persia that, if he wishes, he may come, since he can now capture the Emperor Valentinian, on account of those and other opportunities." He then scattered this letter in the court of the king of Persia; and when it was handed to the king of Persia, he at once sent it to the Emperor Valentinian. The emperor, however, summoned Damascene to himself, showed him the letter, and asked why he had written these things. Looking carefully at the letter, he said: "Lord Emperor, I recognise my hand, and I cannot deny it; but I solemnly swear that I never thought of such a thing, and much less wrote it." The emperor said: "You cannot deny it, for it is your hand." So, overcome in this way, he was maimed in his right hand. This is the favour and reward that the ungrateful disciple gave to his teacher.

units.la: INGRATITVDO ERGA bene meritos.
units.tr: INGRATITUDE TOWARDS THOSE WHO HAVE DESERVED WELL.

units.la: Clitum, cuius mater nutrix Alexandri Magni fuit, à quo idem in bello seruatus erat, Alexander tandem interfecit. In prima pugna Alexander pugnauit cum Persico duce, qui decusserat ei galeam, & erat iam uictor: periisset Alexander nisi Clitus interuenisset, & ducè Persicum interfecisset: ita fuit ita fuit Clitus seruator uitæ Alexandri. Hunc Cli‐tum interfecit Alexander, in uino liberius loquen‐tem pro patre Alexandri Philippo. Putabat enim eam parrhisiam sibi licere apud suum μετέχνον. Alexandrum uero illud factum sæpe pœnituit, ita ut non diu postea uiueret.
units.tr: Clitus, whose mother had been nurse to Alexander the Great, and by whom the same Alexander had been saved in war, Alexander at last killed. In the first battle Alexander fought with a Persian commander, who had knocked off his helmet and was already the victor. Alexander would have perished had Clitus not intervened and killed the Persian commander. Thus Clitus was the saviour of Alexander's life. Alexander killed this Clitus when, speaking rather freely over wine, he spoke on behalf of Alexander's father Philip. For he thought he might use such frankness with his own child [τέκνον]. But Alexander often regretted that deed, so much so that he did not live long afterwards.

units.la: Prouerbium medicorum est: Accipe dum dolet: quia bene sciunt medici se postea negligi, sed sacræ literæ ferunt: Honora medicum, quia Deus eum creauit propter necessitatem. Sic homines affecti sunt, ut quando alicuius opera indiget, simulato ipsum honore afficiant: simulatq; uero non amplius indigent, contemnant.
units.tr: There is a proverb among physicians: "Take him while he is in pain." For physicians know well that they are neglected afterwards. But Holy Scripture says: "Honour the physician, for God created him because of need." People are so disposed that when they need someone's services, they honour him with feigned respect, but as soon as they no longer need him, they despise him.

units.la: Serpens erat ingressus in antrum ibi quidam obdiderat lapidem antro. Venit uiator & ibi casu dormit. Serpens ubi cognouisset adesse hominem: Mi homo, inquit, libera me ex hoc antro, & reuol‐ue inde lapidem: quia ualde premor siti, sicut serpentes ualde sitiunt, sitimq; ferre non possunt. At ille: Non audeo, uereor ne perdas me. Respondit serpens: Libera me ex hoc carcere, dabo tibi summam mercedem, quam mundus benemeritis largitur. Ille aperit: Egresso iam serpente ex antro, ipsum se interfecturum esse dicit. Talem enim gratiam mundus bene meritis solere reddere affirmat. Ille hanc mundi ingratitudinem negat, & rem ad iudices deferre iubet. Annuit serpens, & interrogat alios de mun‐di gra‐ di gratitudine. Incidunt forte in equum senio iam confectum, qui in campum aliquem erat detrusus, quem serpens de mundi ingratitudine interrogās: respondit equus: Multis iam annis domino meo servivi, iam me vetulum domo sua fustibus propulsavit in hunc campum, ut fame peream. Audi inquit serpens, hanc etiam gratiam tibi declarabo. Rogemus, inquit viator alios, forsitan suo merito hic equus ex domo sui domini est eiectus. Progressus longius, vetulus canis ipsis obuius fit: à quo idem responsum, quod ab equo audiuerunt. Querebatur enim se senio confectum domo herili prohiberi, et extrusum esse, ut fame periret. Nec huic responso acquiescit viator: petit alium arbitrũ. Incidunt tandem in vulpem, quæ de quæstione proposita se consulturam secum dixit, & viatorem ab ductum à serpente paululum adit: eiq; promittit se ab hoc periculo ipsum liberaturum, hac conditione, ut omnes gallinas suas ipsi concedat. Libenter se id facturum respondit viator. Vulpes inquit, hac ratione eludemus serpentem: petam, ut mihi suum antrum iterum ostendat, quoniam mihi nullum de re ignota iudicium esse potest. Præcedam ego speculaturus antrum, & cum serpens, ut solet, tardè me sequetur, & reptauerit in antrum, qua potero velocitate ex antro recurrã, ut serpens se tam citò inuertere nequeat: Tunc tu rursus antrũ lapide obstruas: Bene, inquit uiator, res processit sicut deliberauerant. Verùm postea galinas etiam uulpes poscit: iubet uiator uulpem usq; ad domum suam sequi, & precium, quod ei promiserat, accipere. Domum ueniens uiator, rem totam, sicut acta fuerat, mulieri exponit, & adijciens quanto in periculo fuisset, ex quo uulpis consilio & opera liberatus esset, hac conditione, ut uulpi galinas suas largiretur. Mulier indignabunda, quæ fortasse galinas magis quàm uirum curauit, re longo tempore deliberata, mulier deniq; uulpi galinas promittit, sed ita ut simul uulpi insidias struat. Dum enim in caueam uulpem intromisit, recludit eam, & in ea uulpem interficit. Ita uulpi summum precium, quod mundus bene de se meritis largitur, datur.
units.tr: A serpent had entered a cave, and a certain man had blocked the cave with a stone. A traveller came by and, by chance, fell asleep there. When the serpent realised that a man was near, it said: "My friend, free me from this cave and roll the stone away, for I am severely oppressed by thirst, as serpents are greatly thirsty and cannot bear thirst." But the man replied: "I dare not; I fear you will destroy me." The serpent answered: "Free me from this prison, and I will give you the greatest reward that the world bestows on those who have deserved well." He opened the cave, and once the serpent had come out, it declared that it would kill him. For it asserted that the world is accustomed to repay those who have deserved well in just such a way. The man denied that this was the world's ingratitude and ordered the matter to be referred to judges. The serpent agreed and questioned others about the world's gratitude. By chance they came upon an old horse, now worn out with age, which had been thrust out into a field. When the serpent asked it about the world's ingratitude, the horse replied: "For many years I served my master; now, being old, he has driven me from his house with clubs into this field, so that I may die of hunger." "Listen," said the serpent, "I will show you this gratitude too." "Let us ask others," said the traveller, "perhaps this horse was cast out of its master's house on account of its own desert." Going on a little further, they met an old dog, and it gave the same answer the horse had given. It complained that, worn out with age, it had been kept from its master's house and thrust out to perish of hunger. The traveller was not satisfied with this answer and sought another arbiter. At last they came upon a fox, which said it would consider the question proposed; it approached the traveller, who was being led about by the serpent, a little apart, and promised to free him from this danger on one condition: that he give it all his hens. The traveller replied that he would gladly do so. "Then," said the fox, "we will outwit the serpent in this way. I will ask it to show me its cave again, since I cannot judge a matter I do not know. I will go ahead to inspect the cave, and when the serpent, as is its habit, follows me slowly and crawls into the cave, I will run back out of it as fast as I can, so that the serpent cannot turn around so quickly. Then you must block up the cave with the stone again." "Good," said the traveller, "the matter has turned out as they planned." But afterwards the fox also demanded the hens. The traveller ordered the fox to follow him to his house and receive the payment he had promised. On coming home, the traveller explained the whole affair to his wife as it had happened, adding how great a danger he had been in and how he had been freed by the fox's counsel and effort, on the condition that he give the fox his hens. The wife was indignant. Perhaps she cared more for her hens than for her husband, but after deliberating for a long time, she at last promised the fox the hens, yet arranged a trap for it at the same time. For when she had let the fox into a cage, she shut it in and killed it there. Thus the fox received the greatest reward that the world bestows on those who have deserved well.

units.la: Ingratus hospes.
units.tr: The ungrateful guest.

units.la: Pater Alexandri Philippus, rex Macedonicus, miserat militem ad explorandum negocium aliquod, qui homo erat audax, sicut plerumq; sunt milites. Cùm itaq; oportere ipsum nauigare sæuis tempestatibus, fecit naufragium, & seruatus est à colono in litore, qui scapha excepit eum, cùm nauis eius esset fracta, transuexit eum domum, & collocans eum in cubiculo tractauit hospitaliter: post tringinta dies instruxit eum uiatico, ut posset redire domum. Miles domum rediens, narrat ff singula regi de naufragio{&}Ccedil; suis periculis: uerùm tacet beneficium hospitis. Rex gratulatur ei reditum, ac lætatur de incolumitate serui, inquiens: Ego ero gratus, daboq; tibi prædiū aliquod. Seruus respondit: Domine rex, quæso ut facias, uidi prædium in littore, quod si in memoriam meorum periculorum mihi possidendum dares, rem mihi gratissimā præstares. Rex præ nimia lætitia, aut fortassis quod multum biberat (multum enim bibit pater Alexandri) iubet ei attribui prædium illud ac mittit ad præfectum Pausaniam, ut scribat in præfectura, prædium esse istius militis. Colonus uidens nullam sibi referri gratiam, uerùm etiam eripi prædium, uenit ad regem, & narrat ei totum negocium, ut gestum erat. Rex audita causa ingeti ira exarsit, & statim militem iussit præhendi, & inuri fronti ipsius stigmata, his literis: Hospes Ingratus. Sic Dauid fuit ingratus Uriæ. Seneca inquit: Omnes sumus ingrati. Ausomius: Sunt homines humeris quos si quis gestat ad urbem Ausoniam, domiti quæ caput orbis erat: Nec tamen ad portā placidè deponat eosdem: Gratia præteriti nulla laboris erit.
units.tr: Philip, the father of Alexander and king of Macedon, had sent a soldier to investigate some matter. He was a bold man, as soldiers usually are. Since he had to sail in violent storms, he suffered shipwreck and was saved by a farmer on the shore, who picked him up in a small boat when his ship had been wrecked. The farmer carried him home, put him in a bedroom and treated him hospitably. After thirty days he provided him with provisions so that he could return home. On returning home, the soldier told the king everything about the shipwreck and his dangers, but he kept silent about the host's kindness. The king congratulated him on his return and rejoiced at the servant's safety, saying: "I will be grateful and will give you some estate." The servant replied: "Lord King, I beg you to do so. I have seen an estate on the shore which, if you were to give it to me to possess in memory of my dangers, would be a most welcome favour." The king, in excessive joy, or perhaps because he had drunk a great deal (for Alexander's father drank heavily), ordered that estate to be assigned to him and sent word to the prefect Pausanias to record in the prefecture that the estate belonged to this soldier. The farmer, seeing that no thanks were offered to him but that the estate was actually being taken from him, came to the king and related the whole affair as it had happened. The king, having heard the case, was seized with great anger and at once ordered the soldier to be arrested and branded on the forehead with the letters: "Ungrateful guest." Thus David was ungrateful to Uriah. Seneca says: "We are all ungrateful." Ausonius: "There are men whom, if one carries them on his shoulders to Ausonian Rome, once the head of the world, yet he does not set those same men gently down at the gate: no gratitude will be felt for the labour that is past."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Demetrius Phalerensis philosophus, qui fuit Theophrasti auditor, princeps reipublicæ Athe-niensis niensis, inuitauerat ad cœnam Philosophos, & de-derat eis de optimo genere uini. Cum uerò ueniret ad quendam Cynicum, ille Demetriũ lagena uini petiuit, inquiens, Philosophis non esse tam bonum uinum dandum. Ista non est fatuitas, sed insania be-nemerentibus malã gratiã reserre. Historia extat apud Athenæum.
units.tr: Demetrius of Phalerum, a philosopher who had been a pupil of Theophrastus and was ruler of the Athenian state, had invited the philosophers to dinner and given them some of the best wine. When he came to a certain Cynic, the man asked Demetrius for a jug of wine, saying that philosophers should not be given such good wine. That is not foolishness but madness, to repay good deeds with bad thanks. The story is found in Athenaeus.

units.la: Alphonsus, cùm ad eum referretur, aliquem ab eo in bello defecisse, cui multa præstiterat benefi-cia, tum ipse multa secum in animo reputans de in-gratitudine istius hominis, tandem ad se revocatus inquit: Quid ego queror de ingratitudine illius? ego multo magis ingratus sum Deo meo, à quo multis maximis beneficijs sum affecțus.
units.tr: When Alphonso was told that someone who had received many benefits from him had deserted him in war, he reflected for a long time within himself on the ingratitude of that man, and then, coming to himself, said: "Why do I complain of his ingratitude? I am far more ungrateful to my God, by whom I have been loaded with so many very great benefits."

units.la: Quidam euaserat tres tyrannos, Caligulam, Claudium & Neronem, qui multos bonos homines interfecerunt. Interrogatus igitur ab aliquo, quo-modo euasisset tantos tyrannos, cum fuisset auli-cus? Responđit ille: Iniurias accipiendo, & insuper gratias agendo. Hæc est doctrina aulica, & alias quoq; doctrina de exercitijs, patientiæ & ingrati-tudinis, quæ Deus à nobis postulat.
units.tr: A certain man had survived three tyrants, Caligula, Claudius and Nero, who had killed many good men. When someone asked him how he had survived such great tyrants, though he had been a courtier, he replied: "By accepting injuries and, on top of that, giving thanks." This is the lesson of the court, and also the other lesson of the exercises of patience and of ingratitude, which God demands of us.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Imperator Iustinianus habuit ducem magnitu-dine animi, alijsq; uirtutibus præstantem, nomine Bellisarium. Hic uir excellens, sua fortitudine to-tum ferè orbem terrarum in ordinem redegit, imperio Iustiniani subiecit. Habuit coniugem formosam, quæ, ut fit, propter uirtutem & præclara facta mariti nonnihil insolens est facta. Hanc insolentiam & istum fastum nō potuit ferre Sophia coniunx Imperatoris Iustiniani. Igitur calumnijs & dolis effecit, ut propter uxoris insolentiam optimè merito uiro Belisario oculi effoderentur. Sic tantus uir, tanta fortitudine præditus, & optimè de Imperatore meritus, postea redactus est ad summam paupertatem, ut coactus sit sedere ad tepla & colligere stipem, unde victum haberet. Omnia sunt ingrata, nihil fecisse benigne est. Item post donationem, celeriter senescit gratia.
units.tr: The emperor Justinian had a general, Belisarius, who excelled in greatness of spirit and in his other virtues. By his courage this outstanding man brought almost the whole world under order and subjected it to the rule of Justinian. He had a beautiful wife who, as often happens, became somewhat proud because of her husband's virtue and distinguished deeds. Sophia, the wife of the emperor Justinian, could not bear this pride and arrogance. So by slander and tricks she brought it about that Belisarius, a man who had deserved very well, had his eyes put out because of his wife's arrogance. Thus this great man, endowed with such courage and who had deserved so well of the emperor, was afterwards reduced to utter poverty, so that he was forced to sit by the warm baths and beg alms in order to get his food. Everything is ungrateful; to have done a kindness is nothing. Likewise, after a gift, favour quickly grows old.

units.la: Senex uir, & honestus nobilis Fridericus à Dön, dicebat ad cancelarium D. Pontanum, cum uideret eum esse sedulum & diligentem in suo officio. Idem precium datur maculanti hypocaustū & purganti.
units.tr: The old and honourable nobleman Friedrich von Dönn used to say to the chancellor, Dr Pontanus, when he saw him being diligent and conscientious in his office: the same reward is given to the one who soils the hypocaust and to the one who cleans it.

units.la: Pindarus: παλαιὰ γὰρ ἐυδλε χάρις, ἀμνάμονες δὲ βροτοί: antiqua gratia dormit, & homines sunt ingrati.
units.tr: Pindar: "For ancient grace sleeps, and mortals are ungrateful" [παλαιὰ γὰρ ἐυδλε χάρις, ἀμνάμονες δὲ βροτοί]: that is, old gratitude sleeps, and men are forgetful.

units.la: Docebo uos rhithmum de ingratitudine: Friß dreck scheiß goldt, sowerde dir die Meidlein holt.Per puellas intellige mundū, in quo si quis excellere et præstās esse uelit,muß er dreck fressen,id est, pati iniurias & nihil contradicere.Vult significare: patere omnes iniurias, & insuper gratias agito,uix tamen consistes.
units.tr: I shall teach you a rhyme about ingratitude: "Eat dirt, shit gold, and the little maidens will come to you." By the maidens understand the world. If anyone wishes to excel and be outstanding in it, he must eat dirt, that is, suffer injuries and not contradict anything. The meaning is: suffer all injuries and, on top of that, give thanks; yet you will hardly hold your ground.

units.la: QVINTVM PRAECEPTUM.
units.tr: QVINTVM PRAECEPTUM.

units.la: AMICICIA ET CANDOR.
units.tr: AMICICIA ET CANDOR.

units.la: In Cæsare reperitur pulcherrimum exemplum duorum militum Romanorum Cottæ & Sabini, inter quos etsi antea fuerat æmulatio, tamen in extremo uitæ periculo fiunt optimi & coniunctissimi amici. Cotta inciderat in periculum. Sabinus accurrit & liberat eum. Sabinus in simile periculum uenit (sicut fit) ut in auxiliatorem uerterentur arma: ibi Cotta rursus liberat eum, & sic depellunt hostes. Ideoq; in utroq; fuit felix euentus, quia fuerunt facti in illo summo periculo concordes amici. Si iam in Germania inter principes & omnes Theologos etiam talis coniunctiones animorum & uoluntatum essent contra externos hostes, ah quàm utiles & pulchræ res fierent.
units.tr: In Caesar we find a very fine example in two Roman soldiers, Cotta and Sabinus. Although there had been rivalry between them earlier, in mortal danger they became the best and closest of friends. Cotta had fallen into peril, and Sabinus ran up and freed him. Then Sabinus found himself in a similar danger, and as often happens, their weapons turned against the one who came to help. At that point Cotta in turn freed him, and so they drove back the enemy. Each of them had a happy outcome because in that great danger the friends were of one mind. If only the princes and all the theologians in Germany were joined in such a bond of minds and wills against foreign enemies, how useful and fine things would become!

units.la: Saluftius: Ea demum uera amicicia est, idem uelle ac nolle. Simile dictum apud Platonem citatur: Non aurum, non adamas fulget splendidius, quàm bonorum mentes consentientes.
units.tr: Sallust: "That is true friendship: to want the same things and to refuse the same things." A similar saying is cited from Plato: "Neither gold nor the diamond shines more brightly than the minds of good men agreeing together."

units.la: Demetrius filius Antigoni, cum sciret & uideret patrem ualde durum, & iratum factum esse Lysimacho, monuit eum ut fugeret irā patris, scripsitq; sua hasta in puluere φσύγε φσύγε. Hic lectis literis, statim cogitauit non esse de nihilo, fugit in Thraciam, ubi paulo pòst factus rex. Et est ille Lysimachus qui ab Alexãdro leoni obiectus, leonem interfecit, homo fortis & animosus. Demetrius autem mortuus est deinceps in acie, octogesimo ætatis suæ anno.
units.tr: Demetrius, son of Antigonus, knew and saw that his father was very harsh and had become angry with Lysimachus. He advised Lysimachus to flee his father's anger, and he wrote in the dust with his spear: "Flee, flee" [φεῦγε φεῦγε]. When Lysimachus had read the letters, he at once thought they were not written for nothing, and he fled into Thrace, where shortly afterwards he became king. This is the Lysimachus who was thrown to a lion by Alexander and killed the lion, a brave and spirited man. Demetrius himself later died in battle, in the eightieth year of his age.

units.la: Aristoteles scribit, Græcos templa Gratiarum in medijs urbibus condere solitos, ut ciues mutuæ beneuolentiæ, amicitiæ atq; gratitudinis admonerentur.
units.tr: Aristotle writes that the Greeks were accustomed to build temples of the Graces in the middle of their cities, so that citizens would be reminded of mutual goodwill, friendship and gratitude.

units.la: Apud Ciceronem & Liuium hoc dictum sæpius reperitur: Amicicias decet esse immortales, inimicicias uerò mortales.
units.tr: In Cicero and Livy this saying is found often: friendships ought to be immortal, but enmities mortal.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Nicolaus de Disbach uir nobilis, ac senator urbis inclitæ Bernensis, non ante multos annos elapsos, in proximo bello Heluetico preclarum & memorabile exemplum suæ initæ & antiquæ amicitiæ in academia Basilienfi erga condiscipulum, hoc tempore ciuem Vriensem declarauit. Cùm is ciuis, olim D. Nicolai de Disbach condiscipulus, captus & in arcem Lentzburg deductus, ut ibi de uerijs hostium concilijs & stratagematibus in tortura examinaretur: ibi ipse fidem suam ueteri amico debitam interposuit, misitq; annulum, in quem sua insignia erant insculpta, ad Capitaneum illius loci, eumq; rogauit, ut suo captiuo amico parceret: adret: addes esse adhuc alias rationes quibus conatus & consilia hostium intelligi possent. Debere enim se illud suo ueteri amico ex foedere inchoatae in academia Basiliensi amicitiae officium, ut pro eo intercederet, ac captiuus intelligeret, se in ipsius calamitate dolere, ac non solum id, ut pro eo intercederet, sed etiam alia beneuolentiae & liberalitatis officia debere. Hac fidelitate in conseruando amicitiae foedere Capitancus & alij moti, huic ciui Vriensi pepercerunt, probaueruntq; consilium huius praestantis uiri, qui amicos suos calamitatibus oppressos non negligeret.
units.tr: Nicolaus von Diesbach, a nobleman and senator of the famous city of Bern, not many years ago, in the recent Swiss war, showed a notable and memorable example of the friendship he had entered into long ago at the academy of Basel, toward a fellow student, now a citizen of Uri. This citizen, once a fellow student of Nicolaus von Diesbach, had been captured and taken to the castle of Lenzburg, where he was to be questioned under torture about the enemy's plans and stratagems. There Nicolaus pledged his faith to his old friend and sent to the captain of that place a ring engraved with his own arms, asking him to spare his captive friend, since there were still other ways by which the enemy's plans and attempts could be understood. He said that he owed this duty to his old friend by the bond of the friendship begun at the academy of Basel: that he should intercede for him, so that the prisoner would understand that Nicolaus grieved at his misfortune, and that he owed him not only this intercession but also other acts of goodwill and generosity. Moved by this loyalty in keeping the bond of friendship, the captain and the others spared this citizen of Uri, and they approved the counsel of this excellent man, who did not neglect friends overwhelmed by misfortune.

units.la: Sic profecto uerum dixit ille Philosophus inquiēs, uices fortunae uarie pingere amicos. Quare si in illo bono nobili non fuisset illa uirtutum integritas, quae amicis uersantibus in periculis opitulatur, potuisset illum ueterem suum amicum deserere: sicut prohdolor multi omnibus temporibus faciunt, qui uerbis magis quam factis amici sunt, postea uero in periculis eosdem amicos reliquunt.
units.tr: Truly that philosopher spoke the truth when he said that fortune's changes paint friends in various colours. Therefore, if that noble man had not had that integrity of virtue which comes to the aid of friends in dangers, he could have abandoned his old friend. Alas, many people in every age do just this: they are friends in words more than in deeds, and afterwards they desert those same friends in peril.

units.la: Francofordiae ad Moenum uidi in pariete uirginem pictam, quae faciebat coronam ex leucrio flore, qui germanice dicitur, ie lenger ie lieber, cui adiunctus erat rhythmus talis: Ie lenger ie lieber ich bin allein, Denn trew und warheit ist worden klein.
units.tr: At Frankfurt on the Main I saw, on a wall, a painted maiden who was making a garland of the flower called leucrium, which in German is named "ie lenger ie lieber." Attached to it was this rhyme: "The longer, the dearer; I am alone, for faith and truth have become small."

units.la: Senatus Vratislauiensis misit mihi pro sua in me beneuolentia magnum fasciculum literarum mearum ad alios missarum, quem ibi reliquerat tabellarius, misitq; per proprium nuncium suis sumptibus. Rescripsi Senatui, & egi gratias pro illo officio, ac significaui eis, me nihil arcani, nec quicquam de rebus principum scribere, sed tantũ controuersias Ecclesiasticas, & disputationes nostras scholasticas, & posse eos, si postea literæ meæ simili modo negligerētur dilacerare. O quato fidelior fuit hic Senatus Anthonio, cui Cicero in Philippicis exprobrat literarum amicè & secretè scriptarum diuulgationem. Dicitq; eum per hoc è uita tollere uitæ societatem, & amicorum absentium inter se colloquia. Memētote hic & hoc quoque: Athenienses cum incidissent in fasciculum literarum regis Macedonici, omnes infregerunt, exceptis illis, quas ad coniugem scripserat.
units.tr: The Senate of Breslau, out of its goodwill toward me, sent me a large bundle of my letters written to others, which the courier had left there, and it sent them by its own messenger at its own expense. I wrote back to the Senate, thanked them for this service, and told them that I write nothing secret and nothing about the affairs of princes, but only about ecclesiastical controversies and our scholarly disputations; and that, should my letters in future be similarly neglected, they could tear them up. O how much more faithful this Senate was than Antony, whom Cicero in the Philippics reproaches for publishing letters written to him as a friend and in confidence. Cicero says that by this he removed from life the companionship of living and the conversations of absent friends. Remember this too, here: when the Athenians had come upon a bundle of letters of the Macedonian king, they broke open all of them, except those which he had written to his wife.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Philippus Macedo pater Alexandri Magni, cùm Olynthum (quam urbem diu magno conatu & periculo obsederat) tandem expugnasset, eaq; potitus esset difficili victoria, dicitur ad exhilarandos amicos ludos celebres instituisse. Quorum ludorum die, cùm sacrificasset & amicos suos ducesq; conuiuio excepisset, in unum & hilaritatem effusus, iussit unumquemq; cōuiuarum à se aliquid petere, quod cuiq; commodum & dignum esse uideretur. Alijs igitur aliud petentibus & impetratibus pro ut cuiq; usus & necessitas erat, solus iam restabat Satyrus Comœdus, qui propter artem & ingenij dexteritatem in magna apud Regem gratia erat. Eum, cum nihil adhuc petiuisset, inuitant caeteri primum, deinde Philippus, ut quemadmodum alij fecissent, ipse quoq; aliquid peteret, nec donū aut beneuolentia Regis aspernaretur. At ille: quando a te iubeor, inquit: O Rex petā id, quod & mihi petere, & tibi largiri maximè honestum iudico. Fuit mihi uetus amicitia & ius hospitalitatis cum Apollophane Pilnensi, qui cum ex insidijs periisset, metuens cognati iram regiam, filias eius paruas Olynthum, ut illis tutior ibi uita esset, transmisit. Hæ nunc expugnata urbe captiuæ tenentur, & ea iam ætate existentes, ut opportunæ sint nuptui. Has igitur a te peto, Rex, ut eas mea pecunia elocem, ne quid turpe aut indignum ipsæ, mortuo parente, propter fortunæ iniquitatem patiatur. Alij quod sibi lucro arbitrati sunt fore, id a te optarunt, & optatū abstulerunt: ego si uoti mei compos fuero, dotem insuper de meo addam, existimans me hanc fidem memoriæ extincti amici, & relictis ab ea filiabus debere. Ad hunc sermonem a toto conuiuio plausus cum approbatione excitatus est, uictusq; Philippus, iussit puellas Satyro adduci, ac in manus tradi, admiratus hominis fidem & con-stantiam in colenda amicicia, & insuper dotem di-gnam rege adiecit.
units.tr: Philip of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great, when he had at last taken Olynthus (a city he had long besieged with great effort and danger) and gained that difficult victory, is said to have held famous games to cheer his friends. On the day of these games, after he had offered sacrifice and entertained his friends and commanders at a banquet, he grew expansive and merry, and ordered each of the guests to ask him for something that seemed to each of them fitting and worthy. So while the others asked for one thing or another, and received it according to each man's use and need, only Satyrus the comic actor remained, who because of his skill and cleverness stood high in the king's favour. When he had asked for nothing so far, the others first invited him, and then Philip, that he too, as the rest had done, should ask for something and not refuse the king's gift or goodwill. And he said: "Since you order me to, O King, I will ask for what I judge both fitting for me to ask and most honourable for you to grant. I had an old friendship and the bond of hospitality with Apollophanes of Pydna, who, after he perished by treachery and feared the king's anger at his kinsman, sent his small daughters to Olynthus, so that their life might be safer there. Now that the city has been taken, they are held captive, and they are of an age to be fit for marriage. I ask you, then, King, to grant them to me, that I may give them in marriage at my own expense, so that they, now their father is dead, may suffer nothing shameful or unworthy through the unkindness of fortune. Others asked you for what they thought would bring them profit, and having asked, carried it off; if I obtain my wish, I will add a dowry out of my own means as well, judging that I owe this loyalty to the memory of my dead friend and to the daughters he left behind." At this speech applause broke out from the whole banquet, with approval, and Philip, won over, ordered the girls to be brought to Satyrus and handed into his hands, and, admiring the man's loyalty and steadfastness in cherishing friendship, he added a dowry worthy of a king.

units.la: Achilles interrogatus ab Aiace, quos sustinuis-set omnium maximos labores? respondit : Susceptos pro amicis. Cumq; pergeret interrogare, quos au-tem iucundissimos sustinuisset? rursus Achilles: Eosdem inquit, significans heroicum uirum flagra-re immensa quadam amicos iuuandi cupiditate.
units.tr: When Achilles was asked by Ajax which of his labours had been the greatest of all, he answered: those undertaken for friends. And when Ajax went on to ask which ones he had endured with the greatest pleasure, Achilles again replied: "The same ones," signifying that a heroic man burns with an immense desire to help his friends.

units.la: BENEVOLENTIAE MVTATIO, seu simulatio amiciciæ & inimiciciæ.
units.tr: THE CHANGE OF GOODWILL, or the pretence of friendship and enmity.

units.la: Cor humanum est ἀψίνοφον καὶ φιλόνχνον, id est, fastidiens præsentia, & est amans nouitatis, inde uersus est:
units.tr: The human heart is ἀψίνοφον καὶ φιλόνχνον, that is, weary of the present and fond of novelty; hence the verse:

units.la: Omnia uertuntur, certè uertütur amores.
units.tr: All things turn, and surely loves will turn too.

units.la: Item: Ille tuas pennas tam citò uertit amor.
units.tr: Likewise: "Love has turned your wings so quickly."

units.la: Sic Plato: φίλος ἐνμετάβαλον ζῷον. Amicus ualde mutabile animal.
units.tr: So Plato: φίλος ἐνμετάβαλον ζῷον, a friend is a very changeable animal.

units.la: Rex Antigonus iußit sacerdotem suum sacrifi-care, ut Deus defenderet eum ab amicis. Interro-gatus, quare non ab inimicis? Respondit: Ab ini-micis possum mihi ipsi cauere, ab amicis uerò nō. Notare uoluit simulatos amicos.
units.tr: King Antigonus ordered his priest to sacrifice so that God would protect him from his friends. Asked why not from his enemies, he replied: "I can guard myself against enemies, but not against friends." He meant to point out feigned friends.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Cum Dionysius iunior eiecißet Diogenem af-finem, qui & ipsius rector antea fuerat: Plato me-tuens tuens sibi quoq; aliquid periculi imminere, pro-pter Diogenis amicicia, auellit se à Dionysio qui-bus modis potest. Dimittitur igitur non sine magno munere. Scribunt enim octoginta talenta ei donata esse, hoc est, octo & quinquaginta mil-lia coronatorum. Forte eo tempore Plato prædi-xit eclipsin futuram. Ibi Aristippus qui unà e-rat, ait, se significationem eius eclipsis diuinatu-rum, ac iocans, inquit: Portendi inimiciciam inter Regem & Platonem. Hoc ioco facetè amiciciæ mutationem ostendit Aristippus.
units.tr: When the younger Dionysius had banished Diogenes, his kinsman by marriage, who had earlier been his tutor, Plato, fearing that some danger was hanging over himself too because of his friendship with Diogenes, withdrew from Dionysius by whatever means he could. He was therefore dismissed, not without a great gift; for they write that eighty talents were given to him, that is, fifty-eight thousand crowns. At that time Plato happened to predict a future eclipse. Aristippus, who was present with him, said that he would divine the meaning of that eclipse, and joking, said: "It portends enmity between the king and Plato." By this jest Aristippus wittily showed the change of friendship.

units.la: DE HOSPITIBVS.
units.tr: CONCERNING HOSPITALITY.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Apud Massilienses lex fuit, ut peregrini urbem ingredi cupientes, arma in porta relinquere iube-rentur. Propter quos mores ciuitas Massilia ualde laudatur. Est autem ea urbs in Gallia Narbonēsi, ab Ionibus qui ex Asia illuc profecti erant condi-ta. Iones porro primi & uetustissimi Graecorum, habuerunt multum doctrinae, & diligenter reti-nuerũt uetustissimorum morum atq; rituum disci-plinam, quam deinceps in hanc urbem transtule-runt. Voluerunt itaq; significare hac lege, hospi-tes debere esse modestos, & simul habere defensi-onem ab illis, qui eos excipiunt.
units.tr: Among the Massilians there was a law that foreigners wishing to enter the city were ordered to leave their arms at the gate. For these customs the city of Massilia is greatly praised. It is in Gallia Narbonensis and was founded by Ionians who had set out there from Asia. The Ionians, moreover, the first and most ancient of the Greeks, had much learning and carefully preserved the discipline of very ancient customs and rites, which they afterwards transferred to this city. By this law, then, they wished to signify that guests ought to be modest and at the same time to have protection from those who receive them.

units.la: Triptolemo regi Attico dicũtur donatae fruges, quòd mœstam Cererem hospicio excepisset. Originem fabulæ eam esse opinor, quòd is fuerit excellenti uirtute & probitate morum præditus, qui frumenta ex Thracia (ut ferunt) uel aliunde aduexerit ac reposuerit, quæ postea tempore famis rursus pauperibus distribuit: quo beneficio clarũ nomen adeptus est.
units.tr: The fruits of the earth are said to have been given to King Triptolemus of Attica because he had received the sorrowing Ceres as a guest. I suppose the origin of the fable is that he was endowed with outstanding virtue and integrity of character; he brought grain from Thrace (as they say) or from elsewhere, stored it, and afterwards distributed it again to the poor in a time of famine. By this benefaction he won a famous name.

units.la: DE CONVIVIIS.
units.tr: On Banquets

units.la: Pulchrum est apud Xenophōtem in conuiuio. Socrates sic dicit ad aliquem: Dic mihi quid sit se turpiter gerere in conuiuio? Respōdet alter. Quid sit non possum dicere: sed quid mihi uideatur dicā. Dicas igitur quid uideatur? Est molestia afficere cōuiuas λυπεῖν τὰς συμπότας. Ad quæ Socrates respōdet: Hoc tu facis, quia tacendo nobis omnib. es molestus. Quare amantes conuiuia, amate etiā eleganter & acutè dicta in conuiuijs.
units.tr: It is a fine thing in Xenophon at a banquet. Socrates says to someone: "Tell me, what does it mean to behave shamefully at a banquet?" The other replies: "I cannot say what it is, but I can tell you what seems so to me." "Then tell me what seems so." "It is to annoy one's fellow drinkers" [λυπεῖν τὰς συμπότας]. To this Socrates replies: "You yourself do this, because by your silence you are a nuisance to all of us. So you who love banquets, love also elegant and witty sayings at banquets."

units.la: Plutarchus nominat cōuiuium uulpis & gruis, ut est in fabulis, quando uulpes inuitât grues, grues uicissim uulpes. Talia sunt conuiuia, aliorum dicta obseruantium, ut carpāt dextra ab alijs dicta: non colloquentium inter se, ubi duo aut tres sedent in conuiuio, ipsi silent omnino, auscultant insidiosè, quid alij loquantur aut conferant, ita ut aliquis magis cum feris conuersari exoptet, quàm cū talibus conuiuari.
units.tr: Plutarch calls it the banquet of the fox and the crane, as in the fables, when the fox invites the cranes and the cranes in turn invite the fox. Such are the banquets of those who watch what others say, snatching up whatever others have said, not joining in conversation with one another. Where two or three sit at table, they themselves keep totally silent and listen furtively to what the others say or discuss, so that someone would rather keep company with wild beasts than dine with such people.

units.la: Et Plutarchus etiam dicit alibi: Non esse uociferandum, sicut ebriosi rustici & inebriati uino, aut cereuisia. Aliqui debent esse uocales, aliqui cõ-sonantes: aliqui loquantur, aliqui non sint mutæ, sed consonantes.
units.tr: And Plutarch also says elsewhere that one should not shout, as drunken peasants do, or men inebriated with wine or beer. Some should be talkative and some should harmonize; some should speak, and some should not be mute, but in accord.

units.la: Bachilidis dicit, quatuor in conuiuijs requiri. 1 Modicus cibi & potus apparatus. 2 Suaue collo-quium. 3 Vera conuiuarum benevolentia. 4 Bonũ uinum, quo maxime delectantur senes. Et alius di-cit ultra duo pocula non esse ebibenda in conui-uio, sanitatis causa.
units.tr: Bachilis says that four things are required at banquets: (1) a modest provision of food and drink; (2) pleasant conversation; (3) true goodwill among the guests; (4) good wine, in which the old especially delight. Another says that no more than two cups should be drunk at a banquet, for the sake of health.

units.la: Conuiuia Cyclopica.
units.tr: Cyclopean Banquets

units.la: Satellites regis Galliæ largius se uino ingurgi-tantes contuderunt uitrea pocula, ac alter alteri præbibit illum puluerem. Elapsis uix duobus men-sibus, omnes mortui sunt. Hæc mihi narrauit quì-dam multis nobis notus, ipsisq; assidens, cui tamen ut homini scholastico pepercerunt.
units.tr: Attendants of the king of France, gorging themselves on wine more than was fitting, smashed their glass cups, and each drank the powder to the others. Scarcely two months had passed when all of them were dead. This was told to me by a certain man well known to many of us, who sat with them himself, but they spared him because he was a scholar.

units.la: Ante paucos annos fuerunt quidam Ambergæ in Bauaria, qui longa potatione inebriētati, tan-dem uasa testacea, è quibus biberant contundunt, seu in puluerem redigunt, & alter alteri illum pul-uerem in uino præbibit: tandem uentum est ad ui-tra, quæ similiter in puluerem redacta sunt, ac in-uicem sibi præbiberunt. Hæc ante paucos annos historia huc scripta est, additumq; erat in literis tres ex nobilium numero eo die esse mortuos, re-liquos ægrotare, & mortem certissimam expe-ctare. Non mirum est, uenire Turcā & alias pœ-nas, cùm nas,cùm tam impiè uiuamus. Es ist zuerbarmen das wir arme elende Teutschen so sewisch und so uihisch leben: Vuir fressen und sauffen uns kräck, todt,und in die heel hinnein. Imo deterius iam ui-uitur,quàm bestiæ,certè bestiæ sibi nociua fugiũt. Ita iam diabolus grassatur in genere humano:credo non fuisse tam nociua illa uasa testacea , quàm sunt uitrà , quæ in aluum demissa intestina arro-dunt,unde homo superstes esse nequit.
units.tr: A few years ago there were some men at Amberg in Bavaria who, made drunk by a long drinking bout, at last smashed the earthen vessels they had drunk from, or reduced them to powder, and one drank that powder in wine to another. At last they came to the glasses, which likewise were reduced to powder and drunk to one another. This story was written down here a few years ago, and it was added in the letter that three of the nobles of that day had died, and the rest were sick and expecting certain death. It is no wonder that the Turk comes, and other punishments, since we live so impiously. It is a pity that we poor wretched Germans live so swinishly and so beastly: we gorge and guzzle ourselves to a crack, to death, and into hell. Indeed, we now live worse than beasts, for beasts at least flee what harms them. So now the devil rages through the human race. I believe those earthen vessels were not as harmful as glasses are, which, once lowered into the belly, gnaw away the intestines, so that a man who has swallowed them cannot survive.

units.la: In quodam episcopatu potauerunt aliqui, adeò ut ex ipsorum numero unus sit mortuus , nihilo-minus tamen reliqui,exemplo iræ Dei non com-moti,mortuo suam partem infuderunt.
units.tr: In a certain bishopric some men drank so much that one of their number died; nevertheless the rest, not moved by the example of God's wrath, poured his share into the dead man.

units.la: PAX, SEV TRANQVI-litas Reipublicæ.
units.tr: Peace, or the Tranquillity of the Commonwealth

units.la: Lex est in Sueuicis urbibus , ut si in rixa aliqui gladios strinxerint , ac uel puer , uel muliercula proculetiã inclamans pacẽ imperet,capite punia tur,qui audito nomine pacis insuper ferire audet.
units.tr: There is a law in the Swabian cities that if in a brawl some men draw their swords, and a boy or a little woman from afar cries out and commands peace, whoever dares to strike after hearing the name of peace is punished with death.

units.la: D.Iacobus Fuggerus senior accersitus in sena-tum Augustanum , cùm deliberarent de inferendo bello ducibus Bauariæ, inquit,se non esse suasorẽ belli,sed pacẽ suadere,ͨ ut res perageretur qua-licunq; modo. Ne autem existimaretur id facere sui commodi causa , sed ob publicam utilitatem: Ego,inquit,dabo decem milia aureorũ, quibus , si fieri possit,pax redimatur , Si uerò res transigi nõ possit, ut ijs senatus uterētur ad bellum gerendum. Hoc profecto non facilè alius priuatus, quantum-uis diues, faceret.
units.tr: Jacob Fugger the Elder, summoned to the Augsburg senate when they were deliberating on waging war against the dukes of Bavaria, said that he was not an advocate of war but urged peace, so that the matter might be settled by whatever means. Lest it be thought he did this for his own advantage rather than the public good, he said: "I will give ten thousand gold pieces, by which peace may be bought, if it can be done. But if the matter cannot be settled, let the senate use them for waging war." Certainly another private citizen, however rich, would hardly do this.

units.la: Quando euertitur currus ouorum, non possunt omnia integra rursus colligi. Sic post turbatum Reipublicæ statum, oportet multa patienter ferre ut consulatur reliquo corpori.
units.tr: When a cart of eggs is overturned, not all of them can be gathered up whole again. So after the state of a commonwealth has been thrown into turmoil, many things must be patiently endured so that the rest of the body may be cared for.

units.la: Cracouiæ quidam adolescentes maledixerũt scorto Episcopi, & factus est tumultus, ut Episco-pus mitteret aliquot satellites, qui interfecerunt a-liquos ex scolasticis: & rursus ex satellitibus qui-dam interfecti sunt. Tantum ualuit Episcopi sæui-tia, ut propter scortum turbarit tranquilitatem pu-blicam, & iusserit scholasticos discedere ex ciui-tate. Discesserunt igitur tam innocentes quàm son-tes, tam qui non interfuerant quàm qui interfue-rant. Videte, quanta miseria illa sit. Multi sunt in-terfecti, & schola est dissipata. Vos igitur sitis mo-destiores, & communem tranquilitatem, quantum fieri potest, tuemini.
units.tr: At Kraków some young men spoke ill of a bishop's mistress, and a tumult arose, so that the bishop sent some attendants, who killed some of the scholars; and in turn some of the attendants were killed. So great was the bishop's cruelty that for the sake of a prostitute he disturbed public tranquillity and ordered the scholars to leave the city. So they departed, the innocent and the guilty alike, those who had not taken part as much as those who had. See how great a misery that was. Many were killed, and the school was broken up. Therefore be more modest, and preserve the common tranquillity as far as you can.

units.la: Audiui Anglum quendam dicentem in conuen-tu: Inter Imperatorem & nostrum regem potest esse pax, sed non amicicia.
units.tr: I heard a certain Englishman say in a gathering: "Between the Emperor and our king there can be peace, but not friendship."

units.la: Thucydides.
units.tr: Thucydides.

units.la: Non est turpe, domesticos domesticis cedere. Vtinã hoc cogitaremus in Ecclesia & Republica. Plautus: Facile est imperium in bonos.
units.tr: It is no disgrace for kinsmen to yield to kinsmen. Would that we thought this way in the Church and in the commonwealth. Plautus: It is easy to rule over good men.

units.la: Quando Thrasibulus recuperauit Athenas, ibi exules bona sua ex illa multiplici confusione & turbatione communis status Reipublicæ ad alios passim translata repetiuerūt. Quod cum absq; uis & magnis perturbationibus fieri non posset, Thrasibulus hinc sumpsit occasionem sanciendi legem de ἀμνησίᾳ. Sicut nobiles Brunsuicenses etiam amissis suis bonis ea repetiuerunt, unde sunt orta noua bella. Quare cum ita res accidit, optimum est seruare quod in ueteribus reperimus historijs ἐχόντες ἂ ἐχθσι.
units.tr: When Thrasybulus recovered Athens, the exiles reclaimed their property, which in the great confusion and upheaval of the common state had been passed on to others everywhere. Since this could not be done without violence and great disturbances, Thrasybulus took the occasion to enact a law of amnesty [ἀμνησίᾳ]. Likewise the noblemen of Brunswick, even after losing their goods, reclaimed them, and from this new wars arose. Therefore, since matters turn out in this way, it is best to keep what we find in the ancient histories, holding what they have [ἔχοντες ἃ ἔχουσι].

units.la: TVRBATIO PVBLICAE tranquillitatis.
units.tr: Disturbance of public tranquillity.

units.la: Habemus tot Lycurgos, id est, lupinos homines, quot habemus ædituos. Sed rectius se hic uersus habet:
units.tr: We have as many Lycurguses, that is, wolfish men, as we have sextons. But the verse stands more rightly thus:

units.la: Moribus antiquis res stat Romana uirisq;.
units.tr: By ancient customs the Roman state and its men stand firm.

units.la: Erat hic Danus, homo doctus & eloquens, procerus & pulchræ staturæ, qui semel percusserat quendam studiosum, qui iam est doctor. Relata uero re ad Rectorem, Danus est absolutus. Conuenerant ipse & alij in cella uinaria, hilariter potantes. Postea cum in illa mensa, apud quam studiosus erat, cæpissent ructus edere & uociferari, illud in altera mensa Danus ægreferens, monuit eos, inquiens: Bibite uos uestrum uinum, & nos nostrum bibemus, & uolumus esse hilares. Tunc studiosus diosius cotumeliosis verbis Danum affecit, & probè exagitauit. Tandem surrexit Danus, & pugione inuerso studiosum castigauit, & ipsius tergum bene demulsit. Res ad Rectorem defertur. Danus respondit: Quia ipse mihi molestus fuit multis conuicijs, & me irritauit, pugionem inuertes, eum modicum castigaui. Ita re iudicata à Rectore, Danus est absolutus.
units.tr: There was here a Dane, a learned and eloquent man, tall and of handsome stature, who once struck a certain student, who is now a teacher. When the matter was referred to the Rector, Dane was acquitted. He and others had gathered in a wine cellar, drinking cheerfully. Afterwards, when at that table where the student was sitting they began to belch and shout, Dane, taking it ill at another table, warned them, saying: Drink your own wine, and we will drink ours, and we want to be merry. Then the student, in insulting words, assailed Dane quite vehemently and abused him. At last Dane rose, turned his dagger around, punished the student, and gave his back a good beating with the hilt. The matter was reported to the Rector. Dane replied: Because he had been troublesome to me with many insults and had provoked me, I punished him a little by turning the dagger round. With the matter judged thus by the Rector, Dane was acquitted.

units.la: Audiui ex Iacobo Sturmio in Argentinensi senatu fuisse senem quendam militem, qui cùm interrogaretur, ut diceret suam sententiam de mouendo bello, respondit nihil aliud, quàm: Optimi charissimiq; Domini, planè nihil boni bellum apportat: Lieben herren, lieben herren, es ist nichts guts am krieg.
units.tr: I have heard from Jacob Sturm that in the Strasbourg senate there was once an old soldier who, when asked to give his opinion on launching a war, answered nothing but: Most excellent and dearest lords, war brings absolutely nothing good: Dear gentlemen, dear gentlemen, there is nothing good in war.

units.la: Comes de Nassau qui mortuus est ante annos 25, aut circiter, cum admoneretur, ipsum habere occasionem ad se trahendi comitatū Kazenelnbogen, respondit: Non tanti facio illum Comitatū, ut propterea uelim turbare Germaniæ pacem.
units.tr: The Count of Nassau, who died some 25 years ago or thereabouts, when he was reminded that he had the opportunity to draw the county of Katzenelnbogen to himself, replied: I do not value that county so highly that I would for its sake wish to disturb the peace of Germany.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Miles quidam impius, cum canere audiret cantilenam, Da pacem Domine in diebus nostris, interpellauit canentes, his uerbis: Vt uos pestis perdat: quid petitis pacem, cùm nos nihil magis quàm pacem auersemur? quapropter quotidie bellum gerimus.
units.tr: A certain impious soldier, when he heard people singing the chant, "Grant peace, O Lord, in our days," interrupted the singers with these words: May the plague destroy you! Why do you ask for peace, when we shun nothing more than peace? That is why we wage war every day.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Plutarchus περὶ φιλαδελφίας scribit, morem Græciæ fuisse ut cum duo fratres una incederent, & ad lapidem aliquem eminentiorem uenirent, non statim seiuncti ab eodem loco discederent, sed ambo una ad idem latus circumirent lapidem. Huiusmodi ritus peculiares singulæ gentes habent, qui apud ipsos recepti conseruantur, ut antiquæ probitatis homines admoneant. Accommodat igitur Plutarchus hunc ritum ad fratrum concordiâ, ac moneri eos hoc exemplo ait, ut caueant, ne quis lapis, nec ulla offensio diuellat animos eorum unà uiuentium: Et si qua inciderit offensio, ut illam coniuncti circumeant, hoc est, dissimulent, deleant, & ex animo extinguant.
units.tr: Plutarch, in his work On brotherly love [περὶ φιλαδελφίας], writes that it was the custom in Greece that when two brothers walked together and came to some rather prominent stone, they did not immediately part from that spot, but both went around the stone together, on the same side. Individual peoples have such peculiar rites, which are preserved among them as received practice, to remind men of former uprightness. Plutarch therefore applies this custom to the concord of brothers, and says that they are to be warned by this example to take care that no stone or any offence should tear apart the hearts of those who live together; and if some offence should arise, that they should go around it together, that is, overlook it, wipe it out, and extinguish it from the heart.

units.la: DE IRA, EIVSQVE moderatione.
units.tr: On Anger and Its Moderation.

units.la: Cum esset Doctor Martinus ualde commotus in aliqua causa, & incenderetur alterius sermonibus, interrumpebā eius sermones, recitās uersum: Vince animos iramq; tuam, qui cætera uincis.
units.tr: When Doctor Martin was very stirred up in a certain matter, and was provoked by another man's speeches, I interrupted his speech by reciting the verse: "Conquer your passions and your anger, you who conquer all else."

units.la: Repressit se & subridens dixit: Non uolumus de his amplius, sed de alijs colloqui. Hunc uersum etiam diligenter obseruauit Ioannes Fridericus Dux Saxoniæ.
units.tr: He restrained himself and, smiling, said: "We do not want to talk any more about these things, but about other matters." John Frederick, Duke of Saxony, also took careful note of this verse.

units.la: Noster Cæsar Carolus V. non facilè irasci solet sti solet, sicut frater eius dixit, vsus Germanico illo prouerbio: Mein brueder ist nicht leichtlich auf den esel zubringen, aber wenn er ein mal auf den esel kumbt, so ist er nicht leichtlich wider herunter zubringen:
units.tr: Our Emperor Charles V is not wont to be easily angered. As his brother said, using that German proverb: "My brother is not easily got onto the donkey, but once he is up on the donkey, he is not easily got down again."

units.la: Audiui semel ex nobili Friderico à Dőn, cùm loqueretur de quodam rege, quem iracundum esse expertus erat in quodam negocio, dici, nihil esse perniciolius in gubernatione, quàm iram.
units.tr: I once heard the noble Friedrich von Dohna, speaking of a certain king whom he had found to be quick to anger in a certain affair, say that nothing is more harmful in government than anger.

units.la: Vix inuenientes unum pagum, ubi consentiant pastor et ædituus, quia regulariter vsuvenit, ut cu stodes sint quasi tribuni plebis, incitantes rusticos & populum contra pastorem. Ideo oportet esse sa pientes, qui inter se norunt cedere. Duobus iratis inter se litigantibus, sapientior est qui tacet, quàm qui contradicit, iuxta Philomenis responsum. Ille enim Athenis obiurgatus, quare ita esset ineptus in cõuiuio. Imò respondit, quare tu ita es ineptus, qui ebrium uis reformare & admonere. Ita qui iratum in ipsa turbatione corrigere conatur, non secus facit, atque qui ebrium è ucstigio reforma re tentat.
units.tr: One can hardly find a village where the minister and the sexton agree, because it regularly happens that the churchwardens act like tribunes of the plebs, stirring up the peasants and the people against the minister. So it is necessary to be wise, and to know how to give way to one another. When two angry men are quarrelling, the wiser is the one who keeps silent rather than the one who contradicts, according to the reply of Philomenes. For when he was rebuked at Athens for being so clumsy at a banquet, he answered: "Rather, why are you so clumsy, you who want to reform and admonish a drunk man?" So whoever tries to correct an angry man in the very heat of the quarrel does no differently from one who tries to reform a drunk man on the spot.

units.la: Cùm princeps quidam uehementius esset iratus, Imperator Fridericus, uir tantæ modestiæ ac pietatis, ut quibusdam ignauus propter singulare & insigne humilitatem uisus sit, fertur ad eum dixisse: Si finis bonus sit, omnia reliqua bona erunt. Vt significaret, ipsius uehementem iram ipsi tandem nocituram esse. Ille postea fecit uestem, uilem linteam ex panno crassiore, cui subiunxit fimbriam plane auream cum magno sumptu. Ita uestitus uenit in Senatum principum, qui dixerunt ei: Domine, quid significat uestis ista? Respondit ille: Si finis bonus sit, omnia reliqua bona erunt. Ita risit Imperatorem, sed fuit Sardonius risus. Postea uero captus in bello, admonitione Imperatoris prudentiæ propemodum serò expertus est.
units.tr: When a certain prince was very vehemently angry, the Emperor Frederick, a man of such modesty and piety that to some he seemed slothful because of his singular and remarkable humility, is said to have said to him: "If the end is good, all the rest will be good," meaning that his vehement anger would in the end harm himself. Afterwards he had a garment made of coarse linen cloth, to which he added a fringe of pure gold at great expense. Dressed in this, he came into the senate of the princes, who said to him: "Lord, what does this garment mean?" He answered: "If the end is good, all the rest will be good." Thus he made the Emperor laugh, but it was a sardonic laugh. Later, however, when he was captured in war, he learned through the Emperor's admonition the value of prudence, though almost too late.

units.la: Scipio uir placatissimus maximè delectatus est lectione Xenophontis. Cyrum enim in moderatione iræ, placabilitate, alijsq; uirtutibus diligenter imitatus est (sicut in tota pædia Cyri nusquam reperitur ipsum fuisse iratum) fuit castus, & continens domi & in castris supra alios omnes cives Romanos. Habuit honestam coniugem, quam dilexit, & uicissim ab ea diligebatur.
units.tr: Scipio, a man of the utmost calm, took the greatest delight in reading Xenophon. For he diligently imitated Cyrus in moderating anger, in placability and in other virtues (as nowhere in the Cyropaedia is it found that Cyrus was ever angry). He was chaste and self-controlled, at home and in the camp, above all the other Roman citizens. He had an honourable wife, whom he loved, and by whom he was in turn loved.

units.la: Quando dux Fridericus fuit iratus, discessit in cubiculum, & dimisit à se omnes cum quibus habebat negocium. Ita solus concoxit ac quasi fregit iram: & post aliquot dies redijt ad consiliarios.
units.tr: When Duke Frederick was angry, he withdrew into his bedchamber and dismissed from himself all those with whom he had business. Alone, he digested his anger and, as it were, broke it, and after some days he returned to his counsellors.

units.la: Seneca postremo libro de ira, inquit: Dum inter homines sumus, colamus humanitatem, non timori cuiquam, non periculo simus, detrimenta, injurias, conuitia, uellicationes contemnamus, & magno animo breuia feramus incommoda, &c.
units.tr: Seneca, in the last book of his work On Anger, says: "While we are among men, let us cultivate humanity. Let us be a cause of fear or danger to no one. Let us despise losses, injuries, insults and taunts, and with a great spirit bear the brief troubles of life," etc.

units.la: Quidam noster amicus, bonus aliâs uir, sed admodum contentiosus, & rixarum cupidus, cùm essemus aliquando unà, mouebat magnum certamen de re non necessaria, & ualde resistebat, nec poterat precibus sedari ipsius contentio. Cùm adhortaremus eum pluribus uerbis, ut taceret, respõdit: An igitur ferendum est tam apertam iniuriam mihi fieri? At alij: Quæ patiëtiæ tuæ laus erit, si dignus & meritus mala patiaris, iuxta uersiculum:
units.tr: A certain friend of ours, otherwise a good man but very contentious and eager for quarrels, once when we were together stirred up a great dispute about a matter that was not necessary, and resisted strongly; nor could his contentiousness be calmed by entreaties. When we urged him with many words to be silent, he replied: "Must such an open injury be done to me, and must I bear it?" But others said: "What praise of your patience will there be, if you, who are worthy and deserving, suffer evils, according to the little verse:"

units.la: Quæ uenit indignè, pœna dolenda uenit.
units.tr: "Whatever comes undeservedly brings a punishment that is to be grieved over."

units.la: Milites quidam liberius quædam inter potandum contra regem Pyrrhum dixerant. Vocati igitur ad Regem, iußi sunt dicere causam. Tũc unus inter eos animosior: Immò, inquit, Rex, ista diximus, & nisi lagena defecisset, nos longe acerbiora contra te dixissemus quibus te interfecissemus. Ita placatus est Rex Pyrrhus, & moderatus iram hoc dicto militis urbano.
units.tr: Some soldiers, while drinking, had spoken rather freely against King Pyrrhus. Therefore they were called before the king and ordered to give their reasons. Then one of them, the bolder of the group, said: "Indeed, King, we said those things, and if the flagon had not run dry, we would have said far harsher things against you, with which we would have killed you." Thus King Pyrrhus was appeased, and he moderated his anger at this witty word of the soldier.

units.la: Fridericus à Dõn dixit: O quàm noxia suppelex in imperio est ira.
units.tr: Friedrich von Dohna said: "Oh, how harmful an article of household equipment anger is in government!"

units.la: Scitis prouerbiũ Germanicum: Klein en leutten ligt der dreck nahe beim hertzen, id est: Parui homines citò irascuntur. Stomachus ideo indignationem significat, quia biliosis statim ascendit bilis in orificium uentriculi, uel stomachi: ibiq; statim exæstuat illis qui sunt ὀξύχολοι, seu præcipitis iræ. Deinde non est magna distantia ab orificio uentriuentriculi ad cor, cæteris paribus. Item quando alii quis est famelicus, tunc citius ira incenditur: quia bilis in orificio uentriculi citius mouetur.
units.tr: You know the German proverb: "Klein en leutten ligt der dreck nahe beim hertzen," that is, little people have their dirt close to the heart: small men are quickly angry. The stomach therefore signifies indignation, because in bilious people the bile at once rises to the mouth of the stomach and there at once boils up in those who are oxycholoi [ὀξύχολοι], that is, prone to sudden anger. Then, other things being equal, there is not a great distance from the mouth of the stomach to the heart. Likewise, when someone is hungry, anger is kindled more quickly, because the bile at the mouth of the stomach is stirred more readily.

units.la: Scripsi aliquando ad quendam principem, & fui deprecator pro alio. Ille misit mihi uolumina, quæ erant contra eum, pro quo intercesi. Respon di: Quòd si singula cõsideranda essent, quæ unusquisq; fecisset, mirabilia in mundo reperirentur. Postea moderatus est iram, eumq; recepit, ac restituit ei bona.
units.tr: I once wrote to a certain prince and acted as intercessor for another man. He sent me volumes of documents against the man for whom I had interceded. I replied: "If each single thing that each man has done were to be considered, wonders would be found in the world." Afterwards he moderated his anger, received the man back, and restored his goods to him.

units.la: Imperator Maximilianus habebat scribam, quem admodum diligebat, propter bonam scripturam. Ille imitatus manum Imperatoris, scripsit chirographa nomine Imperatoris, & petiuit à Iacobo Fuggero pecuniã. Quod cum iterum atq; iterũ fecisset, coepit res esse suspecta Fuggero, qui accessit Imperatorẽ & mõstrauit chirographa, interrogans an iussu Imperatoris hæc facta essent? Imperator inspectis chirographis, dixit: esse quidem hanc suam manũ, sed an eo tempore pecuniã postulauerit, se ignorare. Accersiuit ad se suum scribam, quem interrogat, an hæc chirographa ad Fuggerũ detulerit: Ita, inquit. Quærit denuò Imperator: Quis ergo scripsit? Ibi exanimatus ille, statim ad pedes Imperatoris decidit, ac fatetur se scripsisse, veniamq; petit. Maximilianus Imperator nihil seuerius contra ipsum statuit, quàm iubẽs illũ protinus è toto suo imperio discedere, ne usquam inueniretur in ullo loco, ubi ipse imperaret. Tandem in bello Veneto, adiunxit se Venetis, ubi est interfectus. Hæc fuit bonitas Maximiliani imperatoris, & moderatio iræ, ac nõ indulgētia. Recte etiam Maximilianus fecit, quòd ipse accersiuerit scribam, & ille quod accersitus comparuerit.
units.tr: The Emperor Maximilian had a scribe whom he greatly loved on account of his good handwriting. This man imitated the Emperor's hand and wrote promissory notes in the Emperor's name, and asked Jacob Fugger for money. When he had done this again and again, Fugger became suspicious. He approached the Emperor and showed him the notes, asking whether these things had been done by the Emperor's order. The Emperor, having inspected the notes, said that it was indeed his hand, but he did not know whether at that time he had demanded money. He summoned his scribe and asked him whether he had brought these notes to Fugger. "Yes," he said. The Emperor asked again: "Who then wrote them?" Then that man, struck with terror, at once fell at the Emperor's feet, confessed that he had written them, and begged pardon. Emperor Maximilian decided nothing more severe against him than ordering him at once to leave his whole empire, so that he would not be found anywhere in any place where he himself ruled. Finally, in the Venetian war, he joined the Venetians, and there he was killed. This was the goodness of Emperor Maximilian, and his moderation of anger, and not indulgence. Maximilian also acted rightly in that he himself summoned the scribe, and that the scribe appeared when summoned.

units.la: Dux Fridericus dicebat ad quendam nobilem, cum uidissetipsum excandescere: Quàm turpe est uirum sapientem sic irasci?
units.tr: Duke Frederick said to a certain nobleman, when he saw him grow red with rage: "How shameful it is for a wise man to be angry in this way!"

units.la: Quidam ex amicis nostris, uir aliâs doctus & bonus, erat satis asper & pugnax, & multa etiam mouebat cum suo consule non necessaria. Ibi eum adhortatus sum, ne tot rixas excitaret propter publicæ pacis conseruationem, & sui ipsius conscientiam. Tandem illud solummodo ab eo postulaui, ut saltem per aliquot menses nihil necessarium rixarum moueret: statim enim experturum esse multa cum sibi tum paci publicæ salutaria inde prouentura: promisit mihi se facturum. Post biennium itaque ad me reuersus, cum multa familiariter cum suo consule egisset, atq; propter conceptam animi moderationē quædā obtinuisset, dixit: O Domine Philippe, quantū sensi cōmodi ex illo tuo cōsilio, quantumq; id in omnibus reb. agendis adiumenti præstitit? Verum profecto est quod breuis patiētia longā pacē pariat. Sed hoc breue tempus papus patientiæ tã mihi longũ & molestũ uisum est, ut quãtum quidem ad me attinet, diuturnũ bellum & multiplices rixas sustinere malle, quàm tantas patientiæ molestias decoquere. Et re uera sic se res habet. Nam ita naturæ & ingenia hominum sunt comparata, sicut dixit Achilles: Ira melle dulcior est. Huic aptè respondet uersus Martialis: Aurũ & opes & uasa frequẽs donauit amicus: Qui uelit ingenio cedere nullus erit.
units.tr: One of our friends, otherwise learned and good, was rather harsh and quarrelsome, and with his town clerk he also stirred up many unnecessary disputes. There I urged him not to provoke so many quarrels, for the preservation of public peace and for the sake of his own conscience. At last I asked of him only this: that for at least some months he would stir up no unnecessary quarrels, for he would soon find that many things, both for himself and for public peace, would result from this. He promised me he would do so. After two years he came back to me, having dealt much with his colleague in a friendly way, and having obtained certain things through the moderation of mind he had acquired. He said: "O Master Philip, how much benefit I have felt from that counsel of yours, and how much help it has given me in carrying out all my affairs! It is truly the case that brief patience produces long peace. But that short time of patience seemed to me so long and so troublesome that, as far as I am concerned, I would rather endure a long war and manifold quarrels than digest such troublesome patience. And indeed the matter stands so. For the natures and dispositions of men are so constituted, as Achilles said: "Anger is sweeter than honey." Martial's verse answers aptly: "Though a friend often gave gold, riches and vessels, there will be no one who is willing to give way to his temper."
