units.la: Scipio, etsi in manu habens exercitus, non minus tribunorum petulantiam quàm Iulius Cæsar cohercere poterat: tamẽ amore patriæ, ad quẽ iuuandam & cõseruandam se natũ arbitrabatur, iniurias tribunorum dissimulauit, & iram suã contra eos susceptam moderatus est. Ad huius exemplum nos quoq; priuatas iniurias & iram nostrã dissimulemus, & communi tranquillitati condonemus.
units.tr: Scipio, although he had armies in his hand and could restrain the insolence of the tribunes no less than Julius Caesar could, nevertheless, out of love for his country, to whose service and preservation he judged himself born, overlooked the tribunes' injuries and moderated the anger he had conceived against them. Following his example, let us too overlook our private injuries and our anger, and yield them to the common peace.

units.la: AEMVLATIO.
units.tr: EMULATION.

units.la: Vidimus certamen inter duos consiliarios Imperatoris Caroli V. Granuelum & alium quendam, quorum illius fortuna uel potius patientia uicit. Quamuis enim alter esset in magna gratia apud Cæsarem propter suauitatem in dicendo, ita ut Imperator, si quando laudaretur aliquis ob eloquentiam facundus, dicere solitus sit: Ille quidem facundus est, sed meus consiliarius multo suauior: tamen patientia atq; animi moderatio Granueli effecit, ut alter ex aula eijceretur: quin & multi principes laborabant pro eiecto, sed nihil efficere potuerunt.
units.tr: We saw a contest between two councillors of the Emperor Charles V, Granvelle and another man. Granvelle's fortune, or rather his patience, prevailed. Although the other was in great favour with Caesar because of his charm in speaking, so that the Emperor, whenever someone was praised as an eloquent speaker, used to say: "He is eloquent indeed, but my councillor is much more charming." Nevertheless, the patience and self-control of Granvelle brought it about that the other was driven from the court; indeed, many princes laboured to have him removed, but they could accomplish nothing.

units.la: Alexander habuit duos cubicularios, admodū sibi familiares, Ephestionem & Craterum. Ephestion fuit aulicus, idoneus ad assentandum. In Cratero fuit excellentia virtutis: uterq; voluit esse primus. Craterum oderat Ephestio, ideò quòd erat in eo virtus. Sæpe dimicati sunt inter se interveniente Alexandro, ut etiam minaretur utriq; mortē, nisi cessarent ab istis contumelijs & rixis: & dixit Ephestionem esse φιλολέξανδρα, id est amantem Alexandri, & assentatorem: Craterum verò φιλοβασιλέα. Insuper dixit Ephestioni: Craterus est aliquid sine Alexandro: tu nihil es sine Alexandro.
units.tr: Alexander had two chamberlains, very intimate with him, Hephaestion and Craterus. Hephaestion was a courtier, skilled at flattery. In Craterus there was outstanding virtue. Both wished to be first. Hephaestion hated Craterus because virtue was in him. They often quarrelled with each other, with Alexander intervening, so that he even threatened both with death unless they ceased these insults and brawls. He called Hephaestion philalexandros [φιλολέξανδρος], that is, a lover of Alexander and a flatterer, but Craterus philobasileus [φιλοβασιλεύς], a lover of the king. Moreover, he said to Hephaestion: "Craterus is something without Alexander; you are nothing without Alexander."

units.la: BELLVM, EIVSQVE APparatus & circumstantiæ.
units.tr: WAR, ITS PREPARATIONS AND CIRCUMSTANCES.

units.la: Est antiquum dictum ἴσα πόλεμον ὁ ποιεῖ: Aequalia nō faciunt bellum, sicut est etiam bonum dictum Germanicum: Einem wie dem andern, so geschicht keim vnrecht.
units.tr: There is an old saying: "Equal things do not make war" [ἴσα πόλεμον ὁ ποιεῖ], just as there is also a good German saying: "To one as to the other, so no one is wronged."

units.la: Pindarus: Movere rempublicam cuiuis est: sed sistere eam in tranquillo, solius Dei est. Quisq; potest movere rempublicam, sed non potest eam sedare, sicut ipse vellet.
units.tr: Pindar: To stir up a commonwealth is within anyone's power, but to settle it in tranquillity belongs to God alone. Anyone can stir up a commonwealth, but cannot calm it as he himself would wish.

units.la: Italus quidam secutus castra Imperatoris Caroli V. carmen composuit: Vna gerit bellum, pacem manus altera reddit.
units.tr: An Italian who followed the camp of the Emperor Charles V composed a verse: One hand wages war, the other gives back peace.

units.la: Verùm nemo pacem sine Deo restituet: quia bella geruntur propter pacem, & pax petenda est propter constitutionem reipublicæ.
units.tr: But no one will restore peace without God, because wars are waged for the sake of peace, and peace must be sought for the sake of the constitution of the commonwealth.

units.la: Nos tantum quærimus μυομαχίας, & alienà bella, quæ Alexander appellauit muriũ bella. Christus nominauit rumores bellorum, id est, non bella monarchiarum, qualia Cyrus gessit, qui constituit pacem: nam finis belli debet esse pax & constitutio honesti status. Item, ut sunt Alexandri bella & Romanorum, usque ad tempora Augusti, qui domito iam orbe terrarum, homines in pace legibus coniunxit. Nostri uerò temporis bella ad antiqua bella collata, tantummodo murium certamina uideri possunt, sicut Christus uocat rumores & tumultus. Romani tardè mouerunt bella. Ego credo omnes ordinarios magistratus tardè mouisse bella: sicut noster cæsar Carolus V. inchoauit tantùm duo bella, (quod ego scio) in quibus fuit semper infelix: in alijs uerò, quorum ipse non extitit autor, fuit fortunatus. Vt cùm inuasit regem Galliæ, amisit exercitum, infectũ peste, & confectũ fame. Deinde cum in Africā expeditionē faceret, periit exercitus naufragio.
units.tr: We seek only the wars of mice and other people's wars, which Alexander called the wars of mice. Christ named them "rumours of wars," that is, not the wars of monarchies, such as Cyrus waged, who established peace; for the end of war ought to be peace and the establishment of an honourable condition. So too were the wars of Alexander and of the Romans, up to the times of Augustus, who, once the world had been subdued, joined men together in peace under laws. But the wars of our own time, compared with the ancient wars, can only be seen as contests of mice, just as Christ calls them rumours and tumults. The Romans were slow to begin wars. I think all ordinary magistrates have been slow to begin wars. Our Emperor Charles V began only two wars, as far as I know, and in them he was always unfortunate; in others, of which he was not the author, he was fortunate. Thus, when he invaded the king of France, he lost his army, infected by plague and worn down by famine. Then, when he undertook an expedition into Africa, his army perished in a shipwreck.

units.la: Scipio dixit, nusquam esse dimicandũ nisi cùm aut necessitas esset, aut summa oportunitas, iuxta prouerbiu Germanicu: Es gehort mer zum dantz den rotte hossen, es geboren auch beine darein.
units.tr: Scipio said that one should never fight unless either necessity or the highest advantage required it, in accordance with the German proverb: "The dance is mine as much as the red hose; the legs belong to it too."

units.la: Comestabilis Regis Francisci capitaneus, ante annos uiginti uel amplius dixit, quādo Imperator fuit in Narbonēsi prouincia, se gessisse duplex bellum, unum cum Rege suo, qui uoluit statim dimicare, alterū cum Imperatore, ut falleret eū, sed Comestabilis metuit fortunā Imperatoris & eius exercitū, cui cōmodius stratagemate quodam commeatum eripi posse considerauit, sicut factum est.
units.tr: The constable of King Francis, a captain, said more than twenty years ago, when the Emperor was in the province of Narbonne, that he had carried on a double war: one against his own king, who wanted to fight at once, and another against the Emperor, to deceive him. But the constable feared the Emperor's fortune and his army, and he judged that it would be more convenient to seize their supplies by some stratagem, as indeed happened.

units.la: Lantgrauius huius pater dicebat: Si quis tres inimicos habeat, cum duobus pacem componendam, quò tertius superari possit.
units.tr: The Landgrave, his father, used to say: If someone has three enemies, he should make peace with two, so that the third can be overcome.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLLECTIONS.

units.la: Nobilis uir Vlricus ab Erlach, dux Heluetiorū, cui cùm narraretur iam in ipso conflictu suas copias aliquas recessisse, nihil perterrefactus, dixit: Bonū est separari paleam à granis. Hoc enim modo fit, ut generosi animi admoneantur suæ tantum uirtuti & fortitudini totum certamen incumbere: alioqui enim fieri posset, ut reliqui præsentes, ignauis aliquid cōsiderent, ipsiq; negligentiores facti, nihil transfigerent.
units.tr: The noble man Ulrich von Erlach, leader of the Swiss, was told that in the very heat of the battle some of his troops had withdrawn. Not in the least alarmed, he said: "It is good that the chaff is separated from the grain." For in this way brave spirits are reminded to devote the whole struggle to their own courage and fortitude alone; otherwise it could happen that the rest, who were present, would rely on the cowards, and themselves becoming more careless, would accomplish nothing.

units.la: Cæsar Carolus V. intuens nostrum exercitum ad Ingolstadium, ascendit tumulum aliquem, ac stetit diu cogitabundus & tacens: tandem aliquem quem ex astantibus militib. interrogauit: Sunt'ne hi omnes tantùm Germani? Est pulcher exercitus, & militum delectus: sed postea addit: Cito eis decerit sapientia & pecunia. & ita accidit.
units.tr: Charles V, Caesar, looking at our army near Ingolstadt, climbed a certain hill and stood for a long time pensive and silent. At last he asked one of the soldiers standing by: "Are all these only Germans?" "It is a fine army, and a well-chosen body of soldiers." But afterwards he added: "Soon wisdom and money will fail them." And so it came to pass.

units.la: Aeschines. Præmia in bello perueniunt ad capitaneos: causæ conferuntur in oratores.
units.tr: Aeschines: The rewards in war go to the captains; the causes are entrusted to the orators.

units.la: Persicus Rex miserat legatos ad Spartanos, petens, ut darent aquam & terram. Nam illa fuit forma petendæ deditionis. Spartani abiecerunt legatos in puteum, & dixerunt, se dare eis aquam & terram.
units.tr: The Persian king had sent envoys to the Spartans, asking that they give water and earth. For that was the form of demanding surrender. The Spartans threw the envoys into a well and said that they might take water and earth from there.

units.la: Daniel dicit: Gog & Magog sunt in montibus Israel perituri. quid hoc sit, nescio, nisi quòd Deus sit hostes suos deleturus in extremo iudicio, aut quòd adhuc sint magnam cladem accepturi Turci in mõtibus Israel, id est, in Germania, in illis locis, ubi sunt verae Ecclesiae.
units.tr: Daniel says: Gog and Magog are to perish on the mountains of Israel. What this means I do not know, except that God will destroy his enemies at the last judgment, or that the Turks are yet to receive a great defeat on the mountains of Israel, that is, in Germany, in those places where the true Church is.

units.la: Audiui ex nobili à Lasco Bauarico, qui fuerat legatus Constantinopolim, esse uaticinia Turcorũ, Turcos esse potituros Vngaria, Polonia, cum aliqua parte Germaniæ: & deinde fore inclinationẽ regni Turcici. Non dubium est Turcos in Germaniam paulo post esse uenturos.
units.tr: I heard from the noble Laski of Bavaria, who had been an envoy to Constantinople, that there are prophecies of the Turks: that the Turks will seize Hungary and Poland, with some part of Germany, and that afterwards the Turkish kingdom will decline. There is no doubt that the Turks will come into Germany soon after.

units.la: Carolus Martellus trucidauit triginta millia Saracenorum, & magno terrore liberauit Galliam & Germaniam.
units.tr: Charles Martel slaughtered thirty thousand Saracens and with great terror freed France and Germany.

units.la: Primus filius Turcici Imperatoris est interfectus à patre, delatus falsis criminationibus per generũ, ut hic eo modo traheret ad se regnum. Secundus filius sibi conscium mortem, ut dicitur, dolore fra–tris. Tertius est inutilis regno.
units.tr: The first son of the Turkish emperor was killed by his father, having been denounced by false accusations through his son-in-law, who in this way hoped to draw the kingdom to himself. The second son, as is said, died of grief at his brother's death, being conscious of it. The third is useless to the kingdom.

units.la: Accepi literas in quibus scriptum est, Turcos lætari, quòd non debeant uagari per Persiam, sed per Vngariam. Et in ijsdem scriptum est, matrem quandam defendisse filios duos aduersum Turcum quendam, adeò strenuè, ut utriq;, mater & filij mã serint incolumes, sed mater amisit dextrã, & accepit alia uulnera. Est singulare exemplum. Mater est Vngaria, cui etiamsi præcidatur dextera, tamen aliqui seruabuntur.
units.tr: I have received letters in which it is written that the Turks rejoice that they are not to roam through Persia but through Hungary. And in the same letters it is written that a certain mother defended her two sons against a certain Turk so bravely that the mother and both sons remained unharmed, though the mother lost her right hand and received other wounds. It is a remarkable example. The mother is Hungary, and even if her right hand be cut off, some of her children will nevertheless be saved.

units.la: Est in uaticinijs Methodij: uulpem educturam è clauστris Caucasi rufos Iudæos. Vulpes est Machometus, qui eduxit Turcos in Asiam per occasionem bellorum Persicorum. Turci porrò dicuntur rufi Iudæi, quia sunt cruenti, es sindt bluthunde. Dicuntur Iudæi propter superstitionem, quia est quoddã genus hominũ superstitiosum. Nostri homines, abiecta superstitione, fiũt efferi et barbari.
units.tr: In the prophecies of Methodius it is said that a fox will lead the red Jews out of the gorges of the Caucasus. The fox is Mahomet, who led the Turks into Asia on the occasion of the Persian wars. The Turks are further called red Jews, because they are bloody; they are bloodhounds. They are called Jews on account of superstition, since there is a certain superstitious race of men. Our own people, having cast off superstition, become savage and barbarous.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Recens ante paucos annos quatuor mille robu-stissimi uiri, ueštiti turcico ueštitu, ex Vngaria abducti sunt, & missi ad Turcum.
units.tr: A few years ago, four thousand very robust men, dressed in Turkish clothing, were taken out of Hungary and sent to the Turk.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Bessarion Cardinalis, natione Græcus, uir ualde doctus, edidit orationes, in quibus hortatus est reges & principes ad bellum contra Turcos mo-nendum, fuitq; legatus in Gallia, & sæpe in Ger-maniam. Inter cætera exempla in orationibus e-ius hunc apologum citat: Dicit fuisse bellum ma-gnum inter lupos & canes, & uenisse nuncios ad lupos, qui dixerunt, uenire magnum numerum canum. Ibi unus ex senioribus lupis cohortatus est cæteros, ut sese coniungerent, ac mitterent unum speculatum agmen canum. Ille ascendens montem, uidet magnum agmen canum. Senior lupus inter-rogat, qualis sit color canū? Respondit, esse uariū & diuersum. At senior: Res bene se habet, quia di-uersi coloris sunt, non diu simul manebūt. Ita quā-do diuersæ sunt uoluntates, citò fit dissipatio.
units.tr: Bessarion the Cardinal, a Greek by birth and a very learned man, published orations in which he urged kings and princes to move to war against the Turks. He was also a legate in France and often in Germany. Among other examples in his orations he cites this fable: there was, he says, a great war between wolves and dogs, and messengers came to the wolves saying that a large number of dogs was coming. There one of the older wolves exhorted the rest to join together and send out one scouting party of dogs. That wolf, climbing a hill, sees a large troop of dogs. The old wolf asks what colour the dogs are. He replied that they were of various and differing colours. "Well, then," said the old wolf, "all is well, for since they are of different colours they will not stay together for long. So when wills are divided, dispersal quickly follows."

units.la: Iohannes Hilden monachus Ifenaci prædixit anno 1600 Turcos potituros esse Germania, & Italia. Disputaui cum aliis doctis & honestis uiris, cur non potius Turci appeterent Italiā, ubi essent opes & omniū rerum copia, quàm Germaniam? Responderūt, se disputasse cum Turcis eadē de re, qui tandem responderūt: Si Italiā appeterent, cō-currerēt simul Itali & Germani, ac resisterent eis: sed si Germani uicissent, tunc se ultro potituros esse Italia.
units.tr: John Hilden, a monk at Ifenach, predicted in the year 1600 that the Turks would seize Germany and Italy. I argued with other learned and honourable men about why the Turks would not rather aim at Italy, where there were riches and an abundance of all things, than at Germany. They replied that they had disputed the same matter with the Turks, who at last answered: if they aimed at Italy, the Italians and Germans would run together and resist them; but if the Germans were victorious, then they themselves would readily seize Italy.

units.la: Memini, cum essemus in conuentu Angustano, ibi fuisse etiam legationem Vngaricam, & petiuisse nisse auxilium contra Turcos, qui tum cõtra ipsos in bellum processerant. Sed negligebatur ipsorum querela, & unus ex præcipuis dicebat: Hactenus bellũ Turcis fuisse cum rubris ocreis, quãdo perueniret ad nigras, tunc ipsos multo fortiores uisuros esse uiros. Illud responsum ualde ægrefere-batur à multis: & profectò satis superba & iniqua erat responsio. Quia etiam ad uitanda nostra pericula debemus affici uicinorũ calamitate. Profecto res magnas gesserunt Vngari: duas gentes represserunt, Scythicam & Turcicam. Fuerunt muri Europæ ab illa parte.
units.tr: I remember that when we were at the Diet of Augsburg, a Hungarian embassy was also there, asking for help against the Turks, who had then marched to war against them. But their complaint was neglected, and one of the leading men said: "Hitherto the Turks have waged war with red greaves; when they reach black ones, then they will see the men much stronger." That answer was resented by many, and indeed it was a rather arrogant and unjust reply, since even to avert our own dangers we ought to be moved by the calamity of our neighbours. The Hungarians truly accomplished great things: they repressed two peoples, the Scythian and the Turkish. They were the walls of Europe on that side.

units.la: Scanderbegius princeps Epiri fortissimus fuit, qui ante captam Constantinopolin diu Turcis fortissimè restitit. Huic fuit similis Georgius Fronsbergius, qui fuit duodecies victor. Hic dicitur, post factam pugnam, quasi uersaretur adhuc inter hostium tela, semper uibrasse gladium, donec fessus in terram delaberetur.
units.tr: Scanderbeg, prince of Epirus, was a most valiant man, who resisted the Turks very bravely for a long time before Constantinople was taken. Similar to him was Georg Fronsberg, who was victorious twelve times. It is said that after a battle, as though he were still moving among the weapons of the enemy, he kept brandishing his sword until, weary, he slid down to the ground.

units.la: Vidi literas scriptas ad nostrum Imperatorem de bello Turcico à præfecto Polonico Cracouien-si, sapiête uiro, in quibus agens de constituēdo primo duce, dicit, omnino necessariũ esse, ut Imperator sit dux in illa expeditione, propter autoritatē, & propter discordiã aliorũ regum, consulitq; ipsi adducere sexaginta tantũ millia militũ. Sed miretur aliquis, cur ego tam exiguũ numerũ constituã, càm cùm Imperatores Turcici secum trahant 200000 militum. Hoc ideo se facere scribit, quia illa turba Turcica plerunq; sit inermis, quæ in modum latrunculorum uagetur, & rapiat undecunq; possit. At si uagationes istæ prohiberentur (quod facilè posset fieri) commeatum Turcis citò defuturum. Deinde alteram etiam causam addit, quia non plu ribus posset aduehi commeatus, & rem omnē esse positam in unius cum Turcis prælij uictoria. Quia si semel profligarentur, uno tantum prælio futurā inclinationem multarum gentium in Europæ & alijs terræ partibus. Imperator Carolus V. certis de causis iussit mihi illas literas ostendi.
units.tr: I have seen letters written to our Emperor about the Turkish war by the Polish prefect of Krakow, a wise man, in which, discussing the appointment of a first commander, he says that it is altogether necessary that the Emperor himself be the leader in that expedition, on account of his authority and because of the discord of the other kings, and he advises him to bring only sixty thousand soldiers. But someone may wonder why I set so small a number, when the Turkish emperors drag along 200,000 soldiers with them. He writes that he does this because that Turkish crowd is mostly unarmed, wandering like little bands of robbers and plundering wherever it can. But if these roamings were prevented (which could easily be done), the Turks would soon run short of supplies. Then he adds another reason: supplies could not be brought up for more men, and the whole matter rests on victory in a single battle with the Turks. For if they were once routed, the inclination of many peoples in Europe and in other parts of the world would turn on a single battle. Emperor Charles V, for certain reasons, ordered me to be shown those letters.

units.la: Ipse legatus Turcicus dixit Venetijs, se non satis posse mirari stulticiam regum Occidentalium, quòd cùm uideant Imperatorem Turcicum implicatum bello Persico, & abesse in Persia, non bellum in Hungaria moueant, & eam rursus ad se retrahant.
units.tr: The Turkish envoy himself said at Venice that he could not sufficiently marvel at the folly of the Western kings, that when they saw the Turkish emperor entangled in a Persian war and absent in Persia, they did not stir up war in Hungary and draw it back toward themselves.

units.la: Ante annos sedecim dissuasit capitaneus Imperatoris Caroli V. ulterius persequi Turcam fugientem, quia Turca posset reparare exercitum, nostri uerò non.
units.tr: Sixteen years ago a captain of Emperor Charles V advised against pursuing the fleeing Turk any further, because the Turk could rebuild his army, but we could not.

units.la: Iulius Papa in initio pontificatus mouebat bellum contra Imperatorem, postea non secus atq; mus se compescuit & quieuit: fortasse admonitus à Cardinalibus, inter quos sunt multi sapientes homines mines, qui facilè prouiderunt, non ita cuiuis proposito respondere euentum. Nouerunt uersum Phocylidis : ηκιρῷ λᾶ[ρεύειν μὴ δ' αὐτιπνέειν ἀ-νέμοισι.
units.tr: Pope Julius, at the beginning of his pontificate, stirred up war against the Emperor, but afterwards he kept himself in check and quiet like a mouse, perhaps admonished by the cardinals, among whom are many wise men, who readily foresaw that the outcome does not match every purpose. They knew the verse of Phocylides: "Do not sow on the rock, nor fan the winds against yourself" [ηκιρῷ λᾶ[ρεύειν μὴ δ' αὐτιπνέειν ἀ-νέμοισι].

units.la: Itali sunt sapientes homines. Primò etiam multa mouerunt contra Carolum V. Imperatorem: sed postquam intellexerunt eius fortunam, quieuerunt, nec amplius eum irritauerunt. Nos stolidi Germani putauimus esse somnolentum hominem.
units.tr: The Italians are wise men. At first they also stirred up many things against the Emperor Charles V, but after they understood his fortune, they grew quiet and no longer provoked him. We foolish Germans thought the man was sleepy.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam Dux aliquot annos ante bellum ad Ingolstadium gestum, uenit ad ducem Georgium, & fuit hortator, ut eo tempore bellum moueretur. Sed dux Georgius dissuasit, & dixit: An putas illustrissime princeps, ultra illos montes non esse quoq; uiros? quasi diceret: & ipsi sunt formidabiles. So helt ein schwert das ander in der scheiden.
units.tr: Some years before the battle fought at Ingolstadt, a certain duke came to Duke George and urged him to start war at that time. But Duke George dissuaded him and said: "Do you really think, most illustrious prince, that there are no men beyond those mountains too?" As if to say: they too are formidable. "So one sword holds the other in its scabbard."

units.la: Lantgrauius dicebat ante bellū quod gestum est ad Ingolstadium: Ego nunquā suadeo hoc bellum: quia non succedet noster conatus, eò quod nō regatur uno capite aut consilio.
units.tr: Before the war fought at Ingolstadt, the Landgrave said: "I never advise this war, because our undertaking will not succeed, since it is not directed by one head or one plan."

units.la: Multi boni uiri ante bellum ad Ingolstadium, cùm uiderent illud moueri, dixerunt: Iam moue-tur bellum, sed finis eius quando erit? Et profecto iuxta eorum præsagium, longo post tēpore, nulla pax componi potuit.
units.tr: Before the battle at Ingolstadt, many good men, seeing that war was being stirred up, said: "Now war is being stirred up, but when will it end?" And indeed, as they foresaw, no peace could be made for a long time afterwards.

units.la: Quidam Comes capitaneus, & dux exercitus Caroli V. in proximo bello, cum principibus uo-luit dimicare, idq; indicauit Imperatori, ostendens simul opportunitatem opprimēdi hostes. Cùm ue-rò uehementer urgeret, ut committeret prælium: Imperator omnino id fieri noluit, & dixit: Suffi-cit mihi, si post annum idem minore cum damno consequar. Ibi ille iratus, quòd non consiliū suum approbaret tumultuatus est coram Imperatore, & suam panopliam exuit.
units.tr: A certain Count, captain and commander of the army of Charles V in the coming war, wanted to fight with the princes. He told the Emperor this, pointing out at the same time the chance to crush the enemy. When he pressed hard for the battle to be joined, the Emperor flatly refused and said: "It is enough for me if I achieve the same result a year later with less loss." Angry that his plan was not approved, the Count raged before the Emperor and took off his armour.

units.la: Audiui puer ex patre meo, quòd Albertus, dux Bauariæ, auus huius ducis Alberti dixerit: Et-si post diuturnum bellum mihi mediocrem uisto-riam Deus concesserit, cui maximas ago gratias: tamen nihil meorum consiliorum cōcessit, quem-admodum mecum in rebus agendis constitueram. Sic recte Thucydides inquit: ἄνιϭα ὁ πόλεμος ἐπὶ ῥητοῖς προχωρεῖ, id est: minimè bellum procedit iuxta deliberata.
units.tr: As a boy I heard from my father that Albert, Duke of Bavaria, the grandfather of this Duke Albert, said: "Although after a long war God has granted me a moderate victory, for which I give him very great thanks, nothing has come about according to my plans, as I had settled them in conducting affairs." So Thucydides rightly says: [ἄνισα ὁ πόλεμος ἐπὶ ῥητοῖς προχωρεῖ], that is, war least of all proceeds according to what has been decided.

units.la: Non legitis multas triennales obsidiones, sed multas unius anni, & biennales. Triennales obsi-diones tantum scio tres. Prima est Bisantij, tempo-re Imperatoris Seueri ante Constantinum, qui re-stituit urbem destructā, & prorsus ferè deletā pro-pter opportunitatē loci. Durauit hæc obsidio 3 cū dimidio annos, ibi ingens multitudo fortissimorū uirorū intus & foris perijt. Secunda obsidio Bet-horon, tempore Adriani Imperatoris, durauit etiā tres annos. defensa est à Bencosban Iudæorū Messia. Adrianus scripsit ad senatum Romanum, non fuisse leue bellum cum reliquijs gentis Iudaicæ, sed tandē Bethoron fame coacta est facere deditionē. Tertia obsidio fuit Samariæ, quando decem tribus in Assyriam abductæ, & in illarum locum coloni alij ex gentibus introducti sunt, qui deinde aliquos ritus Iudaicos & quosdam gentiles seruabant. unde Samaritanus erat conuitij nomen, sicut apud maiores nostros Bohemus.
units.tr: You do not read of many sieges lasting three years, but of many lasting one year or two. I know of only three sieges lasting three years. The first is that of Byzantium, in the time of the Emperor Severus, before Constantine, who restored the city, which had been destroyed and almost wholly wiped out, because of the advantage of its position. This siege lasted three and a half years, and a huge number of very brave men perished inside and outside the walls. The second siege, of Bethoron, in the time of the Emperor Hadrian, also lasted three years; it was defended by Bencosban, the Messiah of the Jews. Hadrian wrote to the Roman senate that the war with the remnants of the Jewish nation had been no light matter, but at last Bethoron, forced by famine, was compelled to surrender. The third siege was that of Samaria, when the ten tribes were carried off into Assyria and other colonists from the nations were brought in to take their place. These colonists afterwards kept some Jewish rites and some gentile ones. Hence "Samaritan" became a term of abuse, just as "Bohemian" did among our ancestors.

units.la: Maximiliani usitatum fuit dictum: Facilius est regnum occupare, quàm retinere. Ipse expertus locutus est.
units.tr: A saying of Maximilian was common: "It is easier to seize a kingdom than to keep it." He spoke from experience.

units.la: Interrogaui aliquando quendam capitaneum, egregium uirum, qui erat pulsus à Gallo in bello Iuliacensi, an uerum esset, quòd duces bellorum nostro tempore (sicut ferunt) tam grauatim in certamen cum hoste descendant? Ille, inquit: Profecto uerum est, & dicam tibi tres causas quare sic fiat. Prima & principalis causa est, quia habemus reges & principes, qui non intelligunt bella, & quado postea committitur error in bello, & pugnando, tunc omnis culpa confertur in unum aliquem. Secunda, quia cum sit boni ducis non deuitare pericula, sed cohortari milites, & cum illis etiam in maximis periculis uitæ obequitare, & omnia perlustrare: etiam parcimus libenter nostris corporibus, ribus. Tertiò, ideo non libenter pugnamus, sed differimus bella, ut habeamus plus stipendij. Quia moventes bella eadem temeritate finiunt bella, cum non amplius habent pecuniam, qua inceperunt cum haberent.
units.tr: I once asked a certain captain, an excellent man, who had been driven back by the Frenchman in the war of Jülich, whether it was true, as people say, that in our time the commanders of wars go so reluctantly into battle with the enemy. He answered: "It is indeed true, and I will tell you three reasons why it happens. (1) The first and chief reason is that we have kings and princes who do not understand war, and when an error is afterwards made in the war or in the fighting, all the blame is laid on one man. (2) It is the part of a good commander not to avoid dangers but to encourage his soldiers, to share their lives even in the greatest perils, and to survey everything; so we also gladly spare our own bodies. (3) Therefore we do not gladly fight, but put off wars, so that we may have more pay. For those who start wars in the same rashness end them as soon as they no longer have the money they had when they began."

units.la: Audiui alium capitaneum, cum esset bellum motum inter duos potentes Dominos, idq; ualde metueretur, dicentem: Non est res periculosa, quia potentes tantum mouent bellum stulto quodam affectu, quando abundant pecunia: ubi uero ea est exhausta, tunc faciunt fœdera & conditiones pacis, etiamsi nihil earum rerum sit transactum, propter quas prius bellum mouerunt. Et sic accidit in isto bello, quemadmodum dux ille prædixerat.
units.tr: I heard another captain say, when a war had been started between two powerful lords and people greatly feared it: "There is no real danger, because powerful men start wars only from a certain foolish impulse while they have plenty of money. But when that money is used up, they make treaties and terms of peace, even though nothing has been settled on the very matters for which they first went to war. And so it has happened in this war, just as that commander had foretold."

units.la: Cum dux quidam bellum gereret cum Venetis, incendit aliquas villas, in quibus erat multum frumenti. Veneti admonuerũt ne hoc faceret, cum frumentum tam sibi quàm ipsis posset esse usui. Ille rescripsit, ne docerent ipsum quomodo bellum gerendum esset. Paulo post tanta fuit fames in ipsius castris, ut multi præstantissimi uiri fame morerentur. Postea cum milites reuerterentur, in Heluetia nutriti sunt aliquot dies, & instructi uiatico, unde multi qui longiore fame ægrotabant, sic rursus recreati sunt: aliqui etiam propter nimiam uirium debilitatem alimenta cõcoquere nõ ualentes, mortui sunt.
units.tr: When a certain duke was waging war with the Venetians, he set fire to some villages in which there was a great deal of grain. The Venetians warned him not to do this, since the grain could be useful both to him and to them. He wrote back that they should not teach him how to conduct a war. Shortly afterwards there was such famine in his camp that many outstanding men died of hunger. Later, when the soldiers returned, they were fed for some days in Switzerland and supplied with travel provisions, and so many who had been sick from long hunger were restored again. Some, however, too weakened to digest food, died.

units.la: Cum Hispani Mediolanum occupassent, hospi-tes cogebant singulis discumbentibus apponere co-ronatum, & illam pecuniam nominabāt spilgelt, quod si facere recusarent, diripiebant bona aut in-cendia minabantur, aut illos concutiebant.
units.tr: When the Spaniards had occupied Milan, they forced hosts to set a garland before each diner, and they called that money "spilgelt." If the hosts refused, the Spaniards plundered their goods, threatened them with fire, or beat them.

units.la: Lantgrauius bonus princeps, ipse ad me dixit: Quàm diu habui pecuniam, & militibus tempe-stiuè persolui stipendia, tandiu bonam disciplinā militarem in exercitu conseruare potui: sed si du-ces non possunt soluere, tunc nihil est, & discipli-na militaris strictè seruari non potest.
units.tr: As long as I had money and paid the soldiers their wages on time, the Landgrave, a good prince, told me himself, I was able to keep good military discipline in the army. But if the commanders cannot pay, then there is nothing, and military discipline cannot be strictly maintained.

units.la: Cum Veneti Maximiliano Imperatori bellum indicerent, legatus eorum usus est formula anti-qua Romana: Populus senatusq; Venetus bellum indicit Maximiliano. Respondit ei Imperator: Ite & gerite bellum simili stulticia qua indixistis. Sic eadem ratione postea bellum gesserunt.
units.tr: When the Venetians declared war on the Emperor Maximilian, their envoy used the old Roman formula: "The people and senate of Venice declare war on Maximilian." The Emperor answered him: "Go and wage the war with the same foolishness with which you declared it." And so, on the same principle, they afterwards waged it.

units.la: Epicharmus scripsit, Mineruam præcinuisse sal-tantibus Castori & Polluci. Significauit autem Mi-nerua præcinuisse Lacedæmonijs in pugnis et præ-lijs, hoc est, Lacedæmonios & sapientia & forti-tudine excelluisse in bellis. Hæ enim uirtutes duæ significantur per Mineruam. Item obseruandum est, Lacedæmonios non esse usos tympanis in bel-lis, sed ante exortum pugnæ præcinuisse fidibus.
units.tr: Epicharmus wrote that Minerva sang before Castor and Pollux as they danced. He meant that Minerva had sung before the Lacedaemonians in fights and battles, that is, that the Lacedaemonians excelled in wisdom and courage in war, since these two virtues are signified by Minerva. It is also to be noted that the Lacedaemonians did not use drums in battle, but before the fight began they sang to the lyre.

units.la: Georgius à Fronsberg, quamuis magnanimus miles, tamen etiam adeò benignus ac mitis fuit atq; quisquam aliús suo tempore inuentus est, nulli mi-liti egeno petěti uiaticũ negauit, etiamsi ipsi quo-dammodo carendum esset. Hauddubiè inter suos ita uixit, ut ipse nunquam quemquam offenderit, & tamen in acie fuit leo.
units.tr: Georg von Fronsberg, though a magnanimous soldier, was nevertheless so kind and gentle that no one else of his time was found more so. He never refused travel money to any needy soldier who asked for it, even when he himself had to go without. Without doubt he lived among his own people in such a way that he never offended anyone, and yet in battle he was a lion.

units.la: Memini me presente principem Anhaldinum cum doctore Martino Luthero de transferendo dominio iure belli cŏferre. Proponebat Vuolfgan-gus princeps Anhaldinus, esse ingens bellum inter Imperatorem & Regem Galliæ, & nos interro-gabat, cuius causa iustior esset? addens etiam hoc suæ quæstioni: ambo Reges sunt doctissimi, & am-borum aulæ uiris doctissimis abundant. Vnde fieri potest, ut iurisconsulti Regis, Imperatorem & Im-peratoris in Regem Galliæ disputent. Nos respon-dimus, iudicium esse penes Deum, nec facilè posse hæc ab hominibus dijudicari. Asserebamus etiam ignorantiam notoriæ iniuriæ, aut iniusticiæ sub-ditos excusare.
units.tr: I remember, when I was present, Prince Wolfgang of Anhalt conferring with Doctor Martin Luther on the transfer of dominion by the right of war. Prince Wolfgang of Anhalt put forward that there was a great war between the Emperor and the King of France, and asked us which cause was more just. He added to his question: both kings are most learned, and both their courts abound in most learned men, so it can happen that the jurists of the King and of the Emperor dispute, the one maintaining the Emperor's case against the King of France and the other the King's case against the Emperor. We answered that judgement rests with God, and that such matters cannot easily be decided by men. We also maintained that ignorance excuses subjects from a notorious injury or injustice.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: In pugna Patauiensi Imperatoris cum Rege Galliæ, equitatus Hispanicus, tam miserè profli-gauit cataphractos Regis, ut non secus atq; arbo-res quassatæ uiderentur. Hispanorum enim erant 500, qui cum 800 equitibus Gallicis cŏgressi sunt. Et dicebatur nulla eos misericordia erga quem-quam commotos fuisse in tam lamentabili pugna, ita ut tot præstantes equites non secus atque ollas quasdam contriuerint.
units.tr: In the battle of Pavia between the Emperor and the King of France, the Spanish cavalry so thoroughly routed the king's cuirassiers that they looked like trees shaken by a storm. For there were 500 Spaniards, and they met 800 French horsemen. It was said that they were moved by no pity toward anyone in so grievous a battle, and crushed so many excellent horsemen as easily as if they were smashing pots.

units.la: Audiui adolescens de Palatino Friderico bellatore, quòd fuerit consuetudo ipsius, ut si quando uellet mouere bellum, biennio ante uenaretur apros, quos condiebat. Et inde eius subditi coniectu-ram faciebant, cum aliquid moturum, cùm non quotidianis cibis apros consumeret, sicut fit in aulis, sed conditos seponeret.
units.tr: As a young man I heard about the warlike Count Palatine Frederick that it was his custom, whenever he meant to start a war, to hunt wild boars two years beforehand and pickle them. From this his subjects drew the conjecture that he was about to act, since he did not eat the boars every day as is done at courts, but laid the pickled ones aside.

units.la: Memorabile est quòd quidam magni nominis princeps ante aliquot annos de iunioribus quibusdam ducibus, quorum ætas adhuc feruens erat, dixit: Nihil est committendum iuuenibus, tantum perdunt exercitus. Quare nihil potestatis in exercitum ipsis concedatis.
units.tr: It is worth remembering that a certain prince of great renown said some years ago, of certain younger commanders whose age was still hot-blooded: "Nothing should be entrusted to young men; they ruin armies so quickly. Therefore grant them no authority over the army."

units.la: Non est gesta maior pugna nostro tempore, quàm ad Rauenam, ubi pontifex Iulius fuit instru-ctus electissimo & robustissimo exercitu Hispani-co, Helvetico & Italico, quo bellum inferre tentabat Maximiliano & Ludouico Regi Galliæ, qui se cum Maximiliano coniunxerat. Maximilianus re-cognita, mittit Langium cardinalem Saltzburgen-sem ad pontificem, ut faceret pacem cum eo, qui cum diu Romæ cum eo egisset, tandem simplicissi-mè proponit Pontifici: Sanctissime pater, simpli-citer, bellum aut pax. Respondit Pontifex, ut erat furiosus: Bellum. Langius, hoc responso accepto, celeriter per ueredarios equos properat ad Maximilianum. In uia intelligit pugnam iam commissam esse ad Rauennā, & uictum esse Papæ exercitum. Ibi Pontifex ex uia reuocat Langium, ut cum eo de pacis conditionibus agat, mittēs ei simul munera. Sed Cardinalis omnia illa remisit, ita ut ex eis unum tantum salinum retineret, quo significauit, se non aspernari munera Pontificis, sed alias grauissimas causas habere, quare eas suscipere nō posset. Ita ipse non passus est se retrahi: maluit enim domino suo Imperatori victoriam nunciare. Cùm Papa in illa pugna bene instructus esset bombardis, nostri Germani milites id non ignorantes in terra procubuerunt, ut globi, illæsis ipsis, præteruolarent, eoq; stratagemata periculum globorum declinauerunt. Postea Gallicus quidam dux Namorsa cum ala electissimorū militum alloquitur Germanos: Vos fideles, inquiens, Germani, meo exemplo in hostes qua potestis animi alacritate irruite: quo dicto, primus in hostes impetum fecit, & Germani strenuè eum secuti sunt. Ita Hispanos, qui primam aciem tenebant, ad unum omnes trucidant. Dux autem Namorsa seipsum devouerat pro Imperatore, unde fortissimè in illo conflictu acerrimo interfectus est. Postea uerò Papa quibuscunq; cōditionibus coactus est facere pacē.
units.tr: No greater battle has been fought in our time than the one at Ravenna, where Pope Julius was equipped with a most select and robust army, Spanish, Swiss and Italian, with which he tried to make war on Maximilian and on King Louis of France, who had joined himself to Maximilian. Maximilian, having learned this, sent Cardinal Langius of Salzburg to the Pope to make peace with him. After Langius had negotiated with him for a long time at Rome, he finally put it to the Pontiff quite plainly: "Most holy father, simply put: war or peace?" The Pontiff, being furious, replied: "War." Langius, having received this answer, hurried by post-horses to Maximilian. On the way he learned that the battle had already been joined at Ravenna and the Pope's army defeated. Then the Pope recalled Langius from the road, to discuss the terms of peace with him, and at the same time sent him gifts. But the cardinal sent all of them back, keeping only one salt-cellar, by which he signified that he did not scorn the Pope's gifts, but had other very grave reasons why he could not accept them. Thus he did not allow himself to be drawn back; he preferred to bring the news of victory to his lord the Emperor. Since the Pope was well supplied with bombards in that battle, our German soldiers, who were not unaware of this, threw themselves flat on the ground, so that the cannonballs flew over them unharmed; by this stratagem they avoided the danger of the shot. Afterwards a certain French commander, Namorsa, with a wing of the most select soldiers, addressed the Germans: "You faithful Germans, follow my example and rush at the enemy with all the eagerness of spirit you can." With these words he made the first charge against the enemy, and the Germans bravely followed him. In this way they cut down to a man all the Spaniards who held the front line. Commander Namorsa had devoted himself for the Emperor, and so he was most bravely killed in that fierce and bitter conflict. Afterwards the Pope was forced to make peace on whatever terms were imposed.

units.la: Princeps quidam, cum uellet incipere bellum, dicebat: Aut aliquid, aut nihil. Respondu aliquis ex consiliarijs: Tua celsitudo iam quidem est aliquid, at si uelit, facile nihil fieri potest.
units.tr: A certain prince, when he wished to begin a war, used to say: "Either something or nothing." One of his counsellors replied: "Your Highness is indeed already something, but if you wish, it can easily be made into nothing."

units.la: Quidam dux cum appeteret dignitatem Imperatoriam, mouit bellum contra Imperatorem Heinricum Aucupem, qui suffragijs principu acceperat coronam, contra quem Heinricus coactus est se defendere, ac proficiscitur in ea loca, ubi habebat dux alter exercitum. Ibi Heinricus obtulit conditionem alteri, ne dimicaret, ipsum, si uellent principes, libenter dignitate Imperatoria cessuru esse. Tenuit autem Heinricus Auceps tunc temporis totam Saxoniam a littore Oceani septentrionalis usq; ad Thuringiam. Intercesserunt boni homines, qui suaserunt alteri duci ne dimicaret. Composita postea pace ille dux dixit, se uidisse in uisione seu somnio uirum stantem cum gladio sine capite, unde sumpsit coniecturam, se plane infeliciter dimicaturum.
units.tr: A certain duke, when he aspired to the imperial dignity, made war on the Emperor Henry the Fowler, who had received the crown by the votes of the princes. Henry was forced to defend himself against him, and set out for the region where the other duke had his army. There Henry offered the other man a condition, that he should not fight: if the princes wished, Henry would gladly yield the imperial dignity to him. At that time Henry the Fowler held the whole of Saxony, from the shore of the northern Ocean as far as Thuringia. Good men intervened and persuaded the other duke not to fight. After peace was afterwards made, that duke said he had seen in a vision or dream a man standing with a sword and no head, and from this he drew the conjecture that he would fight quite unluckily.

units.la: STRATAGEMATA.
units.tr: STRATAGEMS.

units.la: Valde usitatum est in Italia, ut præstantissimi duces habeant magna uolumina stratagmatu antiquorum & recentium, quorum lectione commo nefaciunt se de multis rebus. Vetus est stratagema, quo magni sæpe superati sunt exercitus. Isto ueteri stratagemate Galli aliquando dicuntur usi aduersus Cæsarianos milites. Præmiserunt autem currus oneratos serico,& alijs pannis, quos milites Cæsariani auidè & securè imuaserunt. Galli interea illos, dum inter se de præda concertant, suo equitatu incautos imuadunt atq; opprimunt.
units.tr: It is very common in Italy for leading commanders to keep large volumes of the stratagems of the ancients and the moderns, so that by reading them they may instruct themselves in many matters. There is an old stratagem by which great armies have sometimes been overcome. The Gauls are said to have once used this old stratagem against Caesar's soldiers. They sent ahead wagons loaded with silk and other cloth, which the Caesarian soldiers eagerly and carelessly attacked. Meanwhile the Gauls, while the soldiers quarrelled among themselves over the booty, attacked and crushed them with their cavalry while they were off their guard.

units.la: Cymon sapientissimus ac fortissimus dux tanta modestia præditus fuit, ut cùm ex Ionia secum poetã duxisset, qui eius laudes nimis amplas descripsisset, non modò non delectatus sit, uerumetiam id ægerrimè tulerit. Dicebat enim ex nullis rebus suis gestis ullam laudem quærere, nisi tantum ex uno stratagemate. Hoc autem erat tale, quod sine ullius offensione, aut læsione erga suos ciues Lacedæmonios usurpauerat. Cum enim magno prælio Persas uicisset, multosq; captiuos, & immensam prædam ex ea pugna retulisset, quæ omnia simul ipsi cum suis ciuibus erant diuidenda: ibi Cymon non ignarus auariciæ Lacedæmoniorum quicquid erat auri & argenti in unum locum, corpora uerò captiuorum uili uestitu induta ex altera parte collocari iussit, deditq; deinceps Lacedæmonijs electionem. Lacedæmonij uerò auaricia decepti, auidè eam partem elegerunt, in qua aurum & argentum collocatum erat, insuperq; Cymoni pro tam liberali diuisione, optionisq; permissione gratias egerunt. Verùm Cymon non minorem prædã una cum laude est assecutus. Erant namq; inter captiuos multi nobilissimi ac ditissimi uiri, quos cùm ipse se redimere permitteret, ingentem pecuniam, & quidè multo maiorem quàm ipsi Lacedæmo-nes ex eorum redemptione ac liberatione, etiam cum gratia collegit. Quinetiam credo ex hac libe-ratione captiuorum ipsum tantum gratiæ apud hostes iniuiße, ut hæc fuerit præcipua causa, quòd postea tanta Asiæ declinatio ad ipsum facta sit. Sic Cymon hoc eleganti stratagemate & suæ utilitati consuluit, & duplicem gratiam apud Lacedæmonios scilicet liberalitatis, & apud captiuos clementiæ iniuit.
units.tr: Cimon, the wisest and bravest commander, was so modest that when he had brought with him from Ionia a poet who had written very extravagant praises of him, he not only was not pleased but took it very badly. For he said that he sought no praise for any of his deeds except for one stratagem alone. This was of such a kind that he had used it without offence or injury to his fellow citizens of Lacedaemon. When he had defeated the Persians in a great battle and brought back many captives and an immense booty from that fight, all of which was to be shared out between himself and his fellow citizens, Cimon, aware of the greed of the Lacedaemonians, ordered that all the gold and silver be placed in one spot, while the bodies of the captives, dressed in poor clothing, be placed on the other side, and then gave the Lacedaemonians the choice. The Lacedaemonians, deceived by their greed, eagerly chose the side where the gold and silver had been placed, and moreover thanked Cimon for such a generous division and for granting them the choice. But Cimon obtained no less a prize, together with the praise. For among the captives were many very noble and wealthy men, whom, since he allowed them to ransom themselves, he collected a huge sum of money, and indeed much more than the Lacedaemonians themselves gathered from their ransom and release, and he gathered it with their goodwill as well. Indeed I believe that by this release of the captives he gained so much favour with the enemy that this was the chief reason why such a great shift of Asia towards him took place afterwards. Thus Cimon, by this elegant stratagem, served both his own advantage and gained a double favour: that of the Lacedaemonians for his generosity, and that of the captives for his clemency.

units.la: Hannibal multis collectis bobus ad cornua faces alligat, eosq; ad saltum contra Fabium exagitat. Turbato Fabio, saluus euadit cum exercitu Hannibal.
units.tr: Hannibal, having gathered many oxen, tied torches to their horns and drove them against Fabius through a pass. Fabius was thrown into confusion, and Hannibal escaped safe with his army.

units.la: Stratagema ualde usi-tatum.
units.tr: A very common stratagem.

units.la: Cum Imperator Conradus obsedisset oppidum Vueimnsberg, quod quatuor milliaribus distat à mea patria, (credo ibi fuisse munitionem, quia situm habet similem arci Coburgensi. In ea obsidione erat Guelfus dux Bauar æ, erat et ami igy æ-cium, & aliorum dominorũ coniuges, filij & puellæ) & cùm tandem deficeret frumentum, excogitabatur consilium à mulieribus, petendum esse ab Imperatore, ut liceret ipsis egredi ex arce cum ijs rebus, quas asportare possent. Hoc concessit Imperator, quia æquissimum est mulieribus præsta- re beneuolentiam. Mulieres egrediuntur, & ge- stant singulæ aliquos principes,& uiros præci- puæ authoritatis. Egregium sanè stratagema mu- lierum,prætendentium se gestare suas res: quia ma- riti etiam ipsorum erant. Apud Imperatorem con- trà disputabatur,uiolari pacta,non esse intellectū de uiris,sed de ornamentis mulierum. Sed quid c- rat faciendum Imperatori? erat à mulieribus de- ceptus. In meliorem itaq; partem interpretatus est,iussit ut gestarent uiros in tentorium suum,ubi consederunt,pransi sunt,& fecerunt pacem. Pul- chrum quidem & Germanicum stratagema.
units.tr: When the Emperor Conrad had besieged the town of Weinsberg, which is four miles from my homeland (I believe there was a fortress there, since it has a site similar to the citadel of Coburg), and the Duke Welf of Bavaria was in that siege, along with the wives, sons and daughters of the Duke's friends and of other lords, and when at last the grain ran out, the women devised a plan of asking the Emperor that they be allowed to leave the citadel with whatever goods they could carry. The Emperor granted this, since it is most fitting to show goodwill to women. The women came out, and each carried on her back some prince or man of outstanding authority. It was indeed a remarkable stratagem of the women, who pretended that they were carrying their own belongings, since these were their husbands. The Emperor was argued against, that the agreement was being violated, and that it had not been understood to refer to men but to the women's belongings. But what was the Emperor to do? He had been deceived by the women. Taking the matter in the better sense, he ordered that they carry their men into his tent, where they sat down, dined, and made peace. A fine stratagem, and a German one indeed.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam bellum gerens cum episcopo Mogun- tinensi, cum in uindemia uinum conuehi uideret, interrogare solebat,cuius' nam esset illud uinum? Quòd si responderetur,esse Capituli,ipse cepit, & abduxit secum: si uerò diceretur,huius uel alterius esse Canonici,respōdit: Hic est meus amicus:& sic aurigam liberè dimisit, subiecitq; hoc sibi usitatū prouerbium: Domini quidem probi sunt,sed Capi- tulum est nequam.
units.tr: A certain man waging war with the bishop of Mainz, when he saw wine being carried in at the vintage, used to ask whose wine it was. If the answer was that it belonged to the Chapter, he seized it and carried it off with him; but if it was said to belong to this or that canon, he replied: "He is my friend," and so he let the carter go free, adding this common proverb: "The lords are indeed upright, but the Chapter is worthless."

units.la: Lantgrauius cū cepisset secretarium Ducis cu- iusdam,ibi Dux obiecit ei (quod ualde speciosum erat).non esse iustum capere legatos. Lantgra- uius econtrà habebat exceptionem, quòd inueniset exemplum apud Liuium, ubi Romani interce- perant legatos Atheniensium: & iudicatũ est re- ƈte fieri. Simile exemplum est apud Herodotum, ubi Athenienses ceperunt legatos Lacedæmonio- rum,ituros ad regem Persicum, ut fœdera ferirêt, & auxilia impetrarent contra eos, & statim illos interfecerunt.
units.tr: When the Landgrave had captured the secretary of a certain duke, the duke objected to him (which was a very specious argument) that it was not right to seize envoys. The Landgrave on the other hand had a defence, namely that he had found a precedent in Livy, where the Romans had intercepted envoys of the Athenians; and it was judged that he had acted rightly. There is a similar example in Herodotus, where the Athenians captured envoys of the Lacedaemonians who were going to the king of Persia to make treaties and obtain help against them, and they immediately put them to death.

units.la: Paches,cum obsideret Colophonem,nouerat Ar cadicum ducem (cuius erat excellens industria)in urbe esse. Igitur euocat illum, & simulat se uelle cum eo colloqui, promittens ei incolumitatem,& saluum in urbẽ reditum. Egresso ipso Paches expugnat urbem, qui sciebat sine duce nihil effectu- rum esse exercitum. Capta uerò urbe, iterum ducem introduxit, ut sic seruare uideretur quod ipsi promiserat:uerùm postea eum callido hoc sophis- mate elusum inique trucidauit. Quare Paches e- tiam seipsum gladio confodit: quia Deus puniuit iniusticiam illam.
units.tr: When Paches was besieging Colophon, he knew that Arcadicus, the leader of the city (who was of outstanding ability), was inside. So he summoned him and pretended that he wished to speak with him, promising him safety and a safe return into the city. When Arcadicus came out, Paches stormed the city, for he knew that the army would achieve nothing without a leader. But after the city was taken, he brought the leader back in, so as to appear to keep what he had promised; yet afterwards, having been tricked by this clever sophism, he cruelly slaughtered him. Therefore Paches himself also stabbed himself with a sword, because God punished that injustice.

units.la: Romanum sophisma.
units.tr: A Roman sophism.

units.la: Quando Popilius missus fuit legatus ad Antio- chum, hominem uafrum & leuẽ prorsus, uoluit cum Cretensi cretisare. Quare iuxta mandatum senatus paƈtus est, ut dimidium nauium Romani retineret. Postea uerò idem Popilius dissecari om- nes naues curauit,& trabes sectas ita diuidi,ut di- midium relinqueretur Antiocho.
units.tr: When Popilius was sent as envoy to Antiochus, a man utterly crafty and fickle, he wanted to play the Cretan with him. Therefore, in accordance with the senate's instruction, he agreed that the Romans should keep half of the ships. But afterwards the same Popilius had all the ships cut apart and the timbers so divided that only half was left to Antiochus.

units.la: VICTORIA, EIVSDEMQUE moderatio.
units.tr: Victory, and its moderation.

units.la: Episcopus Spirensis uictus ab electore Palatino, cum fuisset hostis eius, uenit ultrò, sibi restim seu laqueum collo circundans ac flexis genibus petiuit mitigationem poenæ. Princeps pro sua clementia hac humilitate motus pepercit ei, dimisitq; eum statim.
units.tr: The bishop of Speyer, defeated by the Elector Palatine, who had been his enemy, came of his own accord. He put a rope or noose around his neck, knelt, and begged for a lessening of his punishment. The prince, moved by this humility and by his own clemency, spared him and let him go at once.

units.la: Laurentius Medices uir magnanimus, sapiens, hostis reipub. Florentinæ, sciens se non esse parem aduersario suo Alfonso, tanto regi, ascendit navim, & non petita publica pace, navigauit ad portum Neapolitanum. Cum uero eò peruenisset, iubet regi indicari, adesse Laurentium Medicem. Rex miratus ipsius aduentum, iussit indicari ipsi, ut ad se ueniret. Sed Laurentius: Nolo, inquit, egredi navim, nisi prius sciam, an ad amicum, an uero ad hostem mihi eundum sit. Rex respondit, hoc penes illum esse, eligat utrum uelit: sed malle se, ut veniret tanquam ad amicum. Hæc fuit uirtus eximia, & laude dignissima in Rege. Ita facto colloquio pacem inter se fecerunt.
units.tr: Lorenzo de' Medici, a magnanimous and wise man and an enemy of the Florentine commonwealth, knew he was no match for his adversary Alfonso, so great a king. He boarded a ship and, without asking for a public safe-conduct, sailed to the port of Naples. When he arrived there, he had word sent to the king that Lorenzo de' Medici was present. The king, surprised by his arrival, ordered word to be sent to him to come to court. But Lorenzo said: "I will not leave the ship until I first know whether I am to go to a friend or to an enemy." The king replied that it was up to him to choose whichever he wished, but he would prefer that Lorenzo come as to a friend. This was an outstanding virtue, most worthy of praise in a king. So a conference was held, and they made peace between themselves.

units.la: Quando Pausanias uicit ad Plateas exercitum Darij, trucidatis decem millibus hominum, singularem modestiam & clementiam erga victos ostendit. Cum enim Aeginetæ hortarentur, ut capita ducum affigeret hastis & circumferret, improbauit ipso-uit ipsouit ipsorum consilium, & dixit, non esse insultandum mortuis, satis est mihi patriæ & Deo placere. Factus est postea præses Bizantij, ubi elatus contrà insolentiæ pœnas dedit.
units.tr: When Pausanias defeated Darius's army at Plataea and slaughtered ten thousand men, he showed singular moderation and clemency toward the vanquished. When the Aeginetans urged him to fix the heads of the commanders on spears and carry them about, he disapproved of their proposal and said that the dead should not be insulted; it was enough for him to please his country and God. He was afterwards made governor of Byzantium, where, puffed up with arrogance, he paid the penalty for his insolence.

units.la: Cùm Palatinus cepisset tres principes, in prima cœna prohibuit eis apponere panem. Illi cùm sederent in mensa, & scirent Palatinum non hostiliter sæuiturũ esse in illorũ corpora, (sicut postea etiam dimisi sunt, factis conditionibus, ubi Palatinus admodum suam clementiam erga illos declarauit ) petiuerunt sibi panem præberi : habere ipsos unde soluerent. Ibi Palatinus iussit ipsis renunciari, se hoc ideo fecisse, ut commonefierent ipsos non gessisse bellum sicut decet bonos principes, propterea quòd non pepercilsent segetibus, sed duxissent exercitus per segetes, non coacti ulla necessitate. In pædia Cyri est, quòd cùm Cyrus faceret expeditionem præcipere solitus sit militibus, ut parcerent agricolis, ne segetes uastarentur.
units.tr: When the Palatine had captured three princes, he forbade bread to be set before them at their first meal. While they sat at the table, and knowing that the Palatine would not rage hostilely against their persons (for they were afterwards released on conditions, when the Palatine showed considerable clemency toward them), they asked that bread be given them, since they had the means to pay for it. Then the Palatine ordered them told that he had done this so that they might be reminded that they had not waged war as good princes should, since they had not spared the crops but had led their armies through the fields, with no necessity compelling them. In the Cyropaedia there is a passage where Cyrus, when undertaking an expedition, used to order his soldiers to spare the farmers, so that the crops would not be laid waste.

units.la: Fridericus Palatinus, qui uixit patrum nostrorum memoria, deuictis his tribus principibus, cùm ueniret Heydelbergam, non statim ascēdit arcem, sed prius ingrediebatur templum, ubi flexis genibus ad aram longo tempore dixit suam precationem ad Deum, & egit gratias pro liberatione ex periculis.
units.tr: Frederick the Palatine, who lived within the memory of our fathers, having defeated these three princes, came to Heidelberg. He did not go up to the citadel at once but first entered the church, where he knelt before the altar for a long time, offered his prayer to God, and gave thanks for his deliverance from danger.

units.la: Quando dux Luneburgensis cepit suum hostē, & captum duxit in arcem Cellensem, uenit ei obuiam coniunx cum gynæcio,& obtulit marito coronam auream tanquam uictori: & hosti capto etiam tradidit coronam auream, propterea quòd fortiter pugnasset. Postea simul ceperunt cibum, familiariter colloquentes,& æquissimis conditionibus factis, ipsum rursus dimisit.
units.tr: When the duke of Lüneburg captured his enemy and led him away prisoner into the citadel at Celle, his wife came to meet him with her women and offered her husband a golden crown as to a victor. To the captured enemy too she gave a golden crown, because he had fought bravely. Afterwards they took food together, talking in a friendly way, and on the fairest terms he was set free again. The duke's wife, meeting him with her women, offered her husband a golden crown as to a victor; and to the captured enemy too she gave a golden crown, because he had fought bravely. Afterwards they ate together, talking familiarly, and on the fairest terms he was released again.

units.la: Alphonsus rex Neapolitamus,uiuens tempore maiorum nostrorum, fuit unus de sapientissimis regibus, ualde doctus,& magnas res cum magna admiratione gessit,fuit eiectus ac expulsus,iterũq; in regnum redijt. Is quando obsedit Caietam, Caietani emiserũt magnam turbam senum, mulierũ, puerorum,& puellarum ex urbe, ut reliqui possent diutius habere in obsidione urbis frumēta& alias res necessarias. Ibi quidam consiliarij consuluerunt regi, ut hanc miseram multitudinem aut saltem partem eius in cõspectu urbis interfici mādaret, quo spectaculo ab inhabitatoribus uiso, citius facerent deditionem. Et historiographus inquit:Deus mihi ignoscat, idem & ego regi consului. Tunc Rex stetit attonitus & cogitabundus, tandemq; post longum silentium in hæc uerba prorupit: Totum regnum Neapolitanum non est mihi tanti, ut impetum in hanc miseram turbam faciam: deditq; statim sæuerissimum mandatum, ut omnes incolumes in uicina oppida & loca distribuerentur. buerentur. Hoc cum aspicerent inhabitatores urbis in muris & turribus, re cognita, statim fecerũt deditionem, moti uirtute & clementia Regis in uictoria ferè parta. sic uidetis quanto plus faciat uirtus, quàm crudelitas. Magis enim flectuntur animi clemētia, quàm immanitate & ferocia. Quare pulchrè dixit Scipio, se malle unum ciuem seruare, quàm totam legationem hostium delere.
units.tr: Alphonso, king of Naples, who lived in the time of our forefathers, was one of the most wise kings, very learned, and accomplished great things to great admiration. He was driven out and expelled, and returned again to his kingdom. When he besieged Gaeta, the Gaetans sent out from the city a great crowd of old men, women, boys and girls, so that the rest could hold out longer in the siege with grain and other necessary supplies. Then some of his counsellors advised the king to order this wretched multitude, or at least part of it, to be killed in sight of the city, so that the inhabitants, seeing the spectacle, would surrender more quickly. And the historian says: "God forgive me, I gave the same advice to the king." Then the king stood astonished and deep in thought, and at last, after a long silence, burst out with these words: "The whole kingdom of Naples is not worth so much to me that I should make an assault on this wretched crowd." And he at once gave a most stern order that they all be distributed unharmed among the neighbouring towns and places. When the inhabitants of the city saw this from the walls and towers, and learned of it, they at once surrendered, moved by the valour and clemency of the king when the victory was almost won. So you see how much more valour achieves than cruelty. For minds are bent more by clemency than by savagery and ferocity. Therefore Scipio rightly said that he preferred to save one citizen than to destroy a whole embassy of enemies.

units.la: Rami oleæ significatio.
units.tr: The meaning of the olive branch.

units.la: Ramus oleæ significat pacem. Vnde olim consuetudo, ut petentes pacem eorum legati ramum oleæ hosti deferrent. Cùm Scipio uicisset Hannibalem & desperata esset defensio Carthaginis, Carthaginenses miserunt nauem cum legatis ad Scipionem petitum pacem. Postquam uerò primum à Romanis conspicerentur, indicatur Scipioni à speculatore, adesse hostium naues. Quòd cùm intellexisset Scipio, iubet suas promoueri naues ad incursandum hosti. Cùm uerò propius in conspectu Romanorum accessissent, uidit speculator ramum oleæ in prora nauis suspensum, indicatq; idem Scipioni. Ibi Scipio statim sistit suas naues, nec eas ulterius in hostes promouet: quia ex oleæ ramo eos cognouit uenire petitum pacem.
units.tr: The olive branch signifies peace. Hence the custom in former times that envoys seeking peace carried an olive branch to the enemy. When Scipio had defeated Hannibal and the defence of Carthage was hopeless, the Carthaginians sent a ship with envoys to Scipio to seek peace. But when the Romans first caught sight of it, a scout reported to Scipio that enemy ships were approaching. When Scipio understood this, he ordered his own ships to advance to attack the enemy. But when they had come closer, in full view of the Romans, the scout saw an olive branch hanging from the prow of the ship and reported this to Scipio too. Then Scipio at once halted his ships and advanced them no further against the enemy, because from the olive branch he recognised that they were coming to seek peace.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Maximilianus in puniendis delictis leuissimus, in uindicanda auaricia militum acerrimus fuit. In bello Veneto, cùm capta Vincentia, quidam iniuf-su suo in aliquot ciuium ædes prædandi causa im-petum fecissent: statim illam totam cohortem op-pressit, & plures ducentis secuti percuti iussit, ut eo exemplo ostenderet, non omnia uictoribus in uictos licere.
units.tr: Maximilian was very lenient in punishing offences, but very severe in restraining the greed of his soldiers. In the Venetian war, after Vicenza was taken, some men acting on their own initiative made an attack on several citizens' houses in order to plunder them. He at once had that whole squad cut down, and ordered more than two hundred of their followers to be beaten, so that by this example he might show that victors are not allowed to do everything to the vanquished.

units.la: Est magna laus & bonitas principis Lantgra-uij Hassiæ Philippi, curans in expeditione Vuir-tembergensi quàm diligentissimè, ne fierent rapi-næ in territorio hostili. Non solum à socijs abfti-nuit, sed etiam à prædis hostium. Illa laus est etiam in historia Bellisarij.
units.tr: The Landgrave of Hesse, Prince Philip, deserves great praise and goodness, for in the Württemberg campaign he took the greatest care that no plundering took place in enemy territory. He refrained not only from his allies' property but also from the spoils of the enemy. The same praise is also recorded in the history of Belisarius.

units.la: Alexander cepit regem Indicum Porum, & interrogauit cum, quomodo se tractari cuperet. Respondit Βασιλικῶς. Alexander uero pro eximia sua clementia reliquit ei regnū, liberumq; eum dimisit, cùm id non potuisset facere: quia iam erat dominus captiui regis Pori. Sic Rex Geticus quem uocant Syrmium, id est defensorem, cum cepisset regem Lysimachum Alexandri satellitem, facta pace cum eo, dedit ei filiam, dimisitq; ipsum incolumem.
units.tr: Alexander captured the Indian king Porus and asked him how he wished to be treated. He replied "royally" [Βασιλικῶς]. Alexander, out of his remarkable clemency, left him his kingdom and let him go free, although he could not have done so, since he was already master of the captive king Porus. Likewise the Getic king, whom they call Syrmius, that is, "defender," when he had captured King Lysimachus, a follower of Alexander, made peace with him, gave him his daughter in marriage, and let him go unharmed.

units.la: Noster Imperator olim capto rege Galliæ, cùm iam dominus eius esset, progressus ei obuiam amplexus est eum amicè, dicens: Mon frere n'aye peur, car tes affaires se porte bien, id est, mi frater habe patientiam, res tuæ non male succedent: egit fraternè cum eo.
units.tr: Our Emperor once captured the king of France, and when he was already his master, went out to meet him, embraced him kindly and said: "My brother, do not be afraid, for your affairs are going well"; that is, my brother, have patience, your affairs will not turn out badly. He treated him in a brotherly way.

units.la: Neapolis à Totila rege Gothorum cincta ob sidione, cum facere deditionem cogeretur, ibi tanta fuit uirtus Totilæ, ut exercitum in urbem illæsis plane ciuibus mitteret, & priusquam ingrederetur exercitus, misit in urbem frumentum, cui milites addidit, qui distribuerent ciuibus, ne diriperentur à prædonibus. Valde prædicatur ille summus rex à Historiographis. In prima uictoria Italica, cùm cepisset magnam multitudinem nobilissimarum matronarum iuuenum & puellarum, diligentissime eas curauit deduci ad parentes. Cum porrò cernerent Neapoli, & in aliis urbibus illam clementiam & uirtutes Totilæ, libentius ei dediderunt. Et magna inclinatio Italiæ facta est ad cum propter ipsius clementiam & uirtutes, cum alias essent petulantes grassatores in Italia.
units.tr: When Naples was besieged by Totila, king of the Goths, and was forced to surrender, Totila showed such great virtue there that he sent his army into the city with the citizens entirely unharmed; and before the army entered, he sent grain into the city and added soldiers to distribute it to the citizens, so that they would not be plundered by robbers. That great king is much praised by the historians. In his first Italian victory, when he had taken a large number of most noble matrons, young women and girls, he took the greatest care to have them escorted back to their parents. When the people of Naples and of other cities saw this clemency and virtue of Totila, they surrendered to him more willingly. And because of his clemency and virtues a great inclination of Italy came over to him, although otherwise there were wanton marauders throughout Italy.

units.la: Cæsar in pugna Pharsalica, cum uideret eam inclinare, clamauit miles: Parce ciuibus.
units.tr: Caesar, in the battle of Pharsalus, seeing that the fight was turning his way, cried out to his soldiers: "Spare the citizens!"

units.la: Pericli datum est uitio, quòd magis erat intentus in feriendos ciues, quàm in hostes. Mul[?] semper huic similes reperiūtur, qui magis intenti sunt in hoc, ut se mutuò perdant quàm ut uincant hostes. Quando imperia sunt ruitura, tum ista fiunt. Athenæ ceciderunt Periclis stultitia, qui hoc agebat ut premeret eminentiores ciues magis quàm hostes, & sic implicuit eos bello exitiali.
units.tr: Pericles had the fault that he was more intent on striking down citizens than on the enemy. Many such men are always to be found, who are more intent on destroying one another than on conquering their enemies. When empires are about to fall, such things happen. Athens fell through the folly of Pericles, who aimed to crush the more eminent citizens rather than the enemy, and so entangled them in a ruinous war.

units.la: An faciens deditionem recte faciat?
units.tr: Whether a commander who surrenders may act rightly

units.la: Quærebam aliquando, an sit capitaneo facienda deditio: sicut accidit in deditione arcis Blasenburg? Et responsum est: Ita. Interrogabam ulterius an habuissent victualia? Responderunt mihi, nihil se habuisse, nisi paululum panis, quo vix potuissent nutriri uno mense. Non fecerunt igitur contra fidem datam facientes deditionem.
units.tr: I once asked whether a commander ought to surrender, as happened in the surrender of the fortress of Blasenburg. The answer was yes. I then asked further whether they had run out of provisions. They told me they had nothing left except a little bread, enough to sustain them for barely one month. So they did not act against the faith they had pledged in surrendering.

units.la: Contrà.
units.tr: On the contrary.

units.la: Capitaneus defensionem arcis anteferre vitæ suæ debet.
units.tr: A commander ought to put the defence of his fortress before his own life.

units.la: Illi defensione arcis non antetulerunt vitæ suæ.
units.tr: They did not put the defence of the fortress before their own lives.

units.la: Ergo: non recte fecerunt: et per consequens non debuissent se dedere propter aliquorum morbos vel famem. Responsum est ad maiorem: Capitaneus debet defensionem anteferre suæ vitæ, donec cum viris certamen est, sed quando certamen est cum natura, tunc debet esse finis belli, quando pereunt illi, quibus bella parcere solent, ut sunt mulieres & senes. Extat pulchrum exemplum in primo libro Xenophontis, de eo, qui Byzantium tenuerat nomine Lacedæmoniorum. Dux Byzantiorum Anaxilaus diu tenuerat urbem à hostibus obsessam, imò tam diu donec uideret milites passim fame mori: quo uiso fecit deditionem. postea Spartæ accusatus propter deditionem urbis, respondit,
units.tr: Therefore they did not act rightly, and consequently they ought not to have surrendered on account of some men's sickness or hunger. To the major premise the reply is this: a commander ought to put the defence before his own life so long as the struggle is with men. But when the struggle is with nature, the war must end, once those perish whom wars usually spare, such as women and old men. There is a fine example in the first book of Xenophon, concerning the man who had held Byzantium in the name of the Lacedaemonians. The leader of the Byzantines, Anaxilaus, had held the city, besieged by the enemy, for a long time, indeed so long that he saw the soldiers dying of hunger on every side. Seeing this, he surrendered. Afterwards, when he was accused at Sparta for surrendering the city, he replied:

units.la: Quintum praeceptum.
units.tr: The fifth precept.

units.la: respondit, se tenuisse urbem, dum bellum fuisset cum hostibus, sed cum bellum esset cum natura, id est, cum fame pereundum esset, se fecisse deditionē. Ephori Lacedæmonici laudabiliter eum fecisse iudicarunt, ipsumq; absoluerunt. Ita illi etiam Blas-senburgenses facientes, deditionem propter necessitatem & famem sunt excusati, nec eos inhoneste fecisse iudicatur. Sed humana uel potius diabolica pertinacia decurrit sæpe ad exempla crudelissima contra naturam humanam: sicut recitantur historiæ harum urbium: Hierosolymæ, Samariæ, & Potideæ in bello Peloponesiaco. &c.
units.tr: he replied that he had held the city while the war was with the enemy, but when the war was with nature, that is, when they had to perish by hunger, he had made a surrender. The Ephors of Lacedaemon judged that he had acted commendably and acquitted him. So too those of Blasenburg, who surrendered on account of necessity and hunger, are excused, and it is not judged that they acted dishonourably. But human, or rather diabolical, obstinacy often runs to the most cruel examples against human nature, as the histories of these cities are recounted: Jerusalem, Samaria, and Potidaea in the Peloponnesian War, etc.

units.la: Quatuor insignes obsidiones.
units.tr: Four notable sieges.

units.la: Scribitur de Potidea, quòd tanta fuerit fames in bello Peloponesiaco, ut uentum sit ad humanas carnes, quibus cœperunt uesci illi, qui erant in præsidio. Deinde scribitur de Duneto in Africano bello, quòd milites sint decimati, id est, decimũ quemq; militum secuerint in partes & devoraverint: hoc enim uocant decimare milites. Tertiò, simile exemplum legitur in historia Iudaica, quan do Titus & Vespasianus urbem die Paschatis obsidione cinxerunt. Quartò, quando Amilcar pater Hannibalis oppugnauit Vticam, sicut Polybius refert, etiam decimatæ sunt legiones, id est, decimum quemq; elegerunt, quæ cæteris comedendum præbuerunt, & nostro tempore in urbe Monasteriesi etiam uentum est ad similes calamitates & mise-rias, (quamuis non ad carnes humanas) ut comederent coria. Quanta est miseria, homines se potius fame perdere, quàm facere deditionem. Sed hi furores sunt diabolici, sicut dicit Polybius eodem in loco. Hæc quatuor exempla tantum memini, in quibus uentum est ad humanas hostias.
units.tr: It is written of Potidaea that in the Peloponnesian War there was such famine that people came to human flesh, which those who were in the garrison began to eat. Then it is written of Dunetum in the African war that soldiers were decimated, that is, that they cut every tenth soldier into pieces and devoured him, for this is what they call decimating soldiers. Thirdly, a similar example is read in the Jewish history, when Titus and Vespasian surrounded the city with a siege at the time of the Passover. Fourthly, when Hamilcar, father of Hannibal, attacked Utica, as Polybius reports, the legions were also decimated: they chose every tenth man and gave them over to be eaten by the rest. And in our own time, in the city of Münster, they came to similar calamities and miseries (though not to human flesh), so that they ate hides. How great a misery it is for men to destroy themselves by hunger rather than make a surrender! But these are diabolical frenzies, as Polybius says in the same place. I remember only these four examples, in which men came to human sacrifices.
