units.la: Cùm obsidione cingeretur urbs Coppenhagen à clementissimo rege Christiano, dux Mechelburgensis Albertus, cum coniuge in urbe magna fame laborabat. Rex uerò Christianus, quotidie cognatæ suæ intra urbem dono mittebat multum cibi & potus, carnes ferinas, & alia edulia, in tanta copia, ut inde multi pascerentur: hoc consilio, ut declararet suam clementiam & beneuolentiam cognatæ suæ principissæ, quæ adhuc uiuit. Interea tamen inde quoq; alebatur dominus cum plurimis alijs, ita ut non facerent deditionem saltem longo tempore. Capitaneus, qui ibidē erat, interdiu dormiebat, ne conspiceretur & interficeretur: noctu uerò ordinabat uigilias, circumibat, & alia ad militarem apparatum pertinentia parabat.
units.tr: When the city of Copenhagen was being besieged by the most merciful King Christian, Duke Albert of Mecklenburg, with his wife, was suffering great hunger within the city. Meanwhile King Christian sent daily to his kinswoman within the city a generous supply of food and drink, venison and other dainties, in such abundance that many were fed on it. He did this with the intention of showing his mercy and goodwill to his kinswoman, the princess, who is still alive. Nevertheless, the lord was nourished in this way along with very many others, so that they did not surrender, at least for a long time. The captain who was there slept by day, so that he would not be seen and killed; but by night he arranged the watches, went his rounds, and made preparations for other matters pertaining to military readiness.

units.la: DE SEDITIONIBVS ET seditiosis.
units.tr: DE SEDITIONIBVS ET seditiosis.

units.la: Pictura seditiosorum.
units.tr: The portrait of seditious men.

units.la: Aristophanes (quem Plautus imitatus) inquit: ut qui anguillas capiunt, prius turbat aquas (quia anguillæ abdunt se infra limũ, quæ turbata aqua, strangulantur in locis fimosis seu paludibus) sic Cleon non potest crescere nisi prius turbata repu-blica. Is Cleon homo turbulentissimus, multa scelerate fecit, fuit causa ut Atthenienses amitterent oram Thraciæ. Ita quemadmodum optimi quiq; semper paci ac tranquilitati reipublicæ student: sic sceleratissimi maximè bellum & perturbationes amant ac desiderant.
units.tr: Aristophanes (whom Plautus imitated) says: just as those who catch eels first stir up the water (because eels hide under the mud, and when the water is stirred they are suffocated in the muddy places or marshes), so Cleon cannot grow great unless the commonwealth is first thrown into turmoil. This Cleon was a most turbulent man. He did many wicked things and was the cause of the Athenians losing the coast of Thrace. So, just as the best men always strive for peace and the tranquillity of the commonwealth, the most wicked men above all love and desire war and disturbances.

units.la: Pœna seditionis.
units.tr: The punishment of sedition.

units.la: Monetarius mouit seditionem in qua admodum miserabiliter perit. Cùm enim comites Stolbergenses suspendissent eius patrem, ipse ob ignominiosam patris necem odio incensus, inuasit illorum comitatum, uolens eum ui ad se transferre. Adhæserunt uero ipsi multi homines, qui propè oppidũ Franckenbaufen trucidati sunt: ipse uero alligatus currui, decollabatur. Cùm unus ex aulicis nostri principis Saxoniæ propius ad eum accessisset, qui ipsi notus erat, petiuit ut sibi afferret potum, quo allato, in tanto dolore & metu mortis duodecim cantharos aquæ exhausit.
units.tr: Monetarius stirred up a sedition in which he perished most wretchedly. When the Counts of Stolberg had hanged his father, he, inflamed with hatred because of his father's shameful death, attacked their retinue, wishing to seize him by force. Many men joined him, and they were cut down near the town of Frankenhausen. He himself was bound to a cart and beheaded. When one of the courtiers of our prince of Saxony, who was known to him, came nearer to him, he asked that water be brought to him. When it was brought, in his great pain and fear of death, he drained twelve cups of water.

units.la: De origine seditionis rusticanæ, & numero interfectorum in eadem.
units.tr: On the origin of the peasants' revolt, and the number of those killed in it.

units.la: In seditione rusticana ultra triginta milia rusticorum sunt interfecta. Schapler concionator MemminMemmingensis duodecim articulos de libertate Christiana composuerat. Struthius Ifenaci & Vuicelius census & uectigalia abolere conabantur. Hic phanaticus furor postea uagabatur fere per totam Germaniam. Ad oppidum Franckenhausen perierunt ultrà quingenti: iuxta Argentoratum uero sexcenti: ad oppidum Mulhausen porrò mille & sexcenti: in ducatu Vuirtenbergensi octingenti. Initium uero huius historiæ erat ex iniustitia Abbatis. Abbas alicuius cœnobij non procul ab Vlma, habuit sub se seruos, quales sunt in Vuestphalia. Cùm autem esset mortuus quidam auriga in pago, accepit Abbas non tantum equum, qui ipsi iure debebatur, uerùm etiam abstulit contra ipsorum iura uinum, quod rusticus emerat de suo peculio. Heredes rustici de illa iniustitia Abbatis apud plurimos conqueruntur. Vnde ingens multitudo, miseratione erga heredes indigne spoliatos commota, paulatim concurrit, mouensq; tumultum, in quo monasterium euertit. Postea veluti contagione quadam indies malũ id latius serpit eba, & undiq; plures concurrerunt, præcipuè ad cellas iniurgitantes sese uino: tandem conabantur omnes facultates diripere, non considerantes egregiam illam sententiam: Quod iustũ est, iustè persequeris.
units.tr: In the peasants' revolt more than thirty thousand peasants were killed. Schappeler, a preacher at Memmingen, had drawn up the Twelve Articles on Christian liberty. Struthius of Ichenhausen and Wicelius tried to abolish taxes and tributes. This fanatical fury then spread over almost all of Germany. At Frankenhausen more than five hundred perished; near Strasbourg, six hundred; at Mühlhausen, moreover, one thousand six hundred; in the duchy of Württemberg, eight hundred. The beginning of this story, however, lay in the injustice of an abbot. The abbot of a monastery not far from Ulm had serfs under him, of the kind found in Westphalia. When a certain carter in the village died, the abbot took not only the horse, which was rightly owed to him, but also, contrary to the peasants' rights, took the wine that the peasant had bought from his own savings. The heirs complained to many people about this injustice of the abbot. Hence a huge crowd, moved by pity for the heirs who had been unworthily despoiled, gradually gathered, and raising a tumult, overthrew the monastery. Afterwards, as if by some contagion, this evil crept more widely day by day, and more and more people came together, especially to the cellars, where they flooded themselves with wine. At last they all tried to plunder the goods, not heeding that excellent saying: What is just, you pursue justly.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: In Franconia circa oppida Kittingam Herbipolè & Vuerthaimũ, etiã aliquot centeni sunt puniti & interfecti. Quantis autẽ in periculis nobilitas Franconiæ eo tempore sæpius fuerit, non satis ex relationibus patris sui, uir nobilis Casparus Zolner mihi & alijs declarare potuit.
units.tr: In Franconia, around the towns of Kitzingen, Würzburg and Wertheim, some hundreds were also punished and put to death. How often the nobility of Franconia was in danger at that time, the noble Caspar Zolner, the father of my own relation, could not fully make clear to me and to others.

units.la: Exemplum punitæ seditionis.
units.tr: Example of a punished sedition.

units.la: Rosa homo priuatus collegit exiguas copias, & se oppositit potestati Mediolanensi. Cùm uero esset captus, extraxit gladium militis, qui eum ducebat, & se transfodit. Exutis autem eius vestibus inuenerunt in marsupio testamentum his uerbis scriptum: Domine Deus, tu causam meam cognouisti, quòd sit iusta, & si in ea mori debeam, tu dabis mihi propter eam uitam æternam, aut locum aliquem apud Catonem.
units.tr: Rosa, a private man, gathered a small force and opposed the power of Milan. When he was captured, he drew the sword of the soldier who was leading him and stabbed himself. When his clothes were taken off, they found in his purse a testament written in these words: "Lord God, you have known my cause, that it is just; and if I must die in it, you will give me for it eternal life, or some place beside Cato."

units.la: Stratagemata, quibus seditiones sunt pacatæ.
units.tr: Stratagems by which seditions were quelled.

units.la: Cùm exercitus Alexandri mouissęt seditionem: Prodeat, inquit, aliquis uestrum, qui ausit dicere, suos fuisse maiores labores, quàm mei fuerunt, qui deduxi uos ex horrendis istis locis in tantam opulentiam Asiæ. Tanta fuit Alexandri authoritas in exercitu suo, ut omnes continuò clamarent, se velle obsequi. Sic quoq; Scipio solo vultu compescuit seditiosos. Augustus item, breuissima voce compescuit tumultuantem exercitum, exclamans: Audite iuuenes senem, quem senes iuuenem audiebant.
units.tr: When Alexander's army had stirred up a mutiny, he said: "Let one of you come forward who dares to say that his labours were greater than mine, I who led you out of those dreadful places into such great wealth in Asia." Alexander's authority over his army was so great that all at once they cried out that they were ready to obey. Likewise Scipio quelled the seditious with a single look. Augustus too quieted a rioting army with a very brief speech, crying out: "Hear, young men, an old man, whom old men used to hear as a young man."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Narrabo uobis historiā de Germanico, factam in castris prope Moguntiā: In exercitu Romano erat orta seditio. Postea cum Germanicus redierat (abfuerat enim) ibi iubet ut uxor ipsius Agrippina unà cum paruis liberis ex tentorio egrederetur, & in conspectu omnium simularet se abituram. Illa enim erat neptis Augusti, cõiunx Drusi, medica, circumibat & curabat ægrotos milites, & opem ferebat pauperibus & tenuioribus. Hic Germanicus alloquitur milites: Videtis, inquit Hæc mulier, quæ est neptis Augusti, & benemerita de toto exercitu, cum paruis liberis iam est abitura in alia loca, quia hic non potest esse tuta. Illi muliere conspecta, uociferantur, & clamãt, se uelle obedire, & ita cessauit seditio.
units.tr: I will tell you a story about Germanicus, which took place in the camp near Mainz. A mutiny had arisen in the Roman army. Afterwards, when Germanicus returned (for he had been away), he ordered his wife Agrippina to come out of the tent with her small children, in the sight of all, and pretend that she was about to leave. She was the granddaughter of Augustus, the wife of Drusus, and a physician: she went around and tended the sick soldiers, and brought help to the poor and humbler folk. Then Germanicus addressed the soldiers: "You see this woman, who is the granddaughter of Augustus and has deserved well of the whole army, now about to depart with her small children to other places, because here she cannot be safe." When the soldiers caught sight of the woman, they cried out and shouted that they were willing to obey, and so the sedition ceased.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Cum plebs Romana à senatu dissideret, secessumá; esset in sacrum montem, nec seueriore ulla oratione flecteretur, missus est Agrippa, qui uniuersam multitudinem lepido apologo, de uentre & membris ita cæpit, ut statim liberet in gratiam cum patribus redire.
units.tr: When the Roman plebs was at odds with the senate and had withdrawn to the Sacred Mount, and could be moved by no sterner speech, Agrippa was sent, who began to speak to the whole crowd with a charming fable about the belly and the limbs, so that they at once willingly returned to favour with the fathers.

units.la: DE HOMICIDIIS, ALIISque tragicis casibus.
units.tr: ON HOMICIDES, AND OTHER TRAGIC CASES.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Nemo est Dominus suorum membrorum. Est optimum dictum Iurisconsultorum quod probatur ex illo fonte: Non occides. Nulla uis igitur aut iniuria etiam proprijs membris est inferenda; nec enim illis est utendum pro nostra libidine, sed iuxta normam in Decalogo nobis à Deo perscriptam. In honore igitur & puritate conseruanda sunt, ne crapula aut alijs illicitis modis ea destruamus, & homicidae (sicut proh dolor multi inueniuntur) nostrorum corporum fiamus,
units.tr: No one is lord of his own members. It is a fine saying of the jurists, and it is proved from that source: "You shall not kill." No violence or injury is therefore to be inflicted even on our own members, nor are they to be used at our pleasure, but according to the rule laid down for us by God in the Decalogue. They are therefore to be kept in honour and purity, lest by gluttony or other unlawful means we destroy them and become (as, alas, many are found to be) murderers of our own bodies.

units.la: Anno 1554. die 30 Iulij, narrauit D. Philippus, sibi scriptum esse hoc horrendum facinus, quod accidit in oppido quodam Misniae: ibi duo nobiles amici una potauerunt. Deinde inter potandum, orta inter eos rixa, alter sauciauit alterum, ut statim moreretur. Cum uero aufugisset homicida, pater cognito interitu filij sui, statim conscendit equum (quia fuit praefectus in eo loco) volens ulcisci necem filij. Inter insequendum excusit eum equus, ut laberetur humi ac ceruicē frangeret. Hae poenae diuinae sequuntur ebrietatem. Huius exempli mementote quis fuerit exitus: causam impulsiuam ipsius litis ignoro.
units.tr: In the year 1554, on 30 July, Dr Philip related that he had been told of this dreadful deed, which happened in a certain town in Meissen. There two noble friends drank together. Then, while drinking, a quarrel arose between them, and one wounded the other so that he died at once. When the killer had fled, the father, learning of his son's death, immediately mounted a horse (because he was the governor of that place), wishing to avenge his son's death. While he was pursuing, the horse threw him, so that he fell to the ground and broke his neck. These divine punishments follow drunkenness. Remember what the outcome of this example was; I do not know the impelling cause of the quarrel itself.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Legitur historia de muliere, quæ ueneno interfecerat uirum & priuignum, eo quòd illi prius alterum filium eius mulieris ex priore genitum marito interemissent. Areopagitæ, causa cognita, iudicarunt post centesimum annum accusatores eius esse redituros, id est, neq; damnauerunt, neq; eam absoluerunt.
units.tr: There is a story of a woman who had poisoned her husband and her stepson, because they had earlier killed her other son, born to her by a former husband. The Areopagites, having heard the case, judged that her accusers would return after a hundred years; that is, they neither condemned her nor acquitted her.

units.la: Valentinus papæ Alexandri filius fuit pessimus nebulo, qui proprium interfecit patrem ueneno, idq; hac occasione: Cum pater & filius conspirassent de dado ueneno cuidam Cardinali, quem ad se uocauerant, minister errans dedit uenenum ipsi Alexandro papæ, & filio Valentino: Cardinalis incolumis seruatus est. Cum porrò ipsi sentirentse hausisse uenenum, ambo inuoluti sunt mulis, ut ille recentis mulæ calor ueneni uim exhauriret. Pater tamen, nihil hoc remedio adiutus, est mortuus: filius uerò est seruatus ad aliam pœnam: qui nequam postea multū turbauit Italiam, cuius symbolum fuit: O Cæsar, ô nulla. Et quidem iuxta symbolum factus est nulla.
units.tr: Valentinus, the son of Pope Alexander, was a most wicked rogue, who poisoned his own father, and this on the following occasion. When father and son had conspired to give poison to a certain Cardinal whom they had summoned to them, a servant made a mistake and gave the poison to Pope Alexander himself and to his son Valentinus. The Cardinal was preserved unharmed. When they then realised that they had drunk the poison, both were wrapped in mule skins, so that the heat of the freshly killed mule might draw out the force of the poison. The father, however, aided by no such remedy, died; but the son was preserved for another punishment. He afterwards greatly troubled Italy, and his motto was: "O Caesar, O nothing." And indeed, according to his motto, he became "nothing."

units.la: Vidi quendam affici supplicio Tubingæ ob unicum ac deplorandum latrocinium. Casu enim latro cum alio quodam peregrino in unum conuenerat diuersorium, amboq; paulò largius biberat: alter ignotus hospes, & uiarum ignarus, dixit: Est mihi iter faciendum per proximam ignotam sylvam & non noui uiam, si quis esset, qui monstraret iter gratum mihi faceret officium. Alter assidens etiam bene potus: Ego, inquit, una ibo tecum: sicut illud genus hominum est officiosum, libenter monstrat vias ac peregrinos comitatur. Cùm veniunt in syluam, præcedit ignarus viæ, alter sequitur, cogitans: Quoniam petiuit sibi monstrari viam, fert secum fortassis pecuniam, ob quam sibi metuit: quare tu occides eum, ut illa potiaris. Ita diabolus impulit eum, ut peregrinum occideret. Sed sçpe sua miserè frustratus, inuenit apud eum tantùm septem vel octo numulos. Redicns itaque in diuersorium edit ingentes gemitus. Hospes malè de eo suspicabatur. Altero die, alij isthac perambulantes inueniunt cadauer interfecti. Quare homicida ex illis conicêturis captus, statim confitetur facinus, inquiens: Non est opus tortura, ego feci. Mox itaq; rapiebatur ad supplicium. Vidi eum morientem & deplorantem in rota suam calamitatẽ, ac valdè dolebat se superatu fuisse à diabolo.
units.tr: I saw a man put to death at Tübingen for a single and lamentable robbery. By chance a robber had met another stranger in the same inn, and both had drunk rather freely. The other guest, unknown there and ignorant of the roads, said: "I have to travel through the nearby unfamiliar forest and I do not know the way. If anyone would show me the way, he would do me a kind service." The other, sitting beside him, also well drunk, said: "I will go with you; that kind of people is obliging, gladly shows the way and accompanies strangers." When they came into the forest, the one ignorant of the road went ahead and the other followed, thinking: "Since he asked to be shown the way, he perhaps carries money with him, and for that he is anxious; so you will kill him and get possession of it." Thus the devil drove him to kill the stranger. But, often wretchedly disappointed, he found on him only seven or eight coins. Returning therefore to the inn, he uttered great groans. The host had a bad suspicion of him. The next day, others walking that way found the corpse of the slain man. So the murderer, seized on the basis of those conjectures, immediately confessed the deed, saying: "There is no need for torture; I did it." Forthwith he was dragged off to execution. I saw him dying on the wheel, lamenting his calamity, and he grieved greatly that he had been overcome by the devil.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Anno 1544 decimoquarto Iunij, Vitus Theodorus ex urbe Norinberga horrendum casum Vuitenbergam scripsit. Vidua quædam à quodam scholastico grauida facta fuit, tandem cùm ad baptismum infans est delatus: ibi sacerdos patrem scire voluit, cum non possent indicare patre, puer est relatus ad matrem sine baptismo. Mater audi-tis ijs, quæ acciderant, mox infantem occidit, ac se- etiam illico suspendit. Scholasticus uero pater pu-eri re comperta seipsum quoq; confodit. Sacerdos item postquam hæc audiuit, se quoque suspendit. Horrendum illum casum Lutherus cum singulari gemitu deplorauit, inquiens: Ah quàm horrenda facinora, corpus & animam perdunt. Ergo ore-mus & uigilemus, Sathan non dormit. Monet etiã hæc historia, sacerdotes esse ministros, & non do-minos sacramentorum.
units.tr: On 14 June 1544, Vitus Theodorus wrote from the city of Nuremberg to Wittenberg about a dreadful case. A widow had been made pregnant by a certain scholar. At last, when the infant was brought to baptism, the priest wished to know the father; since they could not name the father, the child was returned to the mother without baptism. The mother, on hearing what had happened, at once killed the infant and immediately hanged herself as well. The scholar, the father, on learning of the child's fate, also stabbed himself. The priest likewise, after he heard these things, hanged himself too. Luther lamented that dreadful case with singular groaning, saying: "Ah, how horrible deeds destroy body and soul! Therefore let us pray and keep watch, for Satan does not sleep." This story also warns that priests are ministers, and not lords, of the sacraments.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: In Bauaria quidam affectus est supplicio, qui tres coniuges suas ueneno necauit, quantumuis pu-taret se uelle facinus occultare, tamen mirabili Dei iudicio res patefacta est.
units.tr: In Bavaria a certain man was put to death who had poisoned his three wives. Although he thought he could conceal the crime, nevertheless, by God's wonderful judgment, the matter was brought to light.

units.la: Fribergæ in Misnia anno 1550 interfectus est sponsus illa hora, qua debuit deduci ad desponsa-tionem, casu à sodali emisso globo ex bombarda. Hæc fuit fortuita cædes non ex insidijs facta.
units.tr: At Freiberg in Meissen in 1550, a bridegroom was killed at the very hour when he was to be led to the betrothal, by accident: a ball fired from a cannon by a companion. This was an accidental killing, not one done by ambush.

units.la: Quidam ciuis Cygneus profectus est in uallem Ioachimicam ad suum fratrem, propter negocia quædam metallica conficienda, simul etiam allatu-rus inde aliquantulum pecuniæ, puto 100 Ioachi-micos, qui ipsi debebantur ex uenis metallicis. Ve-spteri cum postero die alter frater ex uallibus re-uerteretur. uerteretur Cygneam, metuens fortasse sibi, dixit ad alterum in uallibus habitantē: Queso, ut mecū eas per syluam, quia solitudo est mihi molesta: & sic eum inuitauit, ut ipsum comitaretur. Postquàm uentū est in syluam, frater, qui erat comes, dixit alteri: Des mihi mutuo decem loachimicos. Alter respondet: Non possum, quia debeo & fidem meis creditoribus, me iam ipsis soluturum, sed dabo tibi duos loachimicos. Alter hoc audito, paulo post ab eo recessit, & eiaculato globo ex bombarda, fratrem confodit, ipsoq; spoliato domū reuertitur. Postero uerò die homines ex Vallibus in syluam egressi inueniunt cadauer, & statim magistratui annunciant. Magistratus motus suspicione aliqua, cingunt domum fratris interfecti, ille statim confitetur facinus, orans ut de eo citò summatur supplicium, nam cruciatus conscientiæ suæ se nō posse diutius sustinere. Dicūt postea eum in pia inuocatione esse mortuum, & admonuisse turbam astantem ne uiueret in tanta securitate. Nominatim etiam monuit homines, ne diu abstinerēt se à communione cœnæ Domini, se enim in tali securitate uiuentem à diabolo impulsum esse ad talia scelera perpetranda. Dixit etiam, se audiuisse in egressu syluæ uocē fratris uocantis ipsum. Amborum autem uxores eo tempore grauidæ fuerūt.
units.tr: A certain citizen of Zwickau went to the Joachimsthal to his brother, to settle some mining business and also to bring back a little money, I suppose 100 Joachimsthalers, which were owed to him from the metal veins. In the evening, when the other brother was to return from the valleys to Zwickau the next day, fearing perhaps for himself, he said to another man living in the valleys: "I beg you, go with me through the forest, because solitude is troublesome to me." And so he invited him to accompany him. When they came into the forest, the brother who was the companion said to the other: "Lend me ten Joachimsthalers." The other replied: "I cannot, because I owe my creditors, and I must pay them now, but I will give you two Joachimsthalers." Having heard this, the other, a little later, withdrew from him, and firing a ball from a cannon, stabbed his brother; then, after despoiling him, he returned home. But the next day, men coming out of the valleys into the forest found the corpse and at once announced it to the magistrate. The magistrate, moved by some suspicion, surrounded the house of the murdered brother. He at once confessed the deed, begging that punishment be quickly exacted from him, for he could no longer endure the torments of his conscience. They say that afterwards he died in devout invocation, and admonished the crowd standing by not to live in such security. He also particularly warned people not to abstain for long from communion at the Lord's Supper, for he, living in such security, had been driven by the devil to commit such crimes. He also said that, on leaving the forest, he had heard the voice of his brother calling him. The wives of both men were pregnant at that time.

units.la: Hoc exemplum mementote, ut nos quoq; discatis inuocare Deum, ne uos inducat in tentationem: hoc est, ne sinat uos opprimi seu mergi in uarijs diaboli tentationibus. Diabolus impulit illum miserum hominem ad perpetrandum hoc horribile facinus contra Deum & conscientiam. Pleriq; uiuunt in horribilibus peccatis secure, ac si essent tempora tranquilla, simulq; diabolus acquiesceret. Immo uigilemus solicitiq; simus, ne laxemus frena cupiditatibus: simul rogemus, ut Deus nos spiritu sancto suo regat, & uasa suæ misericordiæ faciat.
units.tr: Remember this example, so that you too may learn to call upon God, lest he lead you into temptation; that is, lest he allow you to be overwhelmed or plunged into the various temptations of the devil. The devil impelled that wretched man to commit this horrible crime against God and his conscience. Many live securely in horrible sins, as if the times were calm and the devil were at rest. Rather let us watch and be anxious, lest we loosen the reins to our desires; and at the same time let us pray that God rule us by his Holy Spirit and make us vessels of his mercy.

units.la: Intra biennium omnes sunt interfecti, qui fuerunt conscij cædis Caij Iulij Cæsaris. Trebonius ille præstantissimus uir, qui etiam fuit socius coniurationis, (credo persuasus sic à Bruto) fuit primus qui necatus est. Dolobella eum cruciauit totum triduum in carcere, posteaq; atrocissimè præcidit ei caput, & publicè abiecit eum in forū. Fuit miserabile spectaculum. Ita perijt ille intimus consiliarius Iulij Cæsaris, qui absente eo fuit prætor, rexit Italiam, cui Cæsar maximè confisus est: præfuit castris solus ad Massiliam.
units.tr: Within two years all who had been accomplices in the murder of Gaius Julius Caesar were killed. Trebonius, that most excellent man, who had also been a partner in the conspiracy (I believe he was persuaded to it by Brutus), was the first to be killed. Dolabella tortured him for three whole days in prison, and afterwards most savagely cut off his head and publicly threw it into the forum. It was a pitiable spectacle. So perished that intimate counsellor of Julius Caesar, who in Caesar's absence had been praetor, had governed Italy, and in whom Caesar trusted most; he alone commanded the camp at Massilia.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: Collectanea

units.la: Quando Iulius in rogo combustus est, imago eius ostensa in igni fuit, tanta arte depicta, ut loca singulorum uulnerum cruentata conspici possent. Ibi tota ciuitas attonita stetit, & inter cæteros Antonius, dicens: optare, se potius interfectum esse, quàm talem uirum, cuius excellentißima uirtus fuißet. Additæ sunt tragediæ, in quibus clamatum est: Méne feruasse, ut essent qui perderent? Populus commonefactus istis spectaculis, quæsiuit statim authores cædis, unde intra biennium (ut iam etiam indicatum est) omnes interfectores Cæsaris, etiam qui auffugerant, interficiuntur.
units.tr: When Julius was burned on the funeral pyre, his image was shown in the fire, painted with such skill that the places of each of his wounds could be seen bloodied. There the whole city stood astonished, and among the rest Antony, saying that he would rather have been killed himself than that such a man, whose outstanding virtue had been so great, should have died. Tragedies were added, in which the cry was raised: "Did I save him only that there might be those who would destroy him?" The people, reminded by these spectacles, straightaway sought out the authors of the murder; and so within two years (as has already been noted) all the killers of Caesar, even those who had fled, were put to death.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: Collectanea

units.la: Fuit lex Aegyptia, quando pater occidit filium suum, tunc pater non est occisus, sed fuit ordinatū, ut triduo sederet apud cadauer. Non voluerunt illi summo dolori addere aliam calamitatem. Cogitauerunt enim illam esse horribilem carnificinā, parentes sedere spectatores necis filij.
units.tr: There was an Egyptian law that when a father killed his son, the father was not put to death, but it was ordained that he should sit for three days beside the corpse. The Egyptians did not wish to add another calamity to the greatest grief. For they judged that it would be a dreadful torture for parents to sit as spectators of their son's death.

units.la: Capnio narrauit de duce Eberhardo Vuirtenbergensi, quòd aliquando Romæ fuerit, & cùm petiturus esset templum, additos illi (ut fit) honoris causa duos Cardinales. Ingressi templum, cum starent spectabundi, uenit quidam (ut uidebatur) mendicus, gestans in capite fasciculum graminū: perueniens ad ipsos, cæpit gramina illa spargere, & occultè promens ex ijs sicam, qua unum Cardinalem, ad latus principis stantem, obtruncauit, statimq; aufugit. Quo uiso spectaculo princeps perterrefactus, dixit: Ego profecto non petam amplius templum Romæ, cùm in eo tanti sit periculi. Et recens in Italia etiam in templo adolescens nobilis germanus interfectus est.
units.tr: Capnio related about Duke Eberhard of Württemberg that once, when he was in Rome and was about to visit the temple, two cardinals were assigned to him, as is the custom, for the sake of honour. When they had entered the temple and were standing about looking around, a certain beggar (as he seemed) came up, carrying a bundle of grass on his head. Coming up to them, he began to scatter that grass, and secretly drawing from it a dagger, he cut down one cardinal who was standing at the prince's side, and at once fled away. The prince, terrified by this sight, said: "Certainly I shall not visit the temple at Rome again, since there is so much danger in it." And only recently in Italy a noble young German was also killed in a church.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Casus tragicus qui accidit Torgæ, anno 1559. die 23 Ianuarij.
units.tr: A tragic event that happened at Torgau, on 23 January 1559.

units.la: Virgo quædam ad nuptias uocata, finitis cho-reis, cùm proprium suum ductorem adolescentem sartorem non uidisset coràm, quando iam domum esset deducendæ uirgines è publico, alloquitur quendam studiosum forte ibi astantem, notum, & familiarem (ut aiunt) admodum sartori: & rogat eum amice, ut se comitetur: ducem enim suum non esse coràm, ne cum dedecore sola cogatur adire domum per plateas. Quod cùm honestè studiosus recusare non posset, eam deduxit, præser-tim cùm amicicia, quæ cum sartore intercesisset, non dissereret. Sartor autem ueniens abductam uirginem esse uidet, ac ducè suæ uirginis alienum inquirit: cogitat magnam sibi hoc esse ignominiâ, concreditam uidelicet non deduxisse. Quare ita mouetur indignitate facti, ut furens ad socij accur-rat ædes noctu cum armis: stat ibi ante ianuam deliberans, pulsat, & petit semel atq; iterû perblan-dis uerbis colloquium studiosi. Qui (animo præ-sagiente tristem illam calamitatem) exire reformidat: sartori respondet, cur non ad se potius introeat, si res ea sit tanti ponderis. Tandē uerò cùm nollet sartor à petendo colloquio foris desistere, & ei sine omni periculo esse pollicetur: egreditur
units.tr: A certain young woman had been invited to a wedding. When the dancing was over, and it was time for the maidens to be escorted home from the public hall, she did not see her escort, a young tailor, anywhere. She spoke to a student who happened to be standing there, a man known and very friendly (as they say) with the tailor, and asked him as a friend to accompany her, since her escort was not there and she did not want to be forced to walk home alone through the streets, which would bring shame on her. The student could not courteously refuse, and he escorted her, especially since the friendship between him and the tailor was not a source of any quarrel. The tailor, however, came and saw that the maiden had been taken away, and looked for the man who was her escort. He thought this a great disgrace to himself, that he had failed to escort the girl entrusted to him. Stirred by the outrage of the act, he ran at night, armed, to his friend's house. He stood there before the door, deliberating, knocked, and asked, once and again, with most coaxing words, for a conversation with the student. The student, whose mind foreboded that sad calamity, was afraid to come out. He replied to the tailor, asking why he did not rather come in to him, if the matter was of such weight. At last, when the tailor would not give up his request for a conversation and desist from standing outside, and promised that the student would be in no danger at all, the student came out,

units.la: studiosus, & quidem inermis, amico nihil diffidēs. Ibi nequam ille confestim de angulo ianuæ prosilit, & strićto gladio studiosum trāsfodit. Hoc uero tanto scelere peraćto, se quàm celerrimè in pedes coniȷcit. Concidit studiosus, cuius cùm lapsum & gemitus audiuissent domestici, accurrunt territi, ac studiosum herilem filium ad chirurgū portant. Etsi autem uiscera per uulnus delaberentur: tamen ita læsus non erat, ut statim expiraret. Loquitur pauca quædam ad domesticos, orans ne patri charissimo seni, suam mortem indicarent, & sic altero statim die placidè in pia confessione & inuocatione filiȷ Dei expirat. Res autem cùm diu latere non posset: pater ciuis senator, & honestis-mus senex, lamentabilem casum charissimi & uni-ci filiȷ Hieremiæ experitur: cuius tristissima mors sic auget dolorem, ut triduo post & ipse contabescat mœrore. Itaq; ambo pater & filius in eodem sepulchro sunt conditi. Perit & dolore ingenti sarćtoris mater, percipiēs tam atrox filij facinus: ciuis enim filius ipse quoque erat. Sarćtor uerò homicida, ipse fatali supplicio in desperationem ruens, seipsum in flumen, quod oppidum uicinum præterlabitur, præcipitē dedit, qui post dies octo aut circiter in flumine à piscatoribus est inuentus. Ita Deus cædem innocentissimi hominis ultus est. Deus nos gubernet & tueatur, contra diaboli in-sidias. sidias, qui circuit sicut leo rugiens, quærens quem devoret. Videte quàm leui arrepta occasione tam attrociter grassatus sit sathan. Oremus filium Dei Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum (qui uenit ut destruat opera diaboli, & qui dixit: Nemo rapiet oues de manibus meis) ut nos custodiat immensa sua misericordia & bonitate, Amen.
units.tr: and indeed unarmed, suspecting nothing from his friend. There that wicked man at once leapt out from a corner by the door, and with a drawn sword ran the student through. Having done this great crime, he threw himself into flight as quickly as possible. The student fell. When the household heard his fall and groaning, they ran out in alarm and carried the student, the master's son, to a surgeon. Although his bowels were slipping out through the wound, he was not hurt so badly that he died at once. He spoke a few words to the household, begging them not to tell his most dear old father of his death, and so on the following day he died peacefully, in a pious confession and invocation of the Son of God. But since such a matter could not remain hidden for long, the father, a citizen, a town councillor and a most honourable old man, learned of the lamentable fate of his dearest and only son Hieronymus. His most sorrowful death so increased his grief that three days later he himself wasted away with mourning. Thus father and son were laid in the same grave. The tailor's mother also perished of great grief, on hearing of her son's so atrocious crime, for her son was in fact a citizen too. The tailor, the murderer, himself rushed into despair at his deserved punishment, and threw himself headlong into the river which flows past the neighbouring town. About eight days later he was found in the river by fishermen. Thus God avenged the slaying of a most innocent man. May God govern and protect us against the snares of the devil, who goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. See how readily, on seizing the occasion, Satan raged so savagely. Let us pray to the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who came to destroy the works of the devil, and who said: No one shall snatch my sheep out of my hands, that he may keep us by his boundless mercy and goodness. Amen.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Imperator Turcicus scripsit ante annos triginta Venetias, petens, ut ei mitterent excellentem pictorem, cuius opera in depingendis quibusdam imaginibus uti posset. Miserunt ei egregium, qui postquam ad Cæsarem Turcicum uenisset, ille iubet sibi pingi caput decollatum. Pictor, quamuis excellens erat in pingendo, tamen Turcicus imperator statim animaduertit errorem: quare iubet ante conspectum pictoris cuidam ex suis satellitibus præcidi caput, quod deinde decollatum monstrat pictori, qui errauerat in collo. Nam cuntis solet fieri breuior ex contractione.
units.tr: Some thirty years ago the Turkish emperor wrote to Venice, asking that they send him an excellent painter whose work he could use in painting certain images. They sent him an outstanding one. When he had come to the Turkish emperor, the emperor ordered him to paint a decapitated head. Although the painter was excellent at painting, the Turkish emperor at once noticed the error. So he ordered one of his guards to have his head cut off before the painter's eyes, and then showed the beheaded body to the painter, who had gone wrong about the neck. For in all such cases the neck tends to look shorter through foreshortening.

units.la: Paucis annis elapsis, piscatores in uicina inuenerunt culeum, in quo fuit insuta uirgo, quæ cùm uociferaretur & eiularet, peteretq; auxilium, isti traxerunt ad se, & aperientes uiderunt pulchræ uecтитam uirginem. Tanti asini, plane omnis humanitatis expertes fuerunt, ut interrogarent pastorem, an deberent eam dimittere? Non scio quid pastor ipsis consuluerit. Isti asini iterum insuunt eam, & fiunt secundò lictores. Deus voluisset eam fortasse hoc pacto redimere.
units.tr: A few years later, fishermen in a nearby place found a sack in which a virgin had been sewn up. When she cried out and wailed and begged for help, they dragged the sack to themselves, opened it, and saw a beautifully dressed young woman. Such asses, utterly without any humanity, were they that they asked the minister whether they ought to let her go. I do not know what advice the minister gave them. These asses sewed her up again, and so they became executioners a second time. Perhaps God wished in this way to redeem her.

units.la: Lipsiæ similiter cùm unus esset suspendendus, & alter decollandus, scholastici coniecerunt lapides in lictorem, qui erraverat in officio. Ibi surgēs, qui erat ligatus, fugit, ucnitq; obuiam uiro nobili, qui interrogat eum, quid fieret, an supplicium esset sumptum de illis peccatoribus? Non inquit, sed ego sum ille suppendendus. Quo audito nobilis, descendens de equo, dissoluit ei uincula ac dixit: Vade, nec cuicquam dicito te esse istum furem. Sic iste fur incolumis euasit.
units.tr: Likewise at Leipzig, when one man was to be hanged and another beheaded, the schoolboys threw stones at the officer who had made the mistake in his duty. Then the man who was bound got up and fled, and met a nobleman, who asked him what was happening, whether punishment had been carried out on those wrongdoers. "No," he said, "I am the one who is to be hanged." On hearing this the nobleman got down from his horse, loosed his bonds and said: "Go, and tell no one that you are that thief." So the thief escaped unharmed.

units.la: Duæ historiæ nostro tempore factæ, in quibus sapientia Salomonis in iudicio mulierum de infante representata est.
units.tr: Two stories from our own time, in which the wisdom of Solomon in the judgment about the infant between the two women is represented.

units.la: Iudex quidam Hispanicus, cum factum esset homicidium, & plures unà affuissent, singuli uerò sese excusarent, surrexit, & iußit singulos nudare pectora, & palpauit ipsorū corda. Cùm uerò sensisset in uno maiorem cordis tremorem: Tu inquit fecisti: etsi alioqui foris ille cæteris audacior uideretur: tamen inde iudicauit malè sibi cōscium esse. Ita statim confessus est scelus, & ductus ad supplicium.
units.tr: A certain Spanish judge, when a homicide had been committed and several men had been present together, while each one excused himself, stood up and ordered them all to bare their chests, and he felt their hearts. When he sensed a greater trembling of heart in one man, he said, "You did it," although otherwise that man seemed bolder than the rest. Nevertheless, he judged from this that the man was badly conscious of himself. So the man at once confessed the crime and was led off to execution.

units.la: Gonsagæ præsuli Mediolanensis singularis est in iudicando dexteritas. Cùm Hispanus, præfectus oppidi imperio ipsius subiecti, teneret nobilem captiuum, & coniunx eius peteret liberationem, oblata pro eo magna pecunia: Hispanus hac conditione promisit se ei redditurum maritum, si prius sui copiā ipsi faceret. Quod cū obtinuisset, deinde reddit mulieri captiuum maritum, sed prius interfectum. Gonsaga, resciens illum tristem casum, capit Hispanum, & cogit cum ducere interfecti mulierem. Ducta illa, & re deliberata, Hispanum capitali supplicio affecit, & omnes eius facultates mulieri attribuit.
units.tr: Gonzaga, the prefect of Milan, has a singular skill in judging. When a Spaniard, the commander of a town subject to Gonzaga's rule, held a noble captive, and the captive's wife sought his release, a large sum of money being offered for him, the Spaniard promised that he would return the husband to her on condition that she first granted him her favours. When he had obtained this, he gave the captive husband back to the woman, but already killed. Gonzaga, learning of that sad event, seized the Spaniard and compelled the slain man's wife to go with him. When the case had been heard and considered, he put the Spaniard to death and assigned all his property to the woman.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Ante annos 25 quidam in Salinis Saxonicis interfecerat uxorem, & euaserat in Heluetiam: ubi tāto dolore cōscientiæ exagitatus est, ut aliquoties ex Heluetia rediret in Salinas. Quando uero peruenerat ad muros ciuitatis, metu pœnæ rursus aufugit. Tandem cùm in Heluetia in caupona sederet, orto tumultu, ipsius cantharus miscetur etiam inter tumultuantes. Lictores autem eiusdem loci, inter seditiosos hunc etiam apprehenderunt, qui statim fatetur facinus suum, dicēs: Libenter me captiuum dedam, iam enim diu etiam grauiora commerui. ac fatetur se interfecisse uxorem. Heluetii uero scribunt ad senatum Halensem, ut uenirent & accu-
units.tr: About twenty-five years ago a certain man in the Saxon salt-works had killed his wife and fled into Switzerland. There he was so tormented by the pain of conscience that several times he returned from Switzerland to the salt-works. But when he came to the walls of the city, he fled again out of fear of punishment. Finally, as he was sitting in a tavern in Switzerland, a tumult arose, and his tankard was caught up even among the rioters. The officers of that place seized him among the seditious, and he at once confessed his deed, saying, "I will gladly give myself up as a prisoner, for I have long deserved even graver things." He also admitted that he had killed his wife. The Swiss wrote to the senate of Halle, asking them to come and accuse him.

units.la: [Catchword absent; text continues on the next page.] & accusarent illum. Illi mittùt legatos, & ita sup-plicio est affectus.
units.tr: [Catchword absent; text continues on the next page.] and accuse him. They sent envoys, and so he was punished with death.

units.la: Ante aliquot annos quidam malus nebulo de-prehensus est in oppido Beltz, qui aliorum pre-cibus pro eo intercedentium dimissus est. Cum esset dimissus, indicit ciuitati bellum, quòd non iu-stè ipsum iudicassent, nec suspendissent: populaba-tur agros, spoliabat ciues illius oppidi: tandem in-cendit oppidum. Non multo pòst deprehensus est Brandeburgi. Significatur hoc senatui Belzensi, qui curat eum comburi.
units.tr: Some years ago a certain wicked scoundrel was caught in the town of Beltz, and was released at the entreaty of others who interceded for him. Once released, he declared war on the town, because they had not judged him justly or hanged him. He laid waste the fields and plundered the citizens of that town, and at last he set the town on fire. Not long afterwards he was caught at Brandenburg. This is reported to the senate of Beltz, which arranges for him to be burned.

units.la: Sudiosus quidam Franfordianus in Italiam pro-secturus erat, satis instructus pecunia. Habuit e-nim apud se quadringentos aureos. Is non satis circumspectus, ut solent adolescentes, cum uenisset Halprunnam Imperialem ciuitatem, inuenit forte in hospitio equitem quendam, quem optimè noui: ei se adiungit, nihil mali ab eo metuens. Eques ui-det illum esse bonum socium, potat cum illo, & fit ipsi familiaris, ita ut adolescens etiam monstret ei pecuniam. Post triduum adolescens uolens abire, rogat equitem, ut sibi uiam indicet. Eques pecu-niæ inhians, in itinere studiosum interficit. Post tres uerò septimanas eques uicissim comprehendi-tur, & in eodem loco, quo alium interfecerat, decollatur.
units.tr: A certain student from Frankfurt was about to set out for Italy, well supplied with money, for he had four hundred gold coins with him. Not being as cautious as young men often are, when he came to the imperial city of Halprunna he happened to find in the inn a certain knight whom he knew very well. He attached himself to him, fearing no harm from him. The knight saw that he was a good companion, drank with him, and became his intimate, so that the young man even showed him the money. After three days the young man, wishing to leave, asked the knight to show him the way. The knight, gaping after the money, killed the student on the road. But three weeks later the knight himself was seized, and in the same place where he had killed the other he was beheaded.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Accidit Heydelbergæ, ut boni aliqui sodales una conuiuarentur, & iocis ac salibus conuiuium condirent.Cum igitur unus inter illos uteretur scõ matibus paulò mordacioribus, ac certum aliquem ex numero conuiuarū notabiliter peteret, qui ea neq; arte eludere, neq; patienter ferre poterat:hic impatientia uictus, surgebat ex cõuiuio, & commotus abibat, cogitans quomodo pari referret. Tandem uero decreuit se eum sumpto gladio in certo quoddam loco, quem ille alter transire cogeretur, cum domum iret, præstolaturum, & uenientem stricto gladio aggressurũ,ac sic territum in fugam conuersurum,ut in posterum haberet,quo illum rursus exagitaret, & quod illi de eius timiditate uicissim obijceret. Vbi igitur alter ignorans harum insidiarum, ex conuiuio domum se conferret,& ad locum insidiarum peruenireт: ibi ille,qui erat in insidijs, euaginato ense, ut proposuerat, minabundus in eum irruit,quasi eum statim essει occisurus, & inuerso gladio semel atque itcrum percusit. Verùm quia hic fortassis natura fuit audacior,& iam quoq; uino incaluerat, quod alias in prælium trudit inermem, fugere non voluit, sed sinistro brachio tunica inuoluto ictus excipere,gladiumq; subire conatus est,& sic cum eo luctari. Quod ubi intellexit,ex insidijs prosiliēs, cogitauit se leuiter eum esse uulneraturum, ut sic quiescere aut fugere cogeretur. Vulnerauit autem ipsius poplitem, ita ut ex illo uulnere paulo post moreretur. Alter uero uulnerans illum, contulit se in academiam Friburgensem, in qua etiā postea factus est doctor Theologiæ, ibiq; cum esset, quotiescunq; illi lictores tantū casu obuiam uenerunt, obstupuit, existimans comprehensuros esse.
units.tr: It happened at Heidelberg that some good companions were dining together and seasoning the meal with jokes and witticisms. One of them used rather biting taunts and repeatedly attacked a certain diner, who could neither parry them skilfully nor bear them patiently. Overcome by impatience, this man rose from the table and left in agitation, thinking how he might pay him back in kind. At last he resolved to take a sword and wait at a certain spot that the other would have to pass on his way home. As he came, he would attack him with drawn sword and so frighten him into flight, giving himself material to harass him again and to throw back at him his cowardice. When the other, unaware of this ambush, made his way home from the dinner and reached the place of the ambush, the man lying in wait rushed at him threateningly with his sword unsheathed, as he had planned, as if about to kill him at once, and struck him once and again with the reversed blade. But because this man was perhaps by nature bolder, and had by now grown warm with wine (which otherwise drives an unarmed man into battle), he would not flee. Instead he tried to take the blows on his left arm wrapped in his cloak, to get in under the sword, and so to grapple with his attacker. When the ambusher saw this, he leapt out of hiding and thought he would wound him lightly, so that he would be forced either to stop or to flee. But he struck him in the back of the knee, so that shortly afterwards he died of that wound. The other, having wounded him, betook himself to the University of Freiburg, where he later became a doctor of theology. While he was there, whenever those officers happened by chance to meet him, he was startled, thinking they were going to arrest him.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Morio, cuius princeps febri laborabat, audierat forsan aliquando subita consternatione febrim remoueri. Cùm igitur aliquando dominum sequeretur in loco, ex quo erat præcipitium, memor eius rei, corripit dominum connixus toto corpore, quasi præcipitaturus eum. Dominus perculsus est supra modum, & liberatus est sic à febri. Iubet nihilominus comprehendi morionem, & conijci in carcerem. Post aliquot dies producitur, & pronunciatur sententia, ut de eo ficte sumatur supplicium capitis. Ducitur ad supplicium, & lictor stringit gladium, ut terronē illi inijciat. Postea, ut ei mandatum erat, accipit baculum, & ferit ceruicē morionis. Ibi morio exanimatus concidit præter omnium expectationem. Quidam iudicant eum terrore extinctum esse. Alij putant læsos esse nervuos ceruicis quinti paris, qui ducuntur in diaphragma.
units.tr: Morio, whose prince was suffering from fever, had perhaps once heard that a fever is driven off by sudden terror. So when he was following his lord in a place where there was a precipice, mindful of this, he seized the lord and strained with his whole body, as if about to throw him over. The lord was struck beyond measure and was thus freed from the fever. Nevertheless he ordered the jester to be seized and thrown into prison. After some days he was brought out, and sentence was pronounced that capital punishment should be feigned against him. He was led to execution, and the executioner drew his sword to strike terror into him. Then, as he had been ordered, he took a staff and struck the jester on the neck. There the jester collapsed lifeless, contrary to everyone's expectation. Some judge that he was killed by fright. Others think the nerves of the neck of the fifth pair, which run to the diaphragm, were injured.

units.la: Accepi à quodam amico ex Austria literas, in quibus est horrendum diabolici furoris exemplū. In quodam enim monasterio, monachi, uicinorum hominum filias & coniuges ad se allexerūt, & eas struprauerunt, strupratasq; interfecerunt. Re pate facta, monachi sunt capti. Quid autē de illis futurū sit, ignoratur. Monasterium illud nō procul distat à Vienna. Hæc 13 Iunij anno 1555. Philippus retulit.
units.tr: I received a letter from a friend in Austria, containing a dreadful example of diabolical madness. In a certain monastery, monks enticed the daughters and wives of the neighbouring people to themselves, raped them, and, having raped them, killed them. When the matter came to light, the monks were captured. What will become of them is not known. That monastery is not far from Vienna. Thus far Philip reported, 13 June 1555.

units.la: Anno 1554 hic Viteberge est lata sententia de quodā scurra, qui furatus est undecim pueros, & uendidit Iudæis Pragensibus: idem adiunxit se mendicis, & simulauit se morbo comitiali laborare, ac sanguinē exspuere, quam prius in os ad decipiendos homines assumpserat.
units.tr: In 1554, here at Wittenberg, sentence was passed on a certain buffoon who had stolen eleven boys and sold them to the Jews of Prague. He had also joined the beggars and pretended to suffer from epilepsy and to spit blood, which he had previously taken into his mouth in order to deceive people.

units.la: Huc allatus est casus memorabilis. Duo nobiles in Lusatia habitauerunt in eodem pago, & altercati inter se de quodam pastore, nescio quid suerit negocij, cœperunt rixari. Vnus currit ad domum suam, & uult se armare, & apprehendere bombardam. Ibi alter sequitur (erant enim affines) Vterq; apprehendit bombardam. Prior uero eiaculatur, & uult alterum interficere, & frustrabatur, ictus non collimat. Alter etiam eiaculatur, & simul eodem ictu interficit suum sororiũ & sororem. Hoc est diabolicū sanè facinus. Allati sunt etiam alij quidam casus, sed ista est recens historia, hoc anno 57 facta.
units.tr: A memorable case was reported here. Two nobles in Lusatia lived in the same village and, quarrelling with each other over some shepherd (I do not know what the business was), began to brawl. One runs to his house, wanting to arm himself and seize a handgun. The other follows him (for they were relatives by marriage), and both seize guns. The first fires and wants to kill the other, but he misses; his shot does not hit its mark. The other also fires and, with the same shot, kills his own brother-in-law and sister. This is indeed a diabolical deed. Other cases were also reported, but this is a recent story, which happened this year, 1557.

units.la: Scriptum est huc, non procul ab Vratislauia filium interfecisse parentem & fratrem, cùm quidem non intercessissent inter illos rixæ aut simultates. Inflammauit uerò diabolus ex leuissima causa eorum corda, & manus impulit. Est profectò opus diaboli, sicut est horribilis illa oratio de Iuda: Diabolus intrauit in eum.
units.tr: It is written here that not far from Breslau a son killed his father and brother, although no quarrels or enmities had existed between them. But the devil inflamed their hearts over the slightest cause and drove their hands. It is truly a work of the devil, like that dreadful saying about Judas: "The devil entered into him."

units.la: Habebamus adolescentem Tubingæ ingenio præstanti & liberali specie corporis, qui interfecit aliū pro quo laborauit tota Academia, doctores & professores, & inter hos etiam Stœflerus, ut ille redimeretur quadringentis florenis. Nam Princeps, qui fuit uir seuerus, uoluit eum capitali supplicio affici. Sed Stœfleri authoritas tanta fuit apud Principem, ut aliquid tamen impetraret. Ille adolescens postea cùm esset liberatus, & punitus pœna scholastica, uidelicet exclusione, ueniens in patriam, post paucos menses interficitur. Ita Deus est uindex scelerum, & non curat pactiones humanas.
units.tr: At Tübingen we had a young man of outstanding talent and attractive bodily appearance, who killed another man. The whole university worked for him, the doctors and professors, and among them Stoeffler, so that he might be redeemed for four hundred florins. For the prince, who was a severe man, wanted him to suffer capital punishment. But Stoeffler's authority with the prince was so great that he nevertheless obtained something. That young man, after he had been freed and punished with academic punishment, namely exclusion, returned to his homeland and, after a few months, was killed. So God is the avenger of crimes, and he does not care for human agreements.

units.la: Ante paucos annos Magdeburgi quidam affectus est supplicio, qui ante triginta annos perpetrauerat cædem, & iam neminem superstitem putauerat conscium istius cædis.
units.tr: A few years ago at Magdeburg a certain man was executed who had committed a murder thirty years earlier, and who had by then thought that no one surviving was aware of that murder.

units.la: Selymus pater huius tyranni Turcici, interfecit suum patrem, & tantum regnauit octo annos. Fuit maximè formidabilis post partam primam uictoriam. riam, etiā Imperatori Maximiliano. Et erat summo ingenio praeditus. Interfectus est autē illo ipso loco, ubi assecutus erat patrem, & eum interfecerat. Hæc narratio paulò aliter habetur in loco de ingratitudine erga parentes.
units.tr: Selim, the father of this Turkish tyrant, killed his own father and reigned only eight years. He was most feared after his first victory, even by the Emperor Maximilian, and he was endowed with very great ability. He was killed in the very place where he had overtaken his father and killed him. This narrative is given somewhat differently in the place on ingratitude towards parents.

units.la: Alfonsus Diasius, qui anno 1546 fratrem suum Ioannem Diasium interfecerat Neoburgi in Bauaria, propter solam Euangelij confessionem, cum ipse Alfonsus uersaretur in aula Pontificis, in iudicio Rotæ. Postea uerò anno 1551 seipsum interemit in concilio Tridentino. Inuentus est enim seipsum suspendisse à collo suæ mulæ.
units.tr: Alfonso Diaz, who in 1546 killed his brother John Diaz at Neuburg in Bavaria, solely because of his confession of the Gospel, was then staying at the court of the Pontiff, in the tribunal of the Rota. Later, in 1551, he killed himself at the Council of Trent, for he was found to have hanged himself from the neck of his mule.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Cuidam ciui in uicinia oppidi Vuitembergæ erat interdictum, ne domo exiret propter contagionem pestis, qua pueri ipsius erant mortui. Exiit autem & voluit sibi à caupone quodam uendi ceruisiam. Cumq; ille recusaret, & cum eo rixaretur, ipse afflatu diaboli accensus, cauponem transfodit. In illo tumultu, cùm consul accurreret, ipse minatur etiam consuli: & nisi alij prohibuissent, consulem oppidi interfecisset. Transfodit quoque illum, qui illud facinus prohibuit. Postea conijcitur in carcerem, & statim sumitur de eo supplicium.
units.tr: A certain citizen in the neighbourhood of the town of Wittenberg had been forbidden to leave his house because of the plague, by which his children had died. Nevertheless he went out and wanted to buy beer from a certain innkeeper. When the innkeeper refused and quarrelled with him, the man, kindled by a breath of the devil, stabbed the innkeeper. In that tumult, when the mayor ran up, he threatened the mayor too; and had others not prevented it, he would have killed the town's mayor. He also stabbed the man who had prevented that crime. Afterwards he was thrown into prison, and punishment was immediately taken of him.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Antuerpiæ quidam homo ualde diues alium quēdam suæ gentis hominem in sua domo, cui multum detum debebat, interficit, sumpto prius ab eo chirographo, quo testaretur ipsum nihil sibi debere. Magistratus uolès scire ubi ille creditor mansisset, curauit inquisitionem in omnibus ædibus fieri. Tandem homicida motus conscientia, timet sibi ne deprehendatur, ex sepulchro recens facto, curat cadauer refodi, ac in proximum puteum abijci. Forte in uicinia uetula quædam stat, uidens cadauer ex domo homicidæ ablatum in uicinum puteum abijci, magistratui indicat. Magistratus abiectum cadauer inquiri per lictores iubet. Quo inuento, authorem homicidij cœperunt, & in illa sella, in qua alterum occiderat, in medio foro, supplicio affecerunt.
units.tr: At Antwerp a very rich man killed another man of his own nation in his house. The victim was deeply in debt to him, and before the killing the murderer had taken from him a written acknowledgment that he owed him nothing. When the magistrate wanted to know where this creditor had last been, he ordered a search of all the houses. The murderer, moved by conscience and afraid of being discovered, had the corpse dug out of the freshly made grave and thrown into the nearest well. By chance an old woman standing nearby saw the body carried out of the murderer's house and thrown into the well across the way, and she reported it to the magistrate. The magistrate ordered the lictors to search for the body. When it was found, they seized the author of the murder and executed him in the middle of the marketplace, in the very chair in which he had killed the other man.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Duo adolescentes egregia indole, cum consortes alicuius sceleris essent, & supplicio afficiendi, ibi satellites cuiusdam Præpositi propter indolem & egregias uirtutes quæ elucebant in eis, Præpositum sollicitarunt, ut pro eis intercederet. Præpositus cum precibus uehementer urgetur, importunitate & petacitate uinceretur, dixit: Obsequar uobis. Accessit iudicem & ab eo impetrauit, ut dimitterētur. Dimissi sunt, & dimissos ad se recepit, ac splendidè uestiuit. Postea ad se uocauit, dicens: Videtis filij, quo beneficio uos affecerim, quòd patrētis loco fuerim in hoc præsenti periculo, in quo nihil nisi mors uobis expectanda fuit. Pro hoc beneficio & pietate, si mihi seruire uolueritis, exacto anno liberaliter & magnifice uobis stipendium soluam. Ibi promittunt, studiumq; operam & fidem reuerenter deferunt, & aliquandiu fidelissimè inseruiunt. Præpositus ubi uideret illos ita fideles, & reliquos satellites sceleratos & helluones esse, cogitauit de illis cuehendis, siquidem bonam de illis spem conceperat, quos uita donasset. Accersiuit itaq; ad se, & consilium suum illis aperuit, scilicet illos cubicularios suos constituere decreuisse, & concedere illis pecuniam, & totam rem familiarem. Illi conditionem accipiunt, pietatem & fidem pollicentur. Sed ut fieri solet, quando animus semel à diabolo obsessus est, qui est homicida & mendax, non cessat instigare & hortari ad scelera. Sæpius itaq; deliberarunt de Præposito tollendo: siquidem de omnibus rebus, domesticis ipsis constabat. Intendunt consilium sæpius, sed semper prohibentur. Accidit autem, ut amicus Præpositi inuiseret eum: quo abeúte, reliquos famulos ei adiunxit, qui eos illa nocte apud se retinuit. Ibi statim illi perfidiosi consilium captâtes de nocte surgunt, & ad ianuam conclauis, in quo dormit, accedunt. Quod cum bifore esset, & Præpositus semper pessulũ obijceret, canemq; in lecto ad pedes haberet, tentant ianuam euellere ex cardinibus. Canis audito dito strepitu latrat, & quo magis præfectus prohi bet ne latraret, eo magis latratum ipse intendit, do nec præpositus surgeret, & dolum statim subolens abigeret canem. Cumq; unam ianuā auulsam esse sentiret, accedit fenestram, & spectat in hortum, ubi forte uidet famulum coqui cum lychno: quem submissè uocabat. Famulus nouitate rei consterna- tus, spectrum se nidisse putabat. Cùm tamen insta- ret Præpositus, ibi famulus ille accersitis alijs mini stris, ad conclaue Præpositi uenit. Hoc cum nebu- lones illi duo audirent, posuerunt se in lectum, al- tumq; somnū finxerunt. Præpositus ubi uideret il- las insidias, accedit lectū ipsorum, uiditq; eos ster- tentes. Vbi uerò excitasset illos, expergefacti ocu- los purgabant, ac si illus nihil constaret. Sed duri- ter eos allocutus est: Vos, inquit, scelerati & nefa- rij latrones, scitis quæ beneficia uobis præstiterim, & talem gratiam mihi referre voluistis? & iussit illos uinciri, & statim illo die decollari. Hæc in Vn garia facta sunt.
units.tr: Two young men of outstanding character were accomplices in some crime and were about to be punished. Because of the good character and remarkable virtues that shone in them, the attendants of a certain Provost urged him to intercede on their behalf. Vehemently pressed with entreaties, and overcome by their importunity and persistence, the Provost said: "I will comply with you." He went to the judge and obtained their release. Once they were released, he took them into his own home and dressed them splendidly. Afterwards he called them to him and said: "You see, sons, what favour I have shown you, in standing in a father's place in this present danger, in which nothing but death awaited you. In return for this kindness and loyalty, if you are willing to serve me, I will pay you a generous and handsome wage when a year has passed." They promised, offered their zeal, labour and loyalty with due respect, and served him very faithfully for some time. When the Provost saw that they were so faithful, and that the rest of his attendants were wicked gluttons, he began to think of promoting them, since he had good hopes of men whose lives he had spared. So he summoned them and disclosed his plan: he had decided to make them his chamberlains and to entrust them with money and the whole management of his household. They accepted the condition and pledged devotion and faithfulness. But, as usually happens when a mind has once been seized by the devil, who is a murderer and a liar, the devil did not stop urging them on to crime. So they often deliberated about removing the Provost, since they knew all his domestic affairs. They repeatedly planned it, but were always prevented. It happened that a friend of the Provost came to visit him, and when he left he took the remaining servants with him, who kept those two that night at his house. Then those treacherous men, seizing the opportunity, rose at night and approached the door of the room where the Provost slept. The door was double, and the Provost always kept it bolted, with a dog lying on the bed at his feet, so they tried to tear the door from its hinges. The dog, hearing the noise, began to bark, and the more the prefect tried to stop it barking, the more fiercely it barked, until the Provost got up, sensed the plot at once, and drove the dog away. When he perceived that one door had been torn off, he went to the window and looked out into the garden, where by chance he saw a cook's servant with a lamp, and called to him quietly. The servant, amazed at the strangeness of the thing, thought he had seen a ghost. But when the Provost pressed him, the servant summoned other attendants and came to the Provost's room. When the two scoundrels heard this, they lay down on the bed and feigned a deep sleep. When the Provost saw through their snare, he went to their bed and saw them snoring. When he woke them, they rubbed their eyes as if they knew nothing of it. But he addressed them sternly: "You wicked and nefarious robbers, you know what benefits I have bestowed on you. Is this how you wanted to repay my kindness?" He ordered them bound, and they were beheaded that same day. These things happened in Hungary.

units.la: Historia de crudelissimo facto Æ- thiopis, recitata Philippo Comiti à Nassau per Damianum Knebel, secretarium Comitis de Hana.
units.tr: Account of the most cruel deed of an Ethiopian, related to Philip Count of Nassau by Damian Knebel, secretary of the Count of Hanau.

units.la: Anno 1556, mense Aprili, quidam prædiues no- bilis, non procul ab Augusta Vindelicorum, à teneris puerum æthiopem usq; ad illum annũ alluerat. Cũ forte fortuna nobilis domo abesset, æthiops de nocte consurgens coniugem totamq; familiam, excepta filiola domini, ad octo homines interemit. Mane altero die cum rediret dominus, uidit ædes suas præter morem clausas, & cum propius adequitasset, apparuit illi in domus summitate æthiops truculentissimo aspectu, qui in hunc modum nobilem alloquitur: Scis homo crudelissime, qualiter me quondam innocuum tractaueris, quòd sanè ad hunc diem memoria retinui: illam iniuriam de tuis nunc demum uindicaui. Ecce enim partem de cadauere tuæ coniugis, quam tibi cum tota familia occidi, excepta filiola, quam unam reliqui, tibiq; restituam, si mihi incolumitatem uitæ promiseris. Pater extremè perturbatus, homicidæ incolumitatem promittit. At ille per fenestram infantem ante pedes patris proijcit, Scio, inquies, quòd mihi non sis seruaturus fidem, non satis in temetipso & tuis illam iniuriam ultus, moriar & ego, & sic se de uestibulo ædium præcipitem dedit. Secretarius Hannensis comitis sibi nobilem familiariter notum esse affirmat. Quo facto quid crudelius, magisq; ex proprijs diaboli instigationibus depromptum cogitari potest?
units.tr: In April 1556 a certain very wealthy nobleman, not far from Augsburg, had brought up an Ethiopian boy from childhood, and had kept him until that year. One night, when the nobleman happened to be away from home, the Ethiopian rose and killed his wife and the whole household, about eight people, except the master's little daughter. The next morning, when the master returned, he saw his house shut up, contrary to custom. As he rode closer, an Ethiopian appeared to him on the top of the house, with a most savage look, and addressed the nobleman in these words: "Do you know, most cruel of men, how you once treated me when I was innocent? I have indeed kept it in memory to this day, and now at last I have avenged that injury on your people. Look, here is a part of your wife's corpse, whom I killed with the whole family, except the little daughter, whom alone I have spared. I will restore her to you if you promise me my life." The father, utterly distraught, promised the murderer his safety. But the Ethiopian threw the infant through the window before her father's feet, saying: "I know you will not keep faith with me. Since I have not avenged that injury sufficiently on you and yours, I too shall die." And so he threw himself headlong from the front of the house. The secretary of the Count of Hanau affirms that he was personally acquainted with the nobleman. What could be imagined more cruel, and more clearly prompted by the devil's own instigation?

units.la: Viennæ pistoris seruus, cum sciret thesaurum & alias pistoris facultates, simulauit discessum à pistore. Post paucos uerò dies iterum noctu in domum clam redit, & dormiente familia initiò tumultum in domo excuscitat. Ibi famulus uolens uidere quid esset, statim ex insidijs nebulo prosilit, & eum intersicit. Simili etiam modo ancillam interemit. Ascendit postea in cubiculum pistoris, & pistorem cum coniuge sua occidit. Venit tandem ad filiolam pistoris, quæ clamat: Ah chare Paule, noli me interficere: sed concede mihi uitam, omnia mea tibi dabo crepundia. Ille commotus primò, quòd eum nosset, postea tamen etiam eam intersecit. Confectis tot cædibus, rapit pecuniam ex cistis fractis, & euadit usq; ad Ratisbonam. Cum autem uicini uiderent postero die, domum integrum diē esse clausam, frangunt ex consilio Senatus fores: ingrediuntur, & inueniunt iacentia tot cadauera. Fama fertur, latronem Ratisbonā uersus esse profectū. Ita statim Senatus aliquos eò misit, qui postea latronem captiuum Viennam duxerunt. Ibi affixus est ueruto, an ein pfal. Clamauit uerò inter dolores, se nullū maiorem cruciatum sustinere, quàm illam uoccm puellæ, cui nō pepercisset: Ach lieber Paul, las mich leben, ich will dir all mein pup-pen geben.
units.tr: At Vienna a baker's servant, knowing where the baker kept his treasure and his other valuables, pretended to have left his master's service. After a few days, however, he secretly returned to the house at night. While the household slept, he first made a noise to rouse the household. The servant, wanting to see what it was, came out, and the villain immediately leapt on him from an ambush and killed him. He killed the maidservant in the same way. Then he went up to the baker's bedroom and killed the baker and his wife. At last he came to the baker's little daughter, who cried out: "Ah, dear Paul, do not kill me! Spare my life, and I will give you all my toys." He was at first moved, because he knew her, but afterwards he killed her too. Having committed so many murders, he snatched the money from the broken chests and made his escape as far as Regensburg. When the neighbours saw the next day that the house had been shut up all day, they broke open the doors on the Senate's orders, went in, and found the many corpses lying there. Rumour had it that the robber had gone towards Regensburg. Immediately the Senate sent men there, who afterwards brought the captured robber back to Vienna. There he was fixed to a stake ("an ein Pfal"). Amid his agony he cried out that he suffered no greater torment than that voice of the girl whom he had spared: "Ach lieber Paul, las mich leben, ich will dir all mein puppen geben."

units.la: Nos meminimus ante annos uiginti, Lipsiæ sceleratum aliquem in proximo pago Colgarten interfecisse patrem & matrem familiâs cum pueris, & accepta pecunia aufugisse. Deinde uero ipso comprehenso, cùm de eo Lipsiæ supplicium sumeretur, dixit: Se fere triduò sedisse sine cibo & potu in latebris sub scalis, & deliberasse an deberet facere cædem illam, ac diu abhorruisse à tanto scelere. Tandem dixit, se audiuisse uocem aliquam susurrante: Fac, fac, far fort, far fort: qua uoce afflatus est & impulsus ut pergeret. Illa uerè fuit uox diaboli. Perpetrato hoc scelere, non potuit fugere: sic postea de eo supplicium est sumptum.
units.tr: Twenty years ago, we remember, at Leipzig, a wicked man in the nearby village of Colgarten killed the father and mother of a household, along with their children, and fled with the money. Later, when he had been caught and was being punished at Leipzig, he said that he had sat for almost three days without food or drink in a hiding place under the stairs, deliberating whether he should commit that murder, and that he had long shrunk from so great a crime. At last, he said, he heard some voice whispering: "Do it, do it! Far fort, far fort!" ("fahr fort"). Inspired and driven on by that voice, he went through with it. That was truly the voice of the devil. Having committed this crime, he could not escape, and so afterwards he was punished.

units.la: Cùm essemus Isenaci, in uisitatione, erat ibi iuuenis pauper, cibum in plateis à bonis hominibus colligens: qui forte fortunà uenit ad domũ cuiusdam senis, quem rogauit, ut ipsi in hac calamitate opem ferret. Senex motus misericordia, iuuenem illum pauperem hospitio excepit. Erat autem senex utcunq; dives, & collegerat aliquam pecuniã: quam cùm pauper ille uideret, impellitur à diabolo, ut optimũ illum senem de se benemeritũ interfeciat. Acceptis itaq; sexaginta aureis, qui erat senis thesaurus, domum claudit, & aufugit. Vicini cùm uiderent domus ianuam esse clausam, & neminem tota die egredientem, aperiunt domum, & senem illum in area domus iacentem mortuum uident: unde statim suspicantur de hoc iuuene mendicante. Illud igitur facinus perpetratum indicant magistratui, qui iussit homicidã per lictores inquiri. Hi quo magis illum quæsiuerunt, eo minus inue-nerunt. Tandem uerò, cùm satis diu quæsiuissent, uident eum absconsum sub scalis portæ ciuitatis. Captus uerò, & cõiectus in carcerẽ, à diabolo horribiliter est in carcere uexatus. Petiuit etiam à nobis, ut pro eo apud principẽ intercederemus. Nos, quoniam scelus erat adeò atrox, hoc à principe iustitiam amante petere non ausi sumus: sed hoc promisimus ei, nos impetraturos esse, ut ipsi pœna supplicij mitigaretur. Et misimus ad eum Fridericum Myconium, ut significaret ipsi quid suo nomine actum esset. Sed miser ille ferè exanimatus præ summo dolore, nihil audiuit: tamen post triduum satis iam à diabolo tentatus, his uerbis alloquitur Fridericũ Myconium: O Domine Friderice, in quatis tentationibus uersatus fui. nunc (Deo auxiliante) libenter moriar: nam mortis metũ iam superaui. Sic cõfirmatus in uera fide, & ardenti inuocatione, placidè mortuus est.
units.tr: When we were at Isenach on a visitation, there was a poor young man there who gathered food in the streets from good people. By chance he came to the house of an old man and asked him to help him in this distress. Moved by pity, the old man took the poor youth in as a guest. The old man was fairly wealthy and had gathered some money. When the poor man saw it, the devil drove him to murder the excellent old man, who had done him good. So he took sixty gold coins, the old man's treasure, locked the house and ran away. When the neighbours saw that the door of the house was shut and that no one had come out all day, they broke in and found the old man lying dead in the courtyard. At once they suspected the beggar youth. They reported the crime to the magistrate, who ordered the lictors to search for the killer. The more they searched for him, the less they found. At last, after searching for a long time, they saw him hidden under the stairs of the city gate. He was seized and thrown into prison, where the devil tormented him horribly. He also asked us to intercede for him with the prince. Since the crime was so atrocious, we did not dare to ask this of the prince, who loves justice. Instead we promised him that we would obtain a milder punishment for him. We sent Friedrich Myconius to him to tell him what had been done on his behalf. But the wretched man, almost lifeless from great grief, took in nothing. Yet after three days, sorely tempted by the devil, he addressed Friedrich Myconius in these words: "O Lord Friedrich, what temptations I have been through! Now, with God's help, I will gladly die, for I have already overcome the fear of death." Strengthened in true faith and in fervent prayer, he died peacefully.

units.la: Quidam prope oppidum Kõthen captus, à quo etiã suppliciũ sumptum fuit, qui suam coniugẽ interfecit, cum paruula filiola. Illa nõ sunt humana. Interrogatus quomodo ad illa tanta scelera impulsus esset? dixit, se cœpisse amare alicubi aliam quandam, & ideo voluisse tollere suam uxorẽ, ut posset alteram ducere. Ita diabolus dementat animos hominum. Interrogatus porrò, quare filiolam interfecisset? terfecisset? Respondit, ut eo facilior esset aditus ad alteram ducendam. Non est quaerēda ratio, nos sciamus esse opera diaboli. In his exemplis debemus considerare nostram infirmitatem, & potentiam diaboli. Vtile enim est de istis rebus cogitare: sed ita, ut crescat in nobis timor Dei, dilectio, & aliæ uirtutes. Præterea cogitate, talia exèpla esse significationes minantes omnibus, & significare disciplinæ laxationem, & carnalem securitatem. Videmus nobis proponi multa exempla. Turca nostris ceruicibus imminet, et fames, aliæq; calamitates nobis sunt præ foribus. Hæc exempla portendunt horribiles secuturas cædes. Memento te [?]di Petri, dicentis: Diabolus tanquam leo rugiens circuit, quærens quem deuoret, cui resistite solidi in fide.
units.tr: A man was captured near the town of Köthen, and he too was executed. He had killed his wife and their little daughter. These are not human deeds. When he was asked how he had been driven to such great crimes, he said that he had begun to love another woman somewhere, and so he had wanted to get rid of his wife so that he could marry the other. So the devil drives people's minds mad. Asked further why he had killed the little daughter, he replied that it would make his way to marrying the other woman easier.
