We should not seek a rational explanation; we know these are works of the devil. In such examples we ought to consider our own weakness and the power of the devil. For it is useful to think about these things, but in such a way that the fear of God, love, and the other virtues grow in us. Moreover, consider that such examples are warnings threatening everyone, and signs of lax discipline and carnal security. We see that many examples are set before us. The Turk hangs over our necks, and famine and other calamities are at our doors. These examples portend terrible slaughters to come. Remember the word of Peter: "The devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour; resist him, steadfast in the faith" (1 Pet. 5).

units.la: Ratisponæ in conuentu, miser quidam homo certabat in quadā platea mittendis globis. iacebat globum, quo forte petiuit Hispani prætereuntis caniculam. Hispanus autem statim stringens gladiū, eum insequitur inermem per spacium aliquod in platea, neq; eum assequi poterat. Tandem ille miser accipit iacentem gladium alicuius collusoris, quo mox ferit Hispanum, ac ita lethale vulnus infligit, unde statim moreretur. Quare ex hoc atroci facto statim illa nocte homicida capitur, ac res ad Imperatorem defertur. Obtinebat tandem miser, ut doctor Amantius, & doctor Plicardus ei in patrocinium causæ adiungerentur. Illi accedentes ad Marschalcum inferiorem, qui præest talibus iudicijs in aula Imperatoris, ipsi totum negocium exponunt. Dicunt illum miserum habuisse causam defensionis. Petunt similiter, ut audiantur testimonia. Respondit Marschalcus: se habere seuerißimū mandatum à domino suo Imperatore, ut administraret iudicia sine respectu ullius hominis, siue Hispanus siue alius sit interfectus. Si ille habuerit excusationem cum iure conuenientem, fore ut dimitteretur: si uero minus habuerit probabilem excusationē, fore ut plecteretur. Causa dicta est, & audita sunt testimonia. Peractis illis, plane liberatus est ille miser homo ab omni periculo, quòd fuisset casus defensionis. Postea dicebam ad eundem, ut discederet ex urbe, ne conspectus ipsius præberet Hispanis noui tumultus occasionem: & tamen ipse mansit post nos. Ibi Imperator etiam potuisset dicere, fuisse extra modum culpatæ defensionis, & summo iure eum plecti. Sed fuit defensio, quia fuit inermis.
units.tr: At Regensburg during the Diet, a certain wretched man was playing at throwing balls in a square. By chance a ball he threw struck the little dog of a passing Spaniard. The Spaniard immediately drew his sword and chased the unarmed man through the square for some distance, but could not catch him. At last the wretched man picked up the sword of one of the players who had been playing with him, and at once struck the Spaniard and inflicted a mortal wound from which he died immediately. Because of this atrocious deed, the killer was arrested that same night, and the matter was referred to the Emperor. The wretched man managed to have Doctor Amantius and Doctor Plicardus added to his defence. They went to the lower Marshal, who presides over such courts in the Emperor's household, and set out the whole business before him. They said that the wretched man had a case for self-defence. They likewise asked that witnesses be heard. The Marshal replied that he had a most severe command from his lord the Emperor to administer justice without regard to any person, whether the one killed was a Spaniard or someone else. If the man had an excuse consistent with law, he would be released; if he had only a weak excuse, he would be punished. The case was argued and the witnesses were heard. When this was done, the wretched man was completely cleared of all danger, since it was a case of self-defence. Afterwards I told him to leave the city, so that his presence would not give the Spaniards occasion for fresh tumult; yet he stayed behind after us. The Emperor could also have said that the defence had exceeded the bounds of what was permitted, and that he should be punished by the full force of the law. But it was a defence, because the man was unarmed.

units.la: Quidam scholasticus furabatur Lipsiæ, qui antea etiam propter ætatem iuuenilem furto perpetrato uirgis cæsus fuerat. Is dicebat ad iudicem: Tamen non audes me suspendere. Respõdit iudex: Tibi nõ dicemus, quid nos facturi simus. Et suspen-dit eum, dit eum, ac recté fecit iuxta dictum Iurisconsultorum: Grassantibus exemplis, pœnæ exasperandæ sunt.
units.tr: A certain scholar at Leipzig was stealing. Earlier, on account of his youth, he had already been beaten with rods for a theft. He said to the judge: "Still you do not dare to hang me." The judge replied: "We shall not tell you what we are going to do." And he hanged him, and rightly so, according to the saying of the jurists: "When examples abound, punishments must be made harsher."

units.la: Diuites emebant per totam Italiam agros & prædia, item arces, villas, pagos opulétissimos: & in illos, seruos suos collocabant, sicut nunc etiam fit in quibusdam locis. Serui autem non relinquebant homines in possessionibus, & fiebat ut homines ex suis facultatibus expellerentur. Ita factum est, ut tota Italia seruis impleretur. Cum autẽ Tyberius ueniret in Italiam, ibi homines cum filijs & filiabus ei occurrerunt, & indicauerunt suam necessitatem: nisi ipsis auxiliaretur, fame omnes perituros esse. Tum Tyberius promisit illis suum auxilium, si domum rediret. Cum autem domum reuersus esset, ibi adiunxit sibi consules, & in medio populi orationem habuit. Cùm uerò consules uiderent diuitibus displicere illud negocium, ipsum deseruerunt: sicut fit in aduersis rebus. Mouit enim hac oratione ualde populum. Interea temporis, quando illa aguntur, cognatus suus Pub. Nasica per populum prorupit, (populo cedente, non solum propter auctoritatem, sed etiam propter cognationem) & Tyberium cognatum suum miserabiliter in conspectu populi intersecit. Quanquã homicida non coactus secessit in exilium propter crudele factum, quod exercuit in suo cognato: tamen men est absolutus à Senatu, ita ut in exilium sece-dere non cogeretur. Deniq; idem homicida est ui-cissim interfectus,iuxta regulam: Qui gladiũ ac-ceperit, gladio peribit. Et propter illam ipsam controuersiam est ortum bellum ciuile, quod ma-gnum negocium Senatui fecit: & tandem nihilo-minus tales ueditiones & emptiones abolitæ sunt. Nam aliàs non potuisset stare Respublica.
units.tr: The rich were buying up fields and estates throughout Italy, and also strongholds, villas and very wealthy villages, and they settled their slaves on them, as is still done in some places today. The slaves did not leave people in possession of their holdings, and it came about that men were driven out of their property. So it happened that all Italy was filled with slaves. When Tiberius came to Italy, men with their sons and daughters met him there and declared their need: unless he helped them, they would all perish of hunger. Then Tiberius promised them his help if he returned home. When he had returned home, he gathered the tribunes around him and delivered a speech in the midst of the people. But when the consuls saw that the business displeased the rich, they abandoned him, as happens in adverse circumstances. For this speech greatly moved the people. Meanwhile, while these things were going on, his kinsman Publius Nasica broke through the people (the people giving way, not only out of respect for his authority but also out of kinship) and in full view of the people wretchedly slew his cousin Tiberius. Although the killer was not compelled to go into exile on account of the cruel deed he had committed against his kinsman, yet he was acquitted by the Senate, so that he was not forced to withdraw into exile. In the end the same killer was himself slain in turn, according to the rule: he who takes the sword shall perish by the sword. And on account of that very dispute a civil war arose, which caused great trouble for the Senate; and in the end, nevertheless, such sales and purchases were abolished. For otherwise the commonwealth could not have stood.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: In urbe Pomeranica, puer duodecim annorum obiurgatus est à matre, aut etiam castigatus, quòd ita gulæ & uoluptatibus operã daret. Puer ægre-ferens castigationem, seu obiurgationem, altero die manè dormiêtis suæ matris pectus cultro per-sodit in lecto. Pater excitatus, exilijt de lecto, & puerum apprehensum interficere uolebat, nisi su-ga sibi consuluisset: puer tamen captus est, & for-tassis de eo sumptum supplicium. Iste puer tam iu-uenili ætate naturaliter tam duro animo non po-tuit esse præditus, ut hoc facinus tam celeriter per petraret: sed diabolus hoc per puerum effecit, qui ita instituit & animauit puerum, ut talia commit-tere auderet. Talia exempla debetis considerare, & quotidie recitare dictũ Christi: Vigilate & o-rate, ne intretis in tentationem. Item: Semper pe-tite, Ne nos inducas in tëtationem. Hæc 17. Martij anno 1553 recitata sunt.
units.tr: In a town in Pomerania, a boy of twelve years was rebuked by his mother, or even chastised, because he devoted himself so much to gluttony and pleasures. The boy, resenting the chastisement or rebuke, early the next morning stabbed his mother's breast with a knife while she lay in bed. The father, roused, leapt out of bed and wanted to kill the boy when he caught him, had the boy not saved himself by flight; the boy was nonetheless captured, and perhaps a punishment was taken from him. That boy, at so young an age, could not naturally have been endowed with so hard a spirit as to carry out such a deed so quickly; but the devil brought this about through the boy, who so instructed and inspired him that he dared to commit such things. You ought to consider such examples and daily recite the words of Christ: Watch and pray, that you enter not into temptation. Likewise: Always pray, Lead us not into temptation. These things were recited on 17 March in the year 1553.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam adolescens nobilis, ex petulantia occiderat seruũ domesticum: ac ueniens Vuitebergam exceptus à docto uiro eius rei ignaro, & in numerum ipsius discipulorũ receptus est, ibiq; se honestè gesit. Interea mater cum amicis interfecti rem componit. Postea eum domum reuocat. Post biennium uerò, mater despondit ei uxorem uiduam, adolescentulam opulentißimam: at inter eos sunt ortæ inimicitiæ. Nam ipsa erat scortũ, & aliquoties ei puluerem, quo mures necantur, in cibũ immiscuerat. Tandem cõspiratione facta cum equite, auriga & sarctore, impetum in eum faciunt in cubili, eumq; interficiunt. At cum esset iuuenis robustus, diu se defendit, & ipsi mulieri, dum os suum obturare nititur, digitos morsu abscidit, dicens: Hæc tibi, scortum, postremò habeto. Quo facinore perpetrato, mulier capitur, & decollatur. Reliqui serui aufugerunt, quorum unus Magdeburgæ rotæ impositus est: alter alibi eodem supplicio affectus: tertius capite truncatus est. Hæc sunt manifesta diuinæ iræ iudicia aduersus homicidium.
units.tr: A certain noble youth, out of wantonness, had killed a household servant. Coming to Wittenberg, he was taken in by a learned man who knew nothing of the affair and was received among his pupils, and there he conducted himself honourably. Meanwhile his mother settled the matter with the dead man's friends, and afterwards she recalled him home. Two years later, however, she betrothed him to a widow, a very wealthy young woman; but enmity arose between them. For she was a whore, and several times she had mixed rat poison into his food. At last, after a conspiracy was formed with a horseman, a coachman and a tailor, they attacked him in his bedchamber and killed him. But since he was a strong young man, he defended himself for a long time, and while the woman tried to stop his mouth, he bit off her fingers, saying: "Take this, whore, and keep it for good." After this deed was carried out, the woman was arrested and beheaded. The other servants fled; one of them was broken on the wheel at Magdeburg, another was given the same punishment elsewhere, and the third was beheaded. These are manifest judgments of divine wrath against murder.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Formosa quædam mulier ætate nondum confecta, cum mortuus esset maritus, propter inopiâ frumenti, desperauit se non posse cum illis duobus filiolis, qui ex marito remanserant, sustentari. Neq; enim labore ac sudore tantum colligere aut mereri potuit, ut victum haberent. Denique, cum non sustineret amplius lamentationes filiorum, & ieiunos clamores audire, quamuis non volens, tamen coacta iuit mendicatum, sperans se collectu-ram aliquid, ut sedaret filios pane & potu. Postea cum totam ciuitatem perambulasset, nec quicquā accepisset, & insuper etiam obiurgata ab aliquibus, dicentibus: Tu mulier, quid mendicas, cum sis tam robusta? Bene posses laborare, si uelles, & tuos paruulos laborando nutrire. Illa respondens dixit: Domine in his infelicibus temporibus non possum tantum colligere, & labore mereri, unde ego & filioli mei uiuant. Nam omnia nimis carè uenduntur. Postquam etiam mendicando uideret se nihil accipere, præsertim à ditioribus, qui potuissent liberaliter conferre, redit domum flens ac dicens: Filij mei, eamus unà ad aquam, ac ibi nos præcipitemus, non enim habemus unde uiuamus. At responderunt filij: Charissima mater, ubi tu, ibi & nos uolumus esse: ac ita sumpsit filios illos ambos, unum ducens, alterum gestans humero: & progressa extra portam, proiecit filios primum in Albin, & ipsa deinde statim secuta est. Ita unà obierunt. Hæc historia 1547, in urbe quadam celebri facta est.
units.tr: A certain beautiful woman, not yet advanced in years, when her husband had died, despaired of being able to support the two little sons who had remained from her husband, because of the lack of grain. For by labour and sweat she could not gather or earn enough to keep them alive. At last, when she could no longer endure her sons' laments and hear their hungry cries, she went out to beg, though unwilling and compelled, hoping to collect something to quiet her sons with bread and drink. Afterwards, when she had walked through the whole city and received nothing, and was moreover scolded by some who said: "You woman, why do you beg, when you are so strong? You could work, if you wished, and feed your little ones by labouring." She answered: "Sir, in these unhappy times I cannot gather enough, nor earn by labour, to keep myself and my little sons alive. For everything is sold at too high a price." Then, seeing that by begging she received nothing, especially from the wealthier, who could have given generously, she returned home weeping and saying: "My sons, let us go together to the water and there throw ourselves in, for we have nothing to live on." But the sons answered: "Dearest mother, wherever you are, there we also want to be." So she took both sons, leading one and carrying the other on her shoulder; and going out beyond the gate, she first threw the sons into the Elbe, and then herself immediately followed them. Thus they died together. This story happened in 1547, in a certain famous city.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Cygneæ puer quidam habens cultrum in manibus, incidit forte in eum, ac seipsum transfodit. Pater ueniens domum, uidens hæc, mox ira commotus interfecit uxorem: postea uero & ipse factum suum perhorrescens, ex desperatione sibi cõ sciscit mortem. Hæc omnia non sunt humana, sed diabolica. Ideo continuè oremus Deum, ut nobis det Spiritum sanctum, qui regat corda & totius uitæ actiones.
units.tr: A certain boy at Cygnea, holding a knife in his hands, by chance fell upon it and stabbed himself. His father, coming home and seeing this, straightway moved by anger killed his wife; afterwards, however, he himself, horrified at his deed, out of despair brought death upon himself. All these things are not human but diabolical. Therefore let us continually pray to God that he may give us the Holy Spirit, who rules the hearts and all the actions of life.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Ante annos 18. in hyeme, est interfectus quidam studiosus inter Dieben & Lipsiam, & cadauer proiectum est in aquam, ubi totas quatuor septimanas congelatum iacuit. Postea uero in eodem loco inuentum & erutum ex glacie, in proximum oppidum deportatum est. quod ubi iudex cum multis ciuibus circumstantibus inspexisset, cœpit recentem sanguinem stillare cadauer. Fuit certissimum signum & diuinum testimonium de præsentia homicidæ: sed iudex tam fatuus & stolidus erat, ut nullam inquisitionem institueret.
units.tr: Eighteen years ago, in winter, a certain student was killed between Dieben and Leipzig, and the corpse was thrown into the water, where it lay frozen for four whole weeks. Afterwards, however, it was found in the same place, drawn out of the ice, and carried to the nearest town. When the judge, with many citizens standing around, had examined it, the corpse began to drip fresh blood. This was a most certain sign and divine testimony of the presence of the murderer; but the judge was so foolish and dull that he instituted no inquiry.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Vuinshemij fuerat quidam, qui aliquot cædes fecerat ante multos annos, & aliquas etiam grauidas mulieres disecuerat. Tandem uero accidit, ut circa pascha emeret tria capita uitulina, eaq; in saccum poneret, qui in modum retis nexus erat. Cùm sic iret per plateas, omnibus quot-quot eum aspexerunt, uisus est portare capita humana cruentata. Defertur res ad Senatum, ac statim missi sunt lictores, ut eum caperent. Adductus in curiam, & interrogatus, ubi nactus esseт capita humana? ipse respondit, se emisse in macello. Accersitus igitur lanius, affirmat se ipsi capita uitulina uendidisse, non humana. Senatus animo perculsus, cogitauit hoc nihil boni portendere: iussitq; eum in carcerem deduci, & examinari per torturam. Ille sic examinatus, statim confessus est cædes perpetratas. Deinde capita ex sacco deprõpta sunt, quæ rursus habuerunt formam capitum uitulinarum.
units.tr: There was once a certain man in Wunsiedel who, many years before, had committed several murders and had also cut open some pregnant women. At last it happened that around Easter he bought three calves' heads and put them into a sack, which was tied in the manner of a net. As he went through the streets, everyone who saw him seemed to be carrying bloodied human heads. The matter was reported to the Senate, and at once officers were sent to seize him. Brought into the council chamber and questioned where he had got human heads, he replied that he had bought them at the butcher's. The butcher was therefore summoned and affirmed that he had sold him calves' heads, not human ones. The Senate, alarmed, thought this portended nothing good; and ordered him to be taken to prison and examined under torture. Thus examined, he at once confessed the murders he had committed. Then the heads were taken out of the sack, and they again had the form of calves' heads.

units.la: SEXTUM PRAECEPTUM. CASTITAS ET CONIVGIUM.
units.tr: THE SIXTH COMMANDMENT. CHASTITY AND MARRIAGE.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Hippolytum filium Thesei, natũ ex priore coniuge, Phedra nouerca inuitauit ad incæstã consuetudinẽ, sumpto ab eo iuramento, ut nouercæ petitioni obsequeretur. Sed mens mãsit iniurata: id est, non potuit, quantumuis sanctè promittẽdo, obligari ad aliquid turpe. Nemo enim potest iurare rem aliquā turpem: & præclarè fecit, quòd auer‑satus sit incæstā nouercæ cõsuetudinem. Sicut Hip‑polytus etiam à se nouercæ illicitas libidines re‑pulit. Sic Peleus recusauit rem habere cum uxore Acasti. unde cùm illa ob repulsam irata falsò accu‑sasset eum apud maritum Acastum, hic male suspi‑cans de eo, obiecit ipsum Centauris: ubi dicunt di‑uinitùs ipsi esse missum gladium, quo uicit Centau‑ros, id est: Deus dans præmia castitati, defendit Pe‑leum in maximis periculis. Sic Bellerophõtem in‑uitauit ad consuetudinē turpem uxor Creti, quam cum negaret, ipsa accusauit eum apud uirum, à quo obiectus est Chimæræ. Verùm diuinitùs missus est ei Pegasus, quo uolans in aere uinceret Chimæ‑ram. Hæc sapientissimi homines tradiderunt, ut o‑stenderent quanta præmia sint castitatis, & Deũ dare testimonia innocentiæ.
units.tr: Phaedra, his stepmother, invited Hippolytus, the son of Theseus born of his earlier wife, to an incestuous liaison, after first making him swear an oath that he would yield to her request. But his mind remained unpolluted: that is, however solemnly he promised, he could not be bound to anything shameful. For no one can swear to do something base, and he acted very nobly in abhorring the incestuous intercourse with his stepmother. In the same way Hippolytus also repulsed his stepmother's unlawful lusts. Likewise Peleus refused to have relations with the wife of Acastus. When she, angered by the rebuff, falsely accused him before her husband Acastus, he, suspecting the worst of him, exposed him to the Centaurs. There, they say, a sword was sent to him by divine means, with which he conquered the Centaurs; that is, God, giving rewards to chastity, defended Peleus in the greatest dangers. Likewise the wife of Cretus invited Bellerophon to a shameful liaison; when he refused, she accused him before her husband, who sent him against the Chimaera. But Pegasus was sent to him divinely, and by flying on it through the air he conquered the Chimaera. The wisest men handed these stories down to show how great are the rewards of chastity, and that God bears witness to innocence.

units.la: Quædam principissa, pia & sancta matrona, dimittens suam ancillam, cùm esset elocata, & mi‑gratura in aliam urbem, hanc admonitionem in‑iunxit, & dixit ei: O’ mea ancilla, time Deum, & sis proba: quod si feceris, Deus non derelinquet te. Nam & ego si id fecissem, in hæc pericula nun‑quam incidissem. Peruenerat enim in aliqua peri‑cula, de quibus non fas est loqui.
units.tr: A certain princess, a pious and holy matron, was dismissing her maidservant, who was about to be married and to move to another city, and she gave her this admonition: "O my maid, fear God and be upright. If you do this, God will not forsake you. For if I had done so, I would never have fallen into these dangers." For she had come into certain dangers, of which it is not right to speak.

units.la: Alia nobilis & pia matrona iniūxit filiæ eloca‑tæ, & iam à matre discedēti, inquiens: Charissima filia, timeas Deum, & sis pia & proba: sicq; erga maritum tuum te geras, ut ille postes ædium aspiciens lætetur, & non exhorrescat.
units.tr: Another noble and pious matron gave this charge to her daughter, who had been married and was now leaving her mother: "Dearest daughter, fear God, and be pious and upright; and conduct yourself toward your husband in such a way that, when he looks at the doorposts of the house, he rejoices and does not shudder."

units.la: Rex quidam incluserat nobilem uirginem in arcem, in qua eodem tempore exceperat Imperatorem Carolum V. Cum uero Imperator ingrederetur cubiculum, inuenit illam lachrymantem, miraturq; quid esset? Ista inquit: Hucducta sum mandato Regis. Imperator illam statim suis, quos norat esse integros, dedit adducendam parentibus. Postea in reditu Imperator illam arcem destrui curauit, & nihil atrocius egit.
units.tr: A certain king had shut a noble virgin up in a citadel, in which at the same time he had lodged the Emperor Charles V. When the Emperor entered the bedchamber, he found her weeping and asked what was the matter. She said: "I was brought here by the king's command." The Emperor at once gave her, to be taken back to her parents, to men of his own whom he knew to be upright. Afterwards, on his return, the Emperor had that citadel destroyed, and he did nothing more severe.

units.la: Strabo dicit, quòd non licuerit homini Germano ducere uxorem, nisi prius offerret caput interfecti hostis. Germani semper præ cæteris gentibus laudati sunt ob castitatem.
units.tr: Strabo says that a German man was not permitted to take a wife unless he first offered the head of a slain enemy. The Germans have always been praised above other peoples for their chastity.

units.la: Apelles Venerem pictam, stantem in testudine, pinxit: significare uolens, sexum muliebrē non debere, neq; posse procul uagari: sed debere se domi continere, & respicere ad eas res proprie, quæ ad gubernationem œconomiæ pertinent. Sicut enim testudo nunquam discedit à domo: sic mulieres in domibus suis se contineant, & non expacientur.
units.tr: Apelles painted Venus standing on a tortoise, wishing to signify that the female sex ought not, and cannot, roam far afield, but ought to keep itself at home and attend to those matters that properly belong to the management of the household. For just as the tortoise never leaves its house, so women should remain within their homes and not go gadding about.

units.la: Idem Apelles, cùm Venerem depingeret, curauit sibi triginta pulcherrimas uirgines eligi, quas intueretur. Similiter fecit Durerus, honestus uir, pictor Norinbergensis: cui gratificati sunt honestissimæ simæ matronæ & uirgines. Inde pater Lucæ pictoris, optimus & honestissimus senex, iocari solebat in gynæcio: Antiquis pictoribus uirgines se nudabant, & contrectando in eis proportiones membrorum inueniebant.
units.tr: The same Apelles, when he was painting Venus, took care to have thirty of the most beautiful virgins chosen, so that he might look at them. Dürer, an honourable man and a painter of Nuremberg, did likewise, and the most honourable matrons and virgins obliged him. Hence the father of the painter Lucas, an excellent and most honourable old man, used to joke in the women's quarters: "The ancient painters used to strip their virgins, and by handling them they discovered the proportions of the limbs."

units.la: Francofordiæ ad Mœnum est præclarissima pictura Dureri, qua expressa est assumptio Mariæ uirginis, cum ornamentis flosculorum.
units.tr: At Frankfurt on the Main there is a most famous painting by Dürer, which depicts the Assumption of the Virgin Mary, with decorations of little flowers.

units.la: Virtutes honestæ & piæ matrisfamiliàs, iuxta Paulum Apostolũ, præcipuæ sunt quatuor: fides, dilectio, castitas, & modestia. Ecce ubi hæ quatuor uirtutes adsunt, ibi omnes adsunt, quæ in proba ac laudabili muliere requiruntur.
units.tr: According to the apostle Paul, the chief virtues of an honourable and pious matron are four: faith, love, chastity and modesty. Where these four virtues are present, there are all the qualities required in an upright and praiseworthy woman.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: In matrimonio contrahendo hæc requiruntur: uidelicet, inuocatio, consilium, circumspectio & cautio, seu consideratio qualitatum.
units.tr: In contracting marriage the following are required: namely, invocation, counsel, circumspection and caution, or consideration of the qualities of the parties.

units.la: Quidam pastor ante uiginti quinq; annos in oppido Kal, robustus & iuuenis uir, insulsè uociferabatur in concionibus de puerperio, dicens: Quoniam mulieres sunt deditæ tantũ gulæ & uoluptastibus in puerperio, satis est seruare puerperiũ per triduum aut quatriduum, nec diutius: postea uerò rursus debent redire ad operas. Quædam mulieres motæ eius publicis concionibus, egressæ sunt statim ex puerperio, & redierunt ad domesticos labores, & tandem mortuæ sunt.
units.tr: About twenty-five years ago, in the town of Kal, a certain pastor, a robust and young man, foolishly harangued his congregations about childbed, saying: "Since women are given over only to gluttony and pleasures during their confinement, it is enough to keep to childbed for three or four days, and no longer; after that they must return to their work." Some women, moved by his public sermons, got up from childbed at once and returned to their domestic labours, and in the end they died.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Sextum præceptum.
units.tr: The Sixth Commandment.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Illustri & celebri facto, ad omnem posterita-tis memoriam, pietatem suam erga coniuges suos declararunt Minyarum uxores. Cùm enim uiri ex ea familia omnes, circiter triginta, propter af-sectati regni suspicione à Spartanis publicæ custo-diæ inclusi, & supplicio capitali iam destinati es-sent, quod ex ueteri instituto Lacedæmoniorũ no-cturno tempore passuri erant, coniuges eorũ ex no-bilissimis familiis natæ, cùm (uelut postremò allo-cuturæ perituros uiros) à custodibus accessum im-petrassent, carcerem ingressæ, commutataq; cum maritis ueste, per simulationem doloris, uelatis ca-pitibus eos abire passæ sunt, sua corpora pro illo-rũ salute supplicio & præsenti periculo offerêtes.
units.tr: By an illustrious and famous deed, the wives of the Minyans showed their devotion to their husbands, to be remembered by all posterity. When about thirty men of that family had been shut up in public custody by the Spartans on suspicion of aiming at kingship, and were already condemned to capital punishment, which under the ancient custom of the Lacedaemonians they were to suffer by night, their wives, all born of the noblest families, obtained access from the guards on the pretext of speaking to their husbands for the last time before they died. They entered the prison, exchanged clothes with their husbands, and, feigning grief with veiled heads, let the men go out, offering their own bodies to punishment and immediate danger for their husbands' safety.

units.la: Non dissimili amoris fidelitate Iason seruatus à Medea dicitur. Rex item Galliæ Ludouicus, proxi-mus ante Francisco, cùm esset captiuus Caroli Gib-bosi, liberatus est beneficio mulieris. Sic Sigismun-dus rex Vngariæ, antequam imperiũ accepisset, fuit aliquando captus à suis nobilibus, & beneficio mu-lieris est dimissus. Paulo post cùm iterum esset in-structus exercitu, ui cæpit illos nobiles, qui eũ te-nuerant, & propè triginta decollauit.
units.tr: A similar faithfulness of love is said to have saved Jason through Medea. King Louis of France, the immediate predecessor of Francis, when he was a captive of Charles the Hunchback, was freed by the kindness of a woman. So too Sigismund, king of Hungary, before he had received the empire, was once captured by his own nobles and released through the kindness of a woman. Shortly afterwards, when he had again gathered an army, he forcibly seized those nobles who had held him and beheaded nearly thirty of them.

units.la: Quidam Comes de Gleichen, multis Erphur-diæ notus, cum uxore sua honestè uixit. Is cum in militia aduersus Turcos prælio captus esset, à
units.tr: A certain Count of Gleichen, well known at Erfurt, lived honourably with his wife. When he had been taken prisoner in battle against the Turks while on military service, he was carried into Turkey by the Sultan king.

units.la: Soldano rege in Turciam transvectus est. Ubi cùm diu in vinculis retentus, faciendis operibus rusticis defatigaretur, accidit ut filia regis voluptatis causa expaciaretur, & ibi forte uideret Comitē suas operas exercentē. quem statim adit, interrogans, qua ratione eò peruenisset? Interea dum sic cum eo colloquitur, hominis forma & industria ita delectata est, ut ipsum inciperet amare. Proponit ei, si uellet ipsam ducere, se facilè eum ex vinculis liberaturam, ac unà cum eo in patriam profectu-ram esse. Cui ille respondit, in sua patria sibi esse coniugem & liberos. At ipsa inquit, nihil obstare, cùm moris sit apud Turcos, ut uni marito duæ uel plures coniungantur uxores. His auditis, acquiescit facilè, pollicetur se fidem præstiturum. Tunc Regina statim, ut ex vinculis dimitteretur captiuus, effecit, & cum Comite abit. Sic Comes liberatus, postquam uenisset Venetias, inuenit ibi suum ministrum, iamdudum ipsum quærentem & expectantem: ex quo cognoscit, coniugem cum liberis & reliqua familia saluam esse. His auditis Comes Romam proficiscitur, & rem omnem Pontifici exponit, vt facta erat, quòd uidelicet alteri fidem dedisset vitæ redimendæ causa, & non ex petulantia aut lasciuia, cùm tamen prior coniunx domi sit salua & incolumis. Quare absolutus est à Papa, & acceptis ab eo literis reuertitur domum.
units.tr: There, after being kept a long time in chains and worn down by forced rustic labour, it happened that the king's daughter went out for pleasure and by chance saw the Count doing his work there. She at once approached him and asked by what means he had come to that place. Meanwhile, as she talked with him, she was so charmed by the man's appearance and diligence that she began to love him. She offered that, if he wished to take her as his wife, she would easily free him from his chains and go back to his homeland with him. He replied that he already had a wife and children in his own country. But she said that this was no obstacle, since it is the custom among the Turks for one husband to be joined to two or more wives. Having heard this, he readily agreed and promised to keep faith with her. Then the queen at once had the captive released from his chains, and he departed with the Count. So freed, the Count came to Venice, where he found his own servant, who had long been seeking and waiting for him. From him he learned that his wife, his children and the rest of his household were safe. Having heard this, the Count set out for Rome and laid the whole matter before the Pope just as it had happened: that he had given his word to another woman in order to ransom his life, and not out of wantonness or lust, while his first wife was safe and sound at home. For this reason he was absolved by the Pope, and receiving letters from him, he returned home.

units.la: Redeunte statim agnoscit uxor, nihil offensa propter Turcicam reginam, & amore magno prosecuta est pellicem, cuius beneficio charißimum maritum receperat. Regina etiam facilè tulit Comitissam, ita ut familiarißimè sine ulla discordia uitam inter se agerent. Deus autem, qui facilè tolerauit hoc matrimonium, ueră seu priorem coniugem multa prole beatam fecit, altera prorsus sterili manente: quæ tanquam famula tractauit & souit alterius liberos. Horum monumentum adhuc hodie Erphurdiæ extat, in quo ex utroque latere uxores Comiti astàt: altera regina, marmorea corona ornata: Comitissa sculpta est nuda, & infantes iuxta pedes eius reptantes.
units.tr: On his return, his wife at once acknowledged him and, taking no offence at the Turkish queen, showed great love to the concubine, by whose kindness she had received back her dearest husband. The queen also bore the Countess easily, so that they lived together most amicably without any discord. God, who had tolerated this marriage, blessed the first wife with a large family, while the other remained entirely barren; she treated and cherished the other's children like a servant. A monument of them still stands today at Erfurt, in which the wives stand beside the Count on either side: the queen, adorned with a marble crown, and the Countess, sculpted naked, with infants crawling at her feet.

units.la: Laudatur etiam pietas & patientia coniugis illustrissimi principis Electoris Friderici Palatini ad Rhenum, quæ multis laboribus & uigilijs illustrissimo principi Electori Friderico ægrotanti suas insignes uirtutes, quas Paulus sanctis matronis attribuit, declarauit.
units.tr: The piety and patience of the wife of the most illustrious prince, the Elector Frederick Palatine on the Rhine, are also praised, who, through many labours and vigils, showed the outstanding virtues that Paul attributes to holy matrons to the most illustrious prince, the Elector Frederick, when he was sick.

units.la: Christiani differunt ab Ethnicis, præcipuè duobus uirtutibus, uidelicet religione & castitate. Ethnici enim sicut fuerunt idololatræ, sic postea horribilibus libidinibus sunt polluti. Conuenimus ergo publicè in Ecclesia, ut hac pompa testemur nos approbare coniugium diuinitùs institutum & sancitũ, ut uitentur prauæ commixtiones, & singuli castitatem tueamur, Ecclesiã amemus, eamqʒ tanquam sponsam Christi ornemus.
units.tr: Christians differ from the heathen chiefly in two virtues, namely religion and chastity. For the heathen, just as they were idolaters, were afterwards polluted by horrible lusts. We therefore gather publicly in the Church, so that by this solemnity we may bear witness that we approve marriage, instituted and sanctioned by God, that foul mixtures may be avoided, that each of us may guard chastity, love the Church, and adorn her as the spouse of Christ.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam Bohemicus dominus, ambiuit honestissimam matronã Comitis Stephani Schlick, cum hic abfuisseт duodecim annos, & fama esset cum esse mortuum. Ad cuius petitionem sic respondere iussit: Quod in hoc breui temporis spacio prioris mariti Stephani nondum obliuisci potuisset: quare illi domino suam petitionem recusauit. Vocauit duodecim annos, quibus affuisset maritus, breue tempus. Sic bene optandum esset, ut in similibus casibus, omnes mulieres huius ornatissimæ matronæ uirtutes imitarentur.
units.tr: A certain Bohemian lord courted the most honourable matron, the wife of Count Stephen Schlick, although the Count had been absent for twelve years and was rumoured to be dead. To his request she ordered this answer to be given: that in so short a span of time she had not yet been able to forget her former husband Stephen; therefore she refused his suit. She called the twelve years during which her husband had been away a short time. So it would be well wished that, in similar cases, all women should imitate the virtues of this most distinguished matron.

units.la: Menander inquit: Ducens uxorem, in medium pelagus nauigat, quasi in medias tempestates.
units.tr: Menander says: "When a man takes a wife, he sails out onto the open sea, as it were into the midst of storms."

units.la: Χειμὼν πατ' ὅιnss ἐσὶν ἀνδράσι γύνη: id est, Tempestas est mulier uiro in domo.
units.tr: "A woman is a winter storm for a man in his house." [Χειμὼν κατ' οἶκον ἐστὶν ἀνδρὶ γυνή] That is, a woman is a tempest to a man in the home.

units.la: Iocus.
units.tr: Joke.

units.la: Accidit in uicinia oppidi Vitebergensis, ut quidam iuuenis solea sua cõiugem percusserit. Quod cùm familia illa ex qua erat coniunx, admodum ægrè ferret, conuenerunt aliqui ex cognatis accersentes ad se maritum, cum quo expostularunt, eo quòd cognatam ipsorum tam indignè tractasset. Ille uerò non commotus, humaniter respõdit: Boni affines, boni consulo uestram admonitionem, sed quaeso ut & me audiatis. Fateor, inquit, me co-motum uerberasse, sed illa me prius multo durius stupario malleo percusserat. Vos igitur iudicate utrum fuerit durius, malleone stupario an crepida percuti. Illi quaerunt, quomiodo sit percussus ab ipsa malleo stupario? Respondit: Sua lingua admo-dum mihi maledixerat.
units.tr: It happened in the neighbourhood of the town of Wittenberg that a young man struck his wife with his slipper. When her family, from which she came, took this very badly, some of her relations gathered and summoned the husband to them, and remonstrated with him because he had treated their kinswoman so shamefully. He, however, was not disturbed and answered courteously: "Good kinsmen, I take your admonition in good part, but I beg you to hear me too. I admit that I struck her in anger, but she had first struck me far harder with a stupid mallet. So you judge for yourselves which is the harder blow, to be struck with a stupid mallet or with a slipper." They asked him how he had been struck by her with a stupid mallet. He replied: "She had abused me very harshly with her tongue."

units.la: DE CONIVGIO SACERDO-tum, & coelibatu eorundem.
units.tr: On the Marriage of Priests, and Their Celibacy.

units.la: In iure Canonico, quod medium uocatur, id est, illud quod est inter primum & ultimum, habetur talis lex: Sacerdos ducens uxorem, suspendatur. Hic quidam indocti simpliciter τὸ ῥητὸν intelle-xerunt: id est, suspendatur laqueo de patibulo. Vnde multi honesti uiri sunt interfecti & suspensi, ut etiam Tubingae unus ex sacrificulorum coetu pu-blicè dixerit de hac tyrannide: Si non est nimium, aut illegitimum, tamen utiq; nimis durum est. Non intellexerunt sensum: quia ius Canonicum hoc uult, suspendatur, id est, ad tempus aliquod ab officio remoueatur: seu mandetur ei, ut aliquantisper remittat officium, donec cum episcopo redeat in gratiam.
units.tr: In the canon law, which is called the "middle" (that is, the part lying between the first and the last), there is this rule: "A priest who takes a wife shall be suspended." Some unlearned men have understood the words literally [τὸ ῥητόν], namely, that he should be hanged from a gallows. Hence many honest men have been killed and hanged. Even at Tübingen one of the petty priests said publicly of this tyranny: "If it is not excessive or unlawful, it is at any rate exceedingly harsh." They did not grasp the sense. Canon law means this: "he shall be suspended," that is, removed from his office for some time, or it is ordered that he give up his office for a while, until he is reconciled with the bishop.

units.la: Staphylus, cum nuper petiuisset episcopatum, & ei dictum esset, quod non posset fieri episcopus, quia haberet coniugem legitimam, ille respon-dit:
units.tr: When Staphylus had recently sought a bishopric, and was told that he could not become a bishop because he had a lawful wife, he replied:

units.la: nm m 2 dn: dit: Apud uos est mihi concubina, at apud Lutheranos est mihi coniunx.
units.tr: "With you I have a concubine; but with the Lutherans I have a wife."

units.la: Cœlibatus est multo commodior ad diuitias coparandas, quàm uita coniugalis. Μεγάλη τυραννὶς ἀνδρὶ, γένναι καὶ γύναι: Magnum impedimentum adferunt uxor & liberi, illis qui ad magnos honores & potentiam aspirant. Cœlibi quidem ac libero, siquidem hic fortuna minus ex uoto succedat, alibi melius succedit: coniugato uerò uxor & liberi sunt instar freni ac uinculi, quo constringatur, ne uel solum uertere uel ad altiora peruenire queat. Nisi enim quis sit perditissimus homo, hoc uinculo patitur se retineri. Quare cœlibatus est ualde commodus, ut dixit papa Pius: Multæ fuerunt causæ adimendi coniuges sacerdotibus, sed maiores sunt restituendi. Magnæ inde ortæ sunt contentiones de successionibus. Imò audio regem quendam Polonicum dixisse: Oportere uiolari alterum præceptum, Non mœchaberis, aut Non furtum facies. Si ego sacerdotibus, inquit, concederem coniugia, tunc fierent furta, id est, ecclesiastica bona diriperentur. Videte, quàm astutè sit dictum.
units.tr: Celibacy is far more convenient for acquiring riches than married life. "A great tyranny for a man: children and a wife" [Μεγάλη τυραννὶς ἀνδρὶ, γένναι καὶ γύναι]. A wife and children are a great hindrance to those who aspire to high honours and power. For the unmarried and free man, if fortune turns out less than he wished in one place, it turns out better in another. But for the married man, wife and children are like a bridle and chain, by which he is held back, so that he cannot leave his post or rise to higher things. Unless a man is utterly abandoned, he allows himself to be held back by this chain. Therefore celibacy is very convenient, as Pope Pius said: "There were many reasons for taking wives from priests, but greater reasons for restoring them." Great quarrels have arisen from this over successions. Indeed, I hear that a certain Polish king said that another commandment must be violated, either "You shall not commit adultery" or "You shall not steal." "If I," he said, "were to grant marriage to priests, there would then be thefts, that is, church goods would be plundered." See how cunningly this was put.

units.la: Quàm callidus prætextus est: Sacerdotes non debent ducere uxores, ut possint uacare studijs, ne impediantur œconomijs & cupiditatibus, quæ plerunq; œconomias comitantur. Profectò uerum est, quòd callidus sit prætextus, & prudëter dictũ. Ita dixit Campegius ad secretarium Palatini: Vos Germani habetis unam causam, qua ualde nos gra-uatis de coniugio, & uerum est: multa enim ma-gna uitia sunt secuta cœlibatum, sed nos profere-mus nostras excusationes in Concilio. Ostendemus illam legem de cœlibatu non esse ortam à nobis: sed nos non potuisse sustinere regum & princi-pum interpellationes, qui petiuerunt ut sanci-remus hanc legem. Videtis etiam hoc tempore, quàm multæ miseriæ sequantur coniugium. Ta-men nihil est ordinandum contra uoluntatë Dei.
units.tr: What a clever pretext it is: priests ought not to take wives so that they may be free for their studies and not be hindered by household affairs and desires, which usually accompany household affairs. Truly it is a clever pretext, and it was wisely said. So Campeggio said to the secretary of the Palatine: "You Germans have one reason by which you greatly burden us about marriage, and it is true: for many great vices have followed celibacy. But we will put forward our excuses at the Council. We will show that the law on celibacy did not arise from us, but that we could not withstand the appeals of kings and princes, who asked that we enact this law. You see even now how many miseries follow marriage. Yet nothing must be ordained against the will of God."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam monachus in finibus Bohemiæ habēs sacerdotium mediocre, iussus est aut relinquere sa-cerdotium, aut coniugem. Miser infirmitate gene-ris humani labitur, ac dimittit coniugem, ut re-tineret sacerdotium: cogitans interim, se uelle postea eam ad se rursus recipere. Sed hic in ma-gnos terrores & tentationes post paucos dies in-cidit: quas ut finiret, mortem sibi consciuit. Non est imusitatum, homines sibi accersere mala, malè curando.
units.tr: A certain monk on the borders of Bohemia, holding a modest priesthood, was ordered either to give up the priesthood or his wife. Wretched through the weakness of the human race, he gives way and dismisses his wife, so as to keep the priesthood, meanwhile thinking that he would later take her back to himself. But within a few days he fell into great terrors and temptations, and to end them he took his own life. It is not unusual for men to bring evils upon themselves by applying bad remedies.

units.la: Eccius ultimum librum edidit de coniugio sa-cerdotum turpissimum. Non fuit cygnea cantio, sed ultimus crepitus: & sicut felis fugiens pedit, sic ille monens hunc crepitum cecinit. Legi librum subinde accipiens partem ad cloacam, alioqui non legissem.
units.tr: Eck published the last book on the marriage of priests, a most shameful one. It was not a swan song but a last fart: and just as a cat, when fleeing, befouls the place, so he, while warning of this fart, sang his song. I read the book, taking a part of it from time to time to the privy; otherwise I would not have read it.

units.la: Faber Viennensis adhuc turpius scripsit, de quo Erasmus hos uersus fecit: Mente cares, si res agitur tibi seria: rursus Fronte cares, si sic ludis, amice Faber.
units.tr: Faber of Vienna wrote even more shamefully, and Erasmus made these verses about him: "You lack sense if the matter is serious to you; again you lack a brow, friend Faber, if you jest like this."

units.la: Sic argumentabatur: Semper habet lites alternaq; iurgia lectus: Ergo sacerdotes non debent ducere uxores. Est fallacia accidentis, uel secundum non causam, ut causam.
units.tr: He argued thus: "The bed always has quarrels and wrangling alternating; therefore priests ought not to take wives." It is a fallacy of accident, or of taking a non-cause for a cause.

units.la: Episcopus Moguntinus dixit: Lutheranos habere unum articulum, qui non possit refutari, scilicet de coniugio: sed tamen concesso hoc unico articulo, concidere totum illum pulcherrimum ordinem Ecclesiasticum.
units.tr: The Bishop of Mainz said that the Lutherans have one article which cannot be refuted, namely the one on marriage; but granted this single article, that whole most beautiful ecclesiastical order collapses.

units.la: Maximilianus dixit: Papa egregiè nos uexauit, ipse nobis concesserit tantum unam uxorem, & ipse habet tot quot uult. Putat autem licere sibi omne quod libet: quia omnia iura habet in scrinio sui pectoris.
units.tr: Maximilian said: "The Pope has harassed us outrageously. He himself granted us only one wife, yet he has as many as he wishes. He thinks it lawful for himself to do whatever he likes, because he has all the laws in the chest of his breast."

units.la: Noui quendam doctorem artis medicæ, quem multi alij quoque nouerunt. Nunc autem mortuus est: qui mihi fuit familiarissimè notus. Ille adolescens amabat uirginem, cui coniugium promisit. Parentes uerò ignari huius sponsationis, coegerunt eum ut susciperet sacerdotium. Ipse proficisci tur Constantiam, ibiq; fit subdiaconus, ut uouocant. statim deinde manifesta fit promissio uir-gini facta, aut ipsa puella patefecit. Illa res fuit inexplicabilis multis cõsistorijs, quòd ipse esset subdiaconus, & simul sponsus. Iubetur itaque proficisci Romam. Ille proficiscitur: ibi cognita re, iussus est uiginem retinere, sicut coniugium promisisset. Duxit ergo illā honestam uirginē, ex qua postea suscepit duos filios, qui similiter ambo sunt artis Medicæ doctores, mihi etiam satis noti. Sed tamen pro satisfactione ei impositum est, ut ipse non haberet ius petendæ consuetudinis coniugalis: quod quid sit, iam non ulterius declarabo. Sed seniores, qui ista intelligunt, conijcere possunt, quàm inepta & iniusta ista fuerint.
units.tr: I knew a certain doctor of medicine, whom many others also knew. He has now died, and he was very intimately known to me. That young man loved a virgin, to whom he promised marriage. But his parents, unaware of this betrothal, forced him to take up the priesthood. He set out for Constance, and there became a subdeacon, as they call it. Soon afterwards the promise made to the virgin became known, or the girl herself revealed it. That matter was baffling to many consistories, that he should be both a subdeacon and a betrothed man. He was therefore ordered to set out for Rome. He went; there, the matter having been learned, he was ordered to keep the virgin, since he had promised her marriage. So he married that honest virgin, and by her he afterwards had two sons, who are likewise both doctors of medicine, well known to me. Yet as satisfaction it was imposed on him that he should have no right to demand conjugal intercourse; what that means I will not explain further. But the elders, who understand these matters, can guess how absurd and unjust these measures were.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: A colloquy

units.la: Officialis citauerat quendam pastorem, quòd ipsi natus esset infantulus, & ei indicit multam quinque florenorum. Miser ille sacerdos primò petit sibi dari spacium. postea cum deberet afferre pecuniam, affert duas scopas. Officialis quærit, quare non pecuniam potius, quàm scopas afferret? Respondit sacerdos: Ego ideo duas scopas affero, ut tu prius una tuam domum purgares: altera deinde ego utar in uerrendis meis ædibus.
units.tr: A church official had summoned a certain minister, because a little child had been born to him, and fined him five florins. The poor priest first asked for time to be given him. Afterwards, when he ought to have brought the money, he brought two brooms. The official asked why he had brought brooms rather than money. The priest replied: "I bring two brooms so that you may first sweep out your own house with one; then I will use the other to sweep my own house."

units.la: DE ADVLTERIIS, SCORTATIONIBUS, LIBIDINIBUS, EARUMQ; POENIS.
units.tr: Of adulteries, fornications, lusts, and their punishments.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Fuit una de pulchris legibus Aegyptiacis, quòd si quis stuprasset uirginem ingenuam, excidebantur ei pudenda: si quæ uerò facta esset adultera, nasus ei præcisus est.
units.tr: One of the fine laws of the Egyptians was this: if anyone debauched a freeborn virgin, his private parts were cut off; but if a woman had become an adulteress, her nose was cut off.

units.la: Pindarus ualde laudat ciuitatem Locrensem, quòd bene fuerit constituta. In ea fuit legislator Zaleucus, ex cuius legibus multa adhuc passim citantur. Dicitur autem is inter cætera tulisse legē, ut oculi effoderentur ei, qui commisisset adulterium. Deinde cùm filius eius contra legem peccasset, pater voluit seruari eam: sed ita, ut filio oculus effoderetur unus, & sibi alter. Hæc est pulchra ἰσονομία.
units.tr: Pindar greatly praises the city of Locri for being well constituted. Its lawgiver was Zaleucus, and many of his laws are still cited here and there. He is said, among other things, to have enacted a law that the eyes of anyone who committed adultery should be gouged out. Later, when his son had broken the law, the father wished it to be kept, but in such a way that one eye was taken from the son and the other from himself. This is a fine [ἰσονομία] equality.

units.la: Athenienses fecerunt legem longe diuersam à Lacedæmoniorum, ut qui corrumperet alterius uxorem, uolentem, non coactam, afficeretur capitali supplicio: qui uerò coactam, impunè dimitteretur. Credo illa sic sanxerunt, non aliam ob causam, nisi ut atroci poena legem Lacedæmoniorum à suis auerterent: quia illi negligentiores fuerunt in puniendis adulterijs.
units.tr: The Athenians made a law quite different from that of the Lacedaemonians: whoever corrupted another man's wife, if she was willing and not forced, was to be punished with death; but if she was forced, he was to be let go unpunished. I believe they decreed this for no other reason than to turn their people away from the harsh penalty of the Lacedaemonians, since the Lacedaemonians were more lax in punishing adulteries.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Timoclea (puto fuisse Pelopidæ filiâ, ciuis Thebani) bani) interfecit unum ex capitaneis Alexandri, qui ei uim uoluit inferre, hac arte. Odio dissimulato, dixit se monstraturam illi thesauros, quos habebat: & ducens eum in hortum ad puteum, in illum præcipitauit eum. Re delata ad Alexandrum, cum audiisset eam esse filiā Pelopidæ, iussit ipsam duci in suum conspectum. nam Philippus pater Alexandri fuerat obses in urbe Thebana, apud ipsum Pelopidem. Illa uerò magnitudine animi freta, uenit in eius conspectum. Itaque absoluit eam Alexäder, & dimisit, iussitq; salvas esse omnes res, addens etiam ei custodes.
units.tr: Timoclea (I think she was the daughter of Pelopidas, a citizen of Thebes) killed one of Alexander's captains, who wanted to force himself on her, by this stratagem. Concealing her hatred, she said she would show him her treasures, and leading him into a garden to a well, she threw him headlong into it. When the matter was reported to Alexander, and he heard that she was the daughter of Pelopidas, he ordered her brought into his presence; for Philip, Alexander's father, had been a hostage in the city of Thebes, in the house of Pelopidas himself. She, however, relying on greatness of spirit, came into his sight. So Alexander acquitted and released her, ordered that all her property be kept safe, and even assigned guards to her.

units.la: Fuit nostro tempore Consaluus, præstantissimus & summus capitaneus inter omnes quos habuit Imperator, tantæ authoritatis, uirtutis & sapientiæ, ut per ipsum factus sit Imperator rex Hispanicus. Cùm enim cæteri nollent, ipse sua prudentia traxit eos, ut contra propositum suum, ipsum facerent regem. Hic cum in direptione Genuæ præteriret ædes, in quibus erant tumultus, intrauit ædes, audiuitq; matronam clamantem, cui uolebat miles quidam uim inferre: quare comperta, ipse statim sua manu confodit eum.
units.tr: In our own time there was Gonsalvo, the most distinguished and highest of all the captains that the Emperor had, of such authority, courage and wisdom that through him the Spanish king was made Emperor. For when the others were unwilling, he by his prudence drew them, against their own intention, to make him king. This man, when in the sacking of Genoa he passed by houses in which there was an uproar, entered one and heard a matron crying out, whom a certain soldier wanted to force. Discovering this, he at once ran him through with his own hand.

units.la: Alexander Farnesius, qui duxit exercitum ad Ingolstadium, ibi in honesto gynæcio turpiter se gesit. Res indicatur Imperatori, qui iussit ipsi dicere: ut statim ex castris discederet. addiditq;:
units.tr: Alexander Farnese, who led the army to Ingolstadt, behaved shamefully there in a respectable women's house. The matter was reported to the Emperor, who ordered word to be sent to him that he should leave the camp at once. And he added:

units.la: Si iam haberem istum nebulonem, statim eum mea manu confoderem. Nunquam tam atrox uox est audita à tam graui uiro, ex nostro Imperatore. Ille igitur audito hoc nūcio, statim aufugit ex castris, & redijt in Italiam.
units.tr: "If I had that scoundrel now, I would run him through with my own hand at once." Never was so fierce a word heard from so grave a man as our Emperor. So when he heard this news, the man at once fled from the camp and returned to Italy.

units.la: Audiui sapientem & excellentem uirum, summo genere natum, sed qui non modestè uiuebat, cùm perijsset ei filius incendio, dicentem: O¹ me miserum, mea peccata punit Deus in semine. Postea cùm se occultasset in aliena domo, ut illius uiri coniugem uitiaret, ipse interfectus est.
units.tr: I heard of a wise and excellent man, of high birth, but who did not live modestly. When his son perished in a fire, he said: "Oh, wretched me! God punishes my sins in my offspring." Afterwards, when he had hidden himself in another man's house in order to defile that man's wife, he himself was killed.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Pausanias dux exercitus Græcorum, ad Plateas uicit Mardonium ingenti prælio. Vnde diu non solum dux fortis & felix, uerum etiam modestus & probus est habitus. Postea uerò cùm esset Byzantij, capitaneus rapuit ciuis honesti filiā, & eam stupratam interfecit. Hoc scelere commisso, statim conspirauit cum Persis. Sed retractus ex Byzantio in patriam, nō potuit in effectum producere consilium proditionis, quo nitebatur facere pacta cum Persis, & Græciam ad Persarum imperium transferre. Nam miles quidam, qui erat intimus Pausaniæ, detulerat eum apud Ephoros. Verùm cùm ille non posset detectam à se proditionem probare, hoc egerunt, ut delator accederet ad Pausaniam in templum, in quod fugerat, rat, & starent post cortinam duo Ephori, audi-rentq; eorum colloquia. Ibi cum audiuissent proditionem, pronunciatum est de eo interficiendo. Ideoq; cum nollet exire, clausum est undique templum, ut fame periret: & mater eius Alcythea primum lapidem posuit ad claudendam ianuam. Hoc scitote esse exemplum poenæ libidinum & incontinentiæ in rebus secundis.
units.tr: Pausanias, commander of the Greek army, defeated Mardonius at Plataea in a great battle. Because of this he was for a long time considered not only a brave and fortunate general but also a modest and upright one. Later, however, when he was at Byzantium, as a captain he seized the daughter of an honest citizen, and after ravishing her he killed her. Having committed this crime, he at once conspired with the Persians. But when he was recalled from Byzantium to his homeland, he could not carry out the plan of treason on which he relied, namely to make a pact with the Persians and transfer Greece to the rule of the Persians. For a certain soldier, who was Pausanias' intimate, had informed against him before the Ephors. Since Pausanias could not prove the treason that had been revealed, they arranged that the informer should approach Pausanias in the temple into which he had fled, and that two Ephors should stand behind a curtain and listen to their conversation. When they had heard the treason there, it was pronounced that he should be put to death. And so, when he would not come out, the temple was walled up on every side so that he would die of hunger; and his mother Alcythea laid the first stone to close the door. Know that this is an example of the punishment of lusts and of incontinence in prosperity.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Hetzer, homo doctus, & etiam Anabaptista, qui uertit ex Hebraicis Bibliis quædam scripta, ut prophetam Esaiam, &c. Constantiæ capitali supplicio est affectus, non propter confessionem doctrinæ, sed propter alia perpetrata scelera. Ille insinuauit se in familiaritatem honestissimarum matronarum, cùm esset concionator, (sicut mulieres facilè decipiuntur simulatione religionis) easq; deinde stuprauit. Cùm afficeretur capitali supplicio, confessus est, se voluisse sæpius agere pœnitentiam: sed ita in vinculis diaboli retentum fuisse, ut non potuerit resipiscere, sed semper relapsum esse. Velle etiam se iam libenter mori, & iusto Dei iudicio in hac pœna obtemperare.
units.tr: Hetzer, a learned man and also an Anabaptist, who translated certain writings from the Hebrew Bible, such as the prophet Isaiah, was executed at Constance. This was not because of his confession of doctrine but because of other crimes he had committed. He insinuated himself into the intimacy of very respectable matrons, since he was a preacher (as women are easily deceived by a pretence of religion), and then he debauched them. When he was about to be executed, he confessed that he had often wished to do penance, but that he had been held so in the chains of the devil that he could not repent, but had always fallen back. He also said that he now willingly wished to die, and to submit to this punishment by the just judgment of God.

units.la: Lantgrauius Thuringiæ Albertus habuit coniugem honestissimam matronam, Friderici secūdi Imperatoris filiā: ex qua habuit duos filios, Theodoricum & Fridericum. Postea tamē nihilominus cœpit amare aliam, & non solum factus est adulter, sed etiam insidiatus est uitæ coniugis suæ, imperatoris filiæ. Vnde pacisciltur tandem cum illo mulione, qui quotidie uehebat aquā in arcem Eisanach, ut interficeret mulierem. Ille promittit, uenitq; ad custodem, & consiliariū Dominæ, narrat ei, quid promiserit. simulq; excusauit suā promissionem, dicens: Si negassem, interfecisset me. nunc uos cogitate, quid uobis sit faciendum. Ibi dominus Præfectus prætorio consuluit, ut aufugeret Domina. Ipsa aufugit, & ueniens Frācoforidiam, ibi transegit biennium in monasterio sola, & postea mortua est. Cùm uerò noctu digressura esset ex arce, clam sese per funem demisit ex fenestra non admodum alta, in subiectum scopulum, unde occultè aufugere posset. Sed antequam egre deretur ex cubiculo ualedictura infantibus, arripuit maiorem natu, & momordit genam, ita ut puer alta uoce clamaret. Ibi magister curiæ, Quid facis, inquit: putans matrem interfecturam esse infantem præ dolore. Ah, respondit mater, putas me posse discedere sine magno dolore? relinquam filio notam in gena. Sed uidete porrò in hoc exemplo, quomodo Deus puniat libidines. Postquàm adoleuissent filij, pater seditione quadam voluit eos eijcere ex Misnia: sed filij bellum gerentes contra patrem, expulerunt illum. Sic expulsus Erphordiā peruenit, ubi in summa paupertate mortuus est. Fridericus filius ille peruenit ad senectutem, & est sepultus Isenaci, cuius sepulchro inscriptum est epitaphium, cuius initium est:
units.tr: Albert, Landgrave of Thuringia, had as his wife a most honourable matron, the daughter of the Emperor Frederick II, and by her he had two sons, Theodoric and Frederick. Afterwards, nevertheless, he began to love another woman, and he not only became an adulterer but also plotted against the life of his wife, the emperor's daughter. Hence he at last made a bargain with a carter who every day carried water to the castle of Eisenach, that he should kill the lady. The carter promised, and came to the castle's guard and the lady's counsellor, and told him what he had promised; at the same time he excused his promise, saying: "If I had refused, he would have killed me. Now you consider what you ought to do." Then the lord prefect of the court advised that the lady should flee. She fled, and coming to Frankfurt, spent two years there alone in a monastery, and afterwards died. When she was about to leave the castle at night, she secretly let herself down by a rope from a window not very high, onto a rock below, from where she could escape unseen. But before she went out of the bedroom, bidding farewell to her infants, she seized the elder child and bit his cheek, so that the boy cried out loudly. Then the chamberlain said, "What are you doing?" thinking that the mother would kill the infant out of grief. "Ah," she replied, "do you think I can leave without great grief? I will leave my son a mark on his cheek." But see further in this example how God punishes lusts. After the sons had grown up, their father wanted to drive them out of Meissen in some rebellion; but the sons, waging war against their father, drove him out. Thus expelled, he came to Erfurt, where he died in the utmost poverty. Frederick, that son, lived to old age, and was buried at Isenach, and on his tomb is inscribed an epitaph, which begins:

units.la: Ecce Fridericus cultor veritatis, amicus Pacis, etc.
units.tr: Behold Frederick, lover of truth, friend of peace, etc.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Initium motus Bohemici ante annos 140. aut circiter. Quidam Abbas rapuerat sororem uiri nobilis: de qua iniuria cum cōquestus esset frater ille apud Ziskam, hic collectis amicis quibusdam fidelibus, & amatoribus iusticiæ, cum illis Abbatem oppressit & interfecit: cæteros uero monachos expulit, & prædam diuisit. Postea statim peruagatus est magnum Bohemiæ tractum. Ziska fuit capitaneus, potuitq; uictoriam moderari.
units.tr: The beginning of the Bohemian disturbance, about 140 years ago or thereabouts. A certain abbot had abducted the sister of a noble husband. When her brother complained of this injury to Žižka, the brother gathered some faithful friends who loved justice, and with them he overpowered the abbot and killed him. He drove out the other monks and divided the plunder. Afterwards he at once spread through a large part of Bohemia. Žižka was the captain, and he was able to moderate the victory.

units.la: Dicunt Constantinopoli tantam fuisse libidinum turpitudinem ante annos centum, aut plures, id est, ante captiuitatem, ut omnes homines dixerint futuram esse ingentem mutationem.
units.tr: They say that at Constantinople, about a hundred years or more before the capture, that is, before the city fell, the shamefulness of lust was so great that everyone said a great upheaval was coming.

units.la: Turci à communione rerum transeunt ad communionem mulierum. Quod quidem accidit tempore Carpocratis, qui contendit esse piam istam communionem omnium, allegans dictum: Da omni petenti te. Sed dicti sensus est: Communica iuxta legem Dei, sit æqualitas, sed ordinata iuxta legem Dei: non talis, qualem tu tibi fingis aut excogitas.
units.tr: The Turks pass from the sharing of goods to the sharing of women. This indeed happened in the time of Carpocrates, who maintained that this shared community of all things was pious, citing the saying: "Give to everyone who asks you." But the meaning of the saying is: share according to the law of God, with equality, but ordered by the law of God, not in the way you imagine or devise for yourself.

units.la: Fuerunt aliquando Persici legati in conuiuio Macer Macedonico, in quo etiam coniuges multæ interierant. Ibi cùm Persæ præberent signa obscœnitatis: Alexander adolescens abduxit uirgines, tanquam secessuras, uolētesq; sese illo secessu paululum recreare. Sed paulo post redit in conuiuiū relictis domi prioribus, & adductis adolescētibus, indutis muliebri uestitu, qui erant moniti & iussi, ut sub uestimētis cingerēt se gladijs. Itaq; cùm iterū Persæ præberent signa obscœnitatis, adolescentes interficiunt eos. Rectè fecerunt: quia permissio securitatis datur illis qui non uiolant iura hospitij: illi uerò uiolauerant.
units.tr: Once there were Persian envoys at a banquet given by Macer the Macedonian, at which many wives had also been present. There, when the Persians showed signs of obscenity, the young Alexander led the virgins away, as if they were going to withdraw, wanting to refresh themselves a little in that retreat. But soon after he returned to the banquet, having left the earlier women at home and brought young men dressed in women's clothing, who had been warned and ordered to gird swords under their garments. So when the Persians again showed signs of obscenity, the young men killed them. They acted rightly, because security is granted to those who do not violate the laws of hospitality; but the Persians had violated them.

units.la: Machometistæ habent satisfactiones: ut si quis commiserit adulterium, qui est pauper, debet uestire duos homines: si uerò sit diues, decem.
units.tr: The Mohammedans have satisfactions: if someone has committed adultery, a poor man must clothe two men, but if he is rich, ten.

units.la: Viteberge fuit homo iocosus & officiosus, ex quo postquā ancilla facta esset grauida, plecteba-tur quidē triginta aureis, sed ita, ut maiores alioqui pœnas dedisset, nisi Senatus pepercisset ei propter eius industriā. Ille uerò iocādo ad hæc dicebat: Tempore papatus, si fecissem adulteriū, potuissem me redimere duabus libris ceræ. Lex Iulia, & Attica, puniuit adulteros capite.
units.tr: Wittenberg was a jocular and obliging man. When a maidservant of his became pregnant, he was indeed punished with thirty gold coins, but in such a way that he would otherwise have received greater penalties, had the Senate not spared him on account of his diligence. He, joking about this, used to say: "In the time of the papacy, if I had committed adultery, I could have redeemed myself with two pounds of wax." The Julian and Attic laws punished adulterers with death.

units.la: Memini nobilem quendam cæpisse mœchū, & fame necasse: sed ita, ut quotidie mitteret assaturā optimā, quò odore augeret dolorem famis. Ille uerò captiuus arrosit utrosq; humeros, & uixit usq; ad nonum diem.
units.tr: I remember a certain nobleman who had captured an adulterer and starved him to death. But he did so in such a way that every day he sent the finest roast meat, so that its smell would increase the pain of hunger. The captive, however, gnawed at both his shoulders and lived until the ninth day.

units.la: Dauid fuit ad minimum quinquagenarius, cùm factus est adulter: quia quadragesimo anno peruenit ad regnum.
units.tr: David was at least fifty years old when he became an adulterer, because he came to the kingdom in his fortieth year.

units.la: Pallas à Neptuno petit, ut submergat classem Græcam. Neptunus causam interrogat, inquiens: Miror te sapientem deam, uelle tātam calamitatē Græcis euenire, quos antea defendisti. Respondit: Quia uiolauerunt templum meum. Nam Cassandra fuit struprata in templo meo, & principes hoc non puniuerunt: ego igitur puniam.
units.tr: Pallas asks Neptune to sink the Greek fleet. Neptune asks the reason, saying: "I am surprised that you, a wise goddess, wish such a calamity to befall the Greeks, whom you formerly defended." She replied: "Because they violated my temple. For Cassandra was ravished in my temple, and the leaders did not punish this; I therefore will punish them."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Carolus Gibbosus ingressus in Italiam, cæpit Neapolim. Cùm itaq; iam teneret Carolus Neapolim, duces in domo principis cuiusdam uiri uoluerunt uim inferre nobilibus matronis: illi indicaue- runt uiris, qui secesserāt in arces. Viri clam redeūt in ciuitatem, ac iusserunt matronas apparare conuiuiū. In quo cùm Galli securè potarēt, & luxuriarent cum mulieribus, interueniūt uiri armati, & præcipuos interficiunt. Deinde equitant ex urbe, abductis unà secum mulieribus.
units.tr: Charles the Hunchback, entering Italy, began to take Naples. When Charles already held Naples, some of his captains in the house of a certain prince wanted to force themselves upon the noble matrons. The women informed their husbands, who had withdrawn into the citadels. The husbands secretly returned to the city and ordered the matrons to prepare a banquet. While the French were drinking safely there and indulging in luxury with the women, armed men came in and killed the leading men. Then they rode out of the city, taking the women away with them.

units.la: Agathias scriptor dicit, quosdā honestos doctos & magni nominis uiros discessisse ex Aegypto, eo quòd uiderint magnam turpitudinē & libidines quæ ibi erant. Filij enim cōcubuerunt cum matribus, & patres cum filiabus: sicut adhuc dicūt fieri in Africa. Redeūtes illi Græci, inuenerūt in Græcia iacere cadauer insepultum: quare affecti miseratione (ut congruit humanæ naturæ) fecerunt ei sepulchrum. Idem cadauer postridie inuenerunt extra sepulchrum. Tunc oblata est eis species uel spectrum, ueniens ad unũ ex illorum numero, ac dicens: Noli humare cadauer, quod heri humasti: quia non decet ut terra subleuet eum, seu præbeat hospitium illi, qui polluit suam matrem. Ibi intelexerunt, naturam terræ abhorrere ab illa turpitudine, sicut his indicatum erat. Est narratio apud Agathium, de moribus Persicis.
units.tr: The writer Agathias says that certain honourable, learned men of great reputation departed from Egypt because they had seen the great depravity and lusts that prevailed there. For sons lay with their mothers, and fathers with their daughters, as they say still happens in Africa. Returning, those Greeks found an unburied corpse lying in Greece; moved with pity (as befits human nature) they made a tomb for it. The next day they found the same corpse outside the tomb. Then an apparition or spectre appeared to one of their number, saying: "Do not bury the corpse which you buried yesterday, because it is not fitting that the earth should lift it up or give it lodging, since it polluted its own mother." Then they understood that the nature of the earth shrinks from that filthiness, as had been shown to them. There is an account of this in Agathias, on Persian customs.

units.la: Conueniebat me quidã Comes, discipulus meus, in conuentu Augustano, cui dicebam: Certè te non amplius præ deformitate agnoui. Respondit: Ah, peccata mea sunt causa istius deformitatis. Postea uerò honestissimè uixit. nam morbus ille præbuit ei occasionem conuersionis. Habuit suam coniugem, honestissimam mulierem (ex qua etiã ipsi filij procreati sunt) & sacras Scripturas diligenter legebat: nihilominus tamen ueniũt pœnæ.
units.tr: A certain count, my pupil, used to meet me at the Diet of Augsburg, and I said to him: "Certainly I no longer recognise you because of your deformity." He replied: "Ah, my sins are the cause of this deformity." Afterwards, however, he lived most honourably, for that illness gave him the occasion of conversion. He had his wife, a most honourable woman, from whom children were also born to him, and he diligently read the holy Scriptures. Nevertheless, the punishment came.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: Collation (COLL.)

units.la: Francofordiæ ad Viadrum senex quidam uir, admodum diues, habuit coniugem iuuenculam, cum qua seruus eius habuerat consuetudinẽ. Mortuo autem domino, seruus uiduam relictam in matrimonium ducit, ac intra octennium omnes facultates atq; opes decoquit, insuperq; etiã 1400 florenos renorum nomina contrahit. Inuenerat autem in dote uiginti duo millia florenorum promptam pe-cuniam, item pagos: ita ut diceret se existimasse, hanc pecuniā sibi & nepotibus suis sufficere posse, etiamsi in magno luxu uiueret.
units.tr: At Frankfurt on the Oder there was an elderly man, very wealthy, who had a young wife with whom his servant had been carrying on an affair. When the master died, the servant married the widow, and within eight years he squandered all her property and wealth, and besides this he also took on debts of 1400 guilders in other people's names. She had brought into the marriage a dowry of twenty-two thousand guilders in ready money, as well as estates; yet he used to say that he had thought this money and these properties would suffice for him and his grandchildren even if he lived in great luxury.

units.la: Eccius sedebat Erphurdiæ in cōuiuio inter honestissimos uiros: qui cum adduxissent suas coniuges, statim cum ijs petulanter ludere cœpit, sicut erat homo impudens. Ibi una ex illis duriter eum reprehendit, inquiens: Es tu doctor? non existimo te in honesta familia, sed in lupanari educatū. Ipse uero non habuit folium fici, quo suam tegeret deformitatem: nec etiam cogitauit dictum Plauti, Seruum hominem decet habere oculos continentes, manus & linguam.
units.tr: Eck was sitting at Erfurt at a banquet among most respectable men. When they had brought in their wives, he at once began to play wantonly with them, being the shameless man he was. Then one of the women rebuked him sharply, saying: "Are you a teacher? I do not think you were brought up in a respectable household, but in a brothel." He, however, did not have a fig leaf to cover his disgrace, nor did he think of the saying of Plautus: "A servant ought to have eyes, hands and tongue under control."

units.la: Noribergæ, quidam leuis homo habebat coniugem, à qua libenter fuisset liberatus. Cùm uerò audiuisset, in renouatione doctrinæ Euangelij licere aliam ducere, propter scortationem: palàm scortabatur. quam ob causam etiam in carcerem coniectus est. Cùm uerò interrogaretur, cur id fecisset? respondit, ut uxor eius ipsum accusaret, propter scortationem, & ita contingeret, ut ab ea liberaretur. Norinbergenses rectè & bene eum puniuerunt. Ita enim cæsus est uirgis, ut elapso triduo moreretur.
units.tr: At Nuremberg a certain frivolous fellow had a wife from whom he would gladly have been freed. But when he heard that, with the renewal of the teaching of the Gospel, it was permitted to take another wife on account of fornication, he openly consorted with prostitutes, and for this reason he was thrown into prison. When he was asked why he had done this, he answered that his wife would accuse him of fornication and so it would happen that he was freed from her. The people of Nuremberg punished him rightly and well: he was beaten with rods so severely that after three days he died.

units.la: Memini, tempore Ludouici regis Galliæ Romæ factam esse dispensationem, ut frater duceret soro-rem in regno Gallico: illi tamen noluerunt con-iungi, quia natura abhorrebat, cùm Rex uellet eos coniungere.
units.tr: I remember that at the time of Louis, king of France, a dispensation was granted at Rome so that a brother might marry his sister in the kingdom of France; yet they did not want to be joined, because nature recoiled, although the king wished to unite them.

units.la: Romæ quidam Cardinalis appetiuit coniugem formosam alicuius pauperis: & promisit marito duo millia coronatorum, ut eam sibi aliquandiu concederet. Maritus accepta pecunia, dimisit uxo-rem. Postea uxor ad maritum redire noluit: dicēs, se iam alteri esse uenditam.
units.tr: At Rome a certain cardinal desired the beautiful wife of a poor man, and he promised the husband two thousand crowns so that he might let him have her for a while. The husband, having accepted the money, sent his wife away. Afterwards the wife refused to return to her husband, saying that she had now been sold to another man.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Legitur in Anatomia Vesalij, de quodam Hispa-no, qui cùm uideret de collo inhonestæ mulieris pendentes gemmas preciosissimas, uniones, sma-ragdos, & alias auro circumdatas: delectatus est illis sic, ut in cõsuetudine, quā cũ illa habebat, om-nes deuoraret. Postea uerò reiecit per inferiora.
