units.tr: We read in Vesalius's Anatomy of a certain Spaniard who, seeing precious gems hanging from the neck of a dishonest woman, pearls, emeralds and other stones set in gold, was so taken with them that, during the intercourse he had with her, he swallowed them all. Afterwards, however, he passed them out by the lower way.

units.la: Quidam dux habuit coniugem, quæ scribens binas literas, alteras ad maritum, alteras ad ama-torem, in inscriptione errauit: ita ut literæ ad a-matorem scriptæ, peruenirēt ad ipsum Ducem: & ad maritum scriptæ, amatori tradercntur. Dux ui-dens & legens has literas, statim profectus est ad coniugem, & in primo conspectu eam interfecit. Postea profectus est Romā, & absolutus à Ponti-fice, impositá ei hac satisfactione, ut conderet mo-nasterium: quod & factum est.
units.tr: A certain duke had a wife who, writing two letters, one to her husband and one to her lover, made a mistake in the addresses, so that the letter written to the lover reached the duke himself, and the one written to the husband was handed to the lover. The duke, seeing and reading these letters, set out at once for his wife and killed her at the first sight of her. Afterwards he went to Rome and, absolved by the Pope, was given this satisfaction: that he should found a monastery. This was also done.

units.la: Dicunt Vincentiam hoc modo uenisse in Venetorum potestatem : quia Vincentiæ dominus iussit ad se adduci ciuis cuiusdam filiam, quam pater ei mittere noluit. Abducta igitur est ui, & post aliquot dies remissa patri dissecta in calatho. Pater re deliberata cum amicis quibusdam & senatoribus, mittit cadauer, ut erat dissectum, senatui Veneto, eiq; pollicetur deditionem urbis. Ita tyrannus oppressus & expulsus est.
units.tr: They say that Vicenza came under the power of the Venetians in this way. The lord of Vicenza ordered the daughter of a certain citizen to be brought to him, and the father refused to send her. So she was taken away by force and, after some days, was returned to her father, cut up in a basket. The father, having deliberated with some friends and senators, sent the corpse, just as it had been cut up, to the Venetian senate, and promised the surrender of the city. Thus the tyrant was overthrown and expelled.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Ante paucos annos, miser homo compressit suã filiam. Mater uolens ocultare infamiam filiæ, interfecit puerum. Re autem patefacta, sumptum est supplicium de illis tribus personis.
units.tr: A few years ago a wretched man raped his own daughter. The mother, wishing to hide her daughter's disgrace, killed the boy. When the affair came to light, punishment was taken on all three persons.

units.la: Pastor quidam erat in oppido Vueiden, nobis omnibus, præsertim seniorib. notus. is habebat cõiugem honestã, & filiolũ, quẽ mihi moriturus commendauit. cûmq; haberet cõsuetudinem cum multis alijs, tandẽ etiam suam ancillã cõpressit. Translatus postea in aliũ pagũ, non procul à Salseld, ibi est cõatus in cãpo quandã grauidã cõprimere: illa euasit tamen, ac cõquesta est marito & fratri suo hoc facinus. Pastor uerò hac de re cõuictus, fugit ad episcopũ Mersburgẽsem, eo tẽpore ibi uersantẽ. Factus est igitur papista, relicta coniuge. Postea post biennĩ equitat per illũ pagũ, quia Deus trahebat illũ ad suppliciũ. Ibi cùm uidet illũ equitantem frater illius mulieris: Ah tu nebulo, inquit, re-ste iam te prehēdo. Tantáne est tua audacia, ut au-deas adhuc trāsire hunc pagum? & apprehenso equi freno, ipsum capit, ac sic statim eum abducit ad arcè Calēsem. Nos eramus tūc Ienæ, tēpore pestis.
units.tr: There was a certain pastor in the town of Vueiden, known to all of us, especially to the elders. He had a respectable wife and a little son, whom he commended to me when he was dying. Since he had a habit of this with many others, he finally also raped his maid. Later he was transferred to another village, not far from Salseld, and there he tried to rape a pregnant woman in the field. She escaped, however, and complained of this crime to her husband and her brother. The pastor, convicted of this matter, fled to the bishop of Merseburg, who was then staying there. So he became a Papist, leaving his wife behind. Two years later he rode through that village, because God was drawing him to punishment. When the woman's brother saw him riding there, he said: "Ah, you rascal, now I have you by the reins! Is your audacity so great that you still dare to pass through this village?" And seizing the horse's bridle, he took him and at once led him away to the castle at Calesem. We were then at Jena, at the time of the plague.

units.la: Eodem tempore & alius quidam Anabaptista erat coniectus in carcerem, propter quem oportuit me quoq; accedere. Cùm igitur huius occasione eò uenissemus, ibi ille scortator exēptus ex carcere, deplorauit suam calamitatem, ac petiuit ut pro eo intercederemus. Intercessimus: sed Princeps, ut erat pius & honestus, noluit ueniam concedere. Itaq; statim est de eo suppliciū capitis sumptum. Erat homo ingeniosus, & satis doctus & industrius. Erat etiam ille, qui primus mihi aduersatus est in uisitatione seu inspectione Ecclesiarum. Stabat iste nebulo, & uociferabatur de necessitate operum: Oportere ista opera ita fieri, cum ipse esset magnus scortator. Erat apud ipsum Antonius Musa, qui eum consolabatur & absoluebat, ad quē dixit: Domine Antoni, ago tibi gratias, quòd me reduxisti ex hac dubitatione ad emendationem vitæ. In primis autem Deo gratias ago, quòd redij ad pœnitentiam. Confessus etiam tunc est, quòd ancillæ admouisset cultrum ad iugulum, ut eam comprimeret. Quare nō immeritò tandem secuta est pœna. Non debetis dubitare, quin tanta scelera cerra certæ pœnæ sequantur. Possem consumere integrum annum commemoratione talium exemplorum. Possem uobis etiam commemorare multas historias, non tantum quas legi, sed etiam quæ mihi experientia sunt notæ, & ipsemet uidi. Ideo timeamus Deum, & nos ab ipso regi petamus.
units.tr: At the same time another Anabaptist was thrown into prison, and on his account I too had to go there. When we had come on this business, that whoremonger, taken out of prison, lamented his calamity and asked us to intercede for him. We interceded, but the Prince, being pious and upright, refused to grant pardon. So capital punishment was at once carried out on him. He was a clever man, fairly learned and industrious. He was also the one who first opposed me during the visitation or inspection of the churches. That rascal stood up and clamoured about the necessity of works, saying that these works had to be done in this way, although he himself was a great whoremonger. Antonius Musa was with him, who consoled and absolved him, and to whom he said: "Master Antony, I thank you that you have led me back from this doubt to an amendment of life. Above all, I thank God that I have returned to repentance." He also confessed then that he had put a knife to the maid's throat in order to rape her. So it was not undeservedly that punishment at last followed. You must not doubt that such great crimes are surely followed by certain punishment. I could spend a whole year recalling such examples. I could also tell you many stories, not only those I have read but also those known to me from experience, and that I saw myself. Therefore let us fear God and ask him to rule us.

units.la: Mandatum de castitate seuerissimum est, ut eui denter probant horribiles pœnæ in genere humano. Nō est quòd dubitetis de eo: Scriptura dicit expressè: Omnis anima quæ fecerit has abominationes, eradicabitur. Dicit, Omnis anima: significãs tam reges & principes, quàm infimo loco natos. Ideo considerate familias potentum: quantumuis potentes multum sibi licentiæ permittunt, tamen apud eos uidetis etiam sequi tristissimas calamitates. Inspicite familiam quandam, quæ uobis nota est. Cogitate, quales sint libidinum confusiones in potentibus familijs? quales fuerint? quæ secutæ sint pœnæ? & quæ sequantur aut impendeant? Quia τὰ βασιλέων παθήματα πάντες ἴσασι, inquit Euripides: id est, Regum calamitates omnes norunt. Hæc non dico in cuiusquam contumeliam, sed dico confirmationis & exempli causa. Possem commemorare multa, quæ memini. Vlmæ quidam honestus uir habebat coniugem mœcham, quam cùm accusaret apud familiā, familia ægrè ferebat ipsam fieri infamem. Cùm igitur uideret eam à familia non corrigi, ipse, sicut uir magnanimus, cogitabat quid sibi esset faciendum. Simulabat se profecturū ad mercatū Francofordiensem in ipso die festi Ma-riæ, quo die ibi magnum est festum. Discedit eques suo more, sed equo in proximo pago relicto clam domum redit, cùm alij essent in templo, & oc-cultat se sub scalis. Ibi latuit toto die armatus, à meridie usq; ad uesperam. Ancillæ magnificè coe-perunt apparare cænā: mœchus circa sextam uel septimam horam noctis, cum essent tenebræ, accesf sit. Maritus interea sub scalis latitans, omnia per-tulit: sed dixit, se uix potuisse continere, quò minus ipsum ingredientem, & ascendentem gradus do-mus, interficeret. Sed cogitans se non potuisse tue-ri illud facinus legibus, & quòd fuisset accusatus tanquā homicidia: concedit illis tempus cœnandi, & cubitū eundi. Cùm esset media nox, & cùm pu-taret eos esse sopitos, tūc ipse gradus ascendit. In-terea mulier audiēs strepitum, perterrefacta est, surgitq; & aperit cubiculum, circumspectās num aliquem uideat. Sed ille ita se occultauerat post fo-nacē, ne uideri ab illa posset. Cùm igitur uxor rur-sus ingreditur cubiculū, ibi mox eam maritus se-quitur, quia aliàs nō potuisset ingredi cubiculum: Ecce, inquit, toties accusaui te, & tu negasti: iā ego deprehēdo uos simul. Interea mœchus surgit de le-cto, & arripiēs gladium, parat se ad defensionem.
units.tr: The command concerning chastity is most severe, as the horrible punishments among the human race clearly prove. There is no reason for you to doubt it: Scripture says expressly: "Every soul that commits these abominations shall be cut off." It says "every soul," meaning kings and princes no less than those born in the lowest place. So consider the households of the powerful. However powerful they are, and however much licence they allow themselves, you see that the saddest calamities follow among them too. Look at a certain family that is known to you. Consider what confusions of lust there are in powerful households, what there have been, what punishments have followed, and what follow or hang over them. For "all know the sufferings of kings" [τὰ βασιλέων παθήματα πάντες ἴσασι], as Euripides says; that is, all know the calamities of kings. I say these things not to insult anyone, but for confirmation and as an example. I could recall many things that I remember. A certain honest man of Ulm had an adulterous wife. When he accused her before the household, the household took it badly that she was made infamous. Seeing that she was not corrected by the household, he himself, like a magnanimous man, considered what was to be done. He pretended that he would go to the Frankfurt fair on the very day of the feast of Mary, when there is a great festival there. He departed on horseback as usual, but leaving his horse in the nearest village, he secretly returned home while the others were in church, and hid himself under the stairs. There he lay hidden all day, armed, from midday until evening. The maids began to prepare a lavish dinner. The adulterer came about the sixth or seventh hour of the night, when it was dark. Meanwhile the husband, lurking under the stairs, saw everything, but said he could hardly restrain himself from killing the man as he entered and climbed the steps of the house. But thinking that he could not defend such a deed by the laws, and that he would be accused of homicide, he allowed them time to dine and go to bed. When it was midnight, and he thought they were asleep, he climbed the stairs. Meanwhile the woman, hearing the noise, was terrified, rose and opened the bedroom door, looking round to see whether she could see anyone. But he had hidden himself so well behind the stove that she could not see him. When the wife went back into the bedroom, the husband immediately followed her, since otherwise he could not have entered the room: "Look," he said, "I have accused you so often, and you denied it; now I catch you both together." Meanwhile the adulterer got up from the bed, and seizing a sword, prepared himself to defend himself.

units.la: Maritus cõtrà strictò ense ipsum inuadit. Mulier intẽta uoce exclamàs, uocat ministrũ, ut eis opitu-letur. Sed tota familia sic erat somno sopita, ut nul-lus hominum ueniret. Maritus itaque (Deo ad-iuuante) primùm ipsum adulterum affigit parie-ti, & confodit. postea ipsam aggreditur, dicens: Tu belua, ego coactus sum tam diu ista ferre: nũc te comprehendo: iam quoq; de te sumã supplicium. Ah, inquit illa, concedas mihi tantum spacij, ut a-gam pœnitentiã, & sumã sacramentũ. Non faciã, inquit. Satis est, si dolcs pro perpetratis facinori-bus, ac sic moriaris. Atq; ita illam quoq; intersecit. Postero die iuit ad Senatũ, & dixit se hoc fecisse. Non potuit eũ Senatus reprehendere, nec habuit ius: quia cõceditur iure ciuili, occidere mœchum. Est uera historia, facta non ante multos annos. Memini hanc historiam, & soleo mecum tales considerare. Possem etiam uobis ualde multas si-miles recitare.
units.tr: The husband attacked him in return with his sword drawn. The woman, crying out with a loud voice, called the servants to help them. But the whole household was so sunk in sleep that no one came. So the husband, God helping him, first drove the adulterer against the wall and ran him through. Afterwards he attacked her, saying: "You beast, I have been forced to bear this for so long; now I seize you, and now I will take punishment on you too." "Ah," she said, "grant me only enough time that I may do penance and receive the sacrament." "I will not," he said. "It is enough that you suffer for the crimes you have committed, and so die." And so he killed her too. The next day he went to the Senate and said that he had done this. The Senate could not rebuke him, nor had it any right to, because by civil law it is permitted to kill an adulterer. It is a true story, which happened not many years ago. I remember this story, and I am accustomed to consider such things with myself. I could also recite for you very many similar ones.

units.la: In bello Mediolanensi Gallus quidam, hospes honesti uiri nobilis, cœpit cum uxore eius liberius colludere, & alia inhonesta flagitare. Mulier hæc indicat marito, inquiens: Ego instruã conuiuium, & dabo illi soporiferum: tu uide, ut fortiter illum interficias. Sic illa res processit. Non est disputatio de iure. Illa mulier honestè fecit, & uir generosè & fortiter istum occidit.
units.tr: In the war of Milan a certain Frenchman, a guest of an honourable nobleman, began to make free with his wife and to demand other dishonourable things. The woman told her husband, saying: "I will prepare a banquet and give him a sleeping draught; you see that you kill him boldly." And so the affair went forward. There is no question of right here. The woman acted honourably, and the husband nobly and bravely killed him.

units.la: Tragicus casus punitæ libidinis.
units.tr: A tragic case of lust punished.

units.la: Nepos Pontificis, Cardinalis, habuit consuetudinem cum mediocris ciuis coniuge, qui permittebat illam turpem consuetudinem. Quod facinus ubi resciuit illius mariti frater, grauiter eum accusauit, quòd ita dedecoraret familiam suam. Sed is, quantum potuit, se excusauit. Quomodo autem uterq; punitus sit, breuiter exponā. Cardinalis mittit nuncium eò, & mandat instrui conuiuium: se enim ista nocte uenturum esse. Mulier exequitur mandatum. Sed Cardinalis mirabiliter impeditur, ne illa nocte aduenire posset. Cùm igitur in multā noctem eius aduentum diu expectassent, tandem maritus dixit ad coniugem: Agè eamus unà in cubiculum, quod instructum est Cardinali. Vxor assentitur. Dum simul cubant, mariti frater, qui clā latebat in ædibus, irrumpit in cubiculum, & accedens imprudentius ad lectum, fratrem unà cum coniuge transfodit. Manè cùm cognouisset errorem, antequam in exilium iret, curat per quendam sacerdotem, etiam Cardinalem ueneno extingui. Sic Deus horribiliter libidines puniuit.
units.tr: A nephew of a Pope, a Cardinal, had an affair with the wife of a middling citizen, and the husband allowed this shameful relationship. When the husband's brother learned of this crime, he sharply accused him of disgracing his family in this way. But he excused himself as far as he could. I will briefly set out how each of them was punished. The Cardinal sent a messenger there and ordered a banquet to be prepared, since he would come that night. The woman carried out the order. But the Cardinal was wonderfully prevented from coming that night. When they had waited a long time into the night for his arrival, at last the husband said to his wife: "Come, let us go together into the bedroom, which has been prepared for the Cardinal." The wife agreed. While they lay together, the husband's brother, who had been secretly hiding in the house, burst into the bedroom and, approaching the bed too rashly, ran through his brother together with the wife. In the morning, when he realised his mistake, before he could go into exile he arranged through a certain priest for the Cardinal too to be killed with poison. Thus God horribly punished lusts.

units.la: Noui Comitem, ingeniosum uirum, & Imperatori Maximiliano præ cæteris principibus, propter industriam ualde gratum, qui male regebat uitam suam (erat enim suprà modum libidinosus) cùm cum tamen esset in alijs rebus satis circumspectus. Tandem fuit interfectus à suo scriniario, hac occasione. Cùm aliquādo Comes scriniarium cum literis alìo ablegaret, ille intellexit se ablegari propter uxorem. Quapropter manens domi, se occultabat. Sic postea ex improuiso adortus est Comitem, eumq; interfecit.
units.tr: I knew a count, a clever man, and very dear to Emperor Maximilian above other princes on account of his diligence, who managed his life badly (for he was beyond measure lustful), although in other matters he was quite circumspect. At last he was killed by his secretary, on this occasion. When once the count sent the secretary elsewhere with letters, the man understood that he was being sent away because of his wife. Therefore he stayed at home and hid himself. Afterwards he attacked the count unexpectedly and killed him.

units.la: Cato melancholicus habebat pulchram coniugem, quæ placuit Hortensio, homini docto & elegāti. Petiuit ut Cato sibi eā cederet. Cato putauit esse grauitatem, ut amico petenti uxorem gratificaretur. Ita eam concesìt Hortensio. Mortuo uerò Hortensio, rursum eam ad se recipit.
units.tr: Cato the melancholic had a beautiful wife, who pleased Hortensius, a learned and elegant man. He asked Cato to yield her to him. Cato thought it dignified to gratify a friend who asked for his wife. So he gave her up to Hortensius. But when Hortensius died, he took her back to himself again.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Monetarius, cum esset Cygneæ, uenit ad puellam quandam, dicens, se diuina uoce ad eam missum esse, ut cum ea haberet consuetudinem: quod nisi fieret, non posse uerbum Dei prædicari. Hæc pastori illius loci illa puella confessa est, in periculo mortis.
units.tr: A moneyer, while he was at Cygnea, came to a certain girl, saying that he had been sent to her by a divine voice, so that he might have intercourse with her; unless this happened, the word of God could not be preached. In peril of death, this girl confessed it to the minister of that place.

units.la: Cùm essemus Ratisbonæ, fortè Stigelius uespe-ri rediturus in hospitium nostrum, incidit in Hi-spanum, ducentem alicuius ciuis coniugē. Illa cùm uidet obuiam uenire hominē Germanum, inquit: Iuues me, ille abducit me repugnantem, & nolentem. Ibi Sigelius statim adoritur Hispanum, sicut est fortis & animosus uir, & apprehendit ipsius glagladium, ne cũ stringere posset. Age, inquit, quare abducis alterius coniugem? Auditis illis, statim eam dimisit. Stigelius deinde interrogat eam, quae esset eius domus? Ibi ipsa, et alij ciues præsentes monstrant locum, ad quem etiam ipsam deducũt. Stigelius reuersus ad nos, totā historiam cōmemorauit.
units.tr: When we were at Regensburg, it happened that Stigelius, about to return to our lodging in the evening, came upon a Spaniard leading the wife of some citizen. When she saw a German coming towards her, she said: "Help me! He is dragging me away against my will." Stigelius at once attacked the Spaniard, as he is a brave and spirited man, and seized the Spaniard's sword, so that he could not draw it. "Come now," he said, "why are you leading away another man's wife?" Having heard this, the Spaniard immediately let her go. Stigelius then asked her which was her house. Then she herself and other citizens present pointed out the place, to which they also led her. Stigelius, returning to us, related the whole story.

units.la: Στρατήγημα, quo honesta & pudica uirgo suam pudiciciam tutata est.
units.tr: A stratagem [Στρατήγημα] by which a chaste and modest maiden protected her chastity.

units.la: Quidam dominus admodum libidinosus, cum aliquando in Burgundia iter faceret, à ministris seu curatoribus hospitij, qui eius animum norant, ductus est in quoddā hospitium, in quo erat uirgo præstantissima forma. Cumq; parentes metuerent pudicitiæ ipsius, cogitauerunt eam, antequam dominus ad hospitium ueniret, ad aliquem ex amicis ablegare, ut ibi interea delitesceret. Filia cum esset rogata à parentibus, ut suæ pudicitiæ rationem haberet, & ad aliquē amicorū se conferret, negauit se hoc facturam. ac iussit parentes bono animo esse: se enim fore suæ pudicitiæ custodem. Interea dum Dominus aduenit, ornat se uirgo, ac uenienti obuiam procedit, & blandissimis uerbis excipit.
units.tr: A certain lord, very lustful, once when travelling in Burgundy, was led by the stewards or managers of the inn, who knew his disposition, into a certain lodging in which there was a maiden of outstanding beauty. Since her parents feared for her chastity, they planned, before the lord came to the lodging, to send her away to a friend, so that she might hide there in the meantime. When the parents asked the daughter to look to her chastity and betake herself to one of their friends, she refused to do this and told her parents to be of good cheer, for she herself would be the guardian of her chastity. Meanwhile, when the lord arrived, the maiden adorned herself, went out to meet him as he came, and received him with the most flattering words.

units.la: Dominus, primo aspectu puellæ commotus, statim iussit sibi cubiculum monstrari. Cumq; uirgo cum duxisset in cubiculum, continuò, ut erat peronatus, irruit in eam, ac uoluit eam comprimere. Puella non admodum reluctata, petiit ut prius dimitterentur ministri, ne essent spectatores. Dominus iussit statim omnes discedere. Ibi cum puella esset sola, rogat principem, ut permittat sibi prius detrahi perones. Dominus assentitur, ac porrigit utrumq; pedem. Cum itaq; puella utramq; ocream dimidiā detraxisset, reliquit eum, & fugit per ianuam paruam, ducente ad plateas in altero latere ædium. Dominus, qui erat implicitus ocreis, nō potuit eam sequi. Puella statim depositis omnibus ornamentis, ac sumptis uilibus uestibus, quas prædisposuerat, per posticum clam omnibus aufugit, & apud ciuem quendam latitat, sed nec parentes sciebant quò aufugisset. Postero die, cùm non inueniretur filia, & parentes inciperent metuere, ne quid grauius filia in se perpetrasset: coepit & dominus nonnihil de uita uirginis esse solicitus. & uocatis parentibus, iussit diligenter filiam inquiri: promisitq; bona fide, filiæ nihil à se periculi fore, nec amplius de pudicitia eam apud se periclitaturam. Insuper etiam dotem amplam pollicetur. Nam quantum ad se attineret, se uoluisse eam stuprare, & propterea ei dotem debere. Constituit igitur ei pro dote quatuor millia coronatorum. ac parentes adhortatur, ut quoniam iam nubilis esset puella, statim de aliquo cogitarent, cui eam in matrimonium collocarent. Hæc domini uirtus & liberalitas cùm esset euul-gata, puella rursus prodijt. Cumq; ad ædes paternas parentum iussu redijsset, procidit ante faciem Principis, ac ueniam deprecata est. Dominus humaniter ei respondit, ac dotis loco quatuor millia coronatorum dedit. Statim autem adolescens adductus est, qui eam amare credebatur: cui uirgo desponsata est. & post aliquot dies, præsente illo Domino, nuptiæ cum magna lætitia ipsius & amicorum sunt celebratæ.
units.tr: The lord, moved by the first sight of the girl, at once ordered a bedroom to be shown to him. And when the maiden had led him into the bedroom, he immediately rushed at her, still wearing his riding boots, and tried to force himself upon her. The girl, not struggling much, asked that the attendants be dismissed first, so that they would not be spectators. The lord at once ordered everyone to leave. When the girl was alone with him, she asked the prince to allow her first to pull off his boots. The lord agreed and held out both feet. So when the girl had drawn off half of each boot, she left him and fled through a small door, which led to the streets on the other side of the house. The lord, who was entangled in his boots, could not follow her. The girl at once laid aside all her ornaments, took plain clothes which she had prepared beforehand, and slipped away secretly by the back door, unseen by everyone, and hid at a certain citizen's house; but not even her parents knew where she had fled. On the next day, when the daughter was not found and the parents began to fear that she had done something more serious to herself, the lord too began to be somewhat anxious about the girl's life. Calling the parents, he ordered that the daughter be carefully sought, and promised in good faith that she would come to no harm from him, nor would she again be put at risk to her chastity in his presence. Moreover, he even offered a generous dowry, for as far as he was concerned, he had wished to ravish her, and therefore he owed her a dowry. So he fixed four thousand crowns as her dowry, and urged the parents that, since the girl was now of marriageable age, they should at once think of someone to whom they might marry her. When this virtue and generosity of the lord had been made known, the girl came out again. When she had returned to her parents' house at their command, she fell before the prince's face and begged pardon. The lord answered her kindly and gave her four thousand crowns in place of a dowry. Straightaway a young man was brought in who was believed to love her, and the maiden was betrothed to him. And after some days, with that lord present, the wedding was celebrated with great joy for him and for their friends.

units.la: DE DIVORTIIS.
units.tr: ON DIVORCES.

units.la: Eusebius allegat exemplum ex historia Iustini, qui narrat cuidam matronæ sic consultum esse, ut quoniam maritus crudelis & sceleratus, turpissimè etiam uixerat, peteret diuortium. Et credo magnam seueritatem Ecclesiæ fuisse in ea re. Tale exemplum est et Fabiolæ, quæ nobilis & honesta matrona Romana discessit à uiro mœcho, nupsitq; alteri:id fecit Romanis legibus. Quanquam reprehensa est, tamen Hieronymus defendit, & eam excusat.
units.tr: Eusebius cites an example from the history of Justin, who relates that a certain matron was advised that, since her husband was cruel and wicked and had also lived most shamefully, she should seek a divorce. I believe there was great strictness of the Church in that matter. Fabiola, a noble and respectable Roman matron, provides a similar example: she left her adulterous husband and married another. She did this under Roman law. Although she was criticised for it, Jerome nevertheless defended her and excused her.

units.la: Huc quoq; referri potest exemplum Catonis, qui in amici gratiam fecit diuortium, eiq; coniugē suam credidit, quam mortuo eo recepit. Vide plura in præcedenti loco, de Libidinibus.
units.tr: Here may also be referred the example of Cato, who for the sake of a friend arranged a divorce, and entrusted his wife to him; after his death, he took her back again. See more in the preceding place, on Lusts.

units.la: Alcibiades habuit formosissimam & honestissimam mulierem Atticam, quæ petiuit diuortium. Ille uero cum uenisset in forum, comitatus coetu adolescentium, & grege suorum potatorum, amplectitur eam, ac rursus domum reducit. Sic iocatur, fuit hilaris, & ipsa mansit apud eum. Ita mundus turpiter iocatur, & deridet coniugia. Unde turpes sequuntur etiam euentus.
units.tr: Alcibiades had a most beautiful and virtuous Athenian wife, who sought a divorce. But when he came into the forum, accompanied by a crowd of young men and a throng of his drinking companions, he embraced her and led her back home again. He made a joke of it, was cheerful, and she remained with him. So the world shamefully jests and mocks marriages. From this there follow shameful outcomes as well.

units.la: DE AMORIBUS.
units.tr: ON LOVE.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: In Achaia est statua Iunonis, quæ tenet in una manu malum granatum fissum. ad quam statuā adolat cuculus: quia Iupiter fingitur se convertisse in cuculum, quando appetiuit Iunonem. Est phantasia, excogitata à quodam, uolente depingere amorem: quia omnis amator est cuculus.
units.tr: In Achaia there is a statue of Juno holding a split pomegranate in one hand. A cuckoo is sacrificed before this statue, because Jupiter is said to have changed himself into a cuckoo when he approached Juno. It is a fiction devised by someone who wanted to depict love, since every lover is a cuckoo.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Pindarus: Occultæ sunt claues persuasionis amorum in diis & hominibus, uerecundia tenente, palàm attingere puellas: id est, ex occulta causa.
units.tr: Pindar: The keys to the persuasion of loves, among gods and men, are hidden, since shame holds back from touching girls openly; that is, the cause is hidden.

units.la: Catullus: Odi & amo: quare hoc faciam, fortasse quæris. Nescio, sed fieri hoc sentio, & excrucior.
units.tr: Catullus: I hate and I love. Perhaps you ask why I do this. I do not know, but I feel that it happens and I am tormented by it.

units.la: Propertius:
units.tr: Propertius:

units.la: Quid quæris? Quare, non habet ullus amor.
units.tr: What do you ask? Why? Love has no reason.

units.la: Fuerunt pulchriores uxores in Iudæa, quàm Bersabæa: & tamen Dauid illius accenditur amore.
units.tr: There were more beautiful wives in Judea than Bathsheba, and yet David was inflamed with love for her.

units.la: Ita amor plerunq; tam uulgaria quàm elegantiora prosequitur, iuxta usitatum uersiculum:
units.tr: So love commonly pursues things that are vulgar as well as things that are more refined, according to the common little verse:

units.la: Si quis amat ranam, ranam putat esse Dianam.
units.tr: If someone loves a frog, he thinks the frog is Diana.

units.la: Unde Cicero inquit: Sine unumquemq; sibi scribere: Suum cuiq; pulchrum: suam quisq; sponsam amat.
units.tr: Hence Cicero says: Let each man write for himself: each man thinks his own love beautiful, each man loves his own sweetheart.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Romani admodum appetiuerunt Atticas mulieres, quia hæ fuerunt admodū formosæ, nobiles, eruditæ & medicæ.
units.tr: The Romans greatly desired Attic women, because these were very beautiful, noble, learned and skilled in medicine.

units.la: Musæ cecinerunt Thebis in nuptijs Cadmi: ὅτι καλὸν φίλον ἐστι, ναὶ δ καλὸν δ φίλον ἐστί. Causam esse credo naturalem sympathiam consensus stellarum.
units.tr: The Muses sang at the wedding of Cadmus in Thebes: "What is beautiful is dear, yes, and what is dear is beautiful" [ὅτι καλὸν φίλον ἐστι, ναὶ δ καλὸν δ φίλον ἐστί]. I believe the cause is a natural sympathy, arising from the agreement of the stars.

units.la: Gallus amat celerē pede non remorāte puellā, Quæ levis est certis, ac magis apta modis.
units.tr: The Gaul loves the girl who runs swiftly on her feet and does not linger, who is light for certain things and better suited to particular measures.

units.la: Hispano magis illa placet, cui forma benigna est, Cui Venus ex oculis semper amica ridet.
units.tr: The Spaniard is more pleased by her whose face is kindly, on whom Venus always smiles favourably from her eyes.

units.la: At Italus timidæ lætatur amore puellæ, Dulcia quæ Veneris prælia sæpe fugit.
units.tr: But the Italian rejoices in the love of a timid girl, who often flees the sweet battles of Venus.

units.la: Virgo sed audaci quæ provocat ore magistrum, Illa est Germano dulcis amica viro.
units.tr: But the maiden who challenges her master with a bold face, she is the sweet mistress of the German man.

units.la: Menander.
units.tr: Menander.

units.la: Ἰάλεμος, ἔρως ἄνευ τολμῆς.
units.tr: Ialemos, love without daring [Ἰάλεμος, ἔρως ἄνευ τολμῆς].

units.la: Amor sine audacia, est carmē lugubre.
units.tr: Love without boldness is a mournful song.

units.la: Capnio dicebat: Quando senex vult amare, & ducere uxorē, debet accipere longam furcā, & suspendere de ea crumenas plenas auro, & porrigere per fenestrā amicæ, videreq; num velit aperire, & inspicere quid in ijs contineatur.
units.tr: Capnio used to say: When an old man wants to love and take a wife, he should take a long fork, hang from it purses full of gold, and hold them out through the window to his beloved, and see whether she is willing to open them and look at what they contain.

units.la: Moguntiæ quidam amauit puellã, & impetrauit ut ad eam admitteretur. Asinus ille astãs puellæ, deliberare incipit, dicês: Si attigero te, nascetur puer, quē postea magnis sumptib. enutrire cogar. Respondet illa: Tu fatue, ego te illo honore uolui afficere, ut cognosceres meam erga te beneuolentiam, & tu cupis me dehonestare? Et sic ipsum per gradus præcipitauit, & ex domo expulit.
units.tr: At Mainz a certain man loved a girl and obtained permission to be admitted to her. That donkey, standing before the girl, began to deliberate, saying: "If I touch you, a boy will be born, whom I will then be forced to bring up at great expense." She answered: "You fool, I wanted to honour you so that you would recognise my goodwill towards you, and you desire to dishonour me?" And so she threw him down the stairs step by step and expelled him from the house.

units.la: Doctoris Martini Lutheri de ducendis choreis iudicium.
units.tr: The judgment of Doctor Martin Luther on the leading of dances.

units.la: Chorcæ sunt institutæ & concessæ, ut ciuilitas discatur in frequētia, & discāt adolescentes uenerari femineum sexũ, atq; cōtrahatur amicicia inter adolescentes & puellas honestas, quo postea certius eas ambire possint. Papa dānauit choreas, quia aduersarius fuit nuptijs legitimis. Ideo simul ad nuptias inuitantur etiam honestæ aliquæ matronæ, & uiri qui sunt spectatores, ut omnia modestè fiant. Sed unum est quod mihi in ducēdis choreis displiceat, & uelim id publicè à magistratu prohiberi, ne adolescentes in gyros ducerent puellas, præsertim in publico multis spectantibus.
units.tr: Dances were instituted and permitted so that courtesy might be learned in company, so that young people might learn to respect the female sex, and so that friendship might be formed between young men and respectable girls, by which they might later be able to court them more surely. The Pope condemned dances, because he was opposed to lawful marriages. Therefore respectable matrons and men who are spectators are invited to weddings at the same time, so that everything may be done modestly. But there is one thing about leading dances that displeases me, and I would like the magistrate to prohibit it publicly: that young men should not lead girls in circles, especially in public, with many looking on.

units.la: DE VESTITV, ET MODESTIA in incessu.
units.tr: ON CLOTHING AND MODESTY in bearing.

units.la: Non est de nihilo dictum: Mulier quando uestem deponit, pudorē etiam deponit. quanto magis uir uestem deponens, pudorem simul deponit.
units.tr: It is not said for nothing: when a woman lays aside her clothing, she also lays aside her modesty. How much more, when a man lays aside his clothing, does he at the same time lay aside his modesty.

units.la: Versus Ennij, quem citat Cicero:
units.tr: A verse of Ennius, which Cicero cites:

units.la: Flagitij principium est, nudare corpora inter ciues.
units.tr: It is the beginning of disgrace to bare the bodies among citizens.

units.la: Habui quendam discipulum, qui iam est doctor Iuris, & consiliarius eiusdē Ducis: tum uerò erat pugil. Hic cùm esset reuocatus à patre domum, uenit ad me dicens: Domine præceptor, da mihi pecuniam. Ego itaq; interrogabam: Quid uis pecuniâ facere? Respondit: Curaui mihi caligas, quia non audeo prodire in conspectum patris bisce caligis. Ad hoc ego nonnihil iratus intuli: Quis malus genius tibi illum præposterum & serum pudorem iniecit? Quare antea non es ueritus meos oculos, qui non minus offenduntur?
units.tr: I once had a pupil, who is now a doctor of law and counsellor to the same duke; at that time he was a boxer. When he had been recalled home by his father, he came to me and said: "Master, give me money." So I asked: "What do you want the money for?" He replied: "I have had some hose made, because I do not dare to appear before my father in these breeches." At this I was somewhat angry and said: "What evil spirit has put into you this back-to-front and belated modesty? Why did you not earlier respect my eyes, which are offended no less?"

units.la: Audiui à doctore Iuris de Duce Eberhardo Vuir tembergensi, pio principe. Venit in conspectum eius quidam scholasticus, indutus longa ueste, quem uiderat Princeps aperta tunica habere caligas dissectas. Cùm itaq; hic peteret sacerdotium aliquod, nec quicquâ aut certè parũ Latinè loqui posset, dixit ei princeps: Ira uade, ira uade. quasi diceret: Ego sum iratus tibi, propter uestem, non ad sacerdotium conuenientem: uade, ne tibi aliquid deteriùs accidat.
units.tr: I heard from a doctor of law about Duke Eberhard of Württemberg, a pious prince. A certain scholar came into his presence wearing a long gown, though the prince had seen that under an open tunic he had slashed breeches. Since he was seeking some priesthood, and could speak no Latin, or at least very little, the prince said to him: "Go away in anger, go away in anger," as if to say: "I am angry with you because of your clothing, which does not suit the priesthood; go, lest something worse happen to you."

units.la: Honestissimus dux Saxoniæ Vuilhelmus habuit nobilem apud se, sic uestitum ut nunc est moris, ad quem dixit: Quæso mihi gratificare. eas ad sartorem, & sinas te vestiri ex optimo panno, mco more, & depone scissas istas vestes. Ille inquit: Meo arbitrio me vestiam. Respondit optimus dux: Et meo arbitrio te pellam ex mea aula: & statim oportuit illum discedere ex aula.
units.tr: The most honourable Duke William of Saxony had a nobleman with him, dressed as is now the custom, and said to him: "I beg you to do me a favour. Go to the tailor, and let yourself be dressed in the finest cloth, in the old manner, and put off those slashed clothes." He replied: "I will clothe myself as I please." The excellent duke answered: "And I will expel you from my court as I please." And at once the man had to leave the court.

units.la: Olim in rebus publicis clarissimi cives acerrimè vetera instituta defenderunt. Quoties enim Romæ sumptuariæ leges prolatæ sunt, ut more maiorum vestiret se civitas? Cato quanta contentione tuetur legem Oppiam apud Livium, quæ modum sum-ptibus mulierum præscribebat?
units.tr: In public affairs of old, the most distinguished citizens defended the ancient customs vigorously. For how often at Rome were sumptuary laws proposed, so that the state might dress in the manner of the ancestors? With how much effort does Cato defend, in Livy, the Oppian law, which prescribed a limit on women's expenses?

units.la: Augustus cùm videret Romanos peregrino vestitu delectari, sentiès quantum ea in re mali infes-set, longa oratione cives obiurgauit, & ad togæ usum revocauit, illum etiam Virgilij versiculum citans:
units.tr: When Augustus saw that the Romans delighted in foreign dress, and perceived how much harm this did, he rebuked the citizens in a long speech and recalled them to the use of the toga, citing also that verse of Virgil:

units.la: Romanos rerum dominos, gentemq; togatam.
units.tr: The masters of the world, the toga-wearing race.

units.la: Apud Virgilium, cùm mollitiem objicit Troia nis Turnus, à veste conjecturam facit. Ait enim:
units.tr: In Virgil, when Turnus reproaches the Trojans with effeminacy, he draws a conclusion from their clothing. For he says:

units.la: Et tunicæ manicas, & habet redimicula mitræ.
units.tr: And tunics with sleeves, and he wears the ribbons of a mitre.

units.la: Animadverterunt enim docti viri, sermonem, habitum, incessum, & alios motus corporis, tanquam actionem esse animi, in qua velut in speculo cuiusq; natura cerni posset. Sic & Ecclesiastes dicit: Amictus, risus, & incessus, produnt hominis ingenium.
units.tr: For learned men have observed that speech, bearing, gait and the other movements of the body are, as it were, the actions of the mind, in which a person's nature can be seen as in a mirror. Thus also Ecclesiastes says: Dress, laughter and gait reveal a man's disposition.

units.la: Turcicus Imperator iussit sibi aliquando omnium gentium habitus pingi. Cùm itaque pictor plurimarum gentium uestes depinxisset, tandem pingit nudum hominem, & iuxta eum uarios pannos. Iussus igitur à Rege interpretari illam picturam nudi hominis, cùm exposuisset cæteras imagines, tandè dixit: Nudum illum Germanum esse, cui certa forma uestitus pingi non posset, quòd quotidie nouâ excogitaret.
units.tr: The Turkish emperor once ordered that the costumes of all peoples be painted for him. When the painter had depicted the clothing of very many peoples, at last he painted a naked man, and beside him various cloths. Then, ordered by the king to explain this picture of the naked man, when he had set out the other images, he finally said: that naked figure is a German, for whom no fixed form of clothing can be painted, because he devises a new one every day.

units.la: Socrates calceis Sydonijs contra suam consuetudinem uti noluit, tametsi ipsius confessione aptierant pedibus. Nec ille morosus in re parua uideri debet. Pars quædam grauitatis atq; constãtiæ fuit, ne quidem in paruis rebus sui dissimilem esse.
units.tr: Socrates refused to wear Sidonian shoes, contrary to his custom, although by his own admission they fitted his feet. Nor should he be thought morose in a small matter. It was part of his gravity and constancy not to be unlike himself even in trifling things.

units.la: Homerus ait: honestum habitum ad existimationem augendam conducere.
units.tr: Homer says that respectable dress contributes to increasing esteem.

units.la: Namq; uiro uestis magnum decus addit honesta.
units.tr: For fine clothing adds great honour to a man.

units.la: Non enim gemmæ, aut aurum, aut purpura, quarum rerum usus in ciuitatibus bene constitutis etiam interdictus est honestis hominibus, magnopere ornant uiros: sed quia pro ingenijs ac moribus uestitum ferè quisq; sumit, magnam commendationem habet honestus habitus, quòd eo boni uiri delectari iudicentur.
units.tr: For it is not gems, gold or purple, the use of which has been forbidden even to respectable men in well-ordered states, that greatly adorns men; but because most people dress according to their talents and morals, a respectable appearance earns great commendation, since good men are judged to take delight in it.

units.la: Inter corruptelas rerum publicarum, meritò affectatio siue nouitatis siue peregrinitatis in uestitu numerari debet.
units.tr: Among the corruptions of states, affectation in dress, whether of novelty or of foreignness, ought rightly to be counted.

units.la: Lacedæmonij hospitem Milesium, cùm alijs delicijs affluentem, tum in uestitu sumptuosiorem, quàm pro Spartana consuetudine, iusserunt ciui-tate excedere, ac domi Milesiam exercere.
units.tr: The Spartans, when a Milesian guest abounded in other luxuries and was more extravagant in dress than Spartan custom allowed, ordered him to leave the city and to practise Milesian ways at home.

units.la: Dauid suas gentes, cùm à uicino Rege per con-tumeliam uestes decurtatæ essent, ac barba contra morem rasa esset, iussit extrema regui ipsius oppi-da tenere, nec prodire in publicum donec barba creuisset.
units.tr: David, when his envoys had been humiliated by the neighbouring king, who had cut their garments short and shaved off half their beards contrary to custom, ordered them to remain in the outermost towns of his kingdom and not to appear in public until their beards had grown back.

units.la: Xenophon scribit Lacedæmonios in institutis suis præcepisse, ut pueri in publico manus intra uestes continerent, nec deiicerent oculos ab his quæ ante pedes essent. Et aut hæc duo instituta esse, ut ad uerecundiam, pudorem & modestiam à pri-ma statim puericia assuefierent.
units.tr: Xenophon writes that the Lacedaemonians, in their institutions, ordered boys to keep their hands inside their clothing when in public and not to lift their eyes from what lay before their feet. He suggests that these two rules were meant to train them from earliest childhood in reverence, modesty and self-control.

units.la: Albertus dux Bauariæ, auus huius principis, ualde doctus & honestus, cùm redijsset ex Parisijs in patriâ, & esset factus baccalaureus, credo De-cretorū (nam Lutetiæ eo tempore nullum solebat promouere baccalaureū in iure Ciuili) uenit do-mum in cuculla baccalaurei, & illam cucullā cum alia ueste baccalaurei multos annos gestauit. Si iâ non Princeps, sed aliquis mediocris fortunæ, ueni-ret domū in habitu scholastici modesti, aut ex stu-diosis illius Ducis sic domi appareret, ab alijs dice-retur insanire.
units.tr: Albert, Duke of Bavaria, grandfather of this prince, was very learned and upright. When he returned home from Paris and had become a bachelor (I believe of Canon Law, since at Lutetia at that time no one was usually promoted bachelor in Civil Law), he came home wearing a bachelor's hood, and for many years he wore that hood together with the rest of a bachelor's dress. If someone of moderate means, not a prince, had come home dressed like a modest scholar, or if one of that duke's students had appeared at home in such dress, people would have said he was out of his mind.

units.la: Dicitur communi prouerbio: Vestis non facit monachum, uestis enim non est animi uirtus uel uitium: sed sæpe est signum modestiæ & honestatis, uel econtrà.
units.tr: There is the common proverb: "The clothes do not make the monk." Clothing is not in itself a virtue or a vice of the mind, but it is often a sign of modesty and decency, or the reverse.

units.la: Nihil est pulchrius, quàm uidere uirum cataphractum. Veteres pulcherrima habuerunt arma, distinctos thoraces auro & argento. Sidonius Apollinaris inquit, se inuitatum ad nuptias Burgundiacas, ijsq; præsentem, cùm alijs suæ gentis nobilibus, uidisse spectaculum pulcherrimum chorearum Burgundiacarum: in quibus uir cataphractus, indutus armis pulcherrimè ornatis auro & argento, duceret in chorea procerā uirginē, & saltaret in panoplia tam facilè ac leuiter, atq; si sine ullo onere fuisset.
units.tr: Nothing is more splendid than to see a man in armour. The ancients had very fine arms, with breastplates decorated in gold and silver. Sidonius Apollinaris says that, invited to the Burgundian wedding and present there with other nobles of his people, he saw a most magnificent Burgundian dance, in which an armoured man, dressed in weapons richly adorned with gold and silver, led a tall maiden in the dance and leapt in his armour as lightly and easily as if he carried no burden at all.

units.la: Dux Fridericus, laudatissimus & sapientissimus princeps, si quando accidit ut nactus esset calligas rectè factas & accommodatas suis pedibus, solitus est tam diu illis uti, ut sarctor eas resarcire cogeretur. Quia querebatur sibi raro rectè fieri calligas: idq; nobis omnibus accidit.
units.tr: Duke Frederick, a most praiseworthy and wise prince, whenever it happened that he had got boots well made and fitting his feet, was accustomed to wear them so long that a mender had to be called to patch them. He complained that boots were rarely made properly for him, and this happens to all of us.

units.la: Apud Xenophontem uitio datur Voluptati, quòd sæpius in suā respexerit umbram, & oculos ad uaria loca uolutarit. Sed illa modestia nihilo minus est in nostro Imperatore Carolo V. quòd sicut alijs magnis modestiæ laudibus afficitur, ita præcipuè oculos uagabundos non habeat. Dicam uobis historiam. Cùm post electionem Imperator Antuerpiā ingressus esset, Senatus urbis ut lætari se aduentu Cæsaris, & ipsi gratificari uideretur, ludos & spectacula in plateis, per quas transeundum erat imperatori, exhibuit: inter quæ, pro more ludorum, pulcherrimæ ac uenustissimæ erant uirgines, toto propemodum corpore nudæ, nisi quòd tenuissimo tantum & pellucido uelamento circundatæ essent. Cæsar urbem ingressus, & ad eum locum in quo exhibebantur spectacula delatus (cùm tamen ab aliis undiq; magnus fieret concursus) ne quidem respexit ad uirgines. Narrauit hæc mihi optimus & honestissimus uir Durerus pictor, ciuis Norinbergensis, qui unà cum Cæsare urbem est ingressus. Addebat idem, se quàm libentissimè accessisse, cùm ut agnosceret quid ageretur tum ut perfectionem pulcherrimarum uirginum rectius cõsideraret, dicens: Ego, quia eram pictor, aliquantulum inuerecundius circumspexi.
units.tr: In Xenophon, Pleasure is faulted for looking back at her own shadow too often and for rolling her eyes about in various directions. But our Emperor Charles V has the same modesty, and, while he is honoured with other great praises of modesty, he especially does not let his eyes wander. Let me tell you a story. After his election, when the Emperor had entered Antwerp, the city's senate, wishing to show that it rejoiced at the Emperor's arrival and wished to please him, put on games and shows in the squares through which the Emperor had to pass. Among them, as is the custom at such games, were most beautiful and charming maidens, almost entirely naked, except that they were wrapped in only a very thin and transparent veil. When the Emperor entered the city and was carried to the place where the shows were presented (although a great crowd was gathering from every side), he did not so much as look at the maidens. This was told to me by the excellent and most honourable man Dürer, the painter, a citizen of Nuremberg, who entered the city together with the Emperor. He added that he himself had gone over most willingly, both to see what was going on and to look more carefully at the perfect beauty of the maidens, saying: "I, because I was a painter, looked around a little more shamelessly."

units.la: Quidam Princeps, cum sibi ueste extraneam confici curasset, interrogatus à suo cõsiliario, quare tam peregrina ueste uteretur, dixit: nihil referre, quæ sit uestitus forma. At ille subiecit: Vestis indicat principem esse talem uirum, qui suis consiliarijs nolit obtemperare. Das dorfft er im in das angesicht sagen.
units.tr: A certain prince had a garment made in a foreign style, and when his councillor asked him why he wore such an outlandish dress, he replied that the form of clothing made no difference. But the councillor added: "The garment shows that the prince is the sort of man who will not obey his counsellors. You could tell him that to his face." (German)

units.la: Non sine offensione honesti homines turpem illum uestitum caligarum uidere possunt: & certè deformant tantum corpora, & requirunt magnos sumptus. Præcipuè uerò Saxones non debebant uti illis caligis, qui uolunt habere laudem constantiæ, tibiasq; elegantes ac suris musculisq; bene distinctas habent. Ex hac uestitus leuitate ortus est ignominiosus ille uersiculus: In curta tunica saltat Saxo, quasi pica.
units.tr: Decent people cannot look at that disgraceful style of breeches without offence. They certainly only deform the body and cost a great deal. Especially the Saxons, who wish to have a reputation for seriousness and have shapely legs with well-defined calves, ought not to wear those breeches. From this frivolity of dress arose that shameful little rhyme: "In a short tunic the Saxon dances, like a magpie."

units.la: Sic se deformat turpibus illis, & tanta cum pannositate dependentibus caligis.
units.tr: In this way he disfigures himself with those vile breeches, hanging down so ragged.

units.la: In uicino quodam oppido templum ingredies, uidi quendam cantorem ad pulpitum stantem, & indutum tam breui tunica, ut uix nates tegere posset. Ita impudenter ille nebulo astabat in conspectu Dei, cum honestæ matronæ ad sacram Domini coenam accederent. Si ego fuissem consul illius loci, coniecissem illum scurram in carcerem. Cogitate quantum doleant animi nostri, cum uidemus turpitudinē in uestitu. Luxus in uestitu & in epulis, multa secum uitia trahit.
units.tr: When I entered a church in a certain neighbouring town, I saw a singer standing at the pulpit, dressed in a tunic so short that it could barely cover his buttocks. That scoundrel stood so shamelessly in the sight of God while respectable matrons were coming forward to the Lord's Supper. If I had been the magistrate of that place, I would have thrown that buffoon into prison. Consider how much our minds are hurt when we see indecency in dress. Luxury in clothing and in feasting drags many vices along with it.

units.la: In Italia est consuetudo, ut uiri & mulieres prorsus sine uelamentis ueniant in balnea. Hanc consuetudinem si quis uellet in Germania constituere, ille esset uirgis cædendus.
units.tr: In Italy it is the custom for men and women to go into the baths quite without coverings. If anyone wished to introduce this custom in Germany, he would deserve to be beaten with rods.

units.la: Doctrina de uocatione pertinet ad iusticiam & modestiā. Quidam, quem & ego noui, & multi etiam inter uos, cum esset hospes in alia regione, rogatus ut concionaretur, recusauit: quia dicebat se non posse in illa monastica ueste concionari, sed in sua curta ueste uelle manere. Vestis non sanctificat, sed tamen offendit oculos. Ego credo multos, qui incedunt breuibus uestibus, esse sanctiores quàm ego sum: sed tamen non decet honestos homines. Quia illa leuitas in uestitu est etiam signum & significatio leuitatis in moribus, & in aliis uitæ actionibus.
units.tr: The teaching about vocation pertains to righteousness and modesty. A certain man, whom I too know, and many of you also, when he was a guest in another region and was asked to preach, refused, because he said he could not preach in that monkish dress, but wished to remain in his short coat. Clothing does not make a man holy, yet it offends the eyes. I believe that many who walk about in short clothes are holier than I am, but still it does not befit respectable people. For that frivolity in dress is also a sign and indication of frivolity in morals and in the other actions of life.

units.la: Gregorius Nazianzenus, cùm uideret Julianum Athenis, statim iudicabat ex illius incessu, quanquam humili, qualis esset futurus, dicens: Quantum malum nutrit respublica Romana?
units.tr: Gregory Nazianzen, when he saw Julian at Athens, judged at once from his gait, although it was humble, what sort of man he would become, saying: "What a great evil the Roman state is nourishing!"

units.la: Nuper quidam, cùm priores caligæ ei perijssent, rogatus, ne sibi tales caligas scissas amplius fieri curaret, respondit: Si non curarem mihi fieri similes, à meis socijs deriderer. Sic ille suos socios pluris faciebat, quàm honestorum hominum de se iudicia.
units.tr: Not long ago a certain man, when his earlier boots had worn out, was asked not to bother having such torn boots made for him again. He replied: "If I did not care about having them made like my companions' boots, I would be mocked by my companions." So he valued his companions more highly than the judgements of respectable people about himself.

units.la: SEPTIMVM PRAE-ceptum.
units.tr: SEVENTH PRECEPT.

units.la: DIVITIAE.
units.tr: RICHES.

units.la: Crassus dixit, neminem esse diuitē nisi qui posset alere annuum exercitum. Plutarchus cum reprehendit, & addit: Ad bellum inexhaustæ opes requiruntur: Krieg ist ein bodenloß ding. Crassus fuit tam diues, ut sexaginta thonnas auri possederit. Regno Franciæ esset difficile, annuum exercitum sustentare.
units.tr: Crassus said that no one is rich unless he can support a standing army. Plutarch rebukes him and adds: unlimited resources are needed for war; war is a bottomless thing. Crassus was so rich that he possessed sixty thousand talents of gold. It would be difficult for the kingdom of France to maintain a standing army.

units.la: Pomponius Atticus sic definit diuitias, ut Epi-curus definiuit: Diuitiæ sunt ad legem naturæ com-posita paupertas:id est, Ne uiuas in sordibus, et ha-beas necessaria, non tantum pro sustentatione tui corporis, sed etiam pro tua familia, pro educatio-ne liberorum & aliis rebus necessariis:id est, si re-cte consideras, ut habeas panem quotidianum. Alia huius dicti non multum priori dissimilis expo-sitio. Est conuertibilis propositio: Paupertas ad le-gem naturæ composita, est copia rerum, ut inde tu, tuiq;, commodè, non sordidè contra naturam ui-uant: sunt copiæ rerum, conuenientes naturæ.
units.tr: Pomponius Atticus defined riches as Epicurus did: riches are poverty brought into line with the law of nature. That is, do not live in squalor, but have what you need, not only for the support of your body but also for your household, the education of your children and other necessary things; that is, if you consider rightly, to have your daily bread. Another explanation of this saying differs little from the first. The proposition can be reversed: poverty brought into line with the law of nature is an abundance of things, by which you and yours may live comfortably and not squalidly, contrary to nature; abundances of things agreeing with nature.

units.la: Pythias tam dines fuit, ut potuerit alere decies cētena milia hominum, totum uidelicet exercitum Xerxis. Idem tamen postea factus est tam inops, ut fame tandem mortuus sit. Vuer zům heller ist geborn, der kombt nimmermer zům groschē. Pro-uerbium est, significans quòd Deus uelit aliquos pauperes esse, nec omnes esse diuites. Vult esse di-uersitatem donorum, iuxta prouerbium Salomo-nis: Pauper & diues unà habitabunt.
units.tr: Pythias was so rich that he could have fed a million hundred thousand people, that is, the whole army of Xerxes. Yet he later became so poor that he finally died of hunger. He who is born to a heller will never come to a groschen. This is a proverb, meaning that God wills some to be poor and not all to be rich. He wills a diversity of gifts, according to the proverb of Solomon: the rich and the poor will live together.

units.la: Fridericus à Dōn dixerat ad seniorem domi-num de Orlemunt: (quæ fuit nobilissima familia in Thuringia, iam uerò est extincta) Nobilissime domine, tu es ex nobilissima & antiquissima fami-lia in tota Thuringia, ideoq; sic aut sic te compa-res. Ibi ille respondit: Vnd wenn ich schon so ade-lich,
units.tr: Frederick von Dön had said to the senior lord of Orlemunt (a most noble family in Thuringia, now extinct) : "Most noble lord, you are of the most noble and ancient family in all Thuringia, so therefore you should bear yourself in such and such a way." He replied: "And even if I were so noble that pheasant feathers flew out of my nose,

units.la: Diuitiæ.
units.tr: Riches.

units.la: Pythias. lich wäre, das mir die repphünerfedern aus der nasen flugen, was hülffs es, wenn ich kein gelt hette.
units.tr: what good would it do me if I had no money?"

units.la: Fridericus de Don solitus est dicere: Quid mihi prodesset, etiamsi tam nobilis essem, atq; Alexander Magnus, nec haberem pecuniā? Profectò nullus me non haberet despectui. His quoq; addebat uersiculum:
units.tr: Frederick von Dön was accustomed to say: "What would it profit me, even if I were as noble as Alexander the Great, and had no money? Surely everyone would despise me." To these he also added a little verse:

units.la: Nobilis est ille, quem nobilitat sua uilla. Rectius sic se habet antiquus uersus: Nobilis est ille,quem nobilitat sua uirtus. Iam uerò inuerso ordine iactatur.
units.tr: He is noble whom his estate ennobles. The old verse is better put thus: He is noble whom his virtue ennobles. Now, however, it is tossed about with the order reversed.

units.la: Simile dixit Pflug, pater Iulij episcopi Naumburgensis:
units.tr: Pflug, father of Julius, bishop of Naumburg, said something similar:

units.la: Nobilis est ille,quem nobilitat sua uilla.
units.tr: He is noble whom his estate ennobles.

units.la: Hastu gelt, so tritt hărfür: Hastu nicht geltt,so tritt hinder die thür.
units.tr: If you have money, step forward; if you have no money, step behind the door.

units.la: Habebam aliquando mecum hospitem, Hispanum, bonum uirum, qui, cùm casu loqueremur de præsentibus negocijs, dicebat: Bonum est, semper habere pecuniam in loculis. Respondit ei: Verum est, omnes sic sentiunt de illa propositione.
units.tr: Once I had with me a guest, a Spaniard, a good man, who, when by chance we were talking about current affairs, said: "It is good always to have money in the purse." I replied to him: "True; everyone thinks that about that proposition."

units.la: COLL. Iocus.
units.tr: Joke.

units.la: Narratur historia de Sigismundo Imperatore, cùm eius equus mingeret casu in flumine, ibi quidam ex equitibus suis dixit: Ille equus habet sui domini naturam. Imperator miratus, quærit ex feruo, quid uellet sibi hoc dicto? At ille: In undam spargere equum urinam, ubi antea abundet aqua: sic illum erga cos beneficum esse, qui antea diuitijs abundarent. Animaduertit hoc Imperator, & dixit: Age, experiare tuam fortunam, quando diuerterimus. Postquam uenissent in hospitium, statim Imperator iussit apparari duas pyxides eiusdē formæ & magnitudinis, & deinde etiam impleri, unam auro, alteram plumbo, æquali tamen pondere. Perac̈a hac re, iussit ad se accersi seruū, permittitq; eligere utram malit. Seruus iam hanc, iam illam aspicit, incertus utram malit sumere, tandem arripit plumbeam pyxidem. Tum, inquit Cæsar: Iam uides culpam non esse meam tuæ pauperta-tis & inopiæ, sed fortunam tibi aduersantem.
units.tr: There is a story about the Emperor Sigismund: when his horse by chance made water in a river, one of his horsemen there said: "That horse has its master's nature." The emperor, surprised, asks the servant what he meant by this saying. He replied: that a horse pours its urine into the water where water already abounds; so it is kind to those who already abound in riches. The emperor noticed this and said: "Come, test your fortune when we turn aside." After they had come to the inn, the emperor at once ordered two boxes of the same shape and size to be prepared, and then filled, one with gold, the other with lead, but of equal weight. When this was done, he ordered the servant to be summoned to him and allowed him to choose which he preferred. The servant looked now at this one, now at that, uncertain which he would prefer to take, and at last he seized the leaden box. Then, said Caesar: "Now you see that the fault for your poverty and want is not mine, but that fortune is against you."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: Saying.

units.la: Plautus ait, quòd res secundæ superbiam deceant. Vbi enim quis se opibus aliquibus excellere uidet, statim superbia fastuq; animi inflatur. Sic nanq; usuuenire uidemus, ut qui potens est, & alios ualet cōtemnere ac supprimere, is uerè superbire possit.
units.tr: Plautus says that good fortune becomes pride. For when someone sees himself excelling in some wealth, at once he is puffed up with pride and haughtiness of mind. For we see that it happens in this way, that the man who is powerful and able to despise and crush others may truly be arrogant.

units.la: Quando mendicus euehitur ad honores uelopes, tunc non est sui compos, & plerunq; alijs est insolentior, ut dicitur: Asperius nihil est humili, cùm surgit in altum. Sic aliquando mulier quædam pia & honesta, laboLaborans maxima angustia rei familiaris, ad me dixit: se uiuete marito non fuisse apud se annos quinquedecim, propterea quòd maritus subito fortunæ afflatu nouem milia Ioachimicorum accepisset: qua pecunia cõsumpta à liberis decoctoribus, nunc iterum se mentis compotem factam esse dicebat. Hæc sæpe ad nos iter faciebat, studio audiedi Lutherũ.
units.tr: When a beggar is raised swiftly to honours, then he is not master of himself, and for the most part he becomes more insolent toward others, as the saying goes: nothing is harsher than a lowly man when he rises to the heights. So once a certain pious and honest woman, labouring under the greatest distress in her household affairs, said to me that, while her husband lived, she had not been with him for fifteen years, because her husband had suddenly received, by a gust of fortune, nine thousand Joachimsthalers; when that money had been squandered by the spendthrift children, she said that she had now again become sound of mind. She often came to us, eagerly to hear Luther.

units.la: Recte igitur monet Poeta:
units.tr: The poet rightly advises:

units.la: Fortunam reuerenter habe, quicunq; repente, Diues ab exili progrediêre loco.
units.tr: Respect fortune, whoever you are who suddenly rise rich from a lowly place.

units.la: Seneca: Quid appetis aurum, cùm nihil sit nisi terra sulphurea? Sed facilè fuit illi huiusmodi iactare. Quando enim hæc scripsit de paupertate, habuit sexaginta thonnas auri. Vnusquisq; sanè libens ac patiens talem paupertatem ferret.
units.tr: Seneca: Why do you seek gold, since it is nothing but sulphurous earth? But it was easy for him to talk in this way. For when he wrote these things about poverty, he had sixty thousand talents of gold. Surely anyone would gladly and patiently bear such poverty.

units.la: DE PROFVSIONE.
units.tr: ON EXTRAVAGANCE.

units.la: Cardinalis Augustæ in conuentu inuitauerat Duces & alios quosdam dominos, ad cœnam quandam: quæ ita splendidè apparata erat, ut quando fercula deportabantur, seu leuabantur, ibi aperirentur asseres mensæ, unde aues euolarent, & sic deinceps rursus sternebatur mensa.
units.tr: At a diet in Augsburg a cardinal had invited dukes and other lords to a certain dinner. It was so lavishly prepared that when the dishes were carried in or taken away, the boards of the table were opened, and birds flew out, and then the table was laid again.

units.la: Quando Cleopatra certauit cum Antonio de sumptibus cœnæ, ibi illa facetè lusit cũ isto centauro, ut nihil aliud dicã. Antonius fuit homo solaris, et tamē magnificus, ideoq; præparauit magno sumptu conuiuiũ. Postridie inuitauit Cleopatra rursus AntoAntonium in conuiuium tenuißimi apparatus, sed dempsit de auricula gemmam, seu margaritam, & imposuit aceto, in quo mox soluitur, ut sal (tam mirabilis est συμπαθεια in rerum natura) ac sic Antonio eam propinauit. Postea facta æstimatione gemmæ, hæc longè superauit cœnam Antonij.
units.tr: When Cleopatra competed with Antony over the cost of a dinner, she wittily played a trick on that centaur, to put it no other way. Antony was a man of the sun, yet magnificent, and so he had prepared a banquet at great expense. The next day Cleopatra invited Antony again to a dinner of very meagre fare. But she took a gem or pearl from her ear, dropped it into vinegar, where it soon dissolved like salt (so wondrous is the sympathy [συμπάθεια] in nature), and then offered him the drink. Afterwards, when the gem was valued, it far outdid Antony's dinner.

units.la: Poloni superfluitatem assumunt à Germanis, Italis & Hispanis, ita ut credam nullum talem apparatum esse, qualis est Polonicus. In Germania est etiam superfluitas, ubi dena fercula apponūtur. Noui principem, qui cùm aderant hospites, tantum apponebat eis quadraginta fercula.
units.tr: The Poles have taken up extravagance from the Germans, Italians and Spaniards, so that I believe there is no banquet like the Polish one. There is also extravagance in Germany, where ten courses are served. I knew a prince who, when guests were present, would set forty courses before them.

units.la: Vidi nuper forte matremfamiliàs sedentem & flentem in domo sua, propterea quòd domi suæ tantum octo fercula proponerentur. Quia dominus seu paterfamiliàs cœpisset sumptus aliquantulum diminuere, cùm antea duodecim fercula mensæ apposita fuissent. Flebat ideo, quia illi inutiles sumptus aliquantulum diminuebātur, cùm duo fercula satisfecissent: alsò fressen wir Deütschen vns selbs lamb, kranck, todt vnd in die hell. Illa, proh dolor, passim in mundo fiunt.
units.tr: I recently happened to see a housewife sitting and weeping in her house, because only eight courses were being served there. Her husband, or the head of the household, had begun to reduce expenses a little, when before twelve courses had been set on the table. She wept because those useless expenses were being cut back a little, though two courses would have sufficed. "So we Germans devour ourselves: lamb, sick, dead, and into hell." Alas, such things happen everywhere in the world.

units.la: Iohannes Fridericus dux Saxoniæ, difficultate œconomiæ motus, statuit nō alere amplius priuatis alimentis ministros et aulicos suos: sed singulis certam pecuniam dare, qua alibi cibos caperent, ne haberet necesse tantos sumptus culinæ impendere. dere. Hoc per unũ annũ tentato, mutauit senten-tiam, eo quòd multò plus hac ratione alendis suis impêderet, quàm ipsi priuata culina constaret. Dixit se octingentos florenos plus quàm antea expo-suisse uno anno, in comparando cibo. Tanta est apud Germanos prodigalitas & profusio, ut mutari non possit.
units.tr: John Frederick, Duke of Saxony, moved by the difficulty of household management, decided no longer to feed his ministers and courtiers from his own provisions, but to give each a set sum of money with which to buy food elsewhere, so that he would not need to spend so much on the kitchen. After trying this for one year, he changed his mind, because by this arrangement he spent much more on feeding his people than his own private kitchen cost. He said he had spent eight hundred florins more in one year on buying food. Such is the prodigality and profusion among the Germans that it cannot be changed.

units.la: Nobilis quidam ualde diues, ac mihi bene no-tus, uocauit ad se in oppidum Naumburg suam cõiugem, & alios amicos, ubi magnum conuiuium ipsis instituit. Postquam paululum cõpotassent, ex stulta profusione effregerunt et cõminuerunt for-nacem, atq; etiam lectos diffecuerunt: ita ut postea in subducendis rationibus, uiginti floreni tantum pro damno eo dato, atq; adeò furore, computati sint. Audiui uerò ex hospite, dicente: se nolle centũ florenos accipere, ut illam ἀσωτίαν iterũ uideret.
units.tr: A certain very wealthy nobleman, well known to me, invited his wife and other friends to himself in the town of Naumburg, and gave them a great banquet there. After they had drunk a little too much, in foolish excess they broke and smashed the stove, and even took the beds apart. So when the accounts were reckoned afterwards, the damage was assessed at only twenty florins, given the fury of it. I heard, moreover, from the innkeeper, who said that he would not take a hundred florins, so as not to see that riot [ἀσωτία] again.

units.la: Paulus pontifex dixit, se habere duos filios, unũ prodigum, & alterum frugalem. Prodigum uocauit, regem Galliæ Franciscum: frugalem uerò, nostrum Imperatorem Carolum. Sed rex Galliæ aliquando dixit: Quid profuit nostro patri unquam filius iste frugalis, qui non potest tantum obtinere in suo Imperio, ut reprimat rebelles illos in religione? Ego habeo quietum regnum, in quo omnes repugnantes patri meo Pontifici tollo.
units.tr: Pope Paul said that he had two sons, one prodigal and the other frugal. He called the prodigal one Francis, King of France, and the frugal one our Emperor Charles. But the King of France once said: "What has that frugal son ever profited our father, who cannot obtain so much in his own empire that he can suppress those rebels in religion? I have a quiet kingdom, in which I remove all who resist my father the Pope."

units.la: Noui adolescentes duos nobiles, qui adeò luxu-riosè riosè uiuebant, ut etiam uinum Rheticum uino Rhenano, æstiuali tempore, tanquam sordidæ aquæ, imponerent, ut maiori cum uoluptate biberè possent. Vinum autem Rhenanum aliâs suis, tanquam utilissimum potum bibendum dabant. Hi post aliquot menses in tantam redacti sunt paupertatem, ut etiam cum coniugibus & liberis, non sine maximo uitæ discrimine, ex ciuitate à creditoribus expellerentur: & nisi parentes fecissent, creditores in liberos & coniuges impetum fecissent.
units.tr: I knew two young noblemen who lived so luxuriously that in summer they would mix Rhaetian wine with Rhenish wine, as if it were dirty water, so that they could drink it with greater pleasure. They would give the Rhenish wine to their servants to drink, as if it were most wholesome drink. After some months these men were reduced to such poverty that they were driven out of the city by their creditors, together with their wives and children, at great peril to their lives; and if their parents had not paid, the creditors would have attacked the children and wives.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLLATIONS.

units.la: Vir admodum dives in Borussia petiuit ab Astrologo, ut sibi natiuitatem erigeret, & finem uitæ prædiceret. Quod cum faceret Astrologus, & certum tempus mortis constitueret, ille lautissimè interim cum suis sodalibus uixit, ita ut omnem penè substantiam dilapidasset, cùm finis uitæ instaret. Sedebat autem in sedili expectans mortem, quæ longè adhuc aberat. Et cùm iam parcius uiueret, etiam sanitas augebatur. Cùm autem nihil de patrimonio amplius restaret, coactus est sæpe colligere eleemosynam ad fores templi, nec ullus sociorum eum postea agnouit. Petens autem dicebat: Lieben herren helfft einem der sich im reichtumb verstigen hat. Amici autem nolentes turpitudinem aspicere, effecerunt ut nan ciseretur publicum munus, unde 50. aureos aut plus habebat. Ibi ex dimidia parte uiuebat, dimidiam in alios vsus collocabat, ita ut multum lucrifaceret. Tandem nactus maius officium, plures opes quàm ante habuerat, corrasit. Sic didicit deinde parcius uiuere, & malum sodalitium vitare. Inuenies autem multa milia, quibus non iterum talis fortuna eueniat.
units.tr: A very rich man in Prussia asked an astrologer to cast his horoscope and foretell the end of his life. When the astrologer did so and fixed a certain time of death, the man lived most lavishly in the meantime with his drinking companions, so that he had squandered almost all his substance when the end of his life was at hand. He sat in his chair waiting for death, which was still far off. And when he now lived more sparingly, his health also improved. But when nothing more of his patrimony remained, he was often forced to collect alms at the doors of the church, and none of his companions afterwards recognised him. Begging, he would say: "Dear sirs, help someone who has ruined himself through wealth." His friends, unwilling to look upon his disgrace, arranged that he obtained a public office, from which he had fifty gold coins or more. He lived on half of it and put the other half to other uses, so that he made a great profit. At last, having obtained a higher office, he acquired more wealth than he had before. So he then learned to live more sparingly and to avoid bad company. But you will find many thousands to whom such good fortune never comes again.

units.la: Sedi olim alicubi in conuiuio, ubi quidam honestus uir nobis dixit: Habui ex dote uxoris meæ mille trecentos aureos. Quæ porrò alioqui habeo ex quotidiana practica, illa consumo, nec possum inde multa comparcere. Hanc autem dotem uolui reseruare pro uxore & liberis. Dedi cuidam nobili, sed propter ipsius prodigalitatem perijt mihi. Quid faciam? tulit æquo animo bonus uir, quem adhuc viuere credo. Nobilis quidem ille vera fuit lamia: plurimas uiduas decepit, aliosq; non paucos forte fraudauit. In Anglia certauit cum rege pompis, in apparatu conuiuiorum, ludorum & spectaculorum. Ita permittitur quidem alicui ludere, quandiu pecunia ipsi suppetit: sed postea hac consumpta, audiendum est ipsi illud Ouidij: Si nihil attuleris, ibis Homere foras.
units.tr: I once sat at a banquet somewhere, where a certain honest man told us: "I had 1,300 gold coins from my wife's dowry. Whatever else I have from my daily business, I spend, and I cannot save much from it. But I wanted to keep this dowry for my wife and children. I gave it to a certain nobleman, but through his prodigality it was lost to me. What am I to do?" The good man, whom I believe is still alive, bore it with an even mind. That nobleman was truly a vampire: he deceived many widows and perhaps defrauded not a few others. In England he competed with the king in display, in the splendour of banquets, games and spectacles. Indeed, one is permitted to gamble only as long as money is available; but once that is spent, one must hear those words of Ovid: "If you bring nothing, you will go out, Homer."

units.la: Fuit in aula regis Ferdinandi unus de præcipuis consiliarijs eius, Hispanus, Halomantes, qui prius fuerat decoctor, & (ut uocat) Bancorupto, quum posteaquam peruenire in aulam, sicut sæpe fit, propter ingenij & consilij dexteritatem apud Regem ditescebat: quia tales homines sunt industrij, & fuit in magna Regis gratia. Cùm hoc forte unà sedens in conuiuio Dux Brunsuicensis, frater ducis Henrici, episcopus Mindensis, cùm uideret ipsum esse in magna gratia & authoritate apud regem, interrogat alium quendam assidentem, quomodo uocetur? Ille respondit: Bancorupto. Episcopus non satis intellecto nomine, alloquitur eum, & propinat poculum, inquiens: Domine Bancorupto, ego propino tibi bonum haustum. Ille boni cõsuluit, accepto poculo, ac dissimulat illos sermones. Interpellat uerò unus ex assidentibus Episcopo, dicens, Nõ est hoc ei nomen proprium, sed Bancorupto est nomen contumeliosum. Ibi episcopus irascitur alteri: & parũ absuit quin eum gladio petiuisset.
units.tr: At the court of King Ferdinand there was one of his chief counsellors, a Spaniard named Halomantes, who had formerly been a bankrupt merchant and, as they call it, a "Bancorupto". After he came to court, as often happens, he grew rich through the king's favour, because such men are industrious and skilled in their wit and counsel, and he was in great favour with the king. Once, when he was sitting together at a banquet with Duke Henry of Brunswick, the brother of Duke Henry, and the Bishop of Minden, the bishop saw that he was in great favour and authority with the king. He asked another man sitting nearby what he was called. The man replied, "Bancorupto." The bishop, not having understood the name well, addressed him and offered him a cup, saying: "Lord Bancorupto, I drink to you a good draught." He took the cup graciously and ignored those words. But one of those sitting nearby interrupted the bishop, saying: "That is not his proper name; 'Bancorupto' is an insulting name." Then the bishop grew angry with the other man, and it was a near thing that he did not attack him with his sword.
