units.la: Cùm aliquis probro daret regi Galliæ, quòd soleret parcere pecuniæ, respondit Imperator Carolus V. Credite mihi, si potest bene guardare suam pecuniam, haud stultè facit.
units.tr: When someone reproached the King of France for being accustomed to sparing his money, the Emperor Charles V replied: "Believe me, if he can keep his money well, he is not acting foolishly."

units.la: Dux Fridericus aluit tantum centum equos in aula sua. Et quando ibat ad comitia, habebat comitatum triginta equitum. Dixit enim, impediri consilia magno comitatu. Nunc autem non potentiores ipso, alunt quadringentos, aut plures.
units.tr: Duke Frederick kept only one hundred horses in his court. And when he went to the diet, he had an escort of thirty horsemen. For he said that counsels were hindered by a large retinue. Now, those who are no more powerful than he keep four hundred or more.

units.la: Parsi-
units.tr: Parsi-

units.la: Septimum præceptum. PARSIMONIA.
units.tr: The seventh precept. THRIFT.

units.la: Qui colit Seruatium, coletur à Vincentio: wer bhelt wann er hatt, der nimbt wenn er darff. Item: Bonus Seruatius, facit bonũ Bonifacium. Nemo ex nostris studuit magis parsimoniæ, quàm doctor Augustinus: qui quolibet anni tempore coemebat, conseruabat, & distribuebat ea, quæ ad œconomiam necessaria erant.
units.tr: He who cultivates Servatius will be cultivated by Vincentius; whoever has, keeps; whoever needs, takes. Likewise: Good Servatius makes a good Boniface. None of our people was more devoted to thrift than Doctor Augustine, who at every season of the year bought, saved and distributed the things that were necessary for household management.

units.la: BENEFICENTIA ET liberalitas.
units.tr: BENEFICENCE AND LIBERALITY.

units.la: Nulla est elegantior doctrina de liberalitate & parsimonia, quàm quæ est apud Salomonē: Fontes tui deriuētur foras, et tu dominus eorũ maneto.
units.tr: There is no more elegant teaching on generosity and thrift than that of Solomon: "Let your fountains be dispersed abroad, and do thou be their sole master."

units.la: Deus hanc ipsam ob causam condidit homines & angelos, ut essent creaturæ, quibus se & sua bona communicaret, iuxta dictum: Bonum est communicatiuũ sui. Deus enim sua bonitate omnia condidit, non ut ipse solus illis frueretur, sed ut alijs illa sua bona cōmunicaret. Huc etiam illæ pulchræ regulæ pertinent: Τὸ ἀγαθὸν κοινωνικὸν ἑαυτῆς. Quo natura est præstantior, eo magis est κοινωνικὴ. Item, χρηστὸς ἀνὴρ κοινὸν ἀγαθόν, ὡς φασιν.
units.tr: God created men and angels for this very reason, that they might be creatures with whom he might share himself and his goods, according to the saying: the good is by nature communicative of itself. For God made all things out of his goodness, not so that he alone might enjoy them, but so that he might share those good things of his with others. To this also belong those fine maxims: [Greek: to agathon koinōnikon heautēs]. The nobler a nature is, the more it is communicative [koinōnikē]. Likewise, [Greek: chrēstos anēr koinon agathon, hōs phasin], a useful man is, as they say, a common good.

units.la: Dux Fridericus Palatinus Heydelbergæ humaniter excepit rusticum sibi offerentè pyra, simulq; petentem nescio quid. Princeps benevolus statim accepit donum, quantumuis exiguum: ac id, quod ab ipso petiuerat, perfici mandat. Acceptis ultro citroq; beneficijs, rusticus à principe dimittitur. Illud nõ fuit sordidũ, sed fuit signũ pij Principis, benefici, & beneuoli erga suos etiã infimos subditos.
units.tr: Duke Frederick the Palatine at Heidelberg received kindly a peasant who offered him pears and at the same time asked for something or other. The benevolent prince at once accepted the gift, however small, and ordered that what the man had asked for be carried out. With benefits exchanged on both sides, the peasant was dismissed by the prince. That was not meanness; it was the mark of a pious prince, generous and kind even toward his lowliest subjects.

units.la: Dux Fridericus ante annos triginta, cùm esset magna frumenti difficultas, ita ut modius uende-retur octodecim grosis, dedit multis colonis in Misnia & Franconia ac uicinis locis frumenta. Postea uerò à diuitibus, & illis qui potuerunt reddere, recipit quod dederat: reliquis autem totum do-nauit. Illa fuit concinna liberalitas. Aristoteles e-nim inquit: Liberalitatem debere esse concinnam.
units.tr: Duke Frederick, thirty years ago, when there was a great shortage of grain, so that a bushel was sold for eighteen groschen, gave grain to many farmers in Meissen and Franconia and in neighbouring places. Afterwards, however, he took back what he had given from the wealthy and from those who were able to repay; the rest he gave away entirely. That was a fitting liberality. For Aristotle says that liberality ought to be fitting.

units.la: Credo nostris temporibus non fuisse magis be-neficum & liberalem uirum, quam est D. Iacobus Fuggerus. Audiui à Stigelio, quòd Venetijs, cum ipsum Fuggerum conueniret quidam mercator pauper, peregrinus, petès ab eo duo millia florenorum: ille statim dixit, Veni deinde, isto tem-pore, ad istum locum, tunc hanc pecuniam dabo. Cùm dedisset, dixerunt ad eum ipsius familiares: D. Iacobe, ualde miramur quòd tantum pecuniae huic peregrino & ignoto largiaris. At ille subri-dens, respondit: Bene noui hunc uirum, cuius inte-gritatem & constantiam tanti facio, quanti ul-lius mercatoris in hac tota regione. Idem D. Iacobus Fuggerus per suam beneficentiam & libera-litatem suas facultates adeptus est.
units.tr: I believe that in our times there has not been a more beneficent and generous man than Sir Jacob Fugger. I heard from Stigel that at Venice a certain poor foreign merchant met Fugger himself and asked him for two thousand florins. He at once said, "Come back to this place at this time, and then I will give you the money." When he had given it, his household members said to him: "Sir Jacob, we are greatly surprised that you give so much money to this foreigner, an unknown man." But he, smiling, replied: "I know this man well; I value his integrity and steadfastness as much as that of any merchant in this whole region." The same Jacob Fugger acquired his wealth through his beneficence and liberality.

units.la: Cùm pugna ad Mulbergũ est cõmissa, multi no-biles uiri cum principe Electore Friderico sunt ca-pti, & inter reliquos Cancellarius Iodocus de Hei-de, & Secretarius Vuolfgangus: quibus captis e-repta sunt omnia, quæ secum tunc habebant: ac re-licti sunt vincti ad arborem uicinã pago Pistritzs, ubi cum forte præterisset Secretarius Cæsaris Obernburger, statim expromplsit decem aureos, quos dedit eis: ac promisit se per suum puerũ curà-turũ, ut haberent cibum ex culina Cæsaris, & itá properat ad Imperatorem. Postea uerò in oppido Vuiteberga, cùm essent liberati, uoluit Cancella-rius reddere pecuniam Secretario Obernburger: sed is non accepit, dicens, se tunc cùm daret pecu-niam, propter properationem & uaria negocia, quibus tunc animum occupatum habuerat, non potuisse cogitare: alioqui decuisse in illa amicorũ calamitate alia officia humanitatis & amicicię a-micis præstare. sed statim post doluisse, quòd ami-cis nõ plus pecuniæ dedisset: itaq; orare se, ne hũc quoq; dolorem sibi addant, ut cogant illum pecu-niam expositam recipere. Sic humanissimè factũ & dictum est.
units.tr: When the battle was fought at Mühlberg, many noblemen were captured with the Elector Prince Frederick, and among the rest the chancellor Jodocus von Heide and the secretary Wolfgang. When they were taken, everything they then had with them was snatched away, and they were left bound to a tree near the village of Pistritz. There the secretary of the Emperor, Obernburger, happened to pass by; he at once produced ten gold coins, gave them to the prisoners, and promised that through his boy he would see to it that they had food from the emperor's kitchen; and so he hurried on to the Emperor. Afterwards, however, when they had been freed in the town of Wittenberg, the chancellor wished to return the money to the secretary Obernburger, but he would not accept it, saying that when he gave the money, on account of his haste and the various business that then occupied his mind, he had not been able to think; otherwise, in the misfortune of his friends, he ought to have shown them other acts of humanity and friendship. But afterwards he had grieved that he had not given his friends more money; he therefore asked them not to add this sorrow to him by forcing him to take back the money he had spent. So it was done and said most humanely.

units.la: Menander: χεινὸς αὐὴρ ποινὸν ἀγαθὸν: id est, Bonus & beneficus uir, est publicum bonum. In multis ciuitatibus aliqui tales reperiuntur, qui suis sumptibus priuatim alunt ministros, adiuuat ministeministerium, benefaciunt reipublicæ, fouent scholasticos, aliosq; egenos: tales uiri uere sunt publicum bonum. Talis erat Lipsiæ pius & honestus uir Henricus Schurer. Ille multis benefaciebat pauperibus, credebat illis pecuniam: & qui non poterant restituere, illis donabat. In primis uero beneficus erat erga pauperes scholasticos, ac bene faciebat ministerio Ecclesiastico. Hic primum ipse quoq; pauper fuit: sed postea pro fideli sua dispensatione ac beneficentia, à Deo super plura constitutus, & opibus auctus, agnouit & diuinam benedictionem & gratiam, in diesq; magis ac magis beneficum se erga ministros Ecclesiæ, literarum studiosos, aliosq; egenos exhibuit.
units.tr: Menander: [Greek: chrēstos anēr koinon agathon]: that is, a good and beneficent man is a public good. In many cities there are some such men who at their own expense privately support ministers, aid the ministry, benefit the commonwealth, foster scholars and other needy persons; such men are truly a public good. Such a man was the pious and honourable Henry Schurer at Leipzig. He did good to many poor people, lent them money, and those who could not repay he gave it to outright. Above all he was generous toward poor students, and he did good service to the ecclesiastical ministry. He himself was at first poor too; but afterwards, because of his faithful stewardship and beneficence, he was set by God over more and was enriched with wealth, and he recognised both the divine blessing and grace, and more and more each day he showed himself generous toward the ministers of the Church, students of letters, and other needy people.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: In historijs de uita Germanorum principum & hæc, non contemnenda inter cæteras, habetur, quæ nos merito ad eleemosynas erogandas, omnigenamq; liberalitatem Christianam comouere debet. Episcopus Mediolanensis cum suo ministro iter aliquo faciens, cùm inter eundum in uia mendici ab eo eleemosynam peterent, iussit ministrum omnem pecuniam illis pauperibus dare. Habebat autem tantum tres aureos. Minister diu secum deliberat, an tota substantia mendicis esset danda? Tandem cogitat: Ne mihi meoq; dominoq; deinde uesperi esuriendum, & carendum sit, reseruabo nobis pro uiatico unum aureum. Numerat igitur eis duos aureos, & abijt. Cùm iam paulo ulterius processissent, quidā nobiles pij & boni uiri episco po obuiam ueniunt, quibus hic Episcopus propter suam pietatem & beneuolētiam erga pauperes erat notus: ideoq; mandant, ut ministro episcopi du centi coronati numerarentur, unde Episcopus se sustentaret, & haberet facultates, ex quibus pauperibus uictum praberet. Minister pecuniā læto animo accipit, accurrēs ad Episcopū, ac inquiēs: Domine, hi nobiles mihi ducentos coronatos numerarunt, ut tibi darē. Tunc Episcopus: Ah tu me & te decepisti. Quid ita? ait minister. Nonne (inquit ille) te iussi ut dares omnes tres aureos pauperibus, & tu seruasti unum? nonne ita fecisti? Respondet minister: Confiteor me fecisse. Quia putabam nobis carendum esse: ideo reseruaui unum. Vide, inquit Episcopus, tu mihi & tibi nocuisti. Si enim dedisses tres aureos, accepisses trecentos.
units.tr: In the histories of the lives of German princes this story is also found among the others, and it is not to be despised. It ought rightly to move us to give alms and to every kind of Christian generosity. The Bishop of Milan was once travelling with his minister, and as they went along the road, beggars asked them for alms. The bishop ordered the minister to give all the money to those poor men. The minister had only three gold coins. He thought for a long time with himself whether he should give away his whole substance to the beggars. At last he reasoned: "So that I and my master do not go hungry and lack food this evening, I will keep one gold coin for ourselves as travelling money." So he counted out two gold coins to them and went on. When they had gone a little further, some noble, pious and good men met the bishop. Because of his piety and his kindness to the poor they knew him well. They therefore ordered that two hundred crowns be counted out to the bishop's minister, so that the bishop might support himself and have resources from which to provide food for the poor. The minister took the money gladly and ran to the bishop, saying: "Lord, these nobles have counted out two hundred crowns to me, to give to you." Then the bishop said: "Ah, you have deceived both me and yourself." "How so?" said the minister. "Did I not order you," he said, "to give all three gold coins to the poor, and you kept one? Did you not do so?" The minister answered: "I confess I did. Because I thought we would lack, I kept one back." "See," said the bishop, "you have harmed both me and yourself. For if you had given the three gold coins, you would have received three hundred.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Carolus Magnus semper in sua aula habuit mensam plenam mendicorum. Et si quando Cæsar cibum in aula caperet, ijdem mendici non procul ab ipsius mensa erant collocati. Venit aliquando ad Carolum Magnum quidam Saracenicus princeps, (quia eo tempore multi iter in Germaniam & uicinas regiones faciebant) qui cùm à Cæsare benignè effet acceptus, & ad prandium inuitatus, princeps in aulam ingressus, omnia diligenter explorat. Cùm autem iam ad locum prandendi uenisset, uidet multos Satrapas holosericò & aureis catenis ornatos, aliis mensis assidere: & inferius mensam plenam uiris, annis pannisq; obsitis. Rogat itaq; Imperatorem, quinam isti pannosi & miseri essent? Respondet: Sunt amici & serui nostri Dei, quem nos Christiani colimus. Rursus interrogat Regem, quinam isti alteri essent, putans Satrapas. Rex inquit: Sunt mei ministri. Tunc ille: O', si tuos ministros praefers amicis & seruis Dei tui, ego nolo amplecti uestram religionem, cùm tam pannosi & miseri sint amici Dei tui, ministri uerò tui tam splendidi & ornati sint. Hic reprehendit hypocrisim beneficentiæ Cæsaris, quam erga pauperes exercebat. Etsi autem uerum est, Cæsarem erga hos pauperes suo quodam consilio honesto beneficentiam declarasse: tamen illud principis dictum nõ est probandum, quòd sit offensus his amicis Dei, ut Regis uerba sonabant, quo minus Christianam religionem amplectandam esse censuit. Debet enim discrimen esse inter mendicum & Regis satrapam.
units.tr: Charles the Great always kept at his court a table full of beggars. And whenever the Emperor took his meal in the hall, these same beggars were seated not far from his own table. Once a certain Saracen prince came to Charles the Great (since at that time many travelled to Germany and the neighbouring regions), and when he had been kindly received by Caesar and invited to dinner, the prince entered the hall and examined everything carefully. When he came to the place where they were to dine, he saw many satraps adorned with silk and gold chains sitting at other tables, and lower down a table full of men worn out with years and clad in rags. So he asked the Emperor who those ragged and wretched men were. He answered: "They are friends and servants of our God, whom we Christians worship." Again he asked the King who the others were, thinking they were satraps. The King said: "They are my ministers." Then he said: "O, if you prefer your ministers to the friends and servants of your God, I do not wish to embrace your religion, since the friends of your God are so ragged and wretched, while your ministers are so splendid and adorned." Here he rebukes the hypocrisy of the Emperor's beneficence, which he showed towards the poor. Although it is true that Caesar displayed his kindness to these poor men for some honourable purpose of his own, yet that remark of the prince is not to be approved, that he was offended by these friends of God, as the King's words sounded, and therefore judged that the Christian religion should not be embraced. For there ought to be a difference between a beggar and a king's satrap.

units.la: Brettæ in mea patria, in bello Bauarico, uicini multi, plures quàm trecenti, capti fuerunt: quos omnes, non solum illæsos, sed etiam gratis, sine λύτρῳ, λὐτρῳ, propter uicinitatem dimiserunt. Et cùm dimitterentur, nihil ab eis petitum est, nisi ut huius beneficentiae in simili uicinorum calamitate memores essent.
units.tr: In my homeland of Brettia, during the Bavarian war, many neighbours, more than three hundred, were taken captive. All of them were released, not only unharmed but also freely, without ransom [λύτρον], out of regard for their neighbourhood. And when they were released, nothing was asked of them except that they remember this kindness in a similar calamity of their neighbours.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Magna est benevolentia Turcicorum militum. Si manipulus habet panem pro uno nummo, diuidunt in decem aut undecim esurientes.
units.tr: The Turkish soldiers are very generous. If a company has a loaf of bread for one coin, they divide it among ten or eleven hungry men.

units.la: Imbre Bascha, quem Solymannus, unū ex praecipuis suis consiliarijs interfecit, magnum hospitale in urbe Thessalonica condidit.
units.tr: Imbre Bascha, whom Suleiman put to death as one of his chief counsellors, built a large hospice in the city of Thessalonica.

units.la: Homerus, χαριζόμενος παρεόντων, gratificans pro praesenti copia: nembt für gůt, was das haus ver mag. Item, Λῶσις ἀγαθὸὶ τε φίλη τε, meum mu nusbonum & amabile.
units.tr: Homer: "gratifying with what is at hand," that is, "take in good part whatever the house can provide." Likewise: "A gift that is good and dear" [Λῶσις ἀγαθὸς τε φίλη τε], that is, my gift is good and lovable.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Forte in uia conueniunt caecus & claudus. ubi cùm sine duce progredi caecus non posset, claudo etiam uehiculo opus esset, retinebatur utrq; suo malo. Videt autem claudus caecum ualidos lacertos, firmos pedes, deniq; robur integrum corporis habere, nec quicquam morbi in eo haerere, nisi quòd oculis captus erat. Quare prudenter inijt rationem, ut inter se communicarent operas, & alter farciret id quod deerat alteri: ut caecus tolleret in humeros claudum, claudus monstrator uiae esset. Exponit suum consilium caeco, & suam operam
units.tr: By chance a blind man and a lame man met on the road. Since the blind man could not go forward without a guide, and the lame man needed a conveyance, both were held back by their own misfortune. The lame man, however, saw that the blind man had strong arms, firm feet, and in short the full vigour of his body, and that no sickness clung to him except that he had lost his sight. So he wisely devised a plan by which they might share their labours, each making up for what the other lacked: the blind man would carry the lame man on his shoulders, and the lame man would show the way. He explains his plan to the blind man, and offers his services.

units.la: {y} Exponit suum consilium caeco operam pollicetur.Etsi fortuna imponebatur non leuis cæco : tamen cùm humanitate socij caperetur, non detrectat hanc conditionem. ac sublato in humeros claudo, pergit, & gubernat eum claudus. Ita amanter communicatis operis, iter suscep-tum conficiunt. Hæc est imago beneficentiæ, & beneuolentiæ mutuæ in Republica.
units.tr: He explains his plan to the blind man and offers his services. Although a not light burden was laid on the blind man, yet, being won over by his companion's kindness, he did not refuse this condition. So, lifting the lame man onto his shoulders, he sets off, and the lame man directs him. Thus, sharing their labours in friendship, they complete the journey they had undertaken. This is an image of beneficence and mutual goodwill in the commonwealth.

units.la: SORDES.
units.tr: SORDES.

units.la: Quidam nobilis uolens frugalis uideri, dicebat: Non decebat familiam recenti pane pascere, citò enim multum deuorat: neq; ministris tam bonus potus esset concedendus, ne assuescant se nimium ingurgitare. Item, frugi paterfamilias non debebat equis tam bonum ac recens pabulum proponere, ne nimium absumant. Hæc ita solo lucro intentus ratiocinabatur, nihil pensi habens, quid noceret aut congrueret eorum ualetudini. Nequaquam hæc fuit frugalitas, sed mera auaricia & sordes.
units.tr: A certain nobleman, wishing to seem thrifty, used to say: "It is not right to feed the household with fresh bread, for people quickly eat large amounts of it. Nor should the servants be given such good drink, lest they get used to swallowing too much. Likewise, a thrifty householder should not offer his horses such good and fresh fodder, lest they consume too much." He reasoned this way, intent only on profit and having no regard for what harmed or suited their health. This was not thrift at all, but plain avarice and meanness.

units.la: Noui duos Canonicos, admodum sordidos. Horum alter, nomine Silberberger, qui reliquit plus quàm triginta millia aureorum, homo artheticus, ita sordidus, auriq; cupidus erat, ut si quando ingentes cruciatus, quos ex morbo perpetiebatur, lenire uellet, iuberet sibi afferri peluim aureis impletam, quibus inuoluebat manus, taliq; inuolutione se in maximis doloribus & corporis ipsius cruciatibus oblectabat. Huius uerò mortui hæredes des fuerunt, Episcopus Treuirensis, & alius vicinus princeps, qui pauperi cognato Canonici tria millia aureorum dabāt, & reliquam hæreditatem ipsi inter se partiebantur. Sic sordidus bene collocauit suam parsimoniam, alijsq; satis opulentis reliquit, quæ ipse tanta auaricia comparserat.
units.tr: I knew two canons who were very stingy. One of them, named Silberberger, who left more than thirty thousand gold coins, was a gout sufferer and so miserly and greedy for gold that whenever he wished to ease the great torments he suffered from his illness, he would have a basin filled with gold coins brought to him. He wrapped his hands in them, and by this wrapping he took comfort in the severe pains and agonies of his body. The heirs of this dead man were the Bishop of Trier and another neighbouring prince. They gave a poor relative of the canon three thousand gold coins and divided the rest of the inheritance between themselves. Thus the miser invested his thrift well, leaving to other, already quite wealthy people what he had acquired with such avarice.

units.la: Noui alium Canonicum, viuentem in his terris Saxonicis, qui accepit hæreditatem doctoris Henningi, æstimatam duodecim millibus aureorum: & ipse iam antea ex suis facultatibus plus habebat, ita ut post mortem reliquerit ultra viginti millia aureorum. Miser ille Canonicus in vita tantis suit sordibus præditus, ut supplicationes soleret cōscribere, etiam pro uno grosso. Hæredem autem constituit spuriam quandam, impudicam mulierem, quæ tantam hæreditatem cum suis similibus breui tempore decoxit.
units.tr: I knew another canon, living in these Saxon lands, who received the inheritance of Doctor Henning, valued at twelve thousand gold coins. He already had more from his own means, so that after his death he left over twenty thousand gold coins. That wretched canon was so afflicted with meanness during his life that he used to write petitions even for a single groschen. He appointed as his heir a certain spurious, shameless woman, who within a short time squandered that great inheritance together with others like herself.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam Episcopus Mersburgensis tam sordidus fuit, ut uenderet partem esocum seu salmonum quos ipsi donauerant principes Anhaldini, & aliquam partem sibi reseruabat.
units.tr: A certain Bishop of Merseburg was so stingy that he sold part of the pike or salmon which the princes of Anhalt had given him, and kept a portion for himself.

units.la: Episcopus Saltzburgensis tā auarus & sordidus fuit, ut equitans abscōdere soleret pileū subpallio, ne pluuia madefieret. Potius uoluit caput madefieri, quàm pileum. Et cùm ei donarētur aurea (quæ Arātia nocāt) poma, iterū ea uendere solebat, ut acciacciperet pecuniā, cùm tamen quotannis haberet reditus uiginti millia florenorum.
units.tr: The Bishop of Salzburg was so avaricious and mean that when riding he would hide his hat under his cloak, lest it get wet in the rain. He preferred to have his head get wet rather than his hat. When golden apples (which they call oranges) were given to him, he used to sell them again to get the money, although he had an annual income of twenty thousand florins.

units.la: Romæ Curtisanus quidam, uel parsimoniæ, uel potius auariciæ causa interdicebat suis famulis, ne biberent uinum. & cum mitteret seruum in cellam allatum uinum, cogebat illum sumere aquam in os, ne uinum biberet: & cum reuertebatur, coram se expuere iubebat. Famulus uerò in cella aliam aquam in uase quodam ponens, sumptam aquam coram domino in cella expuit, & bibit quantum uini uolebat: deinde iterum aliam aquam in os sumptam, reuersus coram domino expuit. Sic facetè illum sordidum hominem decepit.
units.tr: At Rome a certain courtier, from thrift or rather from avarice, forbade his servants to drink wine. When he sent a servant to the cellar to bring up wine, he made him take water into his mouth so that he would not drink wine, and when the servant returned, he ordered him to spit in front of him. The servant, however, in the cellar, putting other water into a jug, spat out the water he had taken in his master's presence, and drank as much wine as he wished. Then he took water into his mouth again, and on returning, spat in front of his master. Thus he wittily deceived that stingy man.

units.la: AVARICIA.
units.tr: AVARICIA.

units.la: Cùm Heydelbergæ frigus incidisset, ibi multi ciues precium uini auxerunt. Illud dux Palatinus, ut iustus princeps, ægrè ferebat, ac iubebat singulorum diuitum cellas perquirere: & ex qualibet cella, in qua multum uini erat inuentum, unum uas extrahere. Præcepit etiā, ut illa uasa in cellam ciuitatis ueherentur, & uinū communi precio, quod antea solitum erat, uenderetur. Ita & reipublicæ bene consuluit, & auaros istos fœneratores iustissimè puniuit, pecuniamq; in usum reipublicæ collocauit.
units.tr: When frost struck at Heidelberg, many citizens there raised the price of wine. The Count Palatine, as a just prince, took this badly and ordered that the cellars of each rich man be searched, and that one vessel be taken out of any cellar in which much wine was found. He also commanded that these vessels be carried into the city cellar and the wine sold at the common price that had been customary before. Thus he both provided well for the commonwealth and most justly punished those avaricious moneylenders, and put the money to public use.

units.la: Anno (ni fallor) 43. cùm diu annonæ caritas fuisset, & tandem ea leniretur, quidam rusticus
units.tr: In the year (if I am not mistaken) 1543, when the dearth of grain had lasted a long time and at last eased, a certain countryman

units.la: in Salinis Saxonicis forte circa Pascha frumentum spe lucrandi in urbem uexerat: quod quia uilius spe sua uendiderat, ualde dolebat. Cum ex urbe domum reuerteretur, sedebat mœstus in curru, & seruum insidentem equis increpat, eo quòd canaret. Iuuenis pergit in proposito canendi. Quare canis? inquit rusticus. Respondit iuuenis: Cur non canerem? quia facta est relaxatio annonæ. Quam hilaritatem rusticus ægreferens, præ mœsticia animi retro de curru se suspendit. Seruus non animaduertens heri tragicam mortem, lætus interea pergit. Paulo uerò post homines ei obuiam uenientes, alloquuntur eum, dicentes: Quare tuum herum suspendisti? Respiciês igitur seruus, uidit herũ suum à curru suspensum trahi. Quapropter perterrefactus, orat illos homines, ut ipsi coram iudicio testimonium perhibeant. quod etiam fecerunt.
units.tr: at the Saxon salt-works, who had by chance carried grain into the town around Easter in hope of profit, was very distressed because he had sold it for less than he had hoped. As he was returning home from the town, he sat sadly in the cart and scolded a servant sitting on the horses because he was singing. The youth kept on singing. "Why do you sing?" said the countryman. The youth replied: "Why should I not sing? Because the price of grain has been relaxed." The countryman, annoyed at this cheerfulness, in his gloom of mind hanged himself from the back of the cart. The servant, not noticing his master's tragic death, went on happily meanwhile. Shortly afterwards some men coming towards him spoke to him, saying: "Why have you hanged your master?" Looking back, the servant saw his master being dragged along, hanging from the cart. Terrified, he begged those men to bear witness before the court, which they also did.

units.la: Historia, à doctore Pomerano recitata.
units.tr: Historia, à doctore Pomerano recitata.

units.la: Rusticus quidam auarus, cùm potiretur multo frumento, fore sperauit ingentem annonæ difficultatem: idq; sedulis uotis petebat. Cùm uerò ea secum ita in animo uolueret, cœpit deniq; miser eò omnem spem & fiduciam conijcere, ac molliter eo animo superbo delectabatur. Tum indics quoq; ingressus horreum suum, illud contëplari, & quasi animam suam uisere solebat. Accidit autem non multo post, quàm rusticus hæc facere cõsueuerat, ut ab amico ad cœnam uocaretur. Ibi largius fortè uino ingurgitatus, reuertens domum, non quiescuit, nisi prius uiso frumento: non curans adhortationem suæ coniugis & familiæ, ut à suo instituto desisteret. Accepta itaq; lucerna, frumentum in horreo uisitat. Cum uerò ingrederetur, & perambularet horreum, admirans suam felicitatem, propter frumenti copiam: ibi temulentus imprudens labitur, & candelâ è manibus abijcit, quæ postea frumentum & horreum incendit & absumpsit, ut miser ægrè fuga sine uitæ dispendio euadere potuerit.
units.tr: A certain covetous countryman, when he had a large store of grain, hoped for a great shortage of grain and prayed for it with eager vows. As he turned these things over in his mind, the wretch at last began to place all his hope and trust in them, and took delight in that proud frame of mind. Then he used to go into his granary, look over his grain and gaze at it, as if he were visiting his own soul. It happened not long after the countryman had begun doing this that a friend invited him to supper. There, having drunk rather freely of wine, he returned home and would not rest until he had first seen the grain. Not heeding the urging of his wife and household that he give up this practice, he took a lamp and went to inspect the grain in the barn. As he went in and walked about the barn, marvelling at his own good fortune because of the abundance of grain, he slipped in his drunkenness and heedlessly dropped the candle from his hands. It afterwards set fire to the grain and the barn and consumed them, so that the wretch with difficulty escaped by flight, without losing his life.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam rusticus ex quibusdam signis coniectãs futurã esse annonæ caritatem, retinuerat apud se frumentum, sperans se inde magnum lucrũ & magnas diuitias consecuturum. Cum igitur ascendisset aliquando in granarium, uolens se oblectare aspectu frumenti: ibi diabolus ita uexauit eum, offundens etiam oculis caliginem, ne frumenti quicquam uideret. Qua re subitò terrore perculsus, se in granario suspendit.
units.tr: A certain countryman, conjecturing from some signs that a dearth of grain was coming, had kept his grain back, hoping to gain a great profit and great riches from it. Once, when he had gone up into the granary, wanting to delight himself with the sight of his grain, the devil so tormented him, pouring a darkness over his eyes, that he could see none of the grain at all. Struck suddenly with terror, he hanged himself in the granary.

units.la: Cùm Iudæi rursus in Hasiam reciperentur, forte ad nostrum amicum Dionysium dicebam: Quare permittitis ut concedantur sedes Iudæis in Hasia? Respondit: Profectò ego uehementissimè reprereprehendi & dissuasi, tamen nihil potui efficere. Quare? Tu ille: Quia unctio docet & efficit omnia, uidelicet, quòd manus bene ungātur auro.
units.tr: When the Jews were again being admitted into Hesse, I happened to say to our friend Dionysius: "Why do you allow Jews to be given settlements in Hesse?" He replied: "I strongly objected to it and argued against it, yet I could achieve nothing." "Why?" I asked. He said: "Because ointment teaches and accomplishes everything, namely, that hands are well greased with gold."

units.la: Memini multa exempla, ubi magistratus emit omne sal quod in oppida inuehitur: & postea maiori precio, quando nullum adest, uendit. Prohibet etiam, ne peregrinum sine ipsius consensu uendatur. Hæc est magna auaricia & iniusticia illorum hominum.
units.tr: I remember many examples where a magistrate buys up all the salt that is brought into the towns, and afterwards sells it at a higher price when none is to be had. He also forbids it to be sold to a stranger without his consent. This is the great greed and injustice of those men.

units.la: M. Antonius quadam auaricia aliquando Romæ omne frumentum, quod inuenire poterat, coemebat: postea cùm nullum amplius esset, multo maioris, quàm unquam uenditum erat, uendebat.
units.tr: Through a certain avarice, Marcus Antonius once bought up in Rome all the grain he could find; afterwards, when none was left, he sold it at a much higher price than it had ever been sold for before.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Tanta fuit auaricia Vespasiani, ut etiam census cloacis imponeret: & si potuisseт, etiam uentris crepitibus imposuisset. Quicunq; enim cloacam habuit, illum oportuit Vespasiano quotannis certam pecuniæ summam pro ea soluere. Et cùm aliquando propter istas sordes indignas Imperator à filio reprehenderetur: pater accipiens pugnum plenū aureis, quos ex cloacis collegerat, admhibuit naso filij, inquiens: Fili olfacias, num hæc pecunia oleat cloacam? Sed filij tanta fuit beneficentia & clementia erga subditos ac pauperes, ut si unum diem prætermisisset, in quo nō aliquid beneficij in paupepauperes, uel alios suos subditos collocasset, dixerit, se male illum diem perdidisse.
units.tr: The avarice of Vespasian was so great that he even put a tax on the sewers; and if he could have, he would have put one on the crepitations of the belly. For whoever had a sewer had to pay Vespasian a certain sum of money each year for it. And when the Emperor was once rebuked by his son for these shameful, unworthy dealings, the father took a fistful of gold coins, which he had collected from the sewers, and held it to the son's nose, saying: "Son, smell it: does this money stink of the sewer?" But the son was so generous and merciful towards his subjects and the poor that if he had let a single day pass in which he had not done some kindness for the poor or bestowed some benefit on his other subjects, he used to say that he had wasted that day.

units.la: Olim tempore Rudolphi imperatoris, magnu quidam erat, si quaedam regio (quam propter certas causas non nomino) cogebatur quindecim milia aureorum in una pensione dare. Iam id pro nihilo habetur. Non enim crederem talem pecuniam iam sufficere ad unum conuiuium, seu (ut uocat) ad unam banketam. Si non colligunt ex eadem regione tres thonnas auri, nihil est. Ita crescunt seruitutes, & exhauriuntur regiones, ut aliquando contra communem hostem Turcam nihil facultatum habituri simus. Hæc non malicia quadam in contumeliam ullius dico: sed cum aliis bonis uiris calamitates deploro secuturas.
units.tr: In the time of the Emperor Rudolph, it was a great matter if a certain region (which I do not name, for certain reasons) was compelled to give fifteen thousand gold coins in a single payment. Now that is counted as nothing. I would not believe that such a sum is now enough for one banquet, or (as they call it) one feast. If they do not collect from the same region three tons of gold, it is nothing. Thus burdens grow and regions are drained dry, so that one day we shall have no resources left against the common enemy, the Turk. I say this not out of any malice, to insult anyone, but lamenting, together with other good men, the calamities that will follow.

units.la: COLL. Lectori.
units.tr: COLL. To the reader.

units.la: Hic tria exempla pertinentia ad locum de diuortio (quem in sexto præcepto inuenies) irrepserunt: quae si legeris, ad eundem referto.
units.tr: Three examples concerning the topic of divorce (which you will find under the sixth commandment) have crept in here. If you read them, refer them to that place.

units.la: Turcis est grata licentia ducendi uxores, quot quisq; uoluit, quia apud Machometistas non est coniugium. Ducunt enim quot uolunt: & dimittunt coniuges sine causa, quando uolunt. Sed lex Moysi non concessit diuortia sine causa.
units.tr: The Turks have the freedom to take as many wives as each one wishes, because among the Mohammedans there is no true marriage. For they take as many as they like, and they dismiss their wives without cause whenever they wish. But the law of Moses did not allow divorce without cause.

units.la: Non omnis qui abest à sua coniuge, est desertor, & perfidiosè abest. Vt, cùm absunt quidam propter militiā, alij propter legationes necessa-rias reipublicæ: interdum etiam propter priuatas negociationes, ut mercatores. Habent etiā illa su-um modum. Certè potestas debet uti seueritate in his rebus. Ante paucos annos quidam conciona-tor in oppido Zeitz duxit uxorem. Aliquanto post uenit altera seu prior uxor, & magistratui di-xit, hunc esse suum maritum. Senatus rem domino Episcopo Iulio Pflug exposuit. Hic re intellecta, curauit eum includi in carcerem: & rectè fecit. Potuisset uti maiori seueritate, sed non uoluit fa-cere, ne diceretur odio doctrinæ secisse. Expulit eum deinde, dimisitq; incolumem. Iure usitato in legibus, quarum hodie usus est in Romano iure, po-tuisset decollari. Magna est malicia multorum ho-minum, à suis coniugibus temerè migrantium.
units.tr: Not everyone who is absent from his wife is a deserter, or absent treacherously. For some are absent because of military service, others because of necessary embassies on behalf of the commonwealth, and sometimes also for private business, as merchants are. Even these absences have their limits, and the authorities certainly ought to act with severity in such matters. A few years ago a certain preacher in the town of Zeitz took a wife. Some time later his earlier wife came and told the magistrate that this man was her husband. The council laid the matter before the lord Bishop Julius Pflug. He, having understood the case, had the man shut up in prison, and he did right. He could have used greater severity, but he chose not to, lest it be said that he had acted out of hatred for the doctrine. He then expelled him and let him go unharmed. By the customary law of the statutes, which are in use today in Roman law, he could have had him beheaded. Great is the wickedness of many men who rashly abandon their wives.

units.la: Ante aliquot annos, pastor in Dieben coniun-xerat personas quasdā satis temerè. & scripsit li-teras, in quibus expressè posuerat hanc sententiā: Ego episcopus in Dieben coniunxi has personas, hoc tempore. Si quis petit huius mei propositi ra-tionem, ueniat ad me in meum episcopatum, ubi ipse exponam mcum in hac causa iudicium. Illu-strissimus Princeps collocauit eum in carcerem Torgæ: & sic uenit in ipsius episcopatum. Postea uerò suit pro eo deprecator.
units.tr: Some years ago a minister in Dieben had joined certain persons together rather rashly, and he wrote a letter in which he had expressly set down this statement: "I, the bishop in Dieben, have joined these persons together at this time. If anyone asks for the reason for this my action, let him come to me in my bishopric, where I myself will set out my judgment in this matter." The most illustrious Prince had him placed in prison at Torgau, and so he came into his own bishopric. Afterwards, however, someone interceded on his behalf.

units.la: Cùm Alphonsus rex Hispaniæ iter faceret in regno suo Neapolitano, occurrit ei mulier eiu-lans, & conquerens, quòd pastor illius loci nō uel-let sepelire ipsius maritum, nisi daret tantum pe-cuniæ, quantum non posset soluere. Rex statim iu-bet adduci sacerdotem, & mandat ei fodere sepul-chrum. Sacerdos nihil mali metuens, fodit. Cùm itaq; effodisset, iubet eum descēdere in sepulchrū, & præcipit ministris circa sacerdotem tam mul-tum terræ conijcere, quàm erat egestum, ut ibi te-neretur captiuus. Sic uiuus stetit in sepulchro to-tum diem, & integram noctem. Porrò cùm ille iam putaret sibi iam moriendum esse: postridie iuf-fit Rex refodi terram, ut iterum sacerdos exiret sepulchro: admonuitq; ut meminissët illius pœnæ, & sibi in posterum caueret, ne unquam de ipso ta-lis querela audiretur.
units.tr: When Alphonsus, king of Spain, was travelling through his kingdom of Naples, a woman met him, wailing and complaining that the minister of that place would not bury her husband unless she gave him more money than she could pay. The king at once ordered the priest to be brought and commanded him to dig the grave. The priest, fearing no harm, dug. When he had dug it out, the king ordered him to go down into the grave, and instructed the attendants to throw back around the priest as much earth as had been dug out, so that he would be held there captive. Thus he stood alive in the grave for the whole day and the whole night. But when he already thought he was about to die, the king ordered the earth to be dug out again on the next day, so that the priest might come out of the grave once more; and he admonished him to remember that punishment, and to take care for the future, lest any such complaint about him should ever be heard again.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Antonius, collega Augusti Imperatoris, fuit po-tens dominus: possedit Asiam, Græciam, Aegyptū. Propemodum habuit tantum, quantum Turcicus imperator: & tamen præ nimia auaricia non fuit contentus illis facultatibus, ita ut moueret bella non necessaria: quæ cum non succederent, sibi ipsi mortem consciunt.
units.tr: Antony, colleague of the Emperor Augustus, was a powerful lord. He possessed Asia, Greece and Egypt, and had almost as much as the Turkish emperor. Yet from excessive avarice he was not content with these resources, and so he waged unnecessary wars. When these did not succeed, he brought about his own death.

units.la: Bulgarus, cùm interrogaret auarum principē, quo modo opes ipsius perijssent? respondit: Aua-ricia & temulentia. Sic nos etiam auaricia & te-mu le nmulentia perimus: neq; magnitudinem animorum neq; pecuniam habemus.
units.tr: Bulgarus, when he asked a greedy prince how his wealth had been lost, received the answer: avarice and drunkenness. So we too perish through avarice and drunkenness; we have neither greatness of spirit nor money.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Venetorum prouerbium: Prima pompa parua fuit, & ibi sunt factæ Venetiæ: deinde fuit mediocris, tunc creuerunt Venetiæ: deniq; maxima fuit, in qua iterum Venetiæ sunt euersæ.
units.tr: A proverb of the Venetians: the first pomp was small, and then Venice was founded; then it was moderate, and Venice grew; finally it was at its greatest, and in that state Venice was again overthrown.

units.la: Nouistis fabulam Fortunati, qui reliquit filijs suis duos thesauros. unum marsupium, ex quo poterant proferri decem ducati, quotiescunq; posset for uellet: alterum pileum, quem cùm accipiebat aliquis, erat ubicunque uolebat. Ille, qui hoc figmentum excogitauit, uoluit significare duas maximas cupiditates: unam, appetitione facultatum inexplebilem: alteram, curiositatem. Omnes enim sumus natura auari & curiosi, & hæc est excellentium ingeniorum magis quàm aliorum: auaricia uero magis est sordidorum.
units.tr: You know the fable of Fortunatus, who left his sons two treasures: one a purse, from which ten ducats could be drawn whenever one wished; the other a hat, which whoever wore it could be wherever he wished. The one who devised this fiction meant to signify two very great desires: one, the appetite for wealth, which can never be satisfied; the other, curiosity. For all of us are naturally avaricious and curious, and this is more the case with men of outstanding talent than with others; avarice, however, is more characteristic of the base.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Summum quæstum Papa in religione exercuit. Cæsares, Reges, suas monetas excudunt ex auro & argento. Papa uero ex omnibus creaturis suam monetam cudit: ex indulgētijs, ceremonijs, missis, sacramentis, cibis, pœnitentia, clauibus, & huiusmodi pluribus. Ex solo uero baptismo, nihil potuit mercari, quia infantes nudi & pauperes nascūtur: ideoq; nihil habēt quod possint exponere
units.tr: The Pope has carried on the greatest trade in religion. Caesars and kings strike their coins from gold and silver, but the Pope mints his coin from every creature: from indulgences, ceremonies, masses, sacraments, foods, repentance, the keys, and many other things of this kind. From baptism alone he could make no profit, because infants are born naked and poor, and so have nothing they can put up for sale.

units.la: Non procul à patria mea, noui mangonem, qui emebat pessimos equos, pro vtilissimo precio: eosq; deinde pulchrè ornatos, & assuefactos ad saltationes (sicut illi nebulones facere solent) cum uiatores uel aurigæ præterabularent, producere et in gyrũ agere solebat, ac ita homines decipiebat. Vnde non raro fiebat, ut emens equum ab eo, ut x ad meam patriam perueniret, quin equus cadens morereretur.
units.tr: Not far from my homeland I knew a horse-dealer who bought the worst horses at a very cheap price. He then decorated them handsomely and trained them to dance, as those rascals usually do. When travellers or carters went past, he would bring them out and drive them in a circle, and so deceive people. Hence it often happened that someone who bought a horse from him, in order to get it home to my homeland, found that the horse fell down and died.

units.la: Eremita quidam, cum aliquantum mellis ex alueis apum, quos forte habebat, collegisset, lætatus est istis diuitijs, dicens: Se iturum in urbem, & uenditurum mel illud, ac pro illa pecunia rursus empturum oues: quæ porrò cum ipsi peperissent agnos, se uenditurum eos, & ducturum uxorẽ. Sed econtrà uenit ei in mentem: Quid si illa mulier & liberi, quos ex ipsa genueris, non erunt tibi mori-geri? Sic, inquit, eam & liberos percutiam. simulque sumit baculum, & percutiens ollam, in qua erat mel, fregit eam. Ita stultos spes uana fallere sæpe solet.
units.tr: A certain hermit, having gathered a fair amount of honey from the hives of bees which he happened to have, rejoiced in these riches. He said that he would go into the town and sell the honey, and with that money buy sheep again; and when the sheep had borne lambs, he would sell those too and take a wife. But then it came into his mind: what if that woman and the children he begot from her would not obey him? "So," he said, "I shall strike her and the children." At the same moment he took up a staff, and striking the jar in which the honey was, broke it. Thus empty hope often deceives fools.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Episcopus Pragensis, tempore Ioannis Hus, dictus Albiacus, unicum extremæ auariciæ barathrũ fuit. hic claues cellæ uinariæ nulli alteri quàm sibi ipsi credidit, animalia uiuentia dono accepta mox uendidit: & quia coquus ipsius sumptuosior esse didi dixerat, hoc dimisso, abiectâ anu culinæ suæ præfecit. Interrogatus aliquando, sonorum omnium quem molestissimè audiret? Maxillarum, inquit, ossa frangentium.
units.tr: Albik, bishop of Prague in the time of John Hus, was a unique abyss of extreme avarice. He trusted the keys of his wine cellar to no one but himself, and he soon sold any living animals he received as gifts. Once his cook said that he was too extravagant, so he dismissed him and put a lowly old woman in charge of his kitchen. When he was asked once which of all sounds he found most unbearable, he replied: "The sound of men crunching bones with their jaws."

units.la: DECEPTIONES ET elusiones.
units.tr: Deceptions and evasions.

units.la: Anno 1530. in conuentu Augustano, cùm Carolus V. Imperator eò profecturus esset, facta est contentio inter Electores & Cardinalem Campegium, eo quòd hic uellet equitare ad latus Imperatoris: illi uerò resistentes, sibi eundè honorem vendicarent. Tandem uerò obtinuerunt Electores antiquam & usitatam consuetudinem, ut latus Imperatoris clauderent duo Electores, Moguntinensis & Coloniensis. Postea sequebatur rex Ferdinandus, & ad illius latus Cardinalis Campegius. In itinere autem, antequam ueniret Augustam, fossores Swacenses dono obtulerunt Imperatori amplam & rotundam massam auri, cui insignia imperij artificiosè erant insculpta. Imperator postquam donum grato animo accepisset, statim illum accessit Cardinalis Campegius, orans: Quoniam multis uerbis abundanter Imperator hactenus suum animum erga Romanam curiam declarasset, quòd ipsi optimè uellet: ut hunc suum animum hoc etiā dono ostenderet, & Romanæ curiæ ad pignus quasi beneuolentiæ hanc auri massam (quæ constabat ter mille florenis) donaret. Imperator, qui etiam sciebat, ad quid utilis esset illa massa, & tamen aperte nolebat ipsi denegare, inquit: Hoc donum iam ordinarium esse suæ Cæsareæ Maiestatis coniugi, ideoq; se non posse repetere, ipsiq; in hac re gratificari: promittere se (ut antea) Romanæ curiæ suam benevolentiam in alia quacunque re. Est exemplum ambitionis & auariciæ in Cardinali, & neutrum tamen successit: deinde in facto Imperatoris est pulchrum exemplum parsimoniæ.
units.tr: In 1530, at the Diet of Augsburg, when the Emperor Charles V was about to set out for it, a dispute arose between the Electors and Cardinal Campeggio, because he wished to ride at the Emperor's side. The Electors resisted and claimed that honour for themselves. In the end the Electors secured the ancient and customary arrangement, that two Electors, those of Mainz and Cologne, should flank the Emperor. King Ferdinand followed next, and beside him rode Cardinal Campeggio. On the journey, before he reached Augsburg, the miners of Schwaz presented the Emperor with a large, round mass of gold, on which the insignia of the empire had been artfully engraved. After the Emperor had graciously accepted the gift, Cardinal Campeggio approached him at once and asked that, since the Emperor had already declared his goodwill towards the Roman curia in many words, he should now show that same feeling by a gift, and give this mass of gold, which weighed three thousand florins, to the Roman curia as a pledge of goodwill. The Emperor, who also knew what purpose that mass would serve, yet did not want to refuse him openly, replied that this gift was already set aside for the Empress, his Imperial Majesty's wife, and so he could not take it back or grant the request in this matter. He promised, as before, to show the Roman curia his goodwill in any other matter. This is an example of the ambition and greed of a cardinal, yet neither succeeded; and in the Emperor's action there is a fine example of thrift.

units.la: Eccius in eodem conuentu Augustano, anno 1530. petiuit sacerdotium, quod tunc uacabat Augustæ, à Cardinali Campegio: simulq; dixit, se multum laborare pro Romana ecclesia, & sustinere multa & magna onera, petiuitq; ut iam sui rationem haberet. Respondit Cardinalis: Bene, tu habebis sacerdotium. Eccius abit, putans rem esse certam. Interea uenit alius nobilis, homo uafer, & affert quadringentos florenos, dicens: Domine Cardinalis, ego peto mihi dari hoc sacerdotium. Respondit Cardinalis: Ego iam promisi alteri, idem petenti. Post longam uerò excusationem Cardinalis, ille astutus nobilis dicit: Ah rogo te, ne mihi hoc officium deneges. Facilime componi potest inter te & Eccium: simulq; dat ei consilium, quo utatur in reuocandis promissis. Dicito, inquit, Ducem Bauariæ publicis literis pro alio quodam intercefintercessisse, cui illud sacerdotium præcæteris tradi necesse sit. Eccius post dies tres vel quatuor iterum accedit Cardinalem Campegium, & petit sibi dari testimonium, seu literas quibus certò committeretur ac traderetur ipsi sacerdotium. Cardinalis verò attulit excusationem, quam à nobili edoctus erat. Eccius autem propter eam indignam repulsam, acerrima ira commotus, venit ad Philippum Melanchthonem, aliosq; partis Lutheranæ, simul forte congregatos, & conquestus apud ipsos de tanta contumelia, tandem adiecit: Quid vos mihi dabitis, ut deseram illos nebulones, & vestras partes sequar ac defendam? Ad quæ Philippus: Si causa nostra est vera, cur non sponte tueris veritatem? Ipse verò videns se suo testimonio convictum, primò quidem paululum attonitus & cogitabundus sedit, ac quasi obmutuit. Tandem verò paulum se recolligens, inquit: Non tamen omnia sunt vera quæ defendi possunt. ac sic ab ipsis recessit.
units.tr: At the same Diet of Augsburg in 1530, Eck asked Cardinal Campeggio for the priesthood that was then vacant at Augsburg. At the same time he said that he had laboured hard for the Roman Church and endured many and great burdens, and he asked that the cardinal now take account of him. The cardinal replied: "Good, you shall have the priesthood." Eck left, thinking the matter settled. Meanwhile another nobleman, a shrewd man, came and brought four hundred florins, saying: "Lord Cardinal, I ask that this priesthood be given to me." The cardinal replied: "I have already promised it to another who has asked for it." After a long excuse from the cardinal, that crafty nobleman said: "Ah, I beg you, do not deny me this office. It can very easily be settled between you and Eck." And he gave him a plan to use for withdrawing his promises: "Say," he said, "that the Duke of Bavaria has interceded by public letter on behalf of someone else, to whom that priesthood must be given before all others." Three or four days later Eck again approached Cardinal Campeggio and asked for a testimonial, or a letter, by which the priesthood would be definitely committed and handed over to him. But the cardinal offered the excuse he had been taught by the nobleman. Eck, enraged at this unworthy rebuff, went to Philip Melanchthon and others of the Lutheran party, who happened to be gathered together, and complained to them of such an insult. At last he added: "What will you give me, if I desert those scoundrels and follow and defend your side?" Philip replied: "If our cause is true, why do you not willingly defend the truth?" Eck, seeing himself convicted by his own testimony, at first sat for a little while astonished and deep in thought, as if struck dumb. Then, gathering himself a little, he said: "Yet not everything that can be defended is true." And so he withdrew from them.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam iactans se esse fratrem Maximiliani Imperatoris, venit ad eum, petiturus ut partem bonorum suorum inopi fratri donaret. Quærente Imperatore, quis nam suus pater esset? Respondit: Noster omnium pater Adam fuit. Ibi Cæsar duos crucigeros ipsi numerari iussit. Ægrius autem mendico ferente, tam parum sibi donari: Reliquos quoq; nostros fratres accede, inquit Maximilianus. quòd si singuli tibi tantum dederint, longè meris ditior. Simul quoq; danda est opera, ut sit unde reliquis dem. Longè enim minores sunt meæ opes, quàm ut singulis fratribus tantum largiri queam.
units.tr: A man boasting that he was a brother of the Emperor Maximilian came to him, intending to ask that he give part of his goods to his poor brother. When the Emperor asked who his father was, he replied: "Our common father of all is Adam." Then the Emperor ordered two kreuzers to be counted out to him. The beggar took it badly that he was given so little, and the Emperor said: "Go to our other brothers too. If each of them gives you as much, you will be far richer than I am. At the same time I must also take care to have something to give the others. My means are far too small for me to be able to bestow so much on each brother."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam magni nominis Princeps, in sua aula habuit Doctorem: qui cùm primùm in aulam uenisset, extremæ inopiæ fuit: sed cùm coepisset crescere in aula, ita ut fit, postea tantas opes collegit, ut possideret centena millia florenorum. Dominus autem donauerat ipsi monasterium, reditibus satis multis abundans. Postea verò cùm uideret Princeps, eum cumulare ingentes opum aceruos: tunc libenter illos Ecclesiasticos reditus ad se retraxisset. Dixit itaq; ad Doctorem: Domine Doctor, ego miror, quòd ita secura conscientia possis bona ecclesiastica possidere, postquam ex diuina gratia alioqui satis abundè habes, unde pro statu tuo magnificè uiuas. Respondit Doctor: Ne miretur T. C. quia dulcis est panis Christi. Dominus porrò latius cum eo disceptauit, ratus se ipsi persuasurum, ut monasterium sibi redderet. Subiecit igitur: Domine Doctor, magnum profectò peccatum est, tenere bona Ecclesiastica. Doctor, ut ualebat ingenio, genio, respondit Domino: Si peccatum est metenere bona ecclesiastica, maius peccatum habet is qui mihi hæc tradidit. Ita latenter Dominum ipsum taxabat, & retinebat bona Ecclesiastica.
units.tr: A certain Prince of great renown had a teacher at his court. When he first came to the court he was in extreme poverty, but once he began to rise there, as often happens, he afterwards amassed such wealth that he possessed a hundred thousand florins. The lord had also given him a monastery, which yielded a fairly large income. Later, when the Prince saw him piling up huge heaps of wealth, he wanted to take back those ecclesiastical revenues for himself. So he said to the teacher: "Master Doctor, I am amazed that you can hold church property with a clear conscience, since by God's grace you already have more than enough to live splendidly according to your station." The teacher replied: "Let T. C. not be surprised, for the bread of Christ is sweet." The lord then argued the point further, thinking he could persuade him to give back the monastery. So he added: "Master Doctor, it is truly a great sin to hold church property." The teacher, as far as his wit allowed, answered the lord: "If it is a sin to keep church property, then he who handed it over to me has the greater sin." In this way he tacitly rebuked the lord himself and kept the church property.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Abbas quidam habuit triplex uinum in suo monasterio, unum quidem insigniter bonum, aliud malum, aliud mediocre: prout autem ueniebat ad eum hospites, ita apponebat unum, aut bonum, aut malum, conueniens cuiusq; dignitati. Habebat autem idem Abbas famulum, quem ita instruxit in apportando uino, ut quotiescunq; afferri uellet malum uinum, diceret ad famulum: Quomodo uales famule, heu ut cunq;. Famulus cùm audiret uocabulum Vtcunq;, intelligebat malum sibi esse apportandum. Cùm autem ad famulum, Quid gloriaris? intelligebat, mediocre sibi esse apponendum. Si uero diceret, Noli me tangere: significauit, optimum uinum esse apponendum. Iste Abbas aliquoties ad se inuitabat quendam Poetam, cui semper apponebat mediocre uinum, dicens famulo: Quid gloriaris. Poeta sentiens dolum, cogitat, quid sibi faciendum esset, ut aliquando etiam optimo uino potiretur. Cumq; iterum inuitaretur ab Abbate, & Abbas more solito diceret ad famulum: Quid gloriaris: prorupit Poeta in hæc uerba, inquiens:
units.tr: A certain abbot had three kinds of wine in his monastery: one that was excellent, one that was bad, and one that was middling. Whenever guests came to him, he served one of them, either the good or the bad, according to the dignity of each. This abbot had a servant whom he trained in serving the wine in such a way that whenever he wished the bad wine to be brought, he would say to the servant: "How are you, servant? Alas, however (utcunque)." When the servant heard the word "however" (utcunque), he understood that the bad wine was to be brought. When he said to the servant, "Why do you boast?", the servant understood that the middling wine was to be served. But if he said, "Do not touch me," he signified that the best wine was to be served. This abbot often invited a certain poet to his table, and always served him the middling wine, saying to the servant: "Why do you boast?" The poet, sensing the trick, considered what he must do so as to obtain the best wine at least once. When he was invited again by the abbot, and the abbot, as usual, said to the servant, "Why do you boast?", the poet burst out with these words:

units.la: Non conuertaris, si fers mihi Quid gloriaris: Si fers utcunq;, tollat hunc dæmon utrunq;: Ibis ad astra poli, si fers, me tangere noli.
units.tr: "Do not turn, if you bring me 'Why do you boast'; if you bring 'however', may a demon carry off both; you will go to the stars of heaven if you bring 'Do not touch me'."

units.la: Id est, optimum uinum. His rhythmis seu uersi-bus impetrauit, ut Abbas diceret famulo, Me tan-gere noli: iubens ut optimum uinum proponeret.
units.tr: That is, the best wine. By these rhythms, or verses, he obtained that the abbot told the servant, "Do not touch me," ordering that the best wine be set before him.

units.la: Rex Galliæ, pater Francisci, indigebat subitò pecunia. itaq; per alium quendā ad suum Cancel-larium ex Roma, & per postam mittit ei literas, significans Papam esse mortuum. Lectis literis, mox properat Cancellarius ad Regem, ei nuncia-turus tanquam aliquid noui. Rex legit literas, si-mulans se nescire, & interrogat quid sibi sit faci-endum? Respondit Cancellarius, consultissimum esse mittere Romam Legatum, & aliquem consti-tuere Papam, qui sit à partibus regis Galliæ. At rex: Ad eam rem opus est pecunia, sicut dicitur: Nulla pecunia est satis magna, aspiranti ad Pon-tificatum. Cancellarius dicit, se adhuc habere duas thonnas auri, utrum sufficerent? Respondit Rex: Bene est, & ego aliquid pecuniæ addam. Cura igi-tur unam thonnam auri perferri ad me. Postquam eam Rex acceperat, subornat alium nuncium asse-rentem ei literas, Papam adhuc uiuere, & non esse mortuum. Egregium sanè inuentum, quo quasi cornicum oculos confixit, & auarum per suam a-ariciam decepit.
units.tr: The King of France, father of Francis, suddenly needed money. So, through another messenger, he sent letters by post from Rome to his Chancellor, signifying that the Pope was dead. When the Chancellor had read the letters, he hurried at once to the King, to report it to him as something new. The King read the letters, pretending not to know, and asked what should be done. The Chancellor replied that it would be most advisable to send a legate to Rome and to set up as Pope someone who would be on the side of the King of France. But the King said: "That matter requires money, as the saying goes: no sum is large enough for one who aspires to the papacy." The Chancellor said that he still had two tuns of gold; would they be enough? The King replied: "Good, and I will add some money myself. Have one tun of gold brought to me." After the King had received it, he suborned another messenger, who declared that the Pope was still alive and not dead. A truly excellent invention, by which, as it were, he blinded the eyes of the crows, and through his own cunning deceived the greedy.

units.la: Audiui ex Stœflero, optimo uiro, Mathematico præstanpræstantissimo, qui fuit familiaris Episcopo Constantiensi, quòd Episcopus aliquando allocutus sit ipsum his uerbis: Stœflere, pecunia indigeo, quid consulis? Respõdit Stœflerus: Domine Episcope, habes in tua diœcesi multos sacrificulos & sacerdotes, apud se concubinas alentes. illis præcipe serió ut dimittant eas: & si nolint, redimant eas pecunia. Ita factum est, & Stœflerus fuit unus ex collectoribus illius pecuniæ. Sic magnam pecuniam collegerunt.
units.tr: I heard from Stoeffler, an excellent man and most eminent mathematician, who was on intimate terms with the Bishop of Constance, that the Bishop once addressed him in these words: "Stoeffler, I am in need of money. What do you advise?" Stoeffler replied: "My lord Bishop, you have in your diocese many petty priests and priests keeping concubines at home. Order them earnestly to dismiss them; and if they are unwilling, let them redeem them with money." So it was done, and Stoeffler was one of the collectors of that money. In this way they collected a large sum.

units.la: Cuidam pauperi, casu in hortum incidit lepus: quo capto, invitauit suos vicinos ad venationem in suo horto felicè. Ille postea re manifestata, accusatur in aula. Aula scribit ad Senatum, ut istũ pauperem puniret. Cum id non fecisset Senatus, putàs satis esse pro delicto tali, quòd spacio octo dierum luisset pœnas in carcere: Cancellaria rescisçens nõ gravius ipsum punitum esse, postulat, ut Senatus ducentos florenos pro tanto delicto largiatur: verùm ideo faciebat Cancellaria, ut pecuniam adipisceretur. Quia delinquens erat pauper, & non habebat pecuniam, ideo postulabat à Senatu.
units.tr: A certain poor man had a hare chance into his garden; having caught it, he invited his neighbours to a hunt in his garden, and it went happily. Afterwards, when the matter became known, he was accused at court. The court wrote to the Senate that this poor man should be punished. When the Senate did not do so, judging that eight days' imprisonment was enough punishment for such an offence, the Chancery, learning that he had not been punished more severely, asked the Senate to grant two hundred florins for so great an offence. But the Chancery did this so that it might obtain the money. Because the offender was poor and had no money, it therefore demanded it from the Senate.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Augustæ cùm in concursu hastili forte ex equo delaberetur filius Imperatoris Philippus rex Hispaniarum, ita ut etiam ex lapsu immineret ei periculum: accurrit unus ex cõsiliarijs Imperatoris, & ut commodius eum subleuaret, deponit ab humeris preciosam uestem, qua erat indutus: hanc continuò sustulit quidam Hispanus, & se subduxit.
units.tr: At Augsburg, during a joust, the Emperor's son Philip, king of Spain, happened to fall from his horse when his lance slipped, and the fall put him in real danger. One of the Emperor's counsellors ran up, and to lift him more easily he took off the precious garment he was wearing. A certain Spaniard snatched it up at once and slipped away.

units.la: Cùm essemus Augustæ in conuentu, ibi nobilis quidam intrat in tonstrinam, & ad fores alligat equum. Præteriēs forte Hispanus, soluto statim freno equum ascendit, ac sic discedit, nemine animad-uertente. Hæc fuit elegans ars Hispani. Tale furtum fuit κλοπὴ, non grassatio.
units.tr: While we were at Augsburg for the Diet, a certain nobleman went into a barber's shop and tied his horse to the door. A Spaniard happened to pass by, loosened the bridle at once, mounted the horse and rode off, and nobody noticed. This was the Spaniard's clever trick. Such a theft was stealth [κλοπὴ], not robbery by force.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Venerunt aliqui Hispani ad quendam honestum uirum, ciuem Salitzburgensem, petentes ut ipsis daret pro quingentis coronatis quadringentos Ioachimicos: quos dicebant ipsis maiori usui fore in Germania, quàm coronatos. simulq; stipulati sunt, ut conseruaret coronatos ad annum, ut cùm redirent post annum, ac rursus tot Ioachimicos afferrent, ille recepta sua pecunia, ipsis uicissim coronatos redderet. Si uerò non reuerterentur, ut ipse pecuniam seruaret. Ille homo credens eos nunquam redituros, & inhians pecuniæ, iussit ut Hispani prius suam numerarent pecuniam, & largitur eis tot Ioachimicos. Sed Hispani fecerunt aptè alium quendam saccum, priori similem, & eiusdem ponderis, in quo plumbum posuerunt: eumq; magna celeritate supponunt in locum alterius, & abeunt, ac bonus ille uir feruat saccũ. Elapso uero anno, cum nullus Hispanorũ rediret, aperit saccũ, & inuenit aliquos coronatos in superiore sacci parte positos, in inferiore uero plumbum esse cernit, atq; ita se delusum ab Hispanis intelligit. Tales sunt artifices Hispani, quidã:nam inter ipsos etiã boni aliqui reperiũtur.
units.tr: Some Spaniards came to an honest man, a citizen of Salzburg, and asked him to give them 400 Joachimsthalers in exchange for 500 crowns. They said these coins would be more useful to them in Germany than crowns. They also agreed that he should keep the crowns for a year, so that when they came back after a year and brought as many Joachimsthalers, he would return their crowns after taking back his money. If they did not return, he was to keep the money. The man, believing they would never come back and greedy for the money, ordered the Spaniards to count out their money first, and then handed over the Joachimsthalers. But the Spaniards had cleverly prepared another sack, like the first and of the same weight, filled with lead. They quickly put it in place of the other and left. The good man kept the sack. When the year had passed and none of the Spaniards returned, he opened the sack and found some crowns placed in the upper part, while he saw lead in the lower part, and so he understood he had been fooled by the Spaniards. Such are the Spanish craftsmen, some of them, for among them too some good men are to be found.

units.la: Dionysius Syracusanus, cum indigeret pecunia, uarijs usus est artibus, ut eam à subditis extorqueret. Venit igitur in publicum, dicens: Ceterem ad se uenisse, & iussisse omnes matronas afferre sua ornamenta, ut festum Cereri instituerent, eamq; celebrarent. Cum uero attulissent matronae sua ornamenta, Dionysius ui ipsis eripuit, & nihil ornamentorum eis restituit.
units.tr: Dionysius of Syracuse, when he needed money, used various tricks to extort it from his subjects. So he came before the public and said that Ceres had come to him and ordered all the matrons to bring their ornaments, so that they might establish a festival for Ceres and celebrate it. When the matrons had brought their ornaments, Dionysius took them from them by force and returned none of the ornaments to them.

units.la: Illustrissimus Princeps Dux Saxoniae Elector, donaturus doctori Martino Luthero dolium uini, propositis duobus, iussit eum alterum ex eis eligere. Lutherus uero dedit mihi eligendi potestatem, seu optionem. Nam quando sibi emebat uinum, tunc mihi prius gustandum dare solebat. Saepe enim emebat uinum ex meo iudicio. Dixi igitur ad Principem: Illustrissime Princeps, dicam tuae celsitudini, quid Lysander fecerit apud Dionysium. Lysander cum esset apud Dionysium in Sicilia, & discedere uellet, obtulit ei Dionysius duas stolas, quarum unam eligeret, ac filiae suae daret. Lysander, ut erat Laconicus, respondit, Se harum rerum esse ignarum: sed uelle se suæ filiæ utramq; afferre, ut ipsa eligeret. & utramq; abstulit. Cùm hoc illustrissimo Principi recitassem, intellexit quid uellem, & utrumq; dolium Doctori Martino donauit.
units.tr: The most illustrious Prince, the Elector Duke of Saxony, wishing to give Doctor Martin Luther a cask of wine, offered him two and ordered him to choose one of them. But Luther gave me the power of choice, or the option. For when he bought wine for himself, he used to give it to me to taste first; indeed he often bought wine on my judgment. So I said to the Prince: "Most illustrious Prince, I will tell your highness what Lysander did at the court of Dionysius. When Lysander was with Dionysius in Sicily and wanted to leave, Dionysius offered him two dresses, so that he might choose one and give it to his daughter. Lysander, being a Laconian, replied that he was ignorant of such things, but he wished to take both to his daughter so that she could choose; and he took both away." When I had recited this to the most illustrious Prince, he understood what I meant, and he gave both casks to Doctor Martin.

units.la: VSVRA.
units.tr: USURY.

units.la: Imperatoris lex de usuris est bona, & retinenda: quia non delet uocem Euangelij.
units.tr: The emperor's law on usury is good and should be kept, because it does not blot out the voice of the Gospel.

units.la: Quidam sapiens uir dicebat: Prudens fuit iurisconsultus, qui actionem de eo quod interest excogitauit, & introduxit.
units.tr: A certain wise man used to say: the jurist was shrewd who devised and introduced the action for what is lost through delay (the action de eo quod interest).

units.la: Quidam mecum ueniens, interrogauit num etiam deberet soluere usuras, cum Deus eas prohibeat? Cui respondi: Prohibet accipere usuras, non uetuit ferre iniuriam. Est enim regula uniuersalis: Qui libenter mutuò sumit, eum non libenter soluere. Qui leuiter spondet, nõ multũ soluere curat.
units.tr: A man who came with me asked whether he also had to pay interest, since God forbids it. I replied: God forbids taking usury; he did not forbid suffering wrong. There is a general rule: the man who borrows willingly does not pay willingly, and the man who promises lightly does not care much about paying.

units.la: Alius mercator Augustæ, bonus uir, dixit: Si quis potentioribus aliquam pecuniæ summam dare mutuò uelit, amicitiam & societatem prius ineat cum his tribus hominum generibus, Doctore iuris, Theologo, & Milite. Nam si recusset reddere debitor, à iurisconsulto actio contra illum instituì poterit. Si non obtemperet iudici, à Theologo conscientia eius permoueri potest. Si denique nec tum soluere uult, à milite ui cogi & expugnari potest.
units.tr: Another merchant at Augsburg, a good man, said: if anyone wants to lend a sum of money to powerful people, he should first form a friendship and partnership with three kinds of men: a doctor of law, a theologian and a soldier. For if the debtor refuses to repay, an action can be brought against him through the jurist. If he does not obey the judge, his conscience can be moved by the theologian. If at last he still will not pay, he can be compelled and overpowered by force through the soldier.

units.la: Quando Lucullus uenit in Asiam, fuit tanta mi-seria & usura in Asia, ut nobiles uendere filios & filias coacti sint. Ibi Lucullus restituit ueterem le-gem de centesimis: id est, ut quotannis darentur de centum, duodecim. Quantæ pœnæ uagantur per mundum, omnibus temporibus?
units.tr: When Lucullus came into Asia, there was such misery and usury there that nobles were forced to sell their sons and daughters. There Lucullus restored the old law on centesimae, that is, that each year twelve be paid on every hundred. What penalties wander through the world at all times!

units.la: Tyberius Grachus, quando tulit legem Agra-riam, habuit approbatorem Lelium: qui tamen ar-te se subduxit, postquam uidit se incurrere in odiū. Stetit Tyberius Gracchus in concione, suadens, ut lex ferretur, ne diuites Romani occuparent totam Italiam, eiectis ciuibus, & collocatis in eam seruis. Hortantur uos, inquit, Imperatores, ut dimicetis pro focis & aris, cum principes nostri neque fo-cos neq; aras uobis relinquant. Hoc est singula-re ϖὰθος, quod recitatur à Plutarcho, tanquam sin-gulare lumen orationis, ab absurdo sumptum. Sic Tyberius Gracchus suscipiens causam ciuium, ob eam ipse interficitur: lex tamen post eius mor-tem suscepta est. Hæc in loco De homicidijs paulo aliter sunt recitata.
units.tr: When Tiberius Gracchus proposed the agrarian law, he had Laelius as a supporter, who nevertheless slipped away by a trick once he saw that he was incurring hatred. Tiberius Gracchus stood up in the assembly urging that the law be passed, so that the rich Romans should not occupy all of Italy, with the citizens driven out and slaves settled in their place. "They urge you, commanders," he said, "to fight for hearths and altars, when our leaders leave you neither hearths nor altars." This is a singular touch of character [ἦθος], which Plutarch cites as a remarkable light of oratory, drawn from the absurd. So Tiberius Gracchus, taking up the cause of the citizens, was killed on account of it; yet the law was adopted after his death. These things are recited a little differently in the place On Homicides.

units.la: DISPVTABILES casus.
units.tr: Debatable cases.

units.la: Dux Fridericus amisit annulum in pugna, quæ diligebat propter memoriam aui. Gemma erat in eo ualde pulchra, draconites cæruleus. Postea cum Dux esset in Salinis Saxonicis, in castris Cæsaris,
units.tr: Duke Frederick lost a ring in battle. He valued it because it had been his grandfather's. It set a very beautiful gem, a blue draconites. Later, when the Duke was at the Saxon salt-works in the emperor's camp, after the siege of this town of Wittenberg, it chanced that a famished soldier found the ring.

units.la: post obsidionem huius oppidi Vuitebergæ, casu accidit ut inueniret eum miles famelicus, qui ueniens ad aurifabrum, obtulit illi annulum uenale. Aurifaber uerò suspicabatur esse Ducis: agnoscens illum ex eo, quòd fortasis olim apud Ducem uidisset. Miles petiuit pecuniam, quia esuriebat. Appendit aurum faber, soluit, & adiecit tres Ioachimicos. Miles libenter fuit contentus. Aurifaber statim egreditur in castra Cæsaris ad Ducem, & dixit: Se, quantum agnosceret, afferre annulum Principis: idq; ideo, ut si eius esse deprehenderetur, recuperaret ac retineret ipsum Princeps. Minister ostendit Duci. qui mox agnito suo annulo, fuit exhilaratus. & interrogat aurifabrum de tota actione, reddit̃q; ipsi quantum militi numerauerat. Hic oritur quæstio, an princeps habuerit actionem in rem, seu rei uendicationem: id est, an debuerit reddere aurifabro illā pecuniā, an absq; precij repensione potuerit retinere annulum? Omitto iam hoc de iure belli. Pono casum, quòd aurifaber voluerit soluì: & quæro, an Princeps debuerit soluere? Quòd nō debuerit soluere, sic argumētor: Quicūque emit rem à non domino, non potest à domino rei precium petere. Aurifaber autē hic emit rem non à domino. Nam sicut amissione non perit dominium, ita nec inuentione acquiritur dominium. Ergo aurifaber non potuit precium à Principe reporeposcere. Respondeo: Imò debuit soluere aurifabro pecuniam, quia officiũ non debet nocere præstanti officium. Iste aurifaber emit annulum, ofificij, non quæstus causa, sicut uidebatur etiam Principi. Ergo hoc officium aurifabro illi non debuit esse damnosum. Hæc est demonstratio, reipsa loquendo: quanquam labefactari possit. Nam non sunt semper firmæ demõstrationes in materia morali, quemadmodum in Geometricis & Arithmeticis materijs. Quæ enim pendent ex uoluntate, sunt flexibilia. Probatur autem illud per tale principium, seu demonstrationem: Gratia gratiam parit. Item: Officium nemini debet nocere.
units.tr: He went to a goldsmith and offered the ring for sale. The goldsmith suspected that it belonged to the Duke, perhaps recognising it from having seen it once at the Duke's court. The soldier asked for money, because he was hungry. The goldsmith weighed out gold, paid him, and added three Joachimsthalers. The soldier was happy with this. The goldsmith at once went to the Duke in the emperor's camp and said that, so far as he could tell, he was bringing the Prince's ring.
