He did this so that, if it was found to be the Prince's, the Prince might recover it and keep it. A servant showed it to the Duke, who, recognising his ring at once, was delighted. He asked the goldsmith about the whole affair and repaid him what he had given the soldier. Here arises the question whether the Prince had an action in rem, or a right of vindication. That is, ought he to return that money to the goldsmith, or could he keep the ring without repaying the price? I set aside now the question of the law of war. I posit the case that the goldsmith wanted to be paid, and I ask whether the Prince ought to pay. That he ought not to pay, I argue thus: whoever buys a thing from one who is not the owner cannot demand the price from the owner. But here the goldsmith bought the thing from one who was not the owner. For just as ownership is not lost by losing a thing, so it is not acquired by finding it. Therefore the goldsmith could not reclaim the price from the Prince. I answer: on the contrary, he ought to have paid the goldsmith the money, because an act of duty ought not to harm the one who performs it. This goldsmith bought the ring out of a sense of duty, not for the sake of gain, as the Prince also saw. Therefore this duty ought not to be harmful to him. This is a demonstration, speaking in terms of the facts, although it can be shaken. For demonstrations in moral matters are not always as firm as in geometry and arithmetic, since things that depend on the will are flexible. The point is, however, proved by such a principle or demonstration: grace begets grace. Likewise: duty ought to harm no one.

units.la: Ante 200. annos in ducatu Vuirtembergensi, fuit triennium disputatio de decimis: & interdictum erat, ne templa aperirentur: id est, ne fierent publicæ conciones, &c. Monachi, & alij eis adiunčti litigabant cum Principibus & Comitibus: ac argumĕtabantur ex lege Mosaica, ut decimas ad se retraherĕt, dicentes, Decimas à Deo ordinatas esse sacerdotib. Respõderunt doctiores eo tēpore uiuētes, Aliquotā partĕ, nõ totũ esse dandũ sacerdotibus. Quod hoc modo exponi potest, ut genus, & nõ species, in cõseruatione ministerij obseruetur. Nos debemus necessarios sumptus ad cõseruationĕ ministerij conferre, siue sint decimæ, siue sint aliæ res. Iudæis uerò erat mandatum, ut speciem obseruarent, & decimas ex agris sacerdotibus darent.
units.tr: Two hundred years ago, in the Duchy of Württemberg, there was a three-year dispute about tithes, and an interdict was in force forbidding churches to be opened, that is, forbidding public sermons to be held. Monks and others attached to them litigated with princes and counts, and argued from the Mosaic law that tithes should be drawn back to them, saying that God had ordained tithes for the priests. The more learned men living at that time replied that only a part, not the whole, is to be given to the priests. This may be explained so that the genus, and not the species, is observed in the maintenance of the ministry. We ought to contribute the necessary expenses for the maintenance of the ministry, whether these are tithes or other goods. But the Jews were commanded to observe the species, and to give tithes from the fields to the priests.

units.la: In historia Ambrosij inuenitur, esse ei obiectū, Omnia esse regum: ideo debere ipsum cedere extemplo. Ipse uero contrà constantissimè perseuerauit in concione Christi, dicentis: Domus mea, domus precationis est. Dixit etiam ad Gothos, qui tunc occupauerant Romanum imperium: Vos Gothi, qui olim habitabatis in plaustris, nunc ex templis plaustra facere conamini.
units.tr: In the history of Ambrose we find that he was met with the objection that all things belong to kings, so he ought to yield at once. But he, on the contrary, most steadfastly persevered, citing Christ's words in the temple: My house is a house of prayer. He also said to the Goths, who then held the Roman empire: You Goths, who once lived in wagons, now try to make wagons out of temples.

units.la: Quidam aulicus in nuptijs cuiusdam boni uiri mihi assidebat, qui nactus occasionem à pellibus quibus teguntur Misnenses & Saxonicæ mulieres, mecū disputare coepit de dominio Principum, seu gubernatorum & subditorum, & dicebat: Hodie uidi tot mulieres circundatas istis pellibus, & mecum supputaui precium quo sunt comparatæ, inueniq; ducentis aureis istas pelles non esse emptas. Ad quid hic uestium splendor? Nónne iure potiori Princeps illa bona possideret? Erat igitur tale argumentum: Nos excedimus in luxu uestium: Ergo rectius debentur illi sumptus dominis. Interrogaui ipsum, an uellet concedere, ut Dux ipsius arcè siue splendidè, siue non adeò magnificè extructam, ipsi auferret, & ad se raperet? Respondit, se id non permissurū, cum Princeps sit minimè dominus bonorum, rum, quæ sibi quisq; collegerit. Respōdi: Nec Princeps est dominus eorum quæ subditorum coniuges tenent. Tunc ille sermonem suum repressit.
units.tr: At a wedding of a good man, a certain courtier sat beside me. Seizing the chance offered by the furs in which the women of Meissen and Saxony are wrapped, he began to argue with me about the dominion of princes or rulers over their subjects. He said: Today I saw so many women wrapped in those furs, and I reckoned the price for which they were bought, and I found that those furs were not bought for less than two hundred gold coins. What is the point of this splendour in clothing? Would not the prince have a stronger right to those goods? So his argument ran: we go to excess in the luxury of clothing; therefore those expenses are more rightly owed to the lords. I asked him whether he would concede that the Duke might take from him his house, whether splendidly built or not so magnificently, and seize it for himself. He replied that he would not permit this, since a prince is by no means the lord of the goods that each man has gathered for himself. I replied: nor is the prince the lord of what the wives of his subjects hold. Then he checked his speech.

units.la: Rex Anglicus aliquando in uenatione à uia aberrans, peruenerat in tuguriolum cuiusdam rustici, qui eum pro suis facultatibus satis humaniter excepit. Cùm autem Rex nollet rustico obtemperare, ut de omnibus cibis à rustico propositis comederet, præsertim à quibus Rex nauseam capiebat: rusticus Regi colaphum impegit, dicens, Quòd quisq; esset Rex in sua domo. Rex memor eius dicti, quòd quilibet esset Rex in sua domo, rustico obtemperat, & de cibis parum comedit. Postero uerò die iubet rex uenire rusticum secum in aulā, mandans suis ministris, ut eum adductum collocēt ad mensam suam. Cum uerò uenisset rusticus, & assedisset mensæ, ac proposuissent plurima fercula, tunc Rex alloquitur rusticum: Comede, inquiens, de omnibus: Ego sum Rex in domo mea. Rusticus obtemperat mandato Regio, & comedit de omnibus ferculis. ibi Rex inquit: Tu fecisti sapientius me, quia uitasti colaphum. Ego si de omnibus comedissem, etiam à te sine colapho discessissem.
units.tr: An English king, once while hunting and straying from the road, came to the little hut of a certain peasant, who received him quite kindly according to his means. But when the king would not obey the peasant's urging to eat of all the food set before him, especially the dishes that made the king nauseous, the peasant struck the king a blow, saying that every man is king in his own house. The king, mindful of that saying, that every man is king in his own house, gave in to the peasant and ate little of the food. But the next day the king ordered the peasant to come to the court, instructing his servants to bring him in and seat him at the king's table. When the peasant came and sat at the table, and many dishes had been set out, the King addressed him: Eat of everything, he said; I am king in my own house. The peasant obeyed the royal command and ate of all the dishes. Then the King said: You have acted more wisely than I, because you avoided the blow. If I had eaten of everything, I too would have left you without a blow.

units.la: Habebamus in uisitatione Saxonicarum ecclesiarū quendam Ecclesiæ ministrum, egregium & doctum uirum, & generosi animi, qui conquerebatur nobis, quòd rustici transcenderent sepem, popularentur ipsius hortos: dicebatq;, quòd cum sæpe conquestus esset eadem de causa apud iudicium, iudex noluerit prohibere iniurias illas, sed responderit semper, ut nominatim indicaret, quinam essent facti eius authores: rusticos verò iam indicatos, semper negasse factum coram iudice. Qua iniuria comotus, tandem ille pastor unum in ipso facinore deprehensum bene castigauit. Ille postea accusauit eū apud nos. Inuitabamus pastore ad prandiū, et eū omni molestia liberabamus. diximus rusticū iure percussum esse: quia uniuscuiusq; debet suā domum & facultates defendere.
units.tr: When we were on visitation of the Saxon churches, we had a certain minister of the church, an excellent and learned man of generous spirit, who complained to us that peasants climbed over his hedge and plundered his gardens. He said that he had often complained about this before the court, but the judge had refused to prohibit these wrongs and had always replied that he should name by name who were the authors of the deed. Once the peasants had been named, they had always denied the deed before the judge. Stirred by this injury, the minister at last soundly punished one of them, caught in the very act. The man afterwards brought an accusation against him before us. We invited the minister to dinner and freed him from all his trouble. We said that the peasant had been rightly struck, because each man ought to defend his own house and property.

units.la: Memini ornatissimam urbem ab Hispanis ex mera petulātia incensam esse, ita ut bona pars cōflagrauerit. Cum verò ciues indignè ferrēt, & cōquererētur de iniuria, responderunt: Tamen omnia sunt nostri Domini Imperatoris. Illi non recte dixerūt. non omnia sunt gubernatorū, quod neq; boni gubernatores expetūt: sed ciues habent suas quasdam priuatas facultates, quæ non sunt magistratus. Ac non minus præceptum, Non furtum facies, obligat dominos, quàm ipsos subditos.
units.tr: I remember a most splendid city that was set on fire by Spaniards out of sheer wantonness, so that a large part of it was burned. When the citizens took this badly and complained of the wrong, the Spaniards replied: Yet all things belong to our Lord the Emperor. Those men spoke wrongly. Not all things belong to the rulers, which good rulers themselves do not seek; citizens have certain private goods of their own, which are not the magistrate's. And the precept, You shall not steal, binds lords no less than it binds the subjects themselves.

units.la: Doctus quispiā homo solitus est Iurisconsultorum quorundā sciolorū, disputantiū de Lazaro, an ualuerit ipsius testamentū postquā reuixisset, ineptias huiusmodi festiuo commento deridere. Non procul ab oppido quodā flumē agebat pistrinum, num, ex quo, postquā non ita multo ante aquatū asinus descendisset, cùm in extrema ripa seu lutu-lenta seu tenuior aqua flueret, quàm ut os imbue-ret, in proximam cymbam forte pergit, unde ube-riorem iusti amnis aquā hauriret. Porrò cum in-scendisset nauiculam, impetu detorquet à ripa in medium flumen: quò cùm esset excepta, secundis uentis in scopulum fertur. Hæc postquā impegit, fracta est nauicula: & imperitus ille nauclerus in undis perijt. Doluit molitori (ubi rem resciuit) iactura: & piscatorem, qui nauem ibi collocauerat, in ius uocat: damnum dedisse accusat, quòd eius nauigio iumentū auectum sit. Contrà ille factam ab asino pauperiem, seq; damnū accepisse exclamat, quòd nauigium amiserit, in flumen ab asino impulsum. Vtrinq; acerrimè à conducticiis rabulis certatum est. Iudici causa uisa est intricatior, quàm ut liceret nō consultis iuris professoribus pronūciare: deferūt ad leguleios. His uerò negocū mirū uisum est, dum quisq; pro se asinū uindicare cōtendit: disputationes varias instruūt: rixantur de asino in scholis & conciliabulis pertinacius, opinor, quàm Græcus ille de asini umbra. Ita quorundam disputationes futiliores sunt ista molitoris contentione.
units.tr: A learned man was accustomed to mock, with a witty story, the absurdities of certain half-educated jurists who disputed whether Lazarus's will remained valid after he had come back to life. Not far from a certain town, a mill was driven by a river. Not long before, a donkey had gone down to drink there. At the far bank the water flowed either muddy or too thin to wet its mouth, so the miller happened to go out into the nearest boat, from which he could draw more abundant water from the swift stream. Having got into the little boat, he pushed it by force from the bank into the middle of the river. Once caught there, it was carried by favourable winds onto a rock. When it struck, the little boat broke, and that unskilled boatman perished in the waves. The miller, when he learned of it, grieved at the loss and summoned to court the fisherman who had moored the boat there. He accused him of causing the damage, because his boat had been carried off with the donkey. On the contrary, the fisherman cried out that the poverty had been caused by the donkey, and that he himself had suffered loss, since he had lost his boat, which the donkey had pushed into the river. On both sides the case was contested most fiercely by hired wranglers. The judge thought the matter too tangled to pronounce on without consulting professors of law, so they referred it to the pettifoggers. These found the affair remarkable, and while each man strove to claim the donkey for himself, they set up various disputations. They quarrelled about the donkey in the schools and meeting-places more stubbornly, I suppose, than that Greek over the donkey's shadow. Thus some disputations are more trivial than this contention of the miller.

units.la: Francofordiæ ad Mœnū, cum eius fluminis esset magna inundatio, ut multæ ædes obruerentur & everterentur: ibi forte stans molitor quidam, vidit cunas in aquis natantes: quas cum caperet ut servaret, invenit in iis infantem adhuc vivum: qui tanto gratior & charior ipsi fuit, quod ipse propria sobole careret. Quapropter eum educauit, ac institui curavit. Tandem pater rescisens filium suum vivum pervenisse ad molitorem, profisci-tur ad ipsum, & puerum sibi restitui postulat. Molitor valde rogat patrem, ut sibi relinquat puerum. Sed pater non permittens se exorari, detulit rem ad judicem: qui pronunciauit, ut patri filius restitueretur, simulatq; molitori solvisset sumptus necessarios in alendo filio impensos. Sic dextrè & juste judex causam juxta Jurisconsultorum sententiam decidit.
units.tr: At Frankfurt am Main, when the river was in great flood and many houses were overturned and destroyed, a miller happened to be standing there and saw cradles floating in the water. As he picked them up to save them, he found a baby still alive among them. The child was all the dearer and more precious to him because he had no children of his own. So he brought the boy up and saw to his schooling. Eventually the father, learning that his son had survived and come into the miller's hands, went to him and demanded that the boy be restored to him. The miller earnestly begged the father to leave the boy with him. But the father would not be persuaded and brought the matter before a judge. The judge ruled that the son should be restored to his father, once the father had repaid the miller the necessary costs of feeding and raising the boy. In this way the judge decided the case skilfully and justly, in line with the opinion of the jurists.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Convenerant aliquando leo, equus, vulpes, & asinus, ut quicquid praedando consequerentur, id totum inter se dividerent. Contigit paulo post, ut taurus se illis in praedam offerret: quo dilaniato, leo jussit asinum dividere praedam, & cuiq; partem debitam attribvere. Asinus, ut simplex & rude animal, fecit divisionem secundum proportionem arithmeticam, & cuiq; aequalem attribuit partem. Ibi iratus leo inquit: Quis te ita jussit partiri, & mihi non plus tribvere, qui tamen maximè laboraverim? discerptoq; asino, jussit equum partipartiri. Equus erat æquus: id est, seruabat proportionem Geometricam, & dabat leoni duas partes: alteram quæ sua erat, & alteram discerpti asini. Leo ægreferens hanc etiam diuisionem, innuens sibi plus esse tribuendum, siquidem rex esset, lacerauit etiam equum. Vnde postremò uulpi diuisio est demandata. Vulpes cauta erat, quæ cōgestis omnibus partibus in unum aceruũ, inquit ad leonem: Hæc erit tua pars. Ait leo: Quis te hoc docuit? Respondit, Hi doctores docuerunt: monstrans simul asinum & equum. Queritur, an recte fecerit leo, discerpens equum & asinum? Sed breuiter respondetur: Quòd illa communiter fiât in uita, ut plerunq; potentiores inferiores (si quâ do cum eis ineant familiaritates) premant, iuxta commune prouerbium Germanicũ: Mitt grossen herren ist nicht gůt kirschen essen.
units.tr: Once a lion, a horse, a fox and an ass agreed to share between them whatever they might win by plunder. Shortly afterwards it happened that a bull offered itself to them as prey. When it had been torn apart, the lion ordered the ass to divide the spoil and assign each his due share. The ass, being a simple and blunt creature, made the division by arithmetical proportion and gave each an equal share. The lion, enraged, said: "Who told you to divide it like that, and not to give me more, since I have laboured the most?" He tore the ass apart and ordered the horse to make the division. The horse was fair, that is, it kept to geometrical proportion, and gave the lion two portions: one that was its own, and one of the torn-up ass. The lion, angry at this division too, declared that he ought to receive more, since he was king, and he tore the horse apart as well. Finally the division was handed to the fox. The fox was cautious: having heaped all the portions together into one pile, she said to the lion: "This will be your share." "Who taught you to do this?" said the lion. She replied, "These teachers did," pointing at the ass and the horse. Is the lion right to have torn apart the horse and the ass? The answer, briefly, is this: it is commonly the case in life that the more powerful oppress their inferiors (if they enter into any friendship with them), in line with the common German proverb: "It is not good to eat cherries with great lords."

units.la: In conuentu Spirensi, uenit ad me quidam senex miles, qui dicebat se disputare secum cum sua conscientia, de rapinis in bello, quid facere debeat propter restitutionem. Respondi: Iustum bellum est, iusta causa auferendi res. Ergo possessor illarum rerum est dominus.
units.tr: At the Diet of Speyer a certain old soldier came to me. He said that he was debating with his own conscience about the plunder taken in war, and what he ought to do about restitution. I replied: a war is just, and a just cause for seizing goods exists. Therefore the one who possesses those goods is their owner.

units.la: Est difficile agere cum hominibus, nõ recte institutis. Iudex urbis Augustanæ, alias bonus uir, in conuentu suspendebat furem cum mala conscientia. Dubitabat enim utrũ recte faceret: quan-quam quam multum cum eo disputarë, & conarer eum in uiam reducere, tamen parum efficiebam. Erroris autem sui causa erat, quòd nõ teneret hoc principium & fundamentum: Imperia esse diuinitùs constituta, & magistratum habere potestatem propter probabilem rationem exasperandi poenas, iuxta dictum Iurisconsultorum: Graßantibus delictis, pœnæ exasperandæ sunt.
units.tr: It is hard to deal with men who have not been rightly instructed. A judge of the city of Augsburg, otherwise a good man, was hanging a thief at an assize while troubled in conscience. For he doubted whether he was doing right. Although I argued with him at length and tried to bring him back to the right path, I achieved little. The cause of his error was that he did not hold to this principle and foundation: that governments are established by God, and that the magistrate has power, for a reasonable cause, to make punishments harsher, in line with the saying of the jurists: "When crimes are rampant, penalties must be made harsher."

units.la: Hîc Vuitebergæ, nõ ante multos annos, suspe-debatur quidã fur, qui interrogabat: Est ne iustũ, hominẽ suspendere? Nos uicissim interrogabamus ipsum: An etiam iustum esset furari? Dicebatur, quòd idem antea bis effanuerat, & in loco ipsius stramen pepederat. at hîc ars eius nõ succedebat.
units.tr: Here at Wittenberg, not many years ago, a certain thief was being hanged, and he kept asking: "Is it right to hang a man?" In turn we asked him: "Would it be right to steal?" It was said that he had twice before slipped away in this same way, leaving a bundle of straw behind in his place. But his trick did not work here.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Asinus cuiusdã molitoris, præteriens uineã, ubi premebantur uuæ, cùm in uasa mustũ expressum inueniret, bibit bonũ haustũ. Postea dominus uineæ adueniens, asinũ abigit, & cõquerens de suo damno, molitorẽ in ius uocat. Ibi est lata sententia, ut quandoquidem asinus non consedisset, sed tantum præterçundo unicum haustum bibissel, liber ab actoris accusatione pronunciaretur.
units.tr: The ass of a certain miller, passing by a vineyard where the grapes were being pressed, found some must that had been squeezed into vessels, and drank a good draught of it. Afterwards the owner of the vineyard came up, drove the ass away, and, complaining of his loss, summoned the miller to court. There the sentence was pronounced that, since the ass had not stopped but had drunk only one draught while passing by, the miller should be acquitted of the plaintiff's accusation.

units.la: POENA EIVS QVI NON est soluendo.
units.tr: The punishment of one who is not able to pay

units.la: Scribitur de patre Empedoclis, quòd Thebis sit impositus calatho, & perfusus aqua. Talis fuit ce remoremonia, qua infamia notabatur ille qui non erat soluendo. Aliæ leges nõ mitiores redigebant eum qui non esset soluendo, in seruitutē. Et si uerum est quod historiæ tradunt, Draconis lex fuit, ut obæ-rati corpus distraheretur, & dissectu̇ daretur creditoribus. Quod fuit signum seueræ disciplinæ.
units.tr: It is written of the father of Empedocles that at Thebes he was made to wear a basket and was drenched with water. Such was the ceremony by which the man who could not pay was marked with disgrace. Other laws, no milder, reduced to slavery the man who could not pay. And if what the histories hand down is true, there was a law of Draco that the body of the insolvent debtor was to be cut up and given to the creditors in pieces. This was a sign of severe discipline.

units.la: In oppido Bretta, quando aliquis est decoctor, ita ut non sit soluendo, ille trahitur per ciuitatem, & perfunditur aqua. quod est nota infamiæ.
units.tr: In the town of Bretta, when someone becomes a bankrupt, so that he is unable to pay, he is dragged through the town and drenched with water. This is a mark of infamy.

units.la: Bernæ hæc obseruatur lex, ut cōtrahens plus æris alieni, quàm ut sit soluendo, nulla admissa intercessione aut acceptione personæ, capita-li supplicio afficiatur. Legislatores graues illius legis causas habuerūt, uidelicet ne leuibus hominibus ulla daretur occasio honestos decipēdi. ita pul-chrè utilitas Reipublicæ in illa lege cōsiderata est.
units.tr: At Berne this law is observed: whoever contracts more debt than he is able to pay, without any surety or guarantee being admitted, is punished with capital punishment. The lawgivers had serious reasons for that law, namely so that no occasion would be given to light-minded men to deceive honest ones. In this way the welfare of the commonwealth was admirably taken into account in that law.

units.la: OCTAVVM PRAECEPTUM.
units.tr: OCTAVVM PRAECEPTUM.

units.la: VERITAS.
units.tr: VERITAS.

units.la: Democritus: ἀρχὴ μεγάλης ἀρετῆς, σωτηρία ἀληθείας. id est, Principium magnæ uirtutis, tueri ueritatem.
units.tr: Democritus: ἀρχὴ μεγάλης ἀρετῆς, σωτηρία ἀληθείας [the beginning of great virtue is the preservation of truth]. That is, the beginning of great virtue is to guard the truth.

units.la: Simplex oratio & propria bonis uerbis, est optima, quæ nominatur Attica.
units.tr: A plain style, with proper words and good diction, is the best; it is called Attic.

units.la: Veritas tēporis filia: quia sæpe fit, ut male homines iudicent, incitati aliquo affectu, posteaq; corrigant sententiam alio tempore.
units.tr: Truth is the daughter of time, because it often happens that men judge badly, stirred by some passion, and afterwards correct their opinion at another time.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Pindarus : Ad bonam causam tria uerba sufficiant, nec mendax testis præsideat negocijs.id est, in bona causa non est disputatione opus, quia in uero non multæ sunt intricationes. sicut econtrà Galenus dicit: τὸ ψεῦδος ἐναντα λέγον. Hanc ego iudico simplicissimam & ueram sententiam. Valde sudant hic interpretes, quid uelit Pindarus per illa tria uerba. Dicam meâ opinionem : Tria uerba,id est, maior, minor,& medius terminus. Hæc est Dialectica speculatio.
units.tr: Pindar: For a good cause three words suffice, and a lying witness should not preside over the affairs. That is, in a good cause there is no need of lengthy dispute, because in what is true there are not many entanglements. Galen, on the contrary, says: τὸ ψεῦδος ἐναντα λέγον [falsehood speaks in contradictory ways]. I judge this to be the simplest and truest saying. The interpreters sweat greatly here over what Pindar means by those three words. I will give my own opinion: the three words are the major premise, the minor premise, and the middle term. This is the speculation of dialectic.

units.la: Plato inquit:Satis beatum sibi uideri, cui tandem in senectute contigerit, ut sapientum ueras opiniones assequatur.
units.tr: Plato says: It seems to me a sufficiently happy lot for one who, at last in old age, attains to the true opinions of the wise.

units.la: Χρόνος σωτὴρ ἁπάντων ἀνθρώπων: id est,tempus est seruator iustorum hominum.
units.tr: Χρόνος σωτὴρ ἁπάντων ἀνθρώπων [time is the saviour of all men]: that is, time is the preserver of upright men.

units.la: Veritas (ut est in oratione Fabij ad Aemilium) laborare potest,opprimi non potest.
units.tr: Truth (as it is in the speech of Fabius to Aemilius) can be worn down, but it cannot be crushed.

units.la: Simonidis dictum : Δόξα βιάζεται τὴν ἀλήθειαν: id est,opinio uim affert veritati.
units.tr: Simonides' saying: Δόξα βιάζεται τὴν ἀλήθειαν [opinion does violence to the truth]: that is, opinion does violence to truth.

units.la: CALVMNIA ET OBTRECTATIO.
units.tr: CALUMNY AND DETRACTION.

units.la: Palamedem falsò accusauit Vlysses, eiusq; proditor fuit. Sic Aristidem sui ciues prodiderunt. Cum enim capitali sisteretur iudicio, astitit ei quidam qui non poterat scribere. cui cum daretur testula, ut inscriberet literam condemnationis, alteri astanti eam porrexit, dicēs: Tu pro me scri be. At ille: Quid uis scribi? Respondit: Litera cō demnationis. Et hic: Est' ne condemnatus tibi no tus? Respondit ; Non: sed quia cæteri eum con- demnant, & ego sequar maiorem turbam.
units.tr: Ulysses falsely accused Palamedes, and was himself his betrayer. So too his fellow citizens betrayed Aristides. When he was brought before a capital court, a certain man who could not write stood beside him. When a potsherd was handed to him so that he might inscribe the letter of condemnation, he passed it to another man standing nearby, saying: "You write for me." The other asked: "What do you want written?" He answered: "The letter of condemnation." "Do you know him to be guilty?" "No," he said, "but since the others condemn him, I will follow the greater crowd."

units.la: Cùm cuidam à me petenti scripsissem in librũ, Calumnia turbat sapientē, & frangit robur cor- dis eius: uenit forte ad me quidam bonus uir, con- siliarius præstantis Principis, legēsq; hanc senten tiam, quærebat, Vbi'nam ea inueniretur scripta? Dicebam: In Ecclesiaste, ac monstrabam illi locū. Ad hæc ille: Profecto est egregia sententia.
units.tr: When I had written in a book for a certain man who asked me, "Calumny troubles the wise man and breaks the strength of his heart," a good man, a counsellor of an eminent prince, happened to come to me. Reading this sentence, he asked where it was written. I said: in Ecclesiastes, and I showed him the passage. He replied: "Indeed, it is an excellent saying."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Ex lege duodecim Tabularum, è saxo Tarpeio deijciebatur, qui falsum testimonium dixisse con- uictus erat.
units.tr: By the law of the Twelve Tables, one who had been convicted of giving false testimony was thrown from the Tarpeian Rock.

units.la: Conuiciorum uulnera sunt insanabilia: quia uulnus læsi animi nunquam tam bene curatur, quin maneat cicatrix aliqua. Sic apud Homerum Hector ad Achillem dicit: Timidi solent con- uiciari.
units.tr: The wounds of insults are incurable, because the wound of a wronged spirit is never healed so well that some scar does not remain. So in Homer, Hector says to Achilles that it is cowards who are usually reviled.

units.la: Audiui à præstantissimo uiro, quando edeban tur libri de bello Germanico, esse præsagium a- liarum calamitatum. addebatq;: Si quis hostis fiat, incendijs grassetur, homines abducat, tantummo do à conuicijs abstineat. quia uulnera conuicio- rum manent incurabilia.
units.tr: I heard from a most distinguished man, when the books on the German war were being published, that this was a presage of other calamities. He added: "If an enemy should arise, he would rage with fires and carry off men; only let him abstain from insults, for the wounds of insults remain incurable."

units.la: Memini causas, in quibus aliqui circumuenti iniustis iudicijs oppressi sunt, & post mortem eorum patefiebat iudicium. Tres falsi testes, & accusator in ducatu Vuirtembergensi, cùm essem Tubingæ scholasticus, afficiebantur supplicijs capitalibus, & mittebantur corporum partes in quatuor loca regionis, ut extarent signa punitæ calumniæ, & falsi testimonij. Magna seueritas est. Ille vir qui fuerat oppressus, accesserat Ducem Vuirtembergensem, & dixerat: Domine Princeps, si inueneris me ex diligenti perquisitione veritatis iniquum & iniustum, amputes mihi hoc caput auferre. Princeps motus illa tam constanti interpellatione, rē curauit accuratè inquiri: & postea veritate comperta, usus est illa seueritate.
units.tr: I recall cases in which certain men, circumvented, were oppressed by unjust judgments, and after their death the injustice became plain. When I was a student at Tübingen, in the Duchy of Württemberg, three false witnesses and an accuser were put to capital punishment, and parts of their bodies were sent to four places in the region, so that the signs of punished calumny and false testimony might remain. It was great severity. The man who had been oppressed went to the Duke of Württemberg and said: "Lord Prince, if after a diligent search for the truth you find me unjust and wrongful, let my head be cut off." The prince, moved by such a steadfast appeal, had the matter investigated carefully; and afterwards, when the truth was discovered, he applied that severity.

units.la: Quidam in urbe quadam Marchiæ, die Palmarum in concione sua, similitudine ex Lutheri Postilla desumpta usus est, qua comparauit Christum cum asino. Statim alius quidam insueta comparatione offensus, quærebat occasionem reprehendendi & calumniandi illum: surgensq; clamabat esse rem indignam, Christum conferre cum asino. Ille opponit testimonium Lutheri. Alter, hoc dicto, scribit ad Lutherum, & petit ut emendet suam Postillam. Nos eum ridebamus. Adeò ex leuibus occasionib. oriuntur sæpe dissensiones. Sed aliud est occasio, aliud causa, inquit Polybius. ποιτᾷ δὲ ἐροτόλοιγος ἐρὶς νεν̈εὸν λελαλημνῖα: id est, oberrat seu obambulat homicidialis cõtentio, quæ noua canit. Hoc dictum citat Clemens ex Empedocle.
units.tr: In a certain town of the March, on Palm Sunday, a preacher in his sermon used a comparison taken from Luther's Postil, in which he likened Christ to an ass. At once another man, offended by the unusual comparison, looked for an occasion to rebuke and slander him; rising, he cried out that it was an unworthy thing to compare Christ with an ass. The preacher cited Luther's testimony. The other, upon this reply, wrote to Luther and asked that he correct his Postil. We laughed at him. So often do disputes arise from slight occasions. But occasion is one thing, cause another, says Polybius: [ποιτᾷ δὲ ἐροτόλοιγος ἐρὶς νεν̈εὸν λελαλημνῖα], that is, homicidal strife wanders about and sings new songs. Clement cites this saying from Empedocles.

units.la: Thucydides de suis ciuibus : Estis conteptores usitatarum rerum, & admiratores absurdarum.
units.tr: Thucydides, speaking of his own citizens: You are despisers of familiar things and admirers of absurd ones.

units.la: Lutherus dictum Christi, Pax uobis, uerterat, Habt frid. Illud Emserus calūniatus est, inquiens: Meinstu, das sie einander geschlagem haben? Est calumnia. Vocabulū pax, usurpatur generaliter, sicut nos dicimus Saluete: id est, Deus det nobis omnia fausta, sint omnia fausta & salua: Gott geb eüch alles gütts. Sunt uerba optantis alicui bona, non est imperatiua oratio.
units.tr: Luther translated Christ's words "Peace be with you" as "Habt Frid." Emser slandered this, saying: "Do you think they struck one another?" That is calumny. The word peace is used in a general sense, just as we say "Salute": that is, may God grant us every blessing, may everything be prosperous and well. "Gott geb eüch alles gütts." These are words wishing someone well; they are not an imperative command.

units.la: Concionator in oppido quodā Misniæ, dixerat forte in cõcione, Cõstantinopolin sitam esse in Italia. Id ludi rector reprehendens, dicebat: Esse in Græcia. Quod & ipsum non est uerum. Nam est in Thracia sita. Concionator secutus Germanicum prouerbium, opinatus est, was nicht deütsch sei, das sei welsch.
units.tr: A preacher in a town of Meissen happened to say in a sermon that Constantinople lies in Italy. A schoolmaster rebuked him, saying it lies in Greece. But that too is not true, for it lies in Thrace. The preacher, following the German proverb, judged that whatever is not German is welsch.

units.la: Ego aliquādo cū Erasmo Reinholdo, postquā uxor eius mortua esset, contuli familiares sermones: quib. unà intererat alius quidā, qui minus sincere nostra familiaritate usus est. Cum enim nos ioco proponeremus, quòd in monasteriū aliquod (si adhuc apud nos extarēt) nos cõferre, ibiq; suauiter uiuere ac philosophari uellemus: ille tum quidem in præsentia nihil contradicens, postea cùm à nobis discesisset, iocum nostrum peruersè interpretatus est: & iam scripsit contra me, non secus ac si seriò dixissem, ac multa nunc secus interpretatur quàm olim. Tales hodie multi alij calumniatores reperiuntur: sed nihil refert, Deus in stè iudicabit omnia.
units.tr: Once, after his wife had died, I held friendly conversations with Erasmus Reinhold. Another man was present who used our friendship less sincerely. When we jokingly proposed that, if such places still existed among us, we would join some monastery and live pleasantly there, philosophizing, he said nothing against it at the time. But after he had left us, he twisted our joke perversely, and has now written against me as if I had said it in earnest; and he now interprets many things differently than he once did. Many such slanderers are found today; but it does not matter, for God will judge all things in the end.

units.la: In principum aulis primas tenent gnathones & calumniatores. unde dicā uobis regulā certissimam: Quicunq; uult citò crescere in aulis, tantum uideat quò se domini uoluntas inclinet, & cui nam sit infensus, hūc obseruet: & quicquid is agit, id ad dominum deferat, ac in peiorem partē interpretetur. licet nonnunquam etiam aliquid mendacij de suo addere, modo prætexat aliquam grauitatis & sanctitatis speciem sine affectibus. Talis gnato fuit Ephestion in aula Alexandri Magni. Ibidem quoq; calumniator nominatus est Midias, qui (ut refert Plutarchus) semper dicere solitus est: Calumniare audacter, quia semper aliquid adhæret.
units.tr: In princely courts the first places are held by flatterers and slanderers. So I will give you a most certain rule: whoever wishes to rise quickly at court should only watch where the lord's will inclines, and whom he is hostile to. He should observe that man, report to the lord whatever he does, and interpret it in the worst light. He may sometimes even add a little lie of his own, provided he puts on a show of gravity and holiness without passion. Hephaestion was such a flatterer at the court of Alexander the Great. There was also a calumniator there named Midias, who (as Plutarch reports) used always to say: "Slander boldly, for something always sticks."

units.la: Sunt quidam antagonistæ, qui in omnibus rebus alijs contradicunt. Horum non potestis euidentiora exempla habere, quàm Staphilum & Canisium.
units.tr: There are some antagonists who contradict everything else. You could not have more obvious examples of these than Staphylus and Canisius.

units.la: Disputabant quidam apud Alphonsum regem, quid potissimùm prodesset lippis oculis, & acue-ret ret uisum? Primò alius aliud statuit. Tandem qui dam dixit, nihil ita mederi lippis oculis, quàm inuidentiam: quia inuidus est intentus, & semper occasionem aliquam captat, ut inueniat quod re prehendat, ac etiam optima suis reprehensioni-bus & calumnijs deformat.
units.tr: Some men were disputing before King Alphonso about what would most benefit bleary eyes and sharpen the sight. At first one suggested one thing, another something else. At last someone said that nothing heals bleary eyes so well as envy, because the envious man is intent, always seeking some occasion to find fault, and even distorts the best deeds of others by his rebukes and slanders.

units.la: Non multi sunt anni, cùm quidam nebulo ede-ret teterrimam Caroli Magni uituperationem: in qua uituperatione inter cætera habetur, quòd ipse papistas ditauerit, cùm tamen fuerit præstan-tissimus & optimus Imperator.
units.tr: Not many years ago a certain scoundrel published a most foul disparagement of Charlemagne, in which, among other things, it is claimed that he enriched the papists, although he was a most excellent and distinguished emperor.

units.la: In urbe Northusana duo concionatores inter se multum litigabant de dicto Angeli ad Mariam, Aue gratia plena: ita ut unus contra alterum pu-blicè in suggestu, & priuatim in ædibus pugna-ret. sed uterq; non intellexit quid significet uoca-bulum ἀπεχαρισμένην. Est autem huius uocabuli propria & genuina significatio, esse dilectā per misericordiam, non propter merita, seu opera, ut qualitates in naturalibus uiribus.
units.tr: In the city of Northusen two preachers quarrelled bitterly over the angel's words to Mary, "Hail, full of grace." One fought against the other publicly from the pulpit and privately at home. But neither understood what the word [κεχαριτωμένην] signifies. Its proper and genuine meaning is to be beloved through mercy, not on account of merits or works, as qualities belong to natural powers.

units.la: Illustre discrimē est inter ἀγαπᾶν καὶ χαρίζεσθαι: quorum hoc per misericordiam, illud ordine naturæ diligere significat. sicut apostolus Paulus inquit de æterno patre: ἐχαρίτωσεν ὑμᾶς ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ.
units.tr: There is a clear distinction between [ἀγαπᾶν] and [χαρίζεσθαι]: the latter means to love through mercy, the former to love in the order of nature. So the apostle Paul says of the eternal Father: [ἐχαρίτωσεν ὑμᾶς ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ], that is, he made us accepted in the Beloved.

units.la: Aedituus quidam accusauit suum pastorem, quòd infantem baptizasset indutus chirothecis. Tanta est calumniandi libido, ut non pudeat discipulos, suos doctores etiam ob leuissimam causam palàm accusare.
units.tr: A sexton accused his pastor of having baptized an infant while wearing gloves. So great is the lust for calumny that disciples are not ashamed to accuse their own teachers openly, even for the slightest cause.

units.la: Timon Atheniensis scripsit contra omnes Philosophos, & solitus est de omnibus malè loqui. Idè cùm Respublica uersaretur in periculo, dixit, se magno gaudio affici, quòd iste pessimus populus lueret poenas: & ualde sibi placere ingenium Alcibiadis adhuc iuuenis, & peruersè omnia agentis, ac fore ut aliquando Rempublicā euerteret. Quod postea etiam factum est.
units.tr: Timon of Athens wrote against all the philosophers and was accustomed to speak ill of everyone. So when the commonwealth was in danger, he said he was greatly delighted that that most wicked people was paying the penalty; and he took much pleasure in the temperament of Alcibiades, still a young man, who did everything perversely, and he predicted that Alcibiades would one day overthrow the commonwealth. This indeed happened afterwards.

units.la: Philocrates interrogatus, cur omnibus maledicéret? respondit: Quia omnibus malefacere nō posset. Hæc est responsio [?]. Isocrates enim interrogabat eū de obiecto seu merito, quæ uidelicet esset causa impulsiua, qua in re sic eum omnes læsissent, ut eis offensus esset? Ipse uerò respondit de subiecto, seu morbo animi sui. Est igitur uariatio causæ, ut dictū est. Vt si quis quærat: warumb schabet man den kås? & alter respondeat: wēn er federn hått, so rupffete man in.id est, Quare decrustatur seu circumraditur cascus? & alter respondeat: Quia non habet plumas, alioquin enim deplumaretur.
units.tr: Philocrates, asked why he spoke ill of everyone, replied: "Because I cannot harm everyone." This is the answer [?]. For Isocrates asked him about the object or merit, that is, what the moving cause was, by which everyone had so wronged him that he was offended by them. But he answered about the subject, or the disease of his own mind. There is therefore a variation in the cause, as has been said. It is like asking: "Why do they scrape the Käs?" and another answering: "If it has feathers, one plucks it." That is, why is the cheese scraped or its rind trimmed? Because it has no feathers; otherwise it would be plucked.

units.la: Capnio dicere solitus est de his qui omnia uituperant, eos similes esse muscis: quæ omnia contaminant, & nihil prosunt.
units.tr: Capnio used to say of those who find fault with everything that they are like flies: they contaminate everything and profit nothing.

units.la: Vuicelius & Coeleus dicũt nos prodidisse Rho-dum, & nescio quæ alia fecisse. Hæc impudentia mendacia non opus est refutare: dicant ipsi ta-lia, quo ad uelint.
units.tr: Wicelius and Coelius say that we betrayed Rhodes, and that we did I know not what else. There is no need to refute these shameless lies: let them say such things as they please.

units.la: Scipio iunior ætatis suæ anno 56. est mortuus: sed maior Scipio peruenit ad maiorè senectutem, ac tandem mortuus est in uilla sua. Hic adeò auer-satus est litigare cũ ciuibus, ut ideo relicta Roma in rus abiret. Cum tribuni contra ipsum uocifera-rentur, potuisset facilius imperium rapere, quàm Iulius. sed contétiones fugiēs, hoc unicũ dixit: Ci-ues meministis, me hoc die & hoc anno feliciter pugnasse cõtra Carthaginenses: oro ut mecũ ascē-datis in templũ, & mecum publicè gratias agatis. Et rectè fecit, iuxta dictũ Cypriani: Non est miser qui audit conuicium, sed qui facit. Item Philemo-nis dictum: Nulla carmina magis musica, quàm ferre conuicia hominũ. Idem duobus litigantibus: Altero (ait) maledicente, qui tacet sapientior est. Σιδιόν ἐστι γέγαρ ἢ ἐπαινεῖν: id est, dulcius est uitu-perare quàm laudare.
units.tr: The younger Scipio died in the fifty-sixth year of his age, but the elder Scipio reached a greater old age, and finally died on his country estate. He so much shunned litigation with his fellow citizens that he left Rome and went off to the country. When the tribunes shouted against him, he could more easily have seized power, as Julius did; but avoiding quarrels, he said only this: "Citizens, you remember that on this day and in this year I fought successfully against the Carthaginians. I beg you to come with me to the temple and join me in giving public thanks." And he acted rightly, in line with the saying of Cyprian: "He is not wretched who hears abuse, but he who inflicts it." Likewise the saying of Philemon: "No songs are more pleasing to the ear than men's insults" [sic: ironically, to bear insults]. And to two litigants he said: "When one of you is abusing, the one who keeps silent is the wiser." "It is sweeter to revile than to praise" [Σιδιόν ἐστι γέγαρ ἢ ἐπαινεῖν]: that is, reviling is sweeter than praising.

units.la: Donaui Eobano Hesso ualde elegans Aldinũ exemplar Epigrammatum, quod erat eleganter excusum. Cùm illud à me peteret, facturũ me esse dixi, sed ea cõditione, ut scriberet carmẽ optimũ de re pessima. De qua nam resait. Iussi eum de ca-lumnia scribere. Idq; fecit, ac de hac re iam om-nium pulcherrimũ extat.
units.tr: I gave Eobanus Hessus a very elegant Aldine copy of the Epigrams, which was handsomely printed. When he asked me for it, I said I would do so, but on the condition that he write an excellent poem on the worst of subjects. When he asked what subject, I told him to write on calumny. He did so, and there is now the most beautiful work of all on this theme.

units.la: Plato citat dictum Galeni: Qui amat λογομαχίας, nunquam perueniet ad ueritatem. Sunt autem plurima talia ingenia ἐριστικά.
units.tr: Plato quotes the saying of Galen: whoever loves contentious word-battles [λογομαχίας] will never reach the truth. There are, however, very many such minds that are inclined to wrangling [ἐριστικά].

units.la: ASSENTATIO ET SIMULATIO.
units.tr: ASSENTATIO ET SIMULATIO.

units.la: Seneca.
units.tr: Seneca.

units.la: Adulatores non tantum sunt suorum dominorum arrisores, sed etiam arrisores.
units.tr: Flatterers are not only the mockers of their masters, but also their mockers in turn.

units.la: Cicero:
units.tr: Cicero:

units.la: Nullus Euripus habet tam varias agitationes, ut populi voluntates.
units.tr: No Euripus has such varied currents as the wishes of the people.

units.la: Timon: ἄνθρωποι νεvῆς οἰήσεως ἐμπλεκοι ἀσωοί, Homines vanæ opinionis pleni uentriculi seu sacci.
units.tr: Timon: men full of empty opinion, stomachs or bags of unsteadiness [ἄνθρωποι νεης οἰήσεως ἐμπλεκοι ἀσωοί], that is, men full of empty opinion, bellies or sacks.

units.la: Plato inquit: Cogitationes hominum esse instabiles, ut illæ imagines quæ cernuntur in aquis.
units.tr: Plato says: the thoughts of men are unstable, like those images which are seen in water.

units.la: Memini Ducem Saxoniæ Mauricium de quodam assentatore dixisse: Stercus domini sui comedit, ut canis. Dionysius habuit colacem, qui lingebat eius sputum. Tales omnibus temporibus reperiuntur.
units.tr: I remember Duke Maurice of Saxony saying of a certain flatterer: he eats his lord's dung, like a dog. Dionysius had a flatterer who licked up his spittle. Such men are found in every age.

units.la: Dux Saxoniæ Fridericus acute solitus est dicere, eos maximè esse metuendos, qui proximi essent pedibus, ne calces conculcent: alios non ita posse nocere.
units.tr: Duke Frederick of Saxony used to say shrewdly that those are to be feared most who stand closest to your feet, lest they trample on your heels; others cannot do so much harm.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Cardinalis quidam solitus est dicere, de ijs qui aliud loquuntur & aliud meditantur: Est uox Iacob, & manus Esau.
units.tr: A certain cardinal used to say, of those who say one thing and intend another: "The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: Collectanea.

units.la: In Tripartita historia, libro 6. cap. 28. fit metio Eusebomi, qui fuit rhetor tempore aliquot Imperatorum, & semper se accommodauit ad uoluntates & opiniones de religione, eorum, penes quos summa potestas fuit. Tempore Constantini Principis acerrimè defendit doctrinam Euangelij, & taxauit idololatriam. Postea uerò cùm pio patri succederet impius filius, defensor idololatriæ, ibi rursus strinxit calamum aduersus ueram Ecclesiam.
units.tr: In the Tripartite History, book 6, chapter 28, mention is made of Eusebomius, who was a rhetorician in the time of several emperors, and always accommodated himself to the wishes and opinions about religion of those in whose hands supreme power lay. In the time of the emperor Constantine he defended the doctrine of the Gospel most fiercely and censured idolatry. Afterwards, however, when a pious father was succeeded by an impious son, a defender of idolatry, he again turned his pen against the true Church.

units.la: Menander.
units.tr: Menander.

units.la: In hac uita gaudent improbi potissimùm: sed assentator omnium primas tenet, uiuitq; longè omnium iucundissimè. Deinde sycophantæ proximus est honos: audire enim calumnias, est admodum dulce. At tertius conceditur locus inuido, qui artes noscendi scit astutissimè. Inuidentia enim est proprium φθόνος diaboli, de qua antiquũ dictum est: Virtutem sequitur inuidentia, sicut umbra corpus.
units.tr: In this life the wicked above all rejoice; but the flatterer holds the first place of all, and lives far more pleasantly than all others. Next to him the sycophant has the nearest honour, for it is very sweet to hear slanders. But a third place is granted to the envious man, who knows most cunningly the arts of getting to know people. For envy is the proper vice [φθόνος] of the devil, of which an old saying runs: envy follows virtue as a shadow follows a body.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Cùm Dionysius scripsisset tragœdias, exhibuit eas legendas Philoxeno poetæ. cui cùm non placerent, libero animo id tyranno indicauit: ostendens... ostenditģ; ipsi errata. Ille iratus iussit eum abdu-cere in Latomias. & post aliquot menses inde ex-emit eum, iussitģ; iterum indicare, ut suum iudi-cium de poemate diceret. Cùm & tùc indicare nol-lent, nisi priùs ostensis erratis, iterum eum abdu-xit in carcerem. Ille non fuit assentator, sed for-titer contemptis periculis, tyrannum coràm de uî-tijs admonuit: quod etiamsi ego uel alius non fa-ceremus, tamen laudanda est eius constantia.
units.tr: When Dionysius had written tragedies, he showed them to the poet Philoxenus to be read. When Philoxenus did not like them, he told the tyrant his opinion frankly, pointing out and showing him his errors. The tyrant, angry, ordered him to be taken off to the quarries. After some months he released him from there and ordered him to tell him again, so that he might state his judgment of the poem. When Philoxenus was still unwilling to give his opinion unless the errors had first been pointed out, the tyrant had him led back to prison. Philoxenus was not a flatterer; bravely, despising the dangers, he admonished the tyrant to his face about his faults. Even if I or anyone else would not have done so, his constancy is nonetheless to be praised.

units.la: Demosthenes.
units.tr: Demosthenes.

units.la: Difficilis est assentatio, quando hoc proponi-tur, quod est ingratum cupiditati.
units.tr: Flattery is hard when what is put forward is something unwelcome to desire.

units.la: Plautus:
units.tr: Plautus:

units.la: Odi argutũ ciuẽ sine uirtute, tanquã præficã.
units.tr: I hate a clever citizen without virtue, as a hired mourner.

units.la: MALA CONVERSATIO.
units.tr: MALA CONVERSATIO.

units.la: Κακῆς ὁμιλίας ϐελτερ μεῖζον κακόν: id est, Mala conuersatione nullum malũ maius. iuxta dictum Pauli: Corrũpunt bonos mores colloquia prava. Demosthenes citat hanc sententiam ex Aeschine: Talis est unusquisq;, qualium conuersatione de-lectatur.
units.tr: Nothing is a greater evil than bad company [Κακῆς ὁμιλίας χεῖρον μεῖζον κακόν]: that is, no evil is greater than bad conversation, according to Paul's saying: "Evil communications corrupt good manners." Demosthenes cites this saying from Aeschines: "Each man is such as the company he delights in."

units.la: Sicut basiliscus inficit res quascunq;, ita umbra malorum hominum sæpe nocet bonis.
units.tr: Just as the basilisk poisons whatever things it touches, so the shadow of wicked men often harms good people.

units.la: Κακὸν κακῷ συμφερέγχε: id est, Malum malo computrescit, & colliquescit: malum malo causa destructionis mutuæ.
units.tr: Evil rots and dissolves with evil [Κακὸν κακῷ συμφερέγχε]: that is, evil with evil decays and melts away, evil being the mutual cause of destruction.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Nulla est societas tam parua, in qua non sint aliqui mali. Duodecim fuerunt Christi discipuli, & inter eos Iudas proditor.
units.tr: There is no society so small that some wicked people are not found in it. Christ had twelve disciples, and among them Judas the traitor.

units.la: SOPHISMA.
units.tr: SOPHISM.

units.la: Cùm essemus Smalcaldiæ, uenit eò Legatus Romani pontificis ad Principem Electorem, asse-rens ei literas. Princeps, ut est consuetudo, surre-xit deliberans, & iussit illi per alium responderi: quia Principes non solent loqui latinè. Ille phantasticus dicebat: Quid est opus responsione? Princeps iam est assensus. Et ita argumentabatur: Qui tacet, consentire uidetur. Ego uerò dicebam: Hoc est sophisticum. Incanduit ille, inquiēs: Non sum sophista, sum doctor iuris. Quasi doctor iuris non posset esse sophista. Est regula iuris, sed non ualet in coniecturalibus. Nam dicit, Videtur: Es argumentum, Videtur, soluitur per Non uidetur.
units.tr: When we were at Schmalkalden, the legate of the Roman pontiff came there to the Elector Prince and presented him with a letter. The Prince, as is his custom, rose to deliberate and ordered that he be answered through another person, because princes do not usually speak Latin. That foolish fellow said: "What need is there for a reply? The Prince has already assented." And he argued thus: "Whoever is silent seems to consent." I, however, said: "This is a sophism." He flared up and said: "I am no sophist, I am a doctor of law." As if a doctor of law could not be a sophist! It is a rule of law, but it does not hold in conjectural matters. For he says, "It seems," and the argument from "it seems" is answered by "it does not seem."

units.la: In aditu Franconiæ est sylua, quæ erat Abbatis Fuldēsis, sed oppignorauerat eam alij cuidā Domino. Cùm autem Abbas ante paucos annos suā partem redimere uellet, inuentum est hoc sophisma: non posse sciri pondus aureorum, quos ille olim dedisset.
units.tr: At the edge of Franconia there is a forest which belonged to the Abbot of Fulda, but he had pawned it to another lord. When the abbot wished, a few years ago, to redeem his share, the following sophism was devised: that the weight of the gold coins he had once given could not be known.

units.la: Interfui iudicio, in quo erat Doctor quidā, homo probus uir, cuius antagonista erat rabula indoctissimus. simus. Hic uociferabatur, & sæpe iterabat illa uerba: Domine doctor, uerte folium, ibi inuenies alium textum: Her doctor, keert das blat vmb, da stehets anders. Ita dicunt βωμόλογοι indocti.
units.tr: I was present at a trial in which there was a certain doctor, an upright man, whose opponent was a most unlearned babbler. This fellow kept shouting and often repeated those words: "Herr Doctor, turn the page, there you will find another text" (German: "Her doctor, keert das blat vmb, da stehets anders"). So do the unlearned babblers [βωμόλογοι] talk.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Mit worten deüschet man die leüt. Hoc proverbio Germani significare uolunt, quòd ignorantes proprietates uocabulorum, facilè deciptiantur.
units.tr: "One deceives people with words" (German: "Mit worten deüschet man die leüt"). By this proverb the Germans mean that those who do not know the proper meanings of words are easily deceived.

units.la: Cancer & serpens unà faciebant iter (id est, homo simplex & sophisticus) Videbat cancer, interdum progredi serpentem, interdum facere gyros. Cancer progrediebatur, iubebat serpentem recta uia incedere, ipsumq; sequi. Cùm serpēs non uellet rectè incedere, apprehendit cancer collum eius chelis, & eam strangulat. Sic corrigitur eius perplexus cursus. Iam eris rectus, inquit cancer, cùm te hoc modo punio. Hoc est præmium sophistices.
units.tr: A crab and a snake were travelling together (that is, a simple man and a sophist). The crab saw that the snake sometimes went forward and sometimes made circles. The crab went on ahead and ordered the snake to proceed in a straight path and follow him. When the snake did not want to go straight, the crab seized its neck with its claws and strangled it. In this way its crooked course was corrected. "Now you will be straight," said the crab, "since I punish you in this way." This is the reward of sophistry.

units.la: FOEDERA.
units.tr: COVENANTS.

units.la: Ante paucos annos Imperator Carolus V. & Veneti iniuerant fœdus contra Turcam, cùm Veneti antea confœderati essent Turcico Imperatori: ibi Andreas de Doria deseruit Venetos. Nam naturale odium est inter Venetos & Genuenses. Cōstitit igitur magno Venetis illa discessio à Turcico fœdere. Turcicus enim Imperator noluit eis placaplacari, nisi cederent duabus præstantissimis urbibus, Monembasia uidelicet & Calliopoli. Est autem Monembasia urbs proxima Mycenis, quæ deinde dicta est Epidaurus. In Homero dicitur uitifera. Ibi enim sunt generosissima uina: unde & uinum Maluaticum, quod apud nos habemus, aducbitur. Calliopolis uero paulò superius sita est. Sic Veneti iterum coacti sunt pacem componere, ac nouum fœdus facere cum Turcico Imperatore, quia uidebant se desertos esse ab Andrea de Doria.
units.tr: A few years ago the Emperor Charles V and the Venetians had entered into a covenant against the Turk, although the Venetians had previously been allied with the Turkish Emperor. There Andrea Doria deserted the Venetians, for there is a natural hatred between the Venetians and the Genoese. That defection of the Venetians from the Turkish covenant therefore cost them dearly. For the Turkish Emperor refused to be appeased unless they gave up two most important cities, namely Monemvasia and Gallipoli. Monemvasia is a city near Mycenae, which was later called Epidaurus; in Homer it is called "vine-bearing," for there are very fine wines there, from which also the Malmsey wine that we have here is brought. Gallipoli lies a little further up. Thus the Venetians were once again forced to make peace and to make a new covenant with the Turkish Emperor, because they saw that they had been deserted by Andrea Doria.

units.la: Fridericus Dux Saxoniæ dicebat: Bonum est facere fœdera, sed uæ illi qui seruat.
units.tr: Frederick, Duke of Saxony, used to say: "It is good to make covenants, but woe to him who keeps them."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Fœdera apud omnes gentes sancta atq; inuiolabilia fuerunt. Quibus autem, & quàm uarijs ritibus ab antiquis feriri soleant, passim apud Homerum, aliosq; poetas & historicos uidere licet. Hoc unum impræsentiarum admonendi estis, quòd plerumq; in fœderibus conuiuia in mutuæ beneuolentiæ symbolū adhiberi soleant. Nec solum hostes ad concordiam redeuntes, sed commilitones quoque & socij in præsenti periculo constituti, atq; in hostes ituri, prius hoc sese mutuo beneuolentiæ vinculo obstringere ac deuincire solent. Sic apud Homerum Iliados T. post reconciliationē Agamēnonis & Achillis, elegans ab hoc recitarecitatur uersiculus, Græcos ad præliū præparā-tis: Nunc uerò abite ad cœnam, ut congregemus Martem. Sic etiam mensa Christi tessera quædam esse debet, non solum Christi in nos amoris atque beneficiorum, sed mutuæ quoq; inter nos beneuolentiæ, & sub uno capite Christo in mystico corpore unionis. Verùm hoc, proh dolor, tempore pleriq; contentiosi hoc institutum adeò detorse-runt ac peruerterunt, ut ipsi nos mutuò laceremus atq; conficiamus. Cùm autem omnia fœdera ista sunt cum aliquo ritu, tum præcipuè mensæ debent esse mutuæ beneuolentiæ symbola.
units.tr: Covenants among all nations have been holy and inviolable. Which rites were customarily used by the ancients in striking them, and how varied they were, may be seen everywhere in Homer and other poets and historians. For the present, we should be reminded of this one thing: that in covenants feasts are commonly held as a token of mutual goodwill. Not only enemies returning to concord, but also fellow soldiers and allies placed in present danger and about to go against enemies, are accustomed first to bind and tie themselves to one another by this bond of goodwill. Thus in Homer, Iliad book 19, after the reconciliation of Agamemnon and Achilles, a graceful little verse is quoted, addressed to the Greeks preparing for battle: "Now, however, go away to supper, so that we may gather for Mars." So too the table of Christ ought to be a certain token, not only of Christ's love and benefits toward us, but also of mutual goodwill among us, and of our union under the one head Christ in the mystical body. But, alas, many contentious people in our time have so twisted and perverted this institution that we tear and destroy one another. Since all these covenants have some rite, the table especially ought to be a token of mutual goodwill.

units.la: DECEPTIONES ET elusiones.
units.tr: Deceptions and evasions.

units.la: Sanseuerinus non fuit multò ante nostram ætatem Princeps in regno Neapolitano, & amicus Iouij Pontani. ille profectus est ad montē Sinai, sicut usitatū fuit etiam nostris principibus Germanicis proficisci in terram sanctā: ut dux Fridericus cum duce Christophoro Bauariæ, fuit Hierosolymæ. Oportuit autem in Aegypto iter facere per Idumeam: ibi occurrerūt ei Arabes equites cum magno impetu. Quod uidens deductor, seu interpres corum, dixit: Domini non possum uos protegere cōtra istos latrunculos Arabes, nec publica fides data ab Imperatore uos iuuabit: sed oportet uos redimere pecunia. Bene, inquit Sanseuerinus, nus, uidebimus, descenditq; de equo, ac iubet appa-rare mensam, quasi essent pransuri, promere ua-sa, cibum, potum, & assidere tanquam ad mensam. Cumq; equites accessissent ad eos, iussit Sanseue-rinus per interpretem eis indicare, illos sibi ui-deri militares homines: se etiam esse militarem, & suscepisse istam profectionem, ut cognosceret quale esset genus militiæ, & quales homines mili-tares in illis terris: oratq;, ut descendât de equis, & cum ipso prandeant. Quòd cum factum esset, colloquuntur inuicem de rebus militaribus, de for-mis gerendorum bellorum: & sic unà familiariter prandent. Cum essent pransi, iubet Sanseuerinus promi munera, & illa inter eos distribuit: deditq; uni bombardà, alteri gladiū. Sic distributis mune-ribus incolumes dimittuntur. Elapso triduo in redi-tu, reuertuntur Arabes cum maiori turba, & cap-tiuū Sanseuerinum cum suis abducunt. Ille existi-mat iam actum esse de ipsorum salute, & istos omnino immemores esse prioris beneficij accepti. Illi ducunt eum in arcem, & uicissim honorificè tractant ipsum cum suis comitibus. Elapsis autem aliquot diebus, deducunt ipsum cum suo comitatu incolumē & saluum, præbentq; se defensores & monstratores uiæ. Tantum enim ualet uirtus a-pud Barbaros, iuxta dictū Pindari: Virtus etiam apud hostes in admiratione est.
units.tr: Sanseverinus, a prince in the kingdom of Naples and a friend of Giovanni Pontano, lived not long before our own time. He travelled to Mount Sinai, just as it was customary for our German princes to travel to the Holy Land; Duke Frederick, for example, went to Jerusalem with Duke Christopher of Bavaria. The route had to pass through Idumea in Egypt, and there Arab horsemen came at them with great force. Seeing this, their guide or interpreter said: "Sirs, I cannot protect you against these Arab brigands, and the public safe-conduct given by the Emperor will not help you either. You must buy your way out with money." "Very well," said Sanseverinus, "we shall see," and he dismounted and ordered a table to be set up, as if they were about to dine. He had vessels, food and drink brought out, and they sat down as if at table. When the horsemen came up to them, Sanseverinus had the interpreter tell them that he considered them soldiers, and that he too was a soldier, who had undertaken this journey in order to learn what kind of warfare was practised and what sort of men the soldiers of those lands were. He begged them to dismount and dine with him. When they had done so, they talked together about military affairs and the methods of waging war, and so they dined together in a friendly way. When they had eaten, Sanseverinus ordered gifts to be brought out and distributed them among them: he gave one man a harquebus and another a sword. With the gifts distributed, they were let go unharmed. Three days later, on the return journey, the Arabs came back with a larger band and carried off Sanseverinus as a captive along with his companions. He thought that it was now all over for their safety, and that these men had quite forgotten the earlier favour they had received. But they led him into their stronghold and treated him and his companions with honour in return. After some days, they escorted him and his retinue safely and unharmed, and they offered themselves as guardians and guides of the road. Such is the power of virtue among barbarians, according to the saying of Pindar: "Virtue is admired even among enemies."

units.la: Cùm quidam monachus Dominicaster, concionator Ducis Saxoniæ Friderici (qui admodū à Luthero & alijs doctis uiris laudabatur) aliquando in concione quædam uitia in Principe etiam taxare uellet, nec palàm id facere auderet: arte quadam & stratagemate in populum deriuauit, hac similitudine usus: Amici, inquit concionator, ille textus, eiusq; expositio non est dissimilis ei qui detraxit pellem lepori: & cum à reliquo corpore facilè detrahitur pellis, postquam ad caput uentum est, difficilior est detractio. Ita concionator, cùm populi uicia taxat, ut sunt adulteria, & alia peccata (nominans præcipuè ea quæ in Principe taxare uolebat) non est quòd metuat difficultatem: sed cùm uentum est ad caput (digitis interea monstrans Principem astantem) diabolus pellem à capite abstrahat, da streiff dich der teufel. Fridericus sapiens & bonus Princeps, etsi intelligebat se taxari & reprehendi: tamen sine indignatione adeò tulit modestè, ut monacho etiam nouam uestem dono daret.
units.tr: When a certain Dominican friar, a preacher to Duke Frederick of Saxony (who was much praised by Luther and other learned men), wished at one sermon to rebuke certain vices even in the prince, but did not dare to do so openly, he resorted to a kind of trick and deflected the matter onto the people, using this comparison: "Friends," said the preacher, "that text and its exposition is not unlike a man who strips the skin from a hare. The skin comes off easily from the rest of the body, but once one reaches the head, it is harder to remove. So the preacher, when he rebukes the vices of the people, such as adultery and other sins (naming especially those which he wished to rebuke in the prince), need not fear difficulty; but when he comes to the head (meanwhile pointing with his finger at the prince standing there), the devil strips the skin from the head: da streiff dich der teufel" [then the devil strip it off you]. Frederick, a wise and good prince, although he understood that he was being censured and rebuked, bore it so moderately and without anger that he even gave the monk a new garment as a gift.

units.la: Capnio iter faciens, cùm circa meridiem in oppidū quoddā uenisset, ubi aliquot horas ipsi expectandum erat: cumq; intentissimum esset frigus, & hypocaustum nimia rusticorum multitudine esset occupatum, neminem habebat cum quo colloqui posset: nec ipsi quid, quo tempus falleret, leret, offerebatur: insuper præ nimio rusticorum tumultu & uociferationibus, nihil aut loqui, aut legere poterat. Petijt igitur sibi poculum aqua repletum, nec non particulam cretæ dari. Quæ cum accepisset, duxit circulum in mensæ superficie, cui signum crucis inscripsit: oppositi dextræ poculum, quod aquam continebat: sinistra cultrum in mensa fixum habuit: & librum quem habebat secum, circulo imposuit. Rustici interim omnes oculos & uultum in hunc conuertunt, nihil loquuntur, placidè & quietè quid tandem futurũ sit expectant, Cùm autẽ rustici ita taciti sederent, alter alterum inspiciens, ille interim operam literis nauauit.
units.tr: Capnio, travelling, had come about midday to a certain town, where he had to wait for some hours. It was extremely cold, and the stove room was crowded with an excessive number of country folk, so that he had no one to talk with, and nothing was offered him with which to pass the time. Moreover, because of the great din and shouting of the peasants, he could neither speak nor read. He therefore asked for a cup filled with water and also for a little chalk to be given him. When he had these, he drew a circle on the surface of the table and marked a sign of the cross within it. He placed the cup of water in his right hand, and in his left he held a knife fixed in the table; then he set the book he had with him on the circle. Meanwhile all the peasants turned their eyes and faces upon him, said nothing, and waited quietly and calmly to see what would happen. While the peasants sat thus in silence, looking at one another, he meanwhile devoted himself to his writing.

units.la: In aditu Asiæ fuit templum, in quo pependit nodus uariè colligatus: & fuit dictũ, eum qui soluisset illũ nodum, fore dominum Asiæ. Cùm pluri mi antea uenissent ea de causa in Asiã, ut Lysander, Iason, nec potuissent nodum illũ soluere: tandem Alexander aspiciens illum, statim dissecuit gladio, & sic soluit. Inde inexplicabiles disputationes uocantur nodi Gordij.
units.tr: At the entrance to Asia there was a temple in which hung a knot tied in various ways, and it was said that whoever untied that knot would be lord of Asia. Many had previously come into Asia for this reason, such as Lysander and Jason, but none had been able to untie the knot. At last Alexander, looking at it, immediately cut it through with his sword, and so undid it. Hence inextricable disputations are called "Gordian knots."

units.la: Rabula Norinbergensis alium quendam aduersariæ partis egregiè uolebat traducere & diffamare. Sed legibus Norinbergensis ciuitatis cautum est, ne quis alium conuicijs lacessat coram iudice. Is igitur ut effugeret pœnam, rem ita coponebat. ponebat. Scribebat (ut solet fieri) duo exemplaria, in quorũ altero nihil erat conuiciorum: in altero uero conscripserat aliquas paginas cõuiciorum plenas: sed ea iterum deleuerat, ita tamen, ut adhuc legi possent. Ea ambo exemplaria more usitato iudici exhibet, & curat, ut illud in quo erant conuicia, causidico aduersæ partis daretur. Res procedit. Ille alter perlectis conuicijs, postridie uenit in iudicium accusans alterum, quòd contra leges conuicia scripsisset, quæ coram Senatu & omnibus legi iubet, ac petit de illo funi pœnam. At alter accusatus, Se quidem, inquit, primo calore scripsisse conuicia: sed postea memorem legis, ea rursus deleuisse: deinde tempus etiã describendi breue fuisse, ut describere aliter non potuerit. Se igitur pœnam non debere pro deletis chartis, affirmat. Sic itaq; absolutus est, & nihilominus perfecit id quod uoluit: nempe ut illa conuicia publicè legerentur.
units.tr: Rabula of Nuremberg wished to disgrace and defame an opponent of his party most vigorously. But by the laws of the city of Nuremberg, it was forbidden for anyone to abuse another before a judge. So, to escape punishment, he arranged the matter as follows. He wrote (as is usual) two copies: in one of them there was no abuse; in the other he had written several pages full of insults, but had deleted them again, though in such a way that they could still be read. He handed both copies to the judge in the usual manner, and arranged that the one containing the insults should be given to the advocate of the opposing side. The matter went forward. The other man, having read the insults, came to court the next day, accusing his opponent of having written abuse contrary to the laws. He demanded that the insults be read aloud before the Senate and everyone present, and asked that a penalty be imposed on him. But the accused replied: "I did indeed write insults in the first heat of passion, but afterwards, mindful of the law, I deleted them again. Moreover, the time for copying was short, so I could not copy them otherwise. I therefore maintain that I should not be punished for pages that have been struck out." Thus he was acquitted, and nonetheless he achieved what he wanted, namely that those insults were read out in public.

units.la: Cùm Alexander deleturus esset urbem Lampsacum, & Anaxander deprecari uellet, ne id faceret, accedereq; ad Regem eius rei impetrandæ causa: Alexander ei occurrit, quia intellexerat eum hanc ob causam uenire, ut pro Lampsaco deprecaretur, inquiens: Iuro me non facturũ esse id quod postulas. Tunc Anaxander ait: Precor itaque ô Rex, ut Lampsacũ deleas. Alexander der sancto iuramento perterritus, quia promise-rat se non factURUM esse quæ postularet, ab ex-pugnatione destitit, Lampsacumq; incolumem di-misit. Ita Anaxander urbem seruauit. Hæc fuit uen usta ac salutaris εὐτυχωτέλεια[?] ac clusio.
units.tr: When Alexander was about to destroy the city of Lampsacus, and Anaxander wished to plead with him not to do so, and went to the king to obtain this, Alexander met him, because he had understood that he had come for this purpose, to plead on behalf of Lampsacus. Alexander said: "I swear that I will not do what you ask." Then Anaxander said: "I therefore beg you, O King, to destroy Lampsacus." Alexander, terrified by his solemn oath, since he had promised that he would not do what he was asked, desisted from the assault and let Lampsacus go unharmed. Thus Anaxander saved the city. This was a charming and salutary piece of wit [εὐτραπελία] and conclusion.

units.la: IVDICIA ET MONVMEN-ta de uarijs rebus.
units.tr: Judgements and memorable events concerning various matters.

units.la: Rex Danicus legit multos libros Sibyllinos, & dixit eos continere multa mirabilia: sed non esse bonum eos uenire in manus hominum.
units.tr: The Danish king read many of the Sibylline books and said that they contained many marvellous things, but that it was not good for them to fall into people's hands.

units.la: Valla magnum mouit tumultū, disputans: sym-bolum Apostolorū primùm esse traditū & excogitatum in concilio Niceno. nam non facit discri-men inter symbolū Apostolorum & Nicænum. Allegabat dicta ex iure canonico: & in quibus contra Grammaticam aliquid erratum erat, re-prehendebat. Erat enim bonus Grammaticus.
units.tr: Valla stirred up a great commotion by arguing that the Apostles' Creed was first handed down and devised at the Council of Nicaea, for he makes no distinction between the Apostles' Creed and the Nicene. He cited passages from canon law and corrected whatever had been wrongly written against the rules of grammar, for he was a good grammarian.

units.la: Eramus unà in conuiuio, D. Martinus, D. Hie-ronymus Schurpf, & ego: cùm hic forte esset alius doctus uir. ubi cùm de uarijs rebus, tum etiam de studijs colloqueremur, ille doctus uir dicit: Recès perlegi Odysseam Homeri, quæ erat Germanicè edita: quo libro non quicquā legi ineptius. Certè bellū illud gestū esse, & fuisse etiam ibi præstan-tes Principes in utraq; parte, non dubiū est. Inde aliquæ mutationes secutæ sunt.
units.tr: We were together at a dinner: Dr Martin, Dr Hieronymus Schurpf, and I, and there happened to be another learned man present. As we talked about various matters, and also about studies, that learned man said: "I have recently read through Homer's Odyssey, which was published in German, and I have read nothing more foolish in any book." Certainly that war was waged, and there is no doubt that outstanding princes on both sides took part in it. Some changes followed from it.

units.la: Oda septima Pindarica tantæ fuit admiratiónis apud Rhodios, ut fuerit scripta in templo aureis literis, siue id in pariete, siue in membrana factum sit.
units.tr: The seventh Pindaric ode was so admired by the Rhodians that it was written in golden letters in a temple, whether this was done on a wall or on parchment.

units.la: Ratisbonæ in monasterio est Testamentū nouum, scriptū aureis literis in mēbrana: quod uidi.
units.tr: In the monastery at Regensburg there is a New Testament written in golden letters on parchment; I have seen it.

units.la: Basileæ fuit etiam nouum Testamentum græcum, aureis literis scriptum: quo ego usus sum adolescens. Erasmus eius etiam facit mentionem, quia eo est usus in emendatione noui Testamenti.
units.tr: At Basel there was also a Greek New Testament written in golden letters, which I used as a young man. Erasmus also mentions it, because he used it in the emendation of the New Testament.

units.la: Albertus Durerus, pictor Norinbergensis, sapiens uir, dixit: hoc interesse inter Lutheri & aliorum Theologorum scripta, quòd ipse legens in prima pagina tres uel quatuor periodos scriptorum Lutheri, scire posset, quid esset expectandum in toto opere. Et hanc esse laudem scriptorum Lutheri, uidelicet illam perspicuitatē & ordinem orationis. De alijs uerò dicebat, quòd postquam perlegisset totum librum, oporteret attentè cogitare quid voluisset author dicere, uel de qua re disserat.
units.tr: Albrecht Dürer, the painter of Nuremberg, a wise man, said that there is this difference between the writings of Luther and those of other theologians: when one reads the first page of Luther's writings, after three or four periods one can tell what to expect in the whole work. This, he said, is the praise of Luther's writings, namely that clarity and orderliness of expression. But of the others he said that, after one had read through the whole book, one had to think hard about what the author had wanted to say, or what matter he was discussing.

units.la: Imperator Carolus V. interrogauit legatum Brunsuicensem, dicens: Audiui in curia uestræ urbis multa esse monumenta ueterum Imperatorū. Est'ne hoc ita? Respondit Legatus: Sic esse. & quædam monumenta recitauit. Bene, inquit Imperator: ipse ueniam aliquando, ut ea inspiciam.
units.tr: The Emperor Charles V asked the envoy from Brunswick, saying: "I have heard that there are many monuments of the ancient emperors in the council chamber of your city. Is this so?" The envoy replied that it was so, and he recited some of the monuments. "Good," said the Emperor, "I will come myself sometime to look at them."

units.la: Vidi ibi monumentum Henrici Aucupis, & coniugis eius, quæ fuit comitissa Northeimensis.
units.tr: There I saw the monument of Henry Aucupis and his wife, who was the Countess of Northeim.

units.la: SYMBOLA ET SCVLPTURÆ in numismatibus.
units.tr: Emblems and sculptures on coins.

units.la: Concordia res parvæ crescunt, discordia maximæ dilabuntur. Summi Reges & Principes, sibi & aliis talia breuia præcepta ex sapientum libris electa, sæpe præscripserunt. Sicut Augustus sæpe magistratibus in prouincias misit tales sententias. Et Agrippa Augusti amicus dixit, plurimum sibi profuisse hanc superiorem sententiam ad concordiæ studium cum Augusto.
units.tr: By concord small things grow, by discord the greatest things fall apart. Supreme kings and princes have often prescribed for themselves and for others such brief maxims chosen from the books of the wise.
