Thus Augustus often sent such sayings to magistrates in the provinces. And Agrippa, the friend of Augustus, said that this earlier maxim had greatly helped him in cultivating concord with Augustus.

units.la: Rex Alphonsus Hispanus habuit pro symbolo pellicanum: quam auem dicunt pullos proprio sanguine uiuificare, cum editi sint examines, & adhuc sine motu, si cut etiam catuli leonum. Sed leo ingenti rugitu & halitu catulos animat, & uitam addit. Pellicanus autem sibi fodit pectus, & fundit sanguinem in pullos, quo ipsi uiuific antur. Hoc pinxit Rex, & ascripsit symbolum: Pro lege & grege. Significauit hoc symbolo, bonum Principem debere cum periculo uitæ religionem & subditos defendere. Sic illi heroes dimicarunt: nos tantum quærimus aliena bella.
units.tr: King Alfonso of Spain took the pelican as his emblem. They say this bird revives its young with its own blood, when they are born as shapeless lumps and still without movement, just as lion cubs are (the lion breathes life into its cubs with a mighty roar and breath). But the pelican tears open its breast and pours its blood into the young, by which they are brought to life. The king painted this and added the motto: "For law and flock." By this emblem he signified that a good prince ought, at the risk of his own life, to defend religion and his subjects. Thus those heroes fought; we merely seek other people's wars.

units.la: Medio tutissimus ibis. Medium tenuere beati.
units.tr: "You will go most safely by the middle way." "The blessed have kept to the middle."

units.la: Symbolum Maximiliani Imperatoris est:
units.tr: The emblem of the Emperor Maximilian is:

units.la: TeueTene mensuram, & respice finem. Sic numismatibus suis incudit. Alias scripsit, Tene mensuram, & serua modum. Contraria huic est hæc antiqua sententia: Omne nimiu̇ uertitur in psudich, uel nigrum monachum: id est, Omne nimium conspuitur, aut fit deterius, uertitur in diabolum. Quia diabolus est niger monachus.
units.tr: "Hold fast the measure, and look to the end." This is what he stamped on his coins. At other times he wrote: "Hold the measure and keep moderation." Opposed to this is the old saying: "Every excess turns into a pseudo-monk, or black monk," that is, every excess is spat upon or becomes worse, turning into the devil, because the devil is the black monk.

units.la: Caroli Quinti Imperatoris sunt duæ columnæ Herculis, cum subscriptione: Plus ultra. Quid ipse hoc symbolo significare uoluerit, ignoro: fortasis putat, restare aliam uitam post hanc uitam. Non intelligamus, eum aliquid uelle pro sua sapientia ultra mediocritatem.
units.tr: The Emperor Charles V has the two pillars of Hercules, with the inscription "Further beyond." What he wished to signify by this emblem I do not know; perhaps he thinks there is another life after this one. Let us not suppose that he wishes, by his own wisdom, to go beyond moderation in anything.

units.la: Lysimachi aureus habuit hanc inscriptionem: προνοια και τυχη: id est, prouidentia seu consilium, & successus fortunæ. Hæc enim duo in rebus agē dis debent esse cōiuncta. Agnouit uir fortissimus, professusq; est, ipsum non suo consilio aut uiribus quicquam feliciter transigere potuisse, nisi Deus adiuuisset, & euētus felices addidiset. Deus enim iuuat laborantes.
units.tr: A gold coin of Lysimachus bore this inscription: "providence and fortune [προνοια και τυχη]," that is, foresight or counsel, and the success of fortune. For these two ought to be joined in the conduct of affairs. That most brave man acknowledged and declared that he could accomplish nothing successfully by his own counsel or strength, unless God helped him and granted happy outcomes. For God helps those who labour.

units.la: Augustus habuit capricornū ascendentē in horoscopo, ideoq; ipsum incudit in aureā suam moneta. Vespasianus quoq; habuit capricornū. Noster Imperator Carolus V. etiā habet capricornū, ascendentem in horoscopo. Regula communis habetur: Omnis habens capricornum in horoscopo ascen-
units.tr: Augustus had Capricorn rising in his horoscope, and therefore had it stamped on his gold coin. Vespasian also had Capricorn. Our Emperor Charles V also has Capricorn rising in his horoscope. The common rule is held: everyone who has Capricorn rising in the horoscope...

units.la: Octauum praeceptum.
units.tr: The Eighth Precept.

units.la: ascendentem, facit mutationem in imperio Romano. Dicitur enim esse fatale signum in mutationibus Imperiorum.
units.tr: rising, brings about a change in the Roman empire. For it is said to be the fatal sign in changes of empires.

units.la: Siclus Iudæorum est noster dimidius Ioachimicus: id est, quatuor drachmæ. In uno latere huius Iudaicæ monetæ fuit caliculus thuris, in altero latere uirga Aaronis. Caliculus thuris significat, in illo solo populo fuisse uerā inuocationē: thus enim significat sacrificium & inuocationē. Virga autem Aaronis significat doctrinam legis, & gubernationem sacerdotū: admonet nos hæc, quòd in illo solo populo fuerit uera Ecclesia, sincera uerbi diuini doctrina, & uera inuocatio. Veteres enim voluerunt in numismatibus symbola sculpere, quæ aliquid monerent.
units.tr: The Jewish shekel is our half Joachimsthaler, that is, four drachmas. On one side of this Jewish coin was a little censer of incense, and on the other side Aaron's rod. The censer of incense signifies that true invocation existed in that people alone, for incense signifies sacrifice and invocation. Aaron's rod signifies the doctrine of the law and the government of the priests. It reminds us that the true Church, the pure teaching of the divine Word, and true invocation were to be found in that people alone. For the ancients wished to engrave on their coins devices that would give some admonition.

units.la: Vidi aureum excusum in urbe Monasteriensi, cui inscriptum erat: Rex in templo Dei.
units.tr: I have seen a gold coin struck in the city of Münster, inscribed: King in the temple of God.

units.la: In statua Mercuriali fuerūt hæ sententiæ sculptæ: γνῶχ ι λίπαια φρονῶν: uade, ambula volēs iusta. Altera, μὴ φίλου ἐξαπατᾶν: ne decipias amicū.
units.tr: On a statue of Mercury these sayings were engraved: "Know [γνῶθι] to walk, wishing what is right" (Go, walk willing what is just). The other: "Do not deceive a friend" [μὴ φίλου ἐξαπατᾶν]: do not deceive your friend.

units.la: Fuerunt literæ salui conductus, seu fidei publicæ, quibus promittitur securitas uiatori iusto: nō sis latro, sed iustus, ne decipias amicum.
units.tr: There were letters of safe conduct, or public pledges of good faith, by which security is promised to the upright traveller: Do not be a robber but an upright man; do not deceive a friend.

units.la: Iulianus post Constantinū Magnū rursus amplexus est doctrinā ethnicā: & pinxit suam imaginē in numismate, cui Iupiter imponit coronam, & Pallas injicit ei trabeam, Mercurus verò præbet ei sceptrum.
units.tr: Julian, after Constantine the Great, again embraced pagan teaching, and had his own image struck on a coin, on which Jupiter places a crown on him, Pallas throws a trabea (ceremonial robe) around him, and Mercury gives him a sceptre.

units.la: Octauum præceptum. Symbolum Gostaui, regis Sueciæ.
units.tr: The eighth precept. The device of Gustav, King of Sweden.

units.la: Non nobis Domine, non nobis, sed nomini tuo da gloriam.
units.tr: Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give the glory.

units.la: Eiusdem:
units.tr: By the same:

units.la: Deus dat, cui uult.
units.tr: God gives to whom he wills.

units.la: Vidi nuper monetam ueterem, in cuius altera parte fuit Zopyrus, in altera Zoilus. Fuit imago aulæ. Zopyrus significauit in illo numismate, benè merentem. Nota est enim Zopyri fidelitas erga Darium: qui cùm aliquando haberet malũ granatum, dixit se optare tot habere Zopyros, quot malum haberet grana. Zoilus uerò significat calumniatorem: quia comitantur calumniæ benè merentes.
units.tr: I recently saw an old coin, on one side of which was Zopyrus and on the other Zoilus. It was a court image. On that coin Zopyrus signified one who deserves well. For the loyalty of Zopyrus towards Darius is well known: when Darius once had a pomegranate, he said he wished he had as many Zopyruses as the pomegranate had seeds. Zoilus, however, signifies a slanderer, because slanders accompany those who deserve well.

units.la: Valerianus excudit monetam admodum pulchram, cum inscriptione Cornucopiæ: non uidi pulchriorem aureum.
units.tr: Valerian struck a very handsome coin, with the inscription "Cornucopia." I have never seen a finer gold piece.

units.la: In moneta Theodosij, in uno latere fuit ipsius imago, & in altero latere uexillum crucis, & nõ aquila. Credo ipsum primũ ex Principibus Christianis uexillum in moneta excusum habuisse.
units.tr: On a coin of Theodosius, one side bore his own image and the other side a standard of the cross, not an eagle. I believe he was the first of the Christian princes to have a standard struck on a coin.

units.la: Habui monetam, quæ fuit Ludouici Pij, cuius inscriptio erat: Cludouicus. inde postea fecerunt Clodouicus.
units.tr: I had a coin of Louis the Pious, whose inscription read "Cludouicus"; afterwards they made it "Clodouicus."

units.la: Symbolum Rodolphi, optimi principis in Desaw (qui fui dux Maximiliani Imperatoris, in Italia) pinxit leonem, & ante eum virginem sub quercu nudam, cui leo porrigebat pedem, & uirgo timida semper uerebatur, ne à leone discerperetur. ac inscripsit: Alle zeit mit sorgen.
units.tr: The device of Rudolph, an excellent prince of Desaw (who was a commander under Emperor Maximilian in Italy): he painted a lion and, before it, a naked maiden beneath an oak, to whom the lion held out a paw; the timid maiden always feared lest she be torn to pieces by the lion. And he inscribed it: "Alle zeit mit sorgen" ("Always with care").

units.la: Etiam in Italia quidam recens fecerunt pulchra symbola. Dux Ferrariensis cudit aureum cum inscriptione: Quæ Cæsaris, Cæsari: quæ Dei, Deo. Optarem nos multos aureos posidere, eo ipso, ut Symbola melius consideraremus.
units.tr: Also in Italy some have recently made fine devices. The Duke of Ferrara struck a gold coin with the inscription: "What is Caesar's to Caesar, what is God's to God." I wish we possessed many such gold pieces, so that we might consider these devices better.

units.la: In templo Delphico fuerunt hæ tres sententiæ scriptæ: μηδὲν ἄγαν, Γνῶθι σεαυτὸν: Ἐγγύα, πάρα δ' ἄτη.
units.tr: In the temple at Delphi these three sayings were inscribed: nothing in excess [μηδὲν ἄγαν]; know yourself [Γνῶθι σεαυτὸν]; surety, and ruin is at hand [Ἐγγύα, πάρα δ' ἄτη].

units.la: Regis Hispaniæ Philippi, Caroli V. Imperatoris filij, hoc symbolum esse dicitur: Nec spe, nec metu. Ignoro quid sibi velit hoc symbolo. Magnates eligunt subinde huiusmodi symbola, nescio quo consilio ab ipsis excogitata.
units.tr: The device of Philip, King of Spain, son of Emperor Charles V, is said to be: "Neither by hope nor by fear." I do not know what this device means. Great men from time to time choose such devices, devised by them with some purpose I cannot tell.

units.la: Friderici Imperatoris symbolum est, T. Q. P. Tantum, quantum possum. Significauit, non esse tentanda maiora uiribus.
units.tr: The device of Emperor Frederick is T. Q. P., "As much as I can." It signified that greater things should not be attempted than one's strength allows.

units.la: Ducis Ernesti Luneburgensis fuit, candelabrum cum candela ardente: additis his literis, A. S. M. C. Alijs seruio, mecipsum contero.
units.tr: Of the Duke Ernest of Lüneburg: a candelabrum with a burning candle, with the added letters A. S. M. C., "I serve others, I wear myself out."

units.la: Ducis Henrici Brunsuicensis est: M. Z. M. V. Mein zeit mit vnruw.
units.tr: Of the Duke Henry of Brunswick: M. Z. M. V., "Mein zeit mit vnruw" ("My time with unrest").

units.la: Ducis Mauricij Saxoniæ: V. G. M. A. Vileicht gerets mir auch. Fortes Fortuna adiuuat.
units.tr: Of the Duke Maurice of Saxony: V. G. M. A., "Vileicht gerets mir auch" ("Perhaps it will also turn out well for me"). Fortune helps the brave.

units.la: tt
units.tr: tt

units.la: Regis Daniæ: S.M.C. Spes mea Christus. Reginæ Daniæ: A.G.S.D.VV. Ach Gott schaff deinen willen.
units.tr: The King of Denmark: S.M.C., "Spes mea Christus" (Christ is my hope). The Queen of Denmark: A.G.S.D.VV., "Ach Gott schaff deinen willen" (Ah God, bring about your will).

units.la: Ducis Iuliacensis: Spartā nactus es, hanc orna.
units.tr: Of the Duke of Jülich: "You have obtained Sparta; adorn it."

units.la: Ducis Saxoniæ Ioannis Friderici: Fide, sed cui: Vertrawe, vnd nit zu vil.
units.tr: Of the Duke John Frederick of Saxony: "Fide, sed cui" ("Trust, but in whom"): "Vertrawe, vnd nit zu vil" ("Trust, and not too much").

units.la: Imperatoris Ferdinandi: F.I.E. P. M. Fiat iustitia, & pereat mundus. Item: O.M. D. M. M.
units.tr: Of Emperor Ferdinand: F.I.E. P. M., "Fiat iustitia, & pereat mundus" (Let justice be done, though the world perish). Also: O.M. D. M. M.

units.la: Duces Saxoniæ illud usurparunt: Verbum Domini manet in æternum. Initiò autem electum fuit à duce Friderico, hoc pacto: Cum iussisset dominus Spalatinum colligere aliquot bona dicta ex multis, quæ ille conscripserat, hoc unicum elegit.
units.tr: The Dukes of Saxony adopted this motto: "Verbum Domini manet in æternum" (The Word of the Lord endures for ever). It was first chosen by Duke Frederick, in this way: when he had ordered Spalatin to gather some good sayings from the many that the latter had written down, the duke chose this one alone.

units.la: Idem symbolum, Verbum Domini manet in æternum, usurpauit Georgius Marchio Brandenburgensis: quod quādiu uixit, seruauit. Idem princeps Georgius simile dictum habuit in moneta sua: Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos?
units.tr: The same motto, "Verbum Domini manet in æternum," was used by George, Margrave of Brandenburg, who kept it as long as he lived. The same prince George had a similar saying on his coin: "Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos?" (If God is for us, who is against us?).

units.la: Lutheri: Viuit. scilicet Christus. Si non uiueret, uellem me non unam horam uiuere. & hæ literæ habent mysterium, quod Lutherus explicare noluit.
units.tr: Luther's motto: "Viuit," namely Christ lives. If he did not live, I would not wish to live one hour. And these letters hold a mystery, which Luther did not wish to explain.

units.la: Noua moneta ciuitatis Tigurinæ: Conserua nos Domine in pace. Moneta ciuitatis Schaffhusiensis: Deus spes nostra.
units.tr: A new coin of the city of Zurich: "Conserua nos Domine in pace" (Keep us, Lord, in peace). A coin of the city of Schaffhausen: "Deus spes nostra" (God is our hope).

units.la: ERASMI
units.tr: ERASMI

units.la: Octauum præceptum.
units.tr: The eighth precept.

units.la: COLL. ERASMI SYMBOLVM TERMINVS.
units.tr: ERASMUS'S COLLECTANEA: THE EMBLEM TERMINUS

units.la: ὅρα τέλος μαντεῖ βίε.
units.tr: Look to the end, and foretell your life [ὅρα τέλος μαντεῦ βίε].

units.la: Mors ultima linea rerum.
units.tr: Death is the final boundary of things.

units.la: TERMINVS
units.tr: TERMINUS

units.la: ERASMVS ROTERODAMUS ornatissimo uiro Alfonso Valdesio, Cæsareæ Maiest. Secretario, S. P.
units.tr: Erasmus of Rotterdam to the most distinguished Alfonso Valdés, Secretary to His Imperial Majesty, greetings.

units.la: Quod mihi pro tuo ingenio modestissimè significas, idem ex aliorum literis dilucidè cognoui: excitasse qui Terminum, annuli mei sigillum, in calumniam uocent: uociferantes, intolerabilis arrogantiæ esse, quod adiectum est symbolum, Concedo nulli. Quid est, si hic non est fatalis quidã morbus, calumniandi omnia? Ridetur Momus, qui sandalium Veneris reprehenderit. at isti Momum ipsum superant, qui in annulo quod arrodant, inuenerint. Momos dicerem: sed Momus nihil carpit, nisi quod prius attentè perspexerit. Isti φιλαυτοι, uel sycophantæ potius, clausis oculis carpũt, quod nec uident, nec intelligunt. Tanta est morbi uis. Atq; interim sibi uidentur Ecclesiæ columnæ: quum nihil aliud quàm traducant suam stoliditatem, cum pari malicia coniunctam, iam notiores orbi quàm expedit. Somniant ab Erasmo dici, CONCEDO NVLLI. Atqui si mea scripta legerent, uiderent uix quèquam esse tam mediocrem, ut illi me præferã: citius cõcedens omnibus, quàm nulli. Iam qui me propius ex conuictu familiari nouerunt, quiduis uitij tribuent potius, quàm arrogantiam. meq; fatebuntur propiorem esse illi Socratico, Hoc unum scio, me nihil scire: quàm huic, Concedo nulli. Sed fingant animum tam insolentem esse mihi, ut memet omnibus anteponā: etiam ne tam stultum existimant, ut id symbolo profitear? Si quid haberent Christianæ mentis, interpretarentur ea uerba aut non esse mea, aut aliam habere sententiam. Vident illic sculptam imaginem, inferne saxum, superne iuuenem capillis uolitantibus. An hæc habet aliquid Erasmi? Id si parum est, uident in ipso saxo expressum, Terminus. in quam dictionem si desinas, uersus erit Iambicus dimeter acatalectus, Concedo nulli Terminus. si hinc incipias, erit dimeter trochaicus acatalectus, Terminus concedo nulli. Quid si pinxissem leonem, & addidissem symboli loco, Fuge ni mauis discerpi: num hæc uerba mihi tribuerent pro leone? At nihilo sanius est quod nunc faciunt. Nam similior leoni sum, quàm saxo, ni fallor. Dicent, Non animaduertimus esse carmen, nec novimus Terminum. An igitur posthac crimen erit scripsisse carmen, quoniam illi metricam rationem non didicerunt? Certè cum scirent in huiusmodi symbolis captari etiam obscuritatis aliquid, quod coniecturas intuentium exerceat: si non noverant Terminū, quanquā hoc ex Augustini & Ambrosij libris poterant discere: scisci[?]tari debebant à talium rerum peritis. Olim fines agrorum signo quo quopiam discernebantur: id erat saxum è terra prominès, quod ἀνίνυτον esse iubebant priscorū leges, quarum hæc uox est apud Platonem: Quæ non posuisti, ne tollas. Addita est superstitio, quo magis deterreretur imperita multitudo, à tollendi audacia, dum credit in saxo uiolari Deum, quē Romani Terminum uocant, cui sanum ac festum etiam dicatum Terminalia. Hic Terminus, ut est in Romanis annalibus, solus Ioui noluit concedere: quod quum cæterorum omnium sacellorum exauurationes admitterent, aues in solo Termini fano non addixere. Refert T. Liuius lib. ab Vrbe cond. primo, ac rursus lib. 6. narrat, quòd quum augurato liberaretur Capitolium, Iuuentas Terminusq; moueri se passi non sunt. Id omen magno omnium gaudio exceptum est, quòd existimarent portendi perpetuitatem imperij. Iuuentus ad bellum utilis, & Terminus fixus est. Hic fortè clamabunt, Quid tibi cum fabuloso deo? Obuenit, non ascitus est. Alexander Archiepiscopus titulo S. Andreæ, cum à patre Iacobo Scotiæ rege, Senis, in patriam reuocaretur, mihi Romam euocato, uelut gratus & amicus discipulus, annulos aliquot dono dedit, habitæ inter nos consuetudinis μνημόσυνον. In his erat, qui in gemma sculptum habebat Terminum. Nam hoc prius ignotum, indicauit Italus quidam, rerum rum antiquarum curiosus. Arripui omen: & interpretatus sum, admoneri me, non procul abesse uitæ terminum. Nam id temporis agebam annum circiter quadragesimum. Hæc cogitatio ne posset excidere, literis hoc signum imprimere cœpi. Addidi carmen, ut antè dictum est. Itaq; ex profano deo feci mihi symbolum, adhortans ad uitæ correctionem. Mors enim uerè Terminus est, qui nulli cedere nouit. Atqui in fusili imagine adscriptũ est Græce, ὁρα τέλος μαυρὸν βίχ: id est, Spe finem longæ uitæ: Latinè, Mors ultima linea rerū. Poteras, inquiet, insculpere defuncti craniū. Forsitā accepturus erā, si obuenisset: sed hoc arrisit primùm, quia fortuitò cōtigit: deinde, quòd geminā haberet gratiā. alterā, ex allusione ad priscā ac celebrē historiā: alterā ex obscuritate, quæ symbolis est peculiaris. Habes Apologiā de Termino, seu uerius de lana caprina. Atq; utinā isti tandē calumnijs suis terminū ponerēt. Lubēs enim cũ illis pacisćar, ut mutē symbolū meū, si illi mutēt morbum suū. Ita sanè rectius consuluerint authoritati suæ, quam clamant per bonarū literarum studiosos labefactari. Ego profectò tantū absum à cupiditate lædendi existimationem istorum, ut uehementer dolea, quòd ipsi sese tā stolidis sycophātijs orbi propinēt deridendos, nec erubescāt toties cũ ludibrio confutati. Dominus te seruat incolumem & corpore & animo, amice in Christo charissime. Datum Basileae, Cal. Augusti, Anno 1528.
units.tr: What you have reported to me so modestly, given your good character, I have also learned clearly from other people's letters: certain men have stirred up criticism of my signet ring's device, the Terminus, and they cry out that it is an intolerable arrogance that the motto "I yield to no one" has been added. What is this, if there is not some fated sickness of finding fault with everything? Momus is laughed at because he found fault with Venus's sandal, but these men surpass Momus himself, since they find things to gnaw at even on a ring. I would call them Momuses, but Momus finds fault with nothing without first examining it closely. These men, self-lovers [φιλαυτοι], or rather sycophants, find fault with their eyes shut, with things they neither see nor understand. Such is the power of the disease. Yet meanwhile they think of themselves as the pillars of the Church, when they do nothing but display their own stupidity, joined with equal malice, and they are already better known to the world than is good for them. They dream that Erasmus has said "I yield to no one." Yet if they read my writings, they would see that there is scarcely anyone so mediocre that I would set myself above him; I yield more readily to everyone than to no one. Those who know me more closely from familiar company will attribute to me any fault rather than arrogance, and they will admit that I am closer to that Socratic saying, "I know this one thing, that I know nothing", than to "I yield to no one." But suppose they imagine that I am so insolent that I put myself above everyone: do they also think me so foolish as to profess this in a motto? If they had any Christian mind, they would either interpret those words as not mine, or as having another meaning. They see there an engraved image: a stone below, and above it a youth with flying hair. Does this have anything of Erasmus in it? If that is too little, they see the word Terminus carved on the stone itself. If you end the line with that word, it will be an iambic dimeter acatalectic, "Concedo nulli Terminus"; if you begin with it, it will be a trochaic dimeter acatalectic, "Terminus concedo nulli." What if I had painted a lion and added, in place of a motto, "Flee unless you prefer to be torn apart"? Would they then attribute these words to me as the lion's? Yet what they are doing now is no more sensible. For I am more like the lion than like the stone, unless I am mistaken. They will say, "We did not notice it was a verse, and we do not know what Terminus is." Will it then be a crime from now on to have written a verse, because they have not learned metrical rules? Certainly, since they knew that such devices include some obscurity which exercises the guesses of those who look at them, if they did not know what Terminus was (though they could have learned this from the books of Augustine and Ambrose), they ought to have asked those skilled in such matters. Of old the boundaries of fields were marked by a sign: this was a stone jutting out of the earth, which the laws of the ancients ordered to be inviolable [ἀνίνυτον]. The words of those laws are preserved in Plato: "What you have not set down, do not remove." Superstition was added, so that the unlearned crowd would be more strongly deterred from the daring of removing it, since it believes that God is violated in the stone which the Romans call Terminus, to whom a holy festival, the Terminalia, was also dedicated. This Terminus, as the Roman annals record, alone refused to yield to Jupiter: when the consecrations of all the other shrines were permitted, the birds would not consent to his shrine alone. Titus Livy, in the first book of his history from the founding of the City, reports this, and again in the sixth book he relates that when the Capitol was being cleared by augury, Youth and Terminus did not allow themselves to be moved. This omen was received with great joy by everyone, because they thought it portended the permanence of the empire: youth is useful for war, and Terminus is fixed. Here perhaps someone will cry out, "What have you to do with a fabulous god?" It happened by chance; I did not seek it out. When Alexander, Archbishop with the title of St Andrew, was being recalled to his homeland by his father James, king of Scotland, while he was at Siena, and I had been summoned to Rome, he gave me, as a grateful and friendly pupil, some rings as a gift, a memento [μνημόσυνον] of the familiar intercourse between us. Among them was one which had Terminus carved on a gem. For an Italian, a man curious about antiquities, first pointed out what was not yet known to me. I seized the omen and interpreted it as a reminder that the limit of life was not far off, for at that time I was about forty years old. So that this thought should not slip away, I began to have this sign impressed on my letters. I added the verse, as was said before. Thus out of a profane god I made a motto for myself, urging the correction of life. For death is truly the Terminus, which knows how to yield to no one. Moreover, the cast image has written on it in Greek, ὅρα τέλος μακροῦ βίου [look to the end of a long life], that is, in Latin, "Mors ultima linea rerum" (death is the final line of all things). You may say, "You could have engraved a dead man's skull." Perhaps I would have accepted one, had it come my way; but this pleased me first because it happened by chance, and second because it had a double charm: one from its allusion to an ancient and famous story, the other from the obscurity which is peculiar to mottoes. There you have my apology for the Terminus, or rather an apology about goat's wool. And would that these men would at last set a limit to their accusations! I would gladly make a pact with them, that I would change my motto if they would change their disease. Indeed, they would more properly have consulted their own authority, which they cry out is being undermined among the students of good letters. For my part, I am so far from any desire to harm their reputation that I am deeply sorry they expose themselves to the world as objects of ridicule by such stupid sycophancies, and do not blush at being refuted so often to their disgrace. May the Lord keep you safe in body and mind, most beloved friend in Christ. Given at Basel, on the Calends of August, in the year 1528.

units.la: ORACVLA ET AENIgmata.
units.tr: ORACLES AND RIDDLES.

units.la: Athenienses consulerunt oraculum, num essent feliciter illaturi bellum Syracusanis. Oraculum respondit: Capietis omnes Syracusanos ciues. Ipsi insolentes laetabantur hoc oraculo. Verùm sicut diabolus decipere solet, non iuxta uotum suum homines captiuos abduxerunt, sed hoc modo ceperunt: Venerunt in manus Atheniensium tabulae, quibus inscripta erant nomina Syracusanorum ciuium. Ita caeperunt Syracusanos ciues, sed postea ipsi Athenienses capti & interfecti sunt.
units.tr: The Athenians consulted an oracle about whether they would succeed in waging war against the Syracusans. The oracle replied: "You will capture all the citizens of Syracuse." The arrogant Athenians rejoiced at this oracle. But, as the devil is wont to deceive, the men were not led away captive as they wished. Instead it happened this way: tablets were brought into the hands of the Athenians on which the names of the citizens of Syracuse were written. Thus they "captured" the citizens of Syracuse, but afterwards the Athenians themselves were captured and killed.

units.la: Archimedes cùm specularetur sedẽs[?] in balneo, de proportione ponderis auri & argenti, camq; ex aquae effluxu inuenisset, percurrit nudus per medias plateas clamitans: εὕρηκα, εὕρηκα: inueni, inueni. Quando uis scire quantum auri sit in cyatho deaurato, qui alias est argenteus, pondera primùm cyathum in aere, postea eodem pondere in aqua: tunc deauratus cyathus erit ponderosior: & quo est ponderosior, tantum est auri in eo, vmb deß das er schwerer ist im wasser, dẽn auß ser halb dem wasser, so schwer golt ist dar bey. Haec est ratio, quam Archimedes sedẽs in balneo inuenit: fuitq; sollicitudo uocationis.
units.tr: When Archimedes was sitting in the bath and considering the proportion between the weight of gold and of silver, and had discovered it from the overflow of water, he ran naked through the middle of the squares shouting, "I have found it [εὕρηκα], I have found it!" When you want to know how much gold there is in a gilded cup which is otherwise silver, weigh the cup first in air, then with the same weight in water. The gilded cup will then be heavier, and the more it is heavier, the more gold there is in it: that it is heavier in the water than outside the water, so much gold is in it. This is the principle which Archimedes discovered while sitting in the bath, and this was the concern of his calling.

units.la: Proponi solet in ænigmate, Quæ nam illa res sit, cuius nulla unquam nos capiat satietas? Respo detur: Sola sanitas, seu uita talis est, ut eius per se nullum oboriri possit tædium. Cibo & potu citò satiari solemus: etiā societatis facilè nausea quædam oboritur, iuxta dictum uerissimum Thaletis: Iucundius est parare amicum, quàm retinere.
units.tr: A riddle is often put forward: what is that thing of which we never have enough? The answer is: health alone, or life of such a kind that no weariness of it can arise by itself. We are wont to be quickly satisfied with food and drink; even from company a certain nausea easily arises, in keeping with the most true saying of Thales: it is more pleasant to acquire a friend than to keep one.

units.la: Aliud.
units.tr: Another.

units.la: Homo quidam probus ab alio nequam petebat donum, quod præstantius erat toto mundo. Explicatio ænigmatis talis est: Nicodemus uir bonus petiuit à nequam, nempe Pilato, donum toto mūdo præciosius, uidelicet corpus Christi. In talibus ænigmatibus, in quibus aliquid doctrinæ est, prodest iuniores subinde se exercere, quo ingenium exacuant.
units.tr: A certain upright man asked a wicked man for a gift which was more excellent than the whole world. The explanation of the riddle is this: Nicodemus, a good man, asked of the wicked one, namely Pilate, a gift more precious than the whole world, that is, the body of Christ. In such riddles, in which there is some teaching, it is useful for younger people to exercise themselves from time to time, so that they sharpen their wit.

units.la: Cæsar Maximilianus fuit clemens princeps, erat vilen auf die bein geholffen: id est, quòd ex equitibus facti sint pedites.
units.tr: Emperor Maximilian was a merciful prince. It helped many people onto their feet: that is, from horsemen they became foot soldiers.

units.la: ACVTE FESTIVE, SALSÈ dicta, ac prouerbia.
units.tr: Sharp, witty, and salty sayings and proverbs.

units.la: Est bis apud Demosthenem: Non est dicendū, idem factum est: sed querendum est, an rectè factum sit? Augustinus: Vitiosa consuetudo non est anteferenda ueritati. Dominus enim, inquit: Ego sum uia ueritas & uita: non, inquit, Ego sum consuetudo.
units.tr: Demosthenes has this: "It must not be said, 'It has been done this way before'; rather we must ask whether it has been done rightly." Augustine: "A corrupt custom is not to be preferred to the truth. For the Lord says, 'I am the way, the truth, and the life'; he does not say, 'I am custom.'"

units.la: Erasmus elegantissimè scripsit de Thoma Moro, cùm rex Angliæ Morũ Cancellarium fecisset, ipsum fuisse φιλοβασιλέα: cùm iterum ab officio remouisset, fuisse φιλόμωμον. Est festiua ambiguitas.
units.tr: Erasmus wrote most elegantly about Thomas More: when the king of England had made More Chancellor, he was a φιλοβασιλεύς [lover of the king]; when the king again removed him from office, he was a φιλόμωμος [lover of blame]. It is a witty ambiguity.

units.la: Norinbergæ in curia scriptum est: Vnius uiri oratio dimidia oratio.
units.tr: It was said at Nuremberg, in the council chamber: "One man's speech is half a speech."

units.la: Rex Alphonsus solitus est dicere de mediatoribus, eos similes esse habitantibus in medijs ædibus, qui perfunduntur lotio à superioribus, & lædūtur fimo ab inferioribus. Sic plerunq; mediatores utrinq; lædūtur, sicut uespertilio laceratur à muribus & auibus. Fuit hic Rex ita sapiès & bellicosus, ualès consilio & potentia, ut haberetur unus ex præstantissimis principibus illius ætatis.
units.tr: King Alphonsus used to say of mediators that they are like people living in a house in the middle, who are drenched with slops from above and soiled with dung from below. So mediators are generally harmed from both sides, just as the bat is torn by mice and birds. This king was so wise and warlike, so strong in counsel and power, that he was counted among the most outstanding princes of his age.

units.la: Cùm nunciata esset cuidam Magnati mors filij sui hostis maioris natu, nihil aliud dixit, nisi hoc: Quo plures moriuntur, eo minus habemus hostium. Statuit sibi nō ualde dolendum esse, cum illi essent hostes.
units.tr: When a certain nobleman was told of the death of his elder son's enemy, he said only this: "The more who die, the fewer enemies we have." He judged that there was no great cause for grief, since they had been enemies.

units.la: Extat insignis & memorabilis sententia Friderici Imperatoris, scripta Norinbergæ, in quodam conclaui: Summa felicitas est rerum irrecuperabilium obliuio.
units.tr: There is a notable and memorable saying of Emperor Frederick, written at Nuremberg in a certain room: "The greatest happiness is the forgetting of things that cannot be recovered."

units.la: Dux Albertus, auus huius ducis electoris Augusti, fuit præstās, sapiès & magnanimus uir, qui recreationis causa interdum illas ludorũ ineptias amaamauit, & magnā pecuniā profudit ludo tesserarum. Cū olim forte multa millia aureorū lusu per didisset: conuenientes ipsius cōsiliarij deliberāt de eo, sicut erāt homines sapientes, ipsum q; talis praefatione alloquūtur, dicētes: Ipsis esse notas in omni disciplinarū genere uirtutes illustrissimi principis: tamen optandum esse ut ipse ea in re haberet suae dignitatis rationem, & non ita luderet: non tantum quia profunderet pecuniā, unde magnum incommodū sequeretur, sed etiā quòd posset ei accidere aliquid inter ludendum ab hominibus malis, quod nollent fieri. Ibi princeps respondet: Optimi amici, scio uos candido animo me monere: sed tamen magis debuissetis me reprehendere, quando lucratus fuissem. Iam satis poenae luo, cùm uehementer propter amissam pecuniam doleo.
units.tr: Duke Albert, grandfather of the present Elector Augustus, was an excellent, wise, and magnanimous man, who sometimes, for recreation, indulged in those silly games of chance and spent large sums on dice. Once, having lost many thousands of gold coins at play, his counsellors, who were wise men, met and deliberated about him. They approached him with this address, saying: that the illustrious prince's virtues in every branch of learning were well known; yet it was to be wished that in this matter he would have regard for his dignity and not play so; not only because he was squandering money, from which a great loss would follow, but also because some evil men might bring about something during play that they would not want to happen. The prince replied: "Best of friends, I know you advise me with an honest mind; but you ought rather to have rebuked me when I was winning. Now I am paying enough penalty, since I grieve bitterly over the money I have lost."

units.la: Lantgrauius Vuilhelmus, pater huius Philippi, qui adhuc uiuit, fuit admodum facetus, eruditus, & facundus: quemadmodum & Philippus est, sed continentior patre. Cùm semel principes essent in conuentu, & expectarent Imperatorem Maximilianum ante cubiculum, hic Vuilhelmus, ut princeps adhuc iuuenis, cum caeteris principibus iunioribus suo more iocabatur ante cubiculum. Ibi alius Princeps magnae authoritatis, ualens etiam corporis robore, ad Vuilhelmum dicebat: Domine Lantgraui, ego scirem ad quid prodesses. Domine princeps, re-spondit Vuilhelmus, nescio sane ad quid prodes-sem: sum adhuc iuuenis, neq; tam exercitatus, ut possim intelligere ad quid potissimū prodessem. At alter: Dicam tibi, siquidem cupis scire. Imò di-cito: Ihr weret recht zu meinē lôen, denn ihr habt vil kalb fleisch. Sic solent notare eos, qui se nimis petulanter gerunt, & minus decentes gestus præ se ferunt. Sed Lantgrauius Vuilhelmus celeriter respondit: Domine Princeps, licet & mihi pro-ferre ad quid tua Celsitudo prodesset? Imò ritè po-tes, inquit, dicere. Si vis me audire ac æquo animo ferre, dicam: Ewer Gnaden weren gut, das man iunge affen bey ihr aufzüge, das sie untrew uon ihr lerneten. Et sic salsissimè illum taxauit, qui ta-lis existimabatur. Cæteri astantes Principes tace-bant, & dissimulabant, quia uerè illū taxauerat.
units.tr: Landgrave William, father of this Philip, who is still living, was quite witty, learned, and eloquent, as Philip also is, though more restrained than his father. Once, when the princes were at a gathering and were waiting for Emperor Maximilian before his bedchamber, William, still a young prince, was joking with the other younger princes in his usual way before the chamber. Then another prince of great authority, also strong in bodily vigour, said to William: "Lord Landgrave, I would like to know what use you are." "Lord Prince," William replied, "I really don't know what use I would be; I am still young and not so experienced that I could understand for what use I would be most suitable. But you, the other: 'I will tell you, if you really want to know. Speak plainly: You would be right to be hired by me, for you have plenty of veal (i.e., stupidity).'" Thus people are wont to mark those who behave too impudently and show less seemly manners. But Landgrave William quickly answered: "Lord Prince, may I also state what use Your Highness would be?" "Indeed you may," he said, "speak." "If you want me to hear and bear it calmly, I will say: 'Your Grace would be good for bringing up young monkeys with you, so that they could learn unfaithfulness from you.'" And so he rebuked most wittily the one who was thought to be such a man. The other princes standing by were silent and pretended not to hear, because he had truly hit him.

units.la: Rex Ptolemæus reprehendebat quasdam uo-culas in cantu cuiusdam Musici. Musicus respon-dit: Rex, aliud est plectrum, aliud sceptrum.
units.tr: King Ptolemy found fault with some little notes in the singing of a certain musician. The musician replied: "Your Majesty, a plectrum is one thing, a sceptre another."

units.la: Δσυ τέχαυ φρουτίδες σοφωτέρω.
units.tr: Σὺ τέχνῃ φροντίδες σοφωτέρω [Your art is wiser than cares].

units.la: Erat, me puero, Heydelbergæ sapiens & bonus uir citharœdus, patria Moguntinus, qui optimè canebat testudine. Ille dicebat, sibi nullam canti-lenam satisfacere, nisi quando primùm eius obli-tus, secundò eandem disceret. Et uerum est, ut om-nes, qui sunt sapientes in suo negocio, fateri co-guntur.
units.tr: When I was a boy there was at Heidelberg a wise and good man, a lute-player, a native of Mainz, who played the lute very well. He used to say that no song pleased him unless he first forgot it and then learned it again a second time. And it is true, as all who are wise in their own business are compelled to admit.

units.la: Octauum præceptum.
units.tr: The Eighth Precept.

units.la: Albertus Durerus sæpe dicebat, quòd cùm pin-xisset aliquid, qua potuisset summa cura & dili-gentia, ac deinde post triennium idem inspiceret, mirabiliter displiceret, ita ut vix sine ingenti do-lore intueri posset.
units.tr: Albrecht Dürer often said that when he had painted something with the greatest care and diligence, and then looked at it again three years later, it displeased him so much that he could scarcely look at it without great pain.

units.la: Sic Momus dicit ad Iouem apud Lucianum: ὃ λέγω πάχεις ποιήσω νᾶν, ἂν μὴ προσποιεῖ: nihi pate-ris mali, si non indulgeas affectui, uel, si non assi-ciaris. Melius Germani exprimunt: Es geschicht dir nicht weh, wenn du dichs nicht annimbst. Vt, Christum non lædebant Iudæi, quando ad eum di-cebant: Samaritanus es.
units.tr: So Momus speaks to Jove in Lucian: "What I say, I will make you suffer, unless you pretend: you will suffer no harm if you do not indulge your feeling, or if you are not affected." [ὃ λέγω πάχεις ποιήσω νᾶν, ἂν μὴ προσποιεῖ] The Germans express it better: "It won't hurt you if you don't take it to heart." Just as the Jews did not wound Christ when they said to him, "You are a Samaritan."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Senex quidam, alio ad eum dicente: Lieber freundt, ir habt ein eignen kopf. Verè & graui-ter respondit: Ia lieber freundt ich hab mein kopf, vnd wenn ich den nicht hett, ir wurdt mir den eu-ren nicht leihen.
units.tr: An old man, when another said to him, "Dear friend, you have a head of your own." answered truly and gravely: "Yes, dear friend, I have my head, and if I did not have it, you would not lend me yours."

units.la: ὃ διὰ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ποδὸς ὡς πρὸς λύπην: id est, Non propter erratum pedis in chorea plectitur, aut quòd errauerit in aliquo articulo, sed agitur aliud quiddam. Valde usitatum est in uita aliud agi, aliud ostendi.
units.tr: "That is, one is not punished for a misstep of the foot in the dance, or because one has erred in some point, but something else is at issue. It is very common in life for one thing to be done and another to be shown." [ὃ διὰ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ποδὸς ὡς πρὸς λύπην]

units.la: Quidam habens tentationes spirituales, fuit no-bis molestus, conquerebaturq; se sæpius relabi in adulteria. Nuncius autem eius incusabat eum, quòd sibi non solucret debitā mercedem. Rescripsi illi, cùm haberet tam malam conscientiam de pec-catis commissis, Quare etiam nō haberet malam conscientiam, quòd non solueret mercedem mi-sero nuncio?
units.tr: A certain man troubled by spiritual temptations was a nuisance to us, complaining that he often relapsed into adultery. But his messenger accused him of not paying him the wage he owed. I wrote back to him: since he had such a bad conscience about the sins he had committed, why did he not also have a bad conscience for not paying the wage to the poor messenger?

units.la: Doctor quidam Iurisconsultus, uir honestus & eruditus, cùm pro cliente causam diceret, & ad scriptum contrariæ parti responderet, dixit: Argumenta quæ aduersaria pars contra me addu-xit, sunt argumenta carbonariorum. Audiens hoc contrariæ partis rabula, finita oratione doctoris, ita loqui incipit, & inter cætera quæ pro necessi-tate causæ dicēda erant, etiam hoc adiecit: Quòd autem doctor nobis obijcit, nostra argumenta es-se argumēta carbonariorū, id dominis meis æquis-simis iudicibus iudicandum relinquo, uter no-strûm carbonario sit similior. Erat enim doctor, homo niger. Hæc fuit festiua oratio, ad quam etiā ipse doctor respōdit: Profectò egregiè reddidisti talionem, & par pari retulisti.
units.tr: A learned doctor of law, an honest and learned man, when pleading a case for a client and answering the written brief of the opposing side, said: "The arguments the other side has brought against me are the arguments of charcoal-burners." Hearing this, the opposing side's pettifogger, when the doctor had finished, began to speak, and among the other things that the needs of the case required him to say, he added this: "As for the doctor's charge that our arguments are the arguments of charcoal-burners, I leave it to my most just lords the judges to decide which of us is more like a charcoal-burner, for the doctor is a dark-complexioned man." It was a witty speech, and the doctor himself replied to it: "Truly you have returned the insult splendidly, and paid back like with like."

units.la: Interfui aliquando disputationi acerrimæ pi-ctoris, & alterius cuiusdam, qui cùm diu acriter disputassent, tandem ille alter dixit ad pictorem: Hæc non ita exactè depingi possunt. uolens eum hortari, ut desisteret, nec omnia scrutaretur. Pictor autem excanduit, putans suam artem hoc scōmate taxari. & respondit: Imò tuum pro-positum nec uerbis uerisimiliter exprimi potest.
units.tr: I was once present at a very sharp dispute between a painter and another man. After they had argued fiercely for a long time, the other finally said to the painter: "These things cannot be depicted so exactly," wanting to urge him to stop and not scrutinise everything. The painter flared up, thinking his art was being mocked by this jibe, and replied: "Rather, your proposition cannot even be expressed plausibly in words."

units.la: Ita obijciebat illi artem, in qua alter excellebat, iudicans ea esse obscuriora, quae eloqui non possent, quàm quae pingi nequeunt. Multa enim non possunt pingi, quae tamen uerbis utcunque declarari possunt. Angelus à nemine pingi potest. Pinguntur quidem pueri duabus alis: non tamen sunt angeli, nec ueram angelorum formam referunt. Sed mens cogitare potest, quid sint angeli.
units.tr: In this way he threw in the painter's face the art in which the other excelled, judging things that cannot be spoken to be more obscure than things that cannot be painted. For many things cannot be painted which can nevertheless be declared in words in some way. No one can paint an angel. Boys are indeed painted with two wings, yet they are not angels, nor do they represent the true form of angels. But the mind can think about what angels are.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Piscator ictus sapit, si tamen sapit. Serò sapiũt Phryges. Sic dicitur communi prouerbio: Italus sapit ante factum, Gallus in facto, Germanus post factum.
units.tr: A fisherman is wise when he has been struck, if indeed he is wise at all. The Phrygians are wise too late. So runs the common proverb: the Italian is wise before the deed, the Frenchman in the deed, and the German after the deed.

units.la: Erphurdiæ quidam procurator multas causas solus agens, sine aduocatis, quamuis solus staret in Senatu: tamen plerunq;, quoties erat ei respondendum ad dictam aduersariæ partis intentionē, petiuit spacium ad deliberandum. Festiui interrogauerunt: Cum quo uis deliberare, cùm sis solus? Respondit, Cum isto, cum isto: monstrans ipsis caput.
units.tr: At Erfurt a certain procurator, who conducted many cases alone without advocates, even though he stood alone in the Senate, nevertheless very often, whenever he had to answer the opposing party's claim, asked for time to deliberate. Some wits asked him: "With whom do you want to deliberate, since you are alone?" He replied, "With this one, with this one," showing them his head.

units.la: Dux Fridericus dixit: Nihil magis cauendum est gubernatori, quàm ne subitò respõdeat. Ego recitabam aliquando doctori Pontano hoc dictũ ducis Friderici, unà cum dicto Demosthenis, qui, cùm ei obijceretur, quòd ueniret præmeditatus ad dicendum, respondit: Se uero improbum ciuem iudicare, qui non ueniret præmeditatus in publicum, ad sententiam dicendam: & dicit amplius, Se, si fieri posset, dicturum, non tantum scripta, sed etiam sculpta: id est, sumpturum longam moram ad deliberandum.
units.tr: Duke Frederick said: "Nothing must be guarded against by a governor more than answering on the spur of the moment." I once read this saying of Duke Frederick to Doctor Pontanus, together with the saying of Demosthenes, who, when it was objected to him that he came prepared to speak, replied that he judged a man to be a bad citizen who did not come into public prepared to give his opinion; and he adds that, if it were possible, he would speak not only from written texts but even from carved ones, that is, he would take a long time to deliberate.

units.la: Dux Saxoniæ Iohannes Fridericus sæpè solitus est dicere: Causæ sæpe conciliari possent, si hominum uoluntates possent coniungi.
units.tr: Duke John Frederick of Saxony often used to say: "Causes could often be reconciled if men's wills could be joined together."

units.la: οὐδεὶς ἀνθρώπων ἐστὶν ἄπαντα σοφὸς. Quisq; aliquid fatuitatis habet adiunctum. Doctor Hieronymus Schurpf solebat iocari: Ego ingenuè fatuor, pro fateor. Nos omnes fatuamur satis stolidè.
units.tr: No man is wise in all things. Each of us has some folly attached to him. Doctor Hieronymus Schurpf used to joke: "I freely play the fool (fatuor) for I confess (fateor)." We all play the fool quite foolishly.

units.la: C O L L. Prouerbium ualde usitatum Germanis.
units.tr: COLL. A proverb very commonly used among the Germans.

units.la: Vuer prediger vnd weiber schendet, dem wirdts nimmer mer wolghen: id est, qui cōtemnit ministeriū prædicādi, & personas illo officio fungentes: mulieres, id est unde soboles & politiæ procreantur. Quare contemnentes ministerium & mulieres, contemnunt Deum & homines.
units.tr: "Whoever despises the preacher and the women, will never prosper." That is, whoever despises the office of preaching and the persons who fulfil that office, and women, from whom offspring and commonwealths are produced. Therefore those who despise the ministry and women despise God and men.

units.la: C O L L.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Audiui Basileæ simile referri à honesta & pia persona (quæ optimè de sanitate & ualetudine D. Oporini meretur) dicente: Quòd quisq; in concontractibus matrimonialibus decipiens simplicem foemineum sexum, diuinam ultionem non effugiet: eandem sententiam multis exemplis probauit. Ostenditq; quaedam, vbi Deus in altero coniugio tales deceptores sobole priuasset.
units.tr: At Basel I heard a similar account from an honest and pious person (who has deserved very well of the health of Dr. Oporinus), who said that whoever deceives a simple female in matrimonial contracts will not escape divine vengeance. He proved the same opinion with many examples, and he showed certain cases in which God had deprived such deceivers of offspring in a second marriage.

units.la: ὦ μάκαρς φρόνησις εὐ χρηστῷ τρόπῳ, ὡς ἡδὺ συνέσει χρηστότης πεπαμένη.
units.tr: O blessed prudence joined with a good character, how sweet is goodness when it is combined with understanding. [ὦ μάκαρς φρόνησις εὐ χρηστῷ τρόπῳ, ὡς ἡδὺ συνέσει χρηστότης πεπαμένη.]

units.la: O quàm felix est sapientia cũ bonitate. Quàm iucunda est probitas coniuncta cum consilio. Aliqui sunt boni, sed sunt ignaui, non circumspecti: natura quidem benefici, sed nihil transigentes. Econtrà multi sunt astuti & callidi, sed sunt mali: quod est perniciosum, & lupinum quidam. Sed cõiuncta sapientia cum bonitate, & bonitas habens moderatricem sapientiam, illa est pulcherrima virtutum copulatio. Mercurinus dixit de Imperatore Carolo V. Principes Germaniæ benefecerunt, quòd elegerunt Carolum V. Imperatorē, illi experientur ipsum esse sapientem & bonum principem.
units.tr: How happy is wisdom when it is joined with goodness! How pleasing is uprightness when it is coupled with counsel! Some people are good but idle and careless: they are generous by nature but accomplish nothing. On the other hand, many are shrewd and crafty but wicked, which is harmful and somewhat wolfish. But wisdom joined with goodness, and goodness having wisdom as its guide, is the most beautiful union of the virtues. Mercurinus said of the Emperor Charles V: "The princes of Germany did well in electing Charles V as Emperor; they will find that he is a wise and good prince."

units.la: Monachorum regula: daus eß hat nichts, ses zinck gibt nichts, quater drei, die müsen sich leiden. Eim ieden gefelt sein weise wol: Darumb ist die welt narren vol. Kõnnen wir nich alle dichten: So wollen weir alle richten.
units.tr: The rule of the monks: "Deuce has nothing, six gives nothing, four-three, they must suffer." Everyone is well pleased with his own ways; therefore the world is full of fools. If we cannot all make verses, let us all at least pass judgement.

units.la: Vetustas dixit: Bene olere, est nihil olere. Item, Crede mihi, sapere non est nimium sapere.
units.tr: Antiquity said: "To smell good is to smell of nothing." Likewise: "Believe me, to be wise is not to be too wise."

units.la: Erasmus dicere solebat: Ego non libenter uescor piscibus: nam stomachus est Lutheranus, & mens est Christiana. Venustissimè dictum est, & bella ambiguitas in stomacho, quæ uox hic pro iracundia seu indignatione sumitur. Vult dicere: Ego nō minus irascor sceleribus Papæ, quàm ipse Lutherus.
units.tr: Erasmus used to say: "I do not gladly eat fish, for my stomach is Lutheran, but my mind is Christian." This was said most wittily, and the pun on the stomach is clever, since the word here is taken for anger or indignation. He means: "I am no less angry at the crimes of the Pope than Luther himself is."

units.la: Dux Fridericus dicere solitus est: Colite probitatem, facilè enim desiderabitis, ubi uultis.
units.tr: Duke Frederick used to say: "Cultivate uprightness, for you will easily obtain what you want wherever you wish."

units.la: Plutarchus dicit: eos qui somniant se imitari clarissima facta præstantium uirorum, similes esse pueris, qui induunt thoraces, & alia arma grandiorum parentum. Sicut panoplia parentum non recte potest accommodari ad corpora filiorum parua: sic non conueniunt nostra facta cum heroicis præstantissimorum hominum factis.
units.tr: Plutarch says that those who dream of imitating the most famous deeds of outstanding men are like boys who put on the breastplates and other armour of their grown-up fathers. Just as a father's full panoply cannot properly be fitted to the small bodies of his sons, so our deeds do not match the heroic deeds of the most outstanding men.

units.la: VRBANITATES, SALES, facetiæ, & insulsitates.
units.tr: Witticisms, jests, pleasantries, and dull jokes.

units.la: Quidam ingeniosus homo, interrogabat magistrandum in Academia Friburgensi, Quare fieret nix? Ille simplex respondit: Quia Deus sic uult. At alter inquit: Melius respondit, quàm nos omnes, quia nemo potest sufficientes causas niuis reddere. & sic ab ipso discessit.
units.tr: A clever fellow once asked a candidate for the master's degree at the Academy of Freiburg, "Why does snow fall?" The candidate simply answered, "Because God wills it." The other said, "He answered better than all of us, since nobody can give sufficient causes for snow." And with that he left him.

units.la: Quidam nobilis adolescēs Tubingæ, uolēs exercere ırtere Latinā lingua, delegit sibi carme uerten-dū, quod tunc erat editum de causa Capnionis, cuius primus uersus sic inchoatur: O welt welt, wie bistu so verkert. Hunc ipse sic uertit: O munde mū-de, quàm es peruerse. Rythmus quidem bonus erat, sed constructio non congruebat.
units.tr: A young nobleman at Tübingen, wishing to practise the Latin tongue, chose for a translation exercise a poem that had recently been published about the affair of Capnio (Reuchlin). Its first line begins, "O welt welt, wie bistu so verkert" (O world, world, how perverse you have become). He rendered it thus: "O world, world, how perverse you are." The rhythm was good, but the construction did not agree.

units.la: Parasion elegos aurum Tyriumq; parergum.
units.tr: Parasium, elegies, gold, and Tyrian purple, a sideline.

units.la: Post fato Decker debeo Marce tuo.
units.tr: After death, Decker, I owe you, Marcus, what is yours.

units.la: Hi uersus Erphurdiæ in templo scripti inue-niuntur, quos quidam composuit, uolens etiam ui-deri Poeta. Voluit autem hoc modo interpreta-ri: Ego debeo tibi Marce Deker, post fato, po-suit pro post fatum, id est mortem, parasium, id est picturam: elegos, id est istos duos uersus: tyriū parergum, id est rubeum colorem.
units.tr: These verses are found written in the temple at Erfurt. Someone composed them, wishing also to appear a poet. He wanted them to be read in this way: "I owe you, Marcus Decker, after fate." He put "post" for "post fatum," that is, after death; "parasium," that is, a picture; "elegos," that is, these two verses; and "Tyrian parergum," that is, the red colour.

units.la: Quidam sciolus admodum falsè legebat Ma-gnificat: ac inter cætera, cùm peruenisset ad uer-sum, Dispersit superbos, ibiq; in uoce Superbos, ultima syllaba in priore linea deficeret, quæ in-choata erat in sequēti uersu, dicebat: Proh Deū, non est rectū: oportet esse Super bouem. Hoc est corrigere uelle Magnificat.
units.tr: A half-learned fellow read the Magnificat very wrongly. Among other things, when he came to the verse "Dispersit superbos" (he has scattered the proud), and the last syllable of the word "superbos" was missing from the earlier line, which began in the following verse, he exclaimed, "Good God, that's not right; it ought to be 'Super bouem'." This is to set out to correct the Magnificat.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Amiserat quidam Romæ quinq; capellas, quas suspicabatur uicinum suū esse furatum. Accusat igitur eum, conducens causidicum, qui eius causas in foro ageret. Causidicus ueniens in forū, dicere coepit de bello Punico, de Scipionibus & Annibale, quantas res terra mariq; gesserint: & quòd Scipio sibi, suis, patriæq; usui & ornamento, Annibal autem sibi & suis exitio fuisset. Asistens autem actor tristi vultu: Quæso, inquit, dicas etiam aliquid de meis capellis. Quo audito à populo, causidicus explosus est è foro, cum isto ambitioso ornatu, quia nihil πρὸς ἑαυτὸς erat.
units.tr: A man at Rome had lost five goats, which he suspected his neighbour of having stolen. So he brought an accusation, hiring an advocate to plead his cases in the forum. The advocate came into the forum and began to speak of the Punic War, of the Scipios and Hannibal, and of how much each had achieved on land and sea; and how Scipio had been a benefit and an ornament to himself, his own people, and his country, while Hannibal had been the ruin of himself and his own. The plaintiff, standing by with a gloomy face, said, "I beg you, say something also about my goats." At this the people shouted, and the advocate was hooted out of the forum, with all his showy ornament, because he had nothing to do with the case [πρὸς ἑαυτὸς].

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam nobilis invitauit quondam D. Ioannem Baptistā Bacheleb ad convivium. Cùm idem doctor Iohannes Bacheleb finito convivio nobili valediceret, ibi nobilis prius vocat ad mensam suum morionem, atq; doctorem his verbis alloquitur, inquiens: Domine Bacheleb (monstrans ipsi simul morionem) nonne hic bene exercitatu, uarijsq; artibus instructum doctorem habeo? Ad quæ doctor subitò infert, dicens: Profectò bene me mones: nam ego domi meæ nunc temporis similem alo nobilem, ex tua familia natum. Sic par pari referebat.
units.tr: A nobleman once invited the late Doctor John Baptist Bacheleb to dinner. When the same Doctor John Bacheleb, the dinner finished, was taking his leave of the nobleman, the nobleman first called his jester to the table and addressed the doctor with these words: "Master Bacheleb" (showing him the jester at the same time), "don't I have here a well-trained doctor, instructed in various arts?" To this the doctor at once replied, "You admonish me well indeed, for at home I now keep a similar nobleman, born of your family." So he returned like for like.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Nobilis quidam in aula principis Saxoniæ, videns Principem valde anxium esse de ista pestifera doctrina vulgo Interim dicta, inquit: Clementissime Princeps, quid multum sollicitus es de isto Interim? Ego Interim non solum suscipere, verum etiam comedere & bibere, simulq; cum eo dormire possum. Princeps quærit, quomodo hoc fieri possit? Respondit nobilis: Si quando libum, aut mellipectã comedã, tum neq; panem neq; similã, sed quid aliud interim comedo. Si bibo mulsum, neq; uinum neq; cereuisiam bibo. Cùm porrò inebriatus domum reuertor, concidens in ianuæ limine obdormio: sic interim neq; in domo aut hypocausto, neq; foris iaceo. Ita facetus homo delusit istam doctrinam, & ludêdo tamen uera dixit.
units.tr: A nobleman at the court of the Prince of Saxony saw the prince very anxious about that pestilent doctrine commonly called the Interim, and said, "Most gracious prince, why are you so worried about this Interim? I can not only accept the Interim, I can even eat and drink it, and sleep with it too." The prince asked how this could be done. The nobleman replied, "When I eat a cake or a honey tart, I eat neither bread nor fine flour, but something else, namely interim. If I drink mead, I drink neither wine nor beer. Then, when I come home drunk, I fall asleep on the threshold; so in the interim I lie neither in the house, nor in the hypocaust, nor outside." Thus the witty man mocked that doctrine, and in jest he said true things.

units.la: C O L L.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Morio ducis Friderici Claus narr, stetit ad mensam, & omnes cibos quos habebat canibus proiecit. Interrogatus tandem, cur id faceret? Respondit: Date, & dabitur uobis.
units.tr: Duke Frederick's jester, Claus, the narrator, stood at table and threw all the food he had to the dogs. When at last he was asked why he did this, he replied, "Give, and it will be given to you."

units.la: C O L L.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: In bello contra Turcam, Episcopus quidam exercitum sic consolatus est: Charissimi fortissimiq; milites, hodie uos uiros fortes præbete. Efficiemini enim equites Christi. Et certo uobis promittere possum, quicunq; hodie fortiter occumbant, eos uesperi cum Deo cælesti cœna exceptuiri. Postquam uerò ad prælium deuentum esset, episcopus se subduxit post principia. Quare milites quærentes inuicem causam, cur non Episcopus cum ipsis cœnam in cœlo comedere uellet? Ad hæc quidam respónderunt alij: Hodie sibi ieiunium iunium indixit, idcoq; non uult nobiscum in cœlo cœnare.
units.tr: In a war against the Turk, a bishop encouraged an army with these words: "Dearest and bravest soldiers, today show yourselves to be brave men, for you will become knights of Christ. And I can certainly promise you that whoever falls bravely today will be received by God in heaven at supper this evening." But when they came to battle, the bishop slipped away behind the lines. So the soldiers, asking one another the reason, wondered why the bishop did not want to sup with them in heaven. To this some of the others replied, "Today he has declared a fast for himself, and therefore he does not want to dine with us in heaven."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam Græcus ueniens Romam, cùm ei offerretur honos domini, respondit: ἂν ἐθέλω ἀδύ-νε·ὸ γὰρ ἔχω ἀδύνεναι.
units.tr: A Greek coming to Rome, when a title of lord was offered to him, replied: "I cannot, for I have no power to do so" [ἂν ἐθέλω ἀδύνατον· ὁ γὰρ ἔχω ἀδύνεναι].

units.la: Noui aliquem in cuiusdam domini aula, qui meruit stipendium mille florenorum, hac scurrilitate, cum opinione uirtutis, seu potius fortitudinis. Ascendit uidelicet in mensam, & excremen-ta naturæ reddidit in consessu multorum honestorum hominum. Hoc erat illud egregium factum, ab ipso præstitum, tanto scilicet munere dignū.
units.tr: I know a man in the court of a certain lord who earned a stipend of a thousand florins by this buffoonery, along with a reputation for virtue, or rather for courage. He climbed up onto the table and voided his bowels in the sight of a company of many respectable men. This was that outstanding deed of his, surely worthy of such a reward.

units.la: Quidam obiurgauit ebrium, dicens: Non te pudet sic inebriari? Ille respondit: Nō te pudet ita ebrium obiurgare?
units.tr: Someone rebuked a drunkard, saying, "Aren't you ashamed to get so drunk?" He replied, "Aren't you ashamed to rebuke a man so drunk?"

units.la: Interrogatus aliquando quid boni ex doctrina Euangelij uenisset? Respondi: Multi boni pueri inde uenerunt.
units.tr: Someone once asked him what good had come from the teaching of the Gospel. He answered, "Many good boys have come from it."

units.la: Germanico fertur prouerbio: Bischoff oder bader. Hinc bonus & pius quidam Dux, post bel-lum concedens in thermas, iocari de se solitus est, dicēs: Ich wolt bischoff werden, so bin ich ein ba-der worden.
units.tr: There is a German proverb: "Bischoff oder bader" (bishop or bath-keeper). Hence a certain good and pious duke, after the war, going into the baths, used to joke about himself, saying, "I wanted to become a bishop, and so I have become a bath-keeper."

units.la: Norinbergæ quidam ciuis morosior iusto, ha-bebat famulum facientem multa πωάραγα. Quæ cùm dominus ægre ferens reprehenderet, respondit seruus: Conscribe igitur mihi in charta, ut sciam quæ sint mei officij. Dominus sequens consilium serui, ipsi omnia officia coscribit, ut præter ea nullis parergis distraheretur: postea ipse forte lapsus est in uia. Vocat igitur seruum, inquiens: Cur me non erigis? At seruus: Volo prius uidere an sit in mea charta.
units.tr: In Nuremberg a certain citizen, more morose than is right, had a servant who did many side-tasks [πάραργα]. When the master, taking it badly, reproached him, the servant answered, "Then write down for me on paper what my duties are, so that I may know them." The master, following the servant's advice, wrote out all his duties for him, so that he would not be distracted by any side-tasks beyond them. Afterwards the master himself happened to slip on the road. So he called the servant and said, "Why don't you lift me up?" But the servant said, "I want first to see whether it is on my paper."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Concionator quidam in oppido quodam, sic de furto concionatus est: Sæpe, uos charissimi amici, adhortatus sum, ne quis furtum faceret. Nihilominus intra paucos dies, aliquis uestrum furto aliquid mihi abstulit: quæ bene noui, & nunc hoc libro tangere possem: interim q; gestum minatis iactu præferebat. Ita ille qui fecerat, aufugit e templo, seipsum prodens: cum alioqui illi esset ignotus. Sic fictis nominibus taxantur sæpe in nobis scelera.
units.tr: A certain preacher in a particular town preached on theft in this way: "Dearly beloved friends, I have often urged you not to steal. Nevertheless, within a few days one of you has stolen something from me, which I know well and could now point out in this book." Meanwhile he showed the gesture of throwing a threatening glance. The man who had done it then fled from the church, betraying himself, although he had otherwise been unknown to the preacher. So, under fictitious names, our sins are often rebuked in us.

units.la: Cùm Capnio aliquando esset conuiua Ducis Vuirtenbergensis, Dux appositit illi de serina. Ille cùm uellet esse ciuilior, & excipere cultello, excidit illi in cyathum. Postea illud uolens corrigere alia ciuilitate, & eximere cultro, tunc effudit cyathum in mensam. Sic plerumq; nobis accidit, ut quādo uitia corrigere conamur, in deteriora incidamus.
units.tr: When Capnio was once a guest of the Duke of Württemberg, the Duke set a serving of sausage before him. Wanting to be more refined, he tried to cut it with his knife, but it slipped into his cup. Then, wanting to correct this with another show of refinement and to take it out with the knife, he poured the cup out onto the table. So it often happens to us that when we try to correct our faults, we fall into worse ones.

units.la: Eobanus, uir bonus, ad quendam nostrum semiebriū amicum dixerat: Ey tu es stultus. Ille graviter ferebat, & erat valde ineptus. Postero uero die pœnituit eum, uenitq; ad me, petēs ut rem sopiret: quod me facturum promisi. Cùm igitur uenissemus ad ientaculum, iußi ipsum aliquandiu foris expecta- re. Eobanus cùm uideret ipsum abesse, iußit cum uocari. Ille uenit, dicens: Domine Eobane, appel- lasti me heri meo nomine, quod tunc non intelle- xi, iam uerò intelligo.
units.tr: Eobanus, a good man, had said to one of our friends, who was half drunk: "Hey, you are a fool." The man took it badly, and he was very annoyed. But on the following day he regretted it, came to me, and asked me to settle the matter, which I promised to do. When we had come to breakfast, I told him to wait outside for a while. When Eobanus saw that he was absent, he ordered him to be called in. He came in and said: "Master Eobanus, yesterday you called me by my name, which I did not understand then, but now I do understand."

units.la: Guilhelmus dux Bauariæ habuit quendam cõ- uiuam, quem Marschalcus uoluit collocare supre- mo loco. Cùm autem ille diu repugnaret, tandem Marschalcus ipsi dabat baculum, inquiens: Si es Marschalcus, ipse collocato te in locum tibi conue- nientem. Ipse erubuit, & postea in loco sibi mon- strato aßedit.
units.tr: Duke William of Bavaria had a certain guest, whom the Marshal wished to seat in the highest place. But when the man resisted for a long time, the Marshal finally handed him a staff, saying: "If you are the Marshal, seat yourself in the place that suits you." He blushed, and afterwards he sat down in the place that had been pointed out to him.

units.la: Maximilianus coquum aliquem fidelem lega- uit Carolo V. Imperatori, qui ex fidelitate quen- dam uenenum Imperatori parantem occideret. Neminem enim ad Cæsaris culinaria admittebat. Erat autem natione Sueuus. Cùm igitur in infe- riori Germania in forum prodijßet, uolens uuas paßas emere, interrogauit mulierem, quo precio uenderet? Dicit mulier: &wat wit ghi hewen? At il- le: ich wil nicht heuen, sed uuas. Mulier ait: ick verstaiu nit. Respondit Sueuus: Rede ich doch braite wort.
units.tr: Maximilian sent a certain trustworthy cook to Charles V, the Emperor, so that he might kill anyone who was preparing poison for the Emperor out of loyalty; for he admitted no one to the Emperor's kitchen. He was a Swabian by birth. When he had come out into the marketplace in Lower Germany, wanting to buy raisins, he asked a woman at what price she sold them. The woman said: "And what will you take for them?" He replied: "I don't want to hew, but raisins." The woman said: "I don't understand." The Swabian answered: "But I am speaking plain words."

units.la: Conradus de Rosis Imperatoris Maximiliani miles, homo lepidus (nõ uolo eũ nominare scurrã. gemmæ enim sunt raro inter lapillos) cùm aliqui principrincipes in præsentia Imperatoris Maximiliani cum eo luderet &, ipse haberet duos chartaceos reges: interrogauit eos, an pecuniam uniuersam auferre deberet, qui tres haberet reges? Annuē-tibus illis, uocat Imperatorem Maximilianum, & suis manibus ipsum comprehendit, ac primùm o-stensis suis chartaceis regibus, inquit: Ecce hîc ha-betis duos: deinde monstrato Imperatore (ait) Ille est tertius, ac simul uniuersam pecuniam ab-ripit. Insuper etiam addens: Talem chartaceum Regem tui principem te iudicant. Illud non tam fuit facetum, quàm ironicum.
units.tr: Konrad von Rosen, a soldier of the Emperor Maximilian and a witty man (I do not want to call him a buffoon, for gems are rare among pebbles), once was playing with some princes in the presence of the Emperor Maximilian. He had two paper kings, and he asked them whether he should take the whole stake if he had three kings. When they nodded, he called the Emperor Maximilian, took hold of him with his own hands, and first, showing his paper kings, said: "Here you have two." Then, pointing at the Emperor, he said: "That one is the third," and at the same time he snatched up the whole stake. He added further: "Such a paper king do your princes judge you to be." That was not so much witty as ironical.

units.la: Derisus est iste uersiculus Sardanapali, quem inscripserat sepulchro suo: Hæc habui quæ come-di, quæ bibi, &c. imò non habebat: quia perierat corpus cum multis quæ comederat & biberat.
units.tr: That little verse of Sardanapalus was mocked, which he had inscribed on his tomb: "These things I had: what I ate, what I drank, etc." Indeed, he did not have them, because his body had perished along with the many things he had eaten and drunk.

units.la: Papa Iulius Tertius, qui fuit ante Marcellum, dicitur fuisse turpis belua, dedita libidinibus ob-scœnis & gulæ. Cùm autem libenter comederet pa-uones, fortè sibi iusserat asseruari pauonem, qui utcunq; intactus superfuerat. Ministri uerò non curantes ipsius mandatum, cum comederunt, nec ad mensam domini retulerunt. Postea ipse inter-rogauit, ubi esset? Cùm intelligeret esse absumptũ, coepit commoueri, quòd esset defraudatus tam de-licato cibo. Cardinalis autem astans, uolens ipsius iram lenire, dixit: Sanctissime pater, non decet te ita ob leuem rem irasci. An ego non irascerer[?]ta-men Deus est iratus propter morsum pomi. Voluit esse facetus illo dicto. Ita Epicurei ludunt, qui diuina iudicia profanis iocis immiscent.
units.tr: Pope Julius III, who came before Marcellus, is said to have been a foul beast, given over to obscene lusts and gluttony. Since he eagerly ate peacocks, he happened to have ordered a peacock to be kept for him, which had survived untouched in some way. But the servants, not caring about his command, ate it and did not bring it to the Lord's table. Afterwards he asked where it was. When he learned that it had been eaten up, he began to be stirred up, because he had been cheated of such a delicate dish. But a cardinal standing by, wanting to soothe his anger, said: "Most holy father, it is not fitting for you to be angry over such a trifle. Surely I would be angry too, yet God was angry over a bite of an apple." He wanted to be witty with that saying. So the Epicureans jest, mixing divine judgments with profane jokes.

units.la: Nobilissima quædam domina putabatur esse grauida, sed gerebat molam. Vsitatè nominant molam, massam informem, nõ fœtum. Postea quā do edidit illam massam, honestæ matronæ nobiles missæ sunt ad dominum, ut ipsi casum tristè exponerent. quæ cœperunt uerecundè loqui, & cum quadam commiseratione dixerunt: Illustrissime domine, nos sumus in magna spe tecū, te habitu-rũ esse hæredem, & orauimus Deum, & adhuc oramus ut respiciat te, & cõiugem tuā. (ipsæ hæc erudite & elegãter protulerũt) sed (proh dolor) euētus aliter se declarauit. tua domina nõ iam edidit fœtū, sed massam, ut sæpe accidit mulieribus. At ille: Quomodo igitur nominatur? Respõdent ei uerecũdè: Mã nentsein monkalb. Sic importuna eius interrogatione protulerunt nomen. Ille satis crasse respondit, Hõ,es ist besser ein kalb, als ein kindt, den ein kalb kan man noch essen. Fuit satis insulsa, non digna homine oratio. Discite tamen illa quæ conueniunt hominibus.
units.tr: A certain most noble lady was thought to be pregnant, but she was carrying a mole. People commonly call a shapeless lump a mole, not a foetus. Afterwards, when she had passed that lump, noble matrons were sent to the lord to set out the sad event for him. They began to speak modestly and said with a certain sympathy: "Most illustrious lord, we had great hope with you that you would have an heir, and we prayed to God, and we still pray, that he would look upon you and your wife." (They delivered these words learnedly and elegantly.) But, alas, the outcome turned out otherwise: your lady has not brought forth a child but a lump, as often happens to women. Then he said: "What, then, is it called?" They answered him modestly, and by his blunt questioning they brought out the name: "Man nennt's ein Monkalb" (it is called a moon-calf). He answered quite crudely: "Well, it is better to be a calf than a child, for one can still eat a calf." That speech was rather foolish and not worthy of a man. Yet learn from it what is fitting for men.

units.la: Romæ in quodam conuentu, Principes habebant secum oratorem Bauarum, qui, cùm erat dicendum, iussu Principũ coram Papa, sic incipit dicere: Sanctissime potor, &c. Papa aspiciès cum, putat se ignominiæ causa appellari. Orator perterrefactus obmutescit, ac quærens in pera schedulam (ubi habuerat pyra putrefacta) promit pro schedula putrida pira: unde subito omnibus obortus est magnus risus.
units.tr: At Rome, at a certain gathering, the princes had with them an orator from Bavaria, who, when he had to speak, at the command of the princes, began before the Pope in this way: "Most holy potentate, etc." The Pope, looking at him, thought he was being addressed for the sake of mockery. The orator, terrified, fell silent, and searching his wallet for a slip of paper (where he had some rotten pears), he drew out rotten pears instead of the paper; at once a great laugh arose from all.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam puellæ cuidam obtulit chrysomela, interrogans an etiam antea sæpius huiusmodi uidisset? Respondit: Quidni? uidi sæpe assata. Illud fuit indecorum in sermone. Quia chrysomela non solent assari.
units.tr: Someone offered a girl a golden beetle and asked whether she had often seen such things before. She replied: "Why not? I have often seen them roasted." That was an unseemly remark, because golden beetles are not usually roasted.

units.la: Initio controversiarum Lutheri, duo rustici prope Coburgam convenerunt, cum ambo essent ebrij. Vnus interrogat alterum, cuius nam sit religionis? Respondit alter: Lutheranæ. Ille iratus dicit: Ego sum Martini. Sic unus in alterius crines inuolat.
units.tr: At the start of Luther's controversies, two peasants met near Coburg, both of them drunk. One asked the other what his religion was. The other replied, "Lutheran." The first, angry, said, "I am Martin's." And so one flew at the other's hair.

units.la: Dicebam cuidam de Carolo Magno, illum semel totum anserē comedisse. Ille inquit: Di boni, quoties ego integrum devoraui.
units.tr: I was telling someone about Charlemagne, that he had once eaten a whole goose. He said: "Good gods, how often I have devoured a whole one!"

units.la: Dicunt Delphos fuisse in medio terræ habitatæ: & hoc inde colligitur, quia dicuntur à Ioue emissæ esse duæ aquilæ, altera ab occidente, altera ab oriente, ibiq; convenisse utramq; aquilam.
units.tr: They say Delphi was at the centre of the inhabited earth. This is inferred from the fact that Jupiter was said to have sent out two eagles, one from the west and one from the east, and that the two eagles met there.

units.la: Quòd si rē amissam arte recuperare uelitis, docebo uos artē, qua omnia amissa reperire positis. Nulla opus erit coniuratione, aut alijs diabolicis artibus: sed tantum rei amissæ imponite furfures cum sale, & statim reperietis. Item, Si possis cauere ne pedes retrahas, tutus eris ab omnium canum morsibus.
units.tr: But if you want to recover a lost thing by art, I will teach you an art by which you will find anything lost. No conjuring or other diabolical arts will be needed. Just sprinkle bran mixed with salt on the lost thing, and you will find it at once. Likewise, if you can take care not to draw back your feet, you will be safe from the bites of all dogs.

units.la: Cùm Rex Polonicus aliquando aulico cuidam dixisset, Oportet te cras mecum ire in uenationem: respondit: Nō oportet domine Rex. At rex: Quid? Imo, inquit ille, ego lubens faciam. Iste est iocus aulicus. Vtrunq; oportet, non erat liber à necessi tate, sed à coactione & uiolentia.
units.tr: Once the King of Poland said to a courtier, "You must come hunting with me tomorrow." He replied, "There is no need, my lord King." "What? Indeed you must," said the king. "I will gladly do it," said the courtier. That is a courtly joke. Both answers use "must": the courtier was not free of necessity, but he was free of compulsion and force.

units.la: Albertus dux Saxoniæ in quodam conuiuio, cum alij gloriarentur de suis possessionibus, dixit se habere unam ciuitatem, in qua essent tria magna miracula.
