Tria enim esse in ea ciuitate monasteria. Primum monasterium Prædicatorum, habentium multum frumenti, cùm non haberent agros. Secundum Franciscanorum, qui abundarent pecunia, cùm non haberent reditus. Tertium Thomæ, monachos multos habetes liberos, & tamen carentes coniugibus.
units.tr: At a banquet, when others were boasting about their possessions, Duke Albert of Saxony said that he had a city in which there were three great marvels. For that city had three monasteries. The first was that of the Preachers, who had plenty of grain although they had no fields. The second was that of the Franciscans, who abounded in money although they had no income. The third was that of St Thomas, whose many monks had children, and yet had no wives.

units.la: Poeta quidam, sedens inter bonos sodales, ascendebat mensam, & exerebat pedem extra fenestram, prouocans simul multis execrationibus & maledictionibus diabolum, ut ipsum auferret. Quidam interea præteriens, qui eius mores nouerat, arripuit eius pedē, & protraxit ad se extra fenestram. Ille uerò concidit exanimatus, existimans diabolum præsentem esse, & ipsum comprehendisse. Hinc postquam ad se redijset, risus maximus aliorum est subsecutus.
units.tr: A certain poet, sitting among good companions, climbed onto the table and stuck one foot out of the window, calling down many curses and maledictions on the devil to carry him off. Meanwhile a passer-by who knew his habits seized his foot and pulled him from the window towards himself. The poet collapsed as if dead, thinking that the devil was present and had caught him. When he came to himself, the others burst into great laughter.

units.la: Nobilis quidam uir admodum deditus lusibus in aula Ducis cuiusdam uiuens, cum aliquando luderet cum Duce, amisit multum pecuniæ. quamobrem iratus, chartas lusorias eiecit per fenestrā, & iurauit se posthac nunquam lusurum. Post mensem autem unum atq; alterum, Dux, qui illius ira & consuetudine delectabatur, invitat eum ad balneū, ac eum blandis verbis alloquitur: Non' ne aliquantisper ludemus, ut magis prompti & alacriores in balneo esse possimus? Ille diu recusauit: sed tandem persuasus à Principe incœpit ludere, & multum pecuniæ ludendo perdidit. Ibi denuò iratus, chartas laceravit, easq; per fenestram deiecit, iurauitq; se nunquam lusurum posthac. Illa non fuit constans & perpetua voluntas. Ita multi sunt, qui iurant se temperaturos sibi ab intemperanti illa compotatione: arrepta autem leui occasione, ad ingenium prius, & mores pristinas redeunt.
units.tr: A certain nobleman, much given to gambling, was living at a duke's court. Once, while playing with the Duke, he lost a great deal of money. In anger he threw the playing cards out of the window and swore he would never gamble again. But after a month or two, the Duke, who took pleasure in his anger and his habit, invited him to the bath and addressed him with flattering words: "Shall we not play a little, so that we may be more lively and cheerful in the bath?" He refused for a long time, but at last, persuaded by the prince, he began to play and lost much money at cards. Angry again, he tore up the cards, threw them out of the window, and swore he would never play again. That was not a steady and lasting resolve. So there are many who swear they will abstain from that intemperate drinking, but once a slight opportunity arises they return to their former disposition and habits.

units.la: Sæpe fit, ut quidam stulti imitatores imitentur vanitia præstantium virorum. Erat quidam Orator in aula Maximiliani, cùm ego adhuc essem Tubin‑gæ, qui non poterat R pronunciare, erat enim τραυλὸς.
units.tr: It often happens that foolish imitators copy the vanities of distinguished men. When I was still at Tübingen, there was an orator at Maximilian's court who could not pronounce the letter R, for he was a lisper.

units.la: τραφωλὸς. Hunc omnes doctores in illa pronūcia- tione imitari uolebant, quotquot tunc temporis Tubingæ erāt. Obseruate: hoc exemplū commu- ne est in uita, ut uitia præstantiū uirorū excerpā- tur pro uirtutibus, ab hominib. imeruditis & phā- tasticis. Illa imitatio uocatur ναnoσuλία.
units.tr: He lisped "trafōlos". All the teachers at Tübingen at that time wanted to imitate him in that pronunciation. Note this: it is a common thing in life that the faults of distinguished men are taken up as if they were virtues, by unlearned and fanciful people. Such imitation is called bad emulation [κακοζηλία].

units.la: Studiosus quidam Tubingensis in omni dispu- tatione hoc argumentum afferebat, unde semper quatuor nummos accipiebat.
units.tr: A certain student at Tübingen brought forward this argument in every disputation, and for it he always received four coins.

units.la: Cuiuslibet cōtradictionis altera pars est uera: Lutheri doctrina est contradictionis altera pars.
units.tr: One side of any contradiction is true. Luther's doctrine is the other side of a contradiction.

units.la: Ergo Lutheri doctrina est uera. Et sic possum de qualibet materia inferre.
units.tr: Therefore Luther's doctrine is true. And in this way I can infer the same about any subject whatever.

units.la: Respondeo: Hic non rectè propositiones sub- sumuntur, quia est particularis syllogismus. Eun- dem syllogismū obieci homini contentioso, & de posui cum eo cantharū uini, num posset soluere. Dixit: Video ibi esse aliquid errati, sed ubi sit, ignoro. Iußit ergo cum indignatione uinū afferri, & argumentum solui. Ille syllogismus est tanquā Delphicus gladius ad omnem materiam.
units.tr: I reply: the propositions have not been rightly subsumed here, because this is a particular syllogism. I once put the same syllogism to a contentious man, and set a jug of wine before him, asking whether he could solve it. He said, "I see there is some error here, but I do not know where it is." So, with indignation, he ordered wine to be brought and the argument solved. That syllogism is like the Delphic sword, fit for every subject.

units.la: Romæ Legatus quidā, mittendus in Germaniā, accesit quendam amicū suum Germanū, inquiēs: Audio gentem tuam multas seruare ceremonias in cōgressibus, quæso doceas me, cùm eò mihi pro ficiscendū sit, aliquid earū, ne plane me arbitrētur esse hominem rusticum & agrestem. Respondit Germanus: Nõ potero te nũc eorũ mores docere, sed dabo tibi breuem regulam, qua poteris uti in omnibus congressibus. Quicquid illiiusserint, tu strenuè facere recusès: id nostri putant esse ciui litate, ut in cõuiuijs ad mensam pertrahãtur, vnd reißen solœcismos, vnd grœbe barbarismos: e- uertũt scamna, cantharos, & uitra de mensa pro ijciunt. Postea assidentes mensæ, nihil loquuntur, alter alterum intuetur tacitus, & aliorum sermo- nes obseruat. Hæc sæpißimè in his regionibus ac- cidunt.
units.tr: At Rome a certain legate, who was to be sent to Germany, approached a German friend of his and said: "I hear that your people observe many ceremonies at social gatherings. Please teach me some of them, since I must go there, so that they will not think me a boorish country bumpkin." The German replied: "I cannot teach you their customs now, but I will give you a short rule which you can use at all gatherings. Whatever they do, you should resolutely refuse to do. Our people consider it good manners that at banquets they drag each other to the table, reißen Solœcismos, vnd grœbe Barbarismos [crack solecisms and coarse barbarisms]; they overturn benches, goblets and glasses from the table. Afterwards, seated at the table, they say nothing; one looks silently at another and observes the talk of the rest. These things happen very often in these regions."

units.la: Huttenus cùm in conuentu Augustano febri la boraret, misit febrim schedulæ inscriptam ad Fug gerum, apud quem Cardinalis Sixtus morabatur, quia ibi melius & delicatius tractari posset, quàm apud se. Fuit pulcher iocus.
units.tr: When Hutten was suffering from fever during the assembly at Augsburg, he sent the fever, in a note addressed to Fugger, with whom Cardinal Sixtus was staying, because it could be treated more comfortably and daintily there than with Hutten himself. It was a fine joke.

units.la: In aula Heydelbergensi simplex fatuus mirum in modũ amabat campanas. & quando dicebatur ad eum, Campanam Spirensem esse mortuã, tunc lachrymabatur. Cùm aliquando adueẚta esset no- ua Campana, complexus est ipsam, & dixit: Bis mir willkummen mein liebe glock, ich bin hie, vnnd du bist nun auch hie.
units.tr: At the Heidelberg court there was a simple fool who was wonderfully fond of bells. When it was told him that the bell of Speyer was dead, he wept. Once a new bell was brought, he embraced it and said: "Welcome, my dear bell! I am here, and now you are here too."

units.la: Quidam cùm mensæ apposita esset puls fer- uens, dixit se ita institutũ esse, ne attingeret ferrũ, antequam sputum in illud misisset, & ita explo- rasset, an esset rasset, an esse calidum: idem se in pulte facere. Illud est non in loco uti præceptis.
units.tr: When a hot porridge was set before a certain man, he said he had been taught not to touch metal until he had spat on it, and so had tested whether it was hot; and he did the same with the porridge. That is to use precepts in the wrong place.

units.la: Miles mihi bene notus, Cůntz von der Rosen (qui etiam fuit cum Maximiliano Imperatore in carcere, nec fuit diu post illum superstes) cum obijssset Imperator, dixit: Dominus meus est mortuus, & ego breui moriar. Hic Imperatori in uita fuit admodum iucundus: ferebat ipsius consuetudinem patienter, quia erat ualde facetus, interdum etiam scurrilis. Fuerat comes omnium ipsius itinerum. Hic uidit aliquando pauperem sacerdotem prætereuntem hospitium Imperatoris, & ferentem librum suarum precum, accedit ad eum, & eripit ei librum, dicens: Sequere me, cu rabo ut numos accipias. Sic introducit eum ad Maximilianum Imperatorem, inquiens: Domine Imperator, hic pauper sacerdos amisit librū precationum in lupanari. Da quæso illi, ut redimat librum: alioqui multum bonorum operum & uoluntarum intermittetur. Imperator respondit: Quare crucias miserum hominem (uidebat enim sacrificulum trepidantem) & iussit illi numerari decem florenos.
units.tr: Cuntz von der Rosen, a soldier well known to me (who was also imprisoned with Emperor Maximilian and did not long survive him), said when the Emperor died: "My lord is dead, and I shall die soon." In the Emperor's lifetime he was very pleasant company. He put up with the Emperor's ways patiently, because he was very witty and sometimes even buffoonish. He had accompanied the Emperor on all his journeys. Once he saw a poor priest passing the Emperor's lodging, carrying a book of his prayers. He went up to him, snatched the book from him, and said: "Follow me, and I will see that you get some money." He then led him to the Emperor Maximilian, saying: "Lord Emperor, this poor priest has lost his prayer book in a brothel. Please give him the means to buy back the book, or else much good work and devotion will be interrupted." The Emperor replied, "Why do you torment the poor man?" (for he saw the little priest trembling), and ordered ten florins to be counted out for him.

units.la: In aula Friderici erat duo præstantissimi uiri, Comes de Schwartzenburg, & Friderich Dön. Quorum hic, cum esset aliquando defatigatus negocijs, dixit ad Comitem de Schwartzenburg:
units.tr: At the court of Frederick there were two most outstanding men, the Count of Schwartzenburg and Friedrich Dön. One of them, when he was once worn out by business, said to the Count of Schwartzenburg:

units.la: Tædet me propemodum huius uitæ, & optarem mihi aliam uitam. Comes respondit: Tu nequam (quia erant boni sodales) putas me uoluptatem capere ex illis negocijs? Sed age, quam uitam tibi optares? Respondit Fridericus: Optarem esse aliquis magnus Abbas, in diuiti quodam cœnobio. Tum Comes: Tu nequam, uelles tu solus ita suauiter uiuere? Atqui ego uellem esse monachus, qui regeret illum Abbatem.
units.tr: I am almost weary of this life, and I would wish myself another. The Count replied, "You scoundrel (since they were good companions), do you think I take pleasure in those affairs? But come, what life would you wish for yourself?" Frederick answered, "I would wish to be some great abbot in a rich monastery." Then the Count said, "You scoundrel, would you alone want to live so pleasantly? Indeed, I would wish to be the monk who governed that abbot."

units.la: Materfamilias, cuius filius ex Academia reuersus erat, tria oua filio & patri apposuerat. Ibi paterfamilias obiurgauit ipsam, quòd tantum tria oua apposuisset, præsertim cùm filius domum reuersus esset, quem liberalius accipi conueniret. Filius ostentandi ingenij causa dixit, sex oua esse apposita. Pater miratus, quæsiuit ex filio, qua ratione id fieri posset. Respondit filius: Vnum & duo & tria, sex efficere. Bene, inquit pater, non male collocaui meam pecuniam, cum tam ingeniosum filium habeam. Sed pulchrè illam sophisticam filij refutauit. Ego, inquit, duo oua comedã, & mater tertium, comedas tu reliqua tria. Est fallacia compositionis & diuisionis.
units.tr: A housewife, whose son had come home from the university, had set three eggs before her son and her husband. The householder then scolded her, because she had set out only three eggs, especially since the son had come home and ought to be received more generously. The son, to show off his wit, said that six eggs had been set out. The father, amazed, asked his son by what reasoning this could be so. The son replied, "One and two and three make six." "Good," said the father, "I have not invested my money badly, since I have such a clever son. But he has refuted his son's sophism beautifully. 'I,' he said, 'will eat two eggs, and your mother the third; you may eat the remaining three.'" This is the fallacy of composition and division.

units.la: Homo Saxonicus iter faciens, uenit ad Rhenum in cauponam, & iussit sibi adferri uinum. Caupo appositit ei paruum poculum. Ille sitiens aliquoties ebibit, & iussit sibi rursus infundi.
units.tr: A Saxon man, travelling, came to an inn on the Rhine and ordered wine to be brought to him. The innkeeper set a small cup before him. He, being thirsty, drank it down several times and ordered it to be filled again.

units.la: Caupo miratus bibacitatem hominis, dixit: &wiltu doch gar nichts drinnen haben (quia aliquoties ebibisset.) At ille abiecit poculum, & iratus dixit: wat soll mich dat blakhorn?
units.tr: The innkeeper, amazed at the man's thirst for drink, said, "Do you want to have nothing in it at all?" (because he had drunk it down several times). But the man threw down the cup and angrily said, "What do I want with this little horn?"

units.la: Quidam monachus in ducatu Vuirtenbergensi, Vuigandus dictus, in poetas inuehebatur, præcipuè in Bebelium, quòd is taxaret quantitates, & illuderet monachis. Cùm autē Dux Vuirtenbergensis quosdam operarios fossores piscinarum ex Polonia uocasset, quos ibi Pollecken nominant rustici: ibi monachus cùm nominaret procöcione die Poeten (crassum est) hæreticos, putabant rustici eum inuehere in die Poleken, & eorum noluerunt uti commercio, uocabantq; etiam ipsos hæreticos. Vnde rixæ & tumultus oriebantur. Magistratus autem ignorans quæ esset causa tumultus, tandem resciuit, oriri eum ex concione monachi illius. Sic interdixit Magistratus monacho, ne amplius uel de Poetis, uel de Poleken concionaretur. Est uera historia. Eo tempore fuit Tubingæ.
units.tr: A certain monk in the Duchy of Württemberg, called Wigand, used to inveigh against the poets, especially against Bebel, because he criticised quantities and mocked the monks. When the Duke of Württemberg had summoned certain labourers, diggers of fishponds, from Poland, whom the country people call "Pollecken," then the monk, when on a procession day he named the poets (it is a crude thing) heretics, the country people thought he was attacking the Polish day, and they refused to have dealings with them and even called them heretics themselves. From this quarrels and tumults arose. The magistrate, not knowing the cause of the tumult, at length discovered that it arose from the sermon of that monk. So the magistrate forbade the monk to preach any more either about the poets or about the Pollecken. This is a true story. At that time he was at Tübingen.

units.la: Diligenter est animaduertendum, quæ sit urbanitas, quæ scurrilitas. Vtriusq; exempla habetis in Eülenspiegel. Hic quodam tempore uenit ad Principes, petens sibi dari eleemosynam, eo quòd opificium ipsius non amplius in precio esset apud homines. Ibi interrogatus, quale exerceret opificium manuarium? Respondit: Conficere soleo ocularia, seu perspicilla: sed ea iam non amplius sunt uendibilia, dárumb daß die herren durch die finger sehen.
units.tr: One must carefully note what is urbanity and what is buffoonery. You have examples of both in Eulenspiegel. He once came to the princes, asking to be given alms, on the ground that his trade was no longer valued by people. Asked then what manual trade he practised, he replied: "I used to make spectacles or eyeglasses, but they are no longer saleable now, since the lords look through their fingers" (that is, because the lords overlook things).

units.la: Erat apud nos Tubingæ doctor Eblinger, quē audiuerat doctor Hieronymus Schurpff. De eo alij Doctores dixerunt: Non possumus omnes doctrina æquare Eblingerum.
units.tr: There was at Tübingen among us a teacher Eblinger, whom Doctor Hieronymus Schurpff had heard. Of him the other teachers said, "We cannot all equal Eblinger in learning."

units.la: Rex Alfonsus solitus est dicere de mediatoribus, eos similes esse habitantibus in medijs ædibus, qui perfunduntur lotio à superioribus, & lædruntur fumo ab inferioribus. Sic plerũ q; mediatores utrinq; lædiuntur: sicut uespertilio laceratur à muribus & auibus. Fuit hic rex ita sapiens & bellicosus, ualens consilio & potentia, ut haberetur unus ex præstantißimis principibus illius ætatis.
units.tr: King Alfonso used to say of mediators that they are like people living in a house in the middle, who are drenched with slops from those above and choked with smoke from those below. So mediators are generally hurt on both sides, just as a bat is torn by mice and birds. This king was so wise and warlike, and so strong in counsel and power, that he was regarded as one of the most outstanding princes of his age.

units.la: Cùm essemus in conuentu Augustano apud Episcopum Dantiscanum poetam, qui erat Orator regis Polonici, præstans uir, ego, Eobanus Hessus, & Camerarius, genio indulgentes: interea uenit ad nos Logus, bonus homo, qui etiam nouit Poeticam, & recitat multos uersus, quos in iuuentute memoriæ mandauerat. Eobanus uerò, ut erat modestus, diu sedit tacitus, nihil ei respondens: nõ enim nouerat eum, neq; Logus Eobanum. Tandẽ loquacitatem eius Eobanus ægrè ferens, dixit: Du tropff, meinstu das sonst keiner vers weiß, denn du allein? Aßide, præbibam tibi hoc uitrum uini. (habebamus enim generosum rubrum uinum in mensa) Logus, non agnoscens Eobanum, tacuit, & mutauit uultum. Ibi Episcopus, qui mihi ad dextram sedebat, (in sinistra parte sedebat Eobanus, apud Eobanum Camerarius) dixit: Domine Loge, accipe uitrum uini, & responde ipsi. est enim bonus uir: est Eobanus. Sic non ægre tulit illam responsionem Logus, sed subiunxit: Ego phantasticus, cùm sim ineruditus, uenio huc, & apud homines doctos, & apud ipsos Poetas nugor, uolens uersus recitare. Sic mutatis animis, postea ambo facti sunt hilares.
units.tr: When we were at the assembly of Augsburg, at the house of the Bishop of Danzig, a poet who was ambassador of the Polish king, an outstanding man, I, Eobanus Hessus, and Camerarius were indulging our genius. Meanwhile there came to us Logus, a good man, who also knew poetics and recited many verses that he had committed to memory in his youth. Eobanus, however, being modest by nature, sat silent for a long time, answering him nothing, for he did not know him, nor did Logus know Eobanus. At last, being annoyed at his talkativeness, Eobanus said, "You fool, do you think no one else knows verses but you alone? Sit down, I'll drink this glass of wine to you." (For we had a fine red wine on the table.) Logus, not recognising Eobanus, fell silent and changed countenance. Then the bishop, who sat at my right hand (Eobanus sat on the left, and Camerarius beside Eobanus), said, "Master Logus, take a glass of wine and answer him; for he is a good man, he is Eobanus." Thus Logus did not take that reply badly, but added: "I am a fanciful fellow; though I am unlearned, I come here and play the fool before learned men and before the poets themselves, wanting to recite verses." Thus, with their minds changed, afterwards both became cheerful.

units.la: INSVLSAE ET FALSAE interpretationes.
units.tr: FALSE AND INSIPID INTERPRETATIONS.

units.la: Audiui concionē cuiusdā doctoris Theologiæ, qui interpretabatur hoc dictum: Pietas ad omnia utilis est: Die miltigkeit ist zu allem gůt. Per pietatem intelligebat eleemosynam. Sed pietas hic non significat beneficentiā. Paulus hoc non uult, sed tantum speciem bonorum operum proponit.
units.tr: I heard a sermon by a doctor of theology who explained this saying, "Piety is useful for all things" (German: "Die Mildigkeit ist zu allem gut," that is, "Mildness is good for everything"). He understood "piety" here to mean almsgiving. But piety does not mean beneficence here. Paul does not mean this; he only sets out the appearance of good works.

units.la: Ante octoginta annos uixit Italus, qui uolens Ciceroniano more loqui, si quando utēdum esset uocabulo Episcopi, uocabat ipsum flamē. Episcopus autem non minus purè dicitur, atq; flamen.
units.tr: Eighty years ago there lived an Italian who, wishing to speak in the manner of Cicero, whenever he had to use the word "bishop" called him a "flamen." Yet "bishop" is no less correct Latin than "flamen."

units.la: Longolius non utitur uocabulo Ecclesiæ, sed pro ea substituit nomen Respublica Christiana. idem, fidem nominat persuasionem.
units.tr: Longolius does not use the word "Church," but in its place he substitutes the term "Christian commonwealth." Likewise he calls faith "persuasion."

units.la: Quidam interpretabatur: Propter hæc uenít ira Dei super filios incredulitatis. & mouebat quæstionẽ, num filij incredulorū possent cõuerti?
units.tr: Someone interpreted the verse, "For these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of unbelief," and raised the question whether the sons of unbelievers could be converted.

units.la: In psalmo, Exurgat Deus, hic uersiculus extat: Si dormieritis inter medios cleros. interpretatæ sunt moniales insulsæ, wen ihr bey den pfaffen schlaffet. Sed uera translatio est: Erit exercitus uester in finibus, eritis sicut nitentes columbæ. Iudæi exposuerunt, Cùm dormieritis inter ollas: de ollis Aegyptijs intelligentes. Sed neq; de cleris, neq; de ollis fit mentio: neq; ibi est uerbū dormire, sed accubare.
units.tr: In the psalm "Let God arise" there is this verse: "If you have slept among the middle clergy" (German: "wenn ihr bey den Pfaffen schlaffet," "when you sleep among the priests"), as the foolish nuns rendered it. But the true translation is: "Your army shall be in the borders, and you shall be like doves shining with gold." The Jews explained it, "When you have slept among the pots," understanding the Egyptians by the pots. But there is no mention of clergy or of pots, nor does the word "sleep" occur there, but "lie down."

units.la: In conuentu Tridentino dixerunt, Reddentes rationem fidei uestræ: id est, Scripturam. Hæc autem sunt uerba Petri. Videtis quanta sit fatuitas, quòd exponant rationem pro Scriptura.
units.tr: At the Council of Trent they rendered, "giving an account of your faith," as meaning Scripture. Yet these are the words of Peter. You see how foolish it is to explain "account" as "Scripture."

units.la: In quodam loco concionator quidam aliquot conciones de hac sententia in magna frequentia hominum consumpsit: Peccatum non remittitur, nisi ablatum restituatur. Et mirabiliter illud dictum expositit, ut aliquorum suorum applausum captaret, ex hoc fundamento, quòd esset papisticum. Auditis his concionibus, multi magni & præstantes uiri fremuerunt, ac illas insulsitates ægrè tulerunt: lerunt: inter quos etiam fuit honestus uir, doctor Pontanus.
units.tr: In a certain place a preacher spent several sermons on this saying, before a large crowd: "Sin is not forgiven unless what was taken is restored." He expounded it in a remarkable way, to win the applause of some of his followers, on the ground that it was Papist. When these sermons were heard, many great and distinguished men were indignant and took these insipidities badly; among them was the honourable man, Doctor Pontanus.

units.la: Dixit ad me quidam multis notus, nullum esse uerbum in Scriptura, quod non posset ambiguè intelligi. Cui respondi: Si Scriptura est ambigua, multo magis scriptores, quorum inter-pretationibus tu uis ac-quiescere.
units.tr: A certain man well known to many said to me that there is no word in Scripture which cannot be understood ambiguously. I replied: If Scripture is ambiguous, much more so are the writers whose interpretations you wish to rest in.

IOACHIMO Electori & Archicamerario Romani imperij: GEORGIO FRIDERICO, &c. reuerendißimisq; Principibus ac Dominis, D. VVILHELMO Episcopo Rigensi, &c. atq; SIGISMVNDO Archiepiscopo Magdeburgensi, &c. caeterisq; præstantißimis principibus ex eadem familia originem ducentibus, Marchionibus Brandenburgensibus, Ducibus Pomeraniæ, Rugiæ, Silesiæ, Burggrauijs Norimbergensibus, &c. Dominis suis clementißimis

units.la: S. D.
units.tr: Greetings.

units.la: Tpietate & consolationes plenissima est sententia, quæ legitur apud Paulum his uerbis: Perdam sapientiam sapientum, & prudentiam prudentium reprobabo. ubi sapiens? ubi scriba? ubi inquisitor huius seculi? Nam quia in Dei sapientia non cognouit mundus per sapientiam Deum: placuit Deo, per stulticiam prædicationis saluos facere credentes. 1. Cor. 1.
units.tr: Most full of piety and consolation is the saying read in Paul in these words: "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent. Where is the wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the disputer of this age? For since in the wisdom of God the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe." 1 Cor. 1.

units.la: Proponit enim Apostolus ob oculos iudicium omnium hominum, sinceram
units.tr: For the Apostle sets before our eyes the judgment of all men upon the sincere

units.la: Euangelij doctrinam non recte intelli-gentium, siue sint in Ecclesia, siue extra eam. Præsertim verò sapientiam huius mundi ab Euangelij doctrina seiungit: deinde sapietiam, quæ mundo stultitia est, declarat. Est autem humana sapietia parua quædam particula legis moralis, quod attinet ad externorum membro-rum gubernationem, seu quod alibi Philosophi vocant externam disciplinam: interea nihilominus in mente hærét dubitationes, in voluntate & corde fremitus & furores contra Deum dominatur. Quàm porrò egregios hæc fructus prose-rat, potest nobis exemplo quasi ob oculos ponere Pharisæus ille tumidus, qui commendans suam probitatem, virtute & sapientiam, particulatim recensebat, se de omnibus bonis decimas dare, ieiunare bis in septimana, &c. Huic similes passim Christus in Euangelio taxat. Quamobrem quantumuis pro sapientibus tales habentur & coluntur: tamen omnes naturali sua luce non intelligunt sapientiā Dei: de qua non aliter loquuntur & iudicāt, quàm eam sibi videri stultissimam concionem. Si igitur doctrina ecclesiæ
units.tr: doctrine of the Gospel, of those who do not rightly understand it, whether they are within the Church or outside it. Above all he separates the wisdom of this world from the doctrine of the Gospel, and then declares the wisdom which is foolishness to the world. Human wisdom, however, is a small part of the moral law, insofar as it concerns the governance of the outward members, or what the philosophers elsewhere call external discipline. Yet meanwhile doubts stick in the mind, and in the will and heart murmurings and furies against God hold sway. How remarkable the fruits this produces can be shown to us, as if before our eyes, by that proud Pharisee who, commending his uprightness, virtue and wisdom, listed item by item that he gave tithes of all his goods, fasted twice a week, and so on. Christ everywhere in the Gospel rebukes men like him. Therefore, however much such men are held and honored as wise, they do not, by their natural light, all understand the wisdom of God. Of it they speak and judge no otherwise than that it seems to them a most foolish preaching. If therefore the doctrine of the Church seems foolishness to them, much more are those who teach this mad preaching, according to their opinion, regarded and named fools by them.

units.la: [Note: the words "tamer" and "sapientiā" and "ecclesiæ" are read with some doubt; the ends of several lines are faint.] ecclesię uidetur ipsis stulticia, multo magis ij qui homines iuxta ipsorū opinionem, hac insana prædicatione docent, fatui ab his existimātur ac nominantur. Vnde istæ phantasiæ oriuntur huius seculi prudētum, qui tantum eam ob causam alendos esse ministros Ecclesię somniant, ut populus in disciplina retineatur: ne ue omni religione dissolutus, flagitijs atrocibus rempublicā perturbet. sic & doctores & discipuli studij Theologici coram huius seculi prudentibus iudicantur. Inde audiuntur uulgo aduersus ministros Euāgelij, studiososq; theologiae contumeliosæ exprobrationes & conuicia Pfaff pfaff. Quæ impietas non solùm id incommodū secum adducit, ut contemnatur ministerium, in quo, & per quod Deus semper ab initio usq; ad finem mundi Ecclesiam colligit: sed etiā multi iuuenes ab hoc munere abster- rentur. Cùm tamen illud summū officiū sit, sine quo cętera nec esse nec consistere queunt. Id quod sapientes gubernatores omnibus temporib. intellexerunt. Dauid desiderat Psal. 83, in atrijs Domini potius uersari, quàm in tabernaculis impioimpiorũ. Ezechias etiam 4. Regum 19. 20. & Esaiae 28. moriturus petit, propter conseruationem purae doctrinae, uitam suam prorogari. Simile quiddam ex relatione fide digni hominis accepi de principe Georgio, Marchione Brandenburgensi. Is princeps pientissimus paulò ante agonem mortis, ex intimis sui pectoris gemitibus petiuit, ut omnipotes Deus doctrinam coelestem hoc nostro tempore restitutam, apud posteros conseruare uellet, quò etiam fieret haeredes uitae aeternae. Quantus ergo, optimus princeps, fuerit fautor uerbi diuini, uel ea uox ostendit, quòd etiã in agone mortis tantum in religionis propagatione animum manifestè declarauit. Addatur huic & aliud. Cum cocionator pientissimum hunc principem ex uerbo diuino in extremo uitę discrimine cõsolaretur, & ab alio quodã pio uiro crux & triumphus Christi monstraretur, in haec uerba prorupit: Domine IESV Christe, ego firmiter credo, quòd pro peccatis meis & totius generis humani ipse sis passus, mortuus & resuscitatus: & iam sedeas ad dextram aeterni Patris, ut meum omnium peccatorū corpora resuscites, & tuo conglorificato reddas cōformia. His dictis, Saluatori nostro suam animā commendauit: & paulo post pie & tranquillè in Domino obdormiuit. Sicut ergo hic pijsimus princeps hanc sapientiam diuinam, non iuxta sapientum huius seculi iudicia cōtempsit: sed & in tota uita, & in agone mortis summum gaudium ipsi fuit, doctrinam Euangelij audire & promouere: sic has optimi Principis uirtutes filius eius illustrissim' Princeps Georgius Fridericus Marchio Brandenburgensis, &c. diligeter imitatur, in eo quod non solum Euangeliū suis subditis introductū à patre, per fideles Ecclesiæ doctores doceri permittit: uerùm etiam huic beneficio alia plura beneficia hactenus addere nō dubitauit. Quia ad priora stipendia à patre suo pientissimo Principe pauperibus scholasticis ordinata, noua quædā adiecit: scholamq; in quodam cœnobio instituì curat utiliter, in quam ex singulis suis præfecturis, certis temporibus quosdam suorū subditorum filios introducere, & bonis litteris atq; sumptibus necessariis procurare in animo habet. Quòd uerò illustris-simi illius familię Principes ante hęc no-stra tempora fuerint seduli cultores uer-bi diuini, ipsiusq; ministrorū, toti eccle-siæ Christi non est obscurum. Nam ante nostram ætatem singulis annis, quo ma-ior beneuolētia & mutua copulatio ani-morum inter principes & pastorem Ec-clefiæ illius loci, qui eo tempore erat ca-put ipsorum gubernationis, iniretur, cer-to die pastore accedere, & cū ipso pran-dere nō sunt dedignati: idq; hac ob cau-sam, ut de Ecclesiæ statu doctrinæq; con-trouersijs cum ipso familiariter confer-rent. Sæpius quoq; eadem de causa ad-se uocarunt pastores, aliosq; doctos ui-ros, & de mutatione ac emendatione ce-remoniarum atq; doctrinę cum ipsis cō-tulerunt. Quare illud seculum non mihi dissimile uidetur ei, quo Christus & Iai-rus, aut Centurio in oppido Capernaū, inuicem amicè & familiariter conuenie-bant. Cæterùm quantis beneficijs etiam hodie uiuētes pientissimi Principes, Al-bertus Dux Prufsię, Vuilhelmus Episco-pus Rigéfis, &c. Ioachimus Elector, &c. Sigismundus Archiepiscopus Magde-burgensis, burgensis, &c. cæteriq; eiusdem stirpis Brandenburgicæ Marchiones foueant ecclesias,nemo est qui ignoret. Nam in aduocandis ad se doctis uiris, nulli pecuniæ aut sumptibus parcunt:ad hæc,ec clesiarum ministris,& pauperibus scholasticis,liberalibus sumptibus prospicere sedulò student:ac incumbût in id diligenter,ut sinceram Euangelij doctrinā ad posteros transmittat.Itaq; iustè hanc pietatis & beneuolentiæ erga ecclesiam & suos subditos,illustrissimis principibus Marchionibus dominis meis clementisimis laudé tribuo : ac salua pietate possum affirmare, ex illorum numero ipsos uerè esse, qui sapiētiam Dei per suam sapientiam intelligunt, eamq; in suos subditos transfundere nituntur, quò cum ipsis fiant hæredes æternorum & cœlestium bonorum,ac perpetua Dei cōsuetudine fruantur.Quare,illustrisimi Principes,cùm propter iam recitatas uestri generis uirtutes, & propter gratitudinem,qua mei proaui,aui, parentes, fratres & ego,propter multiplicia beneficia sumus V.C. obligati, hanc sequentem tertiā mei laboris partem, in signū aliquod gratæ erga V. C. mentis meæ, V. C. dedico, & uestro nomine in lucem prodire cupio: oroq́;, ut me meosq; omnes V. C. commendatos habeant. Æternus Pater Domini nostri IESV Christi, unà cum Filio & Spiritu suo sancto, totâ familiam Marchionum Brandeburgensium diu incolumem ac saluam conseruet: & uos etiâ illustrissimos Principes sic gubernet, ut uestra gubernatio ad gloriam nominis sui celebrandam, ac subditorum salutem dirigatur: Amen. Bene & feliciter V. C. ualeant. Datæ Basileæ, 12. Calend. Decembr. anno 1562.
units.tr: To these people the teaching of the Church seems foolishness, and much more so do those who teach it, with this mad preaching, as they see it; these men are regarded and named fools by them. From this arise the fancies of the prudent of this age, who dream that the ministers of the Church must be supported only so that the people may be kept under discipline, lest, released from all religion, they disturb the commonwealth with savage crimes. In this way both teachers and students of theology are judged by the prudent of this age. Hence there are commonly heard insulting reproaches and abuse against the ministers of the Gospel and the students of theology: "Pfaff, pfaff." This impiety brings with it not only the harm that the ministry is despised, the ministry in which and through which God has gathered his Church from the beginning of the world to its end, but also that many young men are deterred from this office, although it is the highest office, without which all the others can neither exist nor stand. Wise governors have understood this in every age. David longs (Psalm 83) to dwell in the courts of the Lord rather than in the tents of the impious. Hezekiah too, about to die, asked (4 Kings 19, 20) and Isaiah (28) asked, that his life be prolonged for the preservation of pure doctrine. I have received something similar from the account of a trustworthy man concerning Prince George, Margrave of Brandenburg. That most pious prince, shortly before the agony of death, asked with groans from the depths of his heart that almighty God would wish to preserve the heavenly doctrine restored in our time for posterity, so that they too might become heirs of eternal life. How great a supporter of the divine Word this excellent prince was, that very phrase shows, since even in the agony of death he clearly declared his mind on the spreading of religion. Add to this another thing. When a preacher was comforting this most pious prince from the divine Word at the extremity of life, and another pious man was showing him the cross and triumph of Christ, he burst out with these words: "Lord Jesus Christ, I firmly believe that you suffered, died and rose again for my sins and for those of the whole human race, and that you now sit at the right hand of the eternal Father, so that you may raise up my body and make it conformed to your glorified body." With these words he commended his soul to our Savior, and a little later fell asleep in the Lord, piously and peacefully. Just as this most pious prince therefore despised this divine wisdom, not according to the judgments of the wise of this age, but throughout his whole life, and in the agony of death it was his greatest joy to hear and advance the doctrine of the Gospel, so his son, the most illustrious Prince George Frederick, Margrave of Brandenburg, diligently imitates these virtues of the excellent prince, in that he not only permits the Gospel, introduced into his subjects by his father, to be taught through the faithful teachers of the Church, but has not hesitated to add many other benefits to this one. For to the earlier stipends that his father, the most pious prince, had established for poor scholars, he has added new ones, and he takes care to have a school founded in a certain monastery, into which he intends to bring, at fixed times, certain sons of his subjects from each of his districts, and to provide them with good letters and necessary expenses. That the princes of that illustrious family were before our times diligent cultivators of the divine Word and of its ministers is not unknown to the whole Church of Christ. For before our age, every year, in order that greater goodwill and mutual union of minds might be entered into between the princes and the minister of the Church of that place, who at that time was the head of their government, they did not disdain on a certain day to approach the minister and dine with him, and this for the reason that they might confer familiarly with him about the state of the Church and the controversies of doctrine. Often too for the same reason they summoned ministers and other learned men to themselves, and conferred with them about the change and correction of ceremonies and doctrine. Wherefore that age seems to me not unlike that in which Christ and Jairus, or the centurion in the town of Capernaum, met together in friendship and familiarity. But by what great benefits the most pious princes who live today, Albert, Duke of Prussia, Wilhelm, Bishop of Riga, and others, Joachim, Elector, and others, Sigismund, Archbishop of Magdeburg, and others, and the other margraves of this Brandenburg stock, cherish the churches, no one is ignorant. For in summoning learned men to themselves they spare no money or expense; besides this, they diligently take care to provide with generous means for the ministers of the churches and for poor scholars, and they labor diligently at this, that they may hand down the pure doctrine of the Gospel to posterity. Therefore I justly give praise for this piety and goodwill toward the Church and their subjects to my most illustrious lords, the most clement Margraves; and without harm to piety I can affirm that they truly are among those who understand the wisdom of God through their own wisdom, and strive to pour it into their subjects, so that with them they may become heirs of eternal and heavenly goods and enjoy the constant fellowship of God. Therefore, most illustrious Princes, since on account of the virtues of your house already recounted, and on account of the gratitude by which my great-grandfathers, grandfathers, parents, brothers and I, on account of manifold benefits, are bound to Your Highnesses, I dedicate to Your Highnesses this following third part of my labor, as a sign of my grateful mind toward Your Highnesses, and I wish it to come forth in your name; and I pray that Your Highnesses hold me and all mine commended to you. May the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, together with his Son and his Holy Spirit, preserve the whole house of the Margraves of Brandenburg safe and sound for a long time, and so govern you also, most illustrious Princes, that your government may be directed to the celebration of his name's glory and the salvation of your subjects: Amen. May Your Highnesses fare well and happily. Given at Basel, 12 days before the Kalends of December, in the year 1562.

units.la: SIncera quæ uerba fide plebs audit IESV, Haud unquam nitida fruge carente fide, Continet, haud ullum doctorum munera uincens Munus: at hi debent non nisi certa loqui.
units.tr: The sincere words that the people hear in faith in Jesus, never lacking the bright fruit of faith, contain a gift surpassing every gift of the learned; but these men ought to speak only what is certain.

units.la: Ab pereant, miseros qui per mala dogmata fallūt: Dogmata, queis iactant certius esse nihil. Decipit incautos iustæ simulatio vitæ, Velleribusq; ovium membra lupina tegit.
units.tr: Let them perish, those who deceive the wretched with wicked doctrines, doctrines by which they boast that nothing is more certain. The pretence of a just life deceives the unwary, and it covers wolfish limbs with sheepskins.

units.la: O' qui regali populos ditione tenetis, Cordi sit uobis concio sacra Dei: Illam protegat atq; exornet uestra potestas: Nulla magis uirtus regia sceptra decet.
units.tr: O you who hold the peoples under royal rule, let the holy assembly of God be dear to your hearts. May your power protect and adorn it; no virtue becomes the royal sceptre more.

units.la: Sic Deus à uobis, quo debet honore, coletur: Diuitis est regum turba ministra Dei. Nam Deus instituit, Deus idem regna tuetur, Atq; idem mutat regna superba Deus.
units.tr: Thus God is to be worshipped by you with the honour he is owed: the crowd of kings is the servant of God. For God establishes kingdoms, God also guards them, and the same God overturns proud kingdoms.

units.la: O' hominum diuûmq; pater, rex maxime regum, Principibus dona pectora iusta uiris: Aequis immenso dominentur legibus orbi, Sit nihil his uera religione prius.
units.tr: O father of men and of gods, greatest of kings, grant princes and men upright hearts. May they rule the whole world with equal laws, and may nothing be placed before true religion.

units.la: DE ECCLESIA.
units.tr: On the Church.

units.la: VEnusta imago est Ecclesiæ halcyonum partus, quæ cum in scopulis maris nidificent, solent incubare ouis & excludere pullos in media bruma: cum quidē matre, tanquam inseruiens illis incubantibus, per illud tempus mitescit & placidum est. Conueniunt Ecclesiæ etiam mores halcyonū, quæ nesciunt adulteria, & extincta coniuge, alter manet cœlebs, ac paulo post consumptus luctu moritur. Mulier etiā senem maritū cherylum gestat humeris suis aquatum. Itaq; ueteres scripserūt honesti coniugij exempla esse. Etiam non male accommodatur ad Ecclesiam, quæ gestare, & fouere omnibus beneficijs & officijs benemeritos pastores, doctores et ministros Euangelij debet.
units.tr: The halcyon's brood is a fine image of the Church. Since they nest on the rocks by the sea, they sit on their eggs and hatch their young in the middle of winter, and the mother, as if serving those who brood, grows calm and still during that time. The Church also shares the habits of the halcyons, who know no adultery: when the mate dies, the other remains unmarried and, wasted with grief, dies soon after. A wife also carries her aged husband, the cheryl, on her shoulders across the water. So the ancients wrote that these are examples of honourable marriage. It also fits the Church well, which ought to carry and cherish with every kindness and service the faithful ministers, teachers and ministers of the Gospel who have deserved well.

units.la: Curruca græcis est hypolais, quia nomen inde habet, quòd humi ad saxa nidificet: talis est uerè Ecclesia, spreta et abiecta in mundo. Hæc dum omnes fouēre & iuuare conatur, etiam supposititios fœtus nutrit, qui cum propter hypocrisin ueniant in admirationem, facilè beneficio Ecclesiæ authoritatem & potentiam consequuntur. Hanc adepti, deinde grassantur in ipsam matrē, eamq; dilacerant, & crudeli tyrannide opprimunt. Cæterum illum feralem & infaustum sonum edunt in Ecclesia, sonant impia & perniciosa dogmata. Arrium eue xit ad honores ecclesia Alexandrina, qui cùm esset suppositititius fœtus, postea Ecclesiam orbis terrarũ horribiliter disipauit.
units.tr: The curruca is called hypolais [ὑπολαΐς] in Greek, because it gets its name from nesting on the ground among rocks. Such truly is the Church, despised and cast down in the world. While it tries to cherish and help everyone, it also nourishes spurious offspring, who, through hypocrisy, win admiration and easily obtain authority and power from the Church's favour. Having obtained it, they then turn against the mother herself, tear her apart, and oppress her with cruel tyranny. Moreover, they utter that baleful and ill-omened sound in the Church: they sound impious and pernicious doctrines. The church of Alexandria raised Arius to honours, and he, though a spurious offspring, afterwards terribly scattered the Church throughout the world.

units.la: Sol est typus Christi, luna est Ecclesiæ. Et sicut luna aliàs est maior alias minor: nonnunquā prorsus etiam occultata sub nubibus: ita Ecclesia aliàs etiam est maior, cùm Deus concesserit ei tranquillitatem & pacem, aliàs est minor, ut quando opprimitur à persequutoribus Euangelij: tum enim, quasi obscurata fit nubibus, id est, calamitatibus et afflictionibus oppressa & obruta, iacet. Præterea quamuis in ipso plenilunio maxima sit serenitas: tamen in ipsa luna etiā reperiuntur maculæ, id est: in ecclesia sunt multæ caligines & tenebræ, quæ omnia in nouissimo die extirpabuntur.
units.tr: The sun is a type of Christ, and the moon is the Church. Just as the moon is sometimes larger, sometimes smaller, and sometimes hidden altogether under clouds, so the Church is sometimes larger, when God grants it tranquillity and peace; at other times it is smaller, as when it is oppressed by the persecutors of the Gospel. Then, as if darkened by clouds, that is, overwhelmed and crushed by calamities and afflictions, it lies low. Moreover, although at the full moon there is the greatest brightness, spots are also found on the moon itself: that is, there are many dark shadows in the Church, and all of them will be rooted out on the last day.

units.la: Quærela Ecclesiæ conferentis se cum Lazaro.
units.tr: The Church's complaint, comparing itself with Lazarus.

units.la: Aeger & ulceribus squalens in corpore toto Hìc iacco, & pereunt tabida membra fame. Diuitis ante fores iacuit, ceu Lazarus olim, Cui fastidito nemo ferebat opem. Vt tamen à cunctis spretus, tua cura tuoq; Exceptus gremio Lazarus ille fuit:
units.tr: Sick, and foul with ulcers over my whole body, I lie here, and my wasted limbs perish with hunger. Like Lazarus of old, I lay before the rich man's gate, and since I was despised, no one brought me help. But though spurned by all, that Lazarus was received into your care and into your bosom.

units.la: De Ecclesia.
units.tr: On the Church.

units.la: Sic æterne Deus tua me clementia seruet, Et miserum dextræ protegat umbra tuæ.
units.tr: So, eternal God, may your mercy keep me, and may the shadow of your right hand protect me in my misery.

units.la: Arca Noe constitit in Armenia, ibi egressus est Noe ex arca. Hodie nulla pars est in oriente tota, quæ habet Ecclesias mediocriter ornatas, sicut Armenia. Armenij autem utuntur Græca lingua in sacris, ut nos Latina, alioquin suam habent linguam peculiarē. Cogitaui sæpè nomen Armeniæ esse nomen Germaniæ. Extant pagellæ de ipsorū ritibus, de Symbolo, de oratione Dominica. Ibi didici, quòd nomen pater est & apud eos nomen Herr, quod quidem est commune omnibus linguis: Hebræis est magister, quod est Græcis ὁ διδάσκαλος.
units.tr: The ark of Noah came to rest in Armenia, and there Noah came out of the ark. Today there is no region in the whole East that has churches moderately well furnished, as Armenia does. The Armenians use the Greek language in their sacred rites, as we use Latin; otherwise they have their own distinct language. I have often thought that the name Armenia is the same as the name Germany. Small pamphlets about their rites exist, on the Creed and on the Lord's Prayer. There I learned that the word "pater" is also in use among them, and the word "Herr," which indeed is common to all languages. For the Hebrews a teacher is "magister," which for the Greeks is ὁ διδάσκαλος [ho didaskalos].

units.la: Existimo nostros homines, ideo in has terras uersus Septentrionem uenisse, ut effugerent Tyrannidem Persarum, uel credo à Iudæis ductos esse nostros homines in has terras religionis causa. Quia tunc multi fuerunt Iudæi in his regionibus, & plures quàm alioqui in toto orbe terrarum.
units.tr: I suppose that our people came to these lands towards the north in order to escape the tyranny of the Persians; or I believe our people were led into these lands by the Jews for the sake of religion. For at that time there were many Jews in these regions, more than anywhere else in the whole world.

units.la: In Africa prorsus exiguæ sunt Ecclesiæ. Etsi ille rex Muleasses, qui fuit in obsidione oppidi Viteberge excæcatus à filijs, quos postea uicissim interfecit, non fuerit professione membrum Ecclesiæ, tamen in illis locis reperiuntur adhuc exigui cœtus Ecclesiæ. Ibidem etiam est tantum superstitionum & confusionum, ut patres concumbant cum filiabus: item circumcidant masculos & femellas, & retineant quoq; baptismum cum circuncisione: retinent etiā diem Sabbathi, & diem Dominicum.
units.tr: In Africa the churches are very few. Although that king Muleasses, who was blinded by his sons during the siege of the town of Viteberge, and whom they afterwards in turn killed, was not a member of the Church by profession, nevertheless small congregations of the Church are still found in those places. There is even so much superstition and confusion there that fathers lie with their daughters; they circumcise both males and females, and they retain baptism together with circumcision. They also keep the Sabbath day and the Lord's day.

units.la: Iohannis decimoquarto inquit filius Dei: Ἐαν τις ἀγαπᾷ με, τὸν λόγον μου τηρήσει, καὶ ὁ πατήρ μου ἀγαπήσει αὐτὸν, καὶ πρὸς αὐτὸν ἐλευσόμεθα, καὶ μονὴν παρ᾽ αὐτῷ ποιήσομεν. Hanc necessariā & dulcissimam consolationem teneamus infixam animis, & sæpè cogitemus. Primùm docet hæc sententia, quæ & ubi sit vera Ecclesia. Affirmat enim esse cœtum visibilem, qui docet, audit, discit, fide amplectitur, amat & propagare studet incorruptam Euangelij doctrinam. In hanc veram Ecclesiam te quoq; includas, ac certò statuas, te veræ ecclesiæ Dei membrū esse, cum audis, discis, fide amplecteris incorruptam Euangelij vocem: nec movearis titulis aut successione ordinaria, ut vocant Episcoporum, qui sunt hostes veræ doctrinæ. Certa enim, & immota veritas docet, non esse membra Ecclesiæ eos, qui scienter oppugnant veritatem, & stabiliunt idola & vitiosos cultus. Nec verba illa τηρεῖν λόγον, intelligenda sunt νομικῶς, sed significant custodes esse doctrinæ, habentes fidem & bonam conscientiam: sicut inquit filius Dei, Apostolos seruasse sermonem, quorū tūc quidē magna infirmitas fuit. & sic loquitur totus Psalmus: Beati immaculati, qui in lege Domini ambulant. Postquam autem didicimus, quæ & ubi sit vera Ecclesia, proponamus nobis etiam dulcissimā promissionem, & cōsolationem, quæ hic recitatur: habitat Deus in hoc suo cœtu, te diligit, regit, protegit, exaudit: & vult opem ferre invocanti, etiam in hac vita, & post hanc vitam vult te socium esse consuetudinis suæ, & filij sui, in æterna vita, sapientia, iustitia & lætitia.
units.tr: In John 14 the Son of God says: "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him" [Ἐαν τις ἀγαπᾷ με, τὸν λόγον μου τηρήσει, καὶ ὁ πατήρ μου ἀγαπήσει αὐτὸν, καὶ πρὸς αὐτὸν ἐλευσόμεθα, καὶ μονὴν παρ᾽ αὐτῷ ποιήσομεν]. Let us hold this necessary and most sweet consolation fixed in our minds, and think on it often. First, this saying teaches what the true Church is and where it is. For it affirms that it is a visible assembly which teaches, hears, learns, embraces the uncorrupted doctrine of the Gospel in faith, loves it, and strives to propagate it. Include yourself also in this true Church, and be certain that you are a member of the true Church of God when you hear, learn, and embrace in faith the uncorrupted voice of the Gospel. Do not be moved by titles or by the ordinary succession of so-called bishops, who are enemies of true doctrine. For the certain and unshaken truth teaches that those who knowingly attack the truth, and set up idols and corrupt worship, are not members of the Church. Nor are the words "to keep the word" [τηρεῖν λόγον] to be understood legalistically; rather they signify being guardians of the doctrine, holding faith and a good conscience. Thus the Son of God says that the apostles kept his word, although their weakness was then indeed great; and so the whole Psalm speaks: "Blessed are the undefiled who walk in the law of the Lord." Now that we have learned what the true Church is and where it is, let us also set before ourselves the most sweet promise and consolation recited here: God dwells in this his assembly, loves you, rules you, protects you, and hears you; he wills to bring help to one who calls upon him, even in this life, and after this life he wills you to be a companion of his fellowship and of his Son, in eternal life, wisdom, righteousness and joy.

units.la: DE DOCTORIBUS, MINISTRIS Ecclesię, eorumq; auditoribus.
units.tr: On the teachers and ministers of the Church, and their hearers.

units.la: Pulchrum dictum est Sophoclis: λόγοι ἀντιπαλαίσοι λόγυς: Rationes reuerberant uel euertunt rationes. Elegās est trāslatio sumpta à gladiatoribus, sicut Germani dicunt: Ein streich vmb den andern. Sic quoq; sunt rationes contra rationes. Dux Fridericus solitus est dicere ante annos quadraginta octo, & præsertim in principio huius doctrinæ: Ego non libenter audio, quando pastores volunt rationibus probare articulos fidei: (sicut habuit pastorem, qui voluit semper adferre & fingere rationes, credo magis ostentatione ingenij sui, quàm cōsilio tuendæ veritatis, qui postea factus est diaconus in quodam alio loco) mihi magis placet proferre testimonia vocis Divinæ: quia rationes possunt rationibus euerti.
units.tr: Sophocles has a fine saying: "Arguments wrestle with arguments" [λόγοι ἀντιπαλαίουσι λόγοις]. Reasons strike or overturn reasons. The metaphor is an elegant one, taken from gladiators, as the Germans say: "One blow after another." So too there are arguments against arguments. Duke Frederick used to say, some forty-eight years ago, and especially at the start of this teaching: "I do not willingly listen when ministers want to prove the articles of faith by reasons. (I once had a minister who always wanted to bring forward and invent reasons, I believe more to display his own cleverness than to defend the truth; he later became a deacon in another place.) I prefer to set forth the testimonies of the divine voice, because reasons can be overturned by reasons."

units.la: Aristoteles dicit de Antisthene, esse quosdam ta les, ut non aliter sit ipsis concionari, quàm si lepo res concionentur leonibus. Plerunq; enim deuo rant eos leones. Est imago piorum & sanctorũ doctorum, Ecclesiæ ueritatem & peccata indican tium leonibus: id est, tyrannis, & persequutoribus piorum hominum, à quibus lacerantur ut lepuscu li à leonibus.
units.tr: Aristotle says of Antisthenes that there are some men for whom preaching is no different from preaching to lions with hares as the audience. For the lions usually tear such preachers apart. This is a picture of the godly and holy teachers who point out the truth of the Church and the sins of men to lions, that is, to tyrants and persecutors of the godly, by whom they are torn to pieces like hares by lions.

units.la: Audiui diaconum Tubingæ concionantem, qui in una concione circiter quadraginta loca ex iure citabat. Volebat ostentare suam eruditionem, cùm neq; ius, neq; Theologiam, intelligeret. Sequeba tur alter diaconus, bonus uir, qui postea factus est Euangelicus concionator, hic ita præfabatur: Bo ni amici, scitis me non esse doctum, ideo non opus est me ostentare: dicam tamen breuem concionem ex qua aliquid discere positis. Textus siue Euan gelium illud, quod recitaui, habet duo capita doc trinalia, uel duos articulos: primus continet hoc, alter illud. Illa tractauit per dimidiam horam, & descendit. Illa concio fuit multo utilior populo, quàm alterius.
units.tr: I once heard a deacon preaching at Tübingen who, in a single sermon, cited about forty passages from the law. He wanted to show off his learning, though he understood neither law nor theology. Another deacon followed, a good man who later became an evangelical preacher. He began by saying: "Good friends, you know that I am not learned, so there is no need for me to show off. I will nevertheless give a short sermon from which you may learn something. The text, the gospel I have just read, contains two doctrinal heads, or two articles: the first contains this, the second that." He treated them for half an hour and then came down. That sermon was far more useful to the people than the other one.

units.la: Est uetus dictũ: Beatus ille pastor, qui nõ habet Nimroth, Abrahã aut Naaman. Der pfarher hatt gütt sach, der nicht hatt ein Nimroth, id est, tyran num: Abraham, id est, Iudæos, qui sunt artifices ad fraudes struēdas et insidias: Naamā, id est leprosos.
units.tr: There is an old saying: "Blessed is that minister who has no Nimrod, Abraham or Naaman." In German: "The parson is well off who has no Nimrod." Nimrod means a tyrant; Abraham means the Jews, who are skilled at contriving frauds and snares; Naaman means lepers.

units.la: Versus in Campana Halensi:
units.tr: Verses on the bell of Halle:

units.la: En ego campana nunquam denuncio uana: Laudo Deum uere, plebem uoco, congrego clerū. Id est: Bonus pastor debet authoritate & doctrina regere auditores. Deinde debet tueri concordiam & mutuam amicitiam inter docentes.
units.tr: Lo, I am the bell that never proclaims empty things; I truly praise God, I call the people, I gather the clergy. That is: a good minister ought to rule his hearers by authority and teaching. Then he ought to maintain harmony and mutual friendship among those who teach.

units.la: Quidam episcopus Ratisbonensis Contareno cardinali dixit: necessario concedendum esse coniugiū presbyteris, quòd alioqui defuturi essent Ecclesijs pastores, et iam multas stare desertas sine ministris. Tum Contarenus miratus, posse se mederi, inquit, huic malo, quia Italia monachis abundaret, quos sit missurus Pontifex ad uacuas Ecclesias. At ille: Quid agent cum linguam nostram nesciant? Contarenus respondet, sacrificaturos esse de more Papistico. Episcopus uerecundè dicit, necessarium munus esse, docere populum, & Euangelij cognitione pietatem esse alendam, ac non sufficere spectacula ceremoniarum.
units.tr: A certain bishop of Regensburg said to Cardinal Contarini that marriage must necessarily be granted to priests, since otherwise the churches would lack ministers, and many were already standing deserted without ministers. Contarini was amazed and said that he could remedy this evil, because Italy had an abundance of monks, whom the Pontiff would send to the empty churches. But the bishop replied: "What will they do, since they do not know our language?" Contarini answered that they would offer sacrifice in the Papist manner. The bishop modestly replied that the duty of teaching the people is necessary, that piety must be nourished by knowledge of the gospel, and that spectacles of ceremonies are not enough.

units.la: Quemadmodum inter politicas personas sunt duo genera, eruditi & practicantes: sic etiam in Theologia, alij sunt facundi & loquaces, nec referunt ad metas suas conciones, sunt tantum declamatores: alij uerò cum consilio concionantur, & eruditè omnia ad certum scopum ac ædificationem referunt.
units.tr: Just as among political figures there are two kinds, the learned and the practical, so too in theology some are eloquent and talkative, and do not direct their sermons to their proper goal; they are mere declaimers. Others, however, preach with judgement, and learnedly refer everything to a fixed aim and to edification.

units.la: Est narratio quædam in historijs Patrū: Quidā pater inter eremitas, uidit sæpè apud sodales suos uagantes pulchros angelos, & lætatus est isto spe-ctaculo. Alio uerò tempore uidit apud eosdem porcos uagantes. Hos cùm uidisset, sæpe accesit propius, & animaduertit, quando loquebantur de rebus bonis, affuisse angelos: quando autem contra alios criminationes aut alias turpitudines proferebant, ibi eis diabolos affuisse.
units.tr: There is a story in the histories of the Fathers. A certain father among the hermits often saw beautiful angels wandering among his companions, and he rejoiced at this sight. At another time, however, he saw pigs wandering among the same men. When he had seen these, he drew nearer and noticed that when they spoke of good things, angels were present; but when they uttered accusations against others or other shameful things, devils were present to them.

units.la: Irenæus citat Polycarpum, qui fuit auditor Iohannis, & Florentino Valentino opponit eius authoritatem. Basilius audiuit Gregorium Neocæsariensem, cuius præcipua fuit authoritas, cùm Pauli Samosateni impietas damnaretur. Nec aliud uetustius testimonium extat post Apostolorum scripta de Trinitate quàm huius Gregorij, cui tantum tribuit Basilius, ut dicat sibi adhuc personare aures uocem Gregorij, eiusq; testimonium opponit Sabellicis perturbantibus ecclesias Neocæsariensium. Hieronymus audiuit Nazianzenum et Epiphanium.
units.tr: Irenaeus cites Polycarp, who was a hearer of John, and sets his authority against Florinus and Valentinus. Basil heard Gregory of Neocaesarea, whose authority was pre-eminent when the impiety of Paul of Samosata was condemned. And no older testimony on the Trinity exists after the writings of the Apostles than that of this Gregory, to whom Basil ascribed so much that he says the voice of Gregory still sounds in his ears, and he sets this testimony against the Sabellians who were disturbing the churches of the Neocaesareans. Jerome heard Gregory Nazianzen and Epiphanius.

units.la: Gener Sebastiani Brand, cuius extant multa scripta bona, habebat consuetudinem, ut suas precationes mane recitaret, sicut multi faciunt. Quando erat in conuentu Schmacaldico, ueni mane ad ipsius hospicium, dicens: Domine Beate (Nam ita erat nomen eius, & ucrè erat beatus) quid tam mane? Respondit: Lego Psalmos. An non, dicebam, es in Concilio? Quid ibi faciam, inquit? Quærebam porrò: Quid est causæ quòd Domini tam mane coueniant? Respondit, dicā tibi: Magno labore quæ-runt cognoscere, quomodo possint esse Christiani, sed nihil tale faciunt.
units.tr: The son-in-law of Sebastian Brand, whose many good writings survive, had the habit of reciting his prayers in the morning, as many do. When I was at the Schmalkaldic assembly, I came early in the morning to his lodging, saying: "Lord Blessed" (for that was his name, and he truly was blessed), "why so early?" He replied: "I am reading the Psalms." "Are you not at the council?" I said. "What should I do there?" he said. I then asked further: "What is the reason that the lords assemble so early in the morning?" He answered: "I will tell you. They labour hard to learn how they might be Christians, but they do nothing of the sort."

units.la: Edidit quidam librum de cura Pastorali: primā uerò quæstionem sic inchoat: Quid est cura pastoralis? Est ars artium, scientia scientiarum. Si modo addidisset, est miseria miseriarum, id est: talis status uitæ, in quo requiritur plurimum eruditionis, sapientiæ & studij, et qui est cumulatus ingentibus miserijs & ærumnis, tunc integram responsionem posuisset.
units.tr: Someone published a book on pastoral care, and he begins the first question thus: "What is pastoral care? It is the art of arts, the science of sciences." If he had only added, "It is the misery of miseries," that is, a condition of life in which very great learning, wisdom and study are required, and which is heaped with immense miseries and hardships, then he would have given a complete answer.

units.la: Officia episcopalia.
units.tr: The duties of a bishop.

units.la: Primum Episcopi officium, est gubernatio studij. Episcopus enim debet esse tanquam inspector studij & doctrinæ, sicut Iohannes fuit summus lector Ephesi.
units.tr: The first duty of a bishop is the oversight of study. For a bishop ought to be, as it were, an inspector of learning and teaching, just as John was the chief reader at Ephesus.

units.la: Secundum, ordinatio, et examen ministrorum.
units.tr: The second is the ordination and examination of ministers.

units.la: Tertium, gubernatio iudiciorum: in Ecclesia enim debent esse iudicia. Igitur sunt ordinata Consistoria, in quibus matrimoniales causæ, & aliæ controuersiæ dijudicantur.
units.tr: The third is the oversight of judicial proceedings, for there must be courts in the Church. Hence consistories have been established, in which matrimonial cases and other disputes are decided.

units.la: Plautus inquit: Ego non seruio libenter, herus meus me non habet libenter: tamē utitur me ut lippis oculis. Eodem ferè modo res procedit in ministerio cum pastoribus per totam Germaniam.
units.tr: Plautus says: "I do not serve willingly, and my master does not keep me willingly, yet he uses me as one uses weak eyes." Much the same thing happens in the ministry with the pastors throughout all Germany.

units.la: Quæstio, Quis sit effectus cōcionis pij ministri? Respondeo. Deus est efficax per uocem ministri, sicut uult efficax esse & non aliter colligere Ecclesiam æternam, nisi uerbo & sacramentis, uerbo fides in corde confirmatur: per uerbum & sacramenta sine ulla dubitatione Deus est efficax. Swan schon alle teüffel darwider schrien.
units.tr: Question: What is the effect of a godly minister's sermon? I answer: God is effective through the voice of the minister, as he wills to be effective, and he does not otherwise gather his eternal Church except by the Word and the sacraments; by the Word faith is confirmed in the heart; through the Word and the sacraments God is unquestionably effective. "Let all the devils cry out against it!"

units.la: Epiphanius.
units.tr: Epiphanius.

units.la: Τὰ θεῖα ῥήματα ὃ πάντα ἀλληγορίας λέγεται, ἀλλὰ ὡς ἐχεῖ θεωρίας ἢ λέγεται, καὶ αἰσθήσεως εἰς τὸ εἰλικρινὲς ἐνάρξης ὑποθέσεως δύναμιν. [?]
units.tr: Τὰ θεῖα ῥήματα ὃ πάντα ἀλληγορίας λέγεται, ἀλλὰ ὡς ἐχεῖ θεωρίας ἢ λέγεται, καὶ αἰσθήσεως εἰς τὸ εἰλικρινὲς ἐνάρξης ὑποθέσεως δύναμιν. [?]

units.la: Deus immensa bonitate se patefecit, & uult in Ecclesia doctrinam suam, quæ in Propheticis & Apostolicis libris scripta est, sermone recte loquen tibus usitato sonare, in linguis Prophetarum et Apo stolorum, qui certè uoluerunt intelligi. Retinenda est igitur natiua significatio sermonis, iuxta phra sin illarum linguarum, nec lex moralis & promis sio gratiæ & articuli fidei, in scriptis Propheticis & Apostolicis sunt transformanda in allegorias. Cur autem dicit Epiphanius opus esse speculatio ne & sensu? Speculationem nominat Dialecticum ordinem membrorum doctrinæ, uidelicet, defini tiones, distinctiones, consequentias recte coagmen tatas quia necesse est considerari, quæ membra ubi in scriptis Prophetis & Apostolicis tradita sunt, & hoc ordine ad docendum accommodato recitan da sunt. Hæc non gignunt peregrinas, sed natiuas sententias recte ordinant. Hæ uiæ non mutant scri-pta, sed illustrant lectionem.
units.tr: God revealed himself in immeasurable goodness, and he wills that his doctrine, which is written in the prophetic and apostolic books, should be sounded in the Church in ordinary and correctly spoken language, in the languages of the prophets and apostles, who surely wished to be understood. The natural meaning of the words is therefore to be retained, according to the idiom of those languages; neither the moral law, nor the promise of grace, nor the articles of faith in the prophetic and apostolic writings are to be turned into allegories. Why, then, does Epiphanius say that there is need of speculation and of sense? By "speculation" he means the dialectical order of the parts of doctrine, namely definitions, distinctions and correctly joined consequences, which must be considered: where these parts are set out in the prophetic and apostolic writings, they must be recited in an order suited to teaching. These methods do not produce foreign opinions but arrange the native meanings correctly. These paths do not change the writings but illuminate the reading.

units.la: Ait itē sensu opus esse, quia ad intelligēda uoca-bula opus est experiētia. Nō intelligūtur uerbo, uita, mors, pœnitētia, timor, fides, cōsolatio, spes, læ-ticia, sine experiētia, id est, sine exercitijs in corde. Quare Epiphanius aptè hæc tria cōiunxit, lectio-nē librorū Propheticorū & Apostolicorū, sensum quo uocabula intelligūtur, & speculationem, quæ forma doctrinæ iuxta Dialecticā ritè cōprehensa.
units.tr: He also says that sense is needed, because experience is needed to understand words. Words such as life, death, repentance, fear, faith, consolation, hope and joy are not understood without experience, that is, without the exercises of the heart. Therefore Epiphanius aptly joined these three things: the reading of the prophetic and apostolic books, the sense by which the words are understood, and speculation, which properly grasps the form of doctrine according to dialectic.

units.la: In Cypro fuit monachus homo eruditus, mihi bene notus, qui scripsit ad me cùm essemus in con-uentu Augustano. Ille multos libros huius linguæ uertit in illam linguam, quia sunt adhuc aliquæ Ec-clesiæ in illis locis.
units.tr: In Cyprus there was a learned monk, well known to me, who wrote to me when we were in the Augsburg assembly. He translated many books of this language into that language, because there are still some congregations in those places.

units.la: Quidam facetus homo dixit, se malle esse epi-scopum Græcum, quàm Lutheranum. Interroga-tus causam, respōdit: quia græca dictio ἐπίσκοπος esset dignior, & maioris authoritatis: Lutherani uero Episcopi essent tantùm superintendentes.
units.tr: A witty man said that he would rather be a Greek bishop than a Lutheran one. When asked the reason, he replied: because the Greek word ἐπίσκοπος is more worthy and of greater authority, whereas Lutheran bishops are merely superintendents.

units.la: In primitiua Ecclesia erant sep-tem ordines.
units.tr: In the primitive Church there were seven orders.

units.la: Primi erant ianitores: Secundi cantores: Tertij ἀκόλουθοι, id est, sectatores, seu pedissequi Episco-porum, per quos uocabant alios: Quarti, diaco-ni, qui præerant ærario, ut Stephanus in Actis, quod uocabulum adhuc retinetur in Ecclesia, sed res mutata est. Quinti, doctores, qui erudiebát populum. Sexti, pastores. Septimi, episcopi.
units.tr: The first were the doorkeepers; the second the singers; the third the acolytes [ἀκόλουθοι], that is, the followers or attendants of the bishops, through whom they summoned others; the fourth the deacons, who had charge of the treasury, as Stephen does in the Acts; this name is still retained in the Church, but the thing has changed. The fifth were the teachers, who instructed the people; the sixth the pastors; the seventh the bishops.

units.la: Cùm aliquando essem in templo, & audirem concionem, stabat apud me aulicus, & interrogabat me: Quomodo placet tibi ille concionator? Benedicebam, placet & est verum: erat bonus concionator. O' inquit: Ille est rusticorum, seu rusticis conueniens, concionator. Dicebam: Melior est concionator simplex, vera prædicans, quàm doctus, qui arte se inflectit ad cupiditates eorum hominũ, quibus concionatur.
units.tr: Once, when I was in church and listening to a sermon, a courtier stood beside me and asked me: "How do you like that preacher?" I said that I approved, and that it was true: he was a good preacher. "Oh," he said, "he is a preacher for peasants, or suited to peasants." I said: "A plain preacher who proclaims true things is better than a learned one who bends his art to the desires of the people he preaches to."

units.la: Dicebam aliquando ad pauperem aliquem hominem, et idoneum ad ministerium, ut præpararet se ad ministerium Euangelij. Respondit ille: Ego sum uir politicus. Putabat esse rem indignam, si fieret diaconus.
units.tr: Once I said to a poor man, who was fit for the ministry, that he should prepare himself for the ministry of the Gospel. He replied: "I am a man of civil standing." He thought it an unworthy thing if he became a deacon.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Apud templum Hierosolymitanum fuerunt mulieres, quæ seruiebant coquendo, lauando, sarciendis uestibus, & educandis instituendisq; liberis ministerio: item eædem subueniebát pauperibus. Hūc morem Apostoli imitati transtulerunt ad Ecclesiã, et iusserũt eligi grandiores natu matronas uiduas, quæ ægrotis aut peregrinis seruirent. Et hæ mercedem habebant ex eleemosynis, quas Ecclesia liberaliter conferebat.
units.tr: At the Temple in Jerusalem there were women who served by cooking, washing, mending garments, and by helping to bring up and instruct the children; likewise these same women assisted the poor. The apostles imitated this custom and transferred it to the Church, and they ordered that elderly widows be chosen, who would serve the sick or strangers. These received their wages from the alms which the Church gave generously.

units.la: Insulsus concionator de S. Petro.
units.tr: A foolish preacher on St Peter.

units.la: Quidam in Salinis, astante eo tempore Episcopo, concionabatur: Vver S. Peter nie ghen hoff komen, so wer er fromb blicben. Sunt propositiones indefinitæ: de multis loquuntur, non de omnibus.
units.tr: Someone preaching in Salzwedel (or at the Salt-works), while the bishop was present at the time, said: "Had St Peter never come to the court, he would have remained pious." These are indefinite propositions: they speak of many, not of all.

units.la: COLL. Alius cuiusdam Monachi iocus.
units.tr: A story of a certain monk's joke.

units.la: Solebat narrare Doctor Martinus de quodam monacho concionaturo in co loco, ubi prandebāt monachi, quòd, cùm inchoaret concionem, præmit tens thema, Ego sum pastor bonus, non potuerit pergere: sed repetiuit iterū, et magis turbatus est, repetiuit & tertiò: tandemq; cum stupore quodam subiecit: Domine doctor setzet eüch nieder, ir seid nicht pastor bonus, ir seid em güts schaff.
units.tr: Doctor Martin used to tell of a monk who was to preach in the place where the monks were dining: when he began the sermon and announced his text, "I am the good shepherd," he could not go on. He started again and was even more confused, tried a third time, and at last, with a kind of astonishment, said: "Doctor, sit down; you are not the good shepherd, you are a good sheep."

units.la: Quidā scripsit defensionem Ciceronis, & uult eum laudare, quòd fuerit uir sanctus & Christianus, eo quòd dicat alicubi Cicero: Reprehendo peccata mea, & magis excrutior dolore peccatorum meorum, quàm euentu. Vult autem Cicero ibi dicere: ideo reprehendo mea peccata, quòd Pompeio confisus, eiusq; partes secutus fuerim. Loquitur de euentis consiliorum suorum, non de peccatis in Deum. Ista ineptiæ sequuntur, non intelle cta phrasi.
units.tr: Someone wrote a defence of Cicero and wants to praise him as a holy and Christian man, because Cicero says somewhere: "I reproach my sins, and I am tormented more by the outcome of my sins than by..." But Cicero there means only this: he reproaches himself for his mistakes because he trusted Pompey and followed his party. He speaks of the outcomes of his plans, not of sins against God. These absurdities follow when a phrase is not understood.

units.la: Quidam dixit de quodam phanatico conciona tore: Per Deum uiuum, est totus Christianus: bibit uobiscum. nobiscum usq; ad secundam noctis horam, & deinde ascendit suggestum, ac egregiè concionatur.
units.tr: Someone said of a certain fanatical preacher: "By the living God, he is a thoroughly good Christian: he drinks with us, with us until the second hour of the night, and then he goes up into the pulpit and preaches splendidly."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: A story.

units.la: Doctor Martinus Lutherus dixit, iuuenes concionatores idem facere, quod illi, qui primùm discunt ludere pyramidibus. Quemadmodũ enim hi confidunt se primo ictu omnes pyramides simul tacturos ac cōstraturos: sic etiam tales nouicij Theologi putāt se primo conatu omnia in ordinem conuenientē redigere, et cuncta uitia extirpare posse.
units.tr: Doctor Martin Luther said that young preachers do the same thing as those who first learn to play with skittles. For just as these trust that with their first throw they will hit and knock down all the pins together, so such novice theologians think that with their first attempt they can bring everything into proper order and root out all vices.

units.la: Vicarius quidam Augustanus, clarus & nobilis uir, qui ualde dilexit Lutherum, Tubingæ doctor Theologiæ factus, & quidem inter primos numeratus, dicebat: se explicasse Tubingæ librum Iob, & cum peruenisset ad decimum & undecimum caput, ibi uisum fuisse Iob magis ipsius enarrationibus cruciari, quàm à suis ulceribus. Tandem finē lectioni imponens dixit, & se & Iob lætari, quòd ab illa lectione desisteret. Significauit se horum nihil intellexisse: quia corpus, seu potius fundamentum doctrinæ Christianæ ignorasset.
units.tr: A certain vicar of Augsburg, a distinguished and noble man who greatly loved Luther, who was made a doctor of theology at Tübingen and counted among the first there, used to say that he had expounded the book of Job at Tübingen, and when he reached the tenth and eleventh chapters, Job seemed to him to be tormented more by his expositions than by his sores. At last, ending the lecture, he said that both he and Job rejoiced that he had stopped reading. By this he indicated that he had understood none of these things, because he was ignorant of the body, or rather the foundation, of Christian doctrine.

units.la: In oppido Stuckardiæ doctor quidā Theologiæ dicebat proconcione, Ecclesiā posse regi ac doceri de Deo, etiā amissis Biblijs, ex Philosophia & ex Ethicis Aristotelis. Non potuit discernere promissiones legis & Euangelij. Ethica Aristotelis sunt pars legis moralis, quòd tamē nō dico in illius uiri contumeliam cōtumelia, cùm fuerit homo doctus & iā mortuus sit, & ante mortē ad veram religionē se cōuerterit.
