units.tr: In the town of Stuttgart a certain doctor of theology said in a sermon that the Church could be ruled and taught about God even if the Bibles were lost, from philosophy and from Aristotle's Ethics. He could not distinguish the promises of the law from those of the gospel. Aristotle's Ethics is part of the moral law. I do not say this to insult that man, since he was learned and is now dead, and before his death he turned to the true religion.

units.la: Eram aliquando die natali in cuiusdam concio ne, ubi dicendū erat de illo mirando & inenarrabi li cōsilio diuinitatis, & quomodo filius Dei assum psit humanam naturam. Item quare illud mirandū fœdus duarum naturarum in Christo unitarum fa- ctum sit, et de illo immenso filij Dei erga genus hu manum amore, & c. ubi (inquam) de illis maximis rebus dicendum erat, ibi concionator sumebat par ticulam ex narratione Euangelij, Exijt decretum à Cæsare Augusto, & c. Et totam horā in maximo frigore consumebat hac unica particula, Obedien dum esse potestatibus, illi dandam esse pecuniam quantam uellet. Erant ⟨Greek⟩, quibus gratifica batur, & assentiebatur quorundam auribus.
units.tr: Once, on my birthday, I was in a sermon where it had to be spoken of that wonderful and unspeakable counsel of the Godhead, and how the Son of God assumed human nature; likewise why that wonderful covenant of the two natures united in Christ was made, and of that immense love of the Son of God toward the human race, and so on. Where (I say) these greatest things had to be discussed, the preacher took up a small passage from the narrative of the gospel, "A decree went out from Caesar Augustus," and so on. And for a whole hour, in the greatest cold, he spent his time on this one small passage: that we must obey the authorities and give them as much money as they wish. There were those whom he pleased, and who gave assent with some ears.

units.la: Turci etiam norunt certamina, quæ nunc sunt in Ecclesia, sicut nos audiuimus à peregrino, qui di cebat, in Armenia esse sermones de doctrinæ emen datione seu repurgatione, qualis est in nostra Ec- clesia. Item ubiq; & passim sunt, qui recta docent. Sunt doctores in Asia, & in Cypro, quorum lite- ras legi. Sunt doctores Constantinopoli, qui rectè docent. Deus mirabiliter docet, & excitat uocem Euangelij, ut exaudiatur à toto genere humano, sicut dicit: Exiuit sonus eorum in omnem terram.
units.tr: The Turks also know of the disputes that now exist in the Church, as we heard from a traveller who said that in Armenia there are sermons about the correction or purging of doctrine, such as there is in our Church. Likewise, everywhere and in many places there are those who teach what is right. There are teachers in Asia and in Cyprus whose writings I have read. There are teachers at Constantinople who teach correctly. God teaches wonderfully and raises up the voice of the gospel so that it may be heard by the whole human race, as it says: "Their sound has gone out into all the earth."

units.la: Quidā nobilis in Silesia cōduxit tres milites ad interficiendum pastorem, sed unus ex militibus te-xit miserum pastorem, ne interficeretur, licet ali-quas plagas acceperit. Postea conuocatis ciuibus ca-pti sunt milites, & narrarunt se conductos esse à nobili ad interficiendum illum pastorem. Est autê imago totius Ecclesiæ, quæ habet hostes, Turcam, Papam, & alios quosdam pessimos homines. Inte-rim tamen Deus dat aliquos, qui defendunt Eccle-siam, sicut hic tertius miles seu minister defendit hunc pastorem.
units.tr: A certain nobleman in Silesia hired three soldiers to kill a minister, but one of the soldiers covered the wretched minister so that he would not be killed, although he received some blows. Afterwards the citizens were called together, the soldiers were seized, and they told how they had been hired by the nobleman to kill that minister. This is indeed an image of the whole Church, which has enemies: the Turk, the Pope, and certain other most wicked men. Meanwhile, however, God gives some who defend the Church, just as this third soldier, or minister, defends this minister.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: A story.

units.la: Nullus erit consensus piorum & impiorum. Quando facis chordam ex neruis lupinis, tunc illa chorda non sonabit uel concordabit cum chordis ouium. Ita nunquã concordabit uera Ecclesia cum hypocritis. Nostræ chordæ semper dissonabunt à fidibus hypocritarum & impiorum.
units.tr: There will be no agreement between the godly and the ungodly. When you make a string from wolf's sinews, that string will not sound or harmonise with the strings of sheep. So the true Church will never agree with hypocrites. Our strings will always be discordant with the lyres of hypocrites and the ungodly.

units.la: DE HYPOCRITIS & sectis.
units.tr: On hypocrites and sects.

units.la: Claus Storck fuit primus author anabaptismi, Cygneæ natus, fulloniam artem exercens, & mihi familiariter notus, uagatus est per magnam Ger-maniæ partem: ille mihi aliquoties retulit, angelũ Gabrielem secum locutum esse, ac promisisse eum sore reformatorem Ecclesiæ, sibiq; esse promissum regnum Ecclesiæ. Nihil fecit palam, sed clam tan-tum uagatus est, homines fraudauit multis modis. Is fuit magister Monetarij, qui seditionem in Thuringia excitauit. Tandem fuit mortuus in hospitali Monasterienſi. ſic fuit eius regni finis.
units.tr: Claus Storck, a fuller by trade, born at Zwickau, and known to me personally, was the first author of Anabaptism. He wandered through a large part of Germany. He often told me that the angel Gabriel had spoken with him, promising that he would be the reformer of the Church and that the kingdom of the Church had been promised to him. He did nothing openly but wandered about in secret, and defrauded people in many ways. He was the teacher of Müntzer, who stirred up sedition in Thuringia. In the end he died in the hospital at Münster. Such was the end of his kingdom.

units.la: Vipera alitur palmis, & interficitur palmis, ut est apud Pausaniam. Palma est generosa arbor, quæ multa significat. Pulchra imago est hæreticorum, qui citant & sumunt ex sacra Scriptura ſententias, quas mutant in uenena, et uincũtur, et occidũtur, seu strãgulãtur postea eadẽ Scriptura.
units.tr: A viper is nourished by palms and killed by palms, as Pausanias reports. The palm is a noble tree that signifies many things. It is a fine image of heretics, who cite and take sayings from Holy Scripture, turn them into poisons, and are overcome and killed, or afterwards strangled, by the same Scripture.

units.la: Impossibile est illam sectam esse Ecclesiam Dei, quæ palàm profitetur se nõ habere Biblia, & damnat libros Propheticos & Apostolicos.
units.tr: It is impossible that a sect is the Church of God if it openly professes that it does not have the Bible and condemns the prophetic and apostolic books.

units.la: Machometistæ non habent libros Propheticos, & Apostolicos, nisi quòd aliquid excerpserunt ex Genesi.
units.tr: The Mohammedans do not have the prophetic and apostolic books, except that they have taken some extracts from Genesis.

units.la: Ergo. Impossibile est eos esse ecclesiam Dei.
units.tr: Therefore it is impossible that they are the Church of God.

units.la: Ipsi dicunt fuisse tres excellentes prophetas, Moysem, Christum & Machometum: & suum Machometum anteferunt cæteris. Quia dicunt Moysen primum populum rexisse, & constituisse pariter politiam, Christum nihil rexisse: Machometum uerò constituisse amplissimum regnum in toto orbe terrarum. Illa magna mutatio totius generis humani, est à secta Machometica orta. Cœpit autem Machometus sub Heraclio hac occasione: Milites illi Agareni & Saraceni, cùm non haberent à Capitaneis Heraclij stipendia, facti sunt prædones: postea illi Arabes milites coniunxerunt se Machometo, et occuparunt Persiam. Inde processerunt in Damascum & Syriam. Et hodie Machometica secta florentissima est in Persia.
units.tr: They say there were three excellent prophets, Moses, Christ and Muhammad, and they place their Muhammad above the others. They say that Moses ruled the first people and likewise established the polity, while Christ ruled nothing; but Muhammad established a most extensive kingdom throughout the whole world. That great change in the whole human race arose from the Muhammadan sect. Muhammad began under Heraclius, on this occasion: those soldiers, the Agarenes and Saracens, when they did not receive their pay from the captains of Heraclius, became robbers. Afterwards those Arab soldiers joined themselves to Muhammad and seized Persia. From there they advanced into Damascus and Syria. And today the Muhammadan sect is most flourishing in Persia.

units.la: Quidam, qui aliquoties fuerat Constantinopoli, uolebat uideri bene sentire de nostra doctrina, dicebat ad me: Non uideo magnam differentiā religionis inter ipsos & nos. Ad quam obiectionem sic respondeo: Machometistæ habent quædam legalia & multa ceremonialia, habent multas lotiones, precationes, &c. Item illi, qui sunt religiosiores, non bibunt uinum: sicut omnes barbari habent legalia: Quia enim lex est natura nota: homines retinēt aliquid de naturali luce. Profitetur iam magna pars generis humani doctrinam Machometicam, quæ nihil aliud est nisi doctrina congruens humanis iudicijs sine uerbo Dei. Non habent articulos doctrinæ difficiles, sed tantum legalia, quæ sunt ad constitutionem imperij accommodata.
units.tr: Someone who had been at Constantinople several times wanted to appear to think well of our doctrine, and said to me: "I do not see a great difference of religion between them and us." To this objection I reply as follows. The Muhammadans have certain legal observances and many ceremonies: they have many washings, prayers, and so on. Likewise, those who are more religious do not drink wine, as all barbarians have legal observances. For since the law is known by nature, men retain something of the natural light. Now a great part of the human race already professes the Muhammadan doctrine, which is nothing other than a doctrine agreeing with human judgments, without the Word of God. They have no difficult articles of doctrine, but only legal matters, which are adapted to the constitution of the empire.

units.la: Turci enim uenientes ex Asia, acceperūt leges religionis Saracenicæ, & illis cōiuncti sunt contra Imperatores Constantinopolitanos. Quia Turci sunt Septentrionales, à mari Caspio, seu à rupibus Caucasi orti.
units.tr: For the Turks, coming from Asia, adopted the laws of the Saracen religion and joined themselves to them against the emperors of Constantinople. The Turks are northerners, born from the Caspian Sea or from the rocks of the Caucasus.

units.la: Hermannus Buschius poeta, uir nobilis, accerrimè se oppositi Rotmanno, quem ualde dilexerat. Erat homo ingeniosus, elegāter facundus, & bene conconcionabatur: docebat Euangelium in oppido Monasterio, quem ego & D. pastor Pomeranus optime nouimus. Quidam uero bonus homo ibidem scriba senatus, patria Lipsensis, fauens Euangelio adiuuit propagatione Euangelij. Hic habebat coniugem mirabilem, quæ coepit insanire amore Rotmanni, quapropter & uirum ueneno interemit, postea Rotmanus duxit eam, eaq; ducta, diabolus intrauit in eã. Postquam enim uidit se uenire in odia hominum, adiunxit se sarctori Holladⁿ o nouo regi, ac tumultuanti multitudini. Coepit furere etiam spiritu, quo uolebat facere Ecclesiam sanctā. Buschius autem ei aduersabatur accerrimè, ac uidens uincere aduersarios, discedebat ex urbe. Sed illi nebulones dederūt pœnas, erupit furor ut conspiceretur.
units.tr: Hermann Busch, a poet and a man of noble birth, most vehemently opposed Rotmann, whom he had greatly loved. Rotmann was a gifted man, elegantly eloquent, and a good preacher. He taught the Gospel in the town of Münster, as I and Pastor Pomeranus knew very well. A certain good man, a scribe of the town senate, a native of Leipzig, who favoured the Gospel, helped in its spreading. This man had a remarkable wife, who began to go mad with love for Rotmann; on account of this she also poisoned her husband. Afterwards Rotmann married her, and once she was married, the devil entered into her. For when he saw that he was coming into the hatred of men, he joined himself to the tailor Holland, the new king, and to the rioting multitude. He began to rage also with that spirit by which he wanted to make a holy Church. Busch, however, opposed him most fiercely, and seeing that his adversaries were winning, he left the city. But those scoundrels paid the penalty, and the fury broke out so that it could be seen.

units.la: Quæstio, an omnes hæretici sint interficiendi?
units.tr: Question: whether all heretics are to be killed?

units.la: Dux Saxoniæ Fridericus diu habuit captiuum anabaptistam in arce Schweinitz, cum quo multi docti cōtulerunt, sed desistere noluit. Tandē in carcere mortuus, fortasse lassitudine: quia tāta fuit moderatio principis, ut ipsum non occiderit.
units.tr: Duke Frederick of Saxony long kept a captive Anabaptist in the castle of Schweinitz, with whom many learned men conferred, but he was unwilling to abandon his views. Finally he died in prison, perhaps from exhaustion, because the prince was so moderate that he did not have him put to death.

units.la: Argētinēsis senatus habuit pellionē captiuū, quē noui, antea diu uagatº fuerat in Liuonia, ibiq; spar- fit Anabaptistica dogmata. Argentinæ annos decē aut amplius fuit in carcere. Auditus est sæpius, tādē sine uiolētia est mortuus. Anabaptistæ sūt seditiosi & blasphemi. Seditiosi, quando dicunt contra ordinem iudiciorum, & contra magistratu. Blasphemi, quando contradicunt primæ tabulæ. Tanta fuit clementia senatus, ut ipsum non interficere voluerit.
units.tr: The senate of Strasbourg held a captive furrier, whom I knew. He had earlier wandered for a long time in Livonia and had there spread Anabaptist doctrines. He was in prison at Strasbourg for ten years or more. He was heard several times, and at last died without violence. The Anabaptists are seditious and blasphemous. They are seditious when they speak against the order of the courts and against the magistracy. They are blasphemous when they contradict the first table of the Law. So great was the clemency of the senate that it was unwilling to put him to death.

units.la: Non iudico omnes Anabaptistas et Christianos interficiendos esse. Quidam in Belgico & Hispania etiam deficientes interficiunt, quod est crudele facto, sine discrimine interficere quosq;, cum Paulus iubeat infirmum recipere in fide. Præcipit vero in illo dicto tam multa, ut illius dicti magnitudine nemo in uno anno exhaurire posset.
units.tr: I do not judge that all Anabaptists and Christians are to be killed. Some in Belgium and Spain even put to death those who have fallen away, which is cruel, to kill everyone indiscriminately, since Paul bids us receive the weak in faith. Moreover, in that saying he enjoins so many things that no one could exhaust the greatness of that single saying in a year.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Parisijs diues Mercator papista ioco dixerat ad Franciscanos: Vos geritis funem circa corpus: quia cum Franciscus suspendendus esset, Papa remisit eum ea lege, ut per omnem vitam funem gereret. Franciscani Parisienses apprehenderunt eum, & in carcerem coniecerunt, iudicatumq; est ut suspenderetur. Ille vero periculum mortis euadere cupiens, cecinit palinodiam, ac dixit: Martinus Lutherus est hæreticus, & ex diaboli instinctu docet. Monachi audientes hæc, recte inquis, dicunt, & si in hac sententia manseris, saluus fies. Igitur iubent pergere, & properare lictores ad patibulum, dum esset in confessione, ne iterum deficeret. Sic suspensus est, propterea, quod per iocum dixerat, cur Franciscani funem gererent.
units.tr: At Paris a rich papist merchant had said in jest to the Franciscans: "You wear a rope around your body." For when Francis was to be hanged, the Pope had released him on the condition that he wear a rope all his life. The Parisian Franciscans seized the merchant, threw him into prison, and it was judged that he should be hanged. Wishing to escape the danger of death, he recanted and said: "Martin Luther is a heretic and teaches at the instigation of the devil." The monks, hearing this, said: "You speak rightly, and if you stay with this opinion you will be saved." So they ordered the constables to hurry to the gallows while he was still confessing, lest he recant again. He was hanged for the very reason that he had jested about why the Franciscans wore a rope.

units.la: Seruetus, qui ante paucos annos est à senatu Ge neuensi intersectus, diu uagatus est in Africa, ubi il la Machometica contra filiū Dei didicit. Postea Ve netijs sparsit suum uenenū, donec uenit Geneuam, & senatus Geneuensis rectè fecit, qui talem bla- sphemum hominem interfecit. Est enim unum ex præcipuis officijs magistratus, facere executio- nem corporalibus pœnis contra deprauatores pri mæ & secundæ tabulæ Decalogi: quando aliquis colit idola, et diabolicum uenenum in homines in- fundit, tunc magistratus iustè facit, si illum tollit. Quia mandatum Dei est, & textus seuerè præci- pit, Ne parcas ei. Debet esse nemesis, & seria dili- gentia. Oportet enim puniri delicta, quod & diui- na uoluntas præcipit. Considerate quæso magnas miserias, plurimaq; scelera in hoc mundo uagātia.
units.tr: Servetus, who a few years ago was put to death by the Senate of Geneva, long wandered in Africa, where he learned Mohammedan teaching against the Son of God. Afterwards he spread his poison at Venice, until he came to Geneva; and the Senate of Geneva acted rightly in killing such a blasphemous man. For it is one of the chief duties of the magistrate to carry out bodily punishments against the corrupters of the first and second tables of the Decalogue: when someone worships idols and pours diabolical poison into men, then the magistrate acts justly if he removes him. For it is God's command, and the text commands severely, "Do not spare him." There must be vengeance and earnest diligence. For crimes must be punished, as the divine will also commands. Consider, I beg you, the great miseries and the many wicked deeds that wander about in this world.

units.la: Egranus sæpè reprehendit Paulum, quòd fuerit homo indoctus, et usus sit declamatorijs uerbis, nõ congruentibus ad rem, ac citasse eum mutilas sen- tentias. Idem sæpe dixit, peccatum originale esse fi gmentum Augustini, & Theologorum, quia illud uocabulum non esset in Scripturis.
units.tr: Egranus often rebuked Paul, because he was an unlearned man and used declamatory words not fitting to the matter, and because he cited passages in mutilated form. He also often said that original sin was an invention of Augustine and the theologians, because that word is not in the Scriptures.

units.la: D. Martinus Lutherus.
units.tr: D. Martinus Lutherus.

units.la: Laurentius Valla in multis libris ita scripsit, et disputare solitus est, ut minimè uideretur uelle præ cipere, nec apparet tam docere illum ueritatem & proprietatem rerum et uocabulorum quàm male- dicere dicere & obtrectare uetustis scriptoribus, atque obloqui. Itaq; Ciceronē uellicabat, Aristotelē carpebat, Virgilio subsannabat, maximos quosq; authores contemnebat: Vni tantū Epicuro assurgebat. Ita quoq; se efferebat, ut, cùm in Dialectica quædā inuenissetcōtra eorū temporū artis magistros, palā diceret, nullā esse Logicā, præter Laurētianā. Imò ne dicere quidē dubitauit, ac palam profiteri, habere se quoq; contra fundamenta fidei errores.
units.tr: Laurence Valla, in many books, wrote and was accustomed to dispute in such a way that he did not seem at all to wish to teach, nor did he appear to teach the truth and proper meaning of things and words so much as to revile and disparage the ancient writers and carp at them. Thus he carped at Cicero, found fault with Aristotle, mocked Virgil, and despised all the greatest authors; he rose up for Epicurus alone. He so exalted himself that, having found certain things in dialectic against the masters of the arts of his time, he openly said there was no logic except Laurentian logic. Indeed he did not hesitate even to say, and to profess openly, that he also had errors against the foundations of the faith.

units.la: Quidam pictores Norimbergæ palàm affirmabant, se esse ethnicos, & non posse credere. Cùm uocarentur à Magistratu, & eadem ab ipsis inquirerentur, dicebant, illam rem non pertinere ad magistratum: credere enim se libenter uelle, si possent ipsis dare fidem? Ita postea ex ciuitate expulsi sunt. Et rectè fecit Senatus expellēs palàm epicureos, et ethnicos homines, negātes se credere symbola. Magistratus enim est custos utriusq; tabulæ, tā primæ quàm secundæ.
units.tr: Some painters at Nuremberg openly declared that they were heathens and could not believe. When they were summoned by the magistrate and questioned about the same things, they said that this matter did not concern the magistrate: they would gladly believe, they said, if they could be given faith themselves? Afterwards they were expelled from the city. And the Senate acted rightly in expelling those who openly professed themselves Epicureans and heathens, denying that they believed the creeds. For the magistrate is the guardian of both tables, the first as well as the second.

units.la: Venit ad nos quidam ualidus nebulo, qui petebat se à nobis ali, quia Christianorum essent omnia communia. Respondi: Nos nō possumus omnes ualidos mendicantes alere, & iussimus eum laborare. Respondebat nobis, se non habere gratiā laborandi. At fustibus gratia laborādi ipsi incudi debuisset.
units.tr: A certain sturdy vagabond came to us, asking to be fed by us, because all things among Christians were held in common. I replied: "We cannot feed all the sturdy beggars, and we have ordered you to work." He answered us that he had no gift for working. But the gift of working should have been hammered into him with cudgels.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam bonus uir in oppido uicino Kemberg uidens quendā suæ uocationis desertorē currū one rantem fimo, uenit ad me, dicēs: Ille habet mentem uerè Christianā. Sic nō intellexit ille bonus uir, di-ctum Pauli: In ea uocatione, in qua quisq; uocatus est, in ea diligenter ambulet.
units.tr: A good man in the town of Kemberg, near us, seeing a certain deserter of his calling loading a cart with dung, came to me and said: "That man has a truly Christian mind." That good man did not understand the saying of Paul: "Let each one walk diligently in the calling in which he was called."

units.la: Quidam professor huius Academiæ uolebat totum ordinem Iurisconsultorū abolere, cui cùm resisterem, dicebat: Quid dicis? nescis cum quo agis? Spiritus loquitur in me. Simulabat se habere motus à Spiritu sancto in suo corde excitatos: sed diabolus ita eum uexabat.
units.tr: A certain professor of this Academy wanted to abolish the whole order of jurists. When I opposed him, he said: "What are you saying? Do you not know with whom you are dealing? The Spirit speaks in me." He pretended to have impulses stirred up in his heart by the Holy Spirit, but the devil was tormenting him in this way.

units.la: Venit huc quidam homo ante annos 26, habēs librum magnum erroribus Anabaptisticis refertū (erat aliâs homo simplex, & deceptus illis furoribus Anabaptisticis) in quibus erant præcipui inter cæteros, quòd adulteria uel scortationes nō esset punienda per hominē, quia textus diceret: Scortatores & adulteros puniet Deus. Sumebam illa, quæ erat crassiora, & cum eo de illis disputabā, quæ ipse nō satis intellexerat. Dicebā: Agnosco tuam in hac re negligētiā. Quādo textus dicit: Scortatores et adulteros iudicabit Deus, tunc sic intellige: Iudicabit Deus, scilicet immediatè, uel mediatè. Lex est uox Dei, & executio legis est opus diuinū. Tū dicebā: Vide quid quærat diabolus. Pono casum q, ista reciperētur: quāta fieret cōfusio, si magistratus ista nō punire deberet? Ita cōferebā cū eo placidè, dabā ei etiam uiaticũ abeunti, & agebat mihi gratias. Ni-hil imposterum resciui, quò peruenerit.
units.tr: A certain man came here about twenty-six years ago, having a large book full of Anabaptist errors. (He was otherwise a simple man, and deceived by those Anabaptist frenzies.) Among these were the chief ones, beyond the rest, that adultery or fornication should not be punished by man, because the text says: "God will punish fornicators and adulterers." I took up those points which were grosser, and disputed with him about them, and about those which he himself had not sufficiently understood. I said: "I recognise your carelessness in this matter. When the text says, 'God will judge fornicators and adulterers,' then understand it thus: God will judge, namely either immediately or mediately. The law is the voice of God, and the execution of the law is a divine work." Then I said: "See what the devil is seeking. Suppose these views were accepted: what great confusion would there be, if the magistrate ought not to punish such things?" So I conferred with him calmly, and I even gave him provision for the journey when he departed, and he thanked me. I have learned nothing since of where he has ended up.

units.la: Epicurus habuit inhonestam mulierem, quam uoluit esse communem omnibus suis auditoribus, & dixit, esse Philosophicum, non esse zelotypum. Postea dicitur esse necatus, quod ego credo esse uerum, hoc modo: Dicitur melle esse oblitus, & rogo impositus, ut hac ratione muscæ et crabones ipsum extinguerent. Fuit pœna conueniens talibus opi-nionibus. Muscæ, id est, opiniones eũ extinxerunt.
units.tr: Epicurus had a dishonourable woman, whom he wished to be common to all his disciples, and he said it was philosophical not to be jealous. Afterwards he is said to have been killed, which I believe to be true, in this way: he is said to have been smeared with honey, and placed on a pyre, so that by this means the flies and hornets might destroy him. It was a punishment fitting such opinions. The flies, that is, the opinions, destroyed him.

units.la: Non debetis ita ludere, sicut quidam facit Christum Epicurum. Epicurus locutus est de illis uoluptatibus, quæ sunt in potu, cibo, & re Venerea. Hæc non in contemptum ullius dico, sed ut adolescentes ob imperitiam rerum absurdas loquãdi formulas caueant.
units.tr: You ought not to jest as some do, making Christ an Epicurus. Epicurus spoke of those pleasures which are in drink, food and sexual love. I say this not in contempt of anyone, but so that young men, because of their inexperience, may beware of absurd ways of speaking.

units.la: An bona opera sint facienda?
units.tr: Whether good works are to be done?

units.la: In hoc nouo Collegio dicebat quidam Anglus ad me, doctus uir: Turpe est in Ecclesia illa quærere, an bona opera sint facienda, uel sint debita. Interrogaui nuper aliquem, an bona opera placeãt Deo? Respondit ille: Deus illa non curat, neq; inspicit. Certè Deus est inspector et iudex bonorũ operum, & bona opera sequuntur etiam præmia.
units.tr: In this new College a certain learned Englishman said to me: "It is disgraceful in that Church to ask whether good works are to be done or are owed. Recently I asked someone whether good works please God. He replied: 'God does not care about them, nor does he look at them.'" Certainly God is the examiner and judge of good works, and good works are followed by rewards.

units.la: Pelagius Britannicus scripsit, peccatũ originale nihil esse. Sunt enim omnibus ætatib. tales multi qui sic sentiunt, sicut sæpè audiui Egranum disentem, cente: Peccatum originale, est figmentum Augustini.
units.tr: Pelagius the Briton wrote that original sin is nothing. For in every age there are many such people who think this way, as I have often heard Egranus saying: "Original sin is a figment of Augustine's."

units.la: Ante aliquot annos cum nostri canerent Rorate, tempore aduentus (ut uocant) quidam hypocrita reprehendit. Ecce inquit, cantant Rorate, adhuc expectant Messiam, sicut Iudaei: Oratio ualde fuit ridicula, quasi post aduentum Christi non sint cantandae aut repetendae prophetiae, quae propter hoc ipsum in Ecclesia semper debent repeti, ut nos cõfirmemur in doctrina, etiamsi loquantur de ijs rebus, quae sunt futurae, aut quae praeterierunt.
units.tr: Some years ago, when our people were singing "Rorate" at the time of Advent (as they call it), a certain hypocrite found fault with it. "Look," he said, "they sing 'Rorate', they still wait for the Messiah, like the Jews." The remark was very foolish, as if prophecies should not be sung or repeated after the coming of Christ, when for this very reason they ought always to be repeated in the Church, so that we may be confirmed in doctrine, even if they speak of things that are yet to come or that have already passed.

units.la: Habuimus hîc duos Anabaptistas, homines rabiosos. Vnus à mercatore quodam circunducebatur, qui eum sicut numen colebat. Erat magna impudentia istius hominis, & contumeliosè contra pios doctores loquebatur. Garriebat post Christi resurrectionem non esse peccatum originale. Non enim erat literatus, tantum poterat Germanicè loqui. Interfui etiam alteri, qui pro stabilitione sui erroris citabat dicta ex Iohanne: Dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri, itè: Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & spiritu, nõ intrabit in regnum Dei. Quorum dictorum genuinam sententiam non intelligebat.
units.tr: We had two Anabaptists here, raging men. One of them was led around by a certain merchant, who worshipped him as a deity. This man was very shameless and spoke abusively against the godly teachers. He babbled that after Christ's resurrection there is no original sin. He was not learned; he could speak only German. I was also present when another man, to support his error, cited words from John: "He gave them power to become children of God," and "Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of God." He did not understand the genuine sense of these sayings.

units.la: Monetarius, cùm esset concionaturus, solitus aliquas matronas eleganti forma ad se accersere, & earum consuetudine dixit se impleri diuino afflatu. Huc congruit dictum Christi: Ex fructibus eorũ cognoscetis eos. Et est regula certissima: confusiones nes libidinum sunt signa cuiuslibet sectæ.
units.tr: Monetarius, when he was about to preach, used to summon some women of elegant appearance to himself, and by their company he said he was filled with the divine breath. The saying of Christ fits here: "By their fruits you will know them." And this is a most certain rule: confusion of lusts is the sign of any sect whatever.

units.la: Duæ puellæ sunt interfectæ in diœcesi Bambergensi ante aliquot annos, quibus erat impositæ coronæ stramineæ, cùm ducerētur ad supplicium. Admodum autem hilares, & ingenti motu animi perpessæ sunt mortem. Inter cætera uerò una dixit ad alteram: Cùm Christus pro nobis tulerit spineā coronā, cur & nos iam non libenter ferremus stra mineam? Quin & in cœlo Deus nobis pro his dabit alias aureis longe præstantiores. Dicebant esse Anabaptisticas. Potuit fieri quòd habuerint aliquid stultitiæ admixtū: tamen habuerūt articulorū fidei fundamentū, & mortuæ sunt feliciter in bona confessione, & agnitione filij Dei. Pauci homines sunt sine erroribus. Non blandimini uobis, existimātes uos sine errore uiuere.
units.tr: Two girls were executed in the diocese of Bamberg some years ago; they had crowns of straw placed on them as they were led to punishment. They endured death very cheerfully and with great firmness of spirit. Among other things, one of them said to the other: "Since Christ bore a crown of thorns for us, why should we not now gladly bear a straw one? Indeed, in heaven God will give us for these others far more excellent ones of gold." They were said to be Anabaptists. It may be that some foolishness was mixed in with them; yet they held the foundation of the articles of faith, and they died happily in good confession and in acknowledgement of the Son of God. Few men are without errors. Do not flatter yourselves, thinking that you live without error.

units.la: PAPATVS, ET VARII eiusdem colores.
units.tr: PAPACY, AND ITS VARIOUS COLOURS.

units.la: In cōuentu Bononiēsi, cui interfuerūt Imperator Carolus V. papa Clemēs, & Mercurinus, disputauit papa Clemēs nō esse cōuocandū Cōciliū, aut nō esse habendā Synodum, quā instituerat Imperator: quia non esset utile pronunciatā iam antea sententiā retractare, cùm de istis rebus iam aliquoties erat disputatū. Ibi Mercurinus graui oratione contrariā sententiā defendit. Unde Papa offensus eius oratione, dixit: Quare tu audes Romano pontifici contracontradicere? Mercurinus respondit: Ego, quæ dixi, dixi ex consilio & mandato Domini mei Imperatoris, qui hic præsens adest, cuius sententia ipse interrogato. Surrexit Imperator & approbàs orationem Mercurini, dixit: Ego ita certò decreui nec uolo hoc mutare, nec quicquam cōtradicas. Illa sic esse acta, narratum est nobis ab ijs qui interfuerũt dicētes, grauissimum illorũ trium fuisse colloquiũ.
units.tr: At the assembly of Bologna, attended by the Emperor Charles V, Pope Clement and Mercurinus, Pope Clement argued that no council should be convened, or that the synod the Emperor had arranged should not be held, because it would be pointless to reopen a judgment already pronounced, since these matters had already been debated several times. There Mercurinus defended the opposite view in a weighty speech. Offended by it, the Pope said: "Why do you dare to contradict the Roman pontiff?" Mercurinus replied: "What I said, I said on the advice and by the command of my lord the Emperor, who is present here; you may ask him his own opinion." The Emperor rose, approved Mercurinus' speech and said: "I have decided this firmly and I do not wish to change it, nor should you contradict anything." We were told how these events went by those who were present, who said that the conversation between those three was most serious.

units.la: Dux Georgius iturus ad conuentum Augustanum, cùm uenissset Ingolstadium, & uocasset ad se Eccium, cum quo multa cōferebat de multis rebus, tandem obiecit dux Georgius Eccio, istum textũ: Reges gentium dominãtur, uos autem non sic. Igitur, inquit, episcopi non habent imperia mundana, & uexauit egregiè Eccium, ita ut ipsi nihil respondere posset, sicut textus non potest cludi.
units.tr: Duke George, about to go to the Diet of Augsburg, came to Ingolstadt and summoned Eck, with whom he discussed many matters. At last Duke George put this text to Eck: "The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, but you shall not be so." Therefore, he said, bishops do not hold worldly power. He so thoroughly vexed Eck that Eck could answer nothing, just as a text cannot be refuted.

units.la: Dux Iohannes Elector senex, optimus & præstãtissimus princeps, cùm essent monachi dissipati, & manerët adhuc monasteria, ac in cõuentib.agereturde restituendis monachis, dixit, se multũ peccasse, quòd nõ in totum deleuissel monasteria igni, ut nõ amplius de restitutione disputari posset.
units.tr: Duke John the Elector, an old, excellent and most distinguished prince, when the monks had been dispersed but the monasteries still stood, and discussion was held in the assemblies about restoring the monks, said that he had sinned greatly in not having burned the monasteries completely to the ground, so that there could be no further debate about restitution.

units.la: Quidã monachus Coloniensis Frãciscanus, contra nostrã cõfessionẽ sic scripsit, tam naturale esse homini concupiscentiã, quàm naturalis est motus solis. Ita iste magnus asinus non intellexit, quid sit cõcupiscentia, cùm sit horribilis confusio actionũ.
units.tr: A certain Franciscan monk of Cologne wrote against our Confession as follows: concupiscence is as natural to man as the motion of the sun is natural. That great donkey did not understand what concupiscence is, since it is a horrible confusion of actions.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Episcopus quidam ad Mœnum habitans pro pallio Papæ uiginti millia aureorum numerare cogitur, alij dicunt, cùm alijs impensis & muneribus ad triginta millia aureorum summam extendi. Simile papa Clemens dixit, nullam pecuniam esse satis magnam aspiranti ad papatum.
units.tr: A certain bishop living by the Main was forced to pay twenty thousand gold pieces for the Pope's pallium. Others say that, with other expenses and gifts, the sum rose to thirty thousand gold pieces. Pope Clement said something similar: no sum of money is large enough for one who aspires to the papacy.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Ex Anglia quotannis Papa accepit à quolibet numisma, quod S. Petri inscribitur, qui nūmus tantum ualuit, quantum nunc dimidius urfiger aut citer: ita ut Angli certò narrent, Papam quotannis ultra nouem tonnas auri ex Anglia accepisse. Adolphus rex id regno suo imposuisse dicitur.
units.tr: Each year the Pope received from England a coin from each person, bearing the inscription of St Peter. This coin was then worth as much as half an urfiger or a citer is now, so that the English reliably report that the Pope received from England over nine tuns of gold each year. King Adolphus is said to have imposed this on his kingdom.

units.la: Quādo rex Persicus procedebat in publicum, præcedebat eum equus gestans ignem, qui apud Persas colebatur pro Deo, & nomen eius erat Ori masda, id est, lumen sanctum.
units.tr: When the Persian king went out in public, a horse carrying fire went before him. Among the Persians this fire was worshipped as God, and its name was Ori masda, that is, holy light.

units.la: Quidam Episcopus statim post suam electionē & confirmationem edidit quoddam mandatum in sua diœcesi, cuius exordium fuit: Sicut regem Persicum præcedebat equus ignem gestans, qui à Persis pro Deo adorabatur: sic nos præcedit consecrata hostia, quam ut uerum corpus Domini coli & adorari ab omnibus nostris subditis mādamus. Sic uoluit suam idololatriam tanquā Christianā probare ex Ethnicorum delirijs. Tanti asini sunt, ut non sciant, quomodo deceat scribere epistolam.
units.tr: A certain bishop, immediately after his election and confirmation, issued a mandate in his diocese, which began: "Just as a horse carrying fire went before the Persian king, and was adored by the Persians as God, so the consecrated host goes before us, and we command that it be worshipped and adored as the true body of the Lord by all our subjects." In this way he wished to prove his idolatry to be Christian by drawing on the follies of the heathen. They are such donkeys that they do not know how it is fitting to write a letter.

units.la: Fuit olim consuetudo ut adolescentes, qui eligebantur in Canonicorum collegia, aliquid legerent in sacris literis, ut ederent specimen suæ eruditionis. Accidit igitur, ut cum quidā iuuenis nobili genere natus, in collegium Bambergēse reciperetur, iussus sit prius à Canonicis legere locum ex epistola Pauli: Expurgate uetus fermentum, &c. Et cùm peruentum esset ad illum locum, Sicut estis azymi, iuuenis, cùm illam uocem non intelligeret, legit: Sicut estis asini. Prudentiores & doctiores Canonici astantes, dicebāt inter se: Cùm à sapiētioribus nolumus huiusmodi audire, à pueris audire cogimur.
units.tr: There was once a custom that young men who were chosen into colleges of canons would read something from Holy Scripture, to display a specimen of their learning. It happened, then, that when a young man of noble birth was being received into the college at Bamberg, he was ordered first by the canons to read a passage from Paul's epistle: "Purge out the old leaven, etc." And when they came to that place, "Sicut estis azymi" (as you are unleavened), the young man, not understanding that word, read "Sicut estis asini" (as you are asses). The more prudent and learned canons standing by said among themselves: "Since we do not want to hear such things from the wiser, we are forced to hear them from boys."

units.la: Deliberabatur inter canonicos Merseburgenses de quodam nobili ex Collegio ipsorum ablegando, eo quòd diceretur parum esse eruditus. Re diu multumq; deliberata, tandem senex quidam iussus dicere suam sententiam, respōdit: Ego uideo ipsum esse nobilē, ergo in hoc nobis par est: & est inerauditus, ergo & in hoc nobis non dissimilis. Quapropter eum minimè abdicandum censeo.
units.tr: The canons of Merseburg deliberated about dismissing a certain noble from their college, because he was said to be little educated. After the matter had been long and much debated, an old man, ordered to give his opinion, answered: "I see that he is noble, and so in this he is equal to us. And he is unlearned, and so in this too he is not unlike us. Wherefore I think he should by no means be dismissed."

units.la: Paulus tertius coegit Polum cardinalem Angliæ contra conscientiā subscribere decretis synodi Tridentinæ. Secesserat enim prætextu ualetudinis Paduam in thermas ad fontem Aponi, ne cogeretur subscribere: postea tamen idipsum facere coactus est.
units.tr: Paul III compelled Cardinal Pole of England to subscribe, against his conscience, to the decrees of the Council of Trent. For he had withdrawn, under pretext of ill health, to Padua, to the baths at the spring of Aponus, so that he would not be forced to subscribe; afterwards, however, he was compelled to do the very same thing.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: Collectanea.

units.la: Quando aliquis Romæ creatur episcopus, & datur ei titulus episcopi in locis remotissimis, tunc vadit in templum, & iurat se conuersuram esse illas gentes ad veram religionem, & fidem catholicam, illisq; prædicaturũ. Postea sumit secum quendam notarium, & testes aliquot, iterum iurans extra ciuitatem se non profecturum, quia sit nimis durum & longum iter, protestaturq; ita de impossibilitate. Postremò redit iterum Romam, & absolutionē à Romano pontifice petit, qui accepta magna pecuniæ summa, illum absoluit.
units.tr: When someone is created bishop at Rome and is given the title of bishop in very remote places, he then goes to the church and swears that he will convert those peoples to the true religion and the Catholic faith and will preach to them. Afterwards he takes with him a certain notary and several witnesses, again swearing that he will not travel beyond the city, because the road is too hard and too long, and he protests thus about the impossibility. Finally he returns to Rome and asks for absolution from the Roman pontiff, who, having received a large sum of money, absolves him.

units.la: Quidã monachus, cùm cõcionaretur de uirgine Maria, applicauit labores Herculis ad Mariam.
units.tr: A certain monk, when preaching about the Virgin Mary, applied the labours of Hercules to Mary.

units.la: Capnio diuites monachos solitus est uocare porcos Dei, vnsers Hergots meistschwein.
units.tr: Capnio used to call the rich monks "the pigs of God," "unsers Herrgotts Mastschwein" (our Lord God's fattened pigs).

units.la: In conuentu Vuormacienfi, cùm Eccius obijceret nobis schisma, dixi, nos necessariò schisma fecisse, ut & Prophetas. Eccius respondebat, quòd illud esset singulare. Imò, dixi: Nos habemus mandatum uniuersale, ut discedamus ab idololatris. Sic plus est habere uniuersale quàm particulare mandatū, sicut nos habemus uniuersale: Fugite idololatriam.
units.tr: At the assembly at Worms, when Eck objected to us the charge of schism, I said that we had necessarily made a schism, as did the prophets too. Eck replied that this was a singular case. Nay, I said: we have a universal command to withdraw from idolaters. So a universal command is greater than a particular one, just as we have a universal command: Flee from idolatry.

units.la: Sic cùm in conuentu Ratisbonensi Contarenus, vir solidè doctus, legatus Pontificius, quædam concederet, ita offendit Romanū pontificem, ut nõ auderet amplius redire Romam, sed Bononiæ in exilio lio mortuus sit. Cùm autem papa Paulus esset moderatior, & sermo incidisset, de eius lenitate, inquit: Ille senex fatuus quædam concessit, cùm nihil sit remittendum propter Pontificiam authoritatem.
units.tr: Likewise, when at the assembly at Regensburg Contarini, a man of solid learning and the papal legate, conceded certain points, he so offended the Roman pontiff that he did not dare to return to Rome again, but died in exile at Bologna. When, however, Pope Paul was more moderate, and the talk had turned to his gentleness, he said: That foolish old man conceded certain things, although nothing ought to be yielded on account of papal authority.

units.la: Episcopus Saltzburgensis dixit ad D. Philippum: Mi Domine Philippe, nos non ignoramus vestram doctrinam esse veram: sed an tu contra ignoras, quòd nullus hactenus papistas superare, aut convertere potuerit? quapropter nec tu primus hoc negotium transfiges.
units.tr: The Bishop of Salzburg said to Master Philip: My Lord Philip, we do not doubt that your doctrine is true; but are you not aware, on the other hand, that no one until now has been able to overcome or convert the Papists? For this reason you will not be the first to carry this business through.

units.la: In papatu citius quis inuenerit aliquâ veterè loricam, quàm antiqua monumenta doctrinæ. Vt cùm imagines circumferre in lustrationibus terminorũ solêt, in quodã papistico loco inter cætera crepudia fuit quoq; uetus & oblongũ corium, iam situ penè et uermib. corrosum: accessit Pirckeimerus cùm alio docto quodã uiro, uolens expiscari quæ nam esset illa pellis: cùm uerò introspicerent, uidêt esse Rhetoricam ad Herennium. Hæ fuerunt illæ sanctissimæ reliquæ, quibus ceu fascinis terminos aegrorum tutiores, hominesq; sanctiores esse futuros putabant.
units.tr: In the papacy one would sooner find some ancient breastplate than an ancient monument of doctrine. For when they are accustomed to carry images around in the processions for marking the boundaries, in a certain papistical place, among other rubbish, there was also an old, oblong piece of leather, now almost eaten away by decay and worms. Pirckheimer came up with another learned man, wishing to fathom what that skin was; when they looked into it more closely, they saw that it was Rhetorica ad Herennium. These were those most holy relics, by which, as by charms, they thought the boundaries of the sick would be safer and men would become holier.

units.la: Heydelbergæ fuit monasterium in suburbio, in quo fuerunt Dominicastri, qui non comederũt carnem in suburbio, sed in oppido. Quasi esset alius Deus, & alius cultus extra urbem, quàm in urbe.
units.tr: At Heidelberg there was a monastery in the suburb, in which there were Dominican friars who did not eat meat in the suburb, but did in the town. As if there were one God and another worship outside the city than within it.

units.la: Episcopus quidã dixit in cõcilio Augustano: Nõ solum credendum est scriptis Apostolorum & Pauli, qui non fuit in ordinaria successione, sed multo magis episcopis, qui sunt in ordinaria successione. Est speciosus prætextus. Sed respondeo, Pauli uocationem maiorem esse, quàm eorum qui sunt episcopi. Quia habuit testimonium diuinitus datum, quod non erat contemnendum.
units.tr: A certain bishop said at the council of Augsburg: We must believe not only the writings of the Apostles and of Paul, who was not in the ordinary succession, but much more the bishops, who are in the ordinary succession. It is a specious pretext. But I answer that the calling of Paul is greater than that of those who are bishops, because he had a testimony given by God, which was not to be despised.

units.la: Dixit quidam alius, si posset Pauli corpus accipere, tunc uellet illud suspendere, quòd author esset tam multorum dissensionum.
units.tr: Someone else said that if he could get Paul's body, he would then wish to hang it up, because he was the author of so many dissensions.

units.la: C O L L.
units.tr: Collectanea.

units.la: Episcopus Saltzburgensis, cùm in quodam publico hospitio diuertisset, ibiq; nouum Testamentum reperisset, aperto libro, forte incidit in locum Pauli ad Romanos, ubi dicit: Arbitramur igitur hominem iustificari fide absq; operibus legis. Ibi ille commotus ira, dixit: O Paule, an tu quoq; Lutheranus factus es? & abiecit librum.
units.tr: The Bishop of Salzburg, when he had put up at a certain public inn, and there had found a New Testament, with the book open, by chance came upon the passage in Paul to the Romans where he says: We therefore conclude that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law. Moved by anger there, he said: O Paul, have you too become a Lutheran? And he threw the book away.

units.la: Bambergæ dedicauit Imperator Heinricus aureum calicem sancto Laurentio. Et fingitur post mortem Heinrici uenisse angelum & ponderasse calicem iuxta peccata Imperatoris. Hoc figmento voluerunt Papistæ confirmare opinionem de bonis operibus. Vidi calicem: sed post bellum nemini amplius ostensus est.
units.tr: At Bamberg the Emperor Henry dedicated a golden chalice to Saint Lawrence. And it is fabled that after Henry's death an angel came and weighed the chalice against the sins of the Emperor. The Papists wished to confirm the opinion about good works by this fiction. I have seen the chalice, but after the war it was shown to no one any more.

units.la: C O L L.
units.tr: Collectanea.

units.la: In historijs Eremitarum scribitur de sancto Antonio, tonio, quòd ualde duriter se exercuerit in eremo. Cum autem in oratione sua optasseт cognoscere quantus esset futurus, aut cui comparandus in regno cœlorũ, in uisione ostensum ipsi fuit, se fore similem coriario cuidam uicino portæ Alexãdrinæ, quē ipse optimè norat. Expergefactus uerò, ingreditur ciuitatem ac interrogat illum coriariũ, qualia ipse haberet pietatis exercitia? Respondit ipse, nulla, nisi quod sua domestica opera faceret, & cùm alijs in congregatione Ecclesiæ oraret. Ibi ille cogitauit de discrimine fidei, & aliorum operum, & fiduciam in filium Dei unicam esse anchoram consequendi uitam æternam: reliqua uerò opera non mereri remissionem peccatorum, aut satisfacere legi diuinæ.
units.tr: In the histories of the hermits it is written of Saint Antony that he exercised himself very harshly in the desert. When, however, in his prayer he wished to know how great he was going to be, or to whom he would be compared in the kingdom of heaven, it was shown to him in a vision that he would be like a certain tanner living near the Alexandrian gate, whom he knew very well. Awakened indeed, he enters the city and asks that tanner what religious exercises he himself had. He replied: none, except that he did his household work, and prayed with others in the congregation of the Church. There he reflected on the difference between faith and other works, and that trust in the one Son of God is the only anchor for obtaining eternal life; the remaining works, however, do not merit the forgiveness of sins or satisfy the divine law.

units.la: Sidonius dixit, Paulũ prædicare mutilatũ Christum, id est, prædicare fidem & omittere opera.
units.tr: Sidonius said that Paul preached Christ mutilated, that is, preached faith and omitted works.

units.la: Monachus Scotus, mala bestia, aliquando sequutus est aulam Imperatoris Caroli V. propter magna sua scelera ex aula est expulsus: scripsit longos commētarios ex aula in epistolas Paulinas, sed nihil horum intellexit.
units.tr: A Scottish monk, an evil beast, once followed the court of the Emperor Charles V, but for his great crimes was expelled from the court. He wrote long commentaries on the Pauline epistles from the court, but understood none of them.

units.la: Quæstor quidam propè meam patriam in Marchiatu Badensi, cùm esset dignus supplicio, protraxit supplicium integrũ annum illo priuilegio, quòd esset ἀπόλυθος. Princeps tam uehementer ob perpetrata facta ipsi irascebatur, ut uellet eum supplicio affici absq; authoritate Pontificis: sed tamen consilio aliorum rem retulit ad Pontificem, & impetrauit hoc ab eo, data magna pecunia. Sic tandem suspensus est.
units.tr: A certain questor near my homeland in the Margraviate of Baden, although he deserved execution, dragged out the punishment for a whole year by that privilege that he was an apolytos. The prince was so violently angry at the deeds he had committed that he wished to have him executed without the authority of the Pope; but nevertheless, on the advice of others, he referred the matter to the Pope, and obtained this from him, with a large sum of money given. Thus at last he was hanged.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Cardinalis Saltzburgensis in comitijs Augustanis, anno trigesimo habitis, dixit: Tria sunt media quibus controuersia in religione componi potest: Primum, ut nos Lutheranis assentiamur, quod facere nolumus. Secundum, ut Lutherani nobis assentiantur, quod facere nō possunt cum Dei causa sit, cui nec adimi nec addi quicquam debet. Cum his duobus modis res componi non possit, ad tertium igitur confugiendum est, ut una pars alteram usque opprimat.
units.tr: The Cardinal of Salzburg at the Augsburg diet held in the year 1530 said: There are three means by which the controversy in religion can be settled. (1) First, that we assent to the Lutherans, which we are unwilling to do. (2) Second, that the Lutherans assent to us, which they cannot do, since the cause is God's, to which nothing may be taken away or added. (3) Since these two ways cannot settle the matter, one must therefore resort to the third, namely that one side crush the other.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Alius episcopus dixit: Etsi uera est doctrina Lutherana, de quo nō dubito, tamen nolo ab addictis huius doctrinæ reformari.
units.tr: Another bishop said: Although the Lutheran doctrine is true, of which I have no doubt, I nevertheless do not want to be reformed by the adherents of this doctrine.

units.la: Cum essemus Ratisbonæ in conuentu, etiā proponebantur nobis moderationes à papistis, quæ postea sunt melius coctæ, Man hatt sie ein wenig besser distilliret. Inter cæteras moderationes proponebant etiam hanc: Vota non sunt temerè facienda, sed tamen si sunt facta, non sunt uiolanda, dicebam: Est perplexitas: Princeps quidam hæc proponebat: Synodis non est temerè contradicendum. Quid hoc est? Quis iubet temerè contradicere Synodis? sed tamen non omnes Synodi fuerunt piæ.
units.tr: When we were at the assembly in Regensburg, moderations were also put before us by the Papists, which have since been distilled a little better (as they say, "Man hat sie ein wenig besser distilliret"). Among the other moderations they also proposed this one: vows must not be made rashly, but once they have been made they must not be broken. I said: this is a contradiction. A certain prince proposed this: one must not rashly contradict synods. What is this? Who orders us to contradict synods rashly? Yet not all synods have been pious.

units.la: Hoc argumentum ualde urgebat quidam Papisticus concionator Augustæ in conuentu, anno 30.
units.tr: A certain Papist preacher at Augsburg in the assembly, in the year 1530, pressed this argument very hard.

units.la: Antiquitati magis est credendum.
units.tr: More credence must be given to antiquity.

units.la: Ecclesia est antiquior doctrina.
units.tr: The Church is the older teaching.

units.la: Ergo: Ecclesiæ magis est credendum.
units.tr: Therefore more credence must be given to the Church.

units.la: Probabat minorem, quia ecclesia fuit longè prior, quàm Scriptura.
units.tr: He proved the minor premise because the Church was far older than Scripture.

units.la: Respondeo: Nego minorem, Ecclesia nõ est antiquior uerbo. Quando loquimur de Scriptura, non intelligimus illas characteres. Dictum enim fuit: Semen mulieris conculcabit caput serpentis, antequam rursus Adam factus est membrum Ecclesiæ. Est enim uerbum, siue scriptum sit, siue non.
units.tr: I reply: I deny the minor premise; the Church is not older than the Word. When we speak of Scripture we do not mean those letters and characters. For it was said: "The seed of the woman shall bruise the head of the serpent" before Adam was made again a member of the Church. The Word exists, whether it is written down or not.

units.la: Cùm episcopus Treuirensis post editum Interim conquereretur apud Imperatorẽ, se nihil posse obtinere, quò subditi reciperent illam doctrinã, & petere, ut sua Cæsarea Maiestas eos armis cogeret ad professionem illius doctrinæ in illo libro comprehensæ. Respõdit Imperator Gallicè: O le mauues pasteur qui ses propres brebis deuore, id est: O quàm malus pastor, qui proprias oues devorat.
units.tr: After the Interim was published, the bishop of Trier complained to the Emperor that he could achieve nothing to make his subjects accept that doctrine, and asked that His Imperial Majesty compel them by arms to profess the doctrine contained in that book. The Emperor replied in French: "O le mauues pasteur qui ses propres brebis deuore," that is, "O what a bad shepherd, who devours his own sheep!"

units.la: Quidam monachus pro concione exponebat Ethica Aristotelis, à quo audiui primam partem primi libri Ethices. Multos autem in hoc authore habebat auditores. Si sacra tradidisset hauddubie pauciores aduenissent. Alius quidam licentiatus Theologiæ dixit: Si amitteremus omnes libros Propheticos & Apostolicos, posse doctrinam Euangelij reparari ex Ethicis Aristotelis.
units.tr: A certain monk, preaching a sermon, expounded the Ethics of Aristotle; I heard from him the first part of the first book of the Ethics. He had many listeners for this author. Had he taught sacred matters, undoubtedly fewer would have come. Another licentiate in theology said: If we lost all the prophetic and apostolic books, the doctrine of the Gospel could be restored from the Ethics of Aristotle.

units.la: De Bonifacio VIII pontifice, tale extat elogiū: Intrauit ut uulpes, regnauit ut leo, mortuus ut canis. Dolo enim peruenit ad Pontificatum, turbauit Germaniā & Galliam: item persecutus est in Italia familiam Comnensem, & quendam ex familia uendidit, ut remos perpetuò duceret. Verùm alius quidā bonus uir redemit eum, non sciens illum esse nobilem. Hic reuersus oppressit Pontificem, ducēs ex Gallia exercitum exiguum Romam, ubi captū pontificem coniecit in carcerem, in quo etiā mortuus est. Ille fuit exitus huius tyranni.
units.tr: There is this epitaph on Pope Boniface VIII: He entered like a fox, reigned like a lion, died like a dog. For he came to the papacy by guile, and he troubled Germany and France. He also persecuted the Comnensian family in Italy, and sold one of that family to be a galley slave for life. But another good man bought him back, not knowing that he was of noble birth. Returning, this man overthrew the pope, leading a small army from France to Rome, where he threw the captured pope into prison, and there he also died. Such was the end of this tyrant.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Heinricus Lutzelburgensis egregius & præstans princeps fuit, cuius potētiam pontifices metuentes, nullum artificiosius uenenum inuenire potuerant, nisi ut, cùm Florentiæ ad cœnam Domini se conferret, in hostia ei uenenum præberent. Sic optimus princeps perfidia & scelere pontificū perijt.
units.tr: Henry of Luxembourg was an outstanding and eminent prince. The popes, fearing his power, could find no more cunning poison than this: when he went to Florence to receive the Lord's Supper, they would offer him poison in the host. Thus that excellent prince perished through the treachery and crime of the popes.

units.la: Latomus Louanienfis, ualens ingenio & erudi-tione tione, fuit præcipuus ex perfequutoribus in Belgi co, scripsit nominatim contra me, quòd posuerim omnes sanctos ab initio post receptionem Adæ & Euæ iustificatos seu saluatos esse fide filiu Dei mediatore apprehendetes. Ille phantasticus mera deliria scripsit, inquiens, non alium fidem fuisse in Abraham, quàm qualis fuerit in Cicerone: cùm Christus dicat: Abraham uidit diem meu, & lætatus est.
units.tr: Latomus of Louvain, a man of talent and learning, was the chief persecutor in Belgium. He wrote against me by name, because I had maintained that all the saints from the beginning, after the reception of Adam and Eve, were justified and saved by faith, laying hold of the Son of God as mediator. That fanciful man wrote sheer nonsense, saying there was no other faith in Abraham than that which was in Cicero, although Christ says: "Abraham saw my day, and rejoiced."

units.la: Dominicus de Sodan Hispanus, homo uerbosus, commentarium in epistolam ad Romanos conscripsit, & ferè decem quaterniones in uocabulo fidei interpretando seu potius calumniando cõsumpsit.
units.tr: Dominicus de Soto, a Spaniard, a verbose man, wrote a commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, and spent nearly ten quires in interpreting, or rather in distorting, the word "faith."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Fuit episcopus Byzantinus adeò ambitiosus & gloriæ cupidus, ut auderet se deuouere diabolo, modò fieret Romanus pontifex. Id cùm impetrasset, et iam designatus esset Romanus pontifex, ideoq; uel let iam proficisci Romam, ibi in itinere ei obuiam uenit diabolus, ablaturus eu ad inferos. Episcopus uidens adesse animarum hostem, signauit se signo crucis, quo se contra hostem generis humani defen deret. Diabolus uerò usus hoc epigrammate eum abstulit: Signa te signa, temerè me tangis & angis. Roma tibi subitò motibus ibit amor.
units.tr: A bishop of Byzantium was so ambitious and eager for glory that he dared to devote himself to the devil, provided he might become Roman pontiff. When he had obtained this, and was already designated Roman pontiff, and was about to set out for Rome, the devil met him on the way, intending to carry him off to hell. The bishop, seeing the enemy of souls near, signed himself with the sign of the cross, by which he might defend himself against the enemy of mankind. But the devil, using this epigram, carried him off: "Sign yourself, sign yourself; you rashly touch and torment me. Rome will soon be yours, with a sudden rush of love."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Suidas optimus Grammaticus Græcus, narrat
units.tr: Suidas, the excellent Greek grammarian, relates

units.la: D. Antonium fuisse Alexandriæ, & de causa soroi ris diu litigasse in foro, postea uenisse Constantino polim. Cumq; uideret se non esse idoneum ad forenses disputationes, quæsiuisse solitudines, ut reliquum uitæ tempus in discendo ac precando consumeret. Quantum autem ab hac imaginatione distant monachorum opiniones, res ipsa satis declarat.
units.tr: that Saint Antony was at Alexandria and for a long time pleaded in the law courts over a matter concerning his sister. He later went to Constantinople. When he saw that he was not fit for the disputes of the forum, he sought solitude, so that he might spend the rest of his life in study and prayer. How far the opinions of the monks depart from this idea, the thing itself makes clear enough.

units.la: Professor Hebraeæ linguæ in Academia Vuitenbergensi dicebat: Cur hic sustineo pro exiguo stipendio magnos labores? conferam me iterum Ratisbonam. Ibi enim habeo victum à Iudæis, & mane valetudinis causa, & quantum sanitati meæ conducit, inambulo parum in templo (alioqui uiuens sine labore) tunc uenit una uetula dans mihi ursigerū: uenit etiam secunda, tertia, & quandoq; quarta accedit: tum demum pro omnibus lego unam missam. Sed cùm in itinere uersaretur consilium eius male succesit: quia Iudæi eo tempore Ratisbona expellebantur. Postea audiui eum Herbipoli apud episcopum uixisse.
units.tr: A professor of Hebrew at the Academy of Wittenberg used to say: "Why do I put up with great labour for a small salary? I will go back to Regensburg. There I have my food from the Jews, and in the morning, for my health, I walk a little in the church, as is good for my well-being (otherwise I live without work). Then a little old woman comes and gives me a jug of beer; a second comes, a third, and sometimes a fourth arrives. Then at last I read one mass for them all." But while he was on this journey his plan went badly, because at that time the Jews were being expelled from Regensburg. Afterwards I heard that he lived at Würzburg with the bishop.

units.la: Tempore Totilæ inceperunt monasteria, & sanctus Benedictus est primum caput monachorum, multi deiecti ex summis locis facti sunt episcopi, alij inclusi sunt in monasteria, cùm illa incoepissent.
units.tr: In the time of Totila the monasteries began, and Saint Benedict was the first head of the monks. Many who were thrown down from high places became bishops; others were shut up in monasteries once those had begun.

units.la: Marchio Albertus iocatus cum Augustano episcopo dixit: O uos episcopi estis multò feliciores nobis laicis. Quia quādo discceditis ex hac uita, habetis betis certum hospitium apud inferos: de nobis uerò laicis ignoro quid agetur. Habemus enim incertum hospitium.
units.tr: Marquis Albert, joking with the bishop of Augsburg, said: "You bishops are far more fortunate than we laymen. When you depart from this life, you have a sure lodging in hell; but as for us laymen, I do not know what will become of us, for we have an uncertain lodging."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam interrogatus unde essent monachi? respondit: Quando Deus raserat sacerdotes, & or dinauerat eos, uolens ipsum imitari diabolus, fecit nimis magnam rasuram: ita facti sunt multi monachi. Sic fit quando magna lux doctrinæ est, tunc diabolus excitat semper sua organa.
units.tr: Someone was asked where monks came from. He answered: "When God shaved the priests and ordained them, the devil, wishing to imitate him, made far too big a shaving; so many monks came into being. So it happens: when there is great light of doctrine, the devil always stirs up his instruments."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam Romanus pontifex dixit: Ego fui dives Episcopus, pauper Cardinalis, mendicus Papa: est bonum dictum.
units.tr: A certain Roman pontiff said: "I was a rich bishop, a poor cardinal, and a beggar as pope." That is a good saying.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Episcopus Moguntinus, profectus Constantiam cum comitatu quadringentorum equitum, uenit in Concilium cataphractus, non secus atq; si equi & arma quoq; disputare debuissent, si modò collocasset equos in Concilium. Noster Imperator Carolus V. odit tam inutilem pompam, & non magnifacit apparatus huiusmodi. Quicunq; sanè magnanimi & prudentes uiri sunt, huiusmodi uanos sumptus & superbam ostentationem contemnunt.
units.tr: The bishop of Mainz set out for Constance with a retinue of four hundred horsemen, and came to the Council in full armour, as if the horses and arms too were to dispute, provided only he had brought his horses into the Council. Our emperor, Charles V, hates such useless pomp and sets no store by display of this kind. Surely whoever are magnanimous and wise men despise such vain expense and proud show.

units.la: Rex Danicus Christianus, cū esset adolescens, in aula Marchionis Electoris Ioachimi uixit, & cum eo simul educatus est. Cum Electore Ioachimi patre anno 21 profectus ad conuentum Vuormatiensem, ibi unà cũ domino suo comitatus est Imperatorem in cõcionem, quam habuit monachus Franciscanus, qui cùm ederet inter concionandum mirabiles gestus Italicos in suggestu, quem ibi utcunq; extruxerant ex asseribus, astans nobilissimus ille adolescens, qui nunc est Rex Daniæ, primùm obstupuit, putauitq; monachum insanire: quia nec uiderat nec audiuerat antea tales ineptias. Cùm sic admirabundus diligenter suspiceret, ac monachus sese (ut solebat) totum inclinaret, ita ut uix conspici posset, ipse forte uidit funem pendentem per rimas duorum asserum, quo monachus ille ex more Franciscanorum erat unctus, eoq; celeriter arrepto, interea dum monachus sic in genua procumberet ut non conspiceretur, nodum satis magnum seu multiplicem fecit, ut finita oratione sese rursus eleuare non posset. Monachus porrò, animaduersa fraude, exclamat: O Domine Imperator uide, hoc faciunt Lutherani te præsente, quid facerent te absente? Imperator existimans id factũ esse ex contumelia, excanduit. Quod cùm uideret Rex Danicus, statim aperuit iterum nodum, & sic monachus rursus se erexit, & concionē suam pertexuit. Finita cõcione, Rex Danicus accedit ad patrem Marchionis, & narrat ei ordine rem, petens ab eo, ut indicet Imperatori, quòd ipse fecisset, admiratus istas ineptias, non propter ullam contumeliam, & se ideò indicare, ne alij ob suum factum in suspicionem uel periculum venirët, seq; petere ab Imperatore veniam. Imperator audito Marchione, arrisit, & admiratus factum & candorem adolescentis, quòd ipse sese detulisset, & ingenuè fassus esset peccatum, ne alij venirent in periculū aut suspicionem, ac æqui boniq; consuluit. Audiui ipse hanc historiam ex Rege Daniæ.
units.tr: Christian, King of Denmark, when he was a young man, lived at the court of the Margrave Elector Joachim, and was brought up there together with him. In his twenty-first year he went with the Elector Joachim his father to the diet at Worms, and there, in the company of his lord, he attended the Emperor at a sermon which a Franciscan monk was giving. While preaching, the monk made amazing Italian gestures on the pulpit, which they had somehow built of planks there. That most noble young man, who is now King of Denmark, standing nearby, was at first astonished and thought the monk was mad, because he had neither seen nor heard such silly things before. While he was looking up at him in wonder and attention, the monk bowed himself low, as he was accustomed to do, so that he could scarcely be seen. By chance the young man saw a rope hanging through the cracks between two planks, by which the monk, according to the custom of the Franciscans, was girded. Quickly seizing it, while the monk knelt down out of sight, he made a knot, big and complicated, so that when the prayer was finished he could not raise himself up again. The monk, noticing the trick, then cried out: "O Lord Emperor, look! The Lutherans do this in your presence; what would they do in your absence?" The Emperor, thinking the insult was intended, flew into a rage. When the King of Denmark saw this, he at once untied the knot again, and so the monk raised himself once more and finished his sermon. After the sermon, the King of Denmark went up to the Margrave's father and told him the whole matter in order, asking him to tell the Emperor that he himself had done it, being amazed at those silly antics and not out of any insult; and that he was telling this so that others should not come under suspicion or danger because of his deed; and that he himself asked the Emperor for pardon. When the Emperor heard the Margrave, he smiled, and, admiring both the deed and the candour of the young man, who had given himself up and openly confessed the fault so that others should not fall into danger or suspicion, he judged it fair and good. I myself heard this story from the King of Denmark.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quãdo uxor ducis Ernesti, boni principis, mortua erat Lipsiæ, ubi sepulta iacet, uenit quidam ex monachis ad principem, referens ipsi, quendam ex fratribus uidisse mortuam coniugem ab angelis in cœlum subuectam esse. Hoc excogitauit: quia sciuit id fore principi gratum.
units.tr: When the wife of Duke Ernst, a good prince, had died at Leipzig, where she lies buried, a certain monk came to the prince and reported to him that one of the brothers had seen his dead wife carried up into heaven by angels. He invented this because he knew it would be pleasing to the prince.

units.la: Quidam sacrificulus in Marchia ex Paulo voluit probare authoritatem Ecclesiæ, in disputatione cū Domino pastore nostro, et citauit caput tertiū ad Romanos: Vbi est gloriatio? Ecclesia est. Legit ecclesia pro exclusa: erat enim abbreuiatum.
units.tr: A certain priest in the Mark, in a disputation with our pastor, wanted to prove the authority of the Church from Paul, and cited the third chapter of Romans: "Where is boasting? Ecclesia is." He read "Ecclesia" for "excluded," because the word was abbreviated.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Abbas quidam dixit, se nolle suos monachos uersari in literis: quia non expediret ullum monachū doctiorem esse suo abbate.
units.tr: A certain abbot said that he did not want his monks to engage in learning, because it was not expedient for any monk to be more learned than his abbot.

units.la: Doctor Martinus Lutherus dixit, se fuisse expatiatum patiatum cum alio quodam monacho, qui debebat celebrare missam, & ipse erat concionaturus in Daibron, cùm legeret Euangelium de minis, initiò legit muas, deinde mias, deniq; decē misericordias. Sic non intellexit ille asinus quid legeret.
units.tr: Doctor Martin Luther said that he had once gone for a walk with another monk who was due to celebrate Mass, while he himself was to preach at Daibron. When that monk read the Gospel about the "minae" (the pounds), he first read "muas", then "mias", and finally "decem misericordias" (ten mercies). That donkey did not understand what he was reading.

units.la: Episcopus Augustanus, cùm ciues cogerentur ad illam nouam reformationem doctrinæ, proposi tam ab Imperatore, quæ uocatur Interim, & in eā consensissent, sequenti die curauit erigi arcus triumphales magnificas, & magnis sumptibus extruendas in honorem Caroli V. Imperatoris, cum hac inscriptione: Inuictissimo diuo Carolo V. Imperatori, semper Augusto, pro restituta in ecclesia concordia, Otto Cardinalis fieri fecit. Vtinam pax ubiq; extaret in uera Ecclesia, non alijs, qui se fingunt esse membra Ecclesiæ, cùm sint manifestè hostes & persecutores Ecclesiæ Christi, & deprauatores diuinæ Scripturæ.
units.tr: When the citizens of Augsburg were compelled to accept that new reform of doctrine proposed by the Emperor, which is called the Interim, and had agreed to it, the Bishop of Augsburg had great triumphal arches erected the next day, built at great expense in honour of the Emperor Charles V, bearing this inscription: "To the most unconquered divine Emperor Charles V, ever Augustus, Otto the Cardinal caused this to be made, for the concord restored in the Church." Would that peace were found everywhere in the true Church, and not among those who pretend to be members of the Church when they are plainly its enemies and persecutors, and corrupters of divine Scripture.

units.la: Concionator Augustanus, dicebat de missis pro mortuis: Si nō prosunt mortuis, tamē nobis uiuen tibus prosunt. Quæ sententia magno cum risu excepta est à populo, qui intelligebat hoc dici de pecunia quæ dabatur sacrificulis.
units.tr: A preacher at Augsburg, speaking of Masses for the dead, said: "If they do not benefit the dead, they nevertheless benefit us who are alive." The people received this saying with great laughter, since they understood that it was said about the money given to the priests.

units.la: Fortes uiri scripti sunt in libris, sed in terris admodum pauci sunt: sicut quidam dicebat, triplices esse monachos: quosdam in cœlis, qui sanctissimi essent: quosdam in parietibus pictos, eosq; esse innocentes. nocentes: ultimos esse malos illos nebulones, qui in monasterio alerentur.
units.tr: Brave men are written about in books, but on earth there are very few of them. As someone used to say, there are three kinds of monks: some in heaven, who are most holy; some painted on walls, and these are innocent; and the last, those wicked rogues who are fed in the monastery.

units.la: Æneas Syluius (qui postea factus est Pontifex) hos uersus de monachis composuit:
units.tr: Aeneas Silvius (who later became Pope) composed these verses about monks:

units.la: Non audet Stygius Pluto tentare, quod audet Effrenis monachus plenaq; fraudis anus.
units.tr: The Stygian Pluto does not dare to attempt what the unbridled monk and the fraud-filled old woman dare.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam monachus Lipsiæ ante annos 15 in præfatione ad ducem Georgium, complurioribus aliquoties posuit. Hanc præfationem doctor Hieronymus Schurpfius recitans, dixit: Quàm placuit fatuo monacho complurioribus compluriora.
units.tr: A certain monk at Leipzig, some fifteen years ago, in a preface addressed to Duke George, repeatedly used the phrase "complurioribus" (very many). Doctor Hieronymus Schurpf, quoting this preface, said: "How pleased the foolish monk was with 'complurioribus compluriora'."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Leo papa Franciscum Galliæ regem elegerat Imperatorem, & illum appellabat Imperatorem Constantinopolitanum. Scribebatq; ad Electores Germaniæ, Carolum V. non posse fieri Imperatorem, quia esset in iuramentis regum Neapolitanorum, ut non appeterent Imperium, ne essent Papæ uicini.
units.tr: Pope Leo had chosen Francis, King of France, as Emperor, and called him the Emperor of Constantinople. He also wrote to the Electors of Germany that Charles V could not be made Emperor, because the oaths of the kings of Naples included a promise not to seek the Empire, lest they should be neighbours of the Pope.

units.la: Accepi literas in quibus scribitur de quodam persecutore Ecclesiæ in Belgico, qui dicitur Pater-greul. Hic horribilem plane exercet crudelitatem, comburens passim homines pios & honestos, apud quoscunq; inuenerit libros sibi non placentes. Et sic uerè dicitur pater abominationis.
units.tr: I have received letters describing a certain persecutor of the Church in the Netherlands, who is called Pater-greul. He practises a truly horrible cruelty, burning everywhere pious and honest men, wherever he finds books that do not please him. And so he is rightly called the father of abomination.

units.la: In quadam inquisitiõe nostro tempore, in quodam regno instituta hæc fiunt, quando aliquis sycophanta accusat amplectentem doctrinam Euangelij, tunc uenit in alteram partem prædæ, & altera pars cedit fisco, etiamsi non convictus fuerit reus. Quòd si uerò sycophanta est industrius, tunc magnam partem facultatum aufert. Faciunt similiter, sicut olim fecerunt Iudaici sacerdotes, qui facultates eripuerunt Christianis, & suis nebulonibus dederũt, quos iudicabãt firmos in factionibus suis. Videte astutiã et malitiã diaboli, & ipsius organorũ.
units.tr: In a certain inquisition in our time, in a certain kingdom, the following is done: when some sycophant accuses a man who embraces the doctrine of the Gospel, then one part of the spoils goes to the informer, and the other part goes to the treasury, even if the accused has not been convicted. But if the sycophant is industrious, then he carries off the greater part of the property. They do similarly to what the Jewish priests once did, who snatched property from Christians and gave it to their own rogues, whom they judged firm in their factions. See the cunning and malice of the devil and of his instruments.

units.la: Cùm Spiræ uenisset in templum S. Bernhardus, ac legisset hunc uersum antiquæ statuæ inscriptũ: O clemens, ô dulcis, ô pia mater, Maria. dicunt statuam sonasse hanc uocem: Salue Bernharde, ac Bernhardum respondisse: Mulierem in ecclesia loqui prohibeo, iudicãs esse diaboli præstigias. Hæc statua Spiræ est collocata post ualuas templi, & est magna & informis.
units.tr: When Bernard came to the church at Speyer and read the verse inscribed on an ancient statue, "O clement, O sweet, O pious Mother Mary", they say the statue sounded out this voice: "Hail, Bernard." And Bernard replied: "I forbid a woman to speak in church, judging these to be the devil's tricks." This statue at Speyer stands behind the doors of the church, and it is large and misshapen.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.
