units.la: Queritur apud papistas, si quis adulter offerret munus aliquod, hac conditione, ut sacrificulus in eodem aut maioribus peccatis suffocatus pro eo missam celebraret, & alius ante sacrificuli adventum ex altari idem munus auferret, quis istorũ trium magis contra Decalogum deliquisset? Hanc subtilem quæstionem, doctis soluendam relinquo.
units.tr: Among the Papists the question is raised: if an adulterer offered some gift on this condition, that a priest, himself strangled in the same or greater sins, should celebrate Mass for him, and another man took the same gift from the altar before the priest arrived, which of these three sinned more against the Decalogue? I leave this subtle question for the learned to solve.

units.la: SCHOLAE, ET STVDIA linguarum, artium ac facultatum.
units.tr: Schools, and the study of languages, arts and faculties.

units.la: Ordo in studijs progrediendi, à D. Philippo nouitijs studiosis præscriptus.
units.tr: The order of progress in studies, prescribed for novice students by D. Philip.

units.la: Mane surgens, dicito precationem, & lege caput in ueteri Testamento, ita ut ordine totam historiam legas, ut textus fiat tibi familiaris, etiamsi nõ omnia intelligis: & adde lectionem unius Psalmi.
units.tr: On rising in the morning, say the prayer and read a chapter of the Old Testament, going through the whole history in order, so that the text becomes familiar to you, even if you do not understand everything. Add the reading of one Psalm.

units.la: Die Lunæ, & Martis.
units.tr: Monday and Tuesday.

units.la: Post precationẽ, lege certum authorem, uel epistolas Ciceronis, uel Terëtium. Postea lectiones audies. Hora octaua lectorem græca prælegentẽ. Hora nona Dialecticen.
units.tr: After prayer, read a set author, either Cicero's letters or Terence. Afterwards you will attend the lectures. At the eighth hour, a lecturer reads Greek beforehand. At the ninth hour, dialectic.

units.la: A meridie.
units.tr: In the afternoon.

units.la: Sphericam doctrinam, et Arithmeticam discito.
units.tr: Learn the doctrine of the sphere and arithmetic.

units.la: Die Mercurij.
units.tr: Wednesday.

units.la: Audies Ethicen.
units.tr: You will attend the lectures on ethics.

units.la: Die Iouis, & Veneris.
units.tr: Thursday and Friday.

units.la: Mane post precationem, unam horam tributo seu Liuio seu Ouidio. Deinde audies lectionem Græcam.
units.tr: In the morning, after prayer, give one hour to either Livy or Ovid. Then attend the Greek lecture.

units.la: A meridie.
units.tr: In the afternoon.

units.la: Spheram, Arithmeticam, & Physicen. Reliquũ tempus tributo interdum lectioni difficilimarum matemateriarum, interdum stilo, interdum iucundæ le-ctioni & recentium aut ueterum scriptorũ. Præci-puè tamen cura sit, artes ordine discere, Dialecti-cen, Arithmeticen, Sphærica elementa, Physica. Quia nisi artes discantur non est certum doctrinæ corpus.
units.tr: Sphere, arithmetic and physics. Give the rest of the time sometimes to reading the most difficult matters, sometimes to writing, and sometimes to the pleasant reading of recent or older writers. Yet above all take care to learn the arts in order: dialectic, arithmetic, the elements of the sphere, physics. For unless the arts are learned, there is no certain body of doctrine.

units.la: Die Saturni.
units.tr: Saturday.

units.la: Exerceas te in Græca lingua, aut in scribendo so-lutam orationem Latinam, aut uersus.
units.tr: Exercise yourself in the Greek language, or in writing Latin prose or verse.

units.la: Diem Dominicā tribue lectioni doctrinæ Chri-stianæ, legito uel locos Theologicos, uel similem summam.
units.tr: Give the Lord's day to the study of Christian doctrine. Read either the Theological Commonplaces or a similar summary.

units.la: COLL. Νόμοι seu Leges.
units.tr: Collection. Rules, or laws [Νόμοι].

units.la: Qui uolet utiliter in studijs literarum uersari, ante omnia & sæpè in memoriam sibi reuocare si-nem studiorum debet: ita & attentius & libentius faciet, et feret omnia, quæ rei magnitudo requirit. Est autem hîc generalis finis propositus omnibus, qui se studijs dediderunt, ut Deum agnoscant ex Verbo, quo se patefecit, & illius Verbi sint custo-des, & propugnatores, pro sua quisq; uirili & uo-catione. Alter finis est, ut se instruant cognitione rerum, quæ ad intelligendam & explicandam cœ-lestem doctrinam, item ad gubernationẽ Ecclesiæ, & Rerumpublicarum requiruntur. Deniq;, quæ ad multas uitæ communis artes necessariæ sunt. Tertius, ut mores regere, & cupiditates frenare assuefaciant disciplina & ratione, ut postea adulti, & in coetus producti, ferre hominum infirmitatē queant, & ipsi aliis hominibus præluceant exemplis modestiæ, iusticiæ, tolerantiæ, & aliarum virtutum necessariarū in communi uita. Hi fines diligenter et sæpè cogitati, sua dignitate excitabunt discentes, & spe ingentium præmiorum urgebunt ad præstandam assiduitatem, & ad perferendas difficultates, quæ in hoc studio offerūtur : sicut nullum uitæ genus non habet aliquas molestias.
units.tr: Whoever wishes to be usefully engaged in literary studies must, before all things and often, call to mind the aim of his studies. He will then work more attentively and more willingly, and will bear everything that the importance of the matter requires. The general aim set before all who have devoted themselves to study is this: that they may know God from the Word by which he has revealed himself, and that they may, each according to his strength and calling, be guardians and defenders of that Word. The second aim is that they equip themselves with knowledge of the things needed for understanding and expounding heavenly doctrine, and likewise for the governance of the Church and of commonwealths, and finally for the many arts necessary to common life. The third is that, by discipline and reason, they accustom themselves to govern their morals and bridle their desires, so that later, as adults and placed in public assemblies, they may be able to bear the weakness of men, and may themselves shine as examples to other men of modesty, justice, patience and the other virtues necessary in common life. These aims, carefully and often considered, will stir up the students by their own dignity, and will urge them with the hope of great rewards to show constant diligence and to endure the difficulties that meet them in this pursuit, just as no kind of life is without some troubles.

units.la: De primo fine.
units.tr: On the first aim.

units.la: Ante omnia puer dabit operam ut doctrinam cœlestem diligenter cognoscat, cùm ex lectionibus publicis & concionibus, tum ex priuata lectione & precatione, & in ea quærat consensum Catholicæ ecclesiæ Christi: discat agnoscere et refutare errores depravantium Scripturas. Et priuatim quidē quotidie, anteq̄ alias operas inchoabit, pexo & nudato capite, Latinè primùm, ac mox, (si libri copia in promptu erit) Germanicè quoq; caput unum in ueteri Testamēto legat. Si qui plures unà habitent, utiliter facient, si collatis pecunijs comparabunt Viti Theodori Norimbergensis summaria in Biblia, quæ ante lectionem capitis Biblici inspecta, monebūt pueros de summa historiæ, ad quos locos cōmunes referenda sit. Eandē quoq; Viti summam uelim denuò post absolutam capitis geminatam lectionem repeti, ut quæ lecta sunt altius in mente infixæ diutius hæreant. VespERI eodem modo, antequam ibit cubitum, puer legat ex nouo Testamento caput unum, adhibitis commentarijs illis breuissimis M. Viti, ut dictum est. Hæc consuetudo præterquam quòd intellectum Scripturæ parit, etiam accendet animum, ut ardentius Deum invocet, & mores studiosius regat ad voluntatem Dei. Vtile erit etiam post sumptu cibum per otium quasi animi causa, psalmos Latinos ordine cantillare, variatis modis illis, quibus in templis canuntur, item Germanicas cantiones usu ediscere, quæ à D. M. Luthero, piæ memoriæ, & alijs pijs uiris erudite compositæ, continent doctrinæ Christianæ summam. Hæc ratio Psalterium reddet pueris notius quod scriptum debet omnibus pijs quàm familiarissimum esse, & uocem exercebit, cuius usus necessarius est in tota uita, maximè ijs, qui publicè docere alios uolent. Et quia Dominicus dies totus debetur tractationi Verbi, uolo, ut qui ex meis discipulis D. Philippum Euangelium enarrantem audire consueuerunt, illam lectionem nullo modo negligant. Reliquos iubeo hora sexta matutina domum meæ conuenire ad explicationem catechesis Christianæ. Qui uerò eam lectionē aut fastidiosè aspernabuntur, aut somno indulgentes sæpius negligent. eos nequaquam feram in numero meorum, ut qui illam partē institutionis contemnere audeant, quæ ut dixi, omnium est præcipua & maximè necessaria, propter quā studia reliqua colimus, imò propter quam conditi sumus, à Deo nutrimur, defendimur, seruamur. Post prandium mei conuenient ad exercendam Musicam, & pijs & artificiose factis carminibus. Hora prima singuli memoriter proferent aliquam insignem sententiam sacræ Scripturæ, quā uel illo die excerpserint, uel per septimanam inter legendum obseruarint. Decet enim pueros sic legere cœlestem doctrinam, ut præcipua dicta memoriæ infigant, eáq; ad arguendos, excitandos, cõsolandos, & cõmonefaciendos sese et alios, cum opus erit, in promptu habeat. Cætera quæ ad primum finem pertinent, uniuscuiusq; pio studio priuatim committo.
units.tr: Above all, the boy shall take pains to know heavenly doctrine carefully, both from public lessons and sermons and from private reading and prayer, and in these he shall seek the agreement of the catholic Church of Christ. Let him learn to recognise and refute the errors of those who corrupt the Scriptures. Privately, indeed, every day, before he begins his other work, with his hair combed and his head bared, let him read one chapter of the Old Testament, first in Latin and soon after (if a copy is at hand) also in German. If several live together, they will do well to pool their money and buy Vitus Theodorus of Nuremberg's summaries on the Bible. Consulted before the reading of a biblical chapter, these will tell the boys the sum of the history and the commonplaces to which it is to be referred. I would also wish this same summary of Vitus to be repeated after the chapter has been read twice through, so that what has been read may stick more deeply and longer in the mind. In the evening, in the same way, before going to bed, the boy shall read one chapter of the New Testament, with the very brief commentaries of Master Vitus at hand, as has been said. This practice, besides producing understanding of Scripture, will also kindle the mind to call upon God more ardently and to govern its morals more diligently according to the will of God. It will also be useful, after the midday meal, for leisure, as it were for the sake of the mind, to sing the Latin Psalms in order, with those varied modes in which they are sung in churches, and likewise to learn by use the German songs, composed learnedly by Dr. Martin Luther of pious memory and other godly men, which contain the sum of Christian doctrine. This method will make the Psalter, which ought to be most familiar to all the godly, better known to the boys, and it will exercise the voice, whose use is necessary throughout life, especially for those who wish to teach others publicly. And since the whole Lord's day is owed to the handling of the Word, I wish that those of my pupils who have been accustomed to hear D. Philip expounding the Gospel by no means neglect that lesson. I order the rest to assemble at my house at the sixth hour of the morning for the exposition of the Christian catechism. Those who either disdain that lesson with distaste or, indulging in sleep, neglect it often, I will by no means keep among my students, since they dare to scorn that part of instruction which, as I have said, is the chief and most necessary of all, the reason for which we cultivate our other studies, indeed the reason for which we were created, nourished, defended and preserved by God. After dinner my pupils shall assemble to practise music, with pious and skilfully made songs. At the first hour each shall recite from memory some notable saying of Holy Scripture, which either he has excerpted that day or has marked during the week while reading. For it is fitting that boys read heavenly doctrine in such a way that they fix the chief sayings in memory and have them ready to hand, to rebuke, encourage and console themselves and others, when need arises. The rest of what pertains to the first aim I commit to each one's pious study in private.

units.la: Secundus finis complectitur linguarum & partium Philosophiæ studium.
units.tr: The second end comprises the study of languages and of the parts of philosophy.

units.la: DE LINGVIS.
units.tr: ON LANGUAGES.

units.la: Græci olim suam tantùm linguam studiosè excolebant: Romani præcipuè suam, et deinde addebant unicam peregrinam linguam, nempe Græcā. Nos, neglecta lingua uernacula, magna cum difficultate simul duas peregrinas linguas discere & comcoplecti, Latinâ primùm, ac Græcâ, si historiarum & artiū cognitionem solidâ nobis cōparare uolu- mus, oporter. Cœlestis doctrinæ explicatio etiam Hebraicæ linguæ peritiâ flagitat, ita nobis saltem plerisq; ut necessariū, ita difficilimū est simul triū peregrinarū linguarum studiū, quod adimit nobis conatū excolēdæ et exercēdæ Germanicæ linguæ, quæ minimè erat negligenda, ijs præsertim qui aliquādo publicè causas agēt, aut cōcionabūtur. Sed obijcitur: Nihil facilius est, q; in sua lingua rectè loqui? At respōdeo tales, Græcos et Latinos stulticiæ et manis curiositatis cōdēnare, quæ gētes à primis statim annis pueros ad certā & uenustā formā dicendi in sua lingua maximo cū labore & solicitudine cōsuefecerūt, & frequētissimas scholas habuerunt, Grammaticorū primùm, deinde etiā Rhetorum, in quibus imūetus uernaculæ linguæ rectum usum longa exercitatione dicēdi & scribēdi addiscebat. Sed fit apud nos temporū iniuria, ut studiū linguæ uernaculæ nō negligatur solùm, sed etiā cō temnatur, & probro detur, si quis id usurpare uideatur. Quare tandem satis graues pœnas damus ignauiæ nostræ, cùm postea producti in cœtus, ubi nobis officij ratio necessitatem dicēdi imponit, aut cōscientia nostræ infantiæ obmutescimus, aut cōsternatione titubantes trepidamus: aut ut illorū nihil cōtingat, tamē impropriè, obscurè, cōfusè dicimus. mus, utpote nulla prius exercitatione exculti aut cõfirmati. Quare hortator sum meis pueris, ut ali quã saltẽ curã etiã maternæ linguæ discẽdæ & exercẽdæ à primis annis suscipiãt, & studiosẽ obseruẽt, ac imitari studeãt illos, qui proprie, elegãter et sine affectatione Germanicè loquũtur. Legãt etiã priuato studio Germanica scripta maximè D. Lutheri, Philippi, Menij: deinde etiã oratorum quorundam, ut D. Pontani, in quibus quid quemque deceat ac ornet obseruent, & affectatam grandiloquentiam, ut alienissimã ab Ecclesiasticis, uitare discant. Proderit ad hoc quoq; argumẽta, quæ latinè scribenda erunt, prius uernacula lingua explicare, ac deinde in peregrinam linguam conuertere. Nec parùm iuuabuntur adolescẽtes, si interdũ duo aut tres per ocium inter deambulandũ, narrationes aliquas ueras uel fabulosas commemorabunt, adhibito studio proprietatis, ordinis & elegantiæ. Hæc de lingua uernacula monuisse satis est.
units.tr: The Greeks of old diligently cultivated only their own language; the Romans chiefly their own, and then added one foreign language, namely Greek. We, having neglected our vernacular, must with great difficulty learn and master two foreign languages at once, Latin first and then Greek, if we wish to acquire a solid knowledge of histories and the arts. The explanation of heavenly doctrine also demands skill in the Hebrew language. Thus for most of us the study of three foreign languages at once is as necessary as it is most difficult, and it takes from us the effort to cultivate and exercise the German language, which was by no means to be neglected, especially by those who will at some time plead causes in public or preach. But it is objected: "Is there anything easier than speaking correctly in one's own language?" I reply that those who think so condemn the Greeks and Romans of foolishness and idle curiosity; these peoples, from their earliest years, trained their boys with the greatest labour and care in a certain elegant form of speaking in their own tongue, and they had very many schools, first of grammarians and then also of rhetoricians, in which the pupil learned the correct use of the vernacular by long practice in speaking and writing. But by the injustice of our times it happens among us that the study of the vernacular is not only neglected but even despised, and it is held up to disgrace if anyone seems to take it up. Therefore at last we pay quite heavy penalties for our idleness: when afterwards we are brought forward into assemblies, where the duty of our office imposes the necessity of speaking, we either fall silent in embarrassment at our own infancy, or we stammer and tremble in confusion; or, if none of these things happens to us, we still speak improperly, obscurely and confusedly, since we were never trained or strengthened by any prior practice. Therefore I urge my pupils that from their earliest years they take up at least some care in learning and practising their mother tongue, and that they attentively observe and strive to imitate those who speak German properly, elegantly and without affectation. Let them also read in private study German writings, chiefly those of Dr Luther, Philip and Mænius, and then also of certain orators, such as Dr Pontanus, in which they may observe what suits and adorns each thing, and learn to avoid affected grandiloquence, as most alien to churchly speech. It will also be useful for this purpose to explain in the vernacular the arguments that are to be written in Latin, and then to turn them into the foreign language. Young men will also be much helped if now and then two or three, while walking at leisure, recount some true or fabulous stories, with attention to propriety, order and elegance. It is enough to have given this advice about the vernacular.

units.la: De lingua Græca.
units.tr: On the Greek language.

units.la: Linguam Græcam sic ferè discũt pleriq;, ut intelligere authores Græcos possint. Ad illud propositum sufficiet diligenter ex Grammatica Græca declinationes nominum & uerborum, & phrases præcipuè indeclinabilium partium cognoscere. Græca scripta partim per interpretationẽ uiuæ uocis, partim collata uersione latina intelligere conari: & cùm eorum sententiâ assecuti sumus, rursus eadem in linguam latinam proprijssimè conuertere. Quod exercitationis genus præter linguæ cognitionem, etiam alias plures utilitates discētibus adsert. Iniungo igitur discipulis meis, ut professorem enarrantem publicè Græcam Grammaticam, & Euripidem, similiter & dominum Philippum Aristotelis Ethica aut alia Græca scripta interpretantem diligenter audiant. Utilissimè feccerint, si qui ex grandioribus natu explicatos uersus Tragici poetæ latinè redderent soluta & liberiore oratione, tanquam ωσραφράσει[?]. Sic enim & linguam persectius discerent, & insignia ornamēta & sententias γνωμικὰς firmius meminissēt, quib. hoc genus scriptı est refertissimum. Mihi hoc tempore priuatim satis uidetur, si die sabbati post concionem uespertinam à certis discipulis expositionem Euangelij Dominicalis exigam, & postulem, ut singularum dictionum Græcarũ themata & flexum indicent: unde intelligant, qua diligentia publicè Grammaticam audierint.
units.tr: Most people learn the Greek language in such a way that they can understand Greek authors. For that purpose it will suffice to know diligently from a Greek grammar the declensions of nouns and conjugations of verbs, and especially the phrases of the indeclinable parts of speech. Greek writings are to be understood partly through the interpretation of the living voice, partly by comparing a Latin version, and when we have grasped their sense, to turn the same back into Latin, as closely as possible. This kind of exercise, besides knowledge of the language, brings many other advantages to learners. I therefore enjoin my pupils to listen diligently to the professor publicly expounding Greek grammar and Euripides, and likewise to Master Philip interpreting Aristotle's Ethics or other Greek writings. They will do best if those of the older ones who are more advanced render the explained verses of the tragic poet into Latin in free and looser prose, as a kind of paraphrase. For in this way they will learn the language more perfectly, and will remember more firmly the striking ornaments and the gnomic sayings, of which this kind of writing is very full. For my part, at this time it seems enough to me privately that, on the Sabbath day after the evening sermon, I require from certain chosen pupils an exposition of the Gospel for the Sunday, and demand that they indicate the stems and inflections of the individual Greek words, so that it may be clear with what diligence they have attended the public grammar lectures.

units.la: De lingua Latina.
units.tr: On the Latin language.

units.la: Sed longè maiori conatu in studium linguæ Latinæ incumbere pueri debebunt: non modò ut latinos scriptores, poetas, oratores, historicos intelligant, uerùm etiam ut eius linguæ proprietatem loquendo & scribendo tam ligata quàm soluta oratione tione exprimere aliquo modo possint. Quandoquidem eius solius usus inter literatos & alibi est plurimus. Cùm autem facultas & copia proprij sermonis Latini non solùm lectione Scriptorum comparetur, sed etiam requirat consuetudinem quotidiani usus in colloquijs familiaribus & exercitatione scribendi, utriq; rei sedulò opera danda est. Quare decreui posthac, Deo iuuante, die Lunæ proponere argumentum in utroq; genere scriptionis, ad quæ excipiëda pueri cõueniat, eaq; interea quinq; dierum spacio absoluta, & grandiusculis literarũ figuris descripta, ita ut in marginibus sit uacua charta, ubi errata indicari & corrigi possint. Die Saturni post cœnam exhibebunt, recepturi eodem tempore, si ullo modo fieri poterit, emendata præcedentis hebdomadis scripta. Sæpè autẽ aliàs commonefiunt pueri de necessitate & diligenti usu crebri stili, quibus impelli debent, ut ultro etiam in ea parte obedientiam & diligentiam præstent. Sed si quem nec officij ratio, nec commodorum magnitudo excitabit, ut obtemperet, is sciat eam contumaciam & socordiam non carituram pœna. Loquendi autem latinè cõsuetudo utinam uel metu pœnarũ, uel præmijs, uel quibuscunq; modis adolescentibus persuaderi ac familiaris reddi possit, quæ necessaria ad linguam discendam, quàm futuro excellenti pugili quotidiana armorũ meditatio est. Sed nimiùm nimium hac in re adolescētia sibi studiorū impedimento indulget, nō æstimās quantū sit & commodum, et ornamentū, posse apud eruditos expeditè, propriè & perspicuè cogitata animi latinè expri mere. Quì felicitatē si quis putet sine exercitatione cōparari, stultè errat. Hortor igitur discipulos meos, qui extra meā domū habitāt, ut cū suis cōtubernalibus colloquētes tantùm Latina utantur lin gua. Iis uerò qui sunt domi meæ idem præcipio, sed hac lege & multa addita, ut si quis uernacula lin gua intra domū usus fuisse deprehēdatur, numulū soluat, ad præmiū in certaminibus uictoribus distribuendū, de quibus infrà dicemus. Eadē lege tenebuntur ij quoq;, qui alibi habitāt, quoties locuti Germanicè fuerint. Cùm aūt Orationis Latinæ initia hauriri cōueniat ex arte Grāmatica, illius præcepta posthac pueris tradā, & rursus exigā horā diurna, die Lunæ, & Martis: alijs duob. Iouis, et Veneris eadē hora explicatur. Terētij comœdias, ut habeāt exēpla purę orationis Latinæ, quæ imitari possint. Vtq; uel æmulatione cōpellātur ad repetitionē assiduā præceptorū Grāmatices, aliquot delectis ex cœtu discipulorū proponetur tēpestiuè aliqua pars carminis Vergiliani ex Bucolicis, in quo dictionum ἐτυμα, origines, flexus, structuras, ita diligēter inuestigabūt delecti illi, ut cæteris suis cōdiscipulis cōuenturis post cœnā die Mercurij, et profectum profectu ipsorum exploraturis, appositis responsionibus satisfacere, et cum eorunde laudatione dimitti possint. Et quia prodest aliquos insignes locos etiam penitus memoriae imprimi, ut scribentib. suppetat bonarum formularum, sententiarum et figurarum copia, singulis septimanis mandabo paucis aliquot, ut ad die Sabbati mane hora sexta memoriter pronuncient in coetu insignes aliquos locos ex bonis autoribus, cum iudicio desumptos. Haec consuetudo, supra utilitates prius dictas, etiam memoriam excolet, pronunciationem formabit, animum addet timidiusculis illis, & rustico saepe pudore praeditis, ut in frequentiore etiam coetu sine deformi trepidatione aut perturbatione animi dicere alacre, distincte & constanter audeat. Ad illam auscultationem volo omnes discipulos adesse, ut & quae cum laude pronunciari audierint, imitari, & quae reprehendi intellexerint, ipsi postea vitare conetur. Supra haec omnia, ad comparandam facultatem Latini sermonis, necessaria est lectio aliquot scriptorum, ad quorum exempla pueri orationem formare assuescant, eorumq; in loquendo et scribendo similitudinem exprimere conetur. Primum igitur domi suae pueri tribuat quotidie horam unam aut dimidiam lectioni Terentij primum, deinde epistolarum Ciceronis, Officiorum, & similium facilium scriptorum. Ex poetis aut legent Vergilij poemata, & Ouidij castiores libros, ut Metamorphosin, Fastos, Tristium, & de Ponto libros, ut in faciendis uersibus habeat quod imitentur. Cùm autem memoria quantumuis felix tenere omnia pariter nõ possit, pueri semper ad manum habebunt libellum ad hoc comparatũ, ut in eo insignes formulas, gnomas, figuras, & si- miles orationis latinè flosculos inter legendum ex- cerptos annotent, ibiq; cõportata ornamenta ora- tionis per totam hebdomadam, die Saturni aliquo- ties relegant, & subinde in memoriam sibi reuo- cent. Hæc de orationis Latinæ facultate comparan- da, & de adminiculis ad eam necessarijs dicta suffi- ciant. Nunc etiam de partibus Philosophiæ pauca dicam.
units.tr: But boys must apply themselves to the study of the Latin language with far greater effort: not only so that they may understand Latin writers, poets, orators and historians, but also so that they may in some measure express the proper idiom of that language in speaking and writing, in bound as well as in free prose. For the use of that language alone is most widespread among the learned, and elsewhere too. Since the ability and abundance of one's own Latin speech is acquired not only by reading the writers, but also requires the habit of daily use in familiar conversation and the exercise of writing, both must be diligently attended to. Therefore I have decided that from now on, God helping, on Monday I will set a subject in each kind of writing, to which the boys are to attend; these they are to complete within a space of five days and write out in fairly large letters, leaving blank paper in the margins where errors may be pointed out and corrected. On Saturday after supper they will hand them in, receiving back, at the same time, if it can in any way be done, the corrected writings of the preceding week. Often at other times the boys are reminded of the necessity and diligent practice of frequent writing, by which they ought to be urged to show obedience and diligence in this matter even unprompted. But if neither the sense of duty nor the greatness of the advantages will rouse anyone to obey, let him know that such obstinacy and laziness will not go unpunished. Would that the habit of speaking Latin could be instilled in young men, and made familiar to them, by fear of punishments, by rewards, or by whatever means: it is as necessary for learning the language as daily practice in arms is for the future excellent fighter. But in this matter young people indulge themselves too much, as an obstacle to their studies, not reckoning how great a benefit and ornament it is to be able to express in Latin, readily, properly and clearly, the thoughts of the mind before learned men. If anyone thinks such felicity can be acquired without practice, he is foolishly mistaken. I therefore urge my pupils who live outside my house to use only the Latin tongue when conversing with their housemates. To those who are in my house I give the same instruction, but under this rule, with much added: that if anyone is caught using the vernacular within the house, he shall pay a small coin, to be distributed as a prize to the winners in the contests of which we shall speak below. The same rule will bind those who live elsewhere, whenever they have spoken German. Since the beginnings of Latin speech ought to be drawn from the art of grammar, I will henceforth teach the boys its precepts, and again I will require them at the daytime hour on Monday and Tuesday; on the other two days, Thursday and Friday, the same hour is devoted to explanation. Terence's comedies are read, so that they may have examples of pure Latin speech to imitate. And so that they may be spurred by emulation to constant repetition of the rules of grammar, some chosen members of the company of pupils will be given in due time some part of a Vergilian poem from the Bucolics, in which those chosen ones shall investigate so diligently the etymologies, origins, inflections and constructions of the words that they can satisfy their fellow pupils, who will be examining them after supper on Wednesday and testing their progress, with prepared answers, and be dismissed with praise. And since it is useful to have certain striking passages fixed deeply in the memory, so that writers have at hand a supply of good formulas, sayings and figures, I will each week assign a few boys to recite from memory in the assembly, at six o'clock on Saturday morning, some striking passages from good authors, chosen with judgement. This practice, beyond the advantages mentioned before, will also cultivate the memory, shape delivery, and give courage to the rather timid and often burdened with a rustic shyness, so that they dare to speak briskly, distinctly and steadily, even before a larger gathering, without unseemly trembling or agitation of mind. I want all the pupils to be present at that hearing, so that they may imitate what they have heard pronounced with praise, and strive to avoid afterwards what they have understood to be blamed. Above all these things, for acquiring the ability of Latin speech, the reading of a number of writers is necessary, on whose examples the boys may learn to shape their style, and strive to express their likeness in speaking and writing. First, therefore, let each boy set aside at home one hour or half an hour daily for reading Terence first, then the letters of Cicero, the Offices, and similar easy writers. Of the poets they shall read the poems of Vergil and the more chaste books of Ovid, such as the Metamorphoses, the Fasti, the Tristia and the books from Pontus, so that they may have something to imitate in making verses. Since no memory, however happy, can retain everything equally, the boys shall always keep at hand a little book prepared for this purpose, in which they note down, as they read, striking phrases, sayings, figures and similar flowers of Latin speech, and then repeat several times during the day of Saturday the ornaments of style gathered there throughout the week, and from time to time recall them to memory. Let these things said about acquiring facility in Latin speech, and about the aids necessary for it, suffice. Now I shall also say a few words about the parts of philosophy.

units.la: De studio partium Philosophiæ.
units.tr: On the study of the parts of philosophy.

units.la: Cùm tres partes Philosophia cõplectatur, quarum prima sermonem in quauis lingua formať, ut eo explicari res, & graues causæ disertè & ornatè exponi possint, secunda rerum in natura noti- ciam tradit, tertia mores instruit: duas dicendi artes Dialecticam & Rhetoricam (nam de Gram- matica, Latina & Græca lingua suprà dictum est) summo studio cognoscant pueri, non tantum ut præcepta discãt, sed etiam ut vsum aliquem sibi artium harum faciant scribendo et disputando. Præ- cepta Dialectices explicabo, qua potero diligëtia, hora secunda dierum Lunæ, Martis, Iouis, & Ve- neris. Rhetoricen publicè prælego, & priuatim addo Quintiliani libros, ut habeant grandiores natu supra elementa Rhetorices accuratiorem etiam explicationem. Quod uero ad usum harum artium attinet, argumenta scriptionum accommodabo fere semper ad exercendam aliquam partem praeceptorum, nunc Dialecticorum, nunc Rhetoricorum. Cumq; animaduertero discipulos, confirmata Grammaticae cognitione, praecepta Dialectices mediocriter tenere de syllogismis faciendis, et soluendis uitiosis argumentis, disputandi quoq; morem instituam. Audiant etiam adolescentes publice elementa eius doctrinae, quae rerum naturas inquirit et patefacit, maxime rudimenta doctrinae cum de motibus corporum coelestium, quae in libello de sphaera traduntur, tum de uiribus et effectibus syderum, quibus in haec inferiora corpora agunt stellae, quam Astrologiam uulgo uocat. Cum autem ad utramq; artem, et postea in tota uita, necessarius et summus usus sit Arithmeticae, magno studio pueri in ea partem, et statim a primis annis usq; incumbent: dabuntq; operam, ut promptam et celerem facultatem recte numerandi etiam difficiliores rationes multo usu sibi comparent. Quare et publice eius artis praecepta audiat, et ego priuatim hora duodecima diei Mercurij eorundem repetitionem et exercitationem instituam. Cumq; aliquid profecisse discipulos uidero, postea, ut exempla habeant exerexercendorum numerorũ, monstrabo illis ratione construendi figuram cœli ad quælibet tempora γε νέσεω, quæ exercitatio voluptate pueris non mediocrem afferet. Et hæc nunc quidem de rerum naturalium cognitione sufficere existimo, quibus cognitis, ad alias Physicæ partes abstrusiores poterunt accedere natu maiores. Ethica præcepta discant pueri publice à D. Philippo. Sed ut communis Iuris quasi summam animo complecti possint, & ut intelligant Iuris formulas, quæ in lectione Latinorum scriptorum ubiq; se offerunt, decreui, Deo iuvante, die Mercurij, hora quinta libellos institutionum tantùm Grammaticè explicare, ut noticiã vocabulorum aliquam acquirant, non profecto arrogantia aliqua adductus, aut ut falcem in alienã messem mittam, cùm facilè agnoscam me nequaquam parem ésse ad Iuris doctrinam docendam, quam ipse non didici: sed tantùm hanc ob causam eam lectionem instituam, ut vocabula, & phrases, quæ Iuris scientiæ sunt peculiares, & tamen à Latinis scriptoribus creberrimè usurpatæ, aliquanto notiora fiant adolescentibus meæ fidei commissis. Res ipsas, quæ ad Iuris ciuilis intellectum pertinet, discant ij, qui se illi studio totos aliquando dedent, ab ijs, qui ex professo Iuris scientiam docent. Pertinet ad Ethicam doctrinam etiam studium colligendi virtutum exempla, negotiorum, & casuum communium, munium, & insignium mutationum in Imperijs, ex Historicorũ & aliorum scriptis. Sed cùm historiæ non facilè propter temporis angustiam pueris enarrari possint, priuato ipsorum studio hanc operam commendo, ut si quando interuallo incidant, ubi à lectionibus publicis aut priuatis uacatio erit, ante omnia perlegant ordine Chronicon Philippi, quod Carionis nomine est uulgatum, in quo summam temporum & præcipuarum rerum gestarũ, item Monarchiarum successionem et durationem, ac causas mutationum diligenter obseruent. Deinde cognoscant Latinas historias ordinè, Plinium, Liuium, Sallustium, Cæsarem, Suetonium. Vtq; cum maiori fructu historias legant, habeāt in promptu librum continentem locos communium locorum Ethicorum, ad quos referant, si quid insigne in historijs ueniat, quod obseruatione dignũ uideatur. Hæc diligentia multas continet utilitates, ut alibi dicetur. Tantum nunc habui, quod de secundo fine dicendum esse arbitrabar, qui est de studio linguarum & artium.
units.tr: Philosophy comprises three parts. The first forms speech in any language, so that things can be explained through it and weighty matters can be set out clearly and elegantly. The second gives knowledge of the things in nature. The third instructs in morals. Boys should learn thoroughly the two arts of speech, Dialectic and Rhetoric (for Grammar, both Latin and Greek, has been discussed above). They should not only learn the precepts but also make some practical use of these arts by writing and disputing. I will explain the precepts of Dialectic as carefully as I can, at the second hour on Mondays, Tuesdays, Thursdays and Fridays. I will lecture publicly on Rhetoric and privately add the books of Quintilian, so that the older boys have a more exact explanation of its elements. As for practice in these arts, I will generally fit the subjects of their written exercises to some part of the precepts, now of Dialectic and now of Rhetoric. When I see that the pupils have a firm grasp of Grammar and hold the precepts of Dialectic reasonably well, I will also set up practice in disputation, including how to form syllogisms and how to refute faulty arguments. Young men will also attend public lessons on the elements of that doctrine which investigates and reveals the natures of things, chiefly the first principles of the motions of the heavenly bodies, as they are set out in the little book on the sphere, and of the powers and effects of the stars by which they act on these lower bodies, which is commonly called astrology. Since Arithmetic is necessary and of the greatest use both for these two arts and for the whole of later life, boys will apply themselves to it with great zeal from their earliest years onward. They will take care to acquire through much practice a ready and quick skill in calculating correctly, even in more difficult reckonings. So they should hear the precepts of this art in public, and I will myself hold a private repetition and exercise in it on Wednesdays at the twelfth hour. When I see that the pupils have made some progress, I will afterwards show them, so that they have examples for working out numbers, how to construct a horoscope figure for any given moment of birth [γενέσεως]; this exercise will give the boys no small pleasure. For now I think enough has been said about knowledge of natural things. Once that is acquired, the older boys can go on to the more abstruse parts of Physics. Boys should learn the precepts of Ethics in public from Dr. Philip. But so that they can grasp, as it were, the sum of civil law and understand the legal formulas that appear everywhere in reading Latin writers, I have decided, God helping, to explain on Wednesdays at the fifth hour only the Institutes, and to do so grammatically, so that they acquire some knowledge of the vocabulary. I am not moved by any arrogance, nor do I mean to put my sickle into another's harvest, since I readily acknowledge that I am by no means equal to teaching the doctrine of law, which I have not myself learned. I undertake this reading only for this reason: that the words and phrases peculiar to the science of law, yet used very frequently by Latin writers, may become somewhat more familiar to the young men entrusted to my care. The subject matter itself, which belongs to the understanding of civil law, those who devote themselves wholly to that study will learn later from those who teach the science of law professionally. To Ethical doctrine also belongs the study of gathering examples of virtues, and of the affairs, common cases, duties and notable changes in empires, from the writings of historians and others. But since histories cannot easily be recounted to boys because of the shortness of time, I commend this task to their private study. If at any time they have an interval, when there is free time from public or private lessons, they should first read through in order the Chronicle of Philip, which is published under the name of Carion, in which they should carefully note the summary of the times and of the principal deeds, likewise the succession and duration of the monarchies, and the causes of the changes. Then they should read the Latin histories in order: Pliny, Livy, Sallust, Caesar, Suetonius. And so that they may read histories with greater profit, they should keep ready a book containing commonplaces of Ethics, to which they can refer whatever striking thing occurs in the histories that seems worthy of notice. This diligence has many advantages, as will be said elsewhere. I have now said what I thought should be said about the second end, which is the study of languages and arts.

units.la: De tertio fine.
units.tr: On the third end.

units.la: Reliquum est, ut de tertio fine aliquid præcipiã, qui ut dictum est, morum etiã gubernationem flagitat, & continet exercitationem maximè earum uirtutũ, quæ nos in cœtu uiuentes regunt & moderantur, ut ipsi tolerari ab alijs, et uicissim nos alios ferre possimus. Sunt autem illæ uirtutes præcipuè: ciuilitas, uerecundia, obedietia, humanitas, candor seu ueritas, modestia, mansuetudo, beneficetia, gra titudo, iusticia, linguæ moderatus usus. Cùm autem hæ uirtutes alibi copiosius describãtur, hìc tantùm extrema singulorum uitia indicare satis esse duxi, ut ea pueri summa diligentia fugienda esse cogitēt.
units.tr: It remains that I say something about the third end which, as stated, also requires the guidance of morals, and which consists chiefly in the practice of those virtues that govern and regulate us as we live in society, so that we may bear with others and in turn be borne with by them. The principal virtues are these: courtesy, modesty, obedience, humanity, candour or truthfulness, moderation, gentleness, beneficence, gratitude, justice, and the moderate use of the tongue. Since these virtues are described more fully elsewhere, I have thought it enough to point out here only the extreme vices of each, so that the boys may consider that they must be avoided with the greatest care.

units.la: Cum ciuilitate pugnat:
units.tr: Against courtesy:

units.la: Rusticitas, sordiũ amor: | Affectatio elegantiæ et ciuilitatis odiosa, qualis est in quibusdam aulicis & mulierculis.
units.tr: Rudeness and love of filth. Also an overdone affectation of elegance and courtesy, such as is found in some courtiers and silly women.

units.la: Cum uerecundia:
units.tr: Against modesty (verecundia):

units.la: Impudentia: | Stupor, rusticus pudor.
units.tr: Shamelessness. Dullness, or a boorish sort of shame.

units.la: Cum obedientia:
units.tr: Against obedience:

units.la: Contumacia, negligentia: | Simulatio obsequij, itè obedientia in re flagitiosa.
units.tr: Obstinacy and negligence. Feigned compliance, or obedience in a shameful matter.

units.la: Cum humanitate:
units.tr: Against humanity (humanitas):

units.la: Durus, aut qui non afficitur alienis rebus, nec libenter fert communia onera, μισανθρωπία: | Adulatio, & nimia facilitas, futilitasq; in amicitiis iungendis: item φιλοφρονοσύνη in suscipienda cura alienarum rerum.
units.tr: Harshness, or a man who is unmoved by others' affairs and unwilling to bear common burdens gladly [misanthropia, μισανθρωπία]. Also flattery and excessive easiness, and frivolity in forming friendships; likewise a fawning eagerness [philophrosyne, φιλοφρονοσύνη] in taking up the care of others' affairs.

units.la: Cum candore seu ueritate:
units.tr: Against candour or truthfulness:

units.la: Suspicacem esse, | Credulitas, non discernens calumnia, | nens recta à prauis, afironia, | fentatio, laudans etiam mendacium: | praua.
units.tr: Being suspicious; credulity, not distinguishing right from wrong; folly; dissimulation; and praising even a lie.

units.la: Cum modestia:
units.tr: Against moderation (modestia):

units.la: Superbia, φιλαυτία, arrogantia, contemptus aliorum: | Abiectio hypocritica, seu extenuatio immodica suorum donorum: item assentatio, omnia aliorũ nostris præferēs.
units.tr: Pride, self-love [philautia, φιλαυτία], arrogance, contempt for others. Hypocritical abasement, or an immoderate belittling of one's own gifts; likewise servility, preferring everything of others to our own.

units.la: Cum mansuetudine:
units.tr: Against gentleness:

units.la: Iracundia, acerbitas, morositas, cupiditas uindictæ: | ἀοργησία, patientia parasitica, simulatio lenitatis occultè captans occasionem ulciscendi.
units.tr: Anger, bitterness, peevishness, and a desire for revenge. Lack of anger [aorgesia, ἀοργησία], parasitic patience, or a pretended mildness that secretly seeks an occasion for revenge.

units.la: Cum beneficentia:
units.tr: Against beneficence:

units.la: Sordes, illiberalitas, tenacitas, maleuolētia, cupiditas lædēdi, premendi, impediendi alios: | Prodigalitas, largitiones officiorum, profusio, facilitas erga quoslibet, neglectis suis reb.
units.tr: Meanness, illiberality, tightfistedness, ill will, and a desire to harm, oppress or hinder others. Prodigality, lavish offers of services, extravagance, and an easy readiness toward anyone at all while neglecting one's own affairs.

units.la: Cum gratitudine:
units.tr: Against gratitude:

units.la: Ingratitudo, nocere benefactori: | Seruitus, cùm quis gratificatur benefacere in re turpi aut impia.
units.tr: Ingratitude, and harming a benefactor. Servility, when someone goes along with a benefactor by doing something base or impious.

units.la: Cum iustitia:
units.tr: Against justice:

units.la: Rapacitas, πλεονεξία, fraudatio: | Rigor iuris, ἀκριβοδι-καιον.
units.tr: Rapacity, greed [pleonexia, πλεονεξία], and fraud. Rigour of the law [akribodikaion, ἀκριβοδίκαιον].

units.la: Cum moderato usu linguæ:
units.tr: Against the moderate use of speech:

units.la: Δυσωπία, occultatio insidiosa, silentium contumax, superbum, fastidiosum: Garrulitas, uanitas, præcipitatia, curiositas, coniuratio, maledicentia, obtrectatio, φιλονενία, scurrilitas, futilitas.
units.tr: Importunity [dysopia, δυσωπία]; treacherous concealment; stubborn, haughty, disdainful silence; chattering, vanity, rashness, curiosity, conspiracy, slander, detraction, contentiousness [philoneikia, φιλονεικία], buffoonery, and frivolity.

units.la: Hæc uitia agnoscere in alijs, & odisse, & acer- rimo conatu uitare iam inde usq; à pueritia scholastici debent, & obseruare, ad quæ uitia singulorum naturæ sint pronæ, ut illas inclinationes ratione & iudicio, uitatis occasionibus, flectere & cohercere assuefiant. Eam ob causam prodest pueros statim ex angulis et solitudine in cœtus et scholas frequentes produci, ubi occasio sit & agnoscendorum uitiorum, & econtrà uirtutis exercendæ.
units.tr: Students ought, from their boyhood onwards, to recognise these vices in others and to hate them, and to avoid them with the sharpest effort. They should also observe to which of these vices each person's nature is inclined, so that they may get used to bending and restraining those inclinations by reason and judgement, by avoiding the occasions. For this reason it is useful to bring boys at once out of corners and solitude into crowded gatherings and schools, where there is an opportunity both to recognise vices and, on the other hand, to practise virtue.

units.la: Quare ut plures fiant causæ pueris meis cõuenien di, utq; facilius ad communia officia humanitatis assuefiant, inter eos, ut in Republica, ordines & gradus secundum profectum & captum constituere decreui, ut interdum aliquas committere, & interdum uel uersuum Gnomicorum recitatione concertent, uel ænigmatis aut obscuris & intricatis constructionibus ingenij uim & celeritatè acuant & exerceãt, unde victi cum pudore, victores præmijs ornati discedant, & hoc modo partim amore laudis, partim metu reprehensionis excitabũtur liberales. berales etiam ad diligentiam in discendo. Tempora autem illis certaminibus tribuenda, satis maturè semper indicabimus. Nec uerò negligi aliæ uirtutes debent, quibus singuli etiam extra cœtus, mores suos & cupiditates ad præscriptum rationis, et imprimis ad uoluntatem Dei regere conabuntur, ut sunt, pietas, temperantia, castitas, uigilantia, fortitudo in tolerandis difficultatibus, sine quibus nec doctrina Ecclesiæ cognosci, nec studia literarum coli possunt. Hæc de ratione uitæ & studiorum secundum tres fines in summa dixi, quæ isti ætati, discentium primas artes cõuenire iudicaui. Si quæ sint prætermissa, illa per sese quisque facilè addet. Cætera ita sunt pro ratione præsentis status & morum attemperata discentium commodis, ut nisi me opinio mea uehementer fallat, existimem, si quis iuxtà præscriptam rationem instituatur, & aliquandiu exerceatur, eum breui tempore non exiguam accessionem morum probitati, eruditioni, & iudicio factam esse, reipsa deprehensurum. Sed tamen ut id facilius fiat, necessariò addenda est admonitio ista, omnia sic demum profutura esse: primùm, si omnes conatus nostros referamus ad obedientiam Deo præstandam, & ad gloriam eius ornandam & celebrandam: deinde, si opem diuinam assiduè & sine intermissione imploremus, & petamus, ut ipse studijs nostris successus felices aspiret. Postremò, si freti conscientia piæ voluntatis & fiducia diuini auxilij, acri studio & indefessa diligentia præscriptam rationem studiorum & uitæ seruare conemur. Vt autem in conspectu pueri habeat breuiter descriptas diuersas operas, breuiter eas ex his legibus decerptas in tabellam aliquam redigant, quàm singulis diebus mane, post finitas preces inspiciant, & de illius diei penso commonefiant, & sub noctem rursus perlustrent, num quid partis studiorum omissum sit.
units.tr: Therefore, so that my boys may have more occasions for meeting together, and so that they may more easily become accustomed to the common duties of humanity, I have decided to set up among them, as in a commonwealth, ranks and grades according to their progress and ability. Sometimes they will compete in some task, sometimes in reciting verses of the Gnomic poets, sometimes in riddles or obscure and intricate constructions, and thereby they will sharpen and exercise the force and quickness of their wits. So the defeated will leave with shame, and the victors will leave adorned with prizes; and in this way the boys will be stirred up, partly by the love of praise and partly by the fear of reproof, and made keen and freely willing to diligence in learning. I will always indicate sufficiently early the times to be given to those contests. Nor indeed should the other virtues be neglected, by which each boy, even outside the gatherings, will try to govern his morals and desires according to the rule of reason, and above all according to the will of God: such as piety, temperance, chastity, watchfulness, and fortitude in bearing difficulties. Without these, neither the teaching of the Church can be known nor the studies of letters cultivated. I have now said, in summary, these things about the plan of life and studies according to the three ends, which I judged suited to this age of pupils beginning their first arts. If anything has been omitted, each person will easily add it for himself. The rest is so adapted to the circumstances of the present state and the manners of the pupils, for their benefit, that, unless my opinion greatly deceives me, I think that if anyone is trained according to the prescribed plan and practised in it for some time, he will in a short while discover in fact that no small addition has been made to his uprightness of character, his learning and his judgement. But so that this may happen more easily, this warning must necessarily be added: all these things will in the end profit only if, first, we refer all our efforts to rendering obedience to God and to adorning and celebrating his glory; then, if we constantly and without interruption implore and ask for divine help, that he himself may breathe happy success on our studies; and finally, if, relying on the consciousness of a pious will and on confidence in divine aid, we try to keep the prescribed plan of studies and life with keen zeal and untiring diligence. So that the boy may have before his eyes the various tasks briefly described, let them reduce them briefly, extracted from these rules, into some small table, which they may look at every morning after the prayers are finished, and be reminded of the day's allotted work; and again at nightfall let them run through it, to see whether any part of the studies has been left undone.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Finis legum, quas excellenti doctrina præstans, & de multorum studijs benemeritus uir, olim Vuitebergæ suis discipulis præscribebat.
units.tr: The end of the rules which a man, outstanding in learning and well deserving of the studies of many, once prescribed to his pupils at Wittenberg.

units.la: Ecclesia non potest carere scholis, quæ semper ipsi fuerunt adiunctæ.
units.tr: The Church cannot do without the schools that have always been joined to it.

units.la: Nunquam uera Ecclesia sine scholis aliquibus fuit, ac ne potest quidem diu conseruari doctrina, nisi scholastici cœtus adiungatur ad ecclesias. Haud dubiè primis patribus, Adæ, Noe, Sem ideo prorogata est uita tot seculis, ut auditores haberent testes ἀξιοπίστους de prima origine generis humani deque initio doctrinæ. Postea familiæ Abrahã, Isaac & Iacob prorsus scholæ fuerunt. Deinde, cùm lex Moysi data est, iam clarum mandatum de scholis additum
units.tr: The true Church has never existed without some schools, and doctrine cannot long be preserved unless a body of scholars is attached to the churches. Surely it was for this reason that the first fathers, Adam, Noah and Shem, were granted such long lives over so many centuries: their hearers would have trustworthy witnesses [ἀξιοπίστους] to the first origin of the human race and to the beginning of doctrine. Afterwards the families of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were altogether schools. Then, when the law was given through Moses, a clear command concerning schools was added

units.la: Ecclesiæ additum est. Constitutum est enim, ut ad tabernaculum semper essent coetus docentium & discentiū. Nam in politia Moysi, ad tabernaculum classes Sacerdotum & Leuitarū constituta fuerunt, non solum ut ibi mactarent pecudes, sed multo magis, ut legem populo enarrarent, responderent ambigentibus animis, & dijudicarent dogmatū controversias, ut clarè testatur caput 17 Deuteronomij, ubi iubet deferri cōtroversias ad sacerdotes Leuiticos, & ad locum tabernaculi, & iudicari res non ex arbitrijs potētum, sed ex lege diuina. Illud Collegiū, uel Academia optimè constituta, usq; ad Christum, circiter 1500 annos, doctrinae diuinae interpres & custos fuit. Illi Collegio traditus est in disciplinam Samuel, perinde ac si esset in Acadamiam bene constitutam missus. Postea cùm negligerent studia sacerdotes, Deus excitauit prophetas, qui magnas cateryas discentium secum traxerunt. Tantum enim agmen erat eruditorū Elisaei, ut cùm antea in Hiericho habitassent, postea propter eius loci angustiā quaererent ad Iordanem aliam sedem. Post Samuelem floruit Nathan: deinde Achias Silonites sub Salomone & Ieroboam: hunc secutus est Ananias Assae tempore. Deinde excitatus est Elias, qui cùm diu res maximas gessisset, & docuisset circiter annos triginta antequā à Deo in cœlum euectus est, successorem Elisēum elegit, qui annos septuaginta cee gubergubernauit Ecclesiam Israel. Vidit hunc adolescens Esaias. Eliseo uero successit Ionas, quem arbitrātur fuisse filium mulieris Sareptanæ, ab Elia reuocatum ex morte. Cæterùm abductis decem tribubus, successit Esaias in Iuda, qui docuit annos octoginta, & liberauit regnū ingentibus bellis. Nam quilibet Propheta habet aliquod insigne ѡολίτευμα. Post Esaiam excitatus est Hieremias, qui annos quadraginta concionatus est. Post Hieremiam, Daniel: qui etsi instituitur doctrina Chaldæorum, tamen hunc uicissim postea reges omnium maximi, tanquam discipuli, audiunt, Nabochdonosor, Euilmerodach, Darius Medus, et Cyrus. Danielem secutus est Zacharias: ipsum uero Esdras & Hieremias, qui attigerū Alexandri Macedonis ætatē. Nehemiam Onias secutus est, celebratus in Ecclesiaste. Postea Simeon Oniæ filius doctrinæ puritatem cōseruauit. Aliquanto post secuta sunt Machabæorū bella, quo tēpore sacerdotes diu iam Ethnicorum more certauerūt ambitione de principatu, et doctrinam ac disciplinā flagitiosè neglexerunt. Accidit enim eo tēpore, quod omnib. temporib. fit, ut si quis unico uerbo autoritatē alicuius in officio uersantis offenderit, certè nō Deū conditorē illius hominis, sed diabolos ipsos læsisse discas, qui nunquā audiuerunt aut docuerūt illam doctrinā in Dominica oratiōe à Deo præscriptā, Remittite, et remittetur mittetur uobis. Sed exortus est tandem Mathatias sacerdos, legis diuinae assertor. Ita Machabaei restituerunt doctrinam. Post hos creuit impudentia in populo Dei: & repudiatis Prophetarum monumentis, coeperunt ingenia prophana amare Graecam philosophiam. Hinc extiterunt sectae diversae Pharisaeorum & Sadducaeorum, qui palam Epicureas opiniones professi sunt. Itaque cum diu horribiles essent tenebrae in populo Dei, Deus rursus excitauit Ichoas per Simeonem & Zachariam, quorum mentio fit in Luca. Deinde per Iohannem baptistam, postquam docere coepit Christus, qui scholam Apostolorum habuit assiduam. Et Hebraei affirmant Mosis institutum (qui septuaginta seniores elegit, ut scribitur capite 11. Numerorum) mansisse in omnem posteritatem, idque postea fuisse collegium doctissimorum hominum, quod nominarunt Sanhedrin, quod pro Graeca voce συνέδριον usurparunt. Sed qualiscunque ille Senatus fuit, Prophetas constat habuisse assidua auditorum agmina. Hunc morem, quem uiderant Apostoli seruatum a Prophetis, Baptista & Christo, retinuerunt & ipsi. Nam hos quoque suas scholas habuisse apparet ex Irenaeo, dicente, Iohannem Apostolum Ephesi habuisse assiduos multos auditores, & in his Polycarpum, qui postea in Ecclesia Smyrnia circiter quinquaginta annos doctrinam ab Iohanne traditam feliciter propagauit.
units.tr: to the Church. For it was ordained that there should always be assemblies of teachers and learners at the tabernacle. In the polity of Moses, companies of priests and Levites were established at the tabernacle, not only to slaughter the cattle there, but much more to expound the law to the people, to answer those whose minds were troubled, and to decide controversies of doctrine. This is clearly attested in chapter 17 of Deuteronomy, where it is commanded that controversies be brought before the Levitical priests and to the place of the tabernacle, and that matters be judged not by the will of the powerful but by the divine law. That college, or academy, was very well constituted, and until Christ, for about 1500 years, it was the interpreter and guardian of divine doctrine. Samuel was handed over to that college for training, just as if he had been sent to a well-ordered academy. Later, when the priests neglected their studies, God raised up prophets, who drew great crowds of learners after them. Indeed, the company of learned men around Elisha was so large that, although they had previously lived in Jericho, they afterwards sought another dwelling by the Jordan because of the narrowness of that place. After Samuel, Nathan flourished; then Ahijah the Shilonite under Solomon and Jeroboam; he was followed by Hanani in the time of Asa. Then Elijah was raised up, who, after he had long accomplished very great things and taught for about thirty years before he was taken up into heaven by God, chose Elisha as his successor, who governed the Church of Israel for seventy years. The young Isaiah saw him. Jonah succeeded Elisha, whom they think was the son of the Sarepta woman, recalled from death by Elijah. Moreover, when the ten tribes were carried off, Isaiah succeeded in Judah; he taught for eighty years and freed the kingdom by great wars. For every prophet has some distinctive political achievement [πολίτευμα]. After Isaiah, Jeremiah was raised up, who preached for forty years. After Jeremiah came Daniel, who, although he was trained in the learning of the Chaldeans, was in turn heard afterwards by the greatest kings, as though they were his pupils: Nebuchadnezzar, Evil-Merodach, Darius the Mede, and Cyrus. Zechariah followed Daniel; Ezra and Jeremiah, who reached the time of Alexander the Great, came after him. Onias followed Nehemiah, celebrated in Ecclesiasticus. Afterwards Simon, the son of Onias, preserved the purity of doctrine. Not long after came the wars of the Maccabees, at which time the priests had long been contending for leadership in the manner of the Gentiles, out of ambition, and had shamefully neglected doctrine and discipline. For at that time, as at all times, it happened that if anyone offended the authority of one holding office by a single word, you may be sure that it was not God, the creator of that man, who was injured, but the devils themselves, who never heard or taught that doctrine prescribed by God in the Lord's Prayer: "Forgive, and you will be forgiven." But at last Mattathias the priest arose, a defender of the divine law. Thus the Maccabees restored doctrine. After these, impudence grew among the people of God; and, rejecting the records of the prophets, they began to love profane wits and Greek philosophy. From this arose the diverse sects of the Pharisees and Sadducees, who openly professed Epicurean opinions. And so, when the darkness among the people of God had lasted for a long time, God again raised up Jehoash through Simeon and Zechariah, who are mentioned in Luke. Then through John the Baptist, after Christ began to teach, who had a constant school of Apostles. The Hebrews also affirm that the institution of Moses (who chose seventy elders, as is written in chapter 11 of Numbers) remained for all posterity, and that afterwards it was a college of most learned men, which they called the Sanhedrin, taking the name from the Greek word [συνέδριον]. But whatever sort of senate that was, it is certain that the prophets had constant crowds of hearers. This custom, which the Apostles had seen kept by the prophets, by the Baptist and by Christ, they too retained. For it is clear from Irenaeus that these also had their own schools, since he says that the Apostle John at Ephesus had many constant hearers, and among them Polycarp, who afterwards in the Church of Smyrna for about fifty years happily spread the doctrine handed down from John.

units.la: Huius auditor Irenæus doctrinæ riuos in Galliâ et Pannoniam duxit. Ac fuisse tales scholas apparet, ubicunq; frequentiores Ecclesiæ fuerunt. Celebratissimæ fuerūt, Antiochena, Alexandrina, Cæsariensis, in qua Origenes docuit: Byzantina, in qua Basilium didicisse Nazianzenus scribit. Nec aliud fuisse initio Collegia canonicorū certum est, quàm docentium & discentium cœtus. Et in ipsa Germania ante Attilam fuerunt adiunctæ scholæ mediocres Ecclesijs. Nam Irenæus & Epiphanius citant testimonia Germanicarum ecclesiarum. Qua ex re apparet, cito propagatum fuisse Euangelium in Germaniam, & aliqua literarum studia in hac natione fuisse. Legimus etiā Lucium Cyrenæum Pauli discipulum primùm docuisse Euangelium ad Danubium in Augusta Tiberina, quæ nunc est Ratisbona: eaq; in loca uenisse eum cum Romanis exercitibus, qui tenebant Rhetias, consentaneum est. Illuxit Euangelium Argentorati populo, & Agrippinæ Coloniæ Doctore Materno, Petri discipulo Trophimum Arelati fuisse Eusebius testatur. Clemens Metenses ad Christi agnitionem uocauit. Crescentem aiunt uenisse Moguntiam. Marcum Pauli discipulum (antiqua monumenta Ecclesiæ Passauiensis, ad Danubium testantur) cōcionatum esse in urbe Iuliobona, quæ sedes fuit Episcopi in Norico ante collegiū Passauiense. Tot magni & sapientes tes uiri,cùm in Germaniam & Galliam uenissent, hauddubiè praecipuam studiorum curam habuerunt, ut ad posteros per homines rectè institutos et solidè doctos Euangelium rectè propagaretur. Etsi autem postea temporibus Barbaricis cum Vandalicis Hunnica & Francica bella magnas uastitates fecissent, ita ut uetera Collegia euersa essent: tamen qualescunq; reliquiae Ecclesiae, quae supererant, carere literis non potuerunt. Rursus igitur Collegia canonicorum, & monasteria condita sunt. Et cùm in Collegijs canonicorũ studia negligerētur, quòd essent occupati regum & aularum negocijs: munus docendi in monasteria est translatũ. Hæc cùm onerarentur ceremonijs, non potuerunt docendi laborem molestum & difficilem simul sustinere. Exortæ simul sunt Academiæ, in quibus studia literarum utcunq; exercitata sunt. Sed disciplinæ vincula nimium laxata sunt. Ex hac historica commemoratione satis intelligi potest, & semper fuisse adiunctas scholas Ecclesijs, & amissis literis, lucem Euangelij extingui.
units.tr: A hearer of this man, Irenaeus, led streams of this doctrine into Gaul and Pannonia. And it is clear that such schools existed wherever the churches were more numerous. The most famous were those of Antioch, Alexandria and Caesarea, where Origen taught, and Byzantium, where Nazianzen writes that Basil learned. It is certain that at first canonical colleges were nothing other than assemblies of teachers and learners. Even in Germany itself, before Attila, moderate schools were joined to the churches. For Irenaeus and Epiphanius cite testimonies of the German churches. From this it appears that the Gospel spread quickly into Germany, and that there were some studies of letters in that nation. We also read that Lucius of Cyrene, a disciple of Paul, first taught the Gospel by the Danube in Augusta Tiberina, which is now Regensburg; and it is consistent that he came to those places with the Roman armies that held Raetia. The Gospel shone on the people of Strasbourg, and Eusebius testifies that Maternus, the teacher of Cologne Agrippina and a disciple of Peter, and Trophimus at Arles. Clement called the people of Metz to the knowledge of Christ. They say that Crescens came to Mainz. The ancient records of the Church of Passau, by the Danube, testify that Mark, a disciple of Paul, preached in the city of Iuliobona, which was the seat of a bishop in Noricum before the college of Passau. So many great and wise men, when they came into Germany and Gaul, undoubtedly took the greatest care of studies, so that the Gospel might be rightly spread to posterity through men rightly trained and soundly learned. Yet although afterwards, in barbarian times, the Vandal, Hunnic and Frankish wars caused great devastation, so that the old colleges were overthrown, nevertheless whatever remnants of the Church survived could not do without letters. Therefore canonical colleges and monasteries were founded again. And when studies were neglected in the canonical colleges, because they were busy with the affairs of kings and courts, the duty of teaching was transferred to the monasteries. But since these were burdened with ceremonies, they could not at the same time bear the troublesome and difficult labour of teaching. Academies arose at the same time, in which the studies of letters were practised in some fashion. But the bonds of discipline were loosened too much. From this historical account it can be sufficiently understood both that schools were always joined to the churches, and that when letters are lost, the light of the Gospel is extinguished.

units.la: Sint Academiæ aristocratiæ, ut aluceoli[?] apum, suum quisq; officium rectè faciat: doceamus utilia: conferamus operas candidè: iuuemus nos mutuo: tueamur communem quandam concordiam cum quadam philosophica moderatione.
units.tr: Let academies be aristocracies, like hives of bees: let each one rightly do his own duty; let us teach useful things, bring our labours together in good faith, help one another, and maintain a common concord with a certain philosophical moderation.

units.la: Alia ratio studendi, parum dissimilis à priore, cuidam Iuris studioso ante viginti annos aut circiter, à D. Philippo Melanchthone præscripta.
units.tr: Another method of study, little different from the earlier one, prescribed some twenty years ago or thereabouts by Philip Melanchthon to a certain student of law.

units.la: Initiò finis constituendus est studiorum. ut enim in aliis omnibus deliberationibus quæri solet, quâ utilitatem, quem fructum adferre possit, quod suscepimus: ita etiam in studijs initio considerandum est, quâ ad vitam utilitatem adferre queant. Et eligeda sunt ea studia quæ plurimũ conferũt tũ ad vitâ priuatâ, tum ad Reipub. rectè administrandas.
units.tr: The aim of studies must be settled first. As in all other deliberations, we usually ask what benefit or fruit a undertaking can bring, so too in studies we must consider at the outset what use they can be for life. We should choose those studies that contribute most both to private life and to the proper administration of the commonwealth.

units.la: Prima sit cura cognoscendæ doctrinæ Christianæ, iuxta illud: Primum quærite regnum Dei. Sed ad eam cognoscendam satis erit audire unam Lutheri prælectionem: item conciones diebus Dominicis & festis audire sufficit. Item methodũ aliquâ. nam in omnibus artibus oportet tenere summam aliquam: idq; maximè opus est in doctrina religionis. Ad hoc conducent uel epistola ad Romanos, uel ad Colossenses, uel Loci cõmunes à me scripti: neq; totum diem assidere oportet Theologicis libellis. Satis est Dominicam diem in horum conferre lectionem. Et mane cùm surrexeris, aut cum uesperi cubitum ibis, legendum aliquid in Biblijs, quod ad precadum excitet, ita simul multa disces.
units.tr: The first care should be to learn Christian doctrine, according to the saying: Seek first the kingdom of God. To learn it, it will be enough to hear one lecture of Luther's, and it is also sufficient to hear sermons on Sundays and feast days. Also some method is useful, for in every art one must hold to some summary, and this is especially needed in the doctrine of religion. Either the Epistle to the Romans or the Epistle to the Colossians will serve for this, or my Loci communes. Nor should you sit over theological booklets all day; it is enough to devote the Lord's day to reading them. And when you rise in the morning, or go to bed in the evening, read something in the Bible that stirs you to prayer; so you will learn much at the same time.

units.la: Altera pars studiorum nõ minus necessaria est, ut ut tractatio literarum humanarum: nam ad uitam opus est multis alijs artibus. Sed tibi prodest adhuc aliquantisper in studio recte dicendi uersari: quia mediocris ratio benedicendi necessaria est ad religionem, ad ius, & ad omnia ciuilia officia uitae. Audiendi in literis Latinis Ciceronis libri de Officijs, Rhetorica: sed addenda etiam philosophiae scientia. Ideo sunt audienda elementa Mathematum, et die Mercurij Politica. Sic duas Philosophiae partes discess: Naturalem & moralem.
units.tr: The other part of studies is no less necessary, namely the study of humane letters. For life needs many other arts. But it still profits you to spend some time on the study of speaking well, because a moderate skill in speaking is necessary for religion, for law, and for all civic duties of life. Listen in Latin literature to Cicero's books On Duties and his Rhetoric; but the knowledge of philosophy must be added as well. Therefore you should attend the elements of mathematics, and on Wednesdays the Politics. In this way you will learn the two parts of philosophy: natural and moral.

units.la: Tertia pars discitur in Rhetoricis, Dialecticis. Est autem opera danda, ut libelli continentes Methodos, hoc est artium summas, diligenter discantur: ut Dialectica à me scripta, et Rhetorica: Epitome Philosophiae moralis, & Physices: Libellus Sphaericus, Politica, Institutiones Iustiniani. Domi biduu in septimana collocabis in Terentium, quem subinde debes relegere, ac satis est quotidie duas horas ad summum in hoc consumere. Nec uolo te aut multum ante lucem surgere, aut sero cubitum ire: sed omnino habenda ratio ualetudinis & sanitatis. Est item biduu collocandu in Liuiu. Dies unus collocetur in Graecas literas, audias lectore Graecae linguae. Quod superest temporis, conferendu est in exercitatione styli: propter quod intermitti interdu lectio Liuij poterit. Interdu legi etiam Vergilius aut Ouidius loco Liuij potest, ne assiduitas in authore difficili pariat tædium. Neq; enim ita putes te esse alligatum ad Liuium, quasi piaculum sit intermittere eius lectionem: satis est habere certum aliquod domicilium, ad quod te recipias, postquam fueris expatiatus ad Vergilium, Ouidium, aut Horatium. Stylum ita exercebis, ut alias scribas epistolas, alias uersus, alias ex Græco uertas. In authoribus quid sit obseruandum, disces in prælectionibus: uerba, phrases, sententiæ. Nunc ante omnia disces uersus facere, hic sit hoc tempore præcipuus labor. Leges igitur Prosodiam, & aliquid Vergilij, seu Ouidij, omisso Liuio. Tempus partiendum, & distribuendæ horæ, ita minuetur labor, & varietate quadam subinde recreabit se animus: nec tamen illa varietas nimis magna erit, qualis obesse solet in discendo. Dominicum totum diem ponendum censeo in lectionem sacrarum literarum, item totum diem Saturni. Legenda est autem aliqua epistola Pauli ab initio usq; ad finem, ut discas unde summa Christianæ doctrinæ (sicut in aliis studijs, summa quædam seu methodus comprehenditur) informetur. Ita in sacris literis præstandum est, ut totam doctrinam animo complectamur, alioqui fiet si carptim degustetur, ut sæpè in iudicando decipiaris. Lege initio epistolam ad Galatas cum Lutheri commento, uel Colossenses meos, et iterum atq; iterum relegi oportet.
units.tr: The third part is learned in rhetoric and dialectic. Care must be taken to study diligently the little books that contain the methods, that is, the summaries of the arts: such as my Dialectic and Rhetoric; the Epitome of moral philosophy and of physics; the Sphere booklet; the Politics; the Institutes of Justinian. At home, spend two days of the week on Terence, which you should reread from time to time, and it is enough to devote no more than two hours a day to this at most. Nor do I want you either to rise long before dawn or to go to bed late, but health and well-being must be taken fully into account. Likewise set aside two days for Livy. Let one day be given to Greek literature; attend a lecturer in the Greek language. For the remaining time, it should be spent on practice in writing style, for which the reading of Livy may sometimes be interrupted. Sometimes Virgil or Ovid may be read instead of Livy, lest constant attention to a difficult author breed boredom. You should not think yourself so bound to Livy as if it were a sin to skip his reading; it is enough to have a fixed home to return to, after you have wandered off to Virgil, Ovid, or Horace. Exercise your style by writing letters at one time, verses at another, and translating from the Greek at another. You will learn in lectures what should be observed in authors: words, phrases, sentences. Now above all you will learn to write verses; this is to be the chief labour at this time. So read prosody and some of Virgil or Ovid, leaving Livy aside. Divide your time and apportion your hours; in this way the labour will be lessened, and the mind will be refreshed from time to time by a certain variety. Yet this variety will not be too great, of the sort that usually hinders learning. I think the whole of Sunday should be given to reading Holy Scripture, and the whole of Saturday likewise. Some epistle of Paul should be read from beginning to end, so that you may learn from it the sum of Christian doctrine (as in other studies some summary or method is grasped), and be formed by it. In Holy Scripture this must be done, so that we take in the whole doctrine in our minds; otherwise, if it is tasted piecemeal, you will often be deceived in judging. First read the Epistle to the Galatians with Luther's commentary, or my Colossians, and you must read them again and again.

units.la: Die Lunæ collocetur una atq; altera hora in Ciceronis epistolis.
units.tr: On Monday let one or two hours be given to Cicero's Letters.

units.la: Die Martis ponatur una atq; altera in Terentij lectionem, illo prælecto legatur & Liuius.
units.tr: On Tuesday let one or two hours be given to the reading of Terence; after this lecture, Livy is also to be read.

units.la: Dies Mercurij totus collocetur in Græcas literas.
units.tr: Let all of Wednesday be given to Greek literature.

units.la: Dies Iouis et Veneris collocentur in lectionem Terentij & Liuij: his aliquoties prælectis legatur & Vergilius.
units.tr: Let Thursday and Friday be given to the reading of Terence and Livy; after these have been lectured on several times, Virgil is also to be read.

units.la: Reliquum tempus collocetur in exercitationem styli, alias in lectione alicuius poematis, aut aliud quiddam, pro arbitrio, ut tantum uoluptati studiorum seruiat.
units.tr: Let the remaining time be given to practice in writing style, at other times to the reading of some poem, or something else as one pleases, so that it serves only the delight of studies.

units.la: Nemo utiliter discet sine exercitatione styli, sed scribendum est ad alicuius iudicium, qui ostendet quid sit probandum, quid non sit probandum.
units.tr: No one learns profitably without practice in writing style, but one must write under the judgment of someone who will show what is to be approved and what is not to be approved.

units.la: Credo multas sententias Hieremiæ esse dictas ab Elia. Hieremias potuit esse auditor Eliæ, ut Daniel Hieremiæ.
units.tr: I believe many sayings of Jeremiah were uttered by Elijah. Jeremiah may have been a hearer of Elijah, as Daniel was of Jeremiah.

units.la: Clemens ait, se peruagatum esse totam Asiam, & de singulis doctrinæ articulis consuluisse erudi tos ubiq;: sed postquam uenit Alexandriam, fuisse se contentū iudicio Patiani, quem ait eruditione et pietate eximia præditum fuisse, ac ornatū testimo nijs Spiritus sancti, seu miraculis.
units.tr: Clement says that he travelled through the whole of Asia and everywhere consulted learned men on the individual articles of doctrine; but after he came to Alexandria, he was content with the judgment of Pantaenus, whom he says was endowed with outstanding learning and piety, and adorned with the testimonies of the Holy Spirit, that is, with miracles.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Dicitur de lyra Orphei, quòd peruenerit in eee ʒ Lesbum. Credo quòd ibi fuerint excellentia studia, ita ut ob eam causam dicta sit lyra Orphei eò pervenisse. Filius principis in Lesbo cogitauit, si caneret lyra Orphei, se futurum alterum Orpheum. Voluit trahere ad se bestias noctu, & cantauit. Eo igitur canente noctu, canes conuenerunt, & eum dilaniarunt. Iste est exitus ʻαναοξυλίας. Sic omnes iam uolūt esse Lutheri, sed lacerātur à canib. Quia semper ʻαναοξυλία est infelix. Mortuo Iulio Caesare, omnes interfectores eius ipsi conabātur esse pares. Quia unus quilibet cogitabat de Monarchia.
units.tr: It is said of the lyre of Orpheus that it came to Lesbos. I believe excellent studies flourished there, which is why the lyre of Orpheus is said to have arrived there. A prince's son in Lesbos thought that if he played the lyre of Orpheus he would become another Orpheus. He wanted to draw wild beasts to himself by night, and he sang. While he sang by night, dogs gathered and tore him apart. This is the end of ἀναοξυλίας (overreaching). So everyone now wants to be a Luther, but is torn to pieces by dogs, because ἀναοξυλία is always unhappy. After Julius Caesar was killed, all his murderers themselves tried to be his equals, since each of them thought about monarchy.

units.la: Plato, cùm obijceretur Philosophis, ipsos esse corruptores iuuētutis, inquit: Imò nos nō corrum pimus iuuentutem: sed uide theatra, illorum mugitibus implentur animi auditorum, & alienantur à recta doctrina, & uera uia.
