units.tr: When the philosophers were charged with corrupting the young, Plato replied: "No, we do not corrupt youth. Look rather at the theatres: the bellowing there fills the minds of the audience and draws them away from sound doctrine and the true way."

units.la: Noui Comitem, ex optimo & sapiente patre natum, qui propter summā suam sapientiā fuit ualde charus Imperatori. Is nimis amans scurrilitatis, eligebat sibi lectionem Martialis: & uita concurrebat cum Martialis carminibus. Sic corrumpunt bonos mores colloquia praua.
units.tr: I knew a count, born of an excellent and wise father, who was very dear to the Emperor because of his great wisdom. He, too fond of buffoonery, chose to read Martial, and his life ran parallel to Martial's verses. So bad conversation corrupts good morals.

units.la: Socrates apud Platonem in Legibus, etiam hac legem tulit, ut cives cogerentur discere Arithmeticam. Proinde & Romanis magnae curae fuit, ut liberi eorum, cum primis literis etiam Arithmeticen perciperent.
units.tr: Socrates, in Plato's Laws, also enacted this law: that citizens should be compelled to learn arithmetic. For this reason the Romans too took great care that their children, along with their first letters, should learn arithmetic.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Plato in Phædro fingit duplices animas, quarum alteras ait alatas esse, alteris uero alas decidisse. Alatus ait uolitare in cœlum, fruentes congressu colloquioq; Dei, & pulcherrimo spectaculo cursuum cœlestium, & considerare causas omnium mutationum in inferiori natura, in aere, in animantium corporibus, in hominum studijs & moribus, in uarijs imperiorum & ciuitatum casibus. Atque hæ animæ toto uolitantes cœlo, captæ pulchritudine diuinarum rerum, & illius admirandi ordinis,& suavitate doctrinæ, & uirtutis: hac una voluptate perpetuò frui cupiunt, nec onerant se obscœnis voluptatibus, quæ perturbant harmoniam uirtutum in animis, & obijciunt caliginem, ne cœlestia aspicere possint. At illæ animæ, quibus alæ deciderunt humi, uagantur, & voluptates quærunt impuras ex rebus terrenis. nec enim illam pulcherrimam lucem rerum cœlestium inspiciunt. Etsi autem Plato alas intelligit heroicos impetus ingeniorum, tamen ne illi quidem impetus soli animos subuehunt: sed opus est etiam artibus, quibus illi ipsi impetus attollantur. Sunt igitur alæ mentis humanæ Arithmetica & Geometria. Has si alligauerit sibi aliquis ingenio non sordido, facilimè penetrabit in cœlum, ac liberè in cœlestiū cœtu uagabitur, illaq; luce, & sapientia fruetur. Prima est numerorum intelligentia: id sensit Pythagoras, cùm definiuit mentem esse numerum. Significauit enim animam esse rationatricem, quæ discernit res, & ordinem animaduertit. Hæc sunt maximè propria menti, et sunt primæ mentis functiones. Quare aptè definiuit mentem esse numerum, uidelicet, numerantem. Hæc causa est, cur & ueteres Græci mox post Grammaticen tradiderunt Arithmeticam: deinde tertio loco proponebāt Dialecticen: quarto Geometriā. Videbant enim Dialecticen initia sumere ab Arithmetica. Et exercitatio multiplicationis & diuisionis optimè præparat ingenia ad syllogismos. Item, uis demōstrationum melius intelligi potest, cognita Arithmetica, quæ habet maximè illustres demonstrationes.
units.tr: In the Phaedrus, Plato imagines two kinds of souls: one kind, he says, has wings, while the other has lost its wings. The winged soul flies up to heaven, enjoying the company and converse of God, the most beautiful sight of the heavenly courses, and contemplating the causes of all changes in the lower nature: in the air, in the bodies of living things, in human pursuits and customs, and in the various fortunes of empires and states. These souls, flying through the whole heaven, captivated by the beauty of divine things, by that wonderful order and the sweetness of doctrine and virtue, desire to enjoy this one delight forever. They do not burden themselves with obscene pleasures, which disturb the harmony of the virtues in the mind and cast a fog over them so that they cannot behold heavenly things. But those souls whose wings have fallen to the ground wander and seek impure pleasures among earthly things, since they do not see that most beautiful light of heavenly things. Although Plato understands the wings to be the heroic impulses of talents, even those impulses alone do not lift minds aloft; arts are also needed, by which those very impulses are raised up. The wings of the human mind, then, are arithmetic and geometry. If anyone with a talent that is not base binds these wings to himself, he will easily penetrate to heaven and wander freely in the assembly of heavenly beings, and enjoy that light and wisdom. The first is the understanding of numbers. Pythagoras perceived this when he defined the mind as number. For he meant that the soul is the reasoning faculty, which distinguishes things and notices order. These are most proper to the mind, and they are the mind's first functions. So he rightly defined the mind as number, that is, as counting. This is also why the ancient Greeks, right after grammar, taught arithmetic; third, they set dialectic; fourth, geometry. For they saw that dialectic takes its beginnings from arithmetic, and that practice in multiplication and division prepares minds very well for syllogisms. Likewise, the force of demonstrations can be better understood once arithmetic is known, since it contains the most illustrious demonstrations.

units.la: Quidam doctor, cum non didicisset Grammaticam, conducebat sibi priuatum præceptorem, (ambo enim mihi noti erant) cùm uerò præceptor postridie reposceret dictata, ut est usitatum: Domine magister, inquit doctor, non conduxi te, ut dictata reposceres, sed uolo mecum expositas lectiones ruminare. Ita tantum, quantum prius nouerat, profecit.
units.tr: A certain teacher who had not learned grammar hired a private tutor for himself (I knew both of them). When the tutor, as is usual, asked the next day for the dictated material to be recited back, the teacher said: "Master, I did not hire you to demand recitations; I want to chew over the explained lessons with you." And so he progressed only as far as he had known before.

units.la: Plato in Repub. spurios philosophos appellat eos, qui sine Dialectica satisfacere se alijs artibus existimaexistimabant. Idem: Indocti Dialectici lacerant doctrinas, sicut caniculi panniculos. Est insignis similitudo, sicut excellens est in similitudinibus Plato.
units.tr: In the Republic, Plato calls spurious philosophers those who think they can satisfy themselves in other arts without dialectic. Again he says: "Untrained dialecticians tear doctrines to pieces, as little dogs tear up rags." It is a striking comparison, and Plato excels in comparisons.

units.la: Philosophi dixerunt, quòd Stoicorum Dialectica sit similis Polypo, qui tenaciter quidem adhæret, sed in fame arrodit suos digitos. Sic Stoica Dialectica corrumpit & euertit seipsam.
units.tr: The philosophers said that the Stoics' dialectic is like the polyp, which clings tenaciously but, in hunger, gnaws its own fingers. So Stoic dialectic corrupts and destroys itself.

units.la: Audiui Doctorem Hieronymum Schurpfium, perfectum Iurisconsultum, dicere: Nihil est, uelle esse Iurisconsultum sine Dialectica.
units.tr: I heard Doctor Hieronymus Schurpfius, a complete jurist, say: "It is nothing to wish to be a jurist without dialectic."

units.la: Aristoteles dicit quinq; necessaria esse scribenti poema, quanquam dicit de Tragœdia: primò, argumentum, ὑπόθεσις: secundò, λέξις, genus sermonis: tertiò, ἦθος: quartò, διάνοια, sententia: Vt quando Aeolus inclusit uentos in utres, & cùm dormit Vlysses, socij cogitāt magnam ibi esse auri uim Vlysi donatam, eamq; contemplari uolentes, resoluūt utres. Ibi uenti erumpūt, & cient procellas: Sic dum quærit opes cæca spe captus auarus, Accersit uentos & noua damna sibi.
units.tr: Aristotle says that five things are necessary for one who writes a poem, although he speaks about tragedy: first, the plot (hypothesis); second, diction (lexis), the kind of style; third, character (ethos); fourth, thought (dianoia), the sentiment. For example, when Aeolus shut the winds in bags, and Ulysses was asleep, his companions thought there was a great store of gold given to Ulysses there; wanting to look at it, they opened the bags. The winds burst out and stirred up storms: "So while the greedy man seeks wealth, captured by blind hope, he summons winds and new losses upon himself."

units.la: Quintò, ὄψις id est, spectaculum, quod incurrit in oculos. Huius dicti Aristotelis debent omnes qui scribunt, dicunt, aut concionantur, memores esse.
units.tr: Fifth is opsis, that is, spectacle, which strikes the eyes. All who write, speak or preach should remember this saying of Aristotle.

units.la: Accidit seniori bachanto, quod nunc multis scholasticis, qui cùm nō posset ediscere uersus Alexandri, emebat sibi pelliceam uestem candidam, in qua scribebat uersus Alexandri, ut semper ipsi essent sent in conspectu. Semel pertransiens pontem, uer to deijcitur in aquam: ibi totam suam doctrinam amisit.
units.tr: It happened to an elderly bachelor, as it now happens to many schoolboys, that since he could not learn Alexander's verses by heart, he bought himself a white fur coat and wrote Alexander's verses on it, so that they would always be in view. Once, crossing a bridge, he turned round, was thrown into the water, and there lost all his learning.

units.la: Galenus fatetur, se penè in amentiam Pyrrho-niorum delapsum esse, nisi in Geometria uidisset tantam uim esse demonstrationum.
units.tr: Galen confesses that he had almost fallen into the madness of the Pyrrhonists, had he not seen in geometry such great power of demonstration.

units.la: Plato prudenter dixit, eum uirum tantum beatum esse, qui doctrinam Mathematicam didicisset. huius mores posse regi: hunc moderatum, iustum & utilem ciuibus fore. Verba eius hæc sunt: Vnum est naturæ vinculum, doctrina numerorum, figurarum, & motuum cœlestium: ac si quis aliam uiam ad discendum inuenire potest, fortunam inuocet, ut dici solet. Nam sine his nemo in ciuitatibus unquam beatus extitit: hic modus, hæc educatio est, hæc disciplina seu facilis seu difficilis: per hanc ire necesse est. nec fas est negligere Deum, qui gratam de se famam in his artibus generi humano attribuit.
units.tr: Plato wisely said that only the man who has learned mathematical doctrine is truly happy; such a man's character can be governed, and he will be moderate, just and useful to his fellow citizens. His words are these: "There is one bond of nature: the doctrine of numbers, figures and the motions of the heavens. If anyone can find another way to learn, let him call on fortune, as the saying goes. For without these no one has ever been happy in states. This is the method, this is the education, this is the discipline, whether easy or hard; one must pass through it. Nor is it right to neglect God, who has given the human race a welcome reputation through these arts."

units.la: Extenuat Astronomiam Phauorinus apud Gellium, & dicit pauca quædam prouideri, seu (ut ipsius uerbo utar) ϖαχυμερέστερον. Imò sic amplissimo præconio ornauit artem: siquidem quædam in natura aut moribus præcipua animaduerti posse, inquit.
units.tr: Phavorinus, in Gellius, belittles astronomy and says that only a few things can be foreseen, or, to use his own word, παχυμερέστερον (more coarsely). Yet he so greatly praised the art: for he says that certain outstanding things in nature or in morals can be perceived.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Aristoteles citat dictum Alcidamantis oratoris, qui interrogatus quid esset Philosophia, dixit, eam esse murum legum. Et verum est dictum, quia loquitur de demonstrationibus, quid sit ius natu-rae, quare sit firmum. Et illae demonstrationes sunt firmamenta iuris.
units.tr: Aristotle cites a saying of the orator Alcidamas, who, when asked what philosophy was, said that it is the wall of the laws. The saying is true, because philosophy deals with demonstrations: what natural right is, and why it is firm. And those demonstrations are the supports of right.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Capnio, cùm Romam à principe Palatino certi negocij causa missus esset, venit in lectionem Argyropyli, qui tunc Romae magna cum laude docebat Graecè. Cumq; Capnio reuerenter salutato Argyropylo, in consessu multorum doctissimorum hominum exponeret ei, se hominem Germanicum, incensum studio Graecarum literarum, gratulari sibi eam fortunam, quòd occasio audiendi ipsius contigisset, quo illis quidem temporibus nemo in Philosophia & Graeca lingua doctior praedicaretur: orasseq;, ut sibi audiendi ipsum potestatem faceret: delectatus Argyropylus oratione Capnionis, cùm operam suam benignè pollicitus esset, interrogat, an attigisset Graecas literas? Capnio ait se Basileae in Germania audiuisse Graecae linguae elementa. Enarrabat autem tum forte Argyropylus Thucydidem. hunc exhibet illi, ac iubet legere, deinde etiam interpretari. Cùm autem & suauiter pronunciaret Capnio ( fuit enim perstud osus recte pronuncia-tionis ) & sententiam sic satis latinè redderet : ibi Graecus ille admirans, conuertit se ad auditores, et exclamās : Ecce, inquit, Graecia nostro exilio trās-uolauit alpes.
units.tr: When Capnio had been sent to Rome by the Palatine prince on a certain business, he attended the lectures of Argyropylus, who was then teaching Greek at Rome with great distinction. Capnio greeted Argyropylus respectfully and, before a gathering of many learned men, told him that he was a German, inflamed with a passion for Greek letters, and that he counted it a great piece of luck that he had the chance to hear him, since at that time no one was reckoned more learned in philosophy and the Greek language. He asked for permission to attend his lectures. Argyropylus was pleased by Capnio's speech and promised his help willingly, then asked whether he had yet studied Greek literature. Capnio said that at Basel in Germany he had heard the elements of the Greek language. Argyropylus happened to be expounding Thucydides at the time. He handed the book to Capnio and told him to read it, and then to translate it. Capnio read it smoothly (for he was very keen on correct pronunciation) and rendered the sense into Latin well enough. The Greek, amazed, turned to the audience and cried out: "Behold, Greece has flown across the Alps in our exile."

units.la: Vetustas finxit Mercurij uirga animas orco reuocatas esse, & Orphei cytheram syluas & saxa traxisse. Significare uoluerunt uiri sapientes, peculiari quodam dicendi genere rudes mortales, & feros, adhuc mansuefactos esse.
units.tr: Antiquity imagined that by Mercury's wand souls were called back from Orcus, and that Orpheus's lyre drew forests and rocks after it. The wise men meant by this that, by a certain distinctive manner of speaking, rough and savage mortals were tamed.

units.la: Cicero reprehendit Platonem, quòd dixerit philosophos, tametsi abstineant à Reipublicae administratione, tamē iustos esse propter hanc ipsam magnarum rerum inquisitionem. Sed Plato rectissimè sensit. Est enim iustitia suum quemque officium facere, & fructum eius officij conferre ad communem salutem generis humani. Id maximè facit Philosophus, qui religiones, rerum naturalium causas, omnium honestorū officiorum leges explicat, & haec res diuinas caeteris impertit, artes illustrat aut docet: denique qui veritatis & iustitiae doctrinam conferre ad aliorum utilitatem studet. Rectè igitur Plato dixit, iustos esse Philosophos, qui doctrinam utilem uitae tradūt. Non gessit magistratus Isocrates: sed consilijs suis gubernauit Imperatorem laudatissimum Timotheum, & formauit ingenia multorum, qui postea in Republica principes extiterūt.
units.tr: Cicero rebukes Plato for saying that philosophers, although they abstain from the administration of the commonwealth, are nonetheless just because of this very pursuit of great matters. But Plato thought very rightly. For justice is for each person to perform his own duty and to bring the fruit of that duty to the common welfare of the human race. This the philosopher does above all: he explains religions, the causes of natural things, and the laws of all honourable duties; he imparts these divine things to others, illuminates or teaches the arts; and, in short, he strives to share the teaching of truth and justice for the benefit of others. Plato was therefore right to say that philosophers are just when they hand down teaching useful for life. Isocrates did not hold public office, but by his counsels he guided the most praised commander Timotheus, and he shaped the minds of many who afterwards became leaders in the commonwealth.

units.la: Nec melius de Republica meritus est Aeschines causidicus, quàm Aristoteles: qui etsi nec magistratus gesserit, nec causas egit, tamen Alexandrum & multos alios principes finxit ad iusticiam & beneficentiam. Iason Iurisconsultus gubernauit magnā Italiæ partem: nec tamen minus de Republica meretur Bartolus, qui in schola tantum uixit. Philippus medicus Alexandri exercitum secutus est, ac regē ipsum ingenti periculo liberauit. Neq; tamen minus de Republica meretur Galenus, qui nullum exercitum secutus, sed in schola asedit, & scripsit doctrinæ suæ monumenta.
units.tr: The orator Aeschines deserved no less of the commonwealth than Aristotle did. Although Aristotle held no magistracy and pleaded no cases, he formed Alexander and many other princes to justice and beneficence. Jason the jurist governed a great part of Italy, yet Bartolus deserves no less of the commonwealth, though he lived only in the school. Philip the physician followed the army of Alexander and freed the king himself from great danger. Yet Galen deserves no less of the commonwealth, though he followed no army but sat in his school and wrote the monuments of his learning.

units.la: Cicero ait magnā uim in discēdo habere studiū cōferendi, quod συζήτησιν uocat ipse. Et Salomon ait: Vt ferrū ferro acuitur, ita uir excitatur à uiro. Significat enim, ingenia cum admoneri collatione consiliorū atq; opinionū, tum exēplis excitari, iuxta Euripidis dictū: ὁμιλία ἐτέλεσε τὰς τέχνας.
units.tr: Cicero says that in learning there is great power in the study of conferring, which he himself calls syzētēsin (συζήτησιν). And Solomon says: "As iron is sharpened by iron, so a man is sharpened by a man." For he means that minds are stirred up both by the comparison of counsels and opinions and by examples, in accordance with the saying of Euripides: "Companionship perfects the arts" [ὁμιλία ἐτέλεσε τὰς τέχνας].

units.la: Fabius monet, scripta euoluenda esse cum tali sollicitudine, quasi nos ipsi ita scripturi uel dicturi simus: quòd ita fiat, ut uigilantioribus oculis omnia lustremus, nihil nobis elabi patiamur quod obseruatu dignū sit, & ad omnes uirtutes scriptorum expendendas attentiores reddamur.
units.tr: Fabius advises that writings are to be read through with such care as if we ourselves were about to write or speak in the same way; so that we may go over everything with more watchful eyes, allow nothing worth noting to slip from us, and become more attentive in weighing all the virtues of the writers.

units.la: Aristoteles dixit, id primùm certū signum esse quòd aliquis quippiam rectè sciat, si de eo ipse loqui, & alium docere possit.
units.tr: Aristotle said that the first certain sign that someone truly knows something is if he can speak about it himself and teach another.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Tithonus filius Laomedontis regis Troiani, raptus ab aurora, petiuit ab ea immortalitatem. Aurora ipsi dedit eam. Sed ipse oblitus, se non solum debere immortalitatem petere, sed & ἀγηρασίαν, id est, non senescentiam: factus est ita senex, adeoq; debilis, ut immortalitas fuerit ei oneri. Petiuit igitur mutari suam senectam. mutatus est in cicadam. Id est, Poemata senescunt, & sunt immortalia: cum posteritate vero crescit eorum admiratio. Homeri opus crevit diuturnitate temporis apud posteros.
units.tr: Tithonus, son of Laomedon, king of Troy, was carried off by Aurora, and asked her for immortality. She granted it to him. But he forgot that he ought to have asked not only for immortality but also for agērasia [ἀγηρασία], that is, freedom from growing old. He became so old and so feeble that immortality was a burden to him. He therefore asked to have his old age changed, and he was turned into a cicada. That is to say, poems grow old yet are immortal, and their admiration increases with posterity. Homer's work grew in reputation among later generations through the length of time it lasted.

units.la: Plinius.
units.tr: Pliny.

units.la: Non multa, sed multum legendum est. Non multa, id est, non distrahendum studium in diuersissima: sed multum saepe legendum, & una eademq; res saepe iteranda & relegenda est.
units.tr: One should read not many books but much: not many, that is, one should not scatter one's study over very diverse things, but one should often read the same thing and go over it again and again.

units.la: Inspicere tabulas, considerare loca et regiones, debebat uobis ludus esse: sicut Caesari Carolo V. Cum enim hic esset in obsidione oppidi Vitenbergae, tunc in pago Pistriz, quando accesserunt ad eum Principes, suffultus brachijs sedit apud mesam, & inspexit tabulas Cosmographicas. Ita inuentus est incumbere tabulis, & considerare loca & regiones, in quibus ipse cum exercitu uersaretur.
units.tr: Looking at maps and considering places and regions ought to be a pleasure for you, as it was for Charles V. When he was besieging the town of Wittenberg, while he was at the village of Pistriz, the princes came to him, and he sat at a table, propped up on his arms, and studied the cosmographical maps. In this way he was found bending over the maps and considering the places and regions in which he himself was campaigning with his army.

units.la: Osiander scribens Hebraicum Alphabetum, inuertebat cartham: tunc in altera facie carthae erat Graecum Alphabetum.
units.tr: While Osiander was writing the Hebrew alphabet, he turned the sheet over; on the other side of the sheet was the Greek alphabet.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: Collectanea

units.la: Herodotus testatur, quòd antiquæ literæ Ionũ sint similes characteribus Phœnicum: & inde sunt cõiecturæ, quòd literæ Ionũ sint à Phœnicib.ortæ.
units.tr: Herodotus testifies that the ancient letters of the Ionians are similar to the characters of the Phoenicians; and from this conjectures are drawn that the letters of the Ionians arose from the Phoenicians.

units.la: Gregorius Triuernas ante annos 68 uenit Parisios, & à senatu Academiæ stipendium postulauit, quòd ibi Græcas literas docere constituisset. Cumq; nonnullis inciuiliter facere uideretur, quòd stipendium flagitare ausus esset, cum senatus Academiæ neq; accersisset eũ, neq; significasset se ipsius usurũ opera, neq; omnino leƈtorem Græcũ haberet ullũ: (erat enim adhuc in Gallia, ut apud nos, Græcæ literæ ignotissimæ) quare cũ interrogaretur, qua impudẽtia peteret à Senatu stipendiũ? hic uir paratus citauit constitutionẽ de linguarũ studijs, in qua nominatim fit mẽtio scholæ Parisiẽsis. Senatum adeò nõ offendit hæc libertas, ut etiã magnopere collaudauerit hominis cõsiliũ et studiũ. Quare stipendiũ ei magno cõsensu satis honorificum est constitutum.
units.tr: Gregorius Triverna came to Paris about 68 years ago and asked the senate of the Academy for a stipend, because he had resolved to teach Greek letters there. Since it seemed somewhat uncivil to some that he had dared to demand a stipend, when the senate of the Academy had neither summoned him, nor signified that it wanted his services, nor indeed had any Greek reader at all (for at that time Greek letters were, as with us, almost unknown in France), when he was asked with what effrontery he sought a stipend from the senate, this man, ready with an answer, cited the decree concerning the study of languages, in which the school of Paris is expressly mentioned. This frankness did not offend the senate so much that it did not greatly commend the man's plan and zeal. Accordingly, by general consent, a stipend suitably honourable for him was established.

units.la: Romani cũ Græcis toti Italiæ indixerũt disertè, ut Medicos in Italia publicæ salutis causa retinerët.
units.tr: The Romans, together with the Greeks, expressly ordered throughout all Italy that physicians should be retained in Italy for the sake of public health.

units.la: Romani Cæsares bonis medicis in singulos annos 250. sestertia pendebant, id est, octo millia aureorum, & amplius trecentis. Reliquarum uerò disciplinarum professoribus, utpote Rhetoribus & Poetis, centena sestertia modò in annum numerarunt, id est, tria millia aureorum, & trecentos triginta quatuor, ut refert Plinius.
units.tr: The Roman emperors paid good physicians 250 thousand sesterces a year, that is, 8,000 gold pieces and a little more than 300. To the teachers of the other disciplines, such as rhetoricians and poets, they paid only 100 thousand sesterces a year, that is, 3,000 gold pieces and 334, as Pliny reports.

units.la: Cum apud Cæsarem Fridericū legatus sui principis esset Capnio, cumq; Venetæ ciuitatis oratoribus, qui eo etiam venerat, per id tempus frequenter esset, accidit ut aliquando Capnio forte pulcherrimè Græcè scriptum enchiridion noui Testamenti in manibus haberet. quod cum uidisset Venetus orator, & animaduertisset Capnionem non esse rudem Græcarum literarum, conuersus ad suos collegas, ait: Videte quæso, in Germania hunc uirum propter cognitionem literarū in admiratione esse, quam nostri tam pertinaciter contemnunt.
units.tr: When Capnio was envoy of his prince at the court of the Emperor Frederick, and he was frequently in the company of the envoys of the city of Venice, who had also come there, it happened once that Capnio chanced to have in his hands a most beautifully written Greek handbook of the New Testament. When the Venetian envoy saw it, and noticed that Capnio was no novice in Greek letters, he turned to his colleagues and said: "Please look, in Germany this man is admired for his knowledge of letters, which our people so stubbornly despise."

units.la: Quidā morio in culina principis Palatini, qui ex more ligna ferebat, solitus est ex infima strue ea ligna reuellere, quæ moueri sine magno impetu nō poterant. Interrogatus cur id faceret, respondit: se difficilimam laboris partem primùm cōsecturum, ut deinde summa illa ligna facilius mouerentur. nec uidit quantum referret, singula ordinè tollere. Huic persimiles sunt omnes studiosi, qui fastiditis primis artibus, ad sublimia studia se conferunt.
units.tr: A certain fool in the kitchen of the Count Palatine, who carried wood according to custom, used to pull out from the bottom of the pile those logs which could not be moved without great effort. Asked why he did this, he replied that he would first tackle the most difficult part of the work, so that the top logs could then be moved more easily. He did not see how much it mattered to take them away one at a time in order. All students who, having scorned the basic arts, betake themselves to the lofty studies are very much like him.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Dicunt Palladem inuenisse tibiam, imitantem sonum capitis Gorgonis: id est, Musica est inuentum sapientiæ. & uera musica fuit complexa doctrinas & artes, quas poetæ carminibus comprehenderunt. Postea Pallas, postquam uidit intumescere scere genas, abiecit eam: id est, quando sapietia est amissa, tunc non fuit studium musices, uel cantus: seu quādo Satyri sunt musici facti, qui obscœna & amatoria composuerunt, tunc serium musices studium desijt.
units.tr: They say Pallas invented the flute, imitating the sound of the Gorgon's head: that is, music is an invention of wisdom. True music embraced the doctrines and arts that the poets comprehended in their songs. Afterwards Pallas, when she saw her cheeks swell, threw the flute away: that is, when wisdom was lost, there was no longer any study of music or song; or when the Satyrs became musicians and composed obscene and amatory pieces, the serious study of music ceased.

units.la: Quo tempore Homerus, Herodotus & Pindarus uixerint.
units.tr: When Homer, Herodotus and Pindar lived.

units.la: Homerus fuit ante Pindarum 400 annis. Herodotus uixit tempore Pindari, seu tempore belli Xerxis.
units.tr: Homer lived 400 years before Pindar. Herodotus lived in Pindar's time, that is, at the time of Xerxes' war.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Apes cum aduolent ad omnia, tamen nullis nocent floribus: ita uirtus & literæ sic ab alijs sumendæ, ut nihil deterior is sit qui communicauit. Non tamen quiduis ex omnibus colligunt apes: ita non omnia ex eodem petenda autore. Industriam adiuuat Deus.
units.tr: Bees, though they fly to all flowers, harm none of them; so virtue and letters should be taken from others, so that the one who shares them is none the worse. Yet bees do not gather just anything from everything; so we should not seek everything from the same author. God helps diligence.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Sicut apes ab unoquoq; flosculo quicquid est optimum excerpunt, si quid insit ueneni, id araneis exugendum relinquunt: ita nos in Poetis & alijs scriptis, quod est eruditionis & utilis doctrinæ, id nobis rapiamus: si uerò quid obscœnitatis occurrerit, id relinquamus.
units.tr: Just as bees take from each little flower whatever is best, and leave any poison that is present to be sucked out by spiders, so in the poets and other writings let us snatch up whatever is of learning and useful teaching; but if anything of obscenity turns up, let us leave it.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Tanta admiratio fuit tragœdiarum Euripidis, ut multi cives Athenienses, cùm essent captiui in Sicilia, dimissi sint propterea, quòd dominis suis descripserint Euripidis tragœdias.
units.tr: So great was the admiration for the tragedies of Euripides that many Athenian citizens, when they were captives in Sicily, were released for this reason: that they had recited Euripides' tragedies to their masters.

units.la: Causæ, propter quas donum linguarum est attributum Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Reasons why the gift of tongues was given to the Church.

units.la: Principalis & prima causa est, ut propagari Euangelium citò in multis gentibus possit, quarū non est una lingua.
units.tr: The principal and first reason is that the Gospel might quickly be spread among many nations, which do not share one language.

units.la: Secunda, ut hoc ipsum donum esset testimonium Spiritus sancti, & præsentiæ Dei in Ecclesia, sicut & alia miracula.
units.tr: The second is that this very gift might be a testimony of the Holy Spirit and of God's presence in the Church, as with the other miracles.

units.la: Tertia, ut esset signum & testimonium de vocatione gentium, quòd gentes etiam ad Ecclesiæ societatem essent vocatæ.
units.tr: The third is that it might be a sign and testimony of the calling of the Gentiles, that the Gentiles too were called into fellowship with the Church.

units.la: ¶ Quādo Turcicus imperator cæpit Cōstātinopolim, & expulsæ essent gentes Græcæ, eo tēpore uenerūt in Italiā præstātissimi uiri, Theodorus Gaza, uir nusquā satis laudatus, item Trapezuntius, & alij, qui simul & linguā, & alias pulcherrimas artes eò transtulerūt: quorū beneficio magna pars Græcæ linguæ ad nos peruenit, sicut Deus nō sine singulari causa facit tales mutationes. Vult enim alias gentes, ignaras talium rerum, instituì ab hospitibus & peregrinis.
units.tr: When the Turkish emperor began to take Constantinople and the Greeks were expelled, at that time very distinguished men came to Italy: Theodore Gaza, a man nowhere praised enough, also Trapezuntius, and others, who at the same time brought the language and other most beautiful arts there. Through their benefit a great part of the Greek language has come down to us, just as God does not bring about such changes without a singular cause. For He wills other nations, ignorant of such things, to be taught by guests and strangers.

units.la: Bonus quidā uir solebat esse solus, uolebatq; in solitudine omnia perdiscere. Inciderat in Aristotele de Iride, ubi fingebat mirabiles speculationes, scri-bebatq; ad quendam: In omnibus materijs alijs, quamuis obscuris, superaui Aristotelem: sed in ma-teria de Iride meipsum superaui. Postea de eadem re disputabat hic in auditorio, & toto prorsus coe-lo à veritate aberrabat suis phantasijs.
units.tr: A certain good man used to be alone and wanted to learn everything in solitude. He had come upon Aristotle's work on the rainbow, where he imagined wonderful speculations, and he wrote to someone: "In all other subjects, however obscure, I have surpassed Aristotle; but in the subject of the rainbow I have surpassed myself." Afterwards he disputed about the same matter here in the lecture hall, and wandered utterly far from the truth, the whole sky away, by his fancies.

units.la: Dicebat aliquādo D. Philippus ad examinādos ualde rudes: Vos facitis sicut ille qui legebat Græcā Grāmaticā in schola, maleq; pronūciabat uocabula, nec bene poterat legere. Accessit igitur ad eū alius, dicens: Cur nō doces Euclidē? Respōdit: Non scio. Verùm alter inquit: Quare igitur doces Grāmaticam, quam etiam ignoras?
units.tr: Master Philip used to say to candidates being examined who were very unskilled: "You do like the man who read Greek grammar in school, pronounced the words badly, and could not read well. Another came up to him and said: 'Why do you not teach Euclid?' He replied: 'I do not know.' But the other said: 'Then why do you teach grammar, which you yourself do not know?'"

units.la: Eobanus sæpè ad me & alios bonos amicos ioco dicebat, se esse principem philosophorū. Id cùm forte narrassemus alteri, dixit ille: Per deum, ergo est princeps omnium fatuorum.
units.tr: Eobanus often used to say to me and other good friends, in jest, that he was the prince of philosophers. When we had happened to tell this to another man, he said: "By God, then he is the prince of all fools."

units.la: Poetarum tria genera.
units.tr: Three kinds of poets.

units.la: Doctor Milichius dicebat esse tria genera Poetarū. Eobanus solitus est simul gignere & scribere uersus. Nos cogimur ante gignere quàm scribere, ex uno latere positū habentes Calepinū, ab altero uerò Bebelium de uersibus, sic magno cū labore aliquid cōsarcientes. Et dicebat se prius scribere, et deinde gignere. Et referebat hoc eò, quia habebamus amicū, qui scripsit initiū et finē, postea dixit: Date mihi spondæū, aut dactylum, quo expleā carmen.
units.tr: Doctor Milichius used to say there were three kinds of poets. Eobanus was accustomed to beget and write verses at the same time. We are forced to beget before we write, having Calepinus on one side and Bebelius on verses on the other, patching something together with great labour. And he said that he wrote first and begot afterwards. He referred this to a friend of ours who wrote the beginning and the end and then said: "Give me a spondee or a dactyl with which I may fill out the poem."

units.la: Heraclides Ponticus, homo quidem studiosus, sed non ita ingeniosus, scripsit carmen πωρὶ πόνυ, & obtulit regi Euergetæ, uel quicunq; fuerit. Rex accepit librum, & deleuit π in titulo, ut ex πόνυ fieret ὄνυ: uolens significare, eum esse asinum, quia uellet præferre studium & laborem naturæ.
units.tr: Heraclides of Pontus, a studious man but not so gifted, wrote a poem On Toil [περὶ πόνου] and offered it to King Euergetes, or whoever he was. The king took the book and erased the π in the title, so that πόνου became of an ass [ὄνου], wishing to signify that he was an ass, because he preferred study and toil to nature.

units.la: Quidam in Anglia nomine Flatimerus quotannis repetiuit Terentium, & dixit se semper in recenti lectione aliquid noui obseruare.
units.tr: A certain man in England named Flatimerus repeated Terence every year, and said that he always observed something new in each fresh reading.

units.la: Camerarius ad me post bellum ad Ingolstadium gestum dicebat: Ego non amplius possum legere Iliada Homeri, sed Odyssea libentius lego: quia uiderat præsentia bella.
units.tr: Camerarius said to me after the war waged at Ingolstadt: "I can no longer read Homer's Iliad, but I read the Odyssey more willingly, because he had seen the wars at first hand."

units.la: Pastor quidam in uicinia patriæ nostræ, qui sæpius ueniebat ad nos, & nos uicissim ad ipsum, hortabatur nos ad discendum his rhythmis: Lernestu wol, so würstu gebratner hüner vol. Lernstu übel, so můstu mit denn schweinen essen auß dem kübel. Potius dixisset: Lernstu wol, so würstu der plagen vol. Quia contrarium est uerum. Nam Canonici, qui nihil didicerunt, die werden gebratner hüner vol: docti uerò & sapientes pro nihilo habentur, & aliqui quoq; exulare coguntur.
units.tr: A certain minister in the neighbourhood of our homeland, who often came to us and we in turn to him, urged us to learn with these rhymes: "Lernstu wol, so würstu gebratner hüner vol. Lernstu übel, so müstu mit denn schweinen essen auß dem kübel." He would have done better to say: "Lernstu wol, so würstu der plagen vol" (if you learn well, you will be full of troubles), because the opposite is true. For canons, who have learned nothing, become full of roast chickens; but the learned and wise are held to be worth nothing, and some are even forced into exile.

units.la: Noster pastor ita se afflixit uigilijs, ut iam non habeat talem somnum, qualem natura postulat. Erasmus mihi scripsit, ac rogauit, ne attingerem libros à cœna. Quam consuetudinem postea semper seruaui. Stœflerus etiam conquestus est in senectu te sua de somno, cum peruenisset ad septuagesimū annum, quòd eum intempestiuis lucubrationibus amisisset.
units.tr: Our minister has so afflicted himself with wakefulness that he no longer has the sleep that nature requires. Erasmus wrote to me and asked me not to touch books after supper; I afterwards always kept this custom. Stoeflerus also complained in old age about his sleep, when he had reached seventy, that he had lost it through untimely late-night studying.

units.la: Vidi libros, qui ipso die direptionis urbis Con stantinopolitanæ sunt conseruati. Quia ibi fuerūt homines doctissimi.
units.tr: I have seen books that were preserved on the very day of the sack of Constantinople, because there were very learned men there.

units.la: Nil curetis, quòd irrisores omnis eruditionis, si quem artibus operam dare uideant, irridentes di cant: Hæc est Platonica facundia. Nullius sunt mo menti huiusmodi irrisiones. Erasmus re spondit extenuantibus artes, & dicentibus non esse opus facundia: Non est etiam opus solœcissmis et barbarismis.
units.tr: Do not worry that the mockers of all learning, if they see someone devoting himself to the arts, jeer and say: "This is Platonic eloquence." Such mockeries are of no account. Erasmus answered those who belittled the arts and said there was no need of eloquence: "Nor is there need of solecisms and barbarisms."

units.la: Paulus Tertius sedulus Homeri & Horatij lector.
units.tr: Paulus Tertius, the diligent reader of Homer and Horace.

units.la: Paulus Tertius semper solitus est aliquid legere in Homero, cum se cubitum conferre uellet: & optimas, si quæ occurrebant, sententias eligebat, easq; summa diligentia considerabat. Habuit etiam semper in manibus Horatium.
units.tr: Paulus Tertius always used to read something in Homer when he was about to go to bed, and he chose the best sayings he came across and considered them with the greatest care. He also always kept Horace in his hands.

units.la: In disputatione Tubingensi erat senex Iurisconsultus, cuius positionibus alius quidam uolens opponere, dixit, in ipsius thematibus esse nugationē. Senex iam oblitus uocabuli illius Dialectici (nam erat octogenarius) dicit: Domine, dic nobis, quid sit nugatio. Respondit opponens, nugationem esse unius unius rei uariā repetitionem. ibi senex ille respon-dit: Ah Domine, quod bonum & utile est, nun-quam nimium inculcari potest, iuxta Græcam pa-roemiam: Ais ναὶ τεὶς τὸ λαχλὸν.
units.tr: At the Tübingen disputation there was an old jurist, and when another man wanted to object to his positions, he said that there was nugation (triviality) in his theses. The old man, who had forgotten the term used by that dialectician (for he was eighty), said: "Sir, tell us what nugation is." The objector replied that nugation is the varied repetition of one thing. Then the old man said: "Ah, sir, what is good and useful can never be drummed in too often, according to the Greek proverb: [ναὶ ναὶ, εἰς τὸ λάχανον]

units.la: Erat olim tres fratres, qui pröptissimi erat in di-cedo de quacunq; re etiā nō meditati, idq; cum ma-gna admiratione multorum. Hi cum interrogaren-tur, unde haberet illā artē dicēdi, responderūt: Ex arte Lullij. Lullius enim fuit quidā doctus uir, qui cōscripsit illū librū. Hic liber etiā ad me portaba-tur ab amico quodā secretò. Nam tres illi fratres ita amabāt eum librū, ut nō permitterēt cuiquā cō-templari. Inspexi librū, & statim uidi esse Dialecti-cam, quā illi tam magni faciebant, & uelut Deum amplectebantur. Sed ex Dialectica non reddimur eloquētes, quæ saltē de reb. iudicat. Rhetorica uerò uerbis lumē atq; splendorē adfert. Quanq; isti in ea antiquitate putauerunt omnia peti ex Dialectica.
units.tr: There was once three brothers who were very ready in speaking on any subject, even without preparation, and this to the great admiration of many. When they were asked where they got that art of speaking, they replied: "From the art of Lull." For Lull was a learned man who wrote that book. This book was also brought to me secretly by a friend, for those three brothers loved that book so much that they would not allow anyone to look at it. I examined the book and at once saw that it was dialectic, which they valued so highly and embraced as if it were a god. But we are not made eloquent by dialectic, which at least judges things; rhetoric, on the other hand, brings light and splendour to words. Yet those men in that age thought that everything was to be sought from dialectic.

units.la: Fui cum quodā docto uiro prope Rhenū in con-uiuio, qui defendebat sectā Epicureorū. Ad quē di-xi: Quare defendis illas manifestas absurditates, cùm uelis haberi uir bonus? Est (inquit) meus mos, ita contrariū defendere. Dixi: Domine, noli hoc fa-cere apud alios: quia illi di ent esse uanitatem inge-nij: & si interessent iuniores & imperiti, illi exci-perent tuas absurditates, & defenderent. Promisit mihi ille bonus uir, se nunquam hoc deinceps factu-rum rum esse, & non ægrè tulit se admoneri.
units.tr: I was at a dinner near the Rhine with a learned man who defended the sect of the Epicureans. I said to him: "Why do you defend those obvious absurdities, when you wish to be thought a good man?" "It is my habit," he said, "to defend the opposite." I said: "Sir, please do not do this in front of others, because they will say it is a vanity of wit; and if younger and inexperienced people were present, they would take up your absurdities and defend them." That good man promised me that he would never do this again, and he did not take it badly that he was reminded.

units.la: Antonius eremita interrogatus, quare non legeret Biblia, & nō secum haberet alios libros? inquit: Cœlū & terra, & tota rerū natura sunt mei libri. Melius dixit, quàm ille alter: Summa ars Christianorū est, nescire legem, & nihil discere. Sed non satis est. Aliquid in Ecclesia discendū est, quod non apprehēditur naturali lumine. Vox Antonij duriter intellecta, pugnaret cum his dictis: Hunc audite. Item: Scrutamini scripturas. Naturalis noticia non tenet promissionem gratiæ.
units.tr: When Antony the hermit was asked why he did not read the Bible and why he did not keep other books with him, he said: "Heaven and earth and the whole nature of things are my books." He said it better than that other one: "The highest art of Christians is not to know the law and to learn nothing." But that is not enough. Something must be learned in the Church which is not grasped by natural light. The saying of Antony, if understood harshly, would conflict with these words: "Hear him" [Matt. 17.5]. Likewise: "Search the Scriptures" [John 5.39]. Natural knowledge does not hold the promise of grace.

units.la: Capnio de studioso Iuris dicebat: Primo anno scit dijudicare omnes controuersias, secundo incipit dubitare, tertio uidet se nihil scire, & tunc primùm incipit discere.
units.tr: Capnio used to say of a student of law: "In the first year he thinks he can judge all controversies; in the second he begins to doubt; in the third he sees that he knows nothing, and only then does he begin to learn."

units.la: Nostri maiores Germani non dederunt operā litteris, igitur prorsus barbarè loquuti sunt. Et quia non fuerūt exculti disciplina, ideo nec habemus aliquid scriptorū de reb. Germanorū: aut si quid habemus, illud plane est impropriū & barbaricum. Quale est illud in historia Ludouici regis quod incipit: Kǒnig Ludewig war ein demūtiger mann, dann er pletzet selbs sein wammes. Ita ille ineptus putabat humilitatem esse, wen einer sein wammes pletzet. Deinde insulsè hoc loco utitur hoc nomine pletzen. Nam non est intelligendum de sartoris resartione, sed quod ille rex tam fuerit industrius in militia, ut ipse in prælio posset resarcire loricas & arma, quibus utebatur aduersus hostes.
units.tr: Our German forefathers did not devote themselves to letters, and so they spoke quite barbarously. And because they were not trained in learning, we have no writings about German matters, or if we have any, they are plainly improper and barbaric. Such is that passage in the history of King Louis which begins: "König Ludewig war ein demütiger Mann, dann er pletzet selbs sein Wammes" (King Louis was a humble man, for he patched his own doublet). That silly writer thought that humility consists in a man patching his own doublet. Then he uses the word "pletzen" here insipidly. For it is not to be understood of a tailor's mending, but that the king was so industrious in war that he himself could repair in battle the breastplates and arms he used against the enemy.

units.la: Quidam bellus homo, me semper eandem cantilenam iterare dixit. Vtinam uero possem nō tantum ijdem uerbis, sed etiā ijdem syllabis grata Deo & Ecclesiæ salutaria eodem modo canere.
units.tr: Some fine fellow said that I always repeat the same tune. Would that I could sing in the same way, not only with the same words but with the same syllables, things pleasing to God and wholesome for the Church!

units.la: Doctor Martinus Lutherus Eobano Hesso scribere solebat: Poetæ ab ipsis Musis Laureato.
units.tr: Doctor Martin Luther used to write to Eobanus Hessus: "A poet, crowned with laurel by the Muses themselves."

units.la: Baumgartnerus senator Norimbergensis, cùm hic literis operam daret, quanquam esset aliâs sedulus & diligens in studijs, tamen cùm aliquando neglexisset lectionem, ac deinde conuenirent eum condiscipuli, narrantes ei, quàm eruditam & bonam lectionem in ipsius absentia audiuissent, respondit: Nunquam fuit tam bona, quin ego meliorem neglexerim.
units.tr: Baumgartner, a senator of Nuremberg, when he was studying here, although otherwise diligent and assiduous in his studies, once neglected a lecture. Then his fellow students met him and told him how learned and good a lecture they had heard in his absence. He replied: "It was never so good that I have not neglected a better one."

units.la: Facetum dictum, quòd Dialectica non fuerit ante Arithmeticam.
units.tr: A witty saying, that dialectic did not exist before arithmetic.

units.la: Dialectica non fuit ante Arithmeticam: quia homines diligentius numerant pecuniam, quàm genera causarum.
units.tr: Dialectic did not exist before arithmetic, because men count their money more carefully than the kinds of causes.

units.la: Stœslerus sæpè grauiter inuehebatur in auditores, quòd nemo percunctaretur apud eum. & aliquando dicebat: Ego tam ignauos habeo auditores, ut si omnem eruditionem illis possem dimidia hora infundere fundibulo, uix unam horâ possem impetrare ab eis, ut eam infundere permitterent.
units.tr: Stoesslerus often railed heavily against his hearers because no one asked him questions. And sometimes he said: "I have such lazy hearers that, if I could pour all learning into them in half an hour with a sling, I could hardly obtain from them in an hour permission to pour it in."

units.la: Iosquinus, uiuens Cameraci, cùm quidam uclC-let ei in suo cantu adhibere colores seu coloratu-ras, quas ipse non composuerat, ingressus est chorum, & acriter increpauit illum, omnibus audientibus, addens: Tu asine, quare addis coloraturam? si mihi ea placuisset, inseruissem ipse. Si tu uelis corrigere cantilenas recte compositas, facias tibi proprium cantum, sinas mihi meum incorrectum. Quoties nouam cantilenam composuerat, dedit eam cantoribus canendam, & interea ipse circumambulabat, attentè audiens, an harmonia congrueret. Si non placeret, ingressus: Tacete, inquit, ego mutabo. Hoc nostrum aliquis non posset imitari: sed nobis iuxta aliorum praescriptum canendum, siue bene siue male harmonia consonet.
units.tr: Josquin, who lived at Cambrai, when someone dared to add to his song ornaments or coloraturas which he himself had not composed, went into the choir and sharply rebuked him, with everyone listening, adding: "You donkey, why do you add a coloratura? If I had wanted it, I would have put it in myself. If you wish to correct songs that are rightly composed, make your own song and let me keep mine uncorrected." Whenever he had composed a new song, he gave it to the singers to sing, and meanwhile walked around listening attentively to see whether the harmony agreed. If it did not please him, he went in and said: "Be quiet, I will change it." Not one of us could imitate this; we must sing according to the prescription of others, whether the harmony agrees well or badly.

units.la: Doctor Hieronymus Schurpfius, dixit de doctore Crucigero: Hic res stringit. Et talis etiam erat magister Reinholdus. Nullum unquam uidi ingenium magis idoneum ad quasuis artes percipiendas, praecipuè ad mathematica, quàm D. Crucigeri.
units.tr: Doctor Hieronymus Schurpfius said of Doctor Crucigerus: "He gets straight to the point." Master Reinhold was of the same kind. I never saw a mind more suited to grasping any arts whatever, especially mathematics, than that of Doctor Crucigerus.

units.la: Descripsi bis mea manu epistolam ad Romanos Graecè, tunc cùm melius adhuc pingerem, & manus essent faciliores, ac plus otij haberem. Vnum uerò exemplar dedi doctori Hesso Vratislauiensi.
units.tr: I twice wrote out the Epistle to the Romans in Greek with my own hand, when I was still writing better and my hand was more nimble and I had more leisure. But I gave one copy to Doctor Hessus of Breslau.

units.la: Turpe est pingere malas literas. Quidam asini de industria male pingunt literas. Omnis qui de industria male pingit literas, est malus grammaticus. cus. Pulchrum est ita scribere, ut literæ sine offensione legi possint. Omnes ueteres principes scripserunt grandiores literas: sicut etiam habebant magnanimitatem animorum, & reliquarum uirtutū. Dux Fridericus & dux Georgius pulchras literas pingebant. Erasmus, Budæus, Lutherus optimè literas pinxerūt: et omnes illos antecellebat Capnio, qui pulchrè pingebat, & grandiusculas amabat literas. Habes mediocrem manum pingendi literas, is eam retineat: neq; illud nisi de affectatione intelligi uolo.
units.tr: It is shameful to write bad letters. Some donkeys deliberately write letters badly. Anyone who deliberately writes letters badly is a bad grammarian. It is fine to write in such a way that the letters can be read without difficulty. All the ancient princes wrote larger letters, just as they also had greatness of spirit and the other virtues. Duke Frederick and Duke George wrote fine letters. Erasmus, Budé and Luther wrote excellent letters, and Capnio surpassed them all: he wrote beautifully and liked somewhat large letters. You have a moderate hand for writing letters; let him keep it, and I want this to be understood only of affectation.

units.la: Chrysoloras, qui docuit Florentiæ literas Græcas primus, cùm parentes sæpè intrassent scholam, uisuri quid filij proficerent, & inspicerent eorum scripturas, dixit: Inspicite tantùm cultros eorum. Qui habet optimum cultrū, ille etiam optimè pingit: id est, qui uenit paratus. Doctor Casparus Crucigerus poterat quorumcunq; pennis optimè pingere. Qui hoc possunt, aut sunt omnino excellentes, aut Schlüngellini, hoc est ignaui.
units.tr: Chrysoloras, who first taught Greek letters at Florence, when parents often came into the school to see what their sons were making progress in and to inspect their writings, said: "Look only at their pens. Whoever has the best pen also writes best, that is, the one who comes prepared." Doctor Caspar Crucigerus could write excellently with anyone's pens. Those who can do this are either wholly outstanding or are Schlüngellini, that is, lazy.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Abbas quidam Erphurdiæ debebat canere missam tono Herbipolensi. Cùm uerò non didicisset illum tonum, stabat ad altare ædituus, incipiens tonum illius loci canère. Perturbatus ea re Abbas, cōuertit se ad ædituum, & ait: Tace, tu facis ut neq; meum neq; tuum sciam. Sic fit etiam, ubi leguntur multæ uersiones & interpretationes.
units.tr: A certain abbot at Erfurt was supposed to sing the Mass in the Würzburg tone. But since he had not learned that tone, the sacristan stood by the altar and began to sing the tone of that place. The abbot, thrown into confusion by this, turned to the sacristan and said: "Be quiet! You make me know neither mine nor yours." So it also happens where many versions and interpretations are read.

units.la: Multi uariè se detorquerūt in inuenienda quadratura circuli in cœlo, & non inuenerunt. Quidam gloriati sunt, se inuenisse: ut Regiomontanus dicit de suo præceptore Burbachio, qui fuit excellens Astronomus. Hanc propositionem meus præceptor tenuit duodecim annos indubitatam, cuius postea falsitatem ipsum inuenisse affirmauit. Videte, hoc accidit præstantissimis artificibus: quid nobis, non tam excellentibus, fieri potest?
units.tr: Many have twisted themselves in various ways in trying to find the squaring of the circle, and have not found it. Some have boasted that they had found it, as Regiomontanus says of his teacher Burbach, who was an excellent astronomer. My own teacher held this proposition as undoubted for twelve years, and afterwards he himself declared that he had discovered its falsity. See, this happens to the most outstanding craftsmen. What may happen to us, who are not nearly so excellent?

units.la: Quidā Comes breui cōmendatione doctrinæ ad magnā administrationē apud Imperatorē Carolū V. propter eruditionē peruenit. Nullus ex ipsius liberis discit literas & artes liberales, neq; ipse adhibet eos ad illas discendas, neq; etiā uult eos discere. Nunc consilium aliquis capere possit, quale genus uitæ ipsi sit eligendum?
units.tr: A certain count, by a brief recommendation of his learning, rose to a high office under the Emperor Charles V on account of his erudition. None of his children learns letters or the liberal arts, nor does he set them to learn them, nor does he even wish them to learn. Can anyone now advise what kind of life should be chosen for them?

units.la: Quidam nugacissima scripsit cōtra Dialecticā Aristotelis. Dicit enim, Aristotelis Dialectica tantū esse rudera lignorū et lapidū, oder ein hauffen zer fallē steīn vnd kalck. Verū est, illi libri nō sunt integri, & interdū sunt mendosi: sed illa fragmēta et tabulæ reliquæ sunt optimæ, & ratio Syllogismorū apud Aristotelē profectò nequaquā est cōtemnēda.
units.tr: Someone wrote very frivolous things against Aristotle's dialectic. He says that Aristotle's dialectic is nothing but the rubble of wood and stone, "or a heap of fallen stones and lime." It is true that those books are not complete and are sometimes faulty, but the surviving fragments and tables are excellent, and the method of syllogisms in Aristotle is certainly not to be despised.

units.la: Plato.
units.tr: Plato.

units.la: Beatus, qui etiā in senectute veritatē cōsequitur.
units.tr: Blessed is he who attains the truth even in old age.

units.la: Dixi aliquando ad amicum: Ego sæpè aliquod argumentum gumentum non statim soluere possum, ita ut post triduum demum soluā. At ille: Hoc non est gloriosum. Respondi: Nos non quaerimus gloriā & ostentationem, sed veritatem.
units.tr: I once said to a friend: "I often cannot solve some argument at once, so that I only solve it after three days." But he replied: "That is not glorious." I answered: "We are not seeking glory and display, but the truth."

units.la: Lipsiæ Mathematicus doctus & peritus in doctrina Mathematum, adeò miserabiliter uixit, ut ex artificio faciendi atramentū uictum suum quaereret. Extant libri ipsius adhuc quidam, & nominatur Alexander. Ille solitus est dicere: Oportet quemlibet Mathematicū esse aut fatuum, aut pauperem, aut malum Grammaticum. Ego, iocosè inquit, sum omnia tria.
units.tr: At Leipzig there was a mathematician, learned and skilled in mathematics, who lived so wretchedly that he sought his living from the craft of making ink. Some of his books still survive, and his name is given as Alexander. He used to say: "Every mathematician must be either a fool, or a poor man, or a bad grammarian. I," he said jokingly, "am all three."

units.la: Bonus Grammaticus est hæreticus.
units.tr: A good grammarian is a heretic.

units.la: In inferiori Germania, uidelicet in Belgico & Brabantia, monachi & sacrificuli habent in quotidianis sermonibus: Bonus Grammaticus est hæreticus. Non enim potest fieri, ut homo habens bonā conscientiam, si sit bonus Grammaticus, & legat scripta ueteris & noui Testamenti, illa non dijudicet. Ego adolescens, audiui doctos uiros & bonos Grammaticos contra aduersarios disputantes, ac dicentes: Si nos legimus libros Propheticos et Apostolicos, tunc longè aliam doctrinam in eis reperimus, quàm uos sacrificuli nobis exponitis.
units.tr: In Lower Germany, namely in Belgium and Brabant, monks and priestlings have it as a common saying: "A good grammarian is a heretic." For, they say, it cannot happen that a man with a good conscience, if he is a good grammarian and reads the writings of the Old and New Testaments, would not judge them correctly. When I was a young man, I heard learned men and good grammarians disputing against their opponents and saying: "If we read the Prophetic and Apostolic books, we find in them a very different doctrine from the one you priestlings expound to us."

units.la: De Ecclesia.
units.tr: On the Church.

units.la: Effectus artium facetè asignatus à Doctore Martino Luthero.
units.tr: The effects of the arts, wittily assigned by Doctor Martin Luther.

units.la: Medicina } facit { infirmos. Mathematica } facit { tristes. Theologia } facit { peccatores.
units.tr: Medicine makes the sick; mathematics makes the sad; theology makes sinners.

units.la: Plato fuit auditor Socratis, de cuius ingenij ac eruditionis futura magnitudine Socrates non obscurè uaticinatus est, dicens, se pridie quàm ad ipsum uenissęt Plato, somniasse, cygnum se in gremio tenere, qui deinde euolàs in altum dulcissimos cantus ediderit: significans, hunc cygnum Græcis futurum esse Platonem. Cùm igitur Socratem aliquandiu audiuissęt, petiuit Aegyptũ, habuitq; Comites peregrinationis Eudoxum & poetam Euripidem. Platonis autem tanta fuit suauitas loquendi Græcè, ut nonnulli dixerint, Iouem, si Græcè locuturus essęt, Platonis usurum oratione. Et Demosthenes fuit auditor Platonis.
units.tr: Plato was a hearer of Socrates, and Socrates prophesied not obscurely the future greatness of his talent and learning. He said that on the day before Plato came to him he had dreamed that he held a swan in his lap, which then flew up into the air, uttering the sweetest songs; signifying that this swan would be Plato for the Greeks. So when Plato had heard Socrates for some time, he sought Egypt, and his companions on the journey were Eudoxus and the poet Euripides. Plato's manner of speaking Greek was so sweet that some have said that Jupiter, if he were to speak Greek, would use Plato's eloquence. Demosthenes too was a hearer of Plato.

units.la: Bonæ pronunciationis utilitas.
units.tr: The usefulness of good pronunciation.

units.la: Dux Eberhardus Vuirtenbergensis, secum Romæ habebat consiliarium, doctũ uirum, sed in pronunciatione saltem rudem: qui cùm ex mandato principis orationem haberet ad Pontificẽ & Cardinales, ita pronunciabat, ut neq; à Pontifice neq; à Cardinalibus intelligeretur. Pontifex igitur Cardinales petebāt, ut alteri Princeps hoc munus dicendi commendaret. Cùm itaq; idem dux simul secum adduxissẹt adolescentem Capnionem, huic mādauit munus dicendi, qui habebat suauem pronunciationem, ita ut ab omnibus intelligeretur. Ea de causa Capnio duci Eberhardo semper fuit charus, & ualde dilectus. Quare adsuefaciēdi sunt adolescentes à primis annis ad bonam & suauem pronunciationem.
units.tr: Duke Eberhard of Württemberg had with him at Rome a councillor, a learned man but at least rough in his pronunciation, who, when he was to deliver a speech by the prince's command to the Pope and the Cardinals, delivered it in such a way that he was understood neither by the Pope nor by the Cardinals. The Pope therefore asked the Cardinals to recommend to another prince someone to perform this task of speaking. Since the same duke had brought with him the young Capnio, he entrusted the speaking task to him, for he had a pleasant pronunciation, so that he was understood by all. For this reason Capnio was always dear to Duke Eberhard and greatly loved. Wherefore young people should be accustomed from their earliest years to good and pleasant pronunciation.

units.la: Iudicium de Liuio docti uiri, nobilis à Carolwitz.
units.tr: The judgement on Livy of a learned man, the nobleman von Carlowitz.

units.la: Nobilis, uir eruditus D. à Carolwitz diligēter legit Liuium, dixitq; se nullam eloquentiam magis mirari quàm illius: quanquam Herodoti lectio etiam ualde dulcis est.
units.tr: The nobleman, the learned Herr von Carlowitz, read Livy diligently, and said that he admired no eloquence more than his, although the reading of Herodotus is also very pleasant.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLLECTANEA.

units.la: Ingressus studia, non frangatur ullis laboribus, qui tolerandi sunt. Est enim omnium rerum ea conditio, ut non sine difficultate cōparentur. Sic enim natura abstrusit pulcherrima quæq; in ipsa terræ uiscera, rosas circumsepsit spinarū aculeis. Quare muni & obfirma animum aduersus illas molestias, quibus superatis consequēris gloriam immortalē. Qui autem feliciter uult progredi in studijs, omnino non det operam amori. Nam qui amori incumbit, nihil aliud cogitat aut facit, quàm quo modo amori seruiat.
units.tr: Having entered upon studies, one should not be broken by any labours that must be endured. For all things are of such a condition that they are not obtained without difficulty. Thus nature has hidden the most beautiful things deep in the bowels of the earth, and surrounded roses with the prickles of thorns. Therefore fortify your mind against those troubles, and once you have overcome them you will win immortal glory. But he who wishes to advance happily in his studies should by no means give himself over to love. For he who devotes himself to love thinks of nothing else and does nothing else than how he may serve his love.

units.la: Sabini iudicium de orationibus Demosthenis.
units.tr: Sabinus' judgement on the orations of Demosthenes.

units.la: Memini Sabinum dicere, Orationes Ciceronis nihil esse, collatas ad Demosthenicas. Nam Demosthenicæ sapientissimè & accuratissimè excogitatæ sunt. Orationes Demosthenis ab omnibus, qui aliquantulum in Græca lingua versati sunt, propter singularem sapientiam laudantur.
units.tr: I remember Sabinus saying that the orations of Cicero are nothing when compared with those of Demosthenes. For the Demosthenic orations were devised most wisely and most carefully. The orations of Demosthenes are praised by all who have some acquaintance with the Greek language for their singular wisdom.

units.la: ENVMERATIO QVORVNDAM præstantissimorum virorum, cùm ex magnatum, tum ex aliis familiis oratorum, qui vel ipsi literarum cognitione studioq; indefesso, vel liberalitate & aliis beneficijs de Ecclesia benemeriti sunt, & adhuc in id incumbunt.
units.tr: A LIST of certain most outstanding men, both from magnates and from other families, orators, who either by their knowledge of letters and tireless zeal, or by their generosity and other benefits, have deserved well of the Church, and still labour for it.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLLECTANEA.

units.la: Philippus rex Macedoniæ cùm aliquando animadvertisset in filio Alexādro, nõ sanè prauā, sed tamè asperiorē & impatientē in imperādo naturā esse, videretq; cum nõ pati domitore asperū: cepit consiliū, doctrina & philosophia flectēdi eum ad suauitatē & comitatē. Hac ratione adeò correxit & excoluit illā naturā, ut in ipso cursu victoriarū vix quisquā fuerit unq; humanior ac moderatior.
units.tr: King Philip of Macedon, when he once noticed that his son Alexander had a nature not indeed depraved but rather harsh and impatient in command, and saw that he would not tolerate a harsh tamer, resolved to bend him towards gentleness and courtesy by means of teaching and philosophy. By this method he so corrected and refined that nature that, even in the very course of his victories, hardly anyone was ever more humane and moderate than he.

units.la: Ludouicus Pius curauit fieri Monotessaron, id est, concordantias quatuor Euangelistarum, magno sumptu. Quem librum diu habuit apud se Lutherus, & hodie est in Lipsica bibliotheca. Præfatio est partim Latinis uersibus, qualde boni sunt, partim prosa oratione, etiā bene et Latinè scripta.
units.tr: Louis the Pious had a Monotessaron made, that is, a harmony of the four Evangelists, at great expense. Luther kept this book with him for a long time, and today it is in the Leipzig library. The preface is partly in Latin verses, which are really good, and partly in prose, also well and elegantly written in Latin.

units.la: Memini, uiuo pio & optimo duce Eberardo Vuirtenbergensi, illam consuetudinem cōtinenter eum obseruasse, ut audiret nobiles adolescentes in cubiculo recitantes Catechismum: & cùm alicuius negligentiam animaduerteret, cæsus est in conspe-ctu ipsius & reliquorum nobilium.
units.tr: I remember that while the pious and excellent Duke Eberhard of Württemberg was still alive, he constantly observed the custom of having noble young men recite the Catechism in his chamber; and when he noticed someone's negligence, that person was beaten in his presence and in that of the other nobles.

units.la: Carolus Magnus est educatus in Collegio mo-nastico, & habuit principes, qui coacti sunt legere singulis diebus horas matutinas. Et ipse hoc pul-chrè obseruauit, ut si quando animaduerteret ali-quem ebriosum aut adulterum, iusserit eum legere aliqua capita in Biblijs ab ipso monstrata, contra ebriosos aut adulteros: ut sic ipsos de disciplina cō monefaceret. Otto Secundus est educatus in Eccle-sia Hildesheimensi.
units.tr: Charles the Great was educated in a monastic college, and had princes who were compelled to read the morning hours every day. He himself observed this admirably: if at any time he noticed someone given to drunkenness or adultery, he would order him to read certain chapters of the Bible pointed out by himself, against drunkards or adulterers, so that thus he might admonish them about discipline. Otto the Second was educated in the church of Hildesheim.

units.la: Hodie rex Portugalensis est egregiè doctus. Audiui ab Appiano & Humelio, amicis nostris, se miratos esse, nostrum Imperatorem Carolum V. uirū occupatum tanta gubernatione Imperij, tamen domi & militiæ contemplationibus & meditationi-bus in doctrina Astronomiæ adeò deditum esse, ut etiam disputet multa quæ ignorent docti in schola.
units.tr: Today the king of Portugal is excellently learned. I heard from Appian and Humelius, our friends, that they marvelled that our Emperor Charles V, a man so occupied with the great governance of the empire, nevertheless is so devoted at home and in military life to contemplation and meditation on the teaching of astronomy that he even debates many matters which the learned in the schools do not know.

units.la: Audiui dici à sapiente uiro, nec auditum nec lectum esse, ullum principem tam studiosum fuisse literarum, atq; Carolum V. Imperatorem, præcipuècum sit obnoxius multis calamitatibus seu morbis.Ille plurimùm legit Thucydidem, qui admodũ difficiliis est intellectu: bene etiam nouit paternam historiam suam: & est consuetudo cubiculariorumsuorum, ut postquam manè, iuxta consuetudinem,dixerunt precationes, postea singuli aliquid legãt,donec Imperator surgat: alius Thucydidem, aliusHerodotum, alius Liuium, alius Gallicam historiã,alius aliud. Postquam Imperator surrexerit, recI-tatis precibus, interrogat, quid singuli legerint, utsic Imperatorem ad hilaritatem excitent. Impera-tor etiam ipse legit Thucydidem, lectisq; aliquotpagellis, sumit sibi spacium de ijs rebus meditandi.Thucydides lingua Gallica est bene uersus, & in-terpres eius adiutus est à Iano Lascare, qui fuitpræses studiorum Lutetiæ. Granuelus adferens Imperatori Thucydidẽ primò Gallicè uersum, dixit:Hunc librum dono Tuæ Maiestati, sed ea cõditio-ne, ut ea promittat mihi, quòd uelit illum perlege-re. Euolutis uerò in eo libro abImperatore aliquotpagellis, ita placuit, ut tertiò perlegeret.
units.tr: I have heard it said by a wise man that neither has it been heard nor read that any prince was so studious of letters as the Emperor Charles V, especially since he is subject to many calamities and diseases. He reads Thucydides very much, which is extremely difficult to understand; he also knows his own paternal history well. And it is the custom of his chamber attendants that, after they have said the morning prayers in the usual way, each then reads something, until the Emperor rises: one reads Thucydides, another Herodotus, another Livy, another the French history, another something else. When the Emperor has risen and the prayers have been recited, he asks what each has read, so that they may stir the Emperor to cheerfulness. The Emperor himself also reads Thucydides, and after he has read a few pages he takes time to meditate on those matters. Thucydides has been well translated into French, and his translator was assisted by Janus Lascaris, who was president of studies at Paris. Granvelle, presenting to the Emperor the Thucydides first translated into French, said: "I offer this book as a gift to Your Majesty, but on this condition, that you promise me you will read it through." And when the Emperor had turned over a few pages of that book, he was so pleased that he read it through a third time.

units.la: Noster Imperator Carolus Quintus non liben-ter multum pecuniæ profundere dicitur: sed tamẽualde est liberalis erga doctos. Cuidam Poetæ car-men men lingua Italica de navigatione Africana componenti, donavit mille coronatos. Alius quidam in Gallia vertit Psalterium versibus in linguam Gallicam, quod ob facundiam ipsius insignem celebratur. Oblato hoc Psalterio Imperatori, dixit Imperator: Non dabo tibi multum. dedit tamen quadraginta coronatos.
units.tr: Our Emperor Charles V is said not to be willing to pour out much money, but nevertheless he is very generous towards the learned. To a certain poet who was composing a poem in the Italian language about the African expedition, he gave a thousand gold crowns. Another man in France turned the Psalter into French verse, which is celebrated for its remarkable eloquence. When this Psalter was offered to the Emperor, the Emperor said: "I will not give you much." Nevertheless he gave forty gold crowns.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Nero, quamuis tyrannus, tamen conduci iussit (cùm videret in suis scholis satis frigidè docere professores & magistros) alios professores, quos substituit ijs, quibus ex suis reditibus dedit stipendia, ut gratis docerent.
units.tr: Nero, though a tyrant, nevertheless ordered (when he saw that the professors and teachers in his schools taught rather coldly) that other professors be hired. He appointed them in place of those to whom he had given salaries from his own revenues, so that they might teach for nothing.

units.la: Multi ex maioribus nostris, quamuis doctrina de filio Dei valde fuit cõtaminata, habuerũt Spiritum sanctũ, intus docentè. Sicut Eberhardus dux Vuirtenbergensis, quando audiuit aliquem multa de operibus cõcionantem, dixit: Ah, quid mihi multa dicis, ego scio articulum fidei, quòd oporteat meredere, & certò remissionem peccatorum expectare propter Christum. Ille dux quamuis non habebat cognitionem Latinæ linguæ, tamè solitus est in publicis disputationibus Germanicè opponere disputantibus. Idem dux Eberhardus Vuirtenbergensis multas causas dixit in imperio: & quia sciebāt homines nobiles, Comites, Principes, et alij, ipsum delectari laude eloquentiæ, sæpè deferebant causas ad eum. Hic etiam primus habuit duodecim Doctores præstátes in cõuentu, cũ alij tunc nõ multos haberet. Et hoc faciebat propterea: nam quando erat ad ipsum relata alicuius Principis, Comitis uel nobilis causa, & dicenda in senatu Imperij, dabat cā faciendā Doctoribus: iubebat poni diserte propositionē uel statū causæ, & muniri certis legibus seu rationib. Ipse interea, cùm diu de ea meditatus esset, & de elocutioe cogitaret: Quæso, inquit, cogitate, quis nostrûm possit habere pulchrũ exemplum uel fabulã. Deinde ipse etiã recitabat, quæ præmeditatus erat.
units.tr: Many of our ancestors, although the doctrine concerning the Son of God was greatly corrupted, had the Holy Spirit teaching within them. So it was with Duke Eberhard of Württemberg: when he heard someone preaching at length about works, he said: "Ah, why do you tell me so much? I know the article of faith, that one must believe and confidently expect forgiveness of sins on account of Christ." That duke, although he had no knowledge of Latin, was accustomed to object in German to the disputants in public disputations. The same Duke Eberhard of Württemberg pleaded many cases in the empire, and since men knew that nobles, counts, princes and others delighted in the praise of eloquence, they often referred their cases to him. He was also the first to have twelve doctors present at the council, when others then did not have many. He did this for the following reason: when the case of some prince, count or noble had been referred to him and was to be argued before the imperial council, he gave the work of preparing it to the doctors. He ordered the proposition or the state of the case to be set out clearly and fortified with certain laws or arguments. Meanwhile he himself, having pondered the matter for a long time and thought about its style, would say: "Please, think which of us could have a fine example or fable." Then he himself recited what he had prepared beforehand.

units.la: Iason adolescēs fuit traditus Chironi medico in disciplinā. Credo quoq; quòd docuerit eũ præter artē medicā, etiā ratione anni & motuũ cœlestiū: sicut ponitur sagittarius inter signa cœlestia, & ipse sagittarius est Chiron. Breuiter, quæcunq; sunt disciplinæ, quibus magni principes & heroes studere solēt, in ijs omnib. hic institutus fuit: quemadmodũ & de Achille fertur. Postquã adoleuit, redijt in patriã. & cùm uenissęt ad flumē, quòd fuit ante patriã, stetit ibi mulier augusta specie, quæ dicebat se esse sacrificulā Iunonis, cùm esset ipsa Iuno: & petiuit ab ipso, ut se trāsportaret per flumē. ibi Iason motus religione, suscepta humeris traduxit eā. & cũ forte hæreret in luto, amisit alterũ calceũ seu ocream (quia ipsi usi sunt ocreis) & sic uenit in patriam altero tantummodo pede calceatus. Ibi petiuit à ciuibus, ut sibi traderent paternam hereditatem, quam tunc tenebat Pelias. Iste, eo uiso, statim recordatus est oraculi: quare arte uolens eum perdere, suasit ei expeditionem suscipere Colchicā ad tollēdum aureum uellus. Quid autem id fuerit, alij aliter narrant. Plutarchus dicit fuisse uenas metalli cas. Post illam expeditionem redit Iason, et Peliam interfecit. Sic uirtute et literis ad summos honores maximamq; laudem peruenit.
units.tr: As a youth, Jason was entrusted to the physician Chiron for instruction. I believe he taught him, besides the medical art, also the reckoning of the year and the motions of the heavenly bodies, just as the archer is placed among the constellations, and the archer is Chiron himself. In short, whatever branches of learning great princes and heroes are accustomed to study, he was trained in all of them, as is also said of Achilles. When Jason had grown up, he returned to his homeland. When they came to the river that lay before his homeland, a woman of stately appearance stood there, who said that she was a priestess of Juno, though she was Juno herself, and asked him to carry her across the river. Moved by religious scruple, Jason took her on his shoulders and carried her over. When by chance he stuck fast in the mud, he lost one of his sandals or greaves (for they used greaves), and so came into his homeland shod on only one foot. There he asked the citizens to hand over to him his paternal inheritance, which Pelias then held. Pelias, on seeing him, at once recalled the oracle. Wishing to destroy him by cunning, he persuaded him to undertake the expedition to Colchis to carry off the golden fleece. What that fleece was, however, others tell differently; Plutarch says it was veins of metal. After that expedition Jason returned and killed Pelias. Thus by virtue and learning he attained the highest honours and the greatest praise.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Narrantur multa de Acaco: sed credo per illas fabulas significatum, ipsum fuisse studiosum in scrutandis causis rerum naturalium, & inuentorem metallorum ac fodinarum.
units.tr: Many things are told of Acacus, but I believe that through those fables it is meant that he was devoted to investigating the causes of natural things, and that he was the inventor of metals and mines.

units.la: Gregorius Nazianzenus sic laudat praesidem suae patriae: Quis senectam meam fouebit? à te impetraui plurima beneficia ærumnosis. Lachrymas uero nobis relinquis, & laudes scriptas in mentibus nostris tanquam in perpetuis columnis. Quòd si redieris, ut optamus, Deo maiora officia gratitudinis offeremus. Dicit Nazianzenus, se fuisse φιλάνθρωπον humanitatis Olympij, hoc est, pro aliis multa impetrasse.
units.tr: Gregory Nazianzen thus praises the governor of his homeland: "Who will cherish my old age? From you I have obtained very many benefits for the afflicted. You leave us tears, indeed, and praises written in our minds as on everlasting columns. But if you return, as we hope, we shall offer God greater duties of gratitude." Nazianzen says that he was a philanthropist of Olympian humanity, that is, that he obtained many things for others.

units.la: Ingeniosissimus princeps Fridericus Secundus Imperator, ex Arabum monumētis doctrinam Mathematicam in Latinum sermonem transfundi, utcunq; instaurari magno sumptu curauit. Ac multa extant testimonia, quae ostendunt his studijs uetustissimos reges deditos fuisse, ut Atlatem, Orionem, Chironem.
