Ideo enim, nomina eorum stellis in coe-lo grata posteritas attribuit, ut significaret se ab illis doctrinam de motibus coelestibus, & anni descriptionem accepisse. Et Caesar de se inquit apud Lu-canum:
units.tr: The most ingenious prince, the Emperor Frederick II, had mathematical doctrine translated into Latin from Arabic records, and at great expense saw to its restoration in whatever way he could. Many testimonies also exist showing that the most ancient kings were devoted to these studies, such as Atlas, Orion and Chiron. For posterity assigned their names to stars in the heavens, to signify that men had received from them the doctrine of the motions of the heavens and the description of the year. And Caesar says of himself in Lucan:

units.la: —Media inter praelia semperStellarum coelicq; plagis superisq; uacaui.
units.tr: "Amid the battles I always kept myself free for the stars and the regions of heaven above."

units.la: Constat etiam, nostrum Imperatorem Carolum V. diligentissimum esse in quaerenda longitudine et latitudine regionum: in stellis conferendis ad regio-num situs, ut navigans coeli contuitu cursum diri-gere possit. Sedens in thermis, cum pedis curationi vacaret, ocium fefellit interdum horologijs artificio-se describendis.
units.tr: It is also established that our Emperor Charles V was most diligent in seeking the longitude and latitude of regions, and in comparing stars with the positions of places, so that a navigator might direct his course by observing the sky. Sitting in the baths, while he had time for the treatment of his foot, he sometimes beguiled his leisure by skilfully constructing sundials.

units.la: In fine conuentus Ratisbonensis, cum altero die esset discessurus, uocauit me ad se optimus prin-ceps Georgius Marchio Brandenburgensis, enar-rans mihi opus sibi esse medicamentis propter acres dolores in sinistro latere. Ad quem dicebam: Illu-strissime Princeps, celsitudo tua non sit nimis solli-cita hac de re: narrabo illi causas illorum dolorum. C.T. habuit in hoc conuentu multa molesta nego-cia publica et priuata propter multiplices religio-nis controuersias, augentia ipsi atram bilem, quae effunditur in uicina loca, & ea efficit sua agitatio-ne illos ingentes dolorum sensus. Quòd autem ita fit, sentiet C.T. cùm domum redierit ad uenationè: qua ipsa oblectetur, & excutiat ex animo illa ne-gocia, quantum potest. Tum enim statim lenientur illi sensus dolorum. Tum ille: Profectò sentio id es-se, quia si biduum aut triduũ uacauero ab illis negociis, paulatim animaduerto dolores leniri: et uicissim, cùm redeo ad illa negocia, augeri.
units.tr: At the end of the Diet of Regensburg, when I was to depart the next day, the excellent prince George, Margrave of Brandenburg, summoned me to him, explaining that he needed medicines because of sharp pains in his left side. To him I said: "Most illustrious Prince, let your Highness not be too anxious about this matter; I will tell you the causes of those pains. Your Grace had many troublesome public and private affairs at this Diet, on account of the manifold religious controversies. These increase black bile in you, which pours out into neighbouring parts and, by its agitation, produces those great sensations of pain. That this is so, Your Grace will notice when you have returned home to hunting, which delights you and drives those affairs from your mind as far as you can. For then those sensations of pain will at once be relieved." Then he said: "Indeed I feel that this is so: if I have two or three days free of those affairs, I notice the pains gradually easing, and conversely, when I return to those affairs, they increase."

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: De illustrissimo Principe Borussiae, Alberto seniore.
units.tr: On the most illustrious Prince of Prussia, Albert the Elder.

units.la: Nota est multis Principis illius pietas & liberalitas erga ecclesiam & scholas, ita ut profectò uerbis consequi non possim zelum pijssimi principis, quo doctrinam puriorem cupit inuiolatam, & ad posteros esse transmissam. Dixit autem aliquando ad honestum & doctrina excellentem uirum, à se ad docendum in Borussia Euangelium uocatum: se toto pectore lætari, si uideat occasionem benefa[?]ciendi Theologis, & se uerè Theologorum colloquia pro deliciis habere. Respondit ille minister: Hæc uox non solùm principe digna, sed & sancta est, declarans suæ celsitudinis studium & amorem seruandi & prouehendi ministerium. Cui mox princeps: Sanctus ego non sum, at sanctorum consortio & colloquio delector. & o utinam mihi semper ad manum decem sint Theologi vita & doctrina probati: tum & suauius vuerem, & suauius memorisci-rem. Sic vere alter Simeon est, summa voluptate complectens Christum, eiq; dulcissima oscula infigens. Hunc piissimum principem, patrem patriæ Germaniæ, ut Deus diu incolumem et saluum una cum coniuge omnibus virtutibus excellentissima, et filio, qui illustrissimi Principis patris Alberti virtutes imitari studet, conseruet, propter nominis sui gloriam, ecclesiæ & Reipublicæ salutem, toto pectore, propter filium suum dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, omnes pij intimis suis pectoris gemitibus orent.
units.tr: The piety and generosity of that prince towards the Church and the schools are well known to many, so that I truly cannot put into words the zeal of this most godly prince, by which he desires the doctrine to be kept pure and unharmed and handed down to posterity. He once said to a learned and honourable man, who had been called by him to teach the Gospel in Prussia, that he rejoiced with his whole heart whenever he saw an opportunity to do a kindness to theologians, and that he truly regarded conversations with theologians as his delight. That minister replied: "This utterance is not only worthy of a prince but holy too, declaring your Highness's zeal and love for preserving and advancing the ministry." Thereupon the prince said at once: "I am not holy, but I delight in the company and conversation of the holy. And O, that I might always have ten theologians of approved life and doctrine at hand! Then I would both live more pleasantly and remember more pleasantly. Thus he is truly another Simeon, embracing Christ with the greatest joy and pressing the sweetest kisses upon him." May all the godly, from the depths of their hearts, pray that God keep this most pious prince, father of the fatherland of Germany, safe and sound for a long time, together with his wife, most excellent in every virtue, and with his son, who strives to imitate the virtues of his most illustrious father Albert, for the glory of his name and for the salvation of the Church and the commonwealth, for the sake of his Son our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Rex Demetrius cum Rhodum obsideret, murumq; in eo loco, ubi tabula erat Protogenis magna arte picta, quassaturus esset: illo autem rogato à Rhodijs, ut monumento illi parceret: reuocauit inde milites, inquiēs, se nō gerere bellū cum artibus. Eaq; initia fuerūt faciedæ pacis cū Rhodijs.
units.tr: When King Demetrius was besieging Rhodes and was about to batter the wall at the place where Protogenes' great painting was, the Rhodians asked him to spare that monument. He then recalled his soldiers, saying that he was not waging war against the arts. This was the beginning of peace with the Rhodians.

units.la: Iacobus Marchio Badensis, maior natu, fuit episcopus Treuerensis. Debuisset quidem patri succedere in regno, sed Maximilianus Imperator voluit eum esse episcopum propter excellens ingenium, eruditionem, eloquentiam, & omnem ingenij &. & corporis præstantiam. Quia Imperator uole‑bat, ut etiā doctus episcopus inter electores esset, cuius usus in negocijs imperij non minimus foret. Hic in cõuentu Coloniensi post bellum Bauaricũ, anno Christi 1505 nomine Imperij respondit legatis Gallicis Gallicè, legatis Pontificijs Latinè, legatis Venetis Italicè, & Germanicis Germanicè. Fuit excellenter doctus in Iure, bonus musicus, & in omnibus rebus industrius, etiā in re militari: ita ut immaturam ipsius mortem totum Germaniæ imperium luxerit.
units.tr: James, Margrave of Baden, the elder son, was bishop of Trier. He ought indeed to have succeeded his father in the realm, but the Emperor Maximilian wished him to be a bishop because of his outstanding talent, learning, eloquence and every excellence of mind and body. For the Emperor wanted a learned bishop among the electors, whose counsel would be of no small use in the affairs of the empire. At the assembly at Cologne after the Bavarian war, in the year of Christ 1505, he replied in the name of the empire to French envoys in French, to papal envoys in Latin, to Venetian envoys in Italian, and to German envoys in German. He was exceptionally learned in law, a good musician, and diligent in all matters, even in military affairs, so that the whole German empire mourned his untimely death.

units.la: Rex Galliæ Franciscus suo sumptu Romæ & Lutetiæ multos libros describi curauit, è quib. multi editi sunt. Pars magna horum librorũ adhuc Lutetiæ asseruatur.
units.tr: King Francis of France, at his own expense, had many books copied at Rome and at Paris, of which many were published. A large part of these books is still kept at Paris.

units.la: Maximilianus Imperator habuit hanc consuetudinem, ut ad prandium & ad cœnam quidã scriptores utiles ipsi legerentur.
units.tr: The Emperor Maximilian had the custom of having certain useful writers read to him at dinner and at supper.

units.la: Legi fundationem episcopatus Hamburgensis, qui nunc est Bremēsis, ubi Imperator Carolus Magnus dicit: Deus dedit nobis uictorias contra has gentes, ideo uolumus ut ipsi Deo seruiant, non nobis, et libertatem ueterem retineant. Ita reges olim voluerunt fines victoriarum esse salutem animarum, & pacem gentium, & libertatem legibus munitam. Et ex Hamburga uoce episcopi Angari, uiri doctrina & testimonijs Spiritus sancti ornati, latè sparsa est doctrina in Frisiam & Daniam. Ita gens Saxonica veram Dei agnitionem annos fere 800 retinet. Et Heinricus Auceps fundauit episcopatū Schleswicensem.
units.tr: I have read the foundation of the bishopric of Hamburg, which is now that of Bremen, where the Emperor Charlemagne says: "God has given us victories against these peoples; therefore we wish them to serve God, not us, and to keep their ancient liberty." Thus kings of old wished the aim of their victories to be the salvation of souls, the peace of nations, and liberty protected by law. And from Hamburg, by the voice of Bishop Ansgar, a man adorned with learning and with the testimonies of the Holy Spirit, the doctrine was widely spread into Friesland and Denmark. So the Saxon people has kept the true knowledge of God for nearly 800 years. And Henry the Fowler founded the bishopric of Schleswig.

units.la: Quæstio.
units.tr: Question.

units.la: An Carolus Magnus habuerit causam gerendi bellum contra Saxones? Unde sic argumentor.
units.tr: Did Charlemagne have a cause for waging war against the Saxons? I argue as follows.

units.la: Nemo potest mutare corda: quia religio mutat corda.
units.tr: No one can change hearts, because religion changes hearts.

units.la: Ergo non magistratus.
units.tr: Therefore not the magistrate.

units.la: Respondeo ad antecedens: Nemo potest mutare corda; scilicet, cui non est mandatum à Deo. Sed magistratus officiū est, ut curet utramq; Tabulam, primam & secundam, & ut maneat externa professio doctrinæ cum gubernatione externæ disciplinæ. Nimis crasse dictum est, quòd magistratus sit armentarius, & tantum curet corpus.
units.tr: I answer the major premise: no one can change hearts, that is, one to whom God has not given the command. But it is the duty of the magistrate to take care of both tables, the first and the second, and to maintain the outward profession of doctrine together with the governance of outward discipline. It has been said too crudely that the magistrate is a herdsman and cares only for the body.

units.la: Godefridus de Bilion, cum recuperasset terram sanctam, coronatus est ab exercitu corona spinea, capite impositō saxo sepulchri Christi. Ita principes debent vitam & omnes facultates in discrimē adducere propter confessionem doctrinæ, & coronari corona spinea, id est, tolerare afflictiones propter confessionem veræ & sincerę doctrinæ.
units.tr: Godfrey of Bouillon, when he had recovered the Holy Land, was crowned by the army with a crown of thorns, a stone from the Lord's sepulchre being placed on his head. So princes ought to put their lives and all their resources in peril for the confession of doctrine, and be crowned with a crown of thorns, that is, bear afflictions for the confession of true and sincere doctrine.

units.la: Francofordiæ est pictura Caroli Magni: fuit vir grandibus oculis, fuit ei vox grandis, & ita eruditus, ut Græcam linguam intellexerit: quanquā nō fuerit fuerit ea lingua usus. Habuit præceptorem discipulum Bedæ, hominem Saxonicum (quia Angli sunt Saxones) cui nomen fuit Alcuinus: & is fuit, ex cuius consilio instituta est Vniuersitas Parisiensis. Curauit describi lingua Frācica historiæ Euāgelij seriē. Rolānd fuit eius patruelis, cui illud Epitaphiū fecit.
units.tr: At Frankfurt there is a painting of Charlemagne: he was a man with large eyes and a loud voice, and so learned that he understood the Greek language, although he did not actually speak that language. He had as his teacher Bede's pupil, a Saxon man (since the English are Saxons), whose name was Alcuin, and it was on his advice that the University of Paris was founded. He had the history of the Gospel's sequence copied out in the Frankish tongue. Roland was his cousin, for whom he composed that epitaph.

units.la: Caroli Magni epitaphium, in obitum Rolandi demortui in Rincevalle, anno à nato Christo 786.
units.tr: Epitaph of Charlemagne, on the death of Roland, who died at Roncevaux in the year 786 after the birth of Christ.

units.la: Tu patriam repetis, nos tristi in orbe relinquis: Te tenet aula nitens, nos lachrymosa dies. Sed qui lustra geris octo binos super annos, Ereptus terris, iustus ad astra redis.
units.tr: You return to your fatherland and leave us in a sorrowful world. The gleaming hall holds you; a tearful day holds us. But you, who have passed eight times two years, snatched from the earth, go back to the stars as a just man.

units.la: Quando Carolus Magnus domuit Germanos siue Saxones, ibi Rolandus fuit capitaneus Caroli: & inde posuit ipse suam statuam in illis urbibus, ut significaretur esse eas in tutela Imperatoria. Hæc etiam talis statua est, quæ est inclusa: ut significetur, illam libertatem esse amissam.
units.tr: When Charles the Great subdued the Germans, or Saxons, Roland was Charles's captain there. From then on he set up his own statue in those cities, to signify that they were under imperial protection. This statue too is enclosed, to signify that the liberty of those cities has been lost.

units.la: Dux Saxoniæ Iohannes fuit vir honestus, pius & bonus, qui sedulò audiuit conciones, & multas etiam propria manu descripsit, & habuit suos codicillos: et si quid memorabile audiuit ex Luthero, illud annotauit. Pinxit quoq; characteres satis magnos & legibiles.
units.tr: Duke John of Saxony was an honest, pious and good man. He diligently heard sermons, wrote out many of them with his own hand, and kept his own notebooks; if he heard anything memorable from Luther, he noted it down. He also drew characters quite large and legible.

units.la: Fuit Francofordiæ in conuiuio quodam nobiliū, quorum aliqui adhuc uiuut, inter quos fuit Heinr<bl>ych</bl> von Lütter, grauis & præstas uir, qui nunc est Capi-taneus principis Lãtgrauij in Hassia. Ibi cœperunt nugari alij inter se de materijs Theologicis. Ille hoc ægrè ferens, seuerissimè eos obiurgauit: Heu, inquiēs, quare uos ita luditis in rebus diuinis, uos omnes nihil omnino intelligitis de illis serijs rebus. Ego quoq; putabã me esse sapientē, & aliquid in-telligere, sed nihil sciebã de his Theologicis mate-rijs. Cùm aũt nuperrimè ægrotarẽ, tũc incœpi pri-mùm aliquid de istis tentationibus discere.
units.tr: At a banquet of nobles in Frankfurt, some of whom are still alive, there was Heinrich von Lütter, a serious and distinguished man, who is now captain for the Landgrave prince in Hesse. There some of the others began to joke among themselves about theological matters. He, taking this badly, rebuked them very sharply: "Alas," he said, "why do you play like this with divine things? You all understand absolutely nothing of those serious matters. I too thought I was wise and understood something, but I knew nothing of these theological matters. Yet when I was recently ill, then I first began to learn something about these temptations."

units.la: Dux Ernestus Luneburgẽsis, pius et optim^o princeps, cũ toto die fuisset ieiunus, et accepisset nunciũ de negocio cuiusdã, dixit: Se maluisse ut brachium sibi fuisset præcisum, quàm q; illud accidisset. Ita do-lebat optimo principi, doctrinã nostrã deformari.
units.tr: Duke Ernst of Lüneburg, a pious and most excellent prince, had fasted all day and received news of some business. He said that he would have preferred that his arm had been cut off rather than that this had happened. So greatly did the excellent prince grieve that our doctrine was being disfigured.

units.la: Dux Fridericus Saxoniæ, quandocunq; legebat in optimis authoribus sententiam quandam insi-gnem, eam parieti inscripsit, ut semper eam in con-spectu haberet, ne excideret ipsi è mente. Sic ambu-lãs in musæo, talia dicta tacitus secum cõsiderauit.
units.tr: Duke Frederick of Saxony, whenever he read some remarkable saying in the best authors, wrote it on the wall so that he always had it in view and it would not slip from his mind. So, walking in his museum, he would silently ponder such sayings.

units.la: Gubernatio ueri doctoris est omniũ difficilima uocatio.
units.tr: The governance of a true teacher is the most difficult of all callings.

units.la: Memini Lantgrauiũ Hassiæ, bonũ principẽ, di-cere in familiari collatiõe, se malle esse omniũ prin-cipũ monarchã, quàm minimũ cõcionatorẽ uel do-ctorẽ Ecclesiæ: nõ quòd ad dignitates aut honores uel authoritatem, aut etiam potentiam attinet, sed potius quod ad sustinendos labores, & propter illius uocationis difficultatem. Volebat dicere, doctorem Ecclesiæ multo maiores curas et labores oportere sustinere, quàm principem aliquem in tota sua Politica gubernatione.
units.tr: I remember the Landgrave of Hesse, a good prince, saying in familiar conversation that he would rather be the monarch of all princes than the humblest preacher or teacher of the Church. This was not because of dignities, honours, authority or even power, but rather because of the labours to be endured and the difficulty of that calling. He meant that a teacher of the Church must bear far greater cares and labours than any prince in the whole conduct of his political government.

units.la: Ptolemæus Philadelphus habuit instructam Bibliothecam, & curauit Biblia Hebraica in linguam Græcam transferri. Idem curauit multarum gentium historias conscribere, et dicitur in translatione Bibliorum Hebraicorum ex Iudæa accersiuisse Leuitas, qui uerterent Biblia Græce. Hoc potest fieri, quòd ita sit: sed fabula est, quòd Septuaginta uiri sint inclusi in singula loca, & cùm uniuscuiusque codex inspiceretur, uisa sit unius uersio congruere uersioni alterius in Græca lingua.
units.tr: Ptolemy Philadelphus had a well-stocked library and saw to it that the Hebrew Bible was translated into Greek. He also had histories of many nations written. It is said that for the translation of the Hebrew Bible he summoned Levites from Judea to turn the Bible into Greek. This may well be true, but it is a fable that the seventy men were shut up in separate cells, and that when each one's copy was examined, the version of one was found to agree word for word with that of another in Greek.

units.la: Carolus Quartus fundator Academiæ Pragensis, sæpè mansit in disputationibus, & unà disputauit tam longo tempore, ut aliquoties negligeret etiam tempus prandij & cœnæ. Cùm autem uocaretur ad cœnam, dixit: Se magis delectari illis cibis & delicijs, quas ex suauitate illarum collationum perciperet, quàm ex terrenis. Tale nunc nihil est præterquam in paucis nostris principibus.
units.tr: Charles IV, founder of the Academy of Prague, often stayed on in disputations, and disputed together for so long that sometimes he neglected even the time for lunch and supper. When he was called to supper, he said that he took more delight in the food and delicacies he received from the sweetness of those discussions than in earthly ones. Nothing like this now exists, except among a few of our princes.

units.la: Insigne Academiæ Heydelbergensis.
units.tr: The emblem of the Academy of Heidelberg.

units.la: Academia Heydelbergensis habet insigne, Leonem tenentem librum, pulcherrimum Principis & Academiæ insigne. Est insigne testimonium, quòd Principes, & omnes gubernatores debeât esse custodes doctrinarum & scholarum.
units.tr: The Academy of Heidelberg has as its emblem a lion holding a book, a most beautiful emblem of the Prince and the Academy. It is a notable testimony that princes and all governors ought to be guardians of doctrine and of schools.

units.la: Non credo esse in mundo adolescentem, cuius fuerit excellentius ingenium, quam regis Angliæ iunioris Eduardi. Erat natus annos octodecim, & bene Græcè & Latinè loquebatur. Fuit etiam non ignarus Gallicæ & Italicæ linguæ, & bene institutus in artibus. Ita erudite disputavit cum Cardano de multis Mathematicis quæstionibus, ut scribat de eo Cardanus, quòd si uixisset, futurus fuisset alter Salomon. Hic optimus rex moritur in flore ætatis suæ.
units.tr: I do not believe there is a young man in the world whose talent was more outstanding than that of the young King of England, Edward. He was eighteen years old and spoke Greek and Latin well. He was also not ignorant of French and Italian, and was well trained in the liberal arts. He disputed so learnedly with Cardano on many mathematical questions that Cardano writes of him that, had he lived, he would have become another Solomon. This excellent king died in the flower of his age.

units.la: Omnes sapientes gubernatores cognitionem historiarum amant.
units.tr: All wise governors love the study of history.

units.la: Memini Capnionem narrare, se cum Rudolpho Agricola, episcopo Dalburgio, & aliis præstantissimis uiris, quorum aliquos bene noui, fuisse in aula Palatini: quia habuit illa Aula uiros præstantissimos & ingeniosos, ut illum ipsum Dalburgium et alios. Et quia audiuit Princeps eos sæpè colloqui de historijs, & antiquis rebus gestis, petiuit ab illis, ut sibi historiæ Epitomen conscriberent, & redigerent in ordinem annos Monarchiarum: quia non habuerunt illa tempora, sicut nostra, tam concinnas & breues Chronologias. Tradidit etiā Princeps satis liberales sumptus ad collectionem illarūhistoriarum. Illi igitur contulerunt operas, ac Ca-pnio & Agricola ex monumētis ueterum scripto-rum conscripserunt librum quendam propemodūeo ordine, quo nos contexuimus Carionis Chroni-con: & excerpserunt iucundiora, ac tradideruntillum librum Principi: qui ita fuit delectatus eo, utquotidie in eo legeret. Existimo etiam illum librūadhuc extare in Bibliotheca Palatinorum.
units.tr: I remember Capnio relating that he, together with Rudolf Agricola, Bishop Dalberg and other most distinguished men, some of whom I know well, was at the court of the Count Palatine. That court had outstanding and gifted men, such as Dalberg himself and others. Since the prince often heard them talk about histories and ancient deeds, he asked them to write him an epitome of history and to arrange the years of the monarchies in order, because those times did not have, as ours do, such neat and concise chronologies. The prince also provided quite generous funds for the collection of those histories. They therefore pooled their efforts, and Capnio and Agricola compiled from the records of the ancient writers a book in nearly the same order as that in which we have put together Carion's Chronicle. They excerpted the more pleasing material and handed the book to the prince, who was so delighted with it that he read it every day. I think that book still survives in the library of the Palatines.

units.la: Ioannis ducis Saxoniæ pia uoluntas benefaciendi Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: The pious willingness of John, Duke of Saxony, to benefit the Church.

units.la: In prima inspectione Ecclesiarū, cùm nulli certi reditus in plerisq; parochijs essent, ibi cùm nos in inspectione attribuissemus certos reditus Ecclesiæ Gothensi, & Isenacensi, & iterum reuersi essemus in aulam Vimariæ, cumq; acta recēseremus, addentes simul supplicationem, ut pius Princeps hanc cō stitutionē defenderet, & ego inter cætera citassem sententiam Esaiæ, quæ tunc non erat nota multis Reges erunt nutritores tui, & regimæ nutrices: ita placuit optimo seni Duci Ioanni, ut statim iuberet locum indicare, ubi hæc sententia scripta esset. Val de delectatus est illa sententia, in qua commonefeci mus eum sui officij. Curauit etiam statim illa quæ petebamus, & misit certos quosdam uiros ad illa loca, ut illa confirmarent, ne ab quibusdam aulicis perturbarentur:
units.tr: At our first inspection of the churches, since in most parishes there were no fixed revenues, we assigned fixed revenues to the churches at Gotha and Eisenach. Then we returned to the court at Weimar, and while we were going over the proceedings, we added a petition that the pious Prince would uphold this arrangement. Among other things I cited the saying of Isaiah, which was then not well known to many: "Kings shall be your nursing fathers, and their queens your nurses." The excellent old Duke John was so pleased with this saying that at once he ordered us to point out the place where it was written. He was especially delighted with that saying, in which we reminded him of his office. He also at once took care of what we were asking for, and he sent certain men to those places to confirm these arrangements, so that they would not be disturbed by some of the courtiers.

units.la: Laudabile factum Constantini in componenda pace in Ecclesia.
units.tr: The praiseworthy action of Constantine in establishing peace in the Church.

units.la: In synodo Nicaena, cùm esset confessio edenda de illo magno articulo, an λόγος esset ὑφιστάμε-νος, & an duæ naturæ essent in filio : cumq; aduersarij ueræ doctrinæ multa apud Constantinum Imperatorem contra pios doctores & episcopos dicerent, simulq; multa scripta ad ipsum referrent, quibus rectè sentientes de doctrina traducerent & accusarent : Imperator clementissimè accepit omnium literas, accusationes ac delationes, ac promisit se illis clementer responsurum. Cùm uerò iam omnium libellos & literas accusatorias accepisset, illiq; putarent se habere propitium Imperatorem, & iam pios Episcopos & doctores cecidisse causa : Imperator Constantinus die quodam omnes accusatores conuocauit, ac in præsentia eorum omnes istas literas accusatorias nondum etiam resignatas, unà cum libellis nondum lectis in ignem coniecit, dicens : Ego uolo uos, qui alios uultis docere in Ecclesia, concordes esse, & non mouere certamina non necessaria. Iam uerò non
units.tr: At the Council of Nicaea, when a confession was to be published on that great article, whether the logos [λόγος] was subsisting [ὑφιστάμενος], and whether there were two natures in the Son; and when the adversaries of sound doctrine said many things before the Emperor Constantine against the godly teachers and bishops, and at the same time brought many writings to him by which they might slander and accuse those who thought rightly about doctrine; the Emperor most graciously received the letters, accusations and denunciations of all, and promised that he would answer them graciously. But when he had now received the pamphlets and accusing letters of everyone, and they thought they had a favourable Emperor and that the cause of the godly bishops and teachers was already lost, the Emperor Constantine summoned all the accusers on one day, and in their presence threw all those accusing letters, not yet sealed, together with the unread pamphlets, into the fire, saying: "I want you, who wish to teach others in the Church, to be of one mind, and not to stir up unnecessary contests. Indeed, it is not private affairs and hatreds that must be dealt with, but public ones, and indeed the salvation of souls, and the spiritual building up of many nations in the saving faith.

units.la: non de priuatis negocijs & odijs agendum est, sed de publica, & quidem animarum salute, & multarum gentium in salutari spirituali fidei ædifica-tione. addens simul hanc uocem: Quia ministrorum Euangelij errata non prodest esse nota uulgo: Et si ministrum Euangelij in adulterio deprehenderé, pallio iniecto celarem scelus. Hic imperator piè et honestè fecit, quia melius est, unum membrum pe-rire, quàm totum corpus. Huic congruit elegas di-ctum Iasonis Phærei ante Philippum Macedonem regnātis, optimi principis in Thessalia: Tendentis ad iusticiam in summa rei necessitate est, negligere iusticias multas in partibus.
units.tr: He added at the same time this saying: "It is not useful for the errors of the ministers of the Gospel to be known to the common people; and if I caught a minister of the Gospel in adultery, I would hide the crime by throwing my cloak over him." This emperor acted piously and honourably, because it is better that one member perish than the whole body. With this agrees the elegant saying of Jason of Pherae, the best prince in Thessaly, who reigned before Philip of Macedon: "It belongs to one who aims at justice, in the greatest necessity of affairs, to overlook many injustices in particulars."

units.la: Alexander Imperator habuit senatum præstan-tissimorum & doctissimorum uirorū, qui tum flo-ruerunt cognitione iuris, inter quos Vlpianus fuit, eius Cancellarius, siue (ut uocant) magister epi-stolarū. Habetur uerò hoc memorabile de Alexan-dro, quòd, cùm milites (qui oderunt scribas & le-ges) impetum facerent in Vlpianum, Imperator obiecerit suum pallium, & opposuerit suū corpus & uitam ad tegendum Vlpianum. Ita princeps de-bet tueri leges & iudices. Recitatur & illud eius-dem dictū: ὁ πολλὰ λαλέψας, ϰωλίγα δὸς, ἐνφ-ξετααι: id est, Qui multa furatur, & pauca dat, scili-cet iudicibus, ille effugiet. Nostri transtulerunt ad alia: Qui multa furatur, scilicet ex monasterijs bonis Ecclesiasticis: & pauca dat, scilicet ministris Ecclesiæ, & pauperibus scholasticis: ille effugiet pœnas, id est, illum absoluimus. Legit quotidie librum Ciceronis de Republica, qui fuit ipsi loco horarij, seu libelli precationis.
units.tr: The Emperor Alexander had a senate of most outstanding and learned men, who then flourished in the knowledge of law, among whom was Ulpian, his chancellor, or (as they call him) master of letters. This is recorded as a memorable thing about Alexander: when soldiers, who hate scribes and laws, made an attack on Ulpian, the Emperor threw his own cloak over him and exposed his own body and life to cover Ulpian. So a prince ought to protect laws and judges. There is also recited this saying of the same man: "He who steals much and gives little [ὁ πολλὰ κλέψας, ὀλίγα δοὺς] will escape [ἐκφεύξεται]." That is, he who steals much and gives little, namely to the judges, will escape. Ours have applied it to other things: he who steals much, namely from the monasteries' ecclesiastical goods, and gives little, namely to the ministers of the Church and to poor scholars, will escape punishment, that is, we absolve him. He read daily the book of Cicero on the Commonwealth, which was for him the equivalent of a book of hours or a prayer book.

units.la: Alexander misit Aristoteli octingenta talenta, hoc est, quadringenta & octoginta millia coronatorum, ad conducendos venatores, & alendas bestias, ut naturas earum considerare posset. Qua in re non solùm Alexandri liberalitas erga studia est laudāda, sed etiā Aristotelis diligentia, qui illos aureos libros de Historia animalium conscripsit?
units.tr: Alexander sent Aristotle eight hundred talents, that is, four hundred and eighty thousand crowns, to hire hunters and to feed wild beasts, so that he could study their natures. In this matter we should praise not only the generosity of Alexander towards learning, but also the diligence of Aristotle, who wrote those golden books on the History of Animals.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Thesaurus librorum Aristotelis prorsus periisset, nisi Syllæ felicitate nobis hæc, quæ habemus, reliqua fuissent: uidelicet, Bibliotheca in bello parta (nam olim Imperatores & summi gubernatores hanc prædam maximè captabant, ut bona scripta conseruarentur) in qua cùm essent multa Aristotelis uolumina, sed penè obliterata, curauit undiq; in Græcia eius autoris libros cōquiri, et emendatos ab Andronico publicauit. Quemadmodum uiuo Aristoteli amicus fuit regum summus, ita penè extinctum reuocauit in lucem potentissimus militiæ dux Sylla, ætatis suæ (ut fertur) sexagesimotertio anno?
units.tr: The treasury of Aristotle's books would have utterly perished, unless by the good fortune of Sulla those writings which we have had been preserved for us: namely, the library won in war (for formerly emperors and great governors especially sought this booty, so that good writings might be preserved), in which, although there were many volumes of Aristotle but nearly obliterated, he had the books of that author sought out everywhere in Greece, and published them corrected by Andronicus. Just as Aristotle, while alive, was the friend of the greatest kings, so the most powerful commander of the army, Sulla, when he was (as is said) in the sixty-third year of his age, recalled him, almost extinct, to the light?

units.la: De uersione Bibliorum septuaginta interpretum.
units.tr: On the translation of the Bible by the Seventy interpreters.

units.la: Ptolemæus Philadelphus, filius Ptolemæi Lagi, uir ualde prudens & doctus, habuit regnū floren tissimū: nam habuit duodecim millia ciuitatū, cuius laudes passim recitātur in scriptoribus. Hic opes tan ti regni retulit ad sustentandos homines doctos ui ros, & instruendā bibliothecā, quæ omniū in toto orbe terrarū fuit celeberrima, & multiplicibus li bris instructissima. Idem Ptolemæus etiam cōduxit septuaginta uiros, qui inter Iudæos pro doctis ha bebantur, ut ex Hebræo uerterent sacra Biblia in Græcā linguā, quā uersionē adhuc habemus, & sa tis cōmoda est. Inter hos septuaginta interpretes di citur etiā fuisse sanctus Simeon, cuius Euāgelica hi storia facit mentionē, qui debuit Esaiā uertere. Sed cùm ad illū locū peruenisset, Eccc uirgo cōcipiet, & pariet filiū: dubitauit, an deberet uertere, quòd uirgo esset paritura. Putabat enim hoc fore scādalū gentibus, & occasionē, ut doctrinā Iudaicā cōtem nerēt. Cum igitur ualde esset anxius, rogauit Deū, ut significaret, quomodo uertere deberet. Et dici tur illi facta esse reuelatio per angelū, ne uerba te xtus mutaret, sed simpliciter ex Hebræo in Græcū uerteret. Insuper & idem angelus fertur ad eum di xisse, ipsum nō moriturū, nisi priuus uidisset, & in manibus gestasset illū filiū uirginis, de quo hic locus
units.tr: Ptolemy Philadelphus, son of Ptolemy Lagus, a man of great prudence and learning, ruled a very flourishing kingdom. He had twelve thousand cities, whose praises are recited here and there by writers. He devoted the wealth of so great a kingdom to supporting learned men and to furnishing a library, which was the most famous in the whole world and the most richly stocked with many books. This same Ptolemy also hired seventy men, who were regarded as learned among the Jews, to translate the holy Bible from Hebrew into Greek. We still have this translation, and it is quite serviceable. Among these seventy interpreters is said to have been holy Simeon, whom the evangelical history mentions, and who was to translate Isaiah. But when he came to the passage "Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son," he hesitated whether he ought to translate it, since it said that a virgin would bear. He thought this would be a scandal to the Gentiles and an occasion for them to despise Jewish doctrine. Being very anxious, he therefore asked God to show him how he ought to translate. It is said that a revelation was made to him through an angel: he was not to alter the wording of the text, but simply to translate it from Hebrew into Greek. Moreover, the same angel is said to have told him that he would not die until he had first seen and held in his arms that son of the virgin of whom this passage speaks.

units.la: B. Simeon ... 70 interpret. cus Esaiæ diceret. Propter hãc reuelatione dicunt sanctũ Simeonẽ, cùm Christũ in ulnis teneret, ut est Lucæ secundo, hæc uerba protulisse: Nunc dimittis seruum tuum Domine, &c.
units.tr: B. Simeon ... of the Seventy interpreters, when he was to translate Isaiah. Because of this revelation they say that holy Simeon, when he held Christ in his arms, as in Luke 2, uttered these words: "Now lettest thou thy servant depart, Lord," etc.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Dicũt de Seuero Imperatore, quòd primum fue-rit scriba, & homo doctus, peritus linguarũ, opti-mus Mathematicus: & ita per rei militaris scientiã & excellentẽ doctrinã ad summos honores perue-nit, id est, ad imperiũ Romanũ regendũ. Ferũt eun-dem moriturũ dixisse: Omnia fui, et nihil mihi nũc expedit: significãs, nihil perpetuũ in hac uita esse. Omnis enim felicitas huius uitæ est quasi somniũ?
units.tr: They tell of the Emperor Severus that he was first a scribe and a learned man, skilled in languages, an excellent mathematician; and thus, through his knowledge of military affairs and outstanding learning, he attained the highest honours, that is, to rule the Roman empire. They report that he said as he was about to die: "I have been everything, and nothing now profits me," signifying that nothing in this life is lasting. For all the happiness of this life is like a dream.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Multi principes ante hæc tempora nouerũt ar-tes liberales, & simul artes manuarias: ut dux Fri-dericus Saxoniæ optimè nouerat artẽ tornandi. Et ante annos 44. ueniebãt in Germaniã quinq; Prin-cipes, qui erãt capti à Turcis, & petebãt à primci-pibus Germaniæ stipendia, ut possent se & suos cõ-iuges ac liberos à Turcis redimere. Illorũ quinq; quilibet nouerat quoq; suum opificiũ. Nihil quen-quã aggrauat, si inter cæteras artes opificiũ quoq; aliquod nouerit. Sicut etiã habemus exemplum de Apelle, insigni pictore: qui nauigaturus in Aegy-ptũ ex Græcia, fecit naufragiũ. Sed ipse arrepta ta-bula in qua sedebat, euasit tandẽ incolumis, & ad littus littus appulit, ubi incidit in piratas, qui ademptis ipsius preciosis uestibus, & datis uicissim suis pan-nosis & laceratis, ipsum dimiserunt. Miser Apel-les, ut mendicus incedebat: & tandem peruenit in urbem Aegypti, in qua habebatur aula regia, & in hospitio passim ab omnibus tanquam mendicus erat cotemptus. Non enim indicabat quis esset, aut quam fortuna passus esset: sed in angulo se abdens, comedebat, quae passim mendicando collegerat. Interea forte uenit eo satrapa regis, ornatus catenis aureis, & indutus holoserico, qui uidens hunc mi-serum hominem, derisit eum (sicut quidam insolentiores solent facere) tandemq; etiam per illu-sionem dixit: Heus tu homuncio, rex te hodie ad conuiuium uocat. Miser Apelles dicit: Ita, ueniam. Aulicus constituit ei certu coenandi tempus. Apel-les respondet: Certo ueniam. Abijt regis cubicula-rius, nec putat illum uenturum: & sibi gratulatur, quod miseru ita irrisisset. Verum cum iam tempus coenandi instaret, Apelles pannosus ascendit aulam regiam. Ibi cum interrogaretur ab aulicis, quid si-bi uellet mendicus: respondit, regem ipsum uocasse ad coenam. Irridیent aulici hanc uocem: o miser, cur rex te inuitaret? Ita fortasis illusus es. Non, inquit Apelles: Fuit apud me hodie quida aulicus, qui me nomine regis inuitauit. Quaerunt igitur, quod nomen esset illi, qui eum inuitauerat. Respon-dit dit Apelles: nomen se ignorare, sed bene posse se illum pingere. Statim iussit sibi adferri instrumenta, & pinxit istam imaginem cubicularij, quam mente conceperat, ita ut ab omnib. dignosceretur, quis esset. Videbat enim imaginem pictam omnino convenire cum forma aulici, qui erat unus ex cubicularijs regis. Deferunt igitur imaginem pictam ad regem. Rex statim agnouit, quod esset imago sui cubicularij: ac iubet adduci hominem, qui istam imaginem pinxerat. Accessit miser Apelles in suis pannosis & squalore obductis uestibus. Rex collocauit eum iuxta suam mensam, ut coenaret cum eo: & inter coenandum quaesiuit, cuias esset. Respondit, se esse hominem Graecum, & fecisse naufragium, & tamen euasisse incolumem: sed incidisse in piratas, qui ipsum suis uestibus exuissent, & pro illis has pannosas sibi induissent. Postea rex longo tempore Apellem apud se retinuit, & usus est ipsius opera in pingendo. Tandem dimisit illum donatis multis millibus aureorum. Ita sua arte est seruatus, cum alioqui per totam uitam, mendicum & erronem manere ipsum oportuisset. Sed ars ei naufragio non fuit adempta. Sic quoq; in omni fortuna utile est, aliquem literas didicisse. Haec anno 1557 sunt recitata.
units.tr: Many princes before this time knew the liberal arts and also manual crafts, as Duke Frederick of Saxony knew the art of turning very well. And about 44 years ago five princes came into Germany who had been captured by the Turks, and they sought stipends from the princes of Germany so that they could redeem themselves and their wives and children from the Turks. Each of these five also knew his own trade. Nothing burdens anyone if, among his other arts, he also knows some craft. Just as we have the example of Apelles, the famous painter, who, setting out from Greece to sail to Egypt, suffered shipwreck. But he seized the plank on which he was sitting, escaped at last unharmed, and reached the shore, where he fell in with pirates. They took his precious clothes and gave him in exchange their ragged and torn garments, and then let him go. Poor Apelles walked about like a beggar. At last he came to a city of Egypt where there was a royal court, and in an inn he was despised by everyone as a beggar. For he did not reveal who he was or what misfortune he had suffered; hiding himself in a corner, he ate what he had gathered by begging here and there. Meanwhile a courtier of the king happened to come there, adorned with gold chains and dressed in silk. Seeing this wretched man, he mocked him (as some rather insolent people are wont to do) and finally said in jest: "Hey you, little man, the king invites you to dinner today." Poor Apelles said: "Yes, I will come." The courtier appointed a time for dinner. Apelles replied: "I will certainly come." The king's chamberlain left, not thinking he would come, and congratulated himself that he had so mocked the wretch. But when the dinner hour was already at hand, Apelles in his rags went up into the royal hall. When the courtiers asked the beggar what he wanted, he replied that the king himself had invited him to dinner. The courtiers laughed at this: "Oh wretch, why would the king invite you? Perhaps you have been mocked." "No," said Apelles, "a certain courtier was with me today and invited me in the king's name." They then asked what the name was of the man who had invited him. Apelles replied that he did not know the name, but that he could well paint him. Immediately he had the instruments brought to him and painted the likeness of the chamberlain, which he had conceived in his mind, so that everyone could recognise who it was. For he saw that the painted image agreed completely with the appearance of the courtier, who was one of the king's chamberlains. So they carried the painted picture to the king. The king at once recognised that it was the image of his chamberlain, and ordered the man who had painted it to be brought in. Poor Apelles came forward in his ragged clothes, covered with filth. The king placed him beside his table so that he might dine with him, and during the meal he asked where he came from. Apelles replied that he was a Greek, that he had suffered shipwreck and yet escaped unharmed, but had fallen in with pirates, who had stripped him of his clothes and put these ragged ones on him instead. Afterwards the king kept Apelles with him for a long time and made use of his skill in painting. At last he dismissed him, presenting him with many thousands of gold pieces. Thus he was saved by his art, when otherwise he would have had to remain a beggar and wanderer all his life. But the shipwreck did not take away his art. So too in every fortune it is useful for someone to have learned letters. These things were recited in 1557.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: An magnates, reges & principes studere debeant?
units.tr: Whether magnates, kings and princes ought to study

units.la: Cùm casu rex Alphonsus interuenisseт disputationi duorum consiliariorum, quorum alter apud regem Galliæ erat, & Alphonsus quæreret de quare disputatio esset? respondit regis Galliæ consiliarius, Quòd reges non deberent literas discere: uerùm satis esse, si literatos & doctos fouerent. Ibi dixit Alphonsus: Vox bouis est, non hominis.
units.tr: When King Alphonso happened to be present at a dispute between two counsellors, one of whom served the king of France, Alphonso asked what the dispute was about. The counsellor of the king of France replied that kings ought not to learn letters; it was enough for them to foster the learned and educated. Then Alphonso said: "That is the voice of an ox, not of a man."

units.la: Optima uoluntas Imperatoris Caroli V. de Ecclesia bene mereri cupientis.
units.tr: The excellent intention of the Emperor Charles V, who desired to deserve well of the Church

units.la: Imperator Carolus V. dixit, se uelle rem eò perducere, ut posthac ipse in comitijs & disputationibus præses & auditor esset. Sed credo ipsum impeditum esse bellis & malis hominibus, qui illud dissuaserunt.
units.tr: The Emperor Charles V said that he wished to bring the matter to such a point that, from then on, he himself would preside over and attend the diets and disputations. But I believe he was prevented by wars and by wicked men, who dissuaded him from it.

units.la: Sapiētes principes deberēt aliquid cõferre in talē laborē, ut anni historiarũ ex eclipsibus supputarentur. Is enim labor nõ est unius, sed multorũ: & nullus priuatus suis sumptibus illũ laborē utilissimum ecclesiæ & Reipublicæ perficere potest.
units.tr: Wise princes ought to contribute something to such labour, so that the years of history might be calculated from eclipses. For this labour belongs not to one man but to many, and no private individual, at his own expense, can complete a labour so useful to the Church and the commonwealth.

units.la: Popularis meus uiuens Romæ, & me ætate aliquot annos antecedens, egit cũ Capitaneis in proxima direptione urbis Romæ sub Clemente, ne bibliothecæ diriperentur: q; etiā obtinuit. Illud enim Deus ordinauit, & postulat, ut libri tam à potentioribus quàm ab alijs conseruentur.
units.tr: My fellow countryman, who lived at Rome and was some years older than I am, dealt with the captains during the recent sack of Rome under Clement, so that the libraries would not be plundered; and he obtained this. For God has ordained and requires that books be preserved by the powerful and by others alike.

units.la: Cognitio bonarum literarum gubernatoribus necessaria.
units.tr: The knowledge of good letters is necessary for rulers

units.la: Valde multũ refert, ad bonã mentē accedere eruditionē, præsertim in magnis personis. Tunc enim rectius in omnib. cõtrouersijs iudicabitur, & plus iudicij accedet. Tales quoq; rectè instituti, non facilè ab assentatoribus corrumpuntur.
units.tr: It matters greatly that learning should come to a good mind, especially in great persons. For then all controversies will be judged more correctly, and more judgment will be brought to bear. Such people, rightly brought up, are not easily corrupted by flatterers.

units.la: Gubernatorū liberalitas excitat studia.
units.tr: The generosity of rulers stirs up studies

units.la: Vos uidetis, quãdo gubernatores mediocriter fouent literas, tũc multa quærũtur, quæ aliâs ignota māsissēt. Eregione sordes illorũ sunt reprehēdēdæ, q nullis officijs munificētiæ aut beneuolētiæ iuuãt studia: sicut dicitur de papa Sixto, cui cũ dedicauisset Theodor 9 Gaza librũ Aristotelis de natura animaliũ (ubi multa utilissima cõtinetur) pulchrè auro & holoserico ornatū, interrogauit asinus papa Sixtus, quāti ornatus cõstaret? Respõdit Gaza: quadraginta coronatis. Illos tantùm quadraginta ei reddi iussit, cùm ille uir magno honorario propter utilitatē illius laboris fuisset ornādus, qui in tanta paupertate uixit, ut nisi eũ ad se dux Ferrariensis non cassset, fame ipsi moriendum fuisset.
units.tr: You see that when rulers moderately foster letters, many things are sought out which would otherwise have remained unknown. On the contrary, the meanness of those who help studies with no offices of generosity or goodwill is to be rebuked; as is said of Pope Sixtus. When Theodore Gaza had dedicated to him a book of Aristotle's On the Nature of Animals (which contains much most useful material), beautifully adorned with gold and silk, that ass Pope Sixtus asked how much the decoration had cost. Gaza answered: forty crowns. He ordered that only those forty be returned to him, although that man ought to have been honoured with a great reward for the usefulness of his labour. He lived in such poverty that, had the Duke of Ferrara not taken him into his household, he would have died of hunger.

units.la: Dalburgiorum familia semper doctos uiros habuit.
units.tr: The Dalberg family has always had learned men

units.la: Celebrata est familia Rhenanæ nobilitatis DalDalburgiorum, in qua noui duos præstãtes uiros, Iohannem Dalburgium, episcopum Vangionum, & Cancellarium principis Electoris. Apud hunc Dalburgiũ uixerunt, Rodolphus Agricola in Academia Heydelbergensi, & Iohannes Capnio : qui cùm essent eruditissimi, ornabant studia etiam uirtute & dulci concordia. Rodolphus Græcos scriptores iuuentuti interpretabatur. Capnio Hebreæ linguæ semina tradebat, sed paucioribus: quia monachorũ rabie impediebatur, ne publicè doceret. Alterum Dalburgium Theodoricum etiam familiariter noui, qui cùm Philosophiæ admodum studiosus fuisset, postea, cùm Euangelij doctrina nobis illuxisset, ueram etiam pietatem amplexus est. & sæpè dixit, se lætari hac luce doctrinæ: quia antea non uidisset discrimen Philosophiæ, & doctrinæ quæ est Ecclesiæ propria.
units.tr: The family of the Dalbergs, a celebrated family of the Rhenish nobility, is one in which I have known two outstanding men: John Dalberg, bishop of Worms and chancellor of the prince elector. With this Dalberg lived Rudolph Agricola at the Academy of Heidelberg, and John Capnio. Being most learned, they adorned their studies also with virtue and sweet harmony. Rudolph explained the Greek writers to the youth. Capnio passed on the seeds of the Hebrew language, but to fewer students, because the rage of the monks hindered him from teaching publicly. I also knew the other Dalberg, Theodoric, intimately. He was very devoted to philosophy, but later, when the doctrine of the Gospel had dawned upon us, he embraced true piety as well. He often said that he rejoiced in this light of doctrine, because previously he had not seen the difference between philosophy and the doctrine proper to the Church.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Aristeus excellens & sapiens princeps, impetrauit sua precatione Etesias : id est: fuit astronomus, multa docuit de natura. Sic apud ueteres studium Physices fuit sapientia summorum principũ.
units.tr: Aristaeus, an excellent and wise prince, obtained the Etesian winds by his prayer; that is, he was an astronomer and taught many things about nature. Thus among the ancients the study of physics was the wisdom of the greatest princes.

units.la: Aristarchus Grammaticus opera Homeri passim sparsa collegit, quæ postea Solon describi curauit (attributa ad id opus describendũ certa pecunia) iubens ut certis solennitatibus & festis recitarentur, populoq; proponerentur.
units.tr: Aristarchus the grammarian gathered together the works of Homer, which were scattered here and there. Afterwards Solon had them copied out, a fixed sum of money being assigned for the copying of that work, and ordered that they be recited at certain solemn festivals and presented to the people.

units.la: Vir quidam nobilis à Malwitz, ualde studiosus Philosophiæ, qui aliis uituperantibus Philosophiã tanquam rem inutilem hominibus, se ipsis opponebat, ac dicebat: Imò legendam, et quidem studiosè cognoscendā Philosophiam esse. quia hoc prodesset Philosophia, ut collata cum sapientia & doctrina Ecclesiæ, ostendat discrimen inter humanam rationem & doctrinam Ecclesiæ, & ut conspicia- tur humanæ rationis imbecillitas, & quantum à ueris fontibus doctrinæ cœlestis differret.
units.tr: A certain noble man, von Malwitz, was very devoted to philosophy. When others disparaged philosophy as a thing useless to men, he set himself against them and said: "On the contrary, philosophy is to be read and indeed studied diligently, because it is of use in this way: when compared with wisdom and the doctrine of the Church, it shows the difference between human reason and the doctrine of the Church; it lets us see the weakness of human reason and how far it differs from the true sources of heavenly doctrine."

units.la: De liberalitate Senatus Basilien-sis.
units.tr: On the liberality of the Senate of Basel

units.la: Inter eos qui Basileæ facultatibus externis de studijs benemeriti sunt, atq; etiamnum benemeren-tur, primùm quidem occurrit ipse Senatus: qui nõ ignarus huiusmodi Vniuersitates non solùm maxi-mam ciuitatibus gloriam conciliare, & latissimè fa-mam dispergere, uerumetiam ad necessarios usus Rerumpublicarum ingenia omnigena doctrina et prudentia instruere ac præparare, liberalitatem atq; beneuolentiam suam nunquam non studiosis declarat. Nam omissis ijs quæ ante nos gesta sunt, adhuc non solum priuilegia authoritatemq; Aca- demiæ tuetur: uerum etiam pauperes scholasticos fouet, ac stipendia professorum auget & intendit. Viginti namq; tenuioris fortunæ studiosos, tam ex ciuium filijs quàm ex peregrinis, in usum reipublicæ & ecclesiæ sustentat. Anno aut 1561 Consule & Magistro ciuium Casparo Crûg, Proconsule Francisco Oberriet, summis uero tribunis Sebastiano Doppelstein, & Iacobo Rudino: Rectore simul Vniuersitatis D. Doctore Basilio Amerbachio, Prorectore D.Huldricho Iselino, ambobus Iurisconsultis: Senatus considerans precia rerū paulatim intendi, professorū Vniuersitatis stipendijs septē canonicatus adiecit:hoc facto nō solū præsentē munificentiā & liberalitatem ostendēs, uerùm etiā in posterum beneuolum suum animum erga pietatis et literarum studiosos pollicens. Hanc deinde summam Scholarchæ, quos Deputatos nominant(quitum fuerunt, nobilis uir D.Heimricus Petri, Ioannes Meier, et Lucas à Brunn,qui ante paucos dies uitam hanc deserens in Domino obdormiuit) unà cum Rectore Basilio Amerbachio,.ex consilio quoque doctissimorum & pijssimorum uirorum D.D. Bonifacij Amerbachij, & reuerendissimi uiri D. Simonis Sulceri,distribuerunt.
units.tr: Among those who, by external means, have deserved well of studies at Basel, and still deserve well, the Senate itself comes first. Not unaware that such universities not only win the greatest glory for cities and spread their fame very widely, but also prepare and equip minds with every kind of learning and prudence for the necessary uses of commonwealths, it never fails to declare its liberality and goodwill toward students. For, passing over what was done before our time, it still not only protects the privileges and authority of the Academy, but also supports poor scholars and increases and extends the stipends of the professors. For it maintains twenty students of modest means, both sons of citizens and foreigners, for the service of the commonwealth and the Church. In the year 1561, with Caspar Krug as Mayor and Master of the citizens, Francis Oberriet as Deputy Mayor, and Sebastian Doppelstein and James Rudin as chief tribunes, and with Dr. Basil Amerbach, a jurist, as Rector of the University and Dr. Huldrych Iselin, also a jurist, as Pro-Rector, the Senate, considering that the prices of goods were gradually rising, added seven canonries to the stipends of the university's professors. By this act it showed not only its present munificence and liberality, but also pledged its benevolent mind for the future toward those devoted to piety and letters. Then this sum was distributed by the scholarchs, whom they call deputies (who were then the noble man Dr. Heimricus Petri, John Meier, and Lucas von Brunn, who a few days before, leaving this life, fell asleep in the Lord), together with the Rector Basil Amerbach, and also on the advice of the most learned and pious men, Dr. Boniface Amerbach and the most reverend man Dr. Simon Sulzer.

units.la: COLL. Beneficentia Erasmi.
units.tr: COLL. The beneficence of Erasmus.

units.la: Erasmi uero Roterodami bene merita de studijs liberalibus,ut totus ferè mundus nouit,ita eiusdem liberalitas perpetua multis egenis & facultatibus destitutis, liberales tamen prouectus in studijs facientibus,subsidio esse solet in hac Republica. Eorum rum aut beneficiorum distributorem fidelissimum constituit, virum æternis laudibus dignum, D. D. Bonifacium Amerbachium, cuius fidelitatem & beneuolentiam nemo non, qui opem eius implora-uit, est expertus. Nec desijt ea beneficentia, sed adhuc hodie per D. D. Basilium F. commune quasi asylum sunt ædes Amerbachianæ omnibus, qui quocunq; modo paupertatis oncre presi, eas adeunt. Erat autem uir ille (liceat enim non negare manifesta) omni uirtute & eruditione excellen-tissimus. In primis singulari prudentia Iuris prædi-tus, magna cum laude diu publice professus est, & de Iure consulendo cum Reipublicæ, tum priuatim multis profuit. Vnde à multis principibus & ciui-tatibus, non paruis muneribus ad magnos honores sæpè inuitatus fuit: sed maluit patriæ suæ prodesse.
units.tr: Erasmus of Rotterdam deserved well of the liberal studies, as almost the whole world knows, and his generosity, which is ever enduring, is usually a help in this commonwealth to many who are needy and destitute of means, yet who, making liberal progress in their studies, are supported by it. He appointed as the most faithful distributor of these benefits a man worthy of everlasting praise, Dr. Bonifacius Amerbach, whose fidelity and goodwill everyone who implored his aid has found. Nor has this beneficence ceased; even today, through Dr. Basilius, his son, the Amerbach house stands as a common refuge for all who are oppressed by the burden of poverty and come to it by whatever means. That man was (for it is permissible not to deny what is manifest) most excellent in every virtue and learning. Especially endowed with singular prudence in law, he taught publicly for a long time with great distinction, and he benefited many, both the commonwealth and private individuals, by his legal counsel. Hence many princes and cities often invited him to high honours with no small rewards, but he preferred to serve his own homeland.

units.la: Huic egregiarum uirtutū choro pulcherrimo ac-cedebat & ea, quæ optimis quibusq; grata, atq; mi-seris necessaria sunt: nimirū liberalitas, candor, be-neuolētia erga omnes, &c. quibus dignitatē quan-dam addebat comis & modesta grauitas. Sed mors à primo parēte in omnes propagata, eū (proh do-lor) hoc anno 1562. mēse Maio nobis eripuit, quin potius Deus ipsum ex hoc ingrato mundo ad cœ-lestia gaudia trāstulit. Nā in uera fide & agnitione filij Dei Saluatoris nostri, ex hac calamitosa uita emigrauit. Cuius obitū nō sine altissimis gemitib. et Respublica Respublica & schola adhuc tacitè deplorat. Solatio tamen est, quòd non prorsus à suis sit sublatus, sed adhuc hodie uiuere uideatur in doctissimo uiro D. Basilio filio, qui patris uirtutes exprimere sedulò conatur.
units.tr: To this most beautiful company of outstanding virtues there was also added what is pleasing to the best people and necessary to the wretched: namely liberality, candour, goodwill towards all, and so on, to which a certain dignity was given by a courteous and modest gravity. But death, spread to all from the first parent, snatched him from us (alas) this year 1562, in the month of May; or rather God transferred him from this ungrateful world to heavenly joys. For he departed from this calamitous life in true faith and in knowledge of the Son of God, our Saviour. His death is still silently lamented, not without the deepest groaning, by the commonwealth and the school. Yet it is a consolation that he has not been wholly taken from his own, but seems still to live today in the learned Dr. Basilius, his son, who diligently strives to express his father's virtues.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: De liberalitate D. Ludouici Carini.
units.tr: On the generosity of Master Ludovicus Carinus.

units.la: Clarissimus & doctissimus uir, omniq; laude et uirtute obseruandus senex D. Ludouicus Carinus, Fuggerorum olim præceptor (studens bonas artes & studia facultatum ad posteros propagare) aliquot millia florenorum ad ingenuos pueros in bonarum literarum studijs instituēdos destinauit. Pro quo beneficio merito totus ordo scholasticus precari debet, ut Deus ipsi longæuitatem, prosperitatem ualetudinis, aliaq; beneficia impertiri uelit.
units.tr: This most distinguished and learned man, the old gentleman Ludovicus Carinus, deserving of all praise and honour, once tutor to the Fuggers, who strives to hand down good arts and the studies of the faculties to posterity, has set aside several thousand florins for the instruction of well-born boys in the study of the humanities. For this benefaction the whole scholastic order ought rightly to pray that God may grant him long life, good health, and other blessings.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: De beneficijs Typographorum Basiliensium.
units.tr: On the Benefits of the Basel Printers.

units.la: Vnica ea urbs typographicis operis & officinis cum omnibus Germaniæ, imò (si quòd res est fateamur) cum totius Europæ urbibus certat: siue spectes multitudinem optimorum autorum, tam ueterum quàm recentium, siue consideres diligentiam quæ in emendatis librorum editionibus insumitur. Adde quòd tolerabili precio cōparantur. iur boni autores. Tanta est typographorum, præ- sertim in pauperes studiosos, liberalitas.
units.tr: This one city competes in printing works and workshops with all the cities of Germany, indeed (if we admit the truth) with the cities of all Europe, whether you look at the multitude of excellent authors, ancient and recent, or consider the care taken in producing corrected editions of books. Add that they are bought at a reasonable price, so that good authors can be had. Such is the generosity of the printers, especially towards poor students.

units.la: In eo autem vitæ genere, & ijs laboribus hoc tempore celebres sunt hi:
units.tr: Among those who are celebrated at present for this way of life and these labours are the following.

units.la: Hieronymus Frobenius, vir doctus, & Nico- laus Episcopius, vir in historijs & Iure quoq; peri- tus, iudicij publici assessor & iudex, individui amici, adhuc iungunt suam operam in grauissimis au- toribus omnium ferè disciplinarum edendis. Præ- cipuè tamē accepta illis ferenda sunt scripta Theo- logica sanctorum Patrum, & maior pars Iurispru- dentiæ, nec nō Medicinæ: ut historicorum et alio- rum utilium authorum opera taceam.
units.tr: Hieronymus Froben, a learned man, and Nicolaus Episcopius, a man also skilled in history and law, a public assessor and judge, inseparable friends, still devote their labour to publishing the most weighty authors of almost all disciplines. Above all, the theological writings of the holy Fathers, the greater part of jurisprudence, and also medicine are rightly credited to them, not to mention the works of historians and other useful authors.

units.la: Heinrici Petri nobilis viri ob singularem pru- dentiam politicis negocijs & tutela Academiæ oc- cupati, vices gerit gener ipsius Hieronymus Cu- rio, & alij.
units.tr: Heinrich Petri, a nobleman remarkable for his singular prudence, who is occupied with political affairs and the guardianship of the Academy, is represented by his son-in-law Hieronymus Curio, and others.

units.la: Ioannes Oporinus, vir & eruditione singulari præditus, & diligentia solertiaq; in restituendis, emendandis, et publicandis optimis autoribus, ne- mini facilè cedens, qui alioqui proprijs quoq; scri- ptis iam clarus esse posset. Id quod omnibus φιλο- λόγοις notius est, quàm ut referri à nobis opus sit.
units.tr: Johannes Oporinus, endowed with singular learning, and with a diligence and skill in restoring, emending and publishing the best authors that scarcely yields to anyone, could already be famous even for his own writings. This is better known to all lovers of learning than it needs to be reported by us.

units.la: Ioannes vero Heruagius, vir grauis, instructā mira varietate officinam, à patre laudatissimo viro acceptam, subinde illustriorē & auctiorem reddit.
units.tr: But Johannes Herwagen, a serious man, who has received from his most praiseworthy father a workshop furnished with wonderful variety, makes it from time to time more distinguished and larger.

units.la: Nicolai Brillingeri, viri boni, & de literis optimè meriti, industriam & diligentiam tam adultiores quàm etiam studiosa iuuentus quotidie sentit. Huius gener Arnoldus Gymnicus his annis propriam officinam aperiēs, nō dubiam spem diligentis & industrij typographi præbet.
units.tr: The industry and diligence of Nicolaus Brillinger, a good man who has deserved well of letters, is felt daily by both older people and studious youth. His son-in-law Arnold Gymnicus, who this year is opening his own workshop, offers a not doubtful hope of a diligent and industrious printer.

units.la: His annumerari possunt Iacobus Parcus, & Petrus Perna, uiri prudentes & laboriosissimi.
units.tr: Among these can be counted Jacob Parcus and Peter Perna, prudent and most hardworking men.

units.la: Hæc tantorum uirorum nomina potius annotare, quàm laudes describere (quod captum meum longè superaret) hoc uolui: tantum ut scirent, qui ex studiosis bonarum literarum grati uolunt esse, quibus uiris magnam suæ eruditionis & profectus in studijs partê acceptâ ferre debeant: desinant cerebrosi zoili tantorum hominum merita extenuare. Deus misericors pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, hæc tanta ornamenta Basiliensis Reipublicæ & Ecclesiæ gubernet etiam in posterum, & eorum conatus, labores & studia dirigat ad sui nominis gloriam, & multorum hominum emolumentum. Amen.
units.tr: I have wished to note the names of such great men rather than describe their praises (which would far exceed my capacity), only so that those students of good letters who wish to be grateful would know to which men they ought to credit a large part of their learning and progress in their studies; and that the crazy zoili would stop belittling the merits of such men. May the merciful God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, govern these great ornaments of the Basel commonwealth and Church also in future, and direct their endeavours, labours and studies to the glory of his name and the benefit of many people. Amen.

units.la: Iudicium Philippi Lantgrauij Hassiæ de studijs.
units.tr: The judgment of Philip, Landgrave of Hesse on studies.

units.la: Lantgrauius Philippus tempore obsidionis urbis Monasteriensis ad me dicebat: Nunc ego incipio magis diligere studia, quia uideo si homines negligunt studia, et abijciunt libros Propheticos et ApostoApostolicos, fieri perplurimos phanaticos homines, suos enthusiasmos & reuelationes iactantes.
units.tr: Landgrave Philip said to me during the siege of the city of Münster: "Now I am beginning to value studies more, because I see that if people neglect studies and cast aside the Prophetic and Apostolic books, very many fanatical people arise, boasting of their enthusiasms and revelations."

units.la: COLL. Ioannis Alberti, ducis Megapolensis, sedulitas in promouendis iuuenum studijs, & audiendo uerbo diuino.
units.tr: Collection: the diligence of John Albert, Duke of Mecklenburg, in promoting the studies of young people and in listening to the divine word.

units.la: In Italia mos est, ut principes audiant & inspiciant studia, sicut etiam inter principes Germaniæ olim fuit consuetudo. Vix ullum autem hanc consuetudinem imitari uideo, nisi Iohannem Albertū principem Megapolensem, qui quotannis aliqua examina in schola Suerinensi instituit, quibus illustrissimus Princeps ipse interest, & simul pueros examinat: bene quoq; respondentibus munera non exigua largitur. Alias etiam extra examina idem Princeps scholas accedit, & studia ac mores iuuenum considerat. Præterea tanta assiduitate concionies Dominicales & alias annotat, ut post multos annos concionatoribus locos, quos eo tempore tra ctauerint, indicare possit, ac citò negligentiam eorum in studijs deprehendat.
units.tr: In Italy it is customary for princes to hear and inspect studies, just as it was once also a custom among the princes of Germany. Yet I see scarcely anyone imitating this custom except John Albert, Prince of Mecklenburg, who holds several examinations each year in the school at Schwerin. The most illustrious prince himself attends these and examines the boys at the same time, and he bestows no small gifts on those who answer well. At other times, apart from the examinations, the same prince visits the schools and considers the studies and conduct of the young. He also takes such careful notes of the Sunday and other sermons that, after many years, he can name for the preachers the passages they treated at that time, and he quickly detects any negligence in their studies.

units.la: COLL. Mauricij ducis & Electoris Saxoniæ memorabile factum.
units.tr: Collection: a memorable deed of Maurice, Duke and Elector of Saxony.

units.la: Laudādus inter cæteros mihi occurrit Dux et Electoris Elector[?] Saxoniae Mauricius, qui non solum duas celebres Academias Lipsensem & Vuitebergensem in flore retinuit, ac sumptibus auxit: uerumetiã insuper tres optimas particulares scholas, Misnensem, Grimmensem & Portensem, in suo territorio fundauit, ubi tam discipuli plurimi, quàm ipsi praeceptores perpetuò publicis sumptibus sustentantur: in quas ex singulis suis ciuitatibus & oppidulis semper elapsis sex annis alij nouitij scholastici introducuntur. Et hic ordo pulchrè est ordinatus: in ijsdem etiam scholis liberales et conuenientes cum praeceptorib. tum scholasticis sumptus praebentur.
units.tr: Among the others, Duke and Elector Maurice of Saxony comes to my mind as deserving of praise. He not only kept the two famous academies of Leipzig and Wittenberg in a flourishing state and increased them with funds, but in addition he founded three excellent particular schools in his territory, at Meissen, Grimma and Pforta. In these, many pupils as well as the teachers themselves are supported continually at public expense, and every six years new scholars are admitted to them from each of his cities and small towns. This arrangement is finely ordered, and in these same schools generous and suitable maintenance is provided both for the teachers and for the pupils.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: De munificentia Augusti, Ducis & Electoris Saxoniae.
units.tr: On the munificence of Augustus, Duke and Elector of Saxony.

units.la: Laudatur similiter ab inhabitatoribus terrae Misnensis & Saxonicae pia uoluntas illustrissimi principis Electoris ducis Saxoniae Augusti, cuius celsitudo non solum has nominatas celebres Academias cum his tribus scholis coseruat, & omnibus beneficijs cumulatè afficit: sed insuper etiam certò secum conclusit, ac in actum suos consiliarios producere iussit, ut reditus perpetuos ad plurima noua stipendia costituenda ordinent. Sic hic pius princeps omnibus modis Ecclesiae benefacere, & studia liberalium artium & facultatum cum sincera Euangelij doctrina ad posteros transferri desiderat. Quare ipsius subditi, & omnes qui iam dictorum beneficiorum participes facti sunt, aut fiet, merito pro huius pij principis incolumitate, & felici gubernatione Deum precari uelint.
units.tr: Likewise the pious will of the most illustrious prince, the Elector and Duke of Saxony Augustus, is praised by the inhabitants of the land of Meissen and of Saxony. His Highness not only maintains these famous Academies with these three schools and heaps every benefit upon them, but has also firmly resolved with himself, and ordered his councillors to bring the matter into effect, that they should set up perpetual revenues for the founding of many new stipends. Thus this pious prince desires in every way to do good to the Church and to hand down to posterity the study of the liberal arts and faculties together with the sincere doctrine of the Gospel. Therefore his subjects, and all who have already become or will become sharers in the aforesaid benefits, may rightly wish to pray to God for the safety and happy government of this pious prince.

units.la: Ernesti Ducis Saxoniæ liberalitas.
units.tr: The liberality of Duke Ernst of Saxony.

units.la: Ernestus dux Saxoniæ, frater Ioannis Friderici Electoris, etsi haberet exiguos reditus ex sua ditione, tamen adeò fuit munificus & liberalis erga homines doctos & studiosos, ut plurimos in Academijs aleret, & plurimis beneficijs eos afficeret.
units.tr: Ernst, Duke of Saxony, brother of Elector John Frederick, although he had slender revenues from his own domain, was nevertheless so generous and liberal towards learned and studious men that he supported very many in the Academies and favoured them with very many benefits.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Christiani regis Daniæ, & Georgij principis Anhaldini erga ecclesiam liberalitas.
units.tr: The kindness of the Christian King of Denmark and of Prince George of Anhalt towards the Church.

units.la: Ante paucos annos serenissimus & sapientissimus rex Daniæ Christianus, in toto suo regno auxit stipendia pastoribus & ministris ecclesiarum. Simile beneficium præstitit illustrissimus princeps Georgius Anhaldinus præpositus Merseburgensis, qui magna liberalitate quoq; ministros suæ ditionis affecit, ordinans ut illi reditus perpetuò apud ecclesiam permanerent.
units.tr: A few years ago the most serene and wise King of Denmark, Christian, increased the stipends of the pastors and ministers of the churches throughout his whole kingdom. The most illustrious Prince George of Anhalt, provost of Merseburg, conferred a similar benefit, for with great generosity he also favoured the ministers of his domain, ordaining that those revenues should remain permanently with the church.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Caroli Marchionis Badensis erga ecclesiam beneuolentia.
units.tr: The goodwill of Charles, Margrave of Baden, towards the Church.

units.la: Illustrissimus princeps Carolus Marchio Badensis, densis, sedecim stipendiatos in usum Ecclesiæ & Reipublicæ liberalib. sumptibus sustentat. Ad hos, tres etiam alios habet, duos Theologicis & unum Medicis studijs destinatum: quorum singulis octo-ginta florenos annuos impertit. Nec iam mihi tem-pus concedit, ut exponam pientissimum animum, aliaq; beneficia eiusdē illustrissimi Principis, quib. indies doctos uiros & ministros Ecclesiæ afficit, et contra notorias iniurias defendit.
units.tr: The most illustrious prince Charles, Margrave of Baden, maintains sixteen stipendiaries at his own liberal expense for the service of the Church and the commonwealth. Besides these, he has three others, two destined for theological studies and one for medicine, to each of whom he grants eighty florins a year. Nor does time now allow me to set out his most pious spirit and the other benefits of this same most illustrious prince, by which he daily favours learned men and ministers of the Church and defends them against notorious injuries.

units.la: Ducis Luneburgensis beneficentia.
units.tr: The beneficence of the Duke of Lüneburg.

units.la: Princeps Luneburgensis, quanquam non habuit magnos reditus: tamen admodum munificus erga sacerdotes & scholasticos fuit.
units.tr: The Prince of Lüneburg, although he did not have great revenues, was nonetheless quite generous towards priests and scholars.

units.la: Relati mihi etiam sunt in hoc labore uersantes alij illustres Comites & Barones, qui bonis literis opera nauantes liberalitate sua sustentant, ut sunt: Illustris comes D. Conradus de Liechteneck. Illustris Comes de Sultz.
units.tr: Other illustrious counts and barons who labour in this field have also been reported to me, who, devoted to good letters, sustain them by their liberality, namely: the illustrious Count Conrad of Liechtenstein; the illustrious Count of Sulz.

units.la: Illustris Baro D. Egenolphus de Rappoltstein, duos aut tres plerunq; tenuioris fortunæ studiosos sustentat.
units.tr: The illustrious Baron Egenolph of Rappoltstein supports two or three students, usually of humbler fortune.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Neq; non recordari possum pietatis & beneficentiæ illustrium Comitum de Stolberg, & alterius viri nobilis non procul ab Isleben habitantis (cuius nomen iam mihi non occurrit) erga literatos & & doctos homines, qui abolitis abusibus in cœnobijs, illos reditus in fouendis pauperibus scholasticis unà cum doctißimis præceptoribus collocarũt. In collegio illustrium Comitum de Stolberg celebris famæ est Michael Neander, qui quantum utilitatis partim scriptis eruditis edendis & emendandis, partim in instituenda iuuentute afferat, id clarius manifesta luce apparet. Nobilis uir prudentia excellenti et eruditione præditus in gratiam iuuentutis alit quinq; doctos uiros, inter quos mihi unicus nomine M. Heinricus Reutterus Saxo, uir cum in artibus tum in Theologia egregiè exercitatus.
units.tr: Nor can I forget the piety and beneficence of the illustrious Counts of Stolberg, and of another noble man living not far from Eisleben (whose name does not now occur to me), towards learned and erudite men, who, when the abuses in the monasteries had been abolished, applied those revenues to supporting poor students together with most learned teachers. In the college of the illustrious Counts of Stolberg Michael Neander is of great renown, and how much use he brings, partly by publishing and correcting learned writings, partly by instructing youth, appears more clearly than the light itself. A noble man, endowed with excellent prudence and learning, for the benefit of youth supports five learned men, among whom I shall name only Master Heinrich Reutter of Saxony, a man thoroughly trained both in the arts and in theology.

units.la: De liberalitate doctoris Ioannis Neuij. COLL.
units.tr: On the liberality of Dr. Johann Neue. COLL.

units.la: D. Ioannes Neuius doctor Medicinæ illustrißimi principis Augusti Ducis & Electoris Saxoniæ, singulari amore studia & pauperes scholasticos cõplectitur, in quorum gratiã anno 1561 Lipsiæ tria stipendia perpetuis reditibus ordinauit: quam pecuniam nemini, ipso mortuo, repetere liceat. Ea uerò stipendia semel adepti, sexennio uti possunt, & sic (si placet) assumere gradum Doctoris: ad quem gradum commodè assumendum, prudens suum consilium addidit.
