Non dubito, quin utentes cum alijs bonis uiris suam gratitudinem & uerbis & reipsa, si alicubi habeaut occasionem, declaraturi sint: & Deum precaturi, ut huic bono & pio seni Doctori una cum honestissima sua coniuge, et fratre D. Casparo uiro doctissimo longaeuitatem, prosperamq; in omnib. uitae actionibus fortunam concedat.
units.tr: Dr. Johann Neue, doctor of medicine to the most illustrious prince Augustus, Duke and Elector of Saxony, embraces with singular affection both study and poor students. For their benefit, in the year 1561, he established three stipends at Leipzig from perpetual revenues; let no one ever be allowed to reclaim this money after his death. Those who obtain these stipends once may enjoy them for six years, and so (if they wish) may take the doctoral degree; for the easy taking of that degree he has wisely added his counsel. I do not doubt that those who enjoy them will, whenever they have an opportunity, declare their gratitude both in words and in deeds, and will pray that God grant to this good and pious old doctor, together with his most honourable wife and his brother, the most learned Dr. Caspar, long life and good fortune in all the actions of his life.

units.la: COLL. Norinbergensium & Hamburgensiū beneficentia.
units.tr: COLL. The beneficence of the people of Nuremberg and Hamburg.

units.la: Norinbergensium quoq; & Hamburgensium beneficentia ac liberalitas nequaquā silentio praetereunda uidetur: qui exceptis aliis officijs, quae in pauperibus scholasticis & ministris Ecclesiae alendis & sustentandis passim praestant, hoc etiā summa cum misericordia addunt, quòd uiduis & orphanis concionatorum post ipsorum mortem habitationes & sumptus vitae largiuntur: promouetq; etiam eorum filios, quando apti sunt, ad studia aut ad artificia: & filiabus etiam dotem addunt in elocando. Hanc pietatem, qua magistratus suam gratitudinem erga Euangelij doctores quoq; mortuos declarat, Deus & postulat, & compensat.
units.tr: The beneficence and liberality of the people of Nuremberg and of Hamburg seem by no means to be passed over in silence. Besides the other services which they render everywhere in supporting and maintaining poor students and ministers of the Church, they add this also with the greatest compassion: that after the death of the preachers they grant dwellings and means of living to their widows and orphans. They also advance their sons, when they are fit, to studies or to crafts, and add dowries for their daughters on marriage. This piety, by which the magistrates declare their gratitude even towards the teachers of the Gospel who have died, God both requires and rewards.

units.la: COLL. Nobilis familiae Tilgerorum benemeritum.
units.tr: COLL. Of the noble family of the Tilgers, who deserved well.

units.la: D. Antonius Tilger senior, uir nobilis, ciuis & senator urbis inclytae Bernensis, duo millia coronatorum pauperibus scholasticis in suo testamento legauit, çauit, ad quæ patre mortuo, filius eius optimus uir D. Antonius Tilger ducentos adhuc adiecit. Quæ consilia præclara, & in omnem posteritatem laudabilia, illos ambos benemeritos de Ecclesia et Republica uiros mouerint, paucis perstringam. Cogitauerunt hi omni genere uirtutum præstantes ac nobiles uiri, quòd nullum regimen, imò nulla uocatio dextrè, cum utilitate proximi, sine studijs gubernari posit. Quantum præterea bonum sit, iuuentutis ad utiles res institutio, satis monstrant exempla: nã nemo non intelligit quanta diuersitas sit, in oratione, moribus, & in alijs circumstantijs rerum & personarum, inter mediocres doctos ac rudes: uidelicet tanta, quantum lapides, cæmentum et ligna nondum præparata à pulchro ædificio discrepãt. Quapropter merito omnes boni uiri, his benemeritis uiris, cõsulentibus illis modis posteritati, ut in utilibus communi uitæ & Ecclesiæ studijs iuuentus instituatur, doctrinaq; Euãgelij unà cum bonis legibus propagetur, perpetuas agunt gratias.
units.tr: Master Antonius Tilger the elder, a noble man, citizen and senator of the renowned city of Bern, bequeathed in his will two thousand crowns to poor scholars and provided for them. After his death his son, the excellent man Master Antonius Tilger, added two hundred more. I shall briefly set out the reasons that moved these two men, both of whom deserved well of the Church and the commonwealth, to such excellent plans, which deserve praise for all posterity. Men of noble birth, outstanding in every kind of virtue, reflected that no government, indeed no calling, can be carried on properly and for the good of one's neighbour without learning. Moreover, examples sufficiently show how great a benefit it is to train young people for useful things. For everyone understands how great the difference is, in speech, in manners and in the other circumstances of things and persons, between the moderately learned and the untrained: it is as great as the difference between a beautiful building and stones, mortar and timber not yet prepared. Therefore all good men rightly give perpetual thanks to these deserving men, who by these measures look to posterity, so that young people may be trained in the studies useful to common life and to the Church, and so that the teaching of the Gospel may be spread together with good laws.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Laudabili quoq; munificentia hæ tres inclytæ ciuitates, Tigurum, Berna & Schaffusium, sibi posteros deuincire uolunt. Nam quantum ex relationibus bonorum & doctorum uirorum percipio, singulæ harum ciuitatum alunt ex communi ærarij sumptu quindecim aut circiter stipendiatos, qui apud ipsos, & in peregrinis locis liberalibus sumptibus sustentantur. Insuper Tigurinos canonicos multos studiosos alere ferunt. Eædem etiā ciuitates fouent quāplurimos doctos uiros, qui uiuentibus & posteritati multa præclara scripta præbēt. Hæc omnia ab his inclytis ciuitatibus in hūc finem fiūt, ut bonæ artes et doctrinæ Euāgelij puritas cō seruetur. Cōseruari aūt aliter doctrina Euāgelij ct studia bonarū artiū nō possunt, nisi sint docētes & discētes: quamobrē à ueterib. Reipublicæ gubernatoribus ille ordo scholasticus docentiū & discentiū tot & tantis priuilegijs ac immunitatibus ornatus est, ut quàm plurimi ad subeundū, cōtra uulgi iudicia, illū ordinē imuitarētur. Itaq; adhuc ab omnib. sapientib. Reipublicæ præsidib. ille ordo prædicatur: & ijdē priuilegia huic ordini scholastico à maioribus nostris nō sine grauib. causis cōcessa, nullo modo uiolari, aut ipsis auferre cupiunt, sed potius nouis immunitatib. et beneficijs ornare studēt. Deniq; ut Deus omnipotēs omnib. bonis gubernatoribus priuatisq; hominibus, qui de studijs literarū, (sine quib. honesta disciplina & inuiolabilis iustitia inter homines, aliaq; innumerabilia bona in genere humano existere nō possunt) benemereri uolunt, prosperos in gubernatione ipsorū, & omniū suarū actionū successus largiri uelit, omnes horum ingentium beneficiorum intelligentes precantur.
units.tr: These three renowned cities, Zurich, Bern and Schaffhausen, also wish to bind future generations to themselves by a praiseworthy generosity. For, as far as I learn from the accounts of good and learned men, each of these cities supports from the common treasury about fifteen or so stipendiaries, who are maintained at generous expense both at home and in foreign places. In addition, they are said to support many studious canons of Zurich. These same cities also foster very many learned men, who give many excellent writings both to their contemporaries and to posterity. All of this is done by these renowned cities to this end: that the good arts and the purity of the teaching of the Gospel may be preserved. But the teaching of the Gospel and the studies of the good arts cannot be preserved otherwise than if there are teachers and learners. For this reason, by the early governors of the commonwealth, that scholastic order of teachers and learners was adorned with such great privileges and immunities that very many were invited to undertake that order, against the judgments of the common people. Accordingly, that order is still praised by all wise rulers of the commonwealth, and they wish not to violate in any way, or take away from them, the same privileges granted to this scholastic order by our forebears not without serious reasons, but rather they strive to adorn it with new immunities and benefits. Finally, let all who understand these great benefits pray that almighty God may grant prosperous government to all good rulers and private men who wish to deserve well of the studies of letters (without which honest discipline and inviolable justice among men, and countless other goods, cannot exist in the human race), and prosperous success in all their actions.

units.la: DE MAGISTRATV, ET Politica potestate.
units.tr: ON THE MAGISTRACY, AND POLITICAL POWER.

units.la: BONVS MAGISTRATVS.
units.tr: THE GOOD MAGISTRATE.

units.la: Aristoteles, ὁ ἄρχων ἐστὶ φύλαξ τῶν νόμων: id est, Magistratus est custos legis.
units.tr: Aristotle: the magistrate is the guardian of the laws [ὁ ἄρχων ἐστὶ φύλαξ τῶν νόμων], that is, the magistrate is the guardian of the law.

units.la: Xenophon: ἀλλὰ διαφέρει ἄρχων ἀγαθὸς ἀγαθῷ πατρὸς: id est, Non differt bonus princeps à patre bono.
units.tr: Xenophon: a good ruler does not differ from a good father [ἀλλὰ διαφέρει ἄρχων ἀγαθὸς ἀγαθῷ πατρὸς].

units.la: Aristoteles ad Alexandrum: Cogita Imperium non esse ὕβριν, id est temeritatem, petulantiam, seu licentiam afficiendi iniuria quoslibet: ἀλλ' εὐεργεσίαν, sed beneficentiam.
units.tr: Aristotle to Alexander: Consider that empire is not hybris [ὕβριν], that is, recklessness, wantonness, or licence to injure anyone at will, but euergesia [εὐεργεσίαν], beneficence.

units.la: Quales dominæ, tales catellæ. Scilicet in uulgus manant exempla regentum: Regis ad exemplum totus componitur orbis: Vtq; ducũ lituos, mores sic castra sequũtur: Claud. Item: — Sed non inflectere sensus Humanos edicta ualent, ut uita regentis.
units.tr: Such as the mistresses, such the lapdogs. Of course, the examples of rulers spread down to the common people: By the king's example the whole world is ordered; and as the trumpets of the commanders, so the camp follows their manners (Claudian). Likewise: But edicts have no power to bend human minds as the life of the ruler does.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Homerus nominat principes concionatores. Prima enim potestas antiquitùs fuit regia, & sacerdotalis: id est, summa authoritas fuit rex & sacerdos. Idem in Aristotele habetur.
units.tr: Homer calls princes preachers. For in early times the first power was royal and priestly: that is, the highest authority was king and priest. The same is found in Aristotle.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Athenienses diu ad hunc modum Græciæ principatum cipatum tenuerunt, ut cum permitterent alijs ciui-tatibus libertatem, ipsi tamen in excubijs essent, suoq; discrimine omnes tuerentur.
units.tr: For a long time the Athenians held the leadership of Greece in this way: while they allowed the other states their liberty, they themselves kept watch and defended everyone at their own risk.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Populus Romanus non saepè victis gentibus libertatem seu αὐτονομίαν concesit. Graecis tamen id honoris habuit, quòd post bellum cum Philippo Macedone gestum, immunitatem ijs donaret, & ut singulae ciuitates suis legibus uiuerēt permitteret. Ea de re cum decretum à senatu populoq; Romano factum Titus V. Imperator in Nemijs, quo ex more ad spectaculū tota Graecia uenerat, uoce praeconum recitare iußissęt, audiuissentq; gratissimum praeconium uniuersi, quantis honoribus affectus Imperator, quàm gratis sermonibus Romanū nomē celebratum est? esse eam unam in terris gentē, quae sua impēsa, suo labore & periculo, pro libertate aliorum bella gerat: detq; operā ne quòd toto orbe terrarum iniustum imperium sit, & ubiq; fas, lex, potētissima sint. Ita iudicarūt Graeci non aliud maius beneficiū homines hominib. praestare posse, quàm quòd accepissent à Romanis.
units.tr: The Roman people did not often grant liberty, or autonomy, to conquered nations. Yet the Greeks had this honour, that after the war waged against Philip of Macedon he granted them immunity and allowed each city to live under its own laws. When a decree to this effect had been made by the Senate and the Roman people, the Emperor Titus had it read out by heralds at the Nemean games, to which all Greece had come, as usual, for the spectacle. Everyone who heard that most welcome proclamation was delighted: with what honours the Emperor was honoured, and with what gratitude the name of the Romans was celebrated in speech; that this was the one nation on earth which waged wars at its own expense, labour and danger for the liberty of others, and took care that nowhere in the whole world should there be unjust rule, but that right, law and justice should prevail everywhere. Thus the Greeks judged that men could confer no greater benefit on men than what they had received from the Romans.

units.la: Enumeratio praestantissimorum & optimorum Regum ac Principum, imperia tepore maiorum nostrorū gubernantium.
units.tr: A list of the most excellent and best kings and princes who governed empires in the times of our ancestors.

units.la: Ferdinandus rex in Hispania.
units.tr: Ferdinand, king in Spain.

units.la: Alphõsus rex Neapolis,uir sapiēs & prudens.
units.tr: Alphonso, king of Naples, a man wise and prudent.

units.la: Imperator Fridericus, etiamsi non multa gesit in armis:tamen fuit sapiēs,nouit modum sui imperij et regni,ac in omni uita sapiēter imperiū rexit.
units.tr: The Emperor Frederick, although he did not accomplish much in arms, was nonetheless wise; he knew the measure of his empire and kingdom, and ruled his empire wisely throughout his whole life.

units.la: Casimirus rex Polonicus, iustus & excellens uictor.
units.tr: Casimir, king of Poland, a just and excellent victor.

units.la: Rex Mathias Vngarius,asperior aliquantulum, at utilis in armis.
units.tr: King Matthias of Hungary, somewhat harsh, but useful in arms.

units.la: Ioannes Hunniades,præstans princeps,&egregius post Mathiam rex Vngariæ,&c.
units.tr: John Hunyadi, an outstanding prince and, after Matthias, an eminent king of Hungary, etc.

units.la: In Germania Carolus Burgundus,pater Philippi Burgundi,qui est nominatus Bonus:à quo Maximilianus filius etiam Bonus dictus, qui propter multas excellentes uirtutes ualde fuit dilectus in Burgundia.
units.tr: In Germany, Charles of Burgundy, father of Philip of Burgundy, who was called the Good; from him his son Maximilian was also called the Good, and on account of many excellent virtues was greatly loved in Burgundy.

units.la: Marchio Albertus,qui nominatus est Achilles Germanicus,ualuit consilio,prudentia,& alijs uirtutibus. Albertus dux Saxoniæ.
units.tr: Margrave Albert, who was called the German Achilles, excelled in counsel, prudence and other virtues. Albert, duke of Saxony.

units.la: Fridericus Palatinus,egregia uirtute præditus.
units.tr: Frederick the Palatine, endowed with outstanding virtue.

units.la: Sic considerate,quòd Deus semper dederit & dat aliquos bonos et salutares principes,quorũ gubernatio et regimen imperijs est felix & salutaris.
units.tr: Consider in this way that God has always given, and still gives, some good and salutary princes, whose government and rule is happy and beneficial to empires.

units.la: Leo imago boni gubernatoris.
units.tr: The lion as an image of a good governor.

units.la: Sicut leo uenatur lupos, sic ordinaria imperia & gubernatores politici debent tollere latrunculos,& noxios seu sceleratos homines.
units.tr: As the lion hunts wolves, so ordinary empires and political governors ought to remove robbers and harmful or wicked men.

units.la: COLL. Signa bonæ gubernationis.
units.tr: COLL. Signs of good government.

units.la: Bene constitutæ Reipublicæ signa sunt, recte ordinatum horologium, bonum regimen, et bona Ecclesiæ constitutio in concionibus et cæremonijs. Veteres addunt, bonos caminos in ciuitate.
units.tr: The signs of a well-ordered commonwealth are a correctly set clock, good government, and a sound constitution of the Church in its sermons and ceremonies. The ancients add good roads in the city.

units.la: COLL. Acutè dictū Maximiliani Imperatoris, de gubernatione regni Hispaniæ, Galliæ & Germaniæ.
units.tr: COLL. A shrewd saying of the Emperor Maximilian about the government of the kingdoms of Spain, France and Germany.

units.la: Imperator Maximilianus solitus est dicere: Tantum tres reges sunt hoc tempore. unus est rex hominum, alter asinorum, & tertius rex regum. Rex hominum est rex Hispaniæ, ille adhuc moderatè regnat, & sentit se præesse hominibus. Alter rex asinorum, est rex Galliæ, cuius subditi omnia onera ut asini patiuntur, quæ ipsis imponuntur. Tertius rex regum, inquit, ego sum. nam quilibet meorum subditorum uult esse rex, & facere quæ ipse uult.
units.tr: The Emperor Maximilian was accustomed to say: "At present there are only three kings. One is the king of men, another the king of asses, and the third the king of kings. The king of men is the king of Spain; he still reigns with moderation and feels that he is set over men. The other, the king of asses, is the king of France, whose subjects bear all the burdens laid on them like asses. The third, the king of kings, is, he said, I myself; for each of my subjects wants to be king and do what he himself wishes."

units.la: Pensiones debentur magistratui, propter defensionem.
units.tr: Pensions are owed to the magistrate for the sake of defence.

units.la: Debentur pensiones principibus & magistratibus iniustam uim à subditis depellentibus, ut alant equites ac alios seruos, quibus arceant malos, ne incursiones in suam ditionem facientes, subditos diripiant ac spolient: sicut ante paucos annos fecit quidam Episcopus, qui ducens secum famelicam turbam militum, miseros subditos non solum pecunia, uerumetiam uictu, pane, pctasonibus, ac omnibus deniq; facultatibus spoliauit. Ille Episcopus fuit tyrannus. Etiam frater ipsius improbauit hoc: et scripsit ad ciuitates, nihil horum fieri suo consilio, se ualde improbare stulticiā & crudelitatē fratris.
units.tr: Pensions are owed to princes and magistrates who repel unjust violence from their subjects, so that they may maintain horsemen and other soldiers with which to keep off the wicked, lest they make raids into the prince's territory and plunder and despoil the subjects. So a few years ago a certain bishop did, who, leading with him a starving crowd of soldiers, despoiled the wretched subjects not only of their money but also of their food, bread, provisions, and finally of all their goods. That bishop was a tyrant. His own brother disapproved of this too, and wrote to the cities that none of these things were done on his advice, and that he greatly disapproved of his brother's folly and cruelty.

units.la: Differentia inter latrocinia & legitima bella.
units.tr: Difference between brigandage and lawful wars.

units.la: Alexander cæpit piratam, et interrogauit eum quare latrocinium exerceret in mari? At ipse respondit: Quin magis mihi licet latrocinari in mari, quàm tibi in terra. Non recte respondit. Quia latrocinium est ordinis politici confusio: sed bellum legitimum non est latrocinium. Alexander gessit iustum bellum, & puniuit iniustam crudelitatem quam tyranni in suos exercuerant.
units.tr: Alexander captured a pirate and asked him why he practised robbery at sea. He replied: "Why is it more lawful for me to commit robbery at sea than for you on land?" He did not answer rightly, for robbery is a confusion of political order, but a lawful war is not robbery. Alexander waged a just war and punished the unjust cruelty that tyrants had inflicted on their subjects.

units.la: Magistratus non debet esse quæstus, sed λατρεγία.
units.tr: The magistracy should not be a source of profit, but a service [λατρεγία].

units.la: Quidā dominus, cui pater administratione ditionis tradiderat (quia pater maluit alibi uiuere propter suas causas) scripserat patri, sibi non sufficere istos reditus, & uelle uti eius consilio ut peteret superindicta. Illud pater rescisens, gubernationem filij asperrimè tulit: & significauit filio, ut mœnia struerent pro suis opibus: er soll sich strecken, darnach er decke hett.
units.tr: A certain lord, to whom his father had handed over the administration of his domain (because the father preferred to live elsewhere for his own reasons), wrote to his father that these revenues were not enough for him, and that he wished to use his father's advice in order to seek extra taxes. When the father learned of this, he took his son's management very badly, and let him know that he should build his walls according to his means: "er soll sich strecken, darnach er decke hett" [he should stretch himself as far as his blanket reaches].

units.la: Pulchra allusio in dicto sequenti, ad multitudinem gubernatorum.
units.tr: A fine allusion in the following saying, to the multitude of rulers.

units.la: ἐν ἀγαθὴ πολυκοιρανίη, εἷς κοίρανος ἔστω: id est, non est bona multitudo regentium, rex unicus esto. Augustus uenustè deprauauit, ἐν ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίην, id est, nō bona est multitudo Cæsarū.
units.tr: "A multitude of rulers is not good; let there be one ruler" [οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη· εἷς κοίρανος ἔστω]. That is, a multitude of rulers is not a good thing; let there be a single king. Augustus wittily turned it around: "A multitude of Caesars is not a good thing" [οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη, Καίσαρες].

units.la: Consuetudo osculandi pedes & manus unde?
units.tr: Where does the custom of kissing feet and hands come from?

units.la: Est antiqua consuetudo, quæ etiam in Oriente fuit, cœpta in Africa, ut oscularentur pedes. Diocletianus retinuit ipsum morem: ita creuerunt adulationes. Postea Papæ sunt imitati, ut Imperatores sese abijcerent ad pedes Pontificum.
units.tr: It is an ancient custom, which existed also in the East and began in Africa, for people to kiss feet. Diocletian retained the very same custom, and so flattery grew. Afterwards the Popes imitated it, so that emperors cast themselves down at the feet of the Pontiffs.

units.la: Imperator noster Carolus V. cùm prouinciales in Africa uellent osculari eius pedes, seuerè dixit: Caput imperat, nō pedes. Nos Germani præbemus tantum manus: sed in prouincijs erat consuetudo, ut prouinciales osculárentur manus Consulibus.
units.tr: When the provincials in Africa wished to kiss the feet of our emperor Charles V, he sternly said: "The head commands, not the feet. We Germans offer only our hands." But in the provinces it was the custom for provincials to kiss the hands of the consuls.

units.la: Imperator noster Carolus V. sedit in mensa: & uenit ad eum Gardianus Cygneus, uolens accusare nostrum principem Iohannem Fridericū, & prius uoluit Imperatori osculari pedes. Imperator attraxit pedes: ille sequebatur. Tandem significat Imperator ministris, ut ipse fatuus abduceretur, & ipse liberaretur: quia noluit sibi osculari pedes.
units.tr: Our emperor Charles V was sitting at table, and Gardianus Cygneus came to him, wishing to accuse our prince John Frederick, and first wanted to kiss the emperor's feet. The emperor drew his feet away, and the man kept following. At last the emperor signalled to his attendants that the fool should be led away and that he himself should be left free, because the man would not stop trying to kiss his feet.

units.la: Vigilantia & sedulitas decet magistratum.
units.tr: Vigilance and diligence befit a magistrate.

units.la: ἡ χρὴ ϖανννύχιον ἐνδιειν βασιληφόρον αὐδρα, ὢ λαοί τ᾽ ἐπιστετράφεται, καὶ τόσα μέμνηλε.
units.tr: "It is not right for a counsellor-man to sleep all night, to whom the peoples turn and about whom so many cares are concerned." [οὐ χρὴ παννύχιον εὕδειν βουληφόρον ἄνδρα, ᾧ λαοί τε πιστρέφονται καὶ τόσα μέμηλε]

units.la: Hos uersiculos dignos putauit Dux Saxoniæ Fridericus, ut sua manu descriptos, & latinè uersos in suo cubiculo haberet, his uerbis:
units.tr: Duke Frederick of Saxony thought these little verses worthy to be kept in his bedchamber, copied out in his own hand and translated into Latin, with these words:

units.la: Nō decet principem uirum dormire totam noctē, Cui populi gubernacula commissa sunt, & à cuius cura pendent ingentia rerum momenta.
units.tr: A prince ought not to sleep the whole night through, when the reins of the people have been entrusted to him, and on whose care great matters of state depend.

units.la: Origo Electoratus.
units.tr: The origin of the Electorate.

units.la: Origo Electoratus principum Germaniæ, orta est à Persis. Vt enim illorum regi adiuncti fuerunt Principes, sic Imperatoribus Germaniæ adiuncti sunt Electores, qui imperio Romano Senatũ summum constituunt. Si rectè uelimus considerare, regi Persico adiuncti fuerunt Ephori. Penes hos enim fuit summa potestas regem eligendi, capiendi & abdicandi. Sic summa potestas & autoritas est Electorum, qui sæpè ab imperio bestias & tyrannos remouerunt. Hic Electorum status defendit Germaniam, & retinuit moderationem & tranquillitatem annos iam quingentos.
units.tr: The origin of the electoral princes of Germany lies with the Persians. For just as princes were attached to the king of Persia, so electors are attached to the emperors of Germany, and they constitute the supreme senate of the Roman empire. If we consider this rightly, the Ephors were attached to the Persian king. For supreme power to elect, to take and to depose the king lay with them. Thus the supreme power and authority belongs to the electors, who have often removed beasts and tyrants from the empire. This estate of electors has defended Germany and has kept moderation and tranquillity for now five hundred years.

units.la: Bene constitutæ Reipublicæ signa.
units.tr: Signs of a well-constituted commonwealth.

units.la: Fui Brunschuigæ, ubi est optima disciplina: etsi nihil detraho aliis ciuitatibus, tamē nusquam meliorem liorem uidi, præsertim in tam populosa ciuitate. Incedunt ciues pleriq; longis uestibus, sine armis: et nusquam uidi pulchrius tectas mulieres, quàm ibi. Et ciuis apud quē diuertimur, homo fide dignus, dixit mihi, in uiginti annis nullā ibi cædē facta esse.
units.tr: I was at Brunswick, where the discipline is excellent. Although I take nothing away from other cities, I nowhere saw better order, especially in so populous a city. Most citizens walk about in long robes, without arms, and I nowhere saw women more becomingly dressed than there. And the citizen with whom we lodged, a trustworthy man, told me that in twenty years no murder had been committed there.

units.la: Simile.
units.tr: A comparison.

units.la: Rex Ferdinandus, cum esset Noribergæ, interrogauit unum ex præcipuis senatoribus ciuitatis, quo modo tantam multitudinem regerent? Respondit ille: Serenissime rex, blandis uerbis, & atrocibus pœnis. Est sapientissimum responsum hominis ingeniosi. Sic enim debent esse Imperia constituta, ut gubernatores omnibus comiter respondeant, at in pœnis sumendis grauitatem adhibeant.
units.tr: King Ferdinand, while he was at Nuremberg, asked one of the leading senators of the city how they managed so great a multitude. He replied: "Most serene king, with soft words and cruel punishments." It is a most wise answer from an ingenious man. For governments ought to be so constituted that the rulers answer everyone courteously, yet bring gravity to the inflicting of punishments.

units.la: Descriptio trium præcipuarum in hac uita uocationum.
units.tr: A description of the three principal callings in this life.

units.la: In curia Basiliensi aureis literis hic uersiculus scriptus inuenitur:
units.tr: In the court at Basel this little verse is found written in golden letters:

units.la: Tu supplex ora, tu protege, tuq; labora.
units.tr: Pray as a suppliant, protect, and labour.

units.la: In hoc uersiculo tres præcipuæ huius uitæ uocationes proponuntur: Ecclesiasticus, politicus, & subditorum status.
units.tr: In this verse three principal callings of this life are set forth: the ecclesiastical, the political, and the estate of subjects.

units.la: Præcipua ornamenta horum trium regnorum, Angliæ, Galliæ, & Hispaniæ, ante hæc tempora.
units.tr: The chief ornaments of these three kingdoms, England, France and Spain, before these times.

units.la: Capuanus natus ex nobilitate Schönberg Misnensis, factus Cardinalis, missus est in Angliam & Hispaniam, Hispaniâ, ac ad nostrum Imperatorē Carolum V. adolescentem. Cum Romam redijsseт, sic est interrogatus à Cardinalibus: Dic nobis Capuane breuiter (quia ipsi amant argutè dicta) quæ uidisti? Dicam, inquit. In Anglia uidi pulcherrimum regem (sicut fuit Eduardus) in Gallia pulcherrimum regnū, in Hispania sapiens consiliū: hoc tribuit Imperatori.
units.tr: Capuanus, born of the nobility of Schönberg in Meissen, was made a cardinal and was sent to England and Spain, and to our Emperor Charles V while he was still young. When he returned to Rome, the cardinals questioned him thus: "Tell us briefly, Capuanus (for they love pointed sayings), what did you see?" "I will tell you," he said. "In England I saw a most handsome king (such as Edward was); in France a most splendid kingdom; in Spain a wise council. This he ascribed to the Emperor."

units.la: Pictura boni magistratus apud ueteres.
units.tr: The picture of a good magistrate among the ancients.

units.la: Imperatores Germani apud ueteres hoc modo pingi solebant, tenentes altera manu librum, & altera ensem. Quo antiquitas voluit significare, imperatores legum & armorum peritia debere esse instructos. Gladius enim sine lege, est tyrannis. Pictura ista in gratiam uniorum sic proposita est, ut cōmonefieret de præcipuis gubernationis partib. In curia Vuormaciensi hoc distichon argenteis literis est scriptum, admonens gubernatores de suo officio.
units.tr: The German emperors were commonly painted in ancient times in this way: holding a book in one hand and a sword in the other. By this the ancients wished to signify that emperors ought to be furnished with knowledge of the laws and of arms. For a sword without law is tyranny. This picture was so presented for the benefit of the rulers that they might be reminded of the chief parts of government. In the court at Worms this couplet is written in silver letters, admonishing governors of their office:

units.la: Astra Deo nil maius habent, nil Cæsare terra: Sic Cæsar terras, ut Deus astra, regat.
units.tr: The stars have nothing greater than God, the earth nothing greater than Caesar: so may Caesar rule the lands as God rules the stars.

units.la: Aliud principis Ernesti Luneburgensis.
units.tr: Another example from Prince Ernest of Lüneburg.

units.la: Prope oppidū Zell, est præquū Lotharij nominatū, et existimatur locus esse natalis Lotharij. Quæstor in arce oppidi Zell voluit imponere prædio, quod habuit immunitatē, nouā pēsionem. Colonus uenit ad Ernestum principem Luneburgensem, qui clementer audiebat suos, & delectabatur honestarum rerum cōsideratiōe, dicēs: Illustrissime Domine Princeps, prædiū illud semper fuit immune: quia nominatur prædium Lotharij, et nos existimamur eius posteri. Delectatus Princeps ista allocutione, inquisiuit diligenter in rationibus: inuentumq; est, fuisse immune prediū. Quo comperto, duxit Princeps secum colonum in suum conclaue, & percontatus est alia multa, quæ uoluit. Iussit deinde scribi in rationibus: Hoc prædium locum natale esse Lotharij, & esse immune. Hanc historiam ideò recito, ut audietis & cognoscatis historias, quarum magna utilitas & necessitas est in omni uita. Quia nemo potest regere patrimoniū suum sine historia. Oportet scire, unde acceperis feuda: unde tui acceperint: unde uenerint in possessionem.
units.tr: Near the town of Zell there is an estate called the estate of Lothair, and it is thought to be the place of Lothair's birth. The treasurer in the castle of the town of Zell wished to impose a new tax on an estate which had immunity. A farmer came to Ernest, Prince of Lüneburg, who listened kindly to his subjects and took delight in the consideration of honourable matters, and said: "Most illustrious Lord Prince, that estate has always been immune, because it is called the estate of Lothair, and we are thought to be his descendants." The Prince, delighted by this address, enquired carefully into the accounts, and it was found that the estate had been immune. When this was discovered, the Prince took the farmer with him into his private room and questioned him about many other things as he wished. Then he ordered it to be written in the accounts: this estate is the birthplace of Lothair, and it is immune. I recount this story so that you may hear and learn histories, whose great use and necessity is in all of life. For no one can govern his patrimony without history. It is necessary to know where you received your fiefs, from whom your ancestors received them, and how they came into possession.

units.la: Aliud Friderici Ducis Saxoniæ insigne.
units.tr: Another distinguishing mark of Duke Frederick of Saxony.

units.la: Dux Fridericus sæpè maluit petentibus ligna, potius dare pecuniam ex camera, qua emerent ligna ex Bohemia, ut parceretur suis syluis. Quia omnes sapientes gubernatores magni faciūt syluas, & potius dant pecuniam, quàm amittant syluas: cùm tamen alioqui non sit usitatum, ut principes largiantur pecuniam. Habebat etiam Dux syluas uicinas Vuitenbergæ, olim emptas à suis maioribus. Princi-
units.tr: Duke Frederick often preferred, when people asked for wood, to give money from the treasury, with which they might buy wood from Bohemia, so that his woods might be spared. For all wise governors value their woods greatly, and would rather give money than lose their woods, although otherwise it is not customary for princes to bestow money. The Duke also had woods near Wittenberg, formerly bought by his ancestors.

units.la: Principissa Anhaldina, mater horum Principum qui nunc uiuunt, cum & ipsa esset sapiens, & bona œconomissa, repetebat illas syluas: quia erant uenditæ cum pacto de reuendëdo. Etsi autem Princeps difficulter amittebat syluas illas, & malebat adhuc aliquid pecuniæ soluere, uel addere, quia precia lignorum iam creuerant: tamen nolebat honestissimam matronam diu uexare, aut suspensam tenere. & quamuis aliqui consilia & prætextus, quibus eas aliquo iure retinere posset, proponerent: tamen noluit suam conscientiam grauare, nec quicquam huiusmodi prætexere, quo syluas illas posset retinere: sed tanta fuit eius integritas, ut Anhaldinis syluas illas sponte restitueret. Pertinet ad curam boni Principis & gubernatoris, ne syluas inutiliter perdat, aut consumat.
units.tr: The Princess of Anhalt, mother of the princes who are now living, being herself wise and a good housekeeper, demanded those woods back, because they had been sold with an agreement of resale. Although the Prince found it hard to lose those woods, and preferred to pay or add some money, since the prices of wood had now risen, yet he was unwilling to vex that most honourable matron for long, or keep her in suspense. And although some advisers put forward pretexts by which he might retain them by some right, he was unwilling to burden his conscience or to allege anything of that kind by which he could keep those woods; and such was his integrity that he restored those woods to the Anhalt family of his own accord. It belongs to the care of a good prince and governor that he should not uselessly lose or waste his woods.

units.la: Aliud Ioannis Friderici Ducis Saxoniæ.
units.tr: Another example, of John Frederick, Duke of Saxony.

units.la: Cum optimus Princeps Ioannes Fridericus captiuus teneretur in Belgico, ac aliquando proficisceretur in uenationem: accidit ut custodes aberrarent ab eo, ac eum diu frustra quærerent. Ipse uero solus sine comitatu uenit ad portam, ubi expectauit custodes, ne si solus ingrederetur, indignatione & odium Cæsaris custodes incurrerent. Illud cum Imperatori indicaretur, admodum delectatus est illa integritate.
units.tr: When the excellent Prince John Frederick was held captive in the Netherlands, he once set out to hunt. It happened that his guards lost sight of him and searched for him for a long time in vain. He himself came alone, without an escort, to the gate, where he waited for the guards, so that they would not, if he went in alone, incur the indignation and hatred of the Emperor. When this was reported to the Emperor, he was greatly delighted by such integrity.

units.la: Pulchra laus candoris in quolibet magistratu.
units.tr: A fine praise of candour in any magistrate.

units.la: De Marco Antonio dicit Dion: Erat similis si-bi ipsi omni tempore, et nihil erat in eo arte fictum & simulatum. Est pulcherrima laus uniuscuiusli-bet uiri, præsertim boni principis.
units.tr: Dio says of Mark Antony: he was always like himself, and nothing in him was feigned or pretended by art. This is the most excellent praise of any man, especially of a good prince.

units.la: Aliud Francisci regis Galliæ.
units.tr: Another example, of Francis, King of France.

units.la: Imperator Carolus V. cum esset mota seditio in Flandria à Gandauensibus, petiuit transitum per Galliam à rege: qui ipsi concessit. Ibi quidam fue-runt suasores regi, ne seruaret pactum: fore sibi noxiam imperatoris potentiam. Sed regium fuit, ser-uare pactum. Postea spectaculum exhibuerunt re-gi. ceruum immiserunt in hortu speciosum, & emi-serunt qui vastaret hortum (quemadmodum Galli delectantur talibus spectaculis) volentes significare, Imperatorem Galliam vastaturum esse.
units.tr: When a sedition had been stirred up in Flanders by the men of Ghent, the Emperor Charles V asked the king for passage through France, and the king granted it. Some advised the king not to keep the agreement, on the ground that the Emperor's power would be harmful to him. But it was the king's part to keep his word. Afterwards they staged a spectacle for the king: they let a stag into a beautiful garden, and then released a beast to lay waste the garden (as the French delight in such shows), wishing to signify that the Emperor would lay waste France.

units.la: Aliud integritatis, in Ludouico rege Galliæ.
units.tr: Another example of integrity, in Louis, King of France.

units.la: Ludouicus rex Galliæ iudicio Parlamenti assi-dere solitus est, & audire suas causas. Si uero aliqui blandirentur regi, cùm ipsius causa ageretur, ac dicerent causam regis bonam esse: Audiamus, inquit, eam, & ius seu iustitia plus in ea valeat quàm ue-stra beneuolentia. Cùm autem ipsi sententia dicen-da esset, sæpè contra se pronunciauit: & ipsos, si ni-mium suæ causæ tribuerent, duriter obiurgauit. Parlamenti autem (ut uocant) Parisiensis (quo nihil est pulchrius) authorem esse dicunt Pipinum, patrem Caroli Magni.
units.tr: Louis, King of France, was accustomed to sit in on the judgments of Parliament and to hear its cases. If some flattered the king when a case concerning him was being argued, and said that the king's cause was good, he would say: "Let us hear it, and let law and justice count for more in it than your goodwill." When it came to pronouncing sentence, he often ruled against himself, and sharply rebuked those who ascribed too much to his cause. Moreover, they say that the founder of the Parliament of Paris (as it is called, and nothing is finer) was Pepin, the father of Charlemagne.

units.la: Celebratio uirtutum in Imperatore Carolo V.
units.tr: The praise of virtues in the Emperor Charles V.

units.la: Dux Saxoniæ Fridericus aliquando de Carolo V. Imperatore dixit: Deus dedit nobis Cæsarem et clementem, ac terribilem. Magnum est elogium, quasi diceret: Deus dedit nobis talem Imperatorem, qui multa in republica corriget, & sub quo multa bona fient.
units.tr: Duke Frederick of Saxony once said of the Emperor Charles V: "God has given us an emperor who is both merciful and terrible." It is a great eulogy, as if he meant: God has given us such an emperor, who will correct many faults in the commonwealth, and under whom many good things will be done.

units.la: Celebratio candoris in Imperatore Theodosio.
units.tr: The praise of candour in the Emperor Theodosius.

units.la: In laudatione Theodosij Imperatoris inter cæteras uirtutes nominatim etiā illa reperitur, quod animus eius non fuerit suspicax.
units.tr: In the praise of the Emperor Theodosius, among his other virtues, this one is also expressly named: that his mind was not suspicious.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Animositas in Romanis colonijs, temporibus aduersis.
units.tr: Courage in the Roman colonies in adverse times.

units.la: Quando Hannibal occupauerat maximam partem Italiæ, & Romani post Cannensem cladem nihil reliquum præter colonias 25. aut circiter habebant: istas deduxerunt Romam, & ostenderunt formulas seu album conscriptorum militum: proposueruntq; sententias, quid essent facturi: an uellent defendere istam particulam & reliquias Italiæ, an uerò se dedere Hannibali? Responderunt coloni, se ad extremum dimicaturos esse. Nunquã Roma fuit maior, quàm cum fuit pauperrima, & derelicta, ita ut nihil spei esset reliquum. Ita opposuerũt se Hannibali excelsis animis, et recuperarũt uires, ut cùm turpitudine coactus sit Hannibal fugere ex Italia. illa exẽpla uirtutis manifestè ostendunt præsentiam Dei in imperijs, & negocijs gubernationis rerumpublicarum.
units.tr: When Hannibal had occupied most of Italy, and after the defeat at Cannae the Romans had almost nothing left except some twenty-five colonies or so, they summoned these colonies to Rome and showed them the lists or rolls of enrolled soldiers. They put the question to them: what would they do? Would they defend that small remnant and what was left of Italy, or would they surrender to Hannibal? The colonists replied that they would fight to the very end. Rome was never greater than when she was at her poorest and most forsaken, with no hope left at all. So they opposed Hannibal with lofty spirits and recovered their strength, so that Hannibal, against his will, was forced to flee from Italy in disgrace. These examples of virtue clearly show the presence of God in the governing of empires and the management of commonwealths.

units.la: Modesta Imperatoris Caroli V. responsio, de suis laudibus.
units.tr: The modest reply of the Emperor Charles V concerning his own praises.

units.la: Imperator Carolus V. cùm à rege Gallico Parisijs exciperetur honorificētissimè, & tanto triumpho, qualis nusquam ei est exhibitus: postea unus ex consiliarijs regis eum longa & grauissima allocutus esset oratione, in qua multarum uirtutum & rerum gestarum Imperatoris commemoratio fiebat: ille ad hæc omnia breuiter ac modestissimè respondit, Ideo sibi gratã esse orationem, quòd cum commonefecisset, quòd talis esse deberet.
units.tr: When the Emperor Charles V was received at Paris by the French king with the greatest honour, and with a triumph such as had never been shown him anywhere else, one of the king's counsellors then addressed him with a long and very weighty speech, in which the Emperor's many virtues and deeds were recounted. He replied to all of this briefly and with the greatest modesty: he was grateful for the speech, because it had reminded him what kind of man he ought to be.

units.la: Magnanimitas Augusti in defendendo seruo.
units.tr: The magnanimity of Augustus in defending a slave.

units.la: Cum Augustus aliquando conuiua alterius magni domini esset, et seruus huius in porrigendis poculis uitrum crystallinũ frãgeret, Dominus seruo iratus, iussit ut cōijceretur in uiuarium, quo à murenis devoraretur. Augustus ægreferens illam crudelitatem, miserius seru, surgit, & frangit omnia crystallina uitra, quæ in mensa erant collocata. Insuper etiam seruum libertate donauit. Hoc fuit uere regium decus.
units.tr: Once when Augustus was the guest of another great lord, and a slave of that lord, while handing round the cups, broke a crystal glass, the master, angry, ordered that the slave be thrown into the fishpond to be devoured by the lampreys. Augustus, displeased at that cruelty, pitied the slave, rose, and broke all the crystal glasses that had been set on the table. Moreover, he also gave the slave his freedom. This was truly a royal glory.

units.la: Beneficentia Atheniensium in soluendis debitis, pro duce integritate uirtutum præstante.
units.tr: The generosity of the Athenians in paying debts, for a general who excelled in integrity and virtue.

units.la: Dux Atheniensis, qui uicit Mitylenem, cùm ad eum deferretur imperiū, excusauit se, quòd multa deberet, & obæratus non posset imperare cum authoritate. Ibi Senatus tanti eius uirtutes fecit, ut pro eo solueret debitum.
units.tr: The Athenian general who conquered Mytilene, when the command was offered to him, excused himself, saying that he was in debt and, being encumbered, could not command with authority. Then the Senate, so highly did it value his virtues, paid the debt on his behalf.

units.la: Dextrum iudicium Ludouici regis Galliæ, de Imperatore Maximiliano.
units.tr: The sound judgement of Louis, king of France, concerning the Emperor Maximilian.

units.la: Consiliarius quidam regis Galliæ dixit de Imperatore Maximiliano, cum esse consulem Augustanum. Ad ea Ludouicus Tertius, pater Francisci, respondit: Tace tu asine, noli talia loqui de potestatibus. quando hic consul tympanū pulsat, tunc propter ipsius uirtutem tota Gallia tremit.
units.tr: A certain counsellor of the king of France said of the Emperor Maximilian, when he was a consul of Augsburg, something disparaging. To this Louis III, the father of Francis, replied: "Be quiet, you ass, do not speak such things about rulers. When this consul beats his drum, then all of France trembles because of his virtue."

units.la: Virtus in iuuenili ætate cernitur.
units.tr: Virtue is seen in youth.

units.la: Amicus quidam noster ante annos quadraginta à Maximiliano missus erat legatus in aulam Palatini, timi, de Carolo Quinto adhuc adolescēte dixit: O amice, nō possum tibi multa dicere de eo: sed quan docunq; aliquid dicit, hoc habet magnam emphasin. Illud est animaduersum statim in illa prima ætate. Ita indoles in bonis citò eminet.
units.tr: A certain friend of ours, forty years ago sent by Maximilian as ambassador to the court of the Palatine, spoke of Charles V while he was still a young man: "O friend, I cannot tell you much about him, but whenever he says anything, it carries great emphasis." This was noticed at once in that first age. Thus a good disposition soon stands out in good people.

units.la: Audio tam mirabilia dici de Imperatoris Caroli Quinti nepote, ut ego credam aliquid magni fore. Hoc propterea dico, ut cogitetis, qui tunc temporis uicturi estis, quando ille regnabit. Genesis est talis, qualem nunquam uidi præstantiorem. Quis scit, quid'nā Carolus Sextus designaturus sit? Deus suam gratiam ipsi largiatur. Videtur aliquid magni portēdere, & præstiturus esse. Fortasis Turcæ uires labefactabit, aut tale quid simile præstabit.
units.tr: I hear such wonderful things said of the grandson of the Emperor Charles V that I believe something great will come of him. I say this so that you, who are going to live at the time when he reigns, may consider it. His promise is such as I have never seen surpassed. Who knows what Charles VI will bring about? May God grant him his grace. He seems to portend something great and to be going to accomplish it. Perhaps he will weaken the power of the Turks, or will achieve something similar.

units.la: DEFENSIO ET GVBERNATIO diuina Magistratus.
units.tr: The defence and government of the magistrate by divine providence.

units.la: Maximilianus, cum aliqui ipsum sequentes interficerētur, et feriretur globis, dicebat: Non oportet uos meam audaciam imitari. Principes habent suam quandam peculiarem fortunam.
units.tr: When some of those following Maximilian were killed and struck by bullets, he said: "You must not imitate my boldness. Princes have their own peculiar fortune."

units.la: Imperium sedes Dei.
units.tr: Empire is the seat of God.

units.la: Quādo Roma fuit capta, uenit Iulius Pflūg Episcopus Naumburgensis ad Ducem Saxoniæ Georgium ex Italia, & retulit ei historiā Romæ captæ. Cùm uerò diceret, tantam fuisse multitudinem in urbe Roma, ut facilimè potuerit exercitus ab ea repelli: & quòd fames coegisset exercitum prope-rare ad expugnationem: ibi sedit Dux Georgius diu cogitabundus, ac tandem hæc uerba protulit: Nunc demum reipsa cõperio, quodcunq; Deus uolucrit, id certò ac necessariò euenire: quod uerò Deus noluerit, id non posse succedere aut perfici.
units.tr: When Rome was taken, Julius Pflug, bishop of Naumburg, came from Italy to Duke George of Saxony and told him the story of the sack of Rome. When he said that the multitude in the city of Rome was so great that the army could very easily have been driven out of it, and that hunger had forced the army to hurry to the assault, Duke George sat for a long time in thought, and at last uttered these words: "Now at last I see in fact that whatever God has willed, that certainly and necessarily comes to pass; and whatever God has not willed, that cannot succeed or be carried out."

units.la: Aquila est imago Imperatoris, qui diuinitùs custoditur.
units.tr: The eagle is an image of the Emperor, who is preserved by divine providence.

units.la: Dicitur autem aquila ideo ministra fulminis, quia altissimè uolat, & non feritur fulmine: nam diuinitùs seruatur. deinde nõ uescitur alieno labore, ut vultures & corui, sed proprio, ex venatione.
units.tr: The eagle is called the bearer of the thunderbolt because it flies very high and is not struck by lightning; for it is preserved by divine providence. Then, it does not feed on the labour of others, like vultures and crows, but on its own, from hunting.

units.la: Moritur autem fame in senecta. Iam uidetis, quantæ sint conspirationes contra nostrum Imperatorem Carolum. Italia & aliæ regiones consentiunt in interitum aquilæ: sed tamen hæc aquila diuinitùs seruatur à fulmine Gallico, Italico, Turcico, & aliarum conspirationum. Sed Omnia sunt hominum tenui pendentia filo: Et subitò casu, quæ ualuere, ruunt.
units.tr: Yet it dies of hunger in old age. Now you see how great the conspiracies are against our Emperor Charles. Italy and other regions agree in the destruction of the eagle; but nevertheless this eagle is preserved by divine providence from the thunderbolt of France, Italy, Turkey, and other conspiracies. But all things hang by a slender thread, and suddenly, by chance, those things that were strong collapse.

units.la: Tria cuilibet magistratui necessaria.
units.tr: Three things necessary for any magistrate.

units.la: Augustus, cùm mitteret Germanicum in Asiam, optauit ei tria: Virtutem Alexandri: beneuolentiâ hominum tantam, quanta fuit erga Pompeium: & tertiò addit, Opto tibi meam fortunam. Significâs, quòd res gestæ, & victoriæ ab ipso partæ, fuissent diuinitùs gubernatæ.
units.tr: When Augustus sent Germanicus into Asia, he wished him three things: the courage of Alexander; as much goodwill from men as Pompey had enjoyed; and thirdly he added, "I wish you my good fortune." He meant that the deeds done and victories won by Germanicus would be governed by God.

units.la: Quando Franciscus rex Galliæ coiunxerat sibi Venetos, pontificem Romanum & Italiam contra Imperatorē, tunc fœdus illud uocabatur Liga sancta. Sed tamen nihil effecerūt. Rex enim est captus: Veneti sunt facti supplices, procumbētes in genua, & difficulter impetrauerunt pacem, quamuis deprecante pro eis pontifice Romano.
units.tr: When Francis, king of France, had joined the Venetians, the Roman pontiff and Italy against the Emperor, that alliance was called the Holy League. Yet they accomplished nothing. The king was taken prisoner, and the Venetians became suppliants, falling on their knees, and with difficulty obtained peace, although the Roman pontiff interceded for them.

units.la: Fridericus Marchio Misnensis, inuitatus est à Duce quodā in cōuiuiū, in oppidū Madeburgum. Inter prandendum autem uenit percussor, qui debebat interficere Ducem Misniæ, & impetum in ipsum facit. Adest tum forte ciuis quidam Freiburgensis, interjiciens sese inter ducem et percussorē: qui tam fortiter defendit suum dominum, ut ipsius uulnera exciperet, ac tandem ipsum percussorem interficeret. In primis quidem exemplum hoc ostendit, quomodo Deus subinde bonos principes Reipublicæ conseruet, atq; etiā in summis periculis mirabiliter tueatur ac liberet. Deinde in hoc ciue relucet exemplum magnæ fidelitatis subditi erga suū Principem.
units.tr: Frederick, Margrave of Meissen, was invited to a banquet by a certain duke in the town of Magdeburg. During the meal an assassin came in, who was to kill the Duke of Meissen, and made an attack on him. Then a certain citizen of Freiburg, who happened to be present, threw himself between the duke and the assassin. He defended his lord so bravely that he took the wounds meant for him and finally killed the assassin himself. First, this example shows how God from time to time preserves good princes for the commonwealth, and even in the greatest dangers protects and delivers them wondrously. Second, in this citizen shines a notable example of great fidelity of a subject toward his prince.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Omnes politiæ sunt sicut ruinosæ domus, quas diabolus conatur demoliri: sed Deus eas sulcit.
units.tr: All commonwealths are like ruinous houses, which the devil tries to pull down, but God props them up.

units.la: AMOR SVPERIORVM ERGA INFERIORES, & econtra.
units.tr: The affection of superiors toward inferiors, and the reverse.

units.la: Dux Eberhardus Vuirtenbergensis in conuentu tu Vuormacienſi tepore Maximiliani habito, cum singuli principes ſingulas ſuas ditiones laudaret, il le auscultauit. Saxonici principes laudauerũt ſuas uenas metallicas. Duces Bauarici laudauerunt ciui tates: Dux Palatinus ſertilitatem terrę & fœcun-ditatẽ uini. Dux itaq; Eberhardus Vuirtenbergenſis iussus à Friderico Duce Saxoniæ etiam suæ di-tionis laudes prædicare: Nihil est, ait, quod prædi-cem, cùm sim inter vos infimus: sed hoc unum scio, me posse securè dormire in gremio cuiuslibet sub-diti mei, in medio campo, quando quidem libuerit. quasi diceret: Ego ita guberno mea ditione, ut mei subditi me ament. Sic reliqui hanc laudem suis fa-cultatibus prætulerunt.
units.tr: At the diet of Worms held under the emperor Maximilian, when the individual princes praised their own territories, the Saxon princes praised their metal mines. The Bavarian dukes praised their cities; the Palatine duke praised the fertility of his land and the abundance of his wine. Duke Eberhard of Württemberg, ordered by Frederick, Duke of Saxony, to praise the excellences of his own territory too, said: "There is nothing I can praise, since I am the lowest among you. But this one thing I know: I can sleep safely in the lap of any of my subjects, in the middle of a field, whenever I please." As if he were saying, "I govern my territory in such a way that my subjects love me." Thus the others preferred this praise to all their other resources.

units.la: Cum alij Principes iactarent sua χειμήλια in cõuentu aliquot Principum, ibi Comes de Nassau, domi-nus Cattorum, dicebat: Habeo nonaginta ru-sticos, quorum quilibet potest mihi, cùm opus est, sine magna iactura suæ rei familiaris, pendere quadringẽtos florenos. Hunc thesaurum pluris fa-cio, quàm vestros thesauros & χειμήλια: & hic thesaurus est mihi certior, quam si in meis arculis absconditus esset: atq; hi sunt mihi fideliores custo-des huius thesauri, quàm si meis quæstoribus esset commissus.
units.tr: While other princes boasted of their valuables [χειμήλια] at a gathering of several princes, the Count of Nassau, lord of the Catti, said: "I have ninety peasants, any one of whom can, when I need it, lend me four hundred florins without great loss to his household finances. I value this treasure more than your treasures and valuables. This treasure is more certain to me than if it were hidden in my chests, and these men are more faithful guardians of this treasure to me than if it had been entrusted to my treasurers."

units.la: Alius similiter αὐτάρχης, cùm uideret neminem gratulari regi, se uero quoq; in proptu nihil quod tali tali rege dignum foret, habere: proximum fluuiolu forte conspicatus, accurrit, hauftamq; ambabus manibus aquam Artaxerxi sitibundo obtulit. Qua hominis urbanitate et beneficentia motus, illico phialam aureā, atq; mille Daricos nummos pro tali in tempore beneficio exhibito donari curauit.
units.tr: Another, likewise self-sufficient [αὐτάρχης], seeing that no one was congratulating the king, and having nothing ready himself that was worthy of such a king, spotted a little river nearby, ran to it, and, scooping up water in both hands, offered it to the thirsty Artaxerxes. Moved by this man's courtesy and kindness, the king at once had a golden cup and a thousand Darics given to him as a reward for such a timely service.

units.la: ODIVM INTER SVPERIORES & INFERIORES.
units.tr: THE HATRED BETWEEN SUPERIORS AND INFERIORS.

units.la: Est naturalis inimicicia inter cygnum & aquilam. Cygnus nō prouocat aquilam, sed sæpè uincit prouocatus. Cygnus significat oratorem, uel bonū senatorem. Aquila significat atrocem gubernatorem. Est odium inter amantes pacem, quietem, & iusticiam, & inter turbatores quietis. Aquila fuit imperij Babylonici signum. Romani etiam aquilā habuerunt, sed ante Mariū alia habuerūt insignia.
units.tr: There is a natural enmity between the swan and the eagle. The swan does not provoke the eagle, but when provoked it often prevails. The swan signifies an orator or a good senator; the eagle signifies a fierce governor. There is hatred between those who love peace, quiet and justice and the disturbers of quiet. The eagle was the sign of the Babylonian empire. The Romans also had the eagle, but before Marius they had other insignia.

units.la: Memini magni nominis principem alteri conqueri, dicente, se mirari quòd nō diligeretur à suis subditis, cùm tamen nihil in eius morib. reprehendere possent. Ibi alter, cui illa erat conquestus, uocauit ad se puerum, dans ei pomum, ac iubens, ut alius pomum puero eriperet. Quod cùm ille faceret, puer cœpit flere, & ei succensere. Idem, respondit principi, tibi contingit: etsi in uita es honestus, ita ut nemo de tuis moribus conqueri possit: tamen ista βλαμία in te reprehenditur.
units.tr: I remember a prince of great name complaining to another, saying that he wondered why he was not loved by his subjects, since they could find nothing to blame in his conduct. The other man, to whom the complaint was made, called a boy to himself, gave him an apple, and ordered someone to snatch the apple from the boy. When this was done, the boy began to weep and to be angry with the one who took it. The same man replied to the prince: "The same thing happens to you. Although you are so upright in life that no one can complain of your morals, that fault [βλαμία] is nevertheless found in you."

units.la: DE CALAMITATE IMPERIORUM, eorundemq; mutatione.
units.tr: On the calamity of empires, and their change.

units.la: Imperator noster Carolus Quintus in obsidione oppidi Vuitebergæ, cùm audiuisseт multiplicia scelera Hispanorum, inquit: Ah, si quando accipiā magnam calamitatem, ea accidet mihi propter malitiam et petulantiam meorum hominū. Quanquā adeò est seuerus, ut statim puniat enormia delicta.
units.tr: Our emperor Charles V, during the siege of the town of Wittenberg, when he heard of the manifold crimes of the Spaniards, said: "Ah, if ever I suffer a great calamity, it will befall me because of the wickedness and wantonness of my men." Yet he is so strict that he punishes grave offences at once.

units.la: Demosthenes dixit: Si retexenda uita esset, & sibi duæ uiæ proponerentur, quarum altera rectè duceret ad summos honores in republica, altera uerò rectè ad mortem: se commonefactum de periculis, potius ingressurū illam uiam quæ ad mortē duceret, quàm ducente ad honores. Huic nō dissimilis est, quod Erasmus dixit: Miseros esse principes, si intelligant sua mala: miseriores, si non intelligāt.
units.tr: Demosthenes said: if life could be retraced, and two ways were set before him, one of which led rightly to the highest honours in the commonwealth, and the other rightly to death, he, having been warned of the dangers, would rather enter the way that leads to death than the one that leads to honours. Not unlike this is what Erasmus said: princes are wretched if they understand their evils, and more wretched if they do not understand them.

units.la: Septuaginta hebdomades significant aliquid peculiare, quia uniuersaliter septuagies septies est periodus usitata imperiorū. Uniuersaliter habetis mutationes regnorum circa annum 500.
units.tr: The seventy weeks signify something peculiar, because seventy times seven is the usual period of empires in general. In general, you have changes of kingdoms around the year 500.

units.la: Primus annus peregrinationis Abrahæ fuit 2023. Populus uerò egressus est ex Aegypto, et lex tradita est anno 2453. Ergo à peregrinatione Abrahæ ad exitum ex Aegypto, sunt anni 430.
units.tr: The first year of Abraham's pilgrimage was 2023. The people went out of Egypt, and the law was given, in 2453. Therefore from Abraham's pilgrimage to the exodus from Egypt there are 430 years.

units.la: Diluuium anno mundi 1656. Exitus ex Aegypto anno mundi 2453, ergo à diluuio ad exitum ex Aegypto, Aegypto anni 797. Circuncisio uerò instituta est anno mundi 2047. Ergo à diluuio usq; ad circunci sionem sunt anni 391.
units.tr: The Flood was in the year of the world 1656. The exodus from Egypt was in the year of the world 2453; therefore from the Flood to the exodus from Egypt there are 797 years. Circumcision was instituted in the year of the world 2047. Therefore from the Flood to circumcision there are 391 years.

units.la: Templum Hierosolymitanum ædificatum à Salomone anno 2933. Populus egressus ex Aegypto anno 245. Ergo ab exitu usque ad ædificationem templi à Salomone, anni 480.
units.tr: The temple at Jerusalem was built by Solomon in 2933. The people left Egypt in 2453. Therefore from the exodus to the building of the temple by Solomon there are 480 years.

units.la: Templum direptum est, & destructum à Nabuchodonosore anno 3336. conditū à Salomone 2933. Ergo à Salomone usq; ad Nabochodonosorē anni 442. & tot annos stetit templum Solomonis.
units.tr: The temple was plundered and destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar in 3336; it had been founded by Solomon in 2933. Therefore from Solomon to Nebuchadnezzar there are 442 years, and the temple of Solomon stood for that many years.

units.la: Templum instauratū est post captiuitatē Babylonicā anno 3446. Christus natus est anno 3962. Ergo ante natum Christū restitutum est templū annis 516. Hoc templum destruxit Herodes annis 16 ante Christum natum, & aliud ædificauit. Subtractis ergo annis 16, proueniunt præcisè anni 500, quibus templum post restitutionem durauit.
units.tr: The temple was restored after the Babylonian captivity in 3446. Christ was born in 3962. Therefore before Christ's birth the temple had been restored 516 years. Herod destroyed this temple 16 years before Christ's birth and built another. Subtracting those 16 years, there come to exactly 500 years, during which the temple lasted after its restoration.

units.la: Initium monarchiæ Persicæ fuit, quando Cyrus cœpit Babyloniā, anno mundi 3417. Græcorū uerò monarchia cœpit, quando Alexander uicit ultimum Darium, anno mundi 3634. Ergo duravit monarchia Persica 217 annos.
units.tr: The Persian monarchy began when Cyrus took Babylon, in the year of the world 3417. The Greek monarchy began when Alexander conquered the last Darius, in the year of the world 3634. Therefore the Persian monarchy lasted 217 years.

units.la: Initium Romanæ monarchiæ fuit, quando Iulius Cæsar factus est monarcha, anno 3917. Initium Græcæ monarchiæ, ut suprà anno 3634. Ergo duravit Græca monarchia tantum annos 283. Sic duæ monarchiæ, Persica & Græca, compleuerunt annos 500.
units.tr: The Roman monarchy began when Julius Caesar was made monarch, in 3917. The beginning of the Greek monarchy, as above, was in 3634. Therefore the Greek monarchy lasted only 283 years. Thus the two monarchies, Persian and Greek, together completed 500 years.

units.la: Troia capta est anno 2783. Initiū regni Romani cœpit à Romulo, anno 3211. Ergo à capta Troia, usq; ad regnum Romuli, anni sunt 428.
units.tr: Troy was taken in 2783. The beginning of the Roman kingdom, from Romulus, was in 3211. Therefore from the capture of Troy to the reign of Romulus there are 428 years.

units.la: Reges Romani expulsi sunt à Bruto & suis socijs, qui summam potestatem postea ad cōsules contulerunt, anno 3455. Iulius Cæsar ex aristocratia monarchiā fecit, anno 3917. Durauit ergo Consulum potestas annos 462.
units.tr: The Roman kings were expelled by Brutus and his companions, who afterwards transferred supreme power to the consuls, in 3455. Julius Caesar turned the aristocracy into a monarchy in 3917. Therefore the consular power lasted 462 years.

units.la: Initium monarchiæ Romanæ cœpit à Iulio Cæsare, anno 3917. ante Christum natum 451. qui addantur ad initium monarchiæ. Cœpit autem Italia uastari à Vandalis & Gothis, anno Christi 409. Ergo floruit monarchia Romana annos 454. Post illud tempus continuos 139 annos uastata est à Gothis & Vandalis.
units.tr: The beginning of the Roman monarchy, from Julius Caesar, was in 3917, which is 451 years before Christ's birth, and these must be added to the beginning of the monarchy. The Vandals and Goths began to lay waste Italy in the year of Christ 409. Therefore the Roman monarchy flourished for 454 years. After that time it was continuously laid waste for 139 years by the Goths and Vandals.

units.la: Constantinus sedem Imperatoriam transtulit Constantinopolim anno 312. Carolus Magnus rursus eandem trāstulit Romam anno Christi 801. Fuit ergo Constantinopolis Romanorum Imperatorū sedes annos 489.
units.tr: Constantine transferred the imperial seat to Constantinople in 312. Charles the Great again transferred it to Rome in the year of Christ 801. Therefore Constantinople was the seat of the Roman emperors for 489 years.

units.la: Constantinopolis capta à Turcis anno Christi 1453. desijt esse sedes Romani Imperij, anno Christi 801. Ergo post Carolum Magnum Constantinopolis fuit Græcorum Imperatorū sedes, annos 652.
units.tr: Constantinople was captured by the Turks in the year of Christ 1453. It ceased to be the seat of the Roman empire in the year of Christ 801. Therefore after Charles the Great, Constantinople was the seat of the Greek emperors for 652 years.

units.la: Orta Electorū imperij institutio ab Ottone Tertio, anno Christi 1002. nūc uerò agitur annus 1549. Ergo iam durauit annos 547.
units.tr: The institution of the electors of the empire arose from Otto III in the year of Christ 1002. Now the year 1549 is current. Therefore it has already lasted 547 years.

units.la: Initium gubernationis regum in populo Iudaico fuit anno mūdi 2850. Finis eiusdem gubernationis, anno captiuitatis Babylonicæ, incidit in annū 3355. Durauit ergo gubernatio regum annos 505.
units.tr: The beginning of the rule of kings over the Jewish people was in the year of the world 2850. The end of that rule, at the time of the Babylonian captivity, fell in the year 3355. Therefore the rule of kings lasted 505 years.

units.la: Populus redijt ex Babylone soluta captiuitate anno 3426. Herodes ex Idumæorum regum familia Iudæam occupauit, anno 3928. Ergo post captiuitatem præfuerunt populo Iudaico summi sacerdotes ex familia Leui annos 502. Postea trāslata est potestas ad peregrinos reges à Romanis constitutos, quorum primus fuit Herodes.
units.tr: The people returned from Babylon when the captivity was loosed, in 3426. Herod, of the family of the Idumaean kings, seized Judea in 3928. Therefore after the captivity, high priests of the family of Levi governed the Jewish people for 502 years. Afterwards the power was transferred to foreign kings, appointed by the Romans, of whom the first was Herod.

units.la: Ita sunt anni 500. ab exitu ex Ægypto ad regnū Salomonis, inde iterum ad destructionem factam à Nabochodonosor, & inde tot anni ad destructionem factam per Titū. sunt anni 500. A principio regni Vngarici & regni Polonici usq; ad nostrum illud tempus, sunt etiam circiter anni 500.
units.tr: So there are 500 years from the exodus from Egypt to the kingdom of Solomon, then again to the destruction wrought by Nebuchadnezzar, and then as many years to the destruction wrought by Titus: 500 years. From the beginning of the kingdom of Hungary and the kingdom of Poland down to our own time there are also about 500 years.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Seruitutem Capuæ prædicens.
units.tr: Predicting the enslavement of Capua.

units.la: Capuæ fuit uir nobilis, qui assumpsit habitū morionis, & cecinit fistula in plateis. Interrogatus quare id faceret, cum aliâs esset uir grauis & senator? respondit: Ego ante seruitutem uolo declarare me adhuc liberum esse. Sic prædixit illis tristem seruitutem, quæ non multò post secuta est.
units.tr: There was a noble man of Capua who put on the dress of a fool and played the pipe in the public squares. When asked why he did this, since he was otherwise a serious man and a senator, he replied: "Before the slavery I want to declare that I am still free." Thus he foretold to them a sad servitude, which not long afterwards followed.

units.la: Mutatio Imperiorum quando accidit.
units.tr: Change of empires: when it happens.

units.la: Quando numeri degenerant in sonos, id est, quando uirtus extinguitur, tunc etiā deficiunt magistratus & gentes: ut factū est sub Henrico Quarto, ubi cecidit imperium Germanicum.
units.tr: When numbers degenerate into sounds, that is, when virtue is extinguished, then magistracies and nations also fail, as happened under Henry IV, when the German empire fell.

units.la: Infinitæ calamitates Imperiorum.
units.tr: Endless calamities of empires.

units.la: Heydelbergæ in arce picti sunt principes Palatini (sicut & apud nos Vuitebergæ habentur imagines ducum Saxoniæ in arce) & ex ijs unus est habens gremium impletum pane, & appositam cucullam stulti. Propterea quod ille sibi in Palatinatu delegerat oppidum exiguum & amœnissimum, ubi erant uina optima, & poma sapidissima, aliarumq; frugum præstantia & abundantia, ac uitam tranquillam prætulerat Reipub. & gubernationi: adeò ut reliquam suam hæreditatem fratri suo dono daret: cum tamen ille longè fuerit felicior, & sapientior cæteris omnibus, quæres mediocritatem. Et multo suauius uixit fratre, siquidem Imperiorū infinitæ sunt miseriæ.
units.tr: At Heidelberg, in the castle, the Palatine princes are painted (just as at Wittenberg in our own castle there are portraits of the dukes of Saxony). One of them has a lap filled with bread and a fool's cap set beside him. This is because he had chosen for himself a small and most pleasant town in the Palatinate, where the wines were excellent, the fruits most savoury, and other crops outstanding and abundant, and he preferred a quiet life to the commonwealth and its government, so much so that he gave the rest of his inheritance to his brother as a gift. Yet the brother was far happier and wiser than all the others, as one would expect of a man who seeks moderation. And he lived much more pleasantly than his brother, since the miseries of empires are endless.

units.la: Capnio de mutatione Imperiorum.
units.tr: Capnio on the change of empires.

units.la: Quando duplicantur lateres, tunc uenit Moyses: id est, cum onera sunt nimis grauia, tunc mutantur Imperia, & ueniunt pœnæ.
units.tr: When bricks are doubled, then Moses comes: that is, when burdens become too heavy, then empires change and punishments arrive.

units.la: Antiquus est uersus in Oraculis, uidelicet: αὐτὸς, καὶ ϖαῖδες, καὶ ϖαίδῳ ἢν ἔτι ϖαῖδες. id est: Ipse, & filij, filiorum uero filij non amplius.
units.tr: There is an ancient verse in the Oracles, namely: Himself, and sons, and of sons' sons no more [αὐτὸς, καὶ παῖδες, καὶ παίδων ἦν ἔτι παῖδες]. That is: himself, and his sons, and the sons of his sons no longer.

units.la: Sic Constantinus pater regnauit, et post eũ Con- stantinus filius. Post Constantinum uero, nullus ex illa familia relictus est.
units.tr: So Constantine the father reigned, and after him Constantine the son. After Constantine, however, none of that family was left.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Vetus legitur Sibyllæ oraculũ de Athenis, duas ei pestes exitio futuras, fraudes & ignauiam ducũ. Sed si communem hominum uitam et interitus re- gnorum considéremus, non tantũ Athenis, sed etiã omnib. urbibus ac imperijs Sibylla est uaticinata.
units.tr: There is an old oracle of the Sibyl about Athens, that two plagues would bring about its ruin: the frauds and the cowardice of its leaders. But if we consider the common life of men and the ruin of kingdoms, the Sibyl prophesied not only about Athens but about all cities and empires.

units.la: Rudolfus cùm esset Imperator, neglexit Italiã, eo quòd propter paupertatem timeret se non pos- se eam amplius recuperare. Sic Imperij fines defe- cerũt. Tempore Friderici Barbarossæ habuit hoc imperium ad minimum ex reditibus, qui fuerunt proprij Imperij, uiginti tonnas auri: ad quas Ger- mania parum admodum contulit, sed maximã par- tem pepedit Italia. Hæc mihi dixit Peutingerus Au- gustanus, qui fuit consiliarius Maximiliani. Postea mox illi census diminuti sunt. Tempore uero Ru- dolfi penè omnino nobis perierunt.
units.tr: Rudolf, when he was emperor, neglected Italy, because on account of his poverty he feared he would not be able to recover it again. So the borders of the empire shrank. In the time of Frederick Barbarossa this empire had, from the revenues that belonged to the imperial estate, at least twenty tons of gold. Germany contributed very little to these, but Italy paid the greater part. Peutinger of Augsburg, who was a counsellor to Maximilian, told me this. Soon afterwards those revenues were reduced. In the time of Rudolf, however, they had almost entirely been lost to us.

units.la: GVBERNATIO POLITICA, & Consilia in eadem utilia.
units.tr: Political government, and useful counsels concerning it.

units.la: Duo genera sunt aulicorum seu politicorum ho- minum. Alij habent practicã sine doctrina, qui pulchrum putant in negocijs certare ingeniorum acu
units.tr: There are two kinds of courtly or political men. Some have practical skill without learning, and think it a fine thing to contend in affairs with the keenness of their wits.

units.tr: Others are learned, remaining within the limits of their calling,

units.la: cationis, non ludentes ingenio, sed habentes leges
units.tr: not playing with their wit, but keeping to the rules

units.la: suorum consiliorū terminos. Hoc est rectius & sa-
units.tr: and boundaries of their counsels. This is the more correct and

units.la: lubrius. Sic etiam in Theologia, aliqui sunt facun-
units.tr: wholesome course. So also in theology: some are

units.la: di & loquaces, qui non referunt ad metas suas ora-
units.tr: fluent and talkative, and do not refer their speeches

units.tr: to their proper limits. Others, however, are less eloquent and

units.la: qui referūt suas orationes ad certas propositiones,
units.tr: fluent, and they refer their speeches

units.la: quod est utilius.
units.tr: to certain propositions, which is more useful.

units.la: Donatio speculi aulici.
units.tr: The gift of the courtly mirror.

units.la: Est in Ecloga Petrarchæ narratio de pastore in
units.tr: In Petrarch's Eclogue there is an account of a shepherd coming

units.la: aulam ueniēte, cui cum donaretur speculū, illudq;
units.tr: into the court, to whom, when a mirror was given and he looked into it,

units.la: inspiceret, incœpit amare uirgines aulicas: sed ma-
units.tr: he began to love the court maidens; but, roughly handled

units.la: lè ob id tractatus, et deiectus per gradus, ibi in hæc
units.tr: on that account and thrown down the steps, he broke out there into these

units.la: uerba prorupit:
units.tr: words, in verse:

units.la: Aeternum gemit ille miser, pastoribus aulæ
units.tr: That wretch groans for ever, the first to give the courtly shepherds

units.la: Qui primus mala dona dedit, &c.
units.tr: the evil gift, &c.

units.la: Voluit significare, quod illud speculum fuisset
units.tr: He meant to signify that the mirror was an evil gift to the shepherd,

units.la: pastori, id est, nouo aulico malum donum. Sic no-
units.tr: that is, to the new courtier. So, for courtly vices, that courtly mirror,

units.la: uitijs aulicis speculum illud aulicum, id est, admira-
units.tr: that is, the admiration of one's own wisdom, learning and the

units.la: tio propriæ suæ sapientiæ, doctrinæ ac aliarum do
units.tr: doctrines of others, is a deadly gift.

units.la: tum, est exitiosum donum.
units.tr: It is a deadly gift.

units.la: Episcopus Saltzburgensis, Lanio dictus, interro-gauit Hispanum quendā in aula Imperatoris Ma-ximiliani, inquiens: Domine, quomodo placet tibi administratio & constitutio aulæ nostri Imperato-ris? Ille respondit: Quantum animaduerto, centum sunt præcipui uiri, per quos administrantur negocia Reipublicæ: Sed inter illos uix sunt quinq; aut octo, qui promouent negocia: cæteri omnes tantùm impediunt.
units.tr: The Bishop of Salzburg, called Lanio, asked a certain Spaniard at the court of the Emperor Maximilian: "Sir, how do you like the administration and constitution of our Emperor's court?" He replied: "As far as I observe, there are a hundred principal men through whom the affairs of the commonwealth are managed. But among them there are scarcely five or eight who advance the business; all the rest merely hinder it."

units.la: In aulis maximus est labor Cancellariæ, sicut dixit Dux Saxoniæ Fridericus: Cācellariam esse cor Principis.
units.tr: In courts the chancery has the greatest labour, as Duke Frederick of Saxony said: the chancery is the heart of the prince.

units.la: Aulici uersus.
units.tr: Courtiers' verses.

units.la: Non mihi sit seruus medicus, propheta, sacerdos.
units.tr: Let me not have a physician, a prophet or a priest as my servant.

units.la: Non mihi sit seruus medicus: id est, non uolo talem habere, qui moderatam uictus rationem præscribat, aut temperantiā ac sobrietatem præcipiat: sed uolo comedere cibos, & bibere potus, quibus delector. Deinde, non sit mihi seruus propheta: id est, talis consiliarius, qui me in periculosis casibus adhortetur. Vltimò, non uolo ut mihi seruiat sacerdos: id est, qui ex uerbo Dei mea peccata arguat, et indicet mihi quòd contra uerbum Dei uiuam.
units.tr: Let me not have a physician as servant: that is, I do not want one who prescribes a moderate rule of diet, or enjoins temperance and sobriety; I want to eat the foods and drink the drinks that please me. Next, let me not have a prophet as servant: that is, a counsellor who urges me on in dangerous cases. Last, I do not want a priest to serve me: that is, one who from the Word of God rebukes my sins and shows me that I live contrary to the Word of God.

units.la: Alius.
units.tr: Another.

units.la: Da, capias, quæras, plurima, pauca, nihil.
units.tr: Give much, take little, ask for nothing.

units.la: id est, da plurima, capias pauca, quæras nihil: id est, non scisciteris. (sum Ouidij:
units.tr: That is: give much, take little, ask nothing; that is, do not make inquiries. (From Ovid:

units.la: Aulicæ beneuolentiæ raro durabiles, iuxta uerOmnia uertuntur, certè uertuntur amores.
