units.tr: Courtly goodwill seldom lasts. As the verse has it, "All things change; loves surely change."

units.la: Huic respondent Germanica prouerbia: Lieber kittel reiß nicht, Herren dienst erbet nicht. Quidam bonus uir, amicus noster, ex aula scripsit ad nos:
units.tr: The German proverbs answer to this: "A good coat does not tear, but a lord's service is not inherited." A certain good man, our friend, wrote to us from the court:

units.la: O me caula prius, quàm nutriet aula, Poetam.
units.tr: O, let the cottage nourish me as a poet before the court does.

units.la: Archelaus ad Euripidem:
units.tr: Archelaus to Euripides:

units.la: σὺ μὲν ἄξιος λαβεῖν, σὺ ᾗ ἄξιος αἰτεῖν.
units.tr: You are worthy to receive, you are worthy to ask [σὺ μὲν ἄξιος λαβεῖν, σὺ δ᾽ ἄξιος αἰτεῖν].

units.la: Fertur Germanico prouerbio: Lang zû hof lâg zû hell. Id sic sapientes interpretantur: multum est miseriarum, dolorum et anxietatum in hac uita, ac praecipuè in aulis & gubernatione.
units.tr: There is a German proverb: "Long at court, long in hell." Wise men interpret it thus: there is much wretchedness, pain and anxiety in this life, and especially at court and in government.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: Collections.

units.la: Demades, cùm ei obijceretur inconstantia in republica, respondit: Nunquam uobis contraria, mihi sæpè contraria dixi. Est sapiens responsum. noluit enim dicere: Quandoquidem tempora mutantur in republica, fieri non potest ut idem semper dicamus, sed idem semper spectemus.
units.tr: When Demades was charged with inconsistency in public affairs, he replied: "I have never said contrary things to you, but I have often said them to myself." It is a wise answer. For he did not mean to say: since the times change in the commonwealth, we cannot always say the same things, but we must always look to the same ends.

units.la: Iurisconsultorum dictum de donis: Neq; omnia sunt accipienda, neq; semper, neq; ab omnibus. Citatur in digestis Græcè: ὃΔΙ ΠΑΝΤΑ, ὃΔΙΣ ΩΑΥΤΟ ΤΕ, ὃΔΙΣ ΩΑΡΑ ΩΑΥΤΩΝ. Certè multum refert in aulis, intelligere quid accipere, quid petere liceat: multo minus omnia, omni tempore, & ab omnibus petenda.
units.tr: A saying of the jurists about gifts: not everything is to be accepted, nor at all times, nor from everyone. It is cited in the Digest in Greek: [οὐ πάντα, οὐδὲ πάντοτε, οὐδὲ παρὰ πάντων]. Certainly at court it matters greatly to understand what it is lawful to accept and to ask for; much less is everything to be sought at every time and from everyone.

units.la: Dux Saxoniæ Fridericus princeps sapientissimus fuit, curam administrationis solus habuit, nec omnia quæstoribus & curatoribus commisit, sed dixit: Quandiu ego uixero, ipse in mea ditione uolo esse quæstor & procurator. Quod ut commo-dius exequeretur, solitus est, quotiescunq; apud ali-quem suorum procuratorum diuertisset, statim suâ symbolam soluere, ne postea in ratione reddenda ulla fraude uti possent.
units.tr: Frederick, Duke of Saxony, was a most wise prince. He kept the care of administration to himself alone, and did not entrust everything to treasurers and overseers, but said: "As long as I live, I want to be the treasurer and steward in my own domain myself." To carry this out more conveniently, whenever he had lodged with any of his stewards, he was accustomed to pay his reckoning at once, so that afterwards they could not use any fraud in rendering their accounts.

units.la: Aristophanes lepida antonomasia lusit in quæ-stores, quod etiâ Plutarchus citat, ταμίαι λαμίαι, id est, quæstores bubones. Allusit ad nomen simile (sicuti appellarunt Tyberium, Biberium: & Erasmus Eccium nominauit Ieccium) iuxta pro-uerbium Germanicũ: Es ist kein emptlein so klei-ne, es ist henckens werdt.
units.tr: Aristophanes played with a witty antonomasia on the treasurers, which Plutarch also cites: [ταμίαι λαμίαι], that is, the treasurers are owls. He alluded to a similar name, just as they called Tiberius "Biberius," and Erasmus named Eck "Ieckius," following the German proverb: "There is no vessel so small that it is not worth hanging up."

units.la: Quando Solon iuit ad Croesum, dicitur interro-gasse Aesopũ, qui tunc fuit apud Croesum, quomo-do deberet loqui cum rege? Respondit ei Aesopus: Aut quàm minima, aut quàm dulcissima.
units.tr: When Solon went to Croesus, he is said to have asked Aesop, who was then at Croesus' court, how he ought to speak with the king. Aesop replied: "Either as briefly as possible, or as pleasantly as possible."

units.la: Salse & acutè dictum est à Cancellario Ducis Vuirtenbergensis Georgio Lamprecht (qui postea factus est consiliarius Imperatoris Caroli Quinti, cum cuius filio mihi fuit dulcis familiaritas) Opor-tere quemlibet principem habere fatuũ, quem ipse exerceat: & uicissim alium, à quo ipse exerceatur.
units.tr: A witty and sharp saying was made by the chancellor of the Duke of Württemberg, Georg Lamprecht (who later became a councillor to Emperor Charles V, and with whose son I had a pleasant friendship): every prince ought to have a fool whom he may exercise, and in turn another by whom he himself may be exercised.

units.la: Quidã prudens uir ex equestri familia, in aula Vuirtenbergensi, agnatus Ducis, habebat canem, ipsum comitantem ad consilium: qui aliquādo ma-lè acceptus à molossis arcis, memor istius iniuriæ, postea Dominum abeũtem in arcem comitatus est ufq; ad aditum arcis, & deinde domum recurrit. At nobilis ille: Canis meus me multo prudëtior est, inquit: nam cum semel malè mulctatus sit in aula, nõ uult redire eò: Ego qui toties plagas accepi ibi, tamen illuc indies redeo.
units.tr: A certain prudent man of the equestrian family, at the court of Württemberg, a kinsman of the duke, had a dog that accompanied him to council. Once, roughly handled by the mastiffs of the castle, the dog remembered that injury; afterwards, when his master went to the castle, it escorted him as far as the castle gate and then ran home. The nobleman said: "My dog is much wiser than I am. For since he was once badly mauled at court, he does not want to go back there. I, who have received so many blows there, still return there every day."

units.la: Negocia proposita sunt perficienda.
units.tr: Proposed business is to be carried through.

units.la: Qui binos lepores una sectabitur hora,Vno quandoq;, quandoq; carebit utroq;.
units.tr: He who chases two hares in one hour will at some time catch one, and at some time lack both.

units.la: Aulicum dictum est, admonens quòd negocia instituta sint urgenda, & non differenda seu distra henda. Datur vitio gubernatoribus, qui instituta negocia nõ perficiũt, & motis reb. incipiũt nouas.
units.tr: This is a courtly saying, reminding us that begun business should be pressed forward, and not deferred or distracted. It is a fault charged against rulers who do not carry through the business they have begun, and, once matters have been stirred up, start new ones.

units.la: Antequam uentum est ad solennem electionem Caroli V. Imperatoris, omnes Electores iurauerũt se non processuros ad electionem solennem, priusquàm omnes consensissent in unum. Et fuit hoc ducis Saxoniæ Friderici consilium (quia illa magna difficultate agebantur) & priusquam irent ad ultimam suffragationẽ, singuli darent literas sui suffragij. Ita facta est concors electio Caroli Quinti.
units.tr: Before the solemn election of Emperor Charles V, all the electors swore that they would not proceed to the solemn election until they had all agreed on one man. This was the counsel of Duke Frederick of Saxony, because the matter was being handled with great difficulty; and before they went to the final vote, each elector was to hand over a written letter of his suffrage. Thus the unanimous election of Charles V was made.

units.la: Dux Palatinus in conuentu Francosordiensi, de Imperatore Carolo Quinto dixit: Ah, illustres domini, cauete uobis ab hac aquila, quæ cũ semel mihi tantum uolauerit in culmĩ, ad hoc usq; tempus nondum damnum resarcire potui, ita ut nunquam eius obliuiscar.
units.tr: At the Frankfurt assembly the Count Palatine said of Emperor Charles V: "Ah, illustrious lords, beware of this eagle. Once it has flown at me so high, I have not been able until now to make good the loss, and so I shall never forget it."

units.la: Cum essent deliberationes de eligendo Imperatore, tore, & quidam illam summam Imperij gubernationem deferrent ad ducem Fridericum, dux Fridericus honestissimè se excusauit: ac cùm pleraq; alia, tum ætatem non utilem esse imperio affirmauit. Nam paulo post alium eligendum esse, & crebras illas mutationes multa afferre incommoda imperio.
units.tr: When there were deliberations about electing an emperor, and some proposed handing the supreme government of the empire to Duke Frederick, Duke Frederick most courteously excused himself, and among many other reasons he affirmed that his age was not useful to the empire. For shortly afterwards another would have to be elected, and such frequent changes bring many disadvantages to the empire.

units.la: Aristoteles proponit præceptum Poetæ, tuendum his qui populo concionantur in ciuitatibus: μή μοι τὰ ὑροτητὰ λέγε, ἀλλ᾽ ὢν πόλει δεῖ: Non mihi plausibilia dicas, sed quibus est opus ciuitati.
units.tr: Aristotle gives the poet's precept for those who address the people in cities: Do not tell me pleasing things, but what the city needs [μή μοι τὰ ἡδέα λέγε, ἀλλ᾽ ὧν πόλει δεῖ].

units.la: Demosthenes grauis orator, cùm Philippus Macedo ea conditione cum Atheniensibus fœdus facturus esset, ut illi oratores sibi dederent, qui perpetuis concionibus animos ciuium aduersus se exacerbarent: imiquissimam reipublicæ conditionem festiuo quodam apologo dissuasit, quanquam ab ea non ita multum plebs diutino bello uexata abhorreret. Nā cùm docere uellet, in hoc postulari oratores, ut urbs destitueretur oratorū præsidio: mira luce & perspicuitate Macedonis consiliū ante oculos multitudinis posuit, hoc cōmento: Lupos quondam cùm pastoribus esse pactos, nihil se posthac hostile caulis illaturos esse, si sibi canes dederentur. placuit stultis pastoribus conditio, canesq; dediti sunt. Proinde cum lupi uiderent excubias caularū sublatas esse, liberè grassari in gregem coepère. Hac fabula docuit, quanti referret Reipublicæ servare Oratores. Tantisper enim dum hoc consilium valuit, servata est Respublica.
units.tr: Demosthenes, the grave orator, when Philip of Macedon was about to make a treaty with the Athenians on the condition that they hand over those orators who, by constant speeches, stirred up the minds of the citizens against him, dissuaded them from this most unjust condition for the commonwealth by a playful fable, although the common people, worn down by a long war, did not much shrink from it. For when he wanted to show that the demand was that the city be deprived of the protection of its orators, he set the Macedonian's plan before the eyes of the crowd with remarkable clarity, by this contrivance: once wolves made a pact with the shepherds that they would do nothing hostile to the sheepfolds if the dogs were given to them. The foolish shepherds liked the condition, and the dogs were handed over. Accordingly, when the wolves saw the guards of the sheepfolds removed, they began to rage freely against the flock. By this fable he taught how much it mattered to the commonwealth to keep its orators. For as long as this counsel prevailed, the commonwealth was preserved.

units.la: Noster Imperator Carolus Quintus nō subscribebat, nisi prius negocium cognosceret. Quare si quādo vehementer ægrotaret, iubebat differri subscriptiones. Rogauerūt eum aliquādo decumbentē consiliarij, ut pateretur aliū subscribere, qui posset eius manum effingere. Respōdit: Non assuefaciatis ad illud quenquam, ego ipse subscribam.
units.tr: Our Emperor Charles V did not sign anything unless he first knew the business. So if he was seriously ill, he ordered the signing to be postponed. Once, when he lay sick, his counsellors asked him to allow someone else to sign who could copy his hand. He replied: "Do not accustom anyone to that; I will sign myself."

units.la: Contrarium exemplum huic est Imperatoris Arcadij, qui nimis levis fuit in subscribendo. Hanc levitatem animadvertens soror Arcadij, scripsit literas nomine alicuius servi, ut daret sororem servo. Imperator non legēs literas, subscripsit statim. Postea vero venit soror, & expostulat cū eo, quòd eam dare vellet illi nebuloni. Respōdit Imperator: Nequaquam. At illa conuicit ipsum sua manu. Ita hortata est eum, ut vitaret illam levitatem in subscribendo & largiendo, non perlectis prius literis.
units.tr: The opposite example is that of the Emperor Arcadius, who was far too careless in signing. His sister, noticing this levity, wrote letters in the name of some servant asking that he give his sister to the servant. The emperor, without reading the letters, signed at once. Afterwards the sister came and remonstrated with him, because he had wanted to give her to that scoundrel. The emperor replied: "By no means." But she reproached him with his own hand. Thus she urged him to avoid that levity in signing and bestowing without first reading letters through.

units.la: Anni sunt circiter septuaginta, aut octoginta, quando duo potentissimi reges, rex Matthias Hungaricus, & Casimirus rex Polonicus, certauerunt de Silesia, ambo volentes ad se pertrahere Silesiam, & similiter Bohemiam, si bellum processisset. Ibi Electores & principes Germaniæ, in primis Ernestus Elector, auus Ioannis Friderici Electoris nuper mortui, & Ioannes Marchio, iam uiuentis Marchionis & Electoris Ioachimi proauus, uidentes illos motus, præterea uicinitatem tam potentũ regũ fore toti Germaniæ perniciosam: collegerunt exercitum sexcentorum equitum, adiunctis aliorũ Principum copijs, & obuiam ueniunt illis duobus regibus Vratislauiæ. Rex Hungariæ urbem Vratislauiã iam occupauerat, & rex Polonicus extra urbem sua castra locauerat. Ita res erat disposita, ut utrorumq; regum potentia Germaniæ esset metuenda, quoquo modo res procederet. Venerunt igitur Principes, & proposuerunt illis duobus potentissimis regibus pacis conditiones, ita ut se promitterent adiuturos esse illum, qui has conditiones pacis reciperet: & contra illum dimicaturos, qui eas recipere nollet. Casimirus igitur rex Polonicus, qui erat pacis cupidissimus, & alioqui placidus, eas conditiones recipit. Matthias uero paulo inquietior, tardius conditionibus à Principibus propositis assentitur. Ibi causam illam Marchio Ioannes Elector, sapiens & eloquens princeps, aliquot horas dixit, inspectantibus & audientibus illis tribus exercitibus, tanta eloquentia, ut iudicatũ sit à sapientibus, nullius fuisse tantam eloquetiam, qui coram tot regibus & principibus potuisset illã causam explicare. Ita tali coniunctione & concor-dia Principum pacata est Germania, & utrque rex discesit. Haec narratio nusquam est in ueteribus historiographis scripta, sed tantum audita ex Ioanne Electore, et duce Saxoniae, patre Friderici, qui unà cum parente Ernesto in illa expeditione fuit.
units.tr: About seventy or eighty years ago, when two most powerful kings, King Matthias of Hungary and King Casimir of Poland, contended over Silesia, both wishing to draw Silesia to themselves, and likewise Bohemia, should the war go on. There the electors and princes of Germany, especially Elector Ernest, grandfather of the recently deceased Elector John Frederick, and Margrave John, great-grandfather of the still living Margrave and Elector Joachim, seeing these movements, and also that the proximity of such powerful kings would be ruinous to all Germany, gathered an army of six hundred horsemen, joined with the forces of other princes, and went to meet the two kings at Breslau. The King of Hungary had already occupied the city of Breslau, and the King of Poland had pitched his camp outside the city. Matters were so arranged that whichever way things went, the power of either king would be feared by Germany. So the princes came and proposed to the two most powerful kings terms of peace: they would promise to aid whichever king accepted these terms, and to fight against whichever refused them. Casimir, King of Poland, who was most eager for peace and otherwise mild, accepted the terms. Matthias, somewhat more restless, assented to the conditions proposed by the princes more slowly. There Margrave John, the Elector, a wise and eloquent prince, spoke on the case for some hours, while those three armies watched and listened, with such eloquence that the wise judged no one could have explained that case so well before so many kings and princes. Thus Germany was pacified by such a union and concord of the princes, and both kings departed. This story is nowhere written in the ancient historians, but was only heard from Elector John, Duke of Saxony, father of Frederick, who was with his father Ernest on that expedition.

units.la: Recitabo uobis narrationem cuiusdam doctoris Tubingesis, uiri praestantis. Hic in legatione quadam cum aliis duobus fuit, quorum unus eques auratus, alter senex miles eques erat (mihi bene notus) nomine Speter. In itinere autem eques ille auratus coepit disputare de mutando decreto commissso, & utile esse aliquando decreta mutari de graui consilio. Doctor dixit: Et ego cogitabam. Ille prior dixit: Iam tuum erit etiam aliquid addere (ut semper primae partes in consilijs principum, sunt Equitum auratorum) & contrariam sententiam coepit defendere: & quaedam etiam confirmauit, pro ut potuit. Cum autem uentum esset ad tertium, senem illum equitem, hic dixit: O Domini, audiui uos disputates diu de commisso decreto nostri Principis. Noster Princeps habet in sua aula tres gradus consiliariorum. Primus est Cancellarij, qui erat homo magnae autoritatis, doctus, & iam senex, Lamprecht uocatus. Secundus est eorum, quos nominant die Landschreiber, quorum no est ita magna autoritas. Postremus est consiliariorum, in quo nos sumus.
units.tr: I will recite to you an account from a certain doctor of Tübingen, an outstanding man. He was on an embassy with two others, one of whom was a knight of the golden spur, and the other an old soldier and knight named Speter, whom I knew well. On the journey, the knight of the golden spur began to argue about changing the decree entrusted to them, saying that it is sometimes useful to change decrees made after serious deliberation. The doctor said: "I was thinking the same." The first knight replied: "Now it will be your turn to add something too, since the leading role in princes' councils always belongs to the knights of the golden spur." He then began to defend the opposite opinion and also confirmed some points as well as he could. But when it came to the third, the old knight, he spoke: "Gentlemen, I have heard you arguing at length about the decree entrusted to us by our prince. Our prince has three grades of councillors in his court. The first is the chancellor, a man of great authority, learned and already old, named Lamprecht. The second is of those they call the Landschreiber, whose authority is not so great. The last is of the councillors, and to that grade we belong."

units.la: Hi omnes re bene deliberata, et approbante quoq; principe, nobis hanc legationē demandarūt. Quare eam exequamur, nec quicquam immutemus. Sic illi acquieuerunt illius sententiæ.
units.tr: All these men, after the matter had been well deliberated and with the prince also approving, entrusted us with this embassy. Therefore let us carry it out and change nothing. In this way they agreed with his opinion.

units.la: Pontanus scribit de duobus regibus, quorum diuersa fuit consuetudo, de rege Ferdinando, & filio eius Alfonso. Pater Ferdinandus consueuit legatis dicere: Mando uobis, ut hoc negocium rectè administretis: & do uobis potestatem mutandi decreti, sicut uidebitur.
units.tr: Pontanus writes about two kings whose customs differed: King Ferdinand and his son Alfonso. The father Ferdinand used to say to his envoys: "I charge you to carry out this business properly, and I give you the power to change the decree as you see fit."

units.la: Filius Alfonsus, forsan uidens aliquid inesse huic rei incommodi, contrariū seruauit, & res deliberatas committens legatis dixit: Mando uobis negocium, & prohibeo ne quicquam in hoc decreto mutetis.
units.tr: His son Alfonso, perhaps seeing some disadvantage in the matter, took the opposite course. Entrusting the settled decision to his envoys, he said: "I entrust the business to you, and I forbid you to change anything in this decree."

units.la: Dominus de Breitenbach, consiliarius Ducis Georgij, cum esset in legatione comissa sibi à principe, uidensq; quædam male deliberata, ac melius consiliū inueniret: relicto facto decreto, rem suo arbitratu gessit. Postquā aūt rediret ad ducem Georgium, & narraret ei quomodo expediuisset negocium, & decretū mutasset: Princeps diu siletit tacitus, toruo multu illū intuēs. & tandē dixit: Domine Doctor, rectè effecisti negocium, sed nō sicut erat imperatum. Vide, ne posthac idem facias.
units.tr: Lord von Breitenbach, a counsellor of Duke George, was on an embassy entrusted to him by his prince. Seeing that some matters had been badly decided and finding a better plan, he set aside the decree and conducted the business by his own judgment. When he returned to Duke George and told him how he had carried out the business and changed the decree, the prince sat silent for a long time, gazing at him fiercely. At last he said: "Doctor, you have carried out the business well, but not as you were ordered. See that you do not do the same again."

units.la: Palatinus Victoriosus dictus, qui ante annos sexaginta uixit, uenit aliquādo in Senatū suum, quē habebat electū ex optima & florentissima nobilitate: & proponit, se moturū bellū cōtra Episcopū Moguntinū: & petere, ut ipsi de modo copiarum equestriū & pedestriū ac commeatu deliberarent. Consiliarij respondēt: Rem esse magnā, de qua consilium peteret. & orant, ut ipsis tempus deliberandi cōcedat. Princeps cōcedit eis octiduum ad colloquendum inter se, & cōferendum de illo negocio. Elapso uero octiduo, redeunt ad principem. & maximus natu, uel qui primas inter eos tenebat, dissuadet bellum Principi longa, & quidē graui oratione. Quem Princeps placidē audit: & quærit deinde, quæ sit aliorum sententia? At ille qui aliorū nomine iam dixerat, respondit, eandē omniū esse sententiam: & sibi commissum esse, ut omnium nomine loqueretur. Ibi subiratus Princeps dixit, Se etiamsi nouerit eorum uoluntates, & sciat ipsos ea bono animo dicere, tamen hoc non quæsiuisse ex eis an esset mouendum bellum, sed quomodo esset gerendum: & se ea quæstione nolle onerare eorum conscientias. sibi enim commissum esse, ut inferat bellum, uel non: & suum maximum periculum esse, si motum fuerit ipsos, si ex territorio suo expellerentur, posse inuenire alium dominum: se uero, si semel expelleretur ex suo territorio, non posse inuenire aliud territorium. Hæc ab homine sapiente & graui, sapiens uox est. Multa autem ille optimus princeps præclarè & feliciter gessit.
units.tr: The Palatine called "the Victorious," who lived some sixty years ago, once came into his senate, which he had chosen from the best and most distinguished nobility. He announced that he would make war on the Bishop of Mainz, and asked them to deliberate with him about the size of the cavalry and infantry forces and the supplies. The counsellors replied that the matter was important and asked for time to deliberate. The prince granted them eight days to confer among themselves about the business. When the eight days had passed, they returned to the prince, and the eldest, or the one who held first place among them, argued at length and with considerable seriousness against the war. The prince listened calmly and then asked what the opinion of the others was. The man who had already spoken on their behalf replied that all of them shared the same view and that he had been entrusted to speak in the name of all. The prince, provoked, said that even if he knew their wishes, and even if he knew they spoke in good faith, he had not asked them whether war should be undertaken, but how it should be waged. He did not want to burden their consciences with that question: it was his to decide whether to make war or not. If he were to go to war and be driven from his territory, they could find another lord; but if he were once expelled from his territory, he could not find another territory. These are wise and serious words from a sensible man. That excellent prince, however, achieved much, and achieved it brilliantly and successfully.

units.la: Noster Imperator Carolus Quintus ultra quatuor aut quinq; non uocat ad consilium, quorum quemq; iubet suam sententiam dicere. Postea animaduertit quæ sint præcipuæ, & de una ac altera sententia disputat: & non statim concludit, sed differt in aliud tempus. Postea (inquiens) plura colloquemur de hoc negocio.
units.tr: Our Emperor Charles V did not summon more than four or five to his council, and he ordered each of them to state his opinion. Afterwards he noted which points were most important and debated one or two of the opinions, and he did not conclude at once but put the matter off to another time. Afterwards, he said, "We shall talk more about this business."

units.la: Audiui Pontificem Paulum Tertium, sapientem uirum, cum haberet consilia cum Cardinalibus, interrogasse primùm iuniores Cardinales, qui hac de causa semper instructiores accesserunt, quàm aliàs fieret. Illos cùm audiuisset, postea audiuit Senensem Cardinalem Genutiũ, & cum illo disputauit: Imò, inquiens, probo meam sententiam propter hãc & hanc causam. Sederunt cæteri Cardinales audientes illorum duorum præstãtium uirorum cum magna admiratione consilia & disputationes.
units.tr: I have heard that Pope Paul III, a wise man, when he held consultations with the cardinals, first asked the younger cardinals, who for this reason always came better prepared than usual. After he had heard them, he then heard the Sienese cardinal Genuzzi, and debated with him: "Indeed," he said, "I approve my opinion for this reason and that reason." The other cardinals sat listening with great admiration to the counsels and debates of these two distinguished men.

units.la: Norinbergenses habent Senatum Iurisconsultorum, & ante quàm quæstionem proferunt, audiut prius Iurisconsultos: & si est ecclesiastica cõtrouersia, tunc audiunt prius Theologos. Principes Saxoniæ habent admodum pulchrum iudicium, ubi sedent nobiles & doctores.
units.tr: The people of Nuremberg have a senate of jurists, and before they bring a question forward, they first hear the jurists; and if it is an ecclesiastical controversy, then they first hear the theologians. The princes of Saxony have a very fine court, where nobles and doctors sit.

units.la: Ebnerus senator Norinbergensis, uir admodũ bonus, cum hærere uideret consilia ob difficultatẽ gubergubernationis, dicebat: Ich heiß Ebner, aber ich kans nicht alles eben machen. iuxta prouerbium: Non semper feriet, quod minabitur arcus. Non enim semper euentus respondet consilijs.
units.tr: Ebner, a senator of Nuremberg, a very good man, when he saw counsels stuck because of the difficulty of governing, used to say: "I'm called Ebner, but I can't make everything come out right." This accords with the proverb: "The bow does not always hit what it threatens." For the outcome does not always match the counsels.

units.la: In Gallia est talis consuetudo, ut bona feudalia, quæ sunt regis, non transferantur ad hæredes: patre mortuo non succedit filius, sed feudum ex arbitrio regis transfertur ad alium. Credo Constantinum hunc morem introduxisse, ut feuda in familijs conseruarentur, ut ea re sibi deuinciret milites fortes. Constantinus mirabiles mutationes fecit in Imperio, mutauit religiones, &c. Item hunc morem de feudis instituit, quod fuit sapiens consilium, & diuinum opus. In Turcia etiam expelluntur ex bonis feudalibus hæredes, & alij substituuntur: ut si qui uasalli etiam in acie occumbant (sicut solent etiam in uno prælio aliquot centum militum occidi) tunc corum liberi & coniuges eijciuntur ex bonis feudalibus, et alij in illorum bona substituuntur.
units.tr: In France there is a custom that feudal estates belonging to the king do not pass to heirs: when the father dies, the son does not succeed, but the fief is transferred to another at the king's discretion. I believe Constantine introduced this custom so that fiefs would be kept within families, and so bind strong soldiers to himself by this means. Constantine made remarkable changes in the empire, changing religions and so on. He also established this custom concerning fiefs, which was a wise counsel and a divine work. Among the Turks too, heirs are expelled from feudal estates and others are substituted; so that if any vassals fall even in battle (as it often happens that some hundreds of soldiers are killed in a single battle), then their children and wives are cast out of the feudal estates, and others are put in their goods.

units.la: DE IVRE ET LEGIBUS.
units.tr: DE IVRE ET LEGIBUS.

units.la: Disputatio de summo iure præbet occasionem maioribus tumultibus: non enim possunt omnia in integrum restitui. Vt cum summa imperia semel corruunt, tunc nunquam restituuntur in pristinum statum: ut si quis currum ouorum prosternat, non potest omnia oua sine damno recolligere. Domini autem, tem, qui semel in possessionem venerunt, postea nō facile adducuntur, ut ciuitatum aliarum ue ditio- num dominia aliis cedant.
units.tr: A dispute about supreme right gives occasion for very great tumults, for not everything can be restored to its former state. When sovereign powers once collapse, they are never restored to their original condition, just as if someone overturned a cart of eggs, he could not gather up all the eggs without loss. Lords, however, who have once come into possession, are not easily brought to yield the dominion of other cities or territories.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Non ad ciuitatum ocium, & concordiam stabi-liendam quicquam perinde conducit, atq; ueterum legum morumq; conseruatio. quod cum urbium e- xempla passim testantur, tum monet aureus vete-ris Poetæ uersiculus: Moribus antiquis res stat Romana, uirisq;.
units.tr: Nothing contributes as much to the peace and harmony of cities as the preservation of the old laws and customs. Examples from cities everywhere bear witness to this, and the golden little verse of an ancient poet makes the same point: the Roman state stands on ancient customs and men.

units.la: Turci non exercet legitima iudicia iuxta leges. In Vngaria Budæ dicitur esse tanta barbaries, ut li-ceat quēlibet appellare de debito, reum etiā absq; causa & legitimo iudicij processu coram iudice sisti-tere. Ille negat, alter affirmat. Accusator conducit falsos testes, qui affirmēt sic esse. Sic solummodo ex relatione falsorum testium causæ dirimuntur, non consideratis ullis aliis circumstātijs, ut omnino in-nocentes debita soluant.
units.tr: The Turks do not conduct lawful trials according to the laws. In Hungary, at Buda, the barbarism is said to be so great that anyone may bring a charge of debt, and an accused person may even be summoned before a judge without any cause and without lawful judicial process. One denies, the other affirms. The accuser hires false witnesses to swear that it is so. In this way cases are settled solely on the testimony of false witnesses, with no other circumstances considered, so that entirely innocent men pay their debts.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Solonem refert Demosthenes, cum reum age-ret quendā perniciosæ legis authorē, dixisse: Cum capitale sit numisma adulterinum, morte etiā mul-ctandos esse eos qui leges uitiant: propterea quòd ut in priuatis commercijs ac contractib. numisma-te utimur, ita in publicis commercijs & negocijs leges sint numismatis uice.
units.tr: Demosthenes reports that when he was prosecuting a certain man who had proposed a harmful law, Solon said that since counterfeit coin is a capital offence, those who corrupt the laws should also be punished with death. For just as we use coin in private dealings and contracts, so in public commerce and affairs laws take the place of coin.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Legum authores omnes ueteres, quo plus auto ritatis suis legibus adderet, Deorum oraculis probatas asseuerabant. Minos fingebatur nouem annorum spacio Iouis usus familiari consuetudine, ab eoq; constituendae Reipublicae rationem didicisse. Lycurgum ferunt, & ab Apolline Deum appellatum esse, & sua edicta ῥήτρας uocasse, quòd oracula uideri uellet. Numam aiunt cum Aegeria nocturnos habuisse congressus. Fingebantur haec, ut cum diuino iudicio approbatae leges uiderentur, pluris fierent.
units.tr: All the ancient authors of laws, in order to add authority to their laws, asserted that they had been approved by oracles of the gods. Minos was said to have spent nine years in the familiar company of Jupiter and to have learned from him the method of establishing a commonwealth. They say Lycurgus was called god by Apollo and called his edicts rhetras [ῥήτρας], because he wished them to seem like oracles. They say Numa had nocturnal meetings with Egeria. These stories were invented so that laws would seem approved by divine judgement and so be held in greater esteem.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Plato dicit: Hypothesis nostrarum legum est, ut ciues fiant honesti, & inter se amici. Est satis pulchrum dictu. Sed nos habemus simplicius dictu: Primu quaerite regnu Dei, et cætera adijcietur uobis.
units.tr: Plato says: the aim of our laws is that citizens become upright and friendly toward one another. That is a fine thing to say. But we have something plainer to say: Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Sicut Athenis leges uiguerunt, Solone gubernante: sic Romae legum reuerentia mansit, donec Augustus uixit. Sed utroq; loco breui post oppresi sunt ciues tyrannide, & leges conticuerunt. Nam Athenis, Solone etiam adhuc uiuo, Pisistratus rapuit dominationem. Sic post Augustum, mox tyranni aliquot perquam crudeliter grassati sunt in Republica. Haec exempla saepe mouent magnos homines, ut aut nullum, aut exiguum esse usum legum arbitretur, qui quidem dictum illud Ciceronis in ore habent: Inter arma silent leges. Marius dixit, se legū uocem inter classica & tubarū sonos non audiuisse. Et Nazianzenus de Iuliano inquit: Voluntatem principis esse, ius non scriptum.
units.tr: Just as laws flourished at Athens while Solon governed, so reverence for the law remained at Rome as long as Augustus lived. But in both places, shortly afterwards, the citizens were oppressed by tyranny and the laws fell silent. For at Athens, while Solon was still alive, Pisistratus seized power; and after Augustus, soon afterwards, several tyrants raged cruelly in the commonwealth. These examples often move great men to think that laws are of no use, or very little use, and they keep on their lips that saying of Cicero: amid arms the laws are silent. Marius said he had not heard the voice of the laws amid the trumpets and the sound of the bugles. And Gregory of Nazianzus says of Julian: the will of the prince is an unwritten law.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Cicero, cùm de optimo ciuitatis statu disputat, non alias nisi Romanas leges fert, easq; naturæ maxime omnium consentaneas esse censet.
units.tr: Cicero, when he discusses the best state of a commonwealth, cites no laws except Roman ones, and he judges them to be most of all in agreement with nature.

units.la: Difficilis fuit disputatio ante annos aliquot, utrùm liceat litigare in foro? Erat hic bonus homo Anglus, qui non tantum propter hunc articulum, sed etiam propter alios, in Anglia erat coiectus in carcerem, ac disputabat mecū hac de re acerrimè.
units.tr: Some years ago it was a difficult question whether it is lawful to go to law in the courts. There was a good Englishman here who had been thrown into prison in England, not only on account of this point but also on account of others, and he argued with me very fiercely about this matter.

units.la: Doctor Henningus, qui fuit apud Ducem Saxoniæ Fridericū, dicere solebat: Lex sine executione est sicut campana sine clipulo seu pistillo.
units.tr: Doctor Henningus, who was at the court of Duke Frederick of Saxony, used to say: a law without enforcement is like a bell without a clapper or striker.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Locris lex erat, ut si quis contra receptas leges rogationem faceret, is eam inserto in laqueum collo ferret. quæ si uidebatur è Republica esse, salvus euadebat autor: ubi autem oratio displicuisset auditoribus, constricto laqueo strangulabatur.
units.tr: The Locrians had a law that if anyone proposed a measure contrary to the accepted laws, he should bring it with a noose around his neck. If it seemed to be for the good of the commonwealth, the proposer escaped unharmed; but if the speech displeased the hearers, the noose was tightened and he was strangled.

units.la: Quidam in Italia magni nominis professor scripsit, leges esse varias seu contrarias, quia voluntates hominū sunt variæ. Est insulsum dictum: quia in legibus multæ sunt demonstrationes, quæ nascuntur tur ex Decalogo, id est lege naturæ: etiamsi non omnia sunt demonstrabilia.
units.tr: A certain professor of great name in Italy wrote that laws are various or contrary because the wills of men are various. This is a silly remark, for in the laws there are many demonstrations which arise from the Decalogue, that is, from the law of nature, even if not everything is demonstrable.

units.la: Politianus.
units.tr: Politianus.

units.la: Inuentum Actæi dicuntur iura Draconis: Vera est fama nimis, nil nisi uirus habent. Hoc non est uerũ, quòd Draco dicitur inuenisse leges. Quia leges Athenis fuerũt promulgatæ ante Draconẽ: sed curia una, quales multæ fuerũt Athenis, fuit insignita pictura draconis, ad terrendos homines, ne se polluerent scelerib. Hinc Politianus motus esse uidetur, quòd scripserit: Inuentum Actæi dicuntur iura Draconis. Sed hoc uerũ est, quòd Draconis leges fuerunt scueriores: sicut in uniuersum leges antiquæ fuerunt scuerissimæ. Deinde uerò senectus mundi quasdam leges propter humanarum uirium imbecillitatem mitigauit.
units.tr: The laws of Draco are said to have been devised by Actaeus: the report is too true, they have nothing but poison. It is not true that Draco is said to have devised the laws, because laws were promulgated at Athens before Draco. But one curia, of which there were many at Athens, was marked with a picture of a dragon, to frighten men lest they defile themselves with crimes. From this, Politianus seems to have been moved to write: the laws of Draco are said to have been devised by Actaeus. But this is true, that Draco's laws were harsher, just as in general the ancient laws were very harsh. Then indeed the old age of the world softened some laws on account of the weakness of human strength.

units.la: Regimen Norinbergense à quo constitutum.
units.tr: The Nuremberg government, and by whom it was established.

units.la: Audiui regimen Norinbergense temperatum esse per hominem Frisium, quem habucrũt in consilio: & in ijsdem legibus stat adhuc ciuitas, Dei beneficio.
units.tr: I have heard that the government of Nuremberg was tempered by a Frisian man whom they kept on their council, and by the same laws the city still stands today, by God's blessing.

units.la: ELVSIONES VARIORVM negociorum.
units.tr: Evasions in various affairs.

units.la: In Comitijs quibusdam, cùm legati Iuliacensis principis in causa sui Ducis ferè ab omnibus principibus impetrassent, ut omnes eo tempore comparerent: rent: Imperator Carolus V.quoq; eos auditum ue-niens,salissimè ipsos taxauit: Ecce,inquit,sæpisi-mè grauissimas res proposui de religione, de defen-sione Imperij contra Turcos,& coseruatione com-munis Imperij status,et nunquam tantam uestrùm frequentiam impetrare potui.Iam uerò cùm unica causa contra me allata sit, omnes conuenitis. Sic ex consessu ipsorum se abduxit, ipsos in consessu relinquens.
units.tr: At certain assemblies, when the envoys of the Prince of Jülich had obtained from almost all the princes that everyone should attend at that time, the Emperor Charles V, hearing of it as he came, rebuked them most sharply: "Behold," he said, "I have very often proposed most weighty matters concerning religion, the defence of the Empire against the Turks, and the preservation of the common state of the Empire, and I could never secure such a full attendance of you. Now, since a single cause has been put forward against me, you all come together." So he withdrew from their assembly, leaving them sitting there.

units.la: Dissensione orta inter Hispanos et Germanos, ignoro qua de causa, quidam Hispani adeunt Im-peratorem Carolum V.à quo insolenter petunt,ut omnes Germanos ex aula dimittat.Imperator mi-ratus eorum stultam & insolentem petitionem: Bene,inquit,siquidem nõ potestis eos ferre, cura-bo ut liberemini ab illa molestia. Constituit eis cer-tum diem,quo iubet ad se accedere omnes Germa-nos in unum locum. Optimi conterranei, inquit, mei Hispani petiuerunt, ut uos omnes ex mea aula dimittere, quia etiã sum Germanus. Venite igitur abeamus, ne simus illis molesti:& conscenso equo, præcedit eos:illi læti, clamantes sequuntur. Cùm hæc sic Hispani agi uiderent,accurrunt,& ad pe-des Imperatoris se deijciunt, retinentes equi fre-num : orantesq; propter Deum, ne stultam & insolentem petitionem ægreferat. Et sic direm-pta est contentio.
units.tr: When a quarrel arose between the Spaniards and the Germans, for some reason I do not know, certain Spaniards approached the Emperor Charles V and insolently asked him to dismiss all the Germans from his court. The Emperor, surprised at their foolish and insolent request, said: "Very well, since you cannot bear them, I will see to it that you are freed from that annoyance." He set a certain day on which he ordered all the Germans to come to him in one place. "My very good fellow countrymen, the Spaniards," he said, "have asked that I dismiss you all from my court, since I too am a German. Come, then, let us go away, so as not to trouble them." And mounting his horse, he went ahead of them. They followed him, cheerful and shouting. When the Spaniards saw this happening, they ran up and threw themselves at the Emperor's feet, holding the bridle of his horse, and begging him, for God's sake, not to take amiss their foolish and insolent request. And so the dispute was settled.

units.la: Cum Heinrico Lutzelburgensi aliquando equitarunt duo Iurisconsulti, disputantes de quadam arce non procul à Bononia. quorum unus defendit esse Imperatoris, adducens generalem propositionem: Omnia esse Imperatoris. alter uero econtrà, unumquemq; suarum facultatum esse dominum contendebat. Tandem de hac lite constituerunt Heinricum Lutzelburgensem iudicem. Certatum est, ita ut victus solueret equum victori. Cùm uentum esset in urbem Bononiam, Imperator conuocatis aliquot, iußit ferre sententiam pro eo qui dixerat, omnia esse Imperatoris. Hinc homines docti facetè sic luserunt. Alter respondit æquum, sed alter habuit equum. Significatum est eo ioco, quòd dicentes æquum improbent propositionem: omnia esse Imperatoris.
units.tr: Once two jurists were riding with Heinrich of Luxembourg, disputing about a certain fortress not far from Bologna. One of them maintained that it belonged to the Emperor, citing the general proposition: "All things belong to the Emperor." The other, on the contrary, contended that each man is lord of his own property. At last they agreed to make Heinrich of Luxembourg judge of this dispute. They wagered on it, on the understanding that the loser would give his horse to the winner. When they came to the city of Bologna, the Emperor summoned some men and ordered judgement to be given for the one who had said that all things belong to the Emperor. Hence learned men jokingly made their play on it in this way: one said "aequum" (fair), but the other had "equum" (the horse). By that joke it was signified that those who say "aequum" reject the proposition that all things belong to the Emperor.

units.la: Quidam Doctor Tubingensis, adcò doctus, ut alij Iurisconsulti ad eum causas deferrent, quando audiebat leges flecti ad commoda potentum, aut uidit legem latam esse in commodum eius qui tulit eam, sicut in Decretalibus saepè fecerunt: solebat dicere, Das ist des Schuldtheßen kû: addendo fabulâ. In pago quodam læserat uacca prætoris uaccâ alterius rustici: qui accedens prætore, primùm in genere quærit de iure, Si alicuius uacca ab alterius læsa sit, quid sit iuris? Prætor respondit: quòd debeat soluere, quantum interest. Rusticus deinde addit addit Minorem: Tua uacca læsit meà. Tunc ille re-spondit: Das ist das Schuldthessen kũ, damit ists ein anders: id est, Verùm hæc est prætoris uacca, de qua aliter ius interpretandum est.
units.tr: A certain doctor of Tübingen, so learned that other jurists referred their cases to him, whenever he heard that laws were bent to the advantage of the powerful, or saw a law passed for the benefit of the one who proposed it, as they often did in the Decretals, used to say: "Das ist des Schuldtheßen kû" ("That is the mayor's cow"), adding a story. In a certain village a prefect's cow had injured another peasant's cow. The peasant came before the prefect and first asked in general terms about the law: "If one man's cow has been injured by another's, what is the law?" The prefect replied that he must pay what the loss amounts to. Then the peasant added the minor premise: "Your cow injured mine." Then the other answered: "Das ist das Schuldthessen kũ, damit ists ein anders" ("That is the mayor's cow, so it's a different matter"); that is, but this is the prefect's cow, and the law must be interpreted differently in its case.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Venit Athenas Demetrius, regum suæ ætatis florentissimus, Antigoni filius, ut Eleusinijs initiaretur. Venit autem eo mense, quo fieri Eleusinia non licebat: quibus attributi erat menses duo, Nouember & Augustus. Vt igitur regi mos gereretur, nec tamen sacra pollui uiderentur, inuenta est bella ratio, ac lex lata est, ut mensium nomina mutarētur.
units.tr: Demetrius came to Athens, the most flourishing of the kings of his age, son of Antigonus, in order to be initiated into the Eleusinian mysteries. But he came in the month in which the Eleusinian rites were not permitted; two months were assigned to them, November and August. So that the king might be humoured, and yet the sacred rites not seem to be profaned, a clever device was found, and a law was passed that the names of the months should be changed.

units.la: Heydelbergæ quidã legatus habiturus orationem in Cancellaria Palatini, cùm ipsa matrona soror Friderici Victoriosi eũ audiret (sicut erat magnifica matrona) stans ipsa cum gynæcio ex altera parte: ipse perterrefactus initio orationis suæ, ex terrore edidit crepitũ. Virgines hoc audito, inci-picebant ridere. Ille uerò ut factum dissimularet, & pudorem abstergeret, dixit: Domina, celsitudo tua curet, ut circumeat per circulũ (sicut illos aulicos oportet habere multa in promptu) postquā ordo ad me redierit, ego quoq; non prætermittā ea, quæ mei officij erunt. Et sic postea pertexuit orationem suam. Hæc fuit iocosa elusio.
units.tr: At Heidelberg a certain envoy was about to give an address in the chancery of the Palatine. The matron herself, the sister of Frederick the Victorious, was listening to him (as she was a magnificent matron), standing on the other side with her ladies. At the start of his speech he was terrified, and from fright he let out a fart. When the virgins heard it, they began to laugh. But he, to hide the deed and wipe away his embarrassment, said: "Lady, may your highness see to it that it goes round the circle (for courtiers ought to have many things ready to hand). When the order has come back to me, I too will not omit those things that are my duty." And so he went on with his speech. This was a witty evasion.

units.la: Tubingæ quidã præfectus, uir acer, solebat eos qui leuioribus de causis afferebant querelas iniuriarum riarum, in carcere conijcere, donec illis primus im petus iræ deferbuisset, ne affectus admiscerentur suis causis. Qua seueritate effecit, ut paucæ apud eum lites agitarentur, sed ciues potius sponte inui cem controuersias componerent.
units.tr: At Tübingen a certain prefect, a stern man, used to throw into prison those who brought complaints of injury for trivial reasons, until the first rush of anger had cooled, so that passions would not mix with their cases. By this severity he brought it about that few lawsuits were pursued before him, and the citizens rather settled their disputes among themselves of their own accord.

units.la: Noster Imperator Carolus V. est expertus multorum negociorum: nemo in aula ipsius simplicius uestiri solitus est, quàm ipse. Patiëtissimè consueuit omnes audire, & singulis manSuetissimè respondere. Potuit etiam significare offensionem animi sui in audiendo. Marchio Albertus episcopus Moguntinus petiuerat ab eodem nostro Imperatore, ut audiret unum ex consiliarijs, ex aula ab ipso dimissum. Venit itaq; consiliarius constituta die, dixitq; suam causam integras duas horas. Elapsis tandem duabus horis, Imperator dixit: Vis aliquid amplius? Ille respondit: Nihil, nisi quod expectem T. C. M. responsum. At Imperator: No promisi, quòd tibi respondere, sed quòd tantum te audire uelim. sicq; ab ipso dimissus est.
units.tr: Our Emperor Charles V had experience of many affairs. No one at his court was usually dressed more simply than he himself. He was most patient, accustomed to hear everyone and to answer each one most gently. He could also show his displeasure at listening. Marquis Albert, bishop of Mainz, had asked this same Emperor to hear one of the counsellors whom he had dismissed from the court. The counsellor came on the appointed day and spoke his case for two full hours. When two hours had elapsed, the Emperor said: "Do you want anything more?" He replied: "Nothing, except that I await Your Imperial Majesty's answer." But the Emperor said: "I did not promise that I would answer you, but only that I wished to hear you." And so he was dismissed.

units.la: Narratur dictum Alexandri Imperatoris: Fumo pereat, qui fumos uendidit. Dicitur autem fumi uenditor, qui uana spe lactat homines, & promittendo auxilium, pecuniam aut alia beneficia extorquet: interim clàm eos prodit, & maligne desert.
units.tr: The saying of the Emperor Alexander is recorded: "Let him perish in smoke who sold smoke." A seller of smoke is one who feeds men with vain hope and, by promising help, extorts money or other favours; meanwhile he secretly betrays them and maliciously deserts them.

units.la: Talem impostorem idem Imperator fumo combusit.
units.tr: The same Emperor burned such an impostor with smoke. ## ON TYRANTS.

units.la: DE TYRANNIS.
Lucanus nominat Alexandrum prædonem, sic inquiens: Hîc iacet fœlix terrarum prædo.
units.tr: Lucan calls Alexander a robber, saying: "Here lies the happy robber of the lands."

units.la: Non rectè dicit, quamuis poetica licentia est cõ cessa. Nam quãdo adolescêtes legût nõ præmoniti, multũ errãt, detrahentes politico ordini dignitatẽ.
units.tr: He does not speak correctly, though poetic licence is granted to him. For when young people read this without being forewarned, they go badly astray, detracting from the dignity of the political order.

units.la: Descriptio tyranni, à Catullo.
units.tr: A description of a tyrant, from Catullus.

units.la: — Tantum tibi gaudium in omni, In quo aliquid sceleris est. —
units.tr: "So great is your joy in everything in which there is some wickedness."

units.la: Est terribilis descriptio tyranni.
units.tr: It is a terrible description of a tyrant.

units.la: Ad generũ Cereris sine cæde & uulnere pauci Descendunt reges, & sicca morte tyranni.
units.tr: "To the kind of Ceres, few kings descend without slaughter and wound, and tyrants by a dry death."

units.la: Poeta ex naturali luce, ipsa experiëtia edoctᵒ, hos uersus expressit, pulcherrimè conuenientes cum dicto Christi: Qui gladium acceperit, gladio peribit.
units.tr: The poet, taught by natural light and by experience itself, expressed these verses, which agree most beautifully with the saying of Christ: "He who takes the sword will perish by the sword."

units.la: Serpens nisi deuorauerit alterum serpentẽ, nunquam fit draco. ὄφις ἂν μὴ ὄφεις φάγοι, ὸ μὴ γένη- σεταὶ ἀρᾶκων. Aeschines uoluit tollere Demosthenem: ita Romæ multi uolebãt sublatũ Ciceronẽ, & utebantur instrumento Clodio, qui erat factiosus.
units.tr: "Unless a serpent devours another serpent, it never becomes a dragon." [ὄφις ἂν μὴ ὄφεις φάγοι, οὐ μὴ γένηται δράκων.] Aeschines wished to remove Demosthenes; so at Rome many wished Cicero removed, and used Clodius as their instrument, who was a factious man.

units.la: Tyranni apud Senecam descriptio.
units.tr: A description of a tyrant in Seneca.

units.la: Fides, & pietas priuata, bona sunt: Reges, quò uolunt, eunt. Intelligit Reges non esse alligatos ad leges, sed omnia impunè eis licere.
units.tr: "Faith and private piety are good things; kings go wherever they wish." He means that kings are not bound by laws, but that everything is permitted them with impunity.

units.la: Seneca.
units.tr: Seneca.

units.la: Iniustus est, qui depositis armis mentem armatam tam retinet. Aristoteles: Viciosa democratia est ἐχάτη τυραννίς.
units.tr: "He is unjust who, having laid down his arms, still keeps an armed mind." Aristotle: a corrupt democracy is the last [ἐσχάτη] tyranny. ## COLL.

units.la: COLL.

Philippus, postremus rex Macedonicus, cæpit filios & filias omnium à se interfectorum, & postea interfecit eos. Id mouit Theoxinam Thessalicā matronam, ut præberet uenenū filijs & filiabus, ne uenirent in manus tyranni.
units.tr: Philip, the last king of Macedon, began to seize the sons and daughters of all whom he had killed, and afterwards he killed them too. This moved Theoxena, a Thessalian matron, to give poison to the sons and daughters, so that they would not fall into the hands of the tyrant.

units.la: Destructio Sydonis & Tyri.
units.tr: The destruction of Sidon and Tyre.

units.la: Ochus rex Persicus destruxit Sydonem: quanquam apparet ex Prophetis, quòd istæ duæ urbes Tyrus & Sydon antea sint oppugnatæ, & captæ à regibus Syriacis: tam magna destructio secuta est per Ochum, qui ante Darium fuit sæuus tyrannus. interfecit multitudinem triginta millium hominū.
units.tr: Ochus, king of Persia, destroyed Sidon. Although it appears from the Prophets that these two cities, Tyre and Sidon, had been attacked earlier and captured by the Syrian kings, the great destruction that followed came through Ochus, who was a cruel tyrant before Darius. He killed a multitude of thirty thousand men.

units.la: Alexāder sex mensibus Tyrum oppugnauit, cuius incolæ quamuis mirabilibus modis se defenderint in mari, tamen eam tandem cæpit & destruxit.
units.tr: Alexander besieged Tyre for six months. Although its inhabitants defended themselves in marvellous ways at sea, he nevertheless at last captured it and destroyed it. ## Herod's tyranny.

units.la: Herodis tyrannis.
Herodes triginta annos gesserat bellum, cùm nasceretur Ioannes Baptista, & interfecerat florem huius populi. Illam lanienam uiderant parentes Ioannis Baptistæ.
units.tr: Herod had waged war for thirty years when John the Baptist was born, and he had slaughtered the flower of this people. The parents of John the Baptist had seen that slaughter.

units.la: Vrit maturè, quod uult urtica manere.
units.tr: The nettle stings at once.

units.la: Scribitur de Lacedæmonijs, quòd interfecerint filium regis puerum, cùm uidissent eum effodere oculos auiculis. Hinc enim Lacedæmones iudicaverūt naturam fore tyrannicā: & si regnaturus esset, futurum esse crudelem in cives.
units.tr: It is written of the Lacedaemonians that they killed their king's son while he was a boy, when they saw him gouging out birds' eyes. From this the Lacedaemonians judged that his nature would be tyrannical, and that if he were to reign he would be cruel towards the citizens.

units.la: Rabies oratorum.
units.tr: The rage of orators.

units.la: Demades dixit, oratores esse aliis hominib. serpentes, sibi invicem viperas: id est, oratores necant alios homines, à quibus non necātur, sed ipsi se mutuò interficiunt. Sic ipse Demades fecit decretū contra Demosthenem, & sororis Demosthenis filius fecit decretum ut Demades pelleretur. Antipater pater Cassandri postulauit sibi dari Demosthenē, ut interficeretur. Demades interfectus à filio Antipatri, scribente decretum alio oratore, Demosthenis (ut iam dictum est) ex sorore nepote.
units.tr: Demades said that orators are serpents to other men and vipers to one another: that is, orators kill other men, by whom they are not killed, but they destroy each other in turn. So Demades himself passed a decree against Demosthenes, and the son of Demosthenes' sister passed a decree that Demades should be driven out. Antipater, the father of Cassander, demanded that Demosthenes be handed over to him to be put to death. Demades was killed by the son of Antipater, the decree being written by another orator, Demosthenes' nephew on his sister's side, as has already been said.

units.la: Poena tyranno digna.
units.tr: A punishment fit for a tyrant.

units.la: Alexandrum Phereum sua coniunx cum fratribus interfecit: qui cùm insueret homines in pellib. luporum, & adigeret canes, ut ipsos lacerarent: tamen tanta fuit eius vigilantia, ut cives non potuerint convenire ad capienda consilia de eo interficiendo. Pernoctavit semper in turri, & vigiles neminem nisi coniugem ad ipsum admiserunt. hæc autem de die suos fratres in turri abscondit: et noctu, cum ille iam dormiret, vocavit fratres ut ipsum interficerēt. Qui cùm primò perterrefacti hærerēt, ibi ipsa inquit: Nisi ipsum occideritis, excitabo eū ut uos occidat. His uerbis moniti, ipsum strangula runt. Dux quidam etiam talia faciēs, est persossus.
units.tr: Alexander of Pherae was killed by his wife together with his brothers. Although he used to fill men with the skins of wolves and set dogs on them to tear them apart, his watchfulness was so great that the citizens could not meet to take counsel about killing him. He always spent the night in a tower, and the guards admitted no one to him except his wife. But she hid her brothers in the tower by day, and at night, when he was already asleep, she called the brothers to kill him. When at first they hesitated, terrified, she said: "Unless you kill him, I will wake him so that he kills you." Warned by these words, they strangled him. A certain commander who did the same kind of thing was also run through.

units.la: Pictura tyranni.
units.tr: A portrait of a tyrant.

units.la: Demosthenes pingit Aristogitonem circumeun-
units.tr: Demosthenes paints Aristogiton going about in the marketplace,

units.la: tem in foro, et uibrantem spiculū ceu scorpiū, exe-rentem caudam insidiari ciuibus, & circumspe-ctare quem feriat, & aliqua calumnia opprimat.
units.tr: brandishing a dart like a scorpion, raising its tail, lying in wait for the citizens, looking all around for someone to strike, and to crush with some false accusation.

units.la: Deinde qui cum nullo ciue ullius officij societatem habeat, sed cum illis uiuat, quos apud inferos aiunt assidere, impijs uidelicet cum inuidia Furijs, ct alijs pestibus.
units.tr: Then he has no fellowship of duty with any citizen, but lives with those whom they say sit beside one another in the underworld, namely the impious, together with envy, the Furies and other plagues.

units.la: Regni Cyclopici pictura.
units.tr: A picture of the Cyclopean kingdom.

units.la: Vlysses interrogat, quale regnum esset Cyclo-pum? respondit Silenus: νομάδες, ἀνάσα ὀδεὶς ὁ δε ὁὸς: id est, uagabundi, ubi nullus alium audit. Sicut in quodam regno accidit controuersia, ubi quidam pastores non uoluerunt habere Superintendentes, allegantes textum: Sitis sicut pueri. unde consequi putarunt, omnes debere esse pares.
units.tr: Ulysses asked what kind of kingdom the Cyclopes had. Silenus answered: "nomades, anasa, odeis ho de hodos" [νομάδες, ἀνάσα ὀδεὶς ὁ δε ὁὸς]: that is, wanderers, where no one hears another. This is how, in a certain kingdom, a controversy arose when some shepherds did not want to have superintendents, citing the text: "Be like children." From this they thought it followed that all ought to be equal.

units.la: Phocæ tyranni pœna.
units.tr: The punishment of the tyrant Phocas.

units.la: Phocas interfectus est ita, ut detruncata sint ei brachia et pedes. & sic iacuit diu, ut duriter excru-ciaretur, nec citò mori posset. Ita Deus seruat ta-lionem.
units.tr: Phocas was killed in such a way that his arms and legs were cut off. He lay for a long time, so that he was cruelly tormented and could not die quickly. Thus God keeps the law of retaliation.

units.la: Pisonis tyrannicum factum, eiusdemq; tragica mors.
units.tr: The tyrannical deed of Piso, and his tragic death.

units.la: Seneca scribit de Pisone tyranno Hispanico, quòd interfecerit trecentos subditos, posteáq́; in-cesserit per cadauera, dicens hoc regium esse. Sic Piso postea sibi consciuit mortem. Cum esset accu-satus coram Tyberio, dixit, se, quæ fecisset, fecisse iussu Tiberij, quem ad hoc libellum scripsisse sin-xit: cui libello incumbens, mortem sibi cõsciuit.
units.tr: Seneca writes of Piso, the tyrant of Spain, that he killed three hundred subjects and then walked over the corpses, saying that this was kingly. So Piso afterwards brought death upon himself. When he was accused before Tiberius, he said that what he had done he had done by Tiberius' order, feigning that Tiberius had written a little book about this; and leaning on that book, he brought death upon himself.

units.la: Præmia societatis tyrannorum.
units.tr: The rewards of the fellowship of tyrants.

units.la: Aratus præstantissimus princeps, fuit familiaris Philippo Macedonico posteriori: qui postea dedit ipsi uenenum, quod paulatim eum extinxit. Ille uero cùm mane uomuisset, uidens uomitus sicut uenenum, dixit: ταῦτα τῆς φιλίας τίμια τυραννικῆς: id est, hæc sunt præmia amicitiæ tyrannicæ.
units.tr: Aratus, a most excellent prince, was a friend of Philip of Macedon the younger, who afterwards gave him poison, which gradually wore him away. But when Aratus vomited in the morning and saw the vomit as poison, he said: "tauta tes philias timia tyrannikes" [ταῦτα τῆς φιλίας τίμια τυραννικῆς]: that is, these are the rewards of tyrannical friendship.

units.la: Tyrannis & calamitas in Turcico regno.
units.tr: Tyranny and calamity in the Turkish kingdom.

units.la: Narrauit Dominus Iulius Pflůg, se audiuisse ex legatis Austriacis, qui cum essent excepti hospitio ab Imbre Bascha, quem Solymannus interfecit, & colloquerentur de forma Imperij, interrogauit Imbre Bascha, an homines in Romano imperio haberent proprias facultates? Legati dixerūt: Re-ges nostros habere sua certa dominia, & reliquos subditos nobiles: & magnates pleno dominio pos-sidere suas facultates, & alia in quibus haberēt dominium utile, ut feudalia: & nõ licere dominis eri-pere, quæ uelint. Sedit Imbre Bascha cogitabun-dus, tandē sustulit oculos: Ego, inquit, quotānis re-cipio [?]tipio nomine Domini mei sex tonnas auri, unde oportet numerare stipendia: sed quando morior, nō scio an obulus sit peruenturus ad meos hæredes. Tale est regnum Turcicū: est tyrannis & barbaries.
units.tr: Lord Julius Pflug related that he had heard from Austrian envoys who, when they were entertained by Imbrahim Pasha, whom Suleiman killed, and were talking about the form of government, Imbrahim Pasha asked whether men in the Roman empire had property of their own. The envoys said: "Our kings have their own fixed domains, and the rest of the subjects are nobles, and the magnates possess their property with full ownership, and other holdings in which they have useful ownership, such as fiefs; and it is not lawful for lords to seize whatever they wish." Imbrahim Pasha sat pondering, then at last lifted his eyes: "I," he said, "receive every year six tons of gold in the name of my lord, from which the wages must be counted out; but when I die, I do not know whether a single penny will reach my heirs. Such is the Turkish kingdom. It is tyranny and barbarism."

units.la: Vindicta tyrannica.
units.tr: Tyrannical vengeance.

units.la: Dux quidam proprium suum fratrem necauit fame, impositum cancellis ad arduam domum: qui die tandem nono fuit mortuus, in maximis uocifera-tionibus, audiente populo. Hæc est uindicta tyrannica, ut Plutarchus ait: id est, propositio concessa, quod tyrāno licet interficere patres, fratres, & propinquos, quia diabolus istos regit.
units.tr: A certain commander starved his own brother, shut up in a cage in a high house; he died at last on the ninth day, with the greatest outcries, the people hearing. This is tyrannical vengeance, as Plutarch says: that is, a proposition granted that it is permitted to a tyrant to kill fathers, brothers and kinsmen, because the devil rules them.

units.la: Rudis est tyrannus, qui poenam morte exigit, ait ille in tragœdia.
units.tr: A tyrant is cruel, who exacts punishment by death, says that character in a tragedy.

units.la: Phocas prius interfecit filium & filiam. Deinde coniugem Mauricij Imperatoris: deniq; interfi-cit ipsum Mauricium.
units.tr: Phocas first killed his son and daughter. Then the wife of the emperor Maurice, and finally he killed Maurice himself.

units.la: Tyranni deterrimi, & Caligula filius boni uiri Germanici degener.
units.tr: The most wicked tyrants, and Caligula, the degenerate son of the good man Germanicus.

units.la: Nero, Caius, Caligula, & Heliogabalus, fuerunt deterrima monstra in toto terrarum orbe, parrici-dijs, confusione libidinum, & alijs peccatis infinitis contaminati, quæ omnia uix aliquis enarrare posset. Caligula fuit optimi uiri Germanici filius.
units.tr: Nero, Gaius, Caligula and Heliogabalus were the most monstrous creatures in the whole world, defiled by parricides, a confusion of lusts and countless other sins, which no one could possibly recount. Caligula was the son of the excellent man Germanicus.

units.la: Quando Augustus adoptauit Tyberiū, non uoluit eū adoptare, nisi hic prius adoptasset Germanicū, ad quem postea propter eximias eius uirtutes uo-luit transferri Imperium . Hic Germanicus primò domuit Germaniam: cuius coniunx fuit Agrippi-na,ex qua filium genuit Caligulam, ad quem pro-pter uirtutem patris peruenit Imperiū . sed postea adeò à paternis uirtutibus degenerauit,ac talis be-stia factus est,ut uoluerit esse Deus,& statuā suam Romæ in templo iuxta Iouem Capitolinũ colloca-uerit, tanquam Ioui aliquid susurrātem in aurem: cui sacerdotes sacrificia offerre iussit.
units.tr: When Augustus adopted Tiberius, he was unwilling to adopt him unless he had first adopted Germanicus, to whom he later wished the empire to pass, on account of his outstanding virtues. Germanicus first subdued Germany. His wife was Agrippina, by whom he begot a son, Caligula, to whom the empire came because of his father's virtue. But afterwards he so degenerated from his father's virtues and became such a beast that he wished to be a god, and set up his statue in Rome, in the temple beside Jupiter Capitolinus, as if whispering something into Jupiter's ear; and he ordered priests to offer sacrifices to it.

units.la: Dionysij filij tyrannica facta,non man-serunt impunita.
units.tr: The tyrannical deeds of Dionysius' son did not go unpunished.

units.la: Dionysius tyrannus obiurgauit filium suum, corrumpentem filias,& coniuges ciuium. At ille: Tyranni filius nõ essem,nisi ista facerem. Debuis-set nebulonem laqueo strangulasse. Sed pater nihil aliud respondit,nisi hoc : Ista faciens,non habebis tyranni filios. Et ita accidit,ut in exilio postea mo-reretur. Fuit itaq; magna indulgentia patris, non cohercentis,& seueris pœnis punientis filium.
units.tr: Dionysius the tyrant rebuked his son for corrupting the daughters and wives of citizens. But he replied: "I would not be a tyrant's son if I did not do these things. You should have strangled the scoundrel with a noose." But the father answered only this: "If you do these things, you will not have tyrant's sons." And so it happened that he later died in exile. So there was great indulgence on the father's part, since he did not restrain his son or punish him with severe penalties.

units.la: Cuidam nobili ante paucos annos obuiam uenit rusticus,gestans pennas gallorum in pileo. Nobilis petit pennas. Rusticus inquit: Mi frater,si hoc ossi-cio tibi gratificari possum,libenter tibi tradã. No-bilis ebrius indigne ferens quòd ipsum fratrem uocasset, emittit globum ex bombarda,& sic ru-sticum sticum interficit. Tales sæuas bestias reddit superbia & insolentia, cum stulta persuasione nobilitatis et opulentiæ. Cum maxima uirtus, hoc est uera nobi-litas sit, humilitas, & conseruatio proximi.
units.tr: A few years ago a peasant met a certain nobleman, wearing cock's feathers in his cap. The nobleman asked for the feathers. The peasant said: "My brother, if I can please you in this matter, I will gladly hand them over to you." The nobleman, drunk and indignant that he had been called a brother, fired a ball from a cannon and so killed the peasant. Pride and insolence, together with the foolish belief in nobility and wealth, produce such savage beasts, when the greatest virtue, which is true nobility, is humility and care for one's neighbour.

units.la: Tyrannorum consultationes & familiariates, bonis per-niciosæ.
units.tr: Consultations and close friendships with tyrants are harmful to good men.

units.la: Dionysius cum uellet statuas in templum collocare, inquisiuit qui essent optimi statuarij? Respondit quidam, eos qui fecissent statuas Tyrannicidarum Athenis: significans, tyrannum esse tollendum. Sed fuit illi exitio ea uox.
units.tr: When Dionysius wanted to place statues in the temple, he asked who the best sculptors were. Someone replied that they were those who had made the statues of the tyrant-slayers at Athens, meaning that the tyrant must be removed. But that remark proved fatal to him.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Nemo unquam in Imperio quicquam effecit sæuitia, præter unum Syllam (quod est apud Appia-num, & alioqui nullibi scriptum reperitur) qui etiam hominibus sæuis & barbaris imperauit, apud quos lenitate & mansuetudine nihil efficere potuit. Quare apud illos seuerior disciplina necessaria fuit. Hic dixit, se uidisse aliquando rusticum exercentem operas suas, quem cum pediculi, quibus scatebat, morderent, coactus est exutis uestibus, & relicto labore, inquirere pediculos. Cum uero rur-sus accederet ad operas, coeperunt denuo, ut antea, pediculi eum molestare, ita ut sæpius eum a labore abigerent. Tandem cum nihil se proficere uideret, coniecit uestes in ignem, & combussit. Sic dixit se nulla ratione suos efferos populos cohercere posse, nisi summa asperitate uteretur.
units.tr: No one ever accomplished anything in the empire by cruelty except Sulla alone (which is in Appian, and is not found written anywhere else), who also commanded savage and barbarous men, among whom he could achieve nothing by gentleness and mildness. Therefore a harsher discipline was necessary among them. He said that he once saw a peasant at his work who, when the lice with which he swarmed bit him, was forced to strip off his clothes, leave his labour and hunt for lice. But when he returned to his work, the lice began again, as before, to harass him, so that they often drove him away from his labour. At last, seeing that he made no progress, he threw his clothes into the fire and burned them. Sulla said that he could restrain his savage peoples by no method except by using the utmost severity.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam Episcopus ad Rhenum, omnes pauperes ad se venientes, & eleemosynam petentes, concludebat in unam domunculam, quam deinde incendebat. Cumq; illi miseri homines alta voce clamarent, dixit: Audite vocem murium. Verùm, divina vindicta sic miraculose ordinante, Episcopus deinde à muribus est arrosus. Cum autem non posset ingruentem ad se murium copiam arcere, curauit sibi ædificari turrim in medio Rheni. Facta hac turri, in eam migrauit: sed ne sic quidem poenâ diuinam effugere potuit. at mures transnatarunt Rhenum, & eum interfecerunt. Vestigia illius turris hodie, iterum illis locis facientibus, ostenduntur.
units.tr: A certain bishop on the Rhine used to shut all the poor who came to him begging for alms into a little house, which he then set on fire. When those wretched men cried out loudly, he said: "Listen to the squeaking of the mice." But by divine vengeance, miraculously ordained, the bishop was afterwards gnawed by mice. When he could not keep off the crowd of mice pressing upon him, he had a tower built for himself in the middle of the Rhine. Once the tower was built, he moved into it; but not even so could he escape divine punishment. The mice swam across the Rhine and killed him. Traces of that tower are shown even today, the mice again being active in those places.

units.la: Ante paucos annos huc scribebatur, esse quendam nobilem, qui euulsione dentium pecuniam à suis miseris subditis extorqueret. Capiebat enim eos, ac primò unum dentem euellebat, minitans, ni tantum pecuniæ darent, quantum postularet, se reliquos omnes dentes ipsis extracturum. Hoc plane est barbaricum, Cyclopicum, & tyrannicum: hoc est cõcutere, & concussio seu extorsio, quæ fit per vim. Illi sunt crudeles in suos, sicut de Lacedæmonibus dictum est: Domi leones, foris vulpes. Sic isti ἀγραυλόφαγοι[?] (ut seipsos nominant) in suos sunt leones, id est, sunt crudeles: & in hostes sunt timidi et fugaces. Nam Lacedæmonij uerè fuerunt genus hominũ uulpinũ, & lupinũ: id est, sæuũ & astutũ.
units.tr: A few years ago it was reported here that a certain nobleman extorted money from his wretched subjects by pulling their teeth. He would seize them and first pull out one tooth, threatening that unless they gave as much money as he demanded, he would extract all their remaining teeth. This is plainly barbarous, Cyclopean and tyrannical: it is shaking down and extortion, which is done by force. Such men are cruel to their own, just as it was said of the Spartans: "lions at home, foxes abroad." So these men, agraulophagoi [ἀγραυλόφαγοι] (as they call themselves), are lions to their own people, that is, they are cruel; and toward their enemies they are timid and fleeing. For the Spartans were truly a fox-like and wolf-like race, that is, savage and crafty.

units.la: Quidam præstans uir, uirtute, prudentia, & aliis uirtutibus ornatus, qui fuit in Cæsaris exercitu, quando obsessum fuit Tunethũ, dixit mihi, uersus Occidētem esse miserrimum hominum statum, nullos ordines, nullas ecclesias, nulla studia literarũ, nullos senatus: sed unũ tantũ esse in urbe qui habet sua prædia, et omnia regit sine legibus, ad nutũ suũ. Talis status in politijs, est tyrānis. Et cũ interrogarē de domestica uita, respōdit, esse prorsus nauiticam uitā: cibũ capiũt in terra, nō secus atq; sues.
units.tr: A certain outstanding man, endowed with virtue, prudence and other excellences, who had been in Caesar's army when Tunis was besieged, told me that toward the west is the most wretched state of men: no orders, no churches, no pursuit of letters, no senates; there is only one man in the city who holds his own estates and rules everything without laws, at his nod. Such a state, in politics, is tyranny. And when I asked about domestic life, he replied that it was entirely a seafaring life: they take their food on the ground no differently from pigs.

units.la: C O·L L.
units.tr: C O L L.

units.la: Ciuis Haganēsis nomine Schmaltz, missus legatus ad Turcā, affirmauit Turcicũ Imperatorē quæsiuisse de Luthero, quot annorũ esset? Cum ei respondisset, eũ esse annorũ quinquaginta. ait ille: Vellē ipsum esse iuniorē. habiturus esset me beneficũ Dominũ. Respōdit Lutherus, signo crucis facto: Deus me tueatur à tali benefico Domino.
units.tr: A citizen of Hagenau named Schmaltz, sent as an envoy to the Turk, affirmed that the Turkish Emperor asked about Luther how old he was. When Schmaltz answered that he was fifty years old, the Emperor said: "I wish he were younger; he would have been a benefit to me as lord." Luther replied, making the sign of the cross: "May God keep me from such a beneficent lord."

units.la: Narrant Procopius & Aegesippus de Theodorico rege Gothorum, quòd cùm interfecisset Boetium, & eius generum Symmachum, uiros consulares, propter futilem suspicionem affectatæ libertatis: hanc cædem tantam mæsticiam esse secutam, ut inter paucos dies examinaretur.
units.tr: Procopius and Aegesippus relate of Theodoric, king of the Goths, that after he had killed Boethius and his son-in-law Symmachus, men of consular rank, on the groundless suspicion of aiming at liberty, this slaughter was followed by such grief that he himself died within a few days.

units.la: Episcopus Saltzburgensis, quendam rusticum, a quo captus fuerat ceruus, uiuum insuit in corio cerui, ac in eundē immisit canes, ut eum lacerarent. Illud supplicium per se est maius iusto: praeterea additur singularis species atrocitatis, qua delectatur, unde tamen nihil ei lucri accedit.
units.tr: The Bishop of Salzburg sewed a certain rustic, by whom a stag had been captured, alive into the hide of the stag, and set dogs upon him to tear him apart. That punishment is in itself greater than is just; to it is added a peculiar kind of atrocity, in which he took delight, though he gained nothing from it.

units.la: Cum mandasset rex Astyages, ut Harpalus capitaneus ipsius interficeret puerum Cyrum: rescisces ipsum fouisse eū, & clàm abduci permisisse, interfecit capitanei filium, quem dedit patri comedendū. & postea filij caput, brachia, & quaedam alia membra iubet proferri, & patri mõstrari, dicēs: Quomodo tibi ista placent? Respondit: Quicquid facit rex, illud mihi placet. Sed postea scripsit Cyro, ut istam iniuriam ulciscerētur: qui uenit, & tyrannū interfecit.
units.tr: When King Astyages had ordered his captain Harpalus to kill the boy Cyrus, and learned that he had cherished him and allowed him to be taken away secretly, he killed the captain's son and gave him to his father to eat. Afterwards he ordered the boy's head, arms and certain other limbs to be brought forth and shown to the father, saying: "How do these things please you?" He answered: "Whatever the king does pleases me." But afterwards he wrote to Cyrus, that he should avenge that wrong; he came and killed the tyrant.

units.la: Tyrannis erga Ecclesiam.
units.tr: Tyranny against the Church.

units.la: Regi cuidam exhibuerunt quidam spectaculum. Cùm igitur uenirent in illud conclaue, in quo rex sedebat in conuiuio cum suis, & dicerent se exhibituros Comœdiam, & collocarent in medium tres arculas seu pyxides, statim deinde effugerunt. Rex putat eos foris caetera adornare, quibus opus erat in tali actione, aut uestes mutare. Et cùm longius differrent reditū (subduxerant autem sese, ne comprehensi poenas darent) iubet rex aperire ordine arculas: in quarum prima fuit imago Christi alligati ti columnæ,quæ cædebatur uirgis & flagris à rege.Significabant illo figmento Ecclesiam, & doctrinā uerā à rege crudeliter opprimi. In secunda arcula erat eques,qui agitabat equum concul-cantem miseros homines.
