Significabant autem esse regnum tale,in quo opprimerentur pij homines, & pauperes,in quibus nulla ratio subditorū egentium & pauperū haberetur. Tertia arcula significabat œconomicum regimen regis:quia in ea sedebat rex in conuiuio sui gynæcij.
units.tr: Some people once put on a show for a certain king. When they came into the room where the king was sitting at a banquet with his men, and said that they would perform a comedy, they set down in the middle three little chests or boxes, and then at once slipped away. The king supposed they were outside preparing the other things needed for such a performance, or changing their clothes. And when they delayed their return for a long time (they had withdrawn, in fact, so as not to be caught and punished), the king ordered the chests to be opened in turn. In the first was a picture of Christ bound to a pillar, who was being beaten with rods and whips by the king. By this figure they signified that the Church and the true doctrine were cruelly oppressed by the king. In the second chest was a horseman who drove his horse over wretched men trampling them down. They signified that there was such a kingdom, in which godly men and the poor were oppressed, and in which no consideration was given to needy and poor subjects. The third chest signified the domestic government of the king, because in it the king sat at a banquet with his harem.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.

units.la: EPIGRAMMA DE STATVA Danielis, à Ioanne Stigelio compositum.
units.tr: EPIGRAM ON THE STATUE OF DANIEL, composed by Johannes Stigelius.

units.la: Hæc quicunq; legis Danielis scripta Prophetæ,Qui tibi de Christo nuncia uera canit:Aspice Regnorum seriem, & titubantia fata,Quæq; abijsse diu, quæq; futura docet.Aspice decidua uix stantem mole Gigantem,Quàm titubat fragili languidus ille pede.Scilicet occiduo declinant omnia mundo,Actaq; ad extremum fabula spectat opus.O' quicunq; cupis uenientem cernere Christum,Iudicium expectans discë timere Dei.
units.tr: Whoever you are who read the writings of the prophet Daniel, which sing true tidings of Christ to you: look upon the succession of kingdoms and their tottering fates, and what he teaches has long since passed away and what is yet to come. Look at the giant, scarcely standing on his crumbling mass, how that feeble figure totters on its frail foot. Surely all things are sinking toward the western world, and the play is heading to its last act. O you who desire to see Christ coming, awaiting judgement, learn to fear God.

units.la: Septem principes Electores, his uersi-bus continentur: quorum priores ecclesiastici, cæteri uerò politici sunt.
units.tr: The seven Electors are contained in these verses: of these, the first are ecclesiastical, the rest are secular.

units.la: Moguntinensis, Treuirensis, Coloniensis,Atq; Palatinus Dapifer, Dux portitor ensis:Marchio præpositus Cameræ, pincerna Bohem9,Romanum regem statuendi dant tibi legem.
units.tr: Mainz, Trier, Cologne, and the Palatine, steward of the household, the Duke, bearer of the sword; the Margrave, steward of the chamber, the Bohemian cupbearer, give you the law for appointing the Roman king.

units.la: Regulæ uitæ pro studiosa iuuentute, à Ioanne Stigelio traditæ.
units.tr: Rules of life for studious youth, handed down by Johannes Stigelius.

units.la: Viue tibi, stolidæq; caue commercia turbæ,Consultum uitæ si cupis esse tuæ.Nil facias, fieri nisi quòd debebat honestè:Sitq;
units.tr: Live for yourself, and beware the company of the foolish crowd, if you wish to have a sound life. Do nothing except what ought to be done honourably.

units.la: Sitq; tuæ vitæ regula certa Deus. Nec famæ rebus temerè te ingesseris ullis, Ni sinat officij causa probanda tui. Congressus caueas, nisi cùm tua functio poscit: Illi autem placidi sint simul, atq; breues. Quâ potes officijs orna, nec commoda specta: Pro meritis reddi gratia rara solet. Præcipuè caueas ulli nimis esse sodalis, Hic iacet in viridi frigidus anguis humo. Nunc ego te iubeam cædem vitare minantes: Quos tibi coniunxit spes bona, semper ama. Dulce quidem certè est, & amici nobile nomen: Sæpè sed hic etiam crimen adesse solet. Limina præcipuè fuge suspiciosa potentum, Crede mihi hæc fuco gratia rara caret. Cautus ut euitat blandas Syrenas Vlysses: Illecebris aulæ ne capiare, Vale.
units.tr: Let God be the sure rule of your life. Do not thrust yourself rashly into any affairs of reputation, unless the duty of your office requires it to be undertaken. Avoid gatherings, unless your function demands them; and let those that you attend be calm and brief. Adorn your duties with whatever you can, and do not look to rewards: thanks for services is rare. Above all, take care not to be too much the companion of anyone; the cold snake lies hidden in the green grass. Now I bid you avoid men who threaten violence; always love those whom good hope has joined to you. Friendship is indeed sweet, and the noble name of friend; yet often a crime lurks here too. Above all flee the suspicious thresholds of the powerful; believe me, favour of this kind is rarely free of deceit. As the cautious Ulysses avoided the enticing Sirens, so do not be caught by the allurements of the court. Farewell.

units.la: Eiusdem:
units.tr: By the same author:

units.la: Qui sapere, & durum traducere molliter æuum, Et vacuum sceleris pectus habere cupis: Res age, iustitiæ memor: & qui cunctat gubernat, Omnia præsenti crede regenda Deo. Disce & fortunam placidè superare ferendo, Atq; animum sortis spe melioris ale. Suggerit ingenuas animo patientia vires: Vincere felici spes ratione potest.
units.tr: You who wish to be wise, and to pass your hard life gently, and to have a breast free of crime: act, mindful of justice; and let him who hesitates steer, entrusting all things to be governed by God who is present. Learn also to overcome fortune calmly by bearing it, and nourish your spirit with the hope of a better lot. Patience supplies free-born strength to the mind; hope can conquer by a happy reason.

units.la: Alia regula uitæ, à Paulo Chierle[?]ro Elsterb.
units.tr: Another rule of life, by Paul Chierle[?]rus of Elsterb.

units.la: Vt tibi toto Rideat æuo Vita beatæ Plena salutis:
units.tr: So that life, full of salvation, may smile on you

units.la: Exue culpam, Indue Christum, Dilige casto Numen amore.
units.tr: for your whole age: put off sin, put on Christ, love the divine power with a pure love.

units.la: Postea cauta Mente caueto, Ne tibi pectus Occupet error.
units.tr: Afterwards, with a wary mind, take care that error does not seize your heart.

units.la: Ritè labore Fungere iusso: Auspice Christo Perfice cuncta.
units.tr: Perform the task you are given diligently; with Christ as your guide, finish everything.

units.la: Sors ubi tristis Venerit olim, Pectora uerbi Robore fulci.
units.tr: When sad fortune comes at some time, strengthen your heart with the strength of the Word.

units.la: Sic tibi dulcis Vita fauebit, Aurea donec Ibis ad astra.
units.tr: Thus sweet life will favour you, until at last you go to the golden stars.

units.la: LIBELLVS, QVO
units.tr: A LITTLE BOOK, IN WHICH

units.la: VARIAE TAM SACRA-
units.tr: the various histories, as much sacred

units.la: rum literarum quàm prophana
units.tr: as profane,

units.la: rum historie,tanquam in Calendario,juxta mensium ordinem,

units.la: Tempora percurrunt haec scripta volubilis anni, Et quædam certis gesta diebus habent. Hæc quoq; divino referēte Melanchthone scripsit, Plurima quæ solitæ pondera laudis habent. Cũ sint grata scholis dixit quæcunq; Melãchthon: Vana quid ulterius fundere verba juvat?
units.tr: These writings run through the turning year, and some of them hold events fixed to certain days. Melanchthon, referring to things divine, wrote these too, many of which carry the weight of the praise they usually receive. Since everything Melanchthon said is pleasing to the schools, what further use is it to pour out empty words?

units.la: IANVARIVS:
units.tr: IANUARIUS:

units.la: X. Ianuarij. Anno mundi 3335. urbs Hie-rosolyma ab exercitu regis Babylonici Nabucho-donosor obsessa est: durauitq; obsidio duodecim menses, etiam fame & pestilentia miserabiliter ne-cante inclusam multitudinem Iudæorū: donec tan-dem urbs capta, unà cum templo direpta et exusta est, & populus in triste exilium abductus.
units.tr: On 10 January, in the year of the world 3335, the city of Jerusalem was besieged by the army of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. The siege lasted twelve months, and the enclosed multitude of Jews was wretchedly destroyed by famine and pestilence. At last the city was taken, and together with the temple it was plundered and burned, and the people were led away into a sad exile.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: XII. Ianuarij. Est dies mortis Maxi-miliani Imperatoris, qui in superioris Austriæ op-pidulo Vuels obijt: maximus princeps, ac verum Aemylij illius magni (cuius nomen referebat) imo sapientiæ prudentiæq; suo seculo unicum exemplū. Cuius cadauer ex testamento in Noua ciuitate loco natali, regio more, & cōmuni omnium luctu con-ditum fuit, anno 1519.
units.tr: 12 January is the day of the death of the Emperor Maximilian, who died in the small Austrian town of Wels. He was a most eminent prince, and in his age the unique example of that great Aemilius (whose name he bore), indeed of wisdom and prudence. By his will his body was buried in his birthplace, Wiener Neustadt, with royal ceremony and the common grief of all, in the year 1519.

units.la: XXVIII. Ianuarij. Est dies mortis Caroli Magni, & Othonis Tertij: qui etiamsi non eodem anno, tamen eodem die sunt mortui. Caro-lus Magnus anno Christi 814. ætatis verò 71. Impe-rij 14. regni 46. mortuus: Otho Tertius verò plus centum annis post ipsum vita defunctus est.
units.tr: 28 January is the day of the death of Charlemagne and of Otto III. Although they did not die in the same year, they died on the same day. Charlemagne died in the year of Christ 814, in the 71st year of his age, the 14th of his empire and the 46th of his kingdom. Otto III, however, departed this life more than a hundred years after him.

units.la: FEBRVARIVS.
units.tr: FEBRUARY.

units.la: III. Februarij. Est dies Blasij, id est Basilij (nā quē Germani Blasiū uocāt, idem est qui Latinis Latinis & Græcis Basilius dicitur) qui fuit episcopus in Cæsarea Cappadociæ, natus ibidem ex nobili patre Basilio, & matre Emmalia: sicut olim nobilitas habitare solebat in urbibus. Fuit coætaneus & amicus singularis Nazianzeni, qui ipsi funebrē orationem scripsit. Illi duo, Basilius & Nazianzenus, fuerunt præstantissimi in Ecclesia Orientali, & in eadem propagatores excellentissimi doctrinæ de filio Dei contra Arrianos: propugnauerūt symbolū Nicenū, & fuerunt in magna autoritate. In primis uero nullus scriptor Ecclesiasticus in tota Græca lingua est, qui rectius loquatur quàm Basilius. Iste Basilius est institutus in patria, dum fuit Florens episcopus: postea missus est ad alia celebriora loca. Fuit auditor Libanij, præstantissimi oratoris. Postea uenit Athenas, ubi pepercerunt ei ne illos ludos depositionis cum eo exercerent (ab eo enim tempore durauit ritus et consuetudo illa depositionis studiosorum: de qua fertur, quòd olim adolescentes ducti sunt in balneum, & exagitati, posteáq; recepti.) Venerunt ad eum fratres, Petrus et Gregorius Nyssenus (hic fuit episcopus Nyssæ, & scripsit libellum de anima, qui adhuc extat) & abduxerunt eum ex cathedra, iusseruntq; seruire Ecclesiæ. Ita rediit in patriā, & factus est Lector collegij in sua patria. Ibi incidit simultas inter ipsum & episcopū, sicut sunt res humanæ. Quanquā fuit bonus homo et episcopus Cæsariensis, tamen habuit etiā aliquid humani: ut nihil humani est perfectũ, sicut dicitur: Nõ est iustus in terra, qui nõ aliquan do peccet. Gregorius Nazianzenus dicebat, Basiliũ non voluisse cū suo episcopo contendere, sed ipsius consilio usum secessisse. Habuit itaq; deinceps cœ-tus scholasticos in suo prædio hæreditario, quod cõ uertit in scholam, ubi uixerunt unà in studio. Illo tempore, cùm esset liber, sumpsit tempus ad pere-grinandum. Dicit se peragrasse Asiam, & uidisse ecclesias Palæstinas, & Constantinopolitanam, ut inquireret testimonia de doctrina. Addit, se didicis-se summam doctrinæ Christianæ à sua nutrice, quā affirmat fuisse auditricem Gregorij Neocæsarien-sis clarissimi uiri, cuius confessio extat scripta con-tra Samosatenum. Postea revocatus, factus est epi-scopus Cæsareæ. Eodē tempore ille ipse voluit eum sibi subrogari, qui prius fuerat eius æmulus: & qui antea prægrauauerat eum, tunc tribuit ei testimo-niũ eruditionis. ἀνεγαὶ δὲ φρονέες ἐδλῶν, inquit Homerus. Imperator Valens tũ persequebatur re-cte sentientes de filio Dei, & tuebatur Arianos, ita ut fuerit tunc Ecclesia satis miseribiliter dilacera-ta. Valentinianus tuebatur recte sentientes, & fuit amicus Ambrosio. In oriente regnabat Valens, fra-ter Valentiniani, qui fauebat Arianis, & pellebat recte sentientes. Hunc igitur Cæsareæ ingredientē in templum, Basilius iussit egredi. tanta fuit in eo magnitudo animi. Verum postea rursus à Valente fuit decretum, ut exiret in exilium: sed praefectus quidam intercessit pro eo, ut lateret. Valens postea à Gothis in fugam actus, abdidit se in casam, & sic combustus est. quod periculum ipsi praedictum erat à sancto viro, dicēte: Vade, tu peribis. & sic accidit.
units.tr: III. February. It is the day of Blasius, that is, Basil (for what the Germans call Blasius is the same man who is called Basil by Latins and Greeks), who was bishop in Caesarea in Cappadocia. He was born there to a noble father, Basil, and a mother, Emmelia, since in those days the nobility used to live in the cities. He was a contemporary and a close friend of Gregory Nazianzenus, who wrote his funeral oration. These two, Basil and Gregory Nazianzenus, were the most outstanding men in the Eastern Church, and the most excellent spreaders of the doctrine of the Son of God against the Arians. They defended the Nicene Creed and were held in great authority. Indeed, there is no ecclesiastical writer in the whole Greek language who speaks more accurately than Basil. Basil was educated in his homeland while he was bishop of Florens; afterwards he was sent to other, more famous places. He was a pupil of Libanius, the most distinguished orator. Later he came to Athens, where his fellow students spared him from the hazing of the "deposition" (for from that time the rite and custom of this student "deposition" endured, of which it is said that in former times young men were led to the bath and roughly handled, and afterwards admitted). His brothers Peter and Gregory of Nyssa came to him (Gregory was bishop of Nyssa and wrote the little book On the Soul, which is still extant) and led him away from his chair and ordered him to serve the Church. So he returned to his homeland and became lector of the college in his own country. There a quarrel arose between him and the bishop, as happens in human affairs. Although he was a good man and the bishop of Caesarea, he nonetheless had something human about him, as nothing human is perfect, as it is said: "There is not a just man on earth who does not at some time sin." Gregory Nazianzenus said that Basil had not wished to contend with his bishop, but had withdrawn on his advice. Thereafter he kept a company of scholars on his hereditary estate, which he turned into a school, where they lived together in study. At that time, when he was free, he took the opportunity to travel abroad. He says that he travelled through Asia and saw the churches of Palestine and Constantinople, in order to seek out testimonies concerning doctrine. He adds that he had learned the sum of Christian doctrine from his nurse, who, he affirms, had been a hearer of Gregory of Neocaesarea, that most distinguished man, whose confession is extant, written against Samosatenus. Afterwards he was recalled and made bishop of Caesarea. At the same time, that very man who had earlier been his rival, and who had previously burdened him, wished to be appointed as his successor, and then he bore witness to his learning. "But he who thinks noble things [ἀνεγαὶ δὲ φρονέες ἐδλῶν]," says Homer. The emperor Valens then persecuted those who held the right view concerning the Son of God and defended the Arians, so that the Church was then torn to pieces in a most wretched way. Valentinian defended those who held the right view, and was a friend of Ambrose. In the East reigned Valens, brother of Valentinian, who favoured the Arians and drove out those of right belief. When he entered the church at Caesarea, Basil ordered him to leave, so great was the greatness of spirit in him. But afterwards Valens again decreed that he should go into exile, but a certain prefect interceded for him, so that he might remain in hiding. Afterwards Valens, driven into flight by the Goths, hid himself in a cottage, and so was burned to death. This danger had been foretold to him by the holy man, who said: "Go, you shall perish," and so it came to pass.

units.la: Scripsit profectò Basilius accuratius & melius quàm omnes alij, contra Arrianos: defenditq; doctrinam de filio Dei, quòd sit ὁμοούσιος patri. Dicit quidam Arrianus, Basilium & Gregorium Neocaesariensem non antecelluisse caeteris doctoribus, ut possit Athanasius prior uideri collatus ad istos, quod est uerum. In primo capite Ioannis disputat, quare filius Dei dicatur λόγος: quia genitus est cogitatione. Refutauit etiā Nouatianos, qui in Occidente sic nominati fuerūt, uel in Græcia Καθαροί, qui dixerunt lapsos post poenitentiam non posse iterum recipi aut redire ad poenitentiam. Contrā istos scripsit luculentam orationem in narratione de filio prodigo, ubi ait: Trahit Deus, sed volentē. Reliquit multa testimonia de Trinitate: nam oportet bene confirmatum fuisse de Trinitate.
units.tr: Basil certainly wrote more accurately and better than all others against the Arians, and defended the doctrine concerning the Son of God, that he is homoousios [ὁμοούσιος] with the Father. Some Arian says that Basil and Gregory of Neocaesarea did not surpass the other teachers, so that Athanasius might seem the earlier when compared with them; but this is true. In the first chapter of John he discusses why the Son of God is called the Word [λόγος]: because he is begotten by thought. He also refuted the Novatians, who in the West were so named, and in Greece were called Cathari [Καθαροί], who said that those who had fallen could not after repentance be received again or return to repentance. Against these he wrote an excellent discourse in his exposition of the parable of the prodigal son, where he says: "God draws, but the one who is drawn must be willing." He left many testimonies concerning the Trinity, for it is fitting that the doctrine of the Trinity should be well confirmed.

units.la: MARTIVS.
units.tr: March

units.la: VII. Martij. Narratur fabula de Thoma Aquinate, qui mortuus est anno à nato Christo 1274. septimo Martij, quòd conspecta sit haec species cies ea ipsa hora qua mortuus est. Visum esse Tho-mam ipsum in usitata cathedra legente, & ingres-sum esse Paulum Apostolum in auditorium. Hunc cùm interrogaret Thomas, recte ne interpretatus esset ipsius scripta? respondit Paulus: Rectius cæte-ris omnibus: & tantũ ipsum percepisse ex suis scri-ptis, quantum in hac uita intelligi posset: sed nunc cum secum iturum esse in cœlestem scholã, ubi ma-ior lux fulget. atq; ita cùm Thomas cum Paulo ex auditorio egrederetur, & monachi utrunq; retine-re conarentur, ambos euanuisse fingitur. Postea cõ-pertum est, Thomam eadem hora mortuum esse.
units.tr: 7 March. A story is told about Thomas Aquinas, who died in the year 1274 after the birth of Christ, on 7 March, that this apparition was seen at the very hour he died. Thomas himself was seen lecturing in his usual chair, and Paul the Apostle was seen entering the lecture hall. When Thomas asked him whether he had interpreted his writings correctly, Paul answered: "More correctly than all the others," and that he had grasped from Thomas's writings only as much as can be understood in this life, but that now he was going with him into the heavenly school, where a greater light shines. As Thomas was leaving the lecture hall with Paul, and the monks tried to hold both of them back, both are said to have vanished. Afterwards it was discovered that Thomas had died at that same hour.

units.la: Credibile est, consultò fictam esse hanc narrationẽ à quodam discipulo seu auditore Thomæ, præce-ptorem suum magnificiente. Manifestum est, do-ctrinam Thomæ in multis materijs à Paulo dissen-tire. Iubet enim Paulus probare spiritus an ex Deo sint, quod præcipuè iudicari potest ex dogmati-bus. Scribit alicubi, mortem Christi fuisse sacrificiū pro peccatis ante eum factis: postea oblationem in missa sacrificium esse pro peccatis sequentibus.
units.tr: It is credible that this story was deliberately invented by some disciple or hearer of Thomas who wished to magnify his teacher. It is plain that Thomas's teaching differs from Paul's in many matters. For Paul bids us test the spirits whether they are from God, and this can be judged chiefly from doctrines. Thomas writes somewhere that the death of Christ was a sacrifice for the sins committed before him, and that afterwards the offering in the Mass is a sacrifice for the sins that follow.

units.la: Præcipuè etiam confirmauit ἀφτολάτρειαν, cùm Papa Vrbanus Quartus circumgestationem insti-tuerit. Et sunt alia multa tetra eius errata. Ac moles librorum, & uitæ eius breuitas osten-dunt ei defuisse diligentiam, & iudicium. Vixit tantum quinquaginta annos, & scripsit magnos aceruos librorum. Sed apparet, pleraq; ex alijs descripta & consarcinata esse: & oratio non solum squalida est, uerum ita confusa, ut sæpè non intelligatur. Negligentia autem in exponendo, significat temeritatem in pronunciādo. Quare certissimum sit, Paulum ei non tribuisse honorificum illud testimoniū, quod in somnio illo seu fabula narratū est.
units.tr: He especially upheld idolatry [ἀρτολατρεία], when Pope Urban IV instituted the procession of the host (circumgestatio). And there are many other foul errors of his. The sheer bulk of his books and the brevity of his life show that he lacked care and judgement. He lived only fifty years and wrote great heaps of books, but it is apparent that most of them were copied out and patched together from others; and his style is not only crude but so confused that it is often unintelligible. Carelessness in explaining, moreover, signifies rashness in asserting. Hence it is quite certain that Paul did not grant him that honourable testimony which is recounted in that dream or story.

units.la: XXV. Martij. Hoc die Dominus noster Iesus Christus, filius & λόγος æterni Patris, assumpsit humanam naturam in uirginis utero. Eodem die post annos triginta tres, filius Dei Dominus noster Iesus Christus est factus pro nobis uictima in cruce. Dicitur, eodem die creatos esse Adam & Euam: quod potest esse. Et scriptū est, tunc uesperi ambulasse filium Dei in paradiso. Res profectò mirabilis est, quòd Deus nos isto modo voluit saluare: uidelicet misso suo unigenito filio, qui legi satisfaceret. Ita cogitate, hac septimana initiū fuisse mundi: & hodie inchoatis annum mundi 5521. Hæc scire, est diligentia digna homine. nam filius Dei seruauit discrimina dierum: itaq; et nos discendi causa, etiam dierū discrimina cōsideremus. Hæc dicta sunt anno à nato Christo millesimo quingentesimo quinquagesimo nono.
units.tr: 25 March. On this day our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son and Word [λόγος] of the eternal Father, assumed human nature in the womb of the virgin. On the same day thirty-three years later, the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, was made a victim for us on the cross. It is said that Adam and Eve were created on the same day, which may well be so. And it is written that the Son of God then walked in paradise in the evening. Truly it is a wonderful thing that God wished to save us in this way, namely by sending his only-begotten Son, who would satisfy the law. Consider this: the beginning of the world was in this week, and today the year of the world 5521 begins. To know these things is a diligence worthy of a man, for the Son of God observed the distinctions of the days; so we too, for the sake of learning, should consider the distinctions of the days. These things were said in the year after the birth of Christ 1559.

units.la: XXXI. Martij. Vltimus dies Martij, est dies mortis Hieronymi Stridonensis. Dicitur autem Strido, uel Stridonium, ab Istro. Ister autem dicitur, citur, ut ego credo à Germanico Oster, id est Ori-entalis: quia Ister seu Danubius fluit ad Orientem. Sed Strido aliud oppidum est in Istria. Est autem Istria in Illyrico, seu pars Illyrici. Illyricum nomen factum ab Illyri flumine, ubi fuit Strido. Fuit porrò hic Hieronymus ex gente Heneta, seu Vandalica: quæ est antiqua gens, & latè dominatur, sparsaq; est per Illyricum, Poloniā, Russiam, & magnā partem Germaniæ. Ptolemæus inquit: Heneti sunt pars Sarmatarum. Sarmatæ autem, seu Sauromatæ dicuntur à Sar, qui fuit dux exercitus. Ista historica considerate: nam iucundum est.
units.tr: 31 March. The last day of March is the day of the death of Jerome of Stridon. Strido, or Stridonium, is named after the Ister. The Ister, I believe, is called from the German Oster, that is, eastern, because the Ister or Danube flows toward the East. But Strido is another town, in Istria. Istria is in Illyricum, or is part of Illyricum. Illyricum took its name from the river Illyrus, where Strido was. Moreover, this Jerome was of the Heneti, or Vandalic, race: an ancient people which holds wide sway and is scattered through Illyricum, Poland, Russia, and a large part of Germany. Ptolemy says: the Heneti are a part of the Sarmatians. The Sarmatians, or Sauromatians, are said to be named from Sar, who was the leader of an army. Consider these historical matters, for they are pleasant.

units.la: Et pius est patriæ facta referre labor. In oppido Stridone fuit natus hic Hieronymus. Vixit in Italia, ubi didicit Latinam & Græcam linguam: in Asia verò Hebræam. Estq; optimè de Ecclesia meritus, præcipuè illa translatione ex fontibus Hebræis in linguam Latinam. Transtulit enim libros Moysi, Samuelis, Regum, Palipomenon, Prophetarum & Psalmorum. Nostri Psalmi, qui sunt in Biblijs usitati, sunt uersi ex Græco. Credo etiam quod uerterit proverbia Salomonis, Ecclesiasten, & Cantica canticorum: ista est bona uersio. Ita Hieronymus est conseruator linguæ Hebrææ. Si ipsius trans-latio non conseruasset linguam Hebræam, iam nō haberemus eam, et hanc Iudæi à nobis discunt. Fuit igitur doctus Hieronymus, audiuit doctissimos homines, & nauauit ecclesiæ bona operam: ideo de- betis eum magnificere, non contemnere ipsum, sicut aliqui faciunt. Translatio illius magnificien- da est, licet aliquid uetustatis resipiat. Dicat ali- quis: ipse sæpè errauit. An tu nihil erras? hoc non potest fieri in loquendo, ut non interdum impro- prie loquamur, etiā cum singulariter uolumus ef- ferre nostras cogitationes. Homines eloquentissimi & felicissimi, uberrimiq; in dicendo, natura sculpti & facti ad decus eloquentiæ, intelligunt & experiuntur hanc difficultatem. Ideo debemus boni con- sulere lapsus aliquot magnorum hominum, quos nō potest natura hominū cauere. Interdū enim & bonus dormitat Homerus, inquit Horatius. Hic bo- nus senex est mortuus ultimo die Martij, anno ætatis suæ 91. Cogitate eum modestè temperanterq; ui- xisse, cum ad tantam senectutem peruenerit. Cum esset iunior, fuit Romæ. postea Damasci fuit scriba seu notarius, ideo pingitur sicut Cardinalis: quan- quam tunc non fucrit ea Cardinalium dignitas, quæ nunc est. Vixit magis ex beneficijs locupletum ci- uium, quibus respondit ad multas quæstiones, ex sa- cris literis desumptas, quibus itē dedicauit uersio- nes et enarrationes, quàm ex certis redditibus. Est autem mortuus anno à nato Christo 420. Iam itaq; à morte ipsius effluxerūt anni 1130. Vos legite eius uersionem, quæ est bona: cui adiungite postea uice inter-
units.tr: "And it is a pious labour to recount the deeds of one's country." In the town of Strido this Jerome was born. He lived in Italy, where he learned Latin and Greek, and in Asia he learned Hebrew. He has deserved very well of the Church, especially by his translation from the Hebrew sources into Latin. For he translated the books of Moses, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, the Prophets and the Psalms. Our Psalms, which are in common use in the Bibles, were translated from the Greek. I believe he also rendered the Proverbs of Solomon, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs; that is a good version. Thus Jerome is the preserver of the Hebrew language. If his translation had not preserved the Hebrew language, we would no longer have it, and the Jews now learn it from us. Jerome was therefore learned, heard the most learned men, and did the Church good service; so you ought to honour him, not despise him, as some do. His translation is to be honoured, although it savours somewhat of antiquity. Someone will say that he often erred. But do you make no errors? In speaking it cannot be avoided that we sometimes speak improperly, even when we want to express our thoughts exactly. Men most eloquent and fortunate, rich in speech, formed by nature and made for the glory of eloquence, understand and experience this difficulty. Therefore we ought to pardon the slips of some great men, which human nature cannot guard against; for "sometimes even good Homer nods," as Horace says. This good old man died on the last day of March, in the ninety-first year of his age. Consider that he lived modestly and temperately, since he reached such great old age. When he was younger he was at Rome; afterwards, at Damascus, he was a scribe or secretary, and so he is painted like a cardinal, although the dignity of cardinals was then not what it is now. He lived more from the benefactions of wealthy citizens, to whom he replied on many questions drawn from the sacred letters, and to whom he also dedicated his translations and commentaries, than from fixed revenues. He died in the year after the birth of Christ 420, so 1130 years have now passed since his death. Read his translation, which is good, and afterwards add to it, in turn, the

units.la: [Text of a few words at the right edge belongs to the neighbouring page and is not transcribed.] interpretationis Germanicā Lutheri uersionem. Augustinus præcisè decimo anno post eum mortuus est: id est, anno 430. cum esset egressus annum septuagesimum sextum. Mortuus est autem Hieronymus in Bethlee, quò secesserat, ut effugeret multorum sycophantiam: quare procul iuit in Asiam, ibiq; cōsenuit (ego nusquā esse alibi malim, quàm in illo loco) & fuit ibi familiarissimus Epiphanio, cū quo quotidie per literas collocutus est. sæpè etiā solebant conuenire: sicut et ipse Hieronymus dicit, eum sibi fuisse familiarem. Vixit eodem tempore Nazianzenus in Cappadocia, quem Hieronymus dicit se interrogasse, quid sit sabbathum δευτερόπρωτον, quod in Luca est capite sexto. Pono casum, quòd incidisset dies Paschatos in diem sextū, & proximè sequens dies esset sabbathum. illud sabbathum proximū erat δευτερόπρωτον: quia inchoabat septimanam. Hieronymus dicit Nazianzenum sibi respondisse: In concione audies, ibi nō poteris mihi contradicere. Ita per iocum dixit, quod hodie særiò multi imitantur. Fuit enim quidam lepos illorum hominum, in genere fatentium se quædam ignorare: fuit dulcis familiaritas inter illos viros. fuit igitur Hieronymus in Bethleem tanquā in collegio ecclesiastico (wie in eim stifft, ut sunt apud nos) ubi habuit bibliothecam, & fuit instructum rebus necessariis. Hæc dixit Philippus anno 1550.
units.tr: [Text of a few words at the right edge belongs to the neighbouring page and is not transcribed.] German translation of Luther. Augustine died exactly ten years after him, that is, in 430, having passed his seventy-sixth year. Jerome died in Bethlehem, whither he had withdrawn to escape the sycophancy of many; he went far off to Asia and grew old there (I would wish to be nowhere else than in that place), and he was most intimate with Epiphanius, with whom he conversed daily by letter. They also often used to meet, as Jerome himself says, that he had been intimate with him. At the same time Nazianzen lived in Cappadocia, and Jerome says he asked him what the "second-first" sabbath is, which is in Luke chapter six. Suppose the day of Passover fell on the sixth day, and the next day was a sabbath: that sabbath, the one next after, was the "second-first," because it began the week. Jerome says Nazianzen answered him: "You will hear it in the sermon; there you will not be able to contradict me." He said this in jest, which many today imitate in earnest. For there was a certain charm in those men in confessing that they were ignorant of some things, and there was a sweet intimacy between those men. Jerome was therefore in Bethlehem as in an ecclesiastical college (like a Stift, as we have among us), where he had a library and was provided with what he needed. Philippus said this in the year 1550.

units.la: APRILIS.
units.tr: APRIL.

units.la: XXI. Aprilis. Dies est natalis urbis Romæ, seu initium quo inchoata est urbis Romæ conditio, uel quo die sunt eius mœnia extructa, quo tempore fuit festum Paschæ.
units.tr: 21 April. This is the birthday of the city of Rome, or the beginning from which the founding of the city of Rome is reckoned, or the day on which its walls were built. At that time it was the feast of Easter.

units.la: XXIII. Aprilis. Dies est Georgij. Tres sunt equites in cœlo, Georgius, Martinus, & Christus, qui uectus est asino. Dicunt autem Georgium fuisse martyrem Cappadocum, qui locus est in Armenia. Hodie credo Armenios resistere Turcis. Nulla pars Orientis habet ecclesias ordinatas, in quibus hoc tempore plus est studiorum, præter gentem Armeniorum. Armenij enim primo ample xi sunt Euangelium, ita ut aduersarentur Diocletiano & Maxentio, & defenderent pastores contra illos tyrannos. Doctrina etiam quæ nunc est in nostris Ecclesijs, uenit ad eos. Vngarus quidam, qui aliquando fuit in Armenia, dixit, quòd discant ibi Græcam linguam, sicut nostri Latinam in scholis. Illa historia quæ habetur de Georgio, est fabulosa. Vnde autem sint istæ fabulæ de Georgio, Christophoro, Catharina, incertum est. Potest fieri, quòd fuerint inepti imitatores, qui plura affinxerūt stultè, quibus fuerit voluptas sic deludere populum, enumeratis miraculis illorum sanctorum: sicut hodie fit in Italia, ubi habent impurissimas & obscœnas fabulas de Maria, quæ apparuerit monachis. Nostri monachi fuerunt fatui, & asini magna ex parte: sed nihil potest cogitari sceleris, quod nõ sit in Italicis monachis. Christophori fabulam narrat Apollinaris, uir ualde eloquens, & bonus poeta, quod ostendit eius Psalterium lectu ualde iucundum: annumeratur ijs qui suo tempore ualuerũt ingenio. Fuit amicus & coætaneus Basilij, ac Gregorij Nazianzeni. Credo cum adolescentulũ uidisse Côstantinũ. Scripsit autem Christianis multas tragœdias & comœdias, sumpsitq; exempla martyrum, quibus addit poemata. Hoc ideo fecit, quia fuit coætaneus Iuliani Apostatæ Imperatoris, qui prohibuit publico decreto, ne in scholis ethnicis instituerentur Christianorum filij, ubi tradebantur tragœdiæ Euripidis, Sophoclis, & aliorum (Christiani interim cogebantur instituere priuatas scholas) quia sperauerat fore, si non essent eruditi Christiani, extingui doctrinam, et religionem consilescere: sicut et aliud fecit decretum, ne Christiani admitterentur ad honores militiæ, uel togæ. Cogitauit, si nõ haberent potentiam, tunc Christianos nullam habituros esse defensionẽ. Huius Iuliani tempore uixit Apollinaris, qui ut Christiani haberent poemata & exẽpla pia, scripsit cis comœdias, & multa pulchra poemata. Tale fuit Christophori cõmentum. Quia Christophorus significat Ecclesiæ concionatorem, qui debet esse grandi corpore: id est, debet esse for tis, et magnanimus, qui nõ recusét adire periculá. Circumgestat paruũ puerum, id est, Christi doctrinam circumfert: quã ostendit populo, quæ uidetur esse imbecillis. Et magnum pondus immergit illum magnũ gygantem in undas, id est pericula: & circumnatant cum beluæ, id est tyranni. Gerit tamen panem in pera: id est, Deus vult alere concionatores. & senex ipsum præcedit cum lychno in littore, significat uerbum diuinum, & Prophetas monstrantes doctrinam, & exempla: quæ prælucere debeant Christiano concionatori. quòd & alij sancti sæpè similia passi sunt, & patiuntur. Sic Georgij pictura est allegoria ex imitatione Persei facta. Georgius est imago boni principis. γεωργὸς enim significat agricolam. Illa duo sunt opposita inicē, Agricola & tyrannus, seu Turca. Turca significat proprie deuastatorem, quia etiam imperium Turcarum est uastatio. Sed bonus princeps debet esse γεωργὸς, id est agricola, colens, ornans terram & gentes. Princeps diligês in gubernatione, primum curare debet ut iusta imperet, Ecclesias ornet, non nimium expilet populum, eumq; præsidijs legitimis tueatur. Commentū de Georgio sic se habet. Magnus draco iacuit in Libya ante ciuitatem Sileam, iuxta quam erat stagnū instar maris, in quo draco pestifer latitabat, qui sæpè populum contra se armatum in fugam conuerterat, & quàm plurimos ciuitatis inhabitatores accedens ad ciuitatis muros, flatu suo infecerat. Quare ciues compulsi, duas oues quotidie ad sedandū furorem draconi dabant, ne ciuitatis muros inuaderet, & aerē inficeret, unde multi moriebantur. Deficientibus ouibus, initum est consilium, ut draconi unica ouis cum adiuncto homine, quem sors tetigisset, sine ullius hominis respectu, attribueretur. Cum igitur sorte omnium ciuium filij & filiæ draconi darentur, & sors nemini parceret, quadam uice unica filia regis in Libya sorte deprehensa est, & draconi adiudicata. Cum ea iam ad draconem à ciuibus illius loci educeretur, forte Georgius illum locum praeterequitans, audiuit ploratus & lachrimas illius puellæ, filiæ regis: à qua lachrimarum causas inquirit. quibus auditis, iubet puellam forti animo esse: se enim fore ipsius liberatorem. Draco uero iracundia commotus properat, ut & Georgium & puellam deuoret. Cui Georgius cataphractus insistens, celerrimo equi cursu occurrit, eumq; longa hasta transfodit. Sic liberatam filiam regis in urbem, cum omnium ciuium admiratione, reduxit ad parentes: à quibus honorificè exceptus, & apud eos contra suam voluntatem diu retentus est. Cæterum discedens ex Libya, venit in illa loca, ubi Diocletianus, & Maximianus imperabant (quo tempore tanta persecutio fuit Christianorū,
units.tr: 23 April. This is the day of George. There are three knights in the sky: George, Martin, and Christ, who rode on an ass. They say George was a martyr of the Cappadocians, a place in Armenia. Today I believe the Armenians resist the Turks. No part of the East has well-ordered churches where there is more zeal for learning at this time, except the Armenian people. For the Armenians embraced the Gospel very early, so that they opposed Diocletian and Maxentius and defended their ministers against those tyrants. The teaching that is now in our churches has also come to them. A certain Hungarian, who once was in Armenia, said that they learn Greek there, just as ours learn Latin in schools. The story told about George is fabulous. Where these fables about George, Christopher and Catherine came from is uncertain. It may be that foolish imitators, who stupidly added many things, took pleasure in thus deluding the people by enumerating the miracles of those saints, just as today in Italy they have the most impure and obscene tales about Mary, who appeared to monks. Our monks were foolish, and for the most part asses, but no crime can be imagined that is not found among the Italian monks. Apollinaris, a very eloquent man and a good poet, tells the story of Christopher; his Psalter shows that it is very pleasant to read. He is counted among those who in his time excelled in talent. He was a friend and contemporary of Basil and Gregory Nazianzen. I believe he saw Constantine as a young man. He wrote many tragedies and comedies for the Christians, and took examples from the martyrs, to which he added poems. He did this because he was a contemporary of the emperor Julian the Apostate, who by public decree forbade that the sons of Christians be educated in pagan schools, where the tragedies of Euripides, Sophocles and others were taught. (Christians meanwhile were compelled to set up private schools.) Julian had hoped that if Christians were not educated, their doctrine would be extinguished and their religion would wither. He also made another decree, that Christians not be admitted to honours in the military or the civil service. He reasoned that if they had no power, the Christians would then have no defence. In the time of this Julian lived Apollinaris, who, so that Christians might have poems and pious examples, wrote comedies for them, and many fine poems. Such was the fable of Christopher. Christopher signifies a preacher of the Church, who ought to be of great body, that is, ought to be strong and magnanimous, and not refuse to face dangers. He carries a little boy about, that is, he carries about the teaching of Christ, which he shows to the people, though it seems weak. He plunges that great giant, with its great weight, into the waves, that is, the dangers; and beasts, that is, tyrants, swim around him. Yet he carries bread in his wallet: that is, God wishes to feed preachers. The old man goes before him with a lamp on the shore; he signifies the divine word, and the prophets showing the teaching and the examples, which ought to shine before the Christian preacher. Many other saints have also suffered and do suffer similar things. So the picture of George is an allegory made in imitation of Perseus. George is the image of a good prince, for γεωργός [geōrgos] means farmer. The two are opposed to each other, farmer and tyrant, or Turk. "Turk" properly signifies a devastator, because the Turkish empire is also a devastation. But a good prince ought to be a γεωργός [geōrgos], that is, a farmer, cultivating and adorning the land and its peoples. A prince diligent in government ought first to take care that he rules justly, adorns the churches, does not plunder the people too much, and protects them by lawful safeguards. The story about George goes as follows. A great dragon lay in Libya before the city of Sileÿ, beside which was a pool like a sea, in which the deadly dragon lurked. He often put to flight the people who came armed against him, and, approaching the city walls, he infected very many of the inhabitants with his breath. Therefore the citizens, compelled, gave two sheep each day to appease the dragon's fury, so that it would not invade the city walls and infect the air, whence many died. When the sheep ran short, a plan was adopted: a single sheep, with a man added, whom the lot should touch, would be assigned to the dragon, without regard for any person. So when by lot the sons and daughters of all the citizens were given to the dragon, and the lot spared no one, on one occasion the only daughter of the king in Libya was caught by lot and adjudged to the dragon. As she was being led out by the citizens of that place to the dragon, George happened to ride past that place, heard the wailing and tears of the girl, the king's daughter, and asked the cause of her tears. When he had heard them, he bade the girl be of brave spirit, for he would be her deliverer. The dragon, roused to anger, hastened to devour both George and the girl. George, mounted in armour, met him at full gallop and pierced him with a long spear. So he led the king's daughter, now freed, back into the city to her parents, to the admiration of all the citizens. Honourably received by them, he was against his will detained among them for a long time. But departing from Libya, he came to those regions where Diocletian and Maximian ruled (at which time there was such a persecution of Christians,

units.la: ut in spacio unius mensis ultra septendecim milia piorum hominum sint interfecta) ac forte incidit in quedam ipsorum praesidem nomine Datianum, sub quo pio zelo suam confessionem de Trinitate co-tra Ethnica numina edidit. Praeses vero, audiens ta-xari idololatriam Ethnicam, bonum illum Geor-gium capit, & ad martyrium tale ducit. Coniecit ipsum in dolium, in quo fuerunt inter se oppositae falces, & nouaculae, coq; conclusso, deiectus est de excelso monte, ut corpus illis falcibus seu nouaculis lacerarctur. Verum divina clementia fortiorem se in seruando, quam improbi tyranni sunt ad persequendum, ostendit: quae ipsum inter medias falces, tanto cum periculo volutum, incolumem conserua-vit. Tandem vero, edita confessione pia, quamuis antea saepe liberatus ex multis tormentis & afflictionibus, ab eodem praeside Datiano est decollatus. In antiquis seu vetustis templis, Christophori imago foris ad turres depicta videtur: Georgiũ autem intus ad parietes depinxerunt. Quemadmodū enim Christophorus est speculum boni & pij ministri ecclesiae: ita Georgius bonum principem, defensorem iusticiae, & purae doctrinae denotat: quorum hic foris, ille domi & in templis, Ecclesiam tueri & propagare debet. Talis fortunatus & pius iusticiae cultor, sinceraeq; doctrinae propagator fuit in primis Imperator Constantinus, contra tyran-nos nos illos Maxentium, Maximum & Licinium: à quibus, etsi diu uexatus, & multis insidijs odijsq; multiplicib. sæpè fuerit circumuentus: tamē Deus ipsum defendit, & felices euentus inter illas tempestatum turbas concessit.
units.tr: so that within the space of one month more than seventeen thousand pious men were killed), and by chance he fell in with one of their governors named Datianus, before whom he made, with pious zeal, his confession about the Trinity against the pagan deities. The governor, hearing the pagan idolatry condemned, seized that good George and led him to martyrdom of this kind. He threw him into a cask in which sickles and razors had been set against each other; the lid was shut, and it was cast down from a high mountain, so that his body would be torn by those sickles or razors. But divine mercy showed itself stronger in preserving him than the wicked tyrants were in persecuting him: it kept him unharmed amid the sickles, though he was rolled about with such danger. At last, however, having made his pious confession, though he had often before been freed from many torments and afflictions, he was beheaded by the same governor Datianus. In ancient or old churches, the image of Christopher is seen painted outside on the towers, but George they painted inside on the walls. For just as Christopher is the mirror of a good and pious minister of the Church, so George denotes a good prince, defender of justice and of pure doctrine; of these, the one ought to defend and propagate the Church outside, the other at home and in the churches. Such a fortunate and pious worshipper of justice and propagator of pure doctrine was above all the emperor Constantine, against the tyrants Maxentius, Maximus and Licinius. Though he was long harassed, and often surrounded by many plots and hatreds, God defended him and granted him happy outcomes amid those storms of the times.

units.la: COLL. Lectori.
units.tr: To the Reader.

units.la: Hic forte transpositus est dies, quem tu in 24. Aprilis transferto.
units.tr: Perhaps this day has been transposed here by mistake; you should transfer it to 24 April.

units.la: XXIIII. Aprilis. Doctissimus & clarissimus uir Bonifacius Amerbachius legū doctor, professor Academiæ Basiliensis, qui de multorum, præsertim peregrinorum studiosorum studijs bene meritus est, hora secunda Basileæ post meridiem, piè ex hac uita à Christo Saluatore nostro, cui suam animam commendauit, euocatus est, Anno 1562.
units.tr: 24 April. The most learned and distinguished man Bonifacius Amerbach, Doctor of Laws and professor at the Academy of Basel, who did great service to the studies of many students, especially foreigners, was called piously from this life at the second hour after noon at Basel by Christ our Saviour, to whom he commended his soul, in the year 1562.

units.la: MAIVS.
units.tr: MAY.

units.la: I. Maij. Calendis Maij celebratur memoria sanctorū Philippi et Iacobi. Philippus uixit Hierapoli, ueteri urbe Phrygiæ, ubi sunt thermæ: quæ fuit celebris, clara & magna urbs. Ille Apostolus Phrygiensis habitauit ibi cum filiabus & sorore, & circa ea loca concionatus est. Plura non habentur de eo, nisi quòd ibi fregerit idolum, in quo fuit horribilis draco (sicut recitatur) nescio qua ratione. nos nō habemus integras eas historias. De Iacobo plura scribūtur. Iste Iacobus, de quo fit men-tio tio in hoc festo, est minor Iacobus, qui nominatur frater Domini: quia ex sorore natus est, & fuit ei similis. nam & Christus fuit similis suae matri. Credibile est enim fuisse similitudinem sororum. Hic Iacobus fuit filius Alphaei. Alter Iacobus nominatur Maior, cuius memoria in Augusto celebratur, & est filius Zebedaei. Familiae series recitatur propter Euangelij historiam. Maria soror matris Christi fuit nupta initiò Alphaeo, qui habuit ex illa Maria filium Iacobum. Postea Maria fuit nupta Cleophae, ex quo fuit Simeon. Iste verò Iacobus, Minor nominatur, fuit filius Alphaei, qui mansit Episcopus Hierosolymae, ibiq; inter caeteros dixit sententiam in Synodo Apostolorum, Act. 15.
units.tr: 1 May. The memorial of the saints Philip and James is celebrated on the Kalends of May. Philip lived at Hierapolis, an old city of Phrygia where the hot baths are; it was a famous, bright and great city. That Apostle of the Phrygians lived there with his daughters and his sister, and preached in the surrounding places. Nothing more is recorded of him, except that there he broke an idol in which a terrible dragon was (as is told), for some reason I do not know. We do not have those histories in full. More is written about James. This James, who is mentioned in this feast, is the Younger James, who is called the brother of the Lord, because he was born of his mother's sister and was like him, for Christ too was like his mother; it is credible that the sisters had a likeness. This James was the son of Alphaeus. The other James is called the Greater, whose memorial is celebrated in August, and he is the son of Zebedee. The series of the family is recited on account of the history of the Gospel. Mary, the sister of Christ's mother, was first married to Alphaeus, who had by that Mary a son, James. Afterwards Mary was married to Cleophas, by whom she had Simeon. But this James, called the Younger, was the son of Alphaeus; he remained bishop of Jerusalem, and there among the others gave his judgment in the Synod of the Apostles, Acts 15.

units.la: Cogitate in qualia tempora uitae ipsius curriculum post resurrectionem Christi, uel post Pentecosten inciderit. Fuit annos 30 episcopus, et spectator horribilium motuum, quibus iam ruebat Respublica. Decennio post eius mortem, Hierosolyma deleta est. Quando propinqua est periodus seu finis Imperiorum, tunc magnae confusiones, & perturbationes, ut in quolibet corpore multi magni morbi ante interitum, fiunt. Fuerunt assidui motus in urbe Hierosolyma, multae caedes, seditiones, & distractiones factionum, sicut Christus ipse praedicit: Cùm videritis abominationem, desolationis, id est idolum supra arcam propitiatorij: sicut Caligula iusserat collocari suam statuam in Sanctum sanctorum, in cuius statuæ collocatione et defensione plurimæ cædes fiebant. Harum miserabilium calamitatū spectator fuit ille optimus senex Iacobus. Post eum factus est episcopus frater eius uterinus Simeon, qui uixit tempore excidij Hierosolymitani. Postea affectus est extremo supplicio tempore Traiani, cum esset egressus annū ætatis 120. Illum iussit Deus egredi cum Ecclesia ex urbe Hierosolymitana trans Iordanem, ubi seruatus est. Postea euersa urbe reuersi, habitauerunt in ruinis et casulis. Pulchræ sunt imagines, quomodo Deus inter ruinas regnorum & Imperiorum seruet Ecclesiam. Agite gratias Deo, quòd nunc quoq; seruet inter mirabiles ruinas generis humani Ecclesiam. Postea est interfectus Iacobus scelere Pontificum, cùm magistratus Romanus abesset, ac non haberent pontifices ius administrandi gladij: sed illa occasione usus Pontifex, quòd magistratus Romanus abesset, sanctum uirum interfecit. Philippus diu est concionatus ante supplicium: sic Iacobi frater Simeon longo tempore postea interfectus est, fraude cognatorum Iudæorum. Multa monet nos de generibus doctrinæ historia sanctorum. Postea ostendit testimonia conseruationis Ecclesiæ. Quid aliàs est pulchrius cognitione historiarum? Tenebræ sunt in tota uita, sine luce historiarum Apostolicarum. Primò ab illis discamus doctrinam : sciamus quid docuerint, sicut facit Iacobus, qui pronunciat sententiam in synodo Hierosolymitana. Credimus purificari corda, &c. Secundò cogitemus, quibus temporib. uixerint, & quàm mirabiliter Deus colligat Ecclesiam: imò nõ solum colligat, sed etiam protegat atq; defendat.
units.tr: Consider in what times the course of his life fell, after the resurrection of Christ or after Pentecost. He was bishop for thirty years, and a witness of the dreadful upheavals by which the commonwealth was already collapsing. Ten years after his death, Jerusalem was destroyed. When the end or final period of empires is near, then great confusions and disturbances arise, just as in any body many severe illnesses occur before death. There were constant uprisings in the city of Jerusalem, many slaughters, seditions and divisions of factions, just as Christ himself foretold: "When you see the abomination of desolation," that is, the idol above the mercy seat, as Caligula had ordered his own statue to be set up in the Holy of Holies, and in the setting up and defence of that statue very many slaughters took place. That excellent old man James was a witness of these miserable calamities. After him his uterine brother Simeon was made bishop, who lived at the time of the destruction of Jerusalem. Afterwards he was subjected to the extreme punishment in the time of Trajan, when he was 120 years old. God commanded him to leave the city of Jerusalem with the Church across the Jordan, where he was kept safe. Afterwards, when the city was overthrown, they returned and lived among the ruins and in huts. Beautiful are these images of how God preserves the Church amid the ruins of kingdoms and empires. Give thanks to God that even now he preserves the Church amid the wonderful ruins of the human race. Afterwards James was killed by the crime of the Pontiffs, when the Roman magistrate was absent and the priests did not have the right to administer the sword; the Pontiff took advantage of that occasion, because the Roman magistrate was away, and put the holy man to death. Philip preached for a long time before his punishment; likewise James's brother Simeon was afterwards killed for a long time by the treachery of his Jewish kinsmen. The history of the saints warns us of many kinds of teaching. Afterwards it shows the testimonies of the preservation of the Church. What is more beautiful to know than history? Without the light of the Apostolic histories, the whole of life is darkness. First, let us learn doctrine from them: let us know what they taught, as James does, who pronounces his judgment in the Synod of Jerusalem: "We believe that hearts are purified," etc. Secondly, let us consider in what times they lived, and how wonderfully God gathers the Church; indeed he not only gathers it, but also protects and defends it.

units.la: V. Maij. Est dies ascensionis Domini nostri Iesu Christi in cœlum: numerando ab eo paschate, quo resurrexit Christus ad hunc diem. Nam 25. Martij passus est, 27. Martij resurrexit: numerando 40. dies usq; ad hunc 5 diem: tunc est dies ueræ ascensionis Domini. Cogitate quale seculũ fuerit: quid mirabilius factum in omni tempore mundi, quàm quæ facta sunt in illis 40 diebus? Illa omnia familiarius facta sunt, quàm descripta: quia Apostoli nõ voluerunt omnia describere. Cogitabát enim fore, ut gentes deriderent, uel ethnici illa subsannarent: ideò maluerunt breuiter significare magnitudinem illarum rerum.
units.tr: 5 May. It is the day of the ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ into heaven, counting from that Passover on which Christ rose to this day. For he suffered on 25 March and rose on 27 March; counting forty days up to this fifth day, that is the day of the true ascension of the Lord. Consider what a season it was: what more wonderful thing has happened in all time than what happened in those forty days? All those things were done more familiarly than they were described, because the Apostles did not wish to describe everything; for they thought the Gentiles would mock, or the heathen would scoff at those things, and so they preferred to indicate briefly the greatness of those events.

units.la: XVII. Maij. Noe cum sua familia ingressus est in arcam, & sunt anni ab initio mundi quo ingressus est in arcam, usq; ad hunc quinquagesimũ quartũ 3860. Fuit igitur præcisè in arca annum integrũ. Sed interroget aliquis, quomodo congruit cũ 10. dieb. quòd fuerit in arca integrũ annũ. Respondeo: Adduntur decem dies illi, quia prima ætas distinxit annum in 12 menses lunares. Illi non complent, & congruunt ad integram periodum solis: sed oportet addi decem dies (qui uocantur epactæ) ad menses lunares.
units.tr: 17 May. Noah with his family entered the ark, and from the beginning of the world, when he entered the ark, to this fifty-fourth year there are 3860 years. He was therefore in the ark exactly one whole year. But someone may ask how this agrees with the ten days, given that he was in the ark a full year. I answer: those ten days are added, because the first age divided the year into twelve lunar months. These do not complete and agree with the full period of the sun, but ten days (which are called epacts) must be added to the lunar months.

units.la: XXIX. Maij. Est dies captæ Constantinopolis. Historia insignis, & sæpè cogitāda: cùm dies nos admoneat, necesse est eius facere mentionem.
units.tr: XXIX. May. It is the day on which Constantinople was taken. It is a notable event and one that deserves frequent thought. Since the day reminds us of it, it is right that I mention it.

units.la: Hodie sunt anni 104 ab eius captiuitatis tempore. Est enim capta urbs anno Christi 1453. Celebris urbs, opportunissimo loco sita: & quanquam destructa est, cùm fuisset cincta obsidione trienni, tamē instaurata est propter opportunitatem loci. Et lingua Heneta ferè usq; ad Constantinopolim in usu est. Est autem sita in Thracia, ad Hellespontum. Adhuc hodie credo eam omnium urbium pulcherrimam esse: etiamsi Turci non studen ornare ista eripia, tamen sunt pulchra. Ideò Constantinus suo quodā fatali impetu fecit arcem Imperij. Inde potuit traduci exercitus in Asiam, & in reliquam Europam, Pannoniā, & Italiam: fuit locus opportunissimus, & est uberrima regio.
units.tr: Today it is 104 years since the city was captured, for it was taken in the year of Christ 1453. It was a famous city, set in a most advantageous place. Although it was destroyed after a three-year siege, it was restored because of the convenience of its site. The Venetian language is spoken almost as far as Constantinople. It lies in Thrace, on the Hellespont. I still believe it is the most beautiful of all cities today, even though the Turks, who do not trouble to adorn such things, have not made it so. Constantine therefore, by some fated impulse, made it the citadel of the empire. From there armies could be carried into Asia and the rest of Europe, into Pannonia and Italy. It was a most suitable place, and the region is very fertile.

units.la: Antea dicta est Byzantium, ualde clara & potens urbs ante Romana Imperia: aliàs fuit Lacedæmoniorum socia, aliàs Atheniensium, & multæres ibi gestæ sunt. Anaxilaus tenuit Byzantium nomine Lacedæmoniorum, & Athenienses obsidebant eam. Ille, cùm fames grassaretur in urbe, & multi perirent fame, me, fecit deditionem urbis. Quæstũ est, an recte se cisset, sicut idẽ accidit in obsidiõe arcis Blassēburg. interrogaui quēdã, an habuisset ulterius uictualia? Respõdit mihi, ipsos nihil habuisse nisi pauxillum panis, quo uno mēse uix potuissēt retineri. Nõ sece rũt cõtra fidē datā, q fecerũt deditionē. Cõtrà capi tanē debet anteferre defensionē arcis suæ uitæ: Er go nõ debet se dedere, propter aliorũ morbos uel famē. Respõdeo ad antecedēs: Capitaneus debet an teferre defensionē arcis aut ciuitatis, scilicet tã diu, donec cum natura non est bellum: sed quãdo cum natura est bellum, tunc non contra fidem datam fa cit. Fuerũt aũt anni ııı8 ab instauratiõe facta, usq; adhãc postremã illius urbis sub Turcis captiuitatē. Stetit ergo illa urbs, et habuit Imperatores tã lõgo tēpore, q diu stetit urbs Roma. A Romulo usq; ad Totilã sunt anni ııoo. Hæc cõsiderare prodest ad id, ut expauecscamus cogitatiõe iræ Dei: et cõsidere mus, utcũq; stātes et florētes urbes in bono regimi ne, et floreti statu, esse magnũ beneficiũ Dei. sicut fuit magnũ beneficiũ, q doctrina religionis aliquo modo cõseruata est in ista urbe tã lõgo tēpore. Po stea cõsiderãda uenit horribilis ira, q Deus destru xit illã urbem, sicut Hierosolymã, et alias, propter luxũ & insignia peccata. Esaias dicit: Iniquitates nostræ ut uenti dissipauerunt nos. Est regula cõmu nis de ruinis imperiorũ: Propter iniquitates cor ripis homines, inquit Psalmus. Trucidatus est ipse Imperator Cõstãtinus, raptæ sunt honestissimæ matronæ. Dicũt iã in Liuonia maiorẽ sæuitiã exerceri, q̃ Turcæ exercuerũt. Propter peccata populi multæ principũ mutationes, inquit Salomõ. Peccata sunt causæ magnarũ & horribiliũ mutationũ. Fortasse hoc etiã fuit fatale. Arrius ibi mortuus est, sedẽs in latrina, effuditq; intestina. Iam Machometica pestis est ibi, quasi stercus Arrij. Turca delet doctrinas & leges diuinas: ipsi habẽt suas leges, utiles ad retinendos milites utcunq;: sed domestica disciplina nulla est; omnia sunt plena turpitudinis & crudelitatis. Dicũt, quando Turca dat in Vngaria puellæ donũ, & illa accipit, tũc cogitur esse eius coiunx. Ipsi namq; ducũt quotquot uolũt coiuges, & abijciũt quot & quãdo uolũt. hoc nõ est coniugiũ. Post illud exiliũ, eãq; uastatione Cõstãtinopolis, restitutæ sunt doctrinæ in Italia per exules Græcos, qui intulerũt eruditionẽ in Italiã, inde in Germaniã: ut audiuistis sæpè ex narratione Capnionis, qui missus fuerat legatus Romã. Multum prodest ad excitãda studia doctrinarũ, cognitio Græcæ linguæ: quia Latina est admodum manca sine Græca. Oẽs artes sunt Græcè scriptæ: Doctrina Apostolorũ habet fontes Græcos. Vetera testimonia et certamina ecclesiæ fuerũt Græcè scripta: sic Mathemata, Medicina. Narrãt Rudolfum Agricolam suisse motũ ut proficisceretur in Italiã, & audiret TheoTheodorum Gazam: quia uidebat se Aristotelem non posse intelligere, nisi legeret ipsum in fontib. Hæc anno 1559. recitata sunt.
units.tr: Formerly it was called Byzantium, a very renowned and powerful city even before the Roman empires. At one time it was an ally of the Spartans, at another of the Athenians, and many deeds were done there. Anaxilaus held Byzantium on behalf of the Spartans, and the Athenians besieged it. When famine raged in the city and many were dying of hunger, he surrendered the city. It has been asked whether he acted rightly, as happened also at the siege of the fortress of Blassenburg. I asked a certain man whether they had had any further provisions. He replied that they had had nothing but a little bread, which could scarcely have sustained them for a single month. They did not act against the faith given when they surrendered. Against this, one might argue that a commander ought to prefer the defence of his fortress to his own life; therefore he ought not to surrender on account of others' sickness or famine. I answer the antecedent: a commander ought to prefer the defence of the fortress or city, namely for as long as there is no war with nature; but when there is war with nature, then he does not act against the faith given. There were 1118 years from the restoration until the final capture of that city under the Turks. That city therefore stood, and had emperors for as long a time as the city of Rome stood. From Romulus to Totila there are 1100 years. It is useful to consider these things so that we may be struck with awe at the thought of God's wrath, and so that we may consider that cities which stand and flourish under good government and in a prosperous state are a great blessing of God, just as it was a great blessing that the doctrine of religion was in some measure preserved in that city for so long a time. Afterwards there comes to mind the dreadful wrath by which God destroyed that city, as He did Jerusalem and others, on account of luxury and notorious sins. Isaiah says: "Our iniquities, like winds, have scattered us." It is a common rule concerning the ruin of empires: "For iniquities thou dost chastise men," says the Psalm. The emperor Constantine himself was slain, and the most honourable matrons were carried off. It is said that in Livonia greater cruelty is now practised than the Turks practised. "On account of the sins of the people, many changes of rulers," says Solomon. Sins are the causes of great and dreadful upheavals. Perhaps this too was fated. Arius died there, sitting on the latrine, and his bowels gushed out. Now the Mohammedan plague is there, like the dung of Arius. The Turk destroys doctrines and divine laws; they have their own laws, useful in some measure for keeping soldiers in line, but there is no domestic discipline; everything is full of filth and cruelty. It is said that when a Turk gives a girl as a gift in Hungary and she accepts it, she is compelled to become his wife. For they take as many wives as they wish, and cast them off whenever and as many as they please. This is not marriage. After that exile and devastation of Constantinople, learning was restored in Italy through Greek exiles, who brought scholarship into Italy, and from there into Germany, as you have often heard from the account of Capnion, who had been sent as an envoy to Rome. The knowledge of the Greek language is very helpful for arousing studies of the disciplines, because Latin is quite deficient without Greek. All the arts are written in Greek; the doctrine of the Apostles has Greek sources. The ancient testimonies and controversies of the Church were written in Greek; so too mathematics and medicine. They relate that Rudolf Agricola was moved to go to Italy and hear Theodorus Gaza, because he saw that he could not understand Aristotle unless he read him in the sources. These things were recited in the year 1559.

units.la: IVNIVS.
units.tr: JUNE.

units.la: V. Iunij. Est dies Leuctricæ pugnæ, in qua Lacedæmonij sunt uicti, & fractæ sunt turres & potentia Spartanorum, ita ut semper in posterum urbs Spartana oppressa, et in seruitute fuerit. Memorabilis est historia, propter manifestam libidinum pœnam. Duo nobiles adolescentes profecti sunt ad Delphos, & in itinere hospitio sunt excepti ab Scedaso, habitante in Leucris, ibiq; eius filias sollicitarunt ad stuprum. quæ refragatæ sunt: sed reucrtentes, ui eas stuprarunt, absente patre: dissectasq; in frusta, in puteum proiecerunt. Pater uero, cognita iniuria, miser proficiscitur Spartam, et hos adolescentes nobiles illius notoriæ iniuriæ accusat. Derisus est autem senex ab Ephoris, unde in summo mærore urbem egrediens, diras inhabitatoribus imprecatur. Cum uero Magistratus nollet punire illa scelera, Deus atrociter puniuit. Quia oraculum etiā dixit: Ero memor filiarum Scedasi. Paulo post Lacedæmonij in illo ipso loco ab Epaminunda uincuntur, ita ut tota ipsorum potentia labefactaretur: quam nunquam recuperarunt.
units.tr: 5 June. This is the day of the battle of Leuctra, in which the Lacedaemonians were defeated, their towers were broken down, and the power of the Spartans was crushed, so that from then on the city of Sparta was always oppressed and remained in servitude. The story is memorable for the clear punishment of lust. Two noble young men set out for Delphi, and on the journey they were received as guests by Scedasus, who lived in Leuctra. There they tried to seduce his daughters. The girls resisted, but when the young men came back in their father's absence, they raped them by force, then cut the girls into pieces and threw them into a well. The father, on learning of the outrage, went wretchedly to Sparta and accused these noble young men of the notorious wrong. But the old man was mocked by the Ephors, so, in deep grief, he left the city and called down curses on its inhabitants. When the magistrates refused to punish these crimes, God punished them terribly. The oracle had also said: "I will remember the daughters of Scedasus." Shortly afterwards, the Lacedaemonians were defeated by Epaminondas in that very place, so that the whole of their power was overthrown, and they never recovered it.

units.la: VI. Iunij. Est dies natalis Alexandri Magni, filij Philippi, regis Macedonis, qui cœpit regnare gnare post Cyrum, et post reductionem populi ex Babylone, cùm essent exacti anni ducenti. Initium regni Alexandri Macedonici fuit certò Olympiade centesima undecima, sicut omnes historici cõsentientes narrãt, anno mundi 3628. Regnauit annos duodecim: mortuus est ante natale Christi, 324 annis, ætatis suæ anno 33. Fuit Alexander Heraclides, ab Hercule paterno genere: materno autem genere fuit Aeacides. Mater eius fuit Olympias, regina Epiri, à rege Molossorum oriunda: pulcherrima & nobilissima familia, quæ fuit in Græcia. Frangitur Alexãder voluptatibus, cùm iam esset victor orbis terrarum, vino & ebrietate extinguitur, relinquens bella ducibus, & orbem terrarum inter certamina ferè annos ducentos, donec Romani rursus cõstituerunt monarchiam. Obseruatione dignum est, quòd Alexandrum nemo uicerit dimicando, sed vincitur & capitur voluptatibus: sicut dicitur de regibus Macedonibus, quòd sint pardi.
units.tr: 6 June. This is the birthday of Alexander the Great, son of Philip, king of the Macedonians, who began to reign after Cyrus, and after the return of the people from Babylon, when two hundred years had been completed. The beginning of the reign of Alexander of Macedon was certainly in the hundred and eleventh Olympiad, as all the historians agree, in the year of the world 3628. He reigned twelve years and died 324 years before the birth of Christ, in the thirty-third year of his age. Alexander was a Heraclid on his father's side, and on his mother's side an Aeacid. His mother was Olympias, queen of Epirus, descended from the king of the Molossians, a most beautiful and noble family in Greece. Alexander was broken by pleasures when he was already master of the world; he was extinguished by wine and drunkenness, leaving his wars to his generals, and the world for about two hundred years in strife, until the Romans again established a monarchy. It is worth noting that no one defeated Alexander in battle, but he was conquered and captured by pleasures; and so it is said of the Macedonian kings that they are leopards.

units.la: XXIX. Iunij.
units.tr: 29 June.

units.la: Anno 1555. magnæ fuerunt tempestates: quia sol eo tempore fuit in Asellis, qui immediatè cient tempestates. Fingunt fabulam poetæ, Titanes bella voluisse inferre Dijs: sed territos esse clamore Asellorum, ut desisterent ab incepto: propter quod beneficium relati sunt inter sidera Aselli. Hanc fabulam memētote, propter similitudinem: quia cùm impij putant se maximè victi ros, tunc terrentur clamore asinorum.
units.tr: In the year 1555 there were great storms, because the sun was then in the Asses, which immediately stir up tempests. The poets feign a fable that the Titans wished to make war on the gods, but were frightened away by the braying of the Asses, so that they gave up their undertaking; and for this service the Asses were placed among the stars. Remember this fable for its likeness: when the impious think they are most certainly victorious, then they are terrified by the braying of asses.

units.la: XXV. Iunij. Hodie est annus 1476.
units.tr: XXV. June. Today is the year 1476.

units.la: quando postridie est facta pugna Merspurgensis, ubi Heimricus Quartus uicit Rodolfum, magno prælio, qui fuerat electus Imperator contra eum. In illis bellis ciuilibus attrita est Germania, eiusq; potentia concidit, cùm esset tunc in excubijs pro salute generis humani. Illæ duæ partes robustissimæ dimicarunt. Saxonica fuit coniuncta cum Sueuis & Bohemis, ex una parte: Belgica uerò, & Francica potentia ex altera: ipsiq; duces fuerunt consobrini. Rudolfo præcisa est manus in acie. cùm ductus esset Merspurgum, prolata manu, dixit ad episcopos: Videte, ista est mea manus, qua Imperatori iuraui. Papa enim excitauerat Rodolfum contra Imperatorem. (Et sic Pontifices moliti sunt multa mala, ut omnibus temporibus turbarent imperiū) quia Pontifex non voluit tribui episcopatus à nostris Imperatoribus, sicuti tribuuntur à rege Gallico. Illa eadem consuetudo fuit in Germania, ut non fieret translatio constitutionis à Pontifice. Inde bella orta sunt. Saxones ingeniosi homines, auersati sunt Imperatore. Quanquam uerum est: nostri Imperatores abutebantur quoq; illa potestate transferendi episcopatus. Papa igitur misit Rodolfo coronam, cui inscriptum erat: Petra dedit Petro, Petrus diadema Rodolfo. Petra, id est Christus, dedit Petro, id est Episcopo, eam potestatem imperij: & Petrus, id est Romanus pontifex, dat tibi Rodolfo diadema, id est coronationem imperij. Postea ille idem Heimricus, qui tunc fuit victor, fugatus est à filio: et ille filius qui vicit patrē, magno prælio postea à Saxonibus vincitur. Hæc anno 1556 narrata sunt.
units.tr: On the day after the battle of Merseburg, in which Henry IV, in a great battle, defeated Rudolf, who had been elected emperor against him. In those civil wars Germany was worn down and its power collapsed, though it was then standing guard for the safety of the human race. The two most robust sides fought. On one side the Saxon power was joined with the Swabians and Bohemians; on the other stood the Belgian and French power. The leaders themselves were cousins. Rudolf had his hand cut off in the battle. When he was carried to Merseburg, he held up the hand and said to the bishops: "See, this is my hand, with which I swore allegiance to the emperor." The Pope had stirred Rudolf up against the emperor, and in this way the Pontiffs have devised many evils to disturb the empire at every period, because the Pope would not allow bishoprics to be conferred by our emperors, as they are conferred by the king of France. In Germany the custom was that the transfer of a bishopric was not made by the Pope. From this wars arose. The Saxons, clever men, turned away from the emperor. Yet it is true that our emperors also abused that power of conferring bishoprics. So the Pope sent Rudolf a crown inscribed with the words: "The Rock gave to Peter, Peter gives the diadem to Rudolf." The Rock, that is Christ, gave to Peter, that is to the bishop, that power over the empire; and Peter, that is the Roman pontiff, gives to you, Rudolf, the diadem, that is the coronation as emperor. Afterwards that same Henry, who had then been victor, was put to flight by his son, and that son who had defeated his father was later himself defeated in a great battle by the Saxons. These things were recounted in the year 1556.

units.la: XXVIII. Iunij. Est dies mortis Alexandri, qui potatione & ebrietate nimia, facta apud calumniatorē Medeam, moriebatur. Ita Deus puniuit eius blasphemias. A morte Alexandri usque ad natū Christum, sunt anni 324. Illud tempus bene mementote, propter historias.
units.tr: XXVIII. June. It is the day of the death of Alexander, who died after excessive drinking and drunkenness at the house of the slanderer Medea. Thus God punished his blasphemies. From the death of Alexander to the birth of Christ there are 324 years. Remember that period well, because of the histories.

units.la: IVLIVS.
units.tr: JULY.

units.la: VII. Iulij. Est dies pugnæ ad Chero-neam, ubi admodum acre & insigne commissum est prælium. Fuit autem ea pugna Philippi, patris Alexandri, in qua vicit Thebanam civitatem: ubi fuit victor, non ipse, sed potius filius eius Alexander, qui tunc erat natus annos viginti. Eo die mutatum est imperium Græcorum, & Græcia venit in servitutem, regesq; Macedonici creverunt. Philippus natus annos 45, paulo post interfectus est, ac dedit poenas libidinum. Alexander 12 annos regnavit, & vixit 33.
units.tr: 7 July. This is the day of the battle at Chaeronea, where a very fierce and notable engagement was fought. That battle was Philip's, the father of Alexander, and in it he defeated the city of Thebes. The victor, however, was not Philip himself but rather his son Alexander, who was then twenty years old. On that day the rule of the Greeks was overturned, Greece came into servitude, and the kings of Macedon grew in power. Philip was forty-five years old when he was born, and not long afterwards he was killed and paid the penalty for his lusts. Alexander reigned for twelve years and lived to thirty-three.

units.la: ggg ✶ bbb
units.tr: ggg ✶ bbb

units.la: XII. Iulij. Est dies natalis Iulij Cæsa-ris. Et sunt à natali Christi usq; ad hunc 54 annum, 1652 anni: quia 42 anno Augusti natus est Christus. Iulius interfectus est anno ætatis suæ 56. ea nondū erat senectus: sed adhuc integro corpore, & quasi iuuenilibus uiribus præditus erat. In homine nam-que mediocri ætas sexagenaria est adhuc uigens. Interfectus est autem ab ijs quos seruauerat, ut cla-maret: Me'ne seruasse, ut essent qui me perderent?
units.tr: 12 July. This is the birthday of Julius Caesar. From the birth of Christ to this 54th year there are 1652 years, because Christ was born in the 42nd year of Augustus. Julius was killed in the 56th year of his age. That was not yet old age; he still had a sound body and was endowed with almost youthful strength. For an ordinary man, sixty years is still a vigorous age. He was killed by those whom he had spared, and as he died he cried out: "Did I spare them only so that there would be those who would destroy me?"

units.la: COLLECTOR. Lectori.
units.tr: THE COLLECTOR. To the Reader.

units.la: Tibi etiam Erasmi Roterodami Epitaphium ex-hibeo, quòd in tumulo ipsius marmoreo Basileæ in summo templo his uerbis incisum legitur.
units.tr: I also offer you the epitaph of Erasmus of Rotterdam, which is read carved with these words on his marble tomb in the main church at Basel.

units.la: CHRISTO SALVA-tori S.
units.tr: TO CHRIST THE SAVIOUR, S.

units.la: DES. ERASMO ROTERODA-MO, VIRO OMNIBVS MODIS MA-XIMO, CVIVS INCOMPARABI-LEM IN OMNI DISCIPLINARVM GENERE ERVDITIONEM, PARI CONIVNCTAM PRVDENTIA, PO-STERI ET ADMIRABVNTVR, ET PRAEDICABVNT: BONIFACIVS AMERBACHIVS, HIER. FROBE-NIVS, NIC. EPISCOPIVS, HAERES,
units.tr: To Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam, a man great in every respect, whose incomparable learning in every branch of knowledge, joined with equal prudence, posterity marvels at and proclaims. Bonifacius Amerbach, Hieronymus Froben, and Nicolaus Episcopius, his heirs,

units.la: ET NVNCVPATI SVPREMAE SVAE VOLVNTATIS VINDICES, PATRONO OPTIMO, NON MEMORIAE, QVAM IMMORTALEM SIBI EDITIS LVCVBRATIONIBVS COMPARAVIT, IIS TANTISPER DVM ORBIS TERRARVM STABIT, SVPERFVTVRO, AC ERVDITIS VBIQVE GENTIVM COLLOQVVTVRO, SED CORPORIS MORTALIS, QVO RECONDITVM SIT, ERGO, HOC SAXVM POSVERE. MORTVVS EST IIII. EID. IVL. IAM SEPTVAGENARIVS, ANNO A CHRISTO NATO M. D. XXXVI.
units.tr: and now the guardians of his last will, have set up this stone to their best patron.
