It is not for his memory, which he has won for himself through his immortal publications, and which will survive as long as the world stands and will speak to learned men everywhere among the nations, but for his mortal body, in which he lies hidden. He died on the fourth day before the Ides of July, already seventy years old, in the year of Christ 1536.

units.la: Lapidi, sub quo conditus iacet, hæc insculpta sunt:
units.tr: The following is engraved on the stone under which he lies:

units.la: ERASMVM ROTERODAMVM AMICI SVB HOC SAXO CONDE BANT, QVARTO EIDVS IVLIAS: ANNO M. D. XXXVI.
units.tr: THE FRIENDS BURIED ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM UNDER THIS STONE, ON THE FOURTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF JULY, IN THE YEAR 1536.

units.la: XIIII. Iulij. Dies est, quo celebratur memoria Heimrici Bambergensis, qui est fundator episcopatus Libusiani. Gesit etiam res utiles & salutares: uocaturq; Sanctus Heinricus, pius uir. Otto Primus habuit fratrem Heimricum, ex fami-lia lia Saxonica, quem fecit ducem Bauariæ. Frater Heimricus Auceps (illum alias historici nominant Heinricŭ Humilē) fuit præstantissimus uir, fecit Imperatorem Ottonem filium minorem natu. Sic ueteres imitati sunt exemplum Davidis.
units.tr: July 14. It is the day on which the memory of Henry of Bamberg is celebrated, the founder of the bishopric of Libusia. He also did useful and salutary things, and is called Saint Henry, a pious man. Otto the First had a brother Henry, of the Saxon family, whom he made duke of Bavaria. Brother Henry the Fowler (otherwise the historians call him Henry the Humble) was an outstanding man, and he made the Emperor Otto, his younger son, emperor. Thus the ancients imitated the example of David.

units.la: Porrò hic Otto Primus, rursus fecit Imperatorem minorem natu, eo quòd frater, & filius maior ipsi fuerint rebelles, & regnum appetiuerint.tamē frater factus est ei supplex, quem fecit Ducem Bauariæ. Tunc Bauariæ Ducatus fuit à Bombergâ usq; ad Aquileiā: fuit regnum non contemnendum. Illius Heimrici filius fuit Heimricus Rixosus, rebellis Ottoni Secundo, & longo tempore fuit Treuiri in exilio, usq; ad mortem Ottonis Secundi. Eo mortuo, Otto Tertius adhuc erat paruulus, qui fuit natus patre Saxone, & matre Græca. Heimricus aūt Rixosus, cùm esset potentissimus princeps, & agnatus adolescenti, Ottonem Tertium custodiuit, uolens imuadere Imperium. Sed impediuerunt Principes, qui fuerant apud Ottonem Secundum.
units.tr: Moreover, this Otto the First again made the younger son emperor, because his brother and his elder son had been rebels and had sought the kingdom. Yet the brother became a suppliant to him, and he made him duke of Bavaria. The duchy of Bavaria then extended from Bamberg as far as Aquileia; it was no small kingdom. The son of that Henry was Henry the Quarrelsome, a rebel against Otto the Second, and for a long time he was in exile at Trier, until the death of Otto the Second. When he died, Otto the Third was still a little boy, born of a Saxon father and a Greek mother. Henry the Quarrelsome, however, being a very powerful prince and a kinsman of the young man, kept Otto the Third in custody, wanting to seize the empire. But the princes who had been with Otto the Second prevented him.

units.la: Post mortem Ottonis Tertij fuit filius istius Heimrici Rixosi, Heimricus Claudus, qui est Bombergensis, instituitq; collegium canonicorum Bombergensium & Libusiensiū. Otto autē Tertius primus Imperator factus est iuxta formas electionis: qa fuit sapientissimus princeps, atq; adeò, ut dictus sit mirabilia mundi. Mortis autem causam amores ipsi præbuerunt. buerũt. Romæ enim cœperat quondā qui affectaue rat imperiũ, & impositũ eʃ asino, auersa facie cir cũuexit per urbẽ, et deinde ipsum intersecit. Postea uerò illius intersecti à se cõiugẽ amauit, quæ præ buit ei uenenũ quo cõsumptus est. ita fit, ut dicitur: Luxuriant animi rebus plerunq; secundis:
units.tr: After the death of Otto the Third, the son of that Henry the Quarrelsome was Henry the Lame, who is of Bamberg, and who founded the college of canons of Bamberg and Libusia. Otto the Third was made emperor first, according to the forms of election, because he was a most wise prince, so much so that he was called the wonder of the world. The cause of his death was love affairs. For at Rome a certain man who had aspired to the empire was once put on an ass, face turned backwards, and carried through the city, and then killed. Afterwards Otto loved the wife of the man he had killed, and she gave him poison, by which he was consumed. So it happens, as it is said: Minds luxuriate, for the most part in prosperous circumstances;

units.la: Non facile est æqua commoda mente pati.
units.tr: It is not easy to bear equal fortunes with a calm mind.

units.la: Quare autem Heimricus Bombergensis dictus sit Heimricus Claudus, diuersæ sunt opiniones. Quì-dam alludentes ad historiam Iacobi, scribunt, quòd aduenerit angelus qui eum claudicare fecerit.
units.tr: Why Henry of Bamberg was called Henry the Lame, opinions differ. Some, alluding to the story of Jacob, write that an angel came and made him limp.

units.la: Sed uera est hæc historia, quæ recitatur in episcopi Mersburgensis Chronico, q suit ipsius cõsiliari. Idē dicit etiā fuisse tantā sapientiā & præstantiā ingenij Ottonis Tertij, ut diceretur Mirabilia mũdi. De Heimrico Aucupe narrat hãc historiã, quòd in Italia ex improuiso fuerit circumuentus & imuasus, ut oportuerit eũ desilire ex hospitio, ex quo præcipiti saltu luxauerit coxã, ac inde postea claudicauerit. Hic aureũ calicẽ Mersburgũ attulit, qui in proximo bello ante duodecim annos liquatus, & inter milites distributus est. Ita Heimricus Bombergensis pacauit Germaniã, tumultuantib. quibusdã princi pibus ab altera parte, incitatis à Brunone, qui fuit insolẽs canonicus Augustanus, cui in inferiori Ger mania magna fuerũt certamina cũ Balduino. Illus certamẽ idẽ Heimricus Bõbergẽsis etiã cõposuit, et coegit eum ad obsequium, ut fieret ipsi supplex. Ex Italia expulit Græcos & Sarracenos. Ita tenuit pacatam Italiam, Germaniam & Vngariam. Habuit coniugem Kunigundam, quæ fuit ex Palatina familia, ex stirpe Caroli. Huic mortuæ factus est lapis, cui inscriptum est tale Epitaphium: Kunigund pecc atrix, huius loci dominatrix, obijt anno, &c. Posita sunt etiam & alia carmina addita. Sic antiquitas solet esse modesta, & plena gravitatis: noluit inscribi regina, sed amauit ὁμιοτέλευτα. Scribunt eam uenisse in suspicionem apud uirum, quòd amaret alium: sed ipsa purgauit se, incedens super ferrum ignitum. Potest esse: quia antiquitas habuit maiora uincula disciplinæ, quæ iam sunt abolita. Tunc fuit florens imperium, quando Heinricus Bambergensis dedit suam sororem in coniugem regi Vngarico Stephano, qui prius baptizatus est. Ita fuerunt coniuncta connubio Germania & Vngaria, & utrunq; regnum floruit: & fuerunt tanquam unum regnum, Vngaricum, Germanicum & Polonicum. Videtis quid iam fiat, Vngaria uastatur à Turcis, & fiunt postea accessiones ad nos. fortasse erunt initia, paucis annis elapsis.
units.tr: But the true account is this, which is related in the Chronicle of the bishop of Merseburg, who was his counsellor. He also says that Otto the Third had such wisdom and such excellence of talent that he was called the wonder of the world. Of Henry the Fowler he tells this story: that in Italy he was suddenly surrounded and attacked, so that he had to leap down from his lodging, and by that headlong jump he dislocated his hip, and afterwards limped. He brought the golden chalice to Merseburg, which was melted down in the recent war twelve years ago and distributed among the soldiers. Thus Henry of Bamberg pacified Germany, while some princes on the other side were stirred up, incited by Bruno, an insolent canon of Augsburg, who had great struggles in Lower Germany with Baldwin. The same Henry of Bamberg also settled that dispute and compelled him to obedience, so that he became his suppliant. He expelled the Greeks and Saracens from Italy. Thus he kept Italy, Germany and Hungary at peace. He had as his wife Kunigunde, who was of the Palatine family, of the stock of Charles. When she died, a stone was made for her, on which this epitaph was inscribed: "Kunigund the sinner, mistress of this place, died in the year, etc." Other verses were also added. So antiquity tends to be modest and full of gravity: it did not want to be inscribed as queen, but it loved homoioteleuta. They write that she fell under suspicion with her husband, because she was loving another; but she cleared herself by walking over red-hot iron. It may be so, because antiquity had greater bonds of discipline, which are now abolished. The empire was then flourishing, when Henry of Bamberg gave his sister in marriage to the Hungarian king Stephen, who had first been baptized. Thus Germany and Hungary were joined by marriage, and both kingdoms flourished, and they were as one kingdom, Hungarian, German and Polish. You see what is happening now: Hungary is laid waste by the Turks, and afterwards there are additions to us. Perhaps these will be beginnings, after a few years have passed.

units.la: XVII. Iulij. Est dies confractarum Tabularum, cum Moses ex monte Sinai rediret ad populum Israeliticum, & propter idololatriam uituli aurei tabulas digito Dei scriptas frangeret. Est igitur significatum, quòd nostra natura non seruet legem. Lex data erat, et postea Moses abiecit Tabulas. Simul significatum est, quòd propter idololatriam ille populus sit amissurus legem & politiã. Ante natũ Christum sunt anni 1582. Non existimo tëpus illud finitæ politiæ Mosaicæ longius futurũ esse, quàm quod fuerit stantis politiæ tëpus. Igitur nos nõ procul à fine mũdi abesse, certò statuamus.
units.tr: July 17. It is the day of the broken Tables, when Moses, coming down from Mount Sinai to the Israelite people, broke the tables written by the finger of God because of the idolatry of the golden calf. It is therefore signified that our nature does not keep the law. The law was given, and afterwards Moses threw down the tables. At the same time it is signified that, on account of idolatry, that people was going to lose the law and its polity. Before Christ was born there are 1582 years. I do not think that the time until the end of the Mosaic polity will be longer than the time the polity stood. Therefore let us firmly hold that we are not far from the end of the world.

units.la: XVIII. Iulij. Est dies mortis Gottefridi Bilionei, qui mortuus est anno 1100. Fuit rex Hierosolymæ. quãdo uiginti duo reges pinguntur, tunc etiam ipse inseritur. Ille Gottefridus fuit Capitaneus Heimrici Imperatoris. Dicunt Roma capta, ipsum ægrotum fecisse uotum, quòd non uellet interesse illis ciuilibus bellis. Duxit exercitũ in Asiã, & intra triennium ex Asia repulit Saracenos, & adiunxit sibi Guelsum Ducem Bauariæ. Coronatus est spinea corona rex Hierosolymæ omnium suffragijs, imposito capite in Christi sepulchrũ, quod adhuc extat. Natus est ex illa familia, ex qua sunt principes Iuliacenses & Cliuenses.
units.tr: July 18. It is the day of the death of Godfrey of Bouillon, who died in 1100. He was king of Jerusalem. When twenty-two kings are painted, he too is included. That Godfrey was captain under the emperor Henry. They say that when Rome was taken, he, being sick, made a vow that he would not take part in those civil wars. He led an army into Asia, and within three years drove the Saracens out of Asia, and joined to himself Welf, Duke of Bavaria. By the votes of all he was crowned king of Jerusalem with a crown of thorns, his head having been placed on Christ's sepulchre, which still stands. He was born of that family from which the princes of Jülich and Cleves are descended.

units.la: AVGVSTVS.
units.tr: AUGUST.

units.la: III, Augusti. Dies est pugnæ Mardonij ad Plateas. Is Mardonius fuit capitaneus & cognatus Xerxis, fuitq; incitator & hortator Xerxi ad bellum, ac unus ex magnis principibus in Persia. promiserat Xerxi se magna & multa effecturum {ɛ}turũ esse in Græcia. Xerxes enim mouit bellũ cõtra regulã diuinã: Qui gladiũ acceperit, gladio peribit. Cùm iam fugisset Xerxes in Asiam, cœpit amare cõingẽ fratris, quẽ interfecit. Sed postea ipse quoq; interfectus & cõsõjssus est. Ita peccata peccatis puniũtur. Mardonius fuit amarus index & terribilis tyrãnus, perijt in acie ad Plateas, & cum eo decẽ milia Persicorũ militũ, circiter sesquimiliare à Thebis. Victo Mirdonij exercitu, Græci postea facti sunt insolentiores, & nõ secerũt sicut Pausanias, qui post uictoriã non fuit insolens, sed modestissimus: remisit nobilem matronam honestissimam & pulcherrimam ad suos parentes. Cùm Aeginetæ dicerent, ut faceret crudeliora: Satis, inquit, est, si meis Spartanis placeo. Postea Byzantij indulsit uoluptatibus, quæ ipsi fuerunt exitio. Fuit illa pugna ad Plateas omnium maxima, gloriosissima & nobilissima Græcorum. Sunt autem illius pugnæ Mirdonij ad Plateas anni ante natũ Christum 527, id est, usq; ad hunc diem 2081 anni. Hæc dicta sunt anno 1554.
units.tr: 3 August. The day of the battle of Mardonius at Plataea. Mardonius was a captain and kinsman of Xerxes, and he was the one who urged and encouraged Xerxes to war, and one of the great princes of Persia. He had promised Xerxes that he would accomplish great and many things in Greece. Xerxes, however, began a war against the divine rule: "He who takes the sword will perish by the sword." When Xerxes had already fled into Asia, he began to lust after his brother's wife, whom he then killed. But afterwards he himself was also killed and punished. So sins are punished by sins. Mardonius was a bitter accuser and a terrible tyrant. He perished in battle at Plataea, and with him ten thousand Persian soldiers, about a mile and a half from Thebes. After Mardonius's army was defeated, the Greeks became more insolent, and they did not act as Pausanias did. Pausanias, after the victory, was not insolent but most modest: he sent a noble matron, most honourable and most beautiful, back to her parents. When the Aeginetans told him to act more cruelly, he said: "It is enough if I please my Spartans." Later the Byzantines indulged in pleasures, and these were their ruin. That battle at Plataea was the greatest, most glorious and most noble of the Greeks. The battle of Mardonius at Plataea took place 527 years before the birth of Christ, that is, 2081 years up to this day. These things were said in the year 1554.

units.la: VI. Augusti.
units.tr: 6 August.

units.la: Est dies pugnæ Marathoniæ, ubi Hippias adduxerat magnũ exercitũ Persicum, scilicet 10000. cùm essent 11000 in exercitu Atheniesiũ & Platæensiũ. Fuit aũt hæc causa belli: Atheniẽses expulerãt tyrannũ Hippiã. Is ascendit ad regem Darium, impulitq; eum eò, ut committeret ret exercitum, ad se restituendum.
units.tr: It is the day of the battle of Marathon, where Hippias had brought a great Persian army, namely 10,000, when the Athenians and Plataeans had 11,000 in their army. The cause of the war was this: the Athenians had expelled the tyrant Hippias. He went up to King Darius and persuaded him to send an army to restore him.

units.la: Fuit ne Atheniensibus causa iusta pellendi tyrannum? Hippias est e ciuitate eiectus, quod rapuerat filiam ciuis cuiusdam. Paternus dolor armauit ciuem, ut se coniungeret cum quibusdam, & expelleret tyrannum.
units.tr: Was there a just cause for the Athenians to drive out the tyrant? Hippias was thrown out of the city because he had raped the daughter of a certain citizen. A father's grief armed the citizen, so that he joined with some others and drove out the tyrant.

units.la: Respondeo, quod fuerit iusta causa pellendi, quod probatur etiam hoc argumento.
units.tr: I answer that there was a just cause for driving him out, which is also proved by this argument.

units.la: Contra uiolentiam notoriam defensio, imo etiam poena, est iusta, praesertim in paterno animo.
units.tr: Defence, and indeed punishment, is just against manifest violence, especially in a father's heart.

units.la: Ille pater aduersus notoriam iniuriam coepit arma, cum defensionis, tum poenae causa.
units.tr: That father took up arms against a manifest injury, both for the sake of defence and for the sake of punishment.

units.la: Ergo ille ciuis, & adiuuantes ipsum, recte fecerunt expellentes Hippiam ex urbe.
units.tr: Therefore that citizen and those who helped him acted rightly in expelling Hippias from the city.

units.la: Idem sextus dies Augusti est etiam dies victoriae Hunniadis. Iam vero est centesimus decimus annus ab eo, quo Hunniades, pater Mathiae regis, praestantissimus Ducum postremae aetatis, uicit illum fortissimum & gloriosissimum Imperatorem Turcicum Machometum, qui coperat Constantinopolim, & in illa pugna in qua fuit victus, accepto vulnere fugit, ita ut desperarent de vita ipsius, sed tamen convaluit.
units.tr: The same sixth day of August is also the day of Hunyadi's victory. It is now the 110th year since Hunyadi, father of King Matthias, the most outstanding of the commanders of the last age, defeated that most brave and most glorious Turkish emperor, Mahomet, who had captured Constantinople. In that battle, in which he was defeated, Mahomet was wounded and fled, so that they despaired of his life, but he nevertheless recovered.

units.la: X. Augusti. Est dies Laurentij. Illa eius virtus est manifestissimum opus Dei, & testimonium praesentiae Dei in Ecclesia. Pingitur enim Laurentius, torrefiens & assans in craticula.
units.tr: 10 August. It is the day of Laurence. That virtue of his is the most manifest work of God and a testimony of God's presence in the Church. For Laurence is depicted roasting and broiling on a gridiron.

units.la: Hanc historiam debetis scire: quia homo sine histo-ria multa habet impedimenta, & magnæ sunt tene-bræ nescire historiam. Ideo uetustas distribuit tem-pora in festos dies, ut possit iuuentus commonefie-ri, nō de inuocatione, sed de cōfessione Sanctorum. Alius aliam habuit occasionem, quanquam unam habuerunt Apostoli confessionem: ut Ioannes non est interfectus propter doctrinam, sed quòd repre-hendit incestum Herodis cum Herodiade. Laurentius fuit ciuis Romanus, natus Romæ, & diaconus. Illa uestis, in qua pingitur, est sagum Romanum. Fuit autem diaconus illo tempore, & custos ærarij ecclesiastici. Quanquam illi erat docti, & simul aliquos docebant: tamen diaconum nominabant, qui habebat curationem ærarij ac reditu[?]um: ut in tali urbe habuerunt locupletissimam Ecclesiam, sicut Marcellinus scribit, qui uixit circa ea tempo-ra: dicitq; ijs temporibus fuisse ambitiosam conten-tionem de episcopatu. Passus est autem Laurentius sub Decio Imperatore, ante Cōstantinum regnan-te. Tunc fuit multum tumultuum, & occidebantur nobilissimi homines, ita ut imperium facilius mu-taretur. Ducebātur pij homines ex Gallia in Asiā, & ex Asia Lugdunum, ut ibi afficerentur supplí-cio, & trucidarētur. Occasio autem interfecti Lau-rentij hæc fuit: Imperator petiuit ab ipso, tanquam diacono & custode, sibi dari thesaurū ecclesiastici ærarij.hunc cùm nollet dare, rapitur ad suppliciũ. Quæro an debuerit potius perdere pecuniā, quàm vitam?ut si incideres in latronem, qui à te posceret pecuniam, aut tibi eripere vellet vitam, utrum esses facturus? Hîc teneamus gradus bonorum. Maius malum magis vitandum, quàm minus malum. maius malum est amissio vitæ, quàm pecuniæ Ergo debemus pecuniam magis amittere, quàm vitā. Tu debes quidem notoriam iniuriam repellere: & si potes repellere istos latrones, iustè facis. sed si sis imbecillior, debes dare pecuniam. Cùm igitur iacet Laurentius in craticula, dicit ad carnificem: Ego iam ab uno latere satis sum assatus: inuerte igitur me, ut & ex alio latere æqualiter coquar. Tanta fuit magnitudo animi in cruciatu.
units.tr: You ought to know this history, because a man without history has many hindrances, and great is the darkness of not knowing history. Therefore antiquity distributed the times into feast days, so that youth might be reminded not of invocation but of the confession of the saints. Each had a different occasion, though the apostles had one confession: John, for example, was not killed on account of his doctrine, but because he rebuked the incest of Herod with Herodias. Laurence was a Roman citizen, born in Rome, and a deacon. The garment in which he is painted is a Roman sagum. He was then a deacon and keeper of the church treasury. Although such men were learned and at the same time taught some people, they nevertheless were called deacons if they had charge of the treasury and revenues. In such a city they had a very wealthy church, as Marcellinus writes, who lived around those times, and he says that in those times there was an ambitious contention over the episcopate. Laurence suffered under the emperor Decius, before Constantine reigned. Then there was much turmoil, and the most noble men were killed, so that the empire might change hands more easily. Pious men were led from Gaul into Asia, and from Asia to Lyons, to be punished and slaughtered there. The occasion of Laurence's death was this: the emperor asked him, as deacon and custodian, to hand over to him the treasure of the church. When Laurence refused to give it, he was dragged off to punishment. I ask whether he ought rather to have lost money than his life? Suppose you fell into a robber who demanded money from you, or wanted to take your life: what would you do? Here let us keep the order of goods. A greater evil is to be avoided more than a lesser evil. The loss of life is a greater evil than the loss of money. Therefore we ought to lose money rather than life. Indeed you ought to repel a manifest injury, and if you can repel those robbers, you do right; but if you are weaker, you ought to give up the money. So when Laurence lay on the gridiron, he said to the executioner: "I am now roasted enough on one side; turn me over, so that I may be cooked evenly on the other side." Such was the greatness of his spirit in torment.

units.la: Contrà, quòd Laurentius nō rectè fecerit, sic arguo. Omnia sunt regū. Decius erat rex. Ergo Laurentius debuit ei cedere, et dicere domino: Tu es dominus, accipe claues, & aufer quantū vis. Respondeo: Nego maiorem. Non omnia sunt regum, iuxta præceptum verissimum, obligans omnes homines, tam superiores quàm inferiores: Non furtum facies. Quando magistratus superior postulat tuam tunicam, necesse est ei dari? Non, quia tua est: & sic de aliis. Quādo Achab postulat vineā Naboth, Naboth rectè fecit, nō cedens de suo iure: quia Decalogus tam obligat reges, principes, & alios magistratus, gistratus, quàm nos subditos. Non omnia sunt regum: quia Deus uult esse distinctionē dominio-rum. & Ioannes dicit: Estote contenti stipendijs ue-stris, & non plus exigite.
units.tr: On the contrary, that Laurence did not act rightly, I argue thus. All things belong to kings. Decius was king. Therefore Laurence ought to have yielded to him and said to the lord: "You are lord, take the keys and take away as much as you wish." I answer: I deny the major premise. Not all things belong to kings, according to the most true precept, which binds all men, superiors as well as inferiors: "You shall not steal." When a higher magistrate demands your tunic, is it necessary to give it to him? No, because it is yours; and so with other things. When Ahab demanded Naboth's vineyard, Naboth acted rightly in not yielding his right, because the Decalogue binds kings, princes and other magistrates no less than us subjects. Not all things belong to kings, because God wills that there be a distinction of lordships. And John says: "Be content with your wages," and do not demand more.

units.la: Alia solutio eiusdem argumenti.
units.tr: Another solution to the same argument.

units.la: Omnia sunt regum, uidelicet certo ordine, tan-quam legis: ut quādo lis est de re, tunc res est legis: pronunciat lex, Ego tibi hanc rem attribuo. Vel, Omnia sunt Imperatoris, tanquam iudicis, uel tan-quam legis, ut pronunciet cuius sit res, & faciat executionem. Vt uxor tua, domus tua, non est prin-cipis, sed tamē princeps debet tueri tuam domum, & uxorem. Sic Iurisconsulti respondent: Rex est dominus omnium, quo ad defensionem attinet. Est facilior solutio, quàm cùm dico, lex est iudex. Non enim debet iudicare sicut leo in distributione par-tium. Laurētius rectè fecit, quòd desenderit pos-sessionem bonorum Ecclesiasticorum. Bona Ec-clesiæ non sunt regum: sed reges debent esse defen-sores Ecclesiæ, corporum & bonorum. Princeps debet tueri nos in scholis docentes & discentes, ac defendere pastores, fiscum, &c. Quando dicebatur Ambrosio, ut egrederetur è templo, quando Ar-riani uolebant occupare templum Mediolani, & obijceret ei, Omnia sunt regum, tūc dixit: Domus mea domus precationis est, terram autem dedit fi-lijs hominum, ut alibi habetur.
units.tr: All things belong to the kings, that is, in a certain order, as by law: so that when there is a dispute over a thing, then the thing belongs to the law; the law pronounces, "I assign this thing to you." Or, all things belong to the Emperor, as judge, or as law, so that he may pronounce whose the thing is and carry out the execution. Your wife and your house are not the prince's, yet the prince ought to protect your house and your wife. So the jurists answer: The king is lord of all, as far as defence is concerned. This solution is easier than saying, "The law is judge," for the law should not judge like a lion in the division of shares. Laurentius acted rightly in defending the possession of the Church's goods. The goods of the Church are not the kings', but kings ought to be defenders of the Church, of its persons and its goods. The prince ought to protect us who teach and learn in the schools, and to defend the ministers, the treasury, and so on. When Ambrose was told to leave the church, when the Arians wanted to seize the church at Milan, and they objected to him, "All things belong to the kings," then he said: "My house is a house of prayer," and "the earth he has given to the sons of men," as is said elsewhere.

units.la: Contrà, si incideres in latrones, cogentes te, ac Minicentes[?]: Promitte nobis 100 Ioachimicos, aut te occidemus: non'ne potius amitteres pecuniam quàm uitam? Certè minus malum est magis eligendum. Pecuniam amittere est minus malum, quàm concedere uitam. Ergo Laurentius debuit potius concedere pecuniam, quàm uitam.
units.tr: On the other side: suppose you fell among robbers who forced you and threatened you: "Promise us 100 Joachimsthalers, or we will kill you." Would you not rather lose the money than your life? Surely the lesser evil is the one to be chosen. To lose money is a lesser evil than to yield up one's life. Therefore Laurentius ought rather to have yielded the money than his life.

units.la: Respondeo ad minorem: Cedere pecuniam erat minus malum, sed non depositam, uel publicam, data tam seu commendatam tuae fidei, ut tu sis pecuniae custos, & praesertim Ecclesiae, de illa non debes cedere. Obseruate solutiones concinnas, ut hic fuit simul casus confessionis. non est raptus ad supplicium propterea solum, quòd pecuniam nolebat concedere, sed etiam quia Christianus erat. Est usitatum hominibus malis, aliam causam ostendere, & aliud reipsa agere. iuxta prouerbiu: ὁ διὰ ποδὸς ἁμάρτημα ἐν χορείᾳ[?]: id est, plectimur non propter pedis erratum in chorea. Qui cupiditatem vindictae in aliquo explere desiderant, longè aliam causam facinoris sui praetexunt, atq; intus in animo celatae gerunt. Et ille Laurentius, ut homo Romanus, debuit aliquid Romana magnitudine animi facere.
units.tr: I answer to the minor premise: to yield money was the lesser evil, but not money deposited, or public money, or money entrusted to your faith, so that you are its guardian, and especially the Church's; from that you must not give way. Notice the neat solutions: here there was at the same time a case of confession. He was not dragged to punishment merely because he refused to hand over the money, but also because he was a Christian. It is customary for wicked men to show one cause and in fact do another, according to the proverb: ὁ διὰ ποδὸς ἁμάρτημα ἐν χορείᾳ [the fault of the foot in the dance], that is, we are punished not for a misstep in the dance. Those who wish to satisfy a lust for revenge put forward a quite different cause for their crime, while keeping their real purpose hidden in their hearts. And that Laurentius, as a Roman, ought to have done something with Roman greatness of spirit.

units.la: Item alio modo argumentor.
units.tr: Likewise I argue in another way.

units.la: Maxima fortitudo minus timet. In Christo est maior fortitudo, quàm in Laurentio. Ergo debet minus timere: cùm tamē appareat, Christum esse in tanta consternatione, ut sanguine sudauerit, dixeritq; ipse: Tristis est anima mea usq; ad mortem. Est talis agon in eo, qualis non fuit in ullo homine. In Laurentio est illa celsitudo animi sicut simile exemplum habetis in historijs de Sabina, muliere Romana: quae cum esset in carcere inclusa propter Euangelij confessionem, peperit, & often dit signa doloris, admodum uociferans propter ingetes dolores partus. Lictor ad eam dicit: Quid tu imbecillo animo es? quomodo cras ad supplicium producenda, poteris perferre supplicium, si non potes ferre dolores partus? Respondit, ut magnanima in confessione mulier: Nunc patior ut mulier, secundum naturam: cras patiar ut Christiana.
units.tr: The greatest courage fears less. In Christ there is greater courage than in Laurentius. Therefore he ought to fear less; yet it appears that Christ was in such dismay that he sweated blood, and he himself said: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death." Such a struggle was in him as was in no other man. In Laurentius there is that loftiness of spirit; you have a similar example in the histories of Sabina, a Roman woman, who, shut up in prison on account of her confession of the Gospel, gave birth, and uttered signs of pain, crying out loudly because of the great pains of childbirth. The lictor said to her: "Why are you so weak-spirited? How will you be able to endure the punishment tomorrow, when you are led out to execution, if you cannot bear the pains of childbirth?" She replied, like a woman of great spirit in confession: "Now I suffer as a woman, according to nature; tomorrow I shall suffer as a Christian."

units.la: Respondeo ad argumentum, & ad maiorem: Maxima fortitudo minus timet, scilicet caeteris paribus: id est, cum paria sustinet. Nuper illa mulier misera (haec dicta sunt anno 1559.) de qua sumptu est supplicium in Belga (sicut est necessaria severitas in talibus sceleribus) erat valde animosa: nebulo autem qui eam deceperat, fuit fracto animo. Deus confirmauit eam, ut quae erat decepta ab altero: at ille erat conscius maiorum scelerum, ad id, quod simul incestum commiserat. Declaro minorem: In Christo est maxima fortitudo. Ergo debuisset minus dolere, si non habuisset plura onera quam Laurentius. Quae onera maiora habuit Christus quam quàm Laurentius? Respondeo: Christus patitur propter tua, & mea, & singulorum peccata. Homo quisq; cogitat solùm de se. At Christus deriuat horribilem iram Dei, propter mea, tua, & singulorum peccata in sese: id est, sensit iram Dei aduersus peccata totius generis humani. habet obiectũ infinito maius, quàm Laurētius. Laurentius non patitur propter peccata, sed propter confessionem ueritatis gloriosissimè, iuxta uersiculum: Frangit & attollit uires in milite causa: Quæ nisi iusta subest, excutit arma pudor. Itē: Est aliquid magnis crimen abesse malis.
units.tr: I answer the argument, and the major premise: the greatest courage fears less, namely, other things being equal, that is, when it bears equal burdens. Recently that wretched woman (these things were said in the year 1559), who was executed in Belgium (as severity is necessary in such crimes), was very spirited, but the scoundrel who had deceived her was broken in spirit. God strengthened her, since she had been deceived by another; but he was conscious of greater crimes, in addition to the incest he had committed at the same time. I prove the minor premise: in Christ there is the greatest courage. Therefore he ought to have felt less pain, if he had not had heavier burdens than Laurentius. What greater burdens did Christ have than Laurentius? I answer: Christ suffers on account of your sins, and mine, and the sins of each one. Each man thinks only of himself. But Christ bore in himself the terrible wrath of God on account of my sins, your sins, and the sins of each one: that is, he felt the wrath of God against the sins of the whole human race. He had an object infinitely greater than Laurentius. Laurentius did not suffer on account of sins, but on account of his most glorious confession of the truth, according to the little verse: "A cause breaks and lifts up the strength of the soldier; unless it is just, shame shakes off his arms." Likewise: "It is something to be free from great crimes."

units.la: Laurētius nō uidet peccata, sed ea texit Deus, iuxta dictum Psalmi: Beati quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates, & quorum tecta sunt peccata. Non cerni peccata, est hilari esse animo, iuxta uersum Bembi: Ibat ouans animi, & spe sua damna leuabat.
units.tr: Laurentius does not see sins, but God has covered them, according to the saying of the Psalm: "Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered." Not to see sins is to be of a cheerful mind, according to the verse of Bembo: "He went joyfully, and by his hope lightened his losses."

units.la: Illa argumenta commonefaciunt nos de multis magnis rebus: & illud est celebrare festa Sanctorum, ut uos discatis historias Ecclesiæ necessarias, & simul multas res utiles. Non dico inuocandum esse Laurentium: sumantur ex historijs exempla & doctrinæ.
units.tr: Those arguments remind us of many great matters; and it is to celebrate the feasts of the saints so that you may learn the histories of the Church, which are necessary, and at the same time many useful things. I do not say that Laurentius should be invoked; let examples and doctrine be taken from the histories.

units.la: Eodem die sancti Laurētij, iniectus est ignis in templum Hierosolymitanum, & inflammatũ est templum, postea urbis incendia & uastationes du rauerunt usq; ad Decembrem. Fuerunt in ea urbe magna ædificia, quæ non ita subitò conslagrata sunt: sed in Septembri omnino deleta est urbs.
units.tr: On the same day as St. Laurence, fire was thrown into the temple at Jerusalem, and the temple was set on fire; afterwards fires and devastations of the city continued until December. There were great buildings in that city, which were not burned so suddenly; but in September the city was entirely destroyed.

units.la: Obseruatum autem est, eundem diem inflam- mati templi sub Tito esse, qui fuerat dies destru- ctionis sub Nabuchodonosor: & illa inflammatio sub Nabuchodonosor antecessit annos 617. intra illos sexcentos annos sæpe capta est: fuit bis cap- pa, & non ui expugnata, sed dolo, ac in ea omnia hostilia facta sub Antiocho. Illa direptio uel sæ- uitia quàm exercuit Antiochus, non fuit minor quàm si tota urbs esset deleta. Et ualde mirum est, quòd illi præstantissimi duces Alexander & Iu- lius præterierunt, eam urbem intactam relinquen- tes: sed texerunt Hierosolymam, & nulla in re eam uiolarunt. Alexander cùm accessisset, procef sit ei obuiam Pontifex: tunc Alexander descendit statim de equo, & Pontificem adorauit.
units.tr: It has been observed, moreover, that the same day on which the temple was set on fire under Titus was the day of destruction under Nebuchadnezzar; and that burning under Nebuchadnezzar came 617 years earlier. Within those six hundred years it was often captured: it was taken twice, and not stormed by force but by trickery, and everything hostile was done in it under Antiochus. The plunder and the cruelties which Antiochus practised were no less than if the whole city had been destroyed. And it is very remarkable that those most excellent leaders, Alexander and Julius, passed by, leaving that city untouched; they spared Jerusalem and violated it in no respect. When Alexander drew near, the High Priest came out to meet him; then Alexander at once dismounted from his horse and worshipped the High Priest.

units.la: Ochus ante Darium proximus, magnam sæ- uitiam exercuit aduersus Iudæos.
units.tr: Ochus, the next after Darius, exercised great cruelty against the Jews.

units.la: Titus cùm prius in Iudæa multa oppida solo æquassset, primùm coepit obsidere Hierosolymam in Pascha te, & illa obsidio fuit semestris, seu sex mē- sium. Interea, cùm ibi esset maxima hominum mul- titudo, multi famæ perierunt: maxima pars coxit filios, quibus tamen frui non potuerunt, sed suns eis erepti. Durauit autem ista obsidio usq; ad Septembrem: id est, festum tabernaculorum. Pascha fuit tempus, quando Israelitæ ingressi sunt in terram trans Iordanem. Festum tabernaculorum tale fuit, in quo Deo agerent gratias, quòd eis & patribus ipsorum tradidisset certam & durabilem Ecclesiæ sedem. Ita sub Tito in festo Tabernaculorum, domus & sedes delentur, & tabernacula Hierosolymæ eripiuntur. Illa urbs Hierosolyma, quæ hodie est, non est collocata in ucteri loco, sed ab eo aliquantulum recessit, ubi prius fuit. Nec Roma est hodie, ubi olim fuit: illa pars, quæ olim ornatissima & frequentissima erat, hodie est solitudo: sicut de multis urbibus accidit, quæ etiamsi instauratæ sunt, tamen non in eodem vestigio collocatæ sunt, in quo prius fuerunt. Vt Basilea, Ratisbona, instaurate non in priore sede, sed in reliquijs: sicut & Massilia (quæ iuxta historias est una de laudatissimis urbibus) non est rursus ædificata in priori loco, &c.
units.tr: Titus, having previously levelled many towns in Judea to the ground, first began to besiege Jerusalem at Passover, and that siege lasted half a year, or six months. Meanwhile, since there was a very great multitude of people there, many perished of famine; the greater part cooked their sons, of whom however they could not enjoy the use, since they were snatched from them. But this siege lasted until September, that is, the feast of tabernacles. Passover was the time when the Israelites entered the land beyond the Jordan. The feast of tabernacles was such that in it they gave thanks to God, because he had given to them and to their fathers a sure and lasting seat for the Church. So under Titus, at the feast of Tabernacles, the house and seat are destroyed, and the tabernacles of Jerusalem are snatched away. That city of Jerusalem which exists today is not placed on the old site, but has withdrawn somewhat from the place where it formerly was. Nor is Rome today where it once was: that part which once was most adorned and most crowded is now a wilderness; as has happened to many cities, which, even if they have been restored, nevertheless were not placed on the same footprint on which they formerly stood. As Basel and Regensburg were restored, not on their former site, but on the ruins; and Marseilles too (which according to the histories is one of the most praised cities) was not built again in its former place, and so on.

units.la: XV. Augusti. Festum assumptionis Mariæ.
units.tr: 15 August. The Feast of the Assumption of Mary.

units.la: Mortua est Maria quinquagesimo nono suæ ætatis anno. Vixisse igitur existimatur annos septem, postquam filius ex morte reuixit. Post eius mortem grassata est fames in Asia & Europa, & in Iudæa multi ciues seditionibus sunt interfecti. terfecti. Præcipua uero pars Ecclesiæ Antiochiam migrauit.
units.tr: Mary died in the fifty-ninth year of her age. It is therefore thought that she lived seven years after her son rose from the dead. After her death famine spread through Asia and Europe, and in Judea many citizens were killed in uprisings. The greater part of the Church, however, migrated to Antioch.

units.la: XX. Augusti. Deletio Thebarum.
units.tr: 20 August. The destruction of Thebes.

units.la: Hoc die sunt deletæ Thebæ ab Alexandro, & sunt ultra triginta milia hominũ interfecta: quia ibi fuit magna turpitudo uariorum scelerũ, ideo tam horribilis destructio secuta fuit. Thebæ sunt deletæ anno regni Alexandri 12. Ab initio regni Alexandri ad natum Christum sunt anni 336. Ergo ab hoc anno 1559. ad Thebas deletas, sunt anni 1883. & ad initiũ regni Alexãdri, anni 1895. Factum est decretum, si qui uellent resistere potentiæ Alexãdri, & magnis exercitibus, ut consu gerent ad Thebas: tamen illa ciuitas fuit misetrabiliter capta & deleta. Quis condidit Thebas? Fabius. Illa uastatio & deletio mirabilis Thebarum, est illustre testimonium iræ Dei aduersus peccata generis humani.
units.tr: On this day Thebes was destroyed by Alexander, and more than thirty thousand men were killed, because there was great depravity and a variety of crimes there, and so such a terrible destruction followed. Thebes was destroyed in the twelfth year of Alexander's reign. From the beginning of Alexander's reign to the birth of Christ are 336 years. So from this year 1559 back to the destruction of Thebes is 1883 years, and back to the beginning of Alexander's reign, 1895 years. A decree was issued that if any wished to resist the power of Alexander with great armies, they should gather at Thebes; nevertheless that city was wretchedly captured and destroyed. Who founded Thebes? Fabius. That wonderful devastation and destruction of Thebes is a notable witness of God's wrath against the sins of the human race.

units.la: XXVI. Augusti. Pugna ad Arbelas.
units.tr: 26 August. The battle at Arbela.

units.la: Anno sexto post destructionem Thebarum facta est pugna ad Arbelas. Sunt iam anni 1901. Osee 10. capite fit mentio Arbelarum, in nostris libris habemus: Sicut uastatus est Salman à domo eius, qui uindicauit Baal. Nemo intelligit, quid textus uelit. Totus ille locus est mendosus. PræPrædicit ibi interitum Samariæ: sicut Salman, id est Salmanasar, euertit Arbeel, sic etiā destruet Bethel. Sicut sunt factæ horribiles uastationes in Asia & Græcia per Turcos & alios, sic haud dubiè fient horribiles uastationes in Europa ante finem mundi. Sic tamen dicit Deus, Quid tibi faciā? delebo te sicut Adama & Seboim? non faciam furorē iræ meæ: quia Deus ego sum. Valet consequentia à proprio, quia Dei est misereri, uel misericordiam miscere pœnæ. Item: In ira misericordiæ recordaberis. Quare recordatur misericordiæ erga Ecclesiam? Respondeo: Quia homo non posset sustinere iudicium & iram diuinam. Valet igitur consequentia ab impossibili. Ideo clamamus: Domine, si iniquitates obseruaueris, quis sustinebit? Item: Domine, ne in furore arguas me. Sic inquit Deus: Non faciā furorem iræ meæ: (est dulcis consolatio) quia Deus ego sum. Deus propter multas causas uoluit illas historias scribi, & proponi illa spectacula, et in primis ut reuocet nos ad pœnitentiā. Hæc anno 1559. enarrata sunt.
units.tr: In the sixth year after the destruction of Thebes the battle at Arbela took place. It is now 1901 years. Hosea chapter 10 mentions Arbela; in our books we have: "As Salman was laid waste from his house, who avenged Baal." No one understands what the text means; that whole passage is corrupt. There he foretells the ruin of Samaria: just as Salman, that is Shalmaneser, overthrew Arbel, so he will also destroy Bethel. Just as dreadful devastations have been wrought in Asia and Greece by the Turks and others, so without doubt dreadful devastations will come upon Europe before the end of the world. Yet God says thus: "What shall I do to you? Shall I destroy you as Admah and Zeboiim? I will not execute the fury of my wrath, because I am God." The inference from what is proper holds, because it belongs to God to show mercy or to mingle mercy with punishment. Likewise: "In wrath you will remember mercy." Why does he remember mercy toward the Church? I answer: because man could not endure God's judgment and wrath. The inference therefore holds from the impossible. So we cry: "Lord, if you mark iniquities, who shall stand?" Likewise: "Lord, rebuke me not in your fury." Thus God says: I will not execute the fury of my wrath (a sweet consolation), because I am God. God, for many reasons, willed those histories to be written and those spectacles set before us, and above all to call us back to repentance. These things were expounded in 1559.

units.la: XXVIII. Augusti. Natalis Augustini, eiusdemq; studia ac certamina.
units.tr: 28 August. The birthday of Augustine, and his studies and contests.

units.la: Hic 28. Augusti est dies sancti Augustini, qui fuit natus in oppido Africæ Madauro, quod non procul à Carthagine situm erat. Romæ uero dicit didicit linguam Latinam: quanquam etiam in Africa erat Latinus sermo, tamen sonus Romanus erat elegantissimus. Nunc vero Itali habent suas elegantias, etsi discedunt à Romano sono. Sic Poloni etiam habent suas elegantias. Romanus sonus non multum differt à nostro, nisi quod iste est elegantior nostro. Factus est professor Mediolanensis, docuit Rhetoricam: assuefacit iuuentutem ad consuetudinem declamandi, quae tunc in scholis praecipua cura fuit: in qua aetate etiam audiuit Ambrosium, qui inflexit eum ad puriorē doctrina. Institutus vero fuit in patria, in doctrina Manichaeorum. Manichaei furor conflatus est ex Stoicis phantasijs, & hypocrisi anabaptistica. Duo pariter infinita & aeterna posuerunt, bonum & malum: sicut Stoici duo principia posuerunt, φῶτα & ὕλην, sic ipsi duos deos, φῶς καὶ θεός. Damnauerunt politias, iudicia, & ciuile ordinem. Illud malum venenum fuit uagatum per magnam partem Africae. Gentes enim facile arripiunt dogmata, suis naturis congruentia: eaque transformat ad suam naturam. Itali sunt amantes & intelligentes Imperij: ideo transformaRunt religionem in Imperium, & Pontificatum. Nos Germani sumus beluones, arripimus illa quae augent illa licentia. Ita quisque superstitiosus assumit aliquid praetextu doctrinae. Africanum genus hominum est simile simijs, vel cercopithecis, sicut nostrum strum genus est ursinum: nam plurimum ursa-rum est in his regionib. ad Septentrionē. Ideo ve-nenatos & monstrosos errores defenderūt. Et si⁠u pendū est miraculum, quòd ille error tèpore Au-gustini sit uagatus in maxima parte orbis terra-rū, & in ora Africæ, duraueritq; annos ferè 300. Cogitate quàm magnum hoc fuerit malum. Sed Augustinus conuersus est diligentia & sedulitate Ambrosij, qui multa cum eo disputauit. Est natus matre Christiana, quæ rectè sensit: sed patre ethni-co, qui conuersus est, uidens excellentiam uirtutis in sua coniuge: ita sæpè honesta exempla inuitāt alios ad audiendā doctrinam. Pater fuit homo mi-litaris. Porrò Augustinus postquā factus est Chri-stianus, aliquanto postea rediit in patriā, ac uixit in Ecclesia Hipponensi, qui locus non adeò longè distat àCarthagine: ibi docuit, sicut omnes disci-mus docendo: ut est antiquum distū inter Mimos, Discipulus est prioris, posterior dies.
units.tr: Here 28 August is the day of St Augustine, who was born in the African town of Madauros, which lay not far from Carthage. He learned Latin at Rome, he says; although Latin speech was also in use in Africa, the Roman sound was most elegant. Now indeed the Italians have their own elegances, though they depart from the Roman sound. So too the Poles have their elegances. The Roman sound does not differ much from ours, except that it is more elegant than ours. He became professor at Milan and taught rhetoric; he accustomed young people to the practice of declaiming, which at that time was the chief concern in the schools. In that period he also heard Ambrose, who led him to purer teaching. He had, however, been instructed in his homeland in the doctrine of the Manichaeans. The Manichaean madness was blown together from Stoic fancies and Anabaptist hypocrisy. They likewise posited two infinite and eternal principles, good and evil; as the Stoics posited two principles, light [φῶτα] and matter [ὕλην], so they posited two gods, light and God [φῶς καὶ θεός]. They condemned polities, judgments and the civil order. That evil poison spread through a great part of Africa. For peoples readily seize doctrines congruent with their natures, and transform them to their own nature. Italians are lovers and understanders of empire; therefore they transformed religion into empire and papacy. We Germans are brutes and gluttons: we seize whatever that licence enlarges. Thus each superstitious person takes up something under the pretext of doctrine. The African race of men is like apes or cercopitheci, just as our race is bearish, for there are very many bears in the northern regions. Therefore they defended venomous and monstrous errors. And it is no small wonder that this error wandered in Augustine's time through the greatest part of the world's orb and along the shores of Africa, and endured for almost 300 years. Consider how great an evil this was. But Augustine was converted through the diligence and assiduity of Ambrose, who disputed much with him. He was born of a Christian mother, who thought rightly, but of a heathen father, who was converted on seeing the excellence of virtue in his wife; so often honourable examples invite others to hear the doctrine. The father was a military man. Moreover, after Augustine became a Christian, he returned some time later to his homeland and lived in the church of Hippo, a place not far from Carthage. There he taught, as we all learn by teaching; as the old saying among the mimes goes: "The later day is the pupil of the earlier."

units.la: Sunt autem scripta ipsius dissimilia, sed po-steriora meliora & eruditiora: quia docendo di-dicit, unde edidit Retractiones primorum suo-rum librorum. Factus est etiam collega Episcopi Hipponensis, seu doctor illius ecclesiæ, cui deniq; successit. Habuit multa certamina, primùm cum Manichæis, quos (postquam ueritatem cogno-uit) multis libris refutauit. Deniq; disputauit cum
units.tr: His writings are unlike one another, but the later ones are better and more learned, because he learned by teaching; hence he published the Retractations of his earlier books. He also became colleague of the bishop of Hippo, or teacher of that church, and eventually succeeded him. He had many contests: first with the Manichaeans, whom he refuted in many books after he came to know the truth. Finally he disputed with

units.la: Arrianis, qui etiam passim uagabantur in Asia; accuratiusq; scripsit de Trinitate quàm quisquâ alius. Hoc dico, etiamsi multa extant alia scripta, tamen utile est legere eius explicationē in hoc articulo, qui est magni momenti. Nos reddimus uobis planissimam & simplicissimam eius sententiam, quando eam uobis recitamus. Postea cum Pelagianis, qui senserunt hominem iustum esse bonis operibus, disciplina externa: deleuerunt doctrinam fidei & gratiæ. ibi etiam benemeritus est Augustinus, etiāsi idem non omnia illustrauit: tamen multa sunt testimonia, eum hoc sensisse, quod nos docemus. Miscet aliquid improprij, sicut sua ætas non multum curauit proprie loqui: quia temporis illius erat studium mirabiliter loquendi. Præterea certauit cum Donatistis, quod fuit etiam chaos hominum seditiosorum, qui seiunxerunt se ab Ecclesijs, damnauerunt√q; ministerium propter malos mores docentium: faciebant schismata sine necessitate: exercebant latrocinia: erat pessimi homines, habentes alias multas malas opiniones. sicut dicitur: Error est fœcūdus. item: Error parit errorem. Ita dimicauit sanctus Augustinus, cum quatuor sectis ualde perniciosis. Peruenitq; ad magnam senectutem, uixitq; ad annū nonagesimum. Cogitate igitur quantum æerumnarum pertulerit in uera religione defendenda, & & conseruāda. Obsessa sua urbe Hippone à Vandalis, duce Genserico, ante captam urbem mortuus est. credo illum senem non potuisse præ dolore uidere illas calamitates. Genséricus enim nō tantum diripiebat urbes, sed etiam propagabat Arriani dogma. Matres & filiæ nudæ suspensæ sunt & combustæ, & ita homines passim cruciati sunt, qui non amplecterentur dogma Arrianū. Paulo post est occupatum oppidum. sicut nunc pastor Suueinfurdiensis fuit mortuus, antequam oppidum expugnabatur, haud dubiè præ magnitudine doloris. Augustino defuncto, successerunt: Prosper, qui fuit eius auditor, & conseruator puræ doctrinæ: & Maximus, qui eadem tradidit et propagauit: sicut semper Deus aliquas reliquias ueræ Ecclesiæ seruat. Græci ualdè delectati sunt lectione Augustini, & totū in suam linguā transtulerunt. Planudes uertit Augustinum annis aliquot ante Constantinopolim captam, qui fuit unus ex conseruatoribus linguæ Græcæ: transtulit etiam Catonem. Græci habuerunt Rhodi opera Augustini. Mihi dixit quidam, qui legit ea, & affirmauit admodum eleganter & propriè esse uersa.
units.tr: the Arians, who also wandered everywhere in Asia; and he wrote more accurately about the Trinity than anyone else. I say this: although many other writings exist, it is still useful to read his explanation of this article, which is of great importance. When we recite it to you, we give you his most plain and simple opinion. Afterwards he disputed with the Pelagians, who held that man is justified by good works and external discipline, and so destroyed the doctrine of faith and grace. There too Augustine deserved well, even if he did not illuminate every point; yet there are many testimonies that he held what we teach. He mixes in something improper, since his age did not much care to speak properly, the study of that time being to speak wonderfully. Moreover he contended with the Donatists, who were also a chaos of seditious men: they separated themselves from the churches and condemned the ministry on account of the evil morals of teachers; they made schisms without necessity and practised robberies. They were most wicked men, holding many other bad opinions. As it is said: "Error is fruitful"; and "Error begets error." Thus holy Augustine fought with four very pernicious sects. He reached great old age and lived to ninety. Consider therefore how many hardships he endured in defending and preserving true religion. When his city Hippo was besieged by the Vandals under their leader Genseric, he died before the city was taken. I believe that old man could not, for grief, bear to see those calamities. For Genseric not only plundered cities but also propagated the Arian dogma. Mothers and daughters were hung up naked and burned, and men everywhere were tortured who would not embrace the Arian dogma. Shortly afterwards the town was taken. So now the minister of Schweinfurt died before the town was stormed, undoubtedly from the greatness of his grief. After Augustine's death there succeeded Prosper, who had been his hearer and the preserver of pure doctrine, and Maximus, who handed down and propagated the same teaching; for God always preserves some remnants of the true Church. The Greeks took great delight in reading Augustine and translated the whole of him into their language. Planudes translated Augustine some years before Constantinople was captured; he was one of the preservers of the Greek language, and he also translated Cato. The Greeks had the works of Augustine at Rhodes. Someone told me, who had read them, that they were rendered most elegantly and accurately.

units.la: SEPTEMBER.
units.tr: SEPTEMBER.

units.la: VIII. Septembris.
units.tr: VIII. September.

units.la: Dies est natalis Mariæ, quam Nicephorus scri-bit uixisse annos 59. quæ est ætas Maximiliani Im-peratoris. Ponamus, quòd circa annum uigesimũ suæ ætatis fuerit puerpera, & pepererit Christū. Quanquā idē Nicephorus scribit, peperisse eam anno ætatis suæ decimoquinto: quòd esse potest, sed credo nō adeò iuuenculā fuisse elocatā Ioseph.
units.tr: This is the birthday of Mary, whom Nicephorus writes lived fifty-nine years, the same age as Emperor Maximilian. Let us suppose that she became a mother around her twentieth year and bore Christ. Yet the same Nicephorus writes that she bore him in her fifteenth year. That may be possible, but I do not think she was betrothed to Joseph while still so young.

units.la: Illa enim grauissima ætas non adeò iuuenculas elocauit: sicut apud Hesiodum tempus elocationis annus 18. qui est pubertatis tempus, ut circa annū 20. puerpera fierent. Vixit autem Maria post resurrectionem filij, sex aut septem annos. Po-namus quòd Christus sit passus, inchoante anno 34 suæ ætatis. Cogitate quantarum calamita-tum fuerit spectatrix: considerate eius uitæ cur-riculum, & familiam. Fuit nata ex Regia fami-lia: sed tamen uixit in tali paupertate, ut ne quidē manserit in oppido suæ tribus in Betheleem, sed habitauerit in Galilæa. Cogitate quale tēpus fue-rit pueritiæ & adolescentiæ pulcherrimarũ uir-ginum, Mariæ matris, sororis, & aliarum matro-narum: ubi conspicitur mirabilis bonitas Dei ser-uantis Ecclesiā. isti homines nulla habuerūt præ-sidia, nec potentiam, cum uagarentur per Iudæā, ubi pessimarũ gentiũ latrunculi uersabātur. Cre-do do nec hodie esse in toto orbe terrarum nebulones peiores, quàm sunt in Arabia, Aegypto & Syria, qui sunt petulatissimi & libidinosissimi homines. Contra istos sceleratissimos homines, Deus tamen has familias, & suam Ecclesiam mirabiliter texit & defendit. Ita mirabiliter omnibus temporibus Ecclesia à Deo tegitur & custoditur.
units.tr: For that most serious age did not betroth girls so young. In Hesiod, the time of betrothal is the eighteenth year, which is the age of puberty, so that they would become mothers around the twentieth year. Mary lived on after her Son's resurrection for six or seven years. Let us suppose that Christ suffered in the thirty-fourth year of his life. Consider how many calamities she witnessed. Consider the course and the household of her life. She was born of a royal family, yet she lived in such poverty that she did not even remain in her tribal town of Bethlehem, but lived in Galilee. Consider what the time of childhood and youth was like for the most beautiful of virgins, Mary the mother, her sister, and the other matrons: here the wonderful goodness of God, who preserves the Church, is seen. These people had no protection and no power, as they wandered through Judea, where the little robbers of the worst nations roamed. I believe that even today there are no worse rascals in the whole world than those in Arabia, Egypt and Syria, who are the most wanton and lustful of men. Yet against these most wicked men God wonderfully covered and defended these families and his Church. Thus at all times the Church is wonderfully covered and guarded by God.

units.la: Fuit formosissima iuuēcula Maria: & fuit in ea, apiētia: & nō dubiū mihi est, quin alij multi sint ūsi eius cōsilio: Deus tamē texit eam. Ita non debemus cogitare, nos uiuere nostris uiribus, robore, aut præsidijs: & præsertim qui seruantur in Ecclesia mirabilissimo modo, sicut tres uiri in camino ignis. quare in primis est dulcis cogitatio talium historiarū. Vidit initia Ecclesiae fortasse septē annos post ascensionē filij, sicut credo eam uixisse usq; ad interfectū Iacobū, qui primus inter Apostolos est interfectus. Vidit magna certamina & ipsa haud dubie fuit rectrix Apostolorū, tūc cùm tota Iudæa pessimorum hominum sceleribus & tyrannide perturbaretur.
units.tr: Mary was a most beautiful young girl, and she had wisdom in her; and I have no doubt that many others made use of her counsel. Yet God covered her. So we ought not to think that we live by our own strength, power, or protections, especially those who are preserved in the Church in a most wonderful way, like the three men in the fiery furnace. Therefore first of all the remembrance of such histories is sweet. She saw the beginnings of the Church, perhaps seven years after the Son's ascension. I believe she lived until the killing of James, who was the first of the Apostles to be slain. She saw great conflicts, and she was without doubt herself the guide of the Apostles, at the time when all Judea was thrown into disorder by the crimes and tyranny of the worst men.

units.la: Deletio Hierosolymæ.
units.tr: The destruction of Jerusalem.

units.la: Eodem die etiam deleta est Hierosolyma, videlicet die Laurētij: id est, paulo quidē ante illud tēpus, quo (quia nō omnia uno die cōfici potuerūt) templo sunt iniectæ faces, ac inchoata est templi conflagratio. Deleto tēplo, multū laboris fuit in arce expugnanda, & reliqua urbe delenda. Hoc uero die dicũt opus deletionis esse perfectũ, & ciuitatem penitus totam deletam. Durauit au tem obsidio sex mẽses: & sicut in Paschate ingres sus est populus Iudaicus in illam terram, ita in Pa-schate inchoata est obsidio. & sicut festum Taber naculorum fuit tempus solenne, in quo agebantur Deo gratiæ, pro tradita illa terra: ita festum Ta-bernaculorũ fuit finis istius politiæ. Illo enim te-pore, quo solebat alioqui gratias agere pro terra illa tradita, urbs deleta est: quia Deus uoluit o-stendere finem Tabernaculorum, & quòd non uellet illam politiam diutius seruare. Discite e-tiam illud, quòd politiæ tam diu florentes stant, quandiu Deo placet. Tanti enim sunt furores di-abolorum, nisi Deus seruaret tuguriola, & custo-diret nostra corpora, ac adderet excubias, prote-geretq; domunculas, non essemus incolumes: sicut uidimus ualde mirabilia incendia iam multis an-nis. Simeon fuit episcopus Hierosolymitanus, & Christi cognatus. Fuit enim frater Iacobi, filius so-roris Mariæ. Ante obsidionem duxit Ecclesiam suam trans Iordanem, admonitus diuinitus, ubi habitauit cum suo cœtu in uicinis nidulis. Ro-mani uerò postea cõcesserunt eis rursus loca Hie-rosolymæ. Huius uastationis fuit spectator Io-hannes, qui tunc adhuc uixit in Asia. Nulla fuit pulchrior ciuitas in toto genere humano, & nullibi præstantiores uiri, quàm quales fuerunt Dauid, Nathan, Ezechias, Iosias, Hieremias, Daniel. Roma habuit præstantes uiros, sed bellatores: sed in illa urbe concionatus est ipse filius Dei, ac se patefecit uarijs miraculis. Bethania abfuit di midiũ miliare à Hierosolyma: ibi Lazarus est exuscitatus, & sunt alia multa miracula ibidem in singulis ferè uestigijs illius terræ.
units.tr: On this same day Jerusalem was also destroyed, namely on the day of Laurence; that is, a little before that time when, since not everything could be finished in one day, torches were thrown into the Temple and the burning of the Temple began. Once the Temple was destroyed, there was much labour in storming the citadel and in destroying the rest of the city. On this day they say the work of destruction was completed and the whole city utterly razed. The siege, however, lasted six months, and just as the Jewish people entered that land at Passover, so the siege began at Passover. And just as the Feast of Tabernacles was a solemn time in which thanks were given to God for that land having been handed over, so the Feast of Tabernacles was the end of that polity. For at that very time, when they were accustomed to give thanks for that land delivered to them, the city was destroyed, because God willed to show the end of the Tabernacles and that he did not wish to preserve that polity any longer. Learn also this: flourishing commonwealths stand only as long as it pleases God. For the furies of the devils are so great that, unless God preserved our little huts, guarded our bodies, set his watchmen, and protected our little houses, we would not be safe; as we have seen very wonderful fires for many years now. Simeon was bishop of Jerusalem and a kinsman of Christ. For he was a brother of James, the son of Mary's sister. Before the siege, warned by God, he led his Church across the Jordan, where he lived with his flock in the nearby little nests. Later, however, the Romans again yielded to them the places of Jerusalem. The witness of this devastation was John, who was then still living in Asia. There was no more beautiful city in the whole human race, nor more outstanding men anywhere than such men as David, Nathan, Hezekiah, Josiah, Jeremiah and Daniel. Rome had outstanding men, but warriors; yet in that city the Son of God himself preached, and revealed himself by various miracles. Bethany was half a mile distant from Jerusalem; there Lazarus was raised, and there are many other miracles in that place, almost at every step of that land.

units.la: Causæ destructionis Hierosolymæ.
units.tr: The causes of the destruction of Jerusalem.

units.la: Prima est, quia Deus voluit ostendere iræ suæ aduersus peccatum exemplum, quòd in omnibus hominibus peccatum simili ratione punire uelit. Secunda, illa destructio debet esse testimonium ad uentus Messiæ, qui stante politia Mosaica uenire deberet. Tertia, quòd lex nõ sit iustitia Euãgelij. Ita non tantum facta, sed etiam causæ factorum sunt considerandæ.
units.tr: The first cause is that God wished to show, by this example, his anger against sin, and that he wills to punish sin in the same way in all men. The second is that this destruction ought to be a testimony to the coming of the Messiah, who was to come while the Mosaic commonwealth still stood. The third is that the law is not the righteousness of the Gospel. Thus not only the deeds themselves but also the causes of the deeds must be considered.

units.la: X. Septembris. Dies obitus Ioannis Huniadis, regis Vngariæ.
units.tr: 10 September. The death day of John Hunyadi, king of Hungary.

units.la: Mortuus est hoc die Ioãnes Huniades, pater Mathiæ regis Hungariæ. Ego nõ existimo fuisse præstātiorem ducem his postremis nostris tèporibus. Ille fuit clypeus Hungariæ. Filius Mathias nõ fuit par patri. Accidit ei quòd dicitur de inutilibus canibus venaticis. Quando boni canes venatici conspexerunt feram aliquam, non avertuntur ab illa, etiamsi aliae in occursum ipsorum veniant, antequam priorem ceperunt. De generes contra ingenuam priorem ceperunt. Certò vagantur, & oblata alia priorem deserunt, sicut pulcherrimè hi sequentes versus indicant, simulq; allegoricè notantes eos homines, qui ab institutis laboribus ad alia negocia deflectunt:
units.tr: John Hunyadi, father of Matthias, king of Hungary, died on this day. I do not think there was a more outstanding leader in our own recent times. He was the shield of Hungary. His son Matthias was not equal to his father. What is said of useless hunting dogs applies to him. When good hounds have caught sight of some beast, they do not turn away from it, even if others come into their path before they have taken the first. Useless dogs, by contrast, wander about, and when another is put in front of them they abandon the first. The following verses show this very clearly, and at the same time they allegorically mark those men who turn aside from the labours they have undertaken to other business:

units.la: Qui binos lepores una sectabitur hora,
units.tr: He who will chase two hares in a single hour,

units.la: Vno quandoq;, quandoq; carebit utroq;.
units.tr: will sometimes have one, sometimes neither.

units.la: Sic Mathias non commoratus est in uno proposito. Pater eius habuit tantum unicum hostem, Turcicum Imperatorem, & praeter illum nullos concitauit alios. Fuit ualde egregius Princeps: aliquot magnis praelijs uicit Amuratem: & hoc decimo die Septembris, depulit magnum exercitū à Belgrado: & illo in praelio accepto uulnere mortuus est uictor. Vixit tantisper, donec nuncium est ei, hostes uictos esse. Quo audito, mortuus est alacer: & quod ad uictoriam attinet, sicut Epminundas, obijt. Fuit autem & ipse bonus & sanctus rex, & sine dubio haeres utae aeternae. Deus dedit per hunc praestantem regem, defensionem Hungariae. nunc miserabiliter Hungaria laceratur.
units.tr: So Matthias did not keep to one purpose. His father had only one enemy, the Turkish emperor, and apart from him he stirred up no others. He was a truly outstanding prince: in several great battles he defeated Amurath, and on this tenth day of September he drove a great army away from Belgrade; and in that battle he received a wound and died as a victor. He lived just long enough to hear that the enemy had been defeated, and on hearing it he died cheerful; and as far as victory is concerned, he died like Epaminondas. He was also a good and holy king, and undoubtedly an heir of eternal life. Through this excellent king God gave Hungary its defence. Now Hungary is miserably torn apart.

units.la: XIII. Septembris.
units.tr: 13 September.

units.la: Celebratur festum exaltationis Crucis. In me se Maio celebratur inuentio Crucis, quomodo in uenerit Helena crucem Domini nostri Iesu. Fuit autem Helena mater Constantini Imperatoris. Quòd uerò ipse Constantinus & eius mater crucem inuenerint, credibile est. Festum exaltationis continet historiam receptæ crucis à rege Persico Cosroa, per Heraclium.
units.tr: The feast of the Exaltation of the Cross is celebrated. In May the finding of the Cross is celebrated, how Helena found the cross of our Lord Jesus. Helena was the mother of the emperor Constantine. That Constantine himself and his mother found the cross is credible. The feast of the Exaltation contains the history of the recovery of the cross from the Persian king Chosroes by Heraclius.

units.la: OCTOBER.
units.tr: OCTOBER.

units.la: Natalis Dionysij, & quòd duo Dionysij fuerint.
units.tr: The birthday of Dionysius, and that there were two Dionysiuses.

units.la: IX. Octobris. Dies est sancti Dionysii. Dicamus igitur aliquid de illo, quis fuerit. Vocabulum Dionysij uenit à Διόννυσος, quo vocabulo Græci Bacchū appellarunt. Significat autem Διόνυσος montem Iouis, quo festa Bacchi Dionysia celebrata sunt: quia mali cultus sunt primùm orti à Ioue. nam in mōtibus factæ sunt à Salomone uietimæ, & Bacchanalia sunt celebrata in mōte Nysēo: quæ res in horrendas ac detestandas abominationes excreuit. Sicut in Ecclesia uidemus magnas prophanationes esse factas, cùm paulatim discessu fit ab institutione primæ Ecclesiæ, sicut etiā in Missa accidit. Hic Dionysius nominatur Areopagita: fuit enim Atheniēsis. Ideo uerò addo, nominari ipsum Areopagitā, ut sciamus ipsum fuisse uirū præcipuæ dignitatis. qui cōuersus est à Paulo apostolo, ut habetur in Actis. Areopagita, id est, senator præcipuus, seu unus ex illo summo senatu Atheniensi. Fuit enim illud præcipuum cõsilium, & nomē habet ab Ariopago, id est uico Martis, ubi fuit tumulus, & locus ordinarius, ubi exercebantur iudicia capitalia, ut causæ cædium, & quidem consultò factarum. Nam & alia erant iudicia non concia, ubi tantum iudicabatur de cædibus non consultò factis. & dicitur ideo uicus Martis, quia ibi factum est iudicium Martis. Nam aiunt Martem accusatum esse aliquando à Neptuno, & iudicio Deorum absolutum in hoc uico Areopago, quia Mars interfecerat filium Neptuni, qui suam filiā stuprauerat. Est exemplum, quòd liceat interfi-cere stupratorem filiæ. Extant etiam duæ orationes Libanij, altera est Martis, altera Neptuni. Deinde etiam est facta accusatio Orestis. Sic sapientes homines tradiderunt exemplum, ubi sit facienda ἐπιεικεία[?]. Areopagitæ dicebantur, qui in templo Martis iudicabant: eorumq; iudicium exquisitissimum habebatur. Nam cùm Mars homicidij reus fieret, iudicantibus duodecim dijs in eo pago, sex sententijs absolutus est. Areopagita fuit senator ex summo Senatu Atheniensiū. Vsurpatum quoq; fuit hoc uocabulum prouerbialiter, pro homine tetro & seuero. Porrò de hoc Dionysio Areopagita conuerso à Paulo dicitur, quòd cùm uideret tenebras, quæ factæ sunt in passione Christi pendentis in cruce, dixerit: Aut Deus na-turæ turæ patitur, aut natura rerum dissoluetur. Quia uidit eam eclipsim fieri contra ordinē naturæ. Omnis enim eclipsis Solis fit in nouilunio, aut circiter. Illa eclipsis facta est in plenilunio, quia oportet Pa-scha celebrari in plenilunio, uidelicet quando luna fuit quatuordecim dieru̅. Ergo, &c. Diaconus igi-tur de Dionysio factus est primùm episcopus Athe-niensis, & postea uenit in Gallia, ubi tempore Do-mitiani affectus est supplicio. Diu autem conciona-tus est, nempe à tempore Claudij usq; ad tempora Domitiani. Fuit enim satis longum tempus inter Claudium et Domitianum. Inter illos siquidem re-gnarunt Vespasianus, & Titus filius eius. Interea temporis ipse docuit in patria, et Gallia. Nam Gal-lia tunc temporis fuit plena doctrinarum Græca-rum & Latinarū. Massiliæ enim fuit magna schola. Et dicitur quòd Lazarus Massiliæ condiderit ec-clefiam, Dionysius Lutetiæ. Eodem tempore docuit Marcus, comes Pauli, Ratisbonæ, quia Euangelium citò uenit in Germaniam & Galliam, ibiq; propa-gatum est: quod probatur ex eo, quia Irenæus an-tiquus scriptor, qui in Syrmio affectus est marty-rio, citat illustria testimonia ecclesiarum Gallica-rum & Germanicarū de hac quæstione, quæ tunc & nunc certamina maxima mouet, An Filius Dei sit persona: in tanta causa citat illarum Ecclesiarū testimonia. Post tempora Apostolorū, cùm suissent florēs florentißimæ Ecclesiæ, statim factæ sunt uastatio-nes. Ita Deus puniuit homines propter Euangelij contemptum. Fuit tunc multum confusionum: Gothi, Vandali, Hunni euerterũt Ecclesias. Ita magna fuit confusio Ethnicorum, & Christianorum usq; ad regnum Francicũ, donec se Franci collegerunt, & Germaniam, Italiam, & Galliam occuparunt. Illo tempore effusi sunt ex Scotia iterum homines doĉti, qui restituerunt Ecclesias in Gallia. Per Al-boinum Scotum est Academia Parisiensis instaura-ta, qui fuit præceptor Caroli Magni, & inchoator studiorum. Paulò ante uenit Gallus in Germaniã, & docuit superiorem Germaniam, Heluetios, & Sueuos. Et ita restituta est doĉrina, & ethnicismus repulsus est à temporibus regni Frãcici. Fuit enim squalor Ecclesiæ, qui post Apostolos secutus est, ubi non amplius fuit illæ Apostolorum flos.
units.tr: October 9. It is the feast day of St Dionysius. Let us therefore say something about who he was. The name Dionysius comes from Dionysos [Διόννυσος], which the Greeks used for Bacchus. The word Dionysos means "mountain of Jove," where the feasts of Bacchus, the Dionysia, were celebrated, because the wicked cults first arose from Jove. For sacrifices were offered on the mountains by Solomon, and the Bacchanalia were celebrated on Mount Nysa, a practice that grew into horrible and detestable abominations. In the same way we see great profanations made in the Church, as it gradually drifts away from the institution of the first Church, as also happened with the Mass. This Dionysius is called the Areopagite, for he was an Athenian. I add this so that we may know he was a man of outstanding rank, who was converted by the apostle Paul, as is recorded in the Acts. "Areopagite" means a leading senator, or one of that highest Athenian senate. For that was the chief council, and it took its name from the Areopagus, that is, the hill of Mars, where there was a mound and the regular place where capital trials were held, such as cases of murder committed deliberately. There were also other courts, not of this kind, where judgement was given only on killings not done on purpose. It is called the hill of Mars because the trial of Mars was held there. For they say that Mars was once accused by Neptune and acquitted by the judgement of the gods on this hill of Ares, because Mars had killed the son of Neptune, who had raped his daughter. This is an example that it is lawful to kill a rapist of one's daughter. There are also two orations of Libanius, one of Mars and one of Neptune. Then too the accusation of Orestes was made there. Thus wise men handed down an example of where fairness [ἐπιείκεια] must be shown. Those who judged in the temple of Mars were called Areopagites, and their judgement was regarded as the most exact. For when Mars was made to answer for homicide, the twelve gods sitting as judges in that court acquitted him by six votes. An Areopagite was a senator from the highest senate of the Athenians. The word was also used proverbially for a grim and severe man. Moreover, it is said of this Dionysius the Areopagite, converted by Paul, that when he saw the darkness that came over the passion of Christ hanging on the cross, he said: "Either the God of nature is suffering, or the order of nature will be dissolved." For he saw that eclipse happening against the order of nature. Every eclipse of the sun happens at the new moon, or about then. But that eclipse happened at the full moon, because the Passover must be celebrated at the full moon, namely when the moon is fourteen days old. Therefore, and so on. So Dionysius, first a deacon, became the first bishop of Athens, and afterwards came into Gaul, where in the time of Domitian he was put to death. He preached for a long time, namely from the time of Claudius until the time of Domitian. For there was a fairly long period between Claudius and Domitian, during which Vespasian reigned, and Titus his son. Meanwhile he taught in his homeland and in Gaul. For Gaul at that time was full of Greek and Latin learning. There was a great school at Massilia. And it is said that Lazarus founded the church at Massilia, and Dionysius at Lutetia. At the same time Mark, the companion of Paul, taught at Regensburg, because the gospel came quickly into Germany and Gaul and spread there. This is proved by the fact that Irenaeus, an ancient writer who suffered martyrdom at Sirmium, cites the notable testimonies of the Gallic and German churches on this question, which then and now stirs the greatest disputes, whether the Son of God is a person. In so weighty a matter he cites the testimonies of those churches. After the times of the apostles, when the most flourishing churches had blossomed, devastations at once followed. Thus God punished men for their contempt of the gospel. There was then great confusion: Goths, Vandals and Huns overthrew the churches. So great was the confusion among the heathen and Christians until the Frankish kingdom, when the Franks gathered themselves together and occupied Germany, Italy and Gaul. In that period learned men again poured out of Scotland, who restored the churches in Gaul. Through the Scot Alboin the University of Paris was re-established; he was the tutor of Charlemagne and the initiator of studies. Shortly before, a man named Gall came into Germany and taught Upper Germany, the Helvetii and the Suevi. So doctrine was restored, and heathenism was driven back from the time of the Frankish kingdom. For there was a squalor in the Church which followed the apostles, when that flower of the apostles was no longer there.

units.la: Dicitur autem de Dionysio, quando decollatus est, quòd gestauerit aliquandiu caput: quod quidẽ non impossibile uidetur. Simile exemplũ reperitur in Aristophane, ubi etiam caput post decollationẽ locutũ est, et indicauit latronẽ alium: quod fuit aliquid singulare, et notatu dignũ. Extant hoc tempore libri qui dicuntur huius esse, quod ego non existimo: sed opinor esse libros Dionysij Corinthij, in quibus illud dictũ reperitur: Ne graue onus castitatis uel cœlibatus, tanquã necessariũ, imponatis fra-tribus, tribus, sed infirmitatis plurimorum rationem habeatis. Fuit hic alter quoq; uir admodum præstans: cuius temporibus cœpit imaledcere dogma eorū qui episcoporum & sacerdotum cœlibatum instituere voluerūt. Refutauit hic quoq; Nouatum, qui existimauit hominē renatū, lapsum deinde, nō posse cōuerti, & nō iterū esse recipiendū: ubi ostendit exempla conuersionis. Libros Dionysij misit Michael Imperator Constantinopolitanus ad Carolū Magnū cum instrumēto musico. Existimarūt enim magni Principes, honestū esse sibi inuicē mittere libros. Carolus Magnus curauit eos libros uerti à quodā Scoto, cui sui discipuli effoderūt oculos, qui est primus horum librorū Dionysij interpres. Hoc fuit præmiū pro fideli sua institutioe. Ortus aūt est eo tēpore error de transubstātiatione, ob cuius refutationē causam sumpserūt oculos ipsi effodiēdi.
units.tr: It is also said of Dionysius, when he was beheaded, that he carried his head for some time. This indeed does not seem impossible. A similar example is found in Aristophanes, where a head also spoke after beheading and pointed out another robber. That was something remarkable and worth noting.
