There are books extant at this time which are said to be his, which I do not believe; I think they are the books of Dionysius of Corinth, in which this saying is found: "Do not impose on the brothers the heavy burden of chastity or celibacy as if it were necessary, but take account of the weakness of many." There was also another man of great distinction, in whose times the doctrine of those who wished to establish celibacy for bishops and priests began to be attacked. He also refuted Novatian, who held that a man once reborn and afterwards fallen could not be converted and could not be received again; there he showed examples of conversion. The emperor Michael of Constantinople sent the books of Dionysius to Charlemagne together with a musical instrument. For great princes thought it honourable to send books to one another. Charlemagne had those books translated by a certain Scot, whose own pupils dug out his eyes; he is the first translator of these books of Dionysius. This was his reward for his faithful work. Moreover, an error about transubstantiation arose at that time, and for refuting it the men who gouged out his eyes were themselves moved to do so.

units.la: XVI. Octobris. Dies necis Demosthenis.
units.tr: October 16. The day of Demosthenes' death.

units.la: Hoc die est interfectus Demosthenes. Græci mēses cōputarūt à cōiunctione lunæ, et habebāt lunares mēses: sed intra 18 annos necesse est dies cōgruere.
units.tr: On this day Demosthenes was killed. The Greeks reckoned their months from the conjunction of the moon and so had lunar months, but within 18 years the days must necessarily come back into agreement.

units.la: Cicero, de oratione ὑπὲρ Στεφάνου contra Aeschinem, in qua dicit de suis consiliis, Demosthenis inquit tantam esse eloquentiam in ea oratione, quanta in animis hominum includi possit. Et profecto uerum est: sed fuit inquietus, fuit suasor belli contra
units.tr: Cicero, in his speech on behalf of Stephanus [ὑπὲρ Στεφάνου] against Aeschines, in which he speaks of his own counsels, says that the eloquence of Demosthenes in that speech is as great as can be contained in men's minds. And indeed that is true. But Demosthenes was restless; he was an advocate of war against

units.la: §§§ 2 contra Philippum Macedonicum. Mortuo Alexandro fuit suasor noui belli contra Macedones: ibi Antipater postulauit eum sibi dedi. Suasit uero Demades, ut dederetur: quia erat ualde utile illū dedi. Cùm esset deditus, uenissetq; unus ex ministris Antipatris ut illum abduceret, uiso ipso, fugit in templum. Ex quo cùm nō auderet eum rapere, interea Demosthenes intus hausit uenenum, quod habebat in calamo: & sic mortuus est. Ita magna uis ingenij, & excellens illa eloquentia consumitur in rebus imutilibus & perniciosis patriæ. Hæc exempla commonefaciunt nos de assidua inuocatione, ut Deus faciat nos uasa misericordiæ, & nō iræ: quale fuit Demosthenes, qui monuit Rempublicam aliquoties, & tandem ruinæ incidunt in ipsum, ut miserabiliter sibi conscisçat mortem: sic transit gloria mundi. Est exemplum præstantis ingenij, ornati excellentissimis donis diuinis, cuius dona non conferuntur ad salutem Ecclesiæ, aut Reipublicæ. Sunt anni abhinc, quãdo perit Demosthenes, 1781. quia anno post mortem Alexandri perijt, & a morte Alexandri usq; ad natum Christum sunt anni 324.
units.tr: Philip of Macedon. When Alexander died, he was the advocate of a new war against the Macedonians. Then Antipater demanded that he be handed over to him, and Demades urged that he be surrendered, because it was very useful to hand him over. When he had been surrendered, and one of Antipater's officers came to take him away, Demosthenes fled into a temple as soon as he saw him. Since the man did not dare to drag him out, Demosthenes meanwhile drank the poison he kept in his pen, and so he died. Thus great force of mind and that outstanding eloquence are wasted on useless affairs that are harmful to the fatherland. These examples remind us to call constantly upon God, that He may make us vessels of mercy and not of wrath. Demosthenes, who warned the commonwealth several times, was at last brought to ruin and miserably inflicted death upon himself; so passes the glory of the world. He is an example of an outstanding talent, adorned with excellent divine gifts, whose gifts did not serve the salvation of the Church or the commonwealth. It is 1781 years since Demosthenes perished, for he perished in the year after Alexander's death, and from Alexander's death to the birth of Christ there are 324 years.

units.la: Postea Cassander filius Antipatris postulauit sibi dedi Demadem. Et Demadi interfecti sunt duo filij in conspectu eius, posteaq; ipse interfectus est. Theophrastus interrogatus, qualis esset Demosthenes? [?] dixit: Par Athenis. Interrogatus iterum, qualis effet Demades? dixit: Maior Athenis. Non extant multa Demadis scripta. Fragmentu extat, & quædam eius dicta recitantur. Cùm diceretur de morte Alexandri, & multi disputarent futura noua bella, & quidam metuerent Athenis, dixit Demades: nihil esse metuendum: quia mortuo Alexādro, exercitum eius fore simile Cyclopi effosso oculo: neminē fore, qui ipsos cōcorditer & prudenter duceret, ipsos sese mutuò cōsumpturos. & ita factū est.
units.tr: Afterwards Cassander, son of Antipater, demanded that Demades be handed over to him. Two of Demades' sons were killed before his eyes, and after that he himself was killed. When Theophrastus was asked what sort of man Demosthenes was, he said: "Equal to Athens." Asked again what sort of man Demades was, he said: "Greater than Athens." Few writings of Demades survive. A fragment exists, and some of his sayings are recorded. When people were talking about Alexander's death, and many were debating the new wars to come, and some in Athens were afraid, Demades said that nothing was to be feared: with Alexander dead, his army would be like the Cyclops with his eye put out; there would be no one to lead them with unity and prudence, and they would consume one another. And so it happened.

units.la: Est in fragmentis Demadis, orationes Demosthenis esse ὀνώμαςι nαλαὰς.
units.tr: In the fragments of Demades it is stated that the orations of Demosthenes are "fine words" [ὀνώματα καλά].

units.la: XVIII. Octobris.
units.tr: XVIII. October.

units.la: Est dies Lucæ euangelistæ, patria Antiocheni. Est autē Antiochia urbs Syriæ, quæ terminus siue tractus fuit attributus populo Israel. Antiochus Antiochiam appellauerat à suo nomine, quod fuit Macedonicum: et significat idem quod uindex, assertor seu ultor, ab αὐτὶ nαὶ ἐχειν. Fuit aūt hic Lucas professione medicus, & octuagenarius suspensus est Thebis ab olea. Imperita illa & stolida ciuitas tam sanctum uirum consumpsit. Fuerūt illi populi semper crassi Cyclopes: unde prouerbij loco celebratum est, Sus Bœotica: item, Bœotico more uiuere. Docuit porrò Lucas minorem Asiam à Bithynia usq; in Græciam: fuit comes itinerum Pauli. Exitus cæterorum talis est: Ioānes Euāgelista placida morte est mortuus Ephesi. Matthæus in Aethiopia, infra Aegyptum ptum bitumine perfusus est: cuius flamma incensa cōsumpsit prius idola circumstantia, postea ipsum interemit. Marcus docuit Cyrenæ, infra Africā & Aegyptum (ille tractus fuit colonia Lacedæmoniorum uel Argonautarū) postea redijt Alexandriam, & raptatus per urbem, interfectus est. Ita Matthæus, Marcus, Lucas, violenta morte è medio sublati sunt. Iam considerate quæ sint singulorum propriæ sententiæ. Ioannes Euangelista ideo post cæteros scripsit: quia uoluit addere quasdam conciones Christi: ut resuscitationē Lazari, & alias, quæ sunt omissæ à cæteris. Hæc in Matthæo peculiariter reperiuntur à cæteris omissa: de Magis, de interfectis infantibus: cōcio in mōte, quæ est expositio legis ualde necessaria. item illa memorabilis sententia apud solū Matthæū: Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis, & oneratis estis. item: Ego sum uobiscū usq; ad cōsummationē seculi. Ite: Vbi duo uel tres cōgregati fuerint in nomine meo, in medio eorū sum. item: Non est uoluntas patris, ut pereat unus de his minimis. In Marco solo sunt hæ sententiæ: Credo Domine, sed opē fer imbecillitati meæ: item: Omnis homo igne salietur, & omnis uictima sale salietur. Bona res est sal. In Luca tantū habentur hæc: De Zachæo, de missione angeli ad Mariā, de Samaritano, exemplū de filio prodigo. Ista sunt digna consideratione, ut magis fiat familiaris textus. xtus. Lucas autem fuit professor duarum doctrinarum praecipuarum, doctrinae de Deo, quam uidetis eu eruditissime scripsisse. Deinde fuit medicus, id est, physicus, professor doctrinae de natura rerum. Consideratio enim de natura rerum manuducetrix est ad agnitionem Dei. Unde et primi patres praecipue professioni medicae studiosi fuerunt, ut Abraham, Isaac, & Iacob: & hac occasione peruenerunt ad principes, quos postea simul in doctrina Christiana instituerunt.
units.tr: It is the day of Luke the evangelist, a native of Antioch. Antioch is a city of Syria, which was assigned as the boundary or territory of the people of Israel. Antiochus had named it after himself, and his name was Macedonian; it means the same as avenger, champion or punisher, from "anti" and "echein" [ἀντὶ καὶ ἔχειν]. Now this Luke was by profession a physician, and at the age of eighty he was hanged on an olive tree at Thebes. That unskilled and stupid city destroyed so holy a man. Those peoples were always dense Cyclopes, whence the proverb "Boeotian pig" and the saying "to live in the Boeotian manner." Luke also travelled through Asia Minor from Bithynia as far as Greece, and he was a companion of Paul's journeys. The end of the others was as follows. John the Evangelist died a peaceful death at Ephesus. Matthew, in Ethiopia below Egypt, was drenched in pitch; the flame, once kindled, first consumed the idols standing around him, and afterwards killed him. Mark taught at Cyrene, below Africa and Egypt (that region was a colony of the Lacedaemonians or of the Argonauts); afterwards he returned to Alexandria, and, dragged through the city, was killed. Thus Matthew, Mark and Luke were taken out of the way by violent death. Now consider what are the distinctive opinions of each. John the Evangelist wrote after the others because he wished to add certain discourses of Christ, such as the raising of Lazarus and others, which the rest had omitted. The following are found peculiarly in Matthew and omitted by the others: the account of the Magi, the slaughter of the infants; the sermon on the mount, which is a very necessary exposition of the law. Likewise that memorable saying, found in Matthew alone: "Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened." Also: "I am with you always, to the end of the age." Also: "Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them." Also: "It is not the will of the Father that one of these little ones should perish." In Mark alone are these sayings: "Lord, I believe; help my unbelief." Also: "Everyone will be salted with fire, and every sacrifice will be salted with salt. Salt is a good thing." In Luke alone are found these: the story of Zacchaeus, the angel's mission to Mary, the Samaritan, and the example of the prodigal son. These are worthy of consideration, so that the text may become more familiar. Luke was indeed the teacher of two chief doctrines: the doctrine of God, which you see he wrote most learnedly; and, as a physician, that is a natural philosopher, he was the teacher of the doctrine of the nature of things. For consideration of the nature of things is a guide to the knowledge of God. Hence the first fathers too were especially devoted to the medical profession, such as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; and by this occasion they came to princes, whom they afterwards instructed at the same time in Christian doctrine.

units.la: XXXI. Octobris.
units.tr: XXXI. October.

units.la: Fuit olim consuetudo in ecclesia, ut in festo omnium Sanctorum uenderentur indulgentiae. Ideoq; in profesto omnium Sanctorum sunt primum a Luthero propositiones contra indulgentias, anno 1517. hora 12, ad ianuam templi arcis Vuitebergensis affixae. Ibi primum motae sunt disputationes, & remotae indulgentiae a Papistis venditae. Fuerunt enim indulgentiae res mediae, & tales quae concedebantur: Graeci nominarunt satisfactiones, ἐπιτιμίαν, id est, multam vel poenam, quae delinquenti imponitur. Vocabulum Germanicum Büß, est nomen conueniens satisfactioni: quia cruciabant multos homines istis phantasijs multarum, seu satisfactionum: omne enim nimium uertitur in nigrum monachum, ut dici solet de euidentibus excessibus. Ibi Pontifices & Episcopi instituerunt runt uenditiones indulgentiarum, id est relaxarùt pœnas canonicas, quæ alioqui fuerunt iniustæ, & tantùm ideo uendebant, ut extorquerent pecuniâ. Sicut multum pecuniæ conflabant Papistæ isto modo, ita ut Maximilianus Imperator sæpè deliberauerit de abolitione istarum indulgentiarum, etiam ante doctorem Lutherū: sed quo modo id faceret, ignorabat. Postea Lutherus hoc die, hora 12, publicè Propositionibus affixis in templo arcis, taxauit istos errores, & reduxit populum ad ueram doctrinam. Annus autem nunc est quadragesimus secundus ab eo, quo hæc incepta sunt à Luthero. Videtis quàm fuerit grata causa omnibus eruditis & principibus, quamobrem etiam Principes Luthero fauebãt. Sed iam iterum uidetis ingratitudinem mundi erga ministros & doctores in Ecclesia: sicut Pindarus dicit de ingratitudine hominum, ϖα λαυὰ γὰρ ἐνδεῖα χαρίς, ἀμνάμονες δ' ἀνθρωποι: id est, dormit antiqua gratia, & homines sunt immemores. Itē, Quod dolet meminit, quod placet obliuiscitur. Hæc anno 1559 relata sunt.
units.tr: There was once a custom in the Church that indulgences were sold on the feast of All Saints. Therefore on the eve of All Saints, in the year 1517 at the twelfth hour, Luther first posted propositions against indulgences on the door of the church of the castle at Wittenberg. There the first disputations arose, and the indulgences sold by the Papists were set aside. For indulgences were things indifferent, and were granted as such. The Greeks called satisfactions ἐπιτιμίαν [epitimian], that is, the fine or penalty imposed on the offender. The German word Büß is a fitting name for satisfaction, because by these fantasies of many penances (or satisfactions) they tormented many people; for everything excessive turns into the black monk, as is commonly said of manifest excesses. There the Pontiffs and bishops began to sell indulgences, that is, to remit canonical penalties, which were otherwise unjust, and they sold them only in order to extort money. Just as the Papists gathered much money in this way, so the Emperor Maximilian often deliberated on abolishing these indulgences, even before Doctor Luther; but he did not know how to do it. Afterwards Luther, on this day at the twelfth hour, publicly posted his propositions on the church of the castle, censured these errors and led the people back to the true doctrine. Now it is the forty-second year since these things were begun by Luther. You see how welcome the cause was to all learned men and princes, which is why even the princes favoured Luther. But again you see the ingratitude of the world towards ministers and teachers in the Church, just as Pindar says of human ingratitude: παλαιὰ γὰρ ἐνδεῖα χάρις, ἀμνάμονες δ' ἄνθρωποι [palaia gar endeia charis, amnamones d' anthrōpoi], that is, old grace sleeps, and men are forgetful. Likewise: what grieves a man he remembers, what pleases he forgets. These things were recorded in 1559.

units.la: NOVEMBER.
units.tr: NOVEMBER.

units.la: V. Dies Nouembris. Dies necis Zachariæ.
units.tr: V. November. The day of Zechariah's death.

units.la: Dicunt hoc die interfectum esse Zachariam, de quo in Euangelio dicitur: Veniet super uos omnis sanguis qui effusus est ab Abel usq; ad Zachariã.
units.tr: They say that on this day Zechariah was killed, of whom the Gospel says: "Upon you will come all the blood shed from Abel to Zechariah."

units.la: Quanquam alij aliter scribunt: tamen Basilius scribit esse traditum in Ecclesia à veteribus, quòd intelligendum sit de Zacharia patre Ioannis Bapti-stæ, quem interfecerunt sacerdotes, testificante hūc Christum esse Messiam. & credo ita esse. Quanquā Ioannes interfectus est post patrem ab Herode, tamen credo fieri mentionē Zachariæ propter atrocitatem insignem, quia in templo est interfectus: & quòd Ioannes non ab isto populo, sed ab Herode interficiebatur, sicut & alij multi post illum sunt interfecti. Quàm multi perierunt tempore Machabæorū? Cogitate quanta res fuerit, istum senem Zachariam interfici? quia non dubium est, eius ætatē fuisse admodum senilem, & ipsum octogesimum, nec nonagesimum annum excessisse. Hunc Zachariam Deus voluit esse testem de se: quia præcipua lumina in Ecclesia oportet similia fieri imaginis filij Dei. Cogitate quale spectaculum fuerit, quando Elizabeth (quam adhuc credo vixisse) vidit interfici maritum? Hæc considerantes bene memen-tote, cur Deus suos electos cruci & afflictionibus subijciat.
units.tr: Others write otherwise, but Basil writes that it has been handed down in the Church from the ancients that the reference is to Zechariah the father of John the Baptist, whom the priests killed, because he bore witness that Christ is the Messiah. And I believe it is so. Although John was killed after his father, by Herod, I believe mention is made of Zechariah because of the outstanding atrocity, since he was killed in the temple. John was not killed by that people but by Herod, just as many others after him were killed. How many perished in the time of the Maccabees? Consider what a great thing it was for that old man Zechariah to be killed. There is no doubt that he was very far advanced in years, and had passed eighty, if not ninety. God wanted this Zechariah to be a witness to himself, because the chief lights in the Church ought to become like the image of the Son of God. Consider what a sight it was when Elizabeth (whom I believe was still alive) saw her husband killed. In considering these things, remember well why God subjects his elect to the cross and to afflictions.

units.la: X. Nouembris. Dies est pugnæ ad Varnam, quando Vladislaus Vngariæ & Poloniæ rex, frater Casimiri, cùm esset accersitus in regnū Vngariæ & Poloniæ, gessit bellum aduersus Tur-cas, vbi habuit socios Venetos ac Romanum pon-tificem. tificem. Factæ sunt induciæ cum Turcis. Aliquanto pòst Turci fuerunt in Asia clade affecti. Voluit autem Papa renouari bellum, & disputauit illam pacem non ualere, quia esset sine Papæ autoritate facta. Quare renunciatum est Turcis, illa pacta irrita esse, quæ inita essent ab Vladislao, nesciente Pontifice. Ibi rursus est motū bellum: & quanquā dissuadente patre Huniade, & rex Vladislaus interfectus est, & cum eo præcipua pars nobilitatis Polonicæ occubuit. Fuit autem disputatio hæc: An illæ induciæ ualerent, an non? Et fuit tale argumentum:
units.tr: November 10. It is the day of the battle at Varna, when Vladislaus, king of Hungary and Poland, brother of Casimir, after he had been summoned to the kingdom of Hungary and Poland, waged war against the Turks, having as allies the Venetians and the Roman pontiff. A truce was made with the Turks. Some time later the Turks suffered a defeat in Asia. The Pope, however, wished the war to be renewed, and argued that the peace was not valid, because it had been made without the Pope's authority. Therefore it was declared to the Turks that those agreements which Vladislaus had entered into, without the Pontiff's knowledge, were void. War was then renewed there; and although his father Hunyadi advised against it, King Vladislaus was killed, and with him the chief part of the Polish nobility perished. The dispute was this: whether those truces were valid or not. The argument ran as follows:

units.la: Pacta facta cum alijs, nescientibus socijs, nõ debent esse rata.
units.tr: Agreements made with others, without the knowledge of their allies, ought not to be binding.

units.la: Socij Vladislai non erant assensi, sed nescierunt illa pacta.
units.tr: The allies of Vladislaus had not consented, but they did not know of those agreements.

units.la: Ergo illa pacta Vladislai sunt irrita.
units.tr: Therefore the agreements of Vladislaus are void.

units.la: Respondeo ad maiorē: Pacta cum alijs facta, nescientibus socijs, non debent esse rata, scilicet paribus socijs: quando tantundem iuris habent socij, tunc illa pacta non ualent. Illud uerò bellum gerebatur à rege Hungarico tanquā principali, etiamsi habebat auxilia aliarum gentium. Minor est distinguenda. Siue sint pares, siue nõ sint pares, aliud est loqui de nescientibus socijs, aliud de scientibus. Illa res disputata est tunc magnis contentionibus: quia fuerunt utrinq; episcopi Polonici & Italici. Hungarici garici & Polonici episcopi bellum dissuaserunt. Est igitur facta magna clades, & prælium cõmissum pridie Martini: id est, hoc die, anno 1444. Sūt ad hunc annum 59, anni 115. Breue tempus est inde usq; ad nostram ætatem. Varna non procul abest à Constantinopoli: sint sanè 20 miliaria, credo tamē propius esse. Sunt fortasse 12 miliaria nostratia.
units.tr: I answer to the major premise: agreements made with others, without the knowledge of their allies, ought not to be binding, namely when the allies are equals: when the allies have equal right, then those agreements are not valid. But that war was waged by the Hungarian king as the principal party, even though he had the help of other peoples. The minor premise must be distinguished: whether the allies are equal or not equal, it is one thing to speak of allies who do not know, and another of those who do know. That matter was then disputed with great contention, since there were Polish and Italian bishops on both sides; the Hungarian and Polish bishops advised against the war. A great disaster therefore followed, and the battle was joined on the day before St. Martin's, that is, on this day, in the year 1444. From this year to the present there are 59 years, and 115 years. It is a short time from then to our age. Varna is not far from Constantinople: it is certainly 20 miles, though I believe it is nearer. Perhaps it is 12 of our German miles.

units.la: XI. Nouembris.
units.tr: XI. November.

units.la: Dies est dicatus Martino, qui fuit è Sabaria. Vos adolescentuli debetis discere Cosmographica: quia ualde utile est cogitare metas terræ: & quòd non sit infinitum quiddam terra, sed certum spacium, in quo voluit Deus uiuere genus humanū, & ostendere filium suum. Non amate illos furores Democriticos, affirmantes esse plures mundos: sed in illo unico mundo cogitate, quo ordine, quibus locis ecclesia propagata sit, ubi edita testimonia. Sic Germania hæc nostra patria habet suas metas & limites, quæ his sequentibus uersibus describuntur.
units.tr: The day is dedicated to Martin, who came from Sabaria. You young men ought to learn cosmography, because it is very useful to consider the limits of the earth, and that the earth is not some infinite thing but a definite space, in which God willed the human race to live and to show forth his Son. Do not love those Democritean frenzies which affirm that there are many worlds; rather, in that one world, consider by what order and in what places the Church has been propagated, and where the testimonies are published. So this our fatherland, Germany, has its bounds and limits, which are described in the following verses.

units.la: Versiculi Philippi Melanchthonis de finibus seu limitibus Germaniæ.
units.tr: Little verses of Philip Melanchthon on the boundaries or limits of Germany.

units.la: ῥλῖνος ἀπὸ ξεφύρς, βιάλεσιο δὲ ῥεῖθρον ἀπ' ἠσς,γόρμανῶν λρατόρῶν γαῖαν ὀέιξα ὅλλν.ἐχατιὰ δ' ἄλπεις νιφόεσσα πρὸς νότον εἰσίν,ἐς βορέαν ὠίματος βαλτινὸς ὠπεανός.
units.tr: The Rhine from the west, the Vistula from the east, the Alps snowy to the south, and the Baltic Ocean to the north, enclose the land of the Germans. [ῥλῖνος ἀπὸ ξεφύρς, βιάλεσιο δὲ ῥεῖθρον ἀπ' ἠσς,γόρμανῶν λρατόρῶν γαῖαν ὀέιξα ὅλλν.ἐχατιὰ δ' ἄλπεις νιφόεσσα πρὸς νότον εἰσίν,ἐς βορέαν ὠίματος βαλτινὸς ὠπεανός.]

units.la: Vel
units.tr: Or:

units.la: εἰς ἡῶ βιαδρος, ῥήνυς δ᾽ ἀπο βαλύτης ὄχθαι, γόρμαναν χώρας τόρματα ἑσίν ὅλης.
units.tr: The Vistula from the east, the Rhine from the west, and the banks of the ... of the whole land of the Germans are the limits. [εἰς ἡῶ βιαδρος, ῥήνυς δ᾽ ἀπο βαλύτης ὄχθαι, γόρμαναν χώρας τόρματα ἑσίν ὅλης.]

units.la: γηέίχθη δ᾽ ἔγνος νιφόεσσαν πρὸς νότον ἄλπεας, ἐς βορέαν ὤνυματος βαλτινὸς ὠκεανός.
units.tr: The snowy Alps to the south, and the Baltic Ocean to the north, have been set as the boundary. [γηέίχθη δ᾽ ἔγνος νιφόεσσαν πρὸς νότον ἄλπεας, ἐς βορέαν ὤνυματος βαλτινὸς ὠκεανός.]

units.la: Rhenus ab occasu, Viadri sed flumen ab ortu, Clauserunt fines Teutona terra tuos.
units.tr: The Rhine from the west, the Oder from the east, have enclosed your borders, German land.

units.la: Aeriæq; alpes immotum limes ad Austrum, Balticus ad Boream terminat Oceanus.
units.tr: The Aerian Alps, an unmoved limit to the south, and the Baltic Ocean bound it to the north.

units.la: Aliquæ sunt factæ mutationes. Germaniæ finis olim erat fistula ad Orientem, ubi nunc est Craco- uia: quæ nunc à gente Polonica, quæ est illa uetus gens Heneta, inhabitatur. Et Strabo dicit Albim fluere per mediam Germaniam. Cornelius Tacitus dicit Germaniæ fines esse ad Austrum alpes, & ad Septentrionem mare Balticum, ad occidente Rhenū. Sic semper est cōstitutus Germaniæ finis. Et nomina fluminū magis durabilia sunt quàm montiū: quia nomina montium mutantur per partes, flumina plerunq; à primo ortu usq; ad finem retinent idem nomē. Ad Orientem dixit Cornelius Tacitus esse montem Cætium, & eum dirimere Noricos à Pannonia. Situs est hic mons non procul à Vienna, quem Germani uocāt Kalenberg, daruon auch der pfaff von Kalenberg ist. Accepit autem Panno nia citò doctrinam Euangelij. S. Martinus docuit Syrmij, ubi Irenæus est passus. Syrmiū est circa Belgradum, gradum, habetq; nomen à Syrmio Getico rege, qui cæpit Lisymachum, cui postea dedit ei suam filiā, ut esset pax.
units.tr: Some changes have been made. The boundary of Germany was once a fistula toward the east, where Cracow now is, which is now inhabited by the Polish people, who are that ancient Veneti. And Strabo says the Elbe flows through the middle of Germany. Cornelius Tacitus says that the boundaries of Germany are the Alps to the south and the Baltic Sea to the north, and the Rhine to the west. So the boundary of Germany has always been fixed. And the names of rivers are more durable than those of mountains, because the names of mountains change in their parts, whereas rivers generally keep the same name from their first source to their end. Cornelius Tacitus said that to the east there is Mount Cætius, and that it separates the Norici from Pannonia. This mountain is not far from Vienna, and the Germans call it Kalenberg, "daruon auch der pfaff von Kalenberg ist." Pannonia, however, quickly received the teaching of the gospel. St. Martin taught at Sirmium, where Irenaeus suffered. Sirmium is near Belgrade, and it has its name from the Getic king Sirmus, who captured Lysimachus, to whom he later gave his daughter, so that there might be peace.

units.la: Laudatur eius bonitas, quòd pepercerit clarissi mo regi, quem Alexander obiecit leoni, qui per-cusso leone vitam conservavit. Fuit verò natus S. Martinus in urbe Sabaria in Pannonia, nō procul à Bresburga, quæ fuit colonia Claudij Imperato-ris, ut Plinius scribit. Quæ urbs nomē (ut opinor) sortita est à flumine: flumen verò dictum esse credo à faucibus montium infra Viennā. Sabaria item flumen est, unde & civitati juxta hoc sitæ idem nomē est inditum. Fuit autem hic Martinus vir nobilis, miles, & civis in illa colonia. Quare etiamsi fuit Christianus, tamē oportuit cum militare sub Juliā-no apostata Imperatore. Diu vixit, videlicet usq; ad Theodosij tempora: viditq; magnas seditiones sub Maximo, qui fuit rebellis imperatori. Et quia amabat virtutem, & veram religionem, non libenter fuit cum exercitu Juliani athei, qui à Christiana doctrina defecerat: contra quem scripserunt cum alij, tum Gregorius Nazianzenus, qui egregiè pingit eum, & eius gestus. Martinus itaq; pertæsus (ut credo) consuetudinis Imperatoris, cum ab eo di-scessisset, studijs applicauit animum: ac in Galliam profectus ad Hilarium, vixit cum eo familiariter.
units.tr: His goodness is praised, because he spared the most famous king, whom Alexander threw to a lion, and who, having struck the lion, preserved his life. St. Martin was born in the city of Sabaria in Pannonia, not far from Pressburg, which was a colony of the Emperor Claudius, as Pliny writes. This city has (as I think) gained its name from the river; and I believe the river was named from the gorges of the mountains below Vienna. Sabaria is also a river, and from it the city situated beside it was given the same name. This Martin was a nobleman, a soldier, and a citizen of that colony. So although he was a Christian, he nevertheless had to serve as a soldier under the apostate emperor Julian. He lived a long life, namely until the times of Theodosius, and he saw great seditions under Maximus, who was a rebel against the emperor. And because he loved virtue and the true religion, he was not willing to be with the army of the atheist Julian, who had defected from Christian doctrine. Against him wrote others, and also Gregory Nazianzen, who portrays him and his deeds admirably. Martin, therefore, weary (as I believe) of the emperor's company, when he had departed from him, applied his mind to study; and setting out for Gaul he went to Hilary and lived intimately with him.

units.la: Cumq; multi essent Arriani, ipse constantissimè restitit Arrianis, eosq; refutauit: retinens Eccle-sias Occidetis in uera cofessione de filio Dei, quod λόγος sit persona. Cum uero esset clarus, & con-stans in ueritate, factus est tandem episcopus Thu-ronensis in Gallia, ibiq; uita defunctus est. Inci-dit senex in calamitatem temporu, cum Maximus regeret Galliam, qui aduersabatur Theodosio. Fuit familiaris Maximo regenti Galliam, qui multa fe-cit ex eius consilio. Ita fuit ille Martinus Pannonius, & gubernauit ecclesiam inter magna pericula.
units.tr: And since there were many Arians, he himself most steadfastly resisted the Arians and refuted them, holding to the churches of the West in the true confession concerning the Son of God, that the Word (λόγος) is a person. Since he was famous and steadfast in the truth, he was at last made bishop of Tours in Gaul, and there he died. The old man fell into the calamities of the times, when Maximus ruled Gaul, who opposed Theodosius. He was a familiar of Maximus, who ruled Gaul, and did many things by his counsel. Thus that Martin was a Pannonian, and he governed the Church amid great dangers.

units.la: Porro, quod ad patriam eius attinet, sciendum est, post mortem Martini multas gentes occupasse Pan-noniam. Nostri homines Gotthi ibi tenuerunt par-tem, & credo illos Transsyluanos esse reliquias ue-rum Germanorum. Carolus Magnus non tenuit Pannoniam, sed represit Vngaros, & cum eis ad Ratisbonam dimicauit: sicut postea Otto Impera-tor represit eos ad Augustam, & Heinricus pater Ottonis ad Mersburgum. Postquam occupata est Pannonia, ubi illae gentes factae sunt mitiores, didi-cerunt doctrinam de Deo. Rex quoq; couersus est ad doctrinam Christianam, duxit uxorem sancti Heinrici Bambergensis. Quapropter deinceps fuit inter eos bona amicitia, & pax propter coniun-ctionem coniugij, & affinitatem.
units.tr: Moreover, as to his homeland, it should be noted that after Martin's death many peoples occupied Pannonia. Our own people, the Goths, held part of it, and I believe those Transylvanians are remnants of the true Germans. Charles the Great did not hold Pannonia, but he checked the Hungarians and fought them at Regensburg, just as afterwards the Emperor Otto repelled them at Augsburg, and Henry, Otto's father, at Merseburg. After Pannonia was taken, those peoples became milder and learned the doctrine of God. The king too was converted to Christian doctrine, and he took as his wife the sister of St Henry of Bamberg. For this reason there was thereafter good friendship between them, and peace through the bond of marriage and kinship.

units.la: XIX. Nouembris. Est dies Elisabe-thae. Est autem eius alia historia, quam matris Ioan-nis. his. Hoc enim die fit mentio matronæ principis Thuringiæ. Et ut prius de uocabulo moneam, Elizabeth dicitur quies dei, seu quies donata à Deo. Fuit etiam hoc nomen coniugis Zachariæ, matris Ioannis baptistæ: sed illa Elizabeth cuius historia hoc tempore recitatur, fuit alia. Et multa sunt memorabilia exempla in hac historia. Hæc enim matrona uixit in exercitijs pietatis insignib°: fuit modesta, postraquam secuta cruce, exhibuit se in ea tolerantissimam. Nata fuit patre Andrea rege Vngarico, admodum præstanti: matre vero Germanica Gertrude. Dicunt alij fuisse Bauaricam, filiam ducis Bauarici: quod non est. In aliquibus libris est, quòd fuerit Morauica: utrunq; affine est. Sed fuerunt duces de Mœran, qui tenuerunt Voitlandiā, cuius hæ fuerūt ciuitates: Culmbach, Blauen, Hoff, &c. Hunc ipsi ducatū uocarūt, das Hertzogthumb zū Mœran, tempore Friderici Barbarossæ: quia post illum ducatus de Mœran facta est diuisio in diuersos præfectus. inde uocari cœpit Voitlandia, & tractus est uetus Varistorum, extrema pars Bohemicorum montium uersus Misniam, & Franconiam. Mater Gertrudis fuit filia ducis de Mœran, nupta regi Vngarico, quæ incidit in magnam calamitatem sua culpa. Fuit apud eam frater, qui procul dubio fuit homo insolens, & ferox. Iste amauit coniugem cuiusdam principis Vngarici, & habuit adiutricē suam sororem reginam, absente marito. Nam rex erat Hierosolymæ in illa expeditione, qua recupe rata fuit Syria. Principes Germanici & Italici fue runt ingressi in Syriam ante annos quadringētos, & eam recuperarūt, represseruntq; Turcas: alio qui multo citius Turcæ occupassent Græcum impe rium, quàm tandem euenit. Fuerunt duæ expedi tiones circa ea tempora: in priore fuit Godef-dus Bilionensis, ex familia ducum Iuliacensium & Cli uensium natus, qui Hierosolymæ spineā coro-na, impositio in sepulchrum Christi capite, fuit coro natus: ubi pulcherrimæ res gestæ fuerunt. In secun da expeditione fuit hic rex Vngaricus Andreas, quo absente, coniunx ipsius habuit secum cuiusdā principis coniugē, quam frater ipsius reginæ ama uit: in qua re usus est sorore adiutrice, cuius fraude negocium perfectum est. Maritus stupratæ mulie ris, interfecit Gertrudē, absente rege. Postea uerò cùm res esset cognita, rex absoluit illum suæ coniu gis interfectorem. Credo illam calamitatem matris fuisse causam, quare filia Elisabeth uixerit in tan ta modestia & humilitate, ita ut ipsa solita sit seruire pauperibus, & curare ægrotos. Isenaci plurimum habitauit, & in oppido Hasiæ Marpurgo, ubi & ostendūtur cubicula in quibus uixerit. Ise naci gynæcium subterraneum excisum est in ipsis faxis, ita ut mirum sit homines potuisse retinere ua-letudinem in illis saxis, sicut ibi uidi. Sic hæc Eliza-beth fuit admodum modesta, temperans, & habuit multa & uaria inuocationis, beneficentiæ, & pie-tatis exercitia, fuitq; benefica erga pauperes. Vidi literas donationis factæ ab ipsa, hospitali, in oppi-do Gottha, quæ simpliciter latinè sunt scriptæ, si-cut tunc fuit consuetudo: non extant ueteres literæ germanicè scriptæ. Hæc Elizabeth habuit maritū præstantissimum virum, Ludouicum Lantgrauiū, qui fuit uicarius imperatoris Friderici Secundi, absente uidelicet Friderico in Asia & Italia. Et tūc nominabatur una ditio Lantgrauiatus Thuringiæ, à Marpurgo inde usq; ad Naumburgum. Fuit itaq; potens princeps, & ualuit equitatu, nec paruam sub Imperio suo habuit regionem. Ille bonus prin-ceps uixit in summa concordia cum coniuge. Mul-tis reb. in Germania gestis uoluit proficisci in Asiā ad resistendum Turcis, sicut tunc fuit usitatum. in qua expeditione hic bonus princeps Brundusij est mortuus. Huic successit agnatus eius Hermannus, quanquam ipsi natus esset Ludouicus filius, & fi-lia Sophia: tamen adolescens Ludouicus est mor-tuus. Scribitur uerò, quòd Hermannus eum sustule-rit ueneno. Sit sanè, sed ille Hermannus post mortē Friderici Secundi appetiuit Imperium, & habuit fauorem Romani pontificis. Postquam eo animo peruenisset
units.tr: 19 November. It is the day of Elizabeth. There is also another story of her, that of the mother of John. For on this day mention is made of the matron, the princess of Thuringia. And first, let me say something about the name: Elizabeth means "rest of God," or rest given by God. This name was also borne by the wife of Zechariah, the mother of John the Baptist, but the Elizabeth whose story is recited at this time was a different woman. And this history contains many memorable examples. This matron lived in outstanding exercises of piety. She was modest, and after she had embraced the cross, she showed herself most patient in bearing it. She was born of her father Andrew, king of Hungary, a most distinguished man, and of her mother Gertrude, a German. Others say that she was Bavarian, the daughter of a Bavarian duke, but that is not so. In some books it is said that she was Moravian; both are close to the truth. But there were the dukes of Meran, who held the Vogtland, whose cities were these: Culmbach, Plauen, Hof, and so on. They called this duchy "das Hertzogthumb zu Meran" in the time of Frederick Barbarossa, because after him the duchy of Meran was divided among various governors. From this the region began to be called the Vogtland, and the old territory of the Varisti, the outer part of the Bohemian mountains toward Meissen and Franconia, was so named. Her mother Gertrude was the daughter of the duke of Meran, married to the king of Hungary, and she fell into great calamity through her own fault. She had a brother, who was without doubt an arrogant and fierce man. He loved the wife of a certain Hungarian nobleman, and in the king's absence he had his sister, the queen, as his helper. For the king was in Jerusalem on that expedition by which Syria was recovered. The princes of Germany and Italy had entered Syria four hundred years ago, recovered it, and held back the Turks; otherwise the Turks would have seized the Greek empire much sooner than they eventually did. There were two expeditions about that time. In the first was Godfrey of Bouillon, born of the family of the dukes of Jülich and Cleves, who was crowned at Jerusalem, a crown of thorns being placed on his head over the sepulchre of Christ; there very splendid deeds were done. In the second expedition was this King Andrew of Hungary, and in his absence his wife had with her the wife of a certain nobleman, whom the queen's brother loved. In this affair he made use of his sister as helper, and by her trickery the business was carried through. The husband of the seduced woman killed Gertrude while the king was away. Afterward, when the matter became known, the king absolved the slayer of his wife. I believe that this calamity of her mother was the reason why the daughter Elizabeth lived in such great modesty and humility, so that she was accustomed to serve the poor and care for the sick. She lived for the most part at Eisenach, and in the town of Marburg in Hesse, where the rooms in which she lived are shown. At Eisenach a subterranean women's chamber has been cut out of the very rock, so that it is remarkable that people could keep their health in those rocks, as I saw there. So this Elizabeth was most modest and temperate, and she had many and varied exercises of prayer, beneficence, and piety, and she was generous toward the poor. I have seen the letters of gift made by her to the hospital in the town of Gotha, which are written simply in Latin, as was the custom at that time; no old letters written in German survive. This Elizabeth had as her husband a most excellent man, Louis, Landgrave, who was the vicar of the emperor Frederick II, namely while Frederick was away in Asia and Italy. And at that time the single lordship called the Landgraviate of Thuringia extended from Marburg as far as Naumburg. He was therefore a powerful prince, strong in cavalry, and he held no small region under his rule. That good prince lived in the greatest harmony with his wife. After many events in Germany he wished to set out for Asia to resist the Turks, as was then the custom; and on this expedition the good prince died at Brindisi. He was succeeded by his kinsman Hermann, although Louis, a son, and a daughter Sophia had been born to him; yet the young Louis died. But it is written that Hermann removed him by poison. Be that as it may, after the death of Frederick II this Hermann aspired to the empire and had the favour of the Roman pontiff. When he had come to Ulm with this purpose,

units.la: ttt peruenisset Vlmā, ibi est interfectus: siue quòd appetiuisset imperium, siue propter alias causas: sicut fuerat inquietus etiam domi. Mortuo adolescente Ludouico, iste Hermannus expulit hanc sanctam & piam matronam Elizabetham in exilium. Sic misera sine comitatu peruenit Bambergam, ubi in monasterio est mortua. Filia uerò Sophia est eloca ta marchioni Hollandiæ. Siquidem nulli erant hæredes ex Lantgrauijs: nam Lantgrauij eo tempore fuerūt etiā Marchiones Misniæ. Venit itaq; ipsa cum marito & filio, petens Lantgrauiatum totius Thuringiæ & Hassiæ. Marchiones enim Misnenses iam ad se attraxerant Thuringiam. Implorauit autem auxilia Ducum Brunsuicensium. Res igitur tandem eò deducta est, ut Marchiones Misnenses retinèrent Thuringiam, Sophia uerò Hassiam. Itaq; facta sunt duo nomina, licet sint eadem insignia. Sic auxilio Ducum Brunsuicensiū hæredes in Hassiam introducti sunt, ac res est composita: hac ratione Landtgrauij Hassiæ habent originem à Sophia, filia Elizabetæ.
units.tr: he was killed there, whether because he aspired to the empire or for other reasons; for he had also been restless at home. After the young Louis died, this Hermann drove this holy and pious matron Elizabeth into exile. So the wretched woman, without an escort, came to Bamberg, where she died in a monastery. Her daughter Sophia was married to the margrave of Holland, since there were no heirs among the Landgraves; for at that time the Landgraves were also margraves of Meissen. So Sophia came with her husband and son, claiming the landgraviate of all Thuringia and Hesse, for the margraves of Meissen had already drawn Thuringia to themselves. She implored the help of the dukes of Brunswick. The matter was therefore at last brought to this point: the margraves of Meissen retained Thuringia, and Sophia Hesse. Thus two titles were made, although the coats of arms remained the same. So with the help of the dukes of Brunswick the heirs were introduced into Hesse, and the affair was settled; in this way the landgraves of Hesse take their origin from Sophia, daughter of Elizabeth.

units.la: XXX. Nouembris.
units.tr: XXX. November.

units.la: Dies est sancti Andreæ: de quo nihil scimus, nisi quòd docuerit in oppido Achaiæ Patris, & quòd ibi crucifixus sit. Narrātur eius miracula, sed qualia sint nescio. Illud miror, si fuerit Patris quando Paulus in Achaia docuit, nullam fieri ipsorum congressuum gressuum mentionem: quia Corinthus uicina est Patris, propter Helicen & Buram, quae urbes terraemotu absorptae sunt. Patrae adhuc stat: sunt pauci anni, quado Andreas de Doria cepit eas, sed no diu retinuit. Turci enim iterum illas recuperarunt. Helice et Bura, sunt duae urbes in Achaia, quae sunt submersae tempore belli Peloponnesiaci, ante pugnam Leuctricam. Et hoc signum antecessit pugna Leuctrica, sicut terraemotus excidia urbium, cometae (sicut nos uidimus) aliaq; signa similia praecedere solent euersionem regnorum. Harum duarum urbium nominatim fit metio apud Scriptores, etiam apud Aristotelem: quae urbes submersae sunt ut Sodoma & Gomorrha. & tamen ex illis, immersis sordibus, Deus pro immensa sua bonitate collegit Ecclesiam.
units.tr: It is the day of Saint Andrew, of whom we know nothing except that he taught in the town of Patrae in Achaia and that he was crucified there. His miracles are related, but I do not know what kind they were. I wonder at this: if he was at Patrae when Paul taught in Achaia, no mention is made of any meeting between them. For Corinth is near Patrae, on account of Helice and Bura, which cities were swallowed up by an earthquake. Patrae still stands. It is only a few years since Andrew Doria took them, but he did not hold them long, for the Turks recovered them again. Helice and Bura are two cities in Achaia which were submerged in the time of the Peloponnesian War, before the battle of Leuctra. This sign preceded the battle of Leuctra, just as earthquakes, the ruin of cities, comets (as we have seen) and other similar signs are wont to precede the overthrow of kingdoms. Mention of these two cities is made by name among the writers, even by Aristotle. These cities were submerged just as Sodom and Gomorrah were. And yet, out of those sunken in filth, God in his immense goodness gathered the Church.

units.la: DECEMBER.
units.tr: DECEMBER.

units.la: VI. Decembris.
units.tr: 6 December.

units.la: Celebratur memoria sancti Nicolai. Est autem hic Nicolaus oriundus ex urbe Patara, quae est in Lycia, in principio Asiae.
units.tr: The memory of Saint Nicholas is celebrated. This Nicholas was a native of the city of Patara, which is in Lycia, at the entrance of Asia.

units.la: Fuit episcopus in oppido Myra, tempore Constantini: & tantae autoritatis, ut cum esset sumendum supplicium de tribus militibus, seu capitaneis, qui fuerant calumnia accusati, ipse interce-deret, deret, & reprimeret lictorē, postraq; scriberet Imperatori fieri illis iniuriam. quo audito, Imperator approbauit eius factum. Dicitur etiam quòd fucrit beneficus & liberalis erga pauperes. Interfuit senex in synodo Nicæna: fuit’que unus qui approbarunt illum articulum fidei, de diuinitate filij Dei.
units.tr: He was bishop in the town of Myra in the time of Constantine, and of such authority that, when three soldiers, or captains, who had been falsely accused, were about to be executed, he interceded, held back the executioner, and afterwards wrote to the Emperor that they were being wronged. When this was heard, the Emperor approved his action. It is also said that he was generous and liberal towards the poor. The old man took part in the Synod of Nicaea, and was one of those who approved that article of faith concerning the divinity of the Son of God.

units.la: XV Decembris.
units.tr: December 15.

units.la: Hoc die collocatum est idolum in templum Hierosolymitanum, quando Antiochus exercuit horribilem seuitiam ad delendum populum Iudaicum, & eius leges. Habebat enim hanc persuasionem: quia sciebat istum populum rebellare regibus propter religionem, & res magnas gessisse, ac extendisse imperium in uicinam Syriam: voluit deducere colonias Ethnicas in illam terram. quod durum admodum & arduū fuit. Deus etiam voluit prædicere, & præmonere tempus vastationis, & finem istius politiæ.
units.tr: On this day an idol was set up in the Temple at Jerusalem, when Antiochus carried out a horrible savagery to destroy the Jewish people and their laws. For he had this reasoning: he knew that this people rebelled against kings on account of their religion, had waged great wars, and had extended their rule into neighbouring Syria, so he wished to settle Gentile colonies in that land. This was a very hard and difficult undertaking. God also willed to foretell and forewarn the time of the devastation and the end of that polity.

units.la: Fuit autem talis vastatio, sicut Daniel testatur, talisq; tribulatio, qualis non fuit ab initio. Templū fuit profanatum, & additum est præsidium. Cogitate quantum scelerum factum sit. In templo facta sunt stupra, raptæ uirgines, senes nonagenarij interfecti sunt, pueri suspēsi, stupratæq; honestæ matronæ: Bacchanalia celebrata in ipsa urbe Hierosolyma, quæ eo tempore habuit pulcherrimum templum plum in toto genere humano. In Bacchanalijs discurrebatur ad publicos concubitus, ita ut Romæ sint collocata præsidia contra Bacchanalia, à quibus multi sic discurrentes sunt interfecti.
units.tr: The devastation was such, as Daniel testifies, and the tribulation was such as had not been from the beginning. The Temple was profaned, and a garrison was added. Consider how many crimes were committed. In the Temple there were acts of fornication; virgins were seized; men of ninety years were killed; boys were hanged; and honourable matrons were violated. Bacchanalia were celebrated in the city of Jerusalem itself, which at that time had the most beautiful temple in the whole human race. In the Bacchanalia people ran about to public couplings, so that at Rome guards were posted against the Bacchanalia, and many who ran about in this way were killed.

units.la: Hunc autem mensem ueteres nominant Cisleu. & puto dictum esse quasi Orientalem, uel Orioneum, ab Orione: quia Cesil Hebræis est Orion. Quecunq; causa appellationis sit, ego credo sic dictum esse hunc mensem Cesil, propter incertas tempestates. Græci dicunt esse ab χειμών, id est urinando. sed mihi magis fit uerisimile, dictū esse ab ὥρας, distinctione temporū, quia ipse Oriens affert æstatem, & Occidens hyemem.
units.tr: The ancients call this month Cisleu, and I think it was named as if "Oriental," or "Orioneus," from Orion, because Cesil is Orion to the Hebrews. Whatever the cause of the name, I believe this month was called Cesil on account of its uncertain weather. The Greeks say it derives from cheimōn [χειμών], that is, "raining" (urinando); but it seems to me more likely that it derives from hōras [ὥρας], the division of the seasons, because the East brings summer and the West winter.

units.la: XVII. Decembris.
units.tr: December 17.

units.la: Celebratur dies trium uirorum, qui fuerunt in fornace Babylonica, quos Deus mirabiliter in illis flammis igneis custodiuit, & ex eis liberauit.
units.tr: The day of the three men who were in the Babylonian furnace is celebrated, whom God wonderfully kept safe in those fiery flames and delivered from them.

units.la: XXV. Decembris.
units.tr: December 25.

units.la: Hoc die celebrata Hierosolymæ Encænia, id est, renoualia, noualia uel dedicationes templi. Vocabulum encæniorū est apud Ioannem, ubi Christus ambulat in porticu Salomonis in encænijs: & deriuatur à καινὸν, quod significat nouum aliquid, ut quādo noua res tribuitur cultui, siue alijs rebus. Celebrata sunt ideo encænia, quia hoc die templum à Iuda Michabæo est recuperatum, cultusq; Dei rursus est repurgatus.
units.tr: On this day the Encaenia, that is, the renewals, new things, or dedications of the Temple, were celebrated at Jerusalem. The word encaenia occurs in John, where Christ walks in Solomon's porch at the Encaenia; it is derived from kainon [καινόν], which signifies something new, as when a new thing is assigned to worship or to other uses. The Encaenia were celebrated because on this day the Temple was recovered from Judas Maccabeus, and the worship of God was purified again.

units.la: In hac tota commemoratione debetis intueri uniuersam historiam temporum Machabæorum. Antiochus rex Syriæ fuit similis Caligulæ, & liben ter suo regno Palæstinam adiecisset, ut minus esset dissensionum: voluit tollere religionem Iudæorū, & instituere Græcos ritus, sicut in ipsa Hierosoly-ma, quæ fuit templū Dei, celebrauit Bacchanalia, multum turpitudinum & libidinū habentia. Idem collocauit idolum Iouis Olympij in templum Dei: addens etiā præsidia, quæ ui illud defenderēt, ne ex templo eijceretur. Ita in templo & circa templum quotidie fiebant stupra, cædes, & homines mactabantur: idq; durauit triennium. Post triennium Iudas Machabæus, deletis aliquot exercitibus Antiochi, recuperauit templum: instituensq; cultus diuinitus ordinatos, curauit recte doceri, et à pijs sacerdotibus sacrificari. quanquam multum difficultatum adhuc superfuit, quia tantū biennio postea uixit: & dimicauit cum exercitu adhuc in urbe, ac in acie periit. Ita nondum fuit finis belli. quanquam post mortem eius minor fuit moles belli, & facilè repressa sunt reliqua præsidia, propter eiectū idolum ex templo: unde & restitutis ueris cultibus, celebrata sunt encænia.
units.tr: In this whole commemoration you ought to consider the entire history of the times of the Maccabees. Antiochus, king of Syria, was like Caligula, and would gladly have added Palestine to his kingdom, so that there would be fewer dissensions. He wished to abolish the religion of the Jews and to introduce Greek rites, and in Jerusalem itself, which was the Temple of God, he celebrated Bacchanalia, full of much filth and lust. The same man set up the idol of Olympian Zeus in the Temple of God, adding also garrisons to defend it by force, lest it be cast out of the Temple. Thus in the Temple and around it, fornication and slaughter took place daily, and men were butchered; and this lasted for three years. After three years Judas Maccabeus, having destroyed several armies of Antiochus, recovered the Temple, and, restoring the worship divinely ordained, saw to it that it was taught correctly and that sacrifices were offered by pious priests. Still, much difficulty remained, since he lived only two years afterwards; he fought with the army still in the city and fell in battle. So the war had not yet ended. Yet after his death the burden of war was lighter, and the remaining garrisons were easily put down, because the idol had been cast out of the Temple; and so, with true worship restored, the Encaenia were celebrated.

units.la: XXXI. Decembris.
units.tr: XXXI. December.

units.la: Vltimus dies anni est, dedicatus Syluestro: de que quo tantū hoc scimus, quòd uixerit tempore Con-stantini. Deinde est fabula, quòd Constantinus donauerit ei urbem Romam, & imperium occiden-tis, Italiam & Galliam. Extat quædam constitutio in libris Decretorū,quæ nominatur Donatio Con-stantini:ubi sic scriptum est,quòd donauerit Con-stantinus Syluestro urbem Romam . Laurentius Valla scripsit refutationem: quanquam non opus erat in tam manifesto mendacio . Quòd autem illa narratio de Constantino non sit uera , sic pro-bo : Librorum enim qui leges continent,præci-pua est autoritas . Aliqui dicunt esse unam pa-leam , quando titulus in Iurisconsultorum li-bris de ista donatione loquitur : sed hæc neque uetus neque uera est, sed mendacium ab aliquo nebulone conflictum, ad uexandos homines. Non est igitur uera ( inquam ) quia est impossibilis. Impossibilia enim non possunt esse uera: ut si quis scribat asinum uolasse.
units.tr: The last day of the year is dedicated to Silvester, of whom we know only this much: that he lived in the time of Constantine. Then there is the fable that Constantine gave him the city of Rome and rule over the West, Italy and Gaul. A certain decree in the books of the Decretals, called the Donation of Constantine, has this written in it: that Constantine gave the city of Rome to Silvester. Laurentius Valla wrote a refutation, though there was no need for one in so manifest a falsehood. That this story about Constantine is not true I prove as follows. The books that contain laws have the chief authority. Some say that this is a single forged passage (a palea), since the title in the jurists' books speaks of this donation; but this is neither ancient nor true, but a lie concocted by some scoundrel to harass people. It is therefore not true, I say, because it is impossible. For impossible things cannot be true, as if someone were to write that a donkey flew.

units.la: Impossibile est aliquem episcopum recipere gu-bernationem Imperij, non habentem exercitum, & non administrantem regnum.
units.tr: It is impossible for a bishop to take up the government of an empire without having an army and without administering a kingdom.

units.la: Syluester est episcopus, & non habet exercitus, nec ui administrat regna.
units.tr: Silvester is a bishop, and he has no army, nor does he govern kingdoms by force.

units.la: Ergo non recipit, etiamsi aliquid tale ei osse-ratur.
units.tr: Therefore he does not accept, even if something of that sort were offered to him.

units.la: Alia probatio.
units.tr: Another proof.

units.la: Rex est persona ordinata à Deo ad conservationem disciplinæ & pacis, instructa potentia corporali,ut possit coercere cõtumaces ui corporali.
units.tr: A king is a person ordained by God for the preservation of discipline and peace, equipped with bodily power, so that he can restrain the stubborn by physical force.

units.la: Syluester non habet potestatem corporalem.
units.tr: Silvester does not have bodily power.

units.la: Ergo illa donatio est planè commenticia.
units.tr: Therefore that donation is plainly fictitious.

units.la: Sic ex pacto recipientis manifesta est impossibilitas. Iurisdictio sine executione est inanis sonitus. Postea est impossibilis ex parte donantis, qui non habet ius transferendi illam gubernationem ab imperio in aliquam aliam autoritatem. Sed alterum est illustrius ex persona recipientis. Exercitus nunquam parucrunt Pontificibus. Et Christus prohibet,ne ipsi gerant imperia mundana,in dicto:Reges gentium dominantur, uos autem nõ sic: id est, prætextu Euangelij non debetis regna constituere.
units.tr: Thus the impossibility is manifest on the side of the recipient, by the terms of the agreement. Jurisdiction without enforcement is an empty sound. Next, it is impossible on the side of the donor, who has no right to transfer that government from the empire to some other authority. But the other point is clearer, from the person of the recipient. Armies never obeyed the Pontiffs. And Christ forbids them to hold worldly empires, in the saying: "The kings of the nations lord it over them, but you shall not be so"; that is, under the pretext of the Gospel you ought not to set up kingdoms.

units.la: COLLECTOR
units.tr: COLLECTOR

units.la: Lectori:
units.tr: To the Reader:

units.la: Hæc tria monumenta reperies Basileæ in summi templi circuitu.et siquidem erant coniuncta cũ inferioribus germanicis rhythmis,neq; à me illi separari debebant: præterea annum mortis,& diem mensis unà cum ætatis tempore,tibi ex diligenti inquisitione in posterioribus adieci, quæ in illis abfuerunt. His placuit adijcere inscriptionem tumuli D. Philippi Bechij Medici,& docti uiri M.Conrad Lycosthenis obitus diem & annum: quamuis utriusq; utriusq; epitaphia duplici carminis genere descri-pserit amicus meus singularis Iacobus Hertelius: quæ, si uoles, Senariorum suorum libello subiun-cta leges.
units.tr: You will find these three monuments at Basel, around the circuit of the great church. Since they were joined with the lower German rhymes, I ought not to have separated them from those. Besides, I have added in the later pages, from careful inquiry, the year and day of death and the age, which were absent from those inscriptions, for you. To these I thought it fitting to add the inscription of the tomb of Dr. Philipp Bech, physician, and the day and year of death of the learned man M. Conrad Lycosthenes; although my singular friend Jacob Hertel has described the epitaphs of both in a double kind of verse, which you will read, if you wish, appended to his little book of Senarii.

units.la: DEO OPT. MAX. ET Christo Saluatori no-stro S.
units.tr: TO GOD, BEST AND GREATEST, AND TO CHRIST OUR SAVIOUR

units.la: Dn. Iacobum Meierum, huius inclytæ urbis cō-sulem prudentissimum consultissimumq; , pietatis sanæ cultorem, ac promotorem primarium omnis honestatis, quod in ipso fuit, instauratorem diligen-tissimum, lapis subiectus contegit.
units.tr: Here lies beneath this stone Herr Jakob Meier, the most prudent and most learned consul of this renowned city, a sound cultivator of piety and the chief promoter of all honesty so far as lay in him, and a most diligent restorer.

units.la: D. Io. Oecolampadius, professione theologus, trium linguarum peritissimus, autor Euangelicæ doctrinæ in hac urbe primus, & templi huius uerus Episcopus, ut doctrina, sic uitæ sanctimonia co-lendissimus, sub breue saxum hoc reconditus iacet.
units.tr: Johannes Oecolampadius, a theologian by profession, most skilled in the three languages, the first author of evangelical teaching in this city and the true bishop of this church, most revered both for his learning and for the holiness of his life, lies buried under this small stone.

units.la: Moritur Cal. Decembris, Anno M. D. XXXI. anno ætatis suæ 49.
units.tr: He died on the first of December, in the year 1531, in the 49th year of his age.

units.la: Dn. Simoni Grynæo almæ huius Academiæ rec-tori, & laude & memoria sempiterna ob linguarum Latinæ, Græcæ, & Hebraicæ peritiam, omnisq; Philosophiæ ad miraculum usq; cognitionem, ob Theologiæ ueræ scientiam & usum digno, monu-mentum hoc dicatum est.
units.tr: To Herr Simon Grynaeus, rector of this nourishing Academy, worthy of everlasting praise and remembrance for his skill in Latin, Greek and Hebrew, for his knowledge of all philosophy to a wonderful degree, and for his grasp and use of true theology, this monument has been dedicated.

units.la: Obdormiuit in Domino Calend. Augusti, Anno Domini 1541. ætatis suæ 47.
units.tr: He fell asleep in the Lord on the first of August, in the year of the Lord 1541, in the 47th year of his age.

units.la: Anno Salutis M. D. XXXXII. F. F.
units.tr: In the year of salvation 1542. F. F.

units.la: So ehr/gut/künst/hulffen in not/ Wer keiner von diesen dreie todt.
units.tr: Whoever helped in need with honour, goods or skill, none of these three is dead.

units.la: Inscriptio tumuli D.Philippi Bechij.
units.tr: Inscription on the tomb of Dr Philipp Bech.

units.la: Hæc mihi prætereat nemo monumenta uiator, Non bene qui cineri uoce precetur huic. Bechius hic medica celeber cubat arte Philippus, Qui decus orbis erat totius, atq; scholæ. Si foret è superis quem ducere sedibus æquum, Hunc foret, ut miseris ferre ualeret opem.
units.tr: Let no passer-by pass these memorials by without speaking a kind word over this ash. Here lies Philip Bech, famous for the medical art, who was the glory of the whole world and of the school. If it were right to call anyone down from the seats above, it would be he, that he might be able to bring help to the wretched.

units.la: Herr Philipp Bech/ beider arztney Licentiat / vnd der freien künsten Doctor / entschlieff im Herrn den iij. Herbstmonat / im 1560 jar.
units.tr: Herr Philipp Bech, licentiate in both medicine and the arts, and Doctor of the liberal arts, fell asleep in the Lord on the 3rd of September in the year 1560.

units.la: Decessus ex hac vita Conradi Lycosthenis.
units.tr: Death of Conrad Lycosthenes.

units.la: Bonus & doctus uir M. Conradus Lycosthenes Rubeaquensis, ecclesiæ Basiliensis, minister, ex hac miseriarum ualle in cælestem patriam emigrauit, octauo Calend. Aprilis, anno Domini 1561, ætatis suæ anno 34. qui ultra illos labores, quibus posteritati profuit, alijs quibusdam incumbebat: quos etiā perfecisset, nisi immatura mors eum nobis abstulisset.
units.tr: A good and learned man, Master Conrad Lycosthenes of Rappoltsweiler, minister of the Church of Basel, departed from this vale of miseries for the heavenly fatherland on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, in the year of the Lord 1561, in the thirty-fourth year of his age. Besides those labours by which he served posterity, he was also occupied with certain other works, which he would have completed had not an untimely death taken him from us.

units.la: AVTHORIS CARMEN, QVOD loco gratiarum actionis composuit, cum discessurus esset Basilea.
units.tr: The author's poem, which he composed as a thanksgiving when he was about to leave Basel.

units.la: Iam mea permenso meruit ratis æquore portum: Magnificoq; schole Rectori dicere grates Sulcero nunc hora iubet, doctoq; pioq;, Dedita cui multum Musis iam pectora debent, Præcipuè queis cœlestis Sapientia curæ est, Quæ solum uehit ad celsi nos sidera cœli. Vix alter melius ueræ docuisse salutis Hoc sene nouit iter. Neq; enim facundior ullus, Nec melior, nec quem mage spiritus augeat almus. Atq; Heinrice tibi Petri, uigilantia cuius Ingens, rara fides, studiorum maxima cura. Et tibi qui nulli modo cedis Oporine, spectem Siue typos nunc ipse tuos, seu maxima dona Doctrinæ, ingeniiq; tui, pietatis & usum. Inde uiris, qui uel de religione, uel acri Doctrina legum: medica uel Apollinis arte, Vel de Socraticis sortiti nomina libris. Cunctis atq; uiris, quibus illa Academia floret, Quæ Basilea tuos intra iacet inclyta muros. Queis me, uitalis dum spiritus hos reget artus, (Debeo ceu multum) multum debere fatebor. Atq; utinam meritis æquari gratia posset: Non ego non certè, dum grates ipse referrem,
units.tr: Now my ship, having crossed the sea, has earned its harbour, and the hour bids me give thanks to the Magnificent Rector of the school, Sulzer, learned and pious, to whom devoted hearts now owe much for the Muses, especially those for whom heavenly Wisdom is a care, since she alone carries us up to the stars of high heaven. Scarcely has any other man in this old age known better how to teach the true way of salvation. For no one is more eloquent, none better, and none whom the nourishing Spirit increases more. And to you, Heinrich Petri, whose vigilance is great, your faith rare, and your care for studies the greatest. And to you, Oporinus, who yield to no one, whether I look at your printed works themselves or at the great gifts of your learning, your talent and your practice of piety. Then to the men who are distinguished either in religion, or in the keen learning of law, or in the medical art of Apollo, or who have won their names from the Socratic books; to all and each of the men by whom that academy flourishes which famous Basel holds within its walls. To these men, while the vital breath governs these limbs, I shall confess that I owe much, as I indeed do owe much. And would that thanks could be matched by merits. Certainly I would not, while I myself gave thanks, wish to pass over anything of care or labour.

units.la: Præterijsse uelim quicquam curæq;, laborisq; At mihi cùm donis longè superata facultas Deficiat: precor ipse Deum, semperq; precabor, Hoc placidè longum cunctos ut seruet in æuum.
units.tr: But since my ability, far surpassed by your gifts, falls short, I pray to God myself, and will always pray, that He keep this gentle state of things long and steadfast for all of you through the ages.

units.la: Basileæ, Anno Christi,1562. Mense Nouembri.
units.tr: Basel, in the year of Christ 1562, in the month of November.

units.la: Rerum Creatori, Deo patri, filio, & spiritui sancto, sit laus & gloria, virtus atque maiestas in omne æuum: Amen.
units.tr: To the Creator of all things, God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, be praise and glory, power and majesty for evermore. Amen.

units.la: Vaticinium Ioannis Regiomontani, de interitu mundi.
units.tr: The prophecy of John Regiomontanus concerning the end of the world.

units.la: Post mille expletos à partu virginis annos, Et post quingentos rursus ab orbe datos. Octogesimus octauus mirabilis annus Ingruet: is secum tristia fata trahet. Si non hoc anno totus malus occidet orbis, Si non in nihilum terra fretumq; ruant: Cuncta tamen mundi sursum ibunt atq; deorsum Imperia: & luctus undiq; grandis erit.
units.tr: After a thousand years have been completed from the virgin's birth, and after five hundred more have been given to the world besides, the wondrous year eighty-eight will come rushing in; it will bring sad fates with it. If the whole evil world does not perish in this year, if earth and sea do not fall into nothing, yet all the empires of the world will rise and fall, going up and down, and great mourning will be everywhere.

units.la: De instabilitate rerum huius mundi.
units.tr: On the instability of the things of this world.

units.la: Omnia sunt mundi, quasi bulla caduca rotundi: In pratis ut flos, sic perit omnis honos. Corpora putrescunt hominũ, post funera crescunt Serpentes: uitam quare homo cerne tuam.
units.tr: All things of the world are like the fragile bubble of a round globe; as the flower in the meadows, so all honour perishes. The bodies of men rot, and after the funeral serpents grow from them. Why, man, do you look upon your life?

units.la: Temporis ratio habenda.
units.tr: The consideration of time to be had.

units.la: Dum licet ingenio ditari, disce iuventus: Iste dabit fruges, iste colendus ager.
units.tr: While you may be enriched by talent, learn, young man; this will yield the fruits, this is the field to be tilled.

units.la: Cætera fide Deo qui pressis subvenit: Ille Excubias nostro pro grege semper agit.
units.tr: In other matters, trust God, who helps the oppressed; He always keeps watch for our flock.

units.la: Quatuor quotidie cogitanda.
units.tr: Four things to be considered daily.

units.la: Mors Christi, tua mors, infernus, gloria cœli: Quatuor hæc semper sunt meditanda tibi.
units.tr: The death of Christ, your death, hell, and the glory of heaven: these four things must always be meditated on by you.

units.la: Precatio Ecclesiæ ad Christum.
units.tr: The Church's prayer to Christ.

units.la: Audi nunc gemitus, & vota precantia Christe: Reijce net surda supplicis aure preces.
units.tr: Hear now our groans and our prayers of supplication, O Christ; do not turn away the prayers of the suppliant with a deaf ear.

units.la: Me tibi commendo, tibi me iam porrigo Christe: Tu clemens famulum protege Christe tuum.
units.tr: I commend myself to you, I now stretch myself out to you, O Christ; gracious Christ, protect your servant.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: END.

units.la: PSALMVS LXXXI.
units.tr: PSALM 81.

units.la: Deus stetit in synagoga, &c.
units.tr: God stands in the congregation, etc.

units.la: STat Deus in media turba, coetuq; deorum, Terribiliq; alios increpat ore deos.
units.tr: God stands in the midst of the crowd and the assembly of the gods, and with a terrible voice he rebukes the other gods.

units.la: Nunc quis erit tandem scelerum modus? omnia iura Oppressa à uobis uiq; doloq; iacent.
units.tr: Now at last, what limit will there be to these crimes? All rights lie crushed by you, by violence and by deceit.

units.la: Nil in iudicijs inopis ualet optima causa, Gratia sed tantum diuitis illa regit.
units.tr: In judgments the best cause of the poor man counts for nothing; only the favour of the rich holds sway.

units.la: Quin uos efficite, ut probitas innoxia semper Præsidio uestro tuta manere queat.
units.tr: Indeed, bring it about yourselves that innocent integrity may always be able to remain safe under your protection.

units.la: Nec circumscribi pupillos fraude sinatis, Iniusti metuant tristia iura fori.
units.tr: Do not allow orphans to be cheated by fraud; let the unjust fear the harsh laws of the court.

units.la: Sed nihil hic monitis regum fera corda mouentur, Nec cæcæ mentes numina summa timent.
units.tr: But here the fierce hearts of kings are moved by no warnings, and blind minds do not fear the highest powers.

units.la: Nulla uoluptates moderantur uincula legum, Miscent arbitrio sanda nefanda suo.
units.tr: No laws restrain their pleasures; they mingle the sacred and the accursed as they please.

units.la: Sed meritas olim dabit ista licentia pœnas, Conuenietq; actis exitus ipse suis.
units.tr: But that licence will one day pay the deserved penalties, and the outcome will fit their own deeds.

units.la: Ecce ego deiiciam celsa de sede tyrannos, Cum manibus terras ipse mouebo meis.
units.tr: Behold, I will cast tyrants down from their high seat; with my own hands I will shake the earth.

units.la: Vos equidem esse Deos iusi, Gnatosq; uocaui, Voce mea uobis regna tenere dedi.
units.tr: I indeed commanded you to be gods, and I called you sons; by my voice I gave you the right to hold kingdoms.

units.la: Sed repetam titulos, & regni iratus honores, Et dabitis pœnas uos aliquando mihi.
units.tr: But in anger I will reclaim the titles and honours of the kingdom, and you will one day pay the penalty to me.

units.la: Vtq; alij exuti regni cecidere tyranni, Qui ueluti plebis pars sine honore iacent:
units.tr: And as the other tyrants, stripped of their kingdoms, have fallen, lying like a part of the common people without honour:

units.la: Sic postquam tituli uobis ego dempsero honorem,
units.tr: so, after I have taken away your titles and honour,

units.la: Lapsaq; cum fuerint sceptra superba manu:Vos ignota eruis, contemtaq; funera, sicutObscura vulgus morte perire solet.
units.tr: and when the proud sceptres have fallen from the hand, you will be carried off, your funerals unknown and despised, just as the obscure common crowd is wont to perish in death.

units.la: At tu summe Deus surgas, terramq; gubernes,Absq; tuo regnum numine stare nequit.Omnes te gentes Dominum metuantq; colantq;,Omnia sunt etenim sub ditione tua.
units.tr: But you, highest God, arise and govern the earth, for the kingdom cannot stand without your power. All nations fear and worship you as Lord, for all things are indeed under your dominion.

units.la: Carmen Ioannis Stigolij, de meditatione mortis, plenius superiore.
units.tr: Poem of John Stigolius, on the meditation of death, more fully than the above.

units.la: Mors tua, mors Christi fraus terræ, gloria cœli,Et dolor inferni sunt meditanda tibi.
units.tr: Your death, the death of Christ, the snare of the earth, the glory of heaven, and the sorrow of hell are to be meditated upon by you.

units.la: Viue diu, sed viue Deo: nam viuere mundo,Mortis opus: viua est viuere vita Deo.
units.tr: Live long, but live to God; for to live to the world is the work of death, and to live to God is the true life.

units.la: Quicquid erit tandē, mea spes est unica Christus:Huic viuo, huic moriar, cætera vero nihil.
units.tr: Whatever may come, my only hope is Christ; I live for him, I shall die for him; other things are nothing.

units.la: Quid valet hic mundus, qd gloria? quid'ue triumph?Post miserum funus puluis & umbra sumus.
units.tr: What is this world worth, what is glory, what are triumphs? After the wretched funeral we are dust and shadow.

units.la: Custodia & cura Dei clementissimi erga nos.
units.tr: The custody and care of the most merciful God towards us.

units.la: Non Deus ostendit se tantum ut corpora curet,Sed cur seruare nos velit, ille monet.Scilicet ut sese nobis communicet ipse,Semper & ut viuant pectora plena Deo.Tunc autem in nobis fulget, tunc pectora complet,Mens pia cum discit munera nosse Dei.
units.tr: God does not show himself only so that he may care for our bodies, but he teaches why he wishes to preserve us. Clearly, so that he may impart himself to us, and so that our hearts may always live full of God. Then indeed he shines in us, then he fills our hearts, when a devout mind learns to know the gifts of God.

units.la: Seriem agnationis & cognationis Domini nostri IESV CHRISTI, à Philippo Melanchthone, & alio quodam docto uiro, ex quatuor Euangelistis & ueteris Ecclesiae doctoribus excerptam, eo consilio ac fine hic inseri curauimus, ut huius postremi libelli, & alibi Prophetarum atque Apostolorum historiae melius intelligerentur.
units.tr: We have taken care to insert here the genealogy of the descent and kindred of our Lord Jesus Christ, excerpted by Philip Melanchthon and another learned man from the four Evangelists and the teachers of the ancient Church, with the purpose and aim that the history of the Prophets and Apostles, both in this last little book and elsewhere, may be better understood.

units.tr: ABRAHAM

Lu. 24. frater Iosephi, teste Epiphanio, pag. 438. Ioseph, sponsus Mariae, matris Christi. Mat. 1. Luc. 2. MATTHAT. HELEI, qui & Ioachim, pater Mariae uirginis. MARIA, uirgo mater: mortua est anno 59. aetatis, 6. annis post Ascensionem. IESVS CHRISTVS ANNA, uxor Eli, ex tribu Leuitica, mater duarum sororum. Elizabeth. Zacharias. IOHANNES Baptista. Luc. 1.3.7. Matth. 3. 14. 11. Ioh. 1. 3. 5. Marci 1. 6. MARIA, soror Mariae uirginis: Iohã. 19. nupta Alphaeo: deinde de Cleophae, fratri Ioseph.
units.tr: Isaac. Jacob. Judah. David. Joash. Zerubbabel. Matthan. Jacob. Salome, sister of Joseph and Cleophas, married to Zebedee, who was the mother of Zebedee. Mark 15. Matt. 27. Cleophas, husband of Mary. Luke 24. Brother of Joseph, according to Epiphanius, p. 438. Joseph, betrothed husband of Mary, mother of Christ. Matt. 1. Luke 2. Matthat. Heli, who is also Joachim, father of the Virgin Mary. Mary, virgin mother: she died in the 59th year of her age, 6 years after the Ascension. Jesus Christ. Anna, wife of Eli, of the tribe of Levi, mother of two sisters. Elizabeth. Zacharias. John the Baptist. Luke 1, 3, 7. Matt. 3, 14, 11. John 1, 3, 5. Mark 1, 6. Mary, sister of the Virgin Mary (John 19), married to Alphaeus, then to Cleophas, brother of Joseph.

units.la: 1. Iacobus Minor, episcopus Hierosolymitanus, interfectus 30. an. post Pentecosten, qua Spiritum sanctum acceperunt Apostoli: cuius festum Caled. Maij. Fuit cosobrinus Christi, seu frater Domini, Galat. 1. 2. Act. 12. 15. 21. Matthaei 10. 13. 27. Marci 3. 15. Luc. 6. 8. 24. Iohannis 7. 1. Corinth. 15. autor Epiphan.
units.tr: 1. James the Less, bishop of Jerusalem, killed 30 years after Pentecost, when the apostles received the Holy Spirit; his feast is on the calends of May. He was a cousin of Christ, or brother of the Lord. Gal. 1, 2. Acts 12, 15, 21. Matt. 10, 13, 27. Mark 3, 15. Luke 6, 8, 24. John 7. 1 Cor. 15. Author: Epiphanius.

units.la: 2. Simon episcopus Hierosolymitanorum, post Iacobum, anno aetatis suae 120 interfectus, tempore Traiani.
units.tr: 2. Simeon, bishop of Jerusalem after James, killed in the 120th year of his age, in the time of Trajan.

units.la: 3. Iuda.
units.tr: 3. Judas.

units.la: 4. Iofes.
units.tr: 4. Joses.

units.la: Hi duo Apostoli, fratres Domini, diem consecratum habet 28. Octobris, quorum mentio fit Matthaei 13. Marci 6.
units.tr: These two apostles, brothers of the Lord, have a consecrated day, 28 October. Mention of them is made in Matthew 13 and Mark 6.

units.la: Iacobus Maior Apostolus, cuius festum 25. Iulij, docuit in Hispania: interfectus ab Herode Agrippa, tempore Claudij, circa quod mortua est Maria uirgo: Actorum 12. Huius fit mentio in Euangelistis, Matth. 4. 10. 17. 20. 26. Marci 1. 3. 9. 10. 13. 14. Lucae 5. 6. 9.
units.tr: James the Greater, apostle, whose feast is 25 July. He preached in Spain and was killed by Herod Agrippa in the time of Claudius, around which time the Virgin Mary died. Acts 12. He is mentioned in the Gospels: Matt. 4, 10, 17, 20, 26. Mark 1, 3, 9, 10, 13, 14. Luke 5, 6, 9.

units.la: Iohannes Euangelista, frater Iacobi, qui uixit 89. annos, cuius mentio fit Matth. 4. 10. 17. 20. 26. Marci 1. 3. 9. 10. 13. 14. Lucae 5. 6. 8. 9. 22. Iohannis 13. 19. 20. 21. Actorum 1. 3. 4. 8. 12. & ad Galatas 2.
units.tr: John the Evangelist, brother of James, who lived 89 years. Mention of him is made in Matt. 4, 10, 17, 20, 26. Mark 1, 3, 9, 10, 13, 14. Luke 5, 6, 8, 9, 22. John 13, 19, 20, 21. Acts 1, 3, 4, 8, 12, and Galatians 2.
