units.la: IOANNIS MANLII AD TEMPERANTIAE & SOBRIETATIS FAUTORES PRAEFATIUNCULA.
units.tr: JOHN MANLIUS' SHORT PREFACE TO THE FRIENDS OF TEMPERANCE AND SOBRIETY.

units.la: GRAVE & insigne dictum diui Pauli est, Habete honorē corpori: quo multiplicem materiam cōplectitur. Præcipuè uerò hoc loco quaeritur, de discrimine inter hominum & reliquorum animalium corpora. Hanc quæstionem ut apposite explicemus, prius generalia quædam præmittēda uidentur, quæ ad meliorem reliquorum intellectū facient. Primum omnium constat, in brutis multiplices esse umbras, & simulchra plurimum cum hominibus cōuenientia, imò in quibusdam longè homini præstantiora. Exempli gratia, equi suum insessorē, & itinera, quæ semel confecerint, agnoscunt: ceruus auditu, aquilæ uisu, canes odore superant homines. Eiusmodi qualitates Deus suo quodam consilio animantibus indidit. Veruntamen in ipsis nō est actus reflexus, quo honesta à turpibus, utilia ab inutilibus discernere ualeant. Adde quòd multo minus quæ honesta sunt, præ turpibus eligant, cùm harum semina non obscura in hominū mentib. deprehendantur. Quæ si quis altius introspiciat, facilè habebit quod ad propositam quæstionem respondeat. Habet autem homo maiora & excellentiora dona: quia ipse est domicilium diuinitatis, in quo Deus habitare vult, sicut pulcherrimè hoc 1. Petri 2. describitur, vbi Apostolus ait: Vos estis domus spiritualis, sacerdotium sanctum, ad offerendas spirituales hostias, acceptabiles Deo per IESVM Christum. Siquidem uero Deus in homine habitet: oportet ut aedificium sanctissimae Trinitatis sit immaculatum ab omnibus huius seculi desideriis, & iniquitatibus: à quibus uas nostrum custodire in sanctitate iubemur à Paulo, 1. Thess. 4. Deinde non omni tempore interitui obnoxia erunt nostra corpora, sed Deus etiam ea transformabit, & filij sui corpori conformia reddet, sicut Paulus ad Philippenses scribit: ubi tum Deus erit omnia in omnibus. Quare si nostris corporibus debitum tribuere honorem uelimus, utamur illis ad celebrationem nominis diuini, & proximi utilitatem. Hoc autem variis modis fieri potest, & debet. Quidam ingenij sui neruos, omniaq; studia eò dirigunt, ut utilibus scriptis nominis diuini celebratio propagetur, & multorum hominum utilitas quaeratur. Alij liberales manus porrigunt egenis, & strenuè iuuant honestos piorum inopumq; hominum conatus & labores: inuitati proculdubio insigni praeconio, quo Christus sua in ipsis opera (ut cum Augustino loquamur) coronabit. Id quod Matthaei 25. capite longo catalogo recenset. Et ut uno uerbo dicam, quiuis suo corpori
units.tr: A grave and remarkable saying of the divine Paul is: "Have honour for the body" [1 Cor. 6? / Habete honorem corpori]. It embraces a manifold matter. Chiefly, however, the question is asked here about the difference between the bodies of men and those of the other animals. To explain this question aptly, some general points seem to need to be set down first, which will make the rest easier to understand. First of all, it is agreed that in the brutes there are many shadows and likenesses which closely resemble those of humans, and indeed in some respects they surpass man by far. For example, horses recognise their rider and the routes they have once travelled; the stag excels man in hearing, the eagle in sight, and dogs in smell. God, by some design of his own, gave such qualities to the animals. Yet in them there is no reflexive act by which they can distinguish the honourable from the base, or the useful from the useless. Add that they are much less able to choose what is honourable in preference to what is base, since the seeds of these things are plainly found in the minds of men. If anyone looks into these more deeply, he will easily have what answers the question proposed. Man, however, has greater and more excellent gifts, because he is the dwelling-place of the divinity, in which God wills to dwell, as is most beautifully described in 1 Peter 2, where the Apostle says: "You are a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ." Since God dwells in man, it is necessary that the building of the most holy Trinity be unstained by all the desires and iniquities of this age, from which we are commanded by Paul to keep our vessel in holiness, 1 Thess. 4. Moreover, our bodies will not always be liable to destruction, but God will also transform them and make them conformed to the body of his Son, as Paul writes to the Philippians, where then God will be all in all. Therefore, if we wish to give our bodies the honour due to them, let us use them for the celebration of the divine name and the benefit of our neighbour. This can and must be done in various ways. Some direct the sinews of their talent and all their zeal so that the celebration of the divine name is spread by useful writings and the good of many people is sought. Others stretch out generous hands to the needy, and vigorously help the honest endeavours and labours of pious and poor people, undoubtedly invited by the remarkable proclamation with which Christ will crown his works in them (as we may say with Augustine). This Matthew 25 recounts in a long catalogue. And to say it in one word, everyone [should use his body...]

units.la: AD LECTOREM.
units.tr: TO THE READER.

units.la: corpori honestatem potest tribuere, quando vocationi, quàm sibi Deus iniunxit et commendauit, sedulam diligentiâ suam ac labores tempestiuos cum temperantia mixtos impertitur. Sic eregione perdimus & quasi occidimus corpora nostra, si excessum diurnis nocturnisq; comessationibus, aut ingurgitationibus, uel etiam immodicis uigilijs faciamus: quod uitium, proh dolor, nostram Germaniam grauissimo damno affecit, datq; locum ueteri dicto: Plures nimirum gula quàm gladio perire. Hac de causa nõ frustra Saluator noster nos ad temperantiam, propter ingentia mala quae ex intemperantia sequûtur, adhortatur: Attendite, inquiês, ne grauentur corda uestra crapula, & ebrietate.
units.tr: Each man can lend honour to his own body when he devotes his diligent care and timely labours, tempered with moderation, to the calling which God has laid upon him and commended to him. On the contrary, we lose and as it were kill our own bodies if we indulge in excess of feasting by day and by night, or in gluttony, or even in immoderate wakefulness. This vice, alas, has done our Germany the gravest harm, and gives occasion to the old saying: more people certainly perish from gluttony than from the sword. For this reason our Saviour does not without cause urge us to temperance, on account of the great evils that follow from intemperance: "Take heed," he says, "lest your hearts be weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness."

units.la: Quod si nihil aliud temperantiam nobis inculcaret, uel infinita eius commoda id obtinere debebant. Hac enim cordis affectus aptiores ad orandum & puriores conseruantur, & industria animi ad quasuis actiones uocationis nostrae obeundas alacrior fit: ut experientia ipsa testis est. Hæc præmittere uolui, Lector, ut mecũ ad maiorem sobrietatem seu temperantiam multos alios inuitem: deinde ut cogitemus, nos non potui, cibo, alijs ue corporalibus uoluptatibus destinatos prorsus esse: sed corporalia bona à Deo in hunc finem esse creata, ut nobis inseruirent. Nos uerò Creatori tribuemus, quod à nobis postulat. Ad eiusmodi rerum considera-
units.tr: Even if nothing else urged us towards temperance, its countless advantages ought to secure it. For by it the affections of the heart are kept fitter and purer for prayer, and the zeal of the mind becomes more eager for performing whatever tasks belong to our calling, as experience itself bears witness. I have wished to set this down first, dear reader, so that I may invite many others with me to greater sobriety or temperance; and then so that we may consider that we were not made wholly for food or other bodily pleasures, but that bodily goods were created by God for this end, that they might serve us. Let us indeed render to the Creator what he asks of us. To the consideration of such matters...

units.la: PRAEFATIO
units.tr: PREFACE

units.la: cõsiderationem optima methodo te ducet Libellus ille noster Medicus. Videbis enim, quàm leuibus ac tenuis momenti medicamentis tuam ualetudinem tueri possis: quæ si negligerentur, facilè ualetudo labefactaretur. Sicut eius rei exèpla singulæ familiæ nobis præbere possunt. Quisquis ergo corporis tui curam & conseruationem habere, illudq; præseruare à uariorum morborum conflictationi bus cupis, hunc nostrum laborem non postremo loco colloca, inter ea studia quæ hac de re possunt tradi. Faciet breuitas compëdiosa, ut longè plures inde percipias utilitates, quàm uno atq; altero uerbo tibi prædicare qucam. Prius ergo cognosce, quàm iudices, aut despicias.
units.tr: The little medical book of ours will guide you in this consideration by an excellent method. For you will see how slight and minor remedies can protect your health, the neglect of which would easily weaken it. Individual households can supply us with examples of this very thing. Whoever therefore wishes to take care of and preserve his body, and to guard it against the assaults of various diseases, should not place our labour in the last rank among the studies that can be handed down on this subject. Its compact brevity will yield far more benefits than I could declare to you in one or two words. Therefore, get to know it before you judge or despise it.

units.tr: Farewell.

units.tr: PREFACE,

units.la: In qua Medicinae laus & utilitas breuiter comprehenditur.
units.tr: In which the praise and usefulness of medicine are briefly summed up.

units.la: QVANTA sit Medicinae praestantia, quamq; honorificè ueteres illi uerè sancti & sapientes homines, de ea iudicarint, uel unus certè Homerus, uates sine dubio rerum humanarum peritiss. abundè testatur, qui hanc artem longè pulcherrimo elogio nobilitauit, inquiens:
units.tr: How great the excellence of medicine is, and how highly those truly holy and wise men of old judged it, is amply attested by Homer alone, undoubtedly the most skilled poet of human affairs, who ennobled this art with a most beautiful eulogy, saying:

units.la: ἰατρὸς γὰρ ἀνὴρ πολλῶν ἀντάξιος ἄλλων.
units.tr: "For a physician is a man worth many other men." [ἰατρὸς γὰρ ἀνὴρ πολλῶν ἀντάξιος ἄλλων]

units.la: Hominem enim Medicū, multis alijs hominibus praestare censuit: quod Poeta acerrimi iudicij nunquam dixisset, si nō uidisset, tantum oportere tribui, tam eleganti rerum naturę cognitioni. Quid quòd Homero non tantum uetustiores, sed etiam grauiores uiri, Medicis diuinos honores habuerūt, eosq; beneficentia & studio in numerum deorum sustulerunt? Quod grauiter quidē illi & constanter stanter fecerunt, ut eorum ferebat religio: iudicabant enim illi, hanc sapientiā non humanam, sed cœlestem esse, quæ tam arcanas rerum uirtutes, in ipsis naturæ uenis reconditas & abstrusas, euoluere, & in lucem proferre posset: neque hominis, sed Dei esse, tanta hominibus commoda adferre. Quare merito apud eos in diuino honore erant, à quibus diuina beneficia percipiebant. Principē deniq; locum ueteres, inter honestissimas disciplinas Medicinæ dederunt: ut interim taceam Græciam, quæ cum omni genere disciplinarū maximè floreret, Hippocrati eos honores habuit, quos prius Herculi monstra tollenti detulerat. Ex quo Medicinæ splendor & dignitas æstimari debet: cum ea regio, què sic uiris sapientibus præstabat, sic optimarum rerum iudicio pollebat, Medicinā tam exquisitis honoribus exornarit, ut dignitate eam Herculi minorum gentiū Deo adæquaret. Quapropter illud studium iam olim fuit tantū regum, principum & nobilium: nec uulgaris homo, aut ex plebeio ordine, potuit in illo uersari. Nobiles certē familiæ hanc insignē doctrinam apud priscos excoluerunt. Exemplum est ipse Hippocrates, qui è magna gente ad Medicinā accesit. Fuit enim natione quidem Cous, Heraclidæ autem & Phænaretes filius, ab Hercule Æsculapioq; genus ducens. Hic igitur cum genere & opibus magnus esset, ad Medicinam se contulit potius, quàm ad aliud institutum ullum: atq; in pulcherrimo hoc campo ita expaciatus est, ut nihil intentatum, nihil inexpertum reliquerit, omnia elaborata & summo iure existimata literis consignarit. Eaq; uersantur in oculis, tenētur manibus, & ad usum omnino à natura exprompta, & quid possint sapore consignata, atq; indicata notis: & à maioribus nostris, ab optimis magistris, nostra memoria explicata sunt, quę iam deserta ac suppressa iacent, quia neglecta. Hic uno atq; altero remedio contentus est, quæ scilicet accepit oraculo, nec ulli reuelanda putat. Sed ego sic arbitror, optima esse remedia quæ plurimis cognita, plurimis probata sunt. Alteri elementa sordent, & quicquid est elementare: hinc noua elementorum soboles: hinc æther & cœ lum Iam ipsum ad remedia exprimenda sunt. Hic abdita naturæ latet, & deliciæ discipliné: nō aliæ sunt salutis opes, & præcia Medicinæ, nisi quæ χυαγοιχείωσις illa, magna indignatione rerum à natura extorqueat. Parum sarta est uita, & ualetudo corporis, nisi quæ magno constat. At cōtrà res habet, quia frugi Medicū oportet curare quàm minimo.
units.tr: He judged that a physician surpasses many other men. A poet of such keen judgement would never have said this unless he had seen that so much honour ought to be given to so elegant a knowledge of nature. Moreover, not only the more ancient writers but also the more serious men gave physicians divine honours, and by their beneficence and zeal raised them to the number of the gods. They did this seriously and steadfastly, as their religion required. For they judged that this wisdom is not human but heavenly, since it can unfold and bring to light the hidden powers of things, concealed and buried in the very veins of nature; and that to bring such great benefits to men belongs not to man but to God. Therefore they rightly held in divine honour those from whom they received divine benefits. Finally, the ancients gave medicine the first place among the most honourable disciplines. I say nothing for the moment of Greece, which flourished most of all in every kind of learning, and which paid to Hippocrates the honours it had earlier paid to Hercules for overcoming monsters. From this the splendour and dignity of medicine must be estimated: that the region which thus excelled in wise men and was so strong in the judgement of the best things, adorned medicine with such exquisite honours that it made it equal in dignity to Hercules, the god of the lesser peoples. For this reason that study was long ago the preserve of kings, princes and nobles alone; an ordinary man, or one of the common people, could not engage in it. Noble families certainly cultivated this distinguished learning among the ancients. Hippocrates himself is an example, who came to medicine from a great family. He was indeed a Coan by birth, son of Heraclides and Phaenarete, and traced his lineage from Hercules and Asclepius. Since he was great by birth and wealth, he turned to medicine rather than to any other calling, and he so ranged over this most beautiful field that he left nothing untried and nothing unexplored, and he set down in writing everything he had worked out and judged of the highest worth. These things are before our eyes, held in our hands, and set forth as wholly fit for use by nature; and what they can do is marked and indicated by signs. They have been explained in our own time by our forebears and by the best masters, while those things which have been neglected now lie abandoned and suppressed. Hippocrates was content with one or two remedies, which he evidently received by oracle and thought should not be revealed to anyone. But I think otherwise: the best remedies are those known to many and approved by many. Others despise the elements and whatever is elemental; hence a new progeny of elements, hence ether and heaven. Even remedies themselves must be drawn out from these. Here lies hidden the secret of nature and the delight of the discipline. The resources of health and the price of medicine are nothing other than what must be wrung from nature with great indignation through that chymical preparation. Life is scarcely secure, and bodily health is scarcely sound, unless it costs dearly. But the matter is the reverse, because a thrifty physician ought to cure at the smallest cost.

units.la: Officinę componuntur magno uaria supellex instruitur, uitrea labra, catini, pyramides, folles, aliaq; plurima: tèperantur ignes, materia quoq; nuncupato uoto, appellato numine, ex ephemeride Mathematica notato cœlo legitur, atq; comparatur: articulantur uasa suoq; luto & argilla compinguntur: alij aurę adi tus oblinuntur: alij uiæ corniculis patent. Itaq; natura prorogatur, solicitatur flabris, uexatur igne, cōflatur, coquitur, exprimitur, donec resoluatur, secumq; diuortium faciat: ac tam perplexa cura, sua Saturno, sua Mercurio & Iovi, sua Soli & Lunæ, ac reliquis Planetis genitura deducitur, atq; hi denuò conflati inter se transformantur. Hinc diuina & cœlo ducta remedia, quæ dij illi euocati cœlo, & iam fornacib. excoēti, suis regibus atq; principibus parturiūt. Putrida uerò abiectaq; iacent exprom pta auxilia,nobiscū nata, & sine impen- dio parata domi: uulgaris est natura, & fœculenta Medicina elementorum,qua uulgus & fæcem hominū uti oporteat. Illiberalis scilicet, atq; euidens natura, omnia salutis instrumenta intus abstru- sit:aut effœta defectaq; succo,nihil con- tra morbos concepit:uel non parit qui- dem,nisi cōflata,cocta,soluta deniq; mi ris artibus exprimatur. Sed hæc uitia sunt & fabulamenta artificū: nulla artis culpa est:quæ à præclaris ingenijs parta excultaq;, magna supellectile rerū Me- dicinā auxit.Fruamur potius, more ma- iorum,natura nobis domestica atq; fa- miliari: legatur materia nobiscū edita, quamq; ultronea natura promit. Alijs autem remedijs ueluti externa manu, & auxiliaribus copijs uti conueniet.
units.tr: Workshops are set up, and a varied stock of equipment is provided: glass lips, bowls, pyramids, bellows and very many other things. Fires are regulated; materials are read and procured with a named vow and an invoked deity, the heavens being consulted as noted in the mathematical ephemeris. Vessels are fitted together and bound with their own lute and clay; some are smeared over the openings of the air, others lie open to the little horns of the way. Thus nature is prolonged, urged on with blasts, vexed with fire, blown, cooked, pressed, until she is dissolved and parts from herself. And with such a perplexing labour the generation is traced: one to Saturn, another to Mercury and Jupiter, another to the Sun and Moon, and to the other planets; and these, once more melted together, are transformed among themselves. Hence the divine remedies drawn from heaven, which those gods, summoned from heaven and now purified in the furnaces, bring forth for their kings and princes. But the putrid and cast-off helps lie exposed, born with us and prepared at home without expense; the nature of the common herd is vulgar, and the dregs of the elements constitute a muddy medicine, which the common people and the dregs of men ought to use. Surely an ungenerous and manifest nature has hidden all the instruments of health within, or else, exhausted and drained of juice, it has conceived nothing against diseases, or it does not bring them forth at all unless they are fused, cooked, dissolved and at length wrung out by marvellous arts. But these are faults and fabrications of the craftsmen, not a fault of the art; the medicine which has been produced and polished by excellent minds has enlarged itself with a great store of things. Let us rather enjoy, after the manner of our ancestors, the nature that is domestic and familiar to us; let the material that nature offers spontaneously, produced with us, be gathered. Yet it will be fitting to use other remedies too, as though by an external hand and with auxiliary supplies.

units.la: In eadem causa sunt,quibus nihil pla cere potest,nisi quod Indiam loquatur, & extremum Oceanum:qui tantum ex- terna probant,& exoticas merces admi rantur. Hunc errore ignoratio primum peperit: deinde quia rudibus ingenijs bonarum rerum consuetudo grauis est. Et bona fide oblatae merces uulgo fordescunt. Quid quòd externa illa longo quaesita mari, grauibus periculis inuenta, insanoq; sumptu comportata, exoleta fere, adulterata, suspecta denique ad nos perueniunt? nec alio saepe momento constant, quàm impostura? An non haec demetia est, ita subscribere alienis: uieta, euanida, ac fere dubia auxilia sic persequi, ut uigentem domi, extemporaneam, certamq; Medicinam deseras? Calcantur multa (quemadmodum Herophilus, clarus in Medicina, sensit) & sunt in oculis, quae conflatis, fusis, recoctis, quae ex India & rubro mari coportatis, recte praeferas. Vernaculae sunt nobis, atq; domestica naturae opes, quibus sanitas conseruari, morbus profligari queat. In faece rerum & excrementis, in carie, in rebus minimis, obsoletis, ac paene nullis, remedia condita sunt. Veluti paucis in hoc Opusculo cernere licet, ubi remedia quaedam uere ἀντιδοτα[?], experta, naturaeq; amica reperiuntur: magnis laboribus, magnisq; uigilijs ex D. Phi-lippi
units.tr: In the same cause are those for whom nothing can please unless it speaks of India and the farthest Ocean, who approve only what is foreign and admire exotic wares. Ignorance first produced this error, and then the habit of good things is burdensome to crude minds. And goods offered in good faith commonly become cheap. What of the fact that those foreign things, sought over a long sea, found with grave dangers and brought in at mad expense, reach us stale, adulterated and finally suspect? And they often stand on no other footing than imposture. Is it not madness to subscribe so to foreign things, to pursue so eagerly such weak, faded and almost doubtful helps, that you abandon the flourishing, ready-to-hand and certain medicine at home? Many things are calcined (as Herophilus, famous in medicine, perceived), and there are things before our eyes which, melted, fused and recooked, you may rightly prefer to those brought in from India and the Red Sea. The resources of nature, both native and domestic to us, by which health can be preserved and disease put to flight, are our own. Remedies are stored away in the dregs and excrements of things, in decay, in the smallest, obsolete and almost worthless things. As a few examples in this little work show, certain remedies that are truly antidotes [ἀντιδοτα?], tested and friendly to nature, are to be found; with great labours and great vigils, from D. Philippus

units.la: AD LECTOREM.
units.tr: TO THE READER.

units.la: lippi Melanchthonis, piæ memoriæ, lectionibus, à Doctiss. uiro D. IOAN. MANLIO, summo studio atq; diligentia collecta, ac coportata: qui suas partes esse duxit, ea in Libello hoc, de abditis nonnullis ac mirandis morborū sanationibus quædā, tumultuaria quasi (ut uidebantur) festinatione, ex tempore potius effusa, quàm à cura diligentius exarata, iterum relegere, utcunq; in ordinem redigere, & in publicum dare: ne si qua in his esset utilitas, cùm præsentis tum futuri seculi hominibus inuideretur.
units.tr: of Philip Melanchthon, of pious memory, collected and arranged with the greatest care and diligence by the most learned man Johann Manlius, who thought it his duty to go through these things again, to some extent put them into order, and publish them. They were written down rather hastily, in a rough and improvised manner, as they seemed at the time, and were poured out extemporaneously rather than carefully composed. He did this so that, if there was any usefulness in them, it would not be withheld from the people of this age and of ages to come.

units.la: Porrò, quantum sit illius uiri aduersus posteritatem omnem officium, uel ex hisce quæ nostro seculo faciunt homines, licet intelligere: quorum si quis uel exiguam habet artis portiunculam, ναὶ μι- πρόμ τι τῶν ἐμπειρίας ἀπομαξομένων φαρμά- κων, quantum gloriatur, quantumq; id celare studet: ut ne amicissimis quidem communicari uelit. Veluti qui experimentum habent aduersus morbum aliquem: id enim alij non expediunt, nisi magno oppositio præmio: aut si promat, minimè tamen cæteris id patefieri uolūt. At noster Manlius ille, quæ multis uigilijs,
units.tr: Moreover, how great Manlius's service to all posterity is can be understood even from what people do in our own age. If anyone has even a small scrap of skill, "Yes, some little part of the remedies drawn from experience" [ναὶ μικρόν τι τῶν ἐμπειρίας ἀπομαξομένων φαρμάκων], how much he boasts, and how eagerly he strives to conceal it, so that he does not want to share it even with his closest friends. For example, those who have a remedy against some disease do not disclose it unless a large reward is offered; or if they do bring it out, they still do not want it made known to others. But our Manlius, by contrast, what he learned through many vigils

units.la: Greek words at the line ends are uncertain: [?] applies to the Greek phrase as a whole. lijs, longo temporis interuallo didicit, posteris uniuersa effundit, & fideliter depromit: quæ profecto est animi quædam magnitudo illius hominis. Siquidë occultatio rerum non aliunde, quàm ex animi deiectione proficiscitur. Quapropter primùm ab omnibus bonis qui aliquid utilitatis ex labore huius Manlij, uel ipsi, uel posteri eorū percipient, meritò laudari & tueri debet: deinde etiam ab iis qui hortatores, & incitatores ipsi extiterunt, ut hæc & priora posteritati committeret, qui à Zoilorū calumniis huic postremo seculo usitatis eū defendere, & patronos se ostendere uelint. Facile enim labor alterius potest uituperari, præsertim à talibus qui non subierūt. Quisq; ergo gratitudinē suam erga hunc bonum uirum, qui in honorem Dei, & utilitatem posteritatis laborauit, declarare studeat. Nā tales certè sunt promouendi, summoq; amore amplectendi, colendi, obseruandi, ac omnibus officijs afficiendi: qui non solùm sibi uiuūt, sed etiam alijs quamplurimis prodesse cupiunt: insuper huius boni uiri diligentia & sedulitas omnibus prodesse poterit, dextrè aliorum labores iudicantibus, quibus haud dubiè rem gratissimam fecit. Si qui verò sunt scioli, quibus argumentum calumniandi nunquam defuturum novimus, ac veluti innatum est optima in peiorem partem interpretari, nullis q; honestis & utilibus laborib. delectari, atq; suam cantilenā (sicut coccyx consueuit) solum admirari: illis dictum esto, quod in inusitato & communi Graeco Prouerbio dicitur: μωμήσεται τις θάσσον ἢ μιμήσεται. Habemus etiam alia, quae alio tempore his ipsis, & auaris seu fucis aliorū laborem ad se arripientibus, abun de declarabimus, sicubi huic bono viro sua maleuolentia uel auaricia obesse studebunt. Hæc erant, Lector, de quibus nunc temporis te commonefaciendum esse duximus. Vale: ac bonorum doctorumq; labore, sicut apis sedula, fruere.
units.tr: over a long stretch of time, pours out for posterity in full and hands down faithfully. This is surely a certain greatness of spirit in that man. For concealment of things arises from nothing else than a dejected spirit. Therefore, first of all, all good men who, whether themselves or their descendants, will gain some benefit from the labour of this Manlius ought rightly to praise and defend him. Next, so should those who were themselves the urgers and encouragers that he should entrust these and earlier works to posterity, and who wish to defend him against the calumnies of the Zoilus-like critics in use in this latter age and to show themselves his patrons. For another's labour can easily be found fault with, especially by those who have not undergone it. Let everyone therefore strive to declare his gratitude towards this good man, who laboured for the honour of God and the usefulness of posterity. Such men are certainly to be advanced and embraced with the greatest love, cherished, respected, and honoured with every kind of service, since they live not only for themselves but also desire to benefit very many others. Moreover, the diligence and industry of this good man will be able to benefit everyone who judges the labours of others fairly, and to them he has certainly done a most welcome service. But if there are any smatterers, for whom we know there will never be lack of a pretext for calumny, and who, as if it were innate, always interpret the best things in the worst sense, delight in no honest and useful labours, and admire only their own song, as the cuckoo is wont to do, let them be told what is said in the unusual and common Greek proverb: "Someone will sooner find fault than imitate" [μωμήσεται τις θᾶσσον ἢ μιμήσεται]. We have also other matters which we shall declare at another time, abundantly, against these very men, and against the greedy or drone-like seizers of others' labour, should they try to harm this good man through their malice or avarice. These things, Reader, were what we thought you should now be reminded of. Farewell, and enjoy the labour of good and learned men as a diligent bee does.

units.la: IN LIBELLVM HVNC Medicum Samuelis Holtzachij ad Lectorem, Carmen.
units.tr: On this medical little book of Samuel Holtzach, a poem to the reader.

units.la: ARtes ad medicas referenda sequentia scripta,Summo ridiculis margine plena iocis:Non uni uoluit, sed multis, optime Manli,Ingenium studijs imigilare tuum.Cunctorumq; capax, quae continet igneus aether,Arctis limitibus se cohibere negat.
units.tr: You will find here writings to be read in connection with medicine, full of jokes at the highest level of wit. Best of Manlius, they wish your talent not to be devoted to one field of study but to many. Able to take in everything that the fiery aether contains, it refuses to be confined within narrow limits.

units.la: Aliud, ad eundem, à quodam docto uiro, deq; studijs benemerito, compositum.
units.tr: Another, to the same, composed by a certain learned man who has deserved well of his studies.

units.la: Quaeris opem medicam si quis, curamq; leuandiLethales morbos, hic medicamen habes.Repperies lepidos hic, dulciloquosq; lepores,Quos tibi collectos MANLIA cura dedit.Saepius ingentes morbi sermone leuantur,Atq; remittenti saepe dolore cadunt.
units.tr: If you seek medical help, and a cure for relieving deadly diseases, here you have a remedy. Here you will find charming jokes and sweet-speaking witticisms, which Manlia's care has gathered and given to you. Often great diseases are relieved by speech, and often they fall away when the pain subsides.

units.la: OBSERVATIONES VTILES pro suorum corporum homicidis.
units.tr: Useful observations for the murderers of their own bodies.

units.la: ANcipiti si uis praeceps occurrere morti,Saepe tibi uenas incidito, saepe lauato.Sit cibus immodicus, numerosaq; pharmaca sume:Sollicitus uiuas, grauibusq; obstringere curis.At uacans studijs, foetensq; habitato cubile,Inuidiaq;
units.tr: If you wish to run headlong to meet a doubtful death, often cut your veins and often bathe. Let your food be excessive, and take plenty of medicines. Live anxious, and bind yourself with heavy cares. But live idle, away from studies, and dwell in a foul-smelling bed, and often consume yourself with envy and anger, living with no companions: in this way you waste your life and your hours.

units.tr: and with anger, often consume yourself, with no

units.la: viuito cum socijs: uitam sic perdis, & horas.
units.tr: companions: in this way you waste your life and your hours.

units.la: Ein nützlich regiment/ für die so vor der zeit zům todt eilen.
units.tr: A useful regimen for those who rush to death before their time.

units.la: Wer vor der zeit wil sterben/Der soll sich vleisig bewerben/Offt baden vnd aderlassen/Fressen vnd sauffen one massen:Vil wachē/ bekümern das leben/Sich in schwăre sorg begeben:In stinckenden gemachē wonen/Mit zorn sich nicht verschonen:Alle gschelschafft vermeiden/Pillulen vnd arzeney offt leidē:Das sein zehen gūtter stuck/Dē gsundē leben zů vnderdruck.
units.tr: Whoever wishes to die before his time should apply himself diligently: bathe often and be bled, eat and drink without measure; keep long watches, trouble his life, and put himself into heavy care; live in stinking rooms, and spare himself no anger; avoid all company, and often endure pills and medicine. These are ten good points for undermining healthy living.

units.la: LIBELLUS MEDICUS.
units.tr: A Little Medical Book.

units.la: SYRACH de arte medica dicit: Dedit Deus scientiam, ut conglorificetur in mirabilibus suis. Quibus verbis significare voluit, quòd illa substantialis efficacia in singulis remedijs sit testimonium de prouidentia diuina, & quòd singulae res ad usus hominum sint conditae. Deinde sunt etiam quaedam res ad animantium conseruationem destinatae. Illud enim verissimum est, multos periculosissimos morbos leui cura, si in principio mediocria, & ferè nullius momenti remedia applicata sint, curatos esse. Quòd uero interdum curationes sint infeliciores, id plerunq; fit malicia hominum, nolentiū fidelib. & doctis medicis obedire, ijsdemq; temperantiam mediocrem, quam curatio requirit, praestare. Cuiusmodi exempla sunt haec sequentia.
units.tr: Sirach says of the medical art: "God has given knowledge, that he may be glorified in his marvels" (Sir. 38.6). By these words he meant that the substantial efficacy of each remedy is a testimony to divine providence, and that individual things were created for the use of men. Moreover, there are also certain things destined for the preservation of living creatures. For it is most true that many very dangerous diseases are cured by a light treatment, if moderate remedies, almost of no importance, are applied at the beginning. But if the cures sometimes turn out less favourably, this usually happens through the wickedness of men who are unwilling to obey faithful and learned physicians and who do not observe the moderation of diet that the cure requires. Examples of this kind are the following.

units.la: Contemptus medicorum poenae.
units.tr: The Punishment of Despising Physicians.

units.la: Quidam ex collocutoribus in conuentu Ratisponensi laborabat febri, iubebatq; sibi adferri aquam: & uno impetu tres cantharos aquæ exhauriebat. Medicis eü obiurgantibus, respondit: Vos medici nostri meam naturam, ego sum robustus Sueuus. At paulo post ex illa intemperantia moritur, quia epar antea ualdè calebat: infusaq; nimia aqua, uehementior pugna per antiperistasin facta, debilitatum epar, et eiusdem epatis uirtus calore febrili, accedente illa infusione aquæ, uincebatur: unde statim epatis putrefactio est sequuta.
units.tr: One of the speakers at the Regensburg assembly was suffering from a fever and kept ordering water to be brought to him. At one go he drained three tankards of water. When the physicians rebuked him, he replied: "You doctors do not know my constitution; I am a robust Swabian." But a little later he died from that excess. His liver had already been running very hot, and the large quantity of water brought on a fiercer conflict through antiperistasis. The liver was weakened, and its natural strength was overcome by the febrile heat, the water poured in adding to the struggle. Putrefaction of the liver followed at once.

units.la: Bonus & honestus uir Bononiæ incidit in febrim, & fide medicorum ualetudini est restitutus. Cum uerò minus diligenter custodiretur à socijs, uidit in mensa poculum uini stare: quo arrepto & exhausto, rursum in morbum incidit, & febri extinguitur.
units.tr: A good and honest man at Bologna fell into a fever and was restored to health through the trust he placed in his physicians. But when he was less carefully watched by his companions, he saw a cup of wine standing on the table; having seized and drunk it, he fell ill again and was extinguished by the fever.

units.la: Impostores, qui prætextu medicinæ homines fallunt.
units.tr: Impostors, who deceive people under the pretext of medicine.

units.la: Quidam Princeps pulcherrimus, robusto etiam corpore, tantum mortuus est scelere (non dicam insscitia) chirurgi: cum alij doĉti medici eum monerent, ne uteretur tur illa medicatione. Ille optimus Prin-ceps cœperat laborare pleuritide, quæ ini-tiò quidem est curabilis, præsertim ante-quam ad eam febris accedit, si tantumodo philosophica ratio adhibeatur: quando uidelicet agrotus (ut postea indicabimus) bi-bit succum chamæleontis, & bonam diæ-tam adhibet. Medicus uerò Principis il-lius, uir excellenti doctrina præditus, & medicinæ non uulgariter expertus, in illo morbo ritè physico more procedebat. Sed Princeps habebat chirurgum, qui obtem-perabat eius affectui. reprimebat enim ca-lorem frigida terra, ad plantā pedis applica-ta. sed ita repressit calorem, ut rediret ad cor: ubi ita auctus est, ut sic inflammatus Princeps ille medicatione, deniq; morere-tur. Hæc sunt nobis à fide dignis, & qui huic medicationi præsentes interfuere, uiris recitata.
units.tr: A certain most excellent Prince, also of robust body, died through the wicked act (I will not say ignorance) of a surgeon, although other learned physicians warned him not to use that treatment. That best of princes had begun to suffer from pleurisy, which at the outset is indeed curable, especially before fever joins it, if only a rational, philosophical method is applied: namely, as we shall indicate later, when the patient drinks the juice of chamaeleon and keeps to a good diet. But the physician of that Prince, a man endowed with excellent learning and not commonly experienced in medicine, was proceeding in that disease in the proper physical manner. The Prince, however, had a surgeon who complied with his inclination. For he repressed the heat by applying cold earth to the sole of the foot; but he repressed the heat in such a way that it returned to the heart, where it was so increased that the Prince, inflamed in this way by the treatment, at last died. These things have been recounted to us by trustworthy men who were present at this treatment.

units.la: Erat hic nobilis Pomeranus de Massauu, qui curabatur uino Maluatico in pleuri-tide: erat enim ab indocto medico sic per-suasus. Tandē bonus ille adolescens sic in-flammatus est, ut spacio tridui moreretur.
units.tr: There was a noble Pomeranian from Massow who was being treated for pleurisy with Malmsey wine, for he had been persuaded of this by an unlearned physician. In the end that good young man became so inflamed that he died within three days.

units.la: Quidam sacerdos non procul à Torga, curabat luscos oculos, scribendo characte res, & appendendo illis de collo, addens uidelicet hæc uerba Germanicè: <bl>Der teuffel kratz dir die augen aus/ vnd scheiss dir in die luckhen.</bl> id est, Diabolus tibi oculos eruat, & cacet in cavitates. Sic illis fantasys multos homines decepit.
units.tr: A certain priest not far from Torgau was curing blind eyes by writing characters and hanging them around the patients' necks, adding these words in German: "May the devil scratch your eyes out and shit into the sockets." That is, "May the devil tear out your eyes and defecate into the cavities." In this way he deceived many people with such fancies.

units.la: Pleuritidis curatio.
units.tr: The Cure of Pleurisy.

units.la: Non est magis præsens & subitaneum remedium contra pleurisin, quàm succus ex chamæleote uulgari herba, Germanicè <bl>Marien distellu</bl> / expressus: quæ si ini tio morbi patiens bibat, tùc statim remis sionē & leuamē illius morbi sentit. Hoc remedio multos adhuc uiuetes curauimus.
units.tr: There is no more present and immediate remedy against pleurisy than the juice pressed from the common chamaeleon herb, which in German is called <bl>Marien distellu</bl> (Mary's thistle). If the patient drinks it at the beginning of the illness, he immediately feels the relief and alleviation of that disease. We have cured many people still living with this remedy.

units.la: Memini optimum quendam uirum no biscum iter in æstu facientem, in conuiuio in calescere (eramus enim apud homines lo cupletes, & lautè cibo & potu pleniore nos excipientes) & laborare pleuritide: cui meus frater dabat pharmacum, quo et iam est usa uxor D. Martini Lutheri. Descendebat frater meus in stabulum equorum, rum,& exprimebat ex stercore equino suc-cum: cui, ad salledum, saccharum inspersit, & ægrotanti hauriendum præbuit, iubens eum simul in lecto dormire. Hac unica curatione ille postridie fuit curatus.
units.tr: I remember a certain most excellent man who, travelling with me in the heat, grew warm at a banquet (for we were among wealthy people who received us with rich food and drink) and was suffering from pleurisy. My brother gave him a medicine, the same one that Dr. Martin Luther's wife has also used. My brother went down into the horse stable and pressed out juice from horse dung. To make it palatable he sprinkled sugar on it and gave it to the sick man to drink, bidding him at the same time to sleep in bed. By this single treatment he was cured the next day.

units.la: Ego sum curatus in pleutitide, tantum contusa maxilla piscis lupi, cocta & pota. Nunc hanc ipsam ob causam tales maxil-las, præsertim in grandioribus lupis, diligē-tius reseruo.
units.tr: I was cured of pleurisy only by a crushed jawbone of a pike, boiled and drunk. For this very reason I now keep such jawbones more carefully, especially those of the larger pike.

units.la: Colici doloris curatio.
units.tr: The Cure of Colic Pain.

units.la: Curaui sæpissimè nostros scholasticos co-lico dolore laborantes, hoc leuissimo reme-dio: ut tantum in locum affectum, saccum auena impletū calefactumq́; imponerent: & ita sunt citò curati.
units.tr: I have very often cured our students suffering from colic pain with this very light remedy: they only had to apply to the affected place a sack filled with oats and warmed, and they were quickly cured.

units.la: Alexipharmaca, siue Alexiteria.
units.tr: Alexipharmaca, or Alexiteria.

units.la: Est mirabilis naturæ terra Lemnia. nam Dioscorides scripsit, hircinum sanguinem misceri Lemniæ terræ. Cuius remedij ma-gnus usus est. Quare Galenus ipse ea loca adiit, ut exploraret certò, quomodo appa-raretur: comperitq́; naturam esse metalli-cam, sine mixtura sanguinis hircini. Est autem hodie in tanto usu, tantaq́; admira-tione
units.tr: Lemnian earth is a wonder of nature. Dioscorides wrote that goat's blood is mixed into Lemnian earth, and its use as a remedy is great. Therefore Galen himself went to those places to find out for certain how it was prepared, and he discovered that its nature is metallic, without any admixture of goat's blood. Today it is in such great use and esteem among the Thracians and Greeks that the Turkish emperor is accustomed to give Lemnian earth among the special gifts to foreign envoys. Lemnian earth is indeed the best and most excellent remedy against plague and dysentery. The Turkish emperor gave Schopper, envoy of the Emperor, several small lumps as a singular gift.

Est enim terra Lemnia optimum & præstan-tissimum remedium in peste ac dysenteria. Turcicus Imperator donauit Schoppero Le-gato Imperatoris aliquot massulas, pro sin-gulari munere.
units.tr: Nothing further printed in the foot notes on this page. ...tion among the Thracians and Greeks, so that the Turkish emperor usually gives Lemnian earth as one of his special gifts to foreign envoys. Lemnian earth is the best and most excellent remedy against plague and dysentery. The Turkish emperor gave Schopper, envoy of the Emperor, several small lumps as a singular gift.

units.la: Contra scorpij ictus.
units.tr: Against the sting of a scorpion.

units.la: Quando scorpius necatur in oleo, illudq; sauciato à scorpio illinitur, tunc sauciatus curatur.
units.tr: When a scorpion is killed in oil, and that oil is smeared on the spot wounded by the scorpion, the one who was wounded is cured.

units.la: Quidam eques apud nos uenit ad medi-cum Vlmensem, Doctorem Stock ( qui erat medicus omniû principum in nostra uicinia, habebatq; suam singularem for-tunam curandi morbos )dicens: Domine Doctor, nescio quem morbum habeam: ma-nè ieiunus uentriculum meum cum magno dolore arrodisentio. Tu nebulo, inquit Doctor (erat enim medico familiaris) for-tè aliquid mali comedisti. & retinuit eum quadriduum, ac pauit eum ordine, simulq; à nimio cibo & potu abstinere iussit. Po-stea uerò, post longam deliberationem (erat enim ualde industrius, & artis suæ peritis- simus) inquit: Tu nequam, uorasti semina serpentum, ex quibus serpentes in tuo uen- triculo procreatæ sunt. Instituit uero curationem hoc modo: collocans eum in lectu, ac admouens eius ori lac ualde calefactu. Serpentes postquam hoc olfecerut, serpere cœperunt ex uentriculo in collum. quarum colla statim chirurgus, iampridem aduocatus, paratusq; cum suis instrumentis, apprehendebat, ac extrahebat aliquot serpentes per interualla. Extractis iam omnibus serpentibus, Doctor indicauit, unde illud malum ipsi accidisset: Tu ualde sitiens, inquit, hausisti strenuè aquam ex aliqua lacuna, ubi fuerunt semina serpentum. Ille fassus est, se bibisse in uere: & ita curatus est.
units.tr: A certain horseman came to us to the Ulm physician, Doctor Stock (who was the physician of all the princes in our neighbourhood and had a singular good fortune in curing diseases), saying: "Sir Doctor, I do not know what disease I have: in the morning, fasting, my stomach gnaws at me with great pain." "You scoundrel," said the Doctor (for he was on familiar terms with the physician), "perhaps you have eaten something bad." And he kept him for four days, fed him in an orderly way, and at the same time ordered him to abstain from too much food and drink. Afterwards, however, following a long deliberation (for he was very diligent and most skilled in his art), he said: "You wretch, you swallowed the seeds of serpents, from which serpents have been born in your stomach." He then undertook the cure in this way: laying him on a bed and bringing to his mouth milk that was very warm. After the serpents had smelled this, they began to creep out of the stomach into the throat. A surgeon, who had been summoned earlier and stood ready with his instruments, seized their necks and drew out several serpents at intervals. Once all the serpents had been extracted, the Doctor indicated how the evil had come upon him: "You, being very thirsty," he said, "drank greedily water from some pool where there were serpents' seeds." He confessed that he had drunk it in the spring, and so he was cured.

units.la: Dominus Stanislaus à Lasco, uirtute & sapientia præstans uir, captus cum rege Galliæ, etiam mortuus est, serpentibus in eius uentriculo innatis: cui nemo opitulari potuit.
units.tr: Lord Stanislaus à Lasco, a man outstanding in virtue and wisdom, was seized along with the King of France and also died, with serpents growing within his stomach; no one could help him.

units.la: Contra serpentum ictus.
units.tr: Against the bites of serpents.

units.la: Scribit Athenæus, se audiuisse ex quodam dam ciue,præfecto Ægypti, mirabilem hi storiā. Cum essent puniendi quidā sontes, & ÿ adducerētur ad aspides : mulier quædam dedit eis, recreandi causa, de pomo Citrio. Cum autem obÿcerentur aspidibus, uenenum non fuit efficax, & morsus aspidum non nocuerunt eis. Præfectus & iudex attoniti, putauerunt eos insontes esse: & iterum quæsiuerunt, num aliquid comedissent? illi responderunt, sibi datum esse pauxillum de pomo Citrio. Hoc audientes, postridie rursus produxerūt eos ad supplicium, & alteri dederunt de Citrio, alteri uerò non. Quare cum iterum obÿcerentur aspidibus, ille qui comederat de Citrio, euasit incolumis: alter uerò extinctus est. Tanta est uis huius pomi aduersus uenenū.
units.tr: Athenaeus writes that he heard a remarkable story from a certain citizen, the prefect of Egypt. Certain guilty men were to be punished, and they were brought to the asps; a certain woman gave them, to refresh them, a little citron. When they were then exposed to the asps, the poison was not effective and the bites of the asps did not harm them. The prefect and the judge, astonished, thought they were innocent, and asked again whether they had eaten anything; they replied that they had been given a little of the citron. Hearing this, on the next day they brought them out again to execution, and gave some citron to one and none to the other. When they were again exposed to the asps, the one who had eaten the citron escaped unharmed, but the other was killed. So great is the power of this fruit against poison.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Scribitur de quodam tyranno Pontico, qui solitus est ad se inuitare suos cives, atq; ita uocatis præbere uenenum. Hoc postquam senserunt cives, quos inuitabat, nec tamen auderent detrectare auctoritatē tyranni, sumpserunt prius pauxillū de Citrio cōdito: sicq; uenenū nō fuit efficax.
units.tr: It is written of a certain Pontic tyrant who was accustomed to invite his citizens to himself and, when they had been invited, to offer them poison. After the citizens whom he invited perceived this, yet did not dare to refuse the tyrant's authority, they first took a little preserved citron; and so the poison was not effective.

units.la: Matricis doloris curatio.
units.tr: Curing of uterine pain.

units.la: Scio honestissimam matronam, adhuc viuentem, laborare morbo periculosissimo matricis: de cuius salute omnes medici desperarunt. Doctor Augustinus, remotis omnibus aliis remedijs, nihil aliud parauit, nisi potionem ex libanotide: quae herba cordiualde prodest. Est enim mirabilis vis illius herbae, iuuandi cerebrum, matricem et cor. Hac curatione magnam sibi laudem & autoritatem in medicina comparauit.
units.tr: I know a most respectable matron, still living, who suffers from a very dangerous disease of the womb, and all the physicians have despaired of her recovery. Doctor Augustinus, setting aside all other remedies, prepared nothing but a drink made from libanotis, an herb that is very good for the heart. For this herb has a wonderful power to help the brain, the womb and the heart. By this cure he won great praise and authority in medicine.

units.la: Καχεξίας curatio.
units.tr: Curing of cachexia [καχεξίας].

units.la: Doctor Pontanus & ego veniebamus in itinere ad quendam senem virum, qui nos hospitio excipiebat, qui habebat initia hydropis, seu quandam καχεξίαν: & conquerebatur se laborare insomnio. De illo accidente quaerebamus, quod nam esset symptoma. Consuluerat vero medicum, qui ipsi dabat potiones frigidas, ad conciliandum somnum. Ille autem querebatur, quanto magis ijs uteretur, tanto se peius dormire. Cogitauimus igitur, quae esset causa morbi. Ac sic tandem ipsi dicebam: Domine hospes, da nobis bonum vinum, & cœna nobiscum, & utere illo bonopotu,nec facias excessum, sed bibe pro siti restinguē-da: & confer te citò cubitum, ac cras dic mihi utrum melius dormiueris: tunc enim de alia causa cogitandum est. Ille obtempe-rat mihi, & statim post cœnā se confert cu-bitum. Manè cum interrogarem, quomo-do dormiuisset? respondit, se multis mensi-bus non ita commodè dormiuisse. Inde ratiocinabar, dicens: Tu habes frigidum uentriculum: iam uerò medicus suffundit frigida, augentia cruditatem. Obtempera igitur mihi, bibe semper bonum vinum, & vesperi maturè te confer cubitum. Ille obtemperauit mihi, ac rectè convaluit, leua-tionemq; morbi sensit: ita ut postea mul-tos annos viveret. Iussi verò etiam, illum interdum uti zingibere.
units.tr: Doctor Pontanus and I were travelling to an old man who was receiving us as guests. He had the beginnings of dropsy, or a certain cachexia [καχεξία], and he complained that he suffered from sleeplessness. We asked him about this condition, what its chief symptom was. He had consulted a physician, who had given him cold drinks to induce sleep. But he complained that the more he used them, the worse he slept. So we considered what the cause of the illness might be. And at last I said to him: "Master host, give us good wine, dine with us, drink a good draught of it to quench your thirst, but do not overdo it. Then go to bed early, and tomorrow tell me whether you slept better. For then we must look for another cause." He obeyed me, and straight after supper he went to bed. In the morning, when I asked him how he had slept, he replied that for many months he had not slept so comfortably. Then I reasoned, saying: "You have a cold stomach. The physician has indeed poured cold remedies into it, which increase indigestion. So obey me: always drink good wine, and go to bed early in the evening." He obeyed me, recovered well, and felt relief from his illness, so that afterwards he lived for many years. I also advised him to take ginger now and then.

units.la: Καρδιακή: quo morbo Martinus Lutherus est ex-tinctus.
units.tr: Cardiaca [καρδιακή]: the disease from which Martin Luther died.

units.la: Doctor Martinus Lutherus, annum ante mortem suam, vocavit me mane circa horam secundam. Casu tunc surrexeram, venio ad eum, interrogans quid esset? O`, in-quit, quit, habeo magnos & periculosos cruciatus. Interrogaui, num esset calculus? Respondit: Non: est adhuc aliquid maius supra calculum. Considerabam arteriam, quæ erat bona. Dicebam: Cor est incolume, non est apoplecticum. At ipse: Magnam habeo constrictionem circa cor, tamen non sentio cor constringi, & neq; aliquid incommodi ex pulsu animaduerto. Ergo argumentabar, nihil potest esse nisi humor, in orificio uentriculi ascendens: unde est tanta compressio. & ille morbus uocatur καρδιακή. Quæsiui igitur morbi initium. Ascenderat (sicut erat admodum uerecundus) cloacam, cum esset magnum frigus: simulq; sensit se frigore affici, & statim illo morbo corripi. nam istud frigus mouerat humores, ut ascenderent. Ibi ego iubebam statim admoueri pannos calefactos, tergi pectus & dorsum, ac mox parari iusculum seu offulam. Prohibui etiam ne biberet mustum: mustum enim tunc biberat. Iussi etiā, ut minister de meo uino afferret: bonum enim tunc habebam Rhenanum. Cumq; gustasset iusculum, mox subsedit humor: & iubebam ut quiescєret, & illis calefactis panniculis uteretur. Postea, quando mortuus est, dicunt eum mortuum esse apoplecticum. At non fuit apoplexia, sed mortuus est illo quo dixi morbo: quia paulo ante mortem mihi scripsit, se eo morbo rursum tentatum esse.
units.tr: Doctor Martin Luther called me one morning about the second hour, a year before his death. I had got up early by chance, and I went to him and asked what was the matter. "Oh," he said, "I have great and dangerous pains." I asked whether it was a stone. He replied: "No, there is something else, worse than a stone." I examined his pulse, which was good. I said: "The heart is sound; it is not apoplectic." But he said: "I have a great constriction about the heart, yet I do not feel the heart being squeezed, and I notice no discomfort in the pulse." So I argued: there can be nothing but a humour rising into the mouth of the stomach, and that causes such great pressure; and this illness is called cardiaca [καρδιακή]. I then asked where the illness had begun. He had gone (as he was very modest) to the privy in great cold, and at the same time he felt himself affected by the cold and at once seized by that illness, for the cold had set the humours moving so that they rose. Then I ordered warm cloths to be applied at once, the chest and back to be rubbed, and soon a broth or a little sop to be prepared. I also forbade him to drink must, for he had been drinking must then. I further ordered the servant to bring some of my wine, for I then had good Rhenish. And when he had tasted the broth, the humour soon settled. I told him to rest and to use those warmed cloths. Afterwards, when he died, they say he died of apoplexy. But it was not apoplexy; he died of the disease I have described, because shortly before his death he wrote to me that he had been attacked by that disease again.

units.la: Catarrhorum facilis curatio.
units.tr: Easy cure for catarrhs.

units.la: Dominus Philippus temperàter viuens, nullo alio remedio usus est, nisi quòd ex pelui singulis diebus quibus laborabat catarrhis, saepenumero ex aqua lauabat manus.
units.tr: Master Philip, living temperately, used no other remedy than this: on each day when he suffered from catarrhs, he often washed his hands in water from a basin.

units.la: Ophthalmiae curatio.
units.tr: Cure for ophthalmia.

units.la: Contra dolores oculorum D. Philippus propria manu cuidam Polono haec sequentia scripsit. Rx. Aquarum Euphragiae Rosarum Rutae } an. ʒ. I. Misce pro collirio.
units.tr: Against pains of the eyes, Dr Philip wrote the following with his own hand for a certain Pole. Rx. Waters of eyebright, roses, rue, of each 1 drachm. Mix for an eye-wash.

units.la: Vtilitates tres insignes Electri, quod uulgo uocant Augstein.
units.tr: Three notable uses of electrum, which the common people call Augstein (amber).

units.la: I. Difficilis partus curatio.
units.tr: I. Cure for difficult labour.

units.la: Habet miram efficaciam in mulieribus partuparturientibus, quæ sunt in summo periculo propter fœtus editionem, quando pauxillum electri in vino contunditur, idq; vino imbibunt, vel quando de decocto pulegii datur: tunc statim ediderunt fœtus. In illis rebus est arcana efficacia, quæ non conspicitur: estq; res mirabilis, quando matrix adiuvatur electro vel pulegio.
units.tr: It has a wonderful effect on women in labour who are in the greatest danger because of the delivery of the foetus: when a little electrum is crushed in wine and they drink it down, or when it is given in a decoction of pennyroyal, they at once bring forth the foetus. In these things there is a hidden power, which cannot be seen; and it is a marvellous thing when the womb is helped by electrum or pennyroyal.

units.la: 2. Calculi & stranguriæ curatio.
units.tr: 2. Cure for stone and strangury.

units.la: Deinde electrum, in primis album, contusum, ac vino coctum, vel cerevisia, detur laborantibus calculo vel stranguria: tunc statim meatus aperit, & materiam calculosam disrumpit, ac expellit.
units.tr: Next, electrum, especially the white kind, crushed and boiled in wine or beer, should be given to those suffering from stone or strangury. Then at once it opens the passage and breaks up the stony matter and expels it.

units.la: 3. Utilitas contra apoplexiam.
units.tr: 3. Usefulness against apoplexy.

units.la: Dux Joannes Saxoniæ, pater ducis Joannis Friderici, optimus princeps, habebat secum iter faciens semper optimum succinum. Accidit forte in arce Altenburg, quòd quidam senex consiliarius, in proxima mensa Principis laboraret apoplexia, idq; animadvertens Princeps, ex lapsu ipsius, mox iussit adferri suum succinum, & accendi: quo fumo ægrotans recreatus est adeò, ut post hoc tempus adhuc multos annos vinos uixerit: si non fuisset recreatus, statim in eodem momento fuisset extinctus.
units.tr: Duke John of Saxony, father of Duke John Frederick, an excellent prince, always carried with him on his travels a very fine piece of amber. It happened by chance in the castle of Altenburg that an elderly councillor sitting at the table next to the Prince was struck by apoplexy. The Prince noticed his fall at once, and immediately ordered his amber to be brought and lit. The sick man was revived by its smoke, so that he lived many years afterwards; if he had not been revived, he would have died in that very moment.

units.la: Stranguriæ & calculi alia curatio.
units.tr: Another cure for strangury and stone.

units.la: Sentiens urinæ difficultates, uel stranguriam, aut si quis omnino non potest reddere urinam, is comedat aliquot grana iuniperi. Sic statim dolorum leuationem sentiet.
units.tr: If someone feels difficulty in passing urine, or strangury, or if anyone cannot pass urine at all, let him eat a few grains of juniper. He will at once feel his pains relieved.

units.la: Simile.
units.tr: Similar.

units.la: Dux Vuirtenbergensis, in conuentu Schmalkaldensi docuit doctore Lutherum præsens remedium contra calculum: uidelicet, ut sumeret recentem ollam, usq; ad dimidium recentibus iuniperis impletam, quam postea compleret uino & aqua, in qua iuniperos decoqueret ad tertiæ partis consumptionem: & de hac potione sumeret haustum unum atq; alterum. Tunc enim secuturam doloris mitigationem, & calculi processionem certò sensurum.
units.tr: The Duke of Württemberg, at the assembly at Schmalkald, showed Doctor Luther in person a ready remedy against stone: namely, that one should take a new pot, filled halfway with fresh juniper berries, then fill it up with wine and water, and boil the juniper in this until a third has been consumed. Of this drink one should take a draught or two. Then, he said, the pain would certainly be eased and the stone would certainly pass.

units.la: Aliud.
units.tr: Another.

units.la: Cygneæ quidam habens maximos calculi cruciatus, nullo alio remedio utebatur nisi lacte caprino, in quo poma cynosbati (Germanicè heinboten, uel butten ) coquebat, quebat, & in locum affectum impone-at. Sicq; statim processit calculus.
units.tr: A certain man of Cygnea, suffering the most severe agonies of stone, used no other remedy than goat's milk, in which he boiled the hips of the dog-rose (in German heinboten, or butten), and he applied them to the affected place. At once the stone came away.

units.la: Comitialis morbus an curabi-lis, nec ne, quomodo in-quirendum.
units.tr: Whether epilepsy is curable or not, and how it is to be investigated.

units.la: Vsitatissimum est in morbo comitiali,imponere smaragdum laborantib. eo mor-bo. aut enim frangitur smaragdus in ali-quot frusta, & tunc morbus est lethalis:ut manente integra gemma, ægrotusconvalescit.
units.tr: It is very common in epilepsy to place an emerald on those suffering from the disease. For if the emerald is broken into several pieces, the disease is fatal; but if the gem remains intact, the patient recovers.

units.la: Pectoris doloris curatio.
units.tr: Cure of pain in the chest.

units.la: Sensi aliquando dolores pectoris ma-ximos, quibus nihil aliud adhibui loco do-lorum nisi corallia. Sic breui tempoxis spa-tio dolor pectoris desiit.
units.tr: I once felt very severe pains in the chest, for which I applied nothing but coral in place of the remedies. So in a short space of time the pain in the chest ceased.

units.la: Pectus quare tegendum.
units.tr: Why the chest should be covered.

units.la: Pectus non tantum propter honesta-tem, sed multo magis propter ualetudinisconseruationem tegimus. Nam quandopectus nudum ita afflatur corrupto aere,accidit ut sæpè magnorum morborumcausa sit.
units.tr: We cover the chest not only for decency, but much more for the preservation of health. For when the bare chest is blown upon by corrupt air, it often happens that this becomes the cause of great diseases.

units.la: Dentium doloris curatio.
units.tr: Cure of toothache.

units.la: Cornu ceruinum ustum, & uino calidomixtum, mixtum, saluat dolorem dentium. Et Doctor Laurentius Lindeman, de utilitate huius cornu ceruini hæc dixit: Cornu ceruinum fore æquandú unicorni & rhinoceroti. Dubitatur enim,utrum rhinoceros adhuc sit in rerum natura.
units.tr: Burnt deer's horn, mixed with warm wine, cures toothache. And Doctor Laurentius Lindeman, speaking of the usefulness of this deer's horn, said this: that deer's horn should be rated equal to the unicorn and the rhinoceros, since it is doubted whether the rhinoceros still exists in nature.

units.la: Melancholiæ curatio.
units.tr: Cure of melancholy.

units.la: Lipsiæ quidam (quem credo multis adhuc uiuentibus esse notum) tanta melancholia laborauit,ut crederet se esse mortuum. Is descendit in cellam, in qua dies noctesq; ambulauit, dicens submissa uoce: Sum mortuus,sum mortuus:easq; uoces sub inde repetiuit. Amici uerò cognatiq; eius descendentes ad eum,uolebant eum ex cella educere. Ibi ille, Quid (inquit) petitis? aut quid uultis? ego sum mortuus.nolens cum ipsis egredi. Tandem excogitatum est à medicis eruditis consilium prudens,ut conduceretur robustus & uorax monachus. Quo adducto, apparataq; in cella lautissima cœna,monachus cellam ingreditur,assidensq; mensæ, ructus edit plurimos, simulq; strenuè uorare incipit. Ibi melancholicus prodiens,accedit mensam, interrogat rogat monachum, quis sit ? Respondit ille submissa uoce: Ego sum mortuus, Ego sum mortuus. Subiungit melancholicus, audita hac responsione: Quis tu es ? Respondit iterum monachus, Ego sum mortuus : Ad hæc melancholicus quærit: Comedunt ne etiam mortui? Respondit: Ita, ueni asside mensæ, & mecum comede: Ita assedit melancholicus mensæ, & strenuè comedit: eaq; facetia curatus est, pristinæq; uatetudini restitutus.
units.tr: At Leipzig a certain man (whom I believe many still living know) suffered from such melancholy that he believed himself to be dead. He went down into a cellar, where he walked day and night, saying in a low voice, "I am dead, I am dead," and he repeated these words from time to time. His friends and relatives came down to him and wanted to lead him out of the cell. He replied, "What do you seek, or what do you want? I am dead," and refused to go out with them. At last the learned physicians devised a shrewd plan: a strong and greedy monk was hired. When he had been brought in, and a most lavish dinner had been laid out in the cell, the monk entered, sat down at the table, belched loudly many times, and at once began to eat voraciously. Then the melancholic man came out, approached the table and asked the monk who he was. The monk answered in a low voice, "I am dead, I am dead." On hearing this reply, the melancholic asked, "Who are you?" The monk again answered, "I am dead." To this the melancholic asked, "Do the dead eat as well?" "Yes," he replied, "come, sit at the table and eat with me." So the melancholic sat down at the table and ate heartily, and by this witty device he was cured and restored to his former health.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Alius quidam eodem morbo melancho- licolaborans,dixit se habere ranas in uen-triculo. Ab hac sententia cum nemo eum abducere posset, uenit ad eum medicus, petens ut urinā redderet: qua uisa, medicus promittit se liberaturum eum, si modò ipsi morem gerere uellet. Iussit itaque medicus sibi adferri ranas uiuas, quas ut sculo imposuit, quod collocauit postea sub sellam, in qua necessitatem naturæ reddebat: simulq; potionem, aliquo modo uentriculum curantem, dabat. Qua sumpta, & naturæ opere peracto, quærit Doctor: Vi-disti ne disti'ne aliquas materias ex uisceribus tuis elapsas ? Respondit: Non . Ibi medicus in medium protulit ollam, ex qua ranæ prosilierunt . Ad hæc ægrotus adiecit: Hactenus non potui ipsis persuadere , me ranis uexatum fuisse:iam reipsa experiütur, rem sic se habuisse . & ita æger sanatus est.
units.tr: Another man, suffering from the same melancholy, said that he had frogs in his stomach. When no one could talk him out of this idea, a physician came to him and asked him to pass urine. Having seen it, the physician promised to free him, provided he would be willing to follow his instructions. The physician therefore ordered live frogs to be brought, which he put in a dish and placed afterwards under the chair in which the man was relieving himself. At the same time he gave him a drink that somehow treats the stomach. When this had been taken and the business of nature was done, the doctor asked, "Did you see any matter slip out from your bowels?" "No," he replied. Then the physician brought a pot into the middle of the room, from which the frogs leapt out. At this the patient added, "Until now I could not persuade them that I had been troubled by frogs; now they see with their own eyes that the thing was so." And so the patient was healed.

units.la: Hydropis curatio.
units.tr: Dropsy cured.

units.la: Audiui Pirckeimerum historiam talem dicentem. Paduæ est consuetudo, ut singulis diebus Doctores medicinæ conueniant in myropolio, & inuicem colloquantur. Ibi accedunt homines, & consulunt medicos . Venit quodam die rusticus hydropicus, & rogauit ut curarent ac sanarent ipsum . Medici aspicientes eum, responderunt, non posse curari, nec esse spem aliquam sanitatis . Abit rusticus plorans: et cum egrederetur ex myropolio, obuiam uenit ei alius Doctor medicus, ac interrogat eum , cur ploret ? Respondet rusticus : Se quidem fuisse apud Doctores, eos q; consuluisse : uerum eos omnem sibi salutis recuperandæ spem denegasse . At statim Doctor: Scis cur tibi denegauerint ? illi nouerunt tuam intemperantiam, & te non obseruare si quid mandent. Si mihi certò promittis, te obedientem fore meis mandatis, ego te sanabo. Rusticus promittit. Medicus respondet: Abstineas decem dies saltem à potu, & melius habebis. Non enim siti morieris. Rusticus discedit, & obedit: & elapso octiduo, reuertitur sanus in myropolium, indicatq́; Medico quis sit: ac interrogat quid ulterius ipsi sit faciendum, an adhuc diutius à potu abstinere debeat: quia iam se esse assuefactum, ut facile sitim ferre possit. Medicus iubet, ut non multum bibat, sed singulis diebus cantharum. Tantum consuetudo valet.
units.tr: I heard Pirckheimer tell this story. At Padua it is the custom for the doctors of medicine to meet every day in an apothecary's shop and talk with one another, and people come there to consult them. One day a country fellow with dropsy came and asked them to cure him. The doctors looked at him and replied that he could not be cured and there was no hope of health. The countryman went away weeping. As he came out of the apothecary's shop, another doctor met him and asked why he was weeping. The countryman replied that he had been to the doctors and consulted them, but they had denied him any hope of recovering his health. At once the doctor said: "Do you know why they denied it to you? They know your intemperance, and that you do not follow what they prescribe. If you promise me for certain that you will obey my instructions, I will cure you." The countryman promised. The doctor answered: "Abstain from drink for at least ten days, and you will be better. You will not die of thirst." The countryman went away and obeyed. When eight days had passed, he came back to the apothecary's shop looking well, told the doctor who he was, and asked what else he should do, and whether he ought to abstain from drink even longer, since he had now grown so used to it that he could easily bear thirst. The doctor told him not to drink much, but to have a tankard (cantharus) each day. So much does habit count for.

units.la: Simile.
units.tr: A parallel case.

units.la: Ioachimus Kirsser, medicinæ Doctor & Physicus principis Ernesti Marchionis Badensis, simili ratione ignoranter rusticum hydropicum curauit. Rusticus conueniens medicum, petiit sibi dari consilium, quod in hydropisi sequi posset. Cui Medicus iocosè his uerbis respondit: Si in semestri spacio à potu abstineres, facile curareris. Rusticus existimans hæc à Doctore seriò dicta dicta esse, abstinet per plurimas septimanas à potu, ac indies meliorem sanitatem recuperat. Elapso quadrante anni spacio, rursus alloquitur medicum rusticus, ac totum ipsi negocium exponit. Medicus facti illius iterum recordari incipit: & ulterius rustico nihil aliud consulit, nisi ut liquidiorib. cibis, veluti iusculis & aliis eiusmodi utatur. sic ille quoq; rusticus omnino pristinæ sanitati restitutus est.
units.tr: Joachim Kirsser, doctor of medicine and physician to Prince Ernst, Margrave of Baden, in a similar way unknowingly cured a country fellow with dropsy. The countryman, meeting the doctor, asked for advice that he could follow in dropsy. The doctor answered him jokingly in these words: "If you were to abstain from drink for half a year, you would be easily cured." The countryman, thinking that the doctor had said this in earnest, abstained from drink for many weeks and recovered his health day by day. When a quarter of a year had passed, the countryman again spoke to the doctor and laid the whole matter before him. The doctor began to recall the joke he had made, and advised the countryman nothing further except to use thinner foods, such as broths and other things of that kind. So that countryman too was restored to his former health entirely.

units.la: Apostematis curatio.
units.tr: Cure of an abscess.

units.la: Rex Galliæ habuit apostema in loco egestionis, quod fuit curatu difficile: tandem vero curatus est chirurgi adustione. In quo morbo tantum fuit periculi, ut Rex post curationem mille coronatos primùm chirurgo donauerit: & quotannis ducentos sit largitus.
units.tr: The King of France had an abscess in the place of evacuation, which was difficult to cure; in the end, however, he was cured by cauterization by a surgeon. The danger in this illness was so great that after the cure the King first gave the surgeon a thousand crowns, and then made him a gift of two hundred every year.

units.la: Febris curatio.
units.tr: Cure of a fever.

units.la: Noui quendam cancellarium episcopi Saltzburgensis, qui fuit meus coterraneus. Ille Romæ incidit in febrim: & cum non posset ferre sitim (ut homo Germanus) dixit ad Doctores: Date mihi ad bibendum, ego malo mori, quàm ita sitire. Illi re deliberata, berata, expresserunt succum ex malis Gra-natis, qui est subacidus: & remedium est in febri, quia suauiter refrigerat. Et sic porrexerunt illi calicem illo succo plenum. Ille statim auidè exhausit, dicens: Bene fecistis, quòd me ita recreastis hoc potu. Ibi unus ex eis explorans pulsum arteriæ, sensit pulsum melius se habere. Deinde ipse petiit adhuc unum calicem. Illi porrexerunt ei, & simul explorant arteriam, sentientes iam mitigari morbum. Porrigunt igitur & tertium calicem, dicuntq; se sperare meliora. Ita in uita hic seruatus, multos annos in posterum uixit.
units.tr: I knew a certain chancellor of the bishop of Salzburg, who was my fellow countryman. He fell ill of a fever at Rome, and since he could not bear thirst (as a German man), he said to the doctors: "Give me something to drink; I would rather die than suffer such thirst." The doctors, after deliberating, squeezed out the juice of pomegranates, which is slightly sour, and is a remedy in fever because it cools pleasantly. They then handed him a cup full of that juice. He drank it off eagerly at once, saying: "You did well to refresh me so with this drink." One of them, feeling the pulse of his artery, found that the pulse was better. Then he asked for another cup. They handed it to him, and at the same time felt his artery, noticing that the illness was now abating. So they gave him a third cup as well, saying they hoped for better things. Thus preserved in life, he lived on for many years.

units.la: Tristitia & mœrore animi extincti.
units.tr: Sadness and grief extinguish the spirit.

units.la: Doctor Aurbachius Lipsiæ quadraginta annos practicam exercuit. is sæpe dicebat: Ego quadraginta annos ægrotos uisita ui: reipsa autem comperi plures homines mœsticia & dolore animi mori, quàm uiolenta morte.
units.tr: Doctor Aurbach of Leipzig practised medicine for forty years. He often used to say: "I have visited sick people for forty years, and in fact I have found that more people die of sadness and grief of mind than of violent death."

units.la: Audiui de quodam magni nominis Principe, cui mortuo cor est exectum, & inuentum in modum tosti pyri, wie ein dürre dürre bieren. Ita emarcuit uis eiusdem cordis, præ nimia mœsticia, & magno animi dolore, qualescunq; illi fuerunt.
units.tr: I heard of a certain prince of great name, whose heart was cut out after his death and was found shaped like a roasted pear, wie ein dürre dürre bieren (like a dry pear). So the strength of that same heart withered away, because of excessive sadness and great grief of mind, whatever those were.

units.la: Est narratio de alio præstanti principe, qui magnas res adhuc nostro tempore gessit: illum etiam in senecta morTuum esse dicitur, præ nimia tristitia, p ropterea quod putauerat, fratrem suum minorem, in quem multiplicia beneficia contulerat, ipsum e regno expulsurum esse.
units.tr: There is an account of another outstanding prince, who in our own time has accomplished great things. He is also said to have died in old age from excessive sadness, because he had thought that his younger brother, on whom he had heaped many benefits, would drive him out of the kingdom.

units.la: Boni uini notæ.
units.tr: Marks of good wine.

units.la: Bonum uinum est, quod primò bene sapit, secundò melius, tertio adhuc melius- das eine am ersten wol schmeckt/ vnd zum anderen mall besser / zum dritten mall noch besser.
units.tr: Good wine is that which tastes good at first, better the second time, and still better the third time (das eine am ersten wol schmeckt/ vnd zum anderen mall besser / zum dritten mall noch besser: one tastes well at first, and the second time better, the third time better still).

units.la: Ratio est, quia sitis primum impedit iudicium: postquam uero defecit sitis, lingua acutius iudicat: quod si quis nimium biberit, tunc omne perit iudicium.
units.tr: The reason is that thirst at first hinders judgement; but once thirst has been satisfied, the tongue judges more keenly. If anyone drinks too much, then all judgement is lost.

units.la: Vina optima unde cognoscenda.
units.tr: How the best wines are to be recognised.

units.la: Vinum quo est plenius, eo est halituosius, & Rhenana uina omnium maximè sunt tolerabilia, & magis aeria quàm Austriaca. Austriaca. Ideo noster Cæsar Carolus V. plerunq; bibit Rhenana uina: quia minus offendunt caput, & alia membra. Ad Rhenum non sunt tam multi podagrici homines, sicut in Franconia, ubi multum bibunt uini, ex quo terrestri uino homines plerunq; podagrici fiunt.
units.tr: The fuller the wine, the more it has body and aroma. Rhenish wines are the most tolerable of all and lighter than Austrian ones. Therefore our Emperor Charles V mostly drank Rhenish wines, because they affect the head and the other limbs less. Along the Rhine there are not as many gouty people as in Franconia, where people drink a lot of wine, and from this earthy wine they often become gouty.

units.la: Varíj sales.
units.tr: Various witticisms.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quum Callimachus, præceptor Sigismundi Regis Poloniæ, & scriptor historiæ de clade Varnensi, ægrotaret morbo periculoso, ita ut nulla spes vitæ superesset, omnes serui & ancillæ, secum quæcunq; potue-runt, clam asportarunt. Id cum uidisset si-mia, puluinar domini sub capite stratum arripuit, illudq; sub pedibus occultauit, & ad domunculã properare cœpit, inq; eam introducere ui puluinar conata est. Hoc spe-ctaculo Callimachus ita exhilaratus est, ut rursus conualesceret.
units.tr: When Callimachus, tutor of Sigismund, King of Poland, and writer of the history of the disaster at Varna, lay ill with a dangerous disease, so that no hope of life remained, all his male and female servants secretly carried off whatever they could. When a monkey saw this, it snatched the master's cushion laid under his head and hid it beneath its feet, and it began to hurry toward the little house and tried to force the cushion inside. At this sight Callimachus was so cheered that he recovered his health.

units.la: Anno1548. cum Imperator Carolus V. laboraret suo usitato morbo articulari, cre-scentibus doloribus, accessit ad eum EleËtor Marchio Ioachimus, & adhortatur ut ipse adhibeat remedia, & medicos, qui suæ Cesareæ Maiestati optimè consulerent, cum tales habere posset. Ibi Imperator respondit: O`, patientia est optimum remedium, & in magnis doloribus aliquantulum uociferari: gedult / vnd ein wenig schreien.
