units.tr: In the year 1548, when the Emperor Charles V was suffering from his usual joint disease, and the pains were increasing, the Elector Margrave Joachim came to him and urged him to use remedies and physicians, who might look after His Imperial Majesty well, since he could have such men. There the Emperor replied: "Patience is the best remedy, and to cry out a little in great pains": patience, and a little shouting.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Quidam bellator fortis & strenuus, tempore ducis Friderici, Vuitenbergæ ægrotabat, & mei præceptoris doctoris Medicinæ opera utebatur. Ad quem cum uenissemus, surrexit, & induit thoracem cum lorica & gladio. Quæsiuimus ex eo, quid his sibi uellet? Respondit, se iter suscepisse in ueterem Marchiam: at reuocatum esse ex itinere, eo quòd audiuisset Turcas aduentare, quibus se obuiam iturum affirmabat. sed paulò post moriebatur. Hæc à quodam Doctore recitari audiuimus.
units.tr: A certain brave and vigorous soldier, in the time of Duke Frederick, was sick at Wittenberg and was being treated by the medical care of my teacher, a doctor of medicine. When we came to him, he got up and put on a breastplate with a cuirass and a sword. We asked him what he meant by this. He replied that he had set out on a journey into the Old March, but had been called back from the road because he had heard that the Turks were coming, and he declared that he would go to meet them. But a little later he died. We heard this related by a certain doctor.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Ante 35 annos fuit Vuitenbergæ operarius peste laborans, qui sic erat consopitus, tus, ut mortuus esse existimaretur. Venit uero pollinctor, afferens pheretrum. itaq; tumultuatur (sicut est illud genus hominum clamosum, moræq; etiam impatiens) iacens in deliquio animæ excitatur: ibiq; uidet ac audit clamorem eorum qui circa pheretrum erant, ac territus aufugit. Pollinctor insequens illũ, reuocat: sed quo magis clamat, eo celerius ipse currit: donec in suburbio exceptus, ac stragula tectus, multum sudaret. sicq; euasit.
units.tr: About 35 years ago there was a workman at Wittenberg suffering from plague, who had sunk into such a stupor that he was thought to be dead. But the undertaker came, bringing a bier. So the man, stirred up (as that noisy sort of people is, and impatient of delay), lying in a swoon, was roused; and there he saw and heard the clamour of those who were around the bier, and in fright he fled. The undertaker, pursuing him, called him back; but the louder he shouted, the faster he ran himself, until he was caught in a suburb and wrapped in blankets, and he sweated greatly. And so he escaped.

units.la: De somno & quiete.
units.tr: On sleep and rest.

units.la: Noui iuuenem Magistrum, pulchro corpore, Tubingæ, egressum ex balneis, ac post cœnam mecum & aliys quibusdam bonis adolescentibus extra portam expaciatum: & hastam aliys duobus tenentibus transiliisse adeò, ut uena pulmonis ipsi rumperetur. Ex qua ruptura & fluxione sanguinis intra triduum est mortuus. Idq; ideo dico, ut adolescentes suis iuuenilibus & tenerrimis corporibus parcant, & corporum fragilitatem agnoscant, debitamq; quietem eis tribuant. Sex horæ tantū rebus tribuantur agendis: Viuere post illas litera Zita monet.
units.tr: I knew a young Master of fine physique at Tübingen, who came out of the baths and, after supper, walked outside the gate with me and some other good young men; and while two others held a spear, he jumped over it so that a vein of his lung burst. From this rupture and loss of blood he died within three days. I say this so that young men will spare their youthful and very tender bodies, recognise the frailty of their bodies, and grant them due rest. Let only six hours be given to work. To live after those hours, the letter Z advises.

units.la: Matutinum tempus est ualde idoneum ad res agendas illis, qui ordine uiuunt. Quando in priore uersiculo dicitur, Sex horæ tantum rebus tribuantur agendis: loquitur de horis inæqualibus, quæ in æstate sunt longiores quàm in hyeme. Primam uerò horam ab aurora seu oriente sole inchoauerunt. Quemlibet enim diem, siue æstiuum siue hyemalem, in duodecim horas distribuerunt. inde euenit, quòd æstiuo tempore, siue circa horam secundam aut tertiam, comederint. Sumpto cibo, reliquum tempus, quod superfuerat, tribuerunt deambulationibus, ac alijs iucundis colloquijs. Postea cubitum se contulerunt. Literæ apud Græcos denotant numeros, & Z septenarium designat. Quare ueteres his uersiculis significarunt, peractis uocationis laboribus, liberius uiuendum esse, & aliquid temporis corpori & ualetudini reficiendæ tribuendum. Est
units.tr: The morning hour is very suitable for doing business for those who live by a schedule. When in the earlier verse it says, "Let only six hours be given to work," it speaks of unequal hours, which in summer are longer than in winter. They began the first hour from dawn or sunrise. For they divided every day, summer or winter, into twelve hours. Hence it happens that in summer they ate about the second or third hour. After taking food, they gave the remaining time that was left to walks and other pleasant conversations. Afterwards they went to bed. Among the Greeks, letters denote numbers, and Z stands for seven. Therefore the ancients indicated by these verses that, once the labours of their calling were finished, one should live more freely and give some time to the body and to restoring health. It is

units.la: Est res omnium perniciosissima, omnis lucubratio, etiam sobria: eoq; magis ingurgitantium sese, & potiones infundentium. Quare fugite omnes lucubrationes uespertinas, etiam studiorum. sunt enim (ut sæpe dixi, & dico) lucubrationes corporibus perniciosissimæ. Natura est composita principio noctis ad quietem, eamq; appetit, quæ ipsi est concedenda. Non concedens naturæ debitam quietem, fit homicida sui corporis. Mane autem, sole oriente, cum reliquis diurnis sideribus nostra corpora rursus concipiunt spiritus & calorem uiuifi-cum: quo etiam tempore omnia membra sunt magis idonea ad omnes labores sustinendos. Ego multos periculosos morbos & miserias huius corpusculi mei uito, hac unica ratione, quòd semper utor illa diligentia citò eundi cubitum. Experiemini hanc rationem, & fatebimini, uobis esse salutiberrimam.
units.tr: It is the most ruinous thing of all, every night-work, even sober; the more so for those who gorge themselves and pour in drinks. Therefore flee all evening work, even study. For night-work is (as I have often said and say) most harmful to the body. Nature is made for rest at the beginning of the night, and seeks it; this rest must be granted to it. One who does not grant nature its due rest becomes a murderer of his own body. But in the morning, when the sun rises, our bodies, together with the other daytime stars, again take in spirits and life-giving warmth; and at this time all the limbs are better fitted to endure all labours. I have avoided many dangerous diseases and miseries of this little body of mine by this one rule, that I always use that diligence of going to bed early. Try this rule, and you will confess that it is most healthful for you.

units.la: Quando mundus claudit suum oculum (quod fit sole occidente) tunc etiam nos debemus nostros oculos claudere, seu dormire: rursus aperiente se mundi oculo, nostros stros etiam oculos aperiamus: id est, mane surgamus. Illud vero est naturæ conue-nientissimum.
units.tr: When the world closes its eye (which happens when the sun sets), then we too ought to close our eyes, or sleep; and again, when the eye of the world opens, let us open our eyes too, that is, let us rise in the morning. That indeed is most in agreement with nature.

units.la: DE SOMNIIS. DVAE QVAESTIONES de somniis D. Martini Lutheri, ad quas adiectæ sunt responsiones D. Philippi Melanthonis.
units.tr: ON DREAMS. TWO QUESTIONS concerning dreams by Dr Martin Luther, to which the answers of Dr Philip Melanchthon are added.

units.la: Prima quæstio.
units.tr: First question.

units.la: Exitici 15 capite, Deus prohibet observare somnia, & iubet somniorum interpretes occidi. Quomodo igitur somnia observari possunt?
units.tr: In the fifteenth chapter of Exodus, God forbids the observing of dreams and commands that the interpreters of dreams be put to death. How, then, can dreams be observed?

units.la: Responsio D. Philippi.
units.tr: Answer of Dr Philip.

units.la: Duplicia sunt somnia. Primum est naturale, quod non tantum hominibus, sed etiam plerisq; animantibus convenit. Somniant & reliqua animantia, ut bos, equus: & hoc somnium est imperfectum, nec habet ullam certam demonstrationem, sed sunt confusissimæ apparitiones: quas etsi conjicere possumus, tamen pro veritate asseuerare non debemus: nec talia somnia curanda sunt. Quoniam si qui somniis decipiantur, & credant uera esse quae somniant, id eis plerunq; permittente Deo propter incredulitatem euenit, quod timuerunt. Somnia igitur naturalia possunt aliquo modo obseruari, si non addatur opinio aut euentus necessitatis, uel superstitionis. Secundum genus est diuinum, in quo nulla est confusio: imò in tali somnio est certissima demonstratio ac revelatio Dei, consentiens cum ipsius verbo, ex qua revelatione homo dicere potest quid futurum sit. Sed quia diabolus aliquando se transformat in Angelum lucis, ideo probandi sunt spiritus. Angelus enim bonus ex iussu Dei revelat bona, quae citra controversiam sunt vera, ut de iis dubitari non possit: Sathan vero sub praetextu boni parat malum. Igitur revelationes factae per Angelos malos sunt fictae, diuagantes sine certis demonstrationibus: quae Christiano refutandae sunt, tantum absit ut eis credat.
units.tr: Dreams are of two kinds. The first is natural, which belongs not only to human beings but also to most living creatures. Oxen and horses dream too. This kind of dream is imperfect and has no sure demonstration, but consists of very confused appearances. Although we may conjecture about them, we must not affirm them as true, and such dreams should not be heeded. For if some people are deceived by dreams and believe that what they dream is true, this often happens, by God's permission, on account of their unbelief, so that they come to suffer what they feared. Natural dreams can therefore in some way be observed, provided that no opinion of necessity or outcome, or superstition, is attached to them. The second kind is divine, in which there is no confusion; indeed, in such a dream there is most certain demonstration and revelation of God, agreeing with his word, and from this revelation a man can say what is going to happen. But because the devil sometimes transforms himself into an angel of light, spirits must be tested. For a good angel, by God's command, reveals good things, which are beyond controversy true, so that no doubt can be raised about them; Satan, however, under the pretext of good, prepares evil. Therefore revelations made through evil angels are feigned, wandering without sure demonstrations, and a Christian must refute them, far from believing them.

units.la: SECVNDA QVAESTIO. Quare Ioseph & Daniel iuxta mandatum Dei propter somnia non sunt occisi?
units.tr: Second question. Why were Joseph and Daniel not put to death on account of their dreams, according to God's command?

units.la: RESPONSIO D. PHILIPPI.
units.tr: Answer of Dr Philip.

units.la: Somniorum interpretes, scioli & exquisitores somniorum, occidebantur ex mandato Dei: quia contempto Deo, somnia tantum curabant, & illis plus fidei attribuebant quàm ipsi Deo: ad quos sciolos in omni angustia populus confugiebat. Propter illam impietatem maximam iussit Deus eos è medio tolli. Cæterùm Iosepho & Danieli non per incantationes somnia apparuerunt: sed certa demonstratione, & diuina ordinatione. Habuerunt enim spiritum, reuelantem ipsis somnia.
units.tr: The interpreters of dreams, the half-learned and the seekers after dreams, were put to death by God's command, because, despising God, they attended only to dreams and gave them more trust than they gave to God himself. To these half-learned men the people fled in every distress. On account of that great impiety God ordered them removed from the midst of the people. But Joseph and Daniel did not have their dreams through incantations; rather, the dreams appeared to them with certain demonstration and by divine ordination. For they had a spirit revealing dreams to them.

units.la: Somnia quæ fiunt circa auroram, uera esse creduntur. Cuius rei sanè Philosophicæ causæ reddi possunt. Alia ingenia sunt magis præsaga aliis: item quidam homines publica, quidam priuata facta præsagiunt.
units.tr: Dreams that occur about dawn are believed to be true. Philosophical causes for this can certainly be given. Some minds are more prophetic than others; likewise some men foretell public events, others private ones.

units.la: Nouimus quendam ministrum Ecclesiæ, Paulum Knot, qui forte in lectione Doctoris Martini Lutheri ob dormiuit, ibiq; somniauit. somniauit bellum inter duos principes esse ortum, ac in ipso aggressu unum ex illis duobus de equo tractum & interfectum esse. Accidit vero, ut post biennium duo praestantes principes bellum sibi invicem indicerent, ubi alter in ipso belli apparatu moriebatur. Etsi vero ille, cum ea somniaret, quidq; secuturum esset ignoraret: tamen euentus postea somno illius respondit.
units.tr: We know a certain minister of the Church, Paul Knot, who, perhaps while reading Doctor Martin Luther, fell asleep there and dreamed that a war had arisen between two princes, and that in the very onset one of those two had been dragged from his horse and killed. Indeed it happened that, two years later, two outstanding princes declared war on each other, and in the very preparation of the war one of them died. And although he, when he dreamed this, did not know what would follow, nevertheless the outcome afterwards corresponded to his dream.

units.la: Anno 1542, pridie eius diei quo filia Doctoris Martini Magdalena moreretur, uidit mater, doctoris Martini coniunx, in somnis duos adolescentes pulcherrime ornatos, ducturos filiam suam ad conuiuium nuptiale. Mane cum accederem matrem, interrogaturus de filiae suae ualetudine, narrauit mihi somnium quod habuerat praecedente nocte. Ego expauescens, nihil dicebam: sed hoc ipsum suspicabar, quod Angeli coelestes ducturi essent filiam ipsius ad coeleste conuiuium, sicut eo die accidit.
units.tr: In the year 1542, on the day before the day on which Doctor Martin's daughter Magdalena died, the mother, the wife of Doctor Martin, saw in a dream two very beautifully adorned young men who were going to lead her daughter to the wedding feast. In the morning, when I approached the mother, meaning to ask about her daughter's health, she told me the dream she had had the previous night. I, alarmed, said nothing, but suspected this very thing: that the heavenly angels were going to lead her daughter to the heavenly banquet, as indeed happened on that day.

units.la: Interrogaui honestum virum, Capitaneum in valle Ioachimica, cuius duo filij erant abducti a Turcis in bello, an etiam in somnis eos uideret? Respondit, se minorem saepe sæpè uidisse, maiorem nunquam. Dixi ei: Videbis illum adhuc uiuere. & paulò pòst ille est reuersus.
units.tr: I asked an honourable man, a captain in the Joachimsthal valley, whose two sons had been carried off by the Turks in war, whether he also saw them in dreams. He replied that he had often seen the younger, but never the elder. I said to him: You will see that one still alive. And shortly afterwards that one returned.

units.la: Coniunx ualde boni uiri, Domini magistri Andreæ pastoris Ihenensis, habuit somniū eo tempore, quo Imperator Carolus V. in suam potestatem Vuitenbergam redigebat. Vidit enim iridem supra hoc oppidum Vuitenbergam, et Christum astante & manu iridem tenentem. Hoc significauit procul dubio, quòd Deus voluerit nos castigare, qui tamen sua manu eam castigationem rexit. Quia magnum miraculum & Dei beneficium fuit, Imperatore usque adeò iritato, & iritatis suorum animis, ipsum, cum iam esset uictor, ita ex his regionibus discedere. Ita Deus in medijs periculis pro sua clementia adest, ac euentus nobis tolerabiles largitur.
units.tr: The wife of a very good man, Master Andreas, minister at Ihenen, had a dream at the time when the Emperor Charles V was bringing Wittenberg under his power. For she saw a rainbow above this town of Wittenberg, and Christ standing beside it and holding the rainbow in his hand. This undoubtedly signified that God wished to chastise us, yet with his own hand he directed that chastisement. It was a great miracle and benefit of God that the Emperor, although already victorious, departed from these regions in such a way, when he had been so enraged and his followers' spirits had been roused. Thus God, in the midst of dangers, in his clemency is present and grants us bearable outcomes.

units.la: Cum mortuus esset Can cellarius ducis Saxoniæ Electoris, pater Christiani Beirs, delatum est illud munus Cancellarij ad virum clarissimum Doctorem Pleicard. Is, ut erat prudens, cùm diu secum deliberaret, recipere ne an recusare tantum onus uellet, nellet; tandem somniauit, se sedere in quodam aulæ conclaui, & plurimos serpentes dextrum suum pedem inuadere. Excitatus igitur à somno, denegauit aulicis suam operam, in isto munere obeundo.
units.tr: When the chancellor of the Elector Duke of Saxony, father of Christian Beier, had died, that office of chancellor was offered to the most distinguished Doctor Pleicard. He, being prudent, when he had long deliberated with himself whether he wished to accept or refuse so great a burden, dreamed nevertheless, as he sat in a certain room of the court, that very many serpents attacked his right foot. Roused therefore from sleep, he refused to the courtiers his services in discharging that office.

units.la: Laboraui ante annos aliquot fluxu satis periculoso in dextro oculo, ac usus sum multiplicibus medicamentis: & tamen nihil me proficere sensi. Somniabã uerò, me consulere Doctorem Philonem Medicum, qui iubebat me uti euphrasia: qua usus, statim intra biduum sum curatus.
units.tr: Some years ago I suffered in my right eye from a rather dangerous discharge, and I used many remedies; yet I felt that I gained nothing from them. But I dreamed that I consulted Doctor Philo, a physician, who bade me use eyebright (euphrasia). When I used it, within two days I was at once cured.

units.la: Cum essemus in conuentu quodam, & nobiscum unà reuerendus uir doctor Ionas, ibi accepi literas, quibus mihi significabatur, Doctoris Ionæ filiam grandiorem natu esse mortuam. simulq; uetabatur ne citò illi hoc indicarem, ne territus in morbum aliquem incideret. Ego itaq; , cum post prandium ad mensam sederemus læti, interrogaui: Domine Doctor, quale hodie habuisti somnium? Ille respondit: Dicam tibi liberè. Visus sum mihi domum redire ad meos liberos, ibiq; ab omnibus porrecta manu salutari, præterquam à filia maxima natu, quam deinde circumspicies nusquam comperi. Ad haec ego respondi: Verum est, D. Doctor, somnium tuum: maior filia tua non nisi in futura vita te excipiet, quia mortua est. Quo audito, intrauit cubiculum, & satis lachrimarum effundebat. Postea rediens dixit: Domine Philippe, habeo tibi gratias pro consolatione. ac deinceps animo hilariori erat praeditus.
units.tr: When we were at a certain gathering, and with us the reverend man Doctor Jonas, I received a letter in which I was informed that Doctor Jonas's elder daughter had died; and at the same time I was forbidden to tell him this quickly, lest, frightened, he fall into some illness. So I, when we were sitting happily at table after dinner, asked: "Lord Doctor, what dream did you have today?" He replied: "I will tell you freely. It seemed to me that I returned home to my children, and there I was greeted by all with an outstretched hand, except by my eldest daughter, whom afterwards, though I looked around, I nowhere found." To this I replied: "True is your dream, Doctor; your eldest daughter will receive you only in the future life, because she has died." When he heard this, he went into his room and shed many tears. Afterwards, coming back, he said: "Lord Philip, I thank you for the consolation." And thereafter he was endowed with a more cheerful spirit.

units.la: Dormienti cuidam duo nobiles in somno apparuerunt, quos uiuos agnouit, cum iampridem essent mortui. Illi eum excitabant, ac promittebant nullum periculum ipsi fore si surgeret. Quo facto, iussus est scribere literas, ex eorum ore dictatas. Deinde mandauerunt ut potenti cuidam offerret, & ita euanuerunt: quas postea potenti illi obtulit.
units.tr: To a certain man sleeping, two noblemen appeared in a dream, whom he recognised as alive, although they had long been dead. They roused him and promised that no danger would befall him if he rose. Having done so, he was ordered to write letters, dictated from their mouths. Then they commanded him to offer them to a certain powerful man, and so they vanished; these letters he afterwards offered to that powerful man.

units.la: Narratur historia de Aspasia, quod laborauerit scabie in facie, cum tamen fuerit eo tempore omnium uirginum pulcherrima: quam scabiem in facie nullus medicorum curare potuit. Tandem ipsa somniat, se debere sumere rosas ex Veneris capite, easq; aqua conspersas suae maculae imponere. Id cum fecisset, rursus convaluit.
units.tr: The story is told of Aspasia that she suffered from a scab on her face, although at that time she was the most beautiful of all maidens; no physician could cure that scab on her face. At last she dreamed that she ought to take roses from the head of Venus, sprinkle them with water, and place them on her blemish. When she had done this, she recovered again.

units.la: Alexandro in somnis apparuit species põ tificis Iudaici, hortatis eum, ut susciperet expeditione contra Asiam. Fuit angelus quispiam, qui fuit ei excitator ut id faceret: Cum venit Hierosolymam, desiliit de equo, & praestitit reverentiam summo sacerdoti euntí sibi obuiam. Omnes duces mirabantur, quare hoc faceret: Ista species, inquit, quam nunc uideo, apparuit mihi in somnis, & me adhuc in patria morantem ad has expeditiones uocauit, dicens, se mihi fore uictorem.
units.tr: To Alexander in a dream there appeared the form of the Jewish high priest, urging him to undertake the expedition against Asia. There was some angel who roused him to do this. When he came to Jerusalem, he leapt down from his horse and paid reverence to the high priest coming to meet him. All the commanders wondered why he did this. "That figure," he said, "which I now see, appeared to me in a dream, and while I was still staying in my homeland called me to these expeditions, saying that it would be I who was victorious."

units.la: Commemorat Ioannes Keisersberg, Theologus quondam Argentinensis, de quadam uenefica, quae concionatorem, tales ludos Diaboli reprehendere, & somnia dicere solitum, domum suam duxerat, probatura ei non esse somnia. Eam igitur, cum lintre pistorio se collocasset, obdormiisse: ac deinceps gesticulatam manibus, capite & toto corpore, tanquam uolaret & saltaret: quoad tandem lintre euersa, caderet in pauimentum, ac non sine uulnere excitatam, narrasse mirabilia quae uidisset, & gessisset interea: sed conuictam esse tandem nul-nere, quòd semper fuisset præsens.
units.tr: John Keisersberg, once a theologian at Strasbourg, tells of a certain witch who used to rebuke the preacher for such devilish games and for talking about dreams. She took him to her house, intending to prove to him that dreams were nothing. So she lay down in a kneading trough and fell asleep; then she began to gesticulate with her hands, head and whole body, as if she were flying and dancing, until at last the trough was overturned and she fell onto the floor. Roused, not without an injury, she told of the wonderful things she had seen and done meanwhile; but when she was finally convicted, she confessed that she had never been absent at all.

units.la: Eiusdem farinæ sunt, qui in locis septe-trionalibus sunt frequentes, qui uidetur sibi in lupos mutari, ac dilaniare passim pecora, duci à suo quodam principe ad horrea, ablatum inde frumentum: sed illusi, nihil reportant. Confessus cuidam fide digno uiro, Rigæ in Liuonia, Lycanthropus est, se clauso carcere, in quo coërcebatur, ipso die Paschatis esse profectum ad suos, uxorem & liberos uisendi causa, per multa milliaria. Quærenti, Quomodo euasisti è carcere? respondebat: Facile. Sed magna flumina erant tibi traijcienda. At ille: Transuolaui flumina. Quid dicebas tu-is? Quid dicerem? circumibam protento rostro, ut lupus, olfactu uisuq; explorans quid rerum gererent. Quare reuersus es in carcerem, semel elapsus? Tum ille: Redire necesse erat. Quis non intelligit hæc esse ludibria & somnia diabolica, quibus Satan illum uirum excæcauit?
units.tr: Of the same kind are those who are numerous in the northern regions, who imagine that they are changed into wolves and tear apart herds everywhere, that they are led by their prince to granaries and bring back grain from there; but when they are mocked, they gain nothing. A werewolf confessed to a man worthy of belief, at Riga in Livonia, that when he was shut up in the prison where he was confined, on the very day of Easter he had gone off to his own people, to see his wife and children, across many miles. Asked how he had escaped from the prison, he answered: "Easily." "But great rivers had to be crossed by you." "I flew over the rivers." "What did you say to them?" "What could I say? I went about with my snout thrust out, like a wolf, sniffing out with smell and sight what they were doing." "Why did you return to the prison, once you had escaped?" Then he said: "I had to go back." Who does not see that these are the mockeries and diabolical dreams by which Satan blinded that man?

units.la: Alexander obsedit Tyrum sex mensibus, & magnis adhibitis machinis, tandem ex pugnauit eam. Semel sopitus interdiu, habuit somnium, in quo uidit Satyrum ante se ludentem: quem cum uellet prehendere, diu non potuit: sed tandem tamen prehendit. Aristander uero eius uates, ab ipso interrogatus quid esset? dixit ridens, Sa Tyrus: id est, tua est Tyrus.
units.tr: Alexander besieged Tyre for six months, and after bringing up great engines, at last took it by storm. Once, overcome by sleep during the day, he had a dream in which he saw a satyr playing before him; when he wanted to seize it, he could not for a long time, but at last he did seize it. His seer Aristander, when asked by him what this meant, said with a laugh, "Sa Tyrus," that is, "Tyre is yours."

units.la: DE SOBRIETATE.
units.tr: DE SOBRIETATE (ON SOBRIETY).

units.la: Augustinus in libro Confessionum scribit de sua matre, hanc in prima aetate mira diligentia ad sobrietatem à nutrice assuefactam esse. Neq; enim licuit ei vinum aut aquam, nisi in iusta cæna aut prandio, bibere. Nutrix interrogata, quo consilio etiam puellis aquæ potu interdiceret? respondit: Nisi ea ætate sitim perferre discant, postea matronas factas, cum copia vini fit, simili intemperantia vino se ingurgitare, qua nunc aquam bibunt. τὰμεσον γὰρ ἐστὶν ἀρετῆς σωφροσύνη βροτοῖς: Id est, Virtutis enim est humanæ sobrietas penus.
units.tr: Augustine, in the book of his Confessions, writes about his mother, that in early childhood she was trained to sobriety by her nurse with remarkable care. She was not allowed to drink wine or water except at a proper supper or lunch. When the nurse was asked with what purpose she also forbade the girls water to drink, she replied: "Unless they learn to endure thirst at that age, once they have become matrons and wine is plentiful, they will gorge themselves on wine with the same intemperance with which they now drink water." [τὰμεσον γὰρ ἐστὶν ἀρετῆς σωφροσύνη βροτοῖς] That is: for sobriety is the mean of human virtue.

units.la: Xenophon scribit, Socratem intemperantes in cibo & potu monuisse, ut cauerent ne uescerentur iis dapibus, neue potu eo uterentur, unde lenocinijs dulcedinis pronocatiu, provocatis, appetentia edendi bibendiq; crescere posset. ὡς ἥδύ τὸ μέτριον, ἡδὲ ὑπερβαλνον: id est, Quàm suave est omne moderatum, & non superfluum seu superabundans.
units.tr: Xenophon writes that Socrates warned the intemperate about food and drink, that they should take care not to eat those dainties or drink that kind of drink, by whose seductive sweetness appetite for eating and drinking, once stirred up, could grow. [ὡς ἥδύ τὸ μέτριον, ἡδὲ ὑπερβαλνον] That is: how pleasant is what is moderate, and not what is excessive or superabundant.

units.la: Attendite, inquit Christus, ne graventur corda vestra crapula & ebrietate, et curis huius vitæ. Significat, hoc postremo tempore futurā barbariem multo maiorem, quàm antea fuit, etiam nostra memoria. Sæpe cogito, quomodo vixerit illa familia Heydelbergæ, ubi etiam comites & nobiles unà cibum capiebant. putabatur tunc esse lautissima mensa, in qua ego etiam eram: sed tamen erat maior frugalitas, quàm nunc est. Memini Capnionem, divitem virum, non pluribus quàm duobus ferculis in prandio uti: vesperi verò, unico erat contentus. Solebam illi adducere scholasticos, meos commilitones: quia delectabatur iuuenum consuetudine. Doctiores mecum ibant propter bibliothecam: habebamus enim pulcherrimam bibliothecam, ubi videbamus veterum monumenta. Visa ad libitum bibliotheca, postea hortum accedentes, dentes, lusu aliquo nos recreabamus. Sic igitur semper ipse erat contentus duobus ferculis, aut ad summum tribus in prandio: & uesperi unico. Ipse bibebat loram: nobis non permittebat bibere eam, sed dabat nobis unum.
units.tr: "Take heed," said Christ, "lest your hearts be weighed down with carousing and drunkenness and the cares of this life." This signifies that in these last times a barbarism will come far greater than before, even within our memory. I often think about how that household at Heidelberg lived, where counts and nobles also took their meals together. At that time the table was thought to be most sumptuous, and I myself was there; yet there was still more frugality than there is now. I remember that Capnion, a wealthy man, used no more than two courses at lunch, and in the evening he was content with a single dish. I used to bring him scholars, my fellow soldiers, because he took pleasure in the company of young men. The more learned came with me on account of the library, for we had a most splendid library where we saw the monuments of the ancients. After we had viewed the library as long as we liked, we would go on to the garden, and there we refreshed ourselves with some game. So he himself was always content with two dishes, or at most three at lunch, and with one in the evening. He himself drank thin wine, but he did not allow us to drink it; he gave us one (cup).

units.la: Nos adolescentuli omnes eramus contenti tota septimana duobus cantharis uini, ita ut quisq; in prandio haberet octauam partem mensuræ, tantundem in cœna. Sic ego uixi, & multi alij: & tamen fortasis non minus pulchri sumus, quàm illi qui totum cantharum uno haustu ingurgitant. Si essem in illis locis, adhuc ita uiuerem.
units.tr: All of us young men were content for a whole week with two tankards of wine, so that each had an eighth part of a measure at lunch and the same at supper. I lived like this, and many others did too; and yet perhaps we were no less handsome than those who gulp down a whole tankard in one draught. If I were in those places, I would still live this way.

units.la: Post pugnam Ducis Saxoniæ Electoris Ioannis Friderici, factam ad Mulberg, in qua multi nobiles sunt capti, dixit mihi quidam, qui tres dies ieiunauerat, quibus nihil comederat neq; biberat, se tunc tam bene dispositum fuisse, quàm nunquam antea fuerat in tota sua uita: quia nunquam fuerat sobrius per multos annos. Corpus uerò alioqui non ægrotum, multo melius facit omnia officia, & multo rectius etiam dormit, quando non adest cruditas: ut nout nobis omnibus satis bene constat.
units.tr: After the battle fought at Mühlberg by the Duke of Saxony, Elector John Frederick, in which many nobles were taken, a certain man who had fasted for three days, during which he had eaten and drunk nothing, told me that he was then in as good a condition as he had never been before in his whole life, because he had not been sober for many years. A body that is otherwise not sick, however, performs all its functions much better and also sleeps much more soundly when there is no indigestion, as we all know well enough.

units.la: Spartæ fuit consuetudo, ut fungentes officio magistratus, per id tempus a vino abstinerent. Existimo etiam in de uenire illud, quòd Turcici Imperatores non bibunt uinum.
units.tr: It was the custom at Sparta that those holding the office of magistrate abstained from wine during that time. I think this also applies to the fact that the Turkish emperors do not drink wine.

units.la: DE INTEMPERANTIA & ebrietate.
units.tr: DE INTEMPERANTIA & ebrietate (ON INTEMPERANCE AND DRUNKENNESS).

units.la: Plato in epistola quadam ad Dionis propinquos, de sua in Siciliam peregrinatione sic scribit: Vita illa beata, quæ fereba tur plena Italicarum Syracusanarumque mensarum, nullo modo mihi placuit, bis in die saturum fieri, neq; unquam pernoctare solum: cæteraq;, quæ comitantur hanc vitam, in qua sapiens nemo efficitur unquam, moderatus verò multo minus.
units.tr: Plato, in a certain letter to the relatives of Dion, writes thus about his journey to Sicily: "That blessed life, which was said to be full of Italian and Syracusan tables, never pleased me: to be stuffed twice a day, and never to spend the night alone; and the other things that go with this life, in which no one ever becomes wise, and still less does anyone become moderate."

units.la: Pittacus Mitylenæus tulit legem, ut si quis per temulentiam aliquid sceleris commisisset, duplo graviore pœna plecteretur: quòd causa ipsa, quæ eum ad peccatum impulisset, gravius etiam peccatum esset.
units.tr: Pittacus of Mytilene passed a law that if anyone committed some crime through drunkenness, he should be punished with a penalty twice as severe, because the very cause that had driven him to sin was a more serious sin.

units.la: In conuentu Ratisbonensi, cum vinum valde bonum cresceret, & multi Germani ex longioribus compotationibus eo anno morerentur, ueniebant quidam ad Imperatorem Carolum V. petentes ut legem sanciret contra compotatores. Respondit Caesar: Quid faciam? Tantum efficiam apud Germanos, prohibendo ebrietatem, quantum si Hispanis prohiberem furta.
units.tr: At the Diet of Regensburg, when wine was growing very good and many Germans were dying that year from long drinking bouts, some men came to the Emperor Charles V, asking him to enact a law against heavy drinkers. Caesar replied: "What can I do? I would achieve as much among the Germans by forbidding drunkenness as I would among the Spaniards by forbidding theft."

units.la: Venerant huc ex Torga duo principes laudatissimi, Dux Ernestus Luneburgensis, & Henricus Megalopolensis. Ernestus dicebat: Domine Doctor, volumus omnes esse Christiani, sed non possumus deponere illud vitium potationis. Doctor Martinus respondit: <bl>Darzu solten die herren thun.</bl> Voluit dicere, Principes deberent curare, ut tolleretur istud vitium. Assidens ei dux Henricus, inquit: Hoc facimus Domine Doctor, <bl>denn wenn wir herre nicht darzu thetten / so wer es lengest abgangen.</bl>
units.tr: Two most praiseworthy princes had come here from Torgau: Duke Ernest of Lüneburg and Henry of Mecklenburg. Ernest said: "Lord Doctor, we all want to be Christians, but we cannot put away the vice of drinking." Doctor Martin replied: "The lords ought to do something about that." He meant that the princes ought to take care that this vice was removed. Duke Henry, sitting beside him, said: "That is what we are doing, Lord Doctor, for if we lords did not do something about it, it would have died out long ago."

units.la: Gregorij Nazianzeni contra ebrietatem uersus, quem omnes Iuuenes scire debent.
units.tr: Gregory Nazianzen's verses against drunkenness, which all young people ought to know.

units.la: Οἶνος παςθενικῶνδ᾽ χόλε πλέον ὅςιρ ὀνδρὸς, non recte exponitur sic: Ebrietas est magis dedecus quam ira. non enim est comparatio paratio ebrietatis& iræ. Sed dicitur de iræ alterius, ut sententia sit: Maius dedecus est, quàm cui aliÿ satis irasci possint. Iuuenalis inquit: Quid enim Venus ebria curat?
units.tr: The line "Wine is a greater disgrace to maidens than anger is to a man" [Οἶνος παρθενικῶν δὲ χόλου πλέον ὅστις ἀνδρός] is not rightly explained as "Drunkenness is more of a disgrace than anger." It is not a comparison between drunkenness and anger. Rather, it is said of the anger of another person, so that the sense is: it is a greater disgrace than any that others could be angry enough about. Juvenal says: "For what does drunken Venus care?"

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Species ebrietatis.
units.tr: Kinds of drunkenness.

units.la: Bis sex, credatis, sunt species ebrietatis: In multis primus sapiens est, alter opimus. Ternus grande uorat, quartus sua crimina plorat. Quintus luxuriat, sextus per numina iurat. Septimus contendit, octauus singula uendit. Nonus nil celat, quod habet sub corde reuelat. Somnum denus amat, uomitumq; facit duodenus.
units.tr: Twice six, believe me, are the kinds of drunkenness: among many, the first is wise, the second is fat. The third devours a great deal, the fourth weeps over his sins. The fifth indulges in lust, the sixth swears by the divine powers. The seventh picks quarrels, the eighth sells off everything. The ninth hides nothing and blurts out whatever is in his heart. The tenth loves sleep, and the twelfth vomits.

units.la: In Salinis Doctor quidam medicinæ minimè curabat temperatiam, quæ præcipua est medica uirtus: ipse (inquam) & alius quidam Iuris prudentiæ Doctor, unà forte ad compotandum sedebant. Cum autem diu potassent, sicut Doctor Iuris prudetiæ plurimum potare assueuerat (bona laus scilicet Doctoris) medicus procidit in mesam. Cum autem Iuris consultus putaret eum dormire, ideoq; excitare uellet: ibi primum animaduertit ipsum esse extinctum. Hæc sanè egregia sunt et doctoralia certamina:
units.tr: In Salinae there was a certain doctor of medicine who cared little for temperance, which is the chief virtue of a physician. I myself, I say, and another doctor of law happened to be sitting together at a drinking bout. When they had drunk for a long time, the doctor of law, who was accustomed to drink very heavily (a fine reputation for a doctor, of course), and the physician collapsed onto the table. When the jurist thought he was asleep and wanted to rouse him, he first noticed that he was dead. These are truly splendid and learned contests:

units.la: Ist schad / daß nit Theologi sein gewesen. Fuit vero unus Iurisconsultus, alter medicus.
units.tr: It is a pity there were no theologians. There was one jurist, and the other a doctor of medicine.

units.la: Concessi sunt bibentibus tres haustus: quorum primus est restinguendæ sitis causa: secundus, somni & salubritatis: tertius, hilaritatis causa (hic per hilaritatem non intelligo ebrietatem, quia non debes bibere ut fias ebrius) postea quartus est furoris & ebrietatis, ab hoc planè abstinendum est. De hac enim re multa veterum dicta extant, sicut & hoc est:
units.tr: Three draughts are allowed to those who drink. The first is for quenching thirst; the second is for sleep and health; the third is for cheerfulness (by cheerfulness I do not mean drunkenness, since you ought not to drink so as to become drunk). After these, the fourth draught is for fury and drunkenness, and from this one must altogether abstain. Many sayings of the ancients exist on this matter, such as this:

units.la: Sint tempestiuæ coenæ, laetæq;, breuesq;. Vos autem econtrà hanc sententiam inuertentes, totas noctes potatis. Insuper etiam nihil boni bibitis, lædit is vestra corpora. potus debet vitæ, somno et salubritati prodesse. Debet etiam exhilarare, præsertim nos seniores: oportet & somni causa, etiam cum non sitimus, aliquando pitissare, ut facilius obrepat somnus, aut retineri somnus possit.
units.tr: Let meals be timely, cheerful and brief. But you, on the contrary, reversing this opinion, drink whole nights. Moreover, you drink nothing good, and it harms your bodies. Drink should serve life, sleep and health. It should also cheer, especially us elders; and for the sake of sleep one should sometimes drink even when not thirsty, so that sleep may creep in more easily or be retained.

units.la: Hoc vero est bibere salubritatis causa. Postea additur haustus hilaritatis causa, si quis bono adsit amico: tunc demum enim conceditur. Sicut nuper dicebam ad Stigelium lium Lipsiæ: Poeticum haustum esse, de bono corde bonum unum mediocriter bibere. In loco igitur paulo hilarius bibere, dummodo mediocritatem non excedat, non est turpe, aut illicitum. Quia Deus vult haberi honorem corporis. Sic omnia procedunt ex hoc principio, HABETE honorem corporis: id est, non perdite corpora vel nimium abstinendo, vel ingurgitando immodico cibo aut potu. Vtrumq; membrum curandum est: honos est habendus corporis, ut sit organum Dei, vitando utrumq; extremum, ne vel superfluitate vel immani abstinentia laedatur. Ex hoc principio procedunt hæ virtutes: temperantia, sobrietas, & id genus reliquæ.
units.tr: This is truly drinking for health. Then a draught for cheerfulness is added, if one is with a good friend, for only then is it allowed. As I was saying recently to Stigelius at Leipzig: it is a poetic draught, to drink one good measure moderately with a good heart. Therefore to drink somewhat more cheerfully on some occasion, provided one does not exceed moderation, is neither shameful nor unlawful, because God wills the honour of the body to be kept. So everything proceeds from this principle, HAVE honour of the body: that is, do not ruin the body either by excessive abstinence or by gorging on immoderate food or drink. Both extremes must be guarded against: the body is to be honoured so that it may be an instrument of God, avoiding both excess and monstrous abstinence, lest it be harmed by either. From this principle proceed these virtues: temperance, sobriety, and the like.

units.la: Bibitur aliquando plus cereuisiæ quàm vini, quia est tenuis. Quanquàm credo nostros Germanos veteres fuisse robustissimos homines, & habuisse valde bonam cereuisiam, quæ fuit saluberrima, auxit sanguinem eum q; optimum generauit. Bonus & salubris potus est cereuisia recte coæta, sicut olim habuimus ante 30 annos. Iam corpora corrumpuntur, quia potus est deterior, terior, res profecto deploratione digna. Magistratus exugunt non tantùm marsupia, sed etiam robur & sanguinem subditorum. nam hæ subditorum exactiones efficiunt, ut non possit amplius bona cereui-sia coqui. Non dico maledicendi causa, sed deploro tantum illas communes & publicas calamitates. Mihi non minus quàm aliis æquo animo ferendum est, publica cum sit calamitas. Ruunt enim regimina in deterius, quod deploremus.
units.tr: Sometimes more beer than wine is drunk, because it is thin. Yet I believe our old Germans were very robust men and had very good beer, which was most wholesome, increased the blood and produced the finest blood. Good and wholesome drink is properly brewed beer, as we had thirty years ago. Now bodies are corrupted because the drink is worse, a matter truly deserving lament. The magistrates drain not only purses but also the strength and blood of their subjects; for these exactions of subjects mean that good beer can no longer be brewed. I do not say this for the sake of cursing, but I merely lament those common and public calamities. For me, no less than for others, they must be borne with an even mind, since the calamity is public. For governments fall into worse, which we should lament.

units.la: Lantgrauius in conuentu quodam manè uenit ad Doctorem Pontanum, & dixit: Domine Doctor Pontane, præbe mihi manum tuam. Pontanus respondit: Quid? Vis ne me capere? Lantgrauius: Non volo, inquit, sed uolo tibi aliquid promittere. Ibi cum porrexisset ei manum, dixit: Pa-omitto tibi, quòd non uelim ita posthac potare uesperi. Nam inter potandum multa liberius dicimus, quorum nos postea pœnitet.
units.tr: The Landgrave, at a certain gathering, came one morning to Doctor Pontanus and said: "Lord Doctor Pontanus, give me your hand." Pontanus replied: "What? Do you want to arrest me?" "No," said the Landgrave, "but I want to promise you something." When Pontanus had held out his hand, the Landgrave said: "I let you off, since I would not wish to drink in this way again in the evening. For while drinking we say many things too freely, and afterwards we regret them."

units.la: Parisÿs, quando purpura præparatur, tunc artifices inuitant Germanicos milites & studiosos, qui libenter bibunt: & eis præbent largiter optimum vinum, ea conditione, ut postea urinam reddant in illam lanam. Sic enim audiui à studioso Parisiensi.
units.tr: At Paris, when purple is being prepared, the craftsmen invite German soldiers and students, who drink willingly, and they give them plenty of the best wine on condition that they afterwards pass urine into that wool. So I heard from a Parisian student.

units.la: COLL.
units.tr: COLL.

units.la: Comes de Shvvarzenburg propinas ali cui Domino bonum hauslum, dixit: Es gilt ein Lutherischen drunckh. Ille non satis dictum assequens, quaerit de illo hausto. ibi Comes dixit: Die Lutherischen sehen auf den grundt. sic ego totum poculum exhauriam, biß ich den grundt lehr sehenthan.
units.tr: The Count of Schwarzenburg, offering a good draught to a certain lord, said: A toast to a Lutheran! That one, not fully understanding the saying, asked about that draught. Then the Count said: The Lutherans look to the bottom. So I will drain the whole cup until I see the bottom.

units.la: Ante annos aliquot crescebat valde bonum vinum, anno videlicet 40. quia erant magni æstus. Computabantur eo anno in ducatu Vvirtebergensi à consiliarijs Ducis 400 homines, & amplius, qui erant interfecti in conuiuijs ab autumno usq; ad primam Dominicam quadragesimæ.
units.tr: Some years ago very good wine grew abundantly, namely in the year 1540, because there were great heats. In that year, in the duchy of Württemberg, the councillors of the Duke counted 400 men and more who were killed at banquets from autumn until the first Sunday of Lent.

units.la: Hispanus quidam, cum Imperator Carolus V. bellum inferret Germaniæ, dixit: Nihil aget nobiscum de religione, quia scit vos esse ebrios. Vult igitur prius vos sobrios facere: id est, castigare: & postea aget de religione.
units.tr: A certain Spaniard, when Emperor Charles V made war on Germany, said: "He will get nothing from us concerning religion, because he knows you are drunkards. So he wants first to make you sober, that is, to chastise you; and afterwards he will deal with religion."

units.la: Pardi & pardales non capiuntur nisi inebriati uino, quod olfacientes ueniunt (in illis enim locis ponuntur cymbae plenae uino) & auidè hauriunt, posteaq; concumbunt: & ita sopiti uino & Venere, capiuntur. Sobrij uerò non capiuntur: quia tanta sunt celeritate, ut omnia tela possint excutere. In prophetia Danielis, Macedonici reges comparantur pardali. Talis enim fuit Alexander Magnus, & pater eius Philippus, & alij acerrimi uiri, quise tandem uoluptatibus dediderunt.
units.tr: Leopards and panthers are caught only when made drunk with wine. They come following the smell (for in those places boats full of wine are set out) and drink eagerly, and afterwards they couple, and so, lulled by wine and love, they are caught. The sober ones, however, are not caught, because they are so swift that they can shake off all weapons. In the prophecy of Daniel the kings of Macedon are compared to a leopard. Such was Alexander the Great, and his father Philip, and other very keen men, who at last gave themselves over to pleasures.

units.la: MEDICAMENTORUM OMNIUM, QUAE nostro tempore ad publica munia, & in communi practicantiu sunt usu, atq; in officinis extant, Tabulae breuissimae: ex antiquorum Medicorum praescripto, cum ijs qui Medicum opus facitant, tum Pharmacopoeis uel maximè utiles ac necessariae.
units.tr: A very brief table of all the medicines that in our time are in public use and common practice and are found in the pharmacies, most useful and necessary both for those who practise medicine, according to the prescriptions of the ancient physicians, and for the pharmacopoeias.

units.la: Tabula prima.
units.tr: First table.

units.tr: They prepare for phlegm. Mild: honey of roses, simple oxymel, compound oxymel, syrup of vinegar. Stronger: of two roots, of five roots, oxymel of squill, syrup of stoechas. Waters: fennel, parsnip, wormwood, sage, catmint, asparagus, mint, parsley, decoction of madder. For yellow bile. Mild: syrup of violets, of rose juice, of endive, of chicory, of chicory with rhubarb, of sorrel juice, of agrestum, of water lily. Waters: violet, endive, sorrel, dodder, lettuce, purslane, water lily, chicory, plantain, nightshade. Stronger: oxysaccharum, syrup of pomegranates, of lemons, of the acidity of citron, quince rob, of currants. For black bile. Mild: honey of roses, syrup of hops, syrup of fumitory, syrup of jujubes, simple oxymel, compound oxymel. Waters: of bugloss, balm, basil, hops, fumitory, wormwood, borage, bugloss, scolopendrium, marjoram, elder flowers, broom flowers. Stronger: syrup of thyme, syrup of epithymum, syrup of apples, syrup of calamint, syrup of scolopendrium.

units.la: SYrupos hodie practici aquis distillatis cōmiscere solent, & ita potandos præbent, obseruantq; ut sit dupla aquarum mensura ad unam syruporum. Syrupo-rum autem & aquarum mixtionis quantitas non transcendere debet· unc. iiij. Exhibentur uero omnes Syrupi magna ex parte summo mane: interdum etiam uesperi, circa ingressum lecti, illi potissimum, qui somni conciliandi gratia sumuntur.
units.tr: Practitioners today are accustomed to mix syrups with distilled waters, and they give them to be drunk in this way, observing that there be two measures of water to one of syrup. The amount of the mixture of syrups and waters ought not to exceed four ounces. All syrups are given for the most part early in the morning, but sometimes also in the evening, around the time of getting into bed, especially those taken to induce sleep.

units.tr: Simple and compound oxymel. Waters of dodder, broom, scolopendrium, calamint, bugloss. For the kidneys: syrup of the two roots, compound oxymel, simple oxymel. Waters of asparagus, saxifrage, fennel. For the womb: syrup of wormwood, syrup of red dyers' madder. Simple and compound oxymel. Waters of wormwood, feverfew, balm, catmint, fennel. Concocting a thin flame in the head: of water lily, of poppy. Waters of lettuce, plantain, water lily. For the chest: syrup of violets, of jujubes, of liquorice, julep of violets, of poppy. Waters of barley, violet, maidenhair, Venus' hair. For the stomach: sorrel, syrup of myrtleberries, of quinces, of agrestum, of sorrel juice. Waters of lettuce, chicory, sorrel, plantain, rose. For the liver: syrup of endive juice, of chicory with rhubarb. Waters of endive, sorrel, simple sorrel, of bysantia. Chicory, purslane, for the spleen. Violet, sorrel, simple. Waters of endive, syrup of two roots, bugloss, borage, scolopendrium. For the kidneys: simple sorrel, compound sorrel. Waters of endive, mallow, violets. Cold seeds, nightshade. For the head: hops, fumitory of the earth, balm, of apples, basil, oxymel, fumitory. For black bile in the stomach: honey of roses. Of thyme. Waters of borage for the liver; of epithymum, bugloss and spleen, oxymel, scolopendrium, marjoram.

units.la: DE MEDICAMENTIS PVRGANTIBUS in forma liquida, unumquemlibet humorem. Tab. III.
units.tr: ON PURGING MEDICINES IN LIQUID FORM, FOR EACH HUMOUR. Tab. III.

units.la: Purgāt Pituitam Clementiora, Hiera picra Gal. Agaricus Turbith Diaphoenicon. Valentiora Electuarium elescoph Electua. Indum Diacytoniten Diacarthami Benedicta. Bilem flauā Clementiora Cassia fistularis Manna Diaprunis sim. Catholicon Rhabarbarum. Valentiora, De succo rosarum Diarhabarba. N. Diaprunis soluti. Stomachum laxati. De psyllio Catharticū imperiale. Atrabilem, Clementiora, Cassia fistularis Diacassia Diasene leni. Catholicon. Valentiora, Confectio hamech Electuarium de epithymo Diacitoniten.
units.tr: They purge phlegm: the milder kinds are hiera picra (Galen), agaric, turbith and diaphoenicon; the stronger are the electuary of elescoph, the electuary of indum, diacytonite, diacarthamum and benedicta. They purge yellow bile: the milder kinds are cassia fistula, manna, diaprunis simple, catholicon and rhubarb; the stronger are rose juice, diarrhubarb, solutive diaprunis, and the medicine that loosens the stomach. Of psyllium, the imperial cathartic. They purge black bile: the milder kinds are cassia fistula, diacassia, lenitive diasenna and catholicon; the stronger are the confection of hamech, the electuary of epithymum and diacitonite.

units.la: A' mitioribus semper inchoandum erit, quae alvum leniter movent, atq; sine tumultu exonerant: quorum dosis erit ad unc. 1. Si de paulò autẽ validioribus, drachmas sex hodie, aut paulò plus minus ue, pro ætatis, sexus, anniq; temporum ratione, & pro sumentis uiribus practici exhibere solent. Sumuntur autem omnia medicamenta purgantia summo mane, cùm uentriculus cibo-rum copia non grauatur.
units.tr: One must always begin with the milder medicines, which move the bowels gently and evacuate without disturbance; their dose is one ounce. For somewhat stronger ones, practitioners today are accustomed to give six drachms, or a little more or less, according to age, sex and the time of year, and according to the strength of the patient. All purging medicines are taken early in the morning, when the stomach is not burdened by a quantity of food.

units.tr: Aggregative, for the whole body; Golden, for the head, as also Arabic; Azaircth; Of aloes. Black bile: milder: Indian; Of fumitory. Stronger: Of lapis lazuli; Of Armenian stone, for the liver and spleen.

units.la: Pilulæ quæ ad caput expurgandum hodie exhibentur, cæteris maiores esse debent: quò diuitiùs uentriculo immoratæ, potentius ad se noxios humores trahant: & hæ uespYeri duabus aut tribus horis à cœna sumuntur. Quædam minori forma parantur, ut sunt elephanginæ & communes dictæ, ut statim in uentriculo dissoluantur. Parum purgant, sed uentriculum magis confortant: & illæ solent exhiberi duabus horis ante cœnam. Quæ uerò ad aluum deijciendam, mediocri forma debent esse, & diluculo sumo exhibētur. Dosis aut pilularū, rarò drachmā unā excedere debet, nisi in corporibus expertis. Volutantur in puluere uel cinnamomi, uel liquiriciæ: nonnunquam etiam auro obducuntur, ut minori molestia accipi possint.
units.tr: Pills that are given today to purge the head ought to be larger than the others, so that, lingering longer in the stomach, they draw the harmful humours more powerfully to themselves; these are taken in the evening, two or three hours after supper. Some are prepared in a smaller form, such as the elephangine and the so-called common pills, so that they dissolve at once in the stomach. They purge little but strengthen the stomach more, and these are usually given two hours before supper. Those meant for emptying the bowels should be of medium size and are given early in the morning, fasting. The dose of the pills should rarely exceed one drachm, unless in bodies accustomed to them. They are rolled in powder of either cinnamon or liquorice; sometimes they are also coated with gold, so that they can be taken with less discomfort.

units.la: DE BOLO
units.tr: ON THE BOLUS

units.la: DE BOLO PVRgatorio.
units.tr: On the Purgative Bolus

units.la: Bolus purgatorius, id est buccella, quantum bucca una uice capere potest, diuersis formatur modis. Aliquando ex simplicibus medicamentis, interdum ex antidotis purgantibus liquidis, quæ excipiuntur saccharo. Nonnunquā etiam ex solidis antidotis, adiectis pulueribus & speciebus, ad uehementiam quorundam corrigendam, atqs syrupo, uel alio liquore excipiuntur, & in formam boli reducuntur. Quantitas autē boli nunquam transfire debet uncias duas. nam una uice devoranda erit.
units.tr: A purgative bolus, that is, a morsel as much as the mouth can take at one time, is formed in various ways. Sometimes it is made from simple medicines, sometimes from liquid purgative antidotes that are mixed with sugar. Sometimes too it is made from solid antidotes, with powders and spices added to temper the harshness of certain ingredients, and then it is bound with syrup or another liquid and shaped into a bolus. The quantity of a bolus should never exceed two ounces, for it must be swallowed in one go.

units.la: DE INFVSIONIBVS, decoctis, clysteribus, & suppsitorijs.
units.tr: On infusions, decoctions, clysters, and suppositories.

units.la: Tabula v.
units.tr: Table 5.

units.la: Infusio hodie dicitur liquor, in quo medicamenta parum trita, uel puluerisata, uel solida, etiam integra macerantur, absque ulla decoctione, per horas plures, noctem totam, biduum, uel triduum, pro natura medicamenti, ut uirtus eius tota in liquorem trahatur & transeat. Diuitibus & delicatis exhibentur, eo quòd gratiores sunt huiusmodi potiones purgatrices, quam ipsa solidorum substantia, citius etiam distribuuntur liquida, quàm erassat. Oseruãdũ est quoq; diligēter, ut semper medica mentis purgantibus adijciantur, quæ uehementiam eorum corrigere possint: & quanto tempore maceranda sint. Hodie duodecim horas, nonnunquam integram noctem & diem macerantur, quæ macerata ualentius colando expriműtur, aut per colum rarius, ut per manicam Hippoc. transmittuntur. nōnunquam à nonnullis medicamenta purgantia liquida & syrupi, ut gratior fiat potio, ijs commiscentur: alij alterant saccharo, aut cinnamomo, ut patiens se medicamentum sumpsisse nesciat. Aliquando uice infusionis, iusculo aliquo supradicta medicamenta nodulo ligata incoquimus. Quidam hodie iuxta humorum redundantiam, decoctum pro medicamentis purgantibus parant: ut si pituita redundat, è seminibus atq; radicibus, quæ lentos & crassos humores incidunt, & obstructiones liberant: si bilis flaua, è uiolis, lactuca, cichorio, & eiusmodi quæ quæ bilis acrimoniam refrenant, decocta faciunt. Primus modus est hodie magis in usu.
units.tr: An infusion today is a liquid in which medicines, lightly crushed or powdered, or even solid and whole, are steeped without any boiling, for several hours, a whole night, two or three days, according to the nature of the medicine, so that its whole virtue is drawn into the liquid and passes into it. They are given to the rich and delicate, because such purgative drinks are more pleasing than the bare substance of the solids; liquids are also taken more quickly than thick preparations. It must also be carefully observed that purgatives are always combined with ingredients able to correct their violence, and for how long they must be steeped. Today they are steeped for twelve hours, sometimes a whole night and day; the steeped material is pressed out more forcefully through a strainer, or passed more thinly through a cloth, as through a Hippocratic sleeve. Sometimes by some people purgative liquid medicines and syrups are mixed with them, to make the drink more pleasant; others sweeten it with sugar or cinnamon, so that the patient does not know he has taken medicine. Sometimes, instead of an infusion, we boil the aforesaid medicines tied in a little cloth in some broth. Today some prepare a decoction of purgatives according to the excess of humours: if phlegm is in excess, they make decoctions from seeds and roots which cut thick, viscous humours and clear obstructions; if yellow bile, from violets, lettuce, chicory and the like, which restrain the sharpness of bile. The first method is more in use today.

units.la: Medicamenta quæ infunduntur seu macerantur liquore aliquo, sunt: Agaricum, Dosis est ad.3.v. Senna, Dosis ad.3.vi. Rhabarbarū, Dosis ad.3 iiij. v.aut sex. Turbith ad.3.i. Scammonium Ǝ. s.uel grana iii. Hermodactylus. Myrobalani ad 3 iij. Tamarindi ad 3. ij. Psyllium ad unc.i.sicut fumus terræ. Aloë, ad 3. ij.
units.tr: The medicines that are infused or steeped in some liquid are these: agaric, dose 3 v.; senna, dose 3 vi.; rhubarb, dose 3 iiij to v. or vi.; turbith, dose 3 i.; scammony, dose 3 s., or three grains; hermodactyl; myrobalans, dose 3 iij.; tamarinds, dose 3 ij.; psyllium, dose one ounce; fumitory; aloe, dose 3 ij.

units.la: Agaricum est familiaris medicina, ubi correcta fuerit. corrigitur autem cum oxymelite scyllitico, aut sale gemmæ, uel zingibere, semper admiscendo tertiam partem: & quia uentriculo aduersatur sua leuitate, debet admisceri aliqua medicina stomachica: sicut Cinnamomum, Garyophy. Mastix, aut calamus aromati. Dantur binæ drachmæ cum oxymelite, uel melle rosæ macerati. dosis ad 3.5. Potest dari in forma liquida, aut pilulari, uel pulueris.
units.tr: Agaric is a familiar medicine once it has been corrected. It is corrected with squill oxymel, or gem salt, or ginger, always adding a third part; and because by its lightness it is hostile to the stomach, some stomachic medicine must be added, such as cinnamon, cloves, mastic, or aromatic calamus. Two drachms are given with oxymel, or with macerated rose honey; dose 3 v. It may be given in liquid form, or as pills, or as powder.

units.la: Senna corrigitur cū zingibere, uel datur cū iure gallinæ, pulli, uel carnium, abstq; trituratione.
units.tr: Senna is corrected with ginger, or is given with broth of hen, chicken, or meats, without trituration.

units.la: Rhabarbarū corrigitur cū tertia parte spicæ nardi, aut cinnamomi, uel iunci odorati, aut mastichis. Datur cū sero lactis, aut succo cichorij, uel cū decoctione purgate bilē flauā. Maceratur in ijsdē decoctis, aut in aquis distillatis, idq; in æstate: hyeme uerò in uino albo optimo. In substātia datur ad 3. iiij usque. Turbith
units.tr: Rhubarb is corrected with a third part of spikenard, or cinnamon, or sweet rush, or mastic. It is given with whey, or chicory juice, or with a decoction that purges yellow bile. It is steeped in the same decoctions, or in distilled waters, and this in summer; but in winter in the best white wine. In substance it is given in doses of 3 iiij and up. Turbith.

units.la: Et alia permulta super cineres calidos tēperantur aliquandiu humore siue liquore idoneo, ut uis uehemēs corrigatur. Turbith corrigitur cum subdupla, aut tertia parte zingiberis. Datur cum Melle rosf. aut Conf. uiol. uel passulárum decocto, pondere drachmæ unius, aut paulo plus, pro sumentis uiribus. Pituitam glutinosam purgat, longis morbis medetur.
units.tr: And many other things are warmed for a while over hot ashes in a suitable moisture or liquid, so that their violent force is corrected. Turbith is corrected with a half or a third part of ginger. It is given with rose honey, or conserve of violets, or a decoction of raisins, in a weight of one drachm, or a little more, according to the strength of the patient. It purges glutinous phlegm and cures long-standing diseases.

units.la: Scammoniū, id est diagrydium, corrigitur decoquendo in citonio. Admiscentur ex ijs quæ iucundum spirant odorem, & stomachum confortant: ut Anisum, mastix, thymus aut pulegium, &c. Datur per se cum melle, aut ptisanæ cremore, uel cū aqua myrobal. citrinorū, cum saccharo uiol. uel ros. syrupo. Alij macerant in oleo uiolato: tunc absque noxa deorsum uergit. Dosis est ad scrup. 1.5.
units.tr: Scammony, that is diagrydium, is corrected by boiling it in quince. Among the things added are those that breathe a pleasant odour and strengthen the stomach, such as anise, mastic, thyme or pennyroyal, etc. It is given alone with honey, or with barley water, or with water of citrine myrobalans, or with sugar of violets or roses, or syrup. Others steep it in violet oil; then it moves downward without harm. The dose is one and a half scruples.

units.la: Myrobalani, quorum genera sunt quatuor: citrina, cepula, inda siue nigra, & emblica. Citrina, bilem flauam: nigra, atram: cepula, pituitam detrahunt: uentriculum & intestina sua adstrictione roborant. trita, usta, aut elota, corriguntur cum saccharo, amygdalis dulcibus, passulis, semine anisi. in forma potabili dantur cum decoctione cōmuni, uel sero caprino. Citrini dantur cum decoctione purgante bilem flauam: nigri, cum ijs quæ atram bilem: alij, cum ijs quæ pituitam. quorum dosis ad drach. iij. aut iiij. trita.
units.tr: Myrobalans, of which there are four kinds: citrine, chebulic, indian or black, and emblic. Citrine myrobalans draw off yellow bile, black ones black bile, chebulic ones phlegm; they strengthen the stomach and intestines by their astringency. Dried, burnt, or washed, they are corrected with sugar, sweet almonds, raisins, and aniseed. In a drinkable form they are given with ordinary decoction or goat's whey. Citrine ones are given with a purgative decoction for yellow bile; black ones with those for black bile; the others with those for phlegm. Their dose is three or four drachms, powdered.

units.la: Tamarindus, noxas omnes à calore natas mitigat. Datur ad febres ardentes cum rhabarba. cassia. Dosis est unc. i. Cōtunditur, contusus in aliquo liquore miscetur, ut in hepatis pass. aqua endiuiæ: uentriculi, membræ. deinde colando exprimitur, ut aliquid substantiæ eius extrahatur.
units.tr: Tamarind mitigates all harms arising from heat. It is given in burning fevers with rhubarb and cassia. The dose is one ounce. It is pounded, and the crushed pulp is mixed in some liquid, such as water of liver-wort, endive, or the wall-pennywort of the stomach and membranes; then it is strained and pressed out, so that some of its substance is extracted.

units.la: Aloe, datur ijs qui capitis doloribus à uentriculo afficiuntur: necnon laborantibus oculorum suffusionib. Dosis est ad 3. ij. ex aqua mulsa.
units.tr: Aloe is given to those afflicted by headaches arising from the stomach, and also to those suffering from cataracts of the eyes. The dose is 3 ij, in honeyed water.

units.la: Polypodium. eius radicis purgatæ, dantur 3. ij. ex aqua mulsa. Alij cum odoratis corrigunt eius uim, ut cum zingibere, sem. anisi, gariophillis, cinnamomo, & similibus. Aluum deijcit contra molestiam in gallinaceo iure, tum in ptissanæ cremore radix cocta.
units.tr: Polypody: of its purified root, 3 ij are given in honeyed water. Others correct its force with aromatics, such as ginger, aniseed, cloves, cinnamon, and the like. It loosens the bowels against discomfort in chicken broth; then the boiled root in barley water.

units.la: Epithymū datur adultis tusum, & cribro excussum, ǯ. v. aut 3. ij. cum passo, uel aceto mulso: adiecto pauxillo piperis, uel jalis gemmæ. parum decoquitur.
units.tr: Thyme-seed is given to adults pounded and sifted through a sieve, 3 v. or 3 ij., with raisin wine or mulled vinegar, a little pepper or gem salt being added. It is boiled briefly.

units.la: Elleborus niger corrigitur cum seminibus odoratis: datur ex passo, aut aceto mulso, ad ǯ iij.
units.tr: Black hellebore is corrected with aromatic seeds; it is given in raisin wine or mulled vinegar, at 3 iij.

units.la: Hiera picra, multum de se debilis: per se enim data nō operatur, nisi in debilib. Potest dari in potione: sed propter eius amaritudinē præstabit potius dare in forma pilulari, quāuis in potione potē tius operetur: datur in potione secure ad unc. s.
units.tr: Picra hiera, much weakened in itself: given alone, it does not act, except in weak patients. It can be given in a drink, but because of its bitterness it is better to give it in pill form, although in a drink it acts more strongly; it is given safely in a drink at one ounce, half.

units.la: Mezereon, Esula, & huiusmodi, macerantur in aceto, ut deponant acrimoniam.
units.tr: Mezereon, spurge, and such things are steeped in vinegar, so that they lose their sharpness.

units.la: Armenius lapis, quo pictores utuntur, datur ad ǯ iiij.
units.tr: Armenian stone, which painters use, is given at 3 iiij.

units.la: Decocta parantur ex seminibus, foliis, radicibus, & plantarum floribus Folia & flores manipulis: fructus numero: radices & semina, pondere æstimentur. Radicum quantitas unc. iij ad summum quinq: foliorum, fasciculorum manualium quinq: seminum 3. iiij. aut sex: florum, manipulorum quatuor non excedat. aquæ mensura in qua decoquuntur supradicta, libras tres non debet transfire. Cæterum cuilibet libræ aquæ, libra semis sacchari & mellis admisceatur. Si uero decoctionem odoramentis, ut iucundior fiat, parari opus fuerit, cuilibet libræ decocti 3 ij. odoramentorum commiscendæ erunt.
units.tr: Decoctions are prepared from seeds, leaves, roots, and flowers of plants: leaves and flowers are estimated by handfuls, fruits by number, roots and seeds by weight. The quantity of roots should not exceed three ounces, at most five; of leaves, five small bundles; of seeds, 3 iiij or six; of flowers, not more than four handfuls. The quantity of water in which the aforesaid things are boiled must not exceed three pounds. Moreover, to each pound of water half a pound of sugar and honey is to be added. If indeed it is necessary to prepare the decoction with aromatics, so that it may be more pleasant, 3 ij of aromatics are to be mixed into each pound of the decoction.

units.la: DE CLYSTERIBVS.
units.tr: On Clysters.

units.la: Clysterium uaria sunt genera: ad quorum compositionem, quatuor rebus opus est. Primum aliquo liquore, ut pisorum, cicerum, pulli, gallinæ, capi, castratorum, uel aliarum carnium aut decocti, iuxta morbi naturam uariari solet. aliquando enim abstergendum, adstringendum, glutinādum, &c. Secundò, medicamenta purgantia requiruntur, quæ duplo pondere dantur ad ea quæ deuorantur. Tertiò, sunt olea & pinguedines, quæ etiam pro morbi diuersitate uariantur. Quartò, salis genera, ut facultatem excretoriam excitent: præterea aliquando mel, aut saccharum, aut butyrum, aut uitelli ouorum, prout morbus postulat, adijcium adijciuntur. Estq; communis regula, quòd ad iuris decocti, uel alterius, libram unam, oleorum unc. iiij. uel iij. pinguedinum, mellis, butyri, sachari unc.i. aut s. uitelli ouorum duo, aut tres: salis uerò.3. i. plus minus' ue. Clysterium quidam sunt debiles, quibus utimur in febribus, & in ijs qui longo morbo debilitati, senibus & intestinorum torminibus: uehementiorib.& acrib.in morbis frigid. longis,& qui exitiale uenenum sumpserunt.
units.tr: There are various kinds of clyster, and four things are needed to make them. First, some liquid, such as a broth of peas, chickpeas, chicken, hen, capon, wether, or other meats, or a decoction, which is usually varied according to the nature of the disease: sometimes it must cleanse, sometimes bind, sometimes soothe, and so on. Second, purgative medicines are required, given in twice the weight of those taken by mouth. Third, there are oils and fats, which also vary according to the diversity of the disease. Fourth, kinds of salt to stimulate the excretory faculty; besides these, honey, sugar, butter, or egg yolks are sometimes added, as the disease requires. The common rule is that to one pound of broth, or of some other liquid, one adds four or three ounces of oil or fat, one ounce or half an ounce of honey, butter or sugar, two or three egg yolks, and one drachm of salt, more or less. Some clysters are mild, and we use these in fevers, in those weakened by a long illness, in the old, and in colic of the bowels. Stronger and sharper ones are used in long cold diseases, and in those who have swallowed a deadly poison.

units.la: Malua, Althaea, Mater uiol., Atriplex, Mercurialis. Singulorum quantitas potest esse M.i. decoquatur ad tertias, et colo diffundatur, accipiaturq; iuris decocti lib.1. medullae cassiae uno.1. adijcitur interdum Hierae picrae unc.s.cum mellis rosa.3.iij. olei unc.iij.& salis 3.1.
units.tr: Mallow, marsh mallow, violet, orache, mercury. Of each the quantity may be one handful. Let it be boiled down to a third, and the liquor strained off. Take one pound of this broth, one ounce of cassia pulp, and sometimes half an ounce of hiera picra, with three drachms of rose honey, three ounces of oil, and one drachm of salt.

units.la: Clysteres inijci possunt omni tempore, modo duabus aut tribus horis, uel longius à cibo adhibeantur.
units.tr: Clysters may be injected at any time, provided they are applied two or three hours, or longer, after food.

units.la: DE SVPPOSITORIIS.
units.tr: ON SUPPOSITORIES.

units.la: Suppositoriorum tria sunt genera. Quaedam leuia: & ista nobis sunt familiaria. fiunt enim ex radice betae, caulis, uel mercurialis, lardo, caseo, stercore humano exiccato, melle perunctis, suillo adipe sal consperso, ficu inuersa,& butyro, adiecto sale. Quaedam uerò mediocria, & fiunt è uitello tello oui, croco, additis melle & sale, uel quæ è sale & melle componuntur. Quædam sunt uehementiora, ut quæ recipiunt scammonium, euphorbium, elleborum, & huiusmodi pulueres, quibus magna necessitate utimur in morbis magnis. Danda est opera, ut drach. uni specierum & salis, unc. i. mellis addatur. Pulueres triti & calcinati, cum melle cocto aut cera & oleo, donec in unum coeant, miscentur. Dum subijciuntur, priusquam oleo, butyro, aut alia pinguedine illita esse oportet. Si voluerit medicus fortificare virtutem expulsiuam, subijciat suppositorium Luna in signis existente frigidis: sicut in Cancro, scorpio, & piscibus.
units.tr: There are three kinds of suppositories. Some are mild, and these are familiar to us. They are made from beet root, cabbage or dog's mercury, with lard, cheese, dried human dung, figs smeared with honey, a sprinkling of salt on pig fat, an inverted fig, and butter with added salt. Others are moderate, and are made from the yolk of an egg with saffron, with honey and salt added, or from compounds of salt and honey. Others are stronger, such as those that take in scammony, euphorbium, hellebore and similar powders, which we use in serious illnesses when great necessity requires. Care must be taken that one drachm of the powdered species and a little salt are added to an ounce of honey. The powders, finely ground and calcined, are mixed with boiled honey, or with wax and oil, until they cohere into one mass. When they are inserted, they must first be smeared with oil, butter or some other fat. If the physician wishes to strengthen the expulsive power, let him insert the suppository when the moon is in cold signs, such as Cancer, Scorpio and Pisces.

units.la: DE SPECIEBVS.
units.tr: ON THE SPECIES.

units.la: [illegible, ~40 letters]
