units.la: DE SPECIEBVS AROMATICIS siue confectionibus, unam quamlibet partem roborantibus. Tab. 5.
units.tr: ON AROMATIC SPECIES, OR CONFECTIONS, EACH STRENGTHENING ONE PART. Tab. 5.

units.la: Respiciunt Caput Frigi. Diarhodon abbatis Diacoralli Manus Christi Ad cerebri passiones calidas. Calid. Diambrae Mithridatum Diamarg.calidum Electu.pliris arcotico Apoplexiae, epilepsiae, et affectibus melancholicis medetur. Thorace Frigi. Tragacanthum frigi. Diapapauer Distillationibus ad pectoralia calidis exhibentur. Calid. Diapenidion Tragacanthum calid. Diacalamentum Diaprassyum Diairis Salomonis Ad thoracis et pulmonum vitia, ut sputa leta, crassa, in pectoralibus contenta. Respiciunt Vētriculū, Calid. Rosata nouella Aromaticum rosd. G. Aromatici garyoph. Diatrion pipereon Diagalanga Dianisum Diacyminum Diacynnamomum Diazingiber Confectio de xilaloen. Frigi. Triasantali Diarhodon abbatis Diacitoniten Frigi. Manus Christi Diamarg.frigid. Diacoralli Triasantali Cor, Calid. Diamarg.calidum Confectio de musco dul. Diambra Diacameron Elec.laeticiae Gale, Rosata nouella Mithridatum Theriaca Ad prauam uētriculi coctionē, flatus, acidósq; ructus. Aduersus uētriculi & ïo cinoris calorem. Deiectis uiribus et febribus ardētib. medentur. Aduersus cordis palpitationem. Hepar Frigida Diarrhodon abbatis Triasantali Aduersus iocinoris calores. Calida Dialacca Diacurcuma Ad iocinoris & lienis obstructiones, ac aquam intercutem.
units.tr: These relate to the head: cold: Abbot's Diarrhodon, Diacoral, Christ's Hand. For hot cerebral disorders. Hot: Diambra, Mithridate, Hot Diamargaritum, Electuary of Pliris (Arcoticum). They cure apoplexy, epilepsy and melancholic afflictions. For the chest: cold: Tragacanth (cold). Diapapaver. Hot: distillations for the lungs are given: Diapenidion, hot Tragacanth, Diacalamus, Diaprassium, Iris of Solomon. For faults of the chest and lungs, such as thin or thick sputum held in the breast. These relate to the stomach: hot: New Rose, Aromaticum Rosatum, Aromatic Gariophyllum. Diatrion Pepereon, Diagalanga, Diaanisum, Diacuminum, Diacinnamomum, Diazingiber, Confection of Xylaloes. Cold: Trisantalum, Abbot's Diarrhodon, Diacitonites. Cold: Christ's Hand, cold Diamargaritum, Trisantalum for the heart. Hot: Diamargaritum hot, Confection of Musk Dulcis, Diambra, Diacameron, Electuary of Joy, Galen's, New Rose, Mithridate, Theriac. For a bad digestion in the stomach, wind, and sour belching. Against heat of the stomach and liver. They remedy weakened strength and burning fevers. Against palpitation of the heart. For the liver: cold: Abbot's Diarrhodon, Trisantalum, against heat of the liver. Hot: Dialacca, Diacurcuma, for obstructions of the liver and spleen, and for dropsy under the skin.

units.la: Componuntur magna ex parte confectiones è speciebus multorum antidotorum, adiectis quibusdam nouis & recentibus. Vocantur hodie à nostris practicis rotulæ seu tabulæ: quoniam formam orbicularem accipiunt. Quæ verò forma sunt longa, morselli & lozengiæ dicuntur. Modus exhibitionis 3.1. s.aut 3.ij.pro sumentis habitu & affectu. Dantur diluculò et uespèri, tribus aut quatuor horis à cœna elapsis.
units.tr: Most of these confections are compounded from the species of many antidotes, with some new and recent additions. Our practitioners nowadays call them rolls or tablets, since they take a round form; those that are long in shape are called morsels and lozenges. The dose is 3i s. or 3ij., according to the person taking it and the complaint. They are given in the morning and in the evening, three or four hours after dinner.

units.la: DE CONSERVIS SIVE HODIE conditis uocatis, nec non & trochiscis atq; eclegmatis. Tab. 7.
units.tr: ON PRESERVES, CALLED TODAY CONSERVES, AND ALSO ON TROCHES AND ECLEGMARIES. Tab. 7.

units.la: Respiciunt Caput Anthos Rosmarini. Acori Lauandulæ E bethonica E pœonia. Aduersus comitialem morbū, apoplexiā, & alia capitis & neruorū frigida mala. Frigi. De nenuphare Rosarū E prunella Violarum. Ad uapores in cerebrum irrepètes reprimendos.
units.tr: They are for the head: anthos of rosemary, acorus, lavender, bethony, and peony; against epilepsy, apoplexy, and other cold diseases of the head and nerves. Cold. Of nenuphar, roses, and prunella of violets; for repressing vapours that creep into the brain.

units.la: E 2 Respi{diagram} Respiciunt Thorace { Enulæ campanæ / Capilli Veneris } Ad uiscida & lenta sputa è pectoralibus educenda. Cor { Boragin. / Buglossæ / Acetosæ } Palpitationi, melancholicis, & tristibus auxiliantur. Ventriculum { Absynthij / Gingiber conditū / Acorus conditus / Saluiæ / Citria condita. } Ventriculum firmant, concoctionem iuuant, orisq; suauitatem efficiunt. Ventriculum { Rosarum / Cichorij / Acetosæ / Cotonea condita / De nenuphare. } Acrimoniā bilis obtundunt, uehementioribus febribus subueniunt, doloribus quos bilis creat: et capitis dolores sedant.
units.tr: They are for the chest: elecampane and maidenhair (capillus Veneris), for drawing out viscous and thick phlegm from the breast. For the heart: borage, bugloss, and sorrel; they help palpitations, melancholics, and the sorrowful. For the stomach: wormwood, candied ginger, candied acorus, sage, and candied citron. They strengthen the stomach, aid digestion, and make the mouth sweet. For the liver: roses, chicory, sorrel, candied quince, and nenuphar. They blunt the sharpness of bile, help more violent fevers and the pains that bile produces, and calm headaches.

units.la: Nullus in ijs sumendis præscriptus est modus : usus hodie seruat, ut mane & uesperi nucis iuglandis quantitate exhibeantur.nonnunquā his admiscētur pulueres aromatici, & cum saccharo uel syrupo appropriato, mixtura quam uocant, conficitur.
units.tr: No fixed dose is prescribed for taking these. Current practice keeps to a quantity the size of a walnut, given morning and evening. Sometimes aromatic powders are mixed in, and with sugar or a suitable syrup a mixture, as they call it, is made up.

units.la: DE TRO-
units.tr: ON TRO-

units.la: DE TROCHISCIS.
units.tr: ON TROCHES.

units.la: Trochisci Aperitiui Derhabarbaro | Ad hepatis obstructiones & febrium horrores, quos pituita creat, De eupatorio | necnō aquā intercute. De myrrha. De spodio | Ad febres ardentes, iocinoris calefactionē, atque uentris profiuium. De uesicaria De terra Lēnia De caphura De berberis. Alkeket. Costrictiui,
units.tr: Aperitive troches: of rhubarb (De rhabarbaro), for obstructions of the liver and the shivering fits of fever that phlegm produces; of eupatorium, and for dropsy (aqua intercus); of myrrh; of spodium, for burning fevers, heat of the liver, and diarrhoea; of blistering agents (De uesicaria); of Lemnian earth (De terra Lemnia); of camphor (De caphura); of barberry (De berberis); of alkekengi (Alkeket); astringent troches.

units.la: Trochisci, cū usus postulat, triti ex aqua aut uino, aut alio quouis liquore ebibendi exhibentur. Nonnunquam antidotis, saccharo, pilulis, clysteribus, unguentis, aliisq; huiusmodi cōmiscentur. Trochiscorum, qui sine aliorum medicamentorum mixtione sumuntur, dosis non debet transfire 3.1. uel 3.1.s. & 2. quorum compositionem opium ingreditur. ∋.1. aut 3.s. dantur.
units.tr: Troches, when the need arises, are ground up and given to be drunk in water, wine, or any other liquid. Sometimes they are mixed with electuaries, sugar, pills, clysters, ointments, and similar preparations. The dose of troches taken without being mixed with other medicines should not exceed 3.1 or 3.1.s. Those whose composition includes opium are given at ∋.1 or 3.s.

units.la: DE LOCH, SIVE ECLEGMATIS.
units.tr: On Loch, or Eclegma

units.la: Loch Mitigatora, De pino Me. | Tussi diuturnae & asthmati medentur. De pulmone uulpis Me. De caulibus Gordonij. Valetiora, Sanū & expertū | Asthmati antiquae à crassis et uiscidis humoribus auxiliatur. De squilla. Frigidū. De papaucre. | Tussi à caliditate & siccitate subuenit. Possunt sumi omni hora, præter loch de papauere, qui datur hora post cœnam.
units.tr: Soothing loch, of pine (Me.). Good for chronic cough and asthma. Of fox lung (Me.). Of cabbages (Gordonius). Valetiora, sound and tested. Helps old asthma arising from thick and viscid humours. Of squill. Cooling. Of poppy. Helps cough arising from heat and dryness. They may be taken at any hour, except the loch of poppy, which is given an hour after supper.

units.la: DE STUPEFACIENTIBUS, SOMNUM provocantib. & de ijs quæ uomitū provocant. Tab. 8.
units.tr: ON STUPEFYING DRUGS THAT PROMOTE SLEEP, AND ON THOSE THAT PROVOKE VOMITING. Tab. 8.

units.la: Stupefacientia, somnū provocantia, interius sumēda. Mitiora Sy. uiolaceus Syrupus de papauere Succi: Lactucæ; Semperuiui; Solani; Portulacæ; Cicutæ Conserua Violarum Conserua Nymphææ Valentiora Philonis antidotū Athanasia Dialibanum Diacodyō Micleta
units.tr: Stupefying drugs that promote sleep are to be taken internally. Milder ones: syrup of violets; syrup of poppy; juices of lettuce, houseleek, nightshade, purslane and hemlock; conserve of violets; conserve of water lily. Stronger ones: Philo's antidote; athanasia; dialibanum; diacodium; micleta.

units.la: Vehementiorib. nō nisi maxima necessitate utēdum est: neq; cōtinuis diebus, sed ex intervallis talia sunt dāda. Dosis est à ƽ ij. usq; ad 3.1. cū syrup.rosʃ. Exterius admonēda. Oleum uiolaceum Oleum mandrago. Vnguentum populeonis Decoctū corticis mādrago. Semen hyoscyami Lac muliebre Semen papaueris Decoctum salicis Opium Anethū uiride in oleo coctū
units.tr: The stronger ones must not be used except in the greatest necessity, nor on consecutive days, but such things should be given at intervals. The dose is from 2 drachms up to 1 drachm, with syrup of roses. Applied externally: violet oil; mandrake oil; poplar ointment; decoction of mandrake bark; seed of henbane; women's milk; seed of poppy; decoction of willow; opium; dill boiled in oil.

units.la: Consultius est primo his quæ extrinsecus admouētur, uti (scil. ut tēporibus illinantur) quæ quæ intra corpus sumuntur. Cauendum au, tne unqua membris principalibus, ut cerebro, cordi, iecori adhibeantur: neq; pueris, senioribus, grauidis, ac alijs imbecilioribus applicentur. Mitiora simplicia, uomitu eli cientia Aqua calida Hordei decoctum Ficuu recentiu loga comestio Oleum crudu digitis aut penna in os dimissum. Sumuntur cum unctuosis, uel sine. Mediocria Atriplicis semen & radix Semen: Raparum Nasturtij Erucæ Melonum Cucumer asininus Nasturtium Radix bethonicæ. Ista in aqua decoquuntur, et cum oleo uel unctuosis assumuntur. Composita Sy.acetosus.S.& compos. Oxymel. Hydromel. A cibo sumuntur ad unc. iij. Sumpturis ista uehementiora, confert præsumere paucu cibum: neq; hæc imperari debet nisi ubi stragus latus suspicio imminet. Valentiora Radix rhaphani, & semẽ eius Cæpæ,& semen eius Baurach Vterq; elleborus Radix cucumeris syluestris Flores sparti Nux uomica. Aduertendum, potiones quæ uomitus ciendi gratia bibũ tur, tepidas, affatimq; sumendas esse.
units.tr: It is wiser to use first those things applied from outside (that is, smeared on at the proper times), rather than those taken into the body. Care must be taken never to apply them to the principal organs, such as the brain, heart and liver, nor should they be applied to children, the elderly, pregnant women, or other weaker persons. Milder simple remedies that provoke vomiting: warm water; decoction of barley; eating fresh figs in quantity; crude oil put into the mouth with a finger or a feather. These are taken with fatty substances or without them. Medium ones: seed and root of orache; seed of turnip; of cress; of melon; wild cucumber; watercress; root of betony. These are boiled in water and taken with oil or fatty substances. Compound ones: acetous syrup and compound syrups; oxymel; hydromel. They are taken before food, in doses of 3 ounces. These stronger emetics should be taken after eating only a little food, and they should not be prescribed unless a serious danger of suffocation threatens. Stronger ones: root of radish and its seed; onion and its seed; baurach; both kinds of hellebore; root of wild cucumber; broom flowers; nux vomica. It should be noted that potions taken to induce vomiting must be taken warm and in large quantity.

units.la: DE ERRHINIS, MASTICATO-rijs, odoramentis, & suffumigatio-nibus. Tab. 9.
units.tr: On errhines, masticatories, perfumes, and fumigations. Tab. 9.

units.la: Errhina Miti ora, Aquæ distillatæ capitales Anagallidis utriusq; succus Succus cæparum Succus cyclaminis Succus brassicæ Succus foliorũ enulæ cãpanæ Liquida naribus illinuntur aut injicsiuntur, interdum oleis & speciebus aromaticis admiscentur. Valentiora, Succus struthij Succus rad. nigellæ Succus marrubij Castorium Piper Elleborum album. Quæ sicca sunt, calamo induntur naribus: uel aliquo liquore, aut cera componuntur, & sic naribus induntur.
units.tr: Errhines: milder ones are the distilled waters (Aquae distillatae capitales) of pimpernel, the juice of onions, the juice of cyclamen, the juice of cabbage, and the juice of elecampane leaves. These liquids are poured or injected into the nostrils, sometimes mixed with oils and aromatic spices. Stronger ones are juice of struthium, juice of black cumin root, juice of horehound, castoreum, pepper, and white hellebore. Dry ones are placed in the nostrils on a reed, or are compounded with some liquid or wax and so put into the nostrils.

units.la: Liquorum unc .s. una uice infudisse sufficit. Vnicè tamẽ obseruandum, ut qui sumunt, prius os aqua impleant, ne è naribus per uias siue meatus defluât succi, ac caput in posteriora reclinandum: neq; his utendum, nisi corpus prius uacuatum fuerit medicamento deiectorio, aut phlebotomia. Horum usus est in longis capitis morbis, præsertim morbo comitiali, narium obstructionibus, odoratus difficultate, & oculorum affectibus antiquis.
units.tr: Half an ounce of liquid is enough to infuse at one time. There is one thing above all to observe: those who take these should first fill the mouth with water, so that the juices do not run down from the nostrils through the passages, and the head must be tilted back. Nor should they be used unless the body has first been emptied by a purgative medicine or by phlebotomy. Their use is in long-standing diseases of the head, especially epilepsy, obstructions of the nostrils, difficulty of smell, and old disorders of the eyes.

units.la: De masticatorijs, siue apophlegmatismis.
units.tr: On masticatories, or apophlegmatisms.

units.la: Masticatoria Mitiora, Hyssopus, Origanum, Thymum, Pulegium, Cappares. Retinentur in ore, & commãducantur, detibusq; confringuntur, aut contusa & liquore aliquo uel melle excipiuntur, & mansiles pastilli formantur. Valentiora, Sinapi, Mastix, Radix acori, Zingiber, Piper, Pyrethrum.
units.tr: Milder masticatories are hyssop, oregano, thyme, pennyroyal, and capers. They are held in the mouth and chewed, or crushed with the teeth, or bruised and mixed with some liquid or honey, and formed into soft lozenges. Stronger ones are mustard, mastic, sweet flag root, ginger, pepper, and pellitory.

units.la: Vtendum masticatorijs maxime matutino tempore, quum corpus expurgatum est a reliquis excrementis: atq; post illorum usum, os abluendum est aqua, uel melicrato, aut ptissana.
units.tr: Masticatories should be used especially in the morning, when the body has been cleared of its other excrements; and after using them the mouth must be rinsed with water, or with honeyed water, or with barley water.

units.la: De odoramentis.
units.tr: On perfumes.

units.la: Calida odoramenta Styrax, Lignum aloes, Cinamomum, Maceris, Mastix, Muscus, Nigella, Iuniperus, Genista, Maioran., Garyophylli. Ladanum, Maiorana, Caryophylli, Ladanum, Lauandula, Thus, Ocymum.
units.tr: Warm perfumes: storax, aloeswood, cinnamon, macer, mastic, musk, nigella, juniper, broom, marjoram, cloves, ladanum, marjoram, cloves, ladanum, lavender, frankincense, and basil.

units.la: Citra ignis accessione fiunt, suo odore cerebrum alterant, oleo uel aliquo liquore orbiculi ad usum formatur, aut unguenta uel poma trita excipiuntur liquore. Frigida {Nymphaea | Oleum violarum | De papaue} {Rosae | Viola | Satali} {Camphora | Vnguentum populeum | Madrag. (leonis.
units.tr: These are made without the application of fire; their smell affects the brain. They are shaped into little discs with oil or some liquid for use, or the ground unguents or apples are mixed with liquid. Cold perfumes: water lily, oil of violets, oil of poppy; rose, violet, sandalwood; camphor, poplar ointment, mandrake.

units.la: Vsus horum est ad iucundum odorem faciendum, ad pestilentiae contagia arcenda, ad distillationes à capite ad pectoralia: tunc{q} naribus admouentur.
units.tr: Their use is to make a pleasant smell, to ward off the contagion of pestilence, and to check distillations from the head to the chest; they are then applied to the nostrils.

units.la: De suffumigationibus.
units.tr: On fumigations.

units.la: Saluia | Rosmarin. | Macceris | Cinamomum | Thus, Myrrha Maiorana | Basilicon | Garyophyl. | Lignum aloes | Mastix. Trita ista excipiuntur liquore, incenduntur, aut ignitis carboni bus injiciuntur.
units.tr: Sage, rosemary, macer, cinnamon, frankincense, myrrh, marjoram, basil, cloves, aloeswood, mastic. These ground ingredients are mixed with liquid and set alight, or thrown onto glowing coals.

units.la: Vsus est ad odorem gratum comparandum, ad distillationes à capite ad pectoralia, ad pestiletiae contagia arcenda: tunc naribus admouetur. conueniunt Asthmaticis, ubi uapor per os recipiendus.
units.tr: Their use is to produce a pleasant odour, to check distillations from the head to the chest, and to ward off the contagion of pestilence; then it is applied to the nostrils. They suit asthmatics, where the vapour is to be received through the mouth.

units.la: DE OLEIS, VNGVENTIS, LINIMENTIS, Emplastris, & Cataplasmis. Tab.10.
units.tr: On Oils, Ointments, Liniments, Plasters, and Poultices. Tab. 10.

units.la: Repellētia frigida, et adstringentia, {Oleum rosa. omphac. | Oleum myrtinum | Violarum | Nymphaea | Papaueris | Citoniorum.} Refrigerant, adstringunt, incadescentibus inflammationum feruoribus medentur. Digerētia, siue rarefacientia Mitiora Oleū chamæmeli Anethinum Rosatū cōpletum De nucibus Amygd.dul. ista tēperato calore rarefaciunt, ad longas maximè febres discutiendas accommodantur. Valētiora, De iunipero Laurinum Constinum Rutaceum Mastichinum Absynthij Nardinum Vulpinum Amygd. amararū Scorpionum. Calefaciunt, resicant, membra refrigerata & imbecilla roborāt, neruorū morbis medentur.
units.tr: Cooling and astringent remedies: rose oil, omphacine oil (oil of unripe olives), myrtle oil, violet oil, water-lily oil, poppy oil, quince oil. They cool and bind, and they relieve the fervent heat of inflammations that are already burning. Digestive or rarefying remedies, which are milder: chamomile oil, dill oil, the full rose oil, and sweet almond oil. These, with moderate warmth, rarefy, and they are especially suited to dispersing long fevers. Stronger ones: oil of juniper, laurel oil, Constinum oil, rue oil, mastic oil, wormwood oil, spikenard oil, fox oil, and bitter almond oil, with scorpions. They warm and dry, strengthen cold and weak limbs, and cure diseases of the nerves.

units.la: De unguentis.
units.tr: On Ointments.

units.la: Vnguenta repellentia frigi. Populeon Infrigid. Gale. Santalinum De bolo Ad partes refrigerādas accōmodantur: erysipelæ alijsq; calidis inflāmationibus medentur. Calida ualenter rarefaciētia siue digerentia. Aregon Martiatum Agrippa Dialthæa De meliloto Alabastrum Aduersus frigida corporis mala, resolutionem, coxendicem, nephritem, febrium pituitosarum horrores maximè faciunt, emolliunt duricies, &c. Vnguenta componuntur ex speciebus, iuxta morbi naturam, oleis & cera: interdum adhiben tur adipes, medullæ, butyrum, & similia, aliquan do gummi commiscentur, nonnunquam succi. in-gredientia quædam seorsum debent puluerisari. De cera non datur præscriptus modus, nisi ad cō sistentiam unguenti adijcitur. Hodie in compo-nendis unguentis pračlici obseruant, ut unciæ uni oleorum uel alterius liquoris, drachmam unam pulueris & unc. 2. ceræ adhibeamus. Sed præstat arbitrio medici ceræ quantitatem relinquere.
units.tr: Cooling and repellent ointments: Populeon, Infrigidans, Galenic ointment, sandal ointment, and bole ointment. They are suited to cooling parts of the body, and they cure erysipelas and other hot inflammations. Strongly warming and rarefying or digestive ointments: Aregon, Martiatum, Agrippa's ointment, Dialthaea, melilot ointment, and alabaster ointment. They are most effective against cold ailments of the body, against paralysis, sciatica, and kidney stone, against the shivers of phlegmatic fevers, and they soften hardness. Ointments are made from the spices, according to the nature of the disease, with oils and wax; sometimes fats, marrow, butter, and similar things are added, sometimes gum is mixed in, and occasionally juices. Some of the ingredients ought to be reduced to powder separately. No fixed amount of wax is prescribed, except that it is added to give the ointment its consistency. Today practitioners, in making ointments, observe the rule that we take one ounce of oil or other liquid, one drachm of powder, and two ounces of wax. But it is better to leave the quantity of wax to the physician's judgement.

units.la: De Linimentis.
units.tr: On Liniments.

units.la: Linimenta ex eisdem ferè rebus fiunt, quibus unguenta, dempta sola cera: consistentiam paulò molliorem & liquidiorem accipere debent. Hora applicandi unguenta & linimenta laudabiliora, est post uniuersas euacuationes.
units.tr: Liniments are made from almost the same things as ointments, except for the wax alone; they ought to have a somewhat softer and more liquid consistency. The most commendable time to apply ointments and liniments is after all the evacuations.

units.la: De Emplastris.
units.tr: On Plasters.

units.la: Emplastra ex herbis, floribus, radicibus, speci ebus grossa arte cōtusis cum oleis, uel alijs liquo ribus simul mixtis, uel bullitis. Herbæ & flores per M. numerantur: radices per unc. aut drach. similiter pulueres & farinæ. Obseruant hodie in componendis emplastris, ut cuilibet manipulo oleorum aut alterius liquoris unc.1. aut unc. 1.s. commisceatur. Præterea, Emplastrum ex herbis uiridibus & radicibus, si quando Medicus com-ponere ponere intendat, tantum bulliri ista oportet, donec ad spissitudinem veniant: deinde adduntur liquores, ut vel oleum, adipes, butyrum, & huiusmodi iuxta Medici arbitrium, volētis vel digerere, vel suppurare. Si vero cum melle emplastrum sit componendum, pro lib. i. mell. speciērum unc. 4. admiscentur: compositum emplastrum, linteolo affectæ parti adhuc calidum illitum admoveatur.
units.tr: Plasters are made from herbs, flowers, roots, and spices, coarsely crushed, mixed or boiled together with oils or other liquids. Herbs and flowers are counted by the handful; roots by the ounce or drachm; likewise powders and meals. Today, in making plasters, practitioners add one ounce, or one and a half ounces, of oil or other liquid to each handful. Furthermore, when a physician intends to make a plaster from green herbs and roots, these must be boiled only until they reach a thick consistency; then liquids are added, such as oil, fats, butter, and the like, according to the physician's judgement, depending on whether he wishes to disperse or to suppurate. If, however, the plaster is to be made with honey, four ounces of spices are mixed in for each pound of honey. The finished plaster, still warm, is spread on a linen cloth and applied to the affected part.

units.la: De Cataplasmatis.
units.tr: On Poultices.

units.la: Cataplasmata ab emplastris differunt, quæ fiunt tantum è plantis viridibus contusis, vel ipsdem ad mollitudinē usq; in aqua decoctis. Ea absq; aliquo liquore pingui, hypochondrijs adhiberi solent, aliisq; partibus. Quæ suspecta semper sunt, nisi prius corpore vacuato.
units.tr: Poultices differ from plasters: they are made only from green plants, crushed, or the same plants boiled in water until soft. Without any rich liquid they are usually applied to the hypochondria and other parts. They are always to be regarded with suspicion unless the body has first been emptied.
